**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1181: ALEXANDER III, ROMAN PONTIFF**

[Col. 0009]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 865)

[Col. 0009A] Alexander III, named Roland, a native of Siena, having served on an embassy to Emperor Frederick concerning the injury inflicted upon the bishop of London and not avenged, was elected pontiff in the year of the Lord 1159, in the time of Emperor Frederick, from being cardinal-priest of the title of St. Mark, by twenty-three cardinals (whose names are listed in the letter to Emperor Frederick cited by Radevicus, book II, chapter 53 [see below]). Against him, in the schism, a certain Octavian—a Roman by nation and cardinal-priest—was elected by only three cardinals; he was thereafter called Victor III. The emperor, who was then pressing Cremona under siege, was informed by letters from both parties, which Radevicus reports in book II, of this affair, and ordered both men to come to Pavia, promising there to settle their disputes. When Alexander refused to comply with this order, Frederick, angered, became more inclined toward Victor’s party. Alexander, upon receiving this response, departed for France, [Col. 0009B] where, after holding a council at Clermont, he excommunicated Frederick and Victor.

Meanwhile Frederick destroyed Milan, captured for the third time, and levelled it with the ground. He gave the bodies of the Three Magi to Rainald, archbishop of Cologne, who also transferred them to Cologne, as may be seen in his letter received from a very ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Siegburg, which I append here:

> “RAINOLD, by the grace of God elect of the holy Church of Cologne and archchancellor of Italy, to his most beloved sons and friends in Christ, H., provost of the greater church of Cologne, PHILIP, dean, all the priors and the whole clergy, all beneficed ministers of blessed Peter and of the holy Church of Cologne, and all citizens of the nourishing city of Cologne: greeting and affectionate service, with the fullness of heartfelt love.
>
> “We make known to your most beloved community [Col. 0009C] that, from . . . ., we have now by God’s grace attained the happy beginning of our most ardent desire. For, having received the gracious permission of our most serene lord Emperor Frederick, we were joyfully dismissed by him with the fullness of his favor and affection, and were most splendidly honored with such excellent and great gifts that no earthly valuation can be placed upon them. Among the other benefits of his generosity, which he has poured out most abundantly upon us, he has now given us three most precious gifts: namely, the illustrious bodies of the most blessed Three Magi and Kings, who, as the firstfruits of the Gentiles, in figure and foretoken of the Church that was to come [Col. 0010A] from the Gentiles, offered precious gifts to Christ while he still lay in the manger. These most noble bodies, worthy of every reverence, had been solemnly and gloriously deposited at Milan in the church of blessed Eustorgius, confessor and pontiff. Moreover, with God as our guide, we are bringing to you the bodies of the most holy martyrs Nabor and Felix, so that by this inestimable and incomparable treasure—more to be loved than all gold and every precious stone—the most sacred Church and city of Cologne may be most happily enriched and perpetually adorned.
>
> “Since the route through your enemies and ours is dangerous, we have arranged to travel to you through Burgundy and Gaul. We have sent this messenger ahead from the city of Vercelli on the second Ides of June, proceeding that day with the aforesaid most sacred and venerable relics as swiftly as possible toward Turin and the Alps of Mont Cenis. Therefore we earnestly ask and admonish your most sincere affection in the Lord to prepare yourselves, with the devotion and solemnity that you know and that we trust in you, for a worthy reception of such great gifts. Let us also most affectionately and without ceasing pray the Lord God for us, that, together with these relics, for the honor and glory of his name and for the everlasting salvation of all of you and of the entire country, he may deign to restore us to you safe, sound, and unharmed.”

These things are confirmed by a certain instrument of donation made by Archbishop Philip, Rainald’s successor, to the chapter. I faithfully copied it from the archive of the metropolitan church of Cologne, and append it here:

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, PHILIP . . . . archbishop of Cologne, to the sons of the holy Church, present and future, forever.
>
> [Col. 0010C] “The things that are devoutly bestowed upon churches for the salvation of souls, the greater the reward they expect from God, the more fitting it is that they receive the firm strength of rightful confirmation. From the report of many persons we have learned that our predecessor of pious memory, Archbishop Rainald, bestowed upon the greater church of Cologne the alms offered to the holy bodies of the Kings, together with the Kings themselves, moved by the praiseworthy consideration that where the most holy Kings rested bodily and were held in greatest veneration, there also a just and gracious [Col. 0011A] consolation from their offerings should come to the canons. We commend and ratify the act of the aforementioned archbishop, and confirm it by such authority as we can and ought to exercise.
>
> “And lest in future what has been justly done might be changed, we ourselves gave before many witnesses upon the altar of blessed Peter of the greater church that share which we seemed to possess in the offerings of the Kings, granting the brethren of that church free authority to arrange those alms for the augmentation of their prebends, as they might do more diligently and advantageously. After the solemn donation made by us, as was right, we confirmed our act by a ban, so that if anyone should in future presumptuously move against it, he should know himself bound by the ban and subject to the curse of excommunication. We also ordered this charter to be written and fortified with our seal, so that, by inspection of the writing, the things justly done and faithfully expressed might be transmitted to the knowledge of posterity.
>
> [Col. 0011B] “These things were done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1189. Their witnesses are these: . . . . the greater provost and archdeacon; Adolph, greater dean and archdeacon,” etc.

The emperor advised the king of France to deign to come to the council called by him and to bring Alexander with him. When Alexander again refused to do this, he stirred Frederick, ever more inflamed with anger, against himself. Accordingly, intending soon to follow Victor into Italy, he sent him on ahead; when Victor died at Lucca, he installed Guy of Crema as his successor and antipope. Alexander, summoned to Rome with universal consent, was received by all with the greatest rejoicing.

At the same time, the peoples of Cisalpine Gaul took up arms against the emperor, who therefore returned again to Italy. While these things were taking place, the emperor of Constantinople offered every kind of support and aid to the pontiff through envoys, provided that he would in turn unite the empire divided in earlier years. In England Thomas, bishop of Canterbury, received the crown of martyrdom for the liberty of the Church. English envoys, meeting the pontiff on behalf of the king of England, who had been defamed as responsible for the killing of the innocent martyr, maintained that he was free from guilt in the death of the holy martyr. After a silent inquiry, the pope finally absolved the king on these conditions: that he should acknowledge his kingdom as held from the pope and his successors. He also enrolled holy Thomas, made illustrious by most evident miracles, among the saints.

As the pontiff was daily more severely harassed and troubled by the emperor, he went to Venice. There he received the emperor into the favor, peace, and unity of the Church when he humbled himself to kiss the pontiff’s feet, without any intervention of a more arrogant utterance or harsher deed, and without crushing beneath his feet the emperor’s prostrate head—an allegation which heretics injuriously attribute to this most humble pontiff. The honor [Col. 0012B] which Constantine the Great, that emperor far more powerful and holy, showed to Sylvester, Christ’s vicar, and which other kings of the Franks and English bestowed upon this or other pontiffs—namely, that they served the pontiff in the office of groom—Emperor Frederick rightly rendered to that excellent pontiff; and the pontiff, following the example of his predecessors, not undeservedly accepted it. But that he crushed beneath his feet the head of the prostrate emperor and at the same time said, “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk,” etc., is wholly alien both from the pontiff’s humility and from all credibility. After peace had been made and Venice endowed with many privileges, the pontiff came to Rome and was received with the great joy of all. Having held the ecumenical Lateran council for the eradication of schisms, resistance to the Saracens, and reform of Church morals, he died in the year of the Lord 1181, after presiding over the apostolic see for twenty-one years and nineteen days.

[Col. 0011]

## LIFE OF POPE ALEXANDER III, BY THE CARDINAL OF ARAGON

(Muratori, *Italian Writers*, III, I, 448.)

[Col. 0011C] Alexander III, a Tuscan by nation and a native of Siena, son of Raynutius, named Roland, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Mark and chancellor of the apostolic see, sat for eighteen [twenty-one] years. Since he was a cleric of great renown in the church of Pisa, beloved and welcomed by all, he was called to this Roman Church by blessed Eugenius. When Eugenius, through God’s agency, recognized him as suitable, he first ordained him deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, then priest of the title of St. Mark; finally, because he was always advancing from good to better, he made him chancellor of the apostolic see. He was a most eloquent man, sufficiently instructed in divine and human writings and tested by most subtle exercise in their meanings; a learned man, too, polished and fluent in speech; indeed prudent, kindly, patient, merciful, gentle, sober, chaste, constant in the giving of alms, and always attentive to other works pleasing to God. Therefore the Lord caused him to increase among his people and gave him a great priesthood (Sirach 45).

Accordingly, when Pope Adrian had been buried, the bishops and cardinals assembled together in the church of blessed Peter on the second Nones of September, in order to deliberate about appointing a pastor in his place. For three days they discussed the election among themselves, as is customary; at last all who were present, except Octavian, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Cecilia, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Martin, and Guy, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Callixtus, unanimously agreed, under God’s guidance, upon the person of the aforesaid Chancellor Roland. Having invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, and with the assent of clergy and people, they named and elected him Roman pontiff, Pope Alexander III. The two men previously named, John and Guy, promoting Octavian’s election, insolently named him as a second choice.

Then the bishop of Ostia, together with the bishops of Albano, Porto, and Sabina, the remaining cardinal-priests and cardinal-deacons, through the hands of the prior of the deacons, according to the ancient rite of the Church, clothed their chosen one—fleeing, excusing himself, unwilling, and resisting in every way—with the papal mantle, by God’s favor. Thereupon Octavian, who had long aspired to the apostolic chair, when he saw himself thus deprived of his cherished hope, burst into such mad audacity that, like a man possessed, he violently tore the mantle itself from Alexander’s neck with his own hands and tried to carry it away amid tumultuous outcries. But one of the senators present, seeing so great a crime, trembled to the loins and boldly sprang upon the raging man, snatching the mantle from his hands. Octavian, inwardly stricken with anguish of heart, immediately cast his eyes toward his chaplain, who had come prepared and equipped for this purpose, shouting and signaling like a madman that he should quickly bring him the mantle which he had carried with him. When it was brought without delay, since Cardinal Ad. was then with him, he removed his cap, bowed his head, and by the hands of that same chaplain and another of his clerics—alas, shame!—shamelessly put on the mantle. But by divine judgment it happened that the part of the mantle which ought to have covered the front covered his back, in the sight and laughter of all. When he himself zealously tried to correct this absurdity, because in his distraction he could not find the mantle’s hood, he placed its lower fringes around his neck as best he could. Thus it was plainly shown that, just as his mind was twisted and his purpose crooked, so he received the mantle crosswise and askew, as testimony to his condemnation.

As his blind ambition thus proceeded, the gates of that church, which the senators had secured, were opened, and bands of armed men whom he had hired for money immediately ran to the aid of the schismatic [Col. 0013C] with great noise and drawn swords. Since he wholly lacked the support of bishops and cardinals, crowds of armed men surrounded him on every side. The brethren, seeing so execrable a deed, unheard of through the ages, and fearing lest those hired armed men might compel them to adore the idol that had been set up, withdrew together with their elect into the fortified precinct of the aforesaid church. There, so that they could by no means leave, he caused them, with the consent of certain senators whom he had corrupted by money, to be guarded day and night by armed force with every diligence for nine days.

Meanwhile, as the Roman people continually cried out over so monstrous a crime and raged fiercely against those senators, the assembly of the aforesaid brethren with its elect was removed from the custody of that fortified place, but was maliciously transferred by the same senators, after they had received money, to a narrower and safer place across the Tiber. When they had remained there for about three days, the entire city was stirred by so great an injustice and manifest treachery. Children cried out against this invader of the Church, saying: “Accursed one, son of an accursed man, *dismanta* [‘take off the mantle’].” [Note: [Col. 0013D] A. and M. add *conpannum* (“companion”).] “You shall not be pope; you shall not be pope. We want Alexander, whom God chose.” The women likewise blasphemed the heretic, repeated the same words, and sang other mocking words. A certain Briton approached him and boldly said:

> What are you doing, mad Octavian, death of your country?  
> Why have you presumed to divide Christ’s tunic?  
> Soon, soon you will be dust: now you live; tomorrow you will die.

There was great sadness among the clergy, grief among the judges, mourning among the elders, and extraordinary amazement among the people. [Col. 0014A] Therefore the Roman people, no longer able to endure the enormity of such wickedness, came with Oddo Frangipane and other Roman nobles to the place where the brethren were held enclosed. They compelled the aforesaid senators quickly to open the gates of the fortified place and allow those brethren, with Lord Alexander, to depart released and free. Thus, aided by the merits of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, they were rescued from the violence of their persecutor and restored to their liberty.

Passing honorably through the City with praises, while bells rang everywhere amid their joyful procession, and accompanied by many Roman knights and a throng of foot-soldiers, they prosperously reached Nymphae on the vigil of St. Matthew by God’s grace. [Note: [Col. 0013D] A.: “triumphantly.”] There, on that Sunday, all the brethren having assembled—namely, Gregory of Sabina, Hy. of Ostia, B. of Porto, G. of Albano, I. [Note: [Col. 0013D] M.: “Jo.”] of Segni, and S. of Terracina, bishops [Col. 0014B]; the cardinal-priests and deacons; likewise abbots, priors, judges, advocates, notaries, and the primicerius with the school of singers; as well as nobles and a very large part of the Roman people—Lord Pope Alexander, through the hand of the bishop of Ostia, to whom alone the consecration of the Roman pontiff belongs, was consecrated supreme pontiff under the guidance of the Holy Spirit’s grace, and solemnly crowned with the papal crown according to the custom of the Church.

The aforesaid Octavian, while he was at St. Peter’s and after he secretly left the Leonine City, summoned many bishops to confirm his rash undertaking. He sought to draw some to himself by imperial threats [Note: [Col. 0014D] A.: “arms.”], others by lay violence, and some by money and flatteries; but, the Lord hindering him, he made no progress. The false brethren I. [Note: [Col. 0014D] M.: “Jo.”] of Morcone and G. of Crema remained wrapped in the darkness of their blindness, since, [Col. 0014C] as it is written, “when a sinner comes into the depth of vices, he despises” (Prov. 18). They did not repent of their condemnable presumption, but revered with obstinate perfidy that same man whom they had raised up as a statue for themselves; abandoning the unity of the Church—alas, shame!—they bowed down at his feet. He himself, prefiguring the times of Antichrist, raised himself so high above himself that he sat in the temple of God as a shadow-pontiff, showing himself as though he were the true pope. Indeed, many beheld with bodily eyes, not without tears, this abomination standing in the holy place; they beat their breasts and said: “Now is fulfilled what Pope Anastasius is reported to have said face to face, ironically, to this forerunner of Antichrist: ‘Accursed and excommunicated son, you shall never possess this papal mantle, which you so greatly desire and shamelessly seek, except to your confusion and the ruin of many.’”

Moreover, though for four weeks he continually importuned, both personally [Col. 0014D] and through his knights and kinsmen, that bishops should be summoned to him, and all shrank from approaching him, at last a certain bishop of Melfi, called the Fugitive and Exile, hiding in the territory of Ancona, together with the bishop of Ferentino, who opposed Lord Pope Adrian, and John, bishop of Tusculum, who had first agreed to Alexander and afterward turned back—these three, already excommunicated after the second and third admonition—wickedly consecrated that same Octavian. But Octavian would by no means have dared to undertake [Note: [Col. 0014D] M.: “would have attempted.”] this deed, so ruinous to God’s Church, as afterward became clear, unless he had received from Emperor Frederick favor and boldness for obtaining or seizing the papacy; for there was credible evidence that, so that he might ascend the papal chair by any means whatsoever, he was bound to Frederick by an oath of fealty.

Meanwhile Lord Alexander had gone down with his brethren to Terracina, wishing to discover what Otto Count Palatine and Guy Count of Blandrata would do in the affair of the Church. At that time the emperor had sent them to Pope Adrian of blessed memory. Though they fully knew the truth of the matter and did not at all doubt the canonical election of Lord Alexander, nevertheless, fearing to offend their lord, whom they knew to be greatly attached to Octavian and whose mind they perceived to be stirred against the Roman Church, they gave support and strength to Octavian and dealt deceitfully and fraudulently with Alexander.

While these things were taking place, the pontiff, after taking counsel with his brethren, humbly sent envoys with apostolic letters to the same emperor, then besieging Crema in Lombardy, [Col. 0015B] desiring to recall him to love for the Church in all patience and gentleness, according to the saying of the blessed apostle Paul: “Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil by good” (Rom. 12). But Frederick, inflated with excessive pride, not only disdained to receive the letters, but, like a madman, wickedly wished to hang the envoys themselves, had Duke Welf not opposed him with the duke of Saxony. Although, at the counsel and persuasion of his princes, he allowed the envoys to come before him and at last permitted the letters to be read, he nevertheless deigned to give the pontiff no reply.

Thinking that he could nullify the privilege of liberty granted to the Church by the Lord himself, and place a pope in the apostolic see according to his own will, he sent two of his supporters, the bishops of Verden and Prague, to the brethren who had come with Lord Alexander to the city of Anagni. He wrote not as the advocate and defender of the Church but as a superior judge and lord possessing authority over them. [Col. 0015C] They came in haste in a display of arrogance; entering the palace, they stood before the pontiff, all the brethren, and many others, clerical as well as lay, but showed the pontiff no reverence. They recited what their lord had laid upon them and delivered his letters sealed with gold. In these letters, among other [Note: [Col. 0015D] A.: “insults.”] things, it was expressly stated that the emperor, having heard of the dissension which had arisen in the Roman Church, had summoned ecclesiastical persons from five kingdoms. He therefore commanded them in the name of the universal Church to meet in his presence at Pavia on the octave of Epiphany, to hear and receive whatever should be decreed in that court.

Upon hearing this, the brethren were troubled. Fear and excessive anxiety severely afflicted them because of the ever more grievous evils rising on every side. On the one hand, they especially feared the imminent persecution of so powerful a prince; on the other, the liberty of the Church seemed about to be broken and utterly destroyed. [Col. 0015D] [Note: [Col. 0015D] A. and M.: “They likewise feared that a ruinous example would be extended to other churches.”] What distressed the brethren’s minds no little was that the emperor in his letters called Octavian “Roman pontiff” and Alexander “the pope’s chancellor.”

The brethren therefore deliberated long over these matters and disputed among themselves at length. At last, through the inspiration of the Lord, from whom all good things proceed, it was resolved that they should stand firm in the faith of Catholic unity and obedience to their pontiff. Thus all were confirmed and strengthened unanimously, so that, if necessity should require it, every one of them would freely offer himself to the utmost dangers to maintain the Church’s liberty. Then, when the aforesaid bishops urgently demanded a response, Pope Alexander wrote to them before the multitude of clergy, people, and laypersons as follows:

> We acknowledge the lord emperor, by reason of the dignity duly conferred upon him, as advocate and special defender of the most holy Roman Church. Therefore, provided that he himself does not prevent it, we intend to honor him above all the princes of the world and to defer to him in all things in which the honor of the King of kings suffers no loss. But where anything occurs that cannot be carried out without offense to the supreme King, if the earthly emperor appears to deserve honor, [Col. 0016A] then it is fitting [Note: [Col. 0016D] “Perhaps a word is missing: *fas est*, ‘it is fitting.’”] that He rather be feared and His honor rather preserved—the One who is King of kings and Lord of lords, and who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.
>
> “We therefore wonder that, although we sincerely love him as is fitting and seek more earnestly to honor his eminence, we do not perceive from him an affection of sincere love, but see honor due to us—or rather to blessed Peter and the most holy Roman Church—denied us by him. For in the letters which you brought on his behalf to us and our brethren, it was expressly stated, among other things, that, having heard of the dissension which had arisen in the Roman Church, [Col. 0016B] he had summoned ecclesiastical persons from five kingdoms” (and the remainder as above through “upon hearing this”).
>
> “In this he seems to have departed very far from the custom of his predecessors and to have exceeded the limit of his dignity, in summoning a council without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff and ordering us to appear before him as though he were a man possessing authority over us. But blessed Peter—and through him the most holy Roman Church, of which he himself, through God, was master and founder—received this privilege lawfully from the Lord Jesus Christ and the holy Fathers; through prosperity and adversity, even with the shedding of blood when necessary, it has been preserved down to these times: namely, that its authority should examine and settle the cases of all churches whenever circumstances required, while it itself should never be subject to anyone’s judgment.
>
> “Since therefore we now see action taken contrary to the privilege granted to the Church by the very man through whom it ought to have been defended from others’ attacks; and since this has been written to the mother as though she were any subordinate person, we cannot and ought not to bear it without [Col. 0016C] great amazement. Canonical tradition and the venerable authority of the Fathers do not permit us to come to his court or to accept the sentence of his court in this matter. For, even in lesser churches, their advocates and secular princes do not usurp for themselves or their courts the summonses, hearings, and decisions of such cases, but always await the cognizance and determination of their metropolitans or of the apostolic see.
>
> “It therefore appears most worthy of divine judgment, and deserving of rebuke by the whole Church all the more severely because the danger to the universal Church would be greater, if through our ignorance or weakness of spirit this disease should begin in our days from the head—may God avert it!—and if we should allow the Church redeemed by Christ’s precious blood to be reduced to servitude, though our fathers shed their own blood to defend her liberty and we ourselves, following their example, ought, should necessity require, to endure the utmost [Col. 0016D] dangers.”

When this response had been given, the bishops who had been sent were angered. Returning defiantly to Octavian, they came to him at Segni. When the imperial letters had been presented to him, they prostrated themselves at his feet and adored him. Otto Count Palatine, whom the emperor had dispatched with Germans to the region of Rome, did the same. Then the heart of that heresiarch was moderately lifted up; in his madness and blindness he exalted himself greatly [Note: [Col. 0016D] A. and M.: “above himself.”], not knowing that, according to the saying of the blessed martyr Cyprian: “Schismatics cannot always have fervent growth at their beginnings, nor can they increase what they have unlawfully begun, but immediately fail together with their own rivalry.”

The Prophet speaks of such ambitious persons, saying: “Nevertheless, because of their deceits thou hast appointed evils for them; thou hast cast them down while they were being exalted. How have they become desolate! They suddenly failed and perished because of their iniquities, like the dream of one who awakens” (Ps. 72 [Vulgate]). Such persons the apostle John curses and strikes when he says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us” (1 John 2). Thus heresies have often arisen and arise: a perverse mind has no peace, and discordant perfidy does not maintain unity. Yet the Lord permits and suffers these things, while the choice of free will remains, so that, as he tests our hearts and minds by the crisis of unity, the uncorrupted faith of those who have been proved may shine forth in manifest light [Note: [Col. 0017D] A. and M.: “in the light of truth,” etc.]. The Holy Spirit also gives warning through the Apostle and says: “There must be heresies and schisms, that those who are approved may be made manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11). Thus the faithful are proved; thus the faithless are exposed. But now let us return to the matter.

[Col. 0017B] The Emperor Frederick, vainly hoping to bring to fruition the malice he had long conceived of subjecting Christ’s Church to himself, summoned the heretic himself into Lombardy. Having assembled such bishops and other prelates of churches from the territory of his dominion as he could, he went with the same Octavian to Pavia, intending to hold a general court. There, by crafty manipulation, he disclosed his profane intention and detestable purpose. He asserted that Lord Alexander, his brethren, and his associates were enemies both of the empire and of himself, and had conspired with his enemies and adversaries; whereas Octavian had always been faithful and wholly devoted to him and to the empire. Therefore, it seemed to him that Octavian’s election, although made by fewer Catholics, ought nevertheless to possess greater force and the empire’s favor than the rash deed of many conspirators.

Accordingly, in order to induce those who had assembled to obedience and submission to Octavian, he deceived some by flattery and various promises [Col. 0017C] and dragged others unwillingly by threats and terrors. Thus, seeking the destruction of his own soul and the ruin of many, and attempting to tear Christ’s tunic—that is, the unity of the Catholic faith—he himself first bent down at Octavian’s feet and compelled as many others as he could to do the same. Having done this, he sent an edict throughout the empire subject to him, ordering the prelates of the churches to come and worship the statue which he had set up; whoever refused was to depart from his territory and never return.

This harsh and cruel command resounded throughout all Italy. All who burned with spiritual zeal chose rather to suffer exile and persecution for God and for the maintenance of the unity of faith, than peacefully to adhere to schismatics with honors and abound in the riches of this age. Thus there arose the greatest disturbance in God’s Church: Catholics fled and abandoned their churches, relatives, and homeland, while Octavian’s accomplices were violently installed in their places.

When [Col. 0017D] the blessed Pope Alexander, though kindly and repeatedly admonishing that emperor, was altogether unable to recall him from his treachery, at Anagni on Maundy Thursday, with bishops and cardinals, he solemnly bound him with the bond of excommunication as the principal persecutor of God’s Church. In accordance with the ancient custom of the Fathers, his predecessors, he absolved from their oath all those bound to him by an oath of fidelity; and he renewed the sentence of excommunication already long pronounced against Octavian and his accomplices. Since those schismatics, distrusting justice and truth, had deceived prelates of churches and the princes of the world with elaborate fabrications of lies and had attempted to draw them into a share of their error, it seemed useful to the lord pope [Col. 0018A] to send certain of his brethren from his side into various regions of the world, so that, through their effort and labor, an explanation might be given concerning the matter of the apostolic election, and the whole body of the faithful, once the truth was known, might be strengthened in the faith of Catholic unity.

Accordingly, H., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Nereus; W., cardinal priest of Saint Peter in Chains; and Master O., cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in Prison, were sent to the regions of Gaul. To the eastern regions was sent I., of the title of Saints John and Paul; to the Hungarians, I., bishop of Palestrina, and P., cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace; and to the emperor of Constantinople, the bishop of Tivoli with A., cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.

Once the truth of the said election had been published and unmistakably recognized, Louis, the Most Christian king of the Franks—whose kingdom is not remembered ever to have been defiled by schism—together with Henry king of the English, received Lord Alexander, by the Lord’s inspiration, as father and shepherd [Col. 0018B] of their souls. The kings of Spain, Sicily, Jerusalem, and Hungary likewise did the same, as did the emperor of the Greeks with the patriarchs, bishops, princes, and all clergy and people subject to them. Thus, while the entire world recognized him as Christ’s vicar and the Catholic successor of blessed Peter, Frederick, the aforesaid emperor, alone remained with his accomplices in the obstinacy and persistence of his error, violently attacking and fiercely persecuting the same pontiff and those prelates of churches who stood manfully with him.

In the second year of his pontificate Pope Alexander returned to the city of Rome, where, with the Lord as author, he solemnly dedicated the church of Saint Mary the New. But because he could not remain there peacefully for long on account of the great uprising of the schismatics [Note: Col. 0017D, M.: “among”], he returned, persuaded by the prayers of the Roman people, [Col. 0018C] to the regions of Campania. Since the imperial persecution against the Church around Rome had grown so great that the entire patrimony of blessed Peter—apart from the city of Orvieto, Terracina, Anagni, and the fortress of the Castle—from Acquapendente to Ceprano [Note: Col. 0018D, M.: “Cepano”] had been violently occupied and held by Germans and schismatics, he took counsel with the faithful of the Church that he should cross by sea with his brethren to the regions of Gaul.

Having therefore appointed Lord Julius, bishop of Palestrina, as his vicar in Rome, and arranged the other matters which seemed necessary to the Church, he went to Terracina, intending to embark with his brethren. There he found four galleys of the king of Sicily, excellently equipped, which had been sent there for his service. The pontiff’s household and those of his brethren had scarcely embarked in them with the necessary baggage when a strong wind suddenly arose and changed the calm sea into a violent tempest. The vessels, battered by storm-waves and whirlpools, were driven [Col. 0018D] onto the rocky shore, where, without loss of life or damage to other property, they came apart and were completely wrecked. Thus the pontiff’s intended journey at that time remained disrupted and impeded.

But after a short interval, when the ships had been repaired and other things necessary for the voyage prepared, within the octave of the Lord’s Nativity he entered the sea with his brethren near Mount Circeo, at the narrows of Legula; and on the feast of Saint Agnes he reached Genoa, the Lord rowing him onward [Note: Col. 0018D, A. and M.: “returning by sea”]. There, despite the prohibition of Frederick, persecutor of the Church, he was received and treated with glory and honor by all the clergy and people.

He left Genoa on Passion Sunday, sailed with every joy, and came to the island of Liguria on the Saturday before Palm Sunday, where he was compelled by an exceedingly violent storm at sea to celebrate the Lord’s Resurrection. On the following Wednesday he arrived at the church of Magdalene, where, with the Lord as author, he solemnly dedicated the high altar. Since that place was too confined for receiving guests and a vast multitude of ecclesiastical prelates awaited the arrival of the same pontiff beyond the island with intense longing, he judged it fitting to go up to the populous town of Montpellier. Accordingly, when a white palfrey and the other pontifical insignia had been prepared according to custom, Pope Alexander could scarcely mount his horse or keep to a straight path because of the enormous crowd. So excessive and importunate was the press of all who ran to his footsteps that anyone who could touch even the hem of his cloak, not without great effort, considered himself blessed.

When W., lord of that town, met him with barons and a splendid troop of knights, and performed the office of stirrup-holder [Col. 0019B] for a mile, the pope entered the town in a very great procession. There, among the other nobles who came [Note: Col. 0019D, M.: “went before”] to his feet, a certain resourceful Saracen prince approached reverently with his companions. Having kissed his feet, he knelt before him; and, bowing his head, he adored the pontiff as though he were the holy and merciful God of the Christians.

Speaking to the pontiff on behalf of his lord, the king of the “Mathemuci,” who had sent him to those regions, he spoke with considerable magnificence in his barbarous language; but through an interpreter he explained everything that he wished to say. The pontiff answered him kindly and attentively, paid him great honor, and honorably had him seated among the other honored persons near his feet. All who were present before the pontiff saw this, marveled greatly, and said to one another the prophetic saying: “All kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Psalm VII).

When Sunday came [Col. 0019C], the pontiff went to the principal church to celebrate the solemnities of Mass. An immense multitude of men and women flowed in from every side. After his sermon to the people, his truthful account of his election, and the insolent treachery of the schismatics, he solemnly renewed the sentence of excommunication against Octavian the heresiarch, the aforesaid Emperor Frederick, and their accomplices.

At that time a severe famine grew throughout Aquitaine and the surrounding places, to such a degree that, owing to the extreme lack of food, an innumerable multitude of people perished by unavoidable death. Consequently a vehement fear seized all Gauls, lest a similar affliction should invade their own lands.

The pontiff, wishing to announce his arrival to the king of the Franks, sent two of his brethren into the king’s presence: B., bishop of Porto, and I., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. Their task was to learn the king’s will [Col. 0019D] and ascertain in which region of his realm, with the king’s advice, the pope should go to reside. The king received them reverently out of reverence for blessed Peter, treated them honorably, and, after taking counsel, sent them back with a joyful reply and great rejoicing to Lord Alexander, whom he had already received as father and shepherd of his soul.

When they returned to their lord and the college of his brethren, and reported what they had received from the king’s answer, all rejoiced with great joy. The pontiff therefore departed Montpellier in the following month of June and, passing through Alès, Mende, and Le Puy, entered Auvergne. On the vigil of the Assumption of blessed Mary he arrived at Clermont in all prosperity, with the Lord as his guide.

Meanwhile Frederick, seeing the whole world run after Alexander and the orthodox kings [Col. 0020A] and princes of the world render him honor and reverence as Roman pontiff, wasted away within himself and was put to shame and terror by his accusing conscience. Yet he was ashamed to desist from the evil he had begun, because he was stronger and more powerful than his other predecessors and had already subjected nearly all Italy to himself. On the other hand, he greatly doubted and feared the loss of the imperial crown if Alexander should prevail in his day.

Placed in the slippery position of so great an uncertainty, he considered within himself, as a shrewd and crafty man most wise in worldly matters, how he might jointly depose Alexander and his idol by the judgment of the universal Church and install a third person as Roman pontiff. Since it is generally characteristic of each person to wish to associate with himself men like himself, he enlisted Count Henry of Troyes, in whom he had the greatest confidence. Revealing his thoughts to him, he drew him to his own will [Col. 0020B] and made him helper and collaborator in his plan.

Thus instructed and informed by the emperor, the count returned home. Then, approaching his lord, the king of the Franks—a pious man indeed, of dove-like simplicity—as a tempter, he fraudulently proposed to him, on the emperor’s behalf, a feigned good concerning the restoration of peace in the Roman Church, in these words:

“The emperor wishes, for the contemplation of divine love, to undertake this good work with you in this way: that you, the two greatest princes of the world, should meet together at Dijon [Note: Col. 0019D, A.: “division”], on the border of your kingdom and his empire, with the chief persons, both clerical and lay, of the empire and of your kingdom. He will bring with him Octavian and his followers, while you shall likewise have Alexander and his followers with you. After you two, with both parties, have assembled in the presence of so many men, and the election of each has been carefully heard and examined, let the Gallican, Italian, and German Church assembled [Col. 0020C] there decide concerning each whatever shall appear just to decide, and let that be established and ordered in the Roman Church which shall seem better and more useful to establish and order.”

This proposal for restoring the peace of the Church seemed good to the aforesaid king. Like a true [Note: Col. 0020D, M.: “man”] Israelite in whom there is no guile (John I), because many evils were springing up in all the churches from that discord, he consented in his good simplicity to the count’s persuasion, promising that on his side he would give the emperor security concerning the matters proposed to him.

The count, rejoicing in what he had obtained, immediately returned to the same emperor, then in Lombardy, and gave him an oath on behalf of his lord the king, as stated above.

This evil proposal therefore spread through all the provinces of Italy and Gaul. Catholics grieved and feared what would result, unless the Lord should scatter [Col. 0020D] this plan premeditated against the ancient liberty of the Church. As the appointed day approached, Emperor Frederick came to the place with the entire multitude of his princes and armed soldiers, and Octavian followed him with his school of accomplices. The king of the Franks likewise hastened to the same place with his magnates, bishops, and barons; and he met Pope Alexander at Silvanus [Note: Col. 0020D, A. and M.: “Sylvianus”]. There, honoring one another, they discussed for two days how they might proceed together to the conference.

But because it seemed altogether unworthy and contrary to the ordinances of the holy Fathers that the supreme pontiff and the first see should undergo any human judgment, it seemed good to all that some of the leading persons of the Roman Church should be sent there with the king, [Col. 0021A] solely so that through them Lord Alexander’s election might be shown to have been canonical and just, and Octavian’s later act might likewise be proved to have had no validity whatsoever.

The pope therefore sent with the king to the oft-mentioned place B., bishop of Porto; Hu. [Note: Col. 0021D, M.: “Hugh”], cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross; I., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia; I., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin; and A., cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Theodore. When they had departed, the pope withdrew with his remaining brethren to the monastery of Déols in Aquitaine.

The king, accompanied by persons so numerous and eminent, came to Dijon and advanced to the middle of the bridge over the Saône, which separated the Germans from the French, awaiting what the emperor wished to propose to him concerning the Church’s cause. Then Octavian the heresiarch, seeing that the principal persons of the Roman Church had come with the Gallican Church contrary to his expectation and stood most firmly against him, was greatly [Col. 0021B] terrified and began utterly to despair of his cause. Turning to the emperor, he said:

“That adversary of mine has disdained to come here, and do you allow my cause—which has been judged in your presence and approved in the Council of Lodi—to be judged and reconsidered again?”

Then the emperor, observing Octavian’s deeply disturbed face, seemed to be provoked against the king of the Franks. Speaking to him through envoys, he said:

“Now you appear to have deceived me and manifestly violated the oath of our agreement, since you have not brought your pope to this place, as you promised.”

After taking counsel, the king replied:

“Although I can justly and reasonably excuse the pontiff’s absence, nevertheless, lest any derogation be made from the honor of the realm entrusted to me and from my reputation, and lest I incur, justly or unjustly, the charge of deceit, I shall without delay summon the pontiff himself with his brethren to this place, without guile or fraud, and shall cause him to be present.”

Accordingly, as he had promised, the king sent trustworthy messengers with all speed to Alexander, ordering him to come to him with his brethren without delay, unless he wished to be held captive by the emperor, as had been agreed between them. Hearing this, the pontiff and his brethren, perceiving that the king of the Franks had been deceived by crafty machinations, were greatly troubled within themselves. Foreseeing the gravest dangers threatening them from every side, they were seized with great fear. If they went there to submit to human judgment, they saw that the liberty of the Church would be endangered by force. If they did not go, captivity of their persons through the king’s detention and plundering of their possessions seemed certain and imminent.

Indeed, the emperor’s immense power was terrible and greatly to be feared. For he had, it was believed, brought with him thither the kings of Denmark and Bohemia with their dukes and princes and a great multitude of armed soldiers, so that at the conference he might accomplish, according to his desire, the evil he had long devised concerning the aforesaid pontiff and the king of the Franks. [Col. 0021D] But the merciful and compassionate Lord, who does not abandon those who hope in him and scatters the wicked counsels of princes, did not allow the same pontiff and the pious king of the Franks, placed in the greatest distress, to be tested beyond what they could bear; rather, unexpectedly, he made for them with the temptation a way of escape (1 Corinthians X).

For he stirred up the spirit of the glorious king of the English to hasten with the utmost energy to aid and relieve his lord, the king of the Franks, against that emperor, with a very great multitude of valiant warriors. He also inflicted such a torment of famine upon the emperor’s army that, owing to the extreme scarcity of food, a small loaf of bread was bought by the hungry for the price of one silver mark. Therefore, since the emperor could neither remain there nor carry out the evil he bore in his heart, he hastened to find as honorable a pretext as possible [Col. 0022A] for leaving that place.

Thus, through Chancellor Raynald and his other supporters, he addressed the eminent king of the Franks in these words:

“Our lord Frederick, emperor of the Romans and special advocate of the Roman Church, commands you that it pertains to no prelates of churches to render judgment concerning the election of the Roman pontiff, except only those who are within the Roman Empire. Therefore it seems good and just that you should come to him as friend and associate with your bishops and clergy [Note: Col. 0022D, M.: does not read *vestro*, ‘your’], and that you should hear their decision.”

On hearing these words, the king smiled slightly and answered thus:

“I am surprised that a prudent man has sent me such various and fabulous words. Does he not know that, when our Lord Jesus Christ was upon earth, he entrusted his sheep to blessed Peter, and through him to all his successors, to be fed? Has he not heard in the Gospel the Son of God say to that prince of the apostles: [Col. 0022B] ‘If you love me, Peter, feed my sheep’ (John XXI)? Are the kings of the Franks, or any prelates of churches here, excepted? Or are the bishops of my kingdom not among the sheep whom the Son of God entrusted to blessed Peter?”

Having said these things, he turned his reins in contempt of them and immediately rose to arms with his barons and remaining soldiery. He fortified the weaker places of his kingdom and, as a prudent and strong man, returned with glory and honor, the Lord favoring him, to his seat.

The brethren sent by the pontiff returned joyfully to his presence and related all that had been done at that conference, through the energy of the glorious and orthodox king, to the honor of God and the Church. Therefore the college of brethren and all who were present rejoiced and exulted, giving thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ, who had shown them mercy and deigned to deliver them from the hands of so mighty an enemy. The emperor, remaining confounded in his shame, [Col. 0022C] was compelled, through the severe privations of famine, to dismiss his army to their homes; he himself returned sadly to the German kingdom.

In those days the aforesaid king of the English visited Lord Pope Alexander in person at the monastery of Déols and humbly prostrated himself at his feet. But after he had kissed the feet and offered gifts of gold, he was received to kiss the same pontiff’s mouth. At once, declining to sit upon the faldstool prepared for him, he wished humbly to sit upon the ground at the pontiff’s feet with his barons. After three days, greatly delighted by the pleasant sight of the pontiff, and having bestowed great gifts upon him and his brethren, he departed from him with joy.

The pontiff, after dedicating the high altar of the aforesaid monastery, set out toward Tours and, about the feast of blessed Michael, arrived safely at that city with the Lord’s help. There he remained for a long time with his brethren and [Col. 0022D] solemnly celebrated the Lord’s Nativity. When Septuagesima arrived, he went to the city of Paris for a conference. Before he entered the city, the king, as a pious and gentle man, came out to meet him with his barons and knights for two leagues. On seeing him, the king immediately dismounted and hurried to the pope’s stirrup, humbly kissed his feet, and was at once received with devotion to kiss his mouth.

Then, proceeding cheerfully together, they entered the aforesaid city. The clergy met the pontiff with a very great and splendid procession and conducted him amid joy and jubilation to the principal church. He remained in that city throughout the whole of Lent and celebrated the Paschal feast there. Since the time for holding the council which he had convoked at Tours in the octave of Pentecost was approaching, he left Paris and, passing through Chartres, returned swiftly [Col. 0023A] [Note: Col. 0023D, A.: “quickly”] to the city of Tours.

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1164, in the tenth indiction, the fourth year of his pontificate, on 19 May, the aforesaid Pope Alexander held a council in the church of Saint Maurice at Tours. There were present with him seventeen cardinals, one hundred and twenty-four bishops, four hundred and fourteen abbots, and a very great multitude of other clergy and laity. There the apostolic constitutions were confirmed and these new chapters promulgated.

## Chapters promulgated at the Council of Tours

> “While the greater benefices of the Church remain intact, it seems utterly improper that the lesser prebends of clerics should undergo divisions. Therefore, so that the Church may possess firm unity in its least members as well as in its greatest, we prohibit any division of prebends or exchange of dignities.

> “Many clerics—and, as we have sorrowfully learned, even some of those who have renounced this present age by profession, speech, and habit [Note: Col. 0023D, A. and M.: “according to the confession of speech and habit, etc.”]—although they shrink from common usury as more manifestly condemned, lend money to the needy and take their possessions in pledge beyond the principal. Therefore the authority of the general council decrees that no person henceforth established in the clergy shall presume to practice either this or any other kind of usury.

> “If anyone has hitherto, upon giving money, received another’s possession in pledge under this expectation, and has already received from its fruits his principal after deducting expenses, he shall restore the possession unconditionally to the debtor. But if he has any payment still due, once it has been received, the possession shall freely return to its lord. If, after these decrees, anyone in the clergy persists in the detestable profits of usury, he shall incur the penalty of loss of ecclesiastical office—unless perhaps the matter is an ecclesiastical benefice which seems to him capable of being redeemed in this manner from lay hands.

> “Although it is deemed exceedingly grave and worthy of the judgment of divine punishment that laypeople usurp, in ecclesiastical affairs, what belongs to priests, it inspires still greater dread and sorrow that they are sometimes said to find the fuel of their error in God himself. For certain of our brethren and fellow bishops, and other prelates of the Church, grant them tithes and the administration of churches [Note: Col. 0023D, A. and M.: “and the administrations of those churches themselves, etc.”], and drive into the paths of death those who ought to have been recalled to the way of life by their preaching. Of such persons the Lord says through the prophet: ‘They devour the sins of my people and provoke their souls to iniquity’ (Hosea IV).

> “We therefore decree that if anyone grants a church or a tithe to a layperson remaining in the secular world, he shall be cut down from his office like a tree that uselessly occupies the ground, and shall lie under the ruin of his fall until he makes amends, cast down in sorrow [Note: Col. 0024D, A. and M. do not read *dolore*, ‘in sorrow’].

> “In the regions of Toulouse a condemnable heresy has long since arisen, which, spreading gradually like a cancer into neighboring places, has now infected very many people throughout Gascony and other provinces. Since it hides, serpent-like, within its own coils, the more secretly it creeps, the more seriously it destroys the Lord’s flock among the simple. We therefore command bishops and all the Lord’s priests dwelling in those regions to be vigilant against it, and, under threat of anathema, prohibit [Note: Col. 0024D, A.: “we prohibit”] anyone, wherever the adherents of that heresy are recognized, from presuming to provide them lodging in his territory or afford them protection.

> “Nor shall there be any association with them in selling or buying, so that, deprived even of the support of ordinary human intercourse, they may be compelled to come to their senses from the error of their way. Whoever attempts to act contrary to these things shall be struck with anathema as a leader [Col. 0024A] of their iniquity. If they are apprehended, they shall be committed to custody by Catholic princes and punished by loss of all their goods. Since they frequently gather from diverse regions into one hiding place and, having no reason for living together except agreement in error, dwell in one abode, such assemblies are to be searched out more diligently; and, when found, they are to be forbidden with canonical severity.

> “Since an outrageous custom, contrary to the ordinances of the holy Fathers, has grown strong in certain places—namely, that priests are appointed to the governance of churches for an annual price—we forbid this in every way, because when the priesthood is made saleable by such payment, no regard is had for the reward of eternal recompense.

> “Avarice is not very usefully rebuked among the people unless it is avoided in every way by those who seem established in the clergy, and especially by those who, having despised the world, profess the name [Col. 0024B] and rule of religious persons. We therefore forbid any money to be required from persons wishing to enter religion; nor may any priory or chapel of monks or clerics be sold through annual alienation, nor may any price be demanded from the person to whom their governance is entrusted for that entrustment.

> “The authority of the holy Fathers clearly declares this to be simony. Therefore whoever shall presume to attempt it under this decree [Note: Col. 0024D, A. and M.: “henceforth”], whether giver or receiver, must not doubt that he will have his portion with Simon. Nor shall any charge be exacted for burial or for receiving chrism and holy oil; and no one may defend his guilt under the pretext of any custom, since duration does not diminish sin but increases it.

> “Since in certain bishoprics some deans or archpriests are appointed, for an annual price, to act in the place of bishops [Col. 0024C] or archdeacons and to decide ecclesiastical cases—and this undoubtedly results in oppression of priests and the overthrow of judgments—we strictly forbid this practice from continuing. If anyone does it, he shall be removed from the clergy. Likewise, a bishop who tolerates this in his diocese and permits ecclesiastical judgments to be perverted through his negligence shall be punished by canonical severity.

> “The envy of the ancient enemy does not labor merely to cast down the weak members of the Church, but lays hands upon its precious things and strives to overthrow even the chosen [Note: Col. 0024D, A.: “all clerics”], as Scripture says: ‘His food is choice’ (Habakkuk I). He considers that he brings about the fall of many when some particularly precious member of the Church has been drawn away by his craftiness. Hence, transforming himself as usual into an angel of light, he draws certain religious from their cloisters, under the pretext of healing the bodies of sick brethren and of conducting ecclesiastical business more faithfully, to study laws and even to weigh medicinal compounds.

> “Therefore, lest spiritual men, under the pretext of learning, become once more entangled in worldly pursuits and thereby fail in inward things precisely while they think they are providing for others in outward matters, we decree by the present assent that after taking a religious vow and making profession in any religious house, no one at all may be permitted to leave in order to study medicine or secular laws. If he leaves and does not return to his cloister within two months, let him be avoided by all as excommunicated, and, if he attempts to act as advocate, let him be heard in no case. Upon his return, he shall always be last of the brethren in choir, chapter, at table, and in all else; [Col. 0025A] and, unless perhaps through the mercy of the Apostolic See, he shall lose all hope of advancement.

> “Furthermore, we annul the ordinations made by Octavian and other schismatics and heretics, and judge them to be void.”

After the council had been held, Lord Pope Alexander received this response from the aforesaid kings: if he wished to make a continuing residence in any place within their realms, he should choose whatever town or city pleased him most. Accordingly, he went to reside at the city of Sens, since that metropolis was very famous, fertile, and well suited to those arriving [Note: Col. 0025D, M.: “discoveries,” *adinventionibus*]. There, from the Kalends of October until Easter of the second year, he made a prolonged stay, constantly devoting the care and diligence required by his office to the affairs of the universal Church.

At the same time Octavian, the heresiarch of unhappy memory, fell ill at Lucca, where, about the feast of Easter [Col. 0025B], unrepentant and excommunicated, he departed from this world to hell; although some said that he had summoned a Catholic priest, who, being prevented by the schismatics, could not enter to him. The aforesaid Imarus of Tusculum—[Note: A and M: “Ignarus.”]—one of his chief associates—[Note: A and M: “leaders.”]—had already long preceded him in his detestable death and had met a most evil end at Cluny. Thus, of the four false brethren who had withdrawn from the unity of the Church to the ruin of their souls, only two smoking members remained: namely John of San Martino and Guido of Crema. They afflicted themselves with excessive grief and mourning. And, trembling greatly where there was no fear, they said to one another: “If we choose to turn to Alexander, perhaps he will not receive us without unbearable disgrace and perpetual shame. But if he does receive us, afterwards he will do to us the very thing that Pope Innocent [Col. 0025C] did to those cardinals who stood against him with Peter Leonis.”

Accordingly, despairing of being received by the Church, they summoned the other schismatic clergy and laity, both from Italy and from Germany, who had gathered there to bury Octavian. All, therefore, assembling together as obstinate and faithless men, raised the aforesaid Guido of Crema above themselves as an idol; bowing at his feet, they worshipped him. They immediately sent in haste to the emperor, who was then in Germany, asking him to confirm their abominable deed by imperial authority and, lest they be put to shame by Alexander, to aid them swiftly with the power of his support, both through imperial letters and through distinguished envoys.

When the emperor learned with certainty of Octavian’s death, he was greatly sorrowful and grieved. Yet, lest he should seem to be overcome and defeated in his evil purpose, setting aside the fear of God, he immediately consented without delay to so great an iniquity [Col. 0025D], and exerted himself in every way, so far as he could, to revive the extinguished schism. To increase still further the weight of his own damnation, in order to terrify the Catholics forcefully and make his accomplices firmer in that same wickedness, adding sin to sin, he swore with his own mouth upon the holy Gospels that he would always regard the aforesaid Guido and his successors as Catholics, and Alexander and his successors as schismatics. He likewise compelled whatever ecclesiastical men he could coerce to swear the same. What else did he attempt by this execrable deed but to divide the Church of God?

For, as the Creed contains, every Catholic Christian believes not in two but in one holy apostolic Church, and on every Lord’s Day chants and confesses this. Hence it is written elsewhere: “My dove is one, my perfect one; she is the only one of her mother, chosen of her that bore her” [Col. 0026A] (Song of Songs 6). The blessed apostle Paul teaches this unity of the Church and displays the sacrament of unity, saying: “One body and one spirit, one hope of our calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God” (Ephesians 4).

Frederick the emperor, then, does not maintain this unity of the Church, yet believes that he holds the faith. He abandons the chair of Peter, upon which the Church is founded: how can he trust that he is in the Church? For just as no one who was outside the ark in which Noah was could escape, so neither can anyone who is outside the Church escape at all.

Moreover, we have thought it worth recalling that, before the emperor himself came to the conference with the king of France, after the destruction of Tortona, Milan, and Cremona, he had reduced all Lombardy to such servitude that he not only violently took away their other possessions, but even—what among pagans is not presumed without capital punishment [Col. 0026B]—his ministeriales plundered their wives and daughters and did not fear to abuse them with impunity. Therefore, because of these and other unbearable evils, the Venetians, together with the Veronese, Paduans, Vicentines, and the entire adjoining March, secretly assembled. After long consultation concerning such oppression, they finally swore together that, while preserving the ancient right of the empire, they would henceforth render nothing more to the aforesaid emperor than what their ancient forefathers were known to have rendered to his predecessors—namely Charles and the other orthodox emperors.

United unanimously and bound by the sacred obligation of their oath, they began gradually to fortify their places, curb the insolence of the Germans, and more boldly repel those whom they found rebellious against them. When this came to the emperor’s ears, he blazed with excessive anger. Immediately gathering an army, he advanced with the Pavians, Cremonese, and the other Lombards in whom he seemed to have confidence [Col. 0026C], intending to fight against the Veronese. On the other side, the Veronese league, fully confident in the justice of its cause, fearlessly marched out of the city with a very great multitude of armed men and boldly pitched its tents not far from those of the opposing side.

But when both parties were ready to join battle, the emperor, perceiving beforehand that the Lombards who had come with him favored the opposite side, became greatly afraid. Not without shame and much confusion, he withdrew from the field. He did not engage them in battle, but turned his back and fled. From that time he regarded the cities of Italy as wholly suspect; he preferred to be feared by them rather than loved. Therefore, on the advice of marquises, counts, and captains who were hated by the cities, he took impregnable castles and other very strong fortifications into his own hands, and caused them to be held and guarded more carefully by Germans more faithful to himself. He also appointed German princes, lords, and guardians over the Lombards [Col. 0026D], so that thereafter they could have no possibility whatsoever of resisting his will.

Having arranged and ordered these things according to his will, he passed safely to the conference with the king of France, as we have said above, and thence returned to the regions of Germany. Affairs being thus situated, when the cities of Lombardy listed below had learned by certain indications that this emperor’s intention and purpose against them was wholly bitter and evil, they found no sure plan of escape except that all should stand firmly with the city of Verona against everyone in defense of their liberty, and, mutually aiding one another, furnish the necessary support and assistance.

The following cities therefore joined Verona: first, Cremona; the people of Milan, established outside [Col. 0027A] the walls of their city which the emperor had destroyed; likewise Piacenza, Brescia, and Bergamo. Thus the league suddenly grew immensely and became firm and strong. The other cities of Italy, seeing this, rejoiced in their hearts; and although through excessive fear they outwardly obeyed the emperor, in heart and mind they were with the aforesaid cities—[Note: A and M: “the others.”].

While these things were taking place, Julius, bishop of Palestrina, Pope Alexander’s vicar, died at Rome. In his place John, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, was appointed. At his exhortation the Roman people, for the most part, swore their customary loyalty to Pope Alexander, with no small amount of money as the means; and, renewing it, established the senate according to his will and judgment. They also restored into the hands of the same vicar the church of Blessed Peter and the county of Sabina, which at that time were occupied and held by schismatics through the violence of the emperor—[Note: A: “emperors.”] [Col. 0027B]. Thus almost the entire City was peacefully held by the same vicar for the honor and service of Pope Alexander.

Having taken counsel with the faithful of the Church, both clergy and laity, concerning the recalling of the pontiff to the seat of Blessed Peter and the Lateran palace, he sent envoys and letters to him, while he was in the regions of Gaul at Sens. On behalf of the entire Roman clergy and people and of his faithful adherents, he begged and requested him to deign to return to his first see and to the spiritual people—[Note: A: “special.”]—entrusted to him. For the primacy and governance of the Church in that City were undoubtedly established not by another, but by the Lord himself: so that the city which had been more glorious than all others in the works—[Note: A and M: “time.”]—of paganism might likewise, by divine counsel, possess above all others the dignity of teaching in the revelation of the Christian faith.

Many indeed have tried to resist this divine ordering and to lift up their heel against it [Col. 0027C]; yet none, the Lord protecting it, has been able to prevail. Therefore, dearest Father and Lord, it is fitting that in this matter you provide wisely not only for us but for all the churches and peoples of Italy, who hope that, through the Lord’s agency, peace for themselves and tranquillity for the whole world will arise from your return to that City and your enthronement in the chair of Blessed Peter.

Having heard and understood these things, the pontiff discussed his return to the City at length with the bishops and cardinals. Although he foresaw that many serious and difficult dangers threatened him, nevertheless, after taking counsel with the king of France, the other king of England, and the bishops of Gaul, he gave the aforesaid vicar a definite answer concerning his return; and immediately prepared himself in haste for the journey. After celebrating Easter, he left Sens and, passing through Paris, Bourges, and Le Puy, returned safely through God’s grace to Montpellier after the feast of the Apostles.

Accordingly, ships and the other things deemed necessary for sailing having been prepared, within the octave of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary he entered the sea with his brethren. Crossing the immense expanse of ocean, not without great peril, he arrived at Messina under favorable sails [Col. 0027D]. When this reached the ears of William, king of Sicily, of revered memory and most Christian character, at Palermo, he took care that the pontiff should be treated with fitting honor and that great gifts should be presented to him, as to his father and lord, from whom he was known to hold the patrimony of Sicily and all his other land. For transporting the venerable person of the pope, he most diligently ordered one red galley to be made ready, and four for the use of the bishops and cardinals. He also dispatched the archbishop of Reggio [Col. 0028A] and other magnates with the pontiff, to conduct him gloriously, provide for him splendidly, and convey him in honor as far as the city of Rome.

Thus the blessed Pope Alexander set out from Messina in November. Passing through Salerno and Gaeta, on the feast of Saint Cecilia, aided by the merits of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, he entered the mouth of the Tiber and reached Ostia, where that night, under the Lord’s guidance, he rested safely and unharmed with his brethren. At daybreak the senators, together with the nobles and a great multitude of clergy and people, came out from the City to meet him honorably, rendering him, as shepherd of their souls, their due obedience and customary reverence. Then, with olive branches, they conducted him with all joy and gladness as far as the Lateran Gate.

There the whole clergy of the City, solemnly vested according to custom, awaited the long-desired arrival of the same pontiff. There the Jews had assembled according to custom, carrying their Law in their arms [Col. 0028B]. There also gathered the standard-bearers with their banners, the equerries, the notaries, the judges with the advocates, and no small multitude of the same people. What more need be said? Once the splendid procession had begun and lofty voices rang out on every side, he was led with such glory and exultation to the patriarchal residence of the Holy Saviour and the Lateran palace as no Roman pontiff is remembered to have been received with for a long time past.

These things occurred in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1165, in the thirteenth indiction, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December [23 November], in the sixth year of this pope’s pontificate.

While these things were happening in the city of Rome and Lord Pope Alexander sat in the chair of Blessed Peter as Christ’s vicar, Guido of Crema and his accomplices were greatly troubled and confused, for fear and trembling seized them. The Catholics, though they had endured many tribulations for righteousness from Emperor Frederick, nevertheless rejoiced [Col. 0028C] in the Church’s favorable successes and the extreme confusion of the schismatics.

The Lombard league also continued undaunted against the enemies of the Church and assailants of its liberty. It arranged everything that it foresaw would be more useful for its defense, and exerted effort and diligence to the utmost of its powers so that it might destroy the emperor’s cunning schemes and devices, which he had prepared for the confusion of the Lombards. Therefore the Veronese and Paduans, as warlike men and lovers of their own liberty, in order wholly to disrupt the emperor’s coming through their territories and wisely provide for themselves and their entire country in the future, attacked the strongly fortified Castle of Rivoli and the fortress of Appendice—[Note: A: “Appendii.”]—with a strong force, and, besieging them manfully, destroyed them utterly.

At the same time the emperor gathered an army, and for the third time unexpectedly entered Lombardy through Val Camonica, encamping in the territory of Brescia [Col. 0028D]. Although he hated the Lombard cities greatly and had no confidence in them for any reason, nevertheless, because they had all united against him, it was not safe for him to inflict any injury or annoyance upon them. Accordingly, concealing the ferocity he bore in his heart, he showed himself gentle and cheerful toward all. Companies of nobles and citizens continually approached his presence, as is customary at the sight of so great a prince, and rendered him the honor due to him and their customary reverence.

He advanced toward Ferrara and came in complete peace to the vicinity of Bologna, where he resolved to remain for a while because of the fatigue of his army. Meanwhile he sent some of his magnates ahead into Tuscany, that they might bring aid and forces to Guido of Crema, whom he had again set up as an idol against [Col. 0029A] God, and might endeavor to inflict upon Pope Alexander and the Romans whatever injuries and harm they could. He himself descended with his army to Ancona. Since the emperor of the Greeks, having paid an immense sum of money, held that city forcibly occupied through its citizens, Frederick besieged it and strove by every means to take it, in order to avenge the injury done to himself and his empire.

Moreover, the barbarous host of the same emperor which he had sent into Tuscany, because of the dissensions and wars that had arisen between the Pisans and Lucchese, so terrified everyone and subjected them to imperial lordship that in the city of Rome scarcely anyone could be found who dared resist the imperial commands. Then the towns surrounding the City and their captains were invaded by the Germans and separated from their customary loyalty and subjection to Blessed Peter. Thus these wicked men devastated the whole land with many plunderings, burnings, and other oppressions.

Since they could not subject the mother-city Rome itself to the emperor by force of arms, they nevertheless attempted to corrupt it by lavish distributions of money, so that the Scripture of old might be fulfilled [Col. 0029B]. And because Rome, if it found a purchaser, offered itself for sale, there were not lacking many among that people who, having received money, dared to swear allegiance to Guido the heresiarch and to the emperor against all men.

As these grievous evils increased on every side, the kindly pontiff repeatedly admonished the same people with paternal affection: they should be of one mind with himself and the Church, peacefully recall and bind to themselves the neighboring cities and captains, and stand unanimously with him in defense of the Church and the City against their most powerful adversary. He also offered that people money from the Church to be spent on this undertaking according to the Church’s means. But, sins demanding it, he could accomplish nothing with a people which pretended [Col. 0029C] to please both parties and faithfully adhered to neither. Since it neither wished to understand the shepherd’s voice nor to guard against the calamities that were coming, it justly incurred divine vengeance, when it deserved to lose at once the ownership of persons and of property.

In those days, while Emperor Frederick was still besieging Ancona, the Lombard league, strengthened more firmly in the solidity of its liberty, judged it proper to restore the Milanese, with the Lord’s help, to their city and more diligently repair its ruined walls, aided by the merits of Blessed Ambrose. To give its undertaking greater permanence, it also joined Lodi—recently transferred by the emperor to a very fortified place for the oppression of other cities—to these same Milanese by a friendly treaty and bound it by a closer bond of affection. Moreover, with the Lord’s help, it installed bishops and other prelates of churches throughout all its cities and dioceses, after schismatics and intruders had been expelled in disgrace. Therefore, although the emperor was grieved to the depths of his heart [Col. 0029D], he chose rather to endure these things for the time being with dissimulation than to make his wavering cause worse in the present.

At the same time William, the illustrious and glorious king of Sicily, a faithful and devoted son of the Roman Church—whose soul we commend to the Lord—died peacefully at Palermo. Accordingly, William, his elder son, succeeded him—just as in the kingdom, so also in the same loyalty and devotion—through the Lord’s agency.

At the same time Emmanuel, the great and exalted emperor of Constantinople, knowing the troubles and injuries which the aforesaid Frederick was trying to inflict upon the venerable Pope Alexander against God and every principle of justice, sent to the city of Rome Jordan, sebastos of his empire and son of Robert, formerly prince of Capua, for the aid and service of the same pontiff. On arriving, this sebastos humbly bowed to the pontiff; having offered great and precious gifts at his feet, he carefully laid before him [Col. 0030A] everything he had received as instructions.

Among other things, however, one principal matter was contained which appeared most welcome to God and men. He affirmed that the same emperor wished to unite his Church, as it had better been united in ancient times, with the most holy Roman Church, mother of all Churches, so that under one observance of the divine law and one head of the Church both clergy and peoples—namely Latin and Greek—might remain in perpetual firmness. He also requested that, since a just occasion and a fitting and acceptable time had presented themselves, the crown of the Roman empire should be restored to him by the apostolic see, because he asserted that it belonged by right not to Frederick the German but to himself.
