To carry out this undertaking, he firmly promised to provide such riches of gold and silver and such military strength that he could without doubt bring not only Rome but all Italy into the Church’s service and recover for himself the crown of the Church [Col. 0030B].

Though this proposal seemed very difficult and required much deliberation, it nevertheless appeared expedient that the pontiff, having consulted his brethren and the more faithful men of the City, should send the bishop of Ostia and the cardinal of Saints John and Paul from his side with the aforesaid sebastos to treat of the matter in the presence of that emperor.

In the seventh year of his pontificate, the Roman people began, among other neighboring communities, to hate the Albans and Tusculans: both because, amid the urgent wickedness of the time, they adhered to the Germans, and because they did not buy themselves off from the Romans in proportion to the excessive demands imposed on them. Thus, as rivalries increased and grew between them, in May, when the harvests turn white, the people as a whole, armed in all their strength and contrary to their shepherd’s prohibition, marched out against Rayno, lord of Tusculum.

Advancing into his land, they not only hostilely devastated [Col. 0030C] vineyards, crops, and trees, but also labored to destroy the walls of the city of Tusculum. But since Rayno could neither resist such strength by himself nor defend his land, he had to seek refuge in the emperor’s help. The emperor therefore swiftly sent an immense multitude of strong warriors for Rayno’s assistance and protection, both to defend the Tusculan people and restrain Roman insolence.

After that savage German barbarian host, always accustomed to warfare, reached Tusculum, it saw that the Roman people were numerous but improperly arranged for battle. It took courage and boldness to engage them in battle in the field without delay. As the sides approached, after the ninth hour, a mighty cry suddenly rose from both sides to the stars, and, with swords drawn, the enemies rushed most savagely upon their enemies. But at the first clash the Roman people fell beyond recovery. They were so wickedly shattered and routed over fields and through the paths of valleys that scarcely a third of so great an army escaped [Col. 0030D].

That night, therefore, throughout the entire City there arose sudden grief and great wailing: an unheard-of calamity, insatiable mourning, and irreparable loss of men and goods. Indeed, from the time when Hannibal defeated the Romans at Cannae, no one remembers a slaughter of Romans so great. Yet, though in so grave a sorrow and common grief the pontiff himself could in no way restrain his weeping and tears, seeing that the City was deprived at once of the defense of men and arms, he swiftly adopted the more useful counsel of keeping vigilant guard over the City, repairing its weakened walls, and seeking assistance from within.

The enemies, excessively exulting in their prize of victory, were not content with victory itself. Joined by the Tiburtines, Albans, Campanians, and other surrounding peoples, they immediately hastened to the City [Col. 0031A] and, destroying all fortifications and all crops as far as the river Tiber, surrounded the same City up to its gates.

When the emperor learned of so great a slaughter of Romans, he left Ancona and, coming to his army with no small force, encamped at Monte Mario on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August [19 July]. On the following day, seeing the countless multitude of his army assembled, he descended in great strength as far as the gates of the Castle of Saint Angelo, where he made a most violent assault and repeated attacks. But because the household of the supreme pontiff, called by another name the *masnada*, strongly and manfully resisted him face to face through the prayer of Blessed Peter, that day he gained nothing but the loss of his own men and the disgrace of defeat.

Stirred to even greater fury, he violently attacked with crossbows and archers the church of the Prince of the Apostles, which was held in custody by the faithful of the Church. Since he could not take it [Col. 0031B], setting aside reverence for God and for the same keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, he ordered fire to be applied as a sacrilegious and profane man. The guards of the church, fearing that the entire fabric of the church would be consumed by fire, after the church of Saint Mary in the Tower had been burned, together with its bronze doors and the neighboring porticoes, surrendered the basilica of Blessed Peter into the hand and power of the raging prince.

When the blessed pontiff carefully foresaw these and other impending evils, after that destruction of the people which had happened through sins demanding it, he left the Lateran palace with his brethren and their households, went down to the secure houses of the Frangipani, and took refuge with them at Santa Maria Nuova, the Chartularia, and the Colosseum. There, because of the emperor’s threatening malice, bishops and cardinals met daily; cases were considered and answers given.

In those days the aforesaid king of Sicily, hearing how [Col. 0031C] that savage persecutor of the Church held Rome under siege, feared that some graver danger might befall his lord Pope Alexander in person. He sent him two swift galleys with a great sum of money, commanding their crews to endeavor to reach the pontiff; once they had delivered him the money, they were to receive his person and those of his brethren into those galleys and rescue them from Frederick’s power and from the expectation—[Note: A: “assault.”]—of all the schismatics.

Unexpectedly, the galleys sailed up the channel of the Tiber and came to the church of Saint Paul. Word having been sent to the supreme pontiff, under the guidance of the distinguished man Odo Frangipani, the crews of the galleys approached the feet of the same prelate with the money which they carried. Then the venerable pontiff gave thanks to almighty God for these things, graciously accepted the money, and retained the envoys of that most devoted prince with him for eight days in paternal affection.

Having taken counsel concerning the cause of the Church and the City, he sent the galleys back with thanksgiving to that same king, the most devoted and special son of Blessed Peter. With them he sent two of his brethren, namely M., cardinal deacon of Saint George, and P., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro, to the region of San Germano [Col. 0031D]. Of the money received, he gave a portion to the Frangipani and the sons of Peter Leonis, faithful supporters of the Church, so that, being more closely bound to one another, they might assist each other more strongly, uphold and more stoutly encourage the people in defense of the City. For guarding the City, he sent a portion of the same money to each gate with paternal generosity.

But while the Roman citizens stood more firmly than usual against Frederick and inflicted increasingly serious losses upon him each day, he saw that he could not prevail against them by force of arms. Like a cunning fox [Col. 0032A], he turned to the usual devices of more subtle craft. Through Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, who had gone to him with Pope Alexander’s permission, he sent words of peace to the bishops and cardinals in this form:

“If you bring it about with Alexander that, without prejudice to all his arrangements, he ceases to be pope, I will cause Guido of Crema to cease likewise. Then let all ecclesiastical persons assemble together and freely elect a third person as supreme pontiff. I shall grant the Church a firm peace and shall never again interfere in any way in the matter of the election of the Roman pontiff.”

For this reason he also promised the Roman people that he would restore all their captives and whatever remained of their plunder. This proposal was so welcome to the people that all unanimously praised it as something that ought to be done. They said that for the redemption of his sheep the lord pope ought to do something greater than relinquish the papacy.

But the bishops and [Col. 0032B] cardinals, after deliberate consultation, replied most firmly to Frederick with one voice: “It is not for us to judge the supreme pontiff, whom God has reserved to his own judgment; for, as Scripture testifies: ‘The disciple is not above the master’” (Luke 6).

Since the people strongly pressed the pontiff to put their request into effect, the pontiff, looking to what would better serve the Church, spoke privately with a few brethren and vanished from their sight. But, through the Lord’s favor, on the third day he was seen dining with his companions at the foot of Mount Circeo, beside the spring thereafter called the Papal Spring. Proceeding beyond the river Legula, and with crowds of both clergy and laity flocking to him from every side, he passed through Terracina and Gaeta with joy and gladness, and at length, with the Lord’s favor, reached the Beneventan patrimony with a multitude of bishops. The brethren who had remained after him in the City followed in his footsteps and clung to their head [Col. 0032C] as members of his body.

When Frederick learned that Pope Alexander had left the City and escaped his snares, he was greatly distressed, fearing that Alexander might stir the whole world against him and incite the greater princes of the age to his overthrow. But because in all his acts he had not recognized the gentleness and patience of almighty God and Blessed Peter—like the man “who did not make God his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his riches”—the Lord was angry with him together with Blessed Peter, whose Church he had not shrunk from burning, setting aside the fear of God.

For He sent so great a plague of sudden death into Frederick’s army that within seven days nearly all his chief princes who opposed the Church with him fell by sudden death and died miserably. We have judged it proper to name a few of the more famous among them: Frederick, duke of Bavaria; Henry—[Note: M: “Henricum.”]—count of Nassau [Col. 0032D]; Burchard, count of Alremont; Henry—[Note: M: “Henricum.”]—count of Lippe; R., chancellor and intruded occupant of the church of Cologne; and L., his brother, a count; and the bishop of Verden, an obstinate schismatic.

The remaining barons and knights, and the great multitude of other combatants, sickened and, finding no remedy of health, miserably breathed out their spirits; their bodies lay everywhere unburied. What more need be said? Such fear of sudden death had seized everyone that anyone counted himself blessed if he could somehow leave the camp and make his way to his own refuge. Then Frederick himself, realizing that he had been struck by the divine hand, came to some sort of arrangement with the Romans and withdrew, not without manifest shame, on the eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August].

Yet the plague of mortality followed him still. As he attempted to move onward [Col. 0033A], he left behind him with sorrow a trail of the dead. The arms and the remaining precious equipment of the Germans perished together with their lords, and all their glory was reduced to nothing by divine judgment.

When Frederick reached Lucca amid the lamentations of the dying and the groans of the sick, and wished to pass by the public road and over Monte Bardone, the Lombards forbade him to venture into their territory. Therefore, having obtained safe-conduct from Marquis Malaspina—[Note: A: “having obtained a safe-conduct for himself at Montetremulo.”]—at Pontremoli, he turned aside from the public road. Directing his journey thence through the hollows of valleys and over rugged mountains, he passed like a fugitive near Tortona, not without much plundering of his possessions, and finally arrived at Pavia with a few companions.

But, what was very remarkable in the eyes of all, neither the memory of the many evils which he had cruelly committed from his youth, nor the recent blows inflicted upon him by God and Blessed Peter, had softened the hardness and ferocity of his heart [Col. 0033B] or converted him to do good. Indeed, his nature had been inclined to evil from his adolescence and is believed always to have become still more prone to the same. Therefore the cities of Lombardy, which had long experienced his cruelty and savagery—[Note: A and M add: “within themselves.”]—seeing that his purpose and will against them burned more fiercely than usual, resolved in common deliberation that they ought to expel him from all Lombardy, since he strove to reduce all Italy to shameful servitude.

Accordingly, having gathered a force of brave men, they attacked Frederick as he was leaving Pavia. As a violator and destroyer of the laws and constitutions of orthodox emperors, and one excommunicated by the Roman Church, they did not cease to pursue him until they had violently expelled him from all the borders of Lombardy and compelled him to cross the Alps.

Accordingly, Lombardy having been delivered by divine help [Col. 0033C] from his tyranny and restored to its ancient liberty, all the Lombards—except the Pavians and the people of Como—wisely resolved and decreed that, for the future defense of all, they should build a populous city between Pavia and Asti. It was to be a secure defense and safe stronghold for the Lombards in time to come, while offering the Germans a very great obstacle.

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1168, on the Kalends of May [1 May], in the indiction . . . and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander, Cremona, together with the Milanese and Piacenzans, assembled with a strong force against the rebellion of the Pavians and of the marquis of Montferrat, at the settlement called Rovoretum. There, in honor of God, blessed Peter, and all Lombardy, they marked out the circuit of the city to be built and enclosed the place itself with a broad ditch. All the inhabitants dwelling in the surrounding settlements came there to live, with their families and all their goods: namely, those of Marengo, Gamundioforo, Bergulio, Hunilla, and Solestia. Thus a great and strong city suddenly came into being.

That it might everywhere be held more glorious and renowned, all agreed that this city should forever be called Alexandria, in reverence for blessed Peter and Pope Alexander. It is situated in a pleasant and most fertile district beside the public road, fortified on every side by three rivers and abounding in many resources. In its first year, its inhabitants were said to have increased to fifteen thousand fighting men, cavalry and infantry alike. In the second year, the consuls of that city came to Lord Pope Alexander at Benevento, offering the city itself to him—and through him to the Holy Roman Church—as a right and possession; and of their own accord they made it tributary to blessed Peter. Moreover, they swore to him and [Col. 0034A] to his successors that every year the consulship and people of Alexandria should renew it in their own name, as they had promised. [Note: A. reads “invoke” (*invocare*) instead of “renew” (*innovare*).] When these matters had been duly completed, the consuls returned home, under the Lord’s guidance, with the favor, exultation, and blessing of that pontiff.

At the same time the same pontiff deposed the bishops of Vescovio and Gaiacenza, who had been accused and convicted of simony. It also happened that John, cardinal priest formerly of the title of Saint Martin, who from the beginning of this schism had never ceased to persecute the Church together with Octavian and Guido of Cremona, was riding outside Viterbo when he suddenly fell and, his neck broken, ended his impenitent life by a most miserable death. Guido of Cremona likewise, who had succeeded Octavian in the schism, was struck by an incurable affliction in his foot and had to limp for the rest of his life.

Since the Romans could not avenge the cruel injury inflicted upon them by the Germans, they turned on the people of Albano upon this pretext: they had supported the emperor against them and had dared to offend them. The Romans attacked them so relentlessly that they utterly destroyed their city. For a similar reason they also endeavored to do the same to Tusculum and to other stronger neighboring places; but because the Church did not consent to their unjust designs, they reluctantly abandoned such a purpose for a short time.

Meanwhile Manuel, the great emperor of Constantinople, seeing that Frederick, called emperor, was fiercely attacking and persecuting the Roman Church and Pope Alexander together with the schismatics, sent to Benevento an apocrisiary, one of the leading men of his empire, with an immense quantity of money. In the presence of the pontiff he spoke as follows:

> “My lord the emperor has long earnestly desired to honor and exalt the Roman Church, his mother, and your person. Now [Col. 0034C], seeing that Frederick, her advocate—who by virtue of his office ought to protect and defend her against others—has become her attacker and persecutor, he wishes all the more to serve and assist her. And in order that in these times that Gospel saying may be fulfilled, ‘And there shall be one fold and one shepherd’ [John 10], he desires to unite and subject his Greek Church to that Roman Church, in the state in which it is known to have existed of old, provided that you are willing to restore his rights to him.
>
> “He therefore asks and entreats that, once the adversary of the aforesaid Church has been deprived of the crown of the Roman Empire, you restore it to him, as reason and justice require. For the accomplishment of this matter, whatever you judge necessary he is ready to bestow and pay without delay, in a sufficient outlay of money and in military power and strength, according to your good pleasure.”

When he had heard this, the pontiff, having deliberated at length with the bishops, cardinals, and more eminent Romans, answered the said apocrisiary as follows:

> “We give thanks to your lord the emperor, as to a most Christian prince and a most devoted son of blessed Peter, for his devout and frequent attentions and for the manifestation of the good will which he bears toward the holy Roman Church. Therefore we willingly hear his affectionate words and desire, with paternal kindness, to grant those requests in which we can do so according to God.
>
> “But the things which he requests are too lofty and exceedingly difficult; because of their difficulty they conflict with the decrees of the holy Fathers. Under such conditions we can neither give nor ought to give our assent, for it is fitting that we, by the office entrusted to us by God, should be makers and guardians of peace.”

Thus, having received no gift from the pontiff, the aforementioned apocrisiary returned [Col. 0035A] to his lord with all the money he had brought, accompanied by two cardinals whom the pontiff sent to the same emperor.

## On the miserable death of Guido of Cremona and the similar substitution of John of Struma

[Note: A. reads “Scrivinensis”; M. consistently reads “Scriniensis.”]

At the same time, while Guido of Cremona was lingering near the church of Saint Peter and stubbornly persisted in his error once begun, a disease of cancer, sent upon him by that apostle, appeared in his kidneys together with shortness of breath in his lungs. He discharged foul pus until, impenitent, he breathed out his unhappy spirit and succumbed to a most miserable death. Hence a certain poet sang in verse:

> The impious majesty of mad Guido and Octavian has fallen,  
> Their untimely power has fallen.  
> Alexander rises by right, Peter rises as another;  
> He stands now upon the rock, hereafter to be established in heaven.

[Col. 0035B] Thus the two heads of their desolation having been removed, the remaining troop of schismatics stood in the abyss of despair. Since no one from the body of the Church remained alive whom they could set over themselves, they chose a certain John, formerly abbot of Struma [Note: A. reads “Sarmensis.”], an apostate, slippery, gluttonous, and wandering man. Not without laughter and the mockery of many, they raised him as a horned third beast upon the chair of pestilence; perfidious and obstinate as they were, under the devil’s prompting they dared to worship and venerate that very abomination.

When this apostate man was despised and hated by all good people, as his merits deserved, he attached himself to the wicked and criminal, over whom he was long set as superior and leader. His supporters and intimate household were only apostates, pimps, buffoons, fugitives from monasteries, men condemned for their crimes, thieves, and robbers; these brought to him, needy and poor as he was, the spoils of travelers and pilgrims [Col. 0035C].

Meanwhile Emperor Frederick, seeing that the two statues which he had raised had fallen by divine judgment, and that the third had been selected and raised not from the body of the Church but from the fellowship of his accomplices, was grieved to the heart because his party had come to nothing, while Pope Alexander’s cause, growing stronger, was always advancing toward a better state. But lest he should seem to be overcome in his evil purpose and utterly confounded, he pretended, as a clever and very crafty man, to venerate the aforesaid beast, and commanded his supporters to maintain and uphold it.

After a short time, however, returning to his habitual crafty devices so that he might win everyone’s favor, he deceitfully displayed good will and a pious desire to restore peace between Church and empire. Indeed, he so craftily humbled himself that he sent the bishop of Bamberg—who had always been Catholic at heart—to Pope Alexander at Benevento [Col. 0035D]. He gave him authority to establish agreement and peace with the pope according to the form of the articles entrusted to him. He also ordered him to reveal all these matters to that pontiff alone.

As subsequently became clear, he is known to have acted with this cunning in order to sow discord between the Church and the Lombards and separate them from one another. When the pontiff learned with certainty that the bishop was coming, he could not doubt that nothing concerning the Lombards’ cause had been entrusted to him. Foreseeing the intrigues and artifices of the sender, he therefore, after deliberating with bishops and cardinals, quickly dispatched letters and messengers to the Lombards. He strengthened their doubtful and wavering hearts and urged them to send to his presence one prudent and suitable person from each city, representing the community as a whole [Col. 0036A]. With them he wished to discuss the word of peace and agreement which the bishop was bringing, and together with them to arrange and determine whatever should be done concerning it.

Accordingly, certain faithful and wise men were elected by the Lombard community and sent to the same pontiff. The aforementioned bishop came into Campania and announced his arrival to the pontiff, asking and entreating him, since he had been forbidden to enter the kingdom of Sicily, to deign to return to the Campanian patrimony of blessed Peter in order to confer with him. At his request, then, the pontiff was pleased to go up from Benevento into Campania with his brethren and the Lombard envoys, and to await the aforesaid bishop in the city of Veroli.

On the following day, while the pontiff was sitting, as customary, in full consistory, the bishop of Bamberg arrived [Note: A. and M. consistently read “Banbergensis.”] [Col. 0036B]. Reverently approaching before Pope Alexander, he paid him homage and said:

> “My lord Emperor Frederick has sent me to you and strictly commanded me to speak with you privately and reveal to you alone those things which he has entrusted to me to say.”

Although the pontiff repeatedly told him, “It is wholly useless for you to set forth to me alone matters on which I will give you no answer without the knowledge and consent of my brethren and of these Lombards,” he could scarcely at last obtain from him that he should first hear him alone and afterwards communicate what he had heard to whomever he wished. The pontiff therefore heard him carefully in private, as he requested.

After many varied matters which the bishop disclosed to the pontiff, he firmly asserted that the emperor wished to take no further action against the pope personally, but would hold valid all the pope’s ordinations and command others to hold them so. Yet concerning the papacy and the obedience due to it, he spoke so ambiguously and veiledly that [Col. 0036C] no Catholic meaning could at all be gathered from his words. When the pontiff pressed him insistently and strongly to speak concerning these matters not in parables but most openly and truthfully, he confessed that he had been strictly forbidden either to explain or to alter the actual words.

Having heard this, and being unable to draw anything further from the bishop, the pontiff returned to the more private chamber where he had left his brethren with the Lombards. He reported to them all that he had heard; and after some deliberation Pope Alexander answered the bishop as follows:

> “Dear brother in Christ, we greatly marvel at your prudence in bringing to us, as though unaware, such an embassy from one whose stratagems and artifices we do not ignore. For if, as you assert, that emperor now, thanks be to God, wishes to accept the ordinances made by us and have others hold them valid, while not consenting to our person—even though we are unworthy, we have nevertheless canonically succeeded blessed Peter in the apostolic see—what else does he do but venerate and worship God, while in one respect denying Him?
>
> “The whole Church of God, together with other Christian kings and princes, has already judged our cause canonical and obeys us in every respect. If, therefore, he wishes to be numbered among the sheep which God entrusted to blessed Peter to feed, why does he still delay to bend his neck to the Prince of the Apostles and join himself to Catholic unity? For our part, unless he himself prevents it, we are ready and eager above all other princes of the world to honor and love him and to preserve his rights for him in their entirety, provided that he loves with filial devotion his mother, the most holy Roman Church, which raised him to the height of empire, and preserves her liberty for her.”

Thus rebuked and fraternally admonished, the bishop of Bamberg returned to Frederick, escorted by the Lombards.

## On the gift of the city of Tusculum: how Rayno handed it over to Pope Alexander

[Col. 0037A]

While the pontiff was staying at Veroli and the Romans were attacking the Tusculans more fiercely than usual, Rayno, their lord, terrified by excessive fear, acted contrary to the fidelity which he owed to the pontiff. Like a foolish and senseless man, he gave the city of Tusculum in exchange to the accursed John, whom Frederick had made prefect of the City; and he released the Tusculan people from the fidelity by which they were bound to him. Having put the city into John’s hand and power, he received from him Montefiascone and the borough of Saint Flavian, with their dependencies—places known to belong solely by proper right to blessed Peter.

When Pope Alexander saw the patrimony of blessed Peter thus insolently alienated and bestowed, he could not refrain from indignation and grave anger against both parties. Indeed, one half of Tusculum, together with Montefiascone and the borough [Col. 0037B] of Saint Flavian, belongs by right of ownership to the Roman Church alone. On the other hand, the Romans hated both men; but in order that they might gain dominion, they assailed the city of Tusculum itself more violently with continual attacks.

Therefore the accursed John, greatly frightened, abandoned the city and fled. Rayno likewise, realizing that he had been entirely deceived, was scorned and expelled by the knights and people of Montefiascone. He left that land and, overwhelmed with shame, wished to return to the Tusculans whom he had foolishly abandoned. But because he had released them from his lordship and their fidelity, and had rashly subjected them to another lord, they not only refused to receive him but drove him from all their territory.

Thus, bereft of every aid and counsel, he fled to his mother, the Roman Church, which he had rashly injured. Like the prodigal son, he asked Lord Pope Alexander and his brethren for pardon and mercy, placing himself and whatever right he seemed to possess in the city of Tusculum at their good pleasure and mercy. But the Tusculan people had already forestalled Rayno: as far as lay in their power, they had voluntarily handed themselves and their city over under the lordship of blessed Peter and the power of the pontiff. Accordingly Rayno made, by public instrument, a donation of that city to the pope and his successors [Col. 0037C].

## On the murder of blessed Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury

At the same time, a deeply sorrowful report of the murder of Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, in connection with the king of England reached the ears of the Apostolic See. As this report grew, the king not without reason feared that the Roman Church would punish such a crime severely in his person, unless it came to know his innocence more clearly. He therefore sent ecclesiastical and prudent men to the supreme pontiff [Col. 0037D], granting them authority to swear upon his soul that the king himself would personally submit to the command of the pontiff by oath regarding the killing for which he had been accused.

When these envoys came to Tusculum on the Thursday of Holy Week before Easter, as the pontiff was about to go to church according to his customary practice, they presented themselves before the apostolic presence. Having explained what had been imposed upon them by the king, they offered to take the oath, as we have said. The pontiff then, having taken counsel with his brethren, went out into the consistory and, in public audience, received that oath from the envoys, as it had been formulated and determined by the cardinals, and granted the king a truce.

Accordingly the pontiff sent two of his brethren, A., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and T., cardinal priest of the title of Vestina, into Gaul, so that, in their presence, the king’s guilt or [Col. 0038A] innocence might become clear where so detestable a crime had been perpetrated. On learning of the arrival of the legates of the Apostolic See, the king left all his pressing affairs which he was then conducting in Ireland, hastened back to Normandy, and came humbly and reverently before them at Caen on the second day, with his bishops and barons, prepared to obey their commands as had previously been pledged through his envoys.

Since no one appeared to accuse him regarding the crime laid to his charge, the king cleared himself before the legates, in the presence of a multitude of bishops, barons, and others, clergy and laity alike, as follows.

## Oath of innocence by H., king of England, concerning the death of blessed Thomas

> “I, King H., swear upon these holy Gospels of God that I neither planned, knew of, nor commanded the death of Saint Thomas; and when I learned that the deed had been committed, I grieved and was made as sorrowful as if I had learned that my own son had been killed.
>
> “But I cannot excuse myself in this: that, on the occasion of the agitation and anger which I had conceived against that holy man, he was killed. For this guilt, because I appear to have given cause for his death, I shall without delay send two hundred knights at my own expense to Jerusalem for the defense of Christianity. They shall remain there for one year, or I shall pay them enough that the same number of knights may be maintained there for a year.
>
> “I shall also take the sign of the Lord’s Cross for three years and shall go there in person, unless I remain by permission of the Roman pontiff. I wholly abolish the unlawful customs which I have introduced throughout all my land in my time and henceforth prohibit their observance. I shall also permit appeals to the Apostolic See to be made freely from now on, and will prevent no one in this matter [Col. 0038C].
>
> “Moreover, I and my eldest son, the king, swear that we shall receive and hold the kingdom of England from Lord Pope Alexander and his Catholic successors; and that we and our successors shall never consider ourselves true kings of England unless they acknowledge us as Catholic kings.”

While these matters were being conducted in Gaul, the Romans persisted in their folly. Though they desired the shepherd and bishop of their souls to return to them with his brethren, the bishops and cardinals, they did not permit him to enter the City and perform the office due in its churches. Therefore, since they rejected the word of God which ought first to have been preached to them, the pontiff departed Tusculum with his brethren and went to stay in the Campanian patrimony of blessed Peter, until the Lord should provide better times for His Church.

## On Pope Alexander’s canonization of Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury

[Col. 0038D] Meanwhile, while most blessed Thomas, the glory of the English, was shining everywhere, by God’s will, in the great splendor of miracles, and while not only friends but even persecutors were asking pardon for their sins and continually coming to his tomb to seek benefits of salvation, the Roman pontiff, at the request of the Gallican clergy and people, canonized the same martyr by apostolic authority and commanded that he be enrolled among the other saints.

On the day of the Purification of blessed Mary [2 February], having summoned the bishops and abbots of Campania, he celebrated at Segni with special solemnity the Mass in Thomas’s honor and decreed that the anniversary of his passion, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January [29 December], should be observed forever. Therefore the Western Church rejoiced with great joy, and the name of the glorious martyr increased daily through the manifestation of miracles, so that he was held ever more celebrated even among foreign nations.

Through his merits, almighty God manifestly raised the dead; He restored sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf [Col. 0039A], and walking to the lame; cleansed lepers, healed the sick, freed the possessed, and likewise willed to perform many other marvelous works through him. Therefore very many of the faithful built churches in his honor, to the praise and glory of our Creator, and enriched them with their goods and possessions.

## On the war between the king of England and his son after the death of blessed Thomas

Two years and three months after the death of that martyr had passed when, not without the judgment of divine vengeance, as is believed, it happened that the eldest son of the aforesaid king of England—whom his father, in paternal affection, had exalted as king—wickedly rebelled against his father. Together with his mother and brothers, he rashly attempted to expel him from the whole kingdom. Thus the kingdom was divided into two parts, and the armed barons of Aquitaine stood, some with the son and others with the father.

To crown so detestable a calamity, the king of France received under his protection the younger king, to whom he had given his daughter in marriage, and worked with all his strength to aid and support him against his father. Consequently ruinous evils increased on both sides: the son, as sins demanded, sought his father’s death, and the father thirsted for the son’s killing. Then great armies were prepared on either side, and the younger king, together with [Note: A. reads, “with his fellow-king, etc.”] his father-in-law, the king of France, entered Normandy to fight against his father. Conversely, the elder king of England labored with a strong hand to defend his land and strove by every means to repel force with force.

Without delay, fighting men everywhere rushed to arms, committed plunder, burned villages, stormed castles, invaded churches, and did not cease cruelly to perpetrate other deeds of impiety throughout Aquitaine. As these evils increased daily, Lord Pope Alexander, wishing in fulfillment of his office to provide for the devastations and losses of both kingdoms, sent into those regions his legate, P., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus [Col. 0039C]. He ordered him to summon bishops and other religious persons from both sides and diligently devote effort and care to bringing the kings unanimously back to peace and agreement.

Accordingly, when the legate arrived at a suitable time, prelates of the churches and other religious and prudent men, together with him, intervened so earnestly on behalf of their respective sides that, with the Lord’s help, they brought both parties back to the good of unity and peace.

## On Emperor Frederick’s fifth return to Lombardy

At the same time, in the fifteenth year of Pope Alexander’s pontificate, the so-called Emperor Frederick returned for the fifth time to Lombardy in hostility, at the urging of the Pavians and the marquis of Montferrat. He crossed Mont Cenis and, descending to the plain with a great multitude, made camp near Susa on the third day before the Kalends of October [29 September] [Col. 0039D]. On the following day, unable longer to conceal his conceived rage, he burned that city at the outset of his detestable deeds, and thence directed his battle-lines toward Asti in order to carry out his remaining evils.

He had about him a great multitude of barbarian peoples: men practiced in warfare [Note: A. reads “battle-lines” (*aciebus*) for “acts” (*actibus*)], utterly wicked, rapacious, and desperate, whom he had chosen from Flanders and other neighboring places. And because no one loves a madman, the Lombards, united in one spirit and one purpose, had long anticipated Frederick’s return; they had strongly fortified their cities and castles and stood fearless, like powerful fighting men, ready to resist him face to face.

They therefore sent to aid the Asti people, who had long been their confederates [Col. 0040A], able men very prudent in counsel and proven in arms, in order to make the Asti people bolder against the attack of the advancing enemy and that, when necessity required, they might fight more strongly for the maintenance of their liberty at their exhortation. But the Asti people, making worse provision for themselves in the future, imprudently withdrew from the confederation of the Lombard League. Prostrating themselves before the aforementioned Frederick, they delivered their city into his hand and power.

Asti thus having been subdued, Frederick, exalting himself above himself, hastened with the marquis of Montferrat and the Pavians toward the destruction of Alexandria, which the Lombards had newly built in honor of blessed Peter. But because in all his actions he wickedly opposed God and the Church, almighty God wonderfully frustrated his design and thwarted his purpose. He suddenly sent from heaven such a flood of rains that every river overflowed and all the plains [Col. 0040B] were transformed into marshes.

When the people of Alexandria saw help given them from heaven, they recovered strength and courage, although they had already prepared to flee in fear of the terrible prince. Trusting in the aid of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, they put aside their alarm and prepared themselves manfully to resist the injurious [Note: A. reads “countless”; M. reads “numerous.”] multitude of adversaries.

Yet although the severity of winter and the approaching difficulties of rain and snow discouraged Frederick from approaching Alexandria, he nevertheless advanced in his strength and established his camp on both sides near the city, in watery ground. Carefully observing that the city had no protection of walls or towers beyond its ditches and the proximity of the river Tanaro, he despised it, vainly hoping [Note: A. and M. read “vainly” (*inaniter*) for “in advance” (*in anteo*).] that at the first assault he could destroy it entirely.

Having therefore gathered all the strength of his army, he made a most severe attack upon the Alexandrians. He also brought up machines of various kinds to the embankments and fought against them fiercely for a long time. But, with the Lord’s aid, the people of Alexandria prevailed. They captured the enemy’s engines by force and compelled all that barbarian host to flee, not without slaughter, as far as their tents [Col. 0040C].

Since Frederick appeared to be defeated, he burned with greater anger and therefore, against the counsel and will of his princes, resolved to remain in the siege until he obtained victory. But because the severity of winter was imminent and the whole army suffered a lack of necessities, the multitude of horses began to fail altogether and soldiers’ equipment was being sold off cheaply. Yet neither these nor other difficulties caused imperial wrath to cease from attacking the Alexandrians, although he always received a worse repulse from them.

Since he could by no means incline the citizens to surrender through terrors, flatteries, or promises, he secretly caused underground passages to be made, through which he hoped to enter and seize the city unexpectedly. But, God resisting him, he deserved to suffer a ruinous loss from the very means by which he believed he would obtain future victory and triumph. And because the city had already been closely besieged for four months and was suffering many privations, it jointly requested the forces and assistance of the Lombards [Col. 0040D].

## How the Lombards assisted the Alexandrians

Then the vast league of Lombard cities assembled most swiftly in one place and, by the common decision of all, firmly decreed that they should hasten without delay to Alexandria with an abundance of provisions and other necessities, in a strong force. In the middle of Lent, therefore, all the cities and nobles of Liguria, the March, and Emilia assembled at Piacenza [Col. 0041A]. Having duly arranged and ordered everything that appeared pertinent to military needs, they left that city with ships and wagons laden with provisions and arms.

They advanced toward Alexandria in great strength of armed cavalry and infantry, crossbowmen also and archers; and on Palm Sunday they pitched camp near Tortona, no more than ten miles from Frederick’s camp. When the Germans and Lombards caught sight of one another, fear and mental stupefaction seized Frederick as he considered the terrible multitude of armed men standing against him like an ordered battle-line of camps.

He therefore turned to his usual schemes of cunning and spoke deceptively yet gently to the Alexandrians:

> “Tomorrow is the holy day of Friday, which every Christian reveres with the greatest devotion. Therefore, out of reverence for the Crucified One, by imperial favor I grant and bestow upon you a truce and safe-conduct until Monday.”

Having received this assurance, each person of the population, suspecting no evil, slept securely in his home. But their plotter, about the first watch of the night, ordered the stronger armed men to enter the city through the underground passages. He himself stood armed with his whole army at the gates, waiting until those whom he had sent ahead had entered the city and until he heard the cries of alarm, so that, while fighting increased within, he might force his way in from outside through the gate and seize the city as an enemy.

But the Lord brought it about—marvelous in the eyes of all—that the city was delivered in a moment from such wicked treachery and that discovered iniquity was justly turned back upon the head of the wicked. For nothing is more just than that the contrivers of death should perish by their own law. Truth, which cannot lie, speaks thus of the reprobate: “His sorrow shall return upon his own head, and his iniquity shall descend upon his own crown” [Psalm 7]. And again: “He who prepares a pit for his neighbor himself falls into it” [Proverbs 26].

When the watchmen guarding the city saw companies of armed men had entered it, they shouted loudly for the people to rise swiftly to arms and drive out the enemy who had entered. The citizens then rushed quickly to arms and, like lions, boldly fell upon the enemy. Together with blessed Peter—whom they saw riding before them on a white horse in flashing armor—they cast them down and compelled all who had escaped death by the sword to emerge onto the embankments above, from which they were unwillingly thrown down.

Moreover, all who had not yet emerged from the underground passages were suffocated when the ground above collapsed. Once the gates had been opened, the people went out in great force and struck the army of perfidious Frederick with the sword until Saturday, so that heaps of corpses lay everywhere as far as his camp [Col. 0041D]. Furthermore, they manfully assaulted the wooden castle which he had carefully furnished, for the city’s ruin, with stronger and chosen knights, until they forcibly burned it with the knights inside.

## How Emperor Frederick withdrew in confusion from the siege of Alexandria
Frederick, therefore, seeing that the divine majesty was opposing him in all things, feared that he might suffer violence from the army of the Lombards, which was now approaching, and be compelled to abandon the siege in shame. Accordingly, on the following night he had his camp burned, and at dawn on the Sunday of the Resurrection he set out with all his men toward Pavia. But since he could not avoid passing close by the Lombard expedition, he wished, by this stratagem, to encamp near the Lombards in a village called Guiguella [Note: [Col. 0041D] M.: Guignella.], because he was not afraid [Col. 0042A] that they would attack him unless first provoked by him in hostile fashion.

The Lombards, however, did not yet know what the almighty God had wonderfully accomplished the previous day with the Alexandrians. But when they saw Frederick advancing against them with his banners raised, they took up arms and stood before him, manfully armed and ready for battle, waiting to see which course he would choose: whether he would begin war against them—which was scarcely believed possible, since he had far fewer fighting men than they—or whether he would encamp peacefully and injure no one. On that day which the Lord had made, however, he settled peacefully in the aforesaid village.

When the second day dawned, certain nobles, suspected by neither side, first approached Frederick and then the Lombards, speaking as follows: “What greater madness, or what more grievous evil, can be conceived or committed, than that a lord should wholly endeavor to deprive a servant—or servants their lord—of his right, and possess it by force? Let each side therefore be content with its own right; let these such grave evils now cease; and let the peace you desire be restored between you, with the Lord’s help.”

Then the emperor, after sighing and after many arguments had been put forward on both sides, replied thus: “Saving the right of the Empire, I am prepared to submit this dispute to the judgment of good men from both parties.” The community of the Lombards then said: “Saving the liberty of the Roman Church and our own liberty, for which we contend, we do the same.”

Immediately there were chosen by Frederick Philip, elect of Cologne; G. de Pozasca, captain of Turin; and B. [Note: [Col. 0041D] A. and M. read R. instead of B.] de Sancto Nazario of Pavia. By the Lombards were chosen G. Pistis of Milan, G. de Gambara of Brescia, and G. of Verona. To these both parties gladly entrusted themselves by compromise. After this the Lombards reverently approached Frederick and honored him; and he received and honored them kindly [Note: [Col. 0042D] A.: “well.”]. Thus these matters having been completed on both sides, Frederick permitted the army to depart, [Col. 0042C] and went down into the city of Pavia with his wife, children, and household.

As the Lombards returned joyfully to their homes, they encountered near Piacenza the Cremonese with their carroccio and expeditionary force. For they had always been half-hearted in the undertaking of the league of cities, out of regard for their friendship with the Pavians; and they had therefore deliberately delayed leaving until after the others, so that the expedition of the community might be disrupted by their delay. When they learned that the aforesaid agreement had been made without them, they were covered with shame. Then the people of Cremona, fiercely enraged against their consuls, severely avenged the disgrace of their city: they utterly destroyed the consuls’ palaces and houses, plundered all their property, deposed them, and appointed others as consuls in their place.

Although the Lombard cities were negotiating agreement and peace with Frederick, nevertheless, knowing that man’s cunning, they continued thereafter to guard themselves against him. Therefore they renewed more carefully the oaths of their confederation [Col. 0042D] and always exercised greater vigilance in all things.

## How the Emperor Frederick Sought Peace from the Roman Church in Person, Deceptively

While Frederick remained for a long time at Pavia and met with continually adverse outcomes in all his undertakings, he tried, in order to make religious men and his people favorable to himself, to seek in person peace with the Roman Church—a peace which, above all other things, he publicly declared himself to desire.

He therefore sent letters and members of his household to the bishops of Ostia and Porto and to the cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains, asking them to come safely to him for the restoration of peace between Church and Empire, so that they might discuss the matter with one another face to face and, with the Lord’s assistance, bring it to the desired conclusion with honor to the Church [Col. 0043A].

When this message reached the ears of the Apostolic See, it was not without reason suspected by all: both because the performance of the past showed what certainty might be expected in the future, and because Frederick himself seemed in no way inclined toward good works. Nevertheless, because, according to the saying of blessed Augustine, doubtful matters must always be interpreted in the better sense, and because peace is described as something not merely to be sought but pursued, Lord Pope Alexander, by the common counsel of his brethren, honorably sent the aforesaid persons, fully instructed, to the presence of that prince.

As they traveled separately through different regions, all the people rejoiced in the Lord at the welcome sight of them and brought them a great multitude of children for confirmation. The bishop of Porto and the cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains passed honorably through Spoleto, Imola, and Bologna [Col. 0043B], proceeding as far as Piacenza. There they waited several days for the arrival of the bishop of Ostia, who had passed with glory and honor through the cities of Pisa and Lucca. Meanwhile, in order to confer with the rulers of the cities of Lombardy about the matters entrusted to them, they went to Lodi. When that conference had been completed, they heard that the bishop of Ostia had arrived at Piacenza, and they hastened to join him.

Once these three legates of the Apostolic See were together, they announced their arrival to Frederick, asking him immediately to inform them what he wished them to do. He replied kindly, ordering them to cross the river Po and come safely to him. The legates accordingly left Piacenza with a great escort of envoys and knights, proceeded to the bank of the Po, crossed in prepared vessels, and came to the city of Pavia, where they were honorably received and lodged.

On the following day [Col. 0043C], while the emperor sat publicly in state with the princes and a great concourse of people, the legates approached him together. When they entered before him and sat opposite him on their folding seats, the emperor immediately removed the cap which he wore on his head and greeted the legates in German, as the interpreter’s report declared. He added that their coming was very pleasing to him and their presence most welcome, but he cheerfully invited them to set forth the matters which they had come to conduct.

Then the bishop of Ostia stood in the midst and answered before the whole assembly with a cheerful countenance:

“Your greeting, lord emperor, is welcome and most acceptable to us, as proceeding from a most eminent prince and a most excellent power. But in the address of this greeting, one thing bitterly grieves us: at present, because our sins so require, we cannot return your greeting as we wish. May almighty God, through the ineffable mercy of his goodness, bring about between his bride, the most holy Church, and your Empire that harmony and peace of unity, so that what we cannot now do without scruple of conscience, we may soon be able lovingly to perform, with the Lord’s favor [Col. 0043D].

“For the pursuit of this pious work [Note: [Col. 0043D] A.: “this very work.”], so far as lies in us, we have come especially at your invitation, trusting neither in ourselves nor in our merits, but placing our confidence for the success of this undertaking in him who, when he sent his disciples to preach, said: ‘I have chosen you and appointed you, that you should bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain’ (John 15).”

Beginning from the origin of the schism, he lamented all the burdens of the Church and the manifest ruin of the Empire; and he pleaded so fearlessly for concord and peace between the two parties that all who were present marveled at his words and joyfully said to one another in their hearts: “This man does not speak; rather, the Spirit of God the Father, who dwells in him, speaks.”

Then, shortening his speech, he sharply reproved the emperor’s obstinacy especially in this: that after the four persons who had adhered to him in opposition to the body of the Church had been removed from the midst by God’s judgment, and the whole world had received one Roman pontiff as father and shepherd of their souls, he alone ought no longer to resist Catholic unity, but should believe in the one holy apostolic Church and humbly obey it.

After this, the bishop of Porto and the cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains made brief speeches on the same subject and nevertheless tried, now with gentle words and now with stern ones, to incline the emperor’s mind toward the good of peace. Then the emperor, with great show of compunction, gave a favorable answer and promised all assent to the desired peace. He disclosed the pain of his heart, declaring that he was inwardly consumed with distress [Col. 0044B] because the Church of God was tossed amid so great a peril of tribulation. With this said, all returned together to their lodgings.

Soon afterward, the legates frequented Frederick’s court and for many days discussed the good of peace: how it might be restored between him and the Roman Church and its supporters, namely the Lombards, the king of Sicily, and the emperor of Constantinople—now with Frederick alone, now with him and his counselors. So that negotiations with the Lombards might proceed more conveniently without his own personal presence, the emperor delegated his authority to C. [Note: [Col. 0044D] M.: Con.], the chancellor; P., called the elect of Cologne; and A., his protonotary, so that, after discussion of the conflicting articles, they might show whatever moderation they could and report all matters to him. These men very frequently conferred with the legates and the Lombard rulers, now in the suburbs and now in the cities, as seemed most suitable to them, concerning the restoration of peace [Col. 0044C].

But when the reciprocal demands were reported to the emperor, he exceeded all measure in every respect: from the Church, in spiritual matters, he demanded what was never found to have been granted to any layman; and from the Lombards he exacted more than the emperors Charles, Louis, and Otto had been content with. Since Frederick in no way wished to withdraw from his wicked purpose, the legates, unwilling to depart from the Rules and Constitutions of the holy Fathers, left him in the perfidy of his error and returned, under the Lord’s guidance, to the presence of Lord Pope Alexander and the assembly of his brethren. The Lombards, manfully defending the ancient possession of their liberty, resisted Frederick’s wickedness more strongly than usual and harassed the Pavians, together with the marquises and the men of Como, by continual devastations.

## On the Establishment of the Bishopric of Alexandria and the Deprivation of the Church of Pavia of Cross and Pallium

[Col. 0044D] At the same time Pope Alexander, at the request of the archbishop of Milan, the bishops of the province, and the rulers of the Lombard cities, made the Church of Alexandria a bishopric. There he caused Arduin, subdeacon of the Roman Church, to be elected bishop and consecrated by the metropolitan of Milan as his suffragan.

Moreover, he deprived the bishop of Pavia of the dignity of cross and pallium, because his city had adhered to Octavian the heresiarch and to the excommunicated Emperor Frederick; and, after making satisfaction, had presumed to recall that same Frederick into Italy, to the grave injury of the Church and the Lombards. For, as the deeds of the Roman pontiffs declare, this city had from ancient times been a refuge for kings who persecuted the Roman Church and Roman pontiffs.

Aistulf, king of the Lombards, violently took the Exarchate of Ravenna from Pope Stephen II [Col. 0045A], and, as a wicked and utterly evil man, setting aside fear of God and blessed Peter, inflicted other grievous evils upon the Roman Church and the City. Therefore Pepin, king of the Franks, of revered memory, at the request of that pope, entered Lombardy with a great army for a second time and besieged Aistulf, who was resisting in Pavia, until he made satisfaction according to the command and will of the aforesaid pontiff and restored all that had been taken from the Church.

Likewise King Desiderius, who succeeded Aistulf in the kingdom, impiously and cruelly persecuted Pope Adrian I, as well as the Church and the City. Therefore King Charles, at that pope’s request, besieged this same city, in which Desiderius had been received, so rigorously for six months that he forcibly captured both that king and his wife and carried the captive with him into his Frankish kingdom. It is therefore no wonder if in modern times this treacherous [Col. 0045B] city received schismatics and excommunicated men against the unity of the Church, and labored with all its power to uphold them.

## On the Battle of Campale between King Frederick and the Lombards, and the Lombards’ Desired Victory

And it came to pass in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1175, in the seventeenth year of Pope Alexander’s pontificate, about the end of June, that Frederick, while awaiting at the appointed time the army which he had raised in Germany, secretly went to Como with a few men after deliberating with the Pavians. Having there received that army and gathered all the men of Como to himself, he unexpectedly invaded Milanese territory and began to plunder and devastate their villages and estates in hostile fashion.

For he had arranged with the Pavians that, as soon as he entered Milanese territory, the city itself, on receiving the signal agreed between them, should come to his aid in force and violently drive the resisting Lombards from before him. But because

> Good hope is often deceived by its own omen.  
> —Ovid, *Heroides* XVII.234

he was deceived in his purpose, for matters turned out far worse for him than he expected.

The Lombard cities had long perceived his impious purpose and evil intention against them, and therefore all, prepared for war, hastened unanimously to meet him. But when the Milanese learned with complete certainty of their swiftly approaching enemy, they did not wait for the other cities. Rather, with the Piacentines and selected companies of knights from Verona, Brescia, Novara, and Vercelli, they left Milan with their carroccio on the first Saturday of June. At about the third hour they arrived in great numbers at a place suitable for them between Barrano and Brixianum, fifteen miles from the city.

They then sent ahead seven hundred armed knights [Col. 0045D] toward Como, to learn from which direction their most powerful and formidable enemy was coming. When they had advanced nearly three miles, three hundred German knights met them; Frederick followed their tracks with his entire army, equipped to begin battle. Without delay the enemies violently rushed upon one another, striking each other with drawn swords. But when the prince’s more numerous force came up, the Lombard knights unwillingly gave ground; wishing to seek refuge at the Milanese carroccio, they could not remain before the pursuing enemy.

Then the chosen body of Milanese warriors, which stood firmly in the rear line like an impenetrable wall, first prayed to God, his apostle Peter, and blessed Ambrose; then, raising their banners, confidently met Frederick in great strength [Col. 0046A]. In the first encounter, Frederick’s standard-bearer was pierced through, fell to the ground, and remained slain beneath the horses’ feet. The emperor himself, armored among the rest, when he appeared marked out by the splendor of his own arms, was struck hard by the Lombards, fell from his saddle, and immediately disappeared from all eyes.

Pressed by the Lombards, the entire German expedition turned to flight and fled for eight miles in fear of death. Of their multitude, few escaped: some were killed by the sword, others drowned in the Ticino, and the remaining crowd was divided into captivity among different cities. The treacherous people of Como, who had departed with irreverent and unbridled spirit from the unity of the Church and the Lombard confederation, were almost entirely left lying on the field—either killed by the sword or shamefully led away into captive captivity.

After the famous triumph of the desired victory, the victorious Lombard league gladly gathered all the spoils [Col. 0046B], and in peace each possessed what fortune had granted him. Besides a vast quantity of arms and horses, incalculable riches and every best product of the land were found beyond expectation.

For a long time there was the greatest uncertainty among all as to the emperor’s person—whether he had escaped or had remained dead on the field with the others—so much so that his wife, overwhelmed by grief and mourning, even put on mourning clothes. But while all Italy was greatly agitated over this, behold, he suddenly appeared at Pavia, stripped of his immense equipment and valiant soldiery.

In this the Lord plainly showed what he had spoken through Isaiah: “The eyes of the lofty man are humbled, and the height of mighty men is bowed down” (Isaiah 2). Although his cause, from the time he began to persecute God’s Church, had always fared worse through the Lord’s vengeance, and no adversity or hardship had drawn him back from his enterprise, he was now struck and crushed so severely by the heavenly judge [Col. 0046C] that he seemed humbly inclined toward the peace of the Church, which until then he had sought deceitfully. Through the chief persons of the Empire, he earnestly requested it of Lord Pope Alexander and his brethren.

Indeed, all the ecclesiastical and secular princes of the realm who had hitherto followed Frederick in his error told him that, unless he made peace with the Church, they would follow him no longer nor bring him aid. Moreover, the Lord had made the Lombard league so strong and bold against the Germans that whenever it fought against that barbarian people in battle, it emerged victorious in the first engagement and scattered and routed them before it like flying chaff.

## On the Second Negotiation for Peace between Lord Pope Alexander and Emperor Frederick

[Col. 0046D] Emperor Frederick therefore sent to Lord Pope Alexander W. [Note: [Col. 0045D] M.: William.], archbishop of Magdeburg; Christian, elect of Mainz; P. [Note: [Col. 0046D] M.: Peter.], elect of Worms; and Ar., protonotary of the kingdom—leading princes of the Empire—with full authority to complete the peace between Church and Empire.

Having come as far as Tivoli, they informed the pope, who was residing at Anagni, of the reason for their arrival. Having obtained safe-conduct, they were received by two cardinals and the captains of Campania and honorably conducted into the city of Anagni. On the following day, while the pontiff sat in consistory surrounded by a multitude of clergy and nobles, they approached the principal church with their distinguished company and thence entered before the pontiff.

Standing before him in the middle, they spoke with great reverence:

“Our lord [Col. 0047A] the emperor, with great desire desiring to grant true peace to the Roman Church and to you, has sent us to your presence with plenary authority, urgently requesting that the word of concord and peace which your brethren personally negotiated with him in the preceding year, and which has remained incomplete until now because of sins, may now, through us and your assent, so far as lies in him, be completed by the Lord’s authorship.

“For it is known and beyond doubt that from the beginning of the Church’s birth almighty God willed there to be two powers in the world by which this world should principally be governed: priestly dignity and royal power. Unless they were supported by mutual concord, peace could by no means be preserved everywhere, and the world would abound in disputes and the din of wars. Let this hateful disturbance therefore now cease, and through you, the two rulers of the world, let the peace desired by all Churches and the Christian people be restored.”

[Note: [Col. 0047D] M. does not read the Greek article *to* (*τὸ*) before *hic*, “this.”]

After these public representations, the gracious pontiff replied with cheerful and calm countenance:

“We greatly rejoice at your arrival and its welcome report, and for it we give thanks to almighty God. There is nothing in this present age sweeter to our ears than if our lord emperor, whom we recognize as greater than the other princes of the world, is willing, as you assert, to grant us true peace. But if he wishes to grant his whole peace to us and the Roman Church, he must grant it likewise to our supporters—especially the king of Sicily, the Lombards, and the emperor of Constantinople—who stood firmly with us against him in the necessities of the Church.”

The legates, praising and approving the pontiff’s words, said:

“We have received instructions from the lord emperor to speak privately with you and your brethren, so that the hostile man may not learn what is to be discussed and settled between us and you, and that the matters may remain secret until the good of peace is completed, by the Lord’s favor. For we know that there are some on both your side and ours [Col. 0047C] who hate peace and gladly foster this discord.”

After hearing this, the whole assembly withdrew, and the pontiff entered alone into the private council chamber with his brethren and the legates. They began carefully to discuss the matter of peace with one another. But because the business was arduous and very difficult—for many nobles and powerful men had fallen gravely into schism—and because controversy remained concerning certain articles between Church and Empire, the negotiation lasted more than fifteen days. During this time the authorities of the holy Fathers, imperial privileges, ancient customs, and relevant arguments were set forth; they labored long over them and disputed them with subtlety.

At last, through the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, it came about that the pontiff and his brethren unanimously agreed with the aforesaid legates on all articles between Church and Empire. The Lombard cause remained in the state in which it had been [Col. 0047D] until a common conference, because in the Lombards’ absence it neither ought nor could be settled [Note: [Col. 0047D] M.: “determined.”].

Because the peace itself ought not, as stated above, to be made without the bodily presence of the emperor and the Lombards, it was decided that the pontiff, with his brethren, should labor in person for the great good of the desired peace and hasten to Lombardy without long delay. In the meantime, firm security was granted on the emperor’s behalf to all persons and possessions of the Roman Church, to the lands of blessed Peter and the king of Sicily, and to all leading men, until the completion of that peace. These matters having thus been arranged and settled in agreement, the legates returned joyfully to the emperor.

## How Pope Alexander Went into Lombardy for the Peace of the Church

Pope Alexander, in order that he might approach the conference with the emperor without doubt or danger [Col. 0048A], appointed a vicar in the City and set out with his brethren toward the Adriatic Sea. Coming to Benevento, he passed through Troia and Siponto, and by Mount Gargano to the city of Vesta, situated on the seashore.

There the king of Sicily, a devoted son of blessed Peter, had prepared for his service seven galleys equipped with provisions and arms, as time and circumstances required. He also sent two great men of his land—R., namely the archbishop of Salerno, and R., the great count of Andria—to accompany him there more honorably into the presence of that same peace and his lord [Note: [Col. 0048D] A.: “of that same father and lord,” etc.]. To make the emperor and the Lombards more certain of his arrival, the pontiff had sent six cardinals of his brethren ahead from Siponto to Bologna with the mounts of themselves and of the other brethren.

## On the Great Slaughter of Christians by the Pagans in the East

[Col. 0048B] In those days Manuel, emperor of the Greeks, wishing to subjugate to himself the kingdom of the Turks, violently entered their land with a great multitude. Destroying cities and villages, he advanced almost as far as Cuneum, where the royal seat was, plundering and occupying everything.

Then the sultan, the most powerful king of that people, summoned ten thousand Arabs, more skillful in military practice than the other peoples of that country, and met the emperor with a huge multitude of his soldiers and archers. He begged and requested the emperor to leave his land to him in peace and allow him to retain it in his service. He offered great and precious gifts, that he might deserve to obtain the emperor’s love and favor. Finally, he wished faithfully to render him fealty and homage [Note: [Col. 0048D] A. and M.: “homage.”] and to come to his service with his knights and archers whenever the emperor should require it.

But the emperor, trusting excessively in his forces and power—for he had with him an exceedingly strong and very great army [Col. 0048C] by land and sea—despised him and said: “You shall make neither peace nor agreement with me unless you deliver Cuneum into my hands and power.”

Having heard this, the sultan, as a wise and cunning man, pretended to retreat. Ascending the mountains above the mouths of the valleys through which the emperor intended to pass toward Cuneum, he laid ambushes for him, so that he might unexpectedly attack and ruin him. The emperor, believing that the sultan had withdrawn from before him through fear rather than cunning and craft, entered those difficult and narrow passes between two steep mountains with no caution—indeed, rashly and heedlessly. He sent ahead his strongest cavalry, with wagons and the princes of princes; suddenly they all fell into the enemy’s ambush.

Then on both sides a tremendous shout arose, and a terrible, destructive conflict began. Because of the excessive narrowness of the place, our side could neither flee nor resist; all alike were caught together like flocks in one sheepfold [Col. 0048D]. What more need be said? They were savagely cut down by the savagery of Turks and Arabs and stripped of many and diverse riches; yet only a few of that great multitude were led into captivity.

The emperor himself, armored in the rear line and surrounded by many soldiers, was at last discovered. While the impious multitude impiously struck him with swords, the sultan himself came up. Recognizing him, and though able to avenge fully without danger the injury inflicted upon him, he released him out of extraordinary generosity, as a man gentle in his own law and fearing his Creator, and permitted him to depart free. He even deemed it fitting to restore to him the crown and most precious cross which had been captured, together with many and varied gifts. Finally, he made peace with him for a time, and in this manner they departed from each other as friends.

## How the Antipope of Viterbo Grieved over the Peace of the Church

[Col. 0049A]

Meanwhile that ridiculous antipope of Viterbo, descending always from bad to worse, was deeply grieved with his adherents when he learned that peace and concord between Pope Alexander and the emperor were being privately negotiated without him, and when he learned beyond doubt that firm security had been given to all travelers—as though his heart had burst in two.

Before Pope Alexander left Anagni, he had sent H., bishop of Ostia, and R., deacon-cardinal of Saint George, to the emperor for this purpose: that they might openly receive from the emperor, by the taking of an oath, the security which the archbishop of Magdeburg and his companions had pledged. Traveling through Tuscany, they entered Lombardy and found the emperor near Modena quite peaceably disposed. He received them with a cheerful countenance and reverently, [Col. 0049B] honoring them with abundant distinction.

In the presence of many bishops and princes, he caused C., son of the marquis of Montferrat, to swear upon the most holy Gospels, on his behalf, to that same security which the aforesaid legates had undoubtedly pledged at Anagni. Moreover, as a fuller demonstration of the good will he bore toward peace, he likewise caused all the German princes who were present with him to strengthen the same security by oath.

In those days Cremona, shamefully looking back and perjuring itself without compunction, impudently withdrew from the confederation of the other cities and turned to the emperor, not without great dishonor. It therefore justly incurred the indignation of the Church and the hatred and enmity of the other Lombards. Terdona also, not long afterward, reprehensibly did the same and disgracefully involved itself in the same infamy.

Hearing this at Vesta, the supreme pontiff was greatly astonished [Col. 0049C], but he could not doubt the steadfastness of the other cities. But when a strong sea-storm had held him there against his purpose, unwillingly, for thirty days, behold: the long-desired south wind suddenly arose, and the sailors immediately and eagerly urged the pontiff to cross. Rising about midnight, very early at the beginning of the coming Lent, after Mass and the reception of ashes, he joyfully entered the vast sea with eleven galleys and two galleys laden with abundant provisions and white horses.

It was delightful to see that naval and glorious fleet plowing the broad sea under favorable sails and a propitious wind. But about noon the north wind came on, entirely extinguishing the south wind, and immediately the sea was thrown into the greatest turmoil. All were afraid; nor was the pontiff altogether secure, because the violence of the storms threatened no small danger.

Then ten galleys, carrying the pope and his brethren, labored without slackening at the oars toward the nearer islands [Col. 0049D]. At last, aided by the merits of blessed Peter and Paul, they safely reached by nightfall that same day the island called Palatiosa [Note: [Col. 0049D] M.: Palacrosa.], giving thanks to God. But the ships carrying the white horses, with the rearmost galley, returned to the harbor of Vesta because they could not follow the other galleys against the strong wind.

The pontiff, exhausted by fasting and the disturbance of the stormy sea, gladly went ashore; and when the table had been set, he dined abundantly and cheerfully. Soon afterward, when all were already resting, the unexpectedly favorable south wind smiled upon the sailors and strongly encouraged them to resume their voyage. Therefore, as all rejoiced with great joy, every sail was swiftly hoisted aloft, and each person remained watchfully at the task entrusted to him amid the darkness of night.

[Col. 0050A] With the swift galley of the supreme pontiff leading the way with a great light, all sailed eagerly through the whole night. On the following day, about noon, they dined with great joy and gladness on the island called Allexa, after Mass had been celebrated there. Then, passing the other islands of Dalmatia, on the following Sunday, before sunrise, they brought the same pontiff safely and cheerfully, through the merits of blessed Peter, to the city of Jadera, situated at the head of the Hungarian kingdom, together with his brethren: M., bishop of Palestrina; I. [Note: [Col. 0050D] M.: Jo.], priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia; B., priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Pudentiana; O., deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian; V., deacon-cardinal of Saint Eustace; also R., archbishop of Salerno; and R., the illustrious count.

Since no Roman pontiff had yet entered that city, the new arrival of the pope brought shared joy and ineffable exultation among its clergy and people, who praised [Col. 0050B] and blessed the Lord, who in modern times had deigned through his servant Alexander, successor of blessed Peter, to visit the Church of Jadera. They therefore prepared for him a white horse in the Roman manner and conducted him in procession through the middle of the city to the principal church of blessed Anastasia, where that virgin and martyr rests honorably entombed, amid immeasurable praises and songs resounding loudly in their Slavic language.

After the fourth day he left Jadera, passed prosperously through the Slavonic islands and the small maritime cities of Istria, and, with the Lord’s help, arrived in complete joy at the monastery of Saint Nicholas, situated at the mouth of the Rialto.

## On the Time When Pope Alexander First Entered Venice
In the eighteenth year of his pontificate, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth indiction, the blessed Pope Alexander first entered Venice with [Col. 0050C] great honour. The doge, together with the patriarch, bishops, nobles, and clergy, came out to meet him amid a great and varied multitude of ships. When he disembarked at the patriarch’s palace on the Rialto, the aforesaid archbishop of Magdeburg, with the bishop-elect of Worms and the protonotary, approached him and said:

“Our lord the emperor is prepared gladly to fulfil everything which, through our mediation, has been negotiated and put in writing between you and him concerning peace. But he cannot possibly meet with you in the city of Bologna, which his princes regard with excessive suspicion. We therefore humbly beseech Your Clemency to endeavour to choose another place suitable both for him and for you—namely, Ravenna or Venice.”

The pontiff immediately and firmly answered them:
