“It was long ago agreed by the emperor with the Lombards, through the mediation of our brethren, V., bishop of Ostia, and R., cardinal deacon, that he should meet at Imola and we at Bologna [Col. 0050D]; therefore, without the Lombards and the counsel of our brethren, who are awaiting our arrival near Bologna, we cannot and ought not change that place. If, then, he is now displeased with what he previously granted voluntarily, he must attribute this to himself, excuses set aside, and not to us. Nevertheless, so that the good undertaking of peace may more swiftly attain, with the Lord’s help, its desired completion, we shall endeavour to come without delay as far as Ferrara, so that there, with our absent brethren and the rectors of Lombardy, we may fully deliberate and determine what would be more fitting for both sides to do.”

Because this statement pleased the envoys, he ordered by apostolic letters all bishops and rectors of the cities of Lombardy to assemble, God willing, in that city in his presence on the Sunday of the Lord’s Passion.

Meanwhile, since great crowds pressed upon him [Col. 0051A], and a multitude of nobles hastened from the surrounding cities into his presence to see and hear him as one sent like an angel of God, he judged it fitting to go on the following Sunday, when *Laetare Jerusalem* is sung, to the church of St Mark in order to celebrate the solemnities of Mass. Having therefore put on the sacred vestments, and carrying, according to custom, a golden rose, he proceeded most devoutly with the bishops and cardinals to the altar.

> [Note: [Col. 0051D] A. and M.: for *nimis* read *majus* (“the greater”).]

After the Gospel reading he preached pastorally to the people of God gathered from diverse regions; and, when the offices of Mass had been completed, he bestowed the rose which he had brought upon the doge of Venice as a sign of the favour of the Apostolic See. In the same week he departed from Venice with a splendid fleet of galleys, a delightful sight, and, ascending through the mouths of the Po, came with glory and honour to his own city of Ferrara.

## On the first conference of the Lombards and the princes at Ferrara, in Pope Alexander’s presence, for the peace of the Church

[Col. 0051B]

On the following day the principal persons listed below from both sides assembled in the presence of the same pontiff. On the Lombards’ side were the patriarch of Aquileia, the archbishops of Ravenna and Milan and their suffragan bishops, the rectors of the cities with their marquises and counts, and likewise the archbishop of Salerno with R., count of Andria. On the emperor’s side were the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne, Trier, Besançon, Magdeburg, and Salzburg, with certain of their suffragan bishops; likewise the bishop-elect of Worms and A., [Note: [Col. 0051D] M.: *An.*] protonotary.

When they had assembled together, there arose no slight contention between the parties concerning the place where the pope might safely meet the emperor in person. The Lombards asked for Bologna, Piacenza, Ferrara, or Padua; while the emperor’s [Col. 0051C] princes chose Pavia, Ravenna, or Venice. The pontiff, with the envoys of the king of Sicily, selected Venice on this condition: if the doge and people of Venice would provide sworn security that, before the peace had been firmly confirmed, they would by no means permit the emperor to enter Venice without the pope’s consent, and would in no way obstruct those coming there or returning, then both parties would safely come to that place.

> [Note: [Col. 0051D] A. and M.: *papae* is not read.]

This was done in accordance with the pontiff’s words. He therefore left Ferrara with the bishops and cardinals on the seventh day before the Ides of May, and returned to Venice without delay; both parties swiftly followed in his footsteps.

When the princes and Lombards had been placed before the pontiff, they began to negotiate a reconciliation and peace between one another. But because the greatest controversy between them concerned regalian rights and fiefs, and because peace with the Church ought not to be made without peace with those who had stood firmly with the Church against the empire [Col. 0051D], the negotiations, interrupted by many adjournments, continued until the octave of the apostles Peter and Paul.

On that day the peace of the Church was ratified, in the form arranged by consent of the parties and confirmed in writing, by the common consent of the princes then present and by the emperor’s assent. The peace of the king of Sicily, from the coming Kalends of August for fifteen years, was likewise approved. Charters concerning these matters were accordingly drawn up in agreement by both sides and received by each party in good faith.

When these matters had been completed, at the princes’ request the pontiff gave the emperor permission to come as far as Chioggia, so that in that place, not far from the pontiff, with the cardinals and princes present who had nearly [Col. 0052A] completed the terms of peace and truce, the matter might, by imperial authority and with God as its author, receive full effect and unchangeable confirmation. The emperor therefore came there, and the cardinals and princes assembled together in his presence, showing him in agreement everything which they had done with his assent.

Having heard and fully understood everything that had taken place, although he was greatly troubled and disturbed by those who hated peace, nevertheless, because the princes firmly withstood him to his face, he finally accepted as valid everything that had been done and recorded in the pontiff’s presence, and freely promised to confirm it. Consequently, in the hearing of the same cardinals and princes, he ordered Count Dodo, son of Marquis C., to swear publicly in his soul before the lord pope, the envoys of the king of Sicily, and the Lombards, as follows:

## These are the first oaths which Emperor Frederick caused to be made in his soul concerning the peace of the Church

[Col. 0052B]

> “I, Count Dodo, swear that my lord the emperor commanded me to swear in his soul the oath which I am now about to make, and that after giving this command he did not revoke it. And by the emperor’s command I swear in his soul that, once he has come to Venice, all question and contradiction being set aside, he will cause an oath to be sworn in his soul that he will keep in good faith the peace of the Church, as arranged by the mediators and written down; the peace of the king of Sicily for fifteen years, as written; and the truce with the Lombards, as arranged by the mediators of both parties and contained in the written document held by those mediators. And he will cause his princes to swear this same oath.”

In like manner he ordered his chamberlain Sigilboth to swear as follows:

> [Note: [Col. 0052D] A.: *Sigilboch*. M.: *Sigilloth*.]

> “I, Sigilboth, swear that, once my lord the emperor has come to Venice, he will cause the aforesaid oath concerning the peace of the Church, the king of Sicily, and the truce with the Lombards [Col. 0052C] to be made in his soul, and he will likewise cause his princes to swear it.”

When these things had been completed in this manner, the pontiff released the doge and people of Venice from the oath by which they were bound, and commanded them to conduct the lord emperor honourably into Venice. The doge, hastening eagerly to carry this out, caused the emperor to be conducted in six prepared galleys, with glory and honour, as far as the monastery of St Nicholas, situated at the head of the Rialto.

## On the absolution of Emperor Frederick and the peace made between him and Lord Pope Alexander

On the next day, very early in the morning on the vigil of St James, the pontiff sent into the emperor’s presence H., [Note: [Col. 0052D] A.: *Hy.*] bishop of Ostia; E., bishop of Porto; M., bishop of Palestrina; I., cardinal priest of the title of St Anastasia; T., cardinal priest of the title of St Vitalis; P., cardinal priest of the title of St Susanna; and I., [Note: [Col. 0052D] M.: *Jo.*] cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. Having come to him, after he had renounced the schism of Octavian, Guy of Crema, and John of Struma, and after he had promised obedience to the venerable Pope Alexander and to his canonically succeeding successors as a Catholic prince, they jointly absolved him from the sentence of excommunication and restored him to Catholic unity. They did the same, according to the ancient custom of the Church, for his principal princes.

Thereupon the emperor, as an orthodox prince, devoutly approached the pontiff, who was seated before the doors of the church of St Mark with bishops and cardinals, awaiting the union of peace in the presence of the assembled multitude. Laying aside his cloak, he prostrated himself on the ground; after kissing the pope’s feet, as those of the prince of the apostles, he most devoutly gave him the kiss of true peace. Then all were filled [Col. 0053A] with great joy, and, in their exceeding gladness, the cry of those singing *Te Deum laudamus* rang out to the stars.

Immediately the emperor, taking the pontiff’s right hand, led him with chants and praises as far as the choir of the church and, bowing his head, reverently received his blessing. On the following day, when the feast of St James the apostle was celebrated, he returned to the same church. The pontiff, intending to celebrate the solemnities of Mass, proceeded in festive procession to the sacred altar with patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, cardinal priests and deacons, and the other orders of the Church.

While the emperor stood in the choir, the German clergy began to sing the introit of the Mass in loud voices and performed the whole office in song with every expression of joy. After the Gospel and the sermon addressed to the people, the emperor again prostrated himself most devoutly at the feet of the same pontiff with his princes. Opening his treasures, he offered him gold after kissing his feet [Col. 0053B]. When the Mass had been sung, he took the pope’s right hand and led him outside the church as far as the white horse, firmly holding his stirrup. When he took the bridle and wished to perform the office of groom, the pontiff considered the deed accomplished, because the emperor had affectionately wished to render it, since the journey to the sea seemed excessively long.

On the following day, about the ninth hour, the emperor, with a few companions, visited the pontiff with filial affection and gladly sought him out as far as his chamber, where he sat familiarly with the bishops and cardinals. They congratulated one another for a long time; and after affectionate conversations, as well as jokes mingled with serious matters and tempered so as not to impair dignity, the emperor, having asked for and obtained leave, returned cheerfully to his lodging.

## On the completion of the peace and the Lombard truce, and the oaths rendered

On the Kalends of August, after the envoys of the king of Sicily and all the Lombard rectors had been summoned, [Col. 0053C] the pontiff and emperor entered the consistory together. Then, before the pontiff in the public audience, the emperor ordered Count Henry of Des to swear in his soul that he would keep in good faith the peace of the Church and empire, the peace of the king of Sicily for fifteen years, and the Lombard truce from the coming Kalends of August for six years, as had been arranged and written by the mediators of both parties. In the princes’ presence he likewise commanded that they should swear the same peace and truce together and keep them in good faith.

The count immediately swore upon the holy Gospels of God as the emperor had commanded him, and, turning to the emperor, said: “So may God help you, and these holy Gospels.”

The following princes swore as follows:

> “I, C., [Note: [Col. 0053D] A.: *O.*] archbishop of Mainz; I, P., archbishop of Cologne; I, V., [Note: [Col. 0053D] A., B., M.: rather *W.*] archbishop of Magdeburg; I, B., archbishop of Trier; I, D., bishop of Passau; I, C., bishop-elect [Col. 0053D] of Worms; I, Ar., protonotary of the imperial court; I, C., formerly bishop of Mantua; I, G., chancellor; and I, C., count, swear in our souls upon these holy Gospels of God that we shall keep in good faith and without deceit the peace of the Church and empire, the peace of the king of Sicily for fifteen years, and the Lombard truce for six years, as arranged and written by the mediators of both parties. So may God help us, and these holy Gospels.”

On the king of Sicily’s side, R., archbishop of Salerno, and R., count of Andria, swore in the same manner.

> [Note: [Col. 0053D] A. and M.: *episcopus* (“bishop”) for *archiepiscopus*.]

On the Lombards’ side those present swore: from Milan, Gerardus Pistis and Roger Marcellinus, consul; from Piacenza, William [Col. 0054A] Leccacorus;

> [Note: [Col. 0053D] M.: *Guilhelmus Lectacormius*. A.: *Lecacorvus*.]

from Brescia, Albert of Gambara; from Bergamo, Albert Albertonis; from Verona, Cothus, consul;

> [Note: [Col. 0054D] A. and M.: *Cochus*.]

from Parma, Vetulus; from Reggio, Arcemanus; from Bologna, Pinamonte, their podestà; from Novara, William Gibuini; from Alessandria, Ubertus de Foro; from Padua, Tessulinus, podestà; and from Vicenza, Ezulinus.

## On the return of the schismatics to the unity of the Church

After the emperor had been absolved, his adherents—the intruded clergy and schismatics—flocked in companies to the bosom of mother Church, humbly requesting absolution. Upon the holy Gospels they renounced and anathematized every heresy exalting itself against the most holy Roman Church, and especially the schism and heresy of Octavian, Guy of Crema, and John of Struma. Declaring their ordinations void, and promising fidelity and obedience to their lord Pope Alexander and to his Catholic successors, [Col. 0054B] they were reconciled and assigned to Catholic unity.

> [Note: [Col. 0054D] A. and M.: *canonicis* (“canonical”) for *catholicis*.]

Among their number we judged the more notable persons worth naming: C. of Mainz; P. of Cologne; W. of Magdeburg; those of Trier, Passau, and Worms, the last bishop-elect; those of Augsburg, Basel, Strasbourg, Halberstadt, Pavia, Piacenza, Cremona, Brescia, Novara, and Acqui; C., formerly bishop of Mantua; those of Bagnoregio, Pesaro, and Fano; V., promoted by Guy of Crema to the diaconate; V., formerly abbot of Cluny and intruded into St Peter in Ciel d’Oro; and the intruded incumbent of the neighbouring church of St Saviour. We are wholly unable to name the multitude of other schismatics who came to their senses.

## How the pope promulgated a sentence of excommunication against violators of the peace

At the same time, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, Pope Alexander held a synod in the church [Col. 0054C] of St Mark at Venice with archbishops and other prelates of churches from Italy and Germany; the emperor himself sat beside him.

> [Note: [Col. 0054D] A.: *praelibatus* (“aforesaid”).]

There the peace between Church and empire, the peace of the king of Sicily, and the Lombard truce, as arranged above, were strengthened and confirmed by common affirmation. But to give them greater security, the pontiff promulgated this sentence of excommunication: whoever violated that peace or truce would incur the same sentence, all excuse set aside, unless, after being required and warned, he made satisfaction within forty days. The schismatics who had not yet repented he bound under sentence of anathema until they should make satisfaction.

## On the acquisition of the castle of Brectanoro

In those days Count C. of Brectanoro died at Venice without children. For the remission of his own sins and those of his parents, he gave the castle itself of Brectanoro—otherwise called Susubium—and all his land, although it had from ancient times belonged by right to St Peter, to the most holy Roman Church as its own inheritance. To make this gift still more secure, he caused a public instrument to be drawn up for Lord Pope Alexander and his successors.

For this reason, in order to receive investiture of that castle, which is the head and seat of the entire county, the pontiff immediately sent there Cardinal Deacon R., Subdeacon R., and his steward P. Saracenus. Through them he received and retained, with investiture, possession of that county in the power and lordship of the Apostolic See.

## Letter of the princes of the Empire concerning confirmation and observance of peace between Church and empire

[Col. 0055A]

> “To their lord and venerable father, ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff and universal pope of the holy Roman See and Catholic Church: CHRISTIAN, archbishop of Mainz; Philip, archbishop of Cologne; Wiermannus, [Note: [Col. 0055D] M.: *Wienandus*.] archbishop of Magdeburg; Arnold, archbishop of Trier; Conrad, bishop-elect of Worms; Godefridus, chancellor; Worumnus, protonotary; F., [Note: [Col. 0055D] M.: *Fredericus*.] count of Holland; T., marquis of Luzis; his brother Dodo; H., [Note: [Col. 0055D] M.: *Henricus*.] count of Diersa; and R., count of Durna: the service of filial devotion, with due obedience and submission.
>
> “The benefits which come to the whole world from the peace of Church and empire now brought to completion, and the countless evils thereby avoided, plainly demonstrate this. For just as the world is governed toward safety and tranquillity by the harmonious foresight of both, so under their division it was drawn away from the rectitude proper to its due condition [Col. 0055B]. Let the earth, therefore, rejoice, now sprinkled by the longed-for visitation of dew and made fruitful by the flood of such gracious rain: through it the dry thirst of the faithful people is driven away, and the stumbling-blocks of every quarrel and the fires of disputes are extinguished.
>
> “Therefore, most holy Father, rejoicing in so great a fruit of concord, we confirm by the earnestness and force of our consent, and hold valid and inviolable, that most sacred peace between Church and empire, as arranged by the mediators of both parties and set forth in a common written document; the peace of the illustrious king of Sicily for fifteen years; and the Lombard truce from the coming Kalends of August for six years, as arranged by the mediators, secured by our oaths, and jointly committed to writing. That written instrument, namely, has been confirmed on both sides by the mediators’ own subscriptions and strengthened by their seals. We shall endeavour that it be observed in this manner.
>
> “And so that this charter of our confirmation may remain firm and unimpaired in future times [Col. 0055C], we have caused it to be authenticated by our own subscriptions and marked by the affixing of our seals.”

> [Note: [Col. 0055D] A. and M.: *appensione* (“hanging”) for *appositione* (“affixing”).]

> “I, Christian, archbishop of the see of Mainz, have subscribed. I, P., archbishop of Cologne and archchancellor of Italy, have subscribed. I, C., bishop-elect of Worms, have subscribed. I, G., chancellor of the imperial court, have subscribed. I, W., protonotary, have subscribed.”

## Letter sent by the emperor to the pope concerning peace between Church and empire

> “To the reverend father in Christ, Lord Pope Alexander, supreme and universal pontiff of the most holy Roman Church: FREDERICK, by God’s grace emperor of the Romans and ever Augustus, due obedience and the affection of filial devotion.
>
> [Col. 0055D] “Since imperial majesty has been ordained on earth by the King of kings for this purpose, that through its agency the whole world may rejoice in an increase of peace, we, whom God has established upon the throne of the Roman Empire, ought and desire to embrace it more diligently and preserve it more fervently. Therefore, the peace of Church and empire—as arranged and ordered by our princes and the cardinals of the Roman Church, and contained in the written document of our princes marked with their seals—we promise by this present document firmly to observe, confirm, and will to remain binding henceforth, just as we caused an oath concerning it to be sworn through an intermediary person according to the form contained in that document. Thus we shall henceforth firmly [Col. 0056A] observe it, and, with God’s favour, shall cause it to be observed insofar as lies within our power.
>
> “Given at Venice, in the doge’s palace, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the tenth indiction.”

At this time, on the vigil of St Matthew the apostle, Pope Alexander completed the eighteenth year of his pontificate.

## On Alexander’s acts in the nineteenth year of his pontificate

His nineteenth year begins. Once peace had been confirmed, as stated above, all who had assembled returned joyfully to their homes. A few days later, however, certain nobles from the city of Treviso, belonging to the Lombard league, went out and approached the emperor. They spoke with him for a long time in secret and made certain mutual oaths, which caused all the Lombards to regard them with hatred and grave suspicion.

When these men returned home, the people of Treviso, fiercely angered against them, called them with terrible cries perjurers, detestable persons, [Col. 0056B] traitors to their country, and men deserving of a most shameful death. In short: in order to escape danger of death, they immediately swore upon the holy Gospels that they would disclose to the rectors of Lombardy everything which they had said or sworn secretly to the emperor. In addition, they gave their sons as hostages and sufficient sureties that they would firmly abide by the commands of those rectors concerning these matters.

Having been led aside, they disclosed to the rectors of Lombardy in a public document whatever they had sworn or said secretly to the emperor. Once the manifest treachery of such wickedness had been discovered, the Lombard league sharply punished the aforesaid nobles as they deserved; and thereafter it watched more carefully against the snares of its crafty enemy and fortified itself more strongly.

## How the emperor departed from the pope with the kiss of peace

These things being so, as the emperor was about to leave Venice, he approached the supreme pontiff, who was sitting in the patriarch’s palace, in order to receive leave from him. All others having been excluded, he held a conference with the pope, only bishops, cardinals, and his own princes being present, concerning the matters still required for the completion of peace.

Then the pontiff asked the emperor to cause the regalian rights of St Peter and the possessions of the holy Roman Church to be restored to him, as had been determined and confirmed through the cardinal mediators and princes at Anagni. The emperor replied:

“I shall presently restore without restriction the regalian rights of St Peter and the other possessions of the Roman Church, except for the land of Countess Matilda and Brectanoro.”

> [Note: [Col. 0056D] A. and M. do not have *ad praesens* (“at present”).]

“But because these appear to me to belong to the right of the empire, choose three from among our princes, and we shall choose an equal number from among the cardinals to discuss these matters; both parties ought to abide irrevocably by their judgment.”

Although this was very grievous and harsh to the pontiff, since the restoration of Countess Matilda’s land had been expressly included and sworn in the peace terms [Col. 0056D], and since he then possessed the castle of Brectanoro, as has been stated above, he nevertheless finally assented to the emperor’s will, lest peace with the Church be disturbed on this occasion.

He immediately chose for this purpose Christian, archbishop of Mainz; C., bishop-elect of Worms; and A., protonotary, who were present. The emperor in turn chose H., bishop of Ostia; W., [Note: [Col. 0056D] M.: *V.*] bishop of Porto; and J., [Note: [Col. 0056D] M.: *Jo.*] cardinal deacon. As for the restoration of the aforesaid regalian rights and other possessions of the Church, he immediately assigned that same archbishop of Mainz to the pontiff, commanding him, on pain of losing the emperor’s favour, to complete the restoration in full within three months.

[Col. 0057A] These matters having been agreed, ordered, and arranged, the emperor himself bent his knees before the pontiff and, having kissed his feet, departed with the kiss of peace from him and all the cardinals, heading toward Ravenna and Cesena.

After his departure, about the middle of October, the pontiff obtained four galleys from the doge of Venice and sent ahead the greater part of his brethren through the Pentapolis along the coast. Then he again entered the vast sea with the Lord as his guide, and, returning by the same route by which he had come, reached Siponto safely and prosperously on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, through the merits of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Afterwards, passing through Troia, Benevento, and San Germano with glory and honour, he returned, sound and safe, thanks be to God, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January to the city of Anagni, which was greatly devoted to him.

There was therefore the greatest exultation at his peaceful and desired return, both in the city and throughout the Roman world, and a common rejoicing of those blessing and praising the Lord, who through the continual prayer of his key-bearer, blessed Peter, and the labour of the pontiff himself, had deigned wonderfully to restore peace and concord between Church and empire.

It consequently happened that, from the great multitude of schismatics, certain intruded clergy voluntarily returned to obedience to Lord Pope Alexander, while others, leaving the churches to Catholics, took refuge with relatives in their own disgrace and confusion. But when their chief synagogue-leader learned that the emperor had come to kiss Pope Alexander’s feet, his bowels were troubled; such fear and trembling seized him in the shame of his desolation that he secretly left Viterbo and, as a fugitive, vainly sought refuge on Monte Albano under the flimsy protection of John, lord of that castle. When the emperor heard this, he showed himself greatly distressed and, in his own defence, declared that same heretic and his defenders out of his peace, unless they hastened [Col. 0057C] to submit to Pope Alexander’s obedience; he subjected them to the imperial ban.

## How Emperor Frederick seized Brectanoro contrary to the terms of the peace made between Church and empire

We have not judged the following matter fit to pass over in silence. After the emperor arrived at Cesena, taking the advice of wicked men, he came near Brectanoro and summoned to himself the aforesaid envoys: R., cardinal deacon of St George; R., subdeacon of the Apostolic See; and P., steward of the same pontiff. He urgently demanded from them possession of that castle with all its appurtenances.

They answered him kindly and gently that they could not and ought not do this without the leave and command of their lord the Roman pontiff. He immediately declared them out of his peace, gathered an army round about,

> [Note: [Col. 0057D] A.: *collocato* (“stationed”) for *collecto* (“gathered”).]

drove them from the castle, and took the impregnable castle without assault or battle. He caused its inhabitants to swear fealty to himself and to his son the king. Nor was this surprising, since rivalries had already arisen between the Bulgari and the Maynardi, who were the stronger soldiers of that place, and one party of them had supported the emperor.

After this deed came to the pontiff’s ears, he admonished the emperor paternally through the leading persons of the Church and carefully and urgently requested that he restore in peace possession of that castle to him and to his mother, the Roman Church. But the emperor persisted in the hardness of his will and utterly refused to make restoration.

Although this matter was injurious and very grievous to the pontiff and the Church, he nevertheless judged it better for the time being to endure and overlook it than to return hostile measures against the emperor’s hostile act, lest the recent peace, so beneficial to Church and empire, be dissolved by discord on this occasion—until the Lord should soften [Col. 0058A] the emperor’s heart and he should voluntarily restore the rights of His Church.

## Text of the privilege of the king of Hungary, who granted liberty to the churches of Hungary out of reverence for the Roman Church and Lord Pope Alexander

> “B., [Note: [Col. 0057D] M.: *Bernardus*.] by God’s grace king of Hungary, Dalmatia, Croatia, and Rama, to L., by the same grace archbishop of Esztergom; C., archbishop of Kalocsa; all their suffragans; the royal provosts;
>
> [Note: [Col. 0058D] M. and A.: *regularibus* (“regular”) for *regalibus* (“royal”).]
>
> and, universally, all ecclesiastical persons established in the aforesaid archbishoprics, present and future, in perpetuity.
>
> “It is recognized as altogether just and consonant with reason, and is proved by the testimony of Holy Scripture, that those who deserve to receive the summit of royal eminence from the eternal King are bound to direct so much more provident care and caution toward matters known to pertain in any way to the advancement of the Church and Christianity, inasmuch as, in return for the honour bestowed upon them by divine disposition, they ought to show their Creator a fuller devotion than others.
>
> “Therefore, moved by sound reason and more earnestly and attentively admonished by the most salutary exhortations of M., venerable cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, and wishing by every means in our power to imitate the devotion which King G., our father of venerable memory, strove in every way to show toward the most holy Roman Church and our most holy father, Lord Alexander, supreme pontiff, we confirm the enactment concerning the deposition and transfer of bishops which he is known to have granted, for himself and his descendants, to Lord Pope Alexander and his successors: namely, that he would neither depose nor transfer bishops, nor permit this to be done, without the counsel and authority of the pope or his successors. We decree that this shall remain inviolably in force forever, both for ourselves and for our descendants [Col. 0058C].
>
> “Furthermore, abandoning the custom held by our predecessors in former times, we enact with unshaken force, binding upon ourselves and our descendants, that when bishops die we shall henceforth neither appoint nor permit to be appointed lay administrators over episcopal property. Rather, we shall appoint upright clerics there, who shall take moderately from the goods of those churches, not for pleasure but for the necessities of subsistence, and who shall faithfully preserve everything else in good faith and without any fraud for rebuilding the churches themselves and the houses of the bishops or canons, and also for the use of the poor, widows, and orphans. Neither we nor our descendants shall hereafter divert anything whatever from these goods to our own uses, unless perhaps—which God forbid—the enemies of the kingdom enter its borders in force, or some other most urgent necessity requires it; and even then we shall not do this without the counsel of the bishops.
>
> [Col. 0058D] “We further add and establish, with unshaken force, to be observed forever by ourselves and our descendants, that royal provosts or abbots shall henceforth not be deprived of their provostships, abbeys, or dignities, we and our descendants hereby renouncing our ancient custom in this matter, unless it should happen through an unhappy event that they are convicted in canonical order of a definite crime or publicly confess their crime.
>
> “Moreover, C., archbishop of Kalocsa, all bishops, elects, royal provosts, and abbots, considering the generosity and liberty which we have granted out of reverence for blessed Peter, our most holy father Pope Alexander, and M., the venerable cardinal deacon, legate of the Apostolic See, entirely surrendered into the hands of the aforesaid cardinal their former custom, contrary to all canons, which they exercised in appointing and removing provosts, other dignitaries, and ecclesiastical benefices.
>
> [Col. 0059A] “Therefore, by their common consent and their free will, we decree and establish inviolably by this privilege, to remain valid forever, that henceforth no archbishop, bishop, bishop-elect, provost, or abbot shall have licence to remove his own provost from a provostship, or to deprive other ecclesiastical persons of their dignities or ecclesiastical benefices, unless they have been canonically convicted of a crime or have confessed it.
>
> “Let all these provisions be known to have been established and firmly confirmed with the counsel of our glorious queen mother, all archbishops, bishops, elects, royal provosts and abbots, all counts, magnates, and other princes. Done in the city of W., in the year 1169.”

## On the third return of Lord Pope Alexander to the city of Rome

[Col. 0059B]

Meanwhile, the whole clergy and people of the city of Rome, seeing that the Emperor Frederick had, by divine inspiration, prostrated himself at the feet of Pope Alexander, and that the evil of schism had been wholly extinguished by divine power, and observing also that through the absence of that pontiff they had for a long time suffered most grievous loss, both in spiritual and temporal matters, wisely took common counsel to recall the same pontiff to the see of Saint Peter. They therefore sent to him at Anagni seven of the worthier Roman citizens, with letters from the clergy, senate, and people, humbly beseeching him now to deign to return to his own City and to the people specially committed to him, and to take charge of it.

Although their humble and devout invitation greatly pleased the pontiff and all the brethren, he nevertheless recalled the former recall by that same clergy and people from beyond the mountains, and how, shortly afterwards, they had inflicted many injuries and insults upon him and his brethren. Not without reason, therefore, he hesitated to trust their flattering promises and to return, without certain and firm security, to that city which is known to harbour many disturbers of the peace. Accordingly, by agreement of both parties, H., bishop of Ostia, I. [Note: [Col. 0059C] M. Jo.] priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, and V., cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, returned to the City with seven worthy men, to arrange with the senators and people a form of security and peace which would satisfy the lord pope and his brethren.

Although much labour was expended on this matter, at last, through the merits and aid of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, it was established by the counsel and deliberation of the whole Roman people that the senators customarily appointed should render fealty and homage to the lord pope, and should freely restore to his hands and power the church of Blessed Peter and the regalia which they had occupied. They were likewise to observe inviolably peace and security for him, his brethren, their possessions, and all those coming to or returning from him. This having been done, the senators came with the same cardinals and other worthy men into the presence of the supreme pontiff. Received kindly, according to custom, with kisses of feet and mouth, they publicly swore before the pontiff, touching the most sacred Gospels, to all that had been established by the people.

When these things had duly been accomplished with the Lord’s cooperation, all rejoiced with great joy; and from that time the lord pope and his brethren quickly prepared for their return to the City. On the approaching feast of Pope Gregory, before Laetare Jerusalem Sunday, after Mass he left Tusculum and proceeded to the City with no little glory and honour. The Roman clergy came out a long way to meet him with banners and crosses—something not remembered to have been done for any Roman pontiff. The senators and magistrates of the people came with sounding trumpets; the nobles, with their cavalry, in fitting array; and the common people on foot, bearing olive branches and crying aloud the customary praises of the pontiff. Then one could see the eyes of all fixed upon his face as though upon the face of Jesus Christ, whose office he bears on earth.

Because of the immense multitude kissing his footsteps, the white palfrey could scarcely walk, and the rider’s right hand grew very weary from imparting blessings. Thus, amid so great and solemn an exultation, the Roman pontiff proceeded slowly as necessity required, and about the ninth hour arrived, not a little fatigued, at the Lateran Gate. He was then led and received with unspeakable glory and multiplied acclamations into the patriarchal palace of the Lateran Church and to the holy altar of the Holy Saviour, as a true and good shepherd and orthodox successor of Blessed Peter. After giving his blessing to the people, he ascended the palace; and, after all the cardinals had withdrawn to their churches, he rested briefly in bed before eating, fatigued by the journey. The following day he went out to the consistory and received an innumerable multitude of clergy and laity at his feet and with the customary kisses. Thereafter he went, as his office required, to the customary stations of the City: on Laetare Jerusalem Sunday to Holy Cross, and on Passion Sunday to Saint Peter’s; and at Easter he solemnly assumed the regnum.

[Col. 0059]

## LETTER OF THE TWENTY-THREE CARDINALS WHO ADHERED TO ALEXANDER, TO THE EMPEROR FREDERICK

(Radevicus of Freising, book II, chapter 53, in Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, VI, 830.)

[Col. 0059D] “To FREDERICK, by God’s grace glorious, illustrious, magnificent, and exalted Emperor of the Romans: GREGORY, bishop of Sabina; HUBALD, bishop of Ostia; JULIUS, bishop of Palestrina; BERNARD, bishop of Porto; WALTHER, bishop of Albano; HUBERT, priest of the title of Saint Prisca; JOHN, priest of the title of Saints [Col. 0060D] John and Paul; HENRY, priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus; ILDEBERT, priest of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles; JOHN, priest of the title of Saint Anastasia; BONADIES, priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus; ALBERT, priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina; and WILLIAM, priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains; [Col. 0061A] ODDO, deacon of Saint Gregory at the Golden Veil; ROM., deacon of Saint Lucy in the Septa Solis; JACINTUS, deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin; ODDO, deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Prison of Tullius; ARDE., deacon of Saint Theodore; Bo., deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian; C., deacon of Saint Adrian; P., deacon of Saint Eustace; and Jo., cardinal deacons, gathered in the Lord in will and spirit: greeting and glorious victory over your enemies.

“The greater the power bestowed and assigned to Your Excellency by God, and the more exalted the rank of dignity which you are known to hold among mortals, the more it befits the imperial majesty to honour in every respect the most holy Roman Church, your special and unique mother, and always, especially in a time of necessity, to provide for her wisely and advantageously. What has happened in these days in that Roman Church, however, and what unheard-of crime has been perpetrated, after some days had elapsed, by those whom she regarded as sons, it is fitting—indeed, most fitting—that we disclose to the imperial highness by our letter.

“For recently, when our lord Pope Adrian of blessed memory paid the debt of nature at Anagni on the Kalends of September, and, called by the Lord, passed from earth to heaven, from the depths to things above, three false brethren—namely Octavian, John of Saint Martin, and Guido of Cremona—who indeed went out from us but were not of us, transforming themselves into angels of light though they are of Satan,” etc.

And below: “Moreover, let Your Sublime Grace know that Count Otto Palatine, taking occasion from the intrusion of [Col. 0062A] Octavian, grievously harassed our aforesaid lord and all of us, strove to divide the Church of God, and in many ways disturbed it without reasonable cause. With the intruder and apostate Octavian he violently entered Campania and the Patrimony of Blessed Peter, and endeavoured by every means to subject that land to him. We therefore, and with us the whole Church of God, humbly beseech Your Majesty carefully to consider, after understanding and diligently examining this violent intrusion as it is, how you ought to proceed in so great a matter for the salvation of your soul and the honour of the Empire.

“Consider and observe what your conduct ought to be toward the most holy Roman Church and toward her one Bridegroom, our Lord Jesus Christ, without whom no one can either possess an earthly kingdom or acquire an everlasting one; and how, by every means, you ought to protect and defend her, by virtue of the office of imperial dignity, from her assailants, especially schismatics and heretics. For our part, we intend in every way to honour you as the special defender and patron of the Roman Church and, with God’s aid, to promote the increase of your glory by every means in our power. We ask and more urgently entreat that you love and honour your mother, the holy Roman Church; that you labour, as befits imperial excellence, for her peace and tranquillity; and that you in no way support the great wickedness of the aforesaid invader and schismatic.”

[Col. 0061]

## CIRCULAR LETTER SENT TO THE WHOLE CHURCH BY THE CARDINALS WHO STOOD WITH ALEXANDER III, CONCERNING THE ELECTION OF THAT PONTIFF

(August Theiner, *Disquisitiones criticae*, Rome, 1836, quarto, p. 211, from London manuscript 9, B XII.)

[Col. 0061C] GREGORY, by God’s grace bishop of Sabina and the lord pope’s vicar in the City; HUBALD, bishop of Ostia; JULIUS, bishop of Palestrina; BERNO, bishop of Porto; WALTER, bishop of Albano; HUBERT, priest of the title of Holy Cross; ASTI, priest of the title of Saint Prisca; JOHN, priest of the title of Saints John and Paul; HENRY, priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus; ILDEBRAND, priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles; JOHN, priest of the title of Saint Anastasia; BONUS, priest of Saint Chrysogonus; ALBINUS, priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina; WILLIAM, priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, cardinal priests; ODDO, deacon of Saint Gregory at the Golden Veil; RODULF, deacon of Saint Lucy in the Septa Solis; JACOB, deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin; ODDO, deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Prison of Tullius; ARDERIC, deacon of Saint Theodore; Bosso, deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian; CENCIUS, deacon of Saint Adrian; PETER, deacon of Saint Eustace; RAYMOND, deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata; JOHN, deacon of Saint Mary in Portico; MILO, deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro—cardinal deacons—to their venerable brethren the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and all children of the Church to whom this letter shall come: may you abound in the spirit of counsel [Col. 0061D] and fortitude.

We are confounded by grief and shame alike, and can scarcely restrain our tears, because that ancient twisting serpent, who, as Job says, “swallows up a river and is not astonished” (Job 40), has so shamefully swallowed certain of our brethren, as you have already heard; and, trusting that “the Jordan would flow into his mouth” (ibid.), he has sought us also, according to the Lord’s saying, to sift us. Yet we give thanks to God, who has now mercifully fulfilled in us his promise that he would remain with his disciples until the end of the age [Col. 0062C] (Matthew 28), and has made us so steadfast in defence of ecclesiastical unity that neither sword, distress, famine, nor nakedness can separate us from it (Romans 8), knowing indeed that tribulation produces patience, and patience a perfect work (James 1).

We believe that you have heard, and that it has been made widely known both by the letters of our lord and by spreading report, how, when our father Adrian had entered upon the way of all flesh, we assembled in the church of Blessed Peter. Passing over what had preceded, we deliberated there for a long time concerning the appointment of a shepherd. After several persons had been nominated, all of us at last, except Octavian, John of Saint Martin, and Guido of Cremona, were divinely inspired to agree that, putting aside the nomination of others, we should elect our lord, confirm him once elected, and consecrate him once confirmed, in the power of the Holy Spirit. Nor did it seem fitting that, because of the disagreement of those men, who, casting aside shame and abandoning priestly moderation, sought not the things of Jesus Christ but their own, the Apostolic See—whence provision is made for all churches in their necessity—should remain long without a ruler.

Accordingly, after the election had been made and confirmed by all, the senior deacon, upon whom this duty rests by virtue of his office, was charged to hasten with our brother Ildebrand, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, to clothe our summoned lord [Col. 0063A] in the pontifical mantle. When they had, in accordance with the will of all, taken hold of our lord and were clothing him in the pontifical mantle, he behaved like the good and discerning guest who occupies the lowest place at the feast, labouring to withdraw himself from the honour imposed upon him, until he should be advanced by the judgment of the inviting master of the house. Then the aforesaid Octavian intervened. Unable to restrain the speech he had conceived, he forbade him, on the Emperor’s behalf, to yield assent to his brethren’s request; and, having uttered many threats—which we did not fear, though we marvelled at his monstrous presumption—he snatched the mantle from the head of our lord and from the hands of the aforesaid brethren, intending to carry it away with him.

When a certain noble senator present saw this, he struck it from Octavian’s hands and restored it to the power of the aforesaid brethren. As they pressed on with us to clothe our lord, Octavian called out for his own mantle and his cleric. The latter came in response to the call and drew out the mantle that he had carried concealed. Octavian removed his cap, bowed his head, and, after the aforesaid cardinal accomplices had withdrawn to another part, had his cleric place it upon him. Seizing it himself with both hands and wrapping it about his wretched neck, with its hood hanging to the ground and its fringes hanging round his neck, he cried out as best he could, *Te Deum laudamus*: “We praise thee, O God.” When some of us rose against him and wished to strip him of such a mantle, he clung to it with both hands around neck and shoulder.

Then those who had been hiding in corners in support of him rushed together; the doors of the church were suddenly opened; and all his kinsmen and friends, swords drawn, burst into the church, no otherwise than that Jewish crowd, with Judas leading it, rushed together to seize the Lord. While some laughed and others wept at the investiture of that monstrosity, Guido of Cremona came forward and adjusted the mantle upon him. We, however, as though lifeless before our persecutors, returned to the fortress [Col. 0063C] of Saint Peter. There, with many tears, every entreaty, and an invocation of divine judgment, we brought our lord to assent to our request.

Octavian, meanwhile, was continuously supported by imperial envoys, who, in their own words, threatened us and those with us with open war. Many senators, deceived by money distributed among them, likewise sustained his wickedness. Through his kinsmen, through senators corrupted by bargain, and through a section of the common people deceived by error, he besieged us for many days. In the meantime, by letters he had prepared beforehand, through the Emperor’s envoys, through Guido of Cremona, and through his brethren and friends, he summoned all bishops of our province to his consecration. With one mind they abominated his act; neither threats nor blandishments could soften them. All replied fearlessly, except the bishop of Ferentino, who was bound to him by their common schooling and deceived by the promise of half a castle: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5).

Then, seeing that all the bishops shrank from his presence—to pass over how he assessed the senators two hundred pounds for holding us for two days; how, though friends had been summoned and a banquet prepared, the bishops failed him for the consecration; and how, of all whom he had previously counted as intimates, he could then scarcely incline one man to consent to his request—he fled the City by night. We, however, were brought out from the custody in which we were held amid the people’s shouting, the ringing of bells, men and women converging from the whole City, and the unanimous applause of all. Escorted by a great company of Roman nobles, cavalry, and infantry, we left the City and, by God’s grace, arrived safely at Ninfa. There our lord, with neighbouring bishops, abbots, and clergy of the City present—who had hastened thither with every desire—solemnly received from God, according to the ecclesiastical form, [Col. 0064A] the gift of consecration.

When this had been done, we warned the aforesaid schismatics to return to the bosom of the Church, setting them a term of eight days, within which, if they should disdain to return, they were to know that they would be cut off from the body of the Church. Since they persisted in their obstinacy, we bound them in the chain of excommunication. Afterwards we subjected to the same sentence Ymer, formerly bishop of Tusculum, who had first agreed with us but then, his mind alienated, went over to their sect. Meanwhile, when the aforesaid schismatic had wandered through many cities and towns and could not find a third bishop for his consecration, he summoned through his envoys two bishops who had been expelled from their sees and were living in exile through the March; and on the fifteenth day after our lord’s consecration he received from them a curse in place of a blessing.

In all these matters Count Otto Palatine and the other envoys of the Emperor did not fail him. By threats and prayers they drew whatever nobles, knights, and peasants they could into his service. And because, not long afterwards, they received the Emperor’s letters ordering them to support him by every means, they began from day to day to lay a heavier hand on the Roman Church, in proportion as they more certainly learned that this pleased their lord. But while God mercifully protected his Church, “the arrows of the parricides [parmidonum; apparently for parricidarum] became their wounds.” Though they expelled bishops from their sees, laid snares and ambushes for all who came to us, and sent carefully contrived lies throughout diverse regions of the world, still, thanks be to God, they failed in their searching investigations and could not conceal the truth. Truth itself, speaking through its own instrument, declared that it is easier to hold down ashes with one’s mouth than to keep hidden the secret of a manifest deed.

The Emperor, seeing therefore that he was spending his labour in vain, began to hide his purpose beneath the shadow of judicial inquiry; and, like a fowler using a sweet whistle to draw birds to him, he feigned a convocation of bishops from five kingdoms and the awaiting and execution of a judgment. [Col. 0064C]

He accordingly sent two bishops to our lord, wrote to him with us as though we were chancellors—although Octavian had long since written to him as to the Roman pontiff—and commanded us to come into his presence to receive a judgment concerning the Church’s case. What were we to do? On the one hand, the need to seek the favour of so great a prince seemed to urge us; on the other, the violated liberty of the Church and the example dangerous to all churches held us back. Yet we chose rather to fall into the hands of man than of the living God, and judged that our answer should be framed so that neither the Church’s liberty might be injured nor he remain in error through fault of ours.

It was also said—and was true—that whatever dissension had arisen through Octavian had advanced through the Emperor’s favour. Therefore, when we wished to send some of our brethren into his presence to explain the affair so that he could not, through ignorance of the facts, turn to the wrong side, we declared that then, if perhaps any doubt concerning our action should remain with him or with the Church of God—though that seemed impossible once the matter had been fully clarified—we would gladly summon ecclesiastical persons from diverse parts of the world to Rome, in accordance with canonical rule, and, on their counsel, correct anything in our action which might seem to require correction, however hostile our disposition might be.

Those who had been sent refused to receive our answer. Instead, as they had been instructed, they demanded towns and hostages through which an appeal to the Emperor might be made for the observance of the judgment. When they could not force us into this, they withdrew from us without showing any reverence to our lord. They then approached the aforesaid schismatic, prostrated themselves at his feet, and presented him with imperial letters [Col. 0065A] in which he was named Roman pontiff and promised favour and aid for the hasty pronouncement of his judgment.

Although he had now so manifestly rushed to judgment, we nevertheless, lest we be accused of any arrogance, sent three of our brethren to Genoa through various perils by sea and land. If they could obtain safe-conduct, they were to go to the Emperor and set forth before him and all present the Church’s case, and with God’s help recall him to the right way. Since they could not obtain safe-conduct, they shook the dust from their feet; and, finding no son of peace, they went elsewhere. Yet, lest there be wholly absent anyone to disclose to him the truth and the merits of the cause, and lest any ground for excuse remain for his wickedness later, the venerable brother William, cardinal priest of Saint Peter in Chains, was at Pavia and wished to withstand his headlong course.

But he, like a deaf asp stopping its ears (Psalm 57), would not understand so as to do good (Psalm 35). Rather, as the prophet says, he set his heart as adamant, lest he hear the law and the words which God sent him through the Holy Spirit (Zechariah 7). Consequently, after some had assembled in the sanctuary of God, he began, following the example of King Nebuchadnezzar, to deliberate about erecting a gilded statue. When the bishops heard from the mouths of the schismatics themselves the order of the election, they judged our lord’s election canonical, though in a subdued voice, and heaped many curses upon the schismatics. One after another they began to leave the church on finding pretexts.

Seeing this, the Emperor ordered the church doors shut. Threatening the few who remained—not, as you say, more than six or seven Italians—with extreme perils and the destruction of their churches, he urged them to bow before the statue he had set up. Therefore our lord, seeing that the iniquity of the Emperor, who had attempted so tyrannically to trample the most holy [Col. 0065C] Roman Church, could no longer be endured, by our common counsel and that of many others bound him, together with the abominable idol he had erected, in the bond of excommunication on Maundy Thursday; and, as his many deserts demanded, made him an alien from the body of Christ, which is the Church.

We have briefly run through the account of our lord’s election, the purpose of the aforesaid schismatic, and the Emperor’s violence and fraud. To avoid wearying readers, we refrain from telling how much money the same man distributed among the schismatic senators; how it was afterwards offered by the senators appointed in their place; how, while all shouted and uttered curses, the simoniacal money was publicly carried to the Capitol; how, by the common voice of the people, the City’s walls were thereby repaired from it; and the many other abominations committed by the same schismatic. For deeds carried out, as it were, in an open market of merchandise cannot remain hidden from you even if we are silent.

Knowing his ambition and evil pride from these matters, you will not be lukewarm either in detesting them or in obedience and reverence toward our lord—unless perhaps someone has resolved to labour for tearing apart the Lord’s garment, which we do not believe.

Henceforth, therefore, most beloved brethren in Christ, seeing our lord like the tower of Lebanon looking toward Damascus, and having a true prophet who does not seize the highest place at the feast but, when the Lord directs him to lead the people out of Egypt, answers with Mosaic humility: “I am not eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before yesterday, nor since thou hast spoken to thy servant; for I am slower and more hesitant of tongue” (Exodus 4)—remain with us in preserving the traditions of the fathers and defending ecclesiastical unity. Adhere immovably to those advancing the common cause, fearing no deficiency whatever in our humility, since you see the Lord Christ, arbiter of wills, giver of grace, and waterer of his planting. For he himself says: “Everyone who believes in me shall not be put to shame” (Romans 9); and elsewhere: “He who trusts in man will quickly fall, but he who hopes in the Lord shall be raised up” (Proverbs 29).

Indeed, if it should happen that our lord is called from this life—which may the Lord avert!—we would immediately raise another to the office of the apostolate. We do not judge the Church changed if the wind of pride shakes from the abundance of her members four rotten teeth, who went out from us but were not of us (1 John [Col. 0066C] 2). But if either of the two in that sect should fail, all disturbance would immediately cease. Therefore, being altogether certain of its barrenness, hold without hesitation concerning our lord the hope which Holy Scripture commands concerning such men: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence” (Jeremiah 17). “And he shall be like a tree transplanted beside waters” (Psalm 1), which sends its roots toward moisture and shall not fear when heat comes. But concerning that other man hold what the Lord says: “Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up” (Matthew 15).

[Col. 0065]

## DIPLOMATIC NOTICE ON THE LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF ALEXANDER III, ROMAN PONTIFF

(Philipp Jaffé, *Regesta Romanorum Pontificum*, p. 677.)

In the bulls of Alexander III, Florentine years of the Incarnation usually occur, and sometimes the ordinary years. Imperial indictions are customarily included, although papal indictions are also occasionally found.

The following clause is added: “SHOW ME THY WAYS, O LORD.”

## LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF ALEXANDER III, ROMAN PONTIFF, ARRANGED IN CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER (A.D. 1159–1181)

For the books used, see the beginning of volume CLXXIX of the *Patrologia*.

## A.D. 1159

[Col. 0069A]

### I. To the archbishop of Genoa [Syrus] and his suffragans—Concerning his election. (Terracina, 26 September.)

(Caffaro, *Annales Genuenses*, in Muratori, *Scriptores Italici*, VI, 272.)

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, namely the archbishop of Genoa and his suffragans: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

The eternal and immutable providence of the Creator willed that the holy and immaculate Church, from the beginning of her foundation, should be governed according to such a principle and order [Col. 0069B] that she should have one shepherd and ruler, to whom the prelates of all churches should be subject without resistance, and that the members, cleaving to him as to their head, should be joined together in a certain wondrous unity and in no way dissent from him. He who promised his apostles, because of the firmness of their faith, saying, “Behold, therefore, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28), will beyond doubt never allow his Church, whose government the apostles themselves undertook, to be deprived of his promise. Rather, he will cause her to endure forever in her condition and order, although she may sometimes appear to be tossed about like Peter’s little boat.

Thus, although at this time three false brethren, who went out from us [Col. 0069C] but were not of us, transform themselves into angels of light though they are of Satan, and labour to tear and rend Christ’s seamless garment—which he himself, speaking in the person of the Psalmist, prays and asks to be delivered from lions, rescued from the sword, and saved from the hand of the dog—Christ, the author and head of the Church, nevertheless guards her by provident governance as his only bride. And he will not allow the vessel of the excellent Fisherman, though often and repeatedly beaten by the waves, to suffer shipwreck.

[Col. 0070A] Now when our predecessor Pope Adrian of blessed memory paid the debt of nature at Anagni on the Kalends of September, and, called by the Lord, passed from earth to heaven and from the depths to things above, he was brought to Rome and buried, on the day before the Nones of September, in the church of Blessed Peter. Almost all the brethren were present, and he was honourably buried according to custom. The brethren, and we with them, then began diligently to consider, according to the custom of the Church, the appointment of a pontiff in that same church. After deliberating among themselves for three days concerning that election, all the brethren who were present—except only three, namely Octavian, John of Saint [Col. 0070B] Martin, and Guido of Cremona—agreed unanimously and in concord upon our person, inadequate for this burden and utterly unfit for so exalted a dignity. God is witness that we do not invent a falsehood but speak the plain truth as it is. With the assent of clergy and people, they elected us Roman pontiff.

But the other two—namely John and Guido of Cremona, whom we have mentioned—drove a third, Octavian, into such audacity and madness that he violently tore from our neck with his own hands, as though it were something seized, the mantle with which, according to the custom of the Church, the prior of the deacons had clothed us, though we resisted and struggled because we perceived our own insufficiency; and amid tumultuous noise and shouting he carried it away with him. But when certain of the senators [Col. 0070C] saw so great a crime, one of them, inflamed by the divine Spirit, wrested the mantle itself from the raging man’s hand. Octavian immediately turned his blazing, furious eyes upon one of his chaplains, who had come prepared and equipped for this purpose, shouting and clamouring that he should quickly bring the mantle which he had brought with him. When it was brought without delay, the same Octavian, having removed his cap and bowed his head, while all the brethren had withdrawn either from the place or in will, assumed the mantle more ambitiously through the hands of that same chaplain and of another of his clerics; and he himself, since there was no one else for this business, acted as assistant to the chaplain and cleric. Yet we believe it happened by divine judgment that the portion of the mantle which ought to have covered his front covered his back, before many who saw and laughed; and, just as his mind was twisted and his purpose crooked, so the mantle was put on him sideways and crookedly, as testimony to his condemnation. When this had been done, the doors of the church, which had been secured, were opened; bands of armed men, whom, as the event showed, he had hired by lavish payments, rushed in; and that deadly pest, since he had no cardinals or bishops, was surrounded by a troop of armed soldiers.

Consider therefore, venerable brethren in [Col. 0071B] Christ; mark diligently so abominable a crime, so execrable a sacrilege, and see whether there is grief like this grief, and whether from the beginning of the nascent Church such madness was ever attempted by any schismatic or heretic.

When the brethren saw unexpectedly such an immense and unheard-of crime and feared that they might be cut down by hired soldiers, they withdrew together with us into the fortified part of the church. There, for nine continuous days, he caused us, with the assent of certain senators whom he had corrupted by proffering money, to be guarded day and night with armed force and every care, lest we should leave it. But when the people pressed on and cried out without ceasing, raging with great fury against the senators [Col. 0071C] for so great an impiety, we were released from the custody of that stronghold; yet the same senators, having received money for it, placed us across the Tiber in a more confined and secure place.

And when we had remained there for almost three days, since the whole people would by no means thereafter endure such treachery and wickedness, the senators, coming with the nobles and people, conducted us and our brethren magnificently and honourably through the City, with immense praises and acclamations, while bells rang everywhere as we passed. Thus, at last delivered from the violence of persecution and restored to our freedom, on the following Sunday [Col. 0071D], our venerable brethren G., bishop of Sabina; Hub., bishop of Ostia; S., bishop of Porto; G., bishop of Albano; I., bishop of Segni; and B., bishop of Terracina; together with cardinals, abbots, priors, judges, advocates, scriniaries, the primicerius, and the singers of the schola, as well as some nobles and the people of the City, all assembled at Nympha, not far from Rome, we received the rite of consecration and, as is customary in the Roman Church, were there magnificently and solemnly crowned with the pontifical crown.

Moreover, although the aforesaid Octavian had summoned many bishops for his consecration—or rather, his execration—both while he was in the City and after he secretly left it, among so many he could scarcely secure even one to confirm his rashness and madness. He tried to entice some bishops by imperial threats, some by lay violence, and others by money and flattery; but, the Lord preventing him, he accomplished nothing. Hence, even now, though he strives by every means, he cannot find anyone to lay upon him the hands of execration and make himself the author of so great a presumption and impiety. But the aforesaid John and Guido, wrapped in the darkness of blindness, because it is written, “When the sinner has come into the depth of vices, he despises” (Prov. XVIII), do not even thus recover from their damnable presumption. Rather, with obstinate perfidy they venerate that same Octavian, whom they have set up for themselves as a statue; abandoning the unity of the Church, they dare still [Col. 0072B] to worship him as an idol or image. He himself, prefiguring the times of Antichrist, has exalted himself so greatly above himself that he has even entered the temple as though he were God, showing himself to be such; and many have beheld with bodily eyes, not without a copious shedding of tears, the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place.

Indeed, recognizing our own weakness and lack of virtues, we cast our care upon God, hoping and trusting more fully in Christ’s mercy that He will make His holy Church rejoice in the peace it desires—the Church for which He Himself appeared in the substance of our mortality, and which He presents to Himself without wrinkle or blemish—and that, once the inundation of every storm has been stilled, nothing will then be able to oppose her, when her one Bridegroom wills to drive away all clouds and harmful things. [Col. 0072C] Therefore, because we distrust the quality of our own merits but have full confidence in your integrity and religion, we ask that our weakness be aided by your prayers and those of the universal Church. By these apostolic letters we earnestly request and admonish your charity that, as Catholic men, you set yourselves as impregnable walls for the house of the Lord; that you remain steadfastly constant in devotion and fidelity to your holy Roman Church; and that you depart from its unity in no respect. If that aforesaid man of impiety should send into your regions any writings of his condemnation, [Col. 0072D] reject them as they deserve to be rejected, and make every effort to despise and cast them away as vain and sacrilegious.

Let your discernment further know that, on the day of our consecration, we granted Octavian himself and his aforesaid supporters a period of eight days in which to return to the bosom and unity of Mother Church. If they delay to do so, then from that time we shall not delay, by the authority of blessed Peter and our own, to bind both them and all their accomplices and helpers with the bond of excommunication and to separate them from the body of Christ, which is the Church.

Given at Terracina, 26 September 1159.

## II. To Gerard, bishop, the canons and doctors of law, and the other masters residing at Bologna—of the same tenor. (Terracina, 5 October.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 868.]

[Col. 0073A]

“Eternal and unchangeable,” etc., as in the preceding letter.

## III. To Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg—of the same tenor. (Terracina, October [?].)

[Harzheim, *German Councils*, III, 378.]

“Eternal and unchangeable,” etc., as in Letter I, as far as: “Let your discernment further know that we [Col. 0073B] have bound the aforesaid Octavian, apostate and schismatic, on the eighth day after our consecration—for we had fixed this term for him to repent and return to the unity of Mother Church—as disobedient and contumacious; and, by the common will and counsel of our brethren, the bishops and cardinals, we have likewise bound with the bond of anathema and excommunication, candles being lit and an assembly of clergy gathered in church, those who have presumed to lay upon him hands, I do not say of consecration but of execration; and we have condemned them with their author, the devil. We have decreed that the same excommunication and condemnation shall apply to his two aforesaid supporters, namely Ivo of Saint-Martin and Guido of Cremona, and to the bishop of Ferentino, who presumptuously persist in adhering to him, as well as to his other accomplices and principal helpers, and to all who knowingly communicate with them.”

## IV. He receives the Church of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem into protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Terracina, 15 October.)

[Eugène de Rozière, *Cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre*, p. 68.]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ARNALD, prior of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that just requests be granted their effect, especially when piety supports the will of those who ask and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously consent to your just requests; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory—Honorius, Innocent, Celestine, Lucius, and Eugenius, Roman pontiffs—we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid Church of the Holy Sepulchre, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods have been reasonably confirmed to you by authentic writings of our venerable brethren, the patriarchs of the Church of Jerusalem [Col. 0074A], as well as whatever that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings, the bounty of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their own names: namely, half of all offerings made at the Lord’s tomb; the offerings of the Cross, except only on the day of Holy Friday and when the patriarch carries it with him for some necessity; the tithes of the city of Jerusalem and the surrounding places, except the tithes of the *funda*; and the Church of St Peter at Joppa with the entirety of its honour and dignity. We further add that no person whatsoever may alter in your church the order of canonical life which you have professed. Moreover, if you perceive that you are burdened by anyone, you may freely appeal to the Apostolic See. We also decree that you, Prior Arnald, and your successors for the time being, may, after consultation with your brethren, have free authority to dispose, for the honour of God and the benefit of your church, of the possessions and goods that belong to you by your own right.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; [Col. 0074C] but that all be preserved intact for the use, in every way beneficial, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right and reverence due to the Patriarch of Jerusalem. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, should fail to make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord, Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve the rights of that same place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Alexander, Pope III.

I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Astald, cardinal priest of the title of St Prisca. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Anastasia. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto. [Col. 0075A] I, Galterius, bishop of Albano. I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Odo, deacon and cardinal of St Nicholas in the Prison of Tullius. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of St Theodore. I, Boso, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Given at Terracina, through the hand of Herman, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the Ides of October, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1159 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

## V. He confirms to the monastery of Monte Cassino, which he declares first among all Italy, all its goods and liberties, and grants new privileges. (At Nympha, 7 November.)

[Gattula, *History of Monte Cassino*, p. 338, from the original.]

[Col. 0075B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son RAINALD, abbot of the venerable monastery of St Benedict at Monte Cassino, and to his successors regularly appointed: in perpetuity.

Although the care and concern of all churches, by reason of the apostolic office entrusted to us by God, presses upon our solicitude, yet it is fitting that we apply ourselves with a fuller zeal of charity to those known to pertain more specially and familiarly to the ordering of the Roman pontiff. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Raynald [Col. 0075C], granting favourable assent to your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery of blessed Benedict, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Calixtus and Anastasius, Roman pontiffs; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the bounty of kings, the generosity of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s help, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

[Col. 0075D] Among these we have thought fit to specify by their own names: first, the monastery of the Lord Saviour situated at the foot of Mount Cassino; the monastery of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, called Plumbarola; the monastery of St Mary in Cincla; the cell of St Benedict at Capua with its dependencies; St Angelo at Formis; St John of the Maidens; St Rufus; St Benedict of Pizuli; St Angelo at Odaliscos; St Agatha at Aversa; St Peter at Rossano; St Angelo at Capraria; St Januarius and St Martin near Benevento; St Dionysius at Ponte; and St Anastasius; [Col. 0076A] St Mary at Coneto beside the River Trinium; St Benedict and St Lawrence at Salerno; St Liberator in the March with all its dependencies; St Benedict in Marsia; St Mary at Luco; St Cosmas at Civitella; St Angelo at Barregio with all its dependencies; St Mary of the Handmaids of God in the city of Cosenza; St Mary at Banza; St Peter of the Lake; St Peter of Ovellano; St Erasmus; St Benedict and St Scholastica at Gaeta; St Magnus at Fondi; St Stephen, St Benedict, and St Agatha at Terracina; St Peter and St Paul in Foresta; St Mary at Pontecorvo; St Angelo, St Nicander, and St Thomas at Troia; St Eustace at Pantania; St Benedict at Aloriano; St Benedict at Pectinari; St Mary at Casaleplano; St Illuminata at the Castle of Linusano; St Scholastica at Penne; St Saviour at Tave; St Nicholas beside the River Tronto in the Abruzzi, with its dependencies; St John at Scurzone; St Benedict at Tronto; St Benedict on the River Tisino; St Apollinaris at Fermo, called at Oplaniis;
