In the county of Aquino: the cell of St Gregory; St Maurice; St Paul; St Constantius; St Christopher; St Nicholas; St Mary at Albaneta; St Nicholas at Ciconia; St Benedict at Chia; St Nazarius in [Col. 0076C] Comino; St Valentine; St Martin; St Urban; St Angelo; St Paul; St Felix; St Saviour; St Angelo of Vallislucis; St Michael at Oliveto; St Nicholas at Pica; St Angelo at Cannuca; St Mary at Veroli; St Peter at Escleto; St Lucy and St Peter at Curuli; St Sylvester, St Martin, and St Lucy at Arpino; St Mary of the Castle of Zuppone; St Martin at the foot of the Fortress; St Benedict on the hill of Insula; St Mary at Bavuco; St Nicholas at Turrice; St Julian at Frosinone; St Caesarius at Anagni; St Germanus at Saza; St Benedict at Paschesano; St Peter at Morini; St Angelo at Peschocanali; St Pater at Formis; St Angelo at Albe; St Erasmus at Pomperano; St Mary at Cellis; St Pastor in the city of Tivoli; [Col. 0076D] at Venafro, St Benedict, St Nazarius, and St Martin in Furca itself; the estate of St Mary and St Benedict Pizoli; at Calvo Sala, St Benedict at Cesima, St Benedict at Sena, and St Leo; the estate called Lauriana; St Benedict at Teano with its dependencies; St Mary at Calvo; St Nazarius at Anglena; St Adjutor and St Benedict at Alife; St Domnus at Telese; St Martin on the Volturno; at Ancalfi, Holy Cross and St Nicholas; Holy Cross at Isernia; St Mark at Carpinone; St Valentine at Ferentino; St Angelo at Algido; St Mark at Ceccano; St Agatha at Tusculano; St Jerusalem; St Benedict at Albano; at Rome, the monastery of St Sebastian at Palladio; at Lucca, the cell of St George; in the territory of the city of Pilana, St Sylvester and St Saviour at Civitella; in the duchy of Spoleto [Col. 0077A], St Mary at Calena; St Benedict at Trani; St Benedict at Caro; St Peter Imperial at Taranto; in Calabria, the cell of Anastasia, St Mary at Tropea, St Nicholas at Sallectano, and St Euphemia in the March; in the county of Arezzo, the monastery of St Benedict and St Benedict at Crema; on the island of Sardinia, the church of St Mary at Tergo, St Elias at Montesancto, and St Elisha, with all their dependencies; St Mary at Sabucco, St Mary of Toralbo, St Mary of Toncele, St Peter of Trecingle, St Nicholas and St Mary at Sallo with their dependencies, St Nicholas of Talasa, St Michael at Ferrucisi, St George at Ticillo, St Peter at Sinebrano, St Peter at Nurchi, St Nicholas of Nugulbi and St John, St Elias of Sitini, St Mary of Fluminetepido; in the city of Cosenza, St Peter [Col. 0077B] at Buda, St Martin beside the River Arinini, St Columbanus, St Nicholas at Guatanelli, and St Lucy with the island of Viti; in the Palentine region, St Mary at Cellis, St John at Vouaze, St John on the Roman Road, St John of Actangone, and St Peter at Pereto; in the Capitanata, half the castle of Serra, St Luke on Mount Gargano, the pastures of Matese; at Fermo, St Bartholomew in the field of Fullonis; at Todi, St Magnus; at Quatrelli, St Angelo at Galla; in the territory of Anjou, St Maurus at Glannafolio with its cells, villages, and all its dependencies; in Dalmatia, St Mary near the city of Ragusa with its harbour, and St Nicholas at Sansacu near Split; in Spain, St Benedict at Tarragona and St Benedict at Coadgrane near the city of Logroño; [Col. 0077C] likewise, the city called St Germanus, situated at the foot of Mount Cassino; the castle of St Peter, anciently called the Castle of Cassino; the castle of St Angelo; Plumbarola; the junction called Pignataria of Piedimonte; the castle of St Ambrose; of St Apollinaris; of St George; the cold valley of St Andrew; monastic Vantra; comital Vantra; the territory of St Stephen; Fracte; Castronuovo; Mortula with the estate called Casa-Fortini; Cucuruzu; Camino; Suio with all its dependencies on both banks of the river; the tower by the sea near the River Garigliano; the castle of Pontecorvo; St Peter in Flia; Torocello; Cervaro; St Victor; St Elias; the round valley; Saracinisco; Cardeto; Acquafondata; Viticuso; in Calabria, the castle of Cetraro with its churches and [Col. 0077D] all its dependencies; in the Teatine March, the castle of Lastiniano, Mount Alberici, Abacela of St Quiricus with its harbour, Frisa, and St Justa. In the county of Ascoli: the castle called Ottavo; beyond Mount Conioni, Triviliano and Cavino; in the principality, the castle of Ripa Ursa, Montebello, Pietrafracida in Comino, and Vicualbo; in the territory of Carsoli, the castle Auricola, Piretum, Rona in Camerata, and Fossa Caeca; at Amalfi, Fundicum; in the territory of Tergono, the small castle of Baroncello, St Justa, and the village of St Nicholas called Galliciano; on Monte Sant’Angelo, the hospice; in the territory of Capua, Gualdo of Liburia; in the county of Teano, the estate of St Felix with the church of St Hippolytus.

[Col. 0078A] Moreover, following in the footsteps of our fathers, we declare that the aforesaid monastery of St Benedict is to be preferred above the other monasteries throughout the West. We decree that both you and your successors shall sit above all abbots in every assembly of bishops or princes and shall pronounce judgment before all other men of your order in courts. We also grant to you and your successors the use of fastening-bands and gloves, of the dalmatic and mitre, at Masses or in the sitting of a council, on principal feasts and Sundays. We prohibit any bishop or priest, save the Roman pontiff, from presuming to exercise within that venerable monastery itself or in the cells of any of its churches any authority whatsoever of excommunicating, imposing an interdict, or summoning to a synod [Col. 0078B], so that, unless invited by the abbot or prior of the place, he may not even dare to celebrate the solemnities of Mass there.

The brethren of that monastery and its cells may receive, without objection by bishops or any other person, clerics of any order or lay people from any bishopric who come for conversion, whether in health or sickness, together with their property—unless those clerics or lay people have been excommunicated by their diocesan bishops for specified crimes. They may likewise judge, without prohibition from any secular or ecclesiastical authority, monks and nuns subject to their monasteries. The brethren in cells established in cities may, whenever they wish, ring the bells [Col. 0078C] for the celebration of divine offices; and no bishop, except in the case of a general interdict of the whole city or parish, may prevent God’s people from entering either the monastery itself or its cells in order to hear the word of God. When you, now abbot of the same place, or any one of your successors dies, no one shall be placed there by any trick of intrigue or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, have elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff, as is contained in the privilege of our lord predecessor of holy memory, Pope Leo.

Further, opposing the avarice [Col. 0078D] and malice both of those now living and of those to come, by apostolic authority we forbid absolutely all seditions called *laevae*, or plunderings, committed upon the death or election of any abbot. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of clerics from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer; but in your towns and villages baptisms and visitation of the sick shall be performed by your own clerics. We also grant you and your successors the cell of Palladio as a perpetual hospice, so that you may appoint there whomever you wish from your own community. If it should please the Roman pontiff to advance him to be an abbot, we nevertheless decree that he shall remain wholly under your authority as a monk of your community. We remit to your ship, when it arrives bearing its insignia, the duty [Col. 0079A] customarily demanded by our officials at Ostia or the port from ships.

We decree that the burial place of your house and monasteries is entirely free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who have determined to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but all shall be preserved intact for the use, in every way beneficial, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0079B] If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, should fail to make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord, Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve the rights of that same place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 0079C]

HOLY PETER. + HOLY PAUL. ALEXANDER POPE III. “SHOW ME YOUR WAYS, O LORD.”

I, Gualterius, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Ubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Astald, cardinal priest of the title of St Prisca, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St John and St Paul, of the title of Pammachius, have subscribed. I, Hildebrand, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve [Col. 0079D] Apostles, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Prison of Tullius, have subscribed. Given at Nympha through the hand of Herman, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of November, in the year 1159 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eighth indiction [Col. 0080A], and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Alexander III.

## VI. To Henry, Bishop of Beauvais—That, rejecting Octavian’s depravity, he should persevere steadfastly in his devotion. (At Nympha, 8 November.)

[Martène, *Amplified Collection*, II, 663.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Beauvais: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

The prudence of your discernment knows, even if we say nothing, how much you owe in accordance with the dignity of your office to your mother, the most holy Roman Church, and to those who, by the canonical election of the brethren and the Lord’s ordering, minister in her; and with what care you ought to labour for her honour and exaltation. We believe that you have been fully informed, by the letters which we remember having formerly sent to archbishops and bishops and to other prelates of the Church established throughout France, how Octavian, a schismatic, simoniac, and manifest usurper, after our canonical election, and after Odo, the prior of the deacons, by command and will of the brethren, had clothed us while we were unwilling and resisting, intruded himself and covered himself with the mantle by his own hands. Therefore, because the Church of God has needed the help and counsel of religious men, in ages past no less than now, we request, [Col. 0080C] admonish, and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord by apostolic letters that you stand, as we trust and hope concerning you, with unshaken firmness in devotion to your mother, the most holy Roman Church, and to us. Reject in every respect the simoniacal depravity of that apostolic claimant and schismatic, from whom bishops, abbots, other religious men, and almost all ecclesiastical persons flee as from a deadly pest, and to whom they by no means go. Establish the steadfastness of your mind upon the rock of faith and the unity of the Church; strive by continual admonition to lead all subject to you to the same end; and exhort them by every means, so that the talent entrusted to you may not appear to have been idly stored away in a napkin, but usefully expended, through the zeal of perfect discernment, for the honour of God. For we wish to love your person, as that of our dearest brother, with sincere charity in the bowels of Christ, not unmindful of past friendship; and we willingly hear your requests, insofar as we can do so with God.

Given at Nympha, 8 November.

## VII. To B[ertha], Queen of the Franks—Against Victor, the antipope. (At Anagni, 13 November.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 971.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest daughter in Christ, B., illustrious queen of the Franks: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

The higher a rank of dignity divine clemency has conferred upon you [Col. 0081A], and the more it has endowed you beyond other persons in the world with power and nobility, the more it is fitting for your excellency to humble itself under the mighty hand of God—from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift (James I)—to love with all the affection of your mind and venerate with all zeal His only bride, namely the most holy Church, to labour earnestly for the honour and exaltation of those who, by the canonical election of the brethren and the Lord’s ordering, minister in her, and to labour more diligently for the confusion of those who try to oppress and tear her apart. We believe that you have been fully informed, by the letters which we remember having formerly sent to bishops and other prelates of the Church established throughout various provinces, how Octavian, a schismatic, simoniac, and manifest usurper, after our canonical election, and after Odo, the prior of the deacons, by the command and will [Col. 0081B] of the brethren, had clothed us while we were unwilling and resisting, intruded himself and covered himself with the mantle by his own hands.

Therefore, because the Church of God, worn down by many labours and oppressed by no slight pressures, has needed the help and counsel of powerful and noble persons in ages past no less than now, we request, admonish, and exhort your excellency in the Lord by apostolic letters that you stand, as we trust and hope concerning you, with unshaken firmness in devotion to your mother, the most holy Roman Church, and to us. Reject in every respect the simoniacal depravity of that schismatic and apostate, from whom bishops, abbots, other religious men, and nearly all persons, ecclesiastical as well as secular, flee as from a deadly pest and to whom they by no means go. Establish the steadfastness of your mind upon the rock of faith and the unity of the Church; strive by constant exhortation to lead our dearest son Louis, the illustrious king of the Franks, your husband, to the same end, and exhort him by every means. We wish to love your person, as that of our dearest daughter, with sincere charity in the bowels of Christ, and willingly hear your requests insofar as we can do so with God.

Given at Anagni, on the Ides of November.

## VIII. To Henry, Bishop of Beauvais—Concerning the intrusion of Octavian the schismatic. (At Anagni, 12 December.)

[Martène, *Amplified Collection*, II, 654.]

[Col. 0081D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Beauvais: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0082A] **How [Note: [Col. 0081D] Octavian, a Roman noble, created cardinal by Innocent II and employed on several legations under other supreme pontiffs, was at last, after the death of Adrian IV, elected three days later by the votes of eight cardinals against Alexander III; he was called the antipope Victor IV and was confirmed at the assembly at Pavia through the agency of Emperor Frederick.] the schismatic and simoniac Octavian, a manifest usurper, after our canonical election, intruded himself by damnable presumption, and how he himself covered himself with the mantle with his own hands, accompanied by only two of his chaplains [Note: [Col. 0081D] The mantle was a red cloak, an emblem of papal dignity, with which in former times the prior of the cardinal-deacons, when clothing the elect, said: “I invest you with the papacy, that you may preside over the City and the world.”],** we believe has fully come to your knowledge both through public and common report and through the letters which we have repeatedly sent into Gaul.

But so that the matter itself may be made more clearly evident, we have decided to send into the kingdom of France our beloved sons H., [Note: [Col. 0082D] Henry, made cardinal from being a Cistercian monk by Eugenius III.] priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, and O., [Note: [Col. 0082D] Otto of Brescia, admitted to the Sacred College by the same pope.] deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, who will recount the entire course of events more fully. Therefore, because among others we have a special confidence in you, and because we possess full trust in every respect as in our most beloved [Col. 0082B] brother, we especially commend these our brothers to your charity. We earnestly request that, for reverence toward blessed Peter and at our intercession, you receive and honour them kindly, and in the affair of the Church provide them in every way with counsel and assistance.

Given at Anagni, on the second Ides of December.

## IX. To the archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and all prelates of Churches established throughout Liguria, Emilia, Istria, and the duchy of Venice.—Concerning the schism. (Anagni, 13 December.)

[Rubeus, *History of Ravenna*, 341.]

[Col. 0082C] “Eternal and unchangeable,” etc., as in Epistle 1 above. It adds that Octavian, on the fifteenth day after his consecration, the eighth after the excommunication pronounced by him against Alexander (that is, on 4 October), was “exsecrated” [i.e. consecrated] through [Imarus] of Tusculum and the bishops of Melfi and [Ubaldus] of Ferentino, with John and Guy, “former” cardinals, present.

## X. To the bishops of England.—Concerning the schism and Octavian’s excommunication. (Anagni, December.)

[Wilkins, *Councils*, I, 432.]

“Eternal and unchangeable,” etc., as in Epistle 1 above.

## XI. To the bishop of Veroli.—Concerning clerics below the order of subdeacon who take a wife.

[Col. 0082D]

“That you [may be] with your enemies,” etc. Furthermore, because the diligence of your brotherhood asks whether clerics who are below the order of subdeacon, and who, compelled by the defect of the flesh, are unable to remain continent, take wives, may canonically be deprived of an ecclesiastical benefice: we wish your experience to hold as an unquestionable truth that, since they are devoted to pleasures and carnal desires and unworthy to handle the divine and ecclesiastical sacraments, they must beyond doubt be deprived of ecclesiastical benefices. Yet if they are known to have bestowed upon the churches to which they had been assigned anything from their possessions or other goods, once they have been separated from the ministry and benefice of those churches, ownership and property must immediately return to them by right, without any objection.

## XII. To the provost and canons of Sulci [otherwise, of Insula].—Concerning a prebend conferred on a certain priest.

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXII, 429.]

[Col. 0083B]

It has been reported to us that, with common consent and will, you have given one ecclesiastical prebend in your church to a priest [otherwise: “that you have given one prebend to a certain priest”], on these terms: that, unless weighed down by bodily illness, he must celebrate daily the Mass of Saint Mary; that he may not leave your church except with the common consent both of the provost and of the chapter; and that he may not assign the anniversary service attached to that prebend to anyone. We have confirmed this ordinance to the extent that the aforesaid priest must continually render his office to the church unless prevented by bodily illness; must celebrate the solemnities of Mass as fervently as he can, consistently with his honour and due devotion; and may not [Col. 0083C] withdraw himself from this duty by transferring to another church or for the sake of pleasure.

## XIII. To the bishop of Beauvais [otherwise, Benevento].—Concerning releasing from vows a boy not yet fourteen years old.

[Ibid.]

It has been reported to us and demonstrated as certain that Griboldus, not yet beginning his fourteenth year, took the religious habit in the church of Russinis [otherwise, Ressone] out of fear of the master who instructed him in letters; that he left from there as a boy within the year; and that he has now wandered about for six years and more amid worldly vanities. Therefore, since the truth of the matter is not established for us, we command your brotherhood through A. S. [uncertain abbreviation] diligently to investigate the matter. If you find that he was not offered by his parents, that he had not begun his fourteenth year when he entered religion, that before his fourteenth year he repented of the vow and withdrew from the church, and that he wishes to remain in the world, then release him by pontifical authority from the vow which he made, and take care to publish his release both in the church of Russinis and among the people of your city. But if he was perhaps offered by his parents, or had completed his fourteenth year when he entered religion, or after his fourteenth year held ratified the profession made by him, compel him by ecclesiastical constraint to enter that same or another religious order.

## XIV. To the bishop of Paderborn.—Concerning Roger, a canon who seemed to have appealed merely in order to delay.

[Ibid., p. 430.]

[Col. 0084A]

It has come to us that, when you had admonished Roger, son of William, a canon of your Church, to render due residence in that Church, he burst forth in an appeal to our hearing and fixed for his appeal the coming feast of Saint Luke. Since it is unworthy that the aforesaid Church should, through his evasions or those of others, be deprived of the services due to it, when he appears to have appealed for the sake of a futile delay, we command your brotherhood through A. S. [uncertain abbreviation] diligently and carefully to admonish the aforesaid [Col. 0084B] Roger either to take up due residence in that Church, setting aside every delay, or to set out to come to us in order to pursue his appeal by the coming feast of Saint Luke. Meanwhile, entrust the performance of his duties in the aforesaid Church to some honourable person, and, while the appeal is in abeyance, assign him only so much from that benefice as will enable him to be suitably maintained. But if the aforementioned Roger neglects to fulfil either of these alternatives, then deprive him of his prebend, all appeal and objection ceasing, and likewise grant and assign it to some prudent and honourable man, without admitting anyone’s appeal.

## XV. To the bishop of Tournai [otherwise, Tours].—Concerning a woman who had killed her son in order that she might enter a monastery.

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0084C]

A woman bearing the present letter came to us and, in a tearful confession, disclosed that she had borne a son by a certain man, and that he had often reproached her with a scornful expression, saying that the son was not his. Led by the heat of anger and frenzy of mind, she killed that same son. When this became known, the count of Flanders compelled her to abjure his entire land for seven years, unless she should remain by our permission [perhaps: “return”]. When she appeared before us and showed that she had taken the cross and was about to set out [Col. 0084D] for Jerusalem, we saw that her presence in those regions could not be useful but harmful. Recalling her from the journey to Jerusalem, we have decided to send her to your brotherhood, commanding by the authority of this letter that you take pains to induce the aforesaid woman to enter some monastery within your diocese and there bewail her sins in perpetual penance. But if, through the resistance of fleshly weakness, she refuses to be induced to do this, grant her permission to marry in the Lord, because it seems safer to us that she marry in the Lord and attach herself to one man alone rather than to many.

## In the Year 1160.

[Col. 0085A]

## XVI. To the canons of the Church of Rheims.—That, rejecting the simoniacal perversity of the schismatic Octavian, they may remain in the faith. (Anagni, 18 January.)

[Dom Marlot, *Metropolitan Church of Rheims*, II, 374.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all the canons of the Church of Rheims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The prudence of your discernment knows, even if we say nothing, how much, by virtue of your office, you owe to your mother, the most holy Roman Church, and to those who, by the canonical election of the brethren and by the Lord’s ordering, minister in her; and how diligently you ought to devote yourselves to her honour and [Col. 0085B] exaltation. How at this time the man of sin, the son of perdition—namely Octavian, schismatic, simoniac, and manifest usurper—has been revealed, he who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God or worshipped; how already the mystery of iniquity is at work; and how, having taken to himself three accomplices in his wickedness, he wishes to establish himself as Peter’s successor although he attacks Peter’s faith and violates Catholic unity—all this, we judge, has come to your knowledge both through public and common report and through the general letters which we have long since sent throughout all provinces.

[Col. 0085C] Therefore, because the Church of God has needed aid through the help and counsel of ecclesiastical men for many times in the past, but never more than now, we request, admonish, and exhort your charity in the Lord by apostolic letters: as we trust and hope concerning you, remain immovably steadfast in devotion to your mother, the most holy Church, and to us; wholly reject the simoniacal perversity of that apostate and schismatic—from whom bishops, abbots, other religious men, and almost all ecclesiastical persons flee as from a deadly plague, and to whom they do not resort on any ground; establish the steadfastness of your minds upon the rock of faith and in the unity of the Church; and strive, by unceasing admonition [Col. 0085D] and every form of exhortation, to lead all others whom you can to do the same. For we wish to love your persons with sincere charity in the bowels of Christ as those of our beloved and special sons, and more willingly to hear your petitions, insofar as with God we are able.

Given at Anagni, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.

## XVII. Privilege for the monastery of Pontigny. (Anagni, 19 February.)

[Marten, *Treasury of Anecdotes*, III, 1252.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, etc., to his beloved son Wichard, abbot of Pontigny, and his brethren, etc.

Whenever that which is asked of us is seen to accord with religion and uprightness, it befits us willingly to grant it and to afford suitable support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your most just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the monastery of Pontigny, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this document. First, we decree that the monastic order which is recognized as established in that monastery according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict shall be inviolably observed there for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically holds, or may in future acquire, the Lord granting it, by concessions of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit expressly to name: [Col. 0086B] the grange of Bunione with all its appurtenances; the grange of Sainte-Porcaria with all its appurtenances; whatever you possess in the land called Communia; the grange of Acrimont with all its appurtenances; the grange of Villarissicum with all its appurtenances; the grange of Creciacum with all its appurtenances; the grange of Challiacum with all its appurtenances; the grange of Burs with all its appurtenances; whatever you possess in the entire wood of Otta; the estate of Saveia with all its appurtenances; the estate of Camporepertum with all its appurtenances; the estate [Col. 0086C] of Revisiacum with all its appurtenances; the estate of Fulgeriae with all its appurtenances; the estate of Cableia with all its appurtenances; the estate of Agliscoli with all its appurtenances; and the estate at Auxerre. Indeed, no one shall presume to demand tithes from you upon your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or upon the increase of your animals.

We also forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, to leave the cloister on any frivolous pretext without the permission of his prior or abbot; nor may anyone dare to retain one who leaves without a guarantee in letters from the community. We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, wholly serving the benefit of those uses for whose administration and support they were granted, the authority of the Apostolic See being preserved in all things.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he corrects his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself answerable before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Place of the monogram.

SAINT PETER. SAINT PAUL. ALEXANDER POPE III: “LORD, MAKE KNOWN TO ME THY WAYS.”

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, Affaldus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Prisca, have subscribed. I, Bonadteus, priest-cardinal of Saint Chrysogonus, [Col. 0087B] have subscribed. I, Albert, priest-cardinal of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed. I, Oddo, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Jacintus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Arditio, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore, have subscribed. I, Boso, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Milo, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Aquiro, have subscribed.

Given at Anagni through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon of the holy [Col. 0087C] Roman Church and notary of the lord pope, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1159 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Alexander, Pope III.

## XVIII. To the barons and people of Dol.—He commends Hugh, archbishop of Dol. (Anagni, 3 March.)

[Marten, *Treasury*, III, 903.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the noble men, the barons, and all the people of Dol: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It befits your nobility to love Churches and their goods with sincere charity, and to defend them vigorously against the assaults of wicked men, so that you may be able to obtain greater rewards in the future in proportion as you are found more devoted to divine works. Therefore, we earnestly commend to your devotion the Church of Dol, which is known to be greatly diminished and desolated. We earnestly request you, and impose it upon you for the forgiveness of your sins, to love and defend more zealously, out of piety and reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, that Church and our venerable brother H., archbishop of Dol; and, against those who take away or harass that Church and its possessions, and who are rebellious and disobedient to that archbishop, effectively to provide him with counsel and assistance. [Col. 0088A] For your discernment ought to know that all who plunder the goods of Churches and hold them by violence are bound by the bond of excommunication.

Given at Anagni, the fifth day before the Nones of March.

## XIX. To Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux.—Concerning the assembly at Pavia. He announces the excommunication of Emperor Frederick and Octavian. (Anagni, 1 April.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 1124.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ARNULF, bishop of Lisieux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received the letter sent to us by your prudence with so much the greater gladness as we knew it to have proceeded from the richer abundance of charity and the fuller fervour of devotion. We ourselves examined it very attentively and carefully; and, so that the integrity of its declared affection and the certainty of its tested faith might not lie hidden in darkness but become manifest to the uninformed, we caused it to be publicly read in the hearing of our brethren. It indeed contained the purity of a most devoted mind, and likewise breathed a no less lucid eloquence from the depths of the heart.

We know, and are not unmindful, how—as your own letter fully set forth—that schismatic, distinguished in remarkable estimation by nobility of birth, abundance of earthly goods, worldly prudence, and grace of speech, rose in wicked audacity against Innocent, our predecessor of holy and revered memory: the harmful man attacked the innocent, the strong attacked the weak, the armed man the unarmed, the schismatic the Catholic. But to what end the matter came, God having mercy, the devoted and faithful sons of the Church learned through the glory of their merits, while the evil learned through the burden of their punishments. You also set forth in those same letters, with both fruitfulness and elegance, what had often happened before to others who presumed upon similar things. And in our own times the most good God has willed heresies to arise, “that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Corinthians 11); and that, through our effort and labour and that of other Catholics, once the grain has been separated from the chaff in the Lord’s threshing-floor, [Col. 0088D] schisms and heresies may be crushed. For we believe, and trust in divine grace, that soon, when the waves of storms have been calmed and the whirlwind of winds driven away, a clear and brilliant day will smile upon us, and, with the enemies of the Church trampled down, Peter’s little ship will rest in a peaceful harbour.

We render thanks to the Creator of all, proclaiming his praises, because we hear that that magnificent and most serene prince of the world, Henry, king of England, remains firm and steadfast in the unity of the Catholic Church; and because, especially through your guidance, he has confirmed his most noble mind in this holy resolve. We request that you remain ever watchful and solicitous concerning him, [Col. 0089A] lest through the repeated harassments of the emperor and his messengers he should in any way—may it never be!—wish to turn aside from devotion to the Church and to us. We wish you to act with that king, the bishops, and neighbouring persons as a kind of apostle and messenger of truth in those regions. Exhort with effective zeal and every diligence the surrounding and neighbouring bishops, and both ecclesiastical and secular persons, especially the noble and powerful, to the same end. For we do not think the prudence of your discernment is ignorant of how sincerely we love your person in the Lord, and with what ready mind we desire to labour for your honour and advancement, as the fervour of affection which we had for you even before our promotion shows.

Moreover, we do not doubt that, from many indications over a long period, it has come to your knowledge how Frederick, emperor of the Romans, has acted in the present and formerly acted toward the most holy Roman Church, and what mind he bears toward her—he who ought especially to be her patron and defender. From the time of our predecessor Pope Adrian of pious memory, and from the beginning of his dignity, he began tyrannically to oppress and grievously harass the holy Roman Church. He frequently ordered archbishops [Col. 0089C] and bishops returning from the Apostolic See to be disgracefully and dishonourably seized, to the shame and injury of the Church, and had them consigned to prison custody. Nor need we now recount how he treated and how unworthily he received us [Note: [Col. 0089D] B.: “not.”] when we held a lesser office and were sent to him with our venerable brother B., now bishop of Porto, at Besançon, because we believe that you have fully learned this yourself. Even while the aforesaid predecessor of ours was alive, he violently invaded the patrimony of blessed Peter and tried in every way to trample down the Roman Church; so much so that many said, and common report almost maintained, that while Adrian lived he intended, should he obtain the opportunity, to make Otto—who had always been the Church’s domestic enemy—Apostolic, or rather apostate.

But because almighty God did not permit him, while Adrian was alive, to carry out his conceived madness, after Adrian’s death he seized the opportunity and supported in every way in so great an iniquity the aforesaid Otto, a schismatic, simoniac, and most manifest usurper. With only three accomplices in his wickedness, as nearly the whole world recognized, after our canonical and unanimous election, he seized the mantle and thus intruded himself by damnable presumption. We hold without doubt that whatever he did, he did solely by the favour, power, and authority of Frederick and his messengers who were present in the city.

Therefore, to confirm him—or rather, that he might appear to possess all authority in the Church of God—Frederick summoned archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of Churches to Pavia, contrary to the enactments of the sacred canons, as it pleased him. That man, like one who trusted neither in God nor in justice, received the insignia of the pontificate in the emperor’s presence for several days, as we have received as certain; just as he wished to do in the presence of ourselves and our brethren when he had formerly kept us shut up in Rome, thereby acknowledging his own wickedness, provided that we would afterwards restore them to him. When we refused to receive them on that condition, he remained in his obstinacy and damnable presumption.

Furthermore, in order that the aforesaid emperor might appear to subjugate the Church of God and subject her to his dominion, reducing her to the uttermost slavery, he restored the pontifical insignia to the aforesaid apostate, as has been said, and invested him, as is reported, with the papacy by a ring—something unheard of for ages. He also compelled certain bishops to show him reverence by lay force and tyrannical [Col. 0090C] oppression, while other bishops, more prudent and honourable, secretly fled from that assembly. Thus he intended to subjugate kings and princes of different regions to himself by both the spiritual and the material sword, should his most wicked purpose in this matter—may it never be!—prevail.

In accordance with your counsel, we are also sending letters of exhortation to the archbishop of Rouen, his suffragans, and others established throughout Normandy. Moreover, know that, because the said Emperor Frederick received the schismatic Otto and presumptuously persists in adhering to him, we, by the common counsel of our brethren, publicly and solemnly excommunicated him on Maundy Thursday, together with that Otto and his other principal supporters.

[Col. 0090D] Given at Anagni, on the Kalends of April. [Note: [Col. 0089D] On receiving these letters from Alexander, in order to carry out the legation entrusted to him, he wrote to the archbishops and bishops of England concerning what had been done at the assembly at Pavia; these letters are extant among his epistles as no. 23. See *Patrologia*, vol. CI.]

## XX. To the archbishop of Salzburg and his suffragans.—That they stand for the Church against Emperor Frederick and the antipope Victor. (Anagni, 4 April.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 1034.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishop of Salzburg and his suffragans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0091A] Because of the tribulations and oppressions which our mother, the most holy Roman Church, suffers from the sons of Satan, we believe that you have conceived the greater grief and sadness, since it is evident that among other ecclesiastical persons you display more fervent devotion and reverence toward her. We do not doubt that many indications over a long period have brought to your prudent knowledge how Frederick, emperor of the Romans, now conducts himself toward that Roman Church, how he formerly conducted himself, and what mind he bears toward her—he who ought to be her special advocate and defender [the Latin reads utrique, “of each/both,” with an uncertain reference]. From the time of our predecessor Pope Adrian of good memory, and from the beginning of his dignity, he began tyrannically [Col. 0091B] to oppress and grievously harass the holy Roman Church. He often ordered archbishops and bishops returning from the Apostolic See to be disgracefully and dishonourably seized, to the shame and injury of the Church, and had them consigned to prison custody. Nor need we now relate how he treated and how worthily he received us when we formerly held a lesser office and were sent to him at Besançon with our venerable brother Bernard, now bishop of Porto, because we believe that you have fully learned it yourselves. Even during the life of our aforesaid predecessor Adrian, he violently invaded the patrimony of blessed Peter and attempted in every way to trample down the Roman Church.

[Col. 0091C] So much so that many said, and common report almost maintained, that while Adrian lived he intended, if he received the opportunity, to make Octavian—who had always been a domestic enemy of the Church—Apostolic, or rather apostate. But because almighty God did not permit him to perpetrate so great a wickedness while Adrian lived, after Adrian’s death he seized the opportunity and in every way supported in so great an iniquity the aforesaid Octavian, schismatic, simoniac, and most manifest usurper. With only three accomplices in his wickedness, as nearly the whole world recognized, after our canonical and unanimous election, he seized the mantle and thereby intruded himself by damnable presumption. We hold without doubt that whatever he did, he did solely by Frederick’s favour, power, and authority, and that of his messengers who were present in the city.

Therefore, to confirm him—or rather, that he might seem to possess all authority in the Church of God—Frederick summoned archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of Churches to Pavia contrary to the ordinances of the sacred canons. But that man, like one who trusted neither in God nor in justice, as we have received as certain, cast aside the insignia of the pontificate in the emperor’s presence; just as, while he formerly held us enclosed in Rome, he wished to do in the sight of ourselves and our brethren, thereby acknowledging his wickedness, provided that we would afterwards return them to him. But when we refused [Col. 0092A] to receive them on that condition, he remained in his obstinacy and damnable presumption.

Furthermore, that the aforesaid emperor might appear to subjugate the Church of God and subject her to his dominion, reducing her to the uttermost slavery, he restored the pontifical insignia to the aforementioned apostate, as we have been told, and invested him, as is said, with the papacy by a ring—something unheard of for ages. He also compelled certain bishops, while other more prudent and honourable men secretly fled that assembly, to show him reverence by lay violence and tyrannical oppression. Thus he would subjugate to himself by both the spiritual and material sword the kings and princes of different regions, should his most wicked purpose in this matter—may it never be!—prevail.

[Col. 0092B] Let, therefore, the prudence of your discernment consider how Christ’s bride, figured by his seamless tunic, which could neither be divided nor had received a cut, may be delivered from so great a disgrace and unprecedented reproach. Strive diligently and labour by every means to prevent that plague from being transmitted to posterity as an example. As Catholic men, fervent in faith, remain immovably steadfast in devotion to your mother and fidelity to the most holy Roman Church, taking careful care lest the blandishments or threats of anyone in any degree move your minds from the unity of the Church—may it never be!

Indeed, considering the immense wickedness and such great faithlessness of the emperor himself, after taking counsel with our brother bishops and cardinals and other religious men, we have publicly excommunicated both Frederick—who now exercises not the office of emperor but the deeds of a tyrant—and the aforesaid schismatic Octavian, Count Palatine Otto, and all their chief supporters. On Maundy Thursday, with an assembly of clergy and many noblemen gathered in the church and candles lighted, we delivered such persons to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that their spirits might be saved on the day of the Lord. By the common counsel and will of our brethren, we absolve all of you, individually and collectively, by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, from the fidelity which you swore to him and from every obligation owed to the Empire, so [Col. 0092D] that you are henceforth bound to obey him in nothing. Rather, for the remission of your sins, we enjoin upon you that you provide him no counsel or aid against those whom he wishes through his tyranny to subjugate, oppress, and lay waste.

Given at Anagni, the second day before the Nones of April.

## XXI. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Mary of Rievaulx. (Anagni, 20 November.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, I, 731.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons AELRED, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Rievaulx, and his brethren, present and future, who profess the monastic life, in perpetuity.

To assent to religious vows and to bring them to fulfillment by the performance of deeds is an obligation to which the office of government we have undertaken invites us, and which the order of reason seems to require. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid church of Saint Mary of Rievaulx, in which you are devoted to divine service. We decree, first of all, that the monastic order established in your church according to the fear of God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian Order, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, [Col. 0093B] whatever possessions, whatever goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, God being favourable, acquire by grants of popes, by the generosity or gifts of kings and princes, by the offerings of the faithful, or by other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the monastery itself of Blessed Mary of Rievaulx, with all its possessions and appurtenances, according to the boundaries and limits of those same lands and possessions as established by Walter Espec, founder of your house: on the eastern side, from the road called Speragata, which leads to the Rye, as far as the road by which one goes to Bref, to the [Col. 0093C] mill of Sproxton; and from the valley leading to the little enclosure of Tilston as far as the ditch opposite, where the two streams, namely Depedace and Little Beck, meet; and from Kauthepeche as far as the stone cairn called Bacheler, and thence as far as the road coming from Turchilsti; on the southern and western side, as the river Rye flows as far as the boundaries of Antona, and thence the boundaries extend as far as Fangadala, and from there as far as the road coming from Wideris; on the northern side, from the hill called Transhobed through the valley of Landesmara and the stream called Willelmesbech, where lie the boundaries of John Engelram; the land of Brif; the land of Tilston; the land called Bidesdale, with all its appurtenances; in the forest of Delmestac, everything [Col. 0093D] necessary for your use in timber, pasture, and pannage.

By the gift of our son Henry, namely the young king of England: the land called Dulberthermech, with all its appurtenances, and with all the pasture of Wasta below Lichering, as he confirmed by his charter and as his grandfather King Henry held it in his demesne.

By the gift of the bishop of Durham: Cotum and Cronebi, with all their appurtenances, as that bishop granted them to you and confirmed them by his charter.

By the gift of the canons of York: Sanburn, with all its appurtenances.

By the gift of Roger de Malbrai: Welleburn and Hovetun, with all their appurtenances, as Roger himself granted them to you and confirmed them by his own charter; moreover, by his gift, Steintun, with all its appurtenances. [Col. 0094A]

By the gift of Gilbert de Gant: the grange of Dundemanebi, and two bovates of land in the same vill, with all the common pasture of that vill.

[The preceding replacement is not applicable: retain the existing wording, but insert “[Col. 0094A]” immediately before “By the gift of Gilbert de Gant.”] with all its appurtenances.

By the gift of Gilbert de Gant: the grange of Dundemanebi and two bovates of land in the same vill, with all the common pasture of that vill.

By the gift of Beltran de Beclensem: that carucate of land which he held in Villeburn, with all its appurtenances.

By the gift of Ralph de Novavilla: one carucate of land in Kiccum, with all its appurtenances.

By the gift of Odo de Bolthebi: Wastina of Disteicheith, together with the lands and pastures of the neighbouring vills, namely Bolthebi, Kabenestorp, and Gfortum, as Odo himself granted them to you and confirmed them by his charter; and the enlargement made for you by Adam, son of that same Odo.

By the gift of Robert de Flellesei: Gfortum, with all its appurtenances, according to the form of his charter.

By the gift of Adam son of Peter: at Rumblesmora, the place called [Col. 0094B] Faweddre, with all its appurtenances; and in the vill called Stainburch, that assart called Dagge de Wuith, and all the iron mine of the aforesaid vill; and, in the wood of that vill, material and timber for charcoal and other things that may be necessary; and the common pasture of that vill; and the rest, according to the common form of his charter.

By the gift of Torphin and his son Alan: one carucate of land in Albestein, as is contained in their chirograph.

By the gift of the brethren of the hospital of Saint Peter at York: that portion of land which they held in Bolthebi, as is contained in the charter and chirographs.

By the gift of Gervase and his son Benedict: the meadow which they gave you at Kocheberch.

By the gift of [Col. 0094C] Odo de Nes: the meadow which he gave you at Walterholm.

By the gift of Hugh del Tuith: the meadow which he gave you at Kochesberch.

By the gift of Hugh Malebestia: the meadow called Dswaldeshenges.

By the gift of the brethren of the hospital of Whitby: two bovates of land in Dovetun, according to the form of their landholding.

By the gift of Richard Cum[in?]: one and a half carucates at Stainchroff, as Richard himself granted them to you and confirmed them by his charter.

Certainly, from the produce of your labours which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals, let no one whatsoever presume to demand tithes from you. We further forbid by apostolic authority that anyone should dare, without your permission, to receive or retain your brethren—clerics as well as laymen—after they have made profession in your monastery. [Col. 0094D] We also decree that no archbishop, bishop, or person of any order shall interdict your house from divine offices, unless there has been an evident and manifest fault on the part of the abbot or brethren of that house. When, however, a general interdict has been laid upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, with excommunicated or interdicted persons excluded.

Providing also, with paternal concern, for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority that anyone shall dare within the enclosure of your lands or granges to commit violence, robbery, or theft, or to seize a person; and if anyone presumptuously attempts this, let him be judged a [Col. 0095A] sacrilegious person and punished by the penalty of excommunication.

Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority all liberties, immunities, and royal customs granted to you and to your church by our dearest son Henry, king of the English, and ratified by the text of his charter; and we decree that they shall remain perpetually unimpaired. We forbid anyone to harass you or your church concerning all Tmanatala [uncertain place or exemption term], concerning *negeld* [a tax], all assizes, customs, aids, pleas, or any earthly service which belonged to any secular person. Rather, you shall remain free and quit of such exactions and demands, as our aforesaid son King Henry or his grandfather, the elder Henry, [Col. 0095B] reasonably confirmed to you by their charters.

Moreover, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot A., desiring that the religious observance established in the monasteries over which you are known to preside may flourish in the Lord, we decree that in all monasteries which have gone forth from the monastery over which you preside, and in those which have proceeded from houses that went forth from the same monastery, you shall have free authority, in accordance with the institution of the Cistercian brethren, to arrange and regulate matters concerning both persons and the goods of the monasteries.

By this present decree we also enact that the bishops in whose dioceses your monasteries are situated shall never impede the regular and canonical election of your abbot, nor shall they in any way interfere, contrary to the statutes of the Cistercian [Col. 0095C] Order and the authority of its privileges, in removing or deposing the person who may be abbot at the time.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, to take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any other vexations; but that all things shall be kept whole, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, anyone in future knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this page of our decree, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the [Col. 0095D] dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity he has perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject, at the last judgment, to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Anagni by the hand of Herman, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December [20 November], in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1160, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

## XXII. To the Bishop of Beauvais.—Commendation for his enduring attachment to the Roman Church and to the person of Pope Alexander, and exhortation to the same. (Anagni, 29 November.)

[MARTEN, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 664.]

[Col. 0096A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Beauvais: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The wall of your unshaken faith, founded with steadfast solidity upon the rock of the Church, can neither be overthrown by the force of flashing lightning nor softened by the gentle falling of rains. For upon such a foundation, which is Christ, the structure of your edifice rises; if a tempest blows upon it, you are not shaken; if winds rush upon it, you are not moved. For where Christ is the foundation, that which has been firmly built can be displaced by no assault.

Since, therefore, nothing can or could cut you off from the unity of the Catholic Church, nothing can restrain your mind from devotion to our person; rather, setting yourself before others as an impregnable wall for the house of God and opposing schismatics and heretics with the utmost vigour; and graciously receiving and honourably treating our beloved sons, the cardinals and legates of the Apostolic See, to whom we entrusted the conduct of the Church’s business in those regions—you have proved exceedingly useful and necessary in the cause of the Church. We commend the beginning, middle, and end of your purpose, and for such constancy we offer boundless thanks to your prudence. We are indeed ready and resolved always to love you in the Lord with sincere charity as a beloved and special son of the Church, and, with God’s help, to honour your person in every way that we can.

For before our promotion, as you yourself know, we held your person very dear and acceptable; and now that, by the Lord’s ordering, we have been promoted to greater things, we wish to hold you dearer in our inmost affections. Whatever we can accomplish for you without offence to conscience, we shall take care to bring to effect with a ready and willing mind. You also, as before we were raised to the office of apostolic dignity you especially loved our person and showed yourself most faithful and devoted to us, so henceforth be yet more fervent in fidelity and devotion to blessed Peter and to us. As a devoted and special son, devote yourself to the honour, exaltation, and advantage of the most holy Roman Church, knowing that the sincerity of your devotion and the constancy of your faith will never pass from the memory of us and our brethren.

Given at Anagni, on the third day before the Kalends of December [29 November].

## XXIII. He confirms the privilege of the canons of Saint Frigidian at Lucca: cardinal deacons of Saint Mary the New are to be chosen from their number. (Avignon [read Anagni], 21 December.)

[See *Bullarium Lateranense*, p. 41.]

## YEAR 1160–1161

[Col. 0097A]

## XXIV. To Hugh, Archbishop of Palermo.—He confirms him as metropolitan of the bishops of Agrigento, Mazara, and Malta. (Anagni, 26 April.)

[PIRRI, *Sicilia Sacra*, I, 101.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, archbishop of Palermo: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The greater the devotion which we know you show to the most holy Roman Church and to ourselves, the more willingly we hear you in your requests, and the more we bring your petitions to effect, insofar as we can with God’s help. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, Archbishop, concurring gladly in your just requests, whatever is known to be contained in the privilege granted to you by our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Adrian, concerning the concession of three suffragans—namely, the bishops of Agrigento, Mazara, and Malta—we confirm to your devotion by apostolic authority and fortify with the protection of this present writing. We decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever to infringe this page of our confirmation or to oppose it in any way. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May [26 April].

## XXV. To the Bishop of Albano, his vicar.

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXII, 428.]

[Col. 0097C]

From the tenor of your letters we have learned that a certain cleric, N., has sinned so seriously that, if his offence were public, he would be degraded from the order which he has received and could no longer be promoted to higher orders. But because, as you said, the sin itself is hidden and private, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you impose upon him fitting penance and persuade him, after the penance has been performed, to exercise the order he has received; and, being content with that, not to proceed any further to higher orders. Nevertheless, because the sin is hidden, should he desire promotion, you neither can nor ought on any ground to forbid him.

Concerning the young man who knew a certain woman and afterwards joined her daughter to himself in marriage, with whom he has now lived for ten years, we reply to your prudence: if, as you have informed us, his offence is hidden, fitting penance ought to be imposed upon him, and he is not for that reason to be separated from a wife unaware of so great a crime. But if it is known to be public, he must both be separated from his wife and remain without hope of marriage.

## XXVI. To the same.

[Ibid.]

From the report of I., bearer of the present letter, and from the tenor of your letters, we have learned that when the same I. had carnally known his wife’s sister and had remained with her for a long time, you separated them from one another and caused the said I. to be sent to our hearing. Concerning this we said in reply to your brotherhood that you should endeavour to send him to Jerusalem. Then, when he has returned home, lest something worse perhaps result from their abstinence, you may overlook his living with his wife; yet not in such a way as to seem in any degree to grant them permission for this as a favour.

## YEAR 1161

## XXVII. To the people of Thérouanne.—On behalf of Bishop Milo II. (4 January.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, X, Instruments, 405.]

[Col. 0098B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the clergy and people of Thérouanne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received with paternal charity our beloved son Milo, formerly elect and now your bishop, when he came to the Apostolic See; and, rendering him the honour due to him, we took care, insofar as we could with God’s help and justice, to grant his requests and those of his Church. For when his opponent, who was more earnestly intent upon withdrawing the Church of Boulogne and being ordained bishop there, and the clerics of the said elect, whom he had sent beforehand to our presence, were assembled in our court, that opponent failed to pursue the case. With the common counsel of our brethren, we decreed that the aforesaid Church of Boulogne should remain in the condition in which it had been until that time.

Given on the day before the Nones of January [4 January] in the year 1161.

## XXVIII. To Samson, Archbishop of Reims.—For the Church of Thérouanne. (Anagni, 17 January.)

[D. MARLOT, *Metropolis Remensis*, II, 371.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother SAMSON, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son M., formerly elect of Thérouanne, and the canons of the same Church, worn out by many labours, came into our presence, asserting that they had endured many expenses and hardships because the people of Boulogne were attempting to withdraw their church from that bishopric. For when he had been canonically elected by the canons of the aforesaid Church of Thérouanne and, as we learned from the admission of the other party, there was absolutely nothing alleged against him that ought in any way to impede his election, and when, at his Church’s request, you wished to impose upon him the hand of consecration after he had already been shaved and tonsured by your command, the canons of the Church of Reims represented to you and to the aforesaid elect that Baldus and his brother E. . . . . ., canons of the Church of Boulogne, had previously made an appeal, forbidding you on the Apostolic See’s behalf to impose your hand upon him unless he renounced the aforesaid Church of Boulogne.

But you, as a devoted son of the most holy Roman Church, and one who has always been accustomed, as a religious and Catholic man, to honour in all things and through all things that same Roman Church, your Mother, did not wish to consecrate him because of the impediment of the appeal that had been made. But when the opponents of the same elect, who were more earnestly intent upon withdrawing the Church of Boulogne and being ordained bishop there, and the clerics of the said elect, whom he had sent beforehand to our presence, had assembled in our court, that opponent failed to pursue the case. With the common counsel of our brethren, we decreed that the aforesaid Church of Boulogne should remain in the condition in which it had been until that time.

Seeing, therefore, that the aforesaid Church of Thérouanne and the elect himself had laboured greatly in coming to us, and recognizing that there was nothing in the institutions of the sacred canons that ought to obstruct his election, we did not wish to leave them desolate. Rather, compassionating mercifully their labours and expenses, and showing every deference to your honour and dignity, at the urgent request of the canons of that Church who were with the elect, and with the common counsel of our brethren, we conferred upon him the gift of consecration—while preserving in all things both your right and that of your Church.

We therefore send him back from our hands to you and to his Church, so that, as to his metropolitan, he may render you every submission due and show reverence, humility, and honour, as his predecessors were ever more accustomed to show your predecessors. We therefore ask, admonish, and earnestly exhort your charity that, for the reverence of blessed Peter and of ourselves, you receive him with due kindness, treat him charitably, and do not let him perceive that your favour toward him has been diminished on this account. Rather, at our intervention, show him greater affection and familiarity.

For we sincerely love your person in Christ’s inmost affections as one of the chief pillars of the Church and an immovable support of God’s house. Although you saw others, when scandals arose in God’s Church, waver through faintness of spirit, you never fell away from the strength of your steadfastness, but always remained immovable in the unity of the Catholic Church. We have no wish whatsoever to do anything by which your person may in any way be offended. Rather, we purpose and intend to anticipate you, as our venerable and most beloved brother, with blessings of sweetness; and we intend to grant your requests in every way that we can with God’s help.

Given at Anagni, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February [17 January].

## XXIX. To Louis VII, King of the Franks.—He commends the piety and merits of the kings of France, especially Louis, toward the Apostolic See. (Anagni, 17 January.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 983.]

[Col. 0100A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

How devoted and obedient your illustrious and magnificent forefathers and predecessors, the kings of the Franks, always were to the most holy Church, and how great were the benefits and services of devotion which they rendered it, we have clearly learned from the many and splendid advantages which came to God’s holy Church through them. Our brethren who have long lived in the Roman Church have recognized this still more fully.

But you, being a praiseworthy imitator of your forefathers, in order to show yourself truly heir both to your paternal virtues and to the kingdom, have, after the example of those forefathers, loved more earnestly your singular and only mother, the most holy Roman Church, from the time when the kingdom was entrusted by God to your excellence to govern. You have faithfully stood by her in her distresses and necessities, and nothing has ever been able to turn your royal mind from devotion to and support of her. For while Frederick—who, by the duty of his office, ought to be the Church’s advocate and defender—was raging cruelly against her, you, as a most Christian prince, love and honour her and venerate her with sincere affection. In every tribulation she has found, both with your predecessors and with yourself, the longed-for harbour of rest and a refuge always ready to help.

Moreover, among all the other churches of the world, the Gallican Church—although the others had changed amid the scandals that arose in their tribulation [perhaps “had wavered”]—has never departed from the unity of the Catholic Mother Church; never withdrawn itself from her subjection and reverence; but, as a most devoted daughter, has always remained firm and stable in devotion to her. Accordingly, the Roman Church, mother and mistress of all, has loved your forefathers, yourself, and the Gallican Church among the other princes and churches of the world with a special and singular prerogative. She has laboured for your honour, increase, and exaltation; and, in all matters in which she could do so according to God, meeting your wishes, she has especially honoured your persons.

For we believe that there is no prince in the whole world whom our predecessors and we ourselves are bound to love with fuller affection, or to whom we ought to show greater deference, than to your Highness. We keep firmly in the treasury of our heart, and have learned both from public report and from the communications sent by the archbishops and bishops of your kingdom and by our beloved sons, the cardinals H[enry], W[illiam], and Odo—whom we sent into those regions for the Church’s necessity and for the honour and advantage of your kingdom and of yourself—how, as you yourself have indicated to us on this occasion by your own letters, whatever others might do, you effectively induced your royal mind from the very beginning to receive us. By your example others also were more strongly stirred to do the same and inflamed in devotion to us. Therefore, from the Creator of all, by whose grace you so praiseworthily directed your purpose, your excellence will obtain an unfailing reward; and we ourselves, insofar as divine grace permits, shall take care to respond beneficially to your serenity for such devotion.

Accordingly, as we rejoice with inward affection in your prosperity and that of the kingdom entrusted to you, so, if adversity should ever occur—which may God avert—we should grieve greatly and be most deeply troubled. For we have the purpose and a most ready will gladly to attend to your peace and tranquillity and to the governance of the kingdom entrusted to you. Concerning the matters which your excellence has indicated to us in your own letters, we are carefully deliberating among ourselves and shall discuss them with our brethren; whatever we see to pertain to the honour of God, of the Roman Church, and of yourself, we shall gladly take care to carry out. Through our beloved son Brother Guy, monk of Marmoutier, we shall, God willing, shortly give your serenity a fuller oral reply concerning these things.

Furthermore, concerning our venerable brother M[anasses], bishop of Orléans, for whom your royal Highness has interceded with us most affectionately: although some have whispered unfavourable things about him into our ears, even if it were certain to us that he had caused us some injury, yet out of love for you and at your intervention we wish to love him with sincere affection. We intend, insofar as we can with God’s help, to honour him as our dearest brother and more willingly to hear him in his requests.

Given at Anagni, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February [17 January].

## XXX. To Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg.—He reports the prosperous state of the Church and of himself; he exhorts him to remain faithfully constant to the Church and to endeavour to bring back the emperor. (Anagni, 20 January.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1036.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother EBERHARD, archbishop of Salzburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Catholic men, fervent in faith, ought to rise up manfully to cut off heresies and schisms. Defending justice and the Church’s liberty, they ought powerfully to set themselves up as wall and bulwark against the presumption of those who attempt to rend the most holy Church, prefigured in the Gospel by Christ’s seamless tunic, which admits no division. Thus grain is separated from chaff, and those who are approved become manifest, so that they may say with the Apostle: “Neither angel nor archangel, nor distress nor hunger, will be able in any way to separate us from charity” (Romans 8).

We rejoice joyfully in the Lord and give thanks to Almighty God because, as we have learned from the reports of many people and as the bearer of the present letter, sent to the Apostolic See by your brotherhood, has shown us in his own report, you have remained firm and steadfast in the unity of the Catholic Church and in devotion to blessed Peter and to us. You are resolved to labour for the honour of your mother, the most holy Roman Church; and, as a Catholic man fervent in faith, you have not so feared the threats of the prince, who persecutes the Church and ourselves without cause and strives wholly to destroy her liberty, that you could in any way be moved from fidelity to the Roman Church and to us. You say with blessed Peter: “It is necessary to obey God rather than men” (Acts 5).

For the fervour of so great a devotion and the purity of such sincere faith, we greatly commend your prudence in the Lord and offer you such thanks as we owe and can offer. We purpose and intend to love your person with sincere charity in our inmost affections and, as we see fitting, by the Lord’s gift, to honour you and respond to you according to your merit.

Moreover, since it is clearer than daylight how Octavian, a schismatic, heretic, and manifest intruder, thrust himself in with three accomplices of his wickedness and attempted through notorious simony and lay violence to seize the papacy; how Frederick—who ought rather to be called a tyrant than emperor—at the assembly laboriously gathered at Pavia, presumed to erect Nebuchadnezzar’s statue and worship the idol of abomination once it had been raised; and how Catholic men fled from Octavian’s face as from the sight of a dragon—we did not think it necessary to detain you longer with an extended series of words and letters, since divine clemency has caused their days to fail in vanity and we see them deceived by the iniquity they embraced.

For the Eastern Church, in a council solemnly held at Nazareth in the presence of the illustrious king of Jerusalem; the churches of France, England, Spain, and the whole Western Church, with their kings, archbishops, bishops, and all their clergy and people, have condemned the aforesaid schismatic and his chief supporters by perpetual anathema. They have unanimously and magnificently received us as spiritual father and supreme pontiff, as you may clearly learn from common report and the copies of letters which we send you through the bearer of the present letter, humbly offering us all obedience and reverence in word and deed. We disclose all this to you in our letter all the more willingly because we believe that you will conceive greater joy at the unity and progress of the Church, and will grieve all the more at her adversity because you are known to be a firmer pillar in her midst.

Since, therefore, we have the fullest confidence in your religion, integrity, and prudence—as in one who could by no means be polluted by schismatic or heretical perversity, but is firmly established upon the rock of Catholic unity—we ask, admonish, and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord by apostolic letters that, as we have heard you have well and praiseworthily begun, you may persevere with unshaken constancy in devotion and fidelity to the most holy Roman Church and to us; striving with pure mind and all your strength for her honour, increase, and exaltation, and for ours. Let no threats or terrors of anyone be able in any degree to deter you from the service of blessed Peter and of us.

Also endeavour, by frequent admonition and careful vigilance, to recall your suffragans, neighbouring bishops, and other persons, ecclesiastical as well as secular, to the service and devotion of the Church and of us, and to establish them more firmly therein. Take care also diligently to soften the mind of the aforesaid prince, and earnestly admonish and exhort him to return to the bosom of Mother Church and to the way of truth. In this he will be able to obtain both spiritual and bodily benefit.

Furthermore, let not your devotion delay to inform us by your own letters of the condition of your Church and of the German kingdom, and also of the minds and intentions of the people of that kingdom. In these matters and in other things which you know to be advantageous for us and for the Church, show yourself so careful and zealous that you may always obtain in fullest measure the favour of the Apostolic See and of ourselves.

Given at Rome. [Note: At [Col. 0103], Wattenbach showed that in the Vienna manuscript *Anagniae* should be read in place of *Romae*. JAFFÉ.] On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February [20 January].

## XXXI. Privilege for the church of Saint Cuthbert at Radford. (Anagni, 22 January.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, II, 53.]

[Col. 0103C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, prior of the church of Saint Cuthbert of Kadeford, and his brethren, both present and future, who profess the regular life: in perpetuity.
