The granting of effect to just requests is required both by the force of equity and by the order of reason, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wish and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to the divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We establish first of all that the canonical order, known to have been instituted according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being propitious, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and undiminished to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: by the gift of William of Suvetot, founder of that church, and of his heirs, the place itself upon which the church stands, with its lands, tithes, and all their appurtenances; the church of Malcringham, the church of Gringeleia, the church of Normaton, the church of Visson, the church of Coleston, and the church of Willeley; whatever you possess in the churches of Bisterton, Cluverburtet, and Beriswell, with their appurtenances; furthermore, all tithes from the lands of the same William, from the Honour of Blida, and from every thing from which tithe is customarily and ought to be given; at Berdemyc, two bovates of land; at Coleston, two bovates of land with one dwelling from the demesne of the same William; at Burford, four bovates; at Wistron, four bovates of land with one dwelling, and the whole land of the said William at Berteby and Slawic, except one bovate of land; at Bayton, the newly cleared lands of Sotumi; at Dormaton, the land of the oft-mentioned Lord William, with the meadow, Howalia, Ulfac, and Bolum, together with the mills and the newly cleared lands of Ehorp; at Sthirakis, one bovate of land with one dwelling, and the whole land on the southern side of the stream in the same vill, the newly cleared lands of Apelia, and Gravam, as enclosed by the ditch; the mill of Banton with its fishpond; the mill of Sthirakis; at Kampton, one fishery, and the whole site of the vill of Radeford, as enclosed by the ditch; by the gift of Gilbert of Wenis, the land of Brist with a mill and half a bovate of land at Belh; by the gift of Robert of Stivellei, six bovates of land at Renchall; by the gift of Radbriton, the place called Stellera with all its appurtenances; by the gift of Avicia, daughter of William of Taneya, three bovates of land at Termodestone; by the gift of Cecilia, wife of Richard of Suwetot, whatever you possess in the territory of the church of Dinisleja.

We likewise confirm by the page of this present writing the liberties and immunities granted to you by kings or princes in pious devotion. Certainly, no one shall presume to demand tithes from you of your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals. In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose priests from among your brethren and present them to the bishop; they shall answer to that bishop concerning the care of the people, but to you concerning temporal matters belonging to the church itself.

Furthermore, we establish that no ecclesiastical or secular person may impose unjust or undue exactions in the aforesaid church, or inflict undue burdens upon the priests dwelling in those churches. We also grant that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who have chosen to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; saving, nevertheless, the canonical right of the mother church and of the parish churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. Upon the death of you who are now prior of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of subterfuge or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine, provide to be elected.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them by any vexations; but that all things be preserved entire for the use, in every respect beneficial, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second and third time, shall not correct his presumption by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know that he is answerable before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of the Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Anagni by the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February [22 January], in the eighth indiction, in the year 1161 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### XXXII. To Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury, and Hilary, Bishop of Chichester.—That Robert de Valoniis should restore the wood of Northaga to the monks of St Albans.  
*(Anagni, 27 January.)*

*[Matthew Paris, Works, Appendix, p. 83.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable THEOBALD, Archbishop of Canterbury, and HILARY, Bishop of Chichester: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the monastery of St Alban, have shown us by a complaint sent to us that Robert de Valoniis unjustly holds in occupation the wood of Northaga, which those brethren assert belongs to their right. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your brotherhood to take care, with all diligence, to summon the said Robert within thirty days after receiving these letters, so that he either restore the wood itself to the said brethren without difficulty, or render them full justice concerning it in your presence. If he should perhaps refuse to do this, pronounce upon him a sentence of excommunication. If one of you cannot take part in this business, the other shall nevertheless carry it out.

Given at Anagni, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [27 January].

### XXXIII. To Henry, Bishop of Beauvais.—Concerning the affair of Master G. and a priest’s prebend at Soissons.  
*(Anagni, 3 February.)*

*[Marten, Amplissima Collectio, II, p. 656.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Bishop of Beauvais: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We greatly commend in the Lord your prudence for that constancy of devotion and purity of faith which, by many indications and evident proof in events, we have learned that you possess toward the most holy Roman Church and our person; and for this we render you abundant thanks. We have the firm purpose and ardent wish sincerely to love your person with an affection of charity, to reward you according to your merit, and willingly to honour you in all things insofar as this may be done with God and justice.

Therefore, as you have well and laudably begun, let your brotherhood remain firm and steadfast in fidelity and service to blessed Peter and to us. Strive diligently, by every means you can, for the honour of that Roman Church and of ourselves; and strive to induce and firmly establish in this same course our dearest son Louis, the illustrious King of the Franks, your brother.

Furthermore, we believe that your discretion is not unaware how our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Adrian, granted one prebend in the Church of Soissons to Master G., priest and bearer of these letters, and, when investing him with it, caused that prebend to be confirmed to him by apostolic authority. Yet he has not been able to possess it peacefully, because the aforesaid king, as is said, has conceived indignation against him through the evil suggestion of someone. By apostolic letters we ask your brotherhood, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves and in consideration of piety, so effectively to intercede with that king that you secure the restoration of his favour to the said priest and cause him to be protected and supported by the same king in his rights.

Given at Anagni, on the third day before the Nones of February [3 February].

### XXXIV. To the clergy of England.—Concerning the canonization of Saint Edward, King of England.  
*(Anagni, 7 February.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, XXI, p. 871.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable archbishops and bishops, and to the beloved sons, abbots, priors, and other prelates of churches established throughout England: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we consider more closely the constancy of devotion and firmness of faith which you show toward your mother, the most holy Roman Church, we are moved to resolve that we should love you in the Lord with sincere charity as dearest brethren and special sons of the Church, honour you more abundantly, and willingly receive your petitions insofar as we can with God.

Accordingly, concerning the petition which both our dearest son in Christ Henry, the illustrious King of the English, and you yourselves have urgently presented to us for the canonization of Edward, formerly the glorious King of the English, and his enrolment in the catalogue of saints, we held careful deliberation with our brethren. We examined the Book of Miracles—the miracles which the almighty Lord in his mercy displayed through him while he lived in mortal flesh and after he was taken from this present world; we also saw the letters of our predecessor of pious memory, Pope Innocent, and received your testimonies concerning the matter. Although so arduous and lofty a business is not customarily granted often except in solemn councils, nevertheless, by the common counsel of our brethren, in accordance with the vow and desire of our aforesaid son the king and of yourselves, we have judged that the body of that confessor ought to be glorified and honoured upon earth with fitting praises, just as the Lord by his grace has glorified that confessor in heaven. Henceforth, therefore, he is to be numbered among the holy confessors, having merited to obtain this from God himself by signs and miracles.

Since it befits your honourable prudence devoutly to reverence and zealously to venerate him whom your devotion requested should by apostolic authority be venerated and worshipped, by apostolic letters we admonish and exhort all of you in the Lord to strive henceforth to honour him with due observances, so that through his intercessions you may deserve to obtain forgiveness from the strict Judge and find a glorious reward in eternal blessedness.

Given at Anagni, on the seventh day before the Ides of February [7 February].

### XXXV. To Hugh, Bishop of Soissons.—In the greatest straits, he asks for some financial assistance.  
*(Anagni, 17 February.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, XXI, p. 1003.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, Bishop of Soissons: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The integrity of devotion and affection of charity which we believe you bear toward the most holy Roman Church and our person gives us no small confidence that we ought to seek counsel and aid from you in our necessities and confidently disclose to you the matters pressing upon us. We do not doubt that it has come to the notice of your discretion how Frederick—that tyrant and violent persecutor of the Church—persecutes the most holy Roman Church, universal mother of all, and oppresses and assails her without cause. Like a ravening and roaring lion lying in ambush, he has so blocked the approaches of the roads with satellites of barbarous ferocity that those from whom the Roman Church has customarily received timely aid in its necessities can no longer reach us.

Since the Roman Church in these times is therefore distressed and afflicted by many oppressions and weighed down by great and almost countless debts, you ought to rise up more zealously and labour more effectively to bear her burdens and relieve the necessities she suffers, in proportion as that mother Church places greater trust in your devotion and purity of faith. Standing in so critical a moment of need, we thank you for your former assistance; and we earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort your charity to recall how many and how great are the burdens and straits which the Roman Church now suffers in defending her own liberty and that of all churches. Consider also what members owe to the head, and extend anew the hand of generosity for the assistance of the Church and the payment of the debts which burden her; grant us, in this crisis, the help of your consolation, if this can be done without serious detriment to your own church. For benefits and services rendered in necessity are always accustomed to be more welcome to those who receive them.

Exhort likewise, with all diligence, the abbots and other prelates of churches established in your bishopric to do the same. Whatever assistance you are able to give us, we wish you to deliver it to our beloved son . . . , bearer of these letters, and to inform us of this by your letters.

Given at Anagni, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March [17 February].

### XXXVI. To Henry, Bishop of Beauvais.—He asks him to assist the Church oppressed by Emperor Frederick.  
*(Anagni, 18 February.)*

*[Marten, Amplissima Collectio, II, p. 657.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brother HENRY, Bishop of Beauvais: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The integrity of devotion and affection of charity which we believe you bear toward the most holy Roman Church and our person gives us no small confidence that we ought to seek counsel and aid from you in our necessities and confidently disclose to you the matters pressing upon us. We do not doubt that it has come to the notice of your discretion how Frederick—[Note: Frederick I, called Aenobarbus, elected 5 March 1152, whom he here calls a tyrant because of the disastrous schism which he provoked in the Church after the death of Pope Adrian IV.]—that tyrant and violent persecutor of the Church, persecutes the most holy Roman Church, universal mother of all, and oppresses and assails her without cause. Like a ravening and roaring lion lying in ambush, he has so blocked the approaches of the roads with satellites of barbarous ferocity that those from whom the Roman Church has customarily received timely aid in its necessities can no longer reach us.

Since the Roman Church in these times is distressed and afflicted by many oppressions and weighed down by great and almost countless debts, you ought to rise up more zealously and labour more effectively to bear all her burdens and relieve the necessities she suffers, in proportion as that mother Church places greater trust in your devotion and purity of faith. Standing in so critical a moment of need, we earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort your charity to recall how many and how great are the burdens and straits which the Roman Church now suffers in defending her own liberty and that of all churches. Consider also what members owe to the head, and extend the hand of generosity for the assistance of the Church and the payment of the debts which burden her; grant us, in this crisis, the help of your consolation. For benefits and services rendered in necessity are always accustomed to be more welcome to those who receive them.

Exhort likewise with diligence the abbots and other prelates of churches established in your bishopric to do the same. Whatever assistance you are able to give us, we wish you to deliver to our beloved son, the bearer of these letters, whom for this purpose we have thought fit to send into those regions, and to inform us of this by your letters.

Given at Anagni, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March [18 February].

### XXXVII. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saints Facundus and Primitivus of Sahagún.  
*(Anagni, 18 February.)*

*[Escalona, History of Sahagún, p. 542, on the testimony of Jaffé, Registers of the Roman Pontiffs, p. 683.]*

### XXXVIII. To Master Nicholas.—He praises his zeal toward the Apostolic See and exhorts him to persevere in it.  
*(Anagni, 6 March.)*

*[Marten, Amplissima Collectio, II, p. 658.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother MASTER NICHOLAS: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We hold dear and acceptable, and greatly commend in the Lord, the constancy of your devotion and firmness of faith which, through many experiences in affairs and by the very outcome of your actions, we know you possess toward the most holy Roman Church and our person. For we know how you have spared yourself not at all and have laboured very greatly for the Church’s cause. Therefore, we have the purpose and will to love your person in the Lord with sincere charity as a special son of the Church, and always to grant your petitions.

But because a good beginning must be brought to completion by a praiseworthy end, by apostolic letters we admonish and exhort your belovedness in the Lord that, as you have well begun in devotion and fidelity to the Church and to us, you may persevere firmly and immovably; and that you may strive to induce and more firmly establish other persons, ecclesiastical as well as secular, in the same course. On account of your devotion, we are sending letters of recommendation for you to our venerable brethren Hugh, Archbishop of Sens, and Samson, Archbishop of Reims—[Note: “Samson.” From this it may be inferred that this letter was written at the beginning of Alexander III’s pontificate, for Samson, Archbishop of Reims, died in 1161.]—and also to the noble Count Henry [Note: That is, the Count of Troyes, to whom Nicholas was especially welcome.].

Given at Anagni, on the second day before the Nones of March [6 March].

### XXXIX. Privilege for the monastery of Phalempin.  
*(Anagni.)*

*[Buzelini, Gallo-Flandria, p. 374.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons in Christ HEMFRED, abbot of the monastery of Phalempin, and his canonical brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

[lacuna]

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We establish first of all that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that church according to the fear of God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the brethren of Arrouaise, shall be observed there inviolate for all time, etc.

Certainly, no one shall presume to demand tithes from you of your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands and at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, and in a subdued voice.

We also forbid any bishop, archdeacon, or other ecclesiastical or secular person to demand or extort from you a palfrey or anything else on account of the election, blessing, or enthronement of your abbots, since it is manifestly simoniacal for anything to be demanded or paid as due on these grounds. Furthermore, by this present writing we strictly prohibit any bishop, archdeacon, or other ecclesiastical person from imposing new and undue exactions upon you or your church; rather, we decree that the church itself shall henceforth remain in that liberty in which it is known to have remained hitherto.

We also decree that the burial-place of the same house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion or final wish of those who have chosen to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; saving, nevertheless, the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are carried out.

Given at Anagni, in the year 1161 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### XL. To Henry, Bishop of Beauvais.—He praises him for his zeal toward the Apostolic See and in repressing schismatics.  
*(Anagni, 7 April.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, XXI, p. 1149.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Bishop of Beauvais: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The constancy of ardent charity and the affection of most sincere devotion which you faithfully showed toward the most holy Roman Church and our person in a stormy and troubled time admonishes and moves us to extol with the highest praises what you have most profitably accomplished for the Church of God. It causes this service, so welcome to us, never to pass from the memory of ourselves and our brethren.

For our beloved sons Henry [Note: Henry of Pisa, a Cistercian monk enrolled in the sacred college of cardinals by Eugene III.] and Oddo [Note: He seems to be Oddo, or Otto, cardinal deacon of St George in Velabro, who was a principal agent in securing the supreme pontificate for Alexander III.], cardinals of the holy Roman Church and legates of the Apostolic See, have repeatedly reported to us—and we know it more clearly from common and public report and from the very result of the matter—how you set yourself up as an unconquerable wall for the house of God; how you most vigorously refuted schismatics and heretics; and how by many persuasions you strengthened in the unity of the Catholic Church the mind of our dearest son Louis, the illustrious King of the Franks, your brother, and that of others, both secular princes and ecclesiastical men.

From the report of those same cardinals we have also learned how long you retained them and their households in your own house, how widely and generously you provided for them at your own expense, and with what affection of charity you strove to treat them. We attribute our reception, solemnly accomplished at the council held in France, more to you than to any mortal man. By your zeal, vigilance, and labour, the minds of the wavering were recalled to the path of truth, and those who remained in the Church’s devotion were firmly strengthened therein.

Therefore, since the advancement and exaltation of the holy Roman Church undoubtedly pertains to the honour and advancement of yourself and of the Church committed to you, induce and exhort in every way our aforesaid son the king to remain in the devotion to the Church which he has begun, and by royal authority compel those rebels in his kingdom to obedience and fidelity toward the Church and ourselves.

Moreover, because Hugh, called Abbot of Cluny, has departed from the unity of the Church at peril to his soul and has fallen into the heretical and schismatic perversity of the pestilent Octavian, we declare him excommunicated after consultation with our brethren. We have committed the matter to your discretion, commanding your brotherhood by apostolic letters, after taking counsel with and receiving the support of our aforesaid son the king—whose kingdom might, on this account, be assailed and gravely troubled by that abbot—to proceed at once to Cluny upon receipt of these letters. There, all appeal being set aside, depose him by the authority of the Apostolic See; and, with the counsel of the Catholic brethren of that monastery, do not delay to place another in his stead. The privilege granted by the Apostolic See to the Church of Cluny shall offer you no impediment concerning the deposition of that abbot. For it is fitting that one who has withdrawn himself from the unity of the Church should, in accordance with his wickedness, be held deprived of ecclesiastical rank.

But if you should perhaps be unable to proceed to his deposition, and if, abandoning his heretical perversity, he wishes to return to the bosom of mother Church, receive him and his accomplices in our stead, if they too choose to return to our obedience, and absolve them from the sentence of excommunication by which they are bound, after first receiving from them the oath contained below:

> I, H., reject and anathematize Octavian, the heretic and schismatic, and all his principal supporters; and from this hour onward I shall be faithful and obedient to blessed Peter and to Lord Pope Alexander and his successors who enter canonically. So help me God and these holy Gospels!

We further command your experience, by whatever means you can, to strive and secure the capture or complete expulsion from the monastery of Ymarus [Note: Ymarus, of whom Alexander speaks here, was a monk of the Cluniac order at St Martin-des-Champs; subsequently prior of St Arnulf of Crépy, then of La Charité-sur-Loire, and afterwards abbot of the New Monastery at Poitiers. Created cardinal by Innocent II, he successfully carried out many legations; but he was unfortunate in adhering to Octavian, the antipope, and consecrating him. It should therefore not seem surprising if he turned Hugh, Abbot of Cluny, away from the true pontiff.], a schismatic and heretic, formerly Bishop of Tusculum. Bring with you to that monastery our beloved sons R., bearer of these letters, and his companions, who have remained faithful to the Roman Church, and cause them to remain peacefully and quietly in their former position. We ask that our aforesaid beloved son R., monk of the Church of Cluny, be earnestly commended to your charity through our intervention.

Given at Anagni, on the seventh day before the Ides of April [7 April].

### XLI. To the Cluniacs.—Concerning the deposition of Hugh, Abbot of Cluny.  
*(Anagni, 7 April.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, XXXI, p. 1151.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all the brethren of the monastery of Cluny who remain in the communion of the Church and in fidelity and obedience to us: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as the once noble, most honourable, and renowned monastery of Cluny has a special regard for the right and protection of the most holy Roman Church, so it has also been accustomed to cling more ardently to her and always to stand by her in her needs. Especially in times when schisms and heresies have arisen, the monastery, sympathizing with its mother’s anguish and laceration, never departed from her unity upon any occasion; it did not deviate from faith in the Catholic Church through blandishments or terrors, judging it better to be oppressed and afflicted in temporal matters than to be severed from the unity of the Church and the maternal bosom.

But now that same church, by reason of sins, has become a mockery and spectacle of all peoples, a byword to the world—she who formerly shone as the most famous among the Gallican churches. Thus, on account of the schismatic brethren who stain the Church of Cluny, the prophecy of Jeremiah is set forth concerning her: “Her gates have been destroyed; her priests groan; her virgins are in squalor; and she herself is oppressed with bitterness” (*Lamentations* 1). To these same false and heretical brethren, who were once in the Church’s communion but now miserably cling to scaly filth, imitating the author and head of schism, another saying applies: “Those who feasted luxuriously have perished in the streets; those nurtured in saffron robes have embraced dung” (*Lamentations* 4).

He who seemed to be the head and support in that church has become the tail and its ruin. Nor has this head merely been weakened but, as we say in grief, cut off. For while the whole Gallican Church and almost the whole Church throughout the world stand fast in our devotion and obedience and condemn Octavian, the schismatic and heretic, he who is called abbot, cut off from the unity of the Catholic Church, presumptuously clings to him in obstinacy at peril to his soul. We are now compelled to lament for him and his accomplices and to say: “All her splendour has departed from the daughter of Zion; her princes have become like rams finding no pasture; they have gone away without strength before the face of the pursuer” (*Lamentations* 1).

For, as we have learned by report, certain among very many of those brethren, clinging to the said Hugh, called abbot, and to Ymarus, apostate and schismatic, formerly Bishop of Tusculum, to the ruin of their order and souls, have been given over to a reprobate mind. Though formerly regarded as religious and Catholic, they have fallen so far into the snare of error and the path of perversity that the following prophecy fittingly applies to them: “The illustrious sons of Zion, clothed first in gold—how have they been reckoned as earthen vessels, the work of a potter’s hands?” (*Lamentations* 4).

Therefore, recognizing that so great an iniquity has gone forth from Babylon and from elder judges who seemed to govern the people, and being unable to leave it unpunished lest, if it remains long, it defile neighbouring places with its foulness, we have commanded our venerable brother Henry, Bishop of Beauvais—a religious, prudent, and honourable man—to go at once to Cluny, and there, all appeal being set aside, depose by the authority of the Apostolic See the said Hugh, called abbot. With the counsel of the Catholic brethren of the same monastery, he is not to delay to substitute another in his place. The privilege which is said to have been granted to the Church of Cluny by Roman pontiffs shall offer him no hindrance or obstacle concerning that abbot’s deposition. For it is fitting that one who has withdrawn himself from the rock of faith and the unity of the Catholic Church should, in accordance with his wickedness, be held deprived of ecclesiastical rank.

We hold most dear and acceptable the constancy of your devotion and purity of faith which you show toward the most holy Roman Church and particularly toward our person; we greatly commend it in the Lord, as it deserves to be commended. We have the purpose and will to love you with sincere affection in the bowels of Christ as religious, Catholic, honourable men and spiritual sons of the holy Roman Church; to honour you more abundantly; and to grant your petitions. But because it is not the one who begins, but the one who perseveres, who will receive the reward for virtue, by apostolic letters we ask, admonish, and exhort you all in the Lord that, as you have begun well and laudably, you may remain firm and immovable in devotion and fidelity to the Church and to us. Receive honourably our aforesaid brother Henry, Bishop of Beauvais, when he comes there; observe firmly and inviolably whatever he determines concerning the affair entrusted to him; supply him with counsel and aid according to your ability; and reject the aforesaid schismatics as a deadly plague.

Given at Anagni, on the seventh day before the Ides of April [7 April].

### XLII. To H[ilary], Bishop of Chichester.—Mabilla, the daughter, and Richard de Anestia, nephew through a sister, dispute the inheritance of William de Saccavilla. Royal permission having been obtained, an appeal is made to the pope, who delegates the case for decision in England.  
*(Anagni, 8 April.)*

*[Rymer, Foedera, I, p. 19.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother H[ilary], Bishop of Chichester, and to his beloved son L., Abbot of Westminster: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The case between Richard de Anesten and Mabilla de Franceville, because Richard asserts that Mabilla was born of an unlawful marriage and therefore presses his claim to inherit his uncle’s property, has long been in litigation. It has been brought before our hearing, since an appeal in the same case was made from the presence of our brother T., Archbishop of Canterbury, to the Apostolic See.

Because both parties had appeared when summoned, yet had not brought with them the witnesses required for the determination of the matter, we were unable to proceed to a decision in the same cause. Therefore, since we have full confidence in your prudence and discretion, we commit the same controversy to your …tiae, to be heard and brought to its proper conclusion.

Accordingly, by these apostolic letters we command you to summon both parties before you at a suitable place and time [Col. 0115B]; to hear the allegations advanced on every point by either side and … to receive, without impediment from an appeal, the depositions of such witnesses as may appear for either party; and to decide the case according to justice within three months after receipt of these letters.

But if either party, after allegations and witness-depositions have been made on both sides, without recourse to appeal, as stated above, appeals to your hearing before sentence is pronounced, you are in no way to proceed to sentence; rather, you are to put everything in writing and send the same writings, sealed with your seals, to our presence.

[Col. 0115C] Moreover, if, after witnesses have been received and allegations put forward, no appeal has been made as stated, you shall pronounce a definitive sentence in the matter.

But if either party withdraws from your summons or from examination of the case, pronounce by our authority a sentence of excommunication against the person who has presumed to do this.

Given at Anagni, 8 April.

### XLIII. He confirms the dignity of Syrus, archbishop of Genoa, established by Innocent II; subjects to him the bishopric of Albenga; and grants him the overseas legation to be exercised every eighth year, together with the use of a horse with a white *naccus*, the Lord’s cross, and the pallium. (At the Lateran? 9 April.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 867.]

[Col. 0115D]

ALEXANDER, etc., to his venerable brother SYRUS, archbishop of Genoa, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The high and ineffable providence of Majesty established the most holy Roman Church as mother and mistress of all Churches, so that, set above the rest, she might consider the merits of each and, in the likeness of the eternal and just Judge, render to every one according to the quality of his merits. Hence that holy Church is accustomed to treat with more merciful favor those whom she finds faithful sons, and to raise with manifold prerogatives of honor those whom she sees more fervent in her service.

We therefore, who by divine disposition, though our merits do not support us, have succeeded blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in the apostolic see [Col. 0116A], carefully considering how great the devotion, reverence, and diligent service which, amid this stormy and turbulent time, the Church of Genoa and the whole city, laying aside every fear, have shown to us and to our envoys; with what magnificence and honor they received us; and also what increase and advantage may accrue to us and our successors through the eminent and renowned city of Genoa—following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Innocent of happy memory, who raised your person, and after you the Church of Genoa, to the glorious pre-eminence of dignity, in honor of the exalted glory and service which it most faithfully renders to blessed Peter and the holy [Col. 0116B] Roman Church, and in which, as stated, it perseveres most readily for her repose and promises that it will hereafter perform still more readily—we have judged it fitting, by the common counsel of our brethren, to confirm that same dignity to you and to your successors.

For what our aforesaid predecessor Innocent conferred upon you, brother archbishop, adorning you with a privilege and, in advancing you to an archbishopric, granting you a more ample favor, we hold ratified and strengthen by apostolic authority. We subject to you by metropolitan right the bishoprics in Corsica—Mariana, Nebbio, and a third whose see the said Innocent established at the church of St. Peter of Accia, to which he granted one *plebs* from Marana and another from Aleria—as well as the bishopric of Bobbio [Col. 0116C] and that of Brumiate, with its churches which it has around it in its castles; this last our same predecessor newly established. We subject them to you and to your successors, as that predecessor is known to have done.

Nevertheless, we retain the bishopric of Genoa—and, that is, you and your successors—freely in our own hand, released from every subjection. We decree that the archbishop of Genoa shall be consecrated by his suffragan bishops and shall receive from the apostolic see the pontifical pallium, for the fullness of his office.

Furthermore, remembering your own and your city’s most sincere devotion, and the many kinds of service which you have hitherto faithfully and generously rendered us and continually still render, we have judged it fitting, after consultation with our brethren, to grant in perpetuity to you and your successors the overseas legation [Col. 0116D], so that the clergy and people of Genoa may be inflamed all the more fervently toward the service and honor of the Church as they know that the Church and city of Genoa are more highly honored by the apostolic see. Thus, every eight years, you must go overseas with a bishop or cardinal of the Roman Church, receiving from us and from our Catholic successors the same fullness of authority and power as the bishop and cardinal whom we or our successors send there from the body of the Church.

We also grant and, by this present privilege, confirm to you and to those who succeed you in perpetuity the monastery situated on the island of Gallinaria, which belongs specially to the right of the holy Roman Church [Col. 0117A], and the churches in the castle and suburb of Porto Venere, exempting them from the jurisdiction of the bishop of Luni.

Moreover, we grant to you and to your successors the bishopric of Albenga, on the condition that, from two years after it has been restored to the Church, you shall hold that bishopric in perpetuity.

Finally, in order that the city of Genoa—which, aided by the favor of the heavenly divinity, has often won triumph and victory over the enemies of Christ’s cross and has subdued very many of their cities by a certain wondrous and invincible power—may be honored with a loftier eminence of dignity, we give you and your successors permission and free faculty, as our aforesaid predecessor Innocent is known to have granted, to use in processions a horse with a white *naccus* and to carry the Lord’s cross through the province subject [Col. 0117B] to you.

You shall use the pallium within the church on these days: Maundy Thursday, Easter, Ascension, Pentecost, the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, St. John the Baptist, St. Lawrence, the three feasts of Blessed Mary, the solemnity of All Saints, St. Syrus, the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, the anniversary day of your consecration, and likewise at the consecration of bishops and basilicas and at the ordinations of clerics. We have also judged it fitting to commit to you, brother archbishop, and to your successors the abbey of Tyre for its improvement, preserving the ownership and census-right of the holy Roman Church, as the aforesaid predecessor Innocent is likewise known to have done [Col. 0117C].

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this charter of our constitution and confirmation, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes due and fitting amends, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who observe these our enactments may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action [Col. 0117D], and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Hubaldus, priest-cardinal.  
I, John, priest-cardinal of St. Anastasia.  
I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina.  
I, Hubaldus, bishop of Ostia.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto.  
I, Gualterus, bishop of Albano.  
I, Hyacinthus, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Arditius, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore.  
[Col. 0118A] I, Riso, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian.  
I, Cynthius, deacon-cardinal of St. Adrian.  
I, John, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Portico.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of …, 9 April, ninth indiction, in the year 1161 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### XLIV. Privilege for the Church of Grado. (Lateran, 12 June.)

[CORNELII, *Hist. Eccles. Venet.*, XIV, p. 97, from the archive of San Salvatore, Venice.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GUIDO and all the brethren of the Church of St. Saviour: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0118B] Whenever a definitive sentence concerning any matter is reasonably pronounced by our brethren or by other prelates of Churches, it ought to stand firm; and, lest in future times it be shaken from its stability through anyone’s rashness, it is fitting that we strengthen it with the protection of the apostolic see. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, favorably assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, and fortify with the protection of this present writing, the sentence reasonably pronounced, after a controversy long debated, by our venerable brother Henry, patriarch of Grado, and our beloved son Ildebrand, priest-cardinal of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles and legate of the apostolic see. The controversy was between you and the pleban jurisdiction (*dominium plebanum*) of St. Bartholomew concerning certain parochial houses, which each party claimed as its own right [Col. 0118C], as is known to be reasonably contained in their written record made on the matter.

Therefore let absolutely no person be permitted to infringe this charter of our confirmation by rash presumption or to oppose it with rash boldness. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, 12 June.

[Note: [Col. 0117D] We found in the archive of San Salvatore a copy of this diploma, bearing neither year nor indiction. But since it was given to Guido the prior [Col. 0118D], and this Guido was appointed to the Church of Emona in 1161, Alexander III’s diploma must likewise be assigned to that year.]

### XLV. He receives the Church of Grado under the protection of Blessed Peter and adorns it with many privileges. (Rome, at St. Mary the New, 13 June.)

[CORNEL., cited work, vol. III, p. 73, from the original in the patriarchal archive.]

[Col. 0118D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, patriarch of Grado, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

We are shown to perform usefully the duty of apostolic dignity and the obligation of the stewardship entrusted to us when we guard with provident solicitude the dignity bestowed upon each Church and strive to preserve whole and unimpaired the rights of individual Churches. For just as the apostolic see ought not through favor of grace to grant anything to anyone beyond what he deserves [Col. 0119A], so neither ought we in any way deny anyone what is known to belong to his right.

Therefore, the greater the prerogative of heavenly grace by which you have been exalted, the more diligently must you take care that, in correcting subjects, reason has more power with you than authority; that the good may find you gentle, and the evil merciful, as a corrector; that you love persons while pursuing the faults of those subject to you. Otherwise, should you perhaps choose to act differently, correction may turn into cruelty, and you may lose those whom you desire to amend. You must cut away a wound in such a manner that you do not ulcerate what is sound; lest, if the iron is applied more than the case demands, it harm the person whom you hasten to benefit. Rather, let one thing be seasoned by another, so that the good, through love, may have what they should avoid [Col. 0119B], and the evil, through fear, what they should love.

Accordingly, venerable brother Henry, patriarch in Christ, favorably assenting to your petitions, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of Grado, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside, and fortify it with the privilege of this present writing.

Therefore, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, Pelagius, Alexander II, Urban, and Adrian, and especially preserving the tenor of the constitution enacted and confirmed by synodal judgment and by a charter of privilege by our predecessor Pope Leo IX, we grant to you and to your successors canonically appointed the patriarchal dignity [Col. 0119C] and confirm to you the governance of the Church of Grado with its primacy only within those boundaries established for that Church by the aforesaid predecessors.

We also grant that a cross may be carried before you, except when you are at Rome or in the presence or company of the Roman pontiff. We likewise bestow upon your brotherhood, from the generosity of the apostolic see, the pallium—that is, the fullness of the pontifical office. You are to remember to use it within your church in celebrating the solemnities of Mass on those days upon which we do not doubt that your predecessors used it: namely, at the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, Hypapante [Meeting of the Lord], the three feasts of St. Mary, Maundy Thursday, Holy Saturday, the Resurrection of the Lord, Ascension, Pentecost, the Nativity of St. [Col. 0119D] John the Baptist and of all the apostles, likewise on the feasts of St. Mary, St. Stephen the Protomartyr, St. Lawrence, St. Martin, the solemnity of All Saints, and the principal feasts of your church; also at the consecrations of churches, bishops, and other clerics, and on the anniversary of your consecration.

[Note: [Col. 0119D] The Greeks call the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary the Hypapante of the Lord, as the Roman Martyrology observes on 2 February. From this and the following bulls it is plainly evident that this Greek-derived term was also used by the Latin Church.]

Furthermore, lest the aforesaid Church of Grado, entrusted to your governance and administration and enjoying through the kindness of the apostolic see a prerogative of honor arising from the shortness of its patriarchate, should be considered inferior and more lowly among the uninstructed [Col. 0120A], and in order to enlarge its dignity, we grant it by apostolic authority primacy over the archbishopric of Zadar and its bishoprics. We decree that you and your successors shall preside, by the dignity of primacy, over the bishop of Zadar and his bishops for the time being, and confer consecration upon that archbishop, the Roman pontiff’s grant of the pallium being reserved.

We also decree that whatever goods and possessions the Church of Grado now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by lawful means with God’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and to your successors. Moreover, we freely confirm to you and to your successors the churches situated throughout your bishopric which religious men have given to the Church of Grado [Col. 0120B], so that no bishop may, without your consent, celebrate consecrations in them or prohibit divine offices to the priests serving the Lord in those same places, so long as they remain there.

We therefore decree that no one at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be preserved whole and intact for the governance and support of those for whom they were granted, to be of use to them in every way, with the authority of the apostolic see reserved in all things.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this charter of our constitution [Col. 0120C], then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his presumption by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him acknowledge himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
[Col. 0120D] I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of St. Eustachius near the Temple of Agrippa, have subscribed.

Given at Rome, at St. Mary the New, by the hand of Herman, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, 13 June, ninth indiction, in the year 1161 of the Lord’s Incarnation; in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

[Note: [Col. 0120D] From the chronological indications of this diploma we learn that Alexander III had already returned to Rome on 13 June from the city of Veroli, where he had previously resided, as is shown by another diploma issued on 14 May of the same year. *Concil. Labb.*, vol. XIII, col. 238.]

### XLVI. To Henry, patriarch of Grado, and the bishops of the March. He reports that he has been very well received at Rome and is exercising the pontifical office there. He exhorts them to remain steadfast against the schismatics. (Rome, at St. Mary the New, 14 June.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 1036.]

[Col. 0121A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren HENRY, patriarch of Grado, and his suffragans—the bishops of Padua, Verona, Treviso, Ferrara, and Vicenza—and to all bishops, abbots, and other prelates of Churches established throughout the March: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0121B] Although at times the little ship of Blessed Peter is tossed by the waves, and although heretics and schismatics endeavor to oppress the Church of God, divine power nevertheless rises up and works wondrously in its elect; and by its grace things that have hitherto been stormy are made tranquil and serene.

Let the prudence of your discretion know that, divine grace going before us, we took possession of the City on 6 June, and that we were solemnly received with every honor by the Roman clergy and people at the church of St. Mary the New, with psalms, hymns, and praises. There, the opponents of ecclesiastical truth having been wholly refuted, we exercise the office committed to us for the honor of God and of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

[Col. 0121C] On the following Sunday after our entry, with our brethren, clergy, and people assembled in the Lateran church, we celebrated there the solemnities of Mass in complete quiet and peace. Since, therefore, we have the fullest confidence in the steadfastness of your devotion and the purity of your faith, we ask, admonish, and exhort your charity in the Lord through apostolic letters that, as you have begun well and commendably, you may remain firm and immovable in fidelity and devotion to your mother, the most holy Roman Church, and may by every means induce others to do the same. For we trust and hope in the Lord that the author and head of the schism, together with all his followers, has been reduced to nothing and utterly trampled down [Col. 0121D], so that henceforth there may be nothing in which they can even slightly draw breath.

Given at Rome, at St. Mary the New, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of June.

### XLVII. To the abbot of St. Victor. He commends to him the deacon Alexius, residing at Saint-Victor. (Palestrina, 27 June.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 241.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and the whole chapter of the Church of St. Victor: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0122A] Although by reason of the office enjoined upon us we ought to love all Christ’s faithful, we ought to hold especially dear and acceptable those who belong more particularly to the Roman Church, and to provide for them with more earnest care. For this reason we particularly commend to you our beloved son, the deacon Alexius, who has received the habit of canonical profession in your Church and who is now living among you. We ask and exhort you that, both for reverence toward Blessed Peter and ourselves and in view of his own goodness and honorable character, you may love and honor him, and henceforth hold one dear already dear to you even dearer.

Given at Palestrina, 27 June.

### XLVIII. To Hugh, bishop of Soissons. That the rights of the monastery of St. Martin of Épernay be kept intact. (Palestrina, 30 June.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 980.]

[Col. 0122B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, bishop of Soissons: greeting and apostolic blessing.

What is granted to anyone by the apostolic see must be preserved unshaken, nor may it be opposed through any rashness. Therefore, since we wish what has been granted by privileges of the Roman Church to the abbot and brethren of St. Martin of Épernay to be observed inviolably [Col. 0122C], we command you by apostolic letters, in accordance with the tenor of the privileges granted by the apostolic see to the church of the aforesaid abbot, to entrust the care of souls in the church of St. Martin of Montféli, said to belong specially to the right and disposal of that abbot, to one of his brethren; and to take diligent care that you do not presume, for any reason, to act contrary to the tenor of those privileges.

Given at Palestrina, 30 June.

### XLIX. He praises the clergy and people of Salona for treating well Julius, bishop of Palestrina, and Peter, deacon-cardinal of St. Eustachius, apostolic legates; and announces that he has appointed Peter, formerly bishop of Narni, as their archbishop and endowed him with the pallium. (Ferentino, 2 July.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 1015.]

[Col. 0122D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the whole clergy and people of Salona: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The sincerity of devotion and steadfastness of purity which you have toward your mother, the most holy Roman Church, and toward our person is clearly evident in this: that, as they themselves have informed us, you took care to receive kindly and treat honorably our venerable brother J., bishop of Palestrina, and our beloved son P., deacon-cardinal of St. Eustachius [Col. 0123A]. Therefore, rendering you thanks for so great a fervor of charity and steadfastness of faith, and loving you with sincere charity in the bowels of Christ, we have received with due kindness P., abbot of St. Stephen, F. O., and W., your envoys. At their request, wishing beneficially to provide for you and your Church concerning an election, we have granted you as archbishop our venerable brother, formerly bishop of Narni—a learned, honorable, prudent, and discerning man—and have judged that he should be established as your spiritual father and shepherd of your souls. To show the fullness of the pontifical office, we have bestowed upon him a pallium taken from the body of Blessed Peter, so that through his care and providence [Col. 0123B] you may be able to advance in spiritual and temporal growth.

Accordingly, we particularly commend to your entire community this man, coming to you and to the Church entrusted to him by the Lord’s guidance, with the favor of the apostolic see and ourselves and with the fullness of his office. By these apostolic letters we command you to receive him kindly and reverently, to render him humble obedience and honor as your archbishop, and without any contradiction to pay him the tithes and other things which belong to him by parochial right. Indeed, if you remain humbly obedient to him and are willing to heed his wholesome admonitions, you and your Church, as we believe and hope [Col. 0123C], will receive spiritual and temporal increase with the Lord’s help. But if any of you is found contumacious or rebellious against him, we shall, God being the author, hold valid and firm the sentence which that archbishop canonically pronounces against him for this reason.

Given at Ferentino, 2 July.

### L. To the dean and chapter of Dol. That the bishop-elect of Dol shall receive consecration from the archbishop of Tours and promise him obedience. (Palestrina, 12 July.)

[MARTEN., *Thesaur.*, III, 903.]

[Note: [Col. 0123] “From the end of the second book, the sixth quire of the first volume of the Registers of Lord Pope Alexander III.”]

[Col. 0123D] We do not believe that it has escaped the memory of your discretion for how long the controversy between you and the Church of Tours was contested, and how many scandals and losses followed from it. When our predecessor Pope Lucius of blessed memory wished to impose a proper end upon that controversy, with both parties present before him and the arguments and documents on either side examined, he adjudged the Church of Dol to be subject to the Church of Tours by metropolitan right; so that the Church of Dol might henceforth in no way lay claim either to suffragans or to the use of the pallium. Our predecessors of happy memory [Col. 0124A], the Roman pontiffs Eugenius and Anastasius, holding that sentence ratified and firm, confirmed it by privileges of apostolic authority. Subsequently, however, peace having intervened between the two Churches, as is said, Hugh, formerly known to have presided over the aforesaid Church of Dol, came to the apostolic see and, through letters from the archbishop of Tours, obtained from our predecessor Pope Adrian of good memory the use of the pallium, although he had previously received consecration from the archbishop of Tours and had promised him subjection and obedience.

Since, therefore, we desire to preserve your rights in such a way that the dignity of the Church of Tours is in no respect diminished, we command your entire body by apostolic letters that, if you have perhaps unanimously agreed upon a person [Col. 0124B], you shall present him to our venerable brother Jodocus, archbishop of Tours. If he has not yet been confirmed by our legates, and if the archbishop finds the election canonically made, he shall confirm it by the duty of his office and confer consecration upon the elect; provided that, once consecrated, he shall render and promise him the obedience and reverence due according to the custom of the Church.

But if the election has perhaps been confirmed by the legates, and the elect has, by their authority—though we do not believe it—been consecrated, he shall nevertheless go to that archbishop when summoned by him and render him obedience, as set forth above. But if within three months from the time he is summoned by the archbishop he has not come into his presence and rendered obedience as stated, from that time we deprive him by authority of the apostolic see of the administration of temporal affairs and of the exercise of the office which he received after the election [Col. 0124C].

Given at Palestrina, 12 July 1161.

### LI. To Peter, archbishop of Salona. That he shall excommunicate V., who, having been deposed by Eugenius III, has continued to occupy the Church of Croatia (Knin); and shall remove P., who, according to the report of Peter, deacon-cardinal of St. Eustachius, has seized the Church of Trogir. (Ferentino, 1 September.)

[FARLATI, *Illyricum sacrum*, III, 184.]

[Col. 0124D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PETER, archbishop of Salona: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our father and predecessor, Pope Eugenius of pious memory, … pronounced a sentence of deposition against V., formerly bishop of Croatia, because, with only one archbishop and no other bishop present, he presumed—not, we say, to consecrate, but rather to desecrate—another, and against the man consecrated by them. That V., indeed, does not fear, contrary to the commands of our same predecessor, to celebrate divine offices. We, holding that sentence [Col. 0125A] to be ratified and firm, as it was reasonably pronounced, command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to admonish the aforesaid V. to make fitting satisfaction for so great a presumption and not to presume anything contrary to the tenor of that sentence. But if he scorns to obey your admonition, pronounce a sentence of excommunication against him and place under interdict the Church which he presumes to occupy.

Moreover, as we have learned from the report of our beloved son P., deacon-cardinal of St. Eustachius, and of certain others, a man called P., not yet tonsured, when he was still twelve years old and not born of lawful marriage, seized the bishopric of Trogir through the power of laymen and does not cease, at peril to his soul, to occupy that bishopric contrary to canonical enactments. Therefore, by the authority of these present letters, we command you, having diligently investigated the truth of this matter, if it proves to be as set forth above [Col. 0125B], to remove the aforesaid P. from it, setting aside every excuse and delay, and to compel him under penalty of ecclesiastical severity to desist from his presumption.

Given at Ferentino, 2 September.

### LII. To L., archpriest, and all the canons of the Church of Pisa. (Ferentino, 20 September.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 402.]

[Col. 0125C] ALEXANDER, bishop, etc., to his beloved sons L., archpriest, and all the canons of the Church of Pisa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We highly commend in the Lord your zeal for that care and steadfastness of faith which your prudence is known to have toward the honor of the holy Roman Church and ourselves, and because you have gladly wished to fulfill in the evident execution of your deed what you offered us in secret speech. We return thanks to you for this, intending and desiring to love your Church and city with pure purpose of heart and, so far as can be done with God and justice, to honor them in all things.

Moreover, although we know you to be so inclined and fervent in our fidelity toward the exaltation and increase of our mother, the Roman Church [Col. 0125D], that you have no need whatever to be stirred to this by anyone’s persuasion, yet, as an excess of caution, we ask, admonish, and beseech your discretion in the Lord Jesus, whose cause it is, that, as you have hitherto done well and commendably, you may labor with all your strength, in the same spirit and with no less zeal, for the exaltation and liberty of the Church.

As for that secret proposal, the plan having for the present been changed for the better by counsel, with God’s help, we have judged it fitting to defer it; and we do not wish you at present to be burdened in that matter. In addition, we earnestly ask your devotion to strive to find and obtain on loan from your citizens money at reasonable interest, if it cannot be otherwise obtained [Col. 0126A], and to assign it to our beloved son Boson, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, so that the money entrusted to Mane, a citizen of Lucca, may be paid in full without any contradiction or delay.

What you obtain on loan for us, we, or our successors, will, God being the author, repay in full.

Given at Ferentino, 20 September.

### LIII. Privilege for the Church of St. Mary the New. (Terracina, 30 September.)

[GARAMPI, *Illustrazione del uno antiquo sigill.*, etc.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, prior, and the brethren of the Church of St. Mary the New: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0126B] The office of apostleship entrusted to us by God admonishes and exhorts us to make salutary provision for the individual churches, and especially for those which belong in a special way to the jurisdiction of the most holy Roman Church, and to consider usefully their advancement. Since this year we were bound, both by your prayers and those of others, to consecrate your church—which pertains to the right of blessed Peter and to our protection—and after bestowing upon it the gift of consecration we promised, when asked, that at a suitable time we would endow it with the counsel of our brethren, who were then absent: therefore now, having taken the counsel of our brethren, we grant to you and to the aforesaid Church of the Mother of God, by apostolic authority and in perpetuity, the church of Saint Sebastian in the Catacombs, with its possessions and all its appurtenances, to hold, govern, and administer. [Col. 0126C] This we do because we trust and hope that through your care and labour it ought to grow in both spiritual and temporal prosperity, and that both you and your successors may derive benefit and increase from it.

That this our grant may be inviolably observed for all future times, and that no one may rashly violate it by any presumption, we confirm it by the authority of the apostolic see and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing; decreeing that absolutely no person may violate this document of our grant and confirmation, or in any way act against it. But if anyone should attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not amend his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour, and let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and our Redeemer Jesus Christ. But upon those who observe these provisions may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Julius, bishop of Palestrina. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Walter, bishop of Albano. [Col. 0127A] I, Ubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.

Given at Terracina through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of October, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1161 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

LIV. To Louis VII, king of the Franks.—Concerning the affair of the Church of Flavigny. (Terracina, 29 November.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 986.]

[Col. 0127B] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the letters of Your Highness with so much the more kindly a spirit and greater gladness of heart whenever it has happened that you send them and make some request in them, as we love Your Excellency with more sincere affection and, because of the great and abundant devotion which your Serenity has shown toward the most holy Roman Church and our person, are bound more fully to grant your requests.—For through the most sincere fervour of your devotion the holy and venerable Roman Church has received, in this time of necessity, such profit and exaltation, and such benefit, that no oblivion can erase it from the memory of us and our successors, whether in you or in all your posterity, nor can any length of time remove it from our heart.

Accordingly, we received with great joy and gladness of heart the letters sent us by Your Excellency concerning the affair of the Church of Flavigny, and we have endeavoured, so far as we could with God, to grant the prayers contained therein. We have entrusted the hearing of this cause to our venerable brethren H., bishop of Beauvais, and M., bishop of Paris, for determination by a canonical conclusion, with the obstacle of appeal set aside. Therefore we ask Your Serenity, and wish you to be diligent, that if anyone should wish to hinder the observance of the sentence rendered in this cause, [Col. 0127D] you wholly forbid him and, by the authority granted to you in this matter, compel him not to presume to do so.

Given at Terracina, the third day before the Kalends of December.

LV. To Henry, bishop of Beauvais.—Concerning the affair of the Church of Flavigny. (Terracina, 23 December.)

[MARTENE, *Collectanea*, II, 656.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Beauvais: greeting and apostolic blessing.

In the letters which we sent to you and to our brother the bishop of Paris concerning the affair of the Church of Flavigny, we recall that R., the former abbot, was described near the beginning as such, although he had been restored to the abbacy by the sentence of our beloved son W., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains and legate of the apostolic see. Since this occurred not through design but because of the pressure of many affairs, we have sent you the same letters corrected in this point, lest what had been carelessly inserted in the others should inflict any prejudice upon the case.

Given at Terracina, the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

LVI. To Henry, bishop of Beauvais, and Maurice, bishop of Paris.—Concerning the civil and criminal accusation against R., abbot of Flavigny, entrusted to Henry, bishop of Beauvais, and M., bishop of Paris. (Terracina, 23 December.)

[Ibid., col. 655.]

[Col. 0128B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren HENRY, bishop of Beauvais, and [Note: [Col. 0127D] Maurice, who, as is evident both from this letter and from the tenth letter, succeeded Peter Lombard in the see of Paris much earlier than the authors of the *Gallia Christiana* believed; they place the beginning of his episcopate in 1164, when Henry, [Col. 0128D] to whom and to Maurice those two letters are addressed, had already spent his third year in the see of Reims.] M., bishop of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has come to us that, when R., [Note: [Col. 0128D] The monastery of Flavigny, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Autun, which has hitherto remained under the congregation of Saint Maurus.] abbot of Flavigny, had formerly resigned that abbey of his own will and another had been appointed in his place, he again aspired to recover [Col. 0128C] the abbey. But since he could not recover it at his pleasure, the affair was brought before the tribunal of our beloved son W., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains and legate of the apostolic see. Having summoned both parties before him, and the other party displaying contumacy, he adjudged restoration of possession to the aforesaid abbot. This was, however, on the condition that, should any persons later appear wishing to sue him in civil or criminal proceedings, he would be ready to answer before that legate.

When he was subsequently sued and accused both civilly and criminally, proceedings had been taken on certain counts in his accusation, and witnesses had been heard and examined on civil and criminal matters, he appealed to the hearing of the apostolic see. But because, when the other party appeared before us, he neither came nor sent any representative, we could not determine that same affair. We therefore entrust the cause to your discretion, to be heard and concluded by due judgment with appeal set aside. Accordingly, by apostolic writs we command you to summon both parties before you and, after hearing and carefully examining the arguments on both sides, determine the same cause by due conclusion, the obstacle of appeal having been removed as [Col. 0129A] stated above. If it is established that the aforesaid abbot, as is said, communicated with an excommunicated person even after the prohibition of the said cardinal, administer canonical justice concerning him; and concerning J. Buffrant, whom that same abbot is said to be holding in captivity, compel him to render full justice in our presence.

Given at Terracina, the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

IN THE YEAR 1162.

LVII. To Louis, king of the Franks.—He commends the Church of Ferrières. (Genoa, 9 February.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 985.]

[Col. 0129B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, etc., to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It befits the clemency of royal dignity to love churches and ecclesiastical persons with sincere charity, and alike to support and foster them in their rights. Therefore we earnestly commend to Your Highness the Church of Ferrières, which belongs in a special way to the jurisdiction of the most holy Roman Church, and the brethren dwelling there in God’s service. We ask most earnestly that, out of regard for piety and reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, you love, support, and defend those brethren and that Church, [Col. 0129C] and preserve their rights for them entire and unimpaired against the assaults of evil men.

Given at Genoa, the fifth day before the Ides of February.

LVIII. To Henry, bishop of Beauvais, and Maurice, bishop of Paris.—Concerning the controversy between Hugh, archbishop of Sens, and the abbot of Ferrières.

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren HENRY, bishop of Beauvais, and M. [MAURICE], bishop of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We entrust to your discretion for hearing and due determination the controversy known to be pending between our venerable brother Hugh, [Note: [Col. 0129D] Hugh of Toucy, brother of William, bishop of Auxerre, succeeded Henry the Boar as archbishop of Sens in 1144. He placed the diadem upon Constance, wife of Louis VII, at Orléans, and crowned Adelaide of Champagne with the same husband, Louis, at Paris in the church of Blessed Mary. He died in 1168, according to the chronicle of Saint Peter of Sens and the continuation of Sigebert.] archbishop of Sens, and our beloved sons D., [Note: [Col. 0130D] Namely Dodo.] abbot, and the brethren [Col. 0129D] of the Church of Ferrières, [Note: [Col. 0130D] Ferrières was a very ancient and noble monastery, where Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens, anointed Louis and Carloman, sons of King Louis the Stammerer. That great Lupus, called Servatus, renowned for learning and piety, was formerly head of this monastery.] concerning the churches of Giverins, Lanais-villa, Lisirvilla, Prodais-fontana, Gisem-basilica, and Coilo; two parts of the offerings and two parts of the small tithe; Curte-maudo; the churches of Conflans, Mandore, Soraterra, Curia-Erardi, Monte-Cressione, Saint [Col. 0130A] Hilary above the river Pisel, and Saint Lupus; Amiliac; and the chapel of Cantu-Galli. The said abbot and brethren complain that these have been violently taken from them by the archbishop himself. Therefore, by our apostolic writs, we command you to summon both parties before you at a suitable place and time; and, after carefully investigating and ascertaining the arguments pending on both sides, determine this controversy through the mediation of justice in such a manner that no complaint about it may henceforth be repeated before us.

Given at Genoa, the fifth day before the Ides of February.

LIX. To the abbot and brethren of Prémontré.—He rejoices that God has preserved them in Catholic unity, but admonishes them to recall schismatics of their order to the bosom of the Church, under penalty of excommunication. (Genoa, 13 February.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 774.]

[Col. 0130B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, PHILIP, abbot of Prémontré, and his brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks to almighty God, from whom all good things proceed, because He has preserved you in Catholic unity and has not permitted you to be defiled by schismatic perversity. Although the presumption of the schismatics has striven, by diverse artifices and lies, to withdraw you [Col. 0130C] from devotion to blessed Peter and ourselves, your prudence has endeavoured to avoid their wickedness and preserve Catholic unity. Holding this to be most pleasing and welcome, and greatly commending in the Lord the constancy of your faith and the affection of your sincerity, we render you the thanks that we owe; and we have the firm purpose and ready will to love your persons and your church with pure affection of heart, embrace them in the arms of inward love, and preserve its rights unharmed and entire.

Moreover, since it is not enough to begin well unless what has been well begun reaches the end of an excellent consummation, we ask, admonish, and exhort your devotion in the Lord by apostolic writs [Col. 0130D] to add still greater advances to a good beginning; to strive with all your strength for the honour, exaltation, and increase of the holy Roman Church and of yourselves; diligently to endeavour, through admonition, more earnestly to call back the schismatics of your order to the truth, the bosom of mother Church, and obedience to our command; and to make them renounce under oath the schism of Octavian the heresiarch. [Col. 0131A] But if, after your admonition, they scorn to return from their wickedness, bind them with sentence of excommunication and most carefully avoid their company.

Given at Genoa, on the Ides of February.

LX. Privilege for the Church of Saints Peter and Ursus at Aosta (province of Tarentaise). (Genoa, 22 February.)

[*Historiae Patriae Monumenta*, *Chartae*, I, 822.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GAUTER and all the canons of the Church of Saints Peter and Ursus, both present and future, who profess the canonical life: in perpetuity.

[Col. 0131B] The office of the government we have undertaken, and the order of reason itself, invite us to assent to religious petitions and fulfil them by the performance of deeds.
