Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we fortify it with the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the canonical order which is known to have been established in that church according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be inviolably observed there forever.

Further, whatever possessions and goods that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have judged that the following should be expressly named: the church of Saint Alban with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Lawrence of Monte-Giraldi with everything belonging to that church; the hospital of the monastery with all its appurtenances; and the other goods and tithes which our venerable brother Peter, archbishop of Tarentaise, granted out of piety and confirmed by an authentic document.

We also decree that no one may, without reasonable cause, pronounce a sentence of excommunication against your church or persons, or subject them to an interdict. You may likewise receive into your church, for conversion, free and unencumbered clerics and laymen fleeing from the world; according to the custom of your order, they are to promise obedience to no one except the prior of that church. We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall remain intact [lacuna] for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, to be in every way beneficial to their uses, without prejudice in all things to the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop.

[Col. 0132A] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowingly acting against this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to violate it, and, having been warned a second or third time, fails to make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let such a person know that he or she is guilty before divine judgment of the wickedness committed, be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But on all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 0132B] Fare well.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed. I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, have subscribed. [Col. 0132C] I, Walter, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore, have subscribed. I, Boso, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed.

Given at Genoa through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, in the tenth indiction, in the year [Col. 0132D] 1161 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

(Place of the seal.)

LXI. Privilege for the canons of the Church of Piacenza. (Genoa, 27 February.)

[CAMPI, *History of Piacenza*, II, 358.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons FREDERICK, provost, and all the canons of the Church of Piacenza: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The holy Roman Church is accustomed to love with more earnest charity those whom it knows to be more faithful and devoted to itself, and to provide for them with more gracious care in their needs. Therefore, in view of the devotion and fidelity which, in this time of necessity, you have shown toward your mother, the Roman Church, and toward ourselves: since the Church of Saint John of Vico, which our predecessor Pope Innocent of holy memory granted you, is bound to pay the Roman Church annually half an ounce of gold as census, we will and decree, in accordance with your petition, that henceforth it shall be bound to pay only two *molachini* each year to us and our successors.

Given at Genoa, the third day before the Kalends of March.

LXII. To Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg.—That he may win the emperor’s disposition. (Genoa, 16 March.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1038.]

[Col. 0133B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother EBERHARD, archbishop of the Church of Salzburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your past life and religious manner of living, and also that sincerity of devotion and integrity of faith which, in this stormy and troubled time, you are known to have maintained hitherto toward your mother, the most holy Roman Church, and especially toward our person, give us fullest confidence that you must devote yourself in every way, and labour with all diligence, for the honour, increase, and exaltation [Col. 0133C] of the Church. For the greater the rank of dignity which you hold in God’s Church, and the loftier the column which the providence of heavenly Majesty has set you in His building, the more strongly has He reserved you in these times as a bulwark for the defence of His bride: that, like the tower of David with its battlements, you might look out toward Damascus and establish yourself as an impregnable wall against schismatic perversity. Indeed, setting aside every fear and seduction, you have, as we know, done this so praiseworthily hitherto that you are proved to be a true champion and defender of the Church, while the schismatics lament that they have found in you a hard hammer.

[Col. 0133D] Now, because, as we have learned, you have been summoned by the emperor concerning the Church’s cause and are soon to appear before him, we ask, admonish, and exhort your prudence in the Lord by apostolic writs to exhort and persuade that emperor by every means to return to his senses, make salutary provision for his soul, and return to the unity of the Catholic Church. Also carefully set before him and urge him not to prove ungrateful for God’s benefits; rather, the more the regard of divine grace has raised him to a higher eminence, the more earnestly should he love with charity and reverence with sincere affection the one bride of Christ, whom Christ Himself washed and redeemed with His own blood.

For unless he is first reconciled to her, he cannot be saved; and unless he withdraws from that schismatic perversity and returns to the bosom of mother Church, even if he seems to prosper in this world, [Col. 0134A] he will not be able in the world to come to escape the punishment of eternal torment. For what, according to Gospel truth, will it profit him if he gains even the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? (Matthew XVI.) Even if he should abound in all the riches and pleasures of this present life, they would profit him nothing whatsoever if, severed from Christ’s body, which is the Church, and from its communion, he is cast into sulphurous Gehenna and the seats of Tartarus, where there is perpetual night without day, punishment without end, pain without remedy, and inextinguishable torment.

But if almighty God, by His ineffable grace, should inspire him to wish with his whole intention to return to the bosom of mother Church, nothing temporal could happen to us in this world that we would hold more welcome or pleasing; and we would endeavour to love him in the Lord with sincere charity, as so great and exalted a prince, and to honour him in every way. For, desiring wholly to imitate the word of the Prophet, who says, “I will not remember their names upon my lips” (Psalm XV), we have this purpose and entirely this will: if he wishes to be converted and adhere to the Catholic Church, we shall consign to oblivion every injury, attack, and burden inflicted upon us, as though he had in no respect whatsoever offended us or the Church of God.

[Col. 0134C] Given at Genoa, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April.

LXIII. To Robert and the whole chapter of Saint Albans. (Genoa, 16 March.)

[MATTHEW PARIS, *Works*, Appendix, p. 77.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ROBERT, abbot, and the whole chapter of Saint Albans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When last year your messenger came before our apostolic presence, we received him kindly and, according to your request, caused to be confirmed the privilege which our predecessor Pope Adrian of good memory had granted to your church. Afterwards, however, our venerable brother the bishop of Lincoln, in a representation sent to us, showed [Col. 0134D] that the same church belongs specially to his jurisdiction and disposition and ought to answer to him as its bishop.

Therefore, although we desire to love you and your church and preserve the rights of your church entire, nevertheless, because we were unwilling, without injury to conscience, to deny the said bishop his justice or fail him in his right, we granted you leave to bring the matter before suitable judges, so that the cause might be examined in their presence, referred to us, and, after the truth had been learned, determined by us through justice. Since this has not yet been carried into effect, and the bishop himself does not cease to cry out in our hearing for his right, we have thought fit to entrust the cause to our venerable brethren, the bishops of Chichester and Norwich.

[Col. 0135A] Accordingly, by repeated letters we command you that, when summoned by them concerning this matter, you appear before them and endeavour to produce witnesses and to adduce documents and arguments, should any question be raised against you. Nor are you to refuse to show them in your cloister the sealed privileges, both new and old. When everything has been shown to those judges, provide the said bishop with copies of all of it, so that, after careful inspection, he may know whether he ought to yield or proceed in the cause. We have indeed commanded those same judges to send to our presence, under the impression of their own seal, the depositions of witnesses, arguments, reasons, and copies of the privileges of both parties, so that, once the truth is known, we may be able to impose a due end upon that controversy.

Given at Genoa, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April.

LXIV. To King Louis.—Concerning his own condition and that of the Church. (At Montpellier, 20 April.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 985.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The firm hope and full confidence which we have in every matter regarding the excellence of your Majesty induce and urge us in every way to set forth to you all the more willingly the condition of your one mother, the most holy Roman Church, and our own condition, [Col. 0135C] because we know that Your Highness is more solicitous and attentive toward her and toward ourselves. Therefore, that the state of the Church may become more fully known to Your Serenity, we intend, God authorizing, soon to send to your regions one or more of our brother cardinals who are with us.

For the present, however, we do not wish Your Highness to be unaware that, on arriving at Montpellier by God’s guidance, we were honourably and devoutly received there by our beloved sons, the count of Saint-Gilles and W. of Montpellier; and that by God’s grace both we and our brethren are dwelling there healthy and safe. There also we received our beloved son Trencavel and the noblewoman Herm. of Narbonne, [Col. 0135D] together with many other barons of that region who came to us; and we are devoutly revered and splendidly honoured both by them and by the other faithful of God in the surrounding area.

Given at Montpellier, the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.

LXV. To Sirus, archbishop, the canons, consuls, and the whole clergy and people of Genoa.—He gratefully praises their services toward him and confirms them for the future. (At Montpellier, 23 April.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, IV, 866.]

ALEXANDER, etc., to his venerable brother SYRUS, archbishop, [Col. 0136A] and his beloved sons, the canons, consuls, and all the clergy and people of Genoa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

You should attribute the fact that we did not earlier discharge the greeting of apostolic address to you by our letters not in any degree to negligence, but to manifest necessity. For, as we believe you have learned through our beloved sons, your noble fellow citizens who came into our service through your favour, our vessel, with part of our household, remained on the island of Liguria, and the unfavourable weather did not permit us in any way to recover it.

But now, visiting you with apostolic letters as the dearest and special sons of the Church, we render every kind of thanksgiving to your sincerity [Col. 0136B] because you have steadfastly devoted yourselves to the service of blessed Peter and ourselves, so that your most holy mother, the Roman Church, just as she has already received from you very great benefits and advancement, may henceforth place more secure confidence in your integrity and be especially and particularly joined to you among the other Catholic sons of truth. For you honour her not merely with your lips and word, but love her in deed and truth, and strive with all your strength magnificently to exalt her.

Although, therefore, we do not think that this constancy of your sincerity and fervour of your devotion can either be broken or grow lukewarm, we nevertheless have thought it right to strengthen it by these present letters, asking, admonishing, and exhorting you in the Lord through apostolic writs that, trusting in the aid [Col. 0136C] of the highest King, you do not cease, through fear of any terror or the force of any empty threat, from persisting in your resolve, as Catholic men and valiant defenders of the Church, to preserve devotion to her and your own liberty. For we trust and hope that the right hand of the heavenly Creator, which always rules and protects His Church and crushes all its enemies under its feet, will always be with you and will bring it about that, especially through His aid, you overcome all your adversaries.

And we, desiring to love, honour, and exalt in every way your Church and city as the proper and special chamber of blessed Peter and of ourselves, shall not cease to secure through the kings and princes of the earth and other sons of the Church [Col. 0136D] that every counsel and assistance which divine grace grants us may always be most abundantly conferred upon you.

Given at Montpellier, the ninth day before the Kalends of May, 1159. [Note: [Col. 0135D] Thus printed, but erroneously. Read 1162.]

LXVI. To Henry, elect of Reims.—Concerning the transmission of the pallium. (At Montpellier, 30 April.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 665.]

ALEXANDER, etc., to his beloved son HENRY, elect of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more we recognize that your affection and mind toward [Col. 0137A] the most holy Roman Church and our person have been earnest and fervent from the very beginning of our promotion, and that you have happened to labour more diligently and more abundantly than others for its honour and exaltation, the more do we rejoice and take delight in your honour and advancement. Had greater things been granted you by divine dispensation, they would have been most welcome and pleasing to our heart.

From the tenor of the letters of our venerable brother the bishop of Langres, of our beloved sons Hen. and Odd., cardinals of the holy Roman Church and legates of the apostolic see, of the abbot of Clairvaux, and also from your own letters, we have plainly learned of your election in the Church of Reims; and both we and our brethren, as we have said, have rejoiced with joy. But do not let it be burdensome or troublesome to your discretion that we have called you “elect” rather than “archbishop”: just as no one is called a bishop before consecration, so no one is rightly called an archbishop before receiving the pallium.

We have received with due kindness our beloved sons Ans. and the others whom you sent with him to our presence, and through our beloved son the abbot of Grand-Selve, [Note: [Col. 0137D] Grand-Selve, a distinguished Cistercian monastery in the diocese of Toulouse, was founded in 1117, first under the institutions of Gerard of Salles, then, a few years later, joined to the Cistercian Order and the line of Clairvaux. Its abbot at that time was Alexander, later abbot of Cîteaux.] and through these same messengers of yours, we have willingly determined to send you the pallium, that is, the fullness of the pontifical office. We ask, admonish, and exhort your discretion in the Lord by apostolic writs that you believe without any doubt [Col. 0137C] what they set before you on our behalf, and that, when you come to our dearest son in Christ Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, you endeavour, as we trust you will, to carry it out in deed.

Given at Montpellier, the second day before the Kalends of May.

LXVII. To Hugh, bishop of Soissons.—That he may faithfully render him assistance with the king of the Franks. (At Montpellier, 30 April.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 982.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother . . . . . bishop of Soissons: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we can recall, we formerly resolved to inform your belovedness by apostolic letters—whose devotion toward the most holy Church we know, as that of one who has always striven to persevere in the unity of the Catholic faith—that we had arranged to travel into the regions of France for the business and affairs of the universal Church, and for the welfare and peace of the realm; trusting in the Lord that, by the assistance of your prudence and of others who love the Church of Christ, the condition of the most holy Roman Church and of the whole kingdom might be restored to a better state. Indeed, laudably following in the footsteps of our dearest son in Christ Louis, the illustrious king of the Franks, you have always honored the Roman Church, our own person, and, in us, especially blessed Peter, in whose chair, though unworthy, we sit, particularly in this time of persecution. You have fixed your hope upon him who said to the apostles, and in them to the primitive Church: “Behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the age” (Matt. 28); nor have any waves of storms, any persuasions, or any blandishments been able to turn your devotion from proceeding along the royal road and walking the path that leads to the brightness of the heavenly homeland.

Therefore, after, under the Lord’s guidance, we had come to Montpellier, where we were received magnificently and honorably by clergy and people, we had determined to send our venerable brother B., bishop of Porto, and our beloved son I., cardinal deacon—men certainly honorable and prudent—to that same dearest son of ours Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, for the welfare of the Church and the peace of the kingdom. But afterward, having learned more fully the state of that land through our beloved son O. [Odo], cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, who was returning to us, we changed our plan and considered that our venerable brothers Henry, archbishop of Reims, and the bishops of Langres and Senlis should be sent to the aforesaid king. And therefore we ask, admonish, and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord, that you take care to assist them diligently before the said king in our affairs, so that you may merit a fuller favor from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, from us, and from the whole Roman Church. For we intend, insofar as we can with God, to exalt and honor your person, and continually to hold you dearer among the beloved sons of blessed Peter.

Given at Montpellier, 30 April.

### LXVIII. To Louis VII, King of the Franks.—Concerning his own position and that of the Church.  
(At Montpellier, 30 April.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 989.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we can recall, we formerly endeavored to inform Your Excellency by apostolic letters—whose most devoted attachment to the most holy Roman Church we know, as that of one who, among the other princes of the world, has especially and sincerely striven to persevere in the unity of the Catholic faith—that we had arranged to travel to the land and kingdom entrusted to your magnificence, for the business and affairs of the universal Church and for the peace and welfare of the realm. We hope and trust in the Lord that, especially through the counsel and assistance of your magnificence and prudence, and of others who love the Church of God, the condition of your mother, the most holy Roman Church, may be restored to a better state, and that things disturbed by the discord which has arisen may be brought back to the good of peace.

Indeed, laudably following the footsteps of your predecessors, the Catholic kings, you have always honored the Roman Church, our own person, and, in us, blessed Peter especially, in whose chair, though unworthy, we sit, particularly in this time of persecution. You have immovably fixed the anchor of your hope in him who said to the apostles, and in them to the primitive Church: “Behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the age” (Matt. 28); nor have any waves of storms, any persuasions, or any blandishments been able to turn the sincerity of your faith from advancing gloriously as king upon the royal road and walking the path which leads to the brightness of the heavenly homeland.

Therefore, after, under the Lord’s guidance, we had come to Montpellier, where we were received magnificently and honorably by clergy and people, we had determined to send to your presence our venerable brother B., bishop of Porto, and our beloved son I., cardinal deacon of the church of St Mary in Cosmedin. But afterward, from the report of our beloved son O., cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, returning to the Apostolic See and more fully acquainted with the condition of that land, we changed our plan and considered that our venerable brothers Henry, archbishop of Reims, and the bishops of Langres and Senlis should be delegated to you. We ask, admonish, and exhort you in the Lord to receive them mercifully and kindly, and to give credence, as though they had been communicated to your discretion from our own mouth, to those matters which they, together with our beloved son . . . . . abbot of Grandselve, endeavor to convey to your royal prudence on our behalf; and, as we trust in your highness, to strive to put them into useful effect.

Moreover, because the noble man Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, came to meet us magnificently, committed himself and his land to us, and endeavored to honor us—and, in our person, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—with due reverence, we render abundant thanks to your highness; and at a fitting time we shall endeavor to respond to him, as is owed by our office, as far as we are able with God.

Given at Montpellier, 30 April.

### LXIX. To [Adela], Queen of the Franks.—He exhorts her to remain devoted to the Apostolic See and to foster the king’s devotion.  
(At Montpellier, 30 April.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 985.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest daughter in Christ, the illustrious queen of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

In the most holy Roman Church there lives the glorious memory of your forebears. The benefits bestowed upon them in fullest measure by the aforesaid Church declare how devoted and fervent they always were in the service of blessed Peter. Since we constantly keep these things before the eyes of our heart without any forgetfulness, we unceasingly give thanks to Almighty God, who has preserved for us such an heir of theirs [variant: “has preserved you for us”]; from whose magnificence the most holy Roman Church may expect still greater benefits.

Therefore we ask, admonish, and exhort Your Highness by apostolic letters in the Lord that, out of regard for the divine Majesty above, you endeavor to show yourself such toward the Church of God and ourselves that, by the Lord’s help, you may worthily imitate, by a praiseworthy example also of faith and devotion, those whose successors you are through the posterity of most illustrious blood. Strive therefore and labor to foster more earnestly and to strengthen diligently your husband and lord, our dearest son in Christ Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, in devotion toward blessed Peter and ourselves, so that that affection of sincerity which we do not at all doubt he bears toward us and the Church of God, strengthened from good to better through you [variant: “in part”], may attain its perfection and, as we trust, advance daily to still further things.

We wish especially that your prudence should know that, although we had arranged to send our venerable brother B., bishop of Porto, and I., cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin, to the aforesaid king concerning the affairs of the Church, afterward, having learned more fully the state of that land from the report of our beloved son O., cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, returning to us, and perceiving that that land was exceedingly dear to him, we changed our plan and considered that our venerable brothers Henry, archbishop of Reims, and the bishops of Langres and Senlis, together with our beloved son the abbot of Grandselve, should be sent to the presence of the royal dignity. We therefore carefully urge Your Magnificence by every means in our power to endeavor to induce and more earnestly exhort the aforesaid king to believe without hesitation and receive kindly what they shall set before him on our behalf, and, as we hope of him, not postpone carrying it through to a useful completion.

Given at Montpellier, 21 April.

### LXX. Confirmation of the possessions of the monastery of Alet, made for Abbot Bernard, in which its founder is mentioned.  
(At Montpellier, 2 May.)

[*Gallia Christiana Nova*, VI, 109, Documents.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BERNARD, abbot of the church of Blessed Mary of Alet, and his brethren, present and future, professed in the monastery, in perpetuity.

A pious request ought to be brought to its effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth laudably and the requested benefit may undoubtedly gain strength. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously consent to your just petitions; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, Leo IX, Calixtus, and Eugenius, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present document, the aforesaid monastery, in which you are dedicated to divine service, which was offered by its founder, Bera, count of noble memory, to blessed Peter under an annual payment. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, with God’s aid, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have considered it proper to specify the following by their proper names: the monastery of St Paul, called Valliolas, on the bank of the Aude, with its appurtenances; the church of St Polycarp on the Great Stream, with its dependencies, as it was confirmed to your monastery by the judgment of our lord predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory; the church of St Mary of Urbione; the church of St Peter of Escalabra with its dependencies; the church of St Romanus of Librazac; the church of St Mary of Vallelias with its dependencies; the church of St Valerius; the church of St Michael of Rethmol; the church of Pairano; the church of the estate called Terracopulata; the church of Villanova; the church of St James of Villariseveric; the estate of Flacianum with its church; the estate of Ladimanellum with its church; the estate of Lupianum with its church; the estate of Solarium; the church of Donadac; the estate of Comelianellum with its church; the church of the Holy Savior situated beside the bank of the Cornelianus; the church of St Julian; the church of St Saturninus of Fan; two parts of the tithe of Sanz; the church of St Nazarius of Aquiscalidis; the monastery of St Pabuli with its appurtenances; the church of St Martin of Cella; the church of Castroresindo; the castle of Princiacum with its church; the castle of Vezolam with two churches; the castle of Cornelianum; and the castle of Blancaforte.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of intrigue or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, provide to be elected. The person elected shall be consecrated by the diocesan bishop, provided that he is willing to bestow consecration freely and without corruption; otherwise, he shall receive consecration from whichever Catholic bishop he prefers.

We further add this provision to the present chapter: because your place is an offering to blessed Peter and belongs by right to the holy Roman Church, no archbishop or bishop whatsoever shall have authority to pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against it or against you; nor shall any archbishop or bishop be permitted in any way to impose unjust and undue exactions in churches belonging to your jurisdiction. Rather, you shall always remain free and undisturbed under the right and protection of the Apostolic See.

We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, the authority of the Apostolic See being reserved. As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one pound of silver to us and our successors every three years.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against this text of our constitution, after having been admonished a second and third time, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself answerable before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But for all who preserve the rights of this place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and St Rufina, have subscribed.  
I, Gualterius, bishop of Albano, have subscribed.  
I, Hunald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed.  
I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed.  
I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed.  
I, Odo, cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed.  
I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of St Theodore, have subscribed.

Given at Montpellier by the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 2 May, in the tenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1162, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### LXXI. Privilege for the monastery of Aniane.  
(At Montpellier, 5 May.)

[*Gallia Christiana Nova*, VI, 841, in the text.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons RAYMOND WILLIAM, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Aniane, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners. Vows which do not depart from the path of reason ought to be fulfilled in their effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, favorably concurring with your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to your devotion, and strengthen by the protection of this present document, the monastery of Livinhac with all its appurtenances, bestowed upon your monastery from the gift of Arnold, formerly bishop of Rodez, of blessed memory, in consideration of pious devotion, as is contained in the document made concerning this matter.

We also will that, if anyone should presume to seize or steal the goods of that monastery of Livinhac, or should attempt grievously to harm the brethren or lay brothers assigned there to God’s service, then, unless after admonition they repent, they shall be bound by the bond of excommunication. We likewise decree that burial at the aforesaid monastery of Livinhac shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict.

We therefore decree that no person at all may infringe this text of our confirmation or in any way act against it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Montpellier, 5 May.

[lacuna] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, [lacuna] we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery in which you are dedicated to divine service, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Innocent of happy memory, etc.

### LXXIII. To Omnibonus, bishop of Verona.—He announces that he and all his brethren are residing at Montpellier safe and well, etc.  
(At Montpellier, 17 May.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1039.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother O., bishop of Verona, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Considering the devotion which you show toward the most holy Roman Church and ourselves, we hold it most welcome and acceptable, and in the Lord commend it with the highest praise. Therefore we disclose the condition of that Church and our own to your brotherhood all the more willingly because we do not at all doubt that the affection of your uprightness toward it is more solicitous and attentive.

Let the prudence of your discretion therefore know that both we and our brethren are residing at Montpellier, through God’s grace, safe and well; and that we are most earnestly honored and devoutly venerated by archbishops and bishops, kings and princes, and the entire Western Church, both in person and through others and their envoys. In particular, we have counted among us our brothers the archbishops of Sens, Tours, Aix, and Narbonne—one of whom, namely the archbishop of Narbonne, we consecrated there—and the bishops of Auxerre, Saint-Malo, Nevers, Thérouanne, Maguelone, and Toulon. With them, on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, we publicly pronounced the sentence of excommunication against Octavian the schismatic and all his accomplices. We are also expecting our beloved sons Henry and William, cardinals of the Holy Roman Church and legates of the Apostolic See, together with the bishops of Évreux and Bayeux, namely envoys of the illustrious king of the Franks, and the archbishops of Bourges and Reims. We hold firm hope and confidence that the clemency of the supreme Godhead will swiftly grant peace and tranquillity to his Church.

Accordingly, we ask, admonish, and exhort your brotherhood by apostolic letters in the Lord that you strive continually to strengthen yourself and such other sons of the Church as you can in devotion toward blessed Peter and ourselves, so that the sincerity of your affection may deserve to be commended at all times by the outcome of events themselves.

Moreover, you should know that it has come to our attention that your archpriest of the Minerva, and others—indeed, many—from your bishopric presume to associate with those excommunicated by that schismatic Octavian and, against our beloved sons the bishop of Brixen and the noble man T., count of Garba, furnish them counsel and aid with all their strength. Your discretion knows all the more fully how unworthy and foreign to the path of reason this is, because you are known to be more learned and instructed in ecclesiastical and secular disciplines. Therefore, by this present letter, we command your brotherhood diligently to admonish and compel both the aforesaid archpriest and the others established throughout your diocese whom you discover to be guilty of this iniquity, that they may henceforth desist entirely from this wickedness. But if they presume to persist in this obstinate purpose, restrain them by the authority granted to you.

Given at Montpellier, 17 May.

### LXXIV. Privilege for the monastery of St Stephen of Nevers.  
(At Montpellier, 22 May.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, 69.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BERNARD, prior of St Stephen of Nevers, and his brethren, present and future, professed in the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously consent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present document, the monastery of St Stephen of Nevers, in which you are dedicated to divine service. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, with God’s favor, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have considered it proper to specify the following by their proper names: the borough of St Stephen itself, with the people dwelling there and all the revenues and customary dues of that borough, just as William, formerly count of Nevers, with the instruction and assent of Hugh, formerly bishop of Nevers, is known to have granted it free and exempt from every exaction and customary due of himself, his heirs, and his men, to the said monastery and the Cluniac brethren, as is contained in the document of donation and grant made by both parties.

The inhabitants of the same borough shall also have free power to use all their resources in the land of the count of Nevers, in waters, pastures, woods, markets, fairs, roads, and paths, just as the other men of that count do, both in the city and outside it, as has been decreed and sanctioned by the aforesaid William, count of Nevers. They shall also have access and use throughout all the woods of the count of Nevers, for fuel and building, and mast-right for your pigs; likewise, vineyards and the rent, so that all that the same count has reasonably granted you beyond Croa and at St Benignus, with the people and newcomers dwelling there, shall be free from every exaction and customary due of the count, as he himself granted them to you; the vineyards of Clement and those of Bussiliac, which belonged to the mother of that same count; the inheritance of Raynald of Vallano; the allod which that count held at Vernac; and the land of Forgies with its people and customary dues.

Also, the land of Morelliac, near the castle of Mont Onesy, which was in Casamento, and which the same count held in lordship at the castle of Moncellis and granted to you; likewise the allod of Morcilliac, in which is located part of the borough adjoining the castle; the chapels of Moncellis, together with what belongs to the chapels; the tithes of Solomon, of that same count; and the church of Luniac in the diocese of Nevers, with its court and appurtenances; the mill of Moisyac with its watercourse and surrounding land; the allod of Meleravo; and the land given by Boniface the priest, beside your field at Old Croa; in the estate called Chivinias near Alluisiac, half of the tithe; the grange of Assertis with all its appurtenances; at Camp Vert, three *rainatae* in the river Aron; the church of St Peter in the suburb of Nevers, with the land, tithe, and rent which Olivarius held in the aforesaid borough; the cell of Boonac with its lands, meadows, vineyards, mills, and all appurtenances; the estate of Suriac with its lands, meadows, mills, and all appurtenances; the church of St Mary of Limone with its oven, winepress, lands, meadows, vineyards, tithe, and other appurtenances; the church of Uxel with its tithe and appurtenances; the tithe of both wine and grain at Sarmaria and what you possess within the jurisdiction of that estate; a fourth part of the allod of Lupi with its appurtenances; the meadows of Uzzeium; and the church of Chevenum with its tithe and appurtenances.

We further decree that, by the authority of the Apostolic See, the aforesaid monastery shall remain in future times in the same liberty and immunity in which it is known hitherto to have stood.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations. Rather, all things shall be preserved whole and unimpaired for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop being reserved.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against this text of our constitution, after having been admonished a second and third time, unless he corrects his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself answerable before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But for all who preserve the rights of this place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Anastasia.  
I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina.  
I, William, cardinal priest of the title of St Peter in Chains.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto.

Given at Montpellier by the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 22 May, in the tenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1162, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### LXXV. Privilege for the monastery of St Arnulf of Crépy.  
(At Montpellier, 22 May.)

[*Ibid.*, 70.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons THEOBALD, prior of the monastery of St Arnulf the martyr at Crépy, and his brethren, present and future, professed in the regular life, in perpetuity.

Those who choose the religious life ought to receive apostolic protection, lest perhaps the assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—restrict the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously consenting to your just petitions and following in the footsteps of our predecessors of holy memory, John, Paschal, Innocent, and Eugenius, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present document, the aforesaid monastery of Blessed Arnulf the martyr, in which you are dedicated to the Lord’s service. It is known to be subject to no dominion or authority except that of the Roman pontiff and the abbot of Cluny.

First, we decree that all things known to have been granted and conveyed to your monastery by your founders, Walter, namely count of Amiens, and his wife Adela, shall, after the example of those same predecessors of ours, remain always secure and unimpaired to you and your successors, in the same liberty in which they were granted. We also decree that all things which at present appear to belong to that place shall remain undisturbed and whole for you. Among these we have considered it proper to specify the following by their proper names: the monastery of Blessed Arnulf itself, with lands, vineyards, tithes, and all other appurtenances; namely, the market and suburb; the castle of Crépy, with the cultivated land adjoining that castle and upon which part of the castle is built; the altar and estate of Oger, with tithes and all that belongs to it; one mill situated at the foot of the hill of the castle of Crépy, in the estate of Dilucium; one [mill] on the water of the Alturna; one meadow; the vineyards of Chaziacum; the estate situated in the district of Othis, with all its appurtenances, lands, woods, meadows, and mills, and two churches: namely, the mother church of the same estate, founded in honor of blessed Denis, and the chapel of St Arnulf subject to it, with its tithes; and the church of St Martin, situated beside the castle of Pont-Arense, with certain lands and vineyards and all its appurtenances. In accordance with the tenor of your privileges, that church shall be subject both to you and to your successors and shall be administered with your favor and counsel.

In the forest of Blera, the estate called Fagit, with all its appurtenances. In the district of Meaux, one church in the estate called Mallos, with lands, people, and tithes. In the bishopric of Senlis, the church of St Agatha, with the whole parochial right of the entire castle of Crépy and all its appurtenances; the altar of Fenico. In the bishopric of Beauvais, the altar and estate of Locelles with all its appurtenances; likewise the cell of Franceries with all its appendages; the *beneura* of Noitello [reading uncertain], namely the houses, vineyards, and tithes of Gercheri. In the bishopric of Amiens, likewise, the cell called Morandi; the monastery with the grange of Avenis and all its appendages, which we decree shall always remain in the same liberty in which it is known hitherto to have remained; the possessions in the estate of Villers near Mont-Didier; the altar of Villers; the altars of Germiniac, which you possess by the charter of Falcon, bishop of Amiens, with all the parochial right of the same estate and its tithes.

In the bishopric of Soissons: the church of Bonoculo, with its grange, lands, vineyards, meadows, tithes, and other revenues; the church of Reptalio, with lands, tithes, and the other revenues of the same estate; the allod of Guy the knight at Maromont; the allod of Leotard at Erlvenium, with the other things which you possess there; the estate of the valley; the new estate; the estate of Walter the knight; the allod of Frenesta.

Whatever has further been bestowed upon that place by anyone out of his own right, or may hereafter be bestowed, shall always remain firm and unimpaired, to be possessed, governed, and disposed of in perpetuity both by you and by others who may be set over that place through the abbots of Cluny. We further add and, by the authority of the apostolic see, decree this: that, as was established and confirmed by our predecessor Pope John of holy memory, since the place was offered to you by the aforesaid count of Amiens of good memory at the beginning of its foundation, and since that house was adopted by him, as a new planting, as a proper and special daughter of the holy apostolic see, no archbishop or bishop may ever pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict upon that monastery without the assent and mandate of the Roman pontiff or of a legate sent from his side; nor may they exact other customary dues there, celebrate public Masses against your will, or lay a hand upon it for the purpose of imposing any burden. For it is not fitting that those known to belong to the right of the Roman Church, which is the head and mother of all Churches, should be burdened by the injuries or harassed by the incursions of anyone whatsoever.

[Col. 0149A]

[Col. 0149B] Moreover, you may choose priests in your churches and present them to the bishop; if they are found suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them. They shall answer to you without objection in temporal matters, and to the bishop in spiritual matters. Further, in the monastery in which you are devoted to divine service, whatever priest is summoned by you to celebrate divine offices there shall answer to no one ever except you and your Church. No one shall presume to demand from you tithes of your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or of the increase of your animals; rather, you shall henceforth possess these more peacefully, without any opposition from bishops or episcopal officers,

[Col. 0149C] since you distribute your goods to pilgrims and the poor. Nor shall anyone have license to disturb you concerning alms, whether of the living or the dead, entrusted to you for the salvation of souls; rather, you may receive, for the benefit of the uses of your servants of God and poor persons, the gifts and offerings of both living and dead which are brought to you. Further, the same monastery, with all its appurtenances, shall remain under the free ordering and disposition of Cluny, as it is known to have been hitherto by institution and concession of the holy apostolic see.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole and intact for the benefit in every way of the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving, indeed, in all matters the authority of the apostolic see and the rights of the diocesan bishops in the aforesaid chapels.

If, moreover, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person should rashly attempt to act against this decree, having been warned a second or third time, unless he corrects his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment.

[Col. 0150A] But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Gualterius, bishop of Albano. I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. . . . . I, Gilbert, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Cornelius and

[Col. 0150B] Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Peter in Chains. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Ardicio, cardinal-deacon of St. Theodore. I, Anthius, cardinal-deacon of St. Adrian. I, John, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in the Portico.

Given at Montpellier, through the hand of Hermann, deacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1162,

[Col. 0150C] in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

## LXXVI. He receives the castle of Scuria under protection.  
*(At Montpellier, 29 May.)*

[MURATORI, *Antiquities of Italy*, I, 941.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons AMBLARD, BERNARD, and the other lords of the castle of Scuria: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is manifest that the castle called Scuria, in the time of blessed Sylvester, as we have learned by inspection of the letters of our predecessor Pope Sergius of holy memory, was once bestowed upon blessed Peter by royal generosity through his hands; and that it was acknowledged and offered anew by Vedianus, formerly lord of that castle, to the aforesaid Pope Sergius, our predecessor, under an annual payment of ten solidi in Raymondine coinage. Hubert, Raymond, and Sicard, lords of that place, likewise acknowledged and offered that castle to our predecessor Pope Calixtus of blessed memory, and through his hand to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church. Therefore, following in the footsteps of those same predecessors of ours, Sergius and Calixtus, and also Innocent, Roman pontiffs, who received the castle itself—belonging to the right and property of blessed Peter—under the protection and defense of the apostolic see, we receive the aforesaid

[Col. 0151A] castle under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves and fortify it by the protection of this present writing. We decree that neither a count nor any person may have power to take away, diminish, attack, or claim that castle for his own uses; rather, as it has been granted by our aforesaid predecessors and by us, it shall remain undisturbed and intact for you under the right and defense of blessed Peter.

If, indeed, one of you should perhaps commit some more serious offense—which God forbid—then, on account of his fault, unless the others too have shared in that same wrongdoing, the others and their honors shall by no means be barred from the divine offices. We command that this same rule be observed concerning your subject knights. We further decree that no one except the lords and men of that castle may build a castle or construct a fortification within the bounds of your holding.

[Col. 0151B] But if any ecclesiastical or secular person brings a complaint against the men of that castle, he shall seek what is just before your metropolitan or a legate sent from the side of the Roman pontiff. If, therefore, any cleric or layperson should rashly attempt—which God forbid—to act against these provisions, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him suffer the loss of his rank and office, or be punished by the penalty of excommunication. But whoever proves a defender of them shall obtain the grace of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Montpellier, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June.

## XXVII. Bull for the church of St. Eusebius.  
*(At Montpellier, 4 June.)*

[*Gallia Christiana Novissima*, XII, 125, Documents.]

[Col. 0151C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons DODO, abbot, and the brethren of the church of the blessed Lawrence and Hilary of the abbey: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting to grant ready assent to the just desires of petitioners, and to fulfill in their resulting effect vows which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, favorably concurring in your petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority for you and, through you, for the aforesaid Church the grant of prebends, reasonably made by our brother Alan, bishop, and by the whole chapter of the Church of St. Eusebius of Auxerre, belonging to the right of your Church, and confirmed by them in their own writing, as is contained in their authentic letters; and we fortify it by the protection of this present writing.

[Col. 0151D] We decree that no person whatsoever may be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way to oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Montpellier, on the second day before the Nones of June.

## LXXVIII. To Louis VII, king of the Franks—Concerning the affair of the Church of Flavigny.  
*(At Montpellier, 4 June.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 987.]

[Col. 0152A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received with due kindness the letters which Your Highness sent us on behalf of our venerable brother, the bishop of Autun; and in accordance with their tenor we willingly extend honor and favor to the aforesaid bishop, as required by our office and out of regard for your sublimity. The case, however, which was in dispute between him and the abbot of Flavigny was for some time examined before our tribunal. The bishop produced witnesses against that abbot concerning his voluntary renunciation of the abbey; the abbot, asserting that he had made the renunciation not voluntarily but under compulsion, declared that he could produce witnesses concerning this, and also alleged that he had something to say against the bishop’s witnesses.

[Col. 0152B] But because he could not pursue this immediately, he earnestly requested a delay from us in order to carry it out. Since, therefore, we could no more lawfully deny him this than we ought to do so—unwilling that anyone should suffer any prejudice in his right, especially under our own examination—we judged, by the common counsel of our brethren, that a delay should be granted him until the octave of St. Michael. Then he is to return to our presence, sufficiently prepared both upon these matters and upon those charges which had been brought against him in the presence of our beloved son W., priest-cardinal of St. Peter in Chains, so that we may investigate the case more fully and, with the Lord’s approval, bring it to an end through justice.

[Col. 0152C] Meanwhile, lest the castle of Flavigny should in any respect be lost to the Church of Flavigny itself, to Your Serenity, or to the aforesaid bishop, we caused the abbot in our presence to swear—as you may see from the written record of his oath which we send you—that he will surrender the castle into your hands, or into those of a trustworthy messenger delegated by you, while the administration of the abbey remains free to him in both temporal and spiritual matters.

[Col. 0152D] Since that castle appears to concern the honor and jurisdiction of your kingdom, we judged it much more fitting that it should be preserved under the governance of royal magnificence than entrusted to any other keeper. Accordingly, by apostolic writing we ask, admonish, and exhort Your Serenity in the Lord not to delay receiving the aforesaid castle, while reserving, as we have said, the abbot’s free administration; and to ensure, by the Lord’s aid, that it is kept until the conclusion of the case in such a manner that no injury or loss may result from it to either bishop or abbot.

For we have commanded them that during this period neither shall attack the other for any reason,

[Col. 0153A] that those who had been captured shall be freely allowed to depart on either side, and that outsiders who have been excommunicated shall withdraw from the same castle. So that Your Royal Highness may take more diligent care to carry all this out, we have sent to your presence, together with the aforesaid bishop and at his request, our beloved son Stephen, our subdeacon, certainly an honorable and learned man whom we hold especially dear and esteemed. We earnestly ask Your Sublimity that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for ourselves, you receive both him and the bishop with royal kindness, treat them honorably, and believe without hesitation what they communicate to Your Highness on our behalf, just as if it had been declared to Your Majesty from our own mouth.

[Col. 0153B] Given at Montpellier, on the second day before the Nones of June.

## LXXIX. He frees the monastery of Vézelay from the authority of the Church of Cluny.  
*(At Montpellier.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1160.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, abbot of the monastery of Vézelay, and his brethren, present and future, professing the monastic life, in perpetuity.

The most holy Roman Church, which answers to each person according to the quality of his merits, is accustomed to treat more favorably those whom it finds faithful and to adorn with the prerogative of honor those whom it sees more fervent in its service.

[Col. 0153C] Our predecessor Pope Paschal of good memory, as we have learned from the privilege of our predecessor Pope Calixtus of blessed memory, entrusted the monastery of Vézelay, which belongs properly and specially to the right of blessed Peter, to the Church of Cluny, taking account of the fervor of religion then existing there, when religion in the monastery of Vézelay had largely declined. Pope Calixtus confirmed this same arrangement by the privilege of his authority: namely, that, upon the death of the abbot established there at the time, another should be appointed there by the common consent of the brethren, or of the sounder part of the father’s counsel, with the counsel of the abbots of Cluny.

But we, having more diligently considered the constancy of your devotion and the firmness of faith which both you and Pontius, abbot of Vézelay of good memory, have displayed toward the Roman Church in this stormy time, and considering also how manifestly the Church of Cluny has erred during this disturbance, and how, falling from its former religious observance and integrity, it has made itself alien from the unity of the Church,

[Col. 0153D] while your aforesaid monastery has remained most steadfast in devotion and faith toward the Church and religious observance has there, by God’s grace, been fully restored—so that each Church may seem to reap the fruit appropriate to its merits—we have judged, by the common counsel of our brethren, that the commission made by the same Pope Paschal, our predecessor, must be revoked. We decree that the same monastery shall in no respect whatsoever be subject to the Church of Cluny, nor be bound to answer to anyone except the Roman Church alone. You shall have an election free in every respect, so that the counsel or consent of the abbots of Cluny shall in no way be required. Rather, we will that he be given and set over you as abbot whom the brethren, by common consent or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, have elected according to the fear of God and the institution of St. Benedict, and whom the Roman pontiff either judges should be ordained or, upon the suggestion of the monks of that place, consents has been ordained.

[Col. 0154A] In order that this our ordinance may always be observed inviolably in future times, we confirm it by apostolic authority and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our constitution or in any way oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, having been warned a second or third time, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon those who observe it may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

## LXXX. To William, lord of Montpellier—He receives his person and goods under the protection of blessed Peter and himself.  
*(At Montpellier, 1 July.)*

[D. BOUQUET, *Collection*, XV, 779.]

[Col. 0154C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, the nobleman WILLIAM of Montpellier: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Considering and more diligently observing how devoted you are to the Roman Church and to ourselves, we grant favorable assent to your petitions and receive under the protection of the apostolic see and ourselves your person and the goods which you possess or may hereafter acquire by just means. We decree that no one whatsoever, except the Roman pontiff, one whom he has specially commanded, or a cardinal delegated from his side, may bind your person with the bond of excommunication.

[Col. 0154D] Likewise, let no one dare place under interdict your chapel at Montpellier or the other chapel in the castle of Palude, so as to prevent divine offices from being celebrated in them for you and your household, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons. For the two chapels, however, since both were offered to St. Peter by your ancestors, one gold piece shall be paid annually to our Lateran palace; provided that the tithes and first fruits, and other things belonging to parochial right, are preserved for the Church of Maguelone.

[Col. 0155A] Given at Montpellier, on the Kalends of July, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

> **[Note: Col. 0155D]** In the year 1162, when this letter was given, on the Kalends of July, the third year of Alexander’s pontificate had not yet been completed. Alexander granted this favor in return for the services with which William received him at Montpellier [Col. 0156D]. Octavian, moreover, had also given letters to the same William in order to draw him to his own party. (See below in the Appendix to Alexander III.)

## LXXXI. Privilege for the monastery of Cour-Dieu.  
*(At Montpellier, 6 July.)*

[*Gallia Christiana Novissima*, VIII, Documents, 514.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons LOTHAR, abbot of the monastery of Cour-Dieu, and his brethren, present and future, professing the monastic life, in perpetuity.

Apostolic protection ought to be present for those who lead a religious life, lest perhaps an assault of anyone’s rashness either turn them back from their purpose or—which God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and receive the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing.

[Col. 0155B] First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order established in that place according to God and the Rule of St. Benedict, from the institution of the Cistercian order, shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, with the Lord’s assistance, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have judged the following worthy of explicit statement: Joiacum, with all its meadows and level land, mill, and other appurtenances; two arpents of meadowland at Campumbonum, between the hills and the water; at Carrelias, land for two plough-teams with meadows, given by our beloved son Louis, most illustrious king of the Franks; one ploughland at the chapel of Cathiniacum, given by Albert of Pithiviers; half a ploughland at the chapel of Cathiniacum, given by Gossenus of Leugis; four ploughlands in meadows, given by the chapter of Holy Cross, Ralph of Balgenciacum, Henry the seneschal, and Peter of Bugellet; at Champellum, three ploughlands with woodland and meadows;

[Col. 0155D] at Ingrannia, four arpents of meadowland, for which you gave in exchange four—[an uncertain OCR reading: perhaps six]—arpents of meadowland at Marollium; and the meadow of Constantius, given by the bishop of Orléans.

Furthermore, we confirm the woods reasonably granted to you by the aforesaid son of ours, Louis, king of the Franks, for all your uses. We likewise confirm by apostolic authority the woods surrounding Holy Cross, which have reasonably been granted to you for all the uses of yourselves and your animals. We further confirm for you the liberties and immunities justly granted to you and your Church by John, formerly bishop of good memory, and confirmed by the protection both of his writing and of that of Manasses, bishop of the same city, as is contained in their authentic documents and in those of our dearest son Louis, most illustrious king of the Franks.

[Col. 0156A] Certainly, no one shall presume to exact tithes or first fruits from you from the produce of your labors, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, or retain those taken away, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 0156B] I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Henry, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, Albert, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Peter in Chains. I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Gualter, bishop of Albano. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of the title of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Ardicio, deacon of the title of St. Theodore. I, Cinthius, cardinal-deacon of St. Adrian. I, Raymond, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata. I, John, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in

[Col. 0156C] the Portico.

Given at Montpellier, through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the day before the Nones of July, in the tenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1162, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

## LXXXII. Privilege for the church of St. Stephen of Toulouse.  
*(At Montpellier, 8 July.)*

[*History of Languedoc*, II, Documents, p. 586.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BERNARD, provost of the church of St. Stephen of Toulouse, and his brethren, who shall live under rule, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0156D] As with those seeking unjust things, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, favorably granting assent to your just petitions, we fortify by the privilege of the apostolic see the Church of Toulouse, in which you devote yourselves to divine service, following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, Paschal and Innocent, Roman pontiffs. We decree that the canonical and regular order and life established in that Church shall be observed there inviolably in perpetual future times.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with God’s favor, shall remain unimpaired and whole, saving the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. We further add that, so long as the canonical order endures among you, you shall hold in perpetuity and peacefully possess all that you now appear justly to possess for the common support of livelihood through the gift of Isarn, sometime bishop of Toulouse: namely, the entire endowment of the deanery, sacristy, and precentorship; the tithe-right of the church and altar; the offerings and grain customarily brought into and carried out from that church; the archdeaconry from the Narbonne gate to the territory of Carcassonne;

[Col. 0157A]

[Col. 0157B] another [archdeaconry] of Vetimorensis; another beyond the Garonne; and another from the village of Gaernensis, called Brohai; cultivated and uncultivated land, waters, meadows, and woods; the land outside the walls called Feratrax; the entire endowment of the provostship; moreover, all the chapels of the castles throughout the whole bishopric of Toulouse; and also the church of St. Martin of Icio, etc.; the churches of Lumbers, Pumpiacum, and Saboneres with their appurtenances; the churches of Laurac, Fongaldo, Verdfeil, Puillaurensis, Bavato, Murel, and Palies; likewise the church of St. Mary of Galders and that of St. Columba with their appurtenances, and the church of Château-Sarrasin.

We further decree that no monk, canon,

[Col. 0157C] or any other person whatsoever in the bishopric of Toulouse may appoint chaplains, except the bishop, provost, and archdeacons alone. We permit no one else to set over you as provost, dean, archdeacons, schoolmaster, or sacristan anyone except the person elected by the consent of the brethren living under rule. We also will that the appointment of bishops in your church, by God’s grace, be made chiefly by your election.

We also prohibit anyone, after making profession in your church, from possessing anything of his own or from leaving the cloister without the permission of the provost or congregation. Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority for you and, through you, for your Church the agreement reasonably made between you and Hugh, abbot of St. Saturninus, and his canons: concerning the burial of knights of the city of Toulouse, which they relinquished to you of their own will; concerning the payment of twenty solidi, which they are to pay you in a lump sum from the archdeaconry of Villelongue; and concerning certain other matters, as is known to be contained in the authentic instrument made concerning it.

[Col. 0157D] We also decree that no one may destroy, alter, or diminish the rights of churches long established in the bishopric of Toulouse and belonging specially to the bishop of Toulouse, without the will and permission of the bishop of Toulouse. If, therefore, in the future, etc. Amen.

Thus signed at the foot:

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina.

[Col. 0158A] I, Ubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Gualterius, bishop of Albano. I, Ubald, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Henry, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

Given at Montpellier, through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of July, in the tenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation

[Col. 0158B] 1162, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

## LXXXIII. To Louis VII, king of the Franks—Concerning the legates whom he will send.  
*(At Montpellier, 10 July.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 988.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The many benefits which you have bestowed upon us declare with what eager affection of devotion you especially embrace the Church of God and ourselves; and the most unconquerable faith of Your Royal Serenity shows with what arms of sincere charity you cherish and defend Christ’s one bride among the other Catholic princes.

[Col. 0158C] For there is no need—and no passage of time, however long, will ever be able to erase from the memory of the apostolic see—how, from the very beginning of our elevation, you have set yourself as an impregnable wall for the house of Israel; how you have borne Peter’s little ship, tossed upon the waves, securely amid the storm by the anchor of faith and the oars of your prudence. Accordingly, we love you as a Catholic prince and a king truly most Christian, with sincere affection in the bowels of Christ; we willingly give attention to your honor and exaltation; and we continually entreat almighty God with devout prayers for the preservation of the glory of Your Highness.

We have received with due kindness the letters which Your Royal Serenity sent us through our beloved sons I., abbot of St. Germain, and B., your familiar cleric—men indeed industrious, discerning, and most devoted to Your Highness—and both we and our brethren rejoiced greatly at them. Therefore, having more fully understood your will both from the letters themselves and from the report of those aforesaid men, we have judged that we should set forth our own will to you through them. Thus what our beloved son . . . . . abbot of Grand-Selve, whom we had sent to Your Excellency, omitted for some reason unknown to us may be made known to the ears of Your Highness through these men.

[Col. 0159A] We are also immediately preparing to send to the presence of Your Highness two of our brethren, whom we hold especially dear and esteemed among our other brethren. Through them we will take care to make known to you more fully both the state of the Church and our will; and, in return, by the Lord’s aid, we shall learn yours, as that of a prince in whom we place the fullest confidence for the honor and exaltation of God’s Church—so that through you it may reach the harbor of tranquillity and safety.

By this present declaration, therefore, we ask, admonish, and exhort Your Royal Clemency in the Lord that, when they come to be presented before the presence of your royal majesty, you receive them kindly for reverence of blessed Peter and ourselves, treat them honorably, and give assent and a useful effect to the things which they will propose to you on our behalf for the honor of God and for the benefit and exaltation of both the Church and your kingdom.

[Col. 0159B] Thus you may receive from the eternal King the recompense of an unfailing reward, and may be bound perpetually to extend more fully in all things the favor of the apostolic see to yourself and your descendants.

Given at Montpellier, on the sixth day before the Ides of July.
