## LXXXIV. Privilege for the church of St. Aignan of Orléans.  
*(At Montpellier, 12 July.)*

[*Historical Antiquities of the Church of Saint-Aignan of Orléans*, Proofs, p. 116.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, dean of the church of St. Aignan of Orléans, and his brethren, present and future, to be canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0159C]

Since we are bound by the office of apostleship entrusted to us by God to exercise vigilant care and concern for all Churches, we must nevertheless be especially solicitous for those which are known to belong to the right and property of the holy Roman Church, which rely with fuller devotion upon the protection of the Apostolic See, and which ought equally to be fortified by the support of our authority, lest they be harassed by the reckless attacks of any persons upon their goods or even their dignities. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions and, by this written privilege, place the aforesaid Church of Saint Anianus, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves [Col. 0159D]. We decree that whatsoever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favourable, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: namely, the estate of Sentiliacum with its church; the estate of Roem with its church; the estate of Tiliacum with its church; the estate of Caloium with its church; the estate of Herbiliacum with its church and all the tithes and appurtenances of those estates; the church of Old Saint Anianus, which is called the chapel, and the church of Saint Germanus within the city walls; whatever you possess in the estate of Centolium and the church of that estate; whatever you possess in the estate of Fonteneium and its church, with the tithes and other revenues belonging to your right; the water of the Loire from the wall of the old city as far as Saint Lupus, with the mills which you possess on that water and their fisheries; whatever you possess beyond the Loire and in Sologne; whatever you possess in Gâtinais; the estate of Bezziacum with all its appurtenances; whatever you possess at Oscuras; whatever you possess in the forest called Bolonia, and the estate of Setteis.

Moreover, in the aforesaid parish churches which you hold—namely, those of Sentilliacum, Roem, Tilliacum, Fonteneium, Centolium, Calaio, and Herbiliacum—you shall choose priests and present them to the bishops. If they are suitable, the bishops shall entrust the care of souls to them without simony, so that they may answer for the care of the people, while, with respect to temporal matters, they shall render you due obedience and customary subjection. In the other two churches, namely Saint Anianus and Saint Germanus, and for service at the altar of the Crucified in the church of blessed Anianus, you may freely appoint priests, without anyone’s objection or presentation, as hitherto, so also henceforth [Col. 0160B].

Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority the fairs granted to you and your church for the two feasts of blessed Anianus, for procuring lights for that church, both by Louis, the illustrious king of the Franks of blessed memory, and by John, bishop of Orléans, and strengthened by the protection of their written instruments; and we decree that they shall remain forever unimpaired [Col. 0160C]. We also enact and decree by this present ordinance that no archbishop, bishop, or any other person may excommunicate the church entrusted to you, or you, or the clerics of your choir, or place them under an interdict from divine offices.

Furthermore, we prohibit any ecclesiastical person, or person of whatsoever order, from imposing unlawful exactions upon your churches, chapels, or their priests. We therefore decree that no one whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain possessions removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted [Col. 0160D].

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly opposing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to violate it, and, after a second or third warning, does not correct that presumption by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and our Lord Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works [Col. 0161A] and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia.  
I, Gualterius, bishop of Albano.  
I, Hubald, cardinal priest of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.  
I, Henry, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus.  
I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina.  
I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains [Col. 0161B].  
I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin.  
I, Odo, or Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.  
I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.  
I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian.  
I, Raymond, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Via Lata.  
I, John, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Portico.

Given at Montpellier by the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of July, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1162 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III [Col. 0161C].

### LXXXV. To Roger, Archbishop, and the Canons of York.—That the archbishop must not presume to have the cross carried before him in the province of Canterbury. (Sens, January.)

[*Letters of Saint Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 43.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ROGER, Archbishop of York, and to the beloved sons, the canons of York: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

It befits your prudence to leave another’s rights untouched, just as you desire that your own be preserved whole and unimpaired. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we prohibit you, Archbishop, from having your cross carried before you in any manner within the province of the Church of Canterbury [Col. 0161D], or from attempting this upon any pretext of appeal. For this could produce harmful prejudice against such right as you may possess. If you are unwilling to refrain for the present, you and your successors will have to refrain forever.

### LXXXVI. To Hugh, Bishop of Soissons.—He commends the dean of Saint Anianus. (At Montpellier, 14 July.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 981.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, Bishop of Soissons: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0162A] Our beloved son Master P., dean of the church of Blessed Anianus, came to us. Among the other commendable things which he reported to us concerning your prudence, he took care to state that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, you love and honour him.

[Note: [Col. 0161D] Saint Anianus: the celebrated body of canons at Orléans, formerly a distinguished abbey of the Order of Saint Benedict [Col. 0162D], from which Fleury, famous for the body of Saint Benedict, arose in the region of Orléans.]

You should know that this is the more welcome and pleasing to us because we love him with a fuller affection of charity and earnestly desire that he be honoured by those who love the most holy Roman Church and ourselves. Therefore, as we send this our son back to the Church committed to him with the fullness of the favour of the Apostolic See, we have thought fit earnestly to commend him to your brotherhood, asking that you love and honour him in such a way that we may owe you abundant thanks for it.

[Col. 0162B] Given at Montpellier, on the second day before the Ides of June.

### LXXXVII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of Master P., dean of the church of Blessed Anianus. (At Montpellier, 14 July.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 717.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son Master P., dean of the church of Blessed Anianus, came to us. Among the other commendable things which he reported to us concerning your prudence, he took care to state that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, you love and honour him. You should know that this is the more [Col. 0162C] welcome and pleasing to us because we love him with a fuller affection of charity and earnestly desire that he be honoured by those who love the most holy Roman Church and ourselves. Therefore, as we send this our son back to the Church committed to him with the fullness of the favour of the Apostolic See, we have thought fit to commend him most earnestly to your brotherhood, asking that you love and honour him in such a way that we may owe you abundant thanks for it.

Given at Montpellier, on the second day before the Ides of July.

### LXXXVIII. To King Louis.—He complains that the bishop of Orléans unjustly harasses certain canons. (At Montpellier, 14 July.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, II, 990.]

[Col. 0162D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

We know from their repeated complaints, and, as we believe, Your Royal Highness does not fail to know, how bitterly and unreasonably our brother, the bishop of Orléans, has hitherto persecuted our beloved sons Letoldus, M., the chaplain, and Adam, canons of Orléans. For a long time now, while they repeatedly appealed in pursuit of justice, he has compelled them to live in exile from their own district; and when they came to us or stood in our presence, he wholly unjustly and unreasonably despoiled them of their own goods [Col. 0163A]. Although he has often received our letters on this matter, he has entirely scorned and disregarded them: he has been unwilling either to restore to them what was taken away, in accordance with our command, or to render them the fullness of justice. The envoys whom he at one time sent to us about this matter came instructed to seek futile delays rather than to render justice. Thus the aforesaid canons, forced to remain in exile longer for the sake of their right, have followed us by land and sea for a long time.

Accordingly, had we not been appeased by the prayers of Your Highness, we would not have been willing to endure his contumacy with the mildness of the Apostolic See; according to the rigour of the canons, we could and should have punished him severely. Nevertheless, having until now borne his disobedience with all patience in consideration of your prayers, we recently commanded him by repeated letters either to restore in full all that had been taken from the said canons, or, at the forthcoming feast of Saint Luke, to appear before us in person or through a sufficient representative, fully to answer them concerning all these matters [Col. 0163B]. Otherwise, from that point we shall neither allow their right to be diminished in any way nor, by God’s authority, let his contumacy go unpunished.

Given at Montpellier, on the second day before the Ides of July.

### LXXXIX. To the Archbishop of Narbonne and the Chapter of Arles.—That they give aid and counsel to William, lord of Montpellier, and to the people and merchants whom he had received as special sons of blessed Peter. (At Montpellier, 15 July.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 782.]

[Col. 0163C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren the Archbishop of Narbonne (PONS), the chapter of the Church of Arles, and all the suffragans of both; and also to the bishops of Viviers (RAYMOND), Mende (ADALBERT), Le Puy (PETER), and Rodez (HUGH): greeting and the apostolic blessing.

A pious request ought to be fulfilled by a corresponding result, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the requested benefit may unquestionably acquire force. Therefore, dearest brethren in Christ [Col. 0163D], moved by the prayers of our beloved son, the nobleman William of Montpellier, we receive his person and goods, and also the people and merchants of Montpellier, under the protection and defence of blessed Peter and ourselves, and desire to cherish them as special sons of the Prince of the Apostles. [Col. 0164A] Accordingly, by these apostolic letters we command you, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, to support and love them and in no way refuse, as your office requires, to give them aid and counsel, etc.

Given at Montpellier, on the Ides of July, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

[Note: [Col. 0163D] “In the fourth year of our pontificate”: an unusual clause in Alexander’s other letters in brief form, apparently added by copyists; for in July 1162 the third year of his pontificate had not yet been completed.]

### XC. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of the Bishop of the Morini. (Mende, 23 July.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 712.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0164B] Although we ought to stand especially beside all God’s faithful and devoted sons of the Church and cherish them with the sweetness of paternal affection, we should especially love with ready charity our brother bishops, who remain devoted and sincere toward God’s Church and toward ourselves, and should always provide with attentive concern for their interests and burdens. We believe your discretion does not fail to know how our venerable brother [Note: [Col. 0163D] Milo II, who had previously been a monk of Blessed Mary of the Wood, as John of Ypres writes; Robert of Mont likewise says of him in the appendix to Sigebert, under the year 1260: “When the venerable Milo, bishop of Thérouanne, died, Milo, archdeacon of the same church and a regular canon, as his predecessor had been, was elected. When Samson, Archbishop of Reims, wished to consecrate him, the clerics of the city of Boulogne, who had long been under the Bishop of Thérouanne, wishing henceforth to have their own bishop as they had had in ancient times, forbade the archbishop, under apostolic appeal, to consecrate him except solely to the title of the Church of Thérouanne [read: Boulogne]. The aforesaid elect refused this; un-consecrated, he went to Rome against those clerics, and there was consecrated.”] the bishop of the Morini has always been faithful and devoted to the most holy Roman Church and to ourselves; how he was the first among western bishops to come into our presence and received consecration from our hands. Therefore, earnestly commending him to your brotherhood [Col. 0164C], we ask, admonish, and exhort you in the Lord to love, support, and honour both him and his Church, so that he may perceive that our prayers have benefited him and we may owe your discretion most abundant thanks. Moreover, we command your brotherhood diligently to cause Sebrand, a cleric excommunicated by the same bishop, to be avoided as excommunicate. He concealed from us the cause of his excommunication and abused the benefit of our letters.

Given at Mende, on the tenth day before the Kalends of August.

### XCI. To Hugh, Bishop of Soissons.—That he bring it about that the king of the Franks refrain from the meeting which he intended to hold with Emperor Frederick. (Mende, 24 July.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 983.]

[Col. 0164D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother H., Bishop of Soissons: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0165A] Considering the constancy of your faith and devotion, and reflecting inwardly upon how you have set yourself up as an impregnable wall for your one mother, the most holy Roman Church, against schismatic perversity, we love you as our dearest brother with sincere charity in the Lord and embrace you in the arms of pure affection. We confidently invite your diligence to undertake matters that may redound to our exaltation and to the advantage of the Church. For we believe and confidently trust without doubt that, through the sincere affection of devotion which you are known to have conceived toward the universal Church itself and especially toward our person, much advantage will come to us and, by God’s aid, great increase will accrue to that Church [Col. 0165B].

Therefore, with complete confidence, by apostolic letters we ask, admonish, and exhort the prudence of your brotherhood in the Lord to strive with all diligence to warn our dearest son in Christ, Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, that he may remain steadfast and firm in the faith and devotion which he has always displayed toward the Church of God, especially at this time, and, as a Catholic prince and most Christian king, may vigilantly labour for the exaltation of holy mother Church and of ourselves. But especially concerning his plan to hold a meeting with Frederick, called emperor, do not delay to warn him more carefully, so that, since we believe and fear [Col. 0165C] that meeting may be harmful in many ways both to God’s Church and ourselves and also to the king and his kingdom, he may refrain from it and wholly abandon such a purpose.

Given at Mende, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August.

### XCII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—He praises and urges him to meet with the king at Clermont concerning the affair of the Church of Châlons. (Brioude, 1 August.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 171.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims [Col. 0165D]: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Considering with the attention it deserves the zeal of devotion which you are known to have laudably shown at all times, and especially from the beginning of our elevation, toward the most holy Roman Church and our person, we have the firmest purpose and most ready will to love you, as our dearest brother, with sincere charity in the Lord, and we gladly desire to grant your requests in all matters in which, with the Lord’s help, we can do so [Col. 0166A]. As you are, we believe, aware, we have now received again and again the letters of our dearest son in Christ, Louis, king of the Franks, and of Count Henry concerning the affair of the Church of Châlons; nor do we believe that your discretion is unaware how they wish us to proceed in that affair. Certainly, in deference to your brotherhood as much as we ought and can, we have thought fit to defer the matter until we speak with the aforesaid king, with whom, as he has informed us in due time, we are to hold a meeting at Clermont [Col. 0166B].

Therefore, both by other letters and by this present letter, we command your discretion to come into our presence at that place, either together with him or before his arrival; and there, with God’s aid, as far as we can do so with a clear conscience, we shall settle the aforesaid matter for the honour of God and of that Church, with the counsel of the same king and of yourself. Moreover, since it befits your honour and prudence to attach yourself familiarly to that aforesaid son of ours, the king, and to bring it about that, as is his custom, he greatly follows your counsel, we ask, admonish, and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord to go to him and show yourself to him as counsellor and intimate friend in such a way that he may more willingly accept your counsel in matters concerning the Lord and the advancement and exaltation of the Church and his kingdom, and, as usual, hold you dear and acceptable about himself [Col. 0166C].

Furthermore, as we have already indicated to you by other letters, so by this letter we urge your prudence to devote every effort to preventing the meeting which the king himself has planned to hold with Frederick, called emperor, and to strive and labour by every means in your power to ensure that such a purpose is not carried out for any reason.

[Note: [Col. 0165D] This meeting, which writers commonly report was appointed at Besançon, but which Anselm of Salerno asserts was held at Dijon, took place at Pont de Laône on the river Saône—that is, at Latona, between Dijon and Dole—as we learn from Emperor Frederick’s letter to the Archbishop of Lyons in Chesne, vol. IV, *History of France*, p. 502. Frederick summoned his followers to Besançon, whereas Louis summoned his to Dijon; both were then to proceed with their respective parties to Pont de Laône. For an account, if desired, of how prudently Louis conducted himself at that meeting and withdrew from it, see Book IV of the *History of Vézelay*, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 581, and the brief Chronicle of Lobbes, vol. III of the *Anecdota*, from which we learn that it was held on the feast of the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist. Alberic writes the same in his Chronicle and further states that King Louis was then turned away from Emperor Frederick through the counsel of the men of Clairvaux. See also the letter of Henry, Archbishop of Reims, to his brother King Louis in Chesne, vol. IV, *History of France*, p. 576 [Col. 0166D].]

Make haste to inform us by letter of the condition of the aforementioned kingdom and of your counsel in the affairs of the Church.

Given at Brioude, on the Kalends of August.

### XCIII. He receives the Monastery of Poblet under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Near Clermont, 13 August.)

[FINESTRES, *History of the Royal Monastery of Poblet*, Cervera, 1753, quarto, II, 424.—As attested by JAFFÉ, *Regesta of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 687.]

[Col. 0166D]

### XCIV. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—That he compel the clerics of the chapters of Lessedene, Tidringia, etc., to obey William, Archdeacon of Colchester. (At Clermont, 26 August.)

[*Letters of Saint Thomas*, ed. GILLET, II, 37.]

[Col. 0167A]

ALEXANDER, pope, to the lord of Canterbury.

It has come to our hearing that the clerics of the chapters of Lessedene, Tidringia, and Brachestedia, situated within the archdeaconry of our beloved son William, Archdeacon of Colchester, refuse to render him due obedience. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood diligently to admonish the aforesaid clerics to render due obedience humbly and reverently to that archdeacon [Col. 0167B]. If, after your admonition, they refuse to do so voluntarily, you shall compel them to it with all strictness, without impediment from an appeal.

Given at Clermont, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September.

### XCV. To Stephen, Bishop, and the Canons of Clermont.—He confirms the agreement made between them and William, Count of Auvergne, concerning the castle of Montferrand. (At Clermont, 19 August.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 784.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother STEPHEN, bishop, and to all the canons [Col. 0167C] of Clermont: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Things established with reasonable foresight for the good of peace between those in discord and dispute ought to endure in stability and retain the strength of permanence for the future. Therefore, granting our favourable assent to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority the agreement made between you and the nobleman William, Count of Auvergne. Following the examples of our predecessors, we wish it known to present and future alike that the grave and long-lasting dispute which had existed between Clermont, the city of Auvergne, and Montferrand has been brought back to the stability of a lasting peace.

William, Count of Auvergne [Col. 0167D], kinsman of the king of the Franks, desiring to make satisfaction to Bishop Stephen and the Church of Clermont and to settle the complaint which the Church of Clermont had concerning Montferrand, gave, for the redemption of his own soul and those of his fathers, to the said bishop and the chapter of the Church of Clermont an amount of rent-paying grain equal to that which he possessed in the houses of Montferrand.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] This agreement is more clearly understood from another contained in the letters of King Louis, in the year 1145, ibid., p. 61. Its terms are as follows: “The aforesaid W., namely the son of Count Robert, wishing to make peace concerning that controversy which had long been pursued between the Church of Clermont and Montferrand, and for which also . . . . . our father Louis, king of revered memory, had endured many labours everywhere, with the counsel of his barons and prudent men, gave and granted in full, wholly and in every respect forever, to the Church of Clermont—namely, Bishop Aymeric and the canons of the same Church and their successors—the tenth part of all his revenues which now exist or may hereafter exist, from whatever source and in whatever manner they may come to Montferrand, without any reservation [Col. 0168D]. Furthermore, for the fuller integrity of peace and for the salvation of his own soul and those of his ancestors, should he die without an heir, that is, a son or daughter, he gave and granted Montferrand and everything belonging to it to the bishop and canons of the aforesaid Church. In the meantime he gave and granted to them in the aforesaid town two houses, one to the bishop and the other to the canons. He also granted them that the people of Clermont should enjoy at Montferrand, in the market, at the fairs, and in judicial proceedings, the same law, custom, and condition as the people of Montferrand enjoy, etc.”]

The said Count of Auvergne and Archimbald, lord of Bourbon, also secured this gift by the impression of their seals, etc.

Given at Clermont, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October.

### XCVI. To Louis, King of the Franks.—He thanks him for the constancy he displayed at the meeting with Emperor Frederick. He reports that he has acted with the king of England so that he might offer all the strength of his kingdom to the king of the Franks. (At Dole, 17 September.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1015.]

[Col. 0168B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

We have heard through our venerable brethren, the archbishops and bishops who were present with you at the meeting which you had arranged with Frederick, called emperor, what troubles and burdens you endured in that meeting. We have also learned, after their departure, of the discovered wickedness and deceit of the said Frederick and his counsellors, who were striving by every means to corrupt the serenity of your faith. We have heard what constancy of mind and spirit of courage you assumed: you preferred and resolved to stand as an iron wall and impregnable defence for the house of the Lord [Col. 0168C], and to contend even to the shedding of blood, rather than depart from the unity of the Church and consent to such great wickedness. To almighty God, who by His ineffable grace established you as so strong and unconquered a defender, against the counsels of the wicked, on behalf of His spotless bride—the holy Church—which He willed to redeem and honour with His most precious blood; and to you yourself, who, spurning all worldly power, looked to God alone, we offer such acts of thanksgiving as we can and ought. In devout meditation of heart and earnest prayer we beseech almighty God to preserve and protect you and your kingdom for many years and grant you victory and triumph over your enemies and those of the Church [Col. 0168D].

And therefore, to enlarge the glory of your name and strengthen the vigour of your courage, through our venerable brethren [Roger], Archbishop of York, [Rotrou], Bishop of Évreux, and [Arnulf], Bishop of Lisieux, together with his other distinguished envoys, we have carefully urged and exhorted our dearest son in Christ, Henry, illustrious king of the English, and endeavoured by every means to induce him to furnish you, as his lord, with resources and aid, and to labour in all things and through all things in the service of Your Royal Highness. He, greatly delighted and rejoicing in our exhortations, and diligently considering with prudent mind what he owes you, has sent to Your Highness our beloved son, the nobleman R. of Saint-Valery, and other valiant and dear envoys. Through them he has placed himself, his land, and all the forces he possesses at the disposal of the honour, fidelity [Col. 0169B], and exaltation of your kingdom. He directed us to convey this offer of resources and aid to your diligence and, if need be, to make ourselves your sureties for all these things more confidently.

For our part, considering more carefully his devotion and sincerity, with which he is known to burn toward you and ourselves, and strongly desiring that your power be increased and enlarged in every respect both through him and through other great men; and wishing, both through ourselves and through other devoted sons of the Church, effectively to furnish you, as our dearest son, with resources and aid and to bestow on you power and assistance both temporal and spiritual, we make ourselves, if need be, your sureties with complete confidence. Therefore, we ask and earnestly exhort Your Most Excellent Highness to receive the aforesaid envoys with the illustrious kindness befitting so capable and prudent a king, to endeavour to honour them in all things, to give the aforesaid king magnificent thanks for his offer of such affection and loyalty, and to incline your noble mind toward him with ready goodwill on account of these things [Col. 0169C].

For we shall take care, as we always have, to induce and exhort in every way the aforesaid king—whom we expect in our presence on the coming Tuesday—to act for your honour and loyalty and for the advancement of your kingdom. We have thought fit to communicate these matters more fully to Your Highness through our beloved son P., our chaplain and subdeacon, the bearer of this letter [Col. 0169D].

Given at Dole, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October.

### XCVII. To Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg.—He rejoices that he remains steadfastly faithful to the Church; he urges him to come to him and, if the opportunity arises, to bring the emperor back to a sounder mind. (At Dole, 18 September.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, p. 1040.]

ALEXANDER, etc., to his venerable brother, the Archbishop of Salzburg: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

We grieve deeply and are greatly troubled that, though we would wish to do so more often, we do not visit your dearest brotherhood with a word of our blessing, impeded both by the insecurity of the land and by the unsuitability of messengers [Col. 0170A]. For as we carefully observe the fervent constancy of your devotion in this crisis of tribulation; as we repeatedly reflect with earnest thought upon the strong prudence of your mind, by which you powerfully refute and confound the enemies of God and the Church, while you strengthen and guide lovers of the light in unity and Catholic faith through kindly encouragement and prudent gentleness; as we consider also with what strength and severity, disregarding all worldly power and attending to truth alone, you manfully resist the emperor and the supporters of his perversity—we are moved to such affection that we place in you alone a part of our consolation both temporal and spiritual and embrace your person with all charity in the bowels of Christ, as an illustrious and special member of the Church [Col. 0170B].

For whoever in those regions is of sound mind, adheres to us, and remains in the unity of the Church, we see beyond doubt and hold as manifest truth that this has come about through your most distinguished diligence and vigilance. Therefore, to almighty God, who through His ineffable grace has appointed you so unconquered and invincible a defender of His Church against the children of darkness, and to you yourself, whom neither the tempest of the raging sea nor the threat of roaring winds has been able by any means to tear away from reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, we offer all the thanks that we can and ought, praying almighty God with pure heart and earnest words that He may defend and protect you for a longer time for His own honour and that of the Church [Col. 0170C].

We ask, moreover, your brotherhood; we admonish and exhort you in the Lord, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of sins: remain steadfast and immovable in devotion to blessed Peter and to us, and by your diligence bring to the same commitment, and exhort in every way, all whom you can. Furthermore, since our heart would be greatly gladdened by your coming, and we need your person in the affairs of the Church, we earnestly urge your discretion to present yourself before us, so that we may have the counsel of your discernment concerning the peace and preservation of the Church. For we shall receive your person, whom we await with ardent desire, with rejoicing of heart [Col. 0170D], and shall take care to honor you in many ways. But if perchance—though it would grieve us—you should be unable to come into our presence, send us one of your clerics, by whose counsel we may more conveniently avail ourselves of your stead in conducting the affairs of the Church. Meanwhile, if you judge the time favorable, go to Emperor Frederick and strive by every means to restore him to the unity of the Church and to devotion to us; and if he should wish to return to us with a sincere mind, state to him more freely on our behalf that, in accordance with your counsel, we are prepared to forgive him everything that he has done against the Church of God and against ourselves, and shall endeavor to honor him as a most powerful prince.

Given at Dol, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October.

XCVIII. Privilege for the monastery of St. John of Kaltenborn. (At Dol, September 20.)

[Thuringia sacra, p. 308.]

[Col. 0171A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BERNARD, provost, and his brethren in the Church of St. John the Evangelist of Kaldebrun, professing the canonical life, both present and future: for perpetual remembrance.

As the authority of the sacred canons teaches, holy places are to be transferred for three reasons. Of these, Otto, formerly bishop of Alberstadt, of good memory, perceived two to be present in the case of the Church of Revenigne [Col. 0171B], namely the unsuitability of the site and the molestation of robbers. Therefore, for the greater benefit of the divine office, with the common consent of his brethren and of the heirs of the founders of that church, he transferred and relocated to Kaldebrunnen the estates granted to the aforesaid church. We therefore, whose particular concern it is reasonably to confirm what is done by our brethren and to support pious desires with appropriate assistance, confirm by the present decree this transfer made for the aforesaid reasons, and decree that it shall remain valid in future times.

Moreover, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of blessed memory—Calixtus, Honorius, Innocent, Eugenius, and Anastasius, Roman pontiffs—we decree that the order of canonical life which you have professed in that church shall be observed there perpetually, and we fortify that place, with all its appurtenances, under the protection of blessed Peter. Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods have been lawfully granted from their own right to that place by the noblemen Hermann and Wigmann, or by any of the faithful, and whatever may hereafter, God granting, be justly and canonically bestowed, shall remain forever firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. We also confirm for you, and through you for the church itself, by the strength of our favor, the tithes which Rembard, Otto, and Odelricus, bishops of Alberstadt, are known to have granted to your church. Upon the death of you, the present provost of that Church [Col. 0171D], or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any artifice of fraud or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall, according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine, determine ought to be elected.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain offerings, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be preserved whole and intact, for the full benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Alberstadt. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and a third time, unless he correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the last judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of St. Peter in Chains. I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina. I, Hubaldus, bishop of Asti. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and St. Rufina. I, Walter, bishop of Albano. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of St. Theodore. I, Boso, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

[Col. 0172C] Given at Dol by the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1162, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

XCIX. Receives under protection the monastery of St. Mary on the mountain called Wlrideshusen, and confirms its discipline, possessions, and privileges. (At Dol, September 20.)

[JAFFÉ, *Regesta Romanorum pontificum*, 688, “from Pertz’s notes.”]

C. To Louis, king of the Franks.—The castle of Flavigny is to be restored by Odo, duke of Burgundy, either to the king or to the bishop of Autun. (At Dol, September 22.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1015.]

[Col. 0172D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received the letter of your excellence with a mind all the more joyful and gracious, and took note of its tenor, because we understood more clearly that it proceeded from a purer constancy and a more fervent devotion of heart. For, having considered more carefully that firm and complete, memorable and praiseworthy devotion of royal serenity by which the most holy Roman Church receives from day to day great and most abundant increase [Col. 0173A], we have a ready mind and fervent will to love you, as a Catholic king and most Christian prince, with all the affection of our heart; daily to promote with earnest endeavors your honor, exaltation, and kingdom; and more willingly to grant your requests a favorable fulfillment, without prejudice to conscience.

Accordingly, at your royal request we have earnestly asked and commanded the nobleman Odo, duke of Burgundy, to surrender to your highness, or to [Henry], bishop of Autun, the castle of Flavigny, which he has unlawfully usurped and holds by violent occupation. Otherwise, we shall hold valid the sentence which that bishop may canonically pronounce against him and his land on this account, and we shall command the venerable brethren [Geoffrey], bishop of Langres, and [Peter], bishop of Chalon [Col. 0173B], to hold it valid and observe it without opposition.

Given at Dol, the tenth day before the Kalends of October.

CI. To Robert, bishop of Chartres.—Privilege for the Church of Chartres. (At Dol, September 24.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, VIII, Documents, 337.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother ROBERT, bishop of the people of Chartres, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Both the order of reason requires and regard for ecclesiastical advantage invites us to love our brethren and fellow bishops [Col. 0173C] with fuller charity, and more earnestly to fortify, under the protection of the Apostolic See, the Churches entrusted to their governance, so that in carrying out the office they have undertaken they may always be more watchful, the more secure they see themselves to remain from the assaults of the wicked. Therefore, venerable brother Robert, bishop in Christ, consenting graciously to your just requests and following the example of Pope Adrian, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the Church of Chartres, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside. We strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing that whatever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, God being favorable, be able to acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the abbey of St. Andrew; the toll; the rents; and the other possessions and revenues which you hold in the city of Chartres, together with its immunity. Likewise, Fraxinetum, Basoche, Bercherie, Chabloium, Ermenodivilla, Pont-Goeni, Balneolum, Mondonville, Tertre, Goderan, Spinterum Theclin, the Wood of St. Martin, Mungerdeville, Bussey, the Valley of Garengis [Col. 0174A], Caldum of St. Stephen, Loun, and Pont-Ebrard, with all the appurtenances of these villages; also the houses and fiefs, and all else belonging to the right and table of the Church of Chartres.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church; alienate in any way from the bishop’s table the aforesaid abbey and the remaining possessions; grant them in personal benefice; take them away, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations. Rather, let all things be preserved whole and intact, for the full benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving, of course, the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person [Col. 0174B], knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and a third time, unless he correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the last judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that same church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Dol by the hand of Norman, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [Col. 0174C], in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1162, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

The following subscribed this letter: Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem; Henry, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus; Albert, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina; William, cardinal priest of the title of St. Peter in Chains.

Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church; Hubaldus, bishop of Ostia; Bernard, bishop of Porto and St. Rufina; Walter, bishop of Albano; Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin; Odo, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison; Arditio, cardinal deacon of St. Theodore [Col. 0174D]; Boso, cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian; Cinthius, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian; John, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico.

CII. Privilege for the Church of St. Ambrose of Milan. (Tours, October 14.)

[FRIZI, *Memorie Storiche di Monza*, II, 63.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother OBERTO, archbishop of Milan, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

[Note: [Col. 0173D] Concerning this bull, addressed by Alexander III to Oberto I da Pirovano and published, with [Col. 0174D] several errors, by Dr. Sormani in his book *De anathemate contra Gallos*, pp. 232 ff., Count [Col. 0175C] Giulini writes in vol. VI, p. 299: “We have no bulls or diplomas older than this which show us precisely what and how extensive were the jurisdictions and estates of the archbishop of Milan, although we know that he was indeed very rich and powerful. The parchment which we now examine is therefore all the more important, because it indicates in detail everything which our archbishop then possessed.”]

[Col. 0175A] Placed, by the Lord’s disposition, in the exalted watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought, by virtue of the office of apostleship entrusted to us by the Lord, to honor our brethren and fellow bishops more earnestly, love them with sincere charity, and fortify under the protection of blessed Peter the places entrusted to their governance, so that they may be more diligent in carrying out their office the more secure and tranquil they are from the storms of worldly waves. Therefore, venerable brother Oberto, archbishop in Christ, graciously consenting to your just requests and following the example of Pope Adrian, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the Church of blessed Ambrose of Milan, over which, by the Lord’s authority, you are known to preside, and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing [Col. 0175B]. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by reasonable means and with God’s favor, acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

In the diocese of Turin: the abbey of St. Constantius with its chapels. In the city of Albenga: the church of Blessed Mary with its chapels. In the diocese of Asti: the Church of St. Peter of Mazano with its chapels, saving the annual payment to us and our successors of a rent of one gold piece. In the diocese of Albano: the parish church of St. Michael of Verduno with its chapels. In Bergulio: the monastery of St. Peter, and the churches of St. John and St. Stephen with their chapels. In the diocese of Vercelli: the parish church of blessed Ambrose of Fragrenedo, with its chapels.

[Note: [Col. 0175C] The parish church of Frassineto with its churches, then in the territory of Vercelli and now in Monferrato, is still subject to the archbishopric and diocese of Milan.]

In the diocese of Tortona: the abbey of St. Peter of Mola with its chapels. In the territory of Piacenza: the abbey of St. Saviour of Tolla with its chapels.

[Note: [Col. 0175C] Dr. Sormani omits the true name of this [Col. 0175D] abbey.]

The monastery of St. Calocerus of Clavate with its churches; the Church of St. John of Modoetia with its chapels; the abbey of the Holy Trinity of Buzizati with its chapels.

[Note: [Col. 0175D] A small settlement near Lake Varese, not far from which stood this abbey. It was subsequently built up with houses around it and was therefore distinguished from Buguzate by being called *capo di lago*, commonly Codelago.]

The monastery of the blessed martyrs Fininus and Gratianus of Arona with its churches; the monastery of Cremella; the monastery of Bernaga.

[Note: [Col. 0175D] Dr. Sormani writes *Binaga*, but the actual reading is *Bernaga*, a monastery in the parish district of Massaglia, also named by Gotofredo da Bussero: “the monastery of St. Gregory of Bernago.”]

The monastery of St. Victor of Modoetia.

[Note: [Col. 0175D] And not St. Saviour.]

In the diocese of Acqui: the monastery of St. Quintinus of Splegno; the monastery of St. Chrispina near Orona; the place called Sesto, with its district; lodging-right, fishing-right, right of inquiry (*quaeritura*), and other reasonable customary rights; and the chapels of St. Vincent.

[Note: [Col. 0175D] Sesto Calende, where the archbishop of Milan possessed many rights.]

Of St. Gregory of Busernago [Col. 0176B] and of St. Peter of Arcagnago, with their parishes and possessions.

[Note: [Col. 0175D] Arcognano, a locality in the parish district of St. Giuliano. Its neighboring church of St. Gregory, in the parish district of Segrate, is believed to be the one simultaneously named here. Count Giulini writes, in vol. VI, p. 302, under the year 1162, that several places in the Milanese [Col. 0176C] lost their ancient names and retained that of the saint to whom their church was dedicated; shortly he will adduce other entirely certain examples.]

The Genoese March, with four parish churches, namely Reuco, Auguxa, Rapallo, and Camuli, and their chapels, tithes, payments, district, and other reasonable rights. In the city of Genoa: a palace, with the chapel of blessed Ambrose, and a *brolium* [orchard/enclosed garden].

[Note: [Col. 0176C] That our archbishop had in Genoa a palace, a church dedicated to St. Ambrose, and an orchard is quite natural, because in the sixth and seventh centuries many of our prelates, together with a large part of the Milanese clergy, had their residence there and were buried there. But that he possessed the March—that is, the marquisate—of Genoa is highly noteworthy. There is no doubt that in the eleventh century Azzo, illustrious progenitor of the Este family, held by imperial investiture the March of Milan and the March of Genoa; and that, twenty-two years after the year with which we are now dealing, Emperor Frederick confirmed to Marquis Obizzo [Col. 0176D] d’Este all that his grandfather Marquis Azzo had already received from the Empire, and specifically the marquisate of Milan and the marquisate of Genoa. On the other hand, it is not likely that Pope Alexander wished to confirm to the metropolitan of Milan the marquisate of Genoa unless he had had sound claims over it; but what they were cannot now be guessed, because our archbishopric, owing to the fires, disasters, and ruin to which the city was subjected, has lost almost all its ancient records. Thus we would not even have this remarkable bull if the archive of Monza had not preserved it for us.]

In the diocese of Tortona: the bridge of Curione.

[Note: [Col. 0176D] Now Poncurone.]

With its district, lodging-right, and other reasonable rights; Coriana with its chapel.

[Note: [Col. 0176D] Coirana, or Corana, in the district of Pavia.]

Salvanum with its district and lodging-right.

[Note: [Col. 0176D] Probably Salvanegio, a proper name; Sormani printed it as *Salvaticum*.]

Casale with lodging-right and other lawful rights; Bergulium.

[Note: [Col. 0176D] In the preceding document: Bergulium. Near that locality the city of Alessandria was later built.]

With its district, lodging-right, and other reasonable rights; Leuca with its county; Modoetia with its district and other reasonable rights; [Col. 0176C] the banks of the Adda on both sides from Brivio to Cavenago; the banks of the Ticino on both sides from Sesto to Fara; and the place called Palanzzo near Como.

Furthermore, we likewise confirm by apostolic authority for you and your successors the coinage which Lothair, of illustrious memory, formerly king of the Romans, is known to have granted to blessed Ambrose, to Manasseh, your predecessor of pious memory, and to his successors for the good of his soul, as is contained in the privilege which he made concerning this matter [Col. 0177A].

[Note: [Col. 0177D] Mentioning in passing that Sormani read *pretam monetam*, we add that among the other rights of our archbishop omitted in this bull, one must note those which he held over the castles of San Giovanini in Sardinia, Carcano, Corbetta, Gajati, Angera, Brebbia, and Cassano on the Adda. The pontiff did not, however, omit the claims which the same archbishop held upon the mint of Milan, recalling its donor. A note added to the reverse of this parchment in a thirteenth-century hand informs us that the archive of Monza possessed two other bulls of the same tenor as the present one, now lost. The note says: “We have two other privileges of the same tenor, from Pope Celestine and Pope Innocent. The first: 1193, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, indiction XI; the other: 1199, the fifth day before the Kalends of May, indiction II.”]

Moreover, considering, dearest brother in Christ, the devotion of your person toward us, and wishing the reasonable and canonical customs of the Church of Milan to be preserved unimpaired hereafter, we decree that no city presently subject to the said Church of Milan by metropolitan right shall in future times be removed from it. It is therefore your concern in all these matters to appreciate the generosity of the Apostolic See and to respond to its grace with due benefits [Col. 0177B], and always to remain steadfast and immovable in the service of blessed Peter and in unity with your mother, the Holy Roman Church.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church of Milan, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations. Rather, let all things be preserved whole and intact for the full benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, having been warned a second or third time, should not correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction [Col. 0177C], let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the last judgment, to severe vengeance.

But upon all who preserve the rights of that Church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Tours by the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Ides of October, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0177D] 1162, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

CIII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of O., son of the nobleman C. Frangipani. (Tours, October 26.)

[MARTEN, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 677.]

[Col. 0178A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more steadfastly and fervently you persevere in devotion and love toward your mother, the most holy Roman Church, and toward us, the greater is the confidence in your breast that you will labor and strive with greater earnestness, by every means within your power, for the honor and advantage of that Church. Therefore, placing the greatest confidence in your diligence, we have entrusted to your discretion certain matters to be communicated to our beloved sons, the abbots of Fesniac and of L’Aumône, concerning the honor and advancement of the Church of God and of the highest importance to ourselves [Col. 0178B]. We ask that these matters be aided by your diligence and request that they be effectively advanced by your prudence. Let your devotion and prudence, then, endeavor to appear prompt and effective in this business of the Church of God, as in other matters, so that we too may owe your brotherhood the most abundant thanks.

[Note: [Col. 0178D] Fesniac was a notable monastery of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Laon, founded by Bishop Bartholomew in 1121. The monastery of La Charité was likewise founded by Count Theobald of Blois, in the diocese of Chartres.]

Furthermore, we ask that, should our beloved son, the nobleman O., son of the nobleman C. Frangipani, whom we are recalling from the German kingdom, come to you, you receive him kindly and treat him with such honor as befits both you and ourselves, and so that the young man may clearly recognize in this matter also the devotion which you have toward us [Col. 0178C].

Given at Tours [Note: [Col. 0178D] From this letter and those following, we infer that Alexander, after residing at Bourges during August and September, proceeded to Tours and spent the winter there. This is confirmed by a bull of the same pontiff issued at Tours in October 1162 for Marmoutier, in which he had consecrated, a few days earlier, the chapel of the sick in honor of St. Benedict. After the winter he went to Paris, whence he returned to Tours to hold a council. When this had ended, after the feast of St. Jerome he came to Sens, where he remained for a year and a half.] on the seventh day before the Kalends of November.

CIV. Confirms the excommunication pronounced by Ulrich, bishop of Halberstadt, against the provost of Rode and his associates, invaders of the goods of the Church of Kaltenborn. (Tours, October 29.)

[SCHOTTGEN and KREYSIG, *Diplomatarium*, II, 698.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren archbishops, bishops, abbots, provosts, and other ecclesiastical persons established throughout Germany to whom this letter shall come: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0178D] An ecclesiastical sentence canonically pronounced against certain wrongdoers for their offenses [Col. 0179A] ought to remain stable, and it is necessary that it retain the force of our confirmation until worthy satisfaction has been made. Therefore, we hold valid and firm the sentence of excommunication which our venerable brother Ulrich, bishop of Halberstadt, is known reasonably to have pronounced against the provost of Rhoden and his principal supporters, because he has with wicked audacity invaded the goods of the Church of Kaldenborn and refuses to restore them. By apostolic letters we command you to hold this sentence valid, firmly observe it, and cause it to be inviolably observed through your dioceses until worthy satisfaction has been made; nor are you in any way to presume to admit them to divine offices.

[Col. 0179B] Given at Tours, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November.

CV. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—On the business of the Roman pontiff. (Tours, November 1.)

[MARTEN, *Amplissima Collectio*, III, 678.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of the people of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As the Lord wills, we are about to send our venerable brother [Note: [Col. 0179D] Bernard, made cardinal by Eugenius III from being a regular canon, and a most steadfast defender of Alexander III’s party in the schism.] B., bishop of Porto, a man indeed honorable, learned, and religious, continually to the presence of our dearest son in Christ, Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, on the affairs of the Church. We have therefore judged that your devotion should be forewarned on this matter [Col. 0179C], holding such hope and confidence in you that we believe that whatever, at this time, is advantageous to the Church of God, especially in the regions of this kingdom, will be effectively advanced through your diligence.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we ask, admonish, and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord that you yourself go to the presence of the aforesaid king and earnestly attend and persist in obtaining from him what the aforesaid bishop will propose to him on our behalf. Through you also, whatever you learn to be advantageous to the Church of God and to ourselves, in accordance with the instruction which we have charged our beloved son Master W., bearer of the present letter, to convey to you on our behalf, endeavor, with the Lord’s help and with effect following, so to bring to completion [Col. 0179D] that we may render the fullest thanks to your brotherhood and may worthily commend in the Lord your diligence in all things.

Given at Tours, on the Kalends of November.

CVI. To Louis, king of the Franks.—Commends [Bernard], bishop of Porto, his envoy. (Tours, November 2.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1016.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son [Col. 0180A] in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The abundant affection of royal devotion and sincerity toward us and the Church of God has placed our mind in such confidence that, setting aside every doubt, we trust in you as the Church’s sole defender after God. We firmly presume from your magnificence that you will never, on any pretext, fail your mother, the Roman Church—you who, pre-eminent among the princes of the world as a ruler of justice and a lover of truth, have begun manfully to aid her cause. Accordingly, in her affairs and our own we resort all the more confidently to the counsel and help of your royal prudence, because we behold the constancy of your devotion and faith as though set visibly before the eyes of our mind [Col. 0180B].

Moved by the assurance of this security, we have judged it appropriate to send our venerable brother B., bishop of Porto, a man indeed industrious and discerning, to the royal presence on the affairs of the Church. We have preferred to entrust to him the communication of our will to you rather than convey it to your excellence by the present letters. Therefore, by apostolic letters we ask, admonish, and exhort your highness in the Lord to receive kindly our aforesaid brother, whom we hold dear and welcome beyond others, and to give him effective assent in those matters which he shall propose to the royal majesty on our behalf, so that the hope which, as we have said, depends after God upon your highness may attain a useful result in these matters [Col. 0180C] and may receive fuller growth in others. For if what he shall propose to your majesty is, the Lord willing, effectively accomplished, it will be all the more pleasing and welcome to us because through these things your mother, the most holy Roman Church, will receive a greater increase of peace and prosperity.

Given at Tours, on the fourth day before the Nones of November.

CVII. Bull for the monastery of Compiègne. (Tours, November 5.)

[*Gallia Christiana Nova*, X, Documents, 125.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ANSOLD, abbot of the monastery of St. Mary at Compiègne . . . etc., as in the bull of Eugenius III [Col. 0180D].

[Note: [Col. 0180D] *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXX, among the letters of Eugenius, no. 409.]

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the hospice situated at Compiègne; the church of St. Clement, called “the abbey”; the church of St. Maurice; the church of St. Germanus; the church of St. Peter; all chapels situated within the boundaries of Compiègne; and the church of the lepers of the same place. In the diocese of Beauvais: the altar-right of Venette, of Celles, of Longueil, of Canly, of Sacy with its viscounty, of Marest, and of Roy with its appurtenances. In the diocese of Amiens: the altar-right [Col. 0181A] of Faveroles, of Prunestre, of Mediovillari, of Bustellis, of Dolencort, and of Defferciis with its appurtenances. In the diocese of Soissons: the altar-right of Jauzy. We also decree that no archbishop or bishop . . .

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of St. Peter in Chains. I, Hubaldus, bishop of Ostia. [Col. 0181B] I, Walter, bishop of Albano. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of St. Theodore. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian. I, John, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico.

Given at Tours by the hand of Theodore, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of November, in the tenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1162 [Col. 0181C], and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

CVIII. To Louis VII, king of the Franks.—That he protect the monastery of Compiègne. (Tours, November 6.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1027.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

That we so confidently commend holy churches to your Highness, you should know proceeds from the consideration by which we recognize that you labour with especial zeal in matters pertaining to God. Hence it is that we have thought fit to commend to your clemency the monastery of Compiègne, and our beloved sons A., its abbot, and the brethren, there devoted to divine service by the institution of our father and predecessor of holy memory, Pope Eugenius, made with your assent and will, as of a Most Christian king who loves and defends religion. By these apostolic letters we ask, admonish, and exhort Your Royal Majesty in the Lord that, for reverence of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and for the sake of your own religion, you love, support, and honour them, and permit them to be harassed by no persons’ injuries; but rather constantly cherish and defend them in their rights, so that they may perceive that our prayers have benefited them, and you may expect abundant thanks from almighty God and from ourselves.

Given at Tours, 8 Id. November [6 November].

### CIX. Takes under protection and confirms the possessions of the Parthenon of St Mary in the Wood of Nide-Merli.

(Tours, 16 November.)—Only a notice of this privilege survives in Morice, *Mémoires pour servir à l’Histoire de Bretagne*, I, 598.

### CX. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of Letold, provost of Orléans.

(Tours, 16 November.)

[Marten., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 679.]

[Col. 0182B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son Letold, provost of Orléans, appearing in the presence of the Apostolic See, showed us in his complaint that the canons of Liège have for two years now unreasonably withheld from him the revenues of the prebend of St Lambert.

[Note: [Col. 0181] The cathedral church of Liège acknowledges St Lambert as its patron.]

Therefore, since we neither can nor ought to fail this provost in his right, we command your Fraternity by apostolic letters diligently to write to the aforesaid canons, admonishing and, if need be, threatening them, that, if this is so, they restore to him in full the fruits withheld [Col. 0182C] and henceforth by no means presume to trouble him regarding the revenues of that prebend. But if, though admonished and frightened by threats, they should perhaps refuse to do so, take from those revenues which certain of the aforesaid canons ought to collect within your archbishopric as much as is shown to have been unjustly taken from Letold out of his prebend by them.

Given at Tours, 16 Kal. December [16 November].

### CXI. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—Concerning letters to the Bishop of Arras, that he should provide for his soul.

(Tours, 28 November.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0182D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received with ready charity our beloved son, the abbot sent by you into our presence, showing him both the countenance and disposition which it befitted us to show to a religious man delegated to us by so venerable a brother. Accordingly, what he set before us orally on your behalf, and what the tenor of your letters likewise expressed, we immediately pursued effectively as was fitting: namely, writing [Col. 0183A] to that our brother, the Bishop of Arras,

[Note: [Col. 0183D] Namely Godescalc, who, having been made Bishop of Arras from abbot of Mont-Saint-Éloi, governed most holily, and is said to have resigned his episcopate in 1164.]

that, since he is burdened with illness and is known to be inadequate for his own administration, he should provide for his soul and endeavour to make more suitable provision for the Church. But concerning what was suggested to us on your behalf about admonishing the canons to hold an election, we did not think we should proceed so hastily, judging it wholly unfitting that, while he is still living and administering the Church entrusted to him, there should be discussion of another’s election. When, however, we are assured of his resignation, we shall, with the Lord’s help, proceed effectively in that matter according to the counsel of your discretion.

Moreover, we give you abundant thanks for the honourable visit of your distinguished devotion, asking, admonishing, and exhorting your Fraternity in the Lord by apostolic letters that, as you have commendably been accustomed to do, you devote vigilant attention to the welfare and advancement of the Church of God and of ourselves; and, diligently investigating German reports, make an effort frequently to inform us of them.

Given at Tours, 4 Kal. December [28 November].

### CXII. To Louis, King of the Franks.—He admonishes him concerning the holding of a council; other matters.

(Tours, 8 December.)

[Mansi, *Concil.*, XXI, 1017.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We took care to receive with due kindness our beloved sons Barbador and the knight who came with him into our presence, sent by your Highness; and we have endeavoured to answer them sufficiently, point by point, concerning the matters which they put before us on your behalf. The aforesaid envoys of your Magnificence will be able to tell you orally why we have not sent letters concerning these matters to your Serenity.

Furthermore, although we believe that through our venerable brother Maurice, Bishop of Paris, we have informed you both about the holding of a council and about our arrival in those regions, nevertheless, doubting lest this may perhaps not yet have come fully to your knowledge through the report of that bishop, we charged those same men to communicate it to the ears of [Col. 0183D] Your Serenity. Whatever, therefore, they report to your Highness concerning this, you cannot doubt proceeds from our intention.

Given at Tours, 6 Id. December [8 December].

### CXIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On the removal of the abbots of St Mary and St Wulmar and the intrusion of secular canons.

(Tours, 10 December.)

[Marten., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 680.]

[Col. 0184A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When we consider inwardly how unjustly and outrageously

[Note: [Col. 0183D] Matthew, Count of Boulogne, on whom see the note to the following letter.]

M., son of the Count of Flanders, removed our beloved sons, the abbots of St Mary

[Note: [Col. 0183D] St Mary and St Wulmar were two abbeys of regular canons of the Order of St Augustine in the city of Boulogne. The first, after the Morini had been destroyed by Emperor Charles V, was converted into a cathedral church; the other passed to the priests of the Oratory. There is also another monastery of the Order of St Benedict, called St Wulmar of the Wood, in the same diocese.]

and St Wulmar with their brethren from their churches and intruded secular canons into them, we are struck and repeatedly distressed by profound sorrow at their misery. [Col. 0184B] But because the aforesaid M. and the canons, though repeatedly admonished by our authority to desist from so great a wickedness, have added worse things to their former acts and have by no means laid aside the poison of their malice, our venerable brother, the Bishop of Thérouanne, has canonically pronounced a sentence of excommunication against them on this account. Holding this sentence to be valid, we command your Fraternity by apostolic letters that, since those with whom the Roman pontiff does not communicate ought not to be communicated with by your Fraternity either—as it is written, “Those with whom this Clement does not communicate, do not communicate with them either”—you diligently avoid the aforesaid M. and the canons as excommunicated persons and perverse invaders of churches [Col. 0184C], and cause them to be more diligently avoided throughout your whole archbishopric. You should also strive effectively to give the aforesaid abbots both your counsel and assistance, so that they may be able to recover their churches.

Given at Tours, 4 Id. December [10 December].

### CXIV. To the same.—Concerning Matthew, Count of Boulogne, who had married a nun and expelled two abbots from regular churches.

(Tours, 18 December.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0184D] We believe you know in full and manifest truth how

[Note: [Col. 0184D] This is Matthew, son of Theodoric, Count of Flanders, concerning whom the ancient author of the *Genealogy of the Counts of Flanders*, vol. III of the *Anecdota*, no. 15, says: “Matthew, however, commendable for bodily beauty and military prowess, since the principality of Flanders had, as is customary, passed by right to his elder brother, at his father’s compulsion took in marriage Mary, daughter of Stephen, King of England. She, initiated from childhood into the religious habit, since she remained the sole heiress of the county of Boulogne, was brought out of the cloister and, with the pope’s assent, was joined in marriage to Matthew in order to provide legitimate heirs to her paternal inheritance [Col. 0185D]. After she had borne him two daughters, he restored the nun to the cloister and again took as wife the sister of the Countess of Flanders,” etc. But the assertion of this author that Matthew married Mary with the pope’s assent is proved false by this letter.]

M., son of our beloved son, the noble Count of Flanders, joined to himself, wholly wickedly and unlawfully, a nun dedicated to God and consecrated as an abbess, to the danger of his soul. Although he ought to have made satisfaction to God, whom he had offended, for [Col. 0185A] so great an iniquity, he heaped sin upon sin: he violently expelled two abbots of Boulogne and their brethren, regular men who fear God, from their churches; and, having intruded certain dissolute men into them, he wickedly compelled the aforesaid regulars into exile. Therefore, when you came into those parts, you ought diligently to have corrected this wrongdoing; but, as is said, you left it uncorrected and unremedied, out of inability, as we believe, rather than deliberately.

Since, therefore, by the Lord’s ordering, we are established in a position in which we ought both to correct wrongful things and endeavour to strengthen what is pleasing to the Lord, we earnestly admonish and command your Fraternity by apostolic letters that you diligently admonish the aforesaid [Col. 0185B] count not to support him in this wickedness on any ground, but, so far as lies in his power, not delay to correct him concerning this as soon as possible: so that, when those excommunicated clerics have been expelled, the aforesaid religious may be able freely to return to their churches and serve the Lord there in peace. Otherwise, he must fear lest divine vengeance be exacted severely upon him and his whole land, and lest the holy Church of God be unable any longer to overlook this.

Given at Tours, 15 Kal. January [18 December].

### CXV. To the same.—Concerning W.’s case regarding a prebend of the church of Châlons.

(Tours, 20 December.)

[Marten., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, col. 682.]

[Col. 0185C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Moved alike by the age of W., bearer of the present letters, and by the long duration of the labour he endured for a prebend of the church of Châlons, and since we could not with a clear conscience provide for him in that prebend itself, because it is known to have been adjudged away from him by our beloved sons Henry and Odd., cardinals of the Holy Roman Church and then legates of the Apostolic See, we commanded the provost, dean, and whole chapter of that Church to endeavour mercifully to provide the boy, in recompense for such labours and expenses, with some compensation [Col. 0185D] from which he might receive worthy consolation. Therefore we command your Fraternity by apostolic letters that, if they should perhaps neglect to do this, you must by no means allow this, but compel them, supported by our authority, to do it.

Given at Tours, 13 Kal. January [20 December].

### CXVI. To the same.—Concerning the Bishop of Orléans.

(Tours, 20 December.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0186A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We remember both having seen and known you in person on a former occasion; and we think that later you have understood more fully, from the report of our beloved son Henry, the abbot who is staying with you and whom we charged to tell you this, how our dearest son in Christ Louis, the illustrious King of the Franks, has urgently interceded with us on behalf of that Bishop of Orléans
