[Note: [Col. 0185D] The bishop then seated in the church of Orléans was Manasses de Garlande, who had succeeded Elias, when the latter voluntarily resigned, about [Col. 0186D] the year 1146. Whether this letter of Alexander concerns him or rather Elias, who could still have been alive when the pope was at Tours in 1162, is not sufficiently clear. Certainly, the king’s intercession with the pontiff, that he should not be compelled to relinquish the episcopate, proves that Louis was favourably disposed toward Elias.]

and has taken care to repeat his entreaties for [Col. 0186B] him both orally and also through frequent envoys. Following the example of our fathers and predecessors, who took care always to love him with inward charity, to receive his wishes and petitions, and to grant them more readily, we have resolved to comply with him in all matters in which we can do so consistently with God and honour; especially since he has the counsel of our brethren that we ought not to be unduly reluctant to grant him assent even in certain matters known to be burdensome to us.

Know, however, that up to now we have awaited your counsel and will on this subject, so that, just as we have recognized that you have burned fiercely against the same Bishop of Orléans, as though he had sinned particularly against you, [Col. 0186C] we may also see more clearly the judgment of your conscience as to whether it is appropriate and deserved to deal with him dispensatorily in these days at the so earnest prayers of so great a prince. By the import of the present letter, therefore, we have thought fit to request the industry of your discretion concerning these matters, so that what occupies the secret recesses of your counsel may swiftly be expressed to us in the letters of your Fraternity. It seems to us, moreover, that you too ought to incline your mind and will to this, since the efforts of the others appear to agree in yielding in this matter to the aforesaid king.

Furthermore, we wish you to know that, if it can be done without serious difficulty, we desire to have you present after the approaching feast of Christmas has passed.

Given at Tours, 13 Kal. January [20 December].

### CXVII. To Louis VII, King of the Franks.—That P., a knight wishing to go to Jerusalem, may sell his possessions without his wife’s consent.

(Tours, 23 December.)

[Mansi, *Concil.*, XXI, 996.]

[Col. 0186D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest [Col. 0187A] son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your Magnificence ought alike to defend and foster with pious protection those who, taking up the cross, intend to visit the holy and venerable places which the Lord made illustrious by his bodily presence, and there to serve as soldiers against the enemies of the cross of Christ the Lord. P., a knight and bearer of the present letters, coming into the presence of our apostolate, placed his vow before us and steadfastly asserted that he wishes to go to Jerusalem. But because his wife has behaved shamefully and dishonourably toward him, and keeps away from him because of her guilt for a crime committed, he cannot sell or pledge his paternal inheritance without her consent, and is wholly unable to carry out his intended journey. [Col. 0187B] Since, however, his wife has, as is said, defiled the marriage-bed by adultery, provided that he wishes to live continently, he is under no compulsion whatever to return to her. We ask and exhort Your Serenity in the Lord by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you make it lawful for him, for the love of God, to sell his possessions to whomever he wishes or pledge them; and that you do not permit any injury or harassment to be unjustly inflicted concerning this upon those to whom he has sold or pledged them.

Given at Tours, 10 Kal. January [23 December].

### CXVIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—Concerning heretical burgesses and persons corrupted in faith.

(Tours, 23 December.)

[Marten., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 683.]

[Col. 0187C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received rather harshly, as seemed fitting, those heretical burgesses and persons corrupted in the doctrine of the faith, against whom your Fraternity sent letters of its own to our presence; and we showed them the severity which it is fitting for us to show to men of such a kind. Yet the prudence of your discretion should know that it is safer and the lesser evil [Col. 0187D] to absolve persons who are guilty and ought to be condemned than to condemn the lives of innocent persons by ecclesiastical severity; and that it is better for ecclesiastical men to be more lenient even than is proper than to be, and appear, excessively severe in correcting vices. Scripture indeed bears witness, saying: “Do not be excessively righteous,” and elsewhere: “He who squeezes too hard draws out blood.” But, desiring to defer to you, as to our dearest son, both in these matters and in all others in which we can do so according to God, and to honour your person more readily, we shall shortly write back to your Fraternity, with the Lord’s help, concerning what we ought to decide in this matter by the counsel of our brethren.

Given at Tours, 10 Kal. January [23 December].

### CXIX. Confirms the rights of Stephen, Bishop of Meaux.

(Tours.)

[Du Plessis, *Histoire de l’Église de Meaux*, II, proofs, p. 51.]

[Col. 0188A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother STEPHEN, Bishop of Meaux, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

Established, by the Lord’s ordering, in the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, etc. . . . . Therefore, dearest brother Stephen in Christ, making salutary provision for the Church of Meaux, whose care has been committed to you by God, after the example of our father and predecessor of holy memory, Pope Honorius, we decree that all clerics and laypersons dwelling in the towns of Rebais and Jouarre [Col. 0188B] shall be subject to the Church of Meaux by parochial right, and that those things which pertain to parochial right from them shall remain free and unimpaired to you and your successors. We also decree that the Abbot of Rebais and the Abbess of Jouarre shall render canonical obedience to you and your successors. Their blessing likewise shall henceforth be conferred by you and your successors, just as it is established to have been conferred hitherto by your predecessors. The promotion of monks to ecclesiastical orders shall also be administered through the Bishop of Meaux, provided that he is willing to confer them freely and without misconduct, and enjoys the favour of the Apostolic See. But if anyone with rash boldness, etc. . . . .

[Col. 0188C] Given at Tours, in the year of the Lord 1162.

### CXX. To John, Bishop of St Malo.—He confirms to him the church of St Malo, once an episcopal see, restored to him by Eugenius III and Anastasius IV.

[D. Bouquet, *Recueil des historiens*, vol. XV, p. 791.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JOHN, Bishop of St Malo, and to his successors, etc.

As is equitable, etc. Pope Lucius, our predecessor of happy memory, received the complaint of your Fraternity against the monks of Marmoutier, namely that they were unlawfully holding the church of St Malo of the Island, which in the time of your predecessors had been an episcopal see. He summoned them to the judgment of the Apostolic See, prepared fully to answer your petition on this matter. In the meantime, Lucius was removed from the hazards of human frailty by the decree of the divine will; and Eugenius of blessed memory, who succeeded him in the ministry of the apostolate by the Lord’s ordering, heard the case diligently when both you and the monks were present in the court of the Apostolic See, and learned the claims of each party by full inquiry. Since, in order to prove that the same church had been an episcopal see, you produced three lawful witnesses in his presence, the aforesaid monks objected that two of them were not lawful, and said that they would prove this lawfully in those parts. Therefore, although they had been summoned by our above-named predecessor Pope Lucius [Col. 0189A] to come adequately prepared to answer you, yet, lest they might reasonably complain of prejudice done them, our aforesaid predecessor Pope Eugenius judged that both parties should be remitted to the discretion of our venerable brethren Geoffrey, Archbishop of Bordeaux, Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, and Lambert, Bishop of Angoulême. By his letters he commanded them that, if you could lawfully prove in the presence of the other party—unless that party perhaps contumaciously absented itself—that the same church had been an episcopal see by two or three witnesses, they should receive those witnesses, all appeal set aside, and invest you by apostolic authority with that church and all the possessions which it possessed at the time when it was given to the monks.

As clearly appeared from their letters, they summoned both parties before them at Périgueux for a fixed date. On the appointed day and at the appointed place, both you and Garnerius, abbot of Marmoutier, appeared. Yet, while you were awaiting the appointed date, the aforesaid abbot would not wait even one day; nor did he put forward any canonical excuse either personally or through his representatives. Rather, leaving no advocate there on his behalf, he contumaciously absented himself, like one who distrusted the merits of his case. Since the above-named brethren of ours had received a command from the Apostolic See to execute this within two months, lest they appear transgressors of the apostolic command [Col. 0189C], and since they had learned through religious men that public report in those regions held the same church to have been an episcopal see in ancient times, they carefully examined three priests from among the many witnesses whom you had brought with you and whom you had earlier presented to the oft-mentioned abbot and his monks. Having taken the advice of religious and prudent men, they received them; and, touching the most holy Gospels, the priests swore that they had heard and seen that the aforesaid church of St Malo, concerning which the dispute existed, had been an episcopal see. The witnesses having thus been received and sworn, those same brethren invested you, in accordance with the command of our aforesaid predecessor, with the church of St Malo and all the possessions which it had when it was given to the monks. Therefore, once the matter had been heard and established, that same predecessor imposed perpetual silence in this case upon those monks, and confirmed by apostolic authority both this investiture and whatever had been done in this matter by our aforesaid brethren.

After our predecessor Pope Anastasius succeeded him in the office of the apostolate, the aforesaid monks came to the Apostolic See and renewed their complaint against you on this subject, causing you to appear before the hearing of that same predecessor, Anastasius. Although perpetual silence had been imposed upon them, when both you and they stood in his court, he ordered both your documents and theirs to be produced before him. Having heard and understood them with his brethren, he judged their documents on this point to possess no force; and, by the will and counsel of the brethren, following the example of the oft-mentioned Pope Eugenius, he imposed perpetual silence upon them, removing from them and their successors every power to harass you or your successors with renewed litigation on this matter. He confirmed the prescribed judgment by apostolic authority and decreed that it should remain firm and unimpaired for all time.

Confirming the same judgment, Pope Anastasius decreed that the canonical order, known to have been established there by your efforts and by the counsel of the oft-mentioned Pope Eugenius, with the Lord as author, according to the Rule of blessed Augustine and the observance of the brethren of St Victor, should be observed there inviolably for all time. The bishop who is to be ordained there at any given time shall be elected by the brethren of that church from their own congregation, or from another regular congregation of their profession, according to canonical enactments. Nor shall anyone be established as archdeacon in that same bishopric of St Malo, by any artifice of surreption or by force, unless he is a regular canon. We too, following the example of our aforesaid predecessors, confirm to you and your successors by apostolic authority the same things which they confirmed by their privileges. Furthermore, whatever possessions, etc.

## YEAR 1163

### CXXI. Privilege for the monastery of St Mary and St Botolph at Thorney.

(Tours, 9 January.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, I, 249.]

[Col. 0190C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HEREBERT, abbot of the church of St Mary and St Botolph of Thorney, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the religious life, in perpetuity.

The authority of the Apostolic See, which by the Lord’s gift we serve, and the unity of brotherly charity exhort us to assent to the just desires of religious persons and mercifully grant their reasonable petitions. [Col. 0190D] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just requests and take under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid Church, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future, God being favourable, acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Namely, the island of Thorney, on which the monastery itself is situated, with woodland, marshland, and all its appurtenances [Col. 0191A]; the church of Whittlesey; the church of Stanground; the church of Yaxley; the church of Woodston; the church of Haddon; the church of Newton; the church of Stibbington; the church of Twywell; the church of Bolnhurst and the church of Gybaldon, with one hide of land, the tithes of that village, and all offerings; the church of St George of Thetford; two churches of Deeping; the church of Fletton; and whatever right you possess in the church of Wansford. In Cambridgeshire: Whittlesey, and all the reasonable customs which the church of Ely had in its hundreds of Witchford from the land and men of Thorney; the church of Whittlesey, excepting the proper royal customs which may arise concerning that land, which Hervey, first Bishop of Ely, with the assent of his chapter, reasonably bestowed upon your church in alms on the day of that church’s dedication.

In Huntingdonshire: Newton, Woodston, Yaxley, and the market of that village, with sake and soke, toll and team, and infangentheof, with all customs appurtenant to it; half the lake called Whittlesmere; Stanground; Farcet; Haddon; Sibson, with two and a half hides; and, in Stibbington, five virgates belonging to Sibson, and the tithe of one ploughland in Sibson; in Stibbington, Roger’s tithe; in the village called Covington, six hides; in the meadow of Stanton, twenty-eight acres [Col. 0191C] held from various persons; in Coppedthorn, fourteen acres of land and the meadow belonging to that land; in the village called Huntingdon, two houses and the lands on which those houses stand; the right which you have in the church of All Saints from the market of that village; the tithe of Wido son of Goscelin in Chesterton; in Fulkeworth, two and a half virgates of land, and other land in the same village yielding eight shillings annually; by the gift of Andrew Revell, fifteen acres which he gave in alms for himself and all his kinsfolk, living and dead.

In Hampshire: Fawley, two hides and a mill; land in Luffwick. Likewise, in the aforesaid village, half a virgate of land and ten acres of inland; one hide in Rande with its rent, namely twelve shillings; half a hide in Charwelton; the land of Pipewell, given by William d’Aubigny the Breton; and, at Stoke, one ploughland of the demesne of the same village, with its toft, meadow, and all common rights in wood, open land, and pastures. By the gift of Alberic of Fawley, two sheaves of the tithes of six ploughlands in three villages, namely Islip, Drayton, and Addington.

In Warwickshire: Salcebrigg with its appurtenances; one virgate of land in Wolfhamcote; and the mill of Ryton. The service of Edric of Fleckenho with his land, namely five acres in the field and three and a half crofts in the village.

In Bedfordshire: two and a half hides in Bolnhurst; at Wilden, two virgates of land [Col. 0192A] with the men who hold them; at Bedford, one house and the land belonging to it. Likewise, in Norfolk, in the village called Tuameres, one small plot yielding five shillings. Likewise, half of the village called Wenge and half the mill of that village. Moreover, one villein, named Norman, with his land, namely one virgate in the aforesaid village. Likewise, ten shillings from the rent of the mill of Feseburge, with half of whatever increase it may produce. Fishing rights at Welle, Elme, Fillinga, and Frillinga; likewise land at Stamford; likewise the hermitage of Frokenholt; the land which you have in Etune; the land which you have in Fid. By the gift of the Count of Clare, a rent of one hundred shillings promised under oath. By the gift of Hugh son of Ralph of Wildenboef, one virgate of land, and the liberty which blessed Æthelwold, bishop and founder of the aforesaid monastery, with the favour of King Edgar and of holy Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury, Oswald, Archbishop of York, and all the other bishops, abbots, and barons of all England, granted to that place and confirmed by his own written instrument.

Moreover, no one whatsoever shall presume to exact tithes from you of your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the fodder of your animals. Upon the death of the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any deceit or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

We decree, therefore, that no person at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact and serve in every way the needs of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted—saving, of course, the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he corrects his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him recognize himself answerable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subjected to strict vengeance. But to all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Tours, by the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 5 Id. January [9 January], in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0193A] 1162; in the fourth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

### CXXII. To Louis, King of the Franks.—Concerning those accused of heresy in the regions of Flanders.

(Tours, 11 January.)

[Marten., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 684.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received with due kindness the letters sent to us by your Highness concerning the affair of those who are accused of heresy in the regions of Flanders. Having carefully examined their contents, we have thought it proper to inform your Excellence that, when certain of them had presented themselves before us with many letters, asserting themselves to be entirely free from every heretical perversity, we wished to send them, with our letters, for judgment before our venerable brother Henry, Archbishop of Rheims. Since they refused to go to him, two of them departed without letters, while the others have remained with us until now, unwilling for any reason to return, but preferring to be judged by us in a just judgment. Yet, since it is always our purpose and intention to follow your counsel in everything which we can carry out with God and justice, we have not been willing, on any account, to hear them, nor shall we hear them in any way, until we have more fully received your counsel, that of the aforesaid archbishop, and that of other religious men [Col. 0193C] concerning this matter. For it is our will and purpose, as we have said, to accept in all things the counsel of your Sublimity, to attend vigilantly with earnest concern to your honor and advancement, and more readily to heed and in all things honor you, as our dearest son and foremost lord and defender of the Church.

Given at Tours, 3 Ides of January [11 January].

### CXXIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—Concerning Drogo, canon of Saint Timothy. (Tours, 12 January.)

[**Ibid.**, 685.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Drogo, deacon and canon of the church of the holy martyrs [Note: [Col. 0193D] Saints Timothy and Apollinaris at Rheims are a college of twelve canons founded by the abbot of Saint Remigius.] Timothy and Apollinaris, appearing before us, lodged in our court the complaint that Milo, cleric of Largeriac, and the servants of the wife of Baldwin, a knight, acting on the advice of the same Milo, violently threw him from his horse; and that those same servants, together with Hervey the priest, after an appeal had been made to us, presumptuously took the produce of a certain piece of his land at Musion and the horse which he is known to have been riding. They refuse to make satisfaction for the injury inflicted and to restore what was taken.

Therefore, because we neither ought nor can leave uncorrected an offense of such presumption, we command your Fraternity by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you declare those who threw the aforesaid cleric from his horse excommunicated until they restore what was taken, make satisfaction for so great an offense, and present themselves before us. But summon strictly the others who presumed, after the appeal to us, to take the aforesaid produce, so that they either restore in full everything taken or provide him complete justice. If they should perhaps refuse to do so, constrain them to carry this out by ecclesiastical censure.

[Col. 0194B] Given at Tours, 2 Ides of January [12 January].

### CXXIV. To Louis, King of the French.—That he protect a certain poor man. (Tours, 19 January.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1004.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious King of the French, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The eminent clemency of piety has always been accustomed to have compassion upon the oppressed and the poor, and to be moved in spirit by their misery, knowing that it is written: “Blessed is he who understands the needy and poor” (Psalm 40). Moved therefore by this consideration and overcome by the tearful entreaty of this poor man M., bearer of the present letter, who complains that he endures harassment and injuries concerning his possessions from certain more powerful men of yours, we earnestly ask your royal Excellence and your customary piety that, for the love of God, in the interest of justice, and at our intervention, you defend him by royal protection from his adversaries, by whom he declares himself oppressed and burdened, and keep him free from their injury. Thus you may expect from him who, though rich, undertook our poverty in order to free us, an eternal reward.

Given at Tours, 14 Kalends of February [19 January].

### CXXV. To the Abbot of Château-Landon.—That he permit the Victorines peacefully to possess their annual revenues in the church of Saint Saviour. (Tours, 22 January.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, VI, 232.]

[Col. 0194D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Château-Landon [Note: [Col. 0193D] It is commonly called *Castrum-Nantonis*, although in French it is pronounced Château-Landon. It is a monastery of regular canons in the diocese of Sens, founded originally for monks by Saint Severinus in the time of King Clovis.], greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of the office entrusted to us exhorts us diligently to uphold every one of God’s faithful, and especially religious men, in their rights, and to preserve wholly intact and unimpaired what belongs to them. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your Belovedness [Col. 0195A] to permit the abbot and brothers of Saint Victor of Paris, our beloved sons, peacefully and quietly to possess the annual revenues which they are known to have possessed canonically for a long time in the church of Saint Saviour, until you reach an agreement with them concerning these matters. Or, if you are confident of your right, contend with them by lawful examination before a judge chosen by both parties, or even with our assistance.

Given at Tours [Note: [Col. 0195D] Alexander III came to Tours in October 1162 and remained there for three months or more [Col. 0196D]. He then came to Paris, and afterwards, returning to Tours, held a council there.], 11 Kalends of February [22 January].

### CXXVI. To [Guy], Elect of Châlons.—Concerning the case of the church of Saint Remigius and G. de Joinville. (Paris, 10 February.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 685.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother G., elect of Châlons, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The abbot and brothers of the church of Saint Remigius at Rheims, our beloved sons, have informed us that Geoffrey of Joinville, your parishioner, unjustly took from them the village called Curcelles and refuses to restore it. Therefore, since we neither can nor ought to fail that church in its right, we command your Discretion by apostolic letters diligently to summon the said Geoffrey within twenty days after receipt of these letters, so that he either restore the said village without difficulty to the aforesaid abbot and brothers or, in your presence, provide them without delay [Col. 0195C] complete justice. If he should perhaps refuse to do either, restrain him by ecclesiastical censure.

Given at Paris, 4 Ides of February [10 February].

### CXXVII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—For the church of Saint Remigius concerning a certain tract of land. (Paris, 11 February.)

[**Ibid.**, 686.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The abbot and brothers of the church of blessed Remigius at Rheims, our beloved sons, laid a complaint before us, asserting that Witter of Sarnay, your parishioner, took a certain tract of land from them and refuses to restore it. Therefore, since we neither can nor ought to fail that church in its right, we command your Discretion by apostolic letters diligently to summon the said W. within twenty days after receipt of these letters, so that he either restore the aforesaid land without difficulty to the aforesaid abbot and brothers, or in your presence provide them without delay with justice. If he should perhaps refuse to do either, restrain him by ecclesiastical censure.

Moreover, we also command your Discretion diligently to admonish and summon the count of Grandpré, who, as we are told, presumes to withhold thirty shillings every year from the aforesaid brothers [Col. 0196A], so that he restore that money to them and henceforth cease withholding it, or provide them with the fullness of justice in your presence; otherwise, do not delay to exercise strict justice upon him.

Given at Paris, 3 Ides of February [11 February].

### CXXVIII. To the same.—Concerning M., a moneylender of Châlons. (Paris, 19 February.)

[**Ibid.**]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0196B] O., bearer of the present letter, appearing before us, showed us in his complaint that M. of Châlons wickedly compels him to pay excessive interest, contrary to the prohibition of the New and Old Testaments. Although he has already repaid him almost twice the principal, M. still demands something further and presumes unjustly to harass him for payment. Therefore, because we neither can nor ought to pass over without inquiry the audacity of such presumption, we command your Fraternity by apostolic letters, if this is so, to restrain him strictly, without appeal, so that henceforth he does not dare to harass this man concerning the matter.

Given at Paris, 11 Kalends of March [19 February].

### CXXIX. To the same.—For P. Lapillus. (Paris, 19 February.)

[**Ibid.**, 687.]

[Col. 0196C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

P. Lapillus by name, bearer of the present letter, appearing before the Apostolic See, lodged a complaint against P. of Châlons, his father-in-law. He asserts that, while he was at Jerusalem, this same father-in-law unjustly took the proceeds of his possessions and presumed unlawfully to occupy them against the will of his father, to whom he had entrusted the preservation of his own goods. Having at last returned, he made an agreement, as he asserts, with that same [Col. 0196D] father-in-law: the latter was to compensate him for the proceeds received with six and a half pounds in Châlons currency and certain other things. When he demanded performance of the agreement, the other denied that such an agreement had been made. Accordingly, M., his brother, who had undertaken to prosecute the case, was before you to provide justice, as we have learned from your own letters; but the father-in-law appealed to our hearing in order to evade judgment, and then neglected to pursue that appeal.

Therefore, since we neither can nor ought to fail P. in his right, we commit the case to your Discretion to hear and, with the appeal set aside, to bring to its due conclusion. We command your Fraternity by apostolic letters, therefore, to summon both parties before you and, having carefully heard and considered the arguments on both sides, decide that case with justice as your guide.

Given at Paris, 11 Kalends of March [19 February].

### CXXX. Privilege for the monastery of Fontevraud. (Paris, 27 February.)

[NIQUET, *History of the Order of Fontevraud*, p. 415.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all venerable bishops in whose bishoprics monasteries of Fontevraud are established, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0197B] It is altogether fitting and necessary for us to attend diligently to the welfare of all God’s faithful, and we are especially bound to make provision with every care for religious persons in matters pertaining to God. Therefore, lest our beloved daughters in Christ, the sisters of Fontevraud, be deprived of the sacrament of consecration of their virgins through long waiting for the feasts of the Apostles, we command all of you by apostolic letters that, whenever the abbess of the same order, or her vicar, presents her sisters to any of you for reception of this sacrament, he is in no way to defer it on account of an apostolic feast; rather, if no feast of an Apostle occurs, he shall bestow the gift of consecration upon those sisters who are otherwise worthy on any Sunday [Col. 0197C].

Given at Paris, 3 Kalends of March [27 February].

### CXXXI. To all the clergy and people in the German kingdom: he writes that he has appointed Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, legate for the purpose of combating schism. (Paris, 28 February.)

[HANSIZIUS, *Germania Sacra*, vol. II, p. 273.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the bishops, and beloved abbots, provosts, and other prelates of churches, and to all clergy and people established in the German kingdom and remaining in the unity of the Church, greeting and [Col. 0197D] apostolic blessing.

Placed, by the Lord’s disposal, upon the watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought so to extend the gaze of our concern over the whole body of the Church that, in the case of those whom we ourselves cannot visit in person, we are shown to exercise care and solicitude through others in whom we have complete confidence. Accordingly, being solicitous for you—as devoted sons, special members of the Church, and with the concern due from paternal affection for your salvation [Col. 0198A]—we appoint as legate in the German kingdom our venerable brother Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, a man distinguished in religion, learning, and integrity. Since at present we cannot attend to you either ourselves or through persons sent from our side, we have thought fit to entrust our office to him for the present, so that, exercising there the office of legation by our authority, he shall have full power to call back to the unity of the Church and to full devotion to us those polluted by the perversity of schism. It shall also be lawful for him, as legate of the Apostolic See, to summon you before him, investigate cases that arise, and bring them to their due conclusion.

Therefore, by apostolic letters [Col. 0198B], we command you all to show him the reverence and obedience due to a legate of the Apostolic See; when summoned by him, to appear before him; and firmly to accept and observe whatever he judges ought to be established for the honor of God and of the Holy Roman Church.

Given at Paris, on the Kalends of March [1 March].

### CXXXII. To Louis VII, King of the French.—He sends him the golden rose. (Paris, 2 March.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1031.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious King of the French [Col. 0198C], greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is known to have proceeded from an institution of the Roman pontiffs that, in mid-Lent, on the Sunday upon which *Laetare Jerusalem* is sung, they customarily carry in their own hands every year a golden flower [Note: [Col. 0197D] The flower which Alexander here calls a “flower” is commonly called the golden rose. The rite in which the Roman pontiff carries the golden rose amid the sacred mysteries on the fourth Sunday of Lent, and then presents it to some prince as a memorial of good will, is also recorded in the letter of Eugenius III to Alfonso, King of Spain. Eugenius there says that this is done as a sign of Christ’s Passion and Resurrection. See also extracts from the *Life of Pope Alexander III* in Baronius under the year 1177, no. XVIII, and the *History of Vézelay*, book IV.], not for the sake of temporal exaltation but in the recurring annual observance—thereby signifying matters which are known to pertain both to the adornment of the Church and to the instruction of the faithful.

Accordingly, when we, following in the footsteps of those same predecessors of ours, recently carried a like flower in our hands on the appointed day, we found no one to whom we ought so worthily to offer such a flower as to your Excellence, whom we know to excel both in devotion toward the Church of God and toward ourselves, and in the honor of your rank [Col. 0198D]. Since we believe that your Highness desires to learn from our exposition the significance of this flower all the more gladly because you are plainly known to adhere more fervently in heart and deed to divine services and pious works, let the wisdom of your royal Serenity recognize that this flower represents and signifies Christ the King, who speaks of himself, saying: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” [Col. 0199A] (Song of Songs 2).

For gold is rightly said to denote a king, since it was figuratively offered by the Magi to the Savior in order that thereby he might be shown as King of kings and Lord of lords. The redness with which the gold is colored and suffused signifies the Passion of the Redeemer, concerning whom it is written: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (Isaiah 63). And again: “Why is your garment red, and your clothing like that of one treading in the winepress?” (ibid.). The fragrance of this flower prefigures the glory of his Resurrection: just as he, the firstborn of the dead among many brethren, rising from the dead can no longer be held by the bonds of death, by which, in dying, he destroyed our death and, in rising, restored life to the glory of immortality.

Indeed, this world’s winding regions and climes, encrusted with the foulness of every crime, have been so sprinkled with the mighty fragrance of the Lord’s Resurrection that no part of the world perceives itself alien to or deprived of this fragrance. Rather, all rejoice that by this most sweet odor they have now overcome the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places [Col. 0199B]. Moreover, in order figuratively to signify Christ’s very Resurrection, those holy women brought spices to the tomb, prefiguring its glory through the sweetness of fragrant ointments. That Resurrection brought terror to hell, joy to heaven, and holiness to earth.

These, dearest son in Christ, are the things which you should know to be figured in this flower, so that it may be held all the more acceptable and pleasing by you as you have learned, through its threefold meaning, to love it more affectionately and revere it more sincerely. We ask, and desire with all our hearts, that the golden flower who surpasses all kings and princes—indeed, through whom kings reign and the wise set forth justice—may by his ineffable mercy preserve your earthly kingdom for a long time and mercifully bestow upon you the eternal kingdom in that blessed recompense of the righteous.

### CXXXIII. To the same.—The king had asked the pope to relax an interdict imposed by the Archbishop of Rheims. The pope does not wholly excuse it, but thinks it more honorable for the archbishop himself to relax it. (Paris, 9 March.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, p. 1002.]

[Col. 0199D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious King of the French, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having received your Excellence’s letters with due kindness, we graciously grant the requests which your royal Highness presented to us through them, since it is always our purpose and intention willingly to grant your requests and to hear you in them, insofar as we can do so with God. Yet you should know that, concerning this affair, we have judged it more honorable to send letters of request to our venerable brother H., Archbishop of Rheims, as you will be able to see from their text [Col. 0200A], asking him, at our intervention and in consideration of your honor, to relax that interdict until the case receives its due conclusion in his court or even in that of . . . . . the Bishop of Beauvais. But if he does not wish to relax the interdict and answers us that this would not be very burdensome to him, we shall proceed in that affair according to the requests of your concern. For otherwise it would be less honorable for us readily to dissolve, without his knowledge, a sentence canonically pronounced by so great a man. But if you have so little confidence in this our brother [perhaps *non* is missing in the Latin], and the affair weighs greatly on your mind, you may write us once more concerning your will, and, with God as author, we shall take care effectively to fulfill your desire.

[Col. 0200B] Given at Paris, 7 Ides of March [9 March].

### CXXXIV. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—For the city of Beauvais, that it be absolved from the sentence. (Paris, 9 March.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 687.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our dearest son in Christ, Louis, illustrious King of the French, your brother, earnestly begged us by his letters to order the city of Beauvais absolved from the sentence of interdict which your Discretion pronounced against it on account of a controversy [Col. 0200C] known to be litigated between two women concerning a certain house. But, deferring especially to your Fraternity, we have not thought it right to proceed in this matter without your knowledge. We therefore ask and exhort your Charity in the Lord to remit that sentence, at our intervention and in consideration of the aforesaid our son the king, until that controversy receives its due conclusion in your judgment or in that of the Bishop of Beauvais. If, however, you do not wish to relax that sentence and would not take it too heavily if we proceeded to remit it in accordance with the king’s desire, make an effort to inform us of this by your own letter.

Given at Paris, 7 Ides of March [9 March].

### CXXXV. Privilege for the monastery of Savigny. (Paris, 10 March.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 859.]

[Col. 0200D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WILLIAM, Abbot of Savigny, and to his successors professing the regular life, forever.

Whenever a request is made to us which is known to accord with religion and right conduct, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and give suitable assistance to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot William, following the example of our father and predecessor Pope Eugenius of holy memory, we graciously assent to your just petitions. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing, the monastery of Savigny, over which, by God’s grace, you are known to preside [Col. 0201A].

First, we decree that the monastic order which is known to have been established according to the fear of God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institutions of the Cistercian brothers, both in the aforesaid monastery and in the houses subject to its authority and discipline, shall be preserved inviolate in future times. We also decree that the abbeys known to pertain by right to your monastery shall remain in the obedience and subjection of you and your successors. We have thought their names should be expressly stated: the abbey of Furness; the abbey of Bufert; the abbey of Biluwas; the abbey of Noth; the abbey of Careia; the abbey [Col. 0201B] of Strafort; the abbey of Cogherhala; the abbey of Basingwer; the abbey of Cumbremare; the abbey of Behelande; the abbey of Suineshenad; the abbey of Cadrei; and the abbey of the Isle of Man. We therefore confirm these abbeys, with all their appurtenances, to you and your successors forever. We decree therefore . . . . . . .

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, Bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Walter, Bishop of Albano. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. [Col. 0201C] I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Boso, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Cynthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Manfred, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Hericus, cardinal priest of Saint Anastasia. I, Albert, cardinal priest of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, cardinal priest of Saint Peter in Chains.

Given at Paris by the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 4 Ides of March [12 March], indiction 10, in the year 1162 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0201D], in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### CXXXVI. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Mary of Retorta. (Paris, 10 March.)

[HUGO, *Annals, Prologue*, II, Pr., p. 428.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons SANCTIUS, abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Retorta, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

Apostolic protection ought to be at hand for those choosing the religious life, lest an attack of anyone’s rashness either turn them back from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the monastery of Retorta, in which you are devoted to divine service. We fortify it by the privilege of the present writing, decreeing that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with God’s help, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit expressly to state the following by their proper names: whatever you have in the church of Saint John of Sardon, in the village of Vacrin; whatever you possess in Valleblis; whatever you possess in Collar [Col. 0202B]; whatever you possess in Pennafiel; whatever you possess in Trospinedo; whatever you possess in Zorita; whatever you possess in Saint Cecilia; and whatever you possess in Saint Peter of the Mount, with all their appurtenances.

We grant that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; while nevertheless preserving the right of the mother church. We decree therefore that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact and entire for the benefit in every way of the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving of course the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and recognize himself to stand guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and at the last judgment be subject to strict vengeance. But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve the rights of that place, so that they may receive here the fruit [Col. 0202D] of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, Bishop of Ostia. I, Bernold, Bishop of Porto. I, Walter, Bishop of Albano. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Henry, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, John, cardinal priest of Saint Angelo. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Blessed Mary in Cosmedin. [Col. 0203A] I, Odo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Boso, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Manfred, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Paris by the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 6 Ides of March [10 March], indiction 12, in the year 1162 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### CXXXVII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—For a certain woman, that her dower be restored to her. (Paris, 11 March.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 688.]

[Col. 0203B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the statement of M., the woman who bears the present letter, we have learned that Archdeacon S. bound Walter of Luico under a sentence of interdict because he had taken from her the marriage-gift which her husband had made to her. The Bishop of Amiens, however, relaxed the interdict before satisfaction had been made. Therefore, since by the office entrusted to us we are bound to secure justice for all Christ’s faithful and especially for widows and orphans, we command your Fraternity by apostolic letters diligently to summon the said Walter, so that he either restore in full to the aforesaid woman the marriage-gift which he unjustly retains, or provide her without delay complete justice concerning it. If he should perhaps refuse to do so, promptly restore the said Walter to the same sentence of interdict, and do not permit him to be absolved before making worthy satisfaction.

Given at Paris, 5 Ides of March [11 March].

### CXXXVIII. To the same.—Concerning the restoration of the church of Rechem to a certain person. (Paris, 14 March.)

[**Ibid.**]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0203D] brother Henry, Archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The bearer of the present letter, now coming to us for the second time, has shown us in his complaint that he was canonically invested by Simon, formerly Bishop of Tournai [Note: [Col. 0203D] Simon, custodian of Saint Quentin and a prince of royal blood, governed the churches of Tournai and Noyon from 1121 to 1148.], with the church of Rechem; and that he possessed it peacefully and quietly in the days of Simon and of his successor Anselm [Note: [Col. 0203D] Anselm, formerly abbot of the monastery of Saint Vincent at Laon, was elected the first bishop after the restoration [Col. 0204D]. He was succeeded by Gerald, formerly abbot of Villers, who was made bishop—the Gerald mentioned here by Alexander. On him, see the *History of the Monastery of Villers*, vol. III of our *Anecdota*.]. G. [Gerald], Bishop of Tournai, who now presides, then, on the pretext of certain letters issued by our father and predecessor Pope Eugenius of pious memory—which stated that grants of ecclesiastical property made by the aforesaid Bishop Simon were to be annulled—unreasonably despoiled him of that church.

We therefore instructed the said Bishop G. that, if what is asserted were true and nothing else reasonably prevented it, he should restore the church to him without any molestation, those letters notwithstanding. Since he has not yet carried this into effect, we command your Fraternity by apostolic letters that, if this is so and, as we said above, no other matter reasonably prevents it, you do not delay to restore the same church to him, without prejudice from the letters of that same [Col. 0204B] predecessor of ours. Know that the aforementioned predecessor did not mean canonical possessions of this kind, but those which the same bishop had procured to the detriment of the Church and in fraud of the sacred canons. If, however, the aforesaid bishop alleges another cause against him, make him come before you, either personally or through a sufficient representative; hear the case and bring it to its due conclusion.

Given at Paris, 2 Ides of March [14 March].

### CXXXIX. To Henry, King of England, who was to send all archbishops and bishops to the council: he gives thanks; but “decrees that, on this account, no loss or disadvantage ought to accrue to him or his heirs, nor can any new custom be introduced into his kingdom on this occasion, nor may the dignity of his kingdom be diminished in any respect.” (Paris, 18 March.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, I, 44.]

[Col. 0204C]

### CXL. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—For Robert and the priest Gill. (Paris, 18 March.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 689.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son O., cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, explained to us that, when he formerly exercised the office of legate in those regions, he summoned the priest Gill. three times before him concerning the controversy which that priest is known to have with Robert of Courtenay; but the priest refused to appear before him. Since Robert himself has now come before us, asserting that he is willing to stand with him under judgment in our court, we command your Fraternity by apostolic letters [Col. 0205A] diligently to admonish and compel the aforesaid priest to present himself before us at the octave of Easter concerning that matter; otherwise we shall be unable to refrain from proceeding in the case according to justice.

Given at Paris, 15 Kalends of April [18 March].

### CXLI. To Gilbert, Bishop of Hereford.—At the request of Henry, King of England, and Thomas of Canterbury, he grants that he undertake the governance of the Church of London, “provided, however, that the Church of London unanimously requests this.” (Paris, 19 March.)

[*Letters of Gilbert Foliot*, ed. GILES, I, 192.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G., Bishop of Hereford, greeting and [Col. 0205B] apostolic blessing.

From the letters of our dearest son in Christ, Henry, illustrious king of the English, and of our venerable brother T[homas], archbishop of Canterbury, as well as from the report of our beloved son R., archdeacon of London, we have learned that the same king earnestly desires and requests that you be transferred to the Church of London, there to undertake pastoral care and solicitude. The reason and necessity proposed to us by that king is this: that the city of London is a royal seat; that the king himself is accustomed to make a more prolonged and longer stay there; and that frequent assemblies of barons and magnates from the whole kingdom are customarily held there. Moreover, the more noble and renowned [Col. 0205C] the aforesaid royal city is than the other cities of the realm, the more the said king desires and asks that that church be governed by a man of greater distinction and better versed both in divine and human law. For, since he has entrusted to you counsel concerning the salvation of his soul, he wishes to have you present when he needs you.

Therefore, wishing to comply with him as our dearest son in every respect and in all matters in which we can serve him according to God, and having carefully considered your religious devotion, integrity, and learning, we have thought fit to assent in this matter to the wish and purpose of the king—provided, however, that the Church of London unanimously requests this. By these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, in accordance with the admonition of our aforesaid brother [Col. 0205D] the archbishop, setting aside every excuse and pretext, you confidently undertake the care and governance of that church, with the Lord’s help, and provide beneficially for it in spiritual as well as temporal affairs. For although we know you to be of such religious devotion and integrity that you would prefer to serve in lesser offices rather than preside over renowned and great churches, nevertheless do not hesitate to assume a burden known to proceed from the decision of divine dispensation. For although the enactments of the sacred canons forbid the transfer of persons from one church to another without an evident and manifest cause, taking account of the definite necessities and reasons laid before us by the prince, as well as that prince’s wish and desire, we grant the transfer, [Col. 0206A] considering indeed the benefits which, through your diligence, we trust will accrue by divine grace to the aforesaid Church of London.

Given at Paris, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### CXLII. To the Chapter of London

He informs it that he has permitted Henry, king of the English, to have [Gilbert], bishop of Hereford, placed over the Church of London, “provided, however,” he says, “that you unanimously request the same bishop.” (Paris, March [?])

[TWISDEN, *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, I, 534.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable chapter of London, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the letters of our dearest son Henry, illustrious [Col. 0206B] king of the English, and of our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, and from the report of our beloved son Ralph, archdeacon of your church, we have learned that the same king earnestly desires and requests that our venerable brother, the bishop of Hereford, be transferred to your church, there to exercise pastoral care and solicitude. The reason and necessity proposed to us by that king is this: that the city of London is a royal seat; that the king himself is accustomed to make a more prolonged and longer stay there; and that frequent assemblies of barons and magnates from the whole kingdom are customarily held there. Moreover, the more noble and [Col. 0206C] renowned the aforesaid royal city is than the other cities of the realm, the more the said king desires and requests that that church be governed by a man of greater distinction and better versed both in divine and human law. For, since he has entrusted to our aforementioned brother counsel concerning the salvation of his soul, he wishes to have him present when he needs him. Therefore, wishing to comply with him as our dearest son in every respect and in all matters in which we can serve him according to God, and having carefully considered the religious devotion, integrity, and learning of that same brother, our bishop, we have thought fit to assent in this matter to the wish and purpose of the king—provided, however, that you unanimously request that same bishop.

### CXLIII. To Louis VII, King of the Franks

Against the ravagers of the Church of Brioude. (Paris, March 20.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1000.]

[Col. 0206D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have learned that it has come to the knowledge of your highness how the counts of Auvergne and the viscount of Polignac, having irreverently attacked the town of Brioude, which is known to be yours, do not cease to despoil the Church of Brioude itself, which belongs in a special manner to the right and protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves; and, wickedly besieging the dean’s house, they assault it with engines of war as far as they can. Since we are unwilling to leave such audacity in any way uncorrected, [Col. 0207A] in accordance with the duty of our office we are endeavoring by our letters to recall both them and the provost and abbot of Brioude, who incited them, from this damnable venture in wrongdoing. We intend and purpose that, unless they repent in accordance with our admonitions, we shall inflict severe punishment, so far as our office permits, both upon them and upon their lands. We therefore ask, admonish, and exhort your magnificence in the Lord to set yourself effectively to correct this; and, unless they repent, to strive and labor by every means to take vengeance upon them.

Given at Paris, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### CXLIV. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims

On behalf of the count of Namur, that his wife may return to him. (Paris, March 22.)

[MARTÈNE, *Collectio*, II, 690.]

[Col. 0207B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son, the noble count of Namur, has informed us by his letters that his wife, whom he had maintained peacefully and with the Church’s peace for a long time, has left him without reasonable cause and, fleeing from place to place, wholly refuses to return to him. Since, because of this, the bishop of Cambrai, by command of the Church of Reims, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against her, that sentence is not observed sufficiently firmly because she is continually moving from place to place [Col. 0207C]. Therefore by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, if this is so, you diligently admonish that woman and induce her, within thirty days after your admonition and laying aside every pretext, to return to her husband. Afterwards, if she considers that any reasonable cause remains for which she ought not to remain with him, let her come into your presence and state her case before you. You, however, shall hear the case and decide it with due finality. But if, having been lawfully admonished by you, she refuses to return to her husband, declare her excommunicated and ensure that, until she has made fitting satisfaction, throughout your province she is diligently [Col. 0207D] avoided by everyone as an excommunicated person.

Given at Paris, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

### CXLV. Privilege for the Abbey of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete

(Paris, April 6.)

[*Works of Abelard*, p. 354.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, HELOISE, abbess, and the other sisters devoted to divine service in the oratory of the Holy Spirit, situated in the district of Troyes, etc. [“To us,” etc., as in the privilege of Eugenius III (see *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXX, no. 238), as far as:] but the places of Triagnel, Leavalle, Neofort, and Saint-Flavit, which have been reasonably granted to you, together with all their appurtenances, we confirm to you by apostolic authority, etc. [Col. 0208A]

Given at Paris, through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, indiction 10, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1163, in the fourth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

### CXLVI. To Stephen, Abbot of Mortemer

He confirms the privileges of this monastery. (Fragment.) (Paris, April 12.)

[*Neustria pia*, p. 780.]

Whenever that is requested of us, etc.

Given at Paris, through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Ides of April, indiction 10, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1163, in the fourth year of our pontificate. [Col. 0208B]

### CXLVII. Second Dedication of the Basilica of Saint-Germain-des-Prés by Pope Alexander III

(Paris, April 21.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, VII, 71.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1163, Pope Alexander III entered the city of Paris and remained there for some time. While he was staying in that city, I, Hugh III, by the grace of God abbot of Saint-Germain at Paris, approached him and humbly entreated him to deem worthy of the dignity of consecration [Col. 0208C] the church of Blessed Germanus, newly restored in design, since it had not yet been consecrated. The most reverend Pope Alexander graciously assented to our prayers and, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, came to the aforesaid church accompanied by a great company of bishops and cardinals. Among them was Maurice, bishop of Paris. When the monks of that church saw him, they were greatly disturbed at his presence and declared that they would by no means permit the church’s consecration to take place while the aforesaid Bishop Maurice was present.

Accordingly, after hearing and learning of the monks’ disturbance, the lord pope summoned Lord Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin; Lord Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison; and [Col. 0208D] Lord William, cardinal priest of Saint Peter in Chains. Having called them, he commanded them to go to the aforesaid Bishop Maurice, carefully inform him of the monks’ agitation, and, by his command, order him to leave the church; otherwise the monks would altogether refuse to permit the consecration. Maurice, upon hearing the lord pope’s order, withdrew from the church with all the ornaments and vestments he had brought with him.

After his departure, Lord Hubald, bishop of Ostia; Bernard, bishop of Porto; Walter, bishop of Albano; John, bishop of Segni; Geraud, bishop of Cahors; Amalric, bishop of Senlis; and, from Spain, John, archbishop of Toledo and primate of the Spains, Felland, bishop of Asturias, John, bishop of León, Stephen, [Col. 0209A] bishop of Zamora, John, bishop of Lugo, Assuerus, bishop of Coria, and Peter, bishop of Mondoñedo—by order of the lord pope—went round the outside of the church three times, and likewise around the interior, sprinkling it with holy water according to custom; and they dedicated it most honorably, as was fitting.

Then Pope Alexander solemnly consecrated the high altar in honor of the Holy Cross and the holy martyrs Stephen and Vincent. In its middle he made a cross with holy oil, while four of the aforesaid bishops stood at the four corners of the same altar, each likewise making a cross with holy oil in his own place. The lord pope placed relics within the altar and, taking the implement commonly called a *truella* (“trowel”), sealed them [Col. 0209B] inside with cement. When this had been done, Lord Hubald, bishop of Ostia, and three bishops together consecrated the morning altar in honor of the most holy confessor Germanus.

Meanwhile Pope Alexander proceeded in solemn procession to the meadow beside the monastery walls, addressed the people, and publicly declared before all those present that the Church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, being by its own right the possession of blessed Peter, is subject to no archbishop or bishop except the supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church.

The following cardinals were present; their names are subscribed below.

Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross [Col. 0209C] in Jerusalem.

Henry, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus.

John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia.

Alberic, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina.

William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains.

Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin.

Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

Arditio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.

[Col. 0209D] Boso, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, at the *Vicus Agrippae*.

Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace beside the temple.

Manfred, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

I, Hugh, third abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, testify that this consecration was thus performed at my instigation; and therefore, for the assurance of present and future persons, I committed it to writing and confirmed it with my seal.

Sealed with a wax seal on a double tag.

### CXLVIII. Privilege for the Church of Saint Mary of Hérivaux

(Paris, April 22.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, VII, col. 273.]

[Col. 0210A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons RALPH, prior of the Church of Blessed Mary of Hérivaux, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever, etc.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods [Col. 0210B] that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by God’s favor, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms:

By the gift of Renaud of Clermont and Matthew, count of Beaumont: Hérivaux and its wood, and the plain adjoining the place, to the extent that you and your successors can cultivate it at your own expense and with your own animals, wholly free and exempt from every secular exaction.

By the gift of Odo Apri: two sextaries of wheat annually from the Fort mill; and that the brothers of this house, immediately after the first miller and to the extent required for the brothers’ needs, may always grind in that mill free of milling dues. [Col. 0210C]

By the gift of Count Renaud: three sextaries of wheat and three of mixed grain at the Coye mill.

By the gift of the knight Ascelin: one sextary of wheat annually from his house at Fosses, whoever may possess it.

By the gift of Gerald of Atrium: one mina of grain from the allod of Compans, whatever kind of grain may grow there, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. Hubald, cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. Albert, cardinal of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. William, cardinal priest [Col. 0210D] of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, etc.

Given at Paris through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, indiction 10, in the year 1163, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Alexander.

### CXLIX. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims

Concerning the affair of the bishop of Arras. (Paris, April 23.)

[MARTÈNE, *Collectio*, II, 1010.]

ALEXANDER, etc.

As we recently explained to your brotherhood both orally and by letter, when our venerable brother [Godescalc], bishop of Arras, laid down the burden of episcopal dignity, we granted him three altars—namely, those of [Col. 0211A] Monchy, Rémicourt, and Miremont—for the necessary support of life, and took care to confirm them by apostolic authority. We therefore expressly will and command your brotherhood to ensure, so far as lies in you, that this is firmly carried out and inviolably observed.

Given at Paris, the ninth day before the Kalends of May.

### CL. He Confirms the Goods and Rights of the Church of Saint Geneviève at Paris

(Paris, April 24.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, VII, 241.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ALBERT, abbot of the Church of Saint Geneviève, [Col. 0211B] situated near Paris, and to his successors canonically appointed forever.

“The Lord by wisdom founded the earth; he founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers.” Hence the constitution of the Church, which the Prophet calls by the name of earth, is not overthrown by any attacks of enemies or by any duration of time; for the Lord’s firm foundation stands, and the gifts and calling of God are without repentance. By this foundation and this gift, the holy Roman and apostolic Church so surpasses all churches throughout the world that, by divine power, it judges and orders not only earthly matters but heavenly also. Though unworthy, we hold the place and office of this power; therefore we are bound so to administer ecclesiastical affairs [Col. 0211C] that God’s honor everywhere, human salvation, and the Church’s dignity may be provided for.

Moved by this obligation of reason, our predecessor Pope Eugenius, of holy memory, entrusted to Odo, your predecessor, the governance and ordering of the aforesaid Church of Saint Geneviève—in which secular clerics had formerly conducted themselves outrageously and less than honorably—in order to restore in it a state of integrity and religious observance; and he strengthened this arrangement by the privilege of his document. Following the example of our predecessor, we regard this same grant as ratified and firm, and confirm it by the present document. [Col. 0212A]

First, we decree that the canonical order, known to have been instituted according to God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine through our aforesaid predecessor and through the exertions of our dearest son Louis, king of the Franks, shall be preserved there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by God’s favor through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired forever for you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms.

[Col. 0212B] The borough of Saint Geneviève—[Note: [Col. 0211C] The borough of Saint Geneviève includes Garanelles, Grenelles, where the land was at first covered with thickets, according to an old charter: “The Church of Saint Geneviève has lands at Garanelles, which the canons cause to be cultivated at their own expense and labor.” This place lies within the parish of Saint Stephen.]—from the house of Bartholomew to the bridge of Saint Medard, and as far as the royal road—[Note: [Col. 0211D] The royal road is the street of Saint James.]—beside the church of Saint Stephen—[Note: [Col. 0211D] The Church of Saint Stephen is the parish of Saint Stephen de Gressibus.]—with all its jurisdictions and liberties.

The village and church of Saint Medard, with all the jurisdictions of that village.

Rungy—[Note: [Col. 0211D] *Rungiacum*: Rungy, near Paris, a village well known for its waters.]—with every jurisdiction belonging to it.

Épinay—[Note: [Col. 0211D] *Spinolium*: Épinay, below Sénart, including also Quinciacum.]—with its church and all the appurtenances and jurisdictions of that village.

At Draveil—[Note: [Col. 0211D] *Dravernum*: Draveil, an estate in the diocese of Paris granted by King Dagobert, within which lies Champrosay.]—the possessions you have there, with their appurtenances.

At Saint-Germain-sur-École—[Note: [Col. 0211D] *S. Germanus super Scolam*: Saint-Germain-sur-École, in the diocese of Sens near Cély; land alienated to Christophe de Thou, president of the Paris Parlement, for financial assistance.]—the possessions with their appurtenances.

Jossigny—[Note: [Col. 0211D] *Jauciniacum*: Jossigny, diocese of Paris.]—with all its jurisdictions and the church of that village.

At Magny—[Note: [Col. 0211D] *Magniacum*: Magny-le-Hongre, diocese of Meaux, whose parish has Saint Geneviève as titular saint [Col. 0212C].]—lands and woods with all jurisdictions.

At Ebly—[Note: [Col. 0212C] *Ebeliaсum*: Ebly, diocese of Meaux.]—lands and chief rents.

At Tri-le-Bardou—[Note: [Col. 0212C] *Trejectum*: Tri-le-Bardou, diocese of Meaux; its church belongs to the presentation of the abbey of Saint Faron, while Saint Geneviève is titular saint. Her body was brought there in the ninth century.]—chief rents [Col. 0212C] from men as well as women.

At Charmentré—[Note: [Col. 0212D] *Charmentrium*: Charmentré, diocese of Meaux, whose parish falls under the patronage of the abbey of Saint Faron.]—possessions and chief rents from men and women.

Likewise, the men and women whom you have at Meaux, at Lisy—[Note: [Col. 0212D] *Lysiacum*: Lisy, diocese of Meaux, whose pastoral care the bishop of Meaux entrusted in 1269 to the regular canons of Saint Geneviève.]—at Mareuil—[Note: [Col. 0212D] *Mareolum*: Mareuil-la-Ferté, diocese of Meaux. Saint Martin was the titular saint of its church, which was presented by the prior of Saint-Célinie, already in the ninth century, when the relics of Saint Geneviève were brought there.]—and throughout the surrounding territory.

At La Ferté-Milon—[Note: [Col. 0212D] *Firmitas Milonis*: La Ferté-Milon, diocese of Soissons.]—from La Tour, five solidi and a halfpenny, tithes, chief rents from many men and women in that vicinity, and the church of Saint Vedast.

Marisy—[Note: [Col. 0212D] *Marisiacum*: Marisy, diocese of Soissons. Its patron saint is Saint Geneviève, whose body was carried there in the ninth century.]—with the Church of Saint Geneviève, woods, meadows, and all appurtenances of that village.

At Palaiseau [Col. 0213A]—[Note: [Col. 0213C] *Palaciolum*: Palaiseau, diocese of Paris.]—and Chilly—[Note: [Col. 0213C] *Ebarliacum*, in the authentic text *Challiacum*: Chilly, near Palaiseau.]—lands and chief rents, tithes, and field-shares.

At Athis—[Note: [Col. 0213C] *Atheiae*: Athis, diocese of Paris.]—tithes and a halfpenny from each house.

At Bagneux—[Note: [Col. 0213C] *Balneolum*: Bagneux, near Fontenay-aux-Roses, diocese of Paris.]—and Fontenay, lands, woods, and meadows, and the Bièvre mill—[Note: [Col. 0213C] *Molendinum Beveris*: a mill on the River Bièvre, a small stream flowing near Fontenay-aux-Roses.].

At Vanves—[Note: [Col. 0213C] *Vanvae*: Vanves, near Paris.]—the church, lands, vineyards, and chief rents, with every jurisdiction belonging to your lands.

Choisy—[Note: [Col. 0213C] *Sosiacum*: Choisy-aux-Bœufs, diocese of Chartres; formerly a parish within the bounds of the great forest of Versailles, now destroyed; see Stephen of Tournai, Epistle CXVIII.]—and the church of that village.

Trianon—[Note: [Col. 0213D] *Triarnum*: Trianon, a destroyed village, where the royal palace now stands.]—with the wood and adjoining land.

Galy—[Note: [Col. 0213D] *Galia*: Galy, land near Choisy, sold to Louis XIV or exchanged for the lordship of Ver in the diocese of Senlis, from which it takes the name Ver-de-Galy.]—with its enclosed estate, pond, and mill.

The tithe at Maulny—[Note: [Col. 0213D] *Malus-Nidus*: Maulny.]—and five arpents of vineyard at Marly—[Note: [Col. 0213D] *Marliacum*: Marly-le-Roi, diocese of Paris.]—and the pond which Bartholomew the Hairy gave you as alms.

Nanterre—[Note: [Col. 0213D] *Nannetodorum*: Nanterre.]—with the church of that village, possessions, and chief rents from many persons.

At Auteuil—[Note: [Col. 0213D] *Autolium*: Auteuil.]—lands, vineyards, [Col. 0213B] chief rents, and the entire jurisdiction of the land you have there.

Rosny—[Note: [Col. 0213D] *Rodoniacum*: Rosny-sous-Vincennes, through which place the body of Saint Geneviève was brought back to Paris in the ninth century.]—with the church of that village, chief rents, jurisdictions, and all its appurtenances.

At Chennevières—[Note: [Col. 0213D] *Canaveriae*: Chennevières, on the Marne near Champigny and Saint-Maur.]—lands, vineyards, and chief rents.

Borrest—[Note: [Col. 0214C] *Borretum*: Borrest, near Senlis. See Stephen of Tournai, Epistle 129.]—and the water of that village, with all its appurtenances.
