## CCXII. To Louis, King of the Franks.—He gives thanks that the king took no small pleasure in the honor and reverence shown to the Roman Church by the envoys of the Emperor of Constantinople. (Sens, 16 October.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1010.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks [Col. 0269D], greeting and apostolic blessing.

The most devoted sincerity and most sincere devotion of your highness, in all things pertaining to the honor of the most holy Roman Church, has always displayed such fervor of inward affection that you appear to be her true son, true protector, and, in a sense, her bearer. No prince exists in the world to whom, as much as to your highness, the advancement and exaltation of that Church may in these times be attributed. We therefore do not cease to render thanks to Almighty God, for whose regard and love you have moved your royal mind to do these things; and we entreat his mercy in unceasing prayers that he who has preserved you for these times as so worthy an aid and most necessary refuge for his one bride [Col. 0270A] may himself preserve you safe for a long time, and grant you so to reign upon earth that after this earthly kingdom you may attain the unfailing kingdom of heaven.

For we have received and truthfully learned, both from the tenor of your letters and from the report of our beloved son B., your envoy, that, when you and your barons who were present at the council heard from the envoys of our dearest son, the illustrious Emperor of Constantinople, concerning the honor and reverence to be shown by that emperor to us and to the holy Roman Church, you conceived no small joy because of the devotion shown toward us. You judged that they should henceforth be heard concerning the other matters they had brought, and that their words should not otherwise be heard by you apart from the customary clemency of your gentleness [Col. 0270B].

For this, rendering to your royal serenity most abundant thanks as is fitting, and highly commending your highness in the Lord in this matter, as also in all other things pertaining to the honor of the Church, we continually pray that the merciful and compassionate Lord may repay you in the eternal recompense of the righteous, for whose sake and grace you have adopted so kindly and gentle a disposition toward us and the Church. Moreover, we wish your highness to know that, after a response had been formulated in accordance with the counsel of our brethren and set before the aforesaid envoys, whatever answer is given them by us we shall take care to communicate fully to you in our letters, as to a most serene prince and one in whom [Col. 0270C] we have no confidence other than that which we have in ourselves or in our brethren.

Given at Sens, on the seventeenth Kalends of November [16 October].

## CCXIII. To the same.—That he order Geoffrey, knight of Molinons, captured by the burgesses of Sens, to be released. (Sens, 16 October.)

[Ibid., col. 1011.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have been informed by the report of certain persons that, when Iterius, knight of Malonido, came to Sens [Col. 0270D] and attacked with drawn sword an enemy of his whom he happened to find there, the burgesses of that city suddenly resisted him. When he fled, they seized and hold in detention a companion of his, namely Geoffrey, knight of Molinons, who, as we have learned, had done nothing wrong in this matter, having lingered for a little while in the same city; and they do not dare release him without your authorization.

The knight who had been attacked so hostilely by the said Iterius altogether asserts and affirms that the man now held captive had in no way injured him; and he asserts that he had not known beforehand that this aforesaid companion of his would in any way harm him, and promises to swear it. Therefore, since it seems unworthy that one to whose innocence testimony is borne both by the man who suffered the injury and by your provost should be punished with an undeserved penalty [Col. 0271A], we ask your serenity and exhort you in the Lord that, in accordance with the customary mercy of royal clemency—which is accustomed both powerfully to repress the guilty and to keep the innocent unharmed and uninjured—you have the same G. released and set free, unless he is proved to have committed something contrary to the royal majesty.

Given at Sens, on the sixteenth Kalends of November [17 October].

## CCXIV. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—He strengthens him against the king’s persecution, then begun, and at the same time warns him not to concede anything to the king contrary to ecclesiastical liberty. (Sens, 26 October.)

[Letters of Saint Thomas of Canterbury, ed. GILES, II, 4.]

[Col. 0271B]

POPE ALEXANDER TO THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

We have heard with attentive care the letter which your brotherhood sent us and the matters which your messenger set before us orally; and we have fully considered the grave anxieties and bitter distresses by which your mind is continually afflicted. On hearing and learning these things, our spirit was moved and deeply troubled—we who gladly delight in your prosperity, and in your adversity very greatly grieve with you as with a dearest brother.

Therefore, as a steadfast and prudent man, often recalling the saying: “The apostles went rejoicing from the presence of the council,” etc. (Acts 5) [Col. 0271C], endure such straits patiently. Let not your spirit be troubled more than is fitting; rather, receive worthy consolation within yourself, so that we too may be consoled together with you in him who has reserved you for this crisis of necessity, to strengthen Catholic and Christian truth. It is his good pleasure to wipe away and punish through various afflictions the stains of those acts which you have committed less lawfully, lest they seem reserved for punishment at the strict judgment.

Furthermore, let it not be burdensome to you, nor—according to what we have learned from the letter which you sent to your clerk—cause you fear for any reason, that you have been summoned before the Apostolic See. For this is pleasing and welcome to us; and we wish that, if those who summoned you should perhaps come, you yourself, if it seems good to you, prosecute that appeal, setting aside every doubt and delay. Nor may anyone ever, by the authority of the Roman Church, instill fear or hesitation into your steadfastness; for we shall, with God as author, take care most zealously to preserve for you, so far as justice and reason permit, the rights and dignities of the church entrusted to you [Col. 0271D], as for one whom we find steadfast in the cause of the Church and her most courageous defender.

Moreover, we command your brotherhood by injunction that you return to the church of Canterbury, and, retaining only a very few things that are absolutely necessary, travel through that land as little as you can. We especially urge your prudence that, under no pretext of fear or adversity which may befall you, be compelled to renounce the right and dignity of your church [Col. 0272A].

Given at Sens, on the seventh Kalends of November [26 October].

## CCXV. To Gilbert, Bishop of London.—That he restore King Henry’s mind to a state of peace and concord. (Sens, 9 November.)

[Letters of Gilbert Foliot, ed. GILES, II, 92.]

POPE ALEXANDER TO GILBERT, Bishop of London.

Because we have the fullest confidence in your integrity, discretion, and devotion, we unhesitatingly suggest to you such matters as we know to be expedient [Col. 0272B], and disclose our mind concerning them. We know, and have learned truly, that our dearest son in Christ Henry, illustrious King of the English, moved by consideration of your prudence and integrity, requested that you be transferred from one see to another so that he might more fittingly both avail himself of and be supported by your counsel, and always direct his actions toward what might deservedly please in the eyes of the heavenly Creator.

We are confident that those matters which we know to conduce to the peace and tranquillity of the Church, to the welfare, honor, and exaltation of the same king and of the whole kingdom entrusted to him, and especially to the advantage of the English Church itself, can be commended to him through you all the more effectively because we do not doubt that he will comply with your counsels. Therefore, since, as we have learned, a spark of indignation has arisen between him and the English Church, we earnestly admonish and command your brotherhood [Col. 0272C] continually to labor to extinguish it, and by every means restore and bring the king’s mind back to a state of peace and concord.

In particular, urge and set before him that he consider how, for all the princes and powerful men of the world, there is one impregnable defense: namely, the love of their own people. Let him desire not to be feared more than to be loved, lest perhaps, if his subjects are compelled to fear him without love, a most grievous hatred may thereafter arise against him and his heirs—God forbid!—from that from which the perpetual and stable support of his whole kingdom ought to have proceeded. For there is only one perfect fear, namely love mingled with reverence; it alone endures and increases, while the other falls away and leaves its author alone and unprotected [Col. 0272D].

Let the diligence of your uprightness therefore endeavor so to commend all these matters to our aforesaid son the king, and utterly abolish in him that spark of indignation, that the devotion of his people may continually increase toward him, and that he may ever be able to reign in peace and tranquillity, with honor to God and holy mother Church, and with safety to himself and his heirs. Farewell.

Given at Sens, on the fifth Ides of November [9 November].

## CCXVI. To the Master of the Hospital of Jerusalem.—He commends Peter, prior of the hospital of Saint John at Constantinople. (Sens, 9 November.)

[DUCHESNE, *Hist. Franc. Script.*, IV, 626.]

[Col. 0273A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son the master of the hospital house situated at Jerusalem, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We willingly suggest and with paternal concern commend to you matters which we know to pertain to your honor and the benefit of the house entrusted to you. It has come to our hearing that, although our beloved son Peter, called the German, prior of the hospital house of Saint John at Constantinople, has remained there for no small time in God’s service and also for the honor and benefit [Col. 0273B] of our dearest son in Christ, the Emperor of Constantinople, you wish to remove him from that priory and summon him to your presence against the will and good pleasure of that emperor.

Since both the Roman Church and secular princes are accustomed to draw religious men from different houses and retain them in their service—whence many benefits usually accrue to those institutions themselves—we ask your prudence and exhort you in the Lord that, out of reverence for Saint Peter and for us, and in view of future advantage, especially since you have received the prayers of the aforesaid emperor on this matter, you leave that same prior in the aforesaid priory in the emperor’s service [Col. 0273C], and do not compel him to return to you.

Given at Sens, on the fifth Ides of November [9 November].

## CCXVII. To W., Prior, and the Chapter of Canterbury.—He praises them for sympathizing with the tribulations of Archbishop Thomas. (Sens, 16 December.)

[Letters of Gilbert Foliot, ed. Giles, II, 69.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons W., prior, and the brethren of the Church of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother Thomas, your archbishop, has carefully represented to us—and we have learned from the report of our beloved son Odo, your fellow brother, and from common report—that you, as religious men devoted to God, zealously stand beside that same brother of ours in the affairs of the Church. Sympathizing with his tribulations and distresses, you willingly provide him counsel and help, and bear the burdens of the Church with him in a ready spirit [Col. 0273D].

Holding this to be pleasing and welcome, we commend with worthy praise in the Lord the constancy of your religious devotion and ardent fidelity, and render you manifold thanks for it. By apostolic letters we ask, admonish, and exhort your whole body in the Lord that, as you have begun well and laudably, so henceforth, acting faithfully and steadfastly, you take care to persevere in your undertaking and strive to join to so laudable a beginning the completion of an excellent end [Col. 0274A].

For we trust and hope from the immeasurable goodness of the Lord that he, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, will soften the mind of our dearest son in Christ Henry, illustrious King of the English, toward the aforesaid archbishop. When that king more carefully recalls to mind Thomas’s service and the affection which he shows him in many ways, as well as the justice in the case, he will restore to him his favor and fullness of love; and your Church will possess its rights, dignities, and liberties intact. You too shall thereby receive a worthy reward from Almighty God and a fuller favor from the Apostolic See. And, because of the faith and devotion which you show to him, we shall always be ready, so far as we can with God and justice, more effectively to advance the rights and dignities of your same Church [Col. 0274B].

Given at Sens, on the seventeenth Kalends of January [16 December].

## YEAR 1163–1164.

## CCXVIII. To the Abbot of Saint Remigius at Rheims.—Concerning the case of the clerk T. (Sens, 5 October.)

[MARTÈNE, *Collectio*, II, 693.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son the Abbot of Saint Remigius, greeting and apostolic blessing [Col. 0274C].

T., a poor clerk and bearer of the present letter, came to us and complained that his grandfather had pledged a certain piece of land to War. Rem. and A., his son, a canon of the church of Saint Timothy, for eleven solidi. When the aforesaid T., who had succeeded his grandfather in the inheritance, wished to repay the money lent to War. and his son and receive back the pledged land upon payment, they refused either to receive the money or restore the land, although, as the said T. asserts, they had already received both the principal and much more from the fruits of that land.

We formerly entrusted the execution of this matter to our venerable brother the Archbishop of Rheims, but he, detained by a multiplicity of affairs, could not give this matter attention [Col. 0274D]. Since, therefore, by the office imposed upon us we are bound to assist the said clerk in his right and provide for his poverty, we command your discretion by apostolic letters carefully to investigate the matter. If, after expenses have been deducted, it is established that they have received the principal and more from the fruits of the land, strictly compel them to restore the land itself. But if this cannot be done without some additional payment, lest that man’s poverty be burdened beyond measure, after receiving some small sum compel the same men by ecclesiastical censure to restore the aforesaid land.

Given at Sens, on the third Nones of October [5 October].

## CCXIX. To Hugh, Bishop of Soissons.—That justice be done to the Bishop of Senlis concerning vineyards taken from him. (Sens, 8 October.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1004.]

[Col. 0275A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother H., Bishop of Soissons, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother Almaricus, Bishop of Senlis, informed us by his letters that Gil. and his wife Hauguidis, your parishioners, presume to hold by force certain lands and vineyards of that bishop, and refuse to restore them, with the fruits received from them, to the bishop. Although the aforesaid bishop had repeatedly summoned them for this purpose, to render him full justice in his court, they refused to do so [Col. 0275B].

Therefore, since we neither can nor ought for any reason to fail that bishop in his right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if you ascertain that the said G. and his wife Hauguidis ought to answer the aforesaid bishop in his court concerning this matter, you earnestly admonish and strictly compel them to render full justice to him upon this matter in the presence of the same bishop. Otherwise, compel them in the presence of the venerable B., Bishop of Beauvais, to answer that same bishop sufficiently concerning this matter and, setting aside appeal, to render full justice. But should they perhaps refuse to do so, strike them with ecclesiastical censure [Col. 0275C].

Given at Sens, on the eighth Ides of October [8 October].

## CCXX. To Louis, King of the Franks.—That he have what was taken restored to the brethren of Saint Mary of the Gate of Saint Leon. (Sens, 18 October.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1026.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved sons, the prior and brethren of Saint Mary of the Gate of Saint Leon, have complained to us that our beloved son the nobleman Peter, your brother, has seized one of their men, taken from him a horse and eight oxen [Col. 0275D], and refuses either to release the man himself or restore what was taken from him. Therefore, since it is our concern to take care and exercise solicitude lest holy Churches of God suffer any injury through the violence of powerful men, we ask your highness by apostolic letters and exhort you in the Lord, for love of justice and out of reverence for Saint Peter and for us, to have that man released and what was taken from him restored in full.

Given at Sens, on the fifteenth Kalends of November [18 October].

## CCXXI. To the same.—For the Church of Brioude. (Sens, 23 October.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing [Col. 0276A].

Our beloved son . . . , abbot of Saint Genevieve, who, like a new shepherd and diligent administrator, strives and labours in every way for the welfare of his church, has shown us by a communication sent to us that our beloved son G., a nobleman, your butler, under pretext of a certain custom which he asserts obtains in all royal abbeys, demands from him certain things which the aforesaid abbot by no means acknowledges to be owed by that church. Therefore, since the serenity of your highness is accustomed to preserve the liberties of churches uninjured and intact, we ask, [Col. 0276B] admonish, and exhort your clemency by apostolic letters in the Lord that, if this is so, you do not permit that church to be burdened by a new and unjust exaction, and that you wholly recall and turn back your aforesaid butler from this purpose.

Given at Sens, 14 Kalends of January [19 December].

### CCXXII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—Concerning the illness of Lord Henry, Archbishop of Rheims, and that God may restore him to health. (Sens, 5 November.)

[MARTEN., *Coll.*, II, 694.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greeting [Col. 0276C] and the apostolic blessing.

We have heard with hearing what grieves us to have heard, and we have received, not without great disturbance of mind, namely, that you are suffering from bodily illness and do not at present enjoy that sound health which we would wish, and which we desire for you in every way. For we know and hold as certain truth how you, like a true Israelite, have fought bravely and steadfastly for the exaltation and defence of the most holy Church; and, setting yourself against Damascus, the tower of strength, you have diligently sought faithfully to conduct and pursue the cause of that same Church as though it were your own. Therefore, as we and our brethren firmly imprint all these things upon our memory, we sympathize with you, as [Col. 0276D] a most beloved brother and a most valiant champion of the Church, with an inward affection of heart concerning the illness with which the right hand of the heavenly Creator has visited you, and we grieve greatly in the Lord.

Accordingly, being exceedingly anxious and concerned for your health, we have thought fit to visit your most beloved brotherhood through the greeting of the apostolic blessing and by our letters; asking and admonishing your prudence to endeavour to inform us more fully, by your own letters and through the bearer of these presents, of your condition and state. For, if it should please and be acceptable to you, we shall send some of the senior persons among our brethren to visit you; and we ourselves would not hesitate to undertake the labour in person, if we believed it would benefit and help you. That the merciful Lord may restore to you the health you desire [Col. 0277A] and grant healing unto salvation, we beseech Him by earnest intercessions.

Given at Sens, on the Nones of November [5 November].

### CCXXIII. To Louis, King of the Franks.—He in turn commends to the king the prior of Saint-Médard, who had been commended to him by the king. (Sens, 6 November.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 1010.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Since it is known to pertain especially to our office [Col. 0277B] to love religious persons—and above all the heads of churches—with ready charity, and to provide beneficially for them in all things, we rejoice with joy and hold it most pleasing and welcome that the fervour of heavenly fire has so kindled your mind also to this end that you prudently seek by your prayers to induce us ourselves to it and sometimes to anticipate our solicitude. We have therefore graciously received the prayers which your royal highness presented to us through our beloved son R., prior of Saint-Médard; and we have undertaken the will and purpose of loving him for whom you asked with more fervent charity, both by reason of the duty of our office and at the instance of your prayers, and of making useful provision for him, so far as with God we shall be able. [Col. 0277C] We ask your serenity, however, that, just as you took care to commend him to us, so you also keep him commended to yourself and, should need arise, grant him fitting protection and support.

Given at Sens, 8 Ides of November [6 November].

### CCXXIV. To the same.—That he establish a fair at Ferrières on the anniversary of the abbot’s consecration. (Sens, 6 November.)

[Ibid., col. 1012.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and the apostolic blessing.

The more constantly we desire the glory and exaltation of your magnificent [Col. 0277D] name to be increased and extended, the more willingly we have thought fit to suggest to your royal serenity those things by which you may obtain the grace of almighty God and merit the salvation of your soul. Therefore, having received the prayers of our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Ferrières—upon whose earnest request from your magnificence we performed the rite of consecration—we earnestly ask your royal serenity, for the sake of that monastery, that, for reverence for blessed Peter and for us, if you judge this to concern the honour of those brethren and the improvement of that monastery, you establish there a fair on the anniversary of his consecration. Once it has been established, [Col. 0278A] forbid, by royal authority, the princes, barons, and others of your realm that anyone should presume to inflict injury, violence, or any loss upon those who have come to that fair in order to obtain the remission which we establish there annually, or for the purpose of trade; and decree that anyone who does so be punished with a fitting penalty.

Given at Sens, 8 Ides of November [6 November].

### CCXXV. To the same.—That the journey to England of the prior of Cerel. should not be further delayed. (Sens, 9 November.)

[Ibid., col. 996.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, [Col. 0278B] greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Having recently summoned to our presence our beloved prior of the house of the Hospital situated at Cerel., intending to send him to England concerning certain affairs of the Church, we received prayers sent by your highness that we should grant him a postponement for this purpose. But since we recognize it to be burdensome and harmful to us if his journey is delayed further, we earnestly ask your serenity to grant that prior leave to undertake the journey which we have enjoined upon him.

Given at Sens, 5 Ides of November [9 November].

### CCXXVI. To the same.—That he order the dispute between the brothers Adam and Gregory to be judged by an impartial judge. (Sens, 10 November.)

[Ibid., col. 1005.]

[Col. 0278C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and the apostolic blessing.

It befits royal excellence to devote diligent care to those matters by which persons living in your realm under the protection of royal defence may firmly obtain their justice. Accordingly, we earnestly ask your serenity to hear carefully the case which is in dispute between Adam and his brother Gregory concerning a certain house that, as is said, belongs to your lordship; or, according to your judgment, to entrust the hearing and due determination of that case to another person who ought to be suspect to neither party. [Col. 0278D]

Given at Sens, 4 Ides of November [10 November].

### CCXXVII. To the abbots of Saint-Remigius and of Eleemosyna, and to the dean of Rheims.—For the church of Saint-Maurice of Tours and Cluny. (Sens, 5 December.)

[MARTEN., *Collect.*, II, 695.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brethren, the abbots of Saint-Remigius and of [Note: [Col. 0277] Eleemosyna, a Cistercian monastery in the diocese of Chartres, commonly called *le Petit Citeaux*.] Eleemosyna, and to the dean of Rheims, greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Because litigated disputes among ecclesiastical men [Col. 0279A] often customarily bring dangers and inconveniences upon the most holy churches, it is fitting for us to employ vigilant care and solicitous diligence in resolving them. Therefore, we entrust to your discretion, in which we have full confidence, for hearing and due decision, with the obstacle of appeal removed, the case that has long been contested, but has not yet reached its proper conclusion, between our beloved sons the canons of the church of Saint-Maurice of Tours and the abbot and brethren of Cluny, concerning certain estates near the village called [Note: [Col. 0279D] There is a priory, or deanery, of Saint Peter of Turibus in the diocese of Rheims, of the Cluniac order.] Turon., situated on the Marne, transferred to the monks from the men of the canons under whatever title.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your care [Col. 0279B] to meet together at Rheims by the coming feast of the Ascension of the Lord, summon both parties before you, and, after the arguments on each side have been sufficiently heard and examined, conclude the same case, with recourse to appeal set aside, by agreement if possible, or otherwise through the administration of justice. But if it should happen that any one of you—son abbot of Eleemosyna or dean—is absent by some chance, you, son abbot of Saint-Remigius, shall take part in the business and nevertheless pursue it together with the other of them. If either party withdraws itself from your judgment within the appointed term, you shall proceed with the case no less in the manner stated.

[Col. 0279C] Given at Sens, on the Nones of December [5 December].

### CCXXVIII. To Louis, King of the Franks.—He reports that the prior of Châteaufort and his associates have been excommunicated by [Joseio], Archbishop of Tours, [Geoffrey], Bishop of Angers, and the abbot of Marmoutier, because of the slander inflicted upon the abbot of Bourgueil. (Sens, 6 December.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 997.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Because the reputation of the enterprise of royal highness always proceeds in such a manner that, through love of heavenly contemplation, you are shown to devote diligent effort and care to the preservation of Churches, we commend your pious solicitude [Col. 0279D] in the Lord, whom we wish and desire always to be exercised in pious works and, as a most Christian king, to prosper in all your good acts.

Therefore we wish it to come to the knowledge of your greatness that, from the tenor of the letters of our venerable brethren the Archbishop of Tours and Bishop of Angers, and of our beloved son the abbot of Marmoutier, we have learned quite clearly that the prior of Châteaufort and his other associates have utterly failed in their accusation of our beloved son, the abbot of Bourgueil—a religious man indeed and one who fears God—and have been found wholly false; and for that reason they have been bound by the bond of excommunication. [Col. 0280A]

Moreover, since the aforesaid prior presumes to squander the goods of the Church of that place and to take them away by unlawful invasion, we ask, admonish, and exhort your highness in the Lord by apostolic letters that, out of regard for piety and reverence for blessed Peter and for us, you protect, uphold, and preserve the goods and rights of the Church of Bourgueil; and that you in no way support the aforesaid prior, but carefully avoid him as one excommunicated. Also compel the lord of Châteaufort, who is said violently to have seized the goods of the church of Saint Christopher, by the authority entrusted to you in this matter, to restore everything taken to that church and not to presume henceforth to attempt such acts against the aforesaid church [Col. 0280B] or to support the frequently mentioned prior.

Given at Sens, 8 Ides of December [6 December].

### CCXXIX. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—For the case pending between the abbot of Cluny and the canons of blessed Maurice. (Sens, 6 December.)

[MARTEN., *Collect.*, II, 696.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greeting and the apostolic blessing.

We entrust to your discretion for hearing and due determination the case known to be pending between our beloved sons, [Note: [Col. 0280D] Stephen, who in 1161 succeeded Hugh III as abbot of Cluny, as we have already observed.] the abbot of Cluny and the canons of blessed Maurice of Tours, concerning goods and possessions at Turn. [Col. 0280C] on the Marne. By apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, unless the same case has been settled by judgment or agreement, or unless the aforesaid abbot has already preferred our judgment in this matter, you summon both parties before you; and, after hearing and carefully examining the arguments on both sides, decide the case itself through justice, without the obstacle of appeal.

Given at Sens, 7 Ides of December [7 December].

### CCXXX. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—For the cleric B. (Sens, 15 December.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0280D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greeting and the apostolic blessing.

B., a cleric, appearing before us in our presence, made the following complaint: that his brother presumes unjustly to take away from him the portion which comes to him by right of inheritance, and to inflict a grave injury upon him in this matter. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to call the brother of that cleric to account in this matter and, if this is so, earnestly admonish and compel him with every severity to leave the cleric his whole portion, free and unencumbered. [Col. 0281A] Furthermore, concerning Ascelin of La Ferté, who is said violently to hold a certain house belonging to him and to inflict other burdens upon him, likewise ensure that the fullness of justice is rendered to him in your presence regarding these matters.

Given at Sens, 18 Kalends of January [15 December].

### CCXXXI. To Louis, King of the Franks.—That he defend the Parisian church of Saint Genevieve from the injuries of G., his butler. (Sens, 25 December.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 1023.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, [Col. 0281B] greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son . . . , abbot of Saint Genevieve, who, like a new shepherd and diligent administrator, strives and labours in every way for the welfare of his church, has shown us by a communication sent to us that our beloved son G., a nobleman, your butler, under pretext of a certain custom which he asserts obtains in all royal abbeys, demands from him certain things which the aforesaid abbot by no means acknowledges to be owed by that church. Therefore, since the serenity of your highness is accustomed to preserve the liberties of churches uninjured and intact, we ask, admonish, and exhort your clemency by apostolic letters in the Lord that, if this is so, you do not permit that same church to be burdened by a new and unjust exaction [Col. 0281C] and that you wholly recall and turn back your aforesaid butler from this purpose.

Given at Sens, 14 Kalends of January [19 December].

### CCXXXII. He confirms the agreement concerning two prebends made between Hugh, Bishop of Soissons, and his chapter. (Sens, 25 December.)

[Ibid., col. 979.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, Bishop of Soissons, greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Since a serious dispute had arisen between you and your chapter on this account: that the chapter did not permit you freely to dispose of those two prebends formerly held by Gerbert, cantor of that church, asserting that one of them belonged to the office of the chantry. By the consent and good pleasure of both parties the following agreement was reached between you: that, one of those prebends being freely disposed of by you, you granted the other to our beloved son R., cantor of the same church, to hold during his lifetime by reason of the office of cantor, [Col. 0281D] on the condition expressly included that, once R. ceases to be cantor, you or your successors shall have power to assign that prebend, as one of the other prebends, to whomsoever you wish.

Accordingly, holding that agreement ratified, we confirm it by apostolic authority, as it is contained in the authentic instrument made concerning it, [Col. 0282A] and strengthen it with the protection of this present writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the wrath of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Sens, 12 Kalends of January [21 December].

### CCXXXIII. To the abbots of Saint-Remigius and Saint-Nicaise.—For the case of the cleric Odo and his mother, and Hugh the Smith. (Sens, 25 December.)

[MARTEN., *Collect.*, II, 697.]

[Col. 0282B] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbots of Saint-Remigius and Saint-Nicaise, greeting and the apostolic blessing.

We have thought fit to entrust to your examination the case known to be pending between Odo, a cleric, and his mother, and Hugh the Smith, concerning a certain vineyard, which was brought before our hearing by the appeal of one party, because neither party came to the case sufficiently prepared. By apostolic letters we command you, after summoning together before you the aforesaid cleric and his mother and Hugh, to receive their arguments and the depositions of sworn witnesses on both sides, with appeal set aside; and, unless they consider an appeal necessary after this, to proceed also to a definitive judgment. [Col. 0282C] But if an appeal is made from the judgment, inform us by your letters, within the period allowed for appeal, of the arguments and the witnesses’ depositions.

Given at Sens, 8 Kalends of January [25 December].

## YEAR 1164

### CCXXXIV. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—He recalls for reconsideration the concession made to Roger, Archbishop of York, to carry the cross before himself throughout all England. (Sens, 21 January.)

[*Letters of Saint Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 8.]

ALEXANDER, pope, to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

[Col. 0282D] Having formerly received complaints from your brotherhood against our venerable brother the Archbishop of York, that he carried the cross through your diocese contrary to the dignity of your church and ancient custom, we wrote to him at your request, commanding him that, although in the letters of our concession which we had previously granted him we had given him authority to carry the cross throughout all England, he should nevertheless not presume to carry it through your diocese until the case itself had been determined in judicial order. Yet in those same letters of our concession the phrase, namely, “throughout all England,” had not been inserted at all; rather, in the aforesaid letters of our concession it had simply been stated: “We grant you free authority [Col. 0283A] to carry the cross before you, as our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, granted to your predecessors, and as they are known to have used it by ancient custom.”

Thus it happened through forgetfulness rather than design that those later letters contained the phrase “throughout all England.” For we did not remember the tenor of our earlier letters of concession. Therefore, lest any prejudice to your church arise in the course of time on account of that phrase, by the authority of these presents we decree that those later letters shall henceforth have no force against you and your church.

Given at Sens, 12 Kalends of February [21 January].

### CCXXXV. To Roger, Archbishop of York.—That he not use the concession to carry the cross before himself throughout all England until this controversy is resolved. (Sens, January?)

[*Letters of Saint Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 43.]

[Col. 0283B]

ALEXANDER, pope, to ROGER, Archbishop of York.

Because of that sincerity of mind and devotion of faith which you are known to have had toward the most holy Roman Church, and especially toward our person, we have always had the mind and will to show you, as our most beloved brother, due regard and to strive with more earnest zeal for your honour and advancement. This, indeed, was why, at the urgent instance [Col. 0283C] of your prayers, having examined certain rescripts of our predecessors, we remember granting you free authority to carry the cross before you throughout all England.

But since a controversy concerning this is still being pursued and the dispute itself has not yet reached its due conclusion, and since no small scandal might now arise if you exercised the licence granted to you at this time, we will and command that, just as before our concession you did not in fact exercise such a dignity, so you likewise do not use it until the case itself has been more fully investigated and the controversy concerning it receives its proper conclusion.

### CCXXXVI. To Roger, Archbishop, and the canons of York.—That the archbishop should not presume to carry the cross before himself in the province of Canterbury. (Sens, January?)

[Ibid., p. 44.]

[Col. 0283D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ROGER, Archbishop of York, and to his beloved sons, the canons of York, greeting and the apostolic blessing.

It befits your prudence to leave another’s rights untouched, just as you desire your own to be preserved whole and inviolate. Accordingly, by apostolic authority we prohibit you, Archbishop, from carrying your cross in any manner within the province of the Church of Canterbury, nor may you attempt this on any occasion under pretext of any appeal. For this could generate harmful prejudice to whatever right you may have. [Col. 0284A] If you are unwilling to abstain for a time, you and your successors will have to abstain perpetually.

### CCXXVII. He confirms the privileges of the priory of Saint Mary of the Field in the district of Roussillon. (Sens, 22 January.)

[AGUIRRE, *Concil. Hisp.*, III, 374.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PONTIUS, prior of the church of Saint Mary of the Field, and to his brethren, both present and future, to be canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

The principle of law [Col. 0284B] and the force of equity require that just requests be granted, especially when the petitioners’ wishes are supported by piety and truth. [lacuna]

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid church in which you are devoted to divine service. First, we decree that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that church according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be preserved there inviolate for all time. Further, whatever possessions or goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by God’s favour, acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the bounty [Col. 0284C] of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of Paciano, with its freeholds and appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Laurone; the church of Saint Mary of Villare Millariis, as the aforesaid bishop granted them to you; the church of Saint Mary of Villare, with its tithes, first-fruits, freeholds, and offerings, as Peter Bernard, of good memory, bishop of Elne, justly granted it to you, except for the synodal payment which he reserved to the church of Elne; and likewise whatever Ermengaud and Peter Bernard, bishops formerly of Elne, of good memory, reasonably bestowed upon your same church out of piety. Indeed, no one may presume to demand tithes from you from your newly cultivated lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals.

We further add that none of your brethren, after making profession in that place, may leave the cloister without his prior’s permission; and no one may dare retain one who leaves without letters of authorization from the community. We prohibit anyone from presuming to receive in burial the parishioners of your church, without prejudice to the canonical right of your church. Upon the death of you, the present prior of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one may be placed over it by any artifice of deceit or violence, unless he whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren from among your own community or another, [Col. 0285A] shall have provided to be elected according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine.

We also decree that the burial-place of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; without prejudice to the canonical right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole and undiminished, to be beneficial in every way for the governance and support of those for whose use they were granted, [Col. 0285B] saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. As a token of this protection received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay two solidi every year to us and our successors.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ualdus, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Hubaldus, Bishop of Ostia. I, Hyacinthus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. [Col. 0285C] I, Gualterius, Bishop of Albano. I, Albertus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Boso, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Cintius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian.

Given at Sens by the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 11 Kalends of February [22 January], in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1163 of the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Alexander III, pope.

### CCXXXVIII. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—Concerning the office of the apostolic legation, customarily granted to Canterbury but granted to York at the king’s request. (Sens, 27 February.)

[*Letters of Saint Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 1.]

[Col. 0285D]

ALEXANDER, pope, to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

Although, because of the prudence of your mind and the sincerity of your faith, we always wish to love your person with a more abundant sweetness of charity and a more ardent desire, and to strive with a more fervent mind for your honour and exaltation, as for those of our most beloved brother, nevertheless it is fitting for both us and you yourself—who are a great pillar of your church—to give more cautious attention to the condition of the times and, by the prudent moderation [Col. 0286A] of dispensation, to soothe the king’s temper.

For your diligence, to which divine dispensation has granted the gift of great foresight and grace, knows how fervently our dearest son in Christ Henry, illustrious King of the English, is engaged in the governance of his realm, and how he wishes that same arrangement, in order that it may be more firmly established and receive greater favour, to be strengthened by the authority of the Roman Church. Hence, since he had formerly urgently requested through our venerable brother the Bishop of Lisieux and our beloved son the Archdeacon of Poitiers that the legation over all England be granted to the Archbishop of York, and had asked that both you and all the bishops be commanded to preserve the ancient customs and dignities [Col. 0286B] of his realm, after we and our brethren had moderated his requests contrary to his desire, immediately after the return of his messengers, scarcely having heard what they had brought back from us, he sent our beloved sons Geoffrey, your archdeacon, and Master John to our presence, and through them urgently sought from us what he had previously requested, and greater things besides.

And, so that we might show a mind more receptive to his desire, he procured letters to us from your brotherhood and from the aforesaid archbishop. What he had first asked should be commanded concerning the preservation of ancient customs and dignities, he recently requested with great insistence, since you and the others had promised to observe them, to be confirmed to himself and his heirs by the authority of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0286C] But we did not admit this request.

Nevertheless, lest we provoke him to excessive bitterness and more violent disturbance of mind against us and yourself, and lest the matter be thought in any way to be hindered out of consideration for you, wishing to provide more wisely for you and ourselves lest perhaps he should blaze up into greater heat of anger against you, and considering the perilous times, we granted the same king letters of legation to be granted to the aforesaid archbishop.

But because one must yield to the wishes of princes and obey their will, we admonish, counsel, and wholly exhort your prudence that, as a prudent and discerning man, measuring the necessity of the time and faithfully considering the dangers that might result from it for you and [Col. 0286D] your church, you endeavour in all things and through all things, while preserving the honour of ecclesiastical order, to show deference to the aforesaid king and tirelessly seek to recover his favour and affection toward you. Otherwise, you may provoke him into hostility against us and yourselves, and those who do not walk in the same spirit may thereby be able to insult you and us.

For when opportunity is given us, we shall confer diligently and carefully with that king concerning your honour and advancement; and we shall exercise the necessary diligence and caution that ought to be exercised in preserving the rights and dignities of your church.

Given at Sens, 3 Kalends of March [27 February].

### CCXXXIX. To the same and the bishops of England.—That they grant King Henry nothing contrary to ecclesiastical liberty. (Sens, February.)

[*Letters of Saint Thomas*, ed. Giles, II, 1, p. 9.]

[Col. 0287A]

ALEXANDER, pope, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, and all bishops established throughout England, greeting and the apostolic blessing.

You are known to have undertaken the burden of the pontifical office in order to govern the churches entrusted to you in such a way for the honour of God and the advancement and salvation of your subjects that the liberty of those churches may in no way be diminished through you, [Col. 0287B] but be preserved in its condition through your care and labour. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and enjoin upon your brotherhood, under obedience, that if the illustrious King of the English at any time asks of you anything that is contrary to ecclesiastical liberty, you make no attempt whatever to do it for him. Nor are you to bind yourselves to him in anything, and especially not against the Roman Church, or presume to introduce a new form of promise or oath beyond that which bishops are accustomed to make to their kings.

But if you know yourselves already bound to the aforesaid king in any such matter, you must by no means observe what you have promised; rather, take care to revoke it and endeavour to be reconciled to God and the Church from an unlawful promise. [Col. 0287C]

### CCXL. To the same.—That he should not be distressed by the legation granted to Roger of York. (Sens, February.)

[Ibid., p. 3.]

Let not your spirit fail because of the favour of the legation granted, nor be led into the sighs of despair. For before we were brought to this point or gave any consent, the aforesaid messengers firmly promised us on the word of truth, on behalf of the king himself—and even offered, if we wished to receive it, an oath on this matter—that those same letters would never be delivered to the Archbishop of York without your knowledge and consent. Indeed, we wish you to believe without doubt [Col. 0287D] and to hold without any scruple of uncertainty that it has never entered our mind, nor, God willing, shall ever enter it, that we should wish you or your church to be subject to any person in ecclesiastical matters, or to obey anyone but the Roman pontiff alone.

Therefore we admonish and command your prudence that, once you can ascertain that the same king has delivered the letters—which we do not believe he will do without your knowledge—immediately notify us of this by a trustworthy messenger and your letters, so that by apostolic authority we may decree your person, [Col. 0288A] your church, and likewise the city entrusted to you, entirely exempt from every right of legation.

### CCXLI. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims, and Henry, Cardinal.—Concerning the business of the lord pope. (Sens, 21 March.)

[MARTEN., *Collect.*, II, 705.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, and to his beloved son HENRY, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Of your plans and your welfare, beloved son cardinal, whom we have heard to be ill, being exceedingly concerned, we send this courier to you, earnestly requesting and admonishing that, by the counsel of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Franks, you by no means withdraw yourselves until these discussions are broken off.

[Note: [Col. 0287D] Observe here in passing that the pontiff calls bishops “brothers,” but cardinals merely “sons,” and places the name of bishops before that of cardinals, [Col. 0288D] because episcopal dignity surpasses cardinalatial dignity.]

For we know and hold as certain truth that whenever matters concerning the Church are discussed, they are directed and advanced more successfully by your presence. But if it should happen that one of you is unable to attend, we ask your fraternity, brother archbishop, that you on no account depart, and that you do not delay to report to us through the same cardinal—so far as your honour permits—whatever is dealt with there concerning the affairs of the Church; and likewise that you write back to us by this courier what [Col. 0288C] he wishes concerning the matter which we discussed with you about our brother.

Given at Sens, 21 March.

CCXLII. To Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg.—That he should persuade and compel Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, to keep silence concerning certain disputations on the faith. (Sens, 22 March.)

[PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, VI, I, 398.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother E., Archbishop of Salzburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When our beloved son Master G., provost of Reichersberg, sent us his letter, containing certain articles which, through disputes between him and [Col. 0288D] others, had become a matter of perplexing controversy, we thought that no definite answer should be given concerning these articles. For unless we heard him and the others in person, it did not seem right to us so readily to pronounce judgment upon them, and, on the basis of reasons alleged by only one party, to condemn the other unheard and undefended by a rash judgment.

But since we recognize that no benefit follows from disputes of this kind, and that they may rather lead the simple into error than confer any advantage—for such persons ought indeed to be fed like asses alongside oxen—we advised the aforesaid provost and persuaded him in every way that, concerning such disputations on the faith, neither he nor the other party should proceed further under any circumstances. Rather, avoiding in every way profane novelties of language, they should follow the simple truth received by the universal Church from blessed Athanasius and, in accordance with the affirmations of the other Fathers, walk in the doctrine of the Catholic faith. Content with the boundaries established by our fathers, they should presume to go neither beyond nor short of them.

Therefore, by these apostolic letters, we command your fraternity urgently to admonish the aforesaid provost and the others, on your behalf and ours, to abstain henceforth from such disputations, especially in public assemblies, and to compel them to do so with all strictness.

[Col. 0289B] Given at Sens, 22 March.

CCXLIII. To Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg.—He enjoins silence upon him concerning the same disputations on the faith. (Sens, 22 March.)

[PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, VI, 1, col. 399.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Master G., provost of Reichersberg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we give more diligent attention to the integrity of sincere mind and the entire devotion which we believe you and your brethren laudably display toward the most holy Roman Church, and especially toward our person, we have a fervent purpose and ready will gladly to promote your honour and advancement. Whenever an opportunity is afforded by messengers, it is pleasing to us to be able to visit you by apostolic letters. This, indeed, was why we sent you our letters on a previous occasion. And now, through the bearer of the present letter, we likewise send others, from whose tenor we wish you and them to know and truly recognize that we love you as special and devoted sons of the Church with sincere charity in the Lord, and that, insofar as we can with God and honour, we intend and desire to honour your persons.

But the greater the bond of charity by which we are bound toward you, and the more earnestly we seek your honour and advancement, the more willingly we suggest to you those things which we know to concern the salvation of the soul and the honour of the body. Certainly, concerning those articles which, through disputes between you and others, became a matter of perplexing controversy, and which you indicated to us in your letter, we thought that no definite answer should be given; and the rest is as written above in the letter addressed to the archbishop.

For we have instructed our venerable brother the Archbishop of Salzburg to admonish you and the others repeatedly, and restrain you, from further disputations of this kind, especially in public assemblies, lest by such novelty of language the hearts of the unlearned and simple be led astray and compelled to enter upon the path of error—which God forbid.

[Col. 0290A] Given at Sens, 22 March.

CCXLIV. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—He consoles one in mourning and absolves him from an oath. (Sens, 1 April.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1193.]

Let your fraternity know that it has been brought to our ears, and represented to us by certain persons, that, on account of some transgression, you have proposed to cease celebrating Masses and to refrain from consecrating the blood and body of the Lord. Consider with careful reflection how grave this is, especially in so important a person, and how much scandal may arise from it; and let the vigilance of your discretion attend to this very point.

Your diligence ought prudently to observe—since it makes a very great difference—when acts are committed deliberately and by one’s own will, and when through ignorance or some necessity. For one must proceed differently in matters done by voluntary will, and differently in matters done, as stated, through ignorance or under compulsion of necessity. The former and the latter must be treated differently and assessed by discerning and prudent men, as we are taught by the testimonies of Holy Scripture. Your intention gives your act its character. For, as is also read elsewhere, sin is voluntary to such an extent that, unless it is voluntary, it is not sin. And the almighty Lord does not consider the deed of the agent, but rather considers the intention and judges the will.

Therefore, if you remember having committed anything for which your own conscience ought to reproach you, whatever it may be, we advise you to confess it penitently to a priest considered discerning and prudent. When this has been done, the merciful Lord, who looks much more upon the heart than upon the act, will forgive you through the compassion of his accustomed mercy. And we, trusting in the merits of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, absolve you from what has been committed and, by apostolic authority, remit the same to your fraternity, advising and commanding that thereafter you ought not to abstain from celebrating Masses on this account.

Given at Sens, 1 April.

CCXLV. He subjects the monastery of Rasbach to Stephen, Bishop of Meaux. (Sens, 2 April.)

[LAUNOII, *Opera*, III, II, 408.]

[Col. 0290D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother STEPHEN, Bishop of Meaux, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever controversies conducted between ecclesiastical persons reach a canonical conclusion in our presence, it is necessary that they be committed to writing and confirmed by a document of apostolic authority, so that matters decided by apostolic favour and confirmed by written instrument may be impressed upon human memory all the more firmly as they are supported with greater care by the protection of our letters.

Now, a case had long been pending between you and our beloved sons B. . . . , abbot, and the brethren of Rasbach, concerning parochial right which you claimed for yourself both in the village and in the monastery. When you and they appeared in our presence concerning this matter, you demanded the subjection of the abbot and episcopal right in that village and monastery, asserting that you had held undisturbed possession for a long time, and establishing the truth of all this by many documents and the corroboration of numerous witnesses. The other party, on the contrary, claimed liberty for itself, and endeavoured to establish this by many arguments and by producing writings and witnesses.

But after both parties had presented on either side the evidence necessary to settle the doubtful matter, and after a careful comparison of documents and witnesses, we recognized that you had possessed without lawful interruption those things which you claimed in the village and the aforesaid monastery. By the common counsel of our brethren, we therefore adjudged to you, and through you to your Church, the obedience and subjection of the abbot and episcopal right, both in the monastery and in the village.

Wishing, however, usefully to provide for the peace and quiet of the same monastery in fulfillment of the duty imposed upon us, we forbid by apostolic authority that, on this occasion, any new and undue burdens be imposed upon the said monastery or village by you or your successors. Therefore, in order that this our determination may always be observed inviolate in future times, we confirm it by the authority of the Apostolic See and fortify it by the protection of this present writing, decreeing that no person whatsoever may infringe this document of our determination or in any way oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Sens, 2 April . . .

CCXLVI. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—Concerning thanks for Ar., Cardinal Deacon of Saint Theodore, and reports from Italy through Master Od. (Sens, 15 April.)

[MARTEN., *Collectanea*, II, 708.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting [Col. 0291D] and apostolic blessing.

We regard as altogether welcome and acceptable the affection and honour which your devotion took care to show, through yourself and your clerics, to our beloved son Ar., Cardinal Deacon of Saint Theodore, at his reception and afterward; and we commend your generosity on this account with fitting thanksgiving and magnificent praise in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] Ardicione Rivoltella of Milan, who, having been created cardinal by Pope Adrian IV in 1155, was sent by him as legate into Lombardy to make peace [Col. 0292D] between the Milanese and the people of Lodi.]

We ask you with every attention and diligence that, as you have well begun, you love this same son of ours and treat him as honourably as befits your dignity and accords with his rank, so that we and our brethren may always owe you due thanks and may be found ever more zealous and altogether more ready in promoting the honour and exaltation of you and the Church entrusted to you. For the honour and reverence rendered to him are no less welcome and acceptable to us and our brethren than if they had been bestowed especially upon our own person.

Nevertheless, let your prudence and solicitude employ such diligence and caution concerning his honour that every ground for detractors’ lips to disparage him, and us through him, may be removed. Certainly, through our beloved son Master Od., we have taken all the more gladly to inform your discretion of certain matters concerning the condition of Italy because we know you remain especially solicitous to learn of events favourable to the Church. We hold firm hope and confidence that the Church of God, which has taken breath through the support of you and the other faithful of Christ, will, after her enemies have been humbled, soon rejoice in the tranquillity of the peace she desires and, by divine mercy, take breath in the joy of rest and exultation. But do you, as you have well begun, devote yourself to her honour and exaltation, and always strive to labour with diligent concern.

Given at Sens, 15 April.

CCXLVII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Mary of Strata. (Sens, 17 April.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, XI, Instrumenta 135.]

[Col. 0292C] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to GERVASIUS, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Strata, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the religious life, in perpetuity.

Although by the office imposed upon us we are debtors to all ecclesiastical persons, we ought nevertheless to devote ourselves with a more particular zeal of charity to those whom we know to serve almighty God in the habit of true religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Saint Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service. We decree that whatever possessions and goods you now possess justly and canonically, or may hereafter be able to acquire, God favouring, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought it right to specify the following by their proper names:

The land of Strata; the land of Bellovillars; the land by the road of Ver; Grandpré; the other lands and meadows which you possess on both banks of the River Arve; one fisherman on the same river, granted by the lord of the castle of Musi; the grange of Faiel with all its appurtenances; the grange of Meravilla with all its appurtenances; the grange of Champeillum with its appurtenances; the land of Bescochin; whatever you possess in the forest of Crotens; and the grange of Chalet.

We forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, on any frivolous pretext to leave the cloister without permission of his prior or abbot; and no one may dare retain one who has departed without a letter of authorization from the community. Providing with paternal solicitude for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority that within the enclosures of your places or granges anyone dare commit violence, robbery, or theft; set fire; seize or kill a person.

Moreover, let no one presume to exact tithes from you from the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals. We decree, therefore, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Bernard, Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Walter, Bishop of Albano. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere.

Given at Sens, through the hand of . . . , subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 17 April, indiction 12, in the year 1164 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

CCXLVIII. Privilege for the Carthusian Order. (Sens, 17 April.)

[*Nova Collectio Statutorum Ordinis Carthusiensis*, Appendix, p. 6.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BASIL, prior of the Carthusians, and all priors and brethren of the Carthusian Order, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have recently learned from the rescript of the letters of the bishops set around you that they have decreed that those things known to have been established by you in common for the honour of God and the observance of your order should stand ratified and firm, and that they have strengthened them by the authority of their document. Therefore, yielding to your requests, we hold as ratified and firm all your constitutions which have reasonably been made, with the common assent of the chapter, for the religious observance of your order; and we confirm them to you by apostolic authority and fortify them by the protection of this present writing.

[Col. 0294A] Given at Sens, 17 April.

CCXLIX. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of a certain Gil., that money lent to him be repaid. (Sens, 19 May.)

[MARTEN., *Collectanea*, II, 709.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Gil., bearer of the present letter, appearing before us, asserted that when he urgently demanded from Ub., prior of the monastery of Saint Vasle, a sum of money which, having received it from another, he had lent to him, and the same prior delayed payment, a case between them was being heard before the dean of your church. He appealed to our hearing; and when he came, the other party came neither in person nor through a representative.

[Note: [Col. 0293] That is, Saint-Basle, in French *Saint-Basle*, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Reims, three or four miles from the city.]

Therefore, since we cannot and ought not to fail the aforesaid G. in his right, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters urgently to admonish and strictly compel the said prior either to return to this man without trouble the money lent to him, or to render him full justice in the matter under the examination of your discretion.

Given at Sens, 19 May.

CCL–CCLI. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres. (Sens, 3 June.)

[*Collection des Cartulaires*, II, 651.]

[Col. 0294C]

ALEXANDER, servant . . . . We decree that in the parish churches which you hold, you may elect priests and present the elected persons to the bishop; if they are found suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them. Those priests shall answer to the bishop regarding the care of the people, but to you regarding temporal matters. Further, when a general interdict of the land is in force, you may, with the doors closed, bells not rung, excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, and the voice subdued, celebrate divine offices . . . . . . .

Given at Sens, 3 June.

CCLII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of the church of Saint Remigius. (Sens, 4 June.)

[MARTEN., *Collectanea*, II, 709.]

[Col. 0294D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have committed to your discretion for hearing and due determination the case being litigated between our beloved sons, the abbots of Saint Remigius and of Der, concerning certain tithes. But since the abbot of Der asserts that his church is two days’ journey from your city, and that coming there greatly burdens him, especially when the other party is in its own house, we admonish and command your fraternity to assign them a suitable place common to both parties. When both parties have been summoned before you there, and their arguments diligently heard and understood on each side, determine the same case to its proper conclusion according to the tenor of the other letters.

Given at Sens, 4 June.

CCLIII. He receives the monastery of Vallis-Richerii under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Sens, 5 June.)

[*Neustria pia*, 826, from the Black manuscript codex of the cathedral church of Bayeux, fol. 17.]

[Col. 0295B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROBERT, abbot of Vallis-Richerii, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, etc.

The office of the government entrusted to us and the order of reason appear to require us to assent to religious vows and fulfill them by the performance of deeds. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests, receive the aforesaid monastery, in which you are dedicated to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, we decree that the monastic order recognized as instituted in this monastery according to the fear of God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institutions of the Cistercian brethren shall be observed inviolably for all time. Further, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now possesses justly and canonically, or may in future acquire, by the grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, the Lord granting it, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought it right to specify the following by their proper names:

From the gift of Simon of Bosville and his son Geoffrey: the place of Vallis-Richerii, where the abbey itself is situated, and part of the wood called Braffai; from the gift of the same, the land extending through the village of Roger, son of Gislebert, as far as the land of Roger de Bruerio, thence to the land of Richard de Altariis, and as far as Gratapantia; and, on the other side, all the land of Floold; and at Bosville, thirty-four acres of land.

From the gift of Richard de Altariis: the land, as marked out by a furrow, as far as the willow pond.

From the gift of Roger Carbonel: the land from the Thorn of Alden to Gratapantia, and from the new ditch to the valley of Orieldis.

From the gift of Robert de Baisio: the land from the path of the abbey as far as Saint Ouen.

From the gift of Richard de Folmuçone: all the land from the spring, following the ditch as far as Saint Ouen and as far as the road.

From the gift of Robert, son of Milo: twenty acres of land from the path of the house of Burinint to the main road; all the land of Ingulf the terrarius; and the land of Richer of Montreuil, from the land of Gernet to the land of Robert of Montreuil.

From the gift of Alured of the Castle: the land, following the ditch of Eve from the ford of Calvel meadow upward to the wood and to the field of Ervei.

From the gift of William Silvanus: the entire open land and wood, from the road that divides his land and the land of Simon of Bosville as far as the land of Rocha.

From the gift of Simon of Bosville: the whole fief of Ralph Gernet, which he held from Simon at Vallis-Richerii and which that same Ralph granted with the assent of Robert de Montfort.

From the gift of the priest Aitard and his nephew Droelin: all the land which they held from Adam Carbonel, both open land and wood; this was granted by Ralph Libaneis, his son Robert, and Richard son of Turgis, and was likewise approved and confirmed on faith by Robert and Adam Carbonel.

From the gift of Hugh de Rocha: fifteen acres of land near Gratapantia.

From the gift of Walchelin de Corcella: the land of Bruya.

From the gift of Robert, son of Herneisy: a dwelling in the forest of Cingleis; from that dwelling to the fields, all the wood lying in front of it; behind it, three acres of woodland in length and breadth; everything lying between the road leading to the monastery and the road of the Hanging Beech; all necessities, namely pasture for livestock, firewood, fencing, and building material; all his land outside the hazel wood as far as the pyre of Pines; and his own neighbouring land of Balchetot, namely thirty acres of land.

From the gift of Ralph de Boenc: six acres of land.

From the gift of Robert Bacon and his brother Gervase: four acres of land, with the consent of his son Robert.

From the gift of Gislebert de Brielcort: the grange of Favarchis; all the open land between the wood and the land of Ralph de Hamel; the wood from the aforesaid land, following the road from Seifredevilla toward the cross of Malagarda; from the exit of that wood, all the open land and wood by the Great Oak as far as the exit of Boelia, toward the house of Ralph le Colet; thence all the land between the land of the said Ralph and the land of Osbelen de Bosco as far as the forest; thence all his lordship as far as the land of his vassals of Sarnai; in Valle-Tolca, one acre of meadow; and in his forest, pasture for animals throughout the year, except in April, excluding goats. This gift was granted by Walchelin de Ferrariis.

From the gift of Ralph, son of Walter Rosfel: the open land and wood, as divided by the road running above his house, as far as his arable field.

From the gift of Ralph de Hamel: four acres of land.

From the gift of William Silvanus: the grange of Green Valley, with all belonging to it.

No one may presume to exact tithes from you from the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals. Further, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone to dare receive or retain your brethren, clerics or laymen, after they have made profession in your monastery, without your permission. Providing with paternal solicitude for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority that within the enclosure of your places or granges anyone dare commit violence, robbery, or theft, or seize a person.

We therefore decree that no one may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain possessions removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all shall be preserved intact and shall in every respect benefit the uses for whose governance and support they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone, therefore, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, Bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Walter, Bishop of Albano. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Henry, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Boso, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Manfred, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.
