Given at Sens through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Roman Church, on the Nones of June, indiction 12, in the year 1164 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

CCLIV. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of R., the chancellor. (Sens, 6 July.)

[MARTEN., *Collectanea*, II, 710.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Considering the fervour of your spirit and the affection of most sincere purity which, from the beginning of our elevation, the innermost recesses of your breast have borne toward the Church of God and ourselves, we more willingly communicate to your devotion, with all confidence and security, whatever we could ever entrust to anyone.

Know, then, that that author and head of the Church’s disturbance, R., namely the former chancellor of the one called Emperor F., since his approach is wholly obstructed elsewhere, plans to go through Flanders into German territory.

[Note: [Col. 0297D] Rainald, formerly provost of Hildesheim and made Archbishop of Cologne, was a faithful companion of Emperor Frederick [Col. 0298D] in Italy.]

Since, therefore, we have complete confidence in the constancy of your strength in every matter, we request and admonish your prudence in every way that, through yourself, your friends, and your faithful men, you endeavour to harass and altogether impede the aforesaid R.; and, if you can seize him, do not delay under any circumstances. For you could accomplish nothing at present more welcome and acceptable to us and the Church, nor anything by which you might gain greater praise and glory of honour.

Given at Sens, 6 July.

CCLV. To the same.—For the absolution of William the monk. (Sens, 13 July.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When W., your parishioner, appeared in our presence, he asserted to us that, while he was grievously afflicted by illness, the abbot and brethren of Saint Remigius persuaded him, without his wife’s permission, to put on the monastic habit and hand over to them twenty pounds which he had with him. When he recovered and more carefully considered within himself what he had done, as though returning to himself, he took off the monastic habit which he had put on, wholly refused to make monastic profession, and demanded back the money which he had handed over to them.

But the aforesaid monks put him in chains, afflicted him with harsh torments, entirely withheld food from him for two days, and sought to compel him to swear that he would never demand the aforesaid money from them or take any action against them on this account. Since we cannot in any way fail the said W. in his right, we command you by apostolic letters carefully to investigate the matter. If it is established that the aforesaid monks caused the said William to put on the monastic habit without his wife’s permission, then, supported by our authority, absolve him from the claim of the said abbot and his brethren.

Given at Sens, 13 July.

CCLVI. To the same.—For the case of Millesende and R. de Curti. (Sens, 18 July.)

[Ibid.]

[Note: [Col. 0298D] In the text of the letter he is called de Coci.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0299A] brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We formerly committed to your discretion for determination, when we were at Tours, the case known to be litigated between the woman Millesende and Ralph de Coci concerning that woman’s dowry. But since the aforesaid woman, though repeatedly wearied by appearing before you, has not yet been able to obtain her right, we command your fraternity by repeated letters that, within thirty days after receiving these letters, you summon both parties before you in a place where they can safely come, and determine the same case to its proper conclusion according to the tenor of the other letters, so that the woman may not thereafter be compelled to labour on this account.

[Col. 0299B] Given at Sens, 18 July.

CCLVII. To Hugh, Bishop of Soissons.—He commends Rain, Archdeacon of Salisbury, who will pursue studies at Paris. (Sens, 26 July.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 981.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, Bishop of Soissons, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son Rain, Archdeacon of Salisbury, has resolved to reside at Paris and for the present to devote himself there to literary study. Since he is very dear and acceptable to us on account of his worth, we earnestly commend him to your fraternity, in whom we have full confidence. We earnestly request that, for reverence of blessed Peter and ourselves, and in consideration of his devotion, you look upon him with a more gracious eye, love and honour him, and give him suitable counsel and favour whenever he has need; so that he may find our prayers beneficial to him, and we in turn may render abundant thanks to your solicitude.

Given at Sens, 26 July.

CCLVIII. To Louis, King of the Franks.—Concerning the chancellor of Emperor Frederick, by whose command workmen had already begun work on the frontier of France. (Sens, 30 July.)

[Ibid., col. 1017.]

[Col. 0299D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When we weigh with attentive reflection the multitude of benefits which royal serenity has always bestowed upon the most holy Roman Church and upon ourselves, and especially in this time of disturbance, with a tranquil disposition; when we consider also how generously and devoutly you and your kingdom have alike devoted yourselves to the service of blessed Peter and to our good pleasure: unless we loved with our whole affection your honour, advancement, and exaltation, and that of the kingdom itself, and unless we endeavoured in all things, insofar as with God and justice we are able, to show you—as a most Christian king and Catholic prince—zealous regard, we should grievously fear offending God, for whose sake you have magnanimously undertaken to defend the cause of the Church, and we should appear wholly to depart from the duty of our office.

Having therefore received the letters of your Highness with such gladness of spirit and joy of mind as was fitting, and having learned more fully from the tenor of those letters of the fervour of devotion which the inmost parts of your heart bear toward the advancement of the Church and of ourselves, we are moved to render more devoted thanks to your royal Sublimity on this account and to seek more earnestly your advantage and advancement. This is especially so since, as we have learned from the report of our messengers and of your clerics, you received our letters with most ready devotion. Therefore let your Highness learn from this communication that we have obtained quite clear assurance from a certain abbot who came from Burgundy, that, after very many workmen had already been hired by R., formerly chancellor of the said Emperor F., and had begun, it is said, to work at his command on the frontier of your kingdom, our beloved son, the nobleman . . . . . Count of Forez, putting on courage and strength, boldly drove the same workmen from the place; and, fiercely threatening them and others who might attempt these things, struck no slight terror into their minds.

But since the aforesaid chancellor, by no means desisting from his malice, has left a large sum of money in order to bring to effect what he wickedly intends: it concerns you, after taking counsel with the barons and prudent men of your kingdom, utterly to destroy this undertaking lest it proceed further, and completely to thwart the malignity of the wicked. For we, being very ready and prepared to offer counsel and aid in this matter, have firmly instructed the elect of Lyons that he is in no way to consent to this affair, but is to endeavour, as far as he can, to disrupt it.

Given at Sens, the third day before the Kalends of August.

CCLIX. To Louis, King of the Franks.—That the king is not to decide otherwise in a cause which the bishop of Le Mans has judged by apostolic authority. (Sens, August 1.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1028.]

[Col. 0300D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Franbus, canon of the church of Saint Martin at Tours, and Nicholas Burgensis, appearing before us, set forth various complaints against one another. The said Burgensis complained that the same F. had inflicted upon him many injuries and burdens, and had rashly violated the settlement which had formerly been made by command of our father and predecessor Pope Eugenius, of pious memory, and confirmed by a bodily oath sworn.

Since we entrusted the complaint of the same N. concerning damages inflicted to our venerable brother [William], bishop of Le Mans, a religious, prudent, and discerning man, and a canon of the same church, to be brought to its proper conclusion, he, as a diligent investigator of justice, having heard the arguments of both sides, pronounced sentence, although it has not yet been carried into execution. But since the clemency of royal Sublimity has appointed the third day after the Kalends of August for them to appear before your presence, we, always wishing with eager mind to defer to your Serenity in all things in which, with God and justice, we can do so, send them to your presence, earnestly requesting that, because the aforesaid N. wished his affair to be decided by authority of the Apostolic See, your Serenity may not take this ill, may in no way regard it as burdensome, may never endeavour to invalidate the bishop’s act, and may not allow him on this occasion to suffer any loss of his right.

For, since we did not wish to entrust the case to others, but committed it to the aforesaid bishop for determination because he is a learned man and loves the honour of that church with his whole desire, not as an outsider but as its own canon, it would greatly redound to contempt of him if your Excellency were to revoke as void what, relying on our authority, he has reasonably decided. Moreover, if you settle peacefully and amicably between them the injuries inflicted, you will do what is pleasing and acceptable to us.

Given at Sens, on the Kalends of August.

CCLX. He establishes the city of Uppsala as metropolitan see of the bishoprics of Skara, Linköping, Strängnäs, and Århus, etc. (Sens, August.)

[LILJEGREN, *Diplomatarium Suecanum*, I, 70.]

[Col. 0301C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother STEPHEN and his successors canonically appointed: in perpetual remembrance.

Although all the disciples received from the Lord the same power of binding and loosing, although Christ, the one true and unique master, commanded all to preach the Gospel to every creature, nevertheless there was among them a certain distinction of dignity; and blessed Peter received, by a special prerogative, the care of the Lord’s sheep, which rested equally upon all, the Lord saying to him: “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep.” He also obtained among all the apostles the title of primacy and received from the Lord a singular command concerning the strengthening of the brethren, so that posterity might thereby understand in particular that, although many might be ordained to govern the Church, yet one alone held the place and summit of supreme dignity and presided over all in the honour of the power to judge and govern.

Accordingly, under this pattern the distinction of ranks has been preserved in the Church; and, just as in the human body diverse members are ordered for the variety of offices, so in the fabric of the Church different persons in different orders have been established to perform different ministries. Some are appointed for the ordering and government of individual churches, others for that of individual cities; and in each province others are appointed whose judgment is to have primacy among their brethren and to whose examination the disputes and affairs of subordinate persons are to be referred.

Above all, however, the Roman pontiff is known to hold the first place, as Noah did in the ark. By the privilege always bestowed upon him in the Prince of the Apostles, he judges and orders the causes of all, and throughout the whole world ceases not to strengthen the children of the Church in the firmness of Christian faith, taking continual care to show himself such a man as deserves to hear the Lord’s word: “And you, when once converted, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22:32).

Moved, indeed, by this consideration, and when, dearest brother in Christ, you came into our presence, we judged fit to grant you the pallium, that is, the fullness of the pontifical office, in accordance with what had been ordered and established by our predecessors from times past but had not yet been fulfilled in execution; this was done at the request and through the intervention of our dearest son Charles, illustrious king of the Swedes and Goths, of the bishops also, and of Duke Ulf of that kingdom.

And lest the metropolitan care of the province of Sweden should hereafter be lacking, we have ordained the city of Uppsala, entrusted to your governance, to be the perpetual metropolitan see of that province; and we have established that the bishoprics of Skara, Linköping, Strängnäs, and Århus shall be subject to it as to their metropolitan see for all time, and that the bishops of those places, present and future alike, shall obey, as their metropolitan, both you and your successors.

We further decree that, just as you received the grace of consecration by our grant and command from our venerable brother, the archbishop of Lund, so your successors must receive consecration from him and his successors without any contradiction, and must show obedience and reverence to him as to their own primate.

Moreover, since the pallium—that is, the fullness of the pontifical office—has been granted to you, your brotherhood may use it within your church, and throughout your province only at the sacred solemnities of Mass, on the following days alone, which are written below: the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, the Lord’s Supper, the Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, the feasts of the blessed Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, the feast of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul; the Finding and Exaltation of the Holy Cross, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; the feast of blessed John the Evangelist, the commemoration of All Saints, the consecrations of churches or bishops, blessings of abbots, ordinations of priests, the anniversary of the dedication of your church, the feast of Saint Lawrence, and the anniversary day of your consecration.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the church of Uppsala, take away its possessions or retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole and inviolate, entirely available for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the due right and reverence of the bishop of Lund.

CCLXI. Bull concerning the establishment of the metropolitan see of Uppsala. (Sens, August 5.)

[Ibid., p. 72.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all his venerable brothers, the bishops established throughout the kingdom of Sweden: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0303B] We received with due kindness our venerable brother Stephen, formerly elect of the church of Uppsala but now your archbishop, when he came to the Apostolic See; and we bestowed upon him all the favour and honour which it was fitting for us to bestow. Giving favourable assent to his petitions, in accordance with what had been ordered and established by our predecessors from times past but had not yet been fulfilled in execution, and at the request and intervention of our dearest son in Christ Charles, illustrious king of the Swedes and Goths, of yourselves also, and of Duke Ulf of that kingdom, we judged fit to grant him the pallium—that is, the fullness of the pontifical office.

And lest the metropolitan care of the province of Sweden should thereafter be lacking, we have ordained that the city of Uppsala, entrusted to his governance, be the perpetual metropolitan see of that province, and have established that your bishoprics shall be subject to it as to their metropolitan see for all time. Therefore, sending him back to his own country with the fullness of our favour and the blessing of the Apostolic See, we earnestly commend him to your charity, requesting, admonishing, and commanding through these present writings that you receive him kindly as your archbishop, treat him honourably, show him in matters pertaining to God every reverence as your metropolitan, and take care humbly to obey him in all things, so that you may appear worthy of commendation for the virtue of obedience.

Moreover, since the pastoral concern entrusted to us by God requires that we apply watchful care and diligent attention to ecclesiastical traditions, we forbid you by apostolic authority ever to perform unlawful ordinations; never to travel through your parishes merely out of customary practice, for the sake of feasting or pleasure, but solely with a view to wholesome teaching; and not to grant churches to anyone for any payment. Thus, by more diligently observing all these things and whatever else becomes pastoral vigilance, you may remain like shining vessels before the eyes of the Lord and in the sight of men.

Given at Sens, on the Nones of August.

CCLXII. To Abbot Henry and the brethren of Saint Mary of Vitskøl. (Sens, August 2.)

[LANGEBECK, *Rerum Danicarum Scriptores*, V, 241.]

[Col. 0304A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HENRY, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Saint Mary of Vitskøl: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having received with due kindness the letters of your devotion, beloved son Abbot, we have learned from their tenor that Eskil, bishop of Århus, having granted to your church a place unsuitable for religious life—namely, Sabro—afterward gave you in exchange for the aforesaid place a more suitable place, namely Smabeng [perhaps Sminge].

Accordingly, when you, son Abbot, sought our counsel in this matter, because that bishop had at one time consented to an error, though, when placed under strict examination, he rejected his own act, we deliberated sufficiently on this matter with our venerable brother Eskil, archbishop of Lund—Eskil was then with the pope—and with our other brethren. This decision pleased the same archbishop, who likewise gave it his assent and support.

Therefore, wishing with paternal solicitude to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we confirm to you, and through you to your church, that place by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way act against it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed Apostles Peter and Paul.

CCLXIII. Concerning the monks of Tiron, who are to be distributed among various monasteries, with five or four left there, so that meanwhile the debts may be paid. (Sens, August 6.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1020.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When our beloved son . . . . . abbot of Tiron came to the clemency of royal Sublimity to seek counsel for the relief of his church, which is burdened by many obligations, he finally came from there into our presence, asserting that you wished to proceed in the affair itself with the favour of the Apostolic See and to comply with the counsel of our good pleasure.

In this, indeed, and in all other matters, attentively considering the illustrious virtue of your royal devotion and commending it with most devout praises in the Lord, as we have often already done, we have taken care to deliberate diligently and carefully with our brethren concerning the advancement and preservation of the aforesaid church. No surer means appeared to us for relieving its burdens and debts than that the brethren be distributed among different monasteries and, with five or four left there, the revenues be applied toward payment of the debts.

We therefore request, admonish, and exhort your royal Piety in the Lord, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of sins: that, for the sake of the heavenly Creator and for the salvation of your soul, you cause the brethren of the aforesaid church to be received in the monasteries of your kingdom and that their necessities be provided for them temporarily. And since this seemed good to us and the abbot consented, namely that two of the brethren and two citizens—discreet and faithful men—be appointed for this purpose, bound by oath to collect the said revenues faithfully and without fraud and expend them in payment of the debts, we likewise urge your Excellency to take the church itself, its town, and all its goods under royal custody and protection, and for this purpose to send your messengers specifically to that place.

For our part, insofar as pertains to our office, we shall take the aforesaid church and the things belonging to it, together with its town, under our protection; and, if need be, we shall endeavour to send one of our own messengers there with yours, before whom the matters set forth above may be more conveniently arranged. But lest the present revenues should come into the hands of several persons, we suggest to your Magnificence that you undertake to put these arrangements into execution without delay, so that you may thereby receive from God a reward in the eternal recompense of the righteous, happily attain everlasting glory, and the monastery may thus, with the Lord’s help, be freed from the burden of its debts.

[Col. 0305C] Given at Sens, the eighth day before the Ides of August.

CCLXIV. To Hugh, bishop of Soissons.—That a certain hospital may belong to the monastery of Compiègne. (Sens, August 11.)

[Ibid., col. 981.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, bishop of Soissons: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because the truth of the matter is not clear to us concerning a certain hospital, regarding which we have asked our dearest son in Christ Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, and because we cannot give certain counsel concerning an uncertain matter, we have requested the Magnificence of that king by our letters that, if it is established that the aforesaid hospital belongs by right to the monastery of Compiègne, he may permit the aforesaid abbot and brethren of that monastery freely to possess it, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves.

But if it is found to belong to the aforesaid king, provided that royal dignity is not in the least offended thereby and that no injury ought on that account to be inflicted upon another, he should nevertheless grant it to the said abbot and brethren out of piety and through the intervention of our prayers. Therefore, through apostolic writings, we earnestly request and carefully admonish your brotherhood to interpose your efforts diligently with our aforesaid son the king, for the sake of our intervention and in view of the religious life of the said brethren, so that our prayers may obtain a useful effect and we may deservedly commend your devotion for this and render most abundant thanks.

Given at Sens, the third day before the Ides of August.

CCLXV. To Louis, king of the Franks.—Concerning a certain Nicholas who had complained to the pontiff of the canons of Tours. (Sens, August 13.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1011.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0306B] Nicholas of Tours, a man subject to royal majesty, came to the Apostolic See as to a singular refuge because F., canon of the church of Blessed Martin at Tours, had inflicted upon him outrageous violence contrary to the settlement made between them by command of our father and predecessor Pope Eugenius, of pious memory, and confirmed by a bodily oath. He did this not because he believed that he was offending the Magnificence of royal Sublimity, but so that, concerning the peace rashly violated against him, he might obtain full justice from the Roman Church, by whose authority the settlement had been made and strengthened by the sanctity of the oath.

For the authority of the sacred canons has so decreed, and the emperors who were your predecessors and the kings of the Franks have likewise decreed in their enactments, that those to whom an injury is inflicted by clerics must summon them only before ecclesiastical judges. We have learned that the same rule has been observed by the custom of your kingdom down to these times, especially concerning matters in which the injury is committed within sacred orders.

For this reason the aforesaid Nicholas, not believing that he was diminishing the excellence of your Highness or opposing in any respect the law or custom of your kingdom, laid before us his complaint concerning the violation of a peace established under the protection of the Apostolic See. We, however, not considering that this could in any way tend to diminish your honour and exaltation, nor believing that it detracted in any respect from your dignity and magnificence—we who always wish to increase manifoldly the honour and glory of your exaltation and preserve it with ardent desire—committed the case for determination to our venerable brother [William], bishop of Le Mans, a religious, prudent, and discerning man, and a canon of that church. He proceeded in the case as reason dictated and brought it to its proper conclusion.

Therefore, as by other writings, so by these present letters we earnestly request your most serene Clemency that, with the customary kindness which mercifully cherishes the poor and less powerful in their rights, you look favourably upon the aforesaid N. and do not allow him to suffer an undue burden on this account.

Given at Sens, on the Ides of August.

CCLXVI. To the same.—Concerning the monastery of Tiron.—See above, letter 263. (Sens, August 18.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1024.]

[Col. 0307A]

ALEXANDER, etc., to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, etc.

From the letters of royal Serenity sent to us, we have learned of the affection and compassion which your illustrious Magnificence bears toward the advancement and relief from the debts of the church of Tiron, and that you have promised generously to provide necessities for thirty brethren of that place. We regard this as very pleasing and acceptable, and render abundant thanks to royal Majesty for it.

It would, however, have pleased us if your prudence had sent a messenger who could go together with our messenger to the aforesaid monastery. Nevertheless, according to what royal Excellency has communicated to us, we shall take care, with God’s help, to proceed diligently in the affair itself and to apply attentive provision.

Given at Sens, the fourth day before the Kalends of September.

CCLXVII. To the abbots of Saint-Germain and Saint-Victor, the prior and subprior of Saint-Victor, and Odo, former abbot of Saint-Geneviève.—That they investigate the penalties inflicted upon William, canon of Saint-Geneviève. (Sens, August 18.)

[Ibid., col. 1030.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbots of Saint-Germain and Saint-Victor, the prior and subprior also of Saint-Victor, and ODO, [Note: From this passage it is clear that Odo, first abbot of Saint-Geneviève, had long before his death resigned pastoral care and returned to Saint-Victor, from which he had been taken, and there also ended his life.] former abbot of Saint-Geneviève: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that, when William, canon of Saint-Geneviève, came into our presence without permission of his abbot and chapter, and we sent him back to the aforesaid abbot in order humbly to make satisfaction in chapter for such a transgression, that abbot treated him so violently and dishonourably that, stripping him of all his clothes and beating him severely, he made him take his food on the ground with dogs for seven days.

But since we ought not readily to believe anything unfavourable concerning a man so honourable and religious, and because we have fuller confidence in your integrity, we commit this matter to your discernment for execution, commanding you to investigate the affair most diligently and faithfully inform us by your letters of the truth of the matter.

Given at Sens, [Note: Pope Alexander, after holding the council at Tours, came to Sens about the feast of Saint Jerome in 1163, where he remained for a year and a half. From this one may infer that this letter was written in the following year, 1164.] the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September.

CCLXVIII. To Louis, king of the Franks.—What diet he should use on every Friday. (Sens, August 20.)

[Ibid., col. 999.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We consider most pleasing and acceptable, and commend with most worthy praises in the Lord, the desire and devotion which royal Magnificence is known to have concerning service to the heavenly Creator, for obtaining remission of your sins. We have learned, however, from your letters that our other writings did not specify to royal Highness whether, on Fridays in the forty-day fasts, you ought to observe that relaxation which we granted you on Fridays at other times.

We have therefore judged that relaxation to be distinguished as follows: during the Lent called that of Saint Martin, until the Advent of the Lord, on Friday you may take one dish of fish and wine in moderation. During Advent, however, and during the greater Lent, you shall always observe the customary abstinence on Friday. But if bodily infirmity cannot endure that abstinence without grave harm, we will, and by apostolic writings command, your Magnificence to take on Friday, during those periods as during other times, one dish of fish and wine in moderation.

We also counsel and urge your Serenity that, according to the advice of our beloved son . . . , your chaplain, you should increase your alms during those periods. Let royal Sublimity know, moreover, that Lent begins from the octave of All Saints and not before.

Given at Sens, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September.

CCLXIX. He confirms to the brethren of Saint Mary of Vallecrosa the place called Fons-Calidus. (Sens, August 21.)

[HUGO, *Annals of Prémontré*, I, Preface, p. 565.]

[Col. 0308C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons and brethren of Saint Mary of Vallecrosa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to completion by effective action the requests which do not depart from the path of right. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, giving favourable assent to the petitions of Peter Benedict, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and to your church the place called Fons-Calidus, where the church of Saint Mary was founded, granted to you by our venerable brother the archbishop of Narbonne, together with its rights and all its appurtenances, as is shown in the authentic document concerning this transaction; and we strengthen it by the protection of this present writing.

We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way act against it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed Apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Sens, the twelfth day before the Kalends of September.

CCLXX. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. Concerning the case pending between the abbot of Saint-Remi and the abbot of Dervent. (Sens, August 29.)

[MARTENE, *Collections*, II, 711.]

[Col. 0309A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son, the abbot of Dervent, appearing in our presence, informed us that, when he was frequently summoned to court by your predecessor S. [Note: Samson.] of good memory concerning a certain case known to have been long contested between him and our beloved son the abbot of Saint-Remi over a certain tithe, while the same abbot sat at his own table, he was repeatedly wearied by such great labour and expense that, because of the burdens which he endured so often, he was almost compelled wholly to renounce the suit.

Later, when we had formerly committed the same case to your prudence for due determination, he likewise represented that he and his church were oppressed by a similar burden. [Note: Consult letters 209 and 255.] He therefore most urgently requested us to inform you by our letters that you should assign a suitable place to both parties, where both he and the opposing party might bear labour and expense equally.

But, understanding more fully that the case had been delayed for so long not through fraud of the abbot of Saint-Remi, but rather through delays of the abbot of Dervent, we command your brotherhood through apostolic writings to summon both parties before your presence and, having carefully heard and considered the arguments on both sides, to endeavour to bring the same case to a lawful conclusion, all obstacle of appeal removed, within thirty days after receipt of these letters, or at least within forty. But if you cannot attend to the aforesaid case, entrust it for hearing to one of your suffragans who cannot reasonably be regarded as suspect by either party, and for determination according to the tenor which we have prescribed to you.

Given at Sens, the fourth day before the Kalends of September.

CCLXXI. To William, count of Nevers, and Ida his mother.—That they abstain from harassing the monastery of Vézelay. (Sens, September 7.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1042.]

[Col. 0309D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman WILLIAM, count of Nevers, and to IDA his mother: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more especially the monastery of Vézelay is known to belong to the right of blessed Peter and to our direction, the more diligently do we attend to its advancement and benefit, and the more solicitous do we remain for its peace and the preservation of its goods. Therefore, being in every respect zealous for the peace and welfare of the same monastery, we send our beloved son Peter, subdeacon, to your nobility, requesting, admonishing, and exhorting your greatness in the Lord through apostolic writings to attend in every way, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, to the peace and welfare of the aforesaid church and the preservation and defence of its possessions; to take care to hear and heed our said subdeacon in this matter; and completely to restrain the neighbouring nobles and your powerful barons from molesting and injuring the aforesaid monastery.

Thus comply with our prayers and admonitions in this matter, so that we may be bound to hear your prayers and petitions more effectively, grant them a useful result, and seek your honour more earnestly at all times.

Given at Sens, the seventh day before the Ides of September.

CCLXXII. He informs Louis, king of the Franks, that he has received his letters and will execute his commands. (Sens, September 24.)

[DUCHESNE, *Writers of French History*, IV, 628.]

ALEXANDER, etc., to LOUIS, etc.

We have received the letters of your Excellency with the kindness of spirit that was fitting; and what you have communicated to us in those letters we regard as most pleasing and acceptable, and shall take care to carry it into effect according to your request.

Given at Sens, the eighth day before the Kalends of October.

CCLXXIII. At the request of Master Garcia and the brethren of Calatrava, he takes Calatrava under protection and confirms the brethren’s rule, goods, and privileges. (Sens, September 25.)

[MANRIQUE, *Cistercian Annals*, II, 400.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GARCIA, master, and the brethren of Calatrava, present and future, living according to the order of the Cistercian brethren: in perpetuity.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to completion by effective action the vows which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, giving favourable assent to your just petitions, we take under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid place of Calatrava, in which you are devoted to serving God in divine service, and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing.

We also confirm by apostolic authority to your devotion the institution which our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of Cîteaux, are known to have made in that place: namely, that you should firmly observe their order and, girded with military arms, should fight manfully against the Saracens in defence of that place. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that place now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s favour, acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors.

Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority to you the regulations concerning your food and clothing which the aforesaid abbot and Cistercian brethren, and the whole chapter of that order, have decreed that you are to observe. It has thus been ordained that you may use linen only for breeches; that you shall have tunics suitable for riding; short sheepskin garments; mantles lined with sheepskin; capes; and a scapular as the habit of religious life. You shall sleep clothed and girded; and you shall maintain continual silence in the refectory, dormitory, and kitchen. Above all, you shall take care not to be accused of superfluity or reproached for ostentation in any garment whatsoever.

Your clothing, therefore, is to resemble that of the aforesaid brethren in colour and thickness. On three days of the week, namely Tuesday, Thursday, and Sunday, together with the principal feast days, you may eat meat; you shall be content with only one dish and with one kind of meat, and shall everywhere keep silence at table. Furthermore, it has been ordained that no member of the Cistercian order may receive any one of your brethren without your consent; and you likewise shall be bound by the same rule toward their brethren.

When you come to any abbey of the Cistercian Order, since you are less acquainted with their custom, you shall be received not in the community, but honourably and charitably in the guest quarters, and as familiarly as can be done. In fasts you shall observe the same rule as their lay brothers; the aforesaid brethren shall receive chaplains professed in your house into houses of their Order as they receive their own. No one shall presume to exact from you tithes or first-fruits from the labour which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals. We further prohibit any one of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving it without the consent of the entire community; and no one shall dare retain one who has left without a common letter of assurance. [Col. 0311D]

We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid place, seize its possessions, retain what has been seized, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be preserved unimpaired and entire, to be of every benefit for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. Should any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowingly, attempt rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know that he is answerable before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe retribution. But upon all who preserve the rights of that same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Given at Sens, through the hand of Herman, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of October [25 September], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1164, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

## CCLXXIV. He takes under protection the monastery of St Mary of Horta and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Sens, 25 September.)

*[Ibid., p. 402.]*

[Col. 0312B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BLASIUS, abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Horta, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

Those who choose the religious life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, lest the assault of any rash person either turn them back from their purpose or—God forbid—impair the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests, receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of the Blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, decreeing that the monastic order which is known to have been established in the same monastery according to the Lord, the Rule of Blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall there be observed inviolably for all time. [Col. 0312C]

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the working of the Lord, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the place itself of Horta, where the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the grange called Cantavos; the grange called Bonicias, with their appurtenances; the grange of Alcardea, with its appurtenances; the grange called Benvivera, with its appurtenances; the grange called Arandela, with its appurtenances; the grange called Gludea, with its appurtenances; etc. It continues with an exemption from tithes and other common grants, to be specially confirmed to the same monastery. [Col. 0312D]

Given at Sens, through the hand of Herman, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of October [25 September], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1164, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Alexander III. [Col. 0313A]

## CCLXXV. To Louis, king of the Franks.—Concerning certain matters which the welfare of both Church and kingdom requires to be changed in Gaul. (Sens, 3 October.)

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 1012.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have thought fit to notify Your Highness, through our beloved son P., our subdeacon, of certain grave and very difficult matters affecting the Church of God and ourselves, and also you and the kingdom, which, unless altered by wiser counsel—and which, if prudently considered, more diligently guarded against, and changed for the better—would be of great benefit and acceptance both to the Church and to ourselves, and would concern your honour and that of the kingdom. By apostolic letters we ask and exhort the royal serenity that, after hearing and learning them more fully through him, you endeavour to alter them by wiser counsel and guard against them beneficially, so that they may redound to the honour of God and the Church, and to the benefit of the kingdom and yourself. [Col. 0313B]

Given at Sens, on the fifth day before the Nones of October [3 October].

## CCLXXVI. To Louis, king of the Franks.—Concerning the election of the Church of Chartres. (Sens, 8 October.)

*[Ibid., col. 1001.]*

[Col. 0313C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved sons—the dean, subdean, archdeacon, and a great part of the canons of the Church of Chartres—appeared together before us and fully explained how heedlessly and imprudently they had proceeded in the matter of the election of that Church. Therefore, both sympathizing with the misfortunes of that Church and wishing them to recover their integrity of reputation, which has been greatly blackened on this account, we most diligently exhorted them toward the good of peace and concord. We admonished them to meet unanimously as one body, to take care to provide beneficially for their Church, and granted them a term until the next Octave of the Epiphany [13 January 1165] for usefully completing this purpose. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort the diligence of Your Royal Highness that you also carefully and diligently exhort the said canons concerning this very matter, both orally and by letters, and effectively supply them with royal favour and assistance to accomplish it; so that, with you as its protector, the aforesaid Church may enjoy the consolation it desires and rejoice in a life-giving provision. [Col. 0313D]

Given at Sens, on the eighth day before the Ides of October [8 October]. [Col. 0314A]

## CCLXXVII. To the same.—Concerning the hospital at Compiègne. (Sens, 9 October.)

*[Ibid.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having formerly learned the will of Your Highness concerning that hospital established at Compiègne—a matter about which, as we remember, we have often asked Your Serenity—that you wished the truth to be more diligently investigated by religious men as to whether it belonged to the monastery of Compiègne, we entrusted the inquiry to our venerable brethren [Baldwin], bishop of Noyon, etc., and [Amalric], bishop of Senlis, whose integrity and prudence we in no way doubt, nor do we believe that you doubt them in any respect. Having jointly gone to the place itself, they endeavoured to investigate the truth, as you can clearly ascertain from their letters, which we send to Your Royal Highness; and, as those same letters state, they found it. Therefore, by apostolic letters we ask, admonish, and exhort Your Magnificence in the Lord that, after carefully examining the tenor of those letters, you bring about and arrange concerning the said hospital whatever you have learned to be expedient and whatever may please your will; so that, when you pass from the earthly kingdom to the heavenly, you may obtain from the rewarder of all good things the prize of eternal felicity, and we ourselves may owe Your Serenity the fullest thanks for it. [Col. 0314B–C]

Given at Sens, on the second day before the Ides of October [14 October].

## CCLXXVIII. To the same.—He assigns the hospital of Compiègne to the abbey of the same city. (Sens, 20 October.)

*[Ibid.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We commend with magnificent praises in the Lord that most sincere affection of Your Royal Highness which you are known to have in many ways toward the Churches of God; with heartfelt longings we desire that the immaculate Bride of God may present you to her husband Christ in eternal blessedness, she whom on earth, as a Catholic king and most Christian prince, you are known to have honoured more fervently by countless proofs of devotion. We have lately learned from letters of Your Highness that you have left to our judgment the affair of that hospital at Compiègne, concerning which we have often written to Your Royal Highness, and that you have assured us by letter that whatever we should decide in the matter Your Magnificence would hold ratified and firm. [Note: [Col. 0313D] See the preceding letter and Letter 264.]

Since, as has been made known to us from the written report of our venerable brethren Baldwin, bishop of Noyon, and [Amalric], bishop of Senlis, to whom we entrusted this inquiry, the aforesaid hospital has been permanently assigned for the reception of the poor and has often had the canons of the Church of Compiègne as its administrators, we—considering that monasteries and other religious houses customarily possess hospitals for the reception of the poor, and placing great confidence in royal clemency, which, as we have said, is accustomed to love and enlarge the Church of God and has left its disposition to our judgment—have thought fit to confirm the said hospital to the monastery of Compiègne by the protection of an apostolic document. It shall, indeed, remain assigned to the use of the poor and belong for ever, free from every disturbance, to the administration and care of our beloved sons, the . . . . abbot and brethren of that place. [Col. 0314D–0315B]

Therefore, by apostolic letters, we ask, admonish, and exhort Your Serenity in the Lord that, in consideration of piety and out of reverence for Blessed Peter and ourselves, you likewise confirm that hospital to the said monastery by a document of Your Highness, so that no dispute may thereafter arise against them concerning it. But if anyone should presume to molest or disturb them in this matter, do not delay to restrain such presumption by royal power, that you may deserve thereby to obtain the reward of eternal blessedness and that we ourselves may render abundant thanks to Your Magnificence.

Given at Sens, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November [20 October].

## CCLXXIX. He receives under protection the Church of St Mary of Liskes and confirms its possessions. (Sens, 25 October.)

*[HUGO, Annals of Prémontré, II, Preface, p. 30.]*

[Col. 0315C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ROBERT, abbot of the Church of Saint Mary of Liskes, and his brethren of the Premonstratensian Order in the diocese of Thérouanne, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority and fraternal charity of the Apostolic See, in whose service we are placed by the Lord’s bounty, exhort us to consent to the just desires of religious persons and graciously to grant their reasonable petitions. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, granting favourable assent to your just requests, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church in which you are devoted to divine service, following the example of our predecessor Pope Adrian of happy memory, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in the same place according to God, the Rule of Blessed Augustine, and the custom of the Church of Prémontré, shall be observed there inviolably for all time. [Col. 0315D]

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may in future acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the altar of the aforesaid village of Liskes; the whole tithe of the same parish; the woods, lands, and meadows adjoining that village, from the gift of Eustace of Malbesbere; etc. [Col. 0316A]

Given through the hand of Herman, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November [25 October], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1164, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

## CCLXXX. Privilege for the monastery of St John of Réome. (Sens, 30 October.)

*[History of the Monastery of St John of Réome, p. 208.]*

[Col. 0316B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot of the monastery of St John of Réome, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

A desire shown to concern the purpose of religion and the salvation of souls ought, by God’s authorisation, to be fulfilled without delay. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests and, following the example of our fathers and predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Innocent and Eugenius of holy memory, receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Blessed John, in which you are devoted to divine service, fortified by the charters of the glorious men Clovis, Charles, and other kings of the Franks, and strengthened by the documents of our brethren Sigoald, Bruno, Jocerannus, William, and other former bishops of Langres. Together with its possessions and goods, we strengthen it by the privilege of this present document, decreeing that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names. [Col. 0316B–C]

Namely: the church in the village called Corpus Sancti; the church of Atheis; the church of Saint George of Simiriac; the church of Berriac; the church of Vineis; the church of Tultriac; the church of Asiac; the church of Nuits; the church of Asinariis; the church of Cortenniac; the chapel of Mont-Bar; the church of Bunciac; the church of Juliac; the chapel of Saint Médard; the church of Scolis; the church of Camedon; the church of Estivei; the church of Estet; the church of Spissia with its appurtenances; the church of Belaum with the chapel of Reu; the church of Bar with the chapel of Torceio; the church of Pisi with its appurtenances; the church of Marmeians; the church of Satigny; the church of Villamorina with its appurtenances; the church of the monastery of Saint John; and the church of Corumblis. [Col. 0316D–0317A]

Whatever rights you possess in the villages of Saint Remigius—namely Betfontis, Visarney, and Teliac—and likewise whatever our brother Godfrey, bishop of Langres, has justly granted you and confirmed by his document. In the diocese of Autun: the church of Joviac; the church of Simeriac; the church of Saint Germanus of Mondoum; the church of Tisiac; the church of Saint Magnenzia; the chapel of Rouredo; the church of Cadriac with the chapel of the same village; the church of Saint Médard; and the church of Blessed Mary in the village of Jonis. In the diocese of Mâcon, at Saturniac: the church of Saint Andrew with the chapel of Saint Leodegar; the church of Saint Martin of Cereis with the chapels belonging to it; the chapel of Bufariis with its appurtenances. In the diocese of Nevers: the monastery of Saint Peter of Glamio. In the diocese of Toul: the church of Saint Stephen. We further confirm by our protection the agreement between you and the sisters of the Church of Saint Mary of Red Mountain, in the parish of Asiac, made with prudent provision by our brother Godfrey, bishop of Langres, with the consent of both parties. [Col. 0317A–B]

We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, seize its possessions, retain what has been seized, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be preserved entire, to be of every benefit for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of diocesan bishops. Should anyone therefore, etc. [Col. 0317B–C]

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Gualterius, bishop of Albano.  
I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Henry, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus.  
I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia.  
I, Albert, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina.  
I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Peter in Chains.  
I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Odo, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.  
I, Boso, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian.  
I, Cinthius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian.  
I, Mainfred, deacon-cardinal of Saint George in Velabro. [Col. 0317C–D]

Given at Sens, through the hand of Herman, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of November [30 October], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1164, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III. [Col. 0318A]

## CCLXXXI. To Louis, king of the Franks.—He commends to him the monastery of St Maximin. (Sens, 26 November.)

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 1000.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Considering the praiseworthy purpose of piety which Your Royal Highness displays toward the holy Church of God, both in head and members, we formerly commended to your majesty the monastery of Blessed Maximin and the abbot and brethren devoted there to divine service, asking you to love that monastery with your customary piety and defend it from the assaults of the wicked by the protection of royal magnificence. Since we know that you have hitherto fulfilled this well, according to God’s good pleasure and in accordance with our prayers and admonitions, we regard it as exceedingly grateful and welcome, and offer Your Highness our fullest thanks for it, holding the firm hope and confidence that thereby both the honour of earthly glory and power on earth will be increased for you, and that from the eternal rewarder of the just you will be granted an unfading palm in heaven.

But because, as we have learned and as has reached our ears, a citizen of Orléans—namely Theobald Morini—harasses the aforesaid monastery by an unjust demand for repayment of money, while O. of Bestisi and M., a widow, severely molest the monastery by a very sudden exaction of debts, we again ask and exhort Your Highness in the Lord to regard, with your customary kindness, the poverty and miseries of that monastery; according to what justice requires, compel by royal authority the aforesaid claimant of money not owed to desist; and cause those who insist upon the immediate collection of debts, so far as may be done with good will, to await a suitable time. Thus you may receive from God a reward and from us thanks. [Col. 0318B–C]

Given at Sens, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December [26 November].

## CCLXXXII. He assigns to Theobald, prior, and the brethren of the Church of St Martin of the Fields the Church of St Martin of Passo, adjudged away from the canons of St Martin of Tours. (Sens, 13 December.)

*[Dom MARRIER, History of St Martin of the Fields, p. 355.]*

[Col. 0318D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons THEOBALD, prior, and the brethren of the Church of St Martin of the Fields, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whereas a controversy had formerly arisen between you and our beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Blessed Martin of Tours, concerning the Church of St Martin of Passo, and had long been argued in our presence, we at last, after hearing the reasons, allegations, and depositions of witnesses on both sides, adjudged possession of the aforesaid church to those canons, while reserving the question of ownership. We provided that the church should by no means revert to secular status, but that religious life should be established there according to our counsel and disposition and observed for all time. Afterwards, confident, as we believed, in the merits and justice of your case concerning the right of ownership, you summoned the aforesaid canons before us in law, in order to contend with them concerning ownership of the said church.

You and they, repeatedly summoned before us on fixed terms concerning the same case, advanced in our presence many reasons and allegations on both sides, and you requested that the said church be restored to you. Having heard and considered the reasons and allegations of each party, we observed both that the Cluniac Church—to which your church belongs—and the Church of Blessed Martin of Tours especially pertain to the right and ownership of the Roman Church. We also considered that, when we pronounced the judgment on possession for the aforesaid canons, we had reserved in that judgment that religious life should be established in the Church of Passo according to our disposition and counsel and should thereafter be observed there for ever. Therefore, by the common counsel of our brethren—not by an arbitral award or judicial sentence, but by the apostolic authority which we exercise, while the cause still remains doubtful—we restore that church to you and adjudge that complete restitution be made to you of all movables and immovables belonging to it. [Col. 0319A–C]

We decree that the religious observance of the Cluniac brethren shall be observed there for all time, provided nevertheless that you pay the aforesaid canons every year at Tours, in the month of March, three marks of good silver by the weight of Troy; or that they receive annually the fruits of one prebend of the same church, should they perhaps prefer this.

That this our institution may be observed inviolably in future times, we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of this present document, decreeing that absolutely no person may infringe this page of our institution and confirmation or in any way act contrary to it. But should anyone presume to attempt this, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour. But upon those who observe these things may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen. [Col. 0319C–D]

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Gualterius, bishop of Albano.  
I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Henry, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus.  
I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia.  
I, Albert, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina.  
I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Odo, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.  
I, Boso, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian.  
I, Cinthius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian.  
I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of Saint Eustace by the temple of Agrippa.  
I, Manfred, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. [Col. 0320A]

Given at Sens, through the hand of Herman, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of December [13 December], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1164, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III. [Col. 0320B]

## CCLXXXIII. He commends to Louis, king of the Franks, Brother F., his messenger. (Sens, 31 December.)

*[DUCHESNE, Writers of the History of France, IV, 615.]*

ALEXANDER . . . . . to LOUIS . . . . .

We send to Your Royal Highness our beloved son Brother F., a member of our household, through whom we set forth orally to Your Highness certain matters which we have not thought fit to commit to the trust of letters. Therefore, by apostolic letters we ask, admonish, and exhort Your Serenity in the Lord carefully to hear what he will propose to you on our behalf; to endeavour to carry it into effect insofar as may be done consistently with your honour and the government of the kingdom entrusted to you; and, through the same man, to inform us, as Your Magnificence sees fit, what you decide to do in the matter. [Col. 0320C]

Given at Sens, on the second day before the Kalends of January [31 December].

## About the year 1164.

## CCLXXXIV. He commends the monastery of Compiègne to Louis, king of the Franks, and wishes a hospital house to be assigned to it. (10 September.)

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 1013.]*

[Col. 0320D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The affection which we bear toward Your Royal Magnificence with more abundant charity prompts and earnestly urges us to suggest to Your Serenity those things which we know especially concern the honour of God, the salvation of your soul, and also the preservation of the kingdom. Since it is a work of piety and worthy of the glory of eternal blessedness to love the holy Churches of God and religious persons and to foster them with the protection of pious guardianship, it is fitting that Your Highness regard with more earnest care and diligence, and protect with more gracious goodness their rights, those Churches which have received no small benefits from your magnificence and that of your glorious fathers from their very foundation.

Therefore we commend the monastery of Compiègne, and the abbot and brethren devoted there to divine service, all the more earnestly to Your Highness because that monastery has special recourse to the right and protection of Blessed Peter and is known to have been entrusted to royal guardianship with more ample provision. By apostolic letters we ask, admonish, and exhort you in the Lord, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of your sins: that, through regard for divine mercy and for forgiveness of your offences, you love, support, and honour the aforesaid monastery and those serving God there, and defend its rights against the snares of wicked men with your customary protection. [Col. 0321A–B]

We especially ask Your Clemency not to permit the hospital house belonging by right to that monastery to be troubled or impeded in any way by our beloved sons, the . . . . . abbot and brethren of that place, so that they may have free administration of that hospital, which, as Your Discretion knows, is most useful and necessary to that church. Thus may you receive the reward of eternal recompense thereby, while the brethren, supported in temporal matters by the favour of your illustrious highness, may apply themselves more fervently to the religious life they have undertaken and, with the Lord’s help, increase the monastery itself both spiritually and temporally.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of September [10 September]. [Col. 0321B–C]

## CCLXXXV. To Conon, abbot of St Vitonus.—He praises him for zeal for the Apostolic See and exhorts him always to adhere to it devoutly. (Paris, 9 April.)

*[MARTEN., Treasury, I, 455.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of the Church of St Vitonus of Verdun, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the tenor of your letters we have learned that you, as a Catholic man and a praiseworthy defender of the Church, have steadfastly maintained devotion and constancy toward us; and that, nobly resisting the former schismatic bishop of Verdun, you have never wished in any way to turn aside into the error and wickedness of the schismatic Octavian. This we regard as more welcome and more pleasing, inasmuch as, placed in the midst of a perverse generation, you have more strongly fortified the constancy of your virtue in the unity of the Church; and you could never have offered us anything more pleasing to God or dearer and more precious in our eyes.

Therefore, commending your prudence in the Lord, as is fitting, and extolling it with deserved praises, we ask, admonish, and exhort your beloved self in the Lord that, as you have begun well and praiseworthily, you may persevere firmly to the end in devotion to Blessed Peter and ourselves, and may endeavour more earnestly to bring and exhort the Church of Verdun to do the same. In view of the devotion and integrity which you show toward us, we desire to love you as our special son, honour you in many ways, and willingly grant your petitions. [Col. 0321C–0322A]

Given at Paris, on the fifth day before the Ides of April [9 April].

## CCLXXXVI. To Martin, abbot, and the monks of St Vaast.—He confirms the settlement made between them and the abbess of Strumis. (Paris, 13 April.)

*[MARTEN., Enlarged Collection, I, 888.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, to his beloved sons MARTIN, abbot, and the brethren of Saint Vaast, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant consent to the just desires of petitioners, and that wishes which do not depart from the path of reason be fulfilled in effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, granting favourable assent to your just requests, we have thought fit to confirm by apostolic authority the settlement reasonably made between you and [Mary], abbess of Saint Mary of Strumis, through the mediation, by our command, of our venerable brother Walter, bishop of Albano, and our beloved sons O[do] and B[oso], deacon-cardinals of the Holy Roman Church. [Note: [Col. 0321] The abbey of Strumis belonged to the Order of St Benedict, in the diocese of Arras, about two leagues distant from Arras.]

For when both you and the other party had come before us, we entrusted the hearing of this dispute to the aforesaid bishop and cardinals. With both parties appearing before them, you complained against the abbess that she had taken possession of certain properties belonging to your monastery and was retaining those same properties contrary to the right secured by your privileges. The abbess, on the other hand, said that she had done so from a very remote time, had thus taken possession of the properties, had held them and wished to hold them without injury to your monastery, since she was prepared to pay the rent and make relief payments upon changes of abbesses.

When you and the other party had advanced these and other allegations of this kind before them, through the mediation of the cardinals of the Church, with C. and F., archdeacons of the Church of Arras, also intervening, you reached the following agreement by common consent. The abbess shall henceforth hold quietly and peacefully, without any claim, from the donors for as long as they live, retaining possession, all those properties within your territory which she possesses today—that is, at the time of this settlement—or had then received by the donation of any persons; provided, however, that she pay the stipulated rent each year. When the present abbess, or any of her successors, has departed this life, she shall make a relief payment according to the custom applicable to other persons. For this grant which you made to her, the abbess, in the name of her church, undertook to pay one mark of silver annually: one half at the Nativity of the Lord and the other half on the feast of St John the Baptist. [Col. 0322B–0323A]

From this hour onward, if the aforesaid abbess wishes, she may receive properties belonging by right to your Church and hold them for two years; within that period she shall arrange matters so that, at the expiration of the two years, neither she herself nor another on her behalf shall possess them any longer, but she shall transfer them to another, unless she obtains this by the common permission of your chapter. The aforesaid bishop and cardinals reduced this agreement to writing and secured it with their own seals. We also, holding this agreement ratified and firm, strengthen it by the authority of the Apostolic See and fortify it by the protection of this present document, decreeing that absolutely no person may, etc. [Col. 0323A–B]

Given at Paris, on the Ides of April [13 April].

## CCLXXXVII. Ordinance concerning the regulation of the property of the canons of Paris. (Paris, 16 April.)

*[Cartulary of Notre-Dame of Paris, I, 226.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons C[LEMENT], dean, and the entire chapter of Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the letters which our father and predecessor of pious memory, Pope Eugenius of blessed memory, granted to T[heobald], formerly your bishop, [Col. 0323C] we learned that, if you could by no means agree in conferring mayoralties and other benefices which belong to the common disposition of your chapter, he was permitted to arrange these matters with the consent of the sounder part of the chapter. Following in the footsteps of that same predecessor, we subsequently renewed those letters for our venerable brother M[aurice], now your bishop. But since we have learned, from the confession of both parties, that this was contrary to the ancient custom of your church, and that they had not made use of the authority of those letters, we have thought it right to decree by apostolic authority that the letters of our aforesaid predecessor, whether [Col. 0323D] his or ours, shall henceforth be of no prejudice to you, so as to prevent you from freely disposing, according to the ancient custom of your church, of your mayoralties or other benefices which belong solely to your disposition.

Given at Paris, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May [16 April].

YEAR 1164–1165.

CCLXXXVIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of Robert the knight. (Sens, 1 January.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 697.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

While the case between Robert the knight and O., a burgess, concerning a certain meadow was being heard in the presence of our beloved son, the dean of Roscy, Robert himself appealed to our venerable brother the Bishop of Laon, while O. appealed to our hearing, fixing the twentieth day after the approaching feast of the Lord [Christmas]. Robert, however, shortening this to the fifth day after Christmas, nevertheless brought an appeal to the Apostolic See. Afterwards, when the said Robert was present before us at the appointed time, the other neither came nor took care to send any representative to us on his behalf. Therefore, relying fully on the prudence of your discretion, [Col. 0324B] we commit this same case to your judgment, to be concluded with due finality once the appeal has ceased. Accordingly, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to summon both parties before you and, after hearing and examining the arguments on either side, diligently bring this same case, the obstacle of appeal having been removed, to its lawful conclusion.

Given at Sens, on the Kalends of January [1 January].

CCLXXXIX. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of A., Bishop of Arras. (Sens, 6 January.)

[Ibid., col. 698.]

[Col. 0324C] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, greetings and apostolic blessing.

When our venerable brother A., Bishop of Arras, [Note: [Col. 0323] Andrew, made bishop in 1164 from being abbot of Vaux-de-Cernay.] had come into our presence at our summons, our beloved son Henry, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, who knew your wishes, severely and harshly reproved him before us concerning the matters that had been reported to your brotherhood about him. He set before him how you had loved him and promoted him from insignificance to higher rank. We ourselves likewise took care to rebuke that bishop concerning this, in a fatherly, gentle, and stern manner, and to admonish him that he should make dutiful satisfaction to you [Col. 0324D] as to his father and lord, and faithfully comply with your commands.

He, however, receiving our correction and that of the cardinal with sufficient humility and patience, excused himself before us in many ways, declaring that he was ready and prepared in every respect, if he had offended in any matter, to make amends according to your command and good pleasure. Since he is your planting, and you made him, from one of the least, great and exalted in the eyes of men, lest through your indignation he should be considered mean or despised by his clergy and people—which would detract from you more than from anyone else—we ask, admonish, and counsel your brotherhood by apostolic letters not readily to believe the unfavorable things reported to you concerning him. Rather, for the present bear with him equably; for reverence for blessed Peter and for us, and by the duty of your office, in consideration of the devotion which he bears toward you, lay aside all resentment and indignation and restore him fully to your favour and affection. If perhaps through ignorance he has offended against you, correct him cautiously and prudently between yourself and him, as shall be fitting. But if he should perhaps scorn to receive your correction in a spirit of humility and gentleness, and judge that he must persist in his obstinacy, both we and you yourself shall have to rebuke him more sharply and severely, and cut away his hardness and contumacy.

Given at Sens, the eighth day before the Ides of January [6 January].

CCXC. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On the case of the abbess of Bertolcors and the nuns of Saint-Ignatius. (Sens, 7 January.)

[Ibid., col. 699.]

[Col. 0325B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We committed the case pending between the abbess of [Note: [Col. 0325D] Commonly Bertoldi-Curtis, in French Berteaucourt: a convent of virgins, five leagues from Amiens, founded about the year 1092.] Bertolocors and the nuns of Saint-Ignatius to our venerable brothers, the bishops of Laon and Noyon, to be concluded by agreement or judgment; but they have hitherto delayed proceeding in that case.
