We have now again commanded them not to defer concluding it by settlement or judgment from now until the approaching feast of Blessed Vincent; or, if they cannot attend to it, to make this known to your brotherhood. Since it is our office to establish peace among those in discord and to preserve to each person his right, lest this case be prolonged henceforth by delays of this kind, we commit it to your discretion, in which we have complete confidence in all things, to be heard. By apostolic letters we command you that, unless the aforesaid bishops have accomplished this by the beginning of the coming Lent, [Col. 0325D] summon both parties—and the bishops themselves, if it seems fit to you—before you; carefully and diligently investigate the arguments on either side; and, when these have been fully understood and examined, strive either peacefully to establish a concord between the two parties, or to proceed in this business with such deliberation and prudent judgment that each party may rejoice to obtain its justice under your examination, and that we may more sincerely commend your prudence in the Lord.

Given at Sens, the seventh day before the Ides of January [7 January].

CCXCI. To the monks of Saint-Vaast.—That, in electing an abbot, they should choose a person from their own body, not an outsider. (Sens, 13 January.)

[MARTEN., *Collect.*, I, 872.]

[Col. 0326A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son M., [Note: [Col. 0326D] Martin, who was made abbot about the year 1155 and governed the monastery of Saint-Vaast for many years.] abbot, and to the brethren of the church of Saint-Vaast, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We perform a fitting act of our office if we bestow diligent care upon the most holy churches whose care and concern pertain to us, and guard them against future injury. Since great consideration and foresight must be employed in appointing a shepherd, we will and command that, when your church is vacant of its pastor, provided that there is among [Col. 0326B] you some person distinguished in integrity and learning and known to be fit for the rule and governance of that monastery, you should endeavour with one accord to choose him as your pastor and abbot, and not elect an outsider, provided that you agree upon him in common.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we grant you free power to receive in pledge the fiefs, possessions, and tithes of your church, lest they perish to that church through the fault of those who hold them. Certainly, because the Roman Church has often been accustomed, through the negligence of prelates, to lose the rights which it possessed in other churches, by the authority of these letters we command both you, son abbot, and your successors, and strictly forbid you in every way, [Col. 0326C] to presume to promise any subjection or obedience to any archbishop or bishop without the knowledge and permission of the Roman pontiff.

Given at Sens, on the Ides of January [13 January].

CCXCII. To Master F. and Master R., canon of Rheims.—On behalf of Theobald Bigot. (Sens, 13 January.)

[MARTEN., *Collect.*, I, 699.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Master F. and Master R., canon of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0326D] In the case which has long been litigated between Theobald Bigot and his adversary Thomas concerning a certain piece of land, and which, if we remember correctly, we formerly delegated to your judgment for conclusion, you have not proceeded as we are told. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion, setting aside every frivolous delay, to proceed in that case according to the strictness of the canons in such a manner that neither of them may reasonably complain to us of a failure of justice.

Given at Sens, on the Ides of January [13 January].

CCXCIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of the church of Saint-Remi. (Sens, 13 January.)

[MARTEN., *Collect.*, I, 700.]

[Col. 0327A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The impulse of compassion urges us, and the order of charity requires, to provide with paternal care for churches which, under the pressure of persecution, are reduced by poverty, or whose resources have been diminished by a catastrophe which has befallen them, and to raise them with the support of our aid. Having heard, therefore, that the church of blessed Remi, through the onset of present evils, is heavily burdened with much debt, [Col. 0327B] and since, as it is written, “A brother helped by a brother is like a strong city” (Prov. XVIII), and the Apostle admonishes us to bear one another’s burdens (Gal. VI), we command your belovedness by apostolic letters that you should in no way hinder the people of the aforesaid church who dwell on your lands from contributing fitting and timely assistance to the brethren of that church. Rather, take care more earnestly to admonish and urge them to do so, and you yourselves, in brotherly love and for reverence for blessed Peter and for us, as in a like necessity you would wish it done for yourselves, effectively assist that abbot in reducing the aforesaid debts, so that you may thereby deserve to receive both eternal reward in the future and increase in temporal goods from God.

[Col. 0327C] Given at Sens, on the Ides of January [13 January].

CCXCIV. To P., Archbishop of Narbonne, and to the bishops of Nîmes, Uzès, Mende, and Maguelonne.—He praises their diligence in abolishing tolls and customs dues; he punishes Count Bernard of Melgueil, who refuses to obey, with a sentence of interdict. (Sens, 17 January.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 813.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers [PONTIUS], Archbishop of Narbonne; [ADELBERT], Bishop of Nîmes; [RAYMOND], Bishop of Uzès; [ALDEBERT], Bishop of Mende; and [JOHN], Bishop of Maguelonne, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0327D] Having received letters from certain among you, we were exceedingly pleased that you, as their tenor declared, are zealous and vigilant in seeking the abolition of the excessive tolls. For that very reason we sent our letters, though without any greeting, to the nobleman Bernard, Count of Melgueil, who refuses to correct himself in these matters according to your admonitions, attentively admonishing and commanding him to comply with your commands and admonitions both regarding the removal of new tolls and the abolition of the old oath. Otherwise, we hold valid the sentence which you, brother archbishop, pronounced against him, and command that it be firmly observed until fitting satisfaction has been made. We further add and command your brotherhood that, in the town of Alès and [Col. 0328A] throughout all his land, burial be kept continually under interdict, and that in every other place where he is personally present you forbid the celebration of divine offices.

Given at Sens, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February [17 January].

CCXCV. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of the Eastern Church. (Sens, 20 January.)

[MARTEN., *Collect.*, II, 700.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your discretion, we believe, knows more fully both how God has afflicted the Eastern Church and crushed it by the hand of its enemies, and this through the reports of people coming from there. Since, among the other places of those regions, the place called Belmas is struck by the Saracens’ attacks more frequently and, exposed to their assaults, greatly needs the aid of the faithful of God, it has sent the bearers of these letters to these parts to collect alms. Therefore, since it is a work of piety, and highly pleasing to God, to furnish both counsel and assistance to those suffering the diverse oppression of pagans, we earnestly commend them to your charity. We attentively ask and admonish you, for the sake of divine mercy and for reverence for blessed Peter and for us, to regard them with a more merciful eye and grant them help [Col. 0328C] and favour in collecting alms through your province, so that you may thereby be able to receive a worthy reward and attain the blessedness of heavenly felicity.

Given at Sens, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February [20 January].

CCXCVI. To Louis, King of the Franks.—On the case of the Bishop of Cambrai, to whom he grants a further respite. (Sens, 27 January.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 1006.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0328D] When our beloved son, the abbot of Saint-Vincent of Senlis, came to us, he earnestly pressed upon us, with letters from your highness, that we should still grant a respite to that Bishop of Cambrai whom, contrary to the honour of the Church and to his own salvation—and, would that it were not so, to yours as well—we have awaited for a long time. But he, as we believe—and would that the truth of the matter were otherwise—makes such excuses through you, not out of any necessity, but so that he may be able to shelter his error under the protection of your clemency and that of our venerable brother Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.

Yet, seeking not money but his soul, and wishing, out of regard for your serenity and for consideration of our aforesaid brother, to comply with prayers and petitions unless we were manifestly acting against God, [Col. 0329A] we have thought that this bishop should still be awaited until the second Sunday of the coming Lent. If, however, within the prescribed period we do not receive either him, or a messenger, or letters from him concerning his return and a definite promise, from that time onward, all delay removed, we shall publicly excommunicate him and exclude him from the body of Christ, which is the Church. Therefore, by this communication we ask your magnificence not to press us further with any petitions concerning this matter. We also ask your excellence to carry out what, through our beloved son the abbot of Saint-Germain, we asked you to do. For we believe that this will again redound to your honour.

[Col. 0329B] Given at Sens, the sixth day before the Kalends of February [27 January].

CCXCVII. He promises Louis, King of the Franks, that he will not fail [Peter], Archbishop of Bourges. (Sens, 4 February.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 1009.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We have received with due kindness the letters of your highness—as letters from the most Christian king and from that prince whom we love with our whole charity in the Lord, and for whose honour and advantage we strive in all things, so far as with God we are able. Accordingly, although it was more than necessary [Col. 0329C] for you to address earnest prayers to us on behalf of our venerable brother P., Archbishop of Bourges, since merely in view of his uprightness and worth we love him with the sincerest affection and gladly wish to provide for the interests both of him and of the Church entrusted to him, nevertheless we have graciously received the prayers of your highness. We undertake and purpose, with respect to that archbishop, both at your intercession and, as we have said, in consideration of his worth, to exercise beneficial care in all things and, by God’s authorship, preserve intact for him his right, both in the case which he now has and in all other matters.

We also kindly received our beloved son Master R., dean of Saint-Germain, [Col. 0329D] whom your serenity commended to us; and, through your intercession, he effectively obtained from us what he reasonably requested.

Given at Sens, the second day before the Nones of February [4 February].

CCXCVIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of the church of Saint-Remi. (Sens, 12 February.)

[MARTEN., *Collect.*, II, 701.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0330A] brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

While the case between the abbot of Saint-Remi and the peasants of Nogent was being heard in the presence of the dean of that place and certain others, concerning some complaints, the abbot of Saint-Remi appealed to our hearing. When the representative of the said abbot was present before us for this purpose, they neither came nor sent any representative on their behalf. We therefore commit that case to your discretion, to be heard and concluded with due finality. Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command you to summon both parties before you and, after carefully hearing and examining the arguments on either side, decide [Col. 0330B] the case in accordance with justice.

Given at Sens, the eleventh day before the Ides of February [11 February].

CCXCIX. To the abbots of Saint-Remi and Château-Saint-Thierry, and to L., dean of Rheims.—On the case pending between the abbots of Orbais and Igny. (Sens, 13 February.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbots of Saint-Remi and Château-Saint-Thierry, and L., dean of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Having very great confidence in your prudence and integrity, we commit to your judgment the case pending between the abbot of Orbais [Note: [Col. 0329D] The monastery of Orbais, of the Order of Saint Benedict, was founded in the diocese of Soissons by Saint Regulus, Archbishop of Rheims.] and Hugh of Igny [Note: [Col. 0329D] The monastery of Igny, of the Cistercian Order, in the line of Clairvaux, is situated five miles from the city of Rheims.] concerning a certain piece of land, [Col. 0330C] to be concluded by amicable settlement or judgment. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your diligence that, when you are requested concerning this matter, you should meet together and summon both parties before you, applying effort and diligence to make a settlement between them. Otherwise, after hearing and examining the arguments on either side, decide the same case by judicial procedure, without recourse to appeal.

Given at Sens, on the Ides of February [13 February].

CCC. To the abbot of Saint-Remi of Rheims.—On the case pending between the abbot of Saint-Remi and Odd. (Sens, 14 February.)

[Ibid., col. 702.]

[Col. 0330D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Saint-Remi, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We have committed to the abbots of Saint-Memmie and All Saints, our beloved sons, [Note: [Col. 0330D] Saint-Memmie and All Saints are two monasteries of the Order of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine in the city of Châlons.] the case pending between you and the priest Odd. concerning a certain house which, as he asserts, his father and mother left to him by testament, to be heard and concluded with due finality. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, when summoned by them concerning this matter, you attend before them in person or through your representative, [Col. 0331A] and firmly accept and observe whatever they may judge on the matter.

Given at Sens, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of March [14 February].

CCCI. He directs the dean and treasurer of Rheims to commend [Guy], bishop-elect of Châlons, to Archbishop Henry. (Sens, 14 February.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 815.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the dean, treasurer, archdeacon, and the entire chapter of Rheims.

[Col. 0331B] We have been informed by the report of certain persons that our beloved son, the said bishop-elect of Châlons, reflecting that the act of his election was excessively hasty and that the procedure in that election was insufficiently regular, has humbly resolved and intends in every respect to comply with the will and good pleasure of our venerable brother Henry, your archbishop. Since he sees that this occasion has greatly disturbed that archbishop together with the church of Rheims itself, he intends wholly to resign everything into his hands. We therefore ask, admonish, and exhort your whole body in the Lord by apostolic letters earnestly to urge and induce that archbishop to look with gracious favour upon the said bishop-elect, since he has so humbled himself in his presence, [Col. 0331C] and to provide in such a way for the church of Châlons that it may obtain in its governance the desired remedy of consolation, and that the archbishop himself may thereby be found worthy of commendation.

Given at Sens, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of March [14 February].

CCCII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of the abbot of Saint-Remi. (Sens, 15 February.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 702.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0331D] We commit to your discretion, to be heard and concluded with due finality, the case known to be pending between our beloved sons P., abbot of Saint-Remi, and the nobleman R., Viscount of Laon, concerning the village of Germigny. And since, as is reported, the said viscount has in no way observed the agreement made concerning this matter through our beloved son O., deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, then legate of the Apostolic See, we firmly will and command that, if this is so, you hear and decide the case in accordance with justice, without being impeded by that agreement. We further command your diligence not to allow the party of the aforesaid viscount to act maliciously against that abbot contrary to the condition stated above, [Col. 0332A] provided that it is certainly established to you that the matter proceeded as reported.

Given at Sens, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March [15 February].

CCCIII. He asks Louis, King of the Franks, to urge [William], King of Sicily, to receive into favour Florio of Camebotta, whom he has exiled. He desires that the same Florio be commended to the Emperor of Constantinople. (Sens, 16 February.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 1025.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greetings and apostolic blessing.

It belongs to the care of our office to provide aid to the oppressed and needy, and to intervene for them with those in whom we know works of piety and the bowels of mercy abound. We wish, then, that it be known to your royal serenity that our beloved son, the nobleman Florio of Camebotta, who was regarded as one of the greater barons of Calabria, has incurred the anger and indignation of our dearest son in Christ W., the illustrious King of Sicily, and, as is said, has been compelled to go into exile from all his territory.

The occasion was this: a religious and honourable person had repeatedly informed us that certain men of his land were laying plots against that king and were planning to commit the sin of treason against him. We therefore sent our letters a second time to our venerable brother, [lacuna], Archbishop of Capua, [Col. 0332C] whom we knew to be, above others, devoted and faithful to the king, that he might forewarn and make the aforesaid king more cautious concerning this. When he made this known to the king through the said F., his nephew, the latter, not believing that this was said on our behalf but supposing that it was intended to render his men suspect to him, compelled Florio to leave the land and go to the region of Jerusalem.

But because we know that your highness is devoted to works of mercy and, with your customary piety and clemency, comforts the oppressed in their afflictions, we earnestly petition your excellence on behalf of the aforesaid F. We ask, admonish, and urgently exhort you, since we believe there is no king or prince to whom the aforesaid king shows greater reverence and devotion than to you, for the sake of piety and for reverence for blessed Peter and for us, to send letters from your magnificence to that king, earnestly asking him, in consideration of your intervention and affection, to remit his anger and indignation, restore Florio to his favour, restore his land to him, and permit both him and his wife and children to remain there freely. We further ask you to petition the illustrious emperor of Constantinople and earnestly request that he keep the aforesaid F. with him and, until he can be safe in his own land, endeavour, for your sake, to assist and support him. We ask you to send, therefore, letters of intercession for him to the emperor as well, [Col. 0333A] so that, if—though we do not believe it—the aforesaid king should not heed our prayers and yours, Florio may have recourse to that emperor and find from him the desired benefits through your prayers.

Given at Sens, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March [16 February].

CCCIV. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—That G., Count of Rosières, be compelled to return the money which he took from the messenger of the Archbishop of Lyons. (Sens, 27 February.)

[MARTEN., *Collect.*, II, 703.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0333B] From the tenor of the letters which your brotherhood sent us, we have learned how, in accordance with the command you received from us, you summoned G., Count of Rosières, to restore in full to the messenger of our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Lyons, the money which he had taken from him. He replied to you that within fifteen days he would come into our presence and disclose to us the purpose of his intention. Upon hearing this, you were unwilling to proceed further in the matter, desiring to show deference to apostolic reverence.

Since we do not wish him to abuse the benefit of appeal so that you may not exercise canonical justice against him unless, after lawful admonition, he repents, we command your discretion by this communication to summon and admonish the aforesaid G. again, that he restore to that archbishop, without any reduction and all pretext set aside, as much as his messenger can prove by oath that he lost. If within fifteen days after receipt of these letters he has neither returned the stolen goods nor given sufficient pledges into your hands for repayment of the money taken, excommunicate him, all appeal and excuse removed, [Col. 0333C] and prohibit the celebration throughout all his land of every divine office except baptism of infants and penances for the dying.

Given at Sens, the third day before the Kalends of March [27 February].

CCCV. To Maurice, Bishop of Paris.—On remission of the annual payment of one ounce of gold owed by the church of Latiniacum. (Sens, 1 March.)

[Cartulaire de Notre-Dame de Paris, I, 32.]

[Col. 0333D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother MAURICE, Bishop of Paris, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Having found in a certain record among our books that the church of Latiniacum was bound to pay the Lateran palace one ounce of gold every year, we demanded that payment from the abbot and brethren of that place. [Note: [Col. 0333] The words enclosed in brackets have been supplied from the great cartulary, fol. 191v, and the small cartulary, fol. 11.] They replied that they had no memory of this, nor any written record that such a payment had customarily been rendered by their church to the Roman Church by virtue of an obligation. Since, therefore, the Roman Church has never been accustomed to exact payments, but rather to be asked to make other churches tributary to itself, we absolve the said abbot and brethren and their church from such exaction. By the authority of these letters we decree that neither we nor our successors may exact this payment from their church, unless perhaps it should proceed from their own free will and good pleasure. If, however, the abbot or brethren of the aforesaid monastery paid the specified payment to the Roman Church at any time, we do not wish this to create any prejudice to your right or to that of the church committed to you.

Given [at Sens], on the Kalends of March [1 March].

CCCVI. To Louis, King of the Franks.—That he should endeavour to reconcile peace between certain persons. (Sens, 3 March.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 1021.]

[Col. 0334B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Because we know that the clemency of royal piety devotes its whole affection of mind to those things which please God and promote the salvation of souls, we have determined with complete confidence to invite your magnificence to what pertains to the good of concord and peace. Our beloved son Simon, a canon of Sens, declared to us orally [Col. 0334C] that A. and O. of Brie are engaged in grave warfare and discord with P. of Glazy, and that unless your royal highness acts as mediator between them, they cannot incline their minds toward the restoration of peace. Therefore, since the condition of subjects is judged the safer the more that the desirable peace and tranquillity are preserved under the equity of the ruler, we ask, admonish, and exhort your highness in the Lord by apostolic letters, for the sake of piety and for reverence for blessed Peter and for us, to labour carefully and diligently to restore peace and concord among the aforesaid men, and effectively to employ your offices to this end.

Given at Sens, the fifth day before the Nones of March [3 March].

CCCVII. Privilege for the abbey of Fontevraud. (Sens, 11 March.)

[NIQUET, *Hist. de l’ordre de Fontevrault*, 416.]

[Col. 0334D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable archbishops and bishops in whose dioceses the dependencies of Fontevraud are situated, greetings and apostolic blessing, etc.

[lacuna] Therefore, by apostolic letters we command all of you that you do not refuse the gift of blessing to virgins who have vowed chastity to God and entered the sacred order of the monastery of Fontevraud, if they request it, on all solemnities of the Blessed Virgin, on Sundays, and likewise on all feasts of the apostles. Rather, setting aside excessive observance of the appropriate time, endeavour, as required by your office, to consecrate them to the Lord in the customary manner. [Col. 0335A]

Given at Sens, the fifth day before the Ides of March [11 March].

CCCVIII. To Walter, bishop, and Robert, Archdeacon of Langres.—On the church of Sarrinia. (Sens, 14 March.)

[DUCHESNE, *Hist. Franc. Script.*, IV, 614.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WALTER, bishop, and his beloved son ROBERT, Archdeacon of Langres, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Pastoral solicitude strongly admonishes and [Col. 0335B] urges us to cherish those ecclesiastical persons, and more diligently to promote their interests and advancement, whom we know to persist more fervently in devotion to the Church and to us. We therefore ask, admonish, and command your discretion to take care courageously to defend and preserve for our beloved son Peter, kinsman of our venerable brother Hugh, Bishop of Soissons, the church of Sarrinia which, as your letters attest, you have canonically granted to him. Through his suitable and honourable procurator, ensure that he holds that church peacefully and freely; do not permit any clerk or layman unjustly to inflict any disturbance upon him concerning it. Rather, in accordance with the testimony of your letters, defend for him the aforesaid church, so that he may thereby be devoted and bound to you, [Col. 0335C] and that we may commend your prudence in this matter.

Given at Sens, the second day before the Ides of March [14 March].

CCCIX. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of the church of Saint-Memmie. (Sens, 15 March.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 704.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

From the complaint submitted to us by the abbot and brethren of St. Memmius [Note: St. Memmius, first bishop of Châlons, after whose name there is at Châlons an ancient monastery of Canons Regular of the Order of St. Augustine.], we have learned that Henry, knight of Deprigi, with rash audacity presumes to seize their men, strip them of all their goods, keep them in chains after despoiling them, and compel them to ransom themselves. Since we neither can nor ought to fail the aforesaid abbot and brethren in maintaining their right, and since so grave an offence must not be left uncorrected or unpunished, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you shall carefully admonish and strictly compel the aforesaid knight to restore everything taken away, and, if he holds any persons captive or bound by surety for payment of money, to permit them to depart free and released; otherwise, you shall endeavour to bind that knight with the bond of anathema.

Given at Sens, on the Ides of March.

### CCCX. To Louis, King of the Franks.—That a priest R. may have his possessions restored to him by an unjust possessor. (Sens, March 17.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 997.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The pious devotion of your Highness requires you always to attend to those matters which undoubtedly concern the benefit of needy clerics. It has come to us that John Baril, with rash audacity, took from the priest R. a certain house and vineyards which he possessed by hereditary right, and refuses to restore them to him. We therefore ask your Magnificence and, as a most dear son of the Church in Christ, earnestly exhort you that, if this is so, your prudent Highness shall ensure that full justice is rendered to the aforesaid priest in your presence, or in that of another person in whom you can place complete confidence, so that the same priest may rejoice that he has fully obtained his right.

Given at Sens, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### CCCXI. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—For the Cistercian brethren. (Sens, March 23.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 705.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although we ought to extend the gaze of our consideration to all men of religious profession, it is fitting that we should love our beloved sons, the brethren of the Cistercian Order, with so much the more abundant charity, and should with more earnest solicitude promote their welfare and increase, inasmuch as, among other religious persons, they have more wisely defended the cause of the Church, magnanimously upheld Catholic unity, and are known to adhere with greater fervour even to the divine offices.

Therefore we earnestly commend the same brethren and their houses to your charity, asking, warning, and exhorting you in the Lord that, for love of the heavenly Creator, reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, and regard for their religious life, you take care to love and support them and laudably uphold them in their rights; that you preserve with diligent care their institutions and observances, and those things known to have been granted to them by the Roman pontiffs; and that you do not permit these in any way to be violated throughout your parishes. Thus an increase of eternal reward may accrue to you, and we may be bound always to render more abundant thanks to your solicitude on this account. For you could do nothing at present that would be more welcome or acceptable to us.

Given at Sens, the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

### CCCXII. He commends Erm. of Narbonne to Louis, King of the Franks. (Sens, April 3.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1027.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that it has come to the knowledge of your royal Highness how, when we were in those regions, our beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman Er. of Narbonne, took care in many ways to honour and serve us, and endeavoured to demonstrate by manifold deeds the devotion which she laudably bears towards us and the Church. Therefore both we and our brethren wish to love her with sincere charity as a most dear and special daughter of the Church; and, in such matters as we can do with God and justice, to incline our mind to her petitions.

Accordingly, we earnestly commend to your royal Serenity her whom we believe to be most devoted to you and wholly faithful, very earnestly requesting by apostolic letters that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, and in view of her fidelity and worth, you love, support, and honour her as your own faithful subject, and receive her reasonable requests with your customary kindness. Thus we may return most abundant thanks to your Highness on this account, and she herself may remain ever more devoted as one devoted, and ever more faithful as one faithful, to you at all times.

Given at Sens, the third day before the Nones of April.

## In the Year 1165

### CCCXIII. He grants to the Abbot of St. Bertin of Sithiu that “he shall not be bound, in a cause concerning churches situated in different dioceses, to attend the synods of the bishops of those places even when summoned.” (Sens.)

[IPERII, *Chronicle of St. Bertin*, in MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, 656.]

### CCCXIV. To Louis, King of the Franks.—He seeks a meeting and consultation with the king. (Sens, January 13.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 998.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[lacuna] came to us the beloved son P., subdeacon, who by his account set before us how [lacuna] your Clemency received him honourably and fittingly, and took care, out of reverence for God and ourselves, to show him every honour and favour befitting a magnificent and Christian prince; and likewise how the affection of your most sincere kindness heard, with every gentleness and diligence, those matters which he set before the royal Magnificence on our behalf.

Moreover, we received with due kindness our beloved son, the nobleman Hugh, your baron, through whom your Highness answered us; and, giving ready attention to his words, we hold your counsel altogether welcome and acceptable. Yet in this matter the sincerity of your admirable devotion towards us and the Church of God has clearly appeared, since, out of reverence for God, honour for blessed Peter, and regard for ourselves, you have shown so great a favour to one of our clerics. Therefore, both for these things and for the other many benefits bestowed upon us and ours by your Highness, we render every kind of thanksgiving to your sincerity, wishing to make known by this letter to your Magnificence that, as soon as it could conveniently be done, we should gladly wish to have your presence and counsel concerning the matters which you have communicated to us.

Given at Sens, on the Ides of January.

### CCCXV. Privilege for the monastery of Foigny. (Sens, January 22.)

[*Historia Fusniacensis Coenobii*, p. 26.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROBERT, abbot of the monastery of Foigny, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid place, in which you are dedicated to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter, God favouring you, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself of Foigny; that part of the wood of Étréaupont which, according to the defined boundaries, you peacefully possess by proprietary right—for the remaining part you have only a right of use; the tithes of the land of Étréaupont; the place called Aubenton, with all appurtenances belonging to it; one half of the land called Fligny; the land called Ladouzy, with the great tithe and all appurtenances except the men; the holding called Vervins, and the second called Watigny; likewise the third called Agnicourt; the land of Foucouzy, and a fourth part of Tibie; the territory of Villers-Cotterêts, with its tithe and certain other adjacent lands; the place called Évergnicourt; grazing rights throughout the whole land of Robert of Montaigu; the holding called Arenzot; the vineyards of Culpetra; the grant of *vionage* throughout the lands of Thomas of Marle, Robert of Montaigu, Burchard of Guise, Robert Mutel, Walter of Solemnia, Ralph, count of Vermandois, Baldwin, count of Hainaut, Hugh, count of Rosoit, Nicholas, bishop of Cambrai, throughout his entire bishopric, and Nicholas of Avesnes.

Moreover, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce of lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. Adding also, by apostolic authority, we forbid anyone to dare to receive or retain, without your permission, your brethren, clerical or lay, after they have made profession in your monastery.

Providing also with paternal solicitude for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosure of your places or granges to commit violence, robbery, or theft, or to seize a person. We further decree that no one shall ever have authority to summon you before secular courts, etc.

Given at Sens, through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of February, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1163 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the fifth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III. [Note: The chronological data are corrupt; the thirteenth indiction agrees with the year 1165.]

### CCCXVI. Bull by which he confirms all the possessions of Saint Peter already confirmed by his predecessors [Note: See the privileges of Paschal and Honorius.], and further, in the diocese of Chartres, the two manses of Sorel and Niglebold; in the diocese of Sées, the church of Saint Anianus; and, in the diocese of Coutances, the church of Ham and the church of Goetbert’s Ville. (Sens, January 26.)

[*Collection des Cartulaires*, II, 650.]

Given at Sens, through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1164 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

### CCCXVII. To Louis, King of the Franks.—He sends him the letters of the emperor of Constantinople. (Sens, January 26.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1022.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has not escaped our memory how formerly, at our and our brethren’s request, you sent letters from your Highness to our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious emperor of Constantinople. As we have learned from the letters which he sent to our venerable brother Henry, archbishop of Benevento, he received them with due kindness; and, because it was difficult for him to send his own messenger so suddenly, he sends his letters to your Serenity through the messenger of that archbishop. We, however, send these letters to your Highness through the same messenger of the archbishop, the bearer of this letter.

Given at Sens, the eighth day before the Kalends of February.

### CCCXVIII. He receives the monastery of Cîteaux under protection and confirms its privileges. (Sens, February 2.)

[HENRIQUEZ, *Privileges of the Cistercian Order*, p. 55.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GILBERT, abbot of the monastery of Cîteaux, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting that apostolic protection be at hand for those choosing the religious life, lest perhaps the assault of someone’s rashness either turn them back from their purpose or—may it not be so—weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are dedicated to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter, God favouring it, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself of Cîteaux, with its lands, meadows, pastures, waters, woods, and all appurtenances; the abbey of La Ferté; the abbey of Pontigny; the abbey of Clairvaux; the abbey of Morimond; the abbey of Preuilly; the abbey of La Cour-Dieu; the abbey of Bonnevaux; the abbey of La Grâce-Dieu; the abbey of L’Oratoire; the abbey of Bussières; the abbey of Miroir; the abbey of Saint-André; the abbey of Valence; the abbey of Persigne; the abbey of Érival; the abbey of Obazine; by the gift of Otto, duke of Burgundy, full rights of use in every respect in his forest, except clearance of land; and free rights of use throughout all his land wherever he has land; the grange of Salives, with adjacent lands, meadows, waters, woods, pastures, tithe, and all appurtenances, by the gift of the abbot and chapter of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, Aimon lord of Til-Châtel, Guy of Clermont, and the other heirs.

(Thereupon it continues, enumerating the other granges and particular possessions of Cîteaux which it possessed at that time, and is subscribed by thirteen cardinals.)

Given at Sens, through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1164 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

### CCCXIX. Bull for Sainte-Croix of Bordeaux. (Sens, February 4.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, II, *Instrumenta*, 313.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BERTRAND, abbot of the monastery of Sainte-Croix of Bordeaux, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

A petition of pious will ought to be fulfilled by an effect that follows; so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth laudably and the requested benefit may undoubtedly gain force. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Sainte-Croix, in which you are dedicated to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order, known to have been established in the same monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, shall be inviolably observed there in perpetuity. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, the Lord granting it, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of Saint Macarius, as we adjudged it to your monastery by the common counsel of our brethren; whatever William the Good, formerly count of Bordeaux and founder of the same monastery, reasonably granted to that monastery; the church of Saint Michael, situated outside the city of Bordeaux above the river Garonne, with its offerings and liberties; the church of Saint Martin of Sadirac, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Machau, with tithe and the adjacent island; the church of Saint Hilary of Ortulan, with its tithe and appurtenances; the church of Saint George of the Island, with its tithe and appurtenances; the church of Saint Stephen of Wlturna, with its tithe and appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Cambas, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter of Lupiag, with part of the tithe and its appurtenances; the church of Saint Severinus of Marca, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Blancafort, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Albinus of Blanhac; the church of Saint Cyricus of Catirenac, with its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Agen: the church of Saint Mary of Alemans, with its tithe and appurtenances; the church of Saint John of Auriol, with part of the tithe and its appurtenances; the church of Saint Maurice, with its tithe and appurtenances. [Note: A short letter of Pope Celestine III, issued in 1193, adds: “In the diocese of Bordeaux, the church of Sainte-Croix of Mont; the church of Saint Maurice of Aubiag, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint John of Gasnag, with part of the tithe and its appurtenances; the place of Balag with its appurtenances; the oratory of Saint Remigius with its appurtenances.”]

Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority the definitive sentence concerning that dispute which formerly arose between your monastery and the monastery of Saint-Sever concerning the church of Saint Mary of Solac. It was pronounced at the council of Bordeaux by Amatus, formerly bishop of Oloron, and Hugh, formerly bishop of Die, then legates of the Apostolic See, and, when it had been brought before them, was confirmed by our predecessors Urban and Paschal, Roman pontiffs, with the counsel of their brethren, bishops and cardinals, as is known to be contained in their authentic writings made on this matter.

We also grant that the burial-place of the same house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; the rights of the parish churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken being nevertheless preserved. In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose priests and present those chosen to the bishop. If they are found suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them; and those priests shall be answerable to the bishop for the care of the people, but to you for temporal matters.

Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of subreption or violence, except the person whom the brethren by common counsel, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. We therefore decree, etc. As a token of the protection received from the Apostolic See, you or your successors shall pay one *marbotin* annually to us and our successors. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, subscribe.  
I, Ubaldus, bishop of Ostia, subscribe.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, subscribe.  
I, Walter, bishop of Albano, subscribe.  
I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, subscribe.  
I, Cencius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, subscribe.  
I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius beside the temple of Agrippa, subscribe.  
I, Manfred, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, subscribe.  
I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, subscribe.  
I, Henry, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, subscribe.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, subscribe.

Given through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, at Sens, on the second day before the Nones of February, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1164 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

### CCCXX. He receives the monastery of the Dunes, formerly on the seashore and now at Bruges, under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Sens, February 7.)

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, II, 1315.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HIDESBALD, abbot of the monastery of the Dunes, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

The office of the government entrusted to us and the order of reason appear to require us to assent to religious vows and fulfil them by the performance of deeds. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are dedicated to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that monastery according to the fear of God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall be inviolably observed there in perpetuity.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, the Lord granting it, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

By the gift of Thierry, count of Flanders: as much of the land of the Dunes as you wish to cultivate for your own use with your own ploughs, and as much as you need for pasturing your animals, together with the land which you inhabit.

In the parish of Ramskapelle: the new land from the count’s ditch to the Yser, and from the land of the church of Broburg to the Venep, whatever has accrued on every side, and whatever land is held within this boundary; namely, the land of Waldagt, provost Bertulf, Gilbert the castellan and his men; a small portion of land beyond the Venep, by the gift of Thierry, count of Flanders, and Philip his son; the land which belonged to Erembald Crumminck and his brethren, on this side and beyond the ditch; the land of Lambertius, Remelinus Condescura; from knights’ fiefs, whatever they reasonably grant you; from the count’s *Cerquarii*; the land which belonged to the sons of Livild, about seventy measures; and that of the sons of Guitoga, twenty-two measures; and beside these, about thirty measures of the land which belonged to Bruttekini and his brother, sons of Bave, and their associates.

From the land which belonged to Condescure: forty-eight measures, twelve hereditary measures by exchange into *terragium*. In the parish of Vulpam: the land which belonged to Alnoth and her sisters, and Sutdigh; the land which belonged to Slaccapt, Bilmantius and his sons, Walter their nephew, Aluisius, and Walter Prim; and, from the freeholds of Walter Cath, Remfrid, Erckenbald, and others, whatever you reasonably possess there.

In the parish of Veurne: the land called Saint Mary’s, which belonged to Ideslof, Reniger, Renibald Fler, and many others in the same parish.

In the parishes of Sintenes and the chapel of Erembald: the land which belonged to Walter Snoekaert, Elbodon of Dyc, Eustace, Renigot, and Baldwin, brothers of Erembald Bandekin; from their freeholds; and the land which the count received from the aforesaid Erembald and from Walter of Formiselles, and gave to us as an hereditary grant; the land which belonged to Baldwin Taschaert and others bordering thereon; the whole island of Bomne with its tithe; the land in Westfory which Badaloga, castellan of Diksmuide, gave you in alms.

Furthermore, we likewise confirm to you certain reasonable customs granted to you by our beloved son Henry, illustrious king of the English, by Count Thierry and his son Philip, and by the count of Guînes, as is contained in their authentic writings made concerning them.

No one shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce of your fields which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals.

If any free and unencumbered person wishes, for the redemption of his soul, to give himself to your monastery, you shall have full liberty to receive him. Adding also, by apostolic authority, we forbid anyone to dare to receive or retain, without your permission, your brethren, clerical or lay, after they have made profession in your monastery. Providing likewise with paternal solicitude for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosures of your places or granges to commit violence, robbery, or theft, or to seize a person.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, the authority of the Apostolic See being preserved.

If, therefore, etc.

Given at Sens, through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of February, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1165 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

### CCCXXI. Privilege for the monastery of La Roche. (Sens, February 8.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, XII, *Instrumenta*, 132.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, abbot of Saint Mary of La Roche, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It accords with the clemency of apostolic governance to love religious persons and defend their places by the protection of its safeguard. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions and, after the example of our father and predecessor of holy memory, Pope Eugenius, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary, in which you are dedicated to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, the Lord granting it, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place in which the monastery itself is situated, with its appurtenances; the grange of Villegest; the grange of Saint-Loup; the grange of Aligny; the grange of Vieux-Champs and Vaux; the grange of Blancfort; the grange of the wood of Saint Gundulf; the grange of Villeneuve; the land of Landes and Fundelin; all that you possess at Liriac; the land of Chanejo; the grange of the village of Gundulf; the grange of Crientiis, with all woods and pastures belonging to the aforesaid granges.

No one shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce of your lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance [lacuna] they have been granted, the authority of the Apostolic See being preserved. If, therefore, in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Hubaldus, bishop of Ostia.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Walter, bishop of Albano.  
I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Henry, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia.  
I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains.  
I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Odo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.  
I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian.  
I, Manfred, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Sens, through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of February, in the year 1160 [lacuna], and the sixth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III, in the thirteenth indiction.

Given at Sens, through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of March, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1164 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

### CCCXXIII. He receives the monastery of Saint Martin of Autun under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Sens, March 20.)

[BULLIOT, *Essai historique sur Saint-Martin d’Autun*, II, 40.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved sons WILLIAM, abbot of Saint Martin of Autun, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by the almighty Lord for this purpose: that, by the authority and goodwill of the Apostolic See, we should be bound to care for all churches, and should take care with paternal affection that they are not harassed by the vexations of evil men. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions; and, following the example of our predecessors, the eminent teacher Gregory and Innocent, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Saint Martin, constructed in the suburb of Autun by Siagrius, bishop of revered memory, and Queen Brunhild; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, the Lord granting it, acquire by grants of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain most firmly secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

In the diocese of Autun, the church of Thoizy (Thoizy-le-Désert), the church of Châtillon (Chàtillon), the church of Maletat (Maletat), the church of Le Feste (Le Feste), the church of Saint Pantaleon (Saint-Panthaléon), the church of Saint Andrew (Saint-André), [Col. 0347B] the church of the Holy Twins (Les Gémeaux, the polyandry of Saint-Pierre-l’Etrier), the church of Marmagne (Marmagne), half the church of Charbonnat (Charbonnat), the church of Thil (Thil-sur-Arroux), the church of Haut-Pont (Haut-Pont), the church of Haute-Ville (Haute-Ville); in the priory of Saint Martin of Anzy (Anzi), the church of Saint Mary, the church of Avrilly (Avrilly), the church of Busseul (Busseul), the church of Urbiz[e] (Urbize), the church of Chenay (Chenay), the church of Le Lac (Le Lac), the church of La Valette (La Valette), the church of Uxelles (Uxelles), the church of Vindecy (Vindecy), the church of Monceau-l’Étoile (Monceau-l’Étoile), the church of Bragny (Bragny), the church [Col. 0347C] of Clessy (Clessy), the church of Chassy (Chassy), the church of Covello [lacuna], the church of Moûtier (Moûtier), the church of Chinaco [lacuna], the church of Stomaro (Etormet), the church of Tavernay (Tavernay), the church of Sommant (Sommant), the church of La Celle (La Celle), the church of Saint Prix (Saint-Prix), the church of Verrière (Verrière); in the priory of Avallon, the church of Saint Martin, the church of Tarot, the church of Magny (Magny), the church of Girolles (Girolles), the church of Anneot (Anneot), the church of Sermizelles (Sermizelles); in the diocese of Nevers, the church of Sainte-Péreuse (Sainte-Péreuse), the church of James (James), the church of Comagny (Comagny); all the churches of Moulins (Moulins-Engilbert), [Col. 0347D] the church of Aulnay (Aulnay), the church of Saint-Maurice-les-Saint-Saulge (Saint-Maurice-les-Saint-Saulge), the church of Saint-Saulge (Saint-Saulge), the church of Narloux (Narloux), the church of Sanisy (Sanisy), the church of Cisely (Cisely), the church of Saint-Pierre-le-Moûtier (Saint-Pierre-le-Moûtier), the church of Sainte-Babille (Sainte-Babille), the church of Saint-Humbert (Saint-Humbert), the church of Langeron (Langeron), the church of Château-sur-Allier (Château-sur-Allier), the church of Saint-Augustin (Saint-Augustin), the church of Livry (Livry), the church of Précy (Précy), the church of Cougny (Cougny), the church of Azy (Azy), the church of Trenay (Trenay), the church of Mornay (Mornay), the church of Mare (Saint-Martin-de-la-Mer), [Col. 0348A] the church of Toury (Toury); in the diocese of Lyons, the church of Milleyco [lacuna]; in the archdiocese of Bourges, the church of Colombier (Colombier); in the diocese of Chalon, the church of Chenoves (Chenoves); in the archdiocese of Besançon, the church of Saint Hilary (Saint-Illiers); in the diocese of Langres, the church of Saint Julian of Cury (Le Cry).

Upon the death of yourself, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors [lacuna], no one shall be set over it by any trick of subreption or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or a part of the brethren [lacuna] counsel, shall determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. And since, through the deceit of religious persons, many pretexts [Col. 0348B] are afforded to wicked men [lacuna], we decree that the same abbot is by no means to be deprived or deposed, unless [lacuna] requires it; whence it is necessary that, if any such complaint should arise against him, the bishop of the city of Autun shall not only examine the case, but, having associated with himself the neighbouring bishops and other religious and discerning men, shall investigate it by a searching and diligent inquiry. Thus, when all have judged in concord and according to canonical discernment, he may by censure either pronounce him guilty or absolve him innocent.

We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, or to take away its possessions, or retain those taken away, [Col. 0348C] diminish them, or harass them with any vexations or oppressions; but let all things be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, anyone, etc.

I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Henry, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary [Col. 0348D] in Cosmedin. I, Walter, bishop of Albano.

Given at Sens, through the hand of Herman, of the Holy Roman Church, [lacuna] and notary, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1164, in the sixth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

### CCCXXIV. To the Abbot of Cîteaux.—Concerning the affair of the Church of Clairvaux and its abbot.  
(Sens, 27 March.)

[MARTÈNE, *Collection*, II, 706.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son [GILBERT], abbot of Cîteaux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your prudence, beloved son, does not fail to know how renowned [Col. 0349A] and celebrated the monastery of Clairvaux is held to be, and how greatly it has hitherto flourished in religious observance and honourable conduct; this has now become known not only to its neighbours, but even to those far away. Therefore, we conceive in our mind so much the greater sorrow and grief at its loss and injury, the more deeply we love the whole Order and the monastery itself with a certain spiritual preference, and recognize that its decline redounds to the loss and injury of the entire Order.

By the truthful reports of many, however, we have learned that, on account of the abbot presiding over that monastery—who has not earned in the eyes of kings and princes the favour and reverence known to have been earned by his predecessors—the monastery itself is not a little disparaged, [Col. 0349B] and the whole Order consequently endures no slight inconvenience and loss. Therefore, wishing, by the obligation of our office, to make provision for the aforesaid monastery, its honour, and its reputation, and desiring to counsel with paternal affection the person of that abbot himself, whom we love with sincere charity in the Lord, we have decided to send there our venerable brothers [Henry], archbishop of Reims, and [Alan], bishop of Auxerre, for this affair.

Since the correction of the Order and the observance of honourable conduct especially pertain to you, we direct and, in directing, command your discretion by these present letters that you should carefully and diligently approach the same abbot in a paternal and admonitory manner, [Col. 0349C] so that, taking counsel for himself and making salutary provision for so famous a monastery, he may of his own will resign the abbacy into your hands. In accordance with the custom of that Order, we believe that he may readily be induced to do this. For abbots of that Order, when approached concerning resignation, lest they perhaps appear to preside through an ambitious and in some manner covetous desire, customarily readily acquiesce in such matters and willingly lay down the burden resting upon them.

But if he should perhaps refuse to comply with your admonition, then, with the counsel of the aforesaid [Col. 0350A] archbishop and bishop, setting aside every appeal and objection, remove him without delay from the administration of the abbey.

> **Note:** [Col. 0349C] This is that very celebrated Geoffrey, notary and biographer of Saint Bernard, who, having been abbot of Igny, became the fourth abbot of Clairvaux after Fastredus. Aptly relevant here is the brief Chronicle of Clairvaux in Chiflet, under the year 1165: “In the same [Col. 0349D] year, lord Geoffrey, abbot of Clairvaux, seeing that the hatreds of certain persons had been stirred against him, whether justly or unjustly, resigned the abbacy.” And below, under the year 1176: “Lord Henry, abbot of Hautecombe, having been promoted to be abbot of Clairvaux, presided for about four years. As soon as his son, lord Gerald, abbot of Fossanova, had become abbot of Clairvaux before him, he placed lord Geoffrey, formerly abbot of Clairvaux and then devoted to contemplation, over Fossanova. And when the same Henry was transferred from Hautecombe to Clairvaux, he took care to promote the same abbot Geoffrey to Hautecombe in his own place.”

> Henriquez writes in the *Cistercian Annals*, year 1168, chapter 5, that the cause of Geoffrey’s deposition was none other than the Clairvaux monks themselves, and that Frotmund was the chief author of this storm; Frotmund had set out for Reims to summon the archbishop, died there, and was buried in the church of Saint Remigius. Moreover, an old author cited by the same Henriquez relates that Geoffrey did not resign voluntarily [Col. 0350C] but was deposed by Alexander, abbot of Cîteaux; that he appealed to the general chapter; that, subsequently approaching the supreme pontiff, he obtained restoration; and that he was then deposed once more. How can these claims [Col. 0350D] stand with the records of Clairvaux, which state that Geoffrey declined a bishopric offered him and that, while Alexander, abbot of Cîteaux, was ill, Geoffrey was sent in his stead to Emperor Frederick to negotiate the affairs of the Church, as John of Salisbury reports, Letter 234?

And first you should make this known to the brethren of that monastery and exhort them to agree with equal willingness upon another religious, suitable, and honourable person, and elect him as their abbot, through whom both the condition of the monastery itself may be maintained in its strength and every occasion for disparaging so great and religious a house may be removed.

Given at Sens, 27 March.

### CCCXXV. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—Concerning the matter entrusted to the archbishop and the bishop of Auxerre to be conducted at Clairvaux, and how they were recalled to Sens.  
(Sens, 1 April.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 1011.]

[Col. 0350B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

That, concerning the [Note: [Col. 0350D] Here he obscurely indicates the matter of the deposition of the abbot of Clairvaux, which was treated in the preceding letter to the abbot of Cîteaux.] matter for which you went to the monastery of Clairvaux, you and our venerable brother the bishop of Auxerre—

> **Note:** [Col. 0350D] Alan, who was raised from being abbot of Ripatorius to the see of the Church of Auxerre. After he had administered it piously and vigorously for several years, he voluntarily resigned it and returned to his mother-house, Clairvaux, where he died about the year 1178.

—to whom the execution of that matter had been entrusted, could not proceed according to our and your desire because the person whom we instructed did not come, you should know is grievous and distressing to us. Therefore, wishing with more cautious care to avoid a scandal in that monastery, we advise and admonish your brotherhood [Col. 0350C] that, lest a greater disturbance arise on this account, you should for the present desist from this affair and, setting it aside now with a certain dissimulation, return to our presence. For we fear that that man, by his talkativeness, may spread the matter abroad and report it to the brethren; if proceedings were conducted in this way, serious ground for detraction would arise both against us and against you.

When you have returned to our presence, we shall deliberate more cautiously with you, with the aforesaid bishop, and with our beloved sons Henry, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, and G., formerly [Col. 0351A] bishop of Langres—

> **Note:** [Col. 0350D] Geoffrey, who, having been prior of Clairvaux and abbot of Fontenay, became bishop of Langres. After presiding most excellently for many years, he resigned the episcopate in 1163 and returned to the monastery.

—and, with your counsel, shall make salutary provision according to what we see to be expedient for the peace and tranquillity of that monastery.

Given at Sens, on 1 April.

### CCCXXVI. Bull for the monastery of Saint Serenus of Cantumerula.  
(Paris, 14 April.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, XII, Documents, 271.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GREGORY, abbot of the church of Saint Serenus of Cantumerula, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the canonical life.

It is required both by the force of equity and by rational order that just petitioners should be granted their requests, especially when piety assists their desire and truth does not oppose it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following the example of our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Adrian, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order, which is recognized to have been established in the same church according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine, shall be observed there inviolate in perpetuity.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting, by grants of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 0351C] Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms:

The entire parish of the castle of Cantumerula; the churchyard with burials, excepting those who reside in the market of Renaud de Poye; half the tithe of grain and wine of that same castle; the entire small tithe; a fourth part of the *minagium*; half the *stallagium*; and whatever you hold in the jurisdiction of that castle, both in persons, vineyards, lands, and the places written below: namely, one third of the grain-tithe of Sclavolla; whatever you have at Panniacum and Saint Ferreolus; whatever you have in the tithe [Col. 0351D] of the village of Gruis and two parts of the small tithe; also two parts of the offering on the second day after the Nativity of the Lord, and the entire churchyard; whatever you have at the hills of Figulus and at Stinellae, at Mount Genoldus and at Folletteria; likewise, at Carmeia, whatever tithe you possess; whatever you have at Faiel, Cubiti, Nuseium, and Voseium, at Saint Quentin, Saint Saturninus, and the Holy Sepulchre; the estate of Chasnella and of Mount Scopatus with their appurtenances; one third of the tithe of Conflant; and the whole tithe from your cultivation in that same parish; likewise, whatever you have in the territory of the same village, both in persons, lands, meadows, and water; the whole territory of Festo, together with the entire tithe which Henry, bishop of Troyes, gave you; [Col. 0352A] the church of Marcilley, with the greater and lesser tithe and the churchyard; the church of Ponstengium together with its estate, as Hatto, formerly bishop of Troyes, of good memory, granted them to you by a reasonable arrangement and confirmed them by the text of his charter; two parts of the entire tithe of that same village; and the entire tithe of Nusiamentum, Vallibus, and Bannoneriis.

Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority the liberty devoutly granted to you by the two lords of that same castle, namely the count and Odo of Averly, and by the four knights commonly called peers: namely, that you may freely acquire, without their consent or demand, by gift, purchase, or any other lawful title whatever is held of them in chief. Certainly, no one shall presume to exact from you tithes from your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands [Col. 0352B] or at your own expense, nor from the sustenance of your animals.

We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, anyone in the future, etc.

Given at Paris, through the hand of Herman, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0352C] 1165, in the sixth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

### CCCXXVII. He confirms the exemption and temporal goods of the monastery of Saint Walaric.  
(Paris, 17 April.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, X, Documents, 317.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ASSELIN, abbot of the monastery of Saint Walaric, situated in the county of Vimeu, and his brethren, both present and future, to be established according to the Rule, in perpetuity.

Whenever that which accords with religion and honourable conduct is requested of us, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and afford suitable assistance to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory Benedict and Paschal, Roman pontiffs, the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service and which is known especially to belong to the right of the Roman Church; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting, by grants of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 0353A]

Furthermore, no priest shall be permitted to exercise authority in that monastery or to molest its goods on any pretext. We utterly forbid public Masses to be celebrated in the same monastery, or processional stations to be held there, except by the will of the abbot or brethren, lest any occasion for popular gatherings be afforded in the retreat of God’s servants. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, the blessing of the abbot, and the ordinations of monks to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to supply them freely and without wrongful exaction; otherwise, you may have recourse to whichever bishop you choose, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. The neighbouring parish, moreover, together with the church of blessed Martin and its priest, shall remain in the liberty which it has hitherto possessed.

We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice in all things to the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, anyone, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. [Col. 0353C] I, Walter, bishop of Albano.
