I, Henry, cardinal priest of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, William, cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Manfred, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

[Col. 0353D] Given at Paris, through the hand of Herman, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1165, in the sixth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

### CCCXXVIII. He confirms the goods and privileges of the Church of Paris.  
(Paris, 20 April.)

[*Cartulary of Notre-Dame of Paris*, I, 227.]

[lacuna] Given at Paris, through the hand of Herman, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0354A] 1165, in the sixth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

### CCCXXIX. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—For the Church of Blessed Glodesindis at Metz.  
(Étampes, 21 April.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 691.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the complaint of our beloved daughters Agnes, abbess, and the sisters of the monastery of Blessed Glodesindis—

> **Note:** [Col. 0353D] Saint Glodesindis: a celebrated and ancient monastery of virgins of the Order of Saint Benedict in the city of Metz.

—we have learned that the monks of Saint Theobald [Col. 0354B] of Vitry—

> **Note:** [Col. 0354D] The monastery of Saint Theobald of Vitry is a cell, or priory, of the Cluniac Order.

—have taken for themselves, contrary to justice, the church of Narcey and the church of Baraville, which they assert rightfully belong to themselves, in such a way that no priest ought to be instituted in those churches except through the sisters; and the monks are not ashamed to retain them no less unlawfully. We have therefore committed this case to our venerable brother, the bishop of Châlons, to hear and bring it to its proper conclusion. But if he should perhaps be unwilling to accomplish this, hear the case yourself and decide it by a canonical judgment.

Given at Étampes, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March [read: May].

### CCCXXX. To Louis, King of the Franks.—That a certain archdeaconry of Chartres be granted to one of his clerks.  
At Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire, 25 April.

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1023.]

[Col. 0354C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When, on the recent second weekday (19 April) which has passed, we spoke together at Paris, we remember having proposed to your serenity that we should grant a certain archdeaconry of Chartres to one of our clerks, an honourable and learned man who had been stripped of all his goods on account of his fidelity to us and his devotion to the Church. You then replied to us, if we remember correctly, that you would take counsel about this. But afterward we neither sought your answer on the matter, nor did you subsequently give us any answer concerning it. Therefore, by these present letters we address the royal highness, earnestly asking and admonishing your serenity, as we remember having done by word of mouth, that, as we are confident of the purity of your most sincere devotion toward us and the Church of God, you should endeavour to answer us effectively through the bearer of these letters, so that we may render most abundant thanks to the royal magnificence on that account, and that he himself may be bound to remain faithful and devoted to your highness at all times for this reason.

Given at Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

### CCCXXXI. To the monks of Saint Peter of Chartres.  
(Bourges, 28 April.)

[*Cartulary of the Abbey of Saint-Père of Chartres*, vol. II, p. 650.)

[Col. 0355A]

ALEXANDER, servant [lacuna].

[lacuna] We [lacuna] decree that in churches where there is a community of four or five monks, their chaplains shall by no means be allowed, contrary to ancient and reasonable custom, to celebrate Mass solemnities for the people at the high altar; rather, the choir and high altar are to be reserved solely for the monks for the performance of the divine offices.

Given at Bourges, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May.

### CCCXXXII. He commends the Church of Bonneval and Walter, its new abbot, to Theobald, a nobleman.  
(Bourges, 29 April.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 990.]

[Col. 0355B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son THEOBALD, nobleman: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that your nobility should love religious places and honourable persons with so much the closer charity as you know them to labour more fervently in the service of the Creator through the pursuit of religious life and to strive by good works to merit his grace. Therefore, for the Church of Bonneval, and for our beloved son Walter, whom the brethren of that place, after another had resigned [Col. 0355C] the burden of the aforesaid church, unanimously and concordantly elected as their abbot, and for those brethren themselves, we earnestly ask your nobility that, for reverence for blessed Peter and for us, you should love, maintain, and vigorously protect and defend that church, the aforesaid abbot, and the brethren from the assaults of wicked men; so that you may thereby deserve to receive from almighty God the reward of eternal recompense and obtain the favour of the Apostolic See at all times.

Given at Bourges, on the third day before the Kalends of May.

### CCCXXXIII. He exhorts the abbot of Saint Remigius at Reims to restore a certain possession to the prior of Saint Maurice.  
(Bourges, 7 May.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 666.]

[Col. 0355D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Saint Remigius—

> **Note:** [Col. 0355D] Peter was then abbot of the monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims, having been taken from the monastery of Saint Peter of the Cell at Troyes; he was distinguished for piety and learning and later became bishop of Chartres.

—greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son, the prior of Saint Maurice at Reims, represented to us in his account that when the husband of the woman J. received the religious habit in his church, he gave with himself to that church half of a certain vineyard and field belonging to him; the aforesaid woman, after the death of her said husband, granted the other half to that church when she herself took the religious [Col. 0356A] habit there. Although that church had long possessed both portions quietly and peacefully, the aforesaid woman, at the prompting of a certain nephew of hers, who is your monk, gave to the church entrusted to you the portion of vineyard and field which she had granted to the Church of Saint Maurice, even though she had entered the aforesaid church together with that portion and had from that time until the present day received food and clothing from it. Yet you, taking occasion from the second donation which she is said to have made to your church, stripped the aforesaid Church of Saint Maurice of the aforementioned portion of field and vineyard.

Since this appears greatly to detract from your religious character and honour, we admonish your discretion by apostolic letters that you restore the aforementioned [Col. 0356B] portion of field and vineyard intact to the aforesaid prior and henceforth allow him and his church to hold it in peace and quiet; or, when you have been summoned for this purpose by our venerable brother the archbishop of Reims, that you do not delay rendering him sufficient justice in his presence.

Given at Bourges, on the Nones of May.

### CCCXXXIV. Privilege for the monastery of Regniacum.  
(Bourges, 12 May.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, XII, Documents, 129.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ACELIN, abbot of the monastery of Regniacum, and his brethren, both present and future, [Col. 0356C] professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant consent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic Order recognized to have been instituted in that monastery according to the fear of God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall be observed there inviolate in perpetuity.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and [Col. 0356D] canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting, by grants of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms:

The place in which the abbey itself is situated, together with the grange located in the same district and the other granges—namely Fontismes, Uldun, Essarz, Carboneries, Lescheries, Calcz, Bellovidere—the house of Campoleniae, the cellar at Vaux with all its appurtenances, and the house of Vaureta; whatever you rightfully possess by the gift of [Col. 0357A] William, Count of Nevers—namely cultivated and uncultivated land as it is bounded, all the water from the spring of Robore to the water of Milo of Noers, together with the vineyard of Ecclesioles. By the gift of Hugh of Château-Censoir, all the land of that district as it is bounded. By the gift of Rainald Caprarius, whatever he possessed at Bruhalt, cultivated and uncultivated land, and whatever he possessed in the mill of Regniac. By the gift of Ascelin of Château-Censoir, his wife Antissiodora, and his sons, all their land in the valley of Porliac; all the land of Essarz, both level and wooded; and all rights of common in all their land situated between the rivers Coram and Sedana, both level and wooded, without injury to pastures, meadows, and crops, [Col. 0357B] on condition that thereafter, as was established by them, or by their heirs, or by any person, no house or dwelling be made on the aforesaid land, except those now there; the meadow of Robore with the cultivated land adjoining it; the land of the valley of Robore; all the water which they held in common with the monks of Vézelay, from the spring of Robore to their house at Basceium.

By the gift of Joscelin of Arcy, his land of Regniac. By the gift of Hilduerius of Sacy, a part of his allod at Sacy below the village called Saint-Quentin. By the gift of Anseric of Avalon and Guy of Nuceries, whatever they possessed, without any reservation, in the land of Fontismes called Saint Peter’s. By the gift of Landric of Prais and [Col. 0357C] his sons, all their land of Uldun with all its appurtenances, both level and wooded, without any reservation. By the gift of Norgaud, whatever he possessed in the land of Huldun. By the gift of Stephen of Poliac, whatever he possessed in the land of Uldun. By the gift of Belardia, wife of Walter of the Tower, and her sons, all the land which they possessed in the wood of Crinal, both level and wooded, and the meadow between the two woods. By the gift of Hugh of Praiz and his brothers, all the meadows which those brothers possessed adjoining the village of Praiz, as they are bounded. By the gift of Geoffrey of Dunziac and his sons Hervey, Geoffrey, and Guy of Vergey and his brothers, and Hugh of Mont-Saint-Jean, the land of the grange of Lescheries with all its appurtenances, both in [Col. 0357D] woods and in level lands, cultivated and uncultivated, and all rights of common throughout the whole castellany of Château-Censoir, both in woods and on lands, without injury to pastures, meadows, and crops. By the gift of the canons of Château-Censoir, Guy of Asneries, and the other heirs, the land of Bergeries and other lands which you have from them, both in woods and in level lands, cultivated and uncultivated. By the gift of Hugh of the Gate and his brothers, the wood called Caulibus. By the gift of the same persons, Geoffrey of Vilari, and John Robert, the meadows which you possess upon the little stream of Anseny; whatever right you possess in the lands which Rainald Adens gave you.

By the gift of Anseric of Mont-Royal, William Fortis, and Theobald of Scutinei, the land on which are situated the grange [Col. 0358A] and house of Carboneries. By the gift of the same Anseric and Ivo of Avalon, the land beside the grange of Carboneries. By the gift of the same Anseric, the meadow between the ford and the great wood, and all rights of common in his land; the meadows of Cochento, Radice, and Vaurella. By the gift of Theobald of Cutinei and William Fortis, all rights of use and common in the wood of Vaurella for pasture, firewood, and construction of buildings. By the gift of Niard of Montegeleni, his sons, and the sons of Arcardus, the land from the stream of Montegeleni to the spring of Cavannis, and thence to the stream of Grassant, and the meadow of Stannum. By the gift of Framund of Rusi, his countess-wife, and Thiberga of Maniac, all the land which they possessed in the district of Cavannis; the land which you possess [Col. 0358B] from Caina of Mont-Royal, that person's nephew Galeran, and Walter, son of Nivard, called the forest of Guinnemannus. By the gift of Landric of Dracy, a house in the city of Auxerre and land beneath that same house beside the city wall; the meadows which you possess from the canons of Saint Lazarus of Avalon; the land of the grange of Morvient, called Calz, with all its appurtenances, in cultivated and uncultivated lands, as you acquired them.

By the gift of Odo, Duke of Burgundy, his son Artaud of Casteluz, and his wife Rachel, all rights of common in all their woods situated between the Coram and Cosa, for grazing cattle and pigs, free of every payment and pannage. By the gift of William of the Tower, whatever right he had in [Col. 0358C] the land which Niard of Mont-Royal granted you; the grange of Bellovidere with all its appurtenances; the land of Annai, the meadows of Vaureta, and the land which you possess from Richard of Lenset, Iterius Jocerius, and his brother. By the gift of Gibaud of Saint-Veran, his brother Rainald, and their sons, the *gixtum* [extent or tract; reading uncertain] which you possess in the land of Thori, insofar as pertains to the grange of Bellovidere, and whatever you possess in the land of Thori from their fief, as the aforesaid possessions are bounded.

Moreover, we likewise confirm to you the ancient and reasonable customs and immunities granted you by our beloved Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, and Count Henry, as is contained in their authentic instruments made concerning this matter. [Col. 0358D] Assuredly, no one shall presume to demand tithes from you upon the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, nor upon the sustenance of your animals. Should any free and independent person wish, for the redemption of his or her soul, to join your monastery, you shall have unrestricted authority to receive that person. Moreover, by apostolic authority we prohibit anyone from presuming, after profession has been made in your monastery, to receive or retain your brethren, clerical or lay, without your permission. Providing with paternal solicitude also for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone, within the enclosure of your places or granges, from daring to commit violence, robbery, or theft, or to seize a person. [Col. 0359A]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole and intact, to be of every benefit for the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Gualter, bishop of Albano. [Col. 0359B] I, Hubald, cardinal-priest of the title of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme. I, Henry, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. [Lacuna], cardinal-priest of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Boso, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Cynthius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Manfred, cardinal-deacon of Saint George [Col. 0359C] at the Golden Veil.

Given at Bourges, through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth Ides of May [12 May], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1164 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### CCCXXXV. Privilege for the monastery of Bonmont, in the diocese of Geneva.  
*(Bourges, 12 May.)*

*[Monuments of National History, Charters, I, 831, from the original. Cantonal Archives of Lausanne; Bonmont portfolio, no. 4; authenticated copy in the baronial archives of the House of Gingins at La Sarra (F. D. G.).]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, abbot of Bonmont, [Note: [Col. 0359D] Abbey of Bonmont. Certain authors, such as Sainte-Marthe, Besson, and Guichenon, have wrongly attributed the foundation of the monastery of Bonmont (in the Swiss canton of Vaud) to a count of Geneva; the bull above makes no mention of this, nor do any subsequent documents. Walcherius of Divonne, his brother Stephen—thought to descend from a younger son of the counts of Geneva (see Guichenon, *Biblioth. Sebus.*, cent. I, no. 82)—and their mother Helvide were the true founders, as is shown by the act confirming their donations in favour of Moses, the first abbot, issued by Arducius, bishop of Geneva, dated the seventh day before the Ides of June, 1134–1136. (See Buchat, documents in the Library of Bern.) In the bull above this same Stephen is called Stephen of Gingins; he was the direct ancestor of the House of Gingins, which still exists today.] and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life, forever.

The duty of the office we have undertaken invites us to accede to religious vows and to fulfil them by effective action; reason itself seems to require it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the monastery in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in your monastery according to the fear of God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the observance of the Cistercian brethren shall be inviolably observed there for all time. [Col. 0360B] Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s aid, through grants of popes, gifts of kings, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought it proper to specify the following by their own names:

The whole territory of Pellens and the mountain country as far as the Valley of Saccone, by the gift of Walcherius of Divonne [Note: [Col. 0359D] Divonne in the district of Gex.], namely whatever he possessed in the aforesaid territory, at Guillione and at Luncuernet [Note: [Col. 0360D] Lunchvernet, Longverney in the district of Gex.]; by the gift of the monks of Saint Eugendus, whatever they possessed in the same territory; by the gift of Stephen of Gingins [Note: [Col. 0360D] Gingins, district of Nyon, canton of Vaud.], the land of Saviniac [Note: [Col. 0360D] Saviniac: read Avenac, Aveney; the grange of Bugey, Bugis—two villages in the district of Gingins.] and the grange of Bugey; by the gift of [Col. 0360C] Humbert, bishop of Geneva [Note: [Col. 0360D] Humbert of Grammont, bishop of Geneva, who held office from 1120 to 31 October 1134.], and the canons of the Church of Saint Mary of Lausanne, the grange of Chasararium [Note: [Col. 0360D] Chasareium, Chézeray, district of Nyon, canton of Vaud.]; by the gift of the monks of Saint Victor of Geneva, whatever they possessed in the village of Charaium; by the gift of Walcherius and his sons, whatever they possessed in the aforesaid village, together with the vineyards and the grange of Divonne; by the gift of Petronilla of Albona [Note: [Col. 0360D] Albona, Aubonne in the canton of Vaud.], the grange of Clareins [Note: [Col. 0360D] Clareins, Clarens, district of Nyon, canton of Vaud.] and vineyards; by the gift of Humbert of Pringins [Note: [Col. 0360D] Pringins, Prangins, district of Nyon, canton of Vaud.], his son Peter, and Humbert of Albona, the church of Vizo [Note: [Col. 0360D] Vizo, perhaps Vich, district of Begnins, canton of Vaud.] and that of Perr[lacuna], and a grange [lacuna]; by the gift of Guigo of Bignins [Note: [Col. 0360D] Bignins, Begnins.] and of Amadeus, Anselm, and Peter, the grange of Frachavallo; the two parts of the tithes of Altaribus [Note: [Col. 0360D] Altaribus, La Rippe, district of Nyon, canton of Vaud.] which you possess in that place; vineyards at [Col. 0361A] Balens, by the gift of Guimard of Lu[lacuna]ne, Humbert Brutinus, Count of Geneva [Note: [Col. 0361D] “Humbert Brutinus, Count of Geneva.” It is evident that this is not a Humbert, count of Geneva, since the first count bearing that name did not rule until the thirteenth century. The passage concerning him in this bull suggests that he was a relative of his donors, Gaimard of L[lacuna] and Otto of Saint-Symphorien. The epithet *Brutinus* appears to be a corruption of an old Germanic word *Brût*, which properly means *nurus*, “daughter-in-law,” and by extension “son-in-law,” or perhaps “bastard” (*nothus*).]] and Otto of Saint-Symphorien; the entire allod of Peter of Scaneins and his brother William, in vineyards, fields, and woods at Scaneins and Bellomonte.

Assuredly, no one shall presume to demand from you tithes on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, nor upon the sustenance of your animals. If any free and independent person wishes, for the redemption of his or her soul, to join your monastery, you shall have unrestricted authority to receive that person. Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone to dare, after clerics or lay brothers have made profession in your monastery, to receive or retain them without your permission. Providing also with paternal solicitude for [Col. 0361B] your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosure of your places or granges from daring to commit violence, robbery, or theft, or to seize a person.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all shall be kept whole and intact, to be of every benefit for the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

[Col. 0361C] I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, cardinal-priest of the title of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme. I, Henry, cardinal-priest [lacuna]. I, John, cardinal-priest of the church of Saint Anastasia. I, William, cardinal-priest of the church of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Parma and Santa Rufina. I, Gualterius, bishop of Albano. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. [Col. 0361D] I, Otto, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas. I, Boso, cardinal-deacon of Saint Cosmas. I, Cinthius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian.

I, Manfred, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Bourges, through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth Ides of May [12 May], in the thirteenth indiction [Note: [Col. 0362D] The indiction here ought to be XII rather than XIII for the year 1164.], in the year 1164 of the Lord’s Incarnation, [Col. 0362A] in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Alexander III.

### CCCXXXVI. He confirms the possessions of the Church of Saint Mark of Venice.  
*(Bourges, 13 May.)*

*[CORNELIUS, **Ecclesiae Venetae**, X, II, 319.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LEONARD, procurator of the fabric of the church of Blessed Mark of Venice, and to his successors in the same office forever.

The effect of a pious petition ought to be brought to completion, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably, and the requested benefit may assuredly gain force. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, graciously assenting to the petitions of our beloved son in Christ Vitalis, doge, and [Col. 0362B] of the citizens of Venice, we confirm by apostolic authority to the church of Blessed Mark, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the church of Saint Mark in the city of Tyre, together with its houses, mill, oven, square, entire street, fields, lands, and all things belonging to that church and to the fabric of Saint Mark; likewise the church of Saint Mark at Acre, with its mill, houses, square, and street, one end of which street reaches the dwelling formerly belonging to Peter Ziani, while the other abuts on the monastery of Saint Demetrius. This is the street which Baldwin I, king of Jerusalem, of good memory, lawfully granted to Blessed Mark, the doge of Venice, and their successors upon the acquisition of the city of Sidon. We likewise confirm all the lands which, in the cities of Jerusalem, Tripoli, Antioch, and Haifa, the doge and commune of Venice, having received them by grant from the king [Col. 0362C] of Jerusalem, lawfully bestowed upon the aforesaid fabric of Blessed Mark, together with all their appurtenances and revenues, as they were lawfully granted and as it is known that they now possess them peaceably and quietly. We decree that both the aforementioned possessions, as stated above, and all other goods which they now lawfully possess for the benefit of that same fabric, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s aid, through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors, for the benefit of that fabric. [Col. 0362D]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the churches, take away the churches’ possessions or other possessions assigned to that fabric, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass them by any vexations; but that all shall be preserved undiminished and entire, to benefit in every way the uses of the fabric of the aforesaid church for whose advantage they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop. [Col. 0363A] If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly acting against this text of our decree, should rashly attempt to contravene it, and, having been warned a second and a third time, does not correct that presumption by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his or her power and office; let that person know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let that person be subject to stern vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of the fabric of the aforesaid church of Blessed Mark may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. [Col. 0363B] Amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Gualterius, bishop of Albano. I, Ubald, cardinal-priest of the title of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme. I, Henry, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, William, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, James, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. [Col. 0363C] I, Otto, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Nicholas in the Prison. I, Boso, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Cynthius, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Adrian. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Manfred, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Bourges, through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the third Ides of May [13 May], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year one thousand one hundred and sixty-five of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### CCCXXXVII. He exhorts Templars residing in the dioceses of Lyon and Chalon to settle with the brethren of Tournus concerning certain tithes withheld from the monastery.  
*(Bourges, 15 May.)*

*[JUENIN, **New History of Tournus**, proofs, p. 167.]*

[Col. 0363D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the Templars residing in the dioceses of Lyon and Chalon, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The brethren of the Church of Tournus have represented to us that you refuse to pay tithes from certain lands which you cultivate, although their church has been accustomed from ancient times to receive tithes from them. [Col. 0364A] Although it has been granted you in the privileges of the Roman Church that you are bound to pay tithes to no one from the produce of your labour, nevertheless, because they complain that in this matter they are greatly burdened, we ask, advise, and admonish your prudence that, as men of peace, for the good of peace you make some provision for the aforesaid brethren, so that they may receive some consolation for the tithes withheld, and that we may deservedly commend your honourable conduct.

Given at Bourges, on the Ides of May [15 May].

### CCCXXXVIII. Bull for the monastery of Saint Satyrus.  
*(Bourges, 17 May.)*

*[Gallia Christiana, new ed., II, Instruments, 54.]*

[Col. 0364B] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, abbot of the church of Saint Satyrus, which is situated near Sancerre, with the brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life, forever and ever. Amen.

It is fitting that we willingly grant a desire shown to concern religious purpose and the salvation of souls, and give suitable support to the requests of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and, following the example of our father and predecessor of holy memory, Pope Eugenius, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Saint Satyrus, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. [Col. 0364C] First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that church according to the Rule of the Lord and of blessed Augustine shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s aid, through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought it proper to specify the following by their own names:

At Sancerre: namely, [Col. 0364D] the church of Saint Peter, the church of Saint Denis, the church of Saint Iterius, the chapel of Saint Hilary in the Count’s Tower, and everything which you possess in that castle, whether in rents, *lerdes* [a local due], other customary dues, or parish tithes, together with the revenue which by customary right you possess on the River Loire; the church of Talverinac, and everything you possess in that parish, whether in rents or tithes; the holding of Frateium and everything you possess there; the church of Saint Baudel, and everything you possess in that parish in tithes, rents, customary dues, meadows, and arable land; the church of Dergicis and everything you possess in that parish; the church of Herriac and everything you possess in that parish in rents, tithes, arable land, [Col. 0365A] and woodland; the church of Vinomum and everything you possess in that parish in tithes and rents; the church of Joci and everything you possess in that parish; the church of Lugniac and everything you possess in that parish; the church of Grellia and everything you possess in that parish in tithes and rents; the church of Jalonnia and everything you possess in that parish in tithes, rents, arable land, meadows, and woodland; the land and meadows of Bordis and everything you possess there; arable land, rent, and customary dues at Elumolium; men, rent, meadows, woodland, and arable land at the village of Donatus; land and meadows at Genevreia; rent and land at Claumos; vineyard rents and the customary dues which [Col. 0365B] you possess there; the right which you possess in the revenue of the church of Sancio; the church of Jars and everything you possess in that parish in tithes and rents; the allod of Cocciac with every possession belonging to it, whether in lands, meadows, woods, and all customary dues; Salnaium of the allod of the village of Genonis; the chapel of Saint Mary, situated in Concortallum, the castle of Bernard Fulmen; the church of Blanca Forte and the allod of Mont-Morlons, the tithes, and everything you possess in that parish; the church of Barloc and everything you possess in that parish; the church of Petrafitta and everything you possess in that parish; the church of Sariac-in-the-Woods and everything you possess in that parish; the allod of the court of John with all its possessions, whether [Col. 0365C] in lands, meadows, woodland, dependent tenants, and all customary dues; the allod of Mavei; the church of Bella-Villa, with its entire tithe, the village itself with all its possessions, whether in lands, meadows, woods, and dependent tenants, whether held in demesne or in *casamentum* [tenures], and all customary dues which you possess; the church of Saviniac and everything you possess in that parish, whether in tithes, men, meadows, woods, demesne, *casamentum*, and all customary dues; the church of Acigniac and everything you possess in that parish; the church of Saint Gemina and everything you possess in that parish, whether in tithes or land; the allod of Cappis with all its appurtenances; the allod of Lichiac with all its possessions, whether in lands, meadows, woodland, and all customary dues; the church of Saint Denis of the fortress of Humbaud with all its appurtenances; the chapel of the Place of God with all its small holdings; in the district of Auxerre, [Col. 0365D] the estate called Meva and the chapel of Saint Martin situated upon it, and everything belonging to it, whether lands, waters, roads, meadows, woods, rents, or customary dues; the church of Saint John the Evangelist at Bourges with all its appurtenances—namely, the land of Raymond of Faia, called Faita and Puzols, together with the wood, level land, and meadows which Master Hermann, our subdeacon and notary, acquired for the same church of Saint John; and everything which belongs to Raymond himself by hereditary right, both on his father’s side and on his mother’s; [Col. 0366A] also the land called Ferragalli and everything belonging to the possession of that Ferragalli; the chapel of Montellis, with land, meadows, mills, rights of woodland use, and all that belongs to it; the church of Saint Amator of Auxerre, with all its appurtenances, namely the church of Brueria and everything belonging to it; the church of Lansec with the lands and meadows belonging to it; the church of Chavanna with the vineyards, meadows, and tithes belonging to it; the church of Villa Feriol with its appurtenances; [Col. 0366B] the chapel of Saint Mary of Celles.

We confirm by apostolic authority the agreement concerning the bank of the Loire, peaceably relinquished to you in full by Rainald of Montfaucon, and concerning the toll on the water at Decommum, likewise relinquished to you and henceforth not to be granted to any church of yours, as it was lawfully made between you and him through our venerable brother Peter, archbishop of Bourges, and confirmed in writing. The wood beside the River Loire called Vaurella, with its meadows, lakes, rents, and customary dues, and everything which you possess there; the prebend in the church of Saint Stephen of Bourges, as it was assigned to you by the Catholic archbishops and chapter of that church; the remission of the procession which you were accustomed to hold on the Feast of the Finding of Saint [Col. 0366C] Stephen of Bourges, as granted by Alberic of good memory, formerly archbishop of Bourges, and as confirmed by authentic writing both by him and by our venerable brother Peter, now archbishop of Bourges, and by the chapter of that church.

Furthermore, the borough itself in which the church of Saint Satyrus is situated, together with the immunity which it is known to have had until these times, and the adjoining territory within boundaries established of old—that is, from the *Dogium* of the late Gerard, along the road leading on this side of Ulmus-Ricardi, rising through the vineyards a little above the Cross as far as the springs between the two houses; then circling above the houses of Fontenaicum to the Cross of Uldric; proceeding by the White Road to the valley of John of Charnis; thence running between two woods; and descending by the little bridge of Vineis to the Loire—shall be free from every right or exaction of kings and princes. Within that territory are, on one side, the small town called Fontiniac; on the other, the chapel of Saint Theobald with the buildings established there, and the village called Catonis. [Col. 0366D] The wood called Foliolium, which is situated beside Count Theobald’s wood called Carnis, and in which you possess the following customary right in the count’s wood: namely, timber for your own use, half the pannage, and a share for your own pigs.

Moreover, we grant you permission to redeem from the hands of laymen the tithes belonging by right to your churches which are held contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers, and to acquire them by every lawful means available to you. [Col. 0367A] We decree that the agreement lawfully made and confirmed in writing by both sides between you and the nuns of Saint Lawrence at Bourges, concerning tithes jointly acquired or to be acquired from lay hands, shall remain valid. Further, after profession has been made in the aforesaid church, none of the brethren may depart from the cloister without the permission of the abbot and the whole congregation; and no one may dare retain a person who departs without the security of letters from the community. The abbot for the time being may impose canonical sentence upon one who has departed without your knowledge or against your will, if, after a second or third admonition, he refuses to return. [Col. 0367B] Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the place, or of any of your successors, no one may be placed in authority there by any craft of subreption or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or the firm decision of the sounder part of the council, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Augustine, shall determine should be elected from among themselves, or, if expedient, from another community of the same order.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that same church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole and intact, to be of every benefit for the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See [Col. 0367C] and the canonical rights of the archbishop and church of Bourges.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Gualterius, bishop of Albano. I, Hubald, cardinal-priest of the title of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme. I, Henry, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, William, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. [Col. 0367D] I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Boso, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Cynthius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Manfred, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Bourges through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman [Col. 0368A] Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June [17 May], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1164 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Alexander III.

### CCCXXXIX. He praises the abbot and brethren of Pontigny for treating Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, honourably, and commends him to them.

*[MANRIQUE, **Cistercian Annals**, IV, 560.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Pontigny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You have abundantly demonstrated by your deeds the fervour of faith and devotion which you show in many ways toward us and the Roman Church, in that you have treated our venerable brother, the archbishop of Canterbury, so kindly, humanely, and [Col. 0368B] honourably, and have been unwilling in this matter to yield either to anyone’s threats or to inducements. We regard this as wholly welcome and pleasing to us, as though it had been done to our own person; we therefore render to your charity all the thanks we can for it, and commend your disposition in the Lord with countless praises. Yet, because the end of a good work is usually regarded more highly than its beginning, by apostolic letters we ask, admonish, and exhort your discretion in the Lord that you provide the said archbishop, as you are known hitherto to have done praiseworthily, with the assistance of brotherly generosity so decently and honourably that he may always find your fraternal charity [Col. 0368C] more ardent, and may never perceive it to have grown cold through threats or terrors.

### CCCXL. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On the affair of the Church of Clairvaux.  
*(At Clermont, 25 May.)*
[MARTEN., *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 713.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Concerning the affair of the Church of Clairvaux [Note: [Col. 0367D] That is, concerning the deposition of Abbot Geoffrey, discussed above in Letters 246 and 249.], regarding which you recently sent us your letter, we have proceeded upon the advice of our venerable brother, the Bishop of Auxerre, and of our beloved son [Note: [Col. 0367D] This Henry the cardinal, as also Henry the archbishop to whom this letter is addressed, and [Col. 0368D] Alan, Bishop of Auxerre, had been Cistercian monks; and at least these two pontiffs had been taken from Clairvaux. This was perhaps the reason why this affair was entrusted to them.] Henry, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, as seemed expedient to us and to them. If anything remains, we shall gladly endeavor to carry it out as we know to be expedient, both out of regard for your sincerity and in consideration of that same church. But concerning what you wrote us regarding the aforesaid cardinal, we could not comply with your request, since he, being a discerning, prudent man, and most devoted to us, is extremely necessary and useful to us for the great affairs of the Church now pressing upon us; nor can we endure his absence in any way.

Moreover, we return abundant thanks to you for your visitation.

Given at Clermont, the eighth day before the Kalends of June [25 May].

CCCXLI. To the brethren of the Church of Saint Peter at Chartres. (At Clermont, 26 May.)

[*Collection des Cartulaires*, II, 649.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons FULCHER, abbot, and the brethren of the Church of Saint Peter at Chartres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

. . . . . We decree that no bishop shall excommunicate any of your monks, or suspend him from the divine office, without an evident and manifest cause.

[Col. 0369B] Given at Clermont, the seventh day before the Kalends of June [26 May].

CCCXLII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of the priest Everen. (At Clermont, 4 June.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 714.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Everen, a poor priest, coming before the clemency of the Apostolic See, represented to us in his account that Walter, a Premonstratensian canon and provost of Gasnan, has unjustly seized the revenues of his church [Col. 0369C] and presumptuously ventures to retain them. Although the same provost had made a settlement with the aforesaid priest in this matter, he has withdrawn from that settlement and unjustly refuses to return a cloak which the said priest had pledged to him as security. He also presumes to seize a meadow and a certain piece of land belonging to the often-mentioned priest, and, as we are told, to hold them without lawful right.

Therefore, since we stand as defenders in their rights of all the faithful of God, and especially of those devoted to divine worship, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the matter is so, you carefully admonish and strictly compel the aforesaid provost to observe diligently the said settlement, if it was reasonably made; to restore everything taken after the settlement was made; and henceforth to desist from harassing the same priest.

Given at Clermont, the second day before the Nones of June [4 June].

CCCXLIII. He asks Louis, King of the Franks, to deter the Count of Nevers and his mother from harassing the monastery of Vézelay. (At Clermont, 5 June.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1044.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that it has come to the notice of your royal serenity how the noble Count of Nevers and [Col. 0370A] his mother have laid their hands upon the monastery of Vézelay more heavily than usual; and, utterly setting aside fear and reverence for God and for blessed Mary Magdalene, whose body rests in that monastery, they have not feared, through their servants, to seize and carry away horses, oxen, asses, and livestock, both of the monastery and of its outlying dependent houses. The aforesaid count also surrounds the abbot of that place with threats and snares, so that he does not dare to leave the monastery without danger and fear for his own person. He not only obstructs the public and ancient highway, but compels travelers to pass through one of his castles; and under this pretext he has seized certain burgesses returning from the fair.

Therefore, since that monastery is known to belong to the right and property of the Roman Church and to the protection of your royal highness, we ask, admonish, and exhort your serenity in the Lord through apostolic letters that, for the love of God and out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, you urgently admonish the said count and his mother, diligently endeavor to meet with them, and, if necessary, restrain them by royal authority, so that without delay they restore all that was taken to the aforesaid abbot and brethren, make suitable satisfaction for the damages and injuries, and thereafter entirely desist from unjustly molesting and burdening them. Thus may you happily obtain from the almighty Lord an unfailing reward for this, [Col. 0370C] and may we be bound to render your clemency most abundant thanks for it.

For our part, we have admonished the aforesaid count and his mother by our letters to endeavor to correct their wrongdoings and henceforth entirely to desist from such acts.

Given at Clermont, on the Nones of June [5 June].

CCCXLIV. He directs Hugh, Archbishop of Sens, to exhort the Count of Nevers and his mother to make good the damages inflicted on the monastery of Vézelay; should they fail to do so within twenty days, he orders them to be subjected to excommunication. (At Clermont, June.)

[Ibid., col. 1043.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, Archbishop of Sens: [Col. 0370D] greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that it has come to the notice of your brotherhood how the noble Count of Nevers and his mother have laid their hands upon the monastery of Vézelay more heavily than usual; and, utterly setting aside fear and reverence for God and blessed Mary Magdalene, whose body rests in that monastery, they have not feared, through their servants, to seize and carry away horses, oxen, asses, and livestock, both of the monastery and of its outlying dependent houses. The aforesaid count also surrounds the abbot of that place with threats and snares, so that he does not dare to leave the monastery without danger and fear for his own person.

Therefore, since that monastery is known to belong especially to the right and property of blessed Peter and ourselves, [Col. 0371A] and is no small member of the Roman Church, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, as you hold dear the favor of blessed Peter and ours, you endeavor swiftly and with every diligence to meet with the said count and his mother, and to exhort them earnestly that they restore without delay all that was taken to the aforesaid abbot and brethren, make suitable satisfaction for the damages and injuries inflicted, and thereafter entirely desist from unjustly molesting and burdening them. Otherwise, within twenty days after your admonition, you shall completely interdict throughout all their land every divine office, except baptism for infants and penance for the dying; and, if even then they do not come to their senses, you shall not delay to pronounce sentence of excommunication against their persons.

You shall notify by your letters our venerable brethren, the Bishops of Autun, Langres, Auxerre, and Nevers, and firmly enjoin upon them in our name that they endeavor inviolably to observe, until fitting satisfaction is made, the sentence pronounced by you against the land or persons of the aforesaid count or his mother. For we command them by our own letters, once they have received your letters in this matter, faithfully to endeavor to carry this out.

CCCXLV. He commands Henry of Autun, Walter of Langres, Alan of Auxerre, and Bernard of Nevers, bishops, to observe the sentence of excommunication which the Archbishop of Sens may pronounce against the Count of Nevers and his mother. (At Clermont, 5 June.)

[Ibid., 1044.]

[Col. 0371C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers HENRY, Bishop of Autun; WALTER, Bishop of Langres; ALBAN, Bishop of Auxerre; and BERNARD, Bishop of Nevers: greeting and apostolic blessing.

To the notice of your brotherhood, etc., as above as far as these words: “is a member of the Roman Church.” We have commanded our venerable brother the Archbishop of Sens to endeavor swiftly and with every diligence to meet with the said count and his mother, and earnestly to exhort them to restore without delay all that was taken to the aforesaid [Col. 0371D] abbot and brethren, to make suitable satisfaction for the damages and injuries inflicted, and thereafter entirely to desist from unjustly molesting and burdening them. Otherwise, he is to interdict throughout all their land every divine office, except baptism for infants and penance for the dying; and, if even then they do not come to their senses, he is not to delay pronouncing a sentence of excommunication against their persons. He is to notify you by his letters and firmly enjoin upon you in our name that you take care to observe inviolably, until fitting satisfaction is made, the sentence pronounced by him against the land or persons of the aforesaid count or his mother.

Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when you have received his letters concerning this matter, you firmly maintain whatever has been decreed by him, as you hold dear the favor of blessed Peter and ours, and cause it to be inviolably observed throughout your dioceses. Otherwise, by the Lord’s authority, we shall punish more severely whoever transgresses our command.

Given at Clermont, on the Nones of June [5 June].

CCCXLVI. He informs Abbot William and the brethren of Vézelay of the foregoing letters. (At Clermont, 5 June.)

[Ibid., col. 1045.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, abbot, and the brethren of Vézelay: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0372B] Having received your letters and carefully considered the tribulations and distresses which their contents set forth, we have inwardly shared your sorrow with a fatherly affection, since we know that your monastery is the proper patrimony of blessed Peter, love you with a more assured charity in the Lord as special and devoted sons of the Church, and eagerly seek your welfare. Accordingly, concerning your affair we have sent our letters to our dearest son in Christ Louis, illustrious King of the Franks; to our venerable brethren Hugh, Archbishop of Sens, and the Bishops of Autun, Langres, Auxerre, and Nevers; also to the noble Count of Nevers and to his countess mother, as you will learn more fully from copies [Col. 0372C] of them. You, however, should exert diligence and effort to bring about these corrections; and, continually devoting yourselves to prayer through observance of the cloister and religious life, cry out to heaven that almighty God may quickly put an end to these evils and grant you peace and the tranquility you desire.

Given at Clermont, on the Nones of June [5 June].

CCCXLVII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of a certain woman named Hersende. (At Clermont, 5 June.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Coll.*, II, 714.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0372D] brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the complaint transmitted by the noblewoman Hersende, it has come to our hearing that, although our venerable brother Eustace, Bishop of Châlons, had at our command excommunicated Germund and Theobald for the many injuries and damages they inflicted upon the same woman, he afterward did not hesitate to absolve them without any satisfaction having been made. Therefore, since the ecclesiastical sword is drawn against evildoers so that their wickedness may be restrained by fitting punishment, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you admonish the aforesaid men and compel them with every severity to restore all things taken to the said woman [Col. 0373A] and not delay in repairing the damages caused. If they scorn to obey your admonition, you shall restore them to the same sentence of excommunication, setting aside every pretext and excluding appeal.

Furthermore, since orphans and wards stand under the Church’s guardianship and protection, we likewise enjoin upon you by the authority of these present letters to endeavor carefully to admonish and strictly compel her debtors, and those of her sons by her former husband, to pay them in full whatever they acknowledge themselves to owe her and her sons. Concerning those debts which they deny, let them either make satisfaction or, in your presence and with appeal set aside, render them the full measure of justice. Yet the debts of the children are to be assigned to those persons who are known to have been entrusted with their care and who ought to preserve them wholly and faithfully for the children’s benefit. You shall also provide for the debtors in such a way that, once they have paid the money, no one may thereafter bring an action against them concerning it.

Given at Clermont, on the Nones of June [5 June].

CCCXLVIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of C., the lord pope’s nephew. (At Clermont, 7 June.)

[Ibid., col. 715.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims: [Col. 0373C] greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son Master Fulco, a canon of your church, represented to us on your behalf that you would pay us one hundred and fifty pounds for a certain brother of yours, which sum we ordered to be assigned to our beloved son Eustace, master of the brethren of the Order of the Temple. But because we are bound to pay the same 158 pounds to the bearers of these letters for money lent, which we received from them for the needs of the Roman Church, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if you have not yet assigned the sum to the said master, you cause the aforesaid 158 pounds, which your generosity promised to our beloved son C., our nephew, to be assigned, and inform us by your letters what [Col. 0373D] you have done in the matter.

Given at Clermont, the seventh day before the Ides of June [7 June].

CCCXLIX. To Gilbert, Bishop of London.—Concerning the Church of Canterbury. (At Clermont, 8 June.)

[*Letters of St Thomas*, ed. Giles, II, 96.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GILBERT, Bishop of London: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not believe that it has escaped your memory how our dearest son in Christ Henry, illustrious King of the English, long ago urgently entreated us by many prayers to permit your translation from the Church of Hereford, over which [Col. 0374A] you presided, to the Church of London. In order that we might grant our assent to this request, he urged both common necessity and advantage, asserting that that city was, as it were, the seat of his kingdom. Because he believed you to surpass all others in every virtue of religion and discernment, he wished to avail himself of your counsel, both spiritually and temporally, concerning matters conducive to the salvation of his soul and relating to the enlargement and preservation of the kingdom; and therefore he desired to have you nearer and more familiar to him.

Accordingly, considering how usefully your prudence and piety might counsel for the welfare of the same king and kingdom, and how much advantage and benefit for the Church of God might result from this, we gladly granted his prayers and allowed you to be promoted to the Church of London. The more graciously and readily we fulfilled his pleasure and will, and applied ourselves likewise to your advancement and honor, the more your integrity ought to exert itself for the increase and preservation of the Church, and the more attentively and effectively labor in this matter, so that by actual performance and by experience itself we may perceive the fruit which the same king promised us and which we hope for, and so that in his days the Church of the English may serve the Lord God in good peace.

But we do not believe you are ignorant how the aforesaid king has turned his mind and heart away from the devotion which he used to show to the Church, and seems to persecute and assail it in many ways: in our appeals and visitations; in communicating also with schismatics and persons expressly [Col. 0374C] excommunicated, and entering into alliance with them; and likewise in having compelled our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to leave his kingdom.

Therefore we ask, admonish, and command your diligence that, joined by our venerable brother Robert, Bishop of Hereford, you carefully admonish the same king and induce him by earnest exhortation to abandon entirely such a course; to make fitting satisfaction for what he has done wrong; to desist altogether from wrongful acts; to love his Creator with a pure heart; to regard his mother, the holy Roman Church, with his accustomed reverence; not to prevent those who wish to visit her; in no way to obstruct appeals made to her; and, graciously recalling and restoring the aforesaid our brother the archbishop to his see, to stand firm and immovable in reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, and to apply himself to works of mercy and compassion. He must neither burden ecclesiastical persons, whether of his kingdom or his land, as he is said to do, nor permit them to be burdened by anyone; but must love them, uphold them, and preserve them under royal protection, so that He through whom kings reign may preserve for him his temporal kingdom on earth and grant him an everlasting one in heaven.

Although, because of his great devotion and the many services rendered to us in our time of need, we love him with more abundant charity as a most excellent prince and renowned king, and, however differently he may suppose, seek with greater zeal his honor, exaltation, and advancement, you shall nevertheless set before him that, unless he correct these matters more promptly, he must fear lest God be gravely angered with him for all these things, should inflict harsher vengeance upon him and his people, and we ourselves be unable much longer to endure them patiently. We say this not so much for our own sake as for his welfare and benefit, for, recalling the splendid services of devotion and generosity which, as we have said, he has often rendered to us as a most Christian king, we cherish his glory and magnificence and desire with all our hearts the welfare of himself, his kingdom, and his people.

Moreover, having fuller confidence in the prudence of your piety and integrity, we entrust the affairs of the Church more confidently to your experience for execution. Accordingly, we command your brotherhood by the authority of these letters to cause the Peter’s Pence for the present year to be faithfully collected throughout all England and not delay in transmitting them to us as soon as you can. We also ask your discretion, while you collect the said money, to make suitable provision for us in the meantime from your own funds or from money obtained on loan, and to send it to us before the next Kalends of August [1 August], afterward to receive the same sum from the said Peter’s Pence. This will be as grateful and welcome to us as if you had granted the money to us as a gift.

[Col. 0375C] Given at Clermont, the sixth day before the Ides of July [read: June; 8 June].

CCCL. To Henry, King of the English.—On the inviolability of ecclesiastical immunity and the prohibition against bringing clerics before a secular tribunal. (At Clermont? June.)

[*Letters of St Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 115.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ HENRY, illustrious King of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although your filial devotion toward us and your mother, the most holy Church, appears in some measure to have grown cold, we have never at any time abandoned our fatherly affection toward you or the kingdom entrusted to your governance. Therefore let your serenity, carefully observing that the wounds of a friend are better than the kisses of an enemy, consider and attend more earnestly to the fact that, as clerics are distinguished from secular men by their manner of life and dress, so the judgments concerning clerics are proved to be wholly different from the judgments of laypeople. If, therefore, you perversely overturn these things in an order that is unfitting; if, usurping to your own power those things which belong to Jesus Christ, you establish new laws at your pleasure for the oppression of churches and of Christ’s poor; and if you introduce customs which you call ancestral, then you yourself will beyond doubt be judged in like manner at the last judgment, which you cannot escape, and the same measure by which you have measured will be measured back to you.

But lest our admonitions seem somewhat tiresome or harsh to the ears of your highness, recall what is written: “The father corrects the son whom he loves” (Prov. III). Know certainly that the more ardently we love your person in the Lord, and the more often and earnestly we recall the marks of your most sincere devotion which you once displayed to us and to the Church of God in many and magnificent ways, the more gladly we bring these things to your attention, desiring for you with the heartfelt affections of our will spiritual and eternal salvation.

For if fear of the judgment to come moves you in any respect, or the crown of rewards in eternal rest delights you, it would be not merely fitting but advantageous for your serenity to cultivate true justice, which is God; to give to each what is his due; to leave ecclesiastical affairs—especially criminal cases arising from violation of faith or oath—and cases concerning the goods and possessions of churches to be dealt with by ecclesiastical persons; and not to confuse kingship and priesthood. Even if you spent upon feeding the poor or upon other works of piety everything that is diverted to your uses from ecclesiastical property by such exactions, you would not thereby render God a service more pleasing than if, having uncovered one altar, you covered another; or if you crucified Peter in order to rescue Paul from the peril of death.

You ought indeed to remember, and to keep before your eyes as an example in this matter, how King Saul, after defeating Amalek, wished to preserve spoil contrary to the divine command. When, in his own excuse, he alleged that he had preserved these things for sacrifice, he was rejected by the Lord, and another was appointed to royal honor and dignity while Saul was still alive. The sins of the people had made him king, but deprived him of the rule of the kingdom entrusted to him. It is likewise fitting for your salvation to recall how King Uzziah, when he wished to burn incense and usurp for himself the office of priest, was struck with leprosy by the just vengeance of God.

But if you ascribe your successes to your own strength and power rather than to God, and do not withdraw your purpose and mind from oppressing ecclesiastical men and churches, then He who set you over others and established you as a great prince in the world for the governance, not the oppression, [Col. 0376D] of His faithful people, will beyond doubt require from you with grievous interest the talents entrusted to you; and, as is read of Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, who was cast out of the kingdom for his father’s offense, He will transfer the paternal trust to heirs.

Therefore do not yield to the wrongful suggestions of anyone, nor lend your ear to those who always whisper evil; but listen more carefully to what is conducive to your salvation. Govern the kingdom, which you obtained only for the honor of God and for the tranquility and peace of His Church, in such a way, and endeavor profitably to administer it according to what the Lord has entrusted to you, that He through whom kings reign, and whom to serve is to reign, may preserve the temporal kingdom for you and your heirs and afterward grant you a kingdom that endures without end.

CCCLI. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—He consoles him when oppressed by difficulties. (At Clermont? June.)

[Ibid., p. 6.]

[Col. 0377A]

POPE ALEXANDER TO THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

Because the days are evil and much must be endured in accordance with the circumstances of the time, we ask, admonish, counsel, and urge your discretion that, in conducting all your own affairs and those of the Church, you show yourself cautious, prudent, and circumspect; that you do nothing hastily or precipitately, but act with deliberation and gravity; and that, so far as can be done without compromising [Col. 0377B] the liberty of the Church or the honor of your office, you strive and labor by every means to recover the favor and goodwill of the illustrious King of the English. And you are to wait upon the same king until the next Easter, making no attempt to act against him or his land before the stated time. For then the Lord will grant better times, and both you and we will be able to proceed more safely in the matter itself.

CCCLII. To the same.—He declares void the sentence pronounced against him by the bishops and barons of England. (At Clermont? June.)

[Ibid., p. 7.]

POPE ALEXANDER TO THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

Both divine and human laws show that an inferior cannot judge a superior, especially one to whom he is known to be subject by right of prelation and bound by the bond of obedience. This is declared still more clearly in the enactments of the holy Fathers. Accordingly, we, whose duty it is to correct errors and those things which, if left uncorrected, would leave a pernicious example to posterity, having weighed these matters with careful consideration, and also observing that the Church ought not to suffer any loss or detriment because of the offense of an individual, decree to be wholly void the sentence presumptuously pronounced against you by the bishops and barons of England because you did not present yourself at the king’s first summons. By that sentence the aforesaid bishops and barons deprived you of all your movable goods, contrary both to the form of law [Col. 0377D] and to ecclesiastical custom—especially since you had no movable goods except those belonging to your church. We annul it by apostolic authority, decreeing that henceforth it shall have no force and shall be unable in the future to inflict any prejudice or injury upon you, your successors, or the church entrusted to your governance.

CCCLIII. To the abbot of the monastery ***.—Concerning the dispute between E. and the priest A. (At Clermont, 9 June.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Coll.*, II, 715.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0378A] brother [Note: [Col. 0377] An error has crept in here through the copyist’s carelessness, for this letter is addressed to some abbot.] HENRY, Archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From your letters, son abbot, which the bearer of these presents brought us, we recently learned that, when a dispute was being heard in your presence between E. and the priest A. concerning a certain house which the same priest held as a pledge, the said priest, alleging no grievance, appealed to our hearing. Since the representative of the said E. was present before us on the appointed day for the appeal, but the aforesaid priest neither came nor sent anyone to us as his representative, we, having full confidence in your prudence, have—although this is contrary to our usual practice—referred the same case to your judgment for decision. For the aforesaid house is said to be held in fief from your church, son abbot, and the said priest, as we have noted, has in no way pursued his appeal.

We command your discretion by apostolic letters that, when you are asked concerning this matter, you summon both parties before you and, having heard and understood the arguments on both sides, duly bring the case to a conclusion, with the remedy of appeal set aside.

Given at Clermont, the fifth day before the Ides of June [9 June].

CCCLIV. Bull for the monastery of Mozac, received under the protection of the Apostolic See. (At Clermont, 15 June.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, *Instrumenta*, 111.]

[Col. 0378C] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of the monastery of Mozac, and to all the brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: J. N. [reading uncertain] . . . . .

To grant effect to just petitions is required by the vigor of equity and the order of reason, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wish and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and, following the example of our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Adrian, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means through the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to name the following in their proper terms:

The church of Gatteria; the church of Saint Hilary with its chapel; the church of Giaco; the church of Marencalmis; the church of Bortis; the church of Oenc with the parish of Faravel; the church of Rubiac-Royac with its appurtenances, namely the church of Castello and the chapel of Pont-Gibald; the church [Col. 0379A] of Saint Ursus; the church of Montibus with the chapel of Castro; the church of Saint Hippolytus; the church of Wulvico with the chapel of Saint Mary; the church of Martiac; the church of Monestrol; the church of Ceresio; the church of Sana-cultura; the church of Cella; the church of Aluchiis; the church of Saint Andrew of Pathas; the church of Saint Bonitus of Calmis; the church of Rocca-forti with the chapel of Castro; the church of Saint Bonitus of Mont-Pancherii with the chapels of Castro; the church of Bodonia; the church of Saint Germanus with the chapel of Castro; the church of Saint Remigius; the church of Sulec; the church of Crusec; the church of Laurigiis; the church of Cos; the church of Saint Desiderius; the church of Dreituraias with the church of Saint Prejectus and the chapel of Palicia; the chapel of Botiaco; the church of Saint Ambrose; the church of Mont-petrosus; the church of Saint Denis; the church of Saint Leontius near your monastery; the church of Saint Lawrence; the church of Saint Paul; the church of Saint Calmutius; and the church of Saint Martin, with their appurtenances; Primiliacum, Tauriniacum, Mabiliacum, Salziniam, Plunberiam, Amanziacum, and Mirabellum with the adjacent valley.

The lands held in fief from the lord of Crest and the lord of Rochafort in Lubartes; whatever you hold in the fiefs of the lord of Camaleria and the lord of Ponte; the lands held in fief from the lord of Caslucio, the lord of Turnolio, the lord of Tuirriaco, the lord of Monte-Gasconis, [Col. 0379C] the lord of Enaziaco, and the lord of Cabaziaco; and the lands held in fief from the lord of Monte-Pancerio, the lord of Scola, and the lord of the castle of Saint Germanus.

We likewise decree that no one may lawfully impose new and undue customs or exactions upon the same monastery or its churches. We also grant that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while the rights of the mother church remain preserved. Upon the death of you, abbot of the said place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be put in charge there through any artifice of intrusion or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, deprive it of its abbatial dignity, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the complete benefit of those uses for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If therefore any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, Bishop of Ostia. [Col. 0380A] I, Bernard, Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Walter, Bishop of Albano. I, Berald, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Otto, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Boso, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. [Col. 0380B] I, Cinthius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of Saint Eustace near the Temple of Agrippa. I, Manfred, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Clermont, by the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July [15 June], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1165 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### CCCLV. Bull by which the monastery of Saint Illidius and all its possessions are received under the protection of the Roman Church.  
(At Clermont, 15 June.)

*[Ibid., 102.]*

[Col. 0380C]

ALEXANDER, etc., to ARNALD, abbot of the monastery of Blessed Illidius, and to his brethren . . . . .

. . . Whenever a request is made to us which is recognized as consonant with religion and uprightness, it is fitting that we grant it with a willing mind and lend appropriate support to the desires of the petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just requests; and we receive the aforesaid monastery . . . . . under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we establish that the monastic order which is known to have been established in the same monastery according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and whatever goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, by the grant of pontiffs, the benefaction of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, God favouring it, acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.
