Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of Turiacum with its appurtenances; whatever you possess in the village of Grisolo; the church of Vicherium, with the chapels of the same castle and all its other appurtenances; the church of Chasannolas; the church of Belvezer; the church of Saint Peter of Chalmez; the church of Saint Felix; the church of Saint Illidius of Valencha; [Col. 0381A] the church of Neyracum; the church of Blanzacum; the church of Saint Bonitus; the church of Nebesac; the church of Agella; the church of Schevina; the church of Basvilla, with the appurtenances of those same places; the church of Saint Peter the Old; the church of Saint Cassius with its appurtenances.

[Note: [Col. 0381D] In the inventory of the possessions of the monastery of Illidius set forth in this bull, no mention is made of gifts conferred by Gerald the priest around the year 980. Concerning these, the following is read in an old authentic instrument: “One vineyard situated in the estate called Noals; [Col. 0382D] a field at Sedoc; one small plot at the spring of Salvamane; trellised vines at Medium-planetum; in the cultivated land of the estate of Pomerios, one vineyard called ‘at the Plaus.’”]

From the gift of Fulk of Jaliniacum: the lands and revenues of Pont Latgen, as far as Bellummons, and lordship in the village of Saint Ellidius. We also grant that the burial place of that locality shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have resolved to be buried there—unless they are excommunicated or under interdict—while preserving, nevertheless, the right of the parish churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

[Col. 0381B] Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the uses for which they were granted—namely, the governance and support of those concerned—saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, [Col. 0381C] any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. Eleven other cardinals subscribe.

Given at Clermont, by the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July [15 June], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1165 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### CCCLVI. To Louis, king of the Franks.—That the cantor of Saint Anianus had deservedly been deprived by the Apostolic See of his office and benefice.  
(At Clermont, 25 June.)

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 1021.]*

[Col. 0381D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has reached our hearing that it was represented to your magnificence that, relying on no reason, but from our own will and impulse of mind, we deprived our beloved son R., formerly cantor of the church of Blessed Anianus, of his cantorial office and benefice. Therefore we wish your royal magnificence to know with unquestionable certainty that we deposed the same R. from that honour by the strictness of justice and with the counsel [Col. 0382A] of all our brethren who were present, and not through any impulse of mind. Moved by the gentleness of piety and mercy in his case, we left him a prebend and the provostship in the same church of Blessed Anianus, and preserved the integrity of his reputation. We therefore ask your royal serenity not to press us, on any account, by your prayers for restoring that honour to him, nor to heed the prayers of others on this matter.

Given at Clermont, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July [25 June].

### CCCLVII. To Louis, king of the Franks.—He commends to him the archdeacon of Bourges; he bids him hope well concerning German affairs.  
(At Le Puy, 30 June.)

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 1007.]*

[Col. 0382B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have decided to send back to you our beloved son C., archdeacon of Bourges, your cleric, whom we have hitherto retained with us in reliance upon your royal serenity. Commending him earnestly to your excellence, we ask and admonish your magnificence by apostolic letters, for reverence toward Blessed Peter and ourselves, and in view of the devotion and fidelity which he has repeatedly shown toward [Col. 0382C] the royal highness, to resolve to cherish and support him and, in your customary clemency, to uphold him in his right.

Moreover, because we do not in the least doubt that you, as the Church’s dearest and special son, a Catholic prince and most Christian king, are anxious and zealous for the state of the Church and for our own, and that you have conceived some sorrow over those recent reports which have come from Germany, we ask and admonish your greatness that, strengthened by the Lord, you may hope and trust fully that the things which that persecutor of the Church—who has always sought a feigned peace with her—believes will happen against her and to her detriment will undoubtedly recoil to his own shame and confusion. For, as we have received for certain, and as our beloved son the elect of Mainz can more fully make known to your serenity, he was able to compel no more than three men in all his territory to render an unconditional oath. Many others indeed departed without his permission, and those who swore conditionally have now been released from the condition imposed. The aforesaid archdeacon will explain the rest more fully to your highness in person.

Given at Le Puy, on the second day before the Kalends of July [30 June].

### CCCLVIII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—For the priest Ralph, that his church may be restored to him.  
(At Alès, 5 July.)

*[MARTÈNE, Amplified Collection, II, 716.]*

[Col. 0383A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When we were formerly present at Sens, moved by the importunity of the priest Ralph, bearer of these letters, we remember having directed our venerable brother, the bishop of Châlons, that unless Ralph should be assiduous in the church entrusted to him, he should take the said church from him and ordain another priest in it. But the bishop, as Ralph says, considering no other cause, [Col. 0383B] took the church from him and installed a priest in it; and, what is grievous, bound him under sentence of excommunication, forbidding all persons of the deanery of Vertus, under threat of anathema, to receive him for more than one night in the land of his birth, but ordering them to avoid him as excommunicated.

Yet, wearied by him, we gave this direction to the said bishop only to instil fear in Ralph; nor did it enter our mind that, if he wished to maintain regular attendance in the church, he should on the occasion of our mandate be thus despoiled. We therefore direct your brotherhood by apostolic letters to endeavour to meet with the aforesaid bishop on our behalf and yours, and carefully admonish him to restore to the aforesaid priest [Col. 0383C] his church in its entirety, without delay; and, if he is not charged with any notorious crime by which he can lawfully be convicted, to declare publicly that he is absolved and cause all persons of that parish to regard him as absolved.

But if he should perhaps refuse to do this in obedience to our mandate and your admonition, you shall diligently investigate the truth of the matter; and if you find that the said priest was excommunicated without another manifest and reasonable cause, you shall absolve him and cause the church to be restored to him without delay. Moreover, we will and command that you permit no undue annoyance or burden to be imposed upon him in this matter by the dean of Vertus or by Warin of Aulnoy.

Given at Alès, on the third day before the Nones of July [5 July].

### CCCLIX. To Clerembald, elect and monk of Saint Augustine.—That, all appeal being set aside, he make profession to the Church of Canterbury.  
(At Montpellier, 10 July.)

*[Letters of Saint Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 109.]*

[Col. 0383D]

POPE ALEXANDER to CLEREMBALD, elect and monk of Saint Augustine.

Following the footsteps of our predecessors of pious memory, Anastasius and Adrian, Roman pontiffs, as we recall having commanded you, beloved son-elect, by apostolic letters, so we command your discretion again: all appeal being set aside, make profession to our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, [Col. 0384A] and to his church, as your predecessors are known to have done. This shall be so arranged that, should you or your successors at any time afterwards wish to raise a question of right against the Church of Canterbury, no future prejudice shall thereby arise to you or to your church, nor shall any new or undue burden be imposed upon a person or church on the occasion of this profession.

Given at Montpellier, on the sixth day before the Ides of July [10 July].

### CCCLX. To princes, counts, barons, and all the faithful of God.—Concerning the dispatch of aid to the East against the Saracens.  
(At Montpellier, 14 July.)

*[RYMER, Foedera, I, 21.]*

[Col. 0384B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, princes, counts, barons, and all the faithful of God to whom these letters shall come: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the accounts of the ancients and from what we find written in their deeds, we have learned how greatly our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, laboured for the liberation of the Eastern Church.

For our predecessor Pope Urban of blessed memory sounded forth like a trumpet from heaven and took care to summon the sons of the holy Roman Church from diverse parts of the world for its liberation. At his call, countless faithful of Christ, kindled by the ardour of charity, gathered together; having assembled a mighty army, and not without a great shedding of their own blood, with divine aid accompanying them, they delivered from the filth of the pagans that city in which our Saviour chose to suffer for us, and where he left us his glorious sepulchre as a memorial of his passion, and many other places which, to avoid prolixity, we refrain from recounting.

These places, through the grace of God and the effort of our fathers, who at intervals of time exerted themselves to defend them and to spread the Christian name in those regions insofar as they could, remained in Christian possession until our own time; and other cities of the unbelievers [Col. 0384D] were bravely captured by them. But in past times, as the sins of that people required—something which we cannot speak of without great grief and lamentation—the city of Edessa, called Roas in our language, which, as is reported, had served the Lord alone under Christian rule when all the land in the East was formerly held by pagans, was captured by the enemies of Christ’s cross. Many Christian castles were occupied by them; the archbishop of that city with his clerics, and many other Christians, were killed there; and the relics of the saints were abandoned to the trampling of the unbelievers and scattered.

For the recovery of this city, our father and predecessor, Pope Eugenius of holy memory, sent letters of exhortation to diverse parts of the world. At his exhortation, an innumerable multitude of people went to those regions, but, by some hidden judgment of God which we do not know, they accomplished absolutely nothing; the same city remained under the dominion and power of those same enemies of Christ.

Now, however, in our own times the ferocity of the pagans has grown so strong that these Saracens rage cruelly up to the very gates of Antioch. Indeed, the prince of that city, after many noble and valiant men had been captured and killed, has fallen into their power and is still held captive under their control. It is also feared by many that the city of Antioch itself, and even the city of Jerusalem, [Col. 0385B] in which is the most holy sepulchre of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, which you yourselves so often visit with most faithful devotion, may fall into their hands, and that the holy place, most devoutly to be venerated by Christ’s faithful, may be defiled by their filth.

Therefore, since it is better to meet a coming disease vigilantly than, after it has seized the body, to seek medicine and discover a remedy, we ask, admonish, and command you all by apostolic letters, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of sins: let those who belong to the Lord, especially the more powerful and noble, gird themselves manfully. Endeavour so to confront the multitude of unbelievers, who rejoice that they have obtained the time of victory over [Col. 0385C] us; so to defend the Eastern Church, liberated from their tyranny, as we have said, by so great a shedding of our fathers’ blood; and so to rescue from their hands many thousands of captives, our brethren, that the dignity of the Christian name may increase in our time and that your valour, praised throughout the world, may be preserved whole and unblemished.

Let that good Mattathias also be an example to us. To preserve the laws of his fathers, he did not hesitate to expose himself together with his sons and his kinsmen to death, and to leave behind all that he possessed in the world. At length, however, with divine assistance cooperating, he and his descendants alike triumphed manfully over their enemies, though through many sufferings.

Moreover, in fatherly concern for your security and for the distressed state of the same Church, we grant and confirm, by the authority given us by God, to those who have resolved to undertake and complete so holy and necessary a work and labour out of devotion, that remission of sins which our aforesaid predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Urban and Eugenius, established. We decree that their wives and children, likewise their goods and possessions, shall remain under the protection of the holy Church, of ourselves, and of the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of God’s Church.

By apostolic authority we also forbid any question henceforth to be raised concerning anything which those who have taken the cross have possessed peacefully, [Col. 0386A] until their return or death is known with certainty.

Furthermore, because those who wage war for the Lord ought by no means to occupy themselves with costly garments, personal adornment, dogs, hawks, or other things which display frivolity, we admonish your prudence in the Lord that those who have resolved to begin so holy a work shall in no way concern themselves with variegated or grey furs, or with arms of gold or silver; but shall devote all their zeal and diligence to such arms, horses, and other things by which they may more forcefully defeat the unbelievers.

Whoever is burdened by another’s money and begins so holy a work with a pure heart shall not pay interest already due. But if they themselves, or others on their account, are bound by oath or pledge for interest, we release them by apostolic authority.

It shall also be lawful for them, after their kinsmen or lords to whose fief they belong have been notified, whether those kinsmen or lords are willing or unwilling, freely and without any objection to pledge their lands or other possessions as security for money to churches, ecclesiastical persons, or other faithful persons.

By the authority given us by God, of almighty God, and of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we grant remission and absolution of sins in accordance with the enactment of the same our predecessors, on these terms: whoever devoutly begins and completes so holy a journey, or dies there, shall obtain absolution from all sins of which, with a contrite and humble heart, [Col. 0386C] he has made confession, and shall receive the fruit of eternal recompense from the rewarder of all good things.

Given at Montpellier, on the second day before the Ides of July [14 July].

### CCCLXI. Bull addressed to Peter, abbot of Bonnefont.  
(At Montpellier, 21 July.)

*[Gallia Christiana, new ed., I, Instruments, 180.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot of the monastery of Bonnefont, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life in the aforesaid monastery.

The office of the government we have undertaken invites us to assent to religious vows and fulfil them by effective action, [Col. 0386D] and the order of reason appears to require it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions and receive under the firm protection of Blessed Peter the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we establish that the monastic order known to have been instituted in your monastery according to the fear of God, the Rule of Blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall be observed there inviolably for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and whatever goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, through grants of pontiffs, benefactions of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, the Lord granting it, acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to state the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the abbey is situated, from the oak of Genitheus to the stream of Manirera, from Agunta of Silveyra to the summit of Mount Saint Canius, as the straight line goes to Exarlobin; the whole place of Exarlobin; the abbey of Bolbona with its granges and all its appurtenances; the abbey of Charité, called Foleus, with its granges and all its appurtenances; the abbey of Campania with its granges and all its appurtenances; the land of Bofartigua; all the land of Cugurra, Silva, Silveyra, Medas, Grah, Morters, Osan, Saint [Col. 0387B] Mary, and Seih; the church of Seih with all its appurtenances; the place of Labbatut; all the land of Marera; the place of Sol; Aldemar of Castaus; all the land of Gotald Cuguravel; all the land of Ruera; the house of Arnald Bonag of Casanova, of Ardinag, of Rochan, and of Villanova; the land of Luha; the land of Roger of Senadors, of Cassanha-Bella; the grange of Nodas with its appurtenances; the land of Sedni; the granges of Canet, Carbona, Riulan, Laisla, Querelag, Borgal, Rua, and Saint Lawrence, with all their appurtenances; the grange of Bonemayso, of Minag; the whole land of the other Minag with all its appurtenances; the whole land of Quint with all its appurtenances; the house of the count of Comminges at Salvetat of Saint [Col. 0387C] Giles; the grange of Las with all its appurtenances; the whole land of Spinaira; the hamlet of Sagara with all its appurtenances; Boseus with all its appurtenances; the hospital of Boseus with all its appurtenances; Pentengens with all its appurtenances; the grange of Saint Faith with all its appurtenances; the summer pasture of Semestra with all its dependencies; that of Rivo Majori with all its dependencies; the gift of the pastures of Enard, count of Comminges; [the grant] of the *punctis* [meaning uncertain] of Galarda his wife, Bernard of Turre, Bernard of Montald, Raymond William of Beura, and his brothers; and your cultivated lands, whether worked by your own hands or at your own expense, and the sustenance of your animals, from which no one shall presume to demand tithes or first-fruits from you.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone to dare to receive or retain, without your permission, any of your brethren, clerk or layman, after he has made profession in your monastery. Providing in fatherly concern also for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone, within the enclosure of your places or granges, to commit violence, robbery, or theft, or to exact a levy.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things [Col. 0388A] be preserved whole and be of every benefit for the uses for which they were granted—namely, the governance and support of those concerned—saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Eguillin, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Arnald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina. [Col. 0388B] I, Walter, bishop of Albano. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Boso, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Cynthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Raymond, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

Given at Montpellier, by the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and [Col. 0388C] notary of the holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August [21 July], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1164 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III. With the seal of the said lord pope.

### CCCLXII. He receives the monastery of Saint Daniel of Venice under the protection of Blessed Peter, confirms its goods, and grants it other privileges.  
(At Montpellier, 27 July.)

*[CORNELIUS, The Church of Venice, IV, 189.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ARNOLD, prior of the monastery of Saint Daniel of Venice, and his brethren to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

A pious petition should be fulfilled by an effective result, [Col. 0388D] so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth worthily and the requested benefit may undoubtedly take effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, which belongs especially to the right of the monastery of Fructuaria and in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We establish that whatever possessions and whatever goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, through grants of pontiffs, benefactions of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, the Lord granting it, acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

[Col. 0389A] Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the church of Saint Blaise of Canale, with all its appurtenances, in tithes as well as other matters; the chapel of Saint Agatha, with all the possessions of the people of Rimano which you possess; whatever you possess in the bishoprics of Treviso and Padua; whatever you possess in Paralacto or in the estate of Danorius in the bishopric of Ferrara. Nor shall anyone, after having made profession in your monastery, be permitted to leave the cloister without his prior’s permission; and no one shall dare to retain a person who has departed without letters of authorization from the community.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, [Col. 0389B] or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the uses for which they were granted—namely, the governance and support of those concerned—saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubalbus, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. [Col. 0389C] I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Cynthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius by the temple of Agrippa. I, Manfred, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Raymond, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Montpellier, by the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August [27 July], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1165 [Col. 0389D] of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### CCCLXIII. He directs the bishops of Rodez and Cahors to decide the dispute between [William], bishop, and the canons of Albi, and the monks of Aurillac.  
(At Montpellier, 1 August.)

*[BALUZE, Miscellanies, ed. Luc., III, 20.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the bishops of Rodez and Cahors: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We commit to your discretion, in which we have full confidence, for hearing and for due settlement, with the obstacle of appeal removed, the case known to be in litigation between our venerable brother the bishop and the canons of Albi, on the one hand, and the monks of Aurillac, on the other, concerning the church of Viancius and certain [Col. 0390A] other churches, as well as certain other complaints which they bring against one another. Therefore we direct your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when you are requested to do so, you summon both parties before your presence and, after fully hearing and ascertaining the arguments on both sides, decide the same case by means of justice, without recourse to appeal.

Given at Montpellier, on the Kalends of August [1 August].

### CCCLXIV. He informs the monks of Aurillac of the preceding letter.  
(At Montpellier, 1 August.)

*[Ibid.]*

[Col. 0390B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the monks of Aurillac: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have committed for hearing, and for due settlement with appeal removed, to our venerable brethren the bishops of Rodez and Cahors, the case known to be in litigation between you and our venerable brother the bishop and the canons of Albi, concerning the church of Viancius and certain other churches, as well as certain other complaints which they bring against you. Therefore we command you by apostolic letters that, when summoned by them in this matter, you appear before them [Col. 0390C] and, without appeal, firmly accept and observe whatever they shall adjudge between you concerning it.

Given at Montpellier, on the Kalends of August [1 August].

### CCCLXV. To Gislebert of Cîteaux and the rest of that order.—He confirms their institutions and adorns them with privileges.  
(At Montpellier, 5 August.)

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 959.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GISLEBERT of Cîteaux, and the other abbots and monks, present and future, professing in perpetuity the regular life and institutions of the Cistercian order.

The most holy Roman Church, just as in Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, she received from the Lord the promise that she should be the foundation of the universal Church, and received the command to strengthen the professors of Christian faith in faith, religion, and every sanctity, has likewise always shown herself solicitous for the advancement of all Churches. At every time she has zealously promoted the establishment, preservation, and furtherance in all Churches of the worship of holy religion, so that religion has flowed from her as from a fountain to all the children of the Church, and what has been religiously and beneficially instituted by others who received the first fruits of the Spirit has received through her the firmness of immutability.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by the renown of your holy religious observance, like that of a field which the Lord has blessed, we confirm by apostolic authority your religious petitions. We have decreed that these be expressed under the definite chapters appended below:

First, that in all your monasteries, as in the church of Cîteaux, the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be observed for all time; and that no member of your order shall introduce into its reading any interpretation beyond the simple and common understanding. Rather, all things shall be understood uniformly, as each is known to have been defined, and shall be observed inviolably. The same observances in every respect, the same chant, and the same books belonging to the ecclesiastical office shall be maintained throughout all the churches of your order. No church or person of your order shall dare to seek, or in any fashion retain if obtained, any privilege contrary to the common institutions [Col. 0391B] of that order.

Next, no one of your churches shall impose upon the church which gave it birth any exaction of earthly advantage or temporal goods; it shall plan no action against it which burdens it or diminishes its substance, lest, while wishing to abound at another’s poverty, it should be unable to avoid the evil of avarice, which, according to the Apostle, is proved to be the service of idols (Galatians V). Nevertheless, the abbot of the mother church shall retain the care of souls in it in the grace of charity, so that, if it should ever attempt—may this never happen—to depart from its holy purpose and from observance of the holy Rule, it may by his care return to the rightness of life.

[Col. 0391C] Likewise, all abbots of your order shall come every year to the general chapter at Cîteaux, every excuse being set aside, except only those whom bodily illness has prevented from undertaking the labour of the journey. They must nevertheless appoint a suitable messenger through whom the cause of their delay may be reported to the chapter. Also excepted are those living in more remote regions who cannot present themselves at the chapter every year without great and evident difficulty; these must come at whatever time the chapter itself shall prescribe for them.

If any controversy arises between certain abbots of your order, or if a charge against any one of them is so grave as to merit suspension or even deposition, whatever the chapter shall determine in this regard according to your order shall be observed without any reconsideration. But if, owing to diversity of opinions, the case comes into discord, the determination of the abbot of Cîteaux for the time being, together with those who appear of sounder counsel and more suitable, shall be observed without challenge.

I ask this: none of those to whom the case particularly pertains may be present at the determination. But if an abbot, because of his own incapacity or faint-heartedness, sees that he ought to be released from the office of his abbey, he shall humbly ask to be released by the abbot of the house from which his own proceeded. That abbot, however, shall not lightly accede to the request or accomplish anything by his own authority; rather, after gathering several abbots of your order, [Col. 0392A] he shall act with their counsel as they jointly judge ought to be done.

If any abbot of the Order appears contemptuous of the Order, or a transgressor against it, or consenting to the vices of the brethren committed to him, let the abbot of the mother church, either in person or through his prior, or in whatever way he knows better to be expedient, admonish him to amend, up to four times. But if he should perhaps refuse to correct his fault or to resign the office of governance which he has undertaken, let a number of abbots of your Order be assembled in the name of the Lord; and, after consultation, if they judge it expedient, let them remove him from the government of the abbey. Thereafter another worthy man shall be elected by the monks of that house, with the abbots, if any belong to it, by the counsel and will of the father abbot. [Col. 0392B] But if the man deposed, or his monks, should resolve stubbornly to resist the sentence pronounced against him, the abbot of the mother church and the other abbots shall have full power to constrain them by the censure of ecclesiastical discipline. If any of these, however, returning to himself and repenting of his obstinacy, humbly seeks the mercy of his mother, let him be received as a repentant son.

So long as any one of your churches is deprived of its own abbot, the father abbot, from whose house that house proceeded, shall have the entire responsibility for ordering that house, until another abbot is elected there. The man elected, however, is not to be handed over as emancipated or, as it were, released, to any archbishop or bishop. [Col. 0392C] Nor, after making his profession to his own archbishop or bishop, shall he on that account transgress the constitutions of his Order or become in any respect a transgressor against it.

Moreover, should the abbots of your Order perceive that your mother church of Cîteaux has departed from the observance of holy religious life, let them admonish the abbot of that place through the first four abbots—of La Ferté, Pontigny, Clairvaux, and Morimond—to amend and to labour for the amendment of his subjects. Let them carry out with respect to him everything we have said above concerning other abbots, except that, if he does not freely resign, they may neither depose him nor, if he appears contumacious, bind him with a sentence of excommunication, until either in a general chapter [Col. 0392D] or, if it seems that this cannot be awaited without grave danger, after summoning the abbots who proceeded from Cîteaux and also some others, they remove the unsuitable man from the office of abbot; and let both they and the abbots and monks of Cîteaux endeavour to substitute for him another suitable abbot. Against the man who has been deposed, moreover, and his monks, if they presume to rebel, let them not hesitate to pronounce a sentence of ecclesiastical severity. If afterwards any one of them, acknowledging the fault of his obstinacy, withdraws for the sake of salvation to one of the four aforesaid churches, let him be received as one of the household, until he is restored to his own church as may be fitting. In the meantime, the annual assembly of abbots shall be held not at Cîteaux but wherever [Col. 0393A] the four aforesaid abbots shall determine.

Since the church of Cîteaux is the mother of you all and has no other father abbot over it, let an annual visitation there be conducted by those same abbots, as you have established for the safeguarding and preservation of the Order; and, at their recommendation, let whatever is found in need of correction be corrected according to your Order. Moreover, whenever the house of Cîteaux lacks its own abbot, its care shall belong to those four; and a suitable person shall be elected by them and by the other abbots belonging to Cîteaux, who have been summoned for at least fifteen days, together with the monks of Cîteaux.

Let it be lawful for every mother church of your Order [Col. 0393B] to choose as its abbot whomever it wishes, provided he is worthy, whether from among its monks or from the abbots themselves of churches known to have proceeded from it. But let none of your churches choose for itself as pastor a person from another Order, just as no member of your Order is to be appointed abbot of a monastery of another Order.

We have therefore extracted these provisions from among the many institutions of your Order and have taken care to set them out under their own chapters. We add that no bishop shall permit any religious or secular dwelling to be built over or adjacent to your abbeys or granges from which disturbance may arise for you; rather, let bishops in whose dioceses such persons are situated prohibit, under threat of anathema, those who attempt such building from doing it. [Col. 0393C] Nor shall anyone receive your professed monks or lay brothers (*conversi*) without permission from their abbots, or dare to retain them after receiving them. Since, indeed, not every particular provision which you have regularly ordained for the advancement of religious life and the salvation of souls could be appended to the present abridgment, together with what has been prescribed above we confirm by apostolic authority everything contained in your charter called the Charter of Charity, and whatever you have regularly established among yourselves for the sake of religious observance. We decree that these things are to be observed inviolate in perpetuity by you and your successors and by all who have professed your Order. Furthermore, since you firmly intend to choose places for your dwellings apart from secular society, we decree that your granges, like your churches, shall be free and undisturbed from the assaults and violence of evil men; and, by the power of the Holy Spirit, we forbid anyone there to presume to seize, despoil, beat, or rob a person. We further enact that, because of general territorial interdicts, none of your churches shall be compelled to abstain from the divine offices. Again, we forbid absolutely any person to dare to summon brethren of your Order before secular courts. Rather, whoever believes that he has a legal claim against them shall have the right to pursue it under examination by an ecclesiastical judge, without prejudice in all things to the authority of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0394A] Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to violate your aforesaid institutions. If anyone should presume to attempt this, and, after a second or third warning, fails to make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to stern vengeance. But upon those who observe these things may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

CCCLXVI. To Pons, Archbishop of Narbonne, and [William], Bishop of Béziers.—He orders them not to permit Fons Calidus to be taken from the church of Valcrose. (At Montpellier, August 6.)

[HUGO, *Annals of Prémontré*, I, Preface, 566.]

[Col. 0394B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers PONS, Archbishop of Narbonne, and the Bishop of Béziers, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have recently received the complaints of our beloved prior of Valcrose: Bernard and William of Capulis, Berengar also of Nicianum, and Bernard of Durafort, laymen, at the instigation of certain clerics, D. B. and Stephen of Cornelianum, and likewise Arnald [Col. 0394C] and Pons Maurelian, lay brothers, presume to take away from his church a certain estate and place called Fons-Calidus [Hot Spring] [lacuna]. Hence, since we are debtors in justice to all the faithful of God and especially to religious men, we command your brotherhood by these present letters to take care diligently to warn and summon the aforesaid men, so that they may promptly surrender the said estate and place to the aforementioned prior and his church, or undertake, in your presence and without appeal, to make them adequate compensation and indemnity for it. If they neglect to carry either of these alternatives into effect, strike them and their principal supporters with a sentence of excommunication until they make fitting satisfaction.

[Col. 0394D] Given at Montpellier, the eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August].

CCCLXVII. To Louis, King of the Franks.—That he should grant Thomas, while in exile, a bishopric or abbey if one becomes vacant. (At Montpellier, August 6.)

[Letters of St Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 113.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your highness knows well how our venerable brother in Christ Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, has resolved, for the defence of the liberty of the Church and out of devotion to us, to endure exile from his own see [Col. 0395A] rather than consent in any way to our detriment and the loss of the Church; and also to what necessities he, together with the other prudent and discerning men who imitate him so praiseworthily and faithfully even in adversity, must come if the persecution should last long—which God forbid. Therefore, although we know that your royal majesty is always so intent upon works of mercy that, even without our entreaties, prompted by mercy alone, you grant aid and consolation to those suffering persecution for God, justice, and Catholic unity—as we have especially experienced in the case of this our brother—we nevertheless earnestly beseech, admonish, and exhort your royal majesty in the Lord [Col. 0395B] that, for the sake of divine mercy and out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, and considering also that, once peace has been restored by God to us and to him, much service and honour may accrue to your highness through him, if any bishopric or abbey in your realm should in the meantime become vacant, royal generosity should assign it to him for the support of himself and his companions, until the peace we desire is granted to us from heaven. For by this act we firmly believe that you will have God favourable to you, and that we ourselves shall be greatly indebted to you.

Given at Montpellier, the eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August].

CCCLXVIII. To John, Bishop, and the Canons of Maguelonne.—They are to restore to the prior of St Mary the altar and offerings of the church of St Saviour, formerly granted by Adrian IV to Lord William and the people of Montpellier in order to support the church. (At Montpellier, August 8.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 342.]

[Col. 0395C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JOHN, bishop, and his beloved sons the canons of Maguelonne, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we have learned from the letters of our predecessor Adrian of blessed memory, that predecessor granted to our beloved sons, the nobleman William and the people of Montpellier, the offerings of the altar of St Saviour, to be held for five years in order to support the church, [Col. 0395D] on this condition: once that period had elapsed, the altar itself and its offerings were to return, without anyone’s objection, into the hands of our beloved son, the prior of the church of St Mary. But because, although the prescribed term has long since elapsed, those men are said still to retain that altar and its offerings, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, in accordance with the ordinance of our aforesaid predecessor, you cause both the said altar and the offerings to be restored, with every pretext and excuse set aside, into the hands and power of the aforesaid prior—unless perhaps they are able to retain them with his assent and consent.

[Col. 0396A] Given at Montpellier, the sixth day before the Ides of August [8 August], in the fourth year of our pontificate.  
[Note: [Col. 0395] This pontifical dating clause is unusual and erroneous.]

CCCLXIX. To Louis, King of the Franks.—He commends William, bishop-elect of Chartres, to the king; he exhorts him to remain steadfast in defending the cause of the Church against Emperor Frederick. (At Montpellier, August 19.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1018.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When our beloved son W., bishop-elect of Chartres, came into our presence, we received him with paternal kindness, both for the sake of your majesty [Col. 0396B] and in consideration of all his kinship, as well as in view of his honour and integrity. While he was with us, we treated him, as was fitting, honourably and kindly, and readily took care to grant his requests. Therefore, as we send him back to his own country with the fullness of our affection and favour, and commend him most earnestly to your royal highness—although this may in some sense appear superfluous—we ask, admonish, and earnestly exhort your serenity by apostolic letters that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, and in view of his nobility and devotion, you undertake to love, support, and honour him more earnestly, and to sustain him in his right and in the church entrusted to him. Thus may he show himself ever more devoted [Col. 0396C] and faithful toward your royal majesty, and may we likewise be bound to render your highness abundant thanks for this.

In addition, we ask and admonish your highness in the Lord that you strive to uphold and defend vigorously the cause of the Church, which you have undertaken to protect as your own; and that you steadily devote effort and diligence to the exaltation and advancement of the Church, as you are known hitherto to have done with magnanimity, and work toward this by every means as a most Christian king and magnificent prince. Let no commands of the said Emperor F. move you for any reason or disturb you on any pretext. Trust in the Lord and in the power of his might: he will shortly restore peace and tranquillity to his Church, [Col. 0396D] and you, together with the other faithful of the Church, will enjoy the joy of immeasurable gladness.

Given at Montpellier, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September [19 August].

CCCLXX. He confirms the inheritance of Guinard, Count of Roussillon. (At Montpellier, August 19.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1061.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman G., Count of Roussillon, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0397A] The more noble and illustrious persons subject themselves to blessed Peter and to us with greater devotion, the more closely the Roman Church customarily loves them with affection and more earnestly sustains them in their rights and honours. Accordingly, moved by your devotion and by the prayers of your beloved uncle, the nobleman Trencavel, we confirm by apostolic authority, and secure by the protection of this present writing, the land which belongs to you by hereditary right, no claim having been made against you by the adulteress or her son. We decree that no man or woman may ever take your paternal inheritance from you against justice or unlawfully disturb you in its possession. Should anyone rashly presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles, blessed Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0397B] Given at Montpellier, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September [19 August].

CCCLXXI. To Pons of Narbonne and Hugh of Tarragona, archbishops, and [Artald] of Elne and the bishops of Girona.—He orders them not to permit the inheritance of Guinard, Count of Roussillon, to be invaded by his illegitimate brothers. (At Montpellier, August 19.)

[Ibid., col. 1062.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers PONS of Narbonne and HUGH of Tarragona, archbishops, and likewise to the bishops of Elne and Girona, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0397C] It has been represented to us and shown by an apparently reliable report that the father of the nobleman G., Count of Roussillon, having dismissed his lawful wife, joined another to himself in adultery. Hence both he and his adulteress deserved to be bound by the chains of anathema; and, as we believe, our predecessor Pope Eugenius of blessed memory forbade the sons born of the adulteress to succeed to their father’s inheritance. Furthermore, since according to the provisions of law the son is he whom lawful marriage establishes, while he who is born of adultery is called not a son but a bastard, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters strictly to forbid [Col. 0397D] those men from claiming anything from the aforesaid inheritance by right of succession, and the adulteress from claiming anything from it on the ground of a marriage-gift; and you are in no way to permit this to be done. If anyone should presume to inflict injury or molestation upon the same G. in this matter, then, when a complaint concerning it comes before you, render him due and complete justice.

Given at Montpellier, the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September [14 August].

CCCLXXII. To Gilbert, Bishop of London.—He orders him to continue admonishing Henry, King of England, to show devotion to the Roman Church, defend its rights, and receive Thomas of Canterbury into favour and grace. (At Gradus Mercurii, August 22.)

[Letters of St Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 99.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0398A] brother GILBERT, Bishop of London, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because you have devoted effective effort and diligence to the matters we entrusted to your brotherhood, and have taken care faithfully to urge and admonish our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King of the English, concerning the advancement and exaltation of the Church and of ourselves, we regard this as altogether pleasing and welcome. We give you most abundant thanks for it, and commend the prudence of your solicitude with splendid praise in the Lord. Since, however, we love that same king as a most dear son and renowned prince with a closer affection, we have often and repeatedly judged it right to urge him, through you and through our venerable brothers the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Hereford, [Col. 0398B] as well as through our dearest daughter in Christ, the illustrious former Empress of the Romans, his mother, and to invite him by many exhortations to devotion toward the Church. We rejoice and exult in the Lord over the devotion of the same king which you have communicated to us in your letters.

Nevertheless, since we wish him to be devoted to the Church of God and to us as he has been accustomed to be from the beginning, we ask, admonish, and command your brotherhood diligently and often—again and again—to warn him, through yourself and others, to exhort him by every means, and, as is fitting, to induce him to direct his efforts in the customary manner toward the honour and exaltation of that Church; vigorously to foster, uphold, and defend its cause; to love and honour churches and ecclesiastical persons and preserve their rights; and to restore our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Canterbury, to his affection and favour. [Col. 0398C] For if he shows to blessed Peter in us the reverence and honour which he has begun to show, we shall love him with fervent affection and shall devote ourselves in every respect, as he may direct, to his honour and exaltation and to the preservation of the kingdom entrusted to him. For we would rather overcome him through patience and gentleness than burden him in any way, so long as we can endure this.

Furthermore, we ask your integrity that, once you have collected in full St Peter’s penny, to which we wish you to devote effort and diligence, as we have indicated to you in other letters, you should strive to send it with all speed by a trustworthy messenger to our beloved son, the abbot of St Bertin; and that you notify us of this as soon as you can.

Given at Gradus Mercurii, the eleventh day before the Kalends of September [22 August].

CCCLXXIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—Concerning the lord pope: how he escaped by sea from the hands of those lying in wait, who were preparing to seize his possessions, himself, and his companions. (At Maguelonne, September 10.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 718.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0399A] brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Considering the fervour of your devotion and the sincerity of faith which you have diligently displayed toward the Roman Church and our person from the beginning of the schism, we have judged it fitting to inform your discretion of the condition of the Church and of our person—matters about which we in no way doubt that your prudence is concerned. Therefore, we have taken care to relate in order to your affection the things that happened to us before we set out on our journey toward Rome, lest, reported by an unfavourable account, they should unsettle or disturb your mind.

[Note: [Col. 0399D] Concerning Pope Alexander’s return to Rome and the ambushes prepared for him on the journey, Nicholas Trivet writes as follows in his *Chronicle* under the year 1165: “Pope Alexander, leaving Sens, where he had already spent two years, made his way to Montpellier; from there he proceeded by sea to the land of William, King of Sicily, nor did the emperor’s pirates fail to lay ambushes for him even at sea.”]

Know, then, that about the octave of the Assumption of blessed Mary we made every preparation for returning to Rome. When we had already [Col. 0399B] sent ahead of us in a certain ship, as was expedient, our venerable brother the Bishop of Albano and our beloved sons the cardinals Jac., Odo, and W. Jan., we came at the suitable time, with our remaining brethren in two galleys, to the ship of the Hospital in which we intended to cross. Nearly all the cardinals, together with their households and their possessions and ours, had by our command taken refuge in that ship; and we ourselves likewise wished first to embark in it with them. Suddenly, a multitude of Pisan galleys appeared close by. Fearing their attack, we returned safe and unharmed to Maguelonne, whence we had come, with the Archbishop-elect of Mainz and two of our brethren, John of Naples and P., cardinals, and only two servants, who happened to have remained with us in those same galleys.

[Note: [Col. 0399D] Conrad, brother of Otto, Count Palatine of Wittelsbach, a kinsman of Emperor Frederick, whom Alberic praises as an honourable and magnanimous man, always remained attached to Pope Alexander, who made him cardinal.]

[Col. 0399C] The aforesaid ship, however, with our brethren and possessions, made its way safely and without any loss or injury to its intended destination, as we had previously understood from the same Pisans; and we are ready shortly, with the Lord’s help, to follow it. The same companions in the Pisan galleys subsequently declared before us, with many protestations, that they had had no wish to harm our person or any plan to attack our possessions. Take courage, therefore, in the Lord. Do not fear that from this any loss or injury will come to us or to the Church, except for a very brief delay; and let your discretion take care, with diligent concern, to report this matter exactly as it occurred to all your fellow bishops and neighbouring persons and princes whom you know ought to be informed.

Given at Maguelonne, the fourth day before the Ides of September [10 September].

CCCLXXIV. He confirms for Roger, Archbishop of Reggio, and his successors the use of the pallium, already granted by Gregory VII and Eugenius III, and the right of consecrating his suffragan bishops, both Greek and Latin. He confirms the privileges granted to the Church of Reggio by emperors and kings, and decrees that the churches of Gerace, Squillace, Tropea, Nicastro, Bova, Oppido, and Crotone shall henceforth be suffragans of the Church of Reggio and subject to the Apostolic See.—“Given at Gaeta, in the year 1165, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December [19 November].”

[Note: [Col. 0400D] The *Diptychs* of the Church of Reggio mention this privilege. The original, along with its other records and the church itself, was burned by the most impious Turks.]

(UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IX, 235.)

[Col. 0400A]

CCCLXXV. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—Concerning the reception of the lord pope in Rome and a certain woman C. (At the Lateran, November 24.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 719.]

[Col. 0400B] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The manner in which you have remained always firm and steadfast in devotion to blessed Peter and to us, and have taken care to render us no small honour and reverence and abundant services, shall never fade from the memory of ourselves or our successors. Keeping this always before our eyes, we have a firm purpose and ready will to love you, as our dearest brother and an immovable pillar of the Church, with closer affection in the Lord, and to seek with more fervent desire your honour and advancement and that of the church entrusted to you.

[Col. 0400C] Since we know that you greatly rejoice and congratulate us in the prosperity of the Church and of ourselves, learn from this notification that, escaping through divine power and the merits of the apostles the various perils of the sea and the grave attacks of enemies and wicked men, we have at last reached the harbour of safety. Invited most devotedly by the senators and people of Rome, we entered the City on the ninth day before the Kalends of December [23 November], were received with complete peace and tranquillity, and were shown by the aforesaid senators, the nobles of the city, the clergy, and the Roman people such reverence, honour, and devotion toward ourselves and our brethren as, according to the testimony of every tongue, none greater is proved to have been shown to any of our predecessors.

[Note: [Col. 0400D] Alexander’s return to Rome occurred in 1165, as may be seen in Baronius and other authors.]

We therefore believe and hope in the mercy of Christ [Col. 0400D] that the Church of God will enjoy complete peace and the prosperity it desires. We ask and admonish your prudence, therefore, that, strengthened with magnanimity in the fervour of the devotion you have undertaken, you should endeavour by your example to establish others firmly and strengthen them more earnestly in reverence toward blessed Peter and toward us.

Furthermore, G., the bearer of these letters, came to us [Col. 0401A] and lodged before us a grave complaint on behalf of his sister C.: G. of Bald. and certain other parishioners of yours have unjustly taken from her her inheritance, called Bremontelles, and presume unlawfully to retain it. When she summoned them to appear before us on this account at the last feast of St John, they did not come and sent no representative to answer for them. But since we are unwilling, as indeed we ought not, to fail that woman in her right, and since we have confidence in your discretion, we commit this case to your judgment, to be heard and brought to its proper conclusion. We therefore command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when you are requested concerning it, you summon both parties before you; and, after carefully hearing and examining the arguments on each side, decide the same case through justice, setting appeal aside, even if an appeal has been made in it.

Given at the Lateran, the eighth day before the Kalends of December [24 November].

CCCLXXVI. To the clerics established in the diocese of Bangor.—That they elect a bishop whom Thomas of Canterbury may confirm. (Lateran, December 10.)

[Letters of St Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 91.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all the clerics established in the diocese of Bangor, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0401C] If you considered with due care how great the losses and disadvantages that usually arise for churches from the lack of a pastor are, your church would by no means have been without a prelate for so long a time as we have heard it to have been deprived of one. Since it is our office to bear care and solicitude for all churches and to provide, with the eye of paternal consideration, for their destitution, we command you by apostolic letters and enjoin you under obedience that, in accordance with the command and counsel of our venerable brother the Archbishop of Canterbury, within two months after receiving these letters you endeavour to elect, by unanimous vote, a suitable and honourable person as your pastor and bishop, [Col. 0401D] under whose government your church may, with the Lord’s help, advance in both spiritual and temporal prosperity. Present the person elected to the aforesaid archbishop, so that, if he finds it expedient, he may confirm his election and endeavour to promote it at a suitable time. Otherwise, receive as your master and bishop, with every excuse and appeal set aside, the person whom the said archbishop assigns to you, and endeavour humbly to show him the reverence and obedience due to him.

Moreover, we have heard that in the archdeaconry of your aforesaid church a son has succeeded his father almost by hereditary right, and that he holds the same archdeaconry without the authority or knowledge of the aforesaid archbishop. We decree that what has thus been done is invalid, [Col. 0402A] and we wholly annul it by apostolic authority.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Ides of December [10 December].

CCCLXXVII. To the Prior and Brethren of Canterbury.—That they assist the destitution of Thomas in exile.

[Letters of St Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 38.]

POPE ALEXANDER to the prior and brethren of Canterbury.

We cannot sufficiently wonder at your religious profession, since, while our venerable brother, your archbishop, labours for the liberty of yourselves and of the whole English Church and endures exile and many other things unworthy of so great a man, you have hitherto been unwilling to regard him as your father and master with fitting consolation [Col. 0402B] or to assist his necessities. Thus, since you seem in a sense negligent in abandoning the rights and dignities of your church, for you have thus far refused even to assist in a small degree the aforesaid archbishop while he exposes himself to many and various dangers for their sake, we command your whole body by apostolic letters and firmly enjoin you under obedience that, within two months after receiving these letters, you take care to give him assistance so suitable that it ought not to dishonour either him or yourselves. Thus may he experience in you filial affection and your loyalty, and may he be bound ever more fervently to strive in every way for the enlargement of the liberties and rights of your church. We too [Col. 0402C], in this matter, may commend your religious profession with worthy praise in the Lord and, when we see that you are concerned for them, preserve with more earnest care the dignities of your aforesaid church.

CCCLXXVIII. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—He confirms the sentence pronounced by him against certain perverse persons.

[Ibid., p. 11.]

POPE ALEXANDER to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

Because, in accordance with the obligation of your office, you are vigilant and earnest in defending the liberty of the Church and ecclesiastical rights, we pursue the prudence of your solicitude and constancy with deserved praise and commend it in many ways in this respect. Therefore we shall not seek to alter for any reason the ecclesiastical sentence which you have reasonably pronounced against Richard of Ilchester, John of Oxford, and all other corrupters of the Church of God; rather, with the Lord as author, we decree that it shall remain ratified and firm.

CCCLXXIX. To Henry, Bishop of Troyes.—He commends Master Herbert, who remained a companion of Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, in exile.

[Ibid., p. 105.]

To the Bishop of Troyes.

You can provide for the welfare of the church entrusted to you in no more advantageous way [Col. 0403A] than by appointing in it persons who shine in learning and uprightness of conduct, and whose virtues seem to contribute more to that church than they themselves have gained from the benefice bestowed. For then, without doubt, the house of God is adorned, when, in its ordering, zeal for God is so kindled according to knowledge by the one who presides that not flesh and blood or nobility of birth, but rather the merits of persons, are weighed.

We do not think it has escaped your knowledge how highly our beloved son Master Herbert is esteemed for his learning and integrity, and how, because he remained with his lord, our venerable brother the Archbishop of Canterbury, while the latter was in exile for the liberty of the church entrusted to him, he was despoiled, through the prince’s [Col. 0403B] indignation, of all the benefices he possessed. You could already have heard this frequently long ago. We therefore commend most earnestly to your integrity—of which we have certain hope and full confidence that it will not in any respect oppose our requests—this man whom we hold dear and acceptable, and whose provision we willingly intend to promote. We ask and admonish your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, and in consideration of his learning and integrity, as well as of the aforesaid archbishop, his lord, you generously grant and assign to him the provostship which our beloved son William, bishop-elect of Chartres, held in your church. [Col. 0403C] Effectively use your influence with the aforesaid elect so that he may grant you his consent and favour in this matter. Thus the said Herbert may be bound always to devote himself fervently to the welfare and advancement alike of yourself and the church entrusted to you; and, regarding this as altogether pleasing and welcome, we may be bound to offer your generosity manifold thanks and to promote your requests more willingly and effectively.

YEAR 1165?

### CCCLXXX. To Robert, Bishop of Hereford.—He rebukes him for having given less support than he ought to Thomas, archbishop, in defending the liberty of the Church.

*[Letters of St Thomas, ed. Giles, II, 92.]*

[Col. 0403D]

Alexander, pope, to Robert, bishop of Hereford.

We are greatly astonished that, although before your promotion we had heard that you were a religious man devoted to God, after attaining the summit of pontifical dignity you seem to have become somewhat lukewarm in this matter. This is more plainly apparent from the fact that you are proved to have given less support than you ought to our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Canterbury, your metropolitan, in defending the liberty of the Church; and that, contrary to what befitted your religious profession, you are said to have preferred human fear to the fear of God. Since, however, we have heard that this has happened otherwise than we believed, especially since our hope in your promotion seems in some measure disappointed, we command you by apostolic letters and enjoin upon you by virtue of obedience that you render due obedience and fitting reverence to your aforesaid metropolitan; and that, standing by him manfully and steadfastly in the affairs of the Church, you faithfully and devoutly carry out his commands and injunctions. Moreover, we command you to keep this wholly secret until the said our brother has peace with our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the English—which, with the Lord as author, will occur shortly.

### CCCLXXXI. To Gilbert, Bishop of London, and the other bishops.—He rebukes them because they have been lukewarm and negligent in many matters.

*[Letters of Gilbert Foliot, II, 93.]*

[Col. 0404B]

Alexander, pope, to Gilbert, bishop of London, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since we know you to be a man of great learning, much uprightness, and no slight abstinence, although you and your fellow bishops have been slack, lukewarm, and even negligent in many matters, because you are regarded as great among them both in learning and in the virtue of religious devotion, we have thought fit to admonish you before the others. By apostolic letters we ask and admonish you [Col. 0404C] that, when opportunity arises, you diligently and urgently exhort our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the English, with whom you are joined in no slight intimacy, not to confuse ecclesiastical and secular affairs, as he is known hitherto to have done; nor to presume to treat or intermingle them at his own will. Rather, let him leave ecclesiastical matters to be handled by ecclesiastical men, and claim secular matters alone for his own jurisdiction. Let him also receive our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Canterbury, into his love and favour, and restore him, together with the other exiles, to his own see and to the church committed to him. Let him restore to those to whom they belong the possessions of churches occupied by himself and his agents, together with the revenues received from them, [Col. 0404D] and permit them to possess those possessions in peace.

When you find him peaceable and well-disposed, you may communicate these matters to him as you judge expedient. But you must observe and render to the Church of Canterbury the obedience which you know you owe it, in such a way that you appear to render to God what is God’s and to Caesar what is Caesar’s. Unless we learn otherwise concerning you, we shall always wish to love you in the Lord with a closer charity, as our dearest brother and as a religious, learned, and upright man; nor shall we burden your person in any matter, or permit it to be burdened by another.

### CCCLXXXII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—Concerning the dispute between the Church of Erapousmanil and the Church of Roye. (Lateran, 12 December.)

*[Martène, Amplissima Collectio, II, 721.]*

[Col. 0405A]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Henry, archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

While we were still present in the kingdom of the Franks, a dispute had arisen concerning the Church of Erapousmanil between our venerable brother, the Bishop of Noyon, and T., formerly bishop of Amiens, of good memory. Since that church had already been adjudged by us to the aforesaid Bishop of Noyon, the clerics [Note: [Col. 0405] Roye is a town in Picardy, in the district of Santerre, where there is a notable college of canons adorned with the relics of St Florentius.] [Col. 0405B] of Roye persistently asserted that its tithes belonged to them. We therefore committed the case to your judgment for decision, appeals set aside, in accordance with the tenor of our letters which we granted to the people of Noyon concerning the judgment rendered.

When, after hearing the case, you pronounced judgment for the Church of Noyon against that of Roye, and its canons scorned to obey it, you subjected them, as is said, to a sentence of interdict. Although, indeed, we have heard that this sentence was relaxed without any satisfaction having been rendered, they did not observe it at all. Since your authority appears to have been gravely slighted in this matter, we command you by apostolic letters diligently to admonish the aforesaid canons that, within [Col. 0405C] thirty days after receiving this letter, they restore everything taken from Noyon in accordance with your command and make reparation for the damage inflicted. Otherwise, unless they have fully carried out what we have said within the fixed term, declare that they have been restored by us to the aforesaid sentence of interdict. We command that this be firmly observed by you until worthy satisfaction is made, and that you cause it to be inviolably observed by all throughout the whole province.

Given at the Lateran, 12 December.

## Year 1166

### CCCLXXXIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—He asks him to obtain one hundred marks of silver for him and to aid his necessities from the churches of his diocese. (Lateran, 18 January.)

*[Ibid.]*

[Col. 0405D]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Henry, archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Giving careful consideration to your perfect faith and the most sincere purity of your devotion, which from the very beginning of our promotion you have steadily and faithfully shown toward the honour and advancement of the most holy Roman Church and of ourselves; and considering [Col. 0406A] also how, regarding that Church’s cause not as another’s but as your own, you have taken care manfully to defend and uphold it, we offer you the fullest thanks. In our necessities we confidently seek counsel and assistance from your generosity.

We wish your prudence to know that whatever is bestowed upon us as alms is swallowed up by the greed of usurers, depriving us of the means and abundance of necessary things. For we are situated in such a place and dwell among such a people that, even in a time of complete peace, much less in a time of disturbance, they are accustomed to look to the hands of the Roman pontiffs and to impose upon them no small burden and expense. Therefore, since we have very great need of your assistance and that of others to lighten the burdens and necessities [Col. 0406B] of that Church, we ask and admonish you by apostolic letters, in view of the weight and hardship of our necessity, to obtain for us, if it can be done in any way consistent with our honour, one hundred marks of silver from the person in whose name, while we were in the kingdom of the Franks, you offered us one hundred and fifty pounds and another sum to our brethren.

Likewise, since among men of pontifical rank we have full confidence in you above others, we have thought fit to ask and earnestly exhort you to endeavour to find us honourable assistance from the churches of your own diocese. For when, at our departure, we had urged other churches of the kingdom of the Franks [Col. 0406C] to provide aid for us and for the Church, we thought it unworthy then to trouble a person of such nobility and dignity concerning these things. Even now, were urgent necessity not pressing upon us, we would not trouble you in this respect. For the Roman Church will always keep before its eyes both this and your other services of devotion and welcome assistance; and it will at all times effectively and zealously direct itself toward the honour and advancement of you and your church.

We wish you to assign, according to what seems good to your generosity, to our beloved sons, the master and brethren of the Knights Templar at Paris. Whatever you decide to do for me, inform us as swiftly as possible by your letters. So great are the burdens of our debts and the pressure of creditors that, unless the Church [Col. 0406D] of God is now aided by your generosity, we shall scarcely, or never, be able to preserve the state of the City in the peace in which it now stands.

Given at the Lateran, 18 January.

### CCCLXXXIV. To all the bishops of England.—That they adhere to Archbishop Thomas in matters concerning the Church of Canterbury. (Lateran, 28 January.)

*[Letters of St Thomas, ed. Giles, II, 76.]*

Alexander, pope, to all the bishops of England.

As part of the office laid upon us, we are bound to exercise care and solicitude for preserving every person’s right in its integrity, especially the rights of those who have been called by the Lord to share in the burden of solicitude entrusted to us. [Col. 0407A] The higher their rank, the more frequently we ought to turn greater diligence and more earnest care toward them. Therefore, moved by this consideration, we command you by apostolic letters and enjoin you by virtue of obedience that, concerning matters known to belong to the rights, dignities, or liberties of the Church of Canterbury, you must by no means presume to intervene without the knowledge and assent of your venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of that church; nor may you attempt this in any way on the pretext of the appeal which you have made against him to us. If any one of you [Col. 0407B] should presume by any boldness to contravene this command of ours, we shall, with the Lord’s help, take such severe vengeance upon this offence that punishment itself will teach him how dangerous it is to oppose apostolic commands.

Given at the Lateran, 28 January.

### CCCLXXXV. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—He orders him to exhort the clerics of the Church of Bangor to elect a bishop; if they do not, he himself is to do so within three months. (Lateran, 29 January.)

*[Ibid., p. 36.]*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0407C] If the clerics of the Church of Bangor carefully considered how great the losses and inconveniences that commonly arise for churches from the lack of a pastor are, their church would not have been without a prelate for so long a time as we have heard it to have been widowed of a pastor. Therefore, since it is our concern to exercise care and solicitude for all churches and to provide with the eye of paternal consideration for their destitution, we command you by apostolic letters diligently to summon the aforesaid clerics and earnestly endeavour to admonish them to agree, with your counsel, upon some suitable and upright person, and not delay electing him as their pastor and bishop within two [Col. 0407D] months after they receive our letters. If they fail to do this in obedience to our command and your admonition, you shall, within three months after receiving this letter, provide them with someone considered suitable for pontifical office. They are to receive him as father and pastor and, without any contradiction, render him the due reverence and obedience owed to their prelate.

Given at the Lateran, 29 January.

### CCCLXXXVI. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—He commends Thomas in exile. (Lateran, 30 January.)

*[Ibid., p. 52.]*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0408A] father Henry, archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Among the other works of divine operation, we regard as most pleasing to God and to ourselves the fact that you have looked upon our venerable father, the Archbishop of Canterbury, in his straits and anxieties with serene favour, and according to your customary kindness have taken care to show him the favour of both your grace and consolation.
