Since he now has the greatest need of aid and counsel, we ask, admonish, and exhort your magnificence in the Lord by apostolic letters that, out of regard for piety and for reverence for Blessed Peter and ourselves, and in consideration of his religious character and dignity, you anticipate him and his people with favour, honour, and affection, and provide him in his adversities with the comfort of your consolation [Col. 0408B] and favour. Thus you may receive eternal recompense from almighty God; and, considering what you give him as especially given to ourselves, we shall be bound in some measure to give thanks to your brotherhood for it.

Given at the Lateran, 30 January.

### CCCLXXXVII. To the clergy and people of Bangor.—That they elect a bishop. (Lateran, 9 February.)

*[Ibid., p. 90.]*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons and all the clergy and people of the Church of Bangor, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0408C] Since grave dangers to souls commonly result from the lack of a pastor, and many inconveniences and losses thereby befall God’s holy churches, we now, as we have admonished you in other letters, admonish and command your whole community by this repeated letter: if you have not yet agreed, agree together upon some upright, suitable, and learned person, and elect him jointly as your bishop. Take care also to present the man elected to our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Canterbury, for consecration. For if you have already made a canonical election of a suitable person, we ratify it; and whatever the aforesaid archbishop decides in the matter, we shall take care to hold [Col. 0408D] ratified and firm.

Given at the Lateran, 9 February.

### CCCLXXXVIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of the chaplains of Laon. (Lateran, 22 February.)

*[Martène, Amplissima Collectio, II, 725.]*

[Col. 0408D]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Henry, archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It befits your brotherhood to show itself kindly and favourably disposed toward those who desire to have your protection and defence, and to furnish them with the patronage of your favour and guardianship. Moved by this consideration, we earnestly commend the chaplains of Laon [Col. 0409A] to your care, commanding and directing you to receive them and their goods under your protection, diligently to uphold and defend them in their rights, as your office requires; and, if the bishop [Note: [Col. 0409] This was Walter of Mauritania, a learned man, made bishop from being dean of Laon and installed at Rome in 1155.], because they have often complained to us about him, should wish to treat them unlawfully and unjustly or impose upon them any burden contrary to our letter and that of his predecessor, you are not under any circumstances to permit this. Rather, endeavour to restrain him from it, so that they may rejoice in being protected by your care and may be more faithful to you throughout their lives.

Given at the Lateran, 22 February.

### CCCLXXXIX. He receives the monastery of St John at Pescara under protection and confirms its possessions and rights. (Lateran, 18 March.)

*[Muratori, Rerum Italicarum Scriptores, II, II, 901.]*

[Col. 0409B]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Leonatus, abbot of the monastery of St Clement on the island of Pescara, called Casa Aurea, and to his brethren, both present and future, who profess the regular life, for ever.

The office of government which we have undertaken, and the order of reason itself, invite us to assent to religious desires and to fulfil them by effective action. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests. Following the example of our predecessors among the Roman pontiffs—Leo, Calixtus, and Adrian, of blessed memory—we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and our own, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid monastery in which rests the body of Blessed Clement, pope and martyr, and in which you are dedicated [Col. 0409C] to divine service. First, we decree that the monastic order, known to have been instituted in that monastery according to the Lord and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, be inviolably observed there in perpetuity.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s favour, acquire through the grants of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their own names: [Col. 0409D] in the county of Penne, the castle of Insula with the entire island itself; Castiglione, Ubicola, Pescuglia, Rocca di Sutri, Corvaria, Petraminiqua, Betorites, Mandeforum, Casale Piano, Coledunum with its appurtenances; the castle called Casale of St Desiderius in the city of St Angelo; the castle of St Maurus with its port and appurtenances; in the county of Chieti, the castle of Bolognano with its appurtenances; in the county of Abruzzo, the castle of Guardia, the castle of Vetulum, and Monaciscum with its appurtenances; in the county of Valva, the hamlet called Holy Trinity with its appurtenances; in the March, [Col. 0410A] the castle of Loreto with its appurtenances; the church of St Mary at Plesiano; the church of St Mary at Fasinaria; the church of St Quiricus of Monte Silvano with its appurtenances; in the aforesaid county of Chieti, the church of St Mary of Pesilo, the church of St Angelo of Casule, the church of St Caesidius, and the monastery of Holy Trinity of Lapidaria with its appurtenances; at Caramanico, the churches of Holy Cross and St Nicholas with their appurtenances, the church of St Martin at Gricta, the church of St John Iscamari, and the church of St Sylvester near Manoppello with its appurtenances; the cell of St Clement at Lisina with its appurtenances; the monastery of St Maurus of Amiterno with its appurtenances; Mount Ursa, Mount Tarini, and Mount Soti, together with their rocks and woods.

We also [Col. 0410B] grant to you and your successors the tithe of the lands of your church and a share of offerings made for the dead. Moreover, we forbid any bishop to hold a synod there. You may receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of monks or clerics to be promoted to sacred orders, from whichever bishop you prefer. On the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one may be placed over it by any craft of fraud or violence, except the person whom [lacuna]: the brethren by common consent, or the wiser part of the brethren's council, shall provide to be elected according to the Lord and the Rule of Blessed Benedict.

[Col. 0410C] We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be kept whole, to be of every benefit for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, the authority of the Apostolic See being preserved in all things. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Walter, bishop of Albano. I, Hugh, bishop of Tusculum. I, Conrad, archbishop of the see of Mainz and bishop of Sabina. [Col. 0410D] I, Ubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul of Pammachius. I, Henry, cardinal-priest of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, William, cardinal-priest of the title of St Peter in Chains. I, Boso, cardinal-priest of the title of St Pudentiana of Pastor. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Oddo, cardinal-deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. [Col. 0411A] I, Arditio, cardinal-deacon of St Theodore. I, Manfred, cardinal-deacon of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, cardinal-deacon of St Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Vitellius, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Theodinus, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Aquiro.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Ermanno, cardinal-deacon of St Angelo, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April; in the fifteenth indiction; in the year 1166 of the Lord’s Incarnation; and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### CCCXC. To Roger, Archbishop of York, and all the bishops of England.—That none of them “presume to take part in crowning a new king, should such a contingency arise, without the assent of Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.” (Lateran, 5 April.)

*[Letters of St Thomas, ed. Giles, II, 45.]*

[Col. 0411B]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the Archbishop of York and all the bishops of England, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard that from ancient times the Church of Canterbury has possessed such dignity and pre-eminence that the kings of England have always customarily been anointed and crowned at the beginning of their accession by the archbishops of that church. Therefore, since, both by the obligation of our office and out of regard for our venerable [Col. 0411C] brother Thomas, archbishop of that see—a religious, upright, and discerning man—we desire to preserve intact and unimpaired the ancient rights and dignities of the aforesaid Church, we strictly forbid your whole body by apostolic authority that none of you may presume, under any pretext, to take part in crowning a new king, should such a contingency arise, without the assent of the aforesaid archbishop or his successors and of the Church of Canterbury, contrary to its ancient custom and dignity; nor dare in any way to attempt this.

Given at the Lateran, 5 April.

### CCCXCI. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—He grants him the legateship of all England, except the bishopric of York. (Lateran, 24 April.)

*[Letters of St Thomas, ed. Giles, II, 10.]*

[Col. 0411D]

Alexander, pope, to Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury.

The most holy Roman Church is accustomed to embrace with a fuller charity and to favour with grace and honour persons of worth, especially those whom it knows to shine with uprightness, prudence, learning, and the eminence of virtues. Accordingly, considering the constancy of devotion and faith by which you have stood firm for the Church of God like an immovable pillar, the prudence of uprightness, learning, [Col. 0412A] and discernment in which you are known to excel, and also judging it fitting to love and honour your person, adorned with the distinction of such great virtues, by some special privilege and singular prerogative, and to provide for your advantage with our customary kindness and more attentive solicitude: we graciously grant you the legateship of all England, except the bishopric of York. There, in our stead, you are to correct what you find requiring correction and, for the honour of God, the most holy Roman Church, and the salvation of souls, establish, build, and plant what ought to be established and planted.

Therefore we admonish and command your brotherhood to act in all things with prudence and discernment, as God shall direct you; to root out vices; and to endeavour to plant virtues in the Lord’s vineyard.

Given at Anagni, 9 October. [Note: [Col. 0411D] Instead of “Given at Anagni, 9 October,” words which appear to have been wrongly inserted through a copyist’s error, the following letter shows that one should read [Col. 0412D]: “Given at the Lateran, 24 April.” Jaffé.]

### CCCXCII. To bishops, abbots, and other prelates of churches established throughout England outside the bishopric of York.—That they obey Thomas of Canterbury, appointed legate of the Apostolic See. (Lateran, 24 April.)

*[Ibid., p. 80.]*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the bishops, his beloved sons the abbots, and the other prelates of churches established throughout England outside the bishopric of York, greeting [Col. 0412C] and apostolic blessing.

By the office of the pontificate laid upon us by God, in addition to that authority granted to the prelates of the various churches over those subject to them, we must exercise a certain special care and solicitude for all matters known to pertain solely to our own provision, or to that of him to whom we have entrusted the execution of our authority in these matters. Therefore, although we have care and concern for all the churches of God, we cannot everywhere carry out in person what belongs to our office. Carefully considering the prudence and discernment of our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Canterbury, and the affection of his most sincere devotion [Col. 0412D] toward us and the Church of God, the more dearly we hold his person among the others called by the Lord to share in the solicitude entrusted to us, and the more fully proved we find him in all things, the more we have judged him worthy above the other children of the Church to be honoured with the prerogative of a special dignity.

Therefore, considering the constancy of his discernment and uprightness, with the common counsel of our brethren we appoint him legate of the Apostolic See throughout all England except the bishopric of York, and entrust our authority there to his prudence for execution: namely, so that in our stead he may correct matters requiring correction and, by God’s aid, [Col. 0413A] beneficially establish what ought to be established. Accordingly, we command your whole body by apostolic letters humbly to obey him in all things as legate of the Apostolic See; to come to him at his summons without any objection; and fully to answer him in those matters which belong to our office. Receive, firmly observe, and always endeavour to honour with fitting reverence and appropriate honours those things which he shall establish for the honour of God and the salvation of His faithful; so that, through his prudence and care and through your obedience and humility, the churches committed to you may advance, with the Lord’s cooperation, from good to better both spiritually and temporally, and so that through this you may happily attain unending joy.

[Col. 0413B] Given at the Lateran, 24 April.

### CCCXCIII. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—That, if he sees an opportunity, he is not to delay exercising ecclesiastical justice against invaders of the possessions of the Church of Canterbury. (Lateran? April.)

*[Ibid., p. 12.]*

Since we ought not to place a cushion under every elbow and encourage some persons in their wickedness, but must declare his iniquity to the wicked and recall him from it by the rigour of ecclesiastical severity, we command you by apostolic letters that, if those who have inflicted violence or injury upon you or your people in the possessions and goods of your church, when lawfully admonished, refuse to restore what they have taken from you and to render fitting satisfaction, you are not to delay, should you see an opportunity, to exercise ecclesiastical justice against them. Whatever you reasonably do in this matter, we shall, with God’s aid, hold ratified and firm.

But we give you no special command concerning the king’s person; nevertheless, we do not take away from you in any respect the pontifical right which you received in your ordination and consecration, but desire, with the Lord’s aid, to preserve it to you unharmed and entire.

### CCCXCIV. To all the bishops of the province of Canterbury.—He informs them of the preceding letter. (Lateran? April.)

*[Ibid., p. 41.]*

[Col. 0413D]

Alexander, pope, to all the bishops of the province of Canterbury.

Since we ought not to place a cushion under every elbow and encourage some persons in their wickedness, but must declare his iniquity to the wicked and recall him from it by the rigour of ecclesiastical severity, we have instructed our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, by our letters that, if those who have inflicted violence or injury upon him or his people in the possessions and goods of his church, when lawfully admonished, refuse to restore what they have taken from them and to render fitting satisfaction, he is not to delay, should he see an opportunity, to exercise ecclesiastical justice against them. Therefore we command your whole body by apostolic letters to hold wholly ratified and firm the justice which your aforesaid archbishop may reasonably judge fit to promulgate on this matter, and to cause it to be inviolably observed by all throughout your dioceses.

But we give him no special command concerning the king’s person; nevertheless, we do not take away from him in any respect the pontifical right which he received in his ordination and consecration, but desire, with the Lord’s aid, to preserve it to him unharmed and entire. For whatever he shall do canonically in the matter, we shall, with God’s aid, hold ratified and firm.

### CCCXCV. To the abbots and brethren of Cîteaux and Pontigny.—That they are not to permit Thomas of Canterbury “to be removed from the monastery of Pontigny.” (Lateran? April.)

*[Ibid., p. 110.]*

[Col. 0414B]

Alexander, pope, to the abbots of Cîteaux and Pontigny and to all the brethren of the Cistercian Order.

Although we are fully aware that you display toward us and the Church of God the faith and devotion which befit religious men devoted to God, we cannot but wonder at the fact that certain of your number, as we have heard, wished our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Canterbury—a man both religious and upright, altogether dear and welcome to God and to ourselves and to the whole Church—to be removed from the monastery of Pontigny, and that all the support of your order was denied him because of the threats and terrors of certain persons.

Therefore, since true charity casts out fear, and it does not befit a religious man in any way to prefer human fear to divine fear, we command your whole body by apostolic letters not to attempt anything of the kind in future. You, who ought to be a refuge for the oppressed and for those exiled in defence of the liberty of the Church, must not offer others a ruinous example in this matter. Rather, for reverence for Blessed Peter and ourselves, in view of his religious character and uprightness, and because he pleads so favourable a cause, take care diligently to love, uphold, and support the aforesaid archbishop; and when he comes to you, receive him kindly and honourably in your houses and treat him gently. Thus he may find in you the fruit of true charity and be bound always to strive more fervently for the growth and advancement of the whole order. We also, considering the honour and service rendered to him as rendered to ourselves, shall be bound to commend your generosity in the Lord and to return the fullest thanks to your sincerity.

### CCCXCVI. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of Robert, a priest. (Lateran, 1 May.)

*[Martène, Amplissima Collectio, II, 734.]*

[Col. 0415A]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Henry, archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As your prudence knows, the priestly office is neglected and held almost in derision and contempt if someone invested with that ministry is compelled, in order to seek the necessities of life, to wander about like a vagrant and suffer grievous want and poverty. Therefore we ask and admonish your providence diligently to exhort, and by every means induce, our venerable brother [Col. 0415B] [Note: [Col. 0415D] G., Walter, third bishop of Tournai after its restoration.] G., bishop of Tournai, to provide fittingly, as he promised us orally, for our beloved son Robert, a priest deprived of ecclesiastical benefice, in the first of his churches which becomes vacant. Thus we may deservedly commend his solicitude in this matter, and this priest may not be compelled any longer—something altogether absurd—to be without ecclesiastical benefice.

Given at the Lateran, 1 May.

### CCCXCVII. To Gilbert, Bishop of London, and all the bishops of the province of Canterbury.—That they strictly compel, under threat of anathema, invaders of the benefices of the clerics of Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to make full restitution. (Lateran, 3 May.)

*[Letters of St Thomas, ed. Giles, II, 95.]*

[Col. 0415C]

Alexander, pope, to the bishop of London and all the bishops of the province of Canterbury.

To all who are oppressed and burdened by injustice we are bound, by the duty of our office, to bring assistance. Above all, we must suitably provide for ecclesiastics who are compelled to endure exile in defence of their church’s liberty, lest they suffer any loss of their rights. Your discretion knows all the more certainly how the clerics of our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, incurred their lord prince’s indignation for their fidelity to him, and on this account were deprived of their goods [Col. 0415D], since you yourselves were able more fully to observe this in part with your own eyes. Therefore, since it is unworthy that, because of violence inflicted upon them, they should suffer any injury to their benefices, by these apostolic letters we command you strictly, and in commanding command, to compel, under threat of anathema and with all appeal set aside, all who have already, by royal command, received the benefices of the said clerics during their absence, to make full restitution of them; and in carrying this out, do not appear in any respect lax or lukewarm.

[Col. 0416A] Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Nones of May [3 May].

CCCXCVIII. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—He confirms the sentence of interdict pronounced by him against Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury. (Lateran? May.)

[Ibid., p. 13.]

ALEXANDER, pope, to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

We learned some time ago from your letters and from the reliable report of many persons that you pronounced a sentence of interdict against Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury, because he was disobedient to you. Although he appealed to our hearing in this matter and set as the term for his appeal the forthcoming Sunday on which is sung, “I am the Good Shepherd” (John XI), when that day arrived he neither came nor sent anyone to answer for him before us. Therefore, unwilling to support him in his contumacy and rebellion against you, we shall, with God’s authority, hold valid and firm the sentence which you have pronounced against him on this account; and we have judged his entire case to be left to the judgment of your discretion, intending to hold valid, with the obstacle of appeal removed, whatever you shall canonically do in the matter.

CCCXCIX. To the same.—He announces that he has annulled the grant made by Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury, to John of Oxford. (Lateran? May.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0416C] From the copy of the letter which you sent to the Bishop of Salisbury, we learned that you annulled, for two reasons, the grant of the deanery which that bishop unlawfully made to John of Oxford: first, because John himself had entangled himself in the snare of schism; and secondly, because it had been done contrary to our prohibition and command. For we had forbidden that any dean should, on any grounds, be appointed in the aforesaid church without the consent of the canons who were in exile with you and on your behalf. Therefore, by the authority which we exercise, we wholly annul the aforesaid grant and decree it void.

CD. To the Archbishop of Rheims.—Concerning the election of the abbess of Dodoniensis. (Lateran, 14 May.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 735.]

[Col. 0416D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the letters sent to us by your brotherhood we learned that, when the sisters of Dodoniensis [Note: [Col. 0415D] Read: *Donanienses*. Denain is a distinguished convent of nuns of the Order of St Benedict in the diocese of Arras, not far from Lille.] were divided among themselves and had nominated two persons for abbess, a far greater part agreed upon one than upon the other. Yet we heard, both from letters and from the report of various persons, that, after the election of both women who had been nominated had been annulled, the sisters entrusted the authority for their election to the judgment of the Bishop of Arras. Since this was not clearly established for us, and because we had been assured that the sisters had withdrawn from both elections, we committed the case to be heard by our venerable brothers the Bishops of Tournai and Thérouanne, and to be concluded under a fixed procedure with an appropriate settlement. Therefore we admonish and command your brotherhood to regard as valid, and cause to be firmly observed, whatever the aforesaid bishops shall determine in this matter.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Ides of March [14 March].

CDI. He exhorts Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, to act more mildly toward Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury. (Lateran, 16 May.)

[Epistles of St Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 12.]

[Col. 0417B]

Alexander, etc., to his venerable brother THOMAS, etc.

It has been brought to our hearing that the Bishop of Salisbury has committed grave and excessive offences, and has sinned seriously and immoderately against God and the Church. Since we believe that he acted not willingly but under compulsion, through fear and dread such as might overcome any steadfast man, in committing something against the honour of that Church, and since it is written: “Your disposition gives its name to your deed; intention and purpose distinguish crimes,” it seems beyond doubt that, if this is so, he should be treated more mildly. But if it is established that he sinned against God and the Church deliberately and of his own free will, he ought to be punished according to the nature of his offence. Nevertheless, whatever your discretion shall judge should canonically be decreed against him on this account, we shall, with God’s authority, hold valid and firm.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June [16 May].

CDII. To Rotrou, Archbishop of Rouen, and his suffragans.—Concerning the evils inflicted on the Church by Henry, King of England. (Lateran, 16 May.)

[Ibid., p. 53.]

ALEXANDER, pope, to ROTROU, Archbishop of Rouen, and his suffragans.

[Col. 0417D] How great the evils and how many the injuries which have come upon the Roman Church and ourselves through our dearest son in Christ, Henry, illustrious King of the English, since he has in some measure withdrawn himself from devotion to it, is clearly seen from the fact that, by associating with that wicked, treacherous, and cruel man Reginald, former chancellor and teacher of the error of this schism, he supplied, through those whom he sent to Frederick, called emperor, the occasion and material by which Frederick was induced to make that detestable and profane oath—indeed, perjury. Yet, setting all this behind us and keeping always before our eyes the splendid and abundant services of devotion which, from the beginning of this disturbance, he showed to us and the Church, we repeatedly admonished him with paternal kindness through our letters and finally through worthy and honourable men, and tried to soften his spirit with apostolic gentleness, awaiting his recognition of his transgression and the moderation, through royal clemency, of his passionate impulse.

[Col. 0418A] Since, therefore, although he has not fallen into schism, he nevertheless burdens beyond measure the churches and ecclesiastical persons of his kingdom, confounds and disrupts their rights, and strives to draw everything to himself and claim it as his own, by these apostolic letters we command you strictly to set all these matters faithfully before him; admonish and exhort him, by almighty God and on behalf of blessed Peter and ourselves, to acknowledge his mother, the Roman Church, with his customary reverence and devotion; to love and honour the churches and ecclesiastical persons of his kingdom; and to endeavour to recall our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, who is faithful and devoted to him, to his church, and to treat him honourably as is fitting. Let him also maintain and preserve, under royal protection, the rights and goods of Thomas and of the others. But if he refuses to abandon the purpose of his present course, he may without doubt fear that God will severely avenge this upon him and his descendants. Nor can we overlook it or leave it unpunished any longer, [Col. 0418C] “for a father corrects and chastises the son whom he loves” (Hebrews XII).

Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June [16 May].

In the same terms to the Archbishop of Bordeaux and his suffragans.

CDIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—Concerning a subdeacon of Laon who had taken a wife, and the dispute of the Bishop of Laon against the chaplains of Laon. (Lateran, 31 March.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 1075.]

It has been reported to us that R. Belm., a canon of the Church of Laon, although he is ordained in the order of subdeacon, has attempted to join a certain woman to himself in marriage [Col. 0418D] and presumptuously lives publicly with her as a husband with his wife. Since the ancient enactments of the holy Fathers, and the council most recently held in the Lateran church [Note: [Col. 0417D] Under Innocent II, canon 6.], had provided that marriages of this sort must not be contracted and, if contracted, must be wholly invalidated, we instructed our venerable brother G. [Galter II], Bishop of Laon, that, if the matter is as stated, he must not delay in separating in every way the said R. from the woman whom he attempted to join to himself in marriage, nor permit them to cohabit further on any grounds. If they refuse to comply in this, he is to bind them with the bond of excommunication.

Furthermore, you should know that a still more serious matter has reached our ears: that the same bishop compelled the chaplains of Laon wholly to renounce the authentic letters of ourselves and of his predecessor which they possessed, freely to surrender them into his hand, and even to confirm by oath that they would never again bring a complaint concerning them. Since this is plainly known to redound wholly to contempt of us and injury to the Roman Church, by our letters we commanded him strictly and enjoined him, by virtue of obedience, that, if he received the aforesaid documents, he should restore them to the said chaplains without any pretext or excuse, absolve them from their oath, and, in order to make satisfaction for so grave an offence, present himself before the apostolic presence, either in person or through a sufficient representative, without any pretext or excuse.

[Col. 0419B] Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion that, if he refuses to carry into effect what has been said, you are to compel him strictly to perform these things. If you find the allegations true, then, with all pretext, excuse, and appeal removed, suspend him from episcopal office and have him regarded by all as suspended, until he restores the documents to the aforesaid chaplains and comes, in person or through a worthy and sufficient representative, to the Apostolic See to make satisfaction for so grave an offence. Moreover, absolve the aforesaid chaplains from their oath, and separate the said R. from the woman whom he attempted to join to himself in marriage. [Col. 0419C] Further, we enjoin you that, if that bishop or others should wish to inflict indignation or any injury upon the bearer of these letters because he has come to us, you are, so far as lies within your power, to protect, support, and defend him, and permit no injury or burden to be imposed upon him.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of June [31 May].

CDIV. To the same.—Concerning the case pending between G. and Hersende. (Lateran, 24 June.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 738.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims: greeting [Col. 0419D] and apostolic blessing.

From the account of G., the bearer of these letters, we learned that, when a dispute was being heard before you by our command between him and a woman named Hersende concerning a sum of money which the same G. was said to owe to Hugh, formerly that woman’s husband, G., as he asserts, was prepared to prove by sufficient witnesses that he had paid that money in full to the said Hugh before Hugh’s death. Yet, after an appeal to us had been made, you subjected G. and his sureties to a sentence of excommunication, because appeal had been forbidden in the letters.

Nevertheless, even if he had appealed from you to us, wishing gladly to defer to you as our dearest brother, we have judged that he should be remitted to the examination of your discretion. By these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood not to permit him to be judged by your court, which he considers suspect in this respect, but that you yourself, having called in our venerable brother the Bishop of Noyon, should judge him. Thus, if before you he can lawfully demonstrate by suitable and sufficient witnesses that he paid the principal of the aforesaid sum to the said Hugh before his death, you are wholly to absolve him, with appeal set aside, from the woman’s claim; you are not thereafter to condemn him, or any other person, for usury in this matter; and you are to decree void our letters in which appeal is prohibited. Furthermore, we ask your discretion, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, to absolve him and his sureties from the sentence by which you bound them, [Col. 0420B] without any ban.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July [24 June].

CDV. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, and his suffragans.—He announces that Counts H. and W. of Vals have been excommunicated. (Lateran, 7 July.)

[Epistles of St Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 35.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, and all his suffragan bishops: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because the noblemen Count H. and W. of Vals, by rash presumption, occupied the goods and possessions of our beloved sons, the brothers of the church of Pantu, [Col. 0420C] and, despite our and others’ admonitions, refused in any way to restore them to those brothers, but afterwards extended their hands more grievously to the invasion of their property, we publicly declare them, by apostolic authority, excommunicated and separated from the body of Christ, which is the Church. Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command you strictly and enjoin you by virtue of obedience publicly to declare, with lighted candles, the said men bound by us with the bond of anathema, and throughout your dioceses to cause all to avoid them as excommunicates, until they restore in full everything taken from the said brothers and make fitting satisfaction for the injuries inflicted.

[Col. 0420D] For we utterly annul by apostolic authority, and decree to have no force henceforward, the grant which that prior is said to have made, without the knowledge and entirely without the consent of his brethren, from the possessions of the church, and to have conveyed to the said count under the name of a certain exchange; since, by the ordinance of the holy Fathers, it is altogether vain and void.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of July [7 July].

CDVI. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of a certain man concerning a pledge of a mill. (Lateran, 20 July.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 739.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0421A] brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

M., the bearer of these letters, returning from Jerusalem, showed us in his statement that the abbot and brothers of Saint Peter of the Mount [Note: [Col. 0421D] Saint Peter of the Mount, a celebrated Benedictine monastery in the city of Châlons, restored by Bishop Roger in 1043, still exists under the Congregation of Saint-Vanne.] had lent his father-in-law nine pounds and had taken from him as a pledge, payable to them every year, measures of grain from a certain mill which was jointly owned by him and the abbot. The aforesaid abbot received, beyond the principal, as much as twenty pounds in Châlons currency. Since the crime of usury is regarded as detestable not only in a monk but also in any layman, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to admonish and compel strictly the said abbot and his brothers, unless another reasonable cause prevents it, to surrender to the said M., with appeal set aside, whatever they are known to have received beyond the principal from the pledge received, after expenses have been deducted.

[Col. 0421B] Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August [20 July].

CDVII. To the Bishop of Le Mans.—Concerning the affair of Philip, nephew of Henry, Archbishop of Rheims. (Lateran, 1 August.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the Bishop of Le Mans [Note: [Col. 0421D] He was then William of Passavant, of noble birth; for a fuller account of his acts see Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. III, [Col. 0422D]]: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother Henry, [Col. 0421C] Archbishop of Rheims, having sent us a complaint, showed that the clerk Arn. unjustifiably withholds fifty pounds from the revenues of his nephew Philip [Note: [Col. 0422D] Philip, who reigned after his father Louis and was called Augustus because of his illustrious deeds.], and wholly refuses to pay them to him. When our said brother repeatedly demanded that money from Arn., he would neither return it nor submit to judgment with him concerning it. The archbishop therefore summoned him by appeal to our presence. Arn., however, neither came at the stated term of appeal nor sent anyone to answer for him before us. Since we can neither fail nor ought to fail the aforesaid archbishop in his right, we commit the case to your discretion to hear and, with appeal set aside, bring to its due conclusion. Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood, when requested concerning this, to summon both parties before you and, after carefully hearing and considering the arguments on either side, decide the case according to justice, with the remedy of appeal removed, as stated.

[Col. 0421D] Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of August [1 August].

CDVIII. To Philip, Count of Flanders.—He confirms his marriage with Elizabeth, daughter of the Count of Péronne. (Lateran, 25 August.)

[Epistles of St Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 146.]

[Col. 0422A]

To his beloved son in Christ, the nobleman Count PHILIP: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because heavenly grace has exalted you above your ancestors and forebears, many envy your successes; and, as we ourselves have in part perceived, they strive to procure a divorce between you and the noble lady Elizabeth, your wife, formerly the daughter of the Count of Péronne, and together seek to obstruct and disturb your marriage from the spite of envy rather than from love of justice. Since envy alone is without misery, and wishing to provide more wisely for your peace and tranquillity, and observing that they undertake this from will rather than zeal for rectitude, we confirm that marriage by apostolic authority.

[Col. 0422B] Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September [25 August].

CDIX. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of Baldwin, a monk, that he may be received. (Lateran, 19 October.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 740.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Baldwin, bearer of these letters, appearing before us, showed in his account that, after he had received the monastic habit in a certain monastery of the German kingdom, he did not dare to remain there because of the treachery of schismatics. He is therefore now compelled to endure exile. Since by the office entrusted to us we are bound to afford aid and assistance to all, and especially to those who are exiled for Catholic unity, and to provide for their needs with paternal solicitude, we ask, admonish, and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord to admonish and exhort the abbot and brothers of the monastery of Saint Remigius [Note: [Col. 0422D] Saint Remigius, a celebrated Benedictine monastery in the city of Rheims, enriched as with a precious treasure by the body of St Remigius.] kindly to receive Baldwin and, until he can return to his own church and remain there freely, to provide fittingly for his necessities. Thus he may receive from them worthy comfort in his exile, [Col. 0422D] serve God there, and we may be bound to render you abundant thanks for it.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November [19 October].

CDX. To the same.—On behalf of L., prior of Saint Remigius at Rheims. (Lateran, 9 November.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0423A] brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those whom we know to be adorned with uprightness of character and the strength of religious life, we desire to embrace with sincere charity and cherish in the favour of our kindness and gentleness. Therefore, giving particular consideration to the prudence, uprightness, and honourableness of our beloved son L., prior of Saint Remigius, and likewise considering how, from devotion to ourselves and the Church, he declined the abbacy to which he had been elected, we warmly commend him to your charity. We earnestly ask and admonish you, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, to receive him beforehand with favour and affection, and to consider his honour and advancement so effectively and attentively [Col. 0423B] that we may more warmly commend your solicitude on this account, and he may be bound to you in the most sincere devotion.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of November [9 November].

CDXI. Privilege for the monastery of Pontigny. (Lateran, 11 November.)

[MARTEN., *Thesaur. Anecdot.*, III, 1235.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GARINUS, abbot of Pontigny, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Those who choose the regular life ought to enjoy apostolic protection, lest an assault of any rashness turn them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions; and, following the example of our predecessor Pope Eugenius of holy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of the present document.

First, we decree that the monastic order established in that monastery according to God, the Rule of Blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall there be inviolably observed for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically holds, or may in the future acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings and princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means through God’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have judged the following to be specified by their own names: the land of Runcinaci; the level wood; the water and other lands; meadows and woods; and whatever rights you possess in the territory of Pontigny; the grange of Bunnoiz with its appurtenances; the vineyards of Fulceriis with lands and woods; and whatever rights you possess at Saint Porcaria in lands, woods, waters, and meadows; whatever rights you have in the freehold of Revisi and in the wood of Contest; the vineyards, lands, and meadows of Sableia; the island beside the mill of Novis; the lands of Bretonaria with the wood; [Col. 0424A] the lands and woods of Old Burs, which you hold at a rent of five solidi from the monks of Molesme; the right of user in the woods of Hotta granted you by Atto, Bishop of Troyes; the right of user in the wood of Saint Lupus; the right of user in the woods and lands of the hunters of the castle of Witois; whatever rights you possess at Seveias; the right of user granted you by Archbishop Henry in his woods of Otta; the grange of Creceio, with lands, meadows, woods, and waters; the exchange which you made with the abbey of Saint Germanus concerning land which you hold with it at Creceio and Dulceium; the exchange which you made with the canons of Sens in the territory of Creceio; the islands of the Salo; the vineyards, lands, and meadows which you possess at Saint Florentinus; the lands and woods given you by Milo “Collumgelatum”; [Col. 0424B] the land of Saint Martin of Cableia; the lands of Calliacus; the lands of Vallis-Joardis and of the manors; the lands, meadows, and woods of Campus-Trovetus; the woods of Saint Peter for every use except giving and selling; the land of Villarissicum with all its appurtenances and its rights of use in woods and pastures; the land and wood which were in dispute with the monks of Saint Germanus, which you afterwards possess peaceably at a rent of three solidi; the land of Loronium with wood and open ground; the land of Cariellum with wood and open ground; the wood of Canniellum; the land of Nusi with wood and open ground; the meadows of the islands situated on the river Yonne, and other meadows; the vineyards which you possess at Auxerre; and whatever rights you possess in the wood called Otta, whether in ownership or in rights of use.

We further forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your monastery, to leave the cloister without the abbot’s permission; and no one may dare retain anyone who departs without documentary assurance from the community. Moreover, wishing by paternal consideration to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone, within the enclosures of your places or granges, from daring to commit molestation, robbery, or theft; to set fire; or to seize or kill a person. Indeed, no one may presume to demand tithes from you for the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals.

We therefore decree [Col. 0424D] that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the full benefit of those uses for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this text of our constitution, should rashly attempt to contravene it, and, having been admonished a second or third time, should fail to correct the offence by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Redeemer; [Col. 0425A] and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But let all who preserve the rights of that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Saint Peter. Saint Paul. Pope Alexander III.

“Show me thy ways, O Lord.”

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Gauslinus, Bishop of Albano. I, Wli., priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul at Pammachius. [Col. 0425B] I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Boso, priest-cardinal of Saint Pudentiana, title of Pastor. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, Theodinus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Vitalis, title of Vestina. I, Galdinus, priest-cardinal of Saint Sabina and Archbishop of Milan. I, Jacynthus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Oddo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. [Col. 0425C] I, Cinthus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Hugh, cardinal-deacon of Saint Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Vitellus, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Aquirio. I, Jerome, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Gerard, scribe of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Ides of November … in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

CDXII. To the bishops of England.—He announces that, in the case of Thomas of Canterbury, he has sent two legates *a latere* to England with plenary authority. (Lateran, 1 December.)

[Epistles of St Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 77.]

[Col. 0425D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the bishops established throughout England: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Let your prudence know that it has come to our ears how, because of the burdens which our venerable brother the Archbishop of Canterbury had imposed upon our dearest son in Christ, Henry, illustrious King of the English, upon yourselves also, and upon the kingdom entrusted to his governance, you appealed to our hearing and fixed the coming Ascension Sunday as the term of appeal. But, moved by the prayers of the aforesaid king—whom, as a most Christian prince, we are bound to honour in all things insofar as we can with God and justice; whose devotion we have experienced in an urgent necessity; whom, among the other princes of the world, we love in the Lord with especial charity and embrace with a particular prerogative of affection—and wishing to spare the labours and expenses of both parties, we have judged that persons from our side should be sent to the king’s realm with full power to hear this case and others which they shall recognize as requiring attention, and canonically to conclude them as the Lord grants them ability.

Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, when you are summoned concerning this by the aforesaid persons, you shall come before them and firmly accept and observe whatever they decide among you. Meanwhile, should any of those persons whom the said archbishop has bound by a sentence of excommunication happen to be in danger of death, we permit him to be absolved by whichever of you is nearer, after receiving an oath that, if he recovers, he will obey our command in this matter; or by another religious and prudent man, according to the tenor set out above. Yet, when the aforesaid persons are present, he must make known before them that he has sworn this oath.

[Col. 0426B] Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of December [1 December].

CDXIII. To Henry, King of the English.—That the authority of the Archbishop of Canterbury be suspended until he has obtained peace from the king. (Lateran, 20 December.)

[Ibid., p. 136.]

[Col. 0426C]

We received the envoys of your magnificence—namely, our beloved sons John Cumin and Master Rad. of Tamworth, devoted to us and to the Church of God and, as we believe, in every respect most faithful to royal highness—and the letters which your excellence sent us, with a mind all the more gracious, and we received them with all the greater favour and honour, because we knew more fully that they had been sent by a magnificent prince and most Christian king. To him we certainly desire every glory and honour which we can seek with God; and toward his advancement, by every honourable means available to us, we and our brethren and the whole Church strive all the more ardently to lend support, because we have experienced the devotion of your most sincere affection in a time of greater necessity. For the marks of your devotion, displayed to us at so opportune a time, can never thereafter be erased from our memory or obscured before the eyes of the Church by any neglect.

We have also taken care to put into execution, insofar as we could do so with God and our honour, the requests which you sent us through the aforesaid envoys, as they themselves will explain more fully to your magnificence orally. Accordingly, as you requested, we have decided to send persons from our side to your highness, with full power—although at this time it seems particularly burdensome and difficult for us to send anyone away from ourselves, since we need the presence and counsel of our brethren, especially those whom you desire. Yet, mindful of that memorable and magnificent devotion of yours of which we have spoken, they are to take cognizance of, [Col. 0427A] judge, and canonically conclude, as the Lord grants them ability, the ecclesiastical causes pending between you and our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury; the case pending between that archbishop and the bishops of your kingdom concerning their appeal to us; and also such other causes in your realm as they recognize to require consideration.

Moreover, we have in every way forbidden the same archbishop to attempt, until those cases obtain their due outcome, to burden, disturb, or molest you, your people, or the kingdom entrusted to your governance in any respect. But if that archbishop in the meantime has pronounced any sentence against you, the kingdom entrusted to your governance, or persons of the realm, we judge that sentence void and not binding. As evidence of this matter and proof of our will, show these present letters if an emergency should arise. Otherwise, we request and earnestly admonish your serenity not to allow these letters [Col. 0427C], or their contents, to become known to anyone, but to keep them altogether secret. Those members of your household and your counsellors whom the aforesaid archbishop has subjected to a sentence of excommunication shall, God willing, be absolved by the persons sent from our side. But if any of them in the meantime should be in danger of death, we permit him to be absolved by any bishop or other religious and discreet man, after he has taken the customary oath of the Church that, if he recovers, he will obey our command in this matter. Moreover, we have ordered our brethren whom we are sending there to set out before the coming Nativity of the Lord; and, God willing, they will, as we believe, begin their journey in January.

[Col. 0427D] Given at the Lateran, 13 Kalends of January [20 December].

CDXIV. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—He exhorts him to patience. (At the Lateran? In December.)

[Ibid., I, p. 8.]

ALEXANDER, pope, to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

Having received the letters and envoys of our dearest son in Christ, Henry, illustrious king of the English, we have resolved again to admonish him by our letters and envoy, and by earnest exhortations to soften his mind, so that he may be reconciled to you and restore you to his favour and affection. For we trust and hope [Col. 0428A] in the Lord that he will consent to our warnings and exhortations, and will restore your church to you freely and peaceably. Therefore we ask, admonish, and counsel your prudence that, until we see the end and outcome of this affair, you bear with him patiently and meanwhile establish nothing against him or against anyone in his kingdom that he may consider burdensome or offensive. Certainly, if he should refuse to comply with us through our envoys, should we happen to send any, we will take care, insofar as divine grace permits, to preserve for you and your church your right, honour, and dignity. Finally, you will not lack authority, if he cannot otherwise be recalled, to exercise your office freely. We wish, however, that you keep this secret.

CDXV. To Waldemar, King of the Danes.—Concerning the alteration of the monastery of Weng and the recall of Archbishop Eskil.

[Langebeck, *Scriptores Rerum Danicarum*, V, 238.]

[Col. 0428B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ WALDEMAR, illustrious king of the Danes, greetings and apostolic blessing.

When we hear that you are diligent and attentive in matters pleasing to God, befitting royal dignity, and conducive to the salvation of your soul and to the growth of virtue and religion, we rejoice greatly and commend with heartfelt praises in the Lord the zeal of your exalted rank in this matter. [Col. 0428C] For from the tenor of your letters and those of certain bishops established in your kingdom, we have learned how you, moved by love of divine mercy, considered that the monastery of Weng—which your predecessors founded for the remedy of your soul and enlarged with extensive and great possessions—had been worn down and greatly diminished both spiritually and temporally. With the counsel of those bishops, you therefore undertook its reform; and, making its abbot, to whom it had formerly been granted, a disciple from a master, you granted that same monastery to brethren of the Cistercian Order, so that religious observance and uprightness might be restored there. If this is so, since we hope that it has proceeded from the inspiration of divine grace and from the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, [Col. 0428D] we hold it pleasing and acceptable; and we ratify and confirm what is known to have been established by your serenity, with the salutary counsel of those bishops, in this regard. We ask, admonish, and exhort your highness in the Lord—and equally impose it upon you for the remission of sins—that you devote yourself fervently and devoutly to the increase and relief of the aforesaid monastery; that you strive to love and support the religious men whom, with your assent and favour, our beloved son Sueno, elect of Aarhus, has brought there; and that you preserve their goods with your customary clemency and piety.

Furthermore, we likewise ask and admonish your royal excellence that you persevere, firm and immovable, in devotion to blessed Peter and to us, as you have rightly begun since returning to [Col. 0429A] the unity of the Church; that you diligently admonish and exhort the bishops, all the clergy, and the people of your kingdom to do the same; and that you devoutly and honourably recall to his church our venerable brother Eskil, Archbishop of Lund, legate of the apostolic see, a religious and prudent man, and, as we believe, greatly acceptable to God and men, and most faithful also to you and your realm.

> [Note: [Col. 0429D] Bartholin, *Annales*, note to the year 1166: “Without doubt Eskil, who in 1164 was at Sens, did not dare return because he had adhered so firmly to Pope Alexander while the king favoured Victor; indeed, because of the king’s anger, whom he had offended in various ways, he fled from his presence, first into Gothia and afterwards to the Roman see. For this very diploma shows [Col. 0430D] that the king then acknowledged Alexander as the true pope.”]

Render to him the honour and favour appropriate to him as your spiritual father, and defend and preserve, by royal protection, the rights and goods of his church. For we trust and hope in the Lord that through his zeal the honour and glory of your greatness will be increased, and that, by the Lord’s help, very many benefits and advantages will accrue both to you, to your heir, and to the kingdom [Col. 0429B].

> [Note: [Col. 0430D] According to Bartholin in the *Annals*, this diploma is dated to the year 1166.]

CDXVI. To the bishops of Denmark.—On the same subject.

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers ABSALON, Bishop of Roskilde, and TUCO, Bishop of Burgalen, and to the beloved sons RADULPH, elect of Ribe, and SUENO, elect of Aarhus, greetings and apostolic blessing.

From your letters and those recently received from our dearest son in Christ Waldemar, illustrious king of the Danes, we have learned how he, as a Catholic man kindled by love of heavenly contemplation and inspired by divine grace, [Col. 0429C] has considered that the monastery of Weng—which his predecessors founded for the remedy of his soul and enlarged with lavish and extensive benefactions and possessions—had been greatly worn down and diminished both spiritually and temporally. With your counsel he has usefully and fervently undertaken its reform; and, making the abbot of that place a disciple from a master, he has granted the same monastery to brethren of the Cistercian Order, so that religious observance and uprightness may be restored there. Since, if this is so, we trust it proceeded from the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, we hold it pleasing and acceptable; and we ratify and confirm what is known to have been established by you, with the assent and favour of the aforesaid king, through salutary provision [Col. 0429D]. We ask and admonish your prudence to take care to urge and earnestly persuade the same king to devote his royal piety to the increase and advancement of that monastery; and, standing firm and immovable in devotion to blessed Peter and to us, reverently and devoutly to recall to his own church our venerable brother Eskil, Archbishop of Lund, legate of the apostolic see, a religious man acceptable to God [Col. 0430A], and to render him the honour and favour due to him. For we believe and hope in the Lord that with a pure heart and affection he will devote himself to that archbishop’s honour, advancement, and loyalty, and will prove useful and fruitful to the whole kingdom. We likewise command you that those who have been called to the episcopal burden but have not yet attained the summit of that honour, if he has not returned so soon, should approach the same archbishop humbly and devoutly and receive orders and the gift of consecration from his hand. For it is dangerous that the churches of God should for too long lack the support of a pastor.

> [Note: [Col. 0430D] Bartholin assigns this diploma to the year 1166.]

CDXVII. To Gilbert, Bishop of London.—That he must not omit to transmit the penny of blessed Peter “which is owed to him from England.”

[*Letters of St Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 100.]

[Col. 0430B]

ALEXANDER, pope, to GILBERT, Bishop of London.

We are often told many things about you which neither your religious character in any way warrants nor your outward habit displays. If these things indeed are true, they greatly disturb our mind and wholly remove the hope and esteem we had concerning your religious character. For neither favour, affection, nor fear of anyone ought to lead you to neglect your office and set aside ecclesiastical liberty. Rather, for justice’s sake, you ought to set yourself against them manfully and steadfastly, like an immovable pillar of the Church, and place the fear of God before all things [Col. 0430C]. You should indeed be inflamed with such zeal of charity that you ought not merely cry out against vices and the oppression of churches, but continually raise your voice like a trumpet, always keeping before your eyes that prophetic saying: “Unless you announce to the wicked man his wickedness, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3). Therefore, if you recognize in yourself the matters reported to us, strive to amend them promptly, and henceforth show yourself such that no adverse reports about you are brought to us and ecclesiastical justice cannot in any way suffer loss through you. For if we hear with certainty further such things about you, we shall by no means overlook them; rather, though unwillingly, we shall more severely extinguish in you the fire of our [Col. 0430D] indignation.

Furthermore, we have committed, under a fixed procedure and with the obstacle of appeal set aside, the case pending between our son Richard, bearer of these letters, and William his nephew concerning the church of Hardentona and other matters, to our venerable brothers the bishops of Chichester and Worcester for determination. Therefore, by these apostolic writings we command your brotherhood and enjoin it upon you by virtue of obedience [Col. 0431A] to hold ratified and firm, and cause to be firmly observed with every appeal and contradiction removed, whatever the aforesaid bishops jointly determine between them concerning their complaints, those who mutilated that same Richard, and the chapel of Drinford, said to have been built to the grave detriment of the old church of Hardentona; or whatever either of them may determine if the other cannot be present.

In addition, by this present notification we command your discretion to send the penny of blessed Peter owed to us from England to the abbot of Saint-Bertin, in a specified weight and number. We do not wish your discretion to be unaware that our venerable brother Bartholomew, [Col. 0431B] Bishop of Exeter, has informed us by a report sent to us that he has not diminished that penny, but has paid it to you in full, first or among the first, from his bishopric. We therefore wonder that we have not received it. Accordingly, we wish them to make good what was lacking from the past, and for the present to collect it faithfully and in full.

YEAR 1166–1167.

CDXVIII. To John, Bishop of Maguelonne. (At the Lateran, 26 January.)

[GARIEL, *Series of the Bishops of Maguelonne*, I, 205.]

[Col. 0431C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother, the Bishop of Maguelonne, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since, as the petition you laid before us stated, several canons of the Church of Maguelonne of the Order of Saint Augustine have set their feet upon a slippery path: not only within but also outside the diocese of Maguelonne, without obtaining or even seeking your permission, they wander about in a blameworthy fashion and wish to turn toward pride with unbridled heel. Although you have repeatedly warned them in a spirit of gentleness, you humbly petitioned us to grant you authority to restrain such audacity. Therefore, by these apostolic writings we command your brotherhood [Col. 0431D] freely to perform your office’s duty in these matters concerning the aforesaid canons, notwithstanding any privileges or indulgences from which they might derive protection contrary to regular and canonical discipline.

Given at the Lateran, 7 Kalends of February [26 January], in the second year of our pontificate.

CDXIX. To John, Bishop of Maguelonne. (At the Lateran, 26 January.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brother JOHN, Bishop of Maguelonne, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0432A] Your brotherhood has informed us that, although the canons of the Church of Maguelonne of the Order of Saint Augustine, in which you are known to hold ordinary jurisdiction, commit many acts requiring the file of correction, yet under pretext of an apostolic indult which they claim to possess—namely, that the Bishop of Maguelonne may not exercise any ecclesiastical censure upon them without the consent of the chapter of that church—such offences remain uncorrected, to the peril of their souls. You therefore requested that, notwithstanding the aforesaid indult, provision be made through the care of the apostolic see for their salvation. We, therefore, who seek the salvation of each individual, wishing to provide a remedy in this matter and unwilling that the good of correction and reformation in the aforesaid church be impeded on account of such an indult [Col. 0432B], command your brotherhood by apostolic writings: if, according to the custom hitherto observed, correction of the canons’ offences belongs to the said chapter, admonish that chapter diligently to correct those offences within three years, a term to be fixed for them by you; otherwise, from that time onward, with God before your eyes, do not delay to correct them yourself, as care for souls requires, notwithstanding the aforesaid indult and custom, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure.

Given at the Lateran, 7 Kalends of March [23 February], in the second year of our pontificate.

CDXX. He praises Bertrand, Archbishop of Bordeaux, legate of the apostolic see, because he approved the sentence pronounced by Bertrand, Abbot of Holy Cross, against the monks of Saint-Macarius. (At the Lateran, 31 January.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new ed., II, 817, in the text.]

[Col. 0432C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother BERTRAND, Archbishop of Bordeaux, legate of the apostolic see, greetings and apostolic blessing.

As we recently learned from the contents of your letters—

> [Note: [Col. 0431D] See these below, after Alexander’s *Regesta*.]

—you have effectively carried out the tenor of our mandate: you held ratified and firm the sentence which our beloved son Bertrand, Abbot of Holy Cross, pronounced against the monks of Saint-[Col. 0432D]Macarius for their disobedience and rebellion, and you confirmed it by our authority and your own jointly. We therefore commend your diligence as is fitting; and by this present notice we enjoin you to hold that sentence ratified and to cause it to be observed inviolably throughout your diocese until due satisfaction is made. For we shall provide, in accordance with your diligence, for our honour in such a way that, if the said monks come to us, they will, God willing, obtain nothing that they ought to carry away.

Given at the Lateran, 2 Kalends of February [31 January].

CDXXI. To the abbot and brethren of Saint-Remigius.—That they receive William, a fugitive monk. (At the Lateran, 10 February.)

[MARTEN., *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 723.]

[Col. 0433A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of Saint-Remigius of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

On behalf of William, bearer of these letters, we have already for the second time sent you, son abbot, our letters directing you to receive him, with the discipline of your order preserved, and to open the door of mercy. But because, as he has informed us, he has not yet been received, and because we fear shipwreck of his soul if, remaining longer without discipline, he should be forced to return to the pleasures of the world [Col. 0433B], we admonish and command your religious community to receive and treat the aforesaid William kindly, without delay or pretext and with the discipline prescribed by your order preserved; or to restore all his possessions to him in full, and take effective care and pains that he be received in another monastery. Thus hear our warnings and commands in this matter with attentive ears and carry them into effect, so that we may not be compelled to write to you further about it, nor he compelled to trouble himself further by coming to us.

Given at the Lateran, 4 Ides of February [10 February].

CDXXII. To John, Bishop of Maguelonne.—Concerning the canons of the Church of Maguelonne. (At the Lateran, 15 February.)

[GARIEL, *Series of the Bishops of Maguelonne*, I, p. 203.]

[Col. 0433C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother, Bishop of Maguelonne, greetings and apostolic blessing.

From your report it has become known to us that the canons of the Church of Maguelonne of the Order of Saint Augustine, who hold prebends, priories, and administrative offices, trusting that until now they have not customarily been removed from them against their will, nor even made to render a complete account of their administration—which appears contrary to regular propriety and ecclesiastical usefulness—are said sometimes to commit acts offensive to the eyes of divine majesty, at times expending the revenues of those prebends [Col. 0433D] and administrative offices upon illicit uses, to the grave prejudice of the Church of Maguelonne, the scandal of the laity, and the peril of their own souls. You therefore humbly requested us, in paternal concern for the protection of that church and the salvation of souls, to decree that the aforesaid canons be bound, at least once a year, to appear before you and the chapter of that church in respect of the aforesaid prebends, priories, and administrative offices which they hold, where they were installed not by election of the chapter nor canonically in those same prebends and priories, and to render an account of their stewardship; and that they be compelled to do this by you with due discretion.

[Col. 0434A] Thus, if the archdeacons, archpriests, or sacristan—whom in that church you alone appoint according to the custom hitherto observed—or priors, to whom priories belonging to the chapter of that church are customarily committed by you and the provost, are found, when the account is rendered, to deserve removal from the offices or administrations committed to them because of some fault or negligence, you may freely remove such persons, whose offices or administrations you alone have the right to confer, once the accounts have been rendered; or transfer them from place to place, as you see expedient. And after a few words. Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your brotherhood, with the counsel of the provost and such canons of that church as you see fit, to establish by our authority whatever you judge regular, honourable, and consistent with the salvation of souls and ecclesiastical benefit in these matters, restraining opponents by ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside [Col. 0434B].

Given at the Lateran, 15 Kalends of March [15 February], in the second year of our pontificate.

> [Note: [Col. 0433] The words “in the second year of our pontificate” were added by another hand.]

CDXXIII. To Stephen, Bishop of Meaux.—If a convent cannot agree on the election of an abbot, the bishop is to confirm as abbot the person upon whom the greater and sounder part has agreed. (At the Lateran, 18 February.)

[PETIT, *The Penitential of Theodore*, II, 611.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable [Col. 0434C] brother STEPHEN, Bishop of Meaux, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Because of dissension among the brethren, monasteries in your diocese frequently happen, as you assert, to lack a pastor for a long time. Their efforts are greatly drawn in different directions, so that they cannot agree upon one person; and you desire this one remedy to be applied, lest religious houses suffer more grievously through want of a pastor—may God avert it. In due favour of your wish, by these present letters we grant you that, whenever any monastery of your jurisdiction becomes vacant and the brethren or sisters of that place cannot, even upon your admonition, agree within a suitable period to be fixed by you [Col. 0434D] upon a suitable person, it shall be lawful for you, by apostolic authority, to confirm as abbot or abbess—provided the person is suitable—the person upon whom you know the greater and sounder part of the chapter has agreed.

Given at the Lateran, 12 Kalends of March [18 February].

CDXXIV. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of Robert the priest. (At the Lateran, 20 February.)

[MARTEN., *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 724.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0435A] Robert, a priest, has informed us that the canons of Roye granted him two churches for an annual rent, under the jurisdiction of one of which a certain chapel of lepers had been placed; and, by concession of the aforesaid canons, we granted that chapel, as is said, its own liberty. Since he asserts that he has thereby incurred a loss of thirty pounds, and since it is neither just nor consonant with reason that, now that his benefice has been diminished, he should be bound to pay the canons the full rent, we command your brotherhood by apostolic writings to summon both parties before you, hear and ascertain fully the arguments on either side, and endeavour, by justice and with the obstacle of appeal removed, to settle the case within forty days after receiving these letters [Col. 0435B]; namely, to cause the rent to be reduced in proportion as the benefice has been reduced.

Given at the Lateran, 10 Kalends of March [20 February].

CDXXV. To the same.—On behalf of Robert the priest.

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Robert, a priest and bearer of these letters, coming to us at great danger and labour, humbly represented that, although he had obtained from the canons of Roye a certain tithe for a rent of eighty measures of grain annually, [Col. 0435C] when a storm of the weather supervened, he obtained from that aforesaid tithe only forty-one measures; and because he was compelled to pay it in full, he incurred a loss of eighty-eight pounds. Since it seems unworthy and inhumane that, when he has not received the whole yield, he should bear the whole burden, we have thought fit to commit this case to your experience. By apostolic writings we command your brotherhood that, when requested in this matter, you summon both parties before you, fully hear and ascertain the arguments on either side, and endeavour, by justice and with the obstacle of appeal removed, to decide the case within forty days after receiving these letters.

[Col. 0435D] Given at the Lateran, 10 Kalends of March [20 February].

CDXXVI. To the abbot and brethren of Cluny, concerning the election, through necessity and without their counsel and authority, of the abbot of Saint Benedict of Padilirone; it is not to be drawn into precedent. (At the Lateran, 1 March.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, 72.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons, the holy abbot and brethren of Cluny, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother the Patriarch of Grado, our beloved son Iliad., cardinal-priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles and legate of the apostolic see, and the bishops of Brescia and Castellano, informed us by letters sent to us [Col. 0436A] that, after Geru, of good memory, formerly abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict above the Po, had been removed from this life as pleased the Redeemer, their minds were uncertain how they might most fittingly proceed to the election of his successor. They summoned to themselves the Catholic monks of that congregation, after due deliberation, and diligently sought to move and exhort them to agree together upon some person. Divine grace gave them such peace and concord of unanimity in making the election that all, with one vote and common consent, chose as their abbot our beloved son Raim., their prior, who is known to shine with many virtues of religion and discretion [Col. 0436B].
