Yet hardened in their obstinacy, they have refused to acknowledge the guilt of their offence or to take care to return to satisfaction. Therefore it may deservedly be said of them: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1); for they now seem fixed in the deep mire, and the pit of the abyss seems to have shut its mouth over them.

They should certainly know that the virtue of obedience incomparably surpasses every kind of sacrifice, and that by it Almighty God wonderfully restored to heavenly glory the first man, who had fallen miserably through pride. Therefore by apostolic letters we have ordered and commanded them, in the virtue of obedience, to request absolution from the aforesaid archbishop with all humility and patience, [Col. 0464B] and humbly and devoutly to render to him and to his Church the due obedience and reverence required by metropolitan right. But if . . . . . given over to pride and disobedience, they refuse to put away a reprobate mind, we have firmly commanded the legate whom, God favouring us, we are sending to those regions to cause the archbishop’s sentence to be observed unshaken and inviolate, and, if they do not come to their senses even thus, to endeavour to punish them by another means.

Nevertheless, we command you by this injunction that, so long as the aforesaid bishops persist in excommunication, you shall by no means show them filial devotion or any subjection, nor reverence them, until they strive humbly to obey the archbishop as their metropolitan in those matters which are God’s. [Col. 0464C]

CDLXVII. To Henry, King of the English.—He announces that Henry’s letters have been delivered to him by Clarembald, Reginald, Simon de Carcere, and Henry of Northampton.

[Letters of St Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 128.]

Pope ALEXANDER to HENRY, King of England.

We have received with the due kindness the envoys of your Highness, our beloved sons Clarembald, elect of St Augustine’s, Reginald, Archdeacon of Salisbury, Simon de Carcere, Henry of Northampton, and the letters of your royal sublimity sent to us through them. Recalling attentively the ardour of that most fervent charity which your magnificence has, from the beginning of our promotion, so steadfastly and warmly displayed towards us and the Church [Col. 0464D] of God, we have taken care to lend a favourable ear to what the aforesaid envoys discreetly and with all diligence conveyed to us on behalf of your Highness, although those matters were exceedingly arduous and difficult.

Indeed, not forgetting that honour and reverence which royal serenity, at the time when necessity pressed, as we remember having often informed your Highness, bestowed upon us with total devotion, as the greater part of Christendom has known, we are ardently moved to advance your petitions wherever we can do so with God; nor will any favour or honour which we can grant your Highness ever seem sufficient to us. [Col. 0465A]

Nevertheless, considering that you, to whom the almighty Lord has granted abundance among the sons of men in such great wealth and such power in prudence and discernment, will not wish to fight against Him whom to serve is to reign, nor resist His will—especially since He has so often granted your valour triumph over the enemy—we fully trust and hope in His boundless goodness that He will make your mind and will gentler concerning the Church and its affairs, and incline your heart to what is His good pleasure. This is so, although the aforesaid envoys firmly asserted that you were stirred by such disturbance that you would in no way receive our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Canterbury, into favour, nor could your mind be softened towards him.

[Col. 0465B] But we, who cannot forget our fatherly affection toward your person, and who desire to honour and hear you in all things, as a Catholic prince and most Christian king, so far as propriety permits, firmly believing and hoping that your prudent foresight does not fail to know that in matters of God and affairs belonging to the Church it is more glorious to have one’s own will overcome than to overcome it, have commanded and utterly forbidden the aforesaid archbishop, in hope and confidence almost amounting to certainty that He in whose hand are the hearts of kings will deign to soften your mind, to attempt in any way to pronounce against you, your land, or the persons of your realm a sentence of interdict or excommunication, until you receive him into your favour and are reconciled with him; [Col. 0465C] nor may he presume in any respect to burden you.

And since it is established that those letters which we last sent to your magnificence last year through your envoys are henceforth without force if, meanwhile, the aforesaid archbishop should presume to burden you, your land, or persons of your kingdom in any respect, you may show these present letters as evidence of our will and demonstrate that you and yours are immune from his burdens.

You ought not at all to wonder that you found variation in our writings or legates, since even blessed Paul is read to have changed his purpose more than once; although we do not in the least recollect having changed our purpose in this matter. For it had been reliably communicated to us—not indeed on your behalf—and a hope and confidence almost certain had been given us, [Col. 0465D] that the aforesaid archbishop would be reconciled to you through their mediation. This we seemed to understand more fully also from certain writings shown to us. Hence it happened that, on this ground and in accordance with the statement of your envoys, we sent those same legates to your royal Highness. While they were still present before us, we charged them in the presence of certain of our brethren, on the strength of this confidence, that they should in no way proceed by judicial order in the hearing of causes between you and the archbishop, especially since we were, as we have said, almost certain of the reconciliation.

Therefore, if we have so written and commanded, your prudence ought not to be brought to any astonishment, nor should it attribute to any fickleness what we did for your honour and under such hope—especially since we are men and in many matters may be deceived or misled. [Col. 0466A]

CDLXVIII. He rebukes Hugh, Archbishop of Sens, because “without the knowledge and command of [Alan], Bishop of Auxerre, he received his resignation.” He nevertheless permits him to consecrate [William], elected in his place.

[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 1083.]

We believe that it has come to the knowledge of your fraternity with what importunity and insistence of prayers our venerable brother, hitherto Bishop of Auxerre, repeatedly asked us to be relieved of episcopal responsibility, and how we could by no means be induced to assent to his request and wish. [Col. 0466B] Therefore, although he himself, as a religious man, perhaps voluntarily resigned the administration entrusted to him from both humility and weakness of mind and body, nevertheless, unless his resignation is first approved by the Roman pontiff, he has neither been released from that administration nor relieved of the governance entrusted to him.

Accordingly, you had no right whatever, without our knowledge and command, to receive his resignation; nor could the chapter of Auxerre treat of an election or proceed to anyone’s nomination. Therefore, if we wished to preserve the rigour of the canons, the authorities of the holy Fathers, and the statutes, we could sharply rebuke you [Col. 0466C] according to the desert of the deed, severely and strictly punish them for the audacity of so great a presumption, and declare that, because the matter has proceeded neither according to right order nor according to the form of the canons, their election ought to have no force by reason of the act itself.

Yet because you have regarded every deed and cause of the Church as your own, and because we are in many respects bound to you and ought, desire, and are obliged, wherever we can do so with God and justice, to defer to your honour and advancement, we do not make a law for the future but prohibit such things from being done henceforth. By the moderation of apostolic dispensation, and not by reason of the deed, we command your prudence to accept without delay our beloved son W., your brother, whom among our other brethren we hold most dear on account of our affection for your worth [Col. 0466D] and whom, because of his foresight and discernment, we believe will bring the aforesaid church spiritual and temporal increase; to ordain him priest at a suitable time; and finally, with the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit, to consecrate him bishop.

CDLXIX. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—That he cease harassing the canons of Reims.

[D. MARLOT, *Metropolis Remensis*, II, 393.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HENRY, Archbishop, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0467A] The greater the dignity and nobility of blood in which you excel, the more it becomes you to show yourself mild and benevolent toward your subjects, and among your other pursuits to apply the whole attention of your zeal to appearing to treat them gently and kindly. We have learned from our beloved sons, the canons of your Church, that you treat them too harshly and severely, have laid your hand upon them beyond measure, and, to their oppression, have appealed to our dearest son in Christ, your brother the illustrious King of the Franks. This was entirely unbecoming to you: in doing so you have made insufficient provision for ecclesiastical liberty, and have neither considered nor reflected how harmful it may hereafter be to that Church that you caused it to be burdened through the same [Col. 0467B] king, besides the burden imposed by yourself.

For if the aforesaid king, so Catholic and most Christian, and a lover of ecclesiastical liberty, extends his hand to the goods of that Church, his heirs, who perhaps will not be such lovers of ecclesiastical liberty, may, following the example of this act, inflict still graver injuries upon it and the other churches of the realm. If this should happen—which God forbid—it would deservedly result in detriment to your eternal salvation.

Since, therefore, it is fitting that you should have peace and concord with all your subjects, and especially with the clerics of the cathedral Church, and that in view of your power and nobility you should more readily refrain from burdening them—for in every conflict the one who has greater power, even when suffering an injury, seems to inflict it—[Col. 0467C] we admonish, command, and order your fraternity to return to yourself; carefully consider what befits your foresight and nobility; love the aforesaid canons with fatherly charity; and strive, also with the same king, to secure for them his favour and the merciful restoration of all that has been taken away. Thus show yourself kind and generous toward them and all your subjects, so that you may seem more loved than feared. For the aforesaid Church and canons will not endure your burden or injury, nor will discord or scandal between you and them continue, without damage to your reputation.

CDLXX. To Louis, King of the Franks.—That he restore both his favour and the possessions taken away to the canons of the Church of Reims.

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0467D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Among the other works of piety to which the greatness of your royal serenity gives heed, this is what will more abundantly bring you the fullness of everlasting reward and the glory of eternal praise: that, as a most Christian king and Catholic prince, above the other kings and princes of the world you especially advance and preserve ecclesiastical liberty, and that you are zealous and diligent in maintaining the ecclesiastical [Col. 0468A] order. Therefore it becomes your royal prudence, with unfailing care and concern and with the devoted affections of your heart, to imitate this pious and praiseworthy work, and never to allow any persons’ suggestions to draw you away from that which unquestionably prepares eternal salvation for you and everywhere increases the renown of your glorious name.

We have learned that, taking occasion from the discord which is said to have arisen between our venerable brother the archbishop and our devoted sons, the canons of Reims, you exacted from those canons certain things contrary to custom; because they refused them to you, you became angry with them and, at your own will, withdrew certain possessions belonging to them and their Church. [Col. 0468B] Therefore, because we love your person with such fervent charity that we would never wish to do anything by which your royal greatness might deservedly be diminished before God or men, we ask, admonish, and exhort your Highness in the Lord, and impose it upon you for the remission of sins, that, for the sake of divine recompense, reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, and your own salvation, you mercifully restore your favour and love to those canons, restore all that has been taken away, diligently attend to restoring peace between that archbishop and the canons, and preserve the aforesaid Church in its liberty, so that, as that Church is held distinguished and eminent in your realm, it may enjoy peace and tranquillity.

[Col. 0468C] For it is indeed unworthy and utterly unbecoming that, whereas the aforesaid archbishop and canons ought to be of one mind and feeling, scandal should appear to continue between them for so long.

YEAR 1168.

CDLXXI. He commends Tribunus, Archbishop of Ragusa, to the abbots and other Latins, clergy as well as laity. (Benevento, January 3.)

[FARLATI, *Illyricum sacrum*, VI, 81.]

[Col. 0468D] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his sons the abbots and the other Latins, clergy as well as laity, dwelling at Durrës, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Lest care for the Lord’s sheep established in different parts of the world should be lacking, the Roman pontiff has called others to share in the administration entrusted to him, so that through them he may more diligently perform the solicitude and care which, being present, he cannot bestow upon all at once. Therefore, because we cannot visit you in bodily presence, nor can our brother cardinals, who are being sent to the illustrious Emperor of Constantinople through . . . . ., remain with you there for a longer time, we have thought fit to visit you as beloved sons through our venerable brother T., Archbishop of Ragusa, [Col. 0469A] an honourable, prudent, and discerning man; so that in our stead he may root out among you what he finds needs uprooting and plant what he knows should be planted.

Therefore we admonish and command the prudence of you all by apostolic letters that you receive the aforesaid archbishop kindly when he comes among you, and take care humbly to assent and obey his counsels and commands in matters concerning the salvation of your souls. Nor should you presume to communicate with those whom he has excommunicated, especially the bishops of Antivari and Dulcigno, so long as they persist in excommunication; thus we may be able to commend your devotion, and he may be able to plant good seed among you.

[Col. 0469B] Given at Benevento, on the third day before the Nones of January.

CDLXXII. Privilege for the Church of Jerusalem. (Benevento, February 8.)

[Eugène de ROZIÈRE, *Cartulaire du Saint-Sépulcre*, 319.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother AMALRIC, Patriarch of Jerusalem, and his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

The benefits which divine mercy has bestowed upon the whole world in the land of Jerusalem, in proportion as they have profited all nations for salvation, invite the whole world to the praise of God and veneration for the Church of Jerusalem. There was made the bread that came down from heaven, which, when tasted, fattens the souls of the hungry; in whose strength Elijah walked forty days; and by whose nourishment we believe that we shall reach Mount Horeb, the mountain of God. [Col. 0469C] There rose the Morning Star that knows no setting; from there the radiance of eternal brightness shone forth through the whole world; from there flowed the first beginnings of the Christian faith.

It is therefore fitting, and reason requires, that the whole world should applaud that place and venerate the Church of Jerusalem above other places in proportion as it sees that it has received greater benefits from it. Although this duty lies upon all people, it especially belongs to us, who, though our merits do not support us, have received, as God Himself has been pleased to ordain, the care of all the churches; and to whom the receiving of fraternal confirmation is known especially to belong through succession to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. [Col. 0469D]

Moreover, that Church has always cleaved with undivided charity to the Apostolic See; it has never been torn apart by heresies, never lost the radiance of the true light; and the more harshly it has been battered by the waves of encircling storms, the more diligently it has diffused throughout the world the fragrance of its virtue and constancy.

[Col. 0470A] Accordingly, venerable brother in Christ Amalric, Patriarch, embracing your person fully in the arms of charity, both on account of your integrity and out of reverence for the Church entrusted to you, and by the authority of the prince of the apostles granted us from above, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory Paschal, Innocent, Lucius, Anastasius, and Adrian, Roman pontiffs, we decree that all cities and provinces which divine grace restored to Christendom in the times of both Baldwins and Fulk, Kings of Jerusalem, and all honours or dignities, all possessions, and all goods which that Church presently holds by metropolitan, primatial, proprietary, or any other just right or title, or may hereafter acquire by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, the Lord granting it, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your [Col. 0470B] successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the tithes of the Church and the other possessions of Jericho, Daron, and Nablus, and of places in the diocese where bishops once were but are no longer, and of other places which you are presently known justly to possess. Further, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your Church the patriarchal dignity and reverence in the churches subject to the patriarchate of Jerusalem; the rights belonging to the same Church and due to you and your successors; and the good and ancient customs which the Church itself is known to have had in the times of your predecessors or to have received from others, both in church solemnities and in penances, burials, the baptismal font, the blessing of brides, and the purification [Col. 0470C] of women.

Whatever, moreover, was reasonably granted or restored to the Church of Jerusalem through the endeavour and power of Baldwin of good memory, formerly King of Jerusalem, and our dearest son in Christ Amalric, illustrious King of Jerusalem, or may hereafter be restored or granted to the same Church, shall likewise be preserved unshaken and entire for you and your successors.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no one whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be kept unimpaired and entire for [Col. 0470D] the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to their every benefit, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this page of our constitution, attempts rashly to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, does not correct that presumption by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be made a stranger to the most sacred body and blood of God; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of the same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before [Col. 0471A] the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, Bishop of Ostia. I, Bernardus, Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Boso, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, title of Pastor. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint [Col. 0471B] Mark. I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of Saint Vitalis, title of Vestina. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro.

Given [at] Benevento, through the hand of Gerard, notary of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of February, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1167, [Col. 0471C] and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

CDLXXIII. He writes to P[eter], prior, and the brethren of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem, that he has admonished P[atriarch] A[malric] by letter not to “presume for any reason to involve himself in their goods or obediences unless requested by them”; and that, “when they wished to receive someone as a fellow canon, he should grant them favour in this and impose no one upon their community”; nor should he assign prebends in their church “to various persons, against their will, according to his own pleasure.” (Benevento, February 15.)

[Ibid., p. 283.]

[Col. 0471D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, prior, and the brethren of the Holy Sepulchre, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we have learned from the report of our beloved sons P . . . and G . . . , your fellow brethren, our venerable brother Amalric, Patriarch of Jerusalem, does not allow you to have, as you wish, the free administration of your affairs granted you by his predecessors and confirmed by the privileges of ourselves and our predecessors; rather, uninvited, he involves himself in the granting and removal of your obediences. Therefore, since the same patriarch ought so to vindicate his own rights that he does not injure those of others, nor usurp for himself what does not concern him, [Col. 0472A] we command and enjoin him by apostolic letters that henceforth he presume in no way to involve himself in your goods or obediences, contrary to the grants of his predecessors confirmed by the privileges of ourselves and our predecessors, unless he is requested by you concerning the matter; but that he permit you to have that same free administration without contradiction or impediment, as it is known to have been granted to you.

Furthermore, by the authority of our letters we have firmly enjoined the said patriarch that, when you wish to receive as a fellow canon someone suitable and reputable, he grant you his favour and assent in this, and impose no one upon your community, as he is said hitherto to have been accustomed to do, [Col. 0472B] unless that person is distinguished by proven integrity and is such as you or another ought not rightly to reject; and that he do this with your counsel and consent. If he acts otherwise, with the Lord as author, we shall take such care for your Church that henceforth he will be unable to attempt such acts, even if he wishes.

Moreover, know that it has been reported to us that in the aforesaid church, against your will, he assigns prebends to various persons according to his own pleasure and provides for their needs from your affairs and goods, especially since your goods and possessions are altogether distinct and separate from those belonging to the same patriarch. Since it is not fitting that he should be generous from your goods and parsimonious from [Col. 0472C] his own, we have more strictly forbidden him by apostolic authority to do such things hereafter without your counsel and will.

Given at Benevento, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March.

CDLXXIV. He informs P[eter], prior, and the brethren of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem that he has directed P[atriarch] A[malric] “to require from them no more than one third of the wax brought to their church”; that “if he entered any city and stayed there while going to or returning from an expedition, he should allow them to have all offerings made there after the second day”; and that he should not forbid either “the bodies of the dead to be brought before their altars” or “crosses to be held before them on the day of Parasceve [Good Friday].” He also announces that the Hospitallers have been admonished not to “attempt to withhold tithes from them whenever they have any complaint against them.” (Benevento, February 15.)

[Ibid., p. 284.]

[Col. 0472D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, prior, and the brethren of the Holy Sepulchre, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received with fatherly kindness our beloved sons P . . . and G . . . , your fellow brethren, whom you sent to our presence concerning your affairs; and we have lent a favourable ear to what they proposed to us on your behalf with sufficient discernment and diligence. So far as propriety allowed, we have taken care to advance these matters, as you will learn more fully from the spoken account of the aforesaid G . . . and as will become clearer to you through our letters addressed to different persons.

[Col. 0473A] In particular, we have commanded our venerable brother Amalric, Patriarch of Jerusalem, that he require from you, contrary to the tenor of your privileges, no more than a third part of the wax brought to your church; that he be content only with the share due him under the privileges; and that he compel neither you nor the person who administers the wax to pay more to him or others.

Concerning offerings made to the Lord’s Cross, we have directed him that, if he enters any of the cities and stays there while going to or returning from an expedition, he must permit you to have without diminution all offerings that the devotion of the faithful makes to it after the second day, and must henceforth in no way presume to withhold them from you. [Col. 0473B] Concerning also the bodies of the dead which, as we have heard, the aforesaid patriarch forbids to be brought before your altars, and the crosses which he does not permit to be held before those altars on the day of Parasceve [Good Friday], we have further commanded that he must not henceforth do this contrary to the custom of your Church.

If he wishes to conceal from you our letters addressed to him on this matter and to pass over our commands in this respect with deaf ears, keep these present letters at hand and show them for your protection; and you shall not be bound further to answer him in this matter contrary to our written orders.

Henceforth we firmly and strictly command the Hospitallers that, whenever they have any complaint against you, they shall not attempt to withhold tithes from you. Rather, from all their possessions situated in the bishopric [Col. 0473C] of Jerusalem, which they do not cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense but have handed over to others to cultivate, they shall pay you whole tithes, all contradiction and appeal ceasing. From their own labours, cultivated by their own hands or at their own expense, they shall render you tithes without any diminution according to the agreement made between you. They must in every way take care not to presume, on the pretext of any complaint which may arise between you, to withhold or deny those tithes; but if they have anything against you, they must seek their remedy from you in judicial order.

Given at Benevento, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March.

CDLXXV. He informs Peter, prior, and the brethren of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem that he has sent letters to the Hospitallers, ordering them not to deny them tithes; not “to presume to build anew a church in the city of Joppa without the consent of the patriarch and of themselves”; nor, “when Joppa has been placed under interdict, in their church situated within the body of the city, to ring bells or admit excommunicated persons or persons individually named under interdict to the divine offices.” (Benevento, February 15.)

[Ibid., p. 286.]

[Col. 0473D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, prior, and the brethren of the Holy Sepulchre: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received with paternal kindness our beloved sons P . . . and G . . ., your fellow brethren, whom you sent to our presence concerning your affairs; and we have given a willing ear to the matters which they discreetly and diligently set before us on your behalf. So far as propriety permitted, we have taken care to advance them, as you will learn more fully from the spoken report of the aforesaid P . . ., and as will become more plainly known to you through our letters addressed to various persons.

In particular, we firmly and strictly command the Hospitallers that, whenever they have any complaint against you, they shall not venture to withhold tithes from you, but shall pay you in full the tithes from all their possessions situated in the bishopric of Jerusalem which they do not cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense, but have entrusted to others for cultivation—without objection or appeal. From the produce which they cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense, they shall render tithes without any diminution, in accordance with the agreement made between you; taking every precaution not to presume, on the pretext of any complaint arising between you, to withhold or deny those tithes to you. But if they have anything against you, let them seek their justice by due judicial process.

We have likewise forbidden those same Hospitallers to presume to build anew a church in the city of Joppa without the consent of the patriarch and yourselves, especially since it is established that they already possess another church in that city. Moreover, we add that, when the aforesaid city of Joppa has been placed under interdict on account of certain criminal offences, those Hospitallers shall not venture, in their church which stands within the body of the city, to ring bells or to admit excommunicated persons or persons individually named under interdict to the divine offices; but, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, they shall perform the divine offices for their household alone, in a subdued voice. If they henceforth attempt this and a repeated complaint concerning it reaches us, we shall take care to punish it so severely that, even if they wish it, they shall thereafter lack the power to commit such acts.

If they should wish to conceal from you our letters sent to them on this matter, and to pass over our commands in this respect with deaf ears, keep these present letters at hand and produce them for your protection.

Given at Benevento, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March [15 February].

CDLXXVI. He forbids the patriarch of Jerusalem “to presume to appoint or depose abbots, abbesses, or other ecclesiastical persons without the assent and counsel of the prior and canons of the Holy Sepulchre.”

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 433.]

[Col. 0474D]

CDLXXVII. Privilege for the church of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem. (Benevento, March 21.)

[ROZIÈRE, *Cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre*, 278.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, prior of the church of the Holy Sepulchre, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0475A] Whenever something is requested of us which is known to accord with religion and uprightness, it is fitting that we grant it with a willing mind and afford suitable support to the petitioners’ wishes. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, and, following the example of our predecessors of pious memory—Honorius, Innocent, Celestine, Lucius, and Eugenius, Roman pontiffs—we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, we establish that the canonical order which is known to have been instituted in that church according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolate for all time. We further establish that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by name:

Namely, one half of all offerings made at the Lord’s Sepulchre; the offerings of the Cross, except only on the day of Holy Friday [*sancta Parasceve*], and when the patriarch carries it with him for some necessity; the tithes of the city of Jerusalem and of the whole bishopric, by gift of Arnulf, formerly patriarch of Jerusalem; at Neapolis, the land which Amalric, illustrious king of Jerusalem, gave you in the new borough, and the church which you built there, by concession of our venerable brother Amalric, patriarch; likewise the houses and other lands which you possess in the same city; the tithes of the village called Derina, and the orchard between the wall of Tyre and the outer defensive wall, by gift of Peter of blessed memory, formerly archbishop of Tyre; the villages which you purchased from Hugh of Ibelin, namely Bethel, Hudemamel, Dersabe, Huodabes, and Dermursur, with their appurtenances; likewise the villages purchased from John Gothman, namely Betatap and Derasen, in their entirety, that is, with their wastelands and appurtenances; further, the village called Geladia, which the aforesaid king, then count of Ascalon, granted you in return for the expenditure and dispatch which you made for the taking of Ascalon; [Col. 0475D] also the two villages Capharuth and Old Bethoron, and the wasteland of Derfres, purchased from the abbot and monks of Saint Sabas; likewise the land which Vivian, lord of Caypha, gave within and outside the church of the Holy Sepulchre, and the house which you built there, and the land which Roger and John, two brothers, gave to that church.

We likewise confirm to you the church and the tithes of the aforesaid land and its animals, which our venerable brother Ernesius, archbishop of Caesarea, granted to you and confirmed by his own privilege; the church of the Holy Sepulchre at Acre with its appurtenances; by gift of Lambert, the village called Mimas, with two full ploughlands of land; two ploughlands which Girald of Cunin . . . . . gave you; the garden which had belonged to Mainard of Port, which his son Raymond, having become a brother of the Holy Sepulchre, gave to the church; moreover, the two villages Gebul and Hecar with all their adjacent lands; fishing for eight days on the Sea of Tiberias; a day’s compulsory service; and a ship in perpetuity, in the manner in which William of Bures granted these things to the aforesaid church and Walter, prince of that city, confirmed them by his own privilege.

At Calcalia: the house and lands which Fed . . . ., a brother of the Holy Sepulchre, gave you, and whose gift Bartholomew, lord of the town, ratified, adding one ploughland of land. Moreover, all the houses which you possess in the city of Jerusalem, as the aforesaid king confirmed to you in his own document; and we also confirm by apostolic authority the house which the archbishop of Tyre sold to you.

We likewise confirm to you by apostolic authority the stations of the Lord’s Temple, the Mount of Olives, Mount Sion, and the Valley of Jehoshaphat on their feast days, as the church of the Lord’s Resurrection has always been accustomed to hold them; provided that, in the patriarch’s absence, the prior then in office may solemnly celebrate Mass at them and arrange a procession with the canons. We further add that you may lawfully condemn by sentence of interdict and excommunication, in the absence of your patriarch, your malefactors—and especially those who withhold tithes from you—who belong to your parish, whether within or outside Jerusalem, unless, after lawful admonition, they make satisfaction.

[Col. 0476C] We also establish that the patriarch or prior may not dispose of, alienate in any manner, or mortgage the church’s property except by the common counsel of the canons, or of their sounder part. Things already known to have been alienated from your church to its damage and loss may lawfully be reclaimed by you on reasonable grounds. We further decree that it shall not be lawful for the patriarch or prior, without the counsel and assent of the chapter or its sounder part, to send any of you to an overseas obedience, suspend him from his office, or remove him from the fellowship of the canons, except because of a manifest and public fault, or one of which he is confessed or convicted.

Furthermore, the body of the Lord and ecclesiastical burial shall not be denied to your fellow brethren unless they are excommunicated or individually named under interdict. To the foregoing we add that the patriarch shall not dare to demand by obedience from your fellow canons or brethren anything from the property of your church that does not belong to him by right. Certainly, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you of your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals.

Upon the death of the patriarch of that place, no one shall be set over it by any craft of stealth or violence, except the person whom the brethren of that place by common assent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall canonically determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the statutes of the holy Fathers.

We decree, therefore, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right and reverence due to the patriarch of Jerusalem. If anyone therefore, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, have subscribed.  
I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul of Pammachius, have subscribed.  
I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, have subscribed.  
I, Boso, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark, have subscribed.  
I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of Saint Vitalis, of the title of Vestina, have subscribed.  
I, Hyacinthus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed.  
I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore, have subscribed.  
I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, have subscribed.  
I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius beside the Temple of Agrippa, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Acquiro, have subscribed.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Gerard, notary of the holy Roman Church, the sixth day before the Nones of March [2 March], in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1167, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

CDLXXVIII. He upholds for the monastery of Saint Walaric the parochial right of the castle of Saint Walaric, which had been denied to the bishop of Amiens. (Benevento, March 21.)

[*Works of Guibert of Nogent*, ed. Luc d’Achery, p. 571.]

[Col. 0477D]

ALEXANDER . . . . . . . . to ASSELIN, abbot, and the brethren of Saint Walaric . . . . . . . .

It is fitting and consonant with reason that, when questions are referred to the Apostolic See, they should there receive their due determination, and that disputes and litigation should come to an end where Mother Church possesses the dignity of primacy. Since, some time ago, a question had arisen between you and the Church of Amiens concerning parochial right in the castle of Saint Walaric and concerning the installation of an abbot in the seat at the time of election, we entrusted that cause for examination to Baldwin, formerly bishop of Noyon, of good memory. He was to receive the arguments and allegations on both sides and the depositions of sworn witnesses, and, if we remember correctly, bring them before us at a specified time with both parties.

When these matters had been examined by him and brought to us, we took care to send our letters on the matter to our venerable brother, the archbishop of Rheims. Therefore, after the acts of both parties—both the arguments and allegations and the depositions of sworn witnesses—had again been brought to us by him under his seal, and when our beloved sons Arnulf and Fulbert, your fellow brethren and representatives, together with Master Gislebert, who had come on behalf of our venerable brother the bishop of Amiens, stood in our presence, we caused the same arguments and allegations to be recited repeatedly before us and our brethren and examined more closely.

[Col. 0478B] When we had inspected the depositions of the sworn witnesses more carefully, although two persons on behalf of the Church of Amiens testified that R., formerly your abbot, was installed in the chair by a certain archdeacon of Amiens, nevertheless more witnesses appeared in your favour, proving more fully that the said R. and your other abbots had been installed in the chair by another person. Concerning parochial right in the aforesaid castle, when we examined the matter more carefully, we could not find two witnesses in agreement for the Church of Amiens, while several sworn witnesses testified that divorces and other parochial acts had been performed by your abbots during the preceding forty years.

We absolve you from the claim of the said bishop and his church, both concerning the installation of the abbot in the chair and concerning the cure of souls and every other parochial right in the aforesaid castle; and by apostolic authority we impose perpetual silence upon them concerning this matter. In order that this judgment of our determination may be observed inviolate for all future time, we have judged it necessary to strengthen it by apostolic authority and secure it by the protection of this present writing; establishing that no person whatsoever may infringe this document of our determination and confirmation or in any way oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia.  
I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of Saint Vitalis, of the title of Vestina.  
I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius beside the Temple of Agrippa.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April [21 March], first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1168, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

CDLXXIX. He takes under protection the nunnery of Saint Victorinus at Benevento and confirms its property, liberty, and privileges. (Benevento, April 26.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, VIII, 119.]

[Col. 0479A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ FUSCHA, abbess of the monastery of Saint Victorinus, situated in the city of Benevento, and her sisters, present and future, professing the monastic life, in perpetuity.

Whenever something is requested of us which is known to accord with religion and uprightness, it is fitting that we grant it with a willing mind [Col. 0479B] and afford suitable support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, we establish that the monastic order known to have been instituted in the same monastery according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Further, whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to those . . . . . who shall succeed you. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by name:

Within the city of Benevento: houses with rural holdings and all their appurtenances; the church of the Holy Cross at Porta Summa with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Severian with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Saviour of Prata with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Saviour of Alife with its churches, namely the church of Saint Secundinus, the church of Saint Martin, the church of Saint Mary of the Hollowed Sand, the church of Saint Vitalian, the church of Saint Peter of the Old Market, the church of Saint Christopher, the church of Saint Vitus, and the church of Saint Angel of Rapa Canina, with their appurtenances—saving, however, the right which the monastery of Saint Vincent of Monte possesses in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Saviour of Alife; a garden near Saint Erasmus; a garden beside Acqualonga; the vineyard of Casalico; the vineyard of Guardia with their appurtenances; the estate of Mathocca; vineyards and lands at Cupuli with their appurtenances; the vineyard of Faldula with its appurtenances; vineyards and lands of Montore with their appurtenances. At Tina: lands and woods.

Certainly, if merchants and pilgrims wish, out of devotion, to give themselves and their goods to your monastery, you shall have full liberty to receive them. Upon the death of yourself, now abbess of that place, or of any of those who succeed you, no one shall be set over it by any trick of stealth or violence except the woman whom the sisters by common consent, or the sounder part of the sisters, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, choose to be blessed by the Roman pontiff.

And because your monastery is especially of the right and property of blessed Peter and is known to belong directly, without an intermediary, to the care and administration of the Roman Church, we wholly declare void and annul by apostolic authority the condition which you granted to the abbot and brethren of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Vincent in your church—namely, that after your death, daughter abbess, you and those who succeed after you were to elect an abbess by the permission and consent of the abbot of Saint Vincent. For no one could, without consulting the Roman pontiff, impose a new condition upon your aforesaid monastery or alter its status for the worse.

We decree, therefore, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop in the aforesaid churches. If anyone therefore, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, John, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia.  
I, Boso, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark.  
I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of Saint Vitalis, of the title of Vestina.  
I, Hyacinthus, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Andrew, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.  
I, Cynthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian.  
I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius beside the Temple of Agrippa.  
I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Acquiro.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, the sixth day before the Kalends of May [26 April], first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1168, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

CDLXXX. To Henry, king of England.—He urges him to receive Archbishop Thomas of Canterbury into favour. (Benevento.)

[*Letters of Saint Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 126.]

ALEXANDER, pope, to HENRY, king of England.

We do not believe that it has escaped the memory of your royal highness [Col. 0481A] how much we have yielded to you concerning the affair of our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury—would that it had not been against justice. Nor can it be unknown to your highness how often we have restrained his mouth, so that he might be unable to pronounce any sentence against you, your kingdom, or any persons of your kingdom, or to burden you even slightly.

But now, in the hope and confidence that almighty God ought to soften and, in His boundless mercy, calm your mind toward the aforesaid archbishop, although we have endured even what is contrary to ecclesiastical rigour and justice, we ask, admonish, and exhort your serenity through apostolic letters in the Lord; and, for the remission of all your sins, we enjoin upon you that you permit your mind and will to be overcome by the Lord, that you do not desire to fight against God and your own salvation, or deservedly stir up His indignation against you—God forbid!

If, however, you consider more carefully the person of the aforesaid archbishop, or even our own, who, though unworthy, are placed in a higher office, and compare them with your nobility and magnificence, you cannot regard this war or indignation as contributing to your praise and glory, but rather to your dishonour. For you are to show him reverence and honour not because of his nobility or greatness, but solely because of God; and in him you undoubtedly venerate God Himself, who says: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10).

Therefore, if you permit your hardness and purpose in this respect to be overcome, it will lead to your increase and exaltation; and God, before whom you humble yourself, will without any doubt exalt your person. Both spiritually and temporally He will take care to reward your patience and humility, as we signify more fully by word of mouth to you through our venerable brother the bishop of Belley and our beloved son, the Carthusian prior, bearers of these letters—men indeed religious and fearing God. We desire by gentle and mild means to turn the indignation and agitation of your mind from its purpose.

CDLXXXI. To Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury.—Concerning Jocelin, bishop of Salisbury. (Benevento, May 11.)

[Ibid., p. 16.]

[Col. 0481D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We well remember how long ago we loved our venerable brother Jocelin, bishop of Salisbury, and with what devotion and intimacy he was closely attached to us even before the beginning of our elevation; and we believe that this is not unknown to your prudence. Among the other indications of our special favour and affection for him, you can surely remember how, when he had incurred royal anger and wrath, we earnestly and affectionately requested your brotherhood on his behalf to intervene effectively for his reconciliation and to expend diligently every effort and service within your power. You performed this so diligently and commendably that, by God’s grace, our intervention, and your care and effort, he obtained the king’s peace and favour.

Mindful, therefore, both of our affection for him and of his former devotion and intimacy toward us, we have thought fit to commend him particularly to you. Through these present letters we earnestly ask, admonish, and command your sincerity, in which we wholly trust, that, having compassion upon his weakness and old age, and deferring not so much to his age as to our will in his case, and considering also that—as we believe and gather from certain indications—he is not guided by his own spirit but is pressed and compelled against his will by a certain necessity arising from fear of the prince, you shall bear with him kindly in a spirit of patience and gentleness. Until the departure of our envoys, whom we have sent to the same king for your reconciliation, do not in any way whatsoever burden him, just as we also wish you meanwhile to observe this with respect to the king himself and the other persons of that realm.

Thereafter, if peace is restored by God’s agency to you and your church, as we equally desire and hope, then, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, and in order more fully to secure henceforth for ever his own devotion and loyalty and that of his people, lay aside all resentment, if you have conceived any against him; love him, support him, and honour him. Inflict upon him no trouble or burden either through yourself or through the aforesaid king, whose wrath he greatly fears and dreads because he has often experienced it.

He himself will labour effectively, both personally and through his friends and kinsmen, for your peace and reconciliation, and will employ every care and effort he can to this end, so that thereby he may more fully deserve and more abundantly obtain our favour and your goodwill. But if, perchance—may God avert it—the often-mentioned king should decide to persist with hardened heart in his obstinacy, and should not even on this occasion be willing, in your reconciliation and the peace of yourself and your church, to yield to the divine will, our admonition, and his own honour, then, if you judge that the severity of due punishment should be exercised against the kingdom and the persons of the kingdom subject to your jurisdiction by metropolitan or legatine right, and that the injuries done to you and your church should be avenged as you know to be expedient, while preserving episcopal gravity and moderation: because we love the aforesaid bishop, as we have said, with a special and longstanding prerogative of affection, you will do what is wholly pleasing and acceptable to us if you deal with him more gently, so far as you can do so consistently with God and uprightness, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves.

As for the grant of the deanery of the church of Salisbury, which we have certainly learned was granted—indeed, rather extorted—from him, though unwilling and resisting, to John of Oxford at the king’s vehement insistence, it ought not to have incurred your indignation or ill-will. For greater force undoubtedly intervened, and we ourselves gave that same deanery to John by our authority after he had resigned it into our hands.

Given at Benevento, the fifth day before the Ides of May [11 May].

CDLXXXII. To Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury.—He revokes the suspension of his apostolic commission. (Benevento, May 19.)

[Ibid., p. 24.]

[Col. 0483B]

ALEXANDER, pope, to THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury.

We believe that the manner in which Henry, illustrious king of England, sent envoys to us, and how harsh and severe were the things which he requested from us through them—matters that greatly afflicted your mind—has already come to the knowledge of your discretion; he held out terrible threats if we did not yield to his will. But because the persecution of the Church has not yet ceased, nor has the calmness of the times yet smiled upon you as would be fitting, we took care to soften and moderate the onset and blow of his anger, although we did not grant his requests. We were struck by the fear that, in order to hinder and disturb the peace of the Church, he might join himself by some compact of alliance—as he did formerly—to that tyrant and wicked enemy of the Church, or might have grounds for withdrawing from the Church and from devotion to us.

Accordingly, taking account of the evil of the times, and by the common counsel of our brethren, we commanded your brotherhood through apostolic letters, in a certain hope and confidence that he would receive you into his favour and leave the Church of Canterbury to your free administration, not to pronounce a sentence of interdict, excommunication, or suspension against him, the persons of the realm, or the realm itself, unless you received further letters from us. In those letters, should the same king refuse to restore his favour to you, you would have authority to exercise your office against him and his people.

Therefore, because we desire by every means to preserve for you, as a most beloved brother, and for your church its proper honour and liberty, unless he carries into effect by the beginning of the coming Lent what we hope and have proposed to him, but remains hardened in his obstinacy, we henceforth restore your authority to you. You shall then have full liberty, if you judge it fitting and expedient for yourself and your church, to exercise the duty of your office against persons, against the kingdom, and against the king himself, with every obstacle of appeal removed, employing the episcopal gravity and moderation which it is fitting to employ.

Given at Benevento, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June [19 May].

CDLXXXIII. To all the bishops of England.—Against investitures usurped by laymen. (Benevento, May 19.)

[Ibid., p. 78.]

[Col. 0484A]

ALEXANDER, pope, to all the bishops of England.

Common report and the testimony of many have brought to our hearing that, after the recent disturbance which, because of sins, arose between our dearest son in Christ Henry, illustrious king of England, and our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, a certain wicked custom has grown up in those parts: namely, that laymen commonly confer churches and ecclesiastical benefices throughout the kingdom of England upon whomever they wish and invest clerics by their own authority.

Since this is known to be so contrary to the ordinances of the holy Fathers that both giver and receiver from a lay hand are under anathema, and since it undoubtedly results gravely in the ruin of ecclesiastical liberty, we wholly annul by the authority of blessed Peter and ourselves all grants made by laymen, to any persons whatsoever, of any churches during this period of disturbance, and decree them void.

Therefore, through apostolic letters we command and enjoin your whole body under obedience that you diligently admonish and earnestly exhort all those who have received anywhere in England churches, prebends, or other ecclesiastical benefices from a lay hand, especially during this period of disturbance, to resign those churches, prebends, or benefices, with the revenues received from them, into your hands without objection or appeal, and to leave them for disposition by those to whose ordering they belong by ecclesiastical right.

If they fail to do so within forty days after receiving these letters, then, laying aside every fear, favour, and prohibition, and with appeal removed, strike them with sentence of excommunication by our authority; and throughout your dioceses cause all persons to avoid them as excommunicates until they have freely resigned the aforesaid churches [Col. 0484D] and other ecclesiastical benefices to those to whom their grant and ordering belong, left them in peace, and made fitting satisfaction to the Church for the revenues received from them.

But if you are negligent or remiss in carrying these commands out, we decree, by the authority which we exercise, that all those known to have received churches or other ecclesiastical benefices from a lay hand, as stated above, without the assent of the bishops to whom their grant belongs, shall be subject to sentence of excommunication unless they obey our commands within the specified period; and we command that all avoid them as excommunicated by us.

Given at Benevento, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June [19 May].

CDLXXXIV. To John Cumin.—That he restore to Roger, bishop of Worcester, the archdeaconry of Bath which he had seized. (Benevento, perhaps May.)

[Ibid., p. 147.]

[Col. 0485A]

ALEXANDER, pope, to JOHN CUMIN.

It is astonishing, most serious, and altogether grievous to us that you, as has long since become known to us, have presumed by lay authority to claim for yourself the archdeaconry of Bath, and that you have not feared to take it away from our venerable brother, the bishop of Worcester, in the person of Master Baldwin, to whom, while Robert, formerly bishop of Bath, was still living, we confirmed it by the protection of our written instrument [Col. 0485B]. Since we neither ought nor wish to pass over such an offence in silence, we command your belovedness by apostolic letters and enjoin you in virtue of obedience to resign to the aforesaid bishop the said archdeaconry, together with all revenues received from it, all appeal and objection ceasing; to allow him to possess it peacefully and undisturbed; and neither by yourself nor through another to inflict any molestation upon him in this matter or presume to hinder his possession of it. But if you neglect to fulfil our command in this respect within twenty days after receiving these letters, know that we have instructed the aforesaid bishop to declare you excommunicated, with recourse to appeal removed. [Col. 0485C] And if he should perhaps refuse to do this, we have commanded our venerable brother, the archbishop of Canterbury, to declare your person subject to a sentence of excommunication, admitting no appeal whatsoever, and to have you avoided by all as excommunicated until fitting satisfaction has been made. We too shall command that you be held by all the bishops of England to be excommunicated.

CDLXXXV. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—That he absolve Gerard Puella from the sentence by which he is bound. (Benevento, 20 May.)

[Ibid., p. 14.]

[Col. 0485D] ALEXANDER, pope, TO THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

It has been reported to us, and represented on your part, that Gerard Puella, acknowledging his offence, wishes to return to obedience and submission to our command and to renounce in every respect the perversity of schism. Therefore, since we ought always to be imitators of Him who, leaving the ninety-nine in the wilderness, carried the hundredth sheep back upon His own shoulders, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the said Gerard wishes, as has been reported to us, to return to devotion to us and to the Church, you are to receive him after he has taken the oath according to the form which we prescribe for you [Col. 0486A], and in our stead absolve him from the sentence by which he is bound. Yet he must by no means retain the benefice conferred upon him by schismatics, unless perhaps the church in which he holds it, after he has returned to devotion to us and to the Roman Church, should wish to confer it upon him.

Given at Benevento, 13 Kalends of June [20 May].

CDLXXXVI. To Louis, King of the Franks. On behalf of Gerard Puella. (Benevento, 20 May.)

[Ibid., p. 138.]

[Col. 0486B] ALEXANDER, pope, TO LOUIS, King of France.

It has been reported to us that Gerard Puella, acknowledging his offence, wishes utterly to renounce the error of schismatic perversity and to return to obedience to our command and to his lord, our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. Therefore, since it belongs to our office to deal mercifully with offenders and to prefer mercy to judgment, we earnestly request and exhort your serenity by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid Gerard wishes to return to obedience to us, the Church, and his archbishop, and to acknowledge his offence through fitting penance, you permit him to come into your land with your favour, without the rancour of any indignation, and to remain in your kingdom [Col. 0486C] as he had formerly done.

Given at Benevento, 13 Kalends of June [20 May].

CDLXXXVII. To Henry, King of the English.—He grieves that Henry has not yet been reconciled with Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. (Benevento, 22 May.)

[Ibid., p. 130.]

ALEXANDER, pope, to his dearest son in Christ, HENRY, King of England.

Your Highness well knows how fatherly and kindly we have repeatedly approached the royal majesty, and how often through letters and messengers we have exhorted you that you ought to be reconciled with our venerable brother [Col. 0486D] Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, and restore to him and his people the churches together with the other things taken away. For this is public and manifest to almost all Christendom. Therefore, since we have thus far been unable to make any progress in this matter, or to soften the movement of your mind by gentle and mild means, we are made sad and sorrowful. And we grieve that our hope and confidence have been frustrated, especially since we love you more sincerely in the Lord as a most beloved son, and see grave danger threatening you in this matter.

And because it is written: “Cry aloud; do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their crimes” (Isa. 58); and elsewhere: “Unless you declare to the wicked man his wickedness, [Col. 0487A] I shall require his blood at your hand” (Ezek. 3); and again through Solomon, that the slothful man is commanded to be stoned with the dung of oxen, we have judged that we ought no longer to endure, as hitherto, your hardness against justice and our salvation. Nor shall we henceforth for any reason silence the aforesaid archbishop, so as to prevent him freely carrying out the duty of his office and avenging, by the sword of ecclesiastical severity, the injury done to himself and to the church entrusted to him.

What is known to be less fully contained in the letters, both concerning these matters and others, our beloved sons, the prior of Mont-Dieu and Brother Bernard of Corilo—men who indeed revere the countenance of the Lord more than that of man—will set before your serenity more fully by word of mouth. May He whom to serve is to reign, and in whose [Col. 0487B] hand are the hearts of kings, incline your mind and will to heed their admonition, so that you may prefer to yield rather than remain longer, against God and your salvation, fixed in so great an obstinacy of purpose. But if you refuse even then to listen to us in these matters, you may without doubt fear what is to come upon you, as they shall propose to you on our behalf.

Given at Benevento, 11 Kalends of June [22 May].

CDLXXXVIII. To Simon, Prior of Mont-Dieu, and Bernard of Corilo.—On behalf of Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. (Benevento, 25 May.)

[Ibid., p. 113.]

[Col. 0487C]

ALEXANDER, pope, TO SIMON, Prior of Mont-Dieu, and BERNARD OF CORILO.

We wish it to come to the knowledge of your belovedness that we have often and repeatedly admonished, gently and fatherly, our dearest son in Christ, Henry, illustrious king of the English, through messengers and letters, to receive our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, again into his favour and affection, and to recall him to his see and to the church entrusted to him. We have indeed borne with him thus far in the hope and confidence that he ought to soften his mind and will toward the said archbishop. But since [Col. 0487D] we have so far been wholly unable to make progress with him in these matters, and have thereby been made sad and sorrowful, we have judged that he should yet again be admonished through you, who, as we believe and know, revere God more than the countenance of man, as a son whose correction we desire with all the affection of our heart.

Accordingly, we command your belovedness by apostolic letters and enjoin you in virtue of obedience that, assembling together, you are jointly to go to the aforesaid king within two months after receiving these letters, if he is on this side of the sea, all excuse and objection ceasing. You are carefully to admonish and earnestly exhort him, and, on behalf of God and of us, to impose upon him, for the remission of all his sins [Col. 0488A], the obligation of being reconciled with the aforesaid archbishop; of receiving him into his favour and affection with every indignation and rancour set aside; and of not delaying to recall him to the church committed to him. He should carefully consider and attend to how dangerous and destructive alike to soul and body it is to fight against God and His Church, as he may plainly recognize in the enemies of the universal Church, if he will diligently call to mind how Almighty God has humbled them by His just judgment and has this year taken care to weaken the forces in which they chiefly trusted. Nor should he regard it as any disgrace or dishonour if he allows his will and mind in this matter to be overcome and humbles himself before God and his Creator, who, if he does this, will without doubt exalt him.

Having more diligently and frequently set these matters and such other things as you know to be more expedient before him, without any hesitation, you are to deliver to him our letters of admonition and endeavour to join your own admonition to them in a spirit of strength and gentleness [Col. 0488B].

But if he refuses to listen to you even thus, and judges rather that he must persist in his hardness and obstinacy, present to him our threatening letters, adding firmly on our behalf that we shall henceforth for no reason silence the aforesaid archbishop. Nor, unless the same king is willing to fulfil before the beginning of the next Lent—which now seems almost at hand [Col. 0488C]—the things stated above, shall we impose any further prohibition upon him from more severely avenging, with the sword of ecclesiastical severity and as the duty of his office requires, the injuries done to himself, the church committed to him, and his own people. For the king ought not to believe or entertain in his mind that the sleeping Lord will never awaken, or that rust has so consumed blessed Peter’s sword that it cannot be drawn and exercise due vengeance. We wish, however, that you carry these matters out with the diligence stated above, unless our venerable brother the bishop of Beauvais and our beloved son the Carthusian prior carry them out as we have instructed them.

Given at Benevento, 8 Kalends of June [25 May].

CDLXXXIX. To Roger, Bishop of Worcester.—That he return to his church. Concerning messengers sent to King Henry. (Benevento, May?)

[Ibid., p. 107.]

[Col. 0488D]

It would altogether please us, and be most expedient for your welfare, if you returned to the church committed to you, provided that you can freely exercise your office there. But if you fear that there you may be compelled to observe those wicked customs which God, the Church, and we have utterly condemned, or may be forced into some other improper course, we by no means advise you to put your foot in the fetter or in any way thrust yourself into prison [Col. 0489A].

As you know, desiring to overcome the king by patience, as was fitting, and by humility, we have thus far yielded much to him, hoping in Christ’s mercy that He in whose hand are the hearts of kings would soften his will and mind and incline them to His good pleasure. But since things have so far turned out for us in this matter otherwise than we believed, we have judged that he should on this occasion be pressed through our messengers, as will become more fully known to you from the other letters which we have sent you. If he should refuse to listen to us on this occasion, know with certainty that we shall no longer bear with him; nor have we silenced or shall we silence our venerable brother, nor in any way take his authority from him, so as to prevent him freely exercising his office [Col. 0489B].

For we wish you to know and hold as certain that, so long as the breath of life shall have its dwelling in our body, we shall in no respect fail him in maintaining the liberty and justice of his church. Rather, in these matters we shall effectively furnish him counsel and assistance wherever we can honourably do so. And if he himself should prove negligent or remiss, we shall without doubt exert the authority of blessed Peter and our own. Therefore act steadfastly and manfully, and be greatly strengthened in the Lord, holding as more than certain that, since the merciful and compassionate Lord has now looked with His customary clemency so favourably upon the cause of the universal Church that scarcely any schismatic now remains, scandals cannot remain long in the members of that Church [Col. 0489C].

CDXC. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—That one must deal fatherly and kindly with King Henry. (Benevento?)

[Ibid., p. 25.]

ALEXANDER, pope, TO THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

From your letters we have learned that you are violently disturbed and troubled because we do not support you as you think fitting and would wish, and because the illustrious king of the English, on the pretext of the letters which we sent him, ceaselessly insults you and boasts that he has withdrawn himself from your jurisdiction. But if he had read the tenor of the letters [Col. 0489D] from beginning to end, he would surely have found in them nothing on account of which he could justly insult either us or you.

Therefore, since the Roman Church is accustomed rather to endure inconvenience in preserving deliberation than to proceed rashly in any affairs, let not your brotherhood be troubled or moved because we have borne with the same king through so long an expectation, wishing by messengers and letters fatherly and kindly to call him back from his purpose and soften his impatience and hardness by the sweetness of gentleness. For the fervour of charity and affection which we have had toward your person has in no respect grown cold or become remiss, but increases more and more from day to day. For it is always our intention diligently to uphold and preserve your honour [Col. 0490A], dignity, and rights, and those of the church over which, by God’s appointment, you preside. What we have granted you we have in no way changed, nor, God granting, shall we change it; and on the day granted to you we give you full authority to exercise your power freely, without recourse to appeal. But we wish to receive an answer from those religious men through whom we have admonished the aforesaid king by our letters.

CDXCI. To Louis, King of the Franks.—On the same subject. (Benevento?)

[Ibid., p. 141.]

ALEXANDER, pope, TO LOUIS, King of France.

[Col. 0490B] We have learned that the clemency of your royal serenity is greatly moved and troubled because we do not assist our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, according to his wish and desire and as necessity requires; and because the illustrious king of the English, ceaselessly insulting him on the pretext of the letters which we sent him, boasts that he has withdrawn himself from his jurisdiction. But if the tenor of those letters were carefully read aloud before upright men, no one could surely discover in them anything affording matter or occasion for insult.

Moreover, if we have at any time assented to the petition of the aforesaid king and seemed to favour his will, we did so in the manner of a skilled physician [Col. 0490C], who gives to a sick man of whose recovery he despairs whatever contrary things he desires, trying by every means possible to restore him to health. But he refuses to administer all harmful things to the sick man whom he is confident he can cure, and whom he loves more affectionately, even though that man most urgently requests them.

Therefore, since it is the custom of the Roman Church rather often to incur loss and damage in preserving deliberation than to sin through haste, let not your serenity wonder or be moved because we have borne with the aforesaid king through so long an expectation, wishing to recall him from his purpose in the sweetness of kindness and gentleness and to soften his hardness. For the fervour of charity and affection which we have had toward that archbishop has in no respect grown cold [Col. 0490D] or become remiss, but grows more and more day by day. And it is always our purpose and will more zealously to uphold his honour, dignity, and rights, and those of the church committed to him, and diligently to preserve them as the duty of our office requires. Nor have we altered in any respect what we granted him, nor shall we alter it by God’s authority; indeed, on the day granted to him we give him free authority to exercise his office without recourse to appeal and without the impediment of objection. Nevertheless, we wish to receive an answer from those religious men through whom we have undertaken to admonish the aforesaid king by our letters.

CDXCII. Privilege for the monastery of St. Sylvester of Nonantola. (Benevento, 9 June.)

[Tiraboschi, *History of Nonantola*, II, p. 284.]

[Col. 0491A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ALBERT, abbot of the monastery of St. Sylvester of Nonantola, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: perpetual greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the authority and duty of the apostolic see we are compelled to labour for the condition of all churches and, with the Lord’s help, to provide beneficially for the peace of those which adhere more especially to that see. [Note: [Col. 0491] Pope Celestine III later confirmed this privilege. See volume CCVI of the *Patrologia*, under Celestine III.] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we have judged it fitting in due kindness to assent to your just requests [Col. 0491B], and, following the footsteps of our predecessors of blessed memory—Leo, Alexander, Paschal, Calixtus, Innocent, Eugenius, and Anastasius, Roman pontiffs—we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of the apostolic see, the aforesaid monastery of blessed Sylvester of Nonantola. By God’s appointment you are devoted there to divine service; and it was offered to blessed Peter by Aistulf, king of the Lombards and founder of the same place. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God and the Rule of St. Benedict shall be observed there inviolably for all time.
