Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, God granting, by concession of pontiffs, grant of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state the following by their proper names:

[Col. 0491C] That is: the castellany of Nonantola itself; the Old Castle and its church with its chapels; Galliano; Catiliano; Fanano and its church with its chapels; Lisano; Silopano and its church with its chapels; Samone; Campilio; Marano; Mount Olivet; the meadow of Albino; the monastery of St. Lucy with its churches and appurtenances; the church of the Holy Trinity of Somogia; Manzulio; Tavialo; Rastellino; St. Mary in Grumulo; Spina Lamberti; Solaria; Roncaglia and [Col. 0491D] its church with its chapels; Camurana and its church with its chapels; Curtiola and its church with its chapels; Sicco; the castle of Pellavi; Trecentula and its church with its chapels; Bondeno; Nogaria; the castle, cell, and Marchalia with their appurtenances.

Moreover, we confirm in perpetuity to your monastery the castle of the cell, the court of Ragusa, and the castle of Tedaldo, with all the allods which Marquis Boniface possessed as acquired in the county of Ferrara. Countess Matilda is known formerly to have given these to you, from the offering which she had made to blessed Peter and the Roman Church, at an annual rent of one gold coin [Col. 0492A].

In the city of Pavia, the church of St. Quilicus; at Piacenza, the church of St. Sylvester; at Parma, the church of the Holy Cross and the church of St. Benedict; in the suburb of Vicenza, the church of St. Sylvester; the cell of St. Sylvester and the cell of St. Mary at Fabbrica; at Libertino, the church of St. Sylvester; on Monte Silice, the church of St. Daniel with all things pertaining to it; in the suburb of Padua, the church of St. Leonard, canonically granted to you by Belino, bishop of Padua of good memory; in the city of Treviso, the church of St. Mary and St. Fusca, with liberty, chapels, and all things pertaining to it.

[Col. 0492B] Indeed, neither the bishop of Modena nor any bishop or prince whatsoever, nor any ecclesiastical or secular person, may inflict burdens upon the aforesaid monastery, its cells, churches, or other possessions; impose exactions; or summon or hold a judicial assembly or conference without the will of the abbot and brethren. We also grant that burial in the monastery itself shall be free, so that no one may hinder the devotion and final wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be placed over it through any deceitful device or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren [Col. 0492C], shall determine should be elected in accordance with the fear of God and the Rule of St. Benedict; he shall, of course, come to the pontiff of the apostolic see to be consecrated. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, ordinations of monks to be promoted to holy orders, and of clerics belonging to the cells or churches of the same monastery, from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the apostolic see and is willing to supply these freely and without corruption.

For we do not permit any bishop to celebrate public Masses in your monastery against the abbot’s will, or to claim their tithes; nor may anyone obtain by surreptitious means or by any other means a rescript concerning the monastery itself or its property. If this should perhaps be attempted, it shall be held wholly void. Nor may bishops impose a sentence of interdict or excommunication upon clerics of your monastery without your consent.

Furthermore, by the kindness of the apostolic see we grant to your person the insignia of dignity which your predecessors are known to have used in the solemnities of Mass: namely, that on solemn days, when celebrating the offices of Mass, you may be vested in a dalmatic, mitre, gloves [Col. 0493A], and sandals.

Adding these provisions, we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, claim for his own uses things unjustly bestowed, diminish them, or harass them with wanton vexations; but that all things shall remain intact for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, so that in all things it may ever rejoice in the defence and protection of the apostolic see, whose own proper concern it is, without prejudice to the authority of that same holy apostolic see. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, etc.

Signed: Alexander, Pope III.

[Col. 0493B] I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and St. Rufina. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, title of Pammachius. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of St. Vitalis, title of Vestina. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of St. Theodore. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian. I, Manfred, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil [Col. 0493C]. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of St. Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Benevento by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth Ides of June [9 June], in the first indiction, in the year 1168 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Alexander, Pope III.

CDXCIII. He confirms the liberty of the monastery of Nonantola. (Benevento, 9 June.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ALBERT, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery [Col. 0493D] of St. Sylvester of Nonantola: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Things properly settled by the authority of the apostolic see ought not to be infringed by anyone’s presumption, so as to prevent their possessing their proper force of firmness. Since, therefore, there had formerly been many quarrels and wars between the people of Nonantola and Modena, at last, for the sake of peace, an agreement of this sort was established between the inhabitants of the two places: namely, that at the request of the abbot of Nonantola the bishop of Modena should consecrate the church of the Old Castle with its chapels, the church of Sclopano with its chapels, the church of Fanano with its chapels, the church of Camurana with its chapels, the church of Trecentula with its chapels, and the church of Curtiola with its chapels, and [Col. 0494A] should promote their clerics.

After this, however, peace was not kept by the people of Modena; and Ribald, bishop of Modena, without consulting the abbot and against his will, consecrated one of the aforesaid churches by force. Because of this act, Hildebrand, formerly abbot of the said monastery and of good memory, came to the council which our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Innocent, held in the Lateran basilica, and lodged a complaint against that bishop in our predecessor’s presence. The bishop, being brought before him and the brethren and unable to defend himself against the charges made, incurred the following judgment. Since it was evident that that agreement had been made contrary to the privileges granted to the monastery of Nonantola by many Roman pontiffs, [Col. 0494B] our aforesaid predecessor decreed that it lacked force and declared it entirely void. He commanded the same bishop of Modena not to presume henceforth to undertake anything similar, but rather always and everywhere to allow your monastery to enjoy the liberty and peace granted to it.

We, therefore, following in the footsteps of that same predecessor of ours, confirm the aforesaid judgment by apostolic authority and fortify it by the protection of the present writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may in any way harass you and your successors concerning these matters, infringe or alter this page of our confirmation, or inflict upon you any opposition arising from it. But if anyone by rash practice should presume to attempt this, unless he suitably corrects his offence, let him incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and be subject to excommunication [Col. 0494C]. But to all, etc.

Fare well.

(Signature of Alexander III.)

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and St. Rufina. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, title of Pammachius. [Col. 0494D] I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Boso, cardinal priest of St. Pudentiana, title of Pastor. I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of St. Vitalis, title of Vestina. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of St. Theodore. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian. I, Manfred, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of St. Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Benevento by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth Ides of June [9 June], [Col. 0495A] indiction [lacuna], 1168, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Alexander, Pope III.

CDXCIV. To the monks of St. Prosper of Reggio.—That they remove Abbot Guido, guilty of wasting the monastery, from office. (Benevento, 12 June.)

[Muratori, *Antiquities of Italy*, VI, 225.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable [lacuna] of the diocese of Reggio, beloved sons Gand., Grat., Jo., Hard., and the other Catholic monks of St. Prosper.

It has come to our knowledge, and we have learned the same from your letters, sons and monks, that Abbot Guido [lacuna] has wasted the goods of the monastery; that you have none of the necessities of life there [Col. 0495B]; and that through his injury and insolence the monastery is said to have been reduced almost wholly to loss and want. His perversity [lacuna] has gone so far that he is said to have stripped off the lead roof of the monastery and squandered its price in the voracity of his gluttony. Added to this is the fact that he first made that most wicked oath to Octavian, the heresiarch of condemned memory, and finally to Guido Cremando. He was unwilling to sin alone, but did not fear to drag others to ruin.

Therefore, since we do not wish to pass over such grave and enormous offences in silence, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the facts are as reported to our ears, you remove the aforesaid abbot from [Col. 0495C] the said monastery, all pretext and appeal set aside; take care to agree upon another suitable and honourable person; and unanimously elect him as your father and shepherd.

Given at Benevento, 2 Ides of June [12 June].

CDXCV. Privilege for John, Bishop of Catania. (Benevento, 26 July.)

[Pirri, *Sacred Sicily*, I, 530.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JOHN, bishop and abbot of Catania, and to his successors to be canonically instituted in the future.

As we are taught by the truthful writings of the most blessed father and most elegant doctor Gregory I [Col. 0495D], it is established that Catania, the city where blessed Agatha was born and suffered, flourished in ancient times with the glory of episcopal rank. But when the island of Sicily was captured by the peoples of the Saracens, episcopal glory perished there and in the other cities of the entire province, and the dignity of the Christian faith disappeared. Then, after almost four hundred years (scarcely 300), divine mercy looking upon its people, that island was restored to Christian rule through the most valiant Count Roger.

Moreover, that distinguished Count Roger, a most devoted son of the Roman Church, eagerly striving everywhere in due season to restore to the cities the glory of their ancient rank, ordained that the mother church of Blessed Agatha, situated at Catania, should be a monastery, so that brethren devoted there to God’s services might implore Almighty mercy for his salvation, for the soul of his deceased wife, and for the souls of the soldiers who had recovered that land for Christian rule by their blood [Col. 0496A]. Accordingly Pope Urban, of pious memory, considering the devotion of so great a man, blessed as abbot the elect whom that count sent to him, so that thereafter the prerogative might flourish: whoever should be elected abbot there by the monks was also to preside over that people as bishop.

We therefore, following in the footsteps of that same predecessor of ours, receive you, brother Bishop John, consecrated from our, though unworthy, hands as though from the hands of blessed Peter, and receive the same church under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves. We fortify it by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing that, as was instituted by our same predecessor [Col. 0496B], both dignities—namely, abbot and bishop—shall be preserved there in one and the same person; that those elected by the monks of that place shall be blessed and consecrated by the Roman pontiff; and that the church itself shall be subject to no one but the Roman pontiff.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses through the donation of the aforesaid count and his heirs, or may in future acquire, God granting, by concession of pontiffs, grant of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state the following by their proper names.

[Col. 0496C] The city of Catania with all its appurtenances and holdings; the castle of St. Anastasia with its possessions and appurtenances; the town of Mascalara with all its appurtenances; the churches of Adernò with their appurtenances; the churches of Judith [rather, Aci] with their appurtenances; the churches of Centuripe with their appurtenances; the churches of the castle of John with their appurtenances; and the churches of all the lands belonging to that castle, as far as the River Salso, which runs between the castle of John and the city of Agrigento, and as far as the boundaries of the city of Tragina, and on the other sides everywhere as they are divided from the appurtenances of other castles and cities.

We likewise confirm by apostolic authority the liberties justly granted by the aforesaid count [Col. 0496D] to your church, for you and your successors. Likewise, from the liberality of the apostolic see, we have judged that the pallium should be granted to your brotherhood, which your solicitude shall use in celebrating Mass on the solemn days listed below: the Nativity of the Lord; St. Stephen; Epiphany; the Presentation (*Ypapanton*); the Lord’s Supper; the Resurrection; the Ascension; Pentecost; the three solemnities of blessed Mary; the Nativity of St. John the Baptist; the feasts of the apostles Peter and Paul; the Commemoration of All Saints; the feast of blessed Agatha; St. Leo; and the martyr St. Eupulus; at the consecration of churches, of priests, and of deacons; and on the anniversary of the day of your consecration.

Therefore let your brotherhood hasten with all your heart to show yourself humble in prosperity and, when adversities occur, righteous and a friend to the good, an opponent of evils; applying yourself to works of mercy in proportion to your means, yet desiring also to undertake them beyond your means. This, dearest brother, is the dignity of the pallium you have received: if you observe it diligently, you shall possess inwardly what you show yourself to have received outwardly.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact for the benefit, in every way, of the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0497B] If therefore anyone in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ubaldus, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Conrad, archbishop of Mainz and bishop of Sabina. I, Ubaldus, cardinal-priest of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Boso, cardinal-priest of St. Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Theodinus, cardinal-priest of St. Vitalis, of the title of Vestina. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. [Col. 0497C] I, Arditio, cardinal-deacon of St. Theodore. I, Chanchiris, cardinal-deacon of St. Adrian. I, Manfred, cardinal-deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, cardinal-deacon of St. Eustachius beside the temple of Agrippa. I, Vitellius, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at Benevento, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 26 July, first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1168, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

CDXCVI. To the bishops of Soissons, Amiens, and Laon.—On behalf of Constance, Countess of Saint-Gilles, against the Count of Boulogne concerning her dower. (Benevento, 27 August.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 755.]

[Col. 0497D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the bishops of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0497D] Hugh of Chamfleury.], Amiens [Note: [Col. 0497D] Robert.], and Laon [Note: [Col. 0497D] Walter.], greetings and the Apostolic blessing.

Our beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman C., Countess of Saint-Gilles, sister of our dearest son in Christ L., the illustrious king of the French, has informed us by a report sent [Col. 0498A] to us that Eustace, formerly son of King Stephen [Note: [Col. 0497D] That is, king of England; his son Eustace married Constance, daughter of Louis the Fat, in 1139, as Matthew Paris writes.], took her as his lawful wife, granted her the county of Boulogne as a dower, and confirmed this in an authentic written instrument, as is customary. Therefore, since Matthew, brother of the noble Count Philip, and M., formerly an abbess, are said to be holding that county by an unreasonable occupation, and, though frequently required, refuse to restore it: by these apostolic letters we command your fraternity diligently to admonish, on our behalf, the aforesaid Matthew and the nun, either to restore the said county to the aforementioned countess and leave it to her freely and without molestation, or to render her full justice concerning it in your presence, all delay and appeal [Col. 0498B] being set aside. But if, in accordance with your admonition, they should perhaps be unwilling to do either, then, although they have been excommunicated for another reason, publicly declare them excommunicated by our authority for this particular matter throughout the whole county; prohibit every divine office from being celebrated, except baptism of infants and penances for the dying; and cause that sentence to be observed inviolably until full satisfaction has been made. If all of you cannot attend to this business, nevertheless let two of you pursue it diligently as stated, within three months of receiving these letters.

Given at Benevento, 27 August.

CDXCVII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—He explains why he did not comply with his requests concerning the bishop of Arras [Note: [Col. 0498D] See Henry’s letter to Alexander in the matter of Drogo the chancellor, among the letters of various persons to him, below. —Patristic Editor.]. He exhorts him to treat his suffragans kindly. He reports that he has written to the bishops of Soissons, Amiens, and Laon concerning his sister Constance, wife of the Count of Toulouse. He commends Master Pagan. (Benevento, 27 August.)

[MARTÈNE, ibid., col. 753.]

[Col. 0498C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greetings and the Apostolic blessing.

Since you had informed us that we regarded neither your letters nor your messengers with a kindly eye, and that we were unwilling to receive your requests concerning the business of the bishop of Arras, we were greatly surprised as to [Col. 0498D] why this disturbance had arisen in your mind and by what arguments you could infer that our favour and affection towards you had grown cold. For we are not so forgetful of the splendid devotion and most useful service which you readily rendered to us and to the Church at a time of need that we do not love you, as our dearest brother and the Church’s most steadfast pillar, with the most sincere affection of charity; that we do not always receive your messengers and letters gladly; and that we do not gladly wish to do for you whatever we can, consistently with God, justice, and [Col. 0499A] our honour, and whatever we would do for any of our brothers. Nor do we recall ever having opposed your requests when we could grant them while preserving the requirements of justice and our honour. Indeed, we have often taken care, beyond the duty of our office, to show deference to your brotherhood and to satisfy your wishes.

Therefore, do not let these thoughts enter your mind; lay aside every anxiety and concern of this kind; and, if we sometimes do not grant your requests as you wish, attribute this not to our will but rather to the merits of the cases. For, as we have said, we have the desire and will gladly to carry out what is dear to your heart and always to grant a kind and ready favour to your wishes where it is expedient. But you, as a [Col. 0499B] discerning and prudent man, should proceed cautiously and wisely in all your undertakings; treat the suffragans of your church kindly and gently; and do not dispose of the churches of Blessed Peter, the Prince [of the Apostles], which are established in your province as though they were your own, but leave them in their liberty. Furthermore, concerning the affair of our beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman C. [Note: [Col. 0499] Constance, daughter of Louis VI, king of France; see the following letter.], your sister, wife of the Count of Toulouse, we have written effectively, in consideration of your brotherhood, to our venerable brothers, the bishops of Soissons, Amiens, and Laon, as we know to be expedient. But because, as we have learned, witnesses are entered in the instrument of her dower, admonish and induce them by our authority and yours to bear testimony to the truth out of love for justice. For just as it is dangerous to utter falsehood, so it is good to bear testimony to the truth. Moreover, we earnestly commend to your care our beloved son Master Pagan, who is exceedingly devoted and faithful to you, asking that you do him good and hold him in many ways commended, since you know that he has remained with us so long concerning his business. For we have settled, quickly and quite briefly, the business for which you sent him.

Given at Benevento, 27 August.

CDXCVIII. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saints Felix and Fortunatus at Vicenza. (Benevento, 12 September.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, V, 1042.]

[Col. 0499D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ARNULPHUS, abbot of the monastery of Saints Felix and Fortunatus of Vicenza, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

To those choosing the religious life, etc., down to “violate.” Therefore, etc., down to “we confirm the privileges.” We decree that whatever possessions, etc., down to the words to be expressly set out: Whatever you possess in length from the river Retrone and Ursega as far as the High Bridge. Whatever also you possess in breadth from the river Retrone to the other bridge, by which one crosses over the same [Col. 0500A] river to Monticello: at Seledo, one estate called Vuarzonus; at Sarecto, one small holding; at Turre, one small holding; at Magrado, one small holding; at Arserio, another small holding; at Cuculo, one parcel of vineyard and three fields; at Muzone, one small holding; at Rauna, another small holding; at Culpano, one estate with its appurtenances; at Cartusiano, the renders belonging to St. Vitus from the small holding of Penculi; between Scledum and St. Vitus, half of one estate; in the place called Holy Title, at Luvizano, one estate with the chapel of St. Vitus. At Malado, nine small holdings. At Marostica, two estates: one at the place called Provio, with the chapel of St. Apollinaris; the other at Burguliano, with chapel and Gazo. At Angarano, two small holdings and two mountains: one called Mount [Col. 0500B] of Olives, the other called Mount of Chestnut Trees; at Solania, one estate with the chapel of St. Vitus; at Tivido, two small holdings; at Facino, three small holdings; at Pechio, one small holding; at Barbutia, one small holding; at Fulviano, one small holding; at Bubeneto, one small holding; at Secusino, one small holding; at Braido of St. Vitus, four estates with parish church, chapels, appurtenances, and tithes; at Cortolonga, one estate with a chapel. Beside the New River, one estate with the chapel of St. Vitus; at Bragantia, one small holding; at Juvene, one estate; at Bucone, another estate; at Fontana Frigida, one small holding; at Paderno, another small holding; at Carbonaria, two small holdings; at Titulo, one small holding; at Causele, four small holdings; at Ara, one small holding; at [Col. 0500C] Cona, arable land; at Calzade, one parcel of vineyard; at Zulano, one small holding; at Arzignano, another small holding; on Mount Cleda, arable land. Two parcels of vineyard at Monticello and arable land; at Albetone, one farm tenancy; at Vivarolio, one estate with the chapel of St. Peter. Beyond Lake Benacus, in the place called Randena, the enclosed field of St. George; and at Lainedo, vineyards and olive groves; also four alpine pastures—two above Marostica, called Lastaria and Bugnaria, Longera, and also the mountains of Zovenano and Novogino; at Uvisega, one mill; at Altico, another mill; half an estate of St. Apollinaris, with its chapel, and the *vantium* of St. George, with its church; two farm tenancies at Bercia and two at Liseria; at Barbarano [Col. 0500D] one estate and two small holdings; at Basico, one estate.

Moreover, we confirm to you, and through you to the same monastery, by the protection of our written instrument, the offerings coming to the same monastery and all other rights, liberties, and gifts which Rodulfus, Lambertus, Hieronymus, Astulfus, Litherius, Turingius, Eccilinus, Henry, and Lothovicus, bishops formerly of Vicenza, of blessed memory, reasonably granted to your monastery—in tithes, tenure-conditions, labour-services, *escatica* [food-renders], pastures, meadows, woods, rocky lands, mountains, plains, waters, watercourses, mills, fishing rights, and hunting rights belonging to the aforesaid places—and which you have possessed for the past forty years without lawful interruption. [Col. 0501A] Saving, however, what the bishops themselves reserved for themselves in the aforesaid monastery in respect of all these things: namely, that at Christmas and Easter, and on each feast of the aforesaid martyrs Felix and Fortunatus, the abbot or monks of the same place must, every year and with all other objection set aside, bring to the bishop then in office one candle, one loaf, and a flask full of wine. We also prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving the monastery on any pretext without his abbot’s permission. No one may dare to retain one who departs without a letter of authorization from the community. Furthermore, we decree that neither a count nor a prince nor any [Col. 0501B] secular or ecclesiastical person may impose unjust or unlawful exactions upon the aforesaid monastery. And no one may presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cultivated lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your animals. But upon your death, etc. We also grant burial, etc. We therefore decree, etc. [lacuna], saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore, etc. But to all, etc. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Boso, cardinal-priest of St. Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. [Col. 0501C] I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Damaso. I, Theodinus, cardinal-priest of St. Vitalis, of the title of Vestina. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Ardicio, cardinal-deacon of St. Theodore. I, Manfred, cardinal-deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, cardinal-deacon of St. Eustachius beside the temple of Agrippa. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 12 September, first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1168, in the tenth year of the pontificate [Col. 0501D] of Lord Pope Alexander III.

CDXCIX. Privilege for the monastery of St. Reparata at Marradino. (Benevento, 9 November.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, II, 499.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HOMODEUS, abbot of the monastery of St. Reparata of Marrata, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

Whenever something is requested from us that accords with religion, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, [lacuna] we receive the aforesaid monastery of St. Reparata, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, following the example of our predecessor Pope Honorius II of holy memory; and we receive it under the protection of Blessed Peter and [Col. 0502A] ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offering of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to set out these possessions expressly: the church of St. Mary at Crispino; the church of St. Lawrence; the church of St. Cassian at Petrosolo; the church of St. Euphemia; the church of St. Martin; the church of St. Peter at Vizzano; the church of St. Andrew in the same place; and Camortinicella. We likewise confirm to you, and through you to the same monastery, by apostolic authority, the tithes reasonably granted to your monastery by the bishops of Faenza. [Col. 0502B]

We also grant that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, saving the right of the mother church. We therefore decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore, etc. Amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Anastasia. [Col. 0502C] I, Boso, cardinal-priest of St. Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Damaso. I, Theodinus, cardinal-priest of St. Vitalis, of the title of Vestina. I, Arditio, cardinal-deacon of St. Theodore. I, Manfred, cardinal-deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, cardinal-deacon of St. Eustachius beside the temple of Agrippa.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 9 November, first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1168, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

D. He takes under protection the church of Saints Hippolytus and Cassian and of St. John the Baptist at Fosciano, and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Benevento, 23 December.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, VI, 423.]

[Col. 0502D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son JACOB, parish priest of Saints Hippolytus and Cassian and of St. John the Baptist of Fosciano, and to his successors to be canonically appointed for ever.

A pious request ought to be brought to fulfillment by the effect of the will, so that faithful devotion may shine forth worthily and the requested benefit may undoubtedly gain force. Therefore, beloved in the Lord, we gladly assent to your just requests [Col. 0503A] and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside. We strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the liberality of popes, the offering of kings or princes or other faithful servants of God, or by other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to set out expressly: all lands and men which the aforementioned church possesses in the village of Basilica, in the castle of Fosciano, and within their boundaries; and whatever it possesses by right in the village of Fabrio, Marcione, Mount Silico, and the estate of Socrajo. [Col. 0503B] The church of St. George beside the aforesaid church of Campo Foscianese; the chapel of St. Mary of Fosciana; the church of St. Peter; the church of St. Michael of Castilione; the church of St. Quiricus of Fabrio; the church of St. Martin of Montepigulo; the church of St. James of Verucola; the church of St. Bartholomew of Cloja; the hospital of St. Peregrine in the Alps; the hospital of St. Mary of the Alp; the church of St. Michael of Saxorubeo; the church of St. Sixtus of Villa; the church of St. Mary of Maniano; the church of St. Lawrence of Corfino; the church of St. Martin of Sericagnana; the church of St. Lawrence; [Col. 0503C] the church of St. Pantaleon of Bacciano; the church of St. Felicitas of Pontequosi; the church of St. Regulus, the church of St. Lawrence, and the church of St. James of Monteserico; the church of St. Andrew and the church of St. Mary of Milano; the church of St. Martin of Paleroso; the church of St. Michael of Perporo; the church of St. Peter of Fiattono; the church of St. James of Montealtissimo; the church of St. Fridianus of Saxo; the church of St. Peter of Castronovo; the church of St. Mary of Campocastellano; the church of St. Nicholas and the church of St. Justus of Calabaroti; the church of St. Pantaleon of Monte; the church of St. Prosper of Antisorano; the church of St. Donatus of Rontano; the church of St. Michael [Col. 0503D] of Colle; the church of St. Bartholomew of Graniano; the church of Saints Philip and James of Filicaja; the church of St. Mary of Rotano and of St. Nicholas of Silicano.

Moreover, we decree and, by apostolic authority, prohibit that neither the bishop then in office nor the canons of Lucca may impose unbearable burdens and grievances upon you and your parish, or in any way exact new or unlawful payments from you. We therefore decree, etc. [lacuna], saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic See. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. [Col. 0504A] I, Conrad, archbishop of Mainz. I, Ubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Cross. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Anastasius. I, Albert, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Mark. I, Theodore, cardinal-priest of St. Vitalis. I, Andrew, cardinal-deacon of St. Theodore. I, Hugh, cardinal-deacon of St. Eustachius beside the temple of Agrippa.

Given at Benevento through the hands of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 23 December, first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0504B] 1168, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

DI. He takes under protection the Bolognese church of St. Peter and confirms its possessions and rights. (Benevento, 30 December.)

[SAVIOLI, *Annali Bolognesi*, II, II, 7.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BONIFACE, archdeacon, and ALBERT, archpriest, of the church of St. Peter at Bologna, and to their brethren, both present and future, to be canonically appointed for ever.

We grant effect to those who make just requests, as the force of equity and the order of reason require, especially [Col. 0504C] when piety supports the petitioners’ will and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of St. Peter, in which you are devoted to divine service. We strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offering of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to set out expressly: the church of St. John the Baptist; the church [Col. 0504D] of St. Mary of Montovalo; the church of St. Giles beside Savina; the church of St. Peter at Castagnolo; St. Mary of the Vineyards; the church of St. Michael of Argelata; and the parish church of Medicina. The church of St. Mary of the Vineyards and the church of St. Michael which are at Medicina, with all the appurtenances of the aforesaid churches; likewise the land, with houses and without houses, which lies around the church of St. Peter of your bishopric, namely, situated to the south, west, and north; the lands belonging by right to your church, situated northward within the city wall in the place called the Hospital, and outside the wall as far as the road of St. Thomas the Apostle, and from the square leading to that same church as far as the stream called [Col. 0505A] Avesa. All the demesne which you possess and hold; likewise three parts of the tithes of all your parish, namely, of St. Peter’s bishopric, with all appurtenances of the living and the dead, and whatever is offered in your aforesaid episcopal church or placed upon the altar or on the pavement. The tithe of the entire parish of Buida.

Furthermore, as Bishop G. of Bologna, of good memory, released you by apostolic authority from the burden of the expenses which you used to incur in going to Ravenna for the synod and returning, so we decree that both you and your successors shall remain released in the future. We therefore decree, etc. [lacuna], saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the bishop of Bologna. If anyone therefore [Col. 0505B] in the future, etc. [lacuna]

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Albert, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I, Boso, cardinal-priest of St. Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of St. Lawrence in the title of Damaso. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Mark. I, Theodinus, cardinal-priest of St. Vitalis of Vestina. [Col. 0505C] I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Ar…., cardinal-deacon of St. Theodore. I, Hugh, cardinal-deacon of St. Eustachius beside the temple of Agrippa.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 30 December, first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1168, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

**YEAR 1168?**

DII. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—He advises him to overcome the king by humility.

[*Letters of St. Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 19.]

[Col. 0505D]

ALEXANDER, pope, to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

Although the pressures of adversities and labours may seem to weigh more heavily upon you and grow stronger, nevertheless set before yourself the many examples of the holy Fathers, who, like you, suffered many calamities and hardships through zeal for justice and happily deserved to attain the unfading crown and the heavenly kingdom. Therefore we ask and admonish your prudence always to keep before your eyes the saying, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matthew 5); do not break your spirit under any adversities, nor cast it down through any disturbance, but strengthen it by the virtue [Col. 0506A] of fortitude and constancy. But wherever you learn that justice and the liberty of the Church are being lost, do not in any way labour to restore peace with the king of the English at the cost and diminution of ecclesiastical dignity. Nevertheless, so far as can be done without injury to the honour of your office and the liberty of the Church, humble yourself before him and strive by every means to recover his favour and affection. Do not fear him more than is just, nor demand greater assurances than are proper. For, as we believe, once he has been reconciled to you, he would not injure you at all, nor permit anyone else to injure you. For we wish, as we have declared to you orally and by letters, to love you with sincere charity as our dearest one and to strive, insofar as divine grace permits, for the preservation of your honour, liberty, [Col. 0506B] and the increase of your dignity.

**YEAR 1165–1169**

DIII. To the King of Scotland.—He commends to him Thomas in exile.

[Ibid., p. 143.]

ALEXANDER, pope, to the king of Scotland.

When we diligently recall the affection of most sincere devotion which Malcolm, formerly king of the Scots and your brother of revered memory, steadfastly showed towards us and the Church of God throughout his life, and your own most devoted sincerity, by which we have learned from your letters that you burn with zeal toward our person, we confidently offer affectionate requests to your magnificence on behalf of those who are dear and acceptable to us, and we earnestly commend them to royal excellence without any hesitation. We do not believe that it is unknown to your highness how our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Canterbury, did not hesitate to endure exile for the liberty of his church, and how, as a religious, discerning, and honourable man, exceedingly dear and welcome to us and to the whole Church of God, he preferred to suffer loss of temporal goods rather than obey the commands of princes. Since your aforesaid brother and your other forebears were customarily, as we are told, to embrace him, his predecessors, and the church entrusted to him with filial [Col. 0506D] devotion, we ask, admonish, and exhort your serenity in the Lord by apostolic letters to endeavour, for the love of God, reverence for Blessed Peter and ourselves, and regard for the archbishop himself, to love and support the said archbishop; always to take care to honour him and the church entrusted to him with the honours due to them; and graciously to grant him effective counsel and assistance. Thus we shall be bound to render manifold thanks to your magnificence, and the aforementioned archbishop shall be bound always to strive more ardently for your honour and exaltation and for that of the entire realm entrusted to your governance, and to remain under greater obligation to you.

DIV. To Philip, Count of Flanders.—On the same subject.

[Ibid., p. 145.]

[Col. 0507A]

ALEXANDER, pope, to PHILIP, Count of Flanders.

The more fully we have found and tested in every respect the fervour of your most sincere devotion toward us and the Church of God, the more confidently we offer affectionate requests to your diligence on behalf of those who are dear and acceptable to us and to that church, and earnestly invite your prudence to love them. Therefore, commending as much as we can to your greatness our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Canterbury—a man indeed religious, discerning, provident, and honourable, [Col. 0507B] and in every respect dear and acceptable to us and to the whole Church of God—we ask, command, and earnestly exhort your nobility by apostolic letters to endeavour, for the sake of divine mercy, reverence for Blessed Peter and ourselves, and regard for the archbishop himself, through whom many advantages and benefits may come to you, to love, honour, support, and foster him and his people generously and in many ways; and, when an opportunity arises, to direct your efforts, as far as you can, toward his peace. Thus he himself may always strive with all his strength for your honour and advancement; we may be bound to return the richest thanks to your sincerity; and we may advance your prayers and requests more readily [Col. 0507C] and effectively. For whatever honour or benefit your generosity, at our intervention, bestows upon him, we shall consider it especially bestowed upon ourselves.

DV. To Count Henry.—On the same subject.

[Ibid., p. 144.]

ALEXANDER, pope, to the nobleman Count HENRY.

Among the other acts of divine operation, we consider this especially pleasing to God and to ourselves: that you have taken care, with a serene countenance, to look upon our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Canterbury, in his straits and anxieties, and from your accustomed clemency to grant him the favour of your goodwill and consolation. Since he now has the greatest need of aid and counsel, we ask, admonish, and exhort your magnificence in the Lord by apostolic letters, and impose this upon you for the remission of your sins: for the sake of mercy, reverence for Blessed Peter and ourselves, and consideration of his religious standing and dignity, give him and his people precedence in favour, honour, and affection, and grant them in their adversities the comfort of your consolation and support. Thus you may receive eternal recompense from almighty God, and we, considering what you have bestowed on him as especially bestowed on ourselves, may be bound to offer your greatness the richest thanks for it.

DVI. To the Abbot of Clairmarais.—He commends the sister of Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, and her children.

[Ibid., p. 112.]

[Col. 0508A]

ALEXANDER, pope, to the abbot and brethren of Clairmarais.

For the benefits which your generosity has bestowed in many ways upon the sister of our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Canterbury, her children, and those with them, we render immense thanks to your charity and commend your religious community with the praise it worthily deserves in the Lord. For we have the desire and intention willingly to promote your welfare and advancement, as far as we can with God, [Col. 0508B] and to advance your prayers and requests effectively insofar as honour permits. The aforementioned archbishop also, when an opportunity occurs, will take care to repay according to their merit the many and great services of your generosity, and will remain always under greater obligation to your monastery. We too shall attend more willingly to your petitions and take care to grant them more effectively.

DVII. To Stephen, Bishop of Meaux, and the Abbot of St. Crispin.—He orders them to exhort King Henry, without delay, to restore and procure the restoration of the revenues, honours, and possessions of the church of Canterbury.

[Ibid., p. 102.]

[Col. 0508C] ALEXANDER, pope, to the bishop of Meaux and the abbot of St. Crispin at Soissons.

Consideration of the devotion and sincerity with which your prudence burns toward us and the Church of God repeatedly urges and invites us confidently to concern you with the business of the Church, and without hesitation to entrust to you even difficult and arduous matters for execution. Certainly, it is not unknown to your discernment by how many troubles, adversities, burdens, persecutions, and oppressions our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, has been weighed down by his king, through zeal for justice and for the liberty of the church entrusted to him; how he has been worn down by long exile; and how he has been deprived both of the possessions [Col. 0508D] and of the revenues of his church. Indeed, we sympathize with him over these things with the inward affection of our heart, as with a dearest brother and an outstanding member of the Church, and gladly grant him, in whatever ways we can, the comfort of our consolation.

For this reason, by apostolic letters we command and expressly enjoin your prudence to labour by every means to move and induce the aforesaid king on our behalf, so that, as he loves the salvation of his soul, he may restore without delay, and cause to be restored, to the said archbishop the revenues, honours, and possessions taken from his church, and allow them to remain freely and peacefully in his possession, lest thereby he incur peril to his soul or have reason to fear divine vengeance. You should also set before that king, concerning this matter, words both mild and [Col. 0509A] sweet, and, if you see it expedient, harsh and severe, acting as discerning and prudent men.

DVIII. To the Abbots of Cîteaux and Pontigny and all the brethren of the Cistercian Order.—Concerning Brother R.

[Ibid., p. 111.]

ALEXANDER, pope, to the abbots of Cîteaux and Pontigny and all the brethren of the Cistercian Order.

Know that it has come to our hearing—at which we are compelled greatly to wonder—that you have proposed to inflict a penalty upon our beloved son R., your brother, because our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Canterbury, sent him into England on business of the Church, being moved to this by human favor rather than by love of God and justice. Since this would redound to injury of us and of God’s Church, and since we could not, as indeed we ought not, endure it patiently, we command and enjoin your whole community by apostolic letters that you presume on no occasion to inflict this penalty upon the said R., or to show him any resentment or displeasure; rather, treat him kindly and fraternally among yourselves.

## DIX. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—The resignation of Henry, Bishop of Winchester, harassed by King Henry, is invalid.

[Ibid., p. 10.]

ALEXANDER, pope, to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

[Col. 0509C] We pursue with due praise the care and solicitude which you prudently and magnanimously exercise concerning the administration entrusted to you; and we commend in many ways in the Lord your purpose of endurance. But what you have reported to us—namely, that our venerable brother, the Bishop of Winchester, resigned his bishopric on account of injuries and persecutions which the king inflicted upon him harshly and intolerably—we regard as sufficiently grave and distressing. And we cannot regard that resignation as valid or invalid unless we first learn, through his letters or messengers, how it was made.

ANNO 1167–1169.

## DX. He commands the abbot and monks of Vallis Laureae not to obey either the Archbishop of Tarragona or the Bishop of Barcelona until their boundary dispute is adjudicated. (Benevento, September 10.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 1064.]

[Col. 0509D]

Since a question has arisen concerning the parochial right over the place in which you began your monastery, between our venerable brothers the Archbishop of Tarragona and the Bishop of Barcelona, we command you by apostolic letters to render neither of them obedience or reverence in respect of parochial jurisdiction [Col. 0510A] until it has been determined to which of them the aforesaid place ought by right to belong.

Given at Benevento, on the fourth Ides of September [10 September].

## DXI. Concerning the case pending between Ric., the abbot, and Saint Peter’s. (Benevento, October 5.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 760.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, etc.

We entrust to your experience for hearing and due final determination the case known to be in dispute between Ric., bearer of the present letter, and the abbot of Saint Peter of the Mountains, as well as Morand and his son Girard, concerning a certain house. Therefore, we command your discretion by apostolic letters [Col. 0510B] that, when you are requested in this matter, you summon both parties before you; and, after carefully hearing and ascertaining the arguments on either side, decide the same case, as stated, by the means of justice, any obstacle of appeal removed.

Given at Benevento, on the third Nones of October [5 October].

## DXII. To Henry, King of the English.—He threatens him with ecclesiastical censure unless he abstains from sacrileges. (Benevento, October 9.)

[*Epist.* S. Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 124.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ HENRY, illustrious King of the English, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0510C] The more fully we love your person with the affection of charity, on account of the many and great merits of your princely devotion and royal munificence, and the more closely we embrace you in the arms of paternal sincerity, the more often and attentively we lay before your Highness those things which we know certainly pertain to the salvation of your soul and to the increase of your honor and glory; and we take care diligently to induce you to carry them out, and graciously to exhort you with every solicitude and zeal. If it had been granted from heaven that we might enjoy the presence of your person, so dear to us, as we should wish, we would much more gladly urge upon you continually in spoken words the same things which we express in writing, and would zealously impress them upon you as remedies, as it were. [Col. 0510D]

We have learned, moreover, that, among other matters in which we desire royal diligence to be corrected, you retain in your own hands the bishoprics of Lincoln, Bath, and Hereford, vacant and deprived of a pastor’s consolation; and that in Bangor and Llandaff you prohibit, by a certain arrogance and by terror of superior power, the holding of a free election as is fitting. Like another Caesar, striving to be everything alone, you do not fear not only to retain what belongs to Caesar, as is proper, but also unlawfully to usurp, to the peril of your soul, what belongs to God. How unworthy this is, so far above and contrary to the dignity of royal justice, your own prudence, if you will consider carefully, will teach you sufficiently by natural reason as its guide; and certain examples of those who vainly attempted the same thing will nonetheless demonstrate it. [Col. 0511A]

And because, though unworthy, we have been entrusted by the Lord—who even shed his own blood for her—with the care and protection of the universal Church, we neither can nor ought in any way to omit to exert ourselves in every manner with you and with the other children of the Church on her behalf, and, after the example of the most holy Naboth, to defend her dignities and rights against all men, even unto death if necessary. Therefore we admonish, entreat, and beseech your Serenity in the Lord, and impose this upon you for the remission of your sins: as you excel in prudent discernment of divine and human matters, so show yourself prudent and moderate in all things; reverence God, your Creator, before all else more truly than hitherto; honor churches and ecclesiastical persons; and so discreetly claim and defend what is yours that you no longer presume to stretch out your hand toward those things known to belong to divine right. In particular, let royal Highness urge the clerics in the aforementioned churches to make an election both free and canonical, and grant them the necessary aid and favor for this purpose, with ecclesiastical liberty wholly preserved. Nor should you wish to name to those who are to elect the person whom they ought to elect. For that would be for you, rather than they, to carry out their election by their ministry, and would entirely deprive them of liberty to choose in the election itself. [Col. 0511C]

Indeed, if you take care, as you ought, to carry into effect what we have just set forth in a spirit of gentleness and with all humility, you will undoubtedly provide both for your own glory and salvation, and will do what is altogether pleasing and acceptable to God and to us. Otherwise, however much we wish to love you as our dearest son and most Christian prince, and to defer to your greatness, we shall not be able to restrain the hands of blessed Peter and our own from punishing you. Fearing God more than man, as is fitting, we shall take care, by the power divinely granted to us, wholly and inviolably to preserve alike the rights and honor of the Church.

[Col. 0511D] Given at Benevento, on the seventh Ides of October [9 October].

## DXIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of the cleric B., and that his prebend be restored to him. (Benevento, November 2.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 760.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

B., a cleric and bearer of this letter, came to us and stated in a tearful complaint that, although he had canonically obtained a prebend in the church of Saint-Germain-des-Monts, he lost it through lay violence, and that the cleric B. presumes to retain it thus occupied. Therefore, since it concerns us [Col. 0512A] and likewise belongs to your office to uphold and protect ecclesiastical persons and their goods more zealously, and to preserve their rights whole and unimpaired, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters carefully to investigate the truth of the matter. If you find it to be as stated above, cause the aforesaid prebend to be restored to the said B. and left to him in peace, every pretext and appeal having ceased. But if the aforementioned B. should refuse to comply with you in these matters, then, any remedy of appeal removed, deprive him of ecclesiastical office and benefice; and, if he still does not submit, place the aforesaid church of Saint-Germain under interdict, admitting no appeal whatsoever.

Given at Benevento, on the fourth Nones of November [2 November].

## DXIV. He confirms to Abbot Roger and the brethren of the monastery of Ibreium the tithes of Doching, adjudged to them by Henry, Bishop of Winchester, and Gilbert, Bishop of London. (Benevento, November 8.)

[*Epistolae Gilberti Foliot*, ed. GILES, II, 107.]

[Col. 0512B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROGER, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Ibreium, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brothers Henry, Bishop of Winchester, and Gilbert, Bishop of London, informed us by letters sent to us that, when we had entrusted to them, with appeal excluded, for due final determination the case long pending between you and the cleric Herlewin concerning the tithes of Doching, which Herlewin claimed had been granted to him, they heard and fully understood the arguments on either side. Since the aforesaid Herlewin failed in proof, they adjudged the said tithes to you and your church and forever absolved both you and that church from his claim concerning them, as plainly appears from the letters of their judgment, which we ourselves have examined. [Col. 0512C]

Accordingly, when both you, son Abbot, and Herlewin himself were present before us on this matter, and Herlewin, offering us only the letters of the aforesaid Bishop of London, asserted that he had appealed, as those letters contained, and urgently requested that the judgment be rescinded because it had not been rendered within the term of our mandate: observing that the matter had been committed to the said bishops, appeal excluded, with his own consent and at his request; and considering also that, as those bishops informed us by their letters, they had extended the term with his consent, we judged that the aforesaid sentence must stand. By the common counsel of our brethren, we absolve you from the claim of the said Herlewin, impose perpetual silence upon him in this matter, and by apostolic authority confirm to you, and through you to the aforesaid church, the aforementioned tithes; and we strengthen this confirmation by the protection of the present writing. We decree that no person whatever may infringe this page of our confirmation and determination or in any way oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the wrath of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Benevento, on the sixth Ides of November [8 November].

## DXV. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—That he restrain Giderus of Sarnay, who is invading the possessions of the church of Montfaucon, within the bounds of his duty. (Benevento, November 9.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 761.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0513B] Both the office of the apostolate laid upon us by God and the fidelity of our beloved son R., bishop-elect of Verdun, which he maintained toward the Church of God in the time of threatening persecution, render us greatly indebted to him and admonish us to give more anxious thought to restraining wicked men from molesting him and his people.

[Note: [Col. 0513D] Richard of Crissa, a noble lord of Grandpré, elected from the archdeaconry of Laon, who died in the Jerusalem expedition about the year 1162.] 

It has come to us that Giderus of Sarnay presumes to invade and devastate the possessions of the church of Montfaucon [Note: [Col. 0514D] In the diocese of Verdun, where there is a college of canons.] and to inflict various losses upon its people. Therefore, since we ought to regard the possessions of the aforesaid son as our own, we command your brotherhood by the present letters to oppose pontifical authority to the said man and restrain him from this presumption in such a way that you compel him to render due satisfaction to the bishop-elect and his people for the injuries and losses inflicted. Thus may that brother rejoice that he has found brotherly support in you, and those who see it may commend you for your zeal for justice. If anything should perhaps arise in dispute between the parties which requires examination and judgment, we wish it to be heard and settled by your authority.

[Col. 0513C] Given at Benevento, on the fifth Ides of November [9 November].

## DXVI. To the same.—On behalf of the priest Huldred concerning the church of Ponit. (Benevento, November 11.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting [Col. 0513D] and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son R., archdeacon of the Church of Châlons, informed us that when the case pending between Ulred, bearer of this letter, and John, priests, concerning the church of Saint Mary was being heard before you pursuant to our commission, Ulred produced his witnesses, namely the priests Ernulf and Henry, to declare before you the truth which they knew concerning the case. The opposing party alleged that they were less than suitable witnesses and appealed to our hearing against them as though they were persons accused of a crime. When [Col. 0514A] both parties appeared before the same archdeacon, and the aforesaid John acknowledged that he had imputed crimes to those witnesses solely out of anger, because they could not prosecute the appeal owing to the imminence of the short time-limit, the archdeacon, after pledges had been given on both sides, settled the matter between them by mutual consent as follows: if the aforesaid John acknowledged before you what he had confessed to their archdeacon, they would desist from the appeal. But on the appointed day, although the opposing party was present, the said John scorned to present himself before you. The other party, with those same witnesses, then appeared before our tribunal in accordance with the appeal; but the aforesaid John neither came nor sent a representative on his behalf.

Moreover, since no appeal was made concerning the principal matter, we have thought fit to remit the same case to your examination, commanding your brotherhood by the authority of this letter that, after summoning both parties before you, you hear the case more carefully. If it is established to you that the aforesaid John violated the pledge he had given, impose upon him a penance proportionate to the perjury; and, after receiving the aforesaid witnesses with the appeal removed, endeavor to decide the same case within fifteen days after receipt of this letter, every obstacle of appeal and every pretext removed.

[Col. 0514B] Given at Benevento, on the third Ides of November [11 November].

## DXVII. To the same.—That he compel the priest Mainerius to restore to Henry the parish he took away. (Benevento, November 12.)

[Ibid., col. 762.]

[Col. 0514C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc., greeting and apostolic blessing.

Henry, bearer of this letter, came to our presence with no little labor and stated in a humble petition that he had been instituted perpetual vicar in the church of Saint Remigius of Notoncurt and in the church of Saint Mary of Calvomonte, had received the care of souls from the hand of his bishop, and afterward, with that bishop’s permission, had set out for Jerusalem. The priest Mainerius, having expelled his chaplain, violently occupied his parish [Col. 0514D] and presumes to retain what he has occupied. Since we neither wish nor ought to permit ecclesiastical men to suffer oppressions and violences of this kind, we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently and carefully to investigate the truth of this matter. If it is lawfully established to you that the said priest was deprived of the aforesaid parish by the violence and presumption of the aforementioned Mainerius, strictly compel him, every pretext and appeal removed, to leave the said parish to that priest without molestation and in peace, and to make full reparation for the losses; imposing upon him such a penalty [Col. 0515A] that others may fear to usurp the sanctuary of God by unlawful occupation.

Given at Benevento, on the second Ides of November [12 November].

## DXVIII. To the same.—On behalf of the priest P. (Benevento, November 17.)

[Ibid., col. 763.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the complaint of the priest P. it has come to our ears that the Bishop of Châlons unjustly despoiled him of his church, and did so after an appeal had been made to us—something which was not lawful. Since the remedy of appeal ought to come to the aid of all who are oppressed, [Col. 0515B] we have commanded him by our letters that, if he despoiled the aforesaid priest of the said church after the appeal, or otherwise unjustly, he restore it without pretext and leave it to him in peace and quiet. If he should perhaps delay doing this, admonish and exhort him to restore without any contradiction to the said priest the aforementioned church, which he took from him after an appeal had been made to us, or unjustly, and to cause him to possess it in peace. But if he should scorn to obey your admonitions, compel him, with every severity and appeal removed, to do this.

Given at Benevento, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December [17 November].

## DXIX. To the same.—On behalf of the lepers of Cambrai. (Benevento, November 18.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0515C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although by the office of administration and the solicitude of pastoral care which we have undertaken we are bound to defend all our afflicted brethren, the protection of the Apostolic See ought to be more promptly available to infirm brethren in proportion as Almighty God, in His just judgment, has visited them with a graver sickness. Our beloved sons, the sick people of Cambrai, have complained to us that the abbots of Saint Andrew of the Castle and of the Holy Sepulchre at Cambrai, the canons of Saint Géry, and the noble Manasses of Rumigny presume to exact tithes from them on newly cultivated land and on the increase of their animals. [Col. 0515D] We have commanded them and enjoined them by virtue of obedience either to restore in full, within forty days after receiving our letters, the tithes which they have presumptuously taken from them in these matters, or to come to an amicable and peaceable agreement with them concerning them, and henceforth not presume to trouble them regarding these things.

Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid abbots and canons refuse in this matter to comply with our commands, you forbid them entrance into their churches, appeal removed; declare by apostolic authority that the aforesaid abbots are suspended from administration until suitable satisfaction has been made; [Col. 0516A] and, if necessary, strictly compel them by other means to carry out our command. Under threat of anathema, forbid their parishioners to assemble in their churches for divine offices; and publicly pronounce the aforesaid Manasses excommunicated if, after being admonished by you, he does not make satisfaction to them concerning this. For the love of God and in reverence for blessed Peter and for us, uphold and defend the said sick persons in their right, as is required by your office, so that you may thereby deserve to receive eternal rewards and may expect abundant thanks from us.

Given at Benevento, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December [18 November].

## DXX. He communicates the preceding letter to the abbots of Saint Andrew of the Castle and of the Holy Sepulchre, and to the canons of Saint Géry. (Benevento, November 18.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0516B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, etc.

. . . . . To his beloved sons, the abbots of Saint Andrew of the Castle and of the Holy Sepulchre, and the canons of Saint Géry.

Our beloved sons, the sick people of Cambrai, have complained to us that you do not hesitate at all to demand and extort from them tithes on newly cultivated land and on the increase of their animals. At this we greatly wonder and are gravely moved against you, since it has been granted to them by the Roman Church, as to other sick persons, that they are not bound to pay anyone tithes on the things aforementioned. Therefore, because it neither becomes you nor can we in any way endure that those whom the right hand of the heavenly Creator has so afflicted that they suffer from an incurable disease should be burdened by you with any troubles or anxieties—especially in matters which tend to our contempt and are known greatly to derogate from the authority of the Roman Church—we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters and by virtue of obedience that you restore, without any pretext [Col. 0516D] or excuse, the tithes which you have unlawfully withheld from the aforesaid lepers from newly cultivated land or the increase of their animals; or take care to reach an amicable and peaceable agreement with them concerning this; and henceforth presume in no way to trouble them regarding these matters.

But if you should scorn to fulfill our command within forty days after receipt of this letter, we thereupon forbid you entrance into your churches by apostolic authority. We declare you, sons who are abbots, suspended from the office of administration until worthy satisfaction is made; we command divine offices to cease in your churches; and we have instructed our venerable brother Henry, Archbishop of Reims, and the canons of Cambrai to compel you to this with every severity, and not delay under threat of anathema to forbid your parishioners to assemble for offices in those churches. [Col. 0517A]

Given at Benevento, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December [18 November].

## DXXI. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of the church of Saint Martin of Laon. (Benevento, November 19.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

In cases concerning religious men, your office is to be relied upon all the more because, both by their religious profession and by the authority of your episcopate, you are more strictly bound to give them aid and support. On behalf of our sons, the abbot and brethren of the church of Saint Martin of Laon, we have received complaints concerning certain injuries committed against them by Giles, priest of Mont-Hunold; Hugh, knight of Warch.; Guy of Chamelzi; and P., son of Anselm of Montacute. We entrusted these complaints, appeal removed, for final settlement to our venerable brothers B., Bishop of Beauvais, and the Bishop of Noyon, and to our beloved son, the abbot of Ourscamp.

[Note: [Col. 0517D] Bartholomew, who succeeded Henry after the latter’s translation to the see of Reims.]

[Note: [Col. 0518D] The monastery of Ourscamp, of the Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Noyon, of the line of Clairvaux.]

Therefore we command your brotherhood by the present letters to compel those persons to appear when summoned by those judges and to obey their judgment, so that the said brethren may no longer be oppressed through a failure of justice and your brotherhood may be seen to deserve commendation for restraining wicked men. For we have directed those judges that if one of them is unable to be present in these matters, the other two are nevertheless to carry out what has been enjoined.

[Col. 0517C] Given at Benevento, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December [19 November].

## DXXII. To the same.—On behalf of the cleric R., that the Archbishop of Reims provide for him. (Benevento, November 19.)

[Ibid., col. 766.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to H., Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

R., a cleric and bearer of this letter, came to us and stated in a detailed account [Col. 0517D] that you ordained him deacon but did not assign him a title in any church. Therefore, because he says that he suffers from extreme poverty, and because we do not believe your discretion is unaware that an ordination conferred without a certain title is void, we admonish and command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to make provision for the said R., in some church where he may suitably receive the necessities of life, for reverence of blessed Peter and of us and in discharge of your office. Thus may he faithfully serve Almighty God in his order, and we may be bound greatly to commend your solicitude in this respect.

[Col. 0518A] Given at Benevento, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December [19 November].

## DXXIII. He confirms to the abbey of Fontevraud the grant of an annual revenue of fifty pounds from the castle of Dijon, made by Odo, Duke of Burgundy. (Benevento, December 1.)

[See *Gallia Christiana*, new ed., vol. II, 1319.]

## DXXIV. To all archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and other prelates of Spain.—On behalf of the monastery of Ripoll. (Benevento, December 6.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 1064.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, all archbishops and bishops, and to his beloved sons, abbots, priors, and other prelates of churches to whom these letters may come, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not believe your prudent discretion is unaware how our predecessor Pope Innocent, of revered memory, decreed in the general Lateran Council that whoever should lay violent hands upon a cleric, monk, or lay brother of any religious order would incur sentence of excommunication, such that he could obtain the benefit of absolution only from the Roman pontiff or by his command. Moved by this consideration, and likewise constrained by the duty of our office, we command and enjoin your whole body by apostolic letters that, if any of your parishioners lays violent hands upon any monk, cleric, or lay brother of Ripoll, you publicly declare him excommunicated, every contradiction and appeal removed, and order all persons to avoid him as excommunicated until he has made suitable satisfaction to the person injured and comes to the Apostolic See with your letters to make satisfaction. [Col. 0518C]

What we have said above concerning those who lay hands upon a monk, cleric, or lay brother of Ripoll, we wish to be understood in this sense: all who dishonor them by seizing their persons, wounding them, or taking away goods which they have with them are to be avoided by everyone as excommunicated until they restore what was taken, make suitable satisfaction to the injured party, and come to the Apostolic See to make satisfaction. The brethren of the monastery of Ripoll have further represented to us in an earnest account that, living among mountains and in arid places, they transport provisions to the said monastery from elsewhere, not without grave labor, across great distances. It therefore often happens that, if their beasts carrying food are seized by evildoers, they suffer the torments of deprivation through both hunger and thirst. Accordingly, desiring usefully to provide for their security, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters strictly to forbid all your parishioners, in the name of God and of us and under threat of anathema, to attack for any reason the pack animals of the aforesaid monastery, together with their attendants or services, or to dare inflict upon them any injury or molestation. [Col. 0519A]

Also forbid and publicly interdict anyone from presuming to seize or molest any person coming to its market, or his goods, or anyone found within the precinct of that monastery; nor may anyone inflict violence or injury upon him. But if anyone should presume in this respect to act contrary to our prohibition, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of us.

[Col. 0519B] Given at Benevento, on the eighth Ides of December [6 December].

## DXXV. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of Amelius concerning a certain fief. (Benevento, December 6.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 766.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.
