We therefore caused them, after they had made their way to our presence, to be absolved from the sentence by which they were bound, and suitable penance to be imposed upon them.

We send them back to you absolved, commanding your discretion by apostolic letters that, if, as they assert, they rendered reverence and obedience to Malincasa without an intervening pledge of faith and oath, you cause them to abstain from celebrating Mass until the next feast of the Nativity of the Lord; otherwise, let them abstain for a year. But if the resources of their churches do not permit them to be served by other priests, then, adding to the penance imposed upon them as you think fit, restore their office to them. And because the very journey to us was a punishment to them, diligently admonish the aforesaid abbot on our behalf and yours to receive them again into the full possession of their benefice and to treat them kindly and gently.

Furthermore, we wish it to come to the knowledge of your discretion that, when Villanus, priest of Saint James, came to us, he refused to swear that he would abide by our command; therefore he returned home in the clothing in which he had come. We therefore command your prudence by apostolic letters publicly to declare that the same V. is excommunicated as contumacious, proud, and rebellious, until he comes to our presence to make satisfaction with your letters.

Given at Benevento, on the second day before the Ides of June [12 June].

DLXXX. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims. He writes that the wife of the knight Hugh, whom he had repudiated on false grounds, must be restored to her husband. (Benevento, 16 June.)

[MARTEN., *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 815.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the tenor of certain letters of our venerable brother, the bishop of Châlons, we learned some time ago that Hugh, the knight who bears these letters, had hired certain false witnesses and, through their testimony, had caused a divorce to be pronounced between himself and his wife. Afterwards both he and the aforesaid witnesses showed this to the said bishop by their own confession and asked him for mercy for their perjury. We therefore, if we remember correctly, commanded him by our letters that, if it were lawfully established for him by suitable witnesses—of whom it was probable that they would not wish to commit perjury—that the aforesaid witnesses had been hired for money, or that a degree of kinship other than the one they had alleged existed between the spouses, he should restore his wife to the aforesaid Hugh and cause them to remain together, if neither had yet contracted marriage with another; and further, he should impose suitable penance both on Hugh and on the witnesses for what they had done.

Since, however, as the repeated complaint of this man, who has come to our presence with much toil and danger, shows, the bishop has hitherto been unwilling to accomplish anything in the matter, we commanded him by our letters to proceed in this affair according to the tenor of our other letters, setting aside every delay and appeal. If he perhaps refuses to do so, you are to carry it out more swiftly according to the tenor of our letters which we sent him on this matter, with every pretext and appeal removed.

[Col. 0549C] Given at Benevento, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July [16 June].

DLXXXI. He commands Robert, archdeacon of Châlons, and the abbot of Saint Memmius to hear the case between Herbert Medonarius and the clerk Milo. (Benevento, 8 June.)

[Ibid., col. 816.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ROBERT, archdeacon of the Church of Châlons, and to the abbot of Saint Memmius,

[Note: [Col. 0549] The monastery of Saint Memmius belonged to regular canons of the Order of Saint Augustine.]

greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that the clerk Milo urgently charges Herbert, keeper of the church of Saint Mary, with having stolen from that church property worth one hundred pounds; and he accuses the same citizen of Châlons of knowingly communicating with M. while excommunicated. Since we have no small confidence in the prudence of your discretion and integrity, we entrust to your experience for hearing that case, brought to us by appeal from the tribunal of our venerable brother the archbishop of Rheims. We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters that, when requested concerning this matter, you summon both parties before your tribunal and, having carefully heard and considered the arguments on either side, decide the case through the administration of justice, with the remedy of appeal, as stated, removed.

Given at Benevento, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July [18 June].

DLXXXII. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of the church of Silva Major. (Benevento, 22 June.)

[Ibid., col. 818.]

[Col. 0550A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of the people of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved sons, the abbot and brothers of Silva Major, have informed us by letters that your predecessor S., of good memory, long ago granted them the church of Brague, with the consent and at the request of the noble Count of Registet; namely, that, as the canons died, monks of their order should be instituted there by the prior of Noveio. But now, as we have heard, G. de Mazeriis caused the provostship of that same church, together with a certain prebend long possessed by the monks, to be granted for a price by the count to his son John, and presumptuously continues to hold it thus occupied. Certain others also—namely O., M., and G.—have forcibly usurped prebends which the monks had long held, and, after an appeal had been made to us, caused the houses of those monks to be broken into and their possessions carried off.

Since it is unworthy that what was so granted to the said abbot and brothers should be revoked and should again come into secular hands, we commanded our venerable brother the bishop of Soissons and our beloved son the abbot of Saint Remigius by our letters, after summoning the parties before them, carefully to investigate the truth of the matter. If it is established that the aforesaid men received and occupied the benefices of the aforesaid church in this manner, they are diligently to admonish them to restore those benefices without delay to the said abbot and brothers, together with the revenues received, and to permit them to possess them in peace. If they believe that they have any right in these matters, let them proceed judicially with the abbot and brothers before the aforesaid judges.

If they do not comply with the admonition of the aforesaid judges within forty days, the judges are not to delay, with every objection and appeal removed, to bind them with the bond of excommunication; and if they do not even then come to their senses, they are to declare them condemned by a sentence of perpetual deposition. They are also to compel, under the strictness of anathema and without appeal, those who are said to have broken into the monks’ houses and carried off their property after an appeal to us, to restore the property taken and make good the damages.

But if the aforesaid men scorn to appear before the said judges and to accept and observe what they determine, you are to strike them with a sentence of excommunication, setting aside every pretext and appeal, and announce throughout your whole province that all must avoid them as excommunicated persons. Moreover, endeavour, for reverence for blessed Peter and for us, and in consideration of their religious profession, to love and support the brothers of the aforesaid monastery who serve in those regions. Give them your aid and protection in their affairs, especially in preserving the benefices, dignities, and other rights of the church of Brague; and, as far as lies within your power, do not permit anyone unjustly to harass or disturb them in these matters. Do not delay to bind with the bond of excommunication, until full satisfaction is made, all who presume, by their own authority or by a lay grant and without the consent of the aforesaid abbot and brothers, to usurp prebends or dignities of that church contrary to the concession made to them, after stripping them of ecclesiastical offices and benefices.

Given at Benevento, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July [22 June].

DLXXXIII. To Dominic and Heimard.—He confirms the agreement made between them and Theoderic. (Benevento, 10 July.)

[Ibid., col. 745.]

[Col. 0551B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons DOMINIC and HEIMARD, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When a dispute had arisen in our presence between you and Theoderic and his son over twenty pounds, which they asserted that you owed them, we, who are bound to devote ourselves to restoring peace and concord among those at variance, entrusted the dispute to our venerable brother Rod., bishop of Ferentino, to hear and bring to due conclusion. After carefully hearing and considering the arguments of both sides, he established the following agreement between you, with the consent of both parties: namely, that, touching the holy Gospels, you swore that on the feast of Saint Andrew in each year you would pay them twenty shillings until you had paid in full and completely what you owed them. He also added that, if any one of you should depart from this world before payment of the said debt, your heirs would be bound to discharge the debt in the same manner. You likewise promised that you would give them sureties and pledges.

You further swore that henceforth you would inflict upon them no annoyance or harm whatsoever, all disputes which might arise at any time concerning this business being settled. The aforesaid Theoderic and Heimard likewise swore that they would observe this agreement toward you. Holding this agreement to be ratified and firm, we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this charter of our confirmation or in any way to oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Benevento, on the sixth day before the Ides of July [10 July].

DLXXXIV. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of the canons of the Church of Ham. (Benevento, 14 July.)

[Ibid., col. 746.]

[Col. 0552A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because we have great confidence and hope that, from the fervour of devotion and purity of faith which we see you show toward us by clear proofs, you will willingly receive and observe our admonitions and commands, we entrust ecclesiastical business to your discretion for execution. Therefore, when we hear that matters sometimes turn out otherwise than we hoped and expected, it is exceedingly grievous and distressing to us; and we are the more troubled because we love you with a more sincere affection of charity.

For we have learned that, in accordance with the tenor of our command, you have by no means compelled the Premonstratensian canons to observe the judgment which B., formerly bishop of Noyon, of pious memory, pronounced after examination of the dispute between them and the canons of the Church of Ham concerning the mills of Hamel and Pevilla. Indeed, while you bear it with equanimity, they scorn to obey the judgment rendered.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] Baldwin of Boulogne, who was made bishop of Noyon from abbot of Châtillon in 1140, according to Alberic in his *Chronicle*, and held the see until 1157.]

[Note: [Col. 0552D] Ham, or Hamet, is an abbey of regular canons of the Order of Saint Augustine, who succeeded the secular canons in 1108.]

But since we must greatly fear that, if we prove sluggish or remiss in the execution of justice and in the office of the apostolate entrusted to us, we shall be severely punished at the strict judgment before the tribunal of the heavenly Judge; if through you we cannot render justice against their wrongdoers to those of your province who complain before us that they suffer injuries, then reluctantly and sorrowfully we shall have recourse to others, who ought zealously to perform our office in these matters. For we willingly and gladly show deference to you and to your honour where it is proper; but we ought to show still greater deference to Him who has the power to judge us and all men according to His good pleasure.

Accordingly, by repeated letters we command and enjoin your brotherhood, carefully considering and attending, as a discreet and eminent man, to what is expedient for you and your office, to admonish the aforesaid Premonstratensians on our behalf and yours and strictly compel them, within thirty days after receipt of these letters and with every pretext set aside, to obey the aforesaid judgment. Let them restore in full to the canons of Ham all expenses they incurred on that occasion after the judgment was pronounced, and presume no longer, for any reason, to act against the aforesaid judgment. If they scorn to obey our command and yours in this matter, correct and chastise their contumacy and rebellion in such a way that they may learn by certain experience how dangerous it is to oppose a judgment canonically rendered, and thereafter, unwillingly, do what they ought willingly to do.

Given at Benevento, on the second day before the Ides of July [14 July].

DLXXXV. To the same.—That he cause the relics of Saint James, violently taken by the count of Flanders, to be restored to the monastery of Saint Vedast. (Benevento, 15 July.)

[Ibid., col. 747.]

[Col. 0553A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that our beloved son, the nobleman Philip, count of Flanders, violently took from our beloved son the abbot of Saint Vedast relics of Saint James which that abbot was carrying in procession back to his monastery near Arras, and caused them to be taken to one of his own villages. Since it was no work of justice or merit to despoil the aforesaid monastery violently of those relics, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to admonish and induce the same count, on our behalf and yours, to restore the relics taken to the aforesaid monastery without difficulty, and to make no further effort to retain them. Unless he restores them, and it is established to you that he violently took them from the said abbot, prohibit the divine office, with appeal removed, in the church where they are kept until they have been fully restored to the monastery of Saint Vedast.

Given at Benevento, on the Ides of July [15 July].

DLXXXVI. To the dean and chapter of Paris.—That they invest Philip, nephew of the bishop of Meaux. (Benevento, 20 July.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1031.]

[Col. 0553C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the dean and chapter of Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The fervour of devotion and integrity of faith which our venerable brother the bishop of Meaux displays toward us and the Church—as a true worshipper of justice and an outstanding member of that same Church—show by certain indications how greatly we are bound to defer to him in his prayers and petitions. Therefore, carefully considering the grave labours and many dangers of travel which the said bishop is known to have endured in coming to us for the advancement and exaltation of the Church, we have judged that at present we should deny him nothing which we would do for one of our brethren.

Accordingly, induced by the prayers of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Franks, of the queen also, and of other great persons, as well as by the labours of the aforesaid bishop, and moved, as we thought proper, by consideration of his most sincere devotion: for our beloved son Philip, nephew of that bishop and your fellow canon, we admonish, command, and enjoin your whole body by apostolic letters that, with the impediment of appeal removed, you invest him and, when opportunity is received, take care to grant and assign it to him, so that we may thereby owe abundant thanks to your affection, and the aforesaid bishop may for that reason strive more fervently for the honour and advancement

[Note: [Col. 0553D] “of the Church,” or something similar, is missing.]

Given at Benevento, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August [20 July].

DLXXXVII. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of Milo de Thebio against his adversaries, because the authority of law decrees that a matter adjudged must stand. (Benevento, 30 July.)

[MARTEN., *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 751.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of the people of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the complaint submitted to us by Milo de Thebio, we recently learned that, together with his son, he had granted in alms a certain house belonging to his godmother, together with a grange; and that the said M. had already possessed it peacefully for a long time with that son. Certain persons then brought them into court and tried to invalidate the aforesaid alms-gift. While the case was being litigated, the said M. and his son maintain that they obtained that alms-gift by judgment. Since, as we have heard, their adversaries still do not cease to harass them concerning this, although the authority of law decrees that a matter adjudged must stand, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to cause the aforesaid M. and his son to hold the aforesaid alms-gift in peace, as it was reasonably granted to his son and afterwards adjudged to him; and do not allow them to be unjustly harassed or drawn into litigation about it by anyone. If their adversaries refuse to desist upon your admonition, restrain them from their presumption by ecclesiastical censure.

Given at Benevento, on the third day before the Kalends of August [30 July].

DLXXXVIII. He writes to P[eter], prior, and the whole convent of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem that A[malric], patriarch, and A[malric], king, ought not to be impeded from restoring to the church of Joppa “the dignity of a cathedral church and the other things which it had long ago lost through the violence and occupation of the pagans, now that an opportunity has arisen.” Nevertheless, he has admonished the patriarch to “find for them worthy and honourable compensation.” (Benevento, 5 August.)

[Eug. de ROZIÈRE, *Cartulaire du Saint-Sépulcre*, 291.]

[Col. 0554D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, prior, and the whole convent of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have graciously received the letters of your devotion; and although we have not been able to grant all your requests, we have nevertheless taken care, so far as we could, with fatherly affection and due charity, to provide for you and your church and to consult your advantage. Certainly, it accords with goodness and equity beyond doubt, and agrees with the institutions of the holy Fathers and our predecessors, that churches destroyed by an incursion of hostile savagery, or abandoned through fear, and however much deprived of their own honours, liberty, or possessions, should, after peace has subsequently been restored and their former prosperity renewed, be restored, as though by a certain right of return after exile, to all things with the full integrity of their former status; and that all their ancient rights, possessions, and liberties should be surrendered back to them without any hindrance or diminution.

Therefore, if in the case of the church of Joppa—which, you complain, is being thus taken from you by our venerable brother Amalric, patriarch of Jerusalem, and our dearest son in Christ Amalric, illustrious king of Jerusalem—we wished to infringe what ought generally to be observed in all cases, and, at the insistence of your petition, to prevent them from restoring to it the dignity of a cathedral church and the other things which it had long ago lost through the violence and occupation of the pagans, now that an opportunity has arisen, we should appear, forgetful alike of divine and human law, utterly to oppose the apostolic decrees which we ought to uphold, and most openly to contravene the commands of our predecessors which are known to have been issued for the restoration of cathedral churches.

Because it neither becomes us to do this nor is fitting for you to request it, and because we wish, so far as we can consistently with the honour of ourselves and the Church, to assist you in accordance with the duty of our office, we have commanded the aforesaid patriarch, our brother, by our letters that, if he considers it necessary to pursue the proposal, and if the situation so requires and opportunity demands—that is, if the aforesaid church of Joppa ought to be restored to its former dignity and ancient liberty—he should exercise such dispensation toward your church and, with the counsel of the aforesaid king and of the religious persons and wise men of that land, find for you in other matters compensation so worthy and honourable, as is customary in such cases, that, once you have received agreeable consolation, your aforesaid church may not appear to sustain excessive damage or an intolerable loss; nor may that patriarch be praised for the erection or restoration of one church in such a way that he is reasonably condemned for the overthrow or ruin of another. Nor should any complaint on that score have occasion to reach our ears.

[Col. 0555D] Given at Benevento, on the Nones of August [5 August].

DLXXXIX. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of Fulk of the village of Aleran. (Benevento, 11 August.)

[MARTEN., *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 752.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of the people of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We entrust to your experience for hearing and due determination the case known to be pending between Fulk of the village of Aleran and Milo concerning a certain piece of land which Fulk claims as his own and alleges has been held contrary to right by the said Milo for fifteen years. Therefore, when requested on this matter, summon both parties before you and, after carefully hearing and considering the arguments on either side, decide the same case through the administration of justice in such a way that neither party may rightly complain of a failure of his legal right.

Given at Benevento, on the third day before the Ides of August [11 August].

DXC. To the same.—On behalf of the Hospitaller brothers of Jerusalem concerning the village of Bechehem. (Benevento, 15 August.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0556B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of the people of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the complaint transmitted to us by the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem, we have learned that, although the village of Bechehem had long ago been delivered and granted to them under the testimony of the noble duke of Louvain, and had been confirmed by Henry, formerly bishop of Liège, while he was still Catholic [Note: [Col. 0555D] This is Henry of Limburg, the second bishop of Liège of that name; he was consecrated by the archbishop of Cologne in the presence of Innocent II and the Emperor Lothair. Afterward he adhered to the antipope Victor IV [Col. 0556D]; when Victor died, he refused the papacy offered him by the Emperor Frederick. Nevertheless, at the emperor’s command, he consecrated John of Struma, as Alberic testifies under the year 1164.], the aforesaid duke, after they had possessed it peacefully for a long time, forcibly took it from the said brethren and did not hesitate to sell it to a certain knight.

[Col. 0556C] Therefore, since it belongs to our office to defend religious men against the injuries of wrongdoers and to preserve their rights unimpaired and intact, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters diligently and earnestly to admonish the aforesaid duke that, if the facts are as stated, he restore the specified village to the aforesaid brethren, setting aside every pretext and appeal, and allow them to possess it in peace. If perhaps he scorns to comply with your admonition, strike his person and the holder of the aforesaid village with a sentence of excommunication, without remedy of appeal; and throughout all his land situated in your province, forbid the celebration of every divine office, except baptism for infants and penances for the dying.

[Col. 0556D] Given at Benevento, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September.

DXCI. He commends the canons of Pisa for their opposition to the schism. (Benevento, August 27.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 402.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of Pisa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the letter of your devotion with our accustomed kindness; [Col. 0557A] and because you carefully and with particular zeal uphold Catholic unity, courageously oppose the error of schismatic perversity, and apply every effort and diligence to recalling schismatics, we fittingly commend, as is right, the constancy of your faith and courage. When opportunity presents itself, we desire to respond to your merits accordingly.

Moreover, we ask and admonish your whole body that, as you have begun well, you labor by every means and exert all your strength for the expulsion of Malincasa and the restoration of your venerable brother, your archbishop. Furthermore, we judge as having fallen into schism those who are known to have communicated with schismatics by oath or pledged faith, prayer, food, or kiss—if they did this voluntarily, or, though at first unwilling, later made it [Col. 0557B] habitual. Yet we consider that those who have sworn an oath or pledged faith should be punished more severely than others.

Moreover, from your letters we learned, to our great sorrow and distress, that the aforesaid archbishop sent back absolved the chaplain of Visignano, who had taken that wicked oath, and commanded you patiently to tolerate A., prior of Saint James, and R., chaplain of the Most Holy Savior, who, together with the aforesaid R., swore to his execration. We have commanded him that, unless they renounce the schism in your presence, or in his presence with your knowledge, according to the form we prescribed for you, and take another oath [Col. 0557C] that they will obey our command, or at least his own, he is not to delay restoring them to their former sentence. He is also to show you due deference in these matters and in others, as is fitting, and suitably honor your whole body.

Given at Benevento, six days before the Kalends of September.

DXCII. He confirms the monastery of the island of Gallinaria to Hugh, archbishop of Genoa. (Benevento, August 28.)

[UGHELLI, IV, 871.]

ALEXANDER, etc., to his venerable brother HUGH, archbishop of Genoa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

No one more than the Roman pontiff ought to remember service received and to respond to each person according to his merits. For everyone is rendered more steadfast in devotion and more ready in service when he sees his good deeds praised and knows that they are encouraged by worthy recompense.

[Col. 0557D] Therefore, considering the constancy of faith and devotion which your predecessor Syrus, of good memory, and you likewise, together with the clergy and people of your city, bestowed upon us and our brethren with ardent desire when the crisis of necessity was pressing, and which you continually display, we desire to render you a worthy recompense for your merits. We desire also to foster both your Church and your city with a special grace and prerogative of affection in the service of ourselves and of blessed Peter, [Col. 0558A] intending, by the Lord’s gift, to make greater provision for you hereafter.

Accordingly, by the common counsel of our brethren, we grant to you and your successors, and through you to your Church, the monastery on the island of Gallinaria, which until now has been subject to no one except the Roman pontiff, to rule, administer, and govern. We decree that henceforth it shall remain firmly and forever under your disposition and ordering as its own bishop, and we subject it to your authority, establishing that there you may exercise correction and freely exercise pontifical right without anyone’s contradiction.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly infringe this page of our grant or in any way oppose it. [Col. 0558B] But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Benevento, five days before the Kalends of September.

DXCIII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—That a cemetery be granted to the sick brethren of Dampierre. (Benevento, August 29.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 755.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved sons, the sick brethren of the castle of Dampierre, represented to us in a communication sent to us [Col. 0558C] that they had no cemetery in which they could bury their brethren; rather, when any one of them dies, they are obliged to carry his body almost half a league for burial. We therefore commanded our venerable brother, the bishop of Châlons, to permit them to have a cemetery for themselves and their *redditi* [Note: [Col. 0557] *Redditi* were those who devoted themselves to the service of the sick, though without taking solemn vows.], and, when requested, not to delay blessing it. If that bishop neglects to fulfil our command, you shall carry out all the aforesaid matters fully, yourself or through another, as swiftly as you can.

Given at Benevento, four days before the Kalends of September.

DXCIV. He ratifies the sentence of interdict pronounced by Leonatus, abbot of Pescara, against clerics in the territory of Sansonesca and confirmed by I., bishop of Segni. (Benevento, September 4.)

[MURATORI, *Rer. Ital. Script.*, II, II, 1013.]

[Col. 0558D]

DXCV. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—Concerning the knight Paganus. (Benevento, September 6.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 756.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0559A] Our beloved son T., monk of La Celle, came to us [Note: [Col. 0559D] La Celle, a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict near Troyes, founded by Saint Frotbert; it was also called the German Island [Col. 0560D] and still exists under the Congregation of Saint-Vanne.] and showed us on his own behalf that you had subjected your knight Paganus to a sentence of excommunication, because he confessed before you that he had laid violent hands upon a cleric. He therefore urgently entreated us to have him absolved through some bishop from those parts.

Accordingly, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters to absolve the said Paganus from the sentence by which he is bound, after receiving from him the oath customary in the Church, and then impose upon him a penance proportionate to the character of the offence. Thereafter, under force of the oath, enjoin him never again to lay violent hands upon a cleric, monk, Templar, Hospitaller, or lay brother of any religious order, [Col. 0559B] unless he did so in defending himself, or by command of his prelate, or found that person in disgraceful intercourse with his own wife, daughter, or sister.

Given at Benevento, on the eighth day before the Ides of September.

DXCVI. To the same.—For the church of Saint Remigius concerning certain rents. (Benevento, September 6.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the complaint sent to us by the abbot and brethren of Saint Remigius of Reims [Col. 0559C] that Radulf of Courteio has for several years withheld an annual rent of sixty solidi which he owes them, and that H., count of Grandpré, presumes to take from them a rent of thirty solidi. The noble counts of Soissons and Herou, R. of Roset, and G. of Châtillon have also inflicted grave losses and many injuries upon their church.

Therefore, since it belongs to our office to foster religious places with pious protection and more earnestly preserve their rights, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and urgently exhort the aforesaid men to restore without diminution to the aforesaid abbot, brethren, and their church the rent withheld and the other things taken away; to make suitable satisfaction for the losses [Col. 0559D] and injuries inflicted; or to provide them before you with sufficient justice in all these matters. Thus the aforementioned abbot and brethren shall suffer no injury to their right, and no blame can deservedly attach to you on that account.

But if the aforesaid wrongdoers perhaps scorn to comply with your admonition in these matters, pronounce ecclesiastical sentence against them and their land, excluding appeal, and cause it to be observed throughout your province by all persons until worthy satisfaction has been made.

Given at Benevento, on the eighth day before the Ides of September.

DXCVII. To the same.—For the church of Saint Remigius against Stephen and certain others who forcibly hold lands of the church. (Benevento, September 6.)

[Ibid., col. 757.]

[Col. 0560A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved sons P., abbot, and the brethren of Saint Remigius of Reims, in a complaint sent to us, showed that Stephen and certain other of their men, who had long been accustomed to dwell in the village of Saint Remigius called the Island, but moved to a new settlement outside the island, [Col. 0560B] presume forcibly to cultivate lands of the church which they formerly held, and refuse to relinquish them.

Therefore, since we love the aforesaid abbot and brethren with such fervor of charity that we are unwilling, as indeed we ought not, for any reason to fail them in their justice, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters zealously to admonish and, excluding appeal, under the compulsion of anathema, compel the aforesaid men either to return to their former dwelling and there render the church of Saint Remigius its due right concerning its lands, or to leave those lands altogether free to that church.

Moreover, diligently admonish the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem, who are said unjustly to have taken away a certain woman from the aforesaid abbot and brethren, to restore her to them without delay [Col. 0560C] and leave her in peace, or to render them full justice on this matter before you. If they are unwilling to comply with either of these requirements upon your admonition, introduce the aforesaid abbot and brethren, excluding appeal, into possession of that which is in dispute.

And because the said abbot and brethren are said to have suffered grave losses through schismatics, who took from them the revenues and possessions which they had customarily held in Germany, we command and prescribe by the authority of this letter, in reliance upon your discretion, that you assign to them, excluding every contradiction and appeal, such possessions and benefices as schismatics from the kingdom of Germany are known to hold in your province, and cause them to possess these in peace until they recover their own property and receive compensation for what was taken. [Col. 0560D] Remember, however, that not all from the kingdom of Germany are infected with schismatic perversity; some of them remain devoted to us.

Given at Benevento, on the eighth day before the Ides of September.

DXCVIII. To . . . .—For the prior of the Valley of Saint Peter. (Benevento, September 6.)

[Ibid., col. 758.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc.: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0561A] Whenever some occasion of contention arises among religious men, it ought to be cut off all the more quickly, since they have greater need of peace and tranquility in order to preserve their vocation. We have received the complaint of our beloved sons En., prior, and the brethren of the Valley of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 0561D] The Valley of Saint Peter, a monastery of the Carthusian Order in the diocese of Laon.], who assert that they suffer no slight disturbance in their lands and pastures from the brethren of Tenalliis [Note: [Col. 0561D] Tenalliae, or Thenoliae or Thenolium, is a monastery [Col. 0562D] of the Premonstratensian Order near the town of Vervins in Thiérache, founded in 1129 by Bartholomew, bishop of Laon.].

Accordingly, having great confidence in your discretion and desiring that the aforesaid brethren on both sides may pursue the path of their profession without the bitterness of contention, we have thought fit to commit the controversy itself to your discretion. By these present letters we command you, meeting in one place, to summon both parties before you, [Col. 0561B] and, after carefully hearing and understanding the arguments of each, to settle the controversy either by agreement or judgment, so that they may not be wearied by prolonged mutual complaints, nor others who see them derive from their contention matter for reproach.

Given at Benevento, on the eighth day before the Ides of September.

DXCIX. He commands the canons of Pisa, after proclaiming excommunication, to forbid anyone to accept benefices from the intruded and schismatic abbot of the monastery of Sexto. (Benevento, September 14.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 405.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of Pisa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0561C] Your prudence does not need to be told how, as the treachery of schismatics swelled, the monastery of Sexto, formerly eminent in religion, has been crushed and diminished both spiritually and temporally; for you see its daily misery and desolation.

Therefore, because it especially befits you to strive for its restoration, we command your whole body by apostolic letters, under threat of anathema, to forbid publicly in your churches, on our behalf, anyone from your diocese to dare receive from the intruder in the aforesaid monastery anything from its property as a fief or in any other manner, [Col. 0561D] or provide that intruder with support or favor in his wrongdoing. Whoever attempts this, you shall publicly declare excommunicated by our authority, and you shall diligently ensure that he is avoided as excommunicated until full satisfaction has been made. But to those who give counsel and aid to your beloved son A., abbot of the aforesaid monastery, promise the grace of God and our blessing, and firmly enjoin this upon them as remission of their sins.

Given at Benevento, eighteen days before the Kalends of October.

DC. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—For the complaint of Marbelin and his mother Belot. (Benevento, September 17.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 759.]

[Col. 0562A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Marbelin and his mother Belot, coming before the mercy of the Apostolic See, set forth to us in a humble petition that, when the father of the aforesaid A. had pledged a certain house of theirs to a knight as security, D., his uncle, redeemed the specified house from the knight. Yet he refused to accept the money for which the house had been pledged, and did not hesitate to sell the house itself [Col. 0562B] to another for one hundred solidi. Wrongfully withholding a certain piece of their land as well, he does not scruple to take the fruits arising from it. Besides this, he refuses to restore to them a certain ring and fifteen ells of fustian which the father of the aforesaid A. lent him.

When their case concerning all these matters was being heard in the presence of our beloved son John, archdeacon of your Church, they appealed to our hearing; but he neither came nor sent anyone to answer for him. Since we could not settle the case in the absence of the other party, we commit it to your fraternity, in whom we have full confidence, to hear and determine it through justice. By apostolic letters [Col. 0562C] we command that, when requested in this matter, you summon both parties before you and, after fully hearing and understanding the arguments on either side, decide the case with a lawful conclusion, removing the impediment of appeal. If the aforesaid D., lawfully summoned, refuses to come before you or submit to your judgment, strike him with ecclesiastical censure, notwithstanding any appeal, so that, if not willingly, he may at least be compelled unwillingly to abide by justice.

Given at Benevento, fifteen days before the Kalends of October.

DCI. He commands the bishop of Forcona and the canons of Penne, Valva, and Chieti to observe, and to cause Richard, brother of Leonatus, to observe, a sentence of excommunication or interdict pronounced by Leonatus, abbot of Pescara, against certain clerics. (Benevento, September 23.)

[MURATORI, *Rer. Ital. Script.*, II, II, 1013.]

[Col. 0562D]

DCII. He commends the parishioners of Saint Savior at Venice for paying tithes and admonishes them to persevere in such payment. (Benevento, September 24.)

[CORNELII, *Ecclesiae Venetae*, XIV, 100.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all the parishioners and neighbors of the church [Col. 0563A] of Saint Savior: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved sons, the prior and brethren of the aforesaid church, informed us in a communication sent to us that you piously and devoutly pay the tithes of your goods to it and faithfully fulfil the Lord’s ordinance in this respect. We therefore commend the devotion of your affection in the Lord in many ways, and ask, admonish, and command your whole body by apostolic letters that you pay, without any diminution, to the aforesaid prior and his brethren, and to the church in which they are devoted to divine service, the tithes of the goods bestowed upon you by God, as these are known to have been granted to them by the privileges of the Roman Church and the writings of the diocesan bishop. [Col. 0563B] having received from the said prior and his successors the customary assurance that you will never again be compelled to render tithes to that bishop or to any other person.

Given at Benevento, eight days before the Kalends of October.

YEAR 1169.

DCIII. He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint Savior and the sentence rendered in its favor by apostolic delegates. (Benevento, January 4.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons VIVIAN, prior of the church of Saint Savior situated at Rialto, and his brethren, present and future, who profess the canonical life: in perpetual remembrance.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the Provider of all good things, in order that we may love religious persons and strive by every means to promote religion pleasing to God. For no service is ever pleasingly offered to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved in the purity of religious life.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests and take the aforesaid Church of Saint Savior, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, [Col. 0563D] Innocent, Eugenius, and Anastasius, Roman pontiffs; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

Because you have vowed to observe the canonical order and to live according to the Rule of blessed Augustine, we willingly grant your requests and, by apostolic authority, decree that this order shall remain inviolate in that church for all time. We establish that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter obtain, with the Lord’s favor, through the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and undiminished to you, your successors, and the church.

[Col. 0564A] We likewise confirm to you that share of the tithes from your parishioners which belongs to your church according to the sacred canons and constitutions of the holy Fathers. We further add and forbid anyone, by any trickery of surreption or by force, to set a prior over that church except one whom the brethren of the place in common, or the party of sounder counsel, shall canonically determine to elect.

We also grant that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving, nevertheless, the right of the mother church. You may receive, without anyone’s opposition, clerics or laymen who are free and absolved, fleeing from the world.

We forbid [Col. 0564B] any brother, after making profession in that place, without permission of his prior, to depart rashly from the cloister; and no one may dare retain one who departs without a letter of authorization from the community.

Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority the sentence reasonably pronounced by our venerable brother Henry, patriarch of Grado, and our beloved son Ildebrand, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles and legate of the Apostolic See, concerning the controversy between you and Dominic, parish priest of Saint Bartholomew. The dispute, long conducted regarding certain parochial houses—namely, the houses of the *justi* (“just/rightful persons”), the Maurocenis, the Gradonicis, the Greeks, Leonard Fradelli, and Dominic Aureus, which each claimed as belonging to his own right—is known to be contained in their authenticated document made concerning this matter. [Col. 0564C] We establish that no one, without your consent, may dare to give penance to your parishioners when ill, anoint them, or receive them for burial, unless the right of your church established by the sacred canons is preserved.

We therefore decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Conrad, archbishop of Mainz and bishop of Sabina. [Col. 0564D] I, Ubaldus, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Albert, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Boso, priest-cardinal of Saint Pudentiana, title of Pastor. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark. I, Theodinus, priest-cardinal of Saint Vitalis, title of Vestina. I, Ardicio, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of Saint Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa.

[Col. 0565A] Given at Benevento through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Nones of January, in the first indiction, in the year 1168 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

DCIV. He takes the monastery of Cava under the protection of blessed Peter and the Apostolic See, and confirms the privileges of the pontiffs his predecessors. (Benevento, January 30.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullar. Casin.*, II, p. 18.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son MORINUS, abbot of the monastery of Cava, situated near Salerno, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: [Col. 0565B] in perpetuity.

The authority of the Apostolic See entrusted to us urges us to offer the protection of guardianship to places and persons which duly implore its help with devotion. For, just as no effect should be given to those who seek what is unjust, so no request should be delayed for those who desire what is lawful and just—especially those who delight in serving almighty God with honorable life and praiseworthy moral discipline.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, Popes Gregory VII, Urban, Paschal, Callixtus, Innocent, and Eugenius, [Col. 0565C] receive the abbey of Cava, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves. We strengthen it by the privilege of this present document and decree that it shall remain altogether free from every yoke of either ecclesiastical or secular persons, so that it may appear subject only to the holy and Apostolic Roman Church.

We also establish that the monasteries, churches, and cells entrusted to your abbey shall remain firm and undiminished to you and your successors. They are listed by the following names:

Saint Lawrence at Paliperna: just as our aforesaid predecessor Pope Eugenius granted it to you, so that you and your successors might govern it forever and restore the religious life which had perished there, and established this by the confirmation of his decree, we confirm it to you and that monastery by apostolic authority. We also confirm the church of Saint Mary within your settlement, the church of Saint Elijah, and the church of Saint Fortunatus. [Col. 0565D] Whether these churches are parish churches or have no people, we confirm them, with their rights and appurtenances, to you and the said abbey by apostolic authority. In favor of your religious life, so that you may serve the Creator of all more quietly and peacefully for the wholesome condition of the universal Church, we exempt them, and any others you may hereafter canonically acquire, from every episcopal right by special grace and plenitude of power. Thus monks or secular clerics dwelling in your churches shall not be bound to answer diocesan bishops in any episcopal right or contentious jurisdiction.

[Col. 0566A] We also confirm to you and the aforesaid monastery the privileges of donations made to those churches, whether by laymen or ecclesiastics. You presented before us the instruments of these churches as authentic and lawful, to be approved by apostolic judgment. Having carefully seen and understood them, we approved, ratified, and confirmed them with certain knowledge. If anything has perhaps been inserted in them with insufficient force through carelessness or negligence, let it receive the fullest force of authority from this our act.

Likewise, we confirm to you and the aforesaid monastery the privileges of the hundred-year prescription which our predecessor Pope Urban, of happy memory, granted to that monastery through apostolic benevolence. We decree that those who hold occupied the possessions and liberties of that abbey, or the rights and revenues of its vassals, are to be entirely removed from them; that they can acquire or possess no right at all through such detention or possession; and that through this no prejudice has been or can be caused to you or to the right of that abbey, unless it is lawfully established that the said holders are protected by a hundred-year prescription.

[Col. 0566B] But if, by rash presumption, an attempt shall be made by you, your successors, or anyone else, whether concerning lands or legal claims, or through the intervention of any decision, contrary to the tenor of this our decree and without permission of the Apostolic See to invoke such immunity, we decree from now on that it shall be entirely without force. Rather, the aforesaid monastery, with all its present and future members, shall be subject in full right to the Apostolic See, saving the annual payment of three gold solidi owed to the holy Roman Church, as is more fully contained in the privilege of the aforementioned Urban.

Moreover, by the more abundant grace of the Apostolic See, we grant to you and your successors that, if you canonically grant any of your churches, possessions, or revenues to an ecclesiastical person as a benefice or annual rent, it shall be lawful for you and your successors, after the death of that ecclesiastical person, or whenever the benefice itself becomes vacant—regardless of whomever may have granted it to that ecclesiastical person—to apply the benefice or revenues to the use of the same monastery and retain them under its proprietary lordship. [Col. 0566D] No general law issued or to be issued by us or our successors, nor letters to be obtained concerning this from the Apostolic See or our cardinal-legates, shall prevent this, unless express mention has been made of this privilege.

Furthermore, whatever goods your abbey now lawfully possesses through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or offerings of the faithful, or shall hereafter canonically possess, we likewise confirm by apostolic authority to you, your successors, and that monastery.

[Col. 0567A] You may receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of clerics, both in the abbey itself and in the adjacent villages and in the churches of the city and diocese of Salerno, from whichever Catholic bishop you choose. In your other monasteries and obediences, receive these from the diocesan bishop, provided that he enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to bestow them freely and without misconduct. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer, who, relying upon our authority, shall grant what is requested.

Furthermore, no bishop may, without permission of the Roman pontiff, subject your places or the monks or secular clerics residing in them to interdict or excommunication. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any deceitful scheme or force, except one whom the brethren, by unanimous consent or by the sounder part of the brethren, elect according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. The person elected shall go to the Roman pontiff for ordination.

[Col. 0567B] If anyone thinks he has a just complaint against the aforesaid monastery and refuses to settle or determine his suit before the abbot or a monk of that abbey, we establish that the complaint shall be brought before our legates or ourselves, so that, by the equity of judgment and without respect of persons, justice may be rendered to each person, with God as author.

We therefore decree, etc.

Given at Benevento through the hands of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the second indiction, in the year 1168 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ubaldus, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Ubaldus, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. [Col. 0567D] I, Albert, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark. I, Theodinus, priest-cardinal of Saint Vitalis, title of Vestina. I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of Saint Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa.

DCV. He confirms the goods and privileges of the monastery of Saint Nicasius of Reims. (Benevento, February 8.)

[D. MARLOT, *Metropol. Rem.*, II, 397.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, [Col. 0568A] to his beloved sons GUIDO, abbot of the monastery of Saint Nicasius, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

For those choosing the religious life, it is fitting that apostolic protection be at hand, etc. Among these possessions we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the estate of Saint Hilary, as your church is known to have possessed it peaceably and without challenge for one hundred and four years, with the demesne holding, adjoining lands, pastures, and all appurtenances of the estate; with bannal authority and jurisdiction; and with mill-sites, both within and outside the estate, the watercourse, and the whole fishery from [lacuna]sione of Mount Saint Remigius as far as the stone boundary-marker of Saint Hilary toward Saint Martin. All these things Gervasius, formerly archbishop of Rheims, had purchased, entirely free from every human claim and exaction, [Col. 0568B] from certain knights, and had granted to the church of Saint Nicasius, to possess in perpetual right, under the authority of the privilege of Philip, formerly king of the Franks.

Also, the church-house on Mount Saint Remigius; the tithe of Burigny-Mont, redeemed through the archbishop from Peter, knight of Arpi [read perhaps *redemptam*, “redeemed”]; the gift of land or woodland which Peter of Courtenay gave to Saint Nicasius for his mother Helvide, at an annual rent of twelve denarii payable at Easter. The whole wood from the cultivated land of the monks of Ham as far as Perus, which Peter of Montcornet gave to the church of Ham on the day of its dedication. The whole estate of Ham, with its church and mill, bannal authority and jurisdiction, male and female serfs, meadows, lands, woods, and free appurtenances of the same estate; the whole tithe of Arces; the whole church of Clerum and the chaplaincy of Montcornet; the church of Lunis; the chapel of Sulmone; the church of Courte-Monastery with the tithes of Nocument; the church of Villzet with the entire tithe and one hide of arable land.

In the borough of Saint Nicasius: portage toll, road toll (*roagium*), grain-measure dues, sextary dues, and toll (*theonicum*), with bannal authority and jurisdiction, a bannal oven, and newly cleared lands cultivated by their own hands or at their expense. If anyone, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest. [Col. 0568D] I, Ardilio, cardinal deacon. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon, etc. I, Conrad, archbishop of Mainz and bishop of Sabina.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of February, in the second indiction, in the year 1168 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

## DCVI. He directs Peter, abbot of Saint Remigius, and the dean of Rheims to decide disputes between I., abbot of Sainte-Marie de Vertus, and various persons.  
(Benevento, February 9.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 958.]

We have recently received complaints from our beloved son I., abbot of Sainte-Marie de Vertus [Col. 0569A], concerning certain burdens inflicted upon his church. We desire that these be brought to their proper conclusion all the more promptly because the church suffers greater poverty and the abbot is less able, owing to weakness of strength, to sustain the business of the church.

For he complains that Man., a priest, has presumptuously and violently taken from him the church of Alvesiolo, which had been granted to the church of Vertus by B., formerly bishop of Châlons, of good memory; and that, concerning restoration, he has allegedly resorted to the refuge of an appeal, but has taken no care to present himself either personally or through another. He also complains that Eur. of Coloneio unjustly holds the tithes of his labours and the annual rent of his house; and that R. of Coloneio and his brothers unjustly hold lands belonging to the right of the same church. Moreover, G. of Bergeries presumes to take from it twelve sextaries of grain at the mill near Clamanges, and, though often warned, refuses to restore them.

Therefore, because we have great confidence in your discernment and because the aforesaid abbot has no small need to be supported by the protection of the Church, by these present letters we command you to summon the aforesaid men and the abbot’s party before you. Having diligently investigated and understood the church’s complaints and the parties’ arguments, impose upon them such a proper settlement that the aforesaid abbot may not be compelled any longer to suffer for want of justice. But if they disdain either to make themselves available or to abide by your judgment, compel them by ecclesiastical censure, informing their bishop on our behalf that he is to ensure observance of the sentence pronounced against them until fitting satisfaction has been made. Further, because the aforementioned priest M. is said not to have taken care to pursue his appeal, we command that case, if this is established to be so, to be decided with the appeal set aside.

Given at Benevento, on the fifth day before the Ides of February.

## DCVII. He confirms the possessions and rights of the monastery of Vallombrosa.  
(Benevento, February 14.)

[LAMI, *Ecclesiae Florentinae Monumenta*, I, 545.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JAMES, abbot of Vallombrosa, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

A desire recognized as pertaining to the profession of religion and the salvation of souls ought, with the Lord as author, to be fulfilled without delay. Since, therefore, the simplicity of your religious profession, divine mercy going before and following after, has breathed the fragrance of good repute upon those near and far, and since we desire, with the Lord’s consent, to add advancement to your advancement, following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, Paschal and Adrian, Roman pontiffs, we receive your monastery—dedicated in honour of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin—into the ownership, guardianship, and protection of the Roman Church and of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0570A] Strengthening it by the privilege of apostolic authority, we decree that it shall remain free from the yoke of all persons.

First, we establish that the monastic order known to have been instituted there according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods the said monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s aid, shall be preserved to you whole and undisturbed. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The monastery of Saint Salvius; the monastery of the Holy Trinity [Col. 0570B] of Florence; the monastery of Struma; the monastery of Osella and of Saint James of the Castle; the monastery of Passignano; and those of Saint Michael of Lenis, Alphiano, Cultubono, and Monte Pisi; the monasteries of Mount Scalario and Nerano; the monastery of Ficiclo; the monastery of Cappiano; the monastery of Saint Paul of Pisa; the monastery of Saint Venerius in Sardinia; the monastery of Saint Angelo of Pistoia; the monastery of Pacciano; the monastery of Monteplano; the monastery of Fonte Thaonis; the monastery of Musceto; the monastery of Monte Armato; the monastery of Saint Cecilia; the monastery of Saint Reparata; the monastery of Trecento; the monastery of Crispino; the monastery of Razzolo; the monastery [Col. 0570C] of the Caesar’s stream; the monastery of Cuneo; the monastery of Turri; the monastery of Caprilia; the monastery of Piacenza; the monastery of Pavia; the monastery of Capranna; the monastery of Saint Prosper; the monastery of Novara; the monastery of Vercelli; the monastery of Genoa; the monastery of Tortona; the monastery of Turin; the monastery of Brescia; the monastery of Verona; the monastery of Saint Vigilius; the monastery of Bergamo; the monastery of Milan; the monastery of Saint Carpophorus; the monastery of Asti; and the monastery of Saint Angelo Juniperiti.

You may receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, and the ordination of clerics from whichever Catholic bishop you choose who enjoys the favour and communion of the Roman Church, and who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. [Col. 0570D] We further decree that no bishop may pronounce against you a sentence of excommunication or interdict, so that you, who have been received as special sons of the Apostolic See, may not rashly be subjected to another’s judgment. Nor may anyone remove or transfer any monastery of your religious order from the stability of its place without the common consent of its abbot and community.

We establish that the monastery situated in the shaded valley is to be regarded as the head of all the aforesaid monasteries. When, however, your pastor reaches the term appointed him by divine disposition, his successor—since he must also preside over all the others—shall be chosen by the consent and judgment of all who preside over the other monasteries. Should one of those abbots, by God’s ordinance, be elected to this general governance, he shall transfer in due form to your principal monastery; and thereafter, by his judgment, all the other monasteries united to you shall be ordered, as is known to have been done in the days of John, your first abbot of venerable memory. [Col. 0571A]

Therefore we decree, etc., without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. [Col. 0571B] I, Ubaldus, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Conrad, archbishop of Mainz and bishop of Sabina. I, Ubaldus, cardinal priest of the Title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius. I, John, cardinal priest of the Title of Saint Anastasia. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the Title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Boso, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, Title of Pastor. I, Peter, cardinal priest of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. [Col. 0571C] I, John, cardinal priest of the Title of Saint Mark. I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of Saint Vitalis, Title of Vestina. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius beside the Temple of Agrippa.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the second indiction, in the year 1168 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

## DCVIII. To Henry, king of the English.—He announces that he has sent Gratian and Vivian to him, to request that he not violate the Church’s rights and that he be reconciled with Thomas.  
(Benevento, February 28.)

[*Letters of Saint Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 122.]

[Col. 0571D]

POPE ALEXANDER to HENRY, king of England.

We have received with paternal kindness the letters which you transmitted to us through our beloved sons, first Reginald, archdeacon of Salisbury, and then Ranulph, archdeacon of Llandaff—prudent and discerning men, zealous and diligent in the business entrusted to them—and we have taken care to hear their contents attentively and carefully. When the requests of Your Highness had become more fully known to us, both from the tenor of your letters and from the oral statements of your messengers, and when we had deliberated upon the matter at length with our brethren, it did not seem to us that we could carry any of them into effect as you requested without injury to our honour and that of the Church. [Col. 0572A]

Nevertheless, so that we may show deference to Your Sublimity in all matters insofar as this can be done with the honour of God and the Church, and so that you may not believe that we have acted in any respect from choice rather than necessity, we have sent to the presence of Your Royal Highness our beloved sons Gratian, our subdeacon and notary, and Master Vivian—men prudent and discerning, and alike dear and acceptable to us and to the whole Church. Through them we shall consider the wishes of Your Magnificence and your advancement, and we shall more fully make known what ought rightly to please Your Serenity.

Moreover, as we have understood from the letters of Your Magnificence, you have inclined your will and mind so far concerning the affair of our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, that, out of reverence for the Church and for us, you would permit him to return to his own see and to possess his church in peace, provided that he is willing to render what he owes you. We consider this altogether welcome and acceptable, and we offer all the praise and thanks we can to divine mercy, which has without doubt inspired this in your heart. We earnestly ask Your Serenity, and impose this upon you as a means of obtaining forgiveness for your sins: in the aforesaid matter, defer rather to God than to man, and incline your mind to this solely in regard for divine mercy. [Col. 0572B]

As for what, according to your statement, had been reported to Your Magnificence concerning us and an alteration of our intention, your discerning prudence ought not to believe every spirit, since there are many detractors and maligners whose assertions are not in any degree to be credited. We desire and intend to love your person with all affection of heart as that of our dearest son in Christ, and we do not wish to burden you in any matter unless perhaps—may God avert it!—you yourself should compel us to do so.

Given at Benevento, on the second day before the Kalends of March.

## DCIX. To Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury.—On the same subject.  
(Benevento, March 10.)

[Ibid., p. 20.]

[Col. 0572D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the messengers and letters of the illustrious king of the English. Although through those messengers he had requested certain great and difficult matters from us, and his messengers had pressed vigorously and strongly before us to obtain them, they were in no way able to bend our mind to his will. Yet, lest they have any ground or occasion for complaining of our harshness—that we were unwilling to show him deference in any respect—we have resolved, following the footsteps and example of our predecessors, whom we do not doubt were saints, to recall the aforesaid king from his purpose with every kindness, moderation, and gentleness, to soften his mind, and to mollify his hardness.

It was therefore decided, upon the counsel and deliberation of our brethren, that we should send to the presence of the aforesaid king our beloved sons Gratian, our subdeacon and notary—a worthy and learned man, whom, because of the memory of our father and predecessor of holy recollection, Pope Eugenius, and in view of his most sincere loyalty and service, we hold wholly dear and acceptable—and Master Vivian, whom we love with sincere affection of heart because of his long familiarity with us, prudence, and learning. [Col. 0573A] Through them and through our letters we admonish the king himself, with all diligence and concern, more strictly than we can, to restore to you his peace and favour, to recall you honourably to your church, to preserve whole and inviolate the ancient rights, liberties, and honours both of you and of that church, and to permit you and yours to remain in complete peace and tranquillity. [Col. 0573B]

Accordingly, we ask and admonish your brotherhood, carefully considering the malice and distress of the time, and observing how our elders redeemed the times because the days were evil, to strive by every means—so far as may be done without prejudice to your rank and office—to recover the favour and love of the aforesaid king and to labour to soften his mind. Show such patience, gentleness, and kindness that no one can rightly say that anything on your part remained undone by which you ought more fully to obtain his favour and goodwill. [Col. 0573C]

Furthermore, we ask, admonish, advise, and will that, until the departure of our messengers, you pronounce no sentence against either the king, the persons of the realm, or the kingdom. And if perhaps—though we do not believe it—you have already pronounced one, suspend it until that time. We say this in order to remove from them every occasion and ground for complaint and so overcome his hardness. If, however—may it not be!—the matter turns out otherwise, we have no wish whatever to withdraw your authority from you, but rather to preserve it and carefully provide our aid and counsel. We have entrusted the remaining matters to our messengers orally. Place unwavering trust in what they say, and comply with their counsels and exhortations.

Given at Benevento, on the sixth day before the Ides of March.

## DCX. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—Concerning the associates Dominic and Haimard.  
(Benevento, March 11.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 787.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0574A] Since a dispute had some time ago arisen in our presence between the associates Dominic and Haimard, on the one hand, and Theodoric and his son Haideric, on the other, concerning twenty pounds which the latter, Theodoric and Haideric, claimed were owed to them by the aforesaid Dominic and Haimard, we entrusted the investigation of that case to our venerable brother R., bishop of Ferentino. Having diligently heard and understood the arguments on both sides, he established an amicable settlement between them, as will become more plainly known to you from our letters issued concerning it.

Since, however, the aforesaid Theodoric and his son, as we have heard, do not fear to act contrary to the terms of the settlement confirmed by our writing, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to admonish them and, under the constraint of anathema, compel them to observe that settlement firmly and without disturbance, as it was confirmed by the faithful undertaking of both parties and as it is known to be contained in our letters issued concerning it; nor are they henceforth to presume to act contrary to it. [Col. 0574B] We also will and command that in carrying these matters out you show yourself so diligent that the aforesaid Dominic and Haimard shall not henceforth be compelled on this account to come into our presence.

Given at Benevento, on the fifth day before the Ides of March.

## DCX bis. Privilege for the church of Blessed Nicholas of Nugarol.  
(Benevento, March 23.)

[*Chronicle of the Church of Auch*, Proofs, Part III, p. 63.]

[Col. 0574C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons OMION, archpriest of the church of Blessed Nicholas of Nugarol, and his brethren, present and future, to be regularly appointed, in perpetuity.

Whenever something is requested of us that is recognized as befitting religion and uprightness, it is proper for us gladly to grant it and to afford suitable assistance to the desires of those who request it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions. We receive the aforesaid church of Blessed Nicholas of Nugarol, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. [Col. 0574D]

First, we establish that the canonical order known to have been instituted there according to God and the Rule of Saint Augustine shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s aid, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Whatever right your said church is known to possess in the new borough, and the liberty of that church—namely, that, as from its first foundation, it shall be wholly exempt and free from every exaction and service of secular power, being subject solely to the jurisdiction of the church of Auch—we confirm to you by apostolic authority. This is according as Bernard, count of blessed memory, together with his wife Naupasia and indeed his sons Gerald and Otto, granted the aforesaid church of Nugarol to the church of Auch, reserving no right or service in it or its appurtenances either for themselves or for their descendants. They swore upon the holy Gospels that they would firmly preserve their devotion and the aforesaid liberty with its additions.

We likewise confirm: the whole borough of Ferra; the estate of Saint Leonard, with its houses and offerings and the cemetery of its parishioners; the grange of Fajet, with its orchards, gardens, and possessions; [Col. 0575A] the fourth portions of all churches lawfully granted to you, as your church has customarily received from the time of Austind, formerly archbishop of Auch, of blessed memory, and as you now peacefully possess them. We also confirm to you, and through you to your church, whatever you hold by right in your archdeaconry; and whatever you possess within or outside the estate of Nugarol, whether in annual rents or other dues, vineyards, gardens, orchards, cultivated lands, and mills. We strengthen these by apostolic authority, so that they may remain free and undisturbed from every exaction of secular power, as is contained in your authentic documents and as you are known lawfully to possess them. [Col. 0575B]

We also grant that the burial-place of that site shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; without prejudice to the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Therefore we decree, etc., without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, etc.

“Show me your ways.” Saint Peter, Saint Paul, Pope Alexander III.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto. [Col. 0575D] I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the Title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.
