I, Boso, cardinal priest of the Title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the Title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, cardinal priest of the Title of Saint Marcellus. I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of the Title of Saint Vitalis in Vestina. I, James, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. [Col. 0576A] I, Emptius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Vitellius, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the second indiction, in the year 1168 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the ninth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

## DCXI. He confirms the boundaries of the bishopric of Modena and the possessions of its church.  
(Benevento, March 26.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *Memorie Modenesi*, vol. II, p. 94.]

[Col. 0576B] ALEXANDER, bishop, etc. (The remainder is as in the bull of 1167, above, no. 450 bis, except for the following subscriptions:)

Given at Benevento through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the second indiction, in the year 1169 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

## DCXII. Privilege for the church of Saint John of Monza.  
(Benevento, March 31.)

[GIULINI, *Memorie storiche di Milano*, VI, p. 536.]

[Col. 0576C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ OBERTO, archpriest of Monza, and his brethren, present and future, to be canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

A devout request ought to be fulfilled in effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may surely receive strength. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your petitions. Following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, Sixtus, Innocent, Celestine, and Anastasius, Roman pontiffs, we receive the church of Blessed John of Monza, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the patronage of this present document. [Col. 0576D] We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, God being favourable, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church itself of Saint John the Baptist, with all its chapels: namely, the churches of Saint Michael, Saint Saviour, Saint Peter, Saint Victor, Saint Lawrence with its hospital, Saint Alexander of Blandino, Saint Martin, [Col. 0577A] Saint Blaise, Saint Agatha, Saint Maurice with its hospital, Saint Ambrose, Saint Donatus, Saint Fidelis, and Saint Anastasia. In Octavo: the church of Saint Christopher and the church of Saint Mary of Sirtori. In Sexto: the churches of Saint Alexander, Saint Saviour, Saint Michael, Saint Eusebius, Saint Mary of Teneblago, and Saint Mary of Sundri. The parish church of Saint Julian of Colonia with all its chapels: namely, in Albairate, the churches of Saint Martin and Saint Maurice; in the village of Modrone, the church of Saint Remigius; in Colonia, the churches of Saint Gregory and Saint Nazarius; in Coliate, the churches of Saint Carpophorus and Saint Alexander with its hospital; in Concorezio, the church of Saint Eugenius; in Vellate, the churches of Saint Mary and Saint Fidelis; in Cremella, [Col. 0577B] the church of Saint Sisinus and the monastery of Saint Peter.

We also confirm the confirmation of the election of the abbess of Cremella, as this was lawfully granted to you and confirmed by the document of Robald, formerly archbishop of Milan, of blessed memory. We likewise confirm the rights and reasonable customs that you possess in the same church of Saint Peter at Cremella; also the church of Saint Gregory at Ormana; at Blotiano, the church of Saint John; Saint George of Coltiaco; Saint John of Varena; Saint Mary of Sorra; Saint Peter of Sirone; and Saint John of Castro Mortis. We also confirm the tithe of the entire territory of Monza, the tithe of the entire territory of Sexto, excepting the tithe of Teneblago; and the tithe arising from the possessions of the parish church [Col. 0577C] of Colonia—namely, from Colonia itself, from the village of Modrone, and from Albairate. We likewise confirm to you, and through you to your church, the principal estates: the court of Cremella, the court of Bluciaco, the court of Valena, the court of Castromartino, the court of Lavedi, the court of Calpurni, the court of Vellate, and the court of Leucate.

Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority for you and your successors those benefices of fiefs which Jordan, formerly archbishop of the church of Milan, of revered memory, prudently granted to your church in the aforesaid churches for the common maintenance of the brethren. We forbid anyone whatsoever henceforth to remove, withdraw, or alter them in any fashion from the common benefit of the brethren. [Col. 0577D] Furthermore, for your peace and that of your church, we confirm the ordinances and customs known hitherto to have been peacefully maintained, by reasonable deliberation, in your church or in chapels belonging to it.

We forbid anyone within your parish to presume to build a church or chapel without your consent. Therefore we decree, etc., without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the archbishop of Milan. If, therefore, etc.

Fare well.

“Lord, show me your ways.”

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 0578A] I, Hubaldus, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the Title of [lacuna]. I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of Saint Vitalis, Title of Vestina. I, John, cardinal priest of the Title of Saints John and Paul, Title of [lacuna]. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Vitellus, cardinal deacon of Saints George and Bacchus. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy [Col. 0578B] Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of April, in the second indiction, in the year 1169 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

## DCXIII. Confirmatory bull of the privileges and rights of the Church of Ferrara.  
(Benevento, April 17.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, VI, 409.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother AMATUS, bishop of Ferrara, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

We are bound by the duty of the office entrusted to us to honour our brethren and fellow bishops with sincere charity, and to preserve their rights and dignities with careful diligence and concern. Therefore, attentively considering the sincerity of your faith and the fervour of devotion with which you have adhered to Blessed Peter and to us with unwavering constancy, we gladly show deference to your honour and accord generous and gracious assent to your petitions.

Accordingly, we confirm by apostolic authority for you and your successors the ancient and reasonable customs which your predecessors held in the major canonry and in the churches of your bishopric. We decree that no one may receive anyone as a canon or to any prelate’s office in the major church without the consent and permission of you or your successors. Nor may anyone appoint or remove a chaplain in the other churches without your consent, as has been observed for forty years before the beginning of this disturbance. [Col. 0578C] A chaplain appointed by your authority shall receive the care of souls from your hand and shall render you the reverence due and customary. We grant and allow you freely to exercise correction over the canons of your church and to make their appointments, as your predecessors are known to have done.

Furthermore, we likewise strengthen by apostolic authority for you and your successors the hospital situated above the Ravine of Peter Scortus, the Hospital of All Saints, and the hospital of Caudalonga. Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly infringe this our privilege or in any way contravene it. [Col. 0578D] If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should presume rashly to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his presumption by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself to stand guilty before divine judgment for the wrong he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all of you who preserve what is just, may there rest the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. [Col. 0579B] I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the Title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the Title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the Title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, cardinal priest of the Title of Saint Marcellus. I, Theodorus, cardinal priest of [lacuna].

Given at Benevento through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the second indiction, in the year 1169 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the [lacuna] year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

## DCXIV. To the bishops of England.—He rebukes their negligence.  
(Benevento, April 25.)

[*Letters of Gilbert Foliot*, ed. GILES, II, 79.]

[Col. 0579C]

We are greatly compelled to marvel at your discernment: although you are prudent and provident men, you are so negligent in carrying out your office that you scarcely seem to remember it, as is more fully demonstrated by your deeds. We are especially struck with astonishment that you pay little or no heed to the obedience you owe the Church of Canterbury, but appear so forgetful of it as though you wholly did not know what ought to be rendered to God and what to men.

That church indeed stands so bare and desolate of a pastor that the prophetic utterance may rightly be applied to it: “How does the city once full of people sit alone! The mistress of nations has become like a widow” [Lamentations 1]. [Col. 0579D] Nevertheless, whatever fault—let us not say disobedience—you have hitherto committed by such negligence, we have by no means forgotten our paternal affection toward you. We have judged that kindness rather than severity should be employed and that deference should be shown you as our venerable brethren far beyond what you have deserved.

Therefore, induced by the regard, earnest representations, and petition of our dearest son in Christ, Henry, the illustrious king of the English, and wishing to spare your expenses and labours, we release you by apostolic authority from the appeal which you long ago made against our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, lest he burden in any respect either the aforesaid king, yourselves, or the kingdom of England. Thus, neither you nor your representatives are in any way bound to pursue it.

Given at Benevento, 25 April.

DCXV. Privilege for the Monastery of Cormeilles. (Benevento, 27 April.)

[Neustria pia, 599.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROBERT, abbot of the monastery of Cormeilles, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0580B] It is fitting that apostolic protection be present in perpetuity for those choosing the religious life, lest an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we grant favourable assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall there be observed inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions or goods [Col. 0580C] that same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by concession of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of St Peter; the church of the Holy Cross; the church of St Sylvester, with all their appurtenances; the borough of Cormeilles, with its toll, oven, waters, mills, meadows, woods, five fairs, five knights’ fiefs, and all the territory adjoining the monastery itself; the church of St Mary of Ferfol, with the chapel of St Christopher, and with its inhabitants, tithes, and offerings; half the tithe of the church [Col. 0580D] of St German of Folmuchamp, together with the tithe of the mill of that village; half the tithes of the churches of St Albin; Pescarium, with one acre of land, and, from the mill of that village, seven quarters of grain; thirty acres of land at the Chapel of Baynel; one man at Buzeville; the land of Wibrai, with two mills at Falaise; dry Nogent, with its church, wood, and mill; at Romilly, one ploughland of land; at Villambon, two parts of the fishery of Aureafossa on the Seine, with the holding belonging to the monastery of Cormeilles; the mill of the village called Vitry; Martigny, with half the mill of Arques and half the mill of Martigny, with their appurtenances; Osbermenil, with its church; at Gougleville, [Col. 0581A] sixteen shillings; the church of Crépin, with all tithes and eighteen acres of land; the church of Grisros; one measure of grain from the mills of Altariis; a fifth part of all things which come to the monastery of Cormeilles from any source at the borough of Pont-Audemer, or which the monks of that monastery purchase for their own use; a meadow at Corhulene and at Chevilly; the vineyard of Roland; the vineyard of the Enclosure of Hildwin, with half of one house, half of all the produce belonging to that house, and three measures of wine; at Gavelli, half a measure of wine.

In England: the manor of Noent, with all its appurtenances, namely five hides of land and the church, with all tithes, offerings, meadows, [Col. 0581B] mills, and woods; from Larclesdune and Toteswide, Contona, Linda, Ecla, and Meleswica, with mills and meadows; Gisgesleia, with all the assarts belonging to Nuent; Staulinus and Bolesduna, with a chapel; the church of Tedintonus; the chapel of Lanteleia; the church of Dimoc, with all its appurtenances and tithes; the tithe of the whole demesne and one virgate of land, and, in the same village, the church of Belrefort, with chapels, tithes, and its other appurtenances: the tithe of the entire demesne, including the improvements and assarts; half a hide of land; the church of Estana, with chapels and all appurtenances, one virgate of land, and the whole tithe of the demesne. At Tocnitona, [Col. 0581C] the whole tithe of the demesne in all things, and one virgate of land at Anglevilla; the church of [lacuna] at Corona, the entire tithe of the demesne and one virgate of land; at Caldebroc, Ora, and Kalestan, the whole tithe of the demesne; the whole village of Eigestona, with all its appurtenances, namely two hides of land, and the chapel of that village. At Westesteigestan, the tithe of the whole demesne and one virgate of land; the church of Murdim, with all its appurtenances, the whole tithe of the demesne, and one virgate of land; the church of Cigestem, with chapels and all its appurtenances, the whole tithe of the demesne, and one virgate of land; at Pisina, the whole tithe of the demesne and one virgate of land; the church [Col. 0581D] of Succeleia, with chapels and all its appurtenances, the whole tithe of the demesne, and one virgate of land; the church of Merleia, with chapels and all its appurtenances, three virgates of land, and the whole tithe of the demesne at Wigrectum, its saltworks; at Golewei, the whole tithe of the demesne and one virgate of land; at Sideham, the tithe of the demesne and half a hide of land; at Kameham, the whole tithe of the demesne and one virgate of land; at Torristona, the whole tithe of the demesne, half a hide of land, and one meadow; the church of Lediart, with all its appurtenances, the whole tithe of the demesne, and one meadow; the church of Canoel, with all its appurtenances, the whole tithe of the demesne, and two virgates of land; [Col. 0582A] the tithes of the revenues of the village of Munemita, of Troi, Cunicarnam, and Nonavilla; half the tithe of the demesne and of the land of Richard, son of Count Gilbert, between Uscham and Uvaia; half the tithe of his own demesne, in woodland and open country, fisheries and honey, pleas and passage-tolls; and a fourth part of the tithe of Strigulus; and, for the aforesaid manor of Nuent, one Blessagham and Carbone for its wood, to support Blessagham; and his land at Ollas, and his wood of Edulfeshella, to clear as assart-land, if it is not in the king’s forest. The church of Strigulus, with all appurtenances; in the town of Hereford, twelve pounds payable at the king’s Exchequer; at Susdhantona, nine pounds and five shillings; in the same village, the monks of Cormeilles, their men, and the house which you possess there, free from all customary dues; from the tithe of Subreleia and Merleia, seventy-five shillings; at Gloucester and Dimac, forty shillings.

Further, in the churches which you hold, you shall choose priests and present them to the bishops. If they are suitable, the bishops shall commit the care of souls to them, so that they may answer to the bishops for the care of the people, but render to you due subjection in temporal matters. We further decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken being nevertheless preserved. [Col. 0582C] Moreover, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you of your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or of the fodder of your animals. When a general interdict is imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, with bells rung, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, and in a subdued voice.

Upon the death of you, now abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any artifice of subreption or by force, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. [Col. 0582D] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowingly acting against this page of our confirmation, shall rashly attempt to violate it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject, at the last judgment, to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Ubaldus, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Hubaldus, cardinal-priest of the church of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal-priest of the church of Saints John and Paul of Pammachius. [Col. 0583B] I, Albert, cardinal-priest of the church of St Lawrence in Lucina. I, Boso, cardinal-priest of St Pudens and Pastor. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the church of St Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, cardinal-priest of the church of St Mark. I, Theobald, cardinal-priest of the church of Saints Vitalis and Justina in Vestina. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Aymard, cardinal-deacon of St Theodore. I, Cinthius, cardinal-deacon of St Adrian. I, Hugh, cardinal-deacon of St Eustachius, beside the temple of Agrippa. [Col. 0583C] I, Vitellus, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Benevento, by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May [27 April], in the second indiction, in the year 1168 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

DCXVI. Privilege for the Church of Syracuse. (Benevento, 28 April.)

[PIRRI, *Sicilia sacra*, I, 622.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother RICHARD, bishop of Syracuse, and to his successors to be canonically appointed in perpetuity.

[Col. 0583D] By the office of the supreme apostolate entrusted to us by God, it is fitting that we provide with paternal care for individual churches and ecclesiastical persons, so that, as we are called fathers in name, we may likewise be shown such in deed. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the Church of Syracuse over which, by God’s authority, you preside, which is known to be subject by metropolitan right to the Roman Church alone and to no other, and whose bishop must receive the gift of consecration only from the Roman pontiff. Furthermore, considering your prudence and integrity, as well as the devotion which you repeatedly display toward blessed Peter and ourselves, [Col. 0584A] by this page of our privilege we grant, by apostolic authority, the pallium in perpetuity to you and your successors. Your fraternity is to understand that its use within the church is permitted at the solemn celebrations of Mass on the following days: the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, the Lord’s Supper, the Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, the feasts of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, the feast of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, the Nativity of St John the Baptist, the feast of St John the Evangelist, the commemoration of All Saints, the Finding and Exaltation of the Holy Cross, the feast of the Holy Trinity, consecrations of churches, blessings of abbots, ordinations of clerics, the principal feasts and dedication [Col. 0584B] of your church, and the anniversary of your consecration.

Let your discretion therefore endeavour, having received the fullness of so great a dignity, to carry out all things so vigorously that the adornments of your character may correspond to it. Let your life be an example to those subject to you, so that through it they may know what they ought to seek and what they must avoid. Be outstanding in discernment, pure in thought, upright in action, prudent in silence, and useful in speech. Let your concern be more to benefit people than to preside over them; you ought to consider in yourself not power but equality of human condition. Take care lest life destroy teaching, or teaching in turn contradict life. Above all, let it be your endeavour firmly to observe the decrees of the Apostolic See and humbly to obey it as your mother and mistress. [Col. 0584C] You will readily fulfil all this, with Christ’s help, if you possess charity, the teacher of every virtue, and humility; and if what you show yourself to possess outwardly, you possess inwardly.

Moreover, whatever possessions or goods the aforesaid church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through concessions of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The churches of the city of Syracuse and those which were in its territory, with all their appurtenances; [Col. 0584D] the churches of Lentini and those in its territory, with all their appurtenances; the church of St Nicholas of the Three Fountains; the church of Pelagonia and the churches of Calataelfar, with all their appurtenances; the churches of Manea and those in its territory, with all their appurtenances; the churches of Bizini and those in its territory, with their appurtenances; the churches of Bucheria, with their appurtenances; the churches of Calatogeron and those in its territory, with all their appurtenances; the churches of Buscema, with their appurtenances; the churches of Sicli and those in its territory, with all their appurtenances; the churches of Buteria and those in its territory, with all their appurtenances; the churches of Mazarini and those in its territory, with their villagers and [Col. 0585A] appurtenances; the churches of Comicini, with their appurtenances; the churches of Ragusa and those in its territory, with all their appurtenances; the churches of Placeoli, with their appurtenances; the churches of Batte, with their appurtenances; the churches of Mount Fahalmi and those in its territory, with all their appurtenances; the churches of Mohac and those in its territory, with all their appurtenances; the churches within the holding of Spaccafurni, with their appurtenances; and the churches of Nata, with their appurtenances.

Likewise, by this present privilege we have thought fit to confirm to you and your successors the hamlet of Bugubel, which is near the city of Syracuse, with its villagers and all appurtenances, as our dearest son in Christ, William, illustrious king of Sicily, piously granted and confirmed it by his own charter to you and, through you, to the Church of Syracuse; [Col. 0585B] also the hamlet of Trimilia; the hamlet of Chifilim; the hamlet of St Mary Magdalene; the hamlet of Rualsenem; the hamlet of Raalchindin; the hamlet of St Michael; the hamlet of Millarini near Lentini; the hamlet of Judecca, on the boundary of Buteria; the hamlet of St Vincent, near Sophiana, with its holdings and two mills, which Manfred, son of Count Simon, granted and confirmed by charter to the aforesaid church; the hamlet of Renda and the hamlet of Rendetgrebin, situated in the appurtenances of Ragusa, as the noble men Geoffrey, son of Count Roger of good memory, and Count Sylvester, son of the same Geoffrey, granted them to the Church of Syracuse in pious devotion and strengthened the grant by their own charter. [Col. 0585C] We also confirm by apostolic authority in perpetuity to you and your successors all tithes, both in seaports and in any other places whatsoever, which the Church of Syracuse is known to possess.

Furthermore, we forbid anyone to construct anew a church or oratory within the boundaries of your parish without the licence and permission of you or your successors; and, after it has been built, to install a superior there unless he receives investiture from you or one of your successors and renders obedience as to a diocesan bishop, while all privileges of the Roman Church are preserved. [Col. 0585D] We further add that no one may receive parishioners of the Church of Syracuse for burial unless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved. Moreover, by apostolic authority we establish that monks or any others holding parish churches within your diocese shall in no way dare to appoint priests in them without your or your successors’ licence and assent, unless they have received from you the care of souls; so that they are answerable to you in spiritual matters, but in temporal matters to those to whom the church belongs. Nevertheless, if they are protected by privileges of the Roman Church, we wish their own full rights to remain intact. Therefore we decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, anyone, etc.

[Col. 0586A] I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ubaldus, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Ubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints John and Paul of Damasus. I, Albert, cardinal-priest of St Lawrence in Lucina. I, Boso, cardinal-priest of St Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St Mark. I, Theodinus, cardinal-priest of St Vitalis, of the title [Col. 0586B] of Faustus. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Ardericus, cardinal-deacon of St Theodore. I, Cinthius, cardinal-deacon of St Adrian. I, Hugh, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Benevento, by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the aforesaid Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May [28 April], in the second indiction, in the year 1168 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

DCXVII. To Henry, King of the English—That he should receive Thomas of Canterbury into favour. (Benevento, 10 May.)

[Letters of St Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 119.]

[Col. 0586C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ HENRY, illustrious king of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Both natural reason and the form of law, we believe, have taught your providence that, the greater the benefits which one is known to have received from another, the more beholden and obligated he is held to be to that person. Your Excellency knows that, since the merciful and omnipotent Lord has chosen to exalt your person so highly among the children of men as to make you a king and prince so powerful and so magnificent, [Col. 0586D] enriching you beyond others with such wealth and glory, it becomes your diligence always to strive with all your strength toward those things which you know to be pleasing to the will of so great a benefactor. Thus you will seem, by right reflection, to assess his immense and overflowing mercy, and to wish, insofar as lies in your power, to respond to such great benefits.

For, as blessed Gregory says: “Evangelical truth earnestly warns us to consider lest we, who are seen to have received more than others in this world, be judged more severely for that by the Author of the world. For when gifts increase, the account of gifts also grows. Therefore each person ought to be the humbler and readier to serve because of the gift, the more obligated he sees himself to be in rendering account.” It is fitting that both prelates of churches and secular powers [Col. 0587A] recall this to mind in earnest meditation, and, lest they be judged more severely at the final examination concerning the talent entrusted to them, think more diligently of the account to be rendered.

Accordingly, because we love your person with such warmth of charity, and hold you dear and welcome among the other Christian kings in such a manner that we would not wish to deny your magnificence anything which we would do for any mortal, we have considered it necessary to admonish your Highness more carefully concerning the account of the penny entrusted to you. Thus, as a man distinguished by great knowledge and ability, you may so think of eternal things that, when temporal things are ended, you may reign in heaven with him who appointed you so great and magnificent a steward on earth.

We remember that we have often and repeatedly urged your Serenity, by envoys and letters, concerning the affair of our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, [Col. 0587B] that you would permit your will and mind in this matter to be overcome by God—who cannot be overcome, and whom to serve is to reign—rather than overcome him. This, we know, is much more glorious and more conducive to your salvation. Since, however, we have thus far been unable to achieve much in these matters, by what judgment of God we do not know, we are made exceedingly sad and sorrowful about this, no less for your sake than for that of your mother, the most holy Church, which is daily more grievously scandalized by it. For we are frequently reproached by many magnates and by almost the whole Church on account of the lukewarmness and negligence of our office, and we know that we have incurred no small reproach from many who taunt us for an abuse of our patience.

But now, because from the letters most recently sent to us through your envoys we learn that your mind in these matters, through the inspiration of divine mercy, is gentler and has inclined not a little toward that which befits a most Christian king and a pious prince, [Col. 0587C] we rejoice in the Lord. We render immense thanks for this both to him from whom all good things proceed, who without doubt inspired this in your heart, and to your Clemency; and we place all our hope in Christ’s mercy that he who began so great a good will, in his customary compassion, bring it to the desired completion.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we ask, warn, and exhort your Serenity in the Lord; moreover, in remission of your sins, on behalf of Almighty God, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and ourselves, we command you [Col. 0587D] to receive the aforesaid archbishop graciously into your favour and affection, for the sake of God, his Church, your honour, and the honour of your whole kingdom, laying aside all indignation and resentment; and to permit God to overcome in this matter and your own will to be overcome. May that same God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who will undoubtedly regard himself as received by you in him, as he himself says, “Whoever despises you despises me, and whoever receives you receives me” (Luke 10), preserve your earthly kingdom in tranquillity for a longer time, grant you longer days with the joy you desire, and, when temporal things have ended, deign to grant you in that blessed recompense of the righteous a special crown for so great an example of patience, [Col. 0588A] piety, and humility. And, making you his co-heir, may he in his boundless goodness pour the reward of such mercy upon your heirs and descendants.

Nevertheless, so that we may more fully prove in deed the hope and confidence which we have received from your aforesaid letters, we have thought fit to send to the presence of the royal Highness our beloved sons, our subdeacon Gratian, an honourable and learned man, whom, because of his remembrance of our predecessor Pope Eugenius of holy memory and in view of his most sincere faith and service, we hold altogether dear and welcome; and Master Vivian, whom we love with sincere affection of heart because of his long-standing familiarity, prudence, and learning. [Col. 0588B] Through them we shall communicate our will to your Excellency more fully by word of mouth, earnestly asking and warning your Magnificence to receive them graciously, as is fitting, out of reverence for the Church of God and in honour of blessed Peter and ourselves, and to treat them honourably.

You are to give unquestioning credence to what they shall set forth orally on our behalf to the royal Serenity, both concerning these matters and concerning the other matters which you communicated to us through our beloved son Reginald, archdeacon of Salisbury. By their exhortation, you should direct every effort to the honour of God and the Church, and likewise to the perpetual praise and glory of your name and to the advantage [Col. 0588C] and advancement alike of your heirs.

Given at Benevento, 10 May.

DCXVIII. Privilege for the Church of St Mary of Reno. (Benevento, 16 May.)

[TROMBELLI, *Memorie storiche S. Mariae di Reno*, p. 371.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GUIDO, prior of St Mary of Reno, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

To grant effect to just petitioners is required both by the strictness of equity and by the order of reason, especially when piety assists the petitioners’ wish and truth [Col. 0588D] does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Innocent, Lucius, Eugenius, and Anastasius, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid church of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that church according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall there be observed inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, [Col. 0589A] or may hereafter acquire through concessions of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of St Saviour in the city of Bologna; at Turricella, the church of St Andrew; the church of St Domninus near Bagnum; the church of St Mary at Raticosa, with its appurtenances; the church of St James called Casa-Dei, with its appurtenances; and the bridge situated over the Reno beside your church, with its possessions.

We also forbid any brother, after making profession in that place, [Col. 0589B] to depart from that cloister without the voluntary permission of the prior or community; and no one at all may receive a departing brother without letters of authorization from the community. But if any of those brethren dares to remain outside the cloister without the aforesaid permission, and, after a second or third admonition, perhaps scorns to repent, the prior of that place may pronounce against him a sentence of excommunication as against his professed religious. You shall have free authority, without anyone’s opposition, to receive for conversion clerics or free laymen living secular lives.

Moreover, no one at all shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce of your labour, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the fodder of your animals. [Col. 0589C] You shall receive holy oil and the ordinations of clerics who are to be advanced to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these things freely and without any impropriety. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you wish, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. We also grant that the burial-place of that house be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted, while the right of the mother church is preserved.

[Col. 0589D] Furthermore, we decree that no archbishop, bishop, or any person whatsoever may make an exaction in the aforesaid church of blessed Mary or inflict burdens upon the prior and brethren. Upon the death of you, now prior of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any artifice of subreption or by force, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine. Therefore we decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, anyone, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, bishop of Ostia. [Col. 0590A] I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Hubaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of St Pammachius. I, Boso, cardinal-priest of St Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Arditio, cardinal-deacon of St Theodore. I, Cinthius, cardinal-deacon of St Adrian. I, Hugh, cardinal-deacon of St Eustachius beside the temple of Agrippa. I, Vitellus, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

[Col. 0590B] Given at Benevento, by the hand of Gerard, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of June [15 May], in the second indiction, in the year 1169 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

DCXIX. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury—He rebukes him because, before the return of the envoys of the Apostolic See, he had “burdened certain persons in England with a sentence.” He urges him to suspend the sentence. (Benevento, 19 June.)

[Letters of St Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 22.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England, and legate of the Apostolic See: [Col. 0590C] greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since you had sent your envoys to our presence, and our dearest son in Christ Henry, illustrious king of the English, had dispatched his own envoys to the Apostolic See, we are surprised that, without awaiting the return of your envoys or learning our counsel, you burdened certain persons of the kingdom with some sentence. Yet, although we do not doubt that you possess great prudence and discerning judgment, because it often happens that a person sees better in another’s cause than in his own, and because we wish your sentence to be revoked by your own authority, we admonish, advise, will, and exhort your fraternity to suspend that sentence, in order to overcome the king’s hardness and soften his mind, [Col. 0590D] until from the reply of our envoys you learn whether the same king is willing to be reconciled to you and, as is fitting and as hope has been given us, to restore you to your church.

For it is fitting for us and for you yourself to wait two or three months in order to soften his severity, and thus to endure his hardness with kindness and gentleness, so that no opportunity may remain to him by which the good of peace and concord between you and him ought in any manner to be impeded. But if you do not judge our counsel and exhortation to be obeyed, and the matter does not proceed in accordance with your desire and expectation but turns, God avert it, to the contrary, you must attribute this to yourself and not to us. Nevertheless, if, in response [Col. 0591A] to our exhortation and the recommendation of our envoys, you suspend the sentence and the king persists in his hardness and severity, then, before those same envoys depart from you, you may, if it be your counsel and will, undoubtedly revoke the sentence. If you do so, it will not displease us in the least. Indeed, counsel and assistance shall be given you by us as may be fitting.

Given at Benevento, 19 June.

DCXX. To the suffragan bishops of the Church of Palermo—At the request of William, king of Sicily, he permits them to consecrate W[alter], archbishop-elect, and to do so in the presence of John, cardinal-priest of the title of St Stephen, who bears the pallium. (Benevento, 22 June.)

[PIRRI, *Sicilia sacra*, I, 104.]

[Col. 0591B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren, the suffragan bishops of the Church of Palermo: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Venerable brother R., our archbishop, and our beloved sons W., cantor of Reggio, and Dechilles, the royal chamberlain, being—as prudent and discerning men—very solicitous with us, on behalf of the royal majesty and of the same elect, [Col. 0591C] for the honour and exaltation of our beloved son W[alter], elect of Palermo, earnestly and effectively urged us to have him consecrated by you. Yet although we do not recall that any predecessor of the aforesaid elect was ever consecrated except by the Roman pontiff, nevertheless, considering the various reasons from which we have learned that our dearest son in Christ W. (William), the illustrious king of Sicily, has the greatest need of the presence of others, and not least of the aforesaid elect, and wishing also to show favour, insofar as we can do so with God and justice, to the king and queen themselves as our dearest children, and likewise to the same elect, by the common counsel of our brethren we grant that he be consecrated by you in the presence of our beloved son J., priest cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia, through whom we send him the pallium and who urged the matter before us and laboured quite diligently; provided, however, that this is not to be taken as a precedent in future or in any way prejudice the right of the Roman Church. Rather, the elect of Palermo are always to come to the Roman pontiff to receive the office of consecration and the fullness of their office. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, when you are requested by the same cardinal, you bestow upon the aforesaid elect, in his presence, the office of consecration, after invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit; and that, after receiving the pallium, you render and promise him obedience and reverence in all things as to your archbishop, just as you are known to have promised his predecessors.

Given at Benevento, the tenth day before the Kalends of July.

DCXXI. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of Nicholas, concerning a prebend at Amiens. (Benevento, 2 July.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 744.]

[Col. 0592A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, etc., to HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims.

Since we repeatedly addressed letters to R. [Note: [Col. 0591D] Robert, who was ordained bishop about the year 1163.], of good memory, formerly bishop of Amiens, requiring him to grant and assign to our beloved son Nicholas the prebend which his predecessor T. [Note: [Col. 0592D] Theoderic, formerly abbot of Saint Eligius of Noyon.], of happy memory, had granted him at our intervention and which both you and he had confirmed in your own writings, that bishop, closing his ears to our commands, although moreover two prebends had fallen vacant, was unwilling to grant him either of them, but granted them less judiciously to others. Your discretion is by no means unaware how greatly in this matter he transgressed and diminished both the honour and dignity of the Roman Church and your own. But because that bishop was overtaken by death, we were unable to express to him our will on this matter or disclose the indignation which we had also conceived. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to cause the aforesaid Nicholas to be received as a canon of the Church of Amiens within twenty days after receipt of these letters, and to have a stall assigned to him in the choir according to custom. If any prebend falls vacant before a bishop is installed there, you are nevertheless to grant and assign it to him, notwithstanding any opposition or appeal whatsoever. Meanwhile, in order that he may be recognized as a canon of that Church, command the canons jointly to assign him every year some suitable and fitting benefice. But if no prebend falls vacant before the installation of a bishop, compel the bishop once installed promptly to carry out, by our authority and your own, what we have commanded you. Strictly forbid both him and the canons, before Nicholas has a prebend, to presume for any reason to receive anyone as a canon or place anyone in a stall; and, should they attempt it, do not allow it to be done in any way, nor leave unpunished contempt of us and of you.

[Col. 0592D] Given at Benevento, on the sixth day before the Nones of July.

DCXXII. He grants certain privileges to the abbots of the Cistercian Order. (Benevento, 4 July.)

[MANRIQUE, *Annals of the Cistercians*, II, 478.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ALEXANDER, abbot of Cîteaux, and all the co-abbots of the same order, present and future, canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Considering how almighty and merciful God has led you, converted from the broad way of secular life, to the entrance of the narrow gate, and has separated you like fat from flesh, we rejoice and are filled with inward gladness of mind and joyful exultation. At the same time we warn and exhort you to strive with vigilant purpose to carry oil in your vessels, so that, when the cry is made at midnight, with your lamps alight, you may deserve to enter the bridegroom’s chamber and receive the blessedness of righteousness which is reserved for you in heaven (Matthew 25). Therefore, since the Lord has chosen you as his inheritance and has looked down from on high upon your peace and tranquillity, desiring, so far as divine grace grants us, to provide for these, we grant and allow you by apostolic authority:

[Col. 0593B] That abbots of your order who, stained by public report of some crime or publicly convicted, after being admonished by the father abbots according to the form of the order, refuse voluntarily to resign their prelacy, shall not have the right to appeal to the Apostolic See or to defend their offence through any representatives. We further decree that, if bishops, requested three times with the humility and devotion that befit the case, should refuse to bless abbots who have been appointed, those abbots may bless their own novices and exercise the other functions belonging to that office, until the bishops reconsider their hardness and do not refuse to bless the abbots who are to be blessed. Indeed, if bishops demand anything from abbots beyond the obedience due, contrary to the liberty of the order granted by our predecessors and by us, the said abbots are free by apostolic authority to refuse what is demanded, lest on this pretext the order itself, hitherto free, be bound in the snare of perpetual servitude. If bishops promulgate any sentence on that account against your persons or churches, we decree that such a sentence, as issued contrary to the grants of the Apostolic See, shall be void.

We therefore decree that absolutely no person may infringe this page of our constitution or in any way oppose it. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowingly, rashly attempts to act against this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third admonition, unless he corrects his presumption by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who observe this our constitution may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. [Col. 0594A] I, Benard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, etc.

Given at Benevento by the hand of Gerard, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of July, in the second indiction, in the year 1169 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander.

DCXXIII. He exhorts the archbishops, bishops, and abbots assembled at the Cistercian chapter to follow in the footsteps of the fathers of the Cistercian Order. He excuses the abbot of Clairvaux, whom he has retained. (Benevento, 19 July.)

[MANRIQUE, *ibid.*, p. 500.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, the archbishops and bishops, and to his beloved sons, all the abbots assembled at the Cistercian chapter, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Amid the innumerable storms of the worldly tempest which the gale of burning persecution has stirred up against the Church of God and against ourselves, God’s providence has afforded us a great remedy: the most fervent charity of you all, which neither feared dangers nor withheld assistance, destined by the former to attain an abundance of reward and, by the latter, with the Lord as author, triumphs of patience. We clearly remember, and recall with every thanksgiving, with what inviolable steadfastness the anchor of your faith preserved Peter’s storm-tossed little boat in the tempest; and how the frequent urgency of your prayers, as it were, roused the Saviour sleeping again in that same boat when the storm broke. Thus, often astonished by the greatness of the miracle, we glorify him who commands sea and waves, as the hoped-for calm began to smile upon us; and we hold you in the highest veneration, through whose merits aiding us the heavenly majesty is believed to have been appeased.

Added to all this is the commendable and devout concern of our beloved sons, the abbots of Cîteaux and Clairvaux. Moved not by human impulse but by the spirit of heavenly counsel, they have undergone the greatest labours and dangers for the peace of the universal Church. This is all the more pleasing and acceptable to us and to our brethren because we are more confident that their zeal and labour will benefit the whole Church of God. We especially hope that their pious earnestness, continually assisted by your prayers, will advance the honour and welfare of the order and bring an increase of the desired peace. Therefore, made your debtors for so manifold a gift of your charity, we love you and the sacred order which you observe with every affection in our power, and eagerly devote the fullest concern to the progress and increase of that order; for we should seem uselessly to perform the role of the heavenly Husbandman if we ceased to water with seasonable rains the planting which his right hand has planted.

[Col. 0595A] Therefore, by apostolic letters, we ask, warn, and exhort you in the Lord: remembering how this holy planting, this fruitful vine, this vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, sprang up under the first fathers of the order and, sending forth its shoots far and wide, produced flowers and poured out fragrance to drive away the deadly poisons on every side, strive with ever-watchful care to adhere in all things to their footsteps. For by their agency, with the Lord cooperating, such a flower of uprightness was planted in the wilderness of this world. As most strict observers of monastic frugality, placing the best beginning in poverty, they attained the fullness of every sufficiency; they were dear to the Church, acceptable to bishops and prelates, and glorious in reputation and merit before kings and princes. Henceforth we commend ourselves and the whole cause of the holy Church to your devout prayers; and we too pray that the almighty Father, in whose name you are assembled, may order your ordinances and works according to his good pleasure and continually advance you and your subject brethren in spiritual growth. Further, because, for the unavoidable necessity of advancing peace, we have thought it necessary to retain the aforesaid abbot of Clairvaux from attending the chapter, we ask you to excuse him; and we ask you likewise to bear patiently with regard to the abbot of Cîteaux, if it should happen that, because of such necessity, we recall him after the chapter has been held.

[Col. 0595C] Given at Benevento, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August.

DCXXIV. He commands the clergy, judges, and whole people of Benevento not to continue the custom by which “merchants, travellers, and pilgrims received as guests by anyone in that city, if they happen to be burdened there with some illness, are not allowed either to leave the house, make a will concerning their goods, or choose the place of their burial if they die; but their possessions are distributed partly to the apostolic court, partly to the church, and partly to their hosts.” (Benevento, 24 July.)

[BORGIA, *Historical Memoirs of Benevento*, III, 157.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy, judges, and whole people of Benevento, present and future, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0595D] Just as a farmer trusts in vain in the fertility of the earth when, before casting seed, he does not clear away thorns and briars, so too the shepherd of the Church vainly expects the reward of the pastoral office if he does not labour to cut away from the field of the Lord the growths of vice; for he has received from the Lord through the prophet the command to uproot and destroy, to ruin and overthrow, to build and to plant. This indeed is incumbent upon all prelates of the Church; but it is believed to be required all the more strongly of us and our successors because by the Lord’s will we receive broader authority in blessed Peter and are, as it were, summoned in the first place by a clearer command to safeguard those who follow.

But there is said to have existed in your city a certain custom—or rather, usurpation—known to be hostile to divine and human laws, and bringing both those who act and those who consent into danger of divine vengeance: namely, if merchants, travellers, or pilgrims received as guests by someone in that city happen to be afflicted there by some illness, they are not allowed to leave the house, make a will concerning their possessions, or, if they die, choose their burial place, although laws and canons command that the final will of the dying concerning burial and the disposal of their possessions be observed. Instead, their goods are distributed partly to our court, partly to the church, and partly to the hosts. Hence very many suspect that at times the sick are so badly treated by their hosts that their death appears to have been summoned both by their hosts’ greed and by their desire. Therefore our predecessor Pope Eugenius, of blessed memory, inflamed with zeal for his office, lest the Roman pontiff be said to permit what ought to be reproved and corrected by him in others, removed from the city of Benevento this most wicked usurpation, which through long duration had become entrenched as custom, and decreed it to be without force. But after that predecessor of ours entered upon the way of all flesh, the pestilential custom revived anew through human greed, and the root of bitterness germinated again through greater connivance and negligence.

[Col. 0596C] Therefore, by the common counsel and assent of our brethren, we condemn this custom, supported by no right but only by greed and long duration, by a perpetual prohibition; we decree that it shall have no effect whatever; and we place both burial and the disposal of their possessions in the free will of those who depart, removing from both our court and the whole city every stain of such great avarice. Henceforth the aforesaid persons in the city of Benevento and its dependencies are to have lawful power, whenever they wish, to depart, to change their place, to choose burial, or, if they decide to remain there, to make a will concerning their goods; and the aforesaid usurpation is in no respect to hinder them from disposing of their persons and possessions as they determine.

If, however, any of them dies intestate, his goods are to be deposited in some church of the aforesaid city under the supervision of our rector, the archbishop, and suitable witnesses, so that if within a year someone should appear who ought by right to succeed to him, they may be returned whole to that person; otherwise, the former custom concerning them is to be observed. But if anyone attempts to act against this our constitution, if he is a cleric he shall be punished by suspension from ecclesiastical benefice; if a layman, he shall, in addition to restoring what was taken, be liable to a fine of two pounds of silver payable to our court. And, that so great an iniquity may be crushed by a double punishment, if any ecclesiastical or secular person rashly attempts to act against the page of this our constitution, after a second or third admonition, unless he corrects his presumption by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour and know himself guilty, etc.

[Col. 0597A] I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Hubald, priest cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, priest cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Albert, priest cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Boso, priest cardinal of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. [Col. 0597B] I, Hyacinth, deacon cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Arditio, deacon cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Cinthius, deacon cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Hugh, deacon cardinal of Saint Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Peter, deacon cardinal of Saint Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Benevento by the hand of Gerard, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the second indiction, in the year 1169 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

DCXXV. He receives the Church of Asti under protection and confirms the possessions and rights of its canons. (Benevento, 25 July.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 368.]

[Col. 0597C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons NICHOLAS, archdeacon, and GARDULPH, provost of the Church of Asti, and their brethren, present and future, canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The authority of our office admonishes and invites us to labour for the condition of churches and, with the Lord’s help, to provide beneficially for their peace and tranquillity. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Adrian, of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now possesses justly and canonically, or may in future obtain, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The estate called Quartum, with its castle, village, and entire demesne, meadows, grasslands, woods, groves, pastures, waters, and riverbanks as far as the Tanagrum, and the whole jurisdiction of that village; the church of Saint Peter situated in the same place, with its tithes and appurtenances; their estate called Ercule, with its churches, tithes belonging to it, and the whole jurisdiction over its inhabitants; the parish church of Pizentiana, with castle, village, and the chapter of the whole parish district, male and female serfs, the chapel of Saint Michael, the tithes belonging to the aforesaid church, the entire jurisdiction over its inhabitants, the tower and castle of Coningo with its walled house and one sixth part of the commons; three holdings in the same place, with the parish church, the chapel of that castle, and the tithes belonging to it; the church of Podanengo, with its tithes and appurtenances; four holdings in the same place, with male and female serfs; an estate called Mons Tegletus, with male and female serfs; the church of Saint Dalmatius, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Andrew of Fontana Stantia; three holdings at Abarana, with the chapel of Saint George belonging to the parish church of Pizentiana; the church of Saint Genesius of Gobione, with one holding, tithes, and its other appurtenances; the tithe of Saint Martin of Compergulis; the church of Malesco, with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Corebama, with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Cortanseris, with the tithes of the allods and of the valley of Azonis, and its other appurtenances; the church of Sexanto, with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Solio, with its tithes and appurtenances; the parish church of Valliculis, with the tithing of the whole village, except the tithing of the lords’ ancient possessions; the church of Castiglione, with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Cellis, with that which belonged to Hugh and whatever you possess in the same village or its territory on the side of Oberius, who clears vines; also the tithes of the entire city and its adjacent villages, of the valley of Tertia, Mount Boninus, Arpegianum, and the valley of Latro, except those granted to other churches; three holdings at Viniaco, with pastures, grasslands, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters, riverbanks, and the entire jurisdiction over their inhabitants; three holdings in the village, with churches and their appurtenances; the two larger parts of the castle of Corseone, which formerly belonged to Boniface of Cortanseris, and the other half of that share, which belonged to Carbo, with the chapel and the whole jurisdiction over its inhabitants; four holdings in the same place, with the share which belonged to Gualfred of Galandria; and whatever you possess in Anteriso, Stoderda, Lorello, and Magleolo, with waters, riverbanks, and the entire jurisdiction over the inhabitants of Vallefenaria, Vallepeto, Suberico, Curaldia, and Montoso; and everything which you rightfully possess in cultivated and uncultivated land, grasslands, meadows, woods, groves, in the land and vineyard of Vallebella, Orista Maior, Chrispizen, and Ecclopleno; and everything you have beyond the Tanarus at Mount Prevello, Lauretto, Saxo Canulro, Calocio, Aglano, Mecedo, Corticellis, Spalvariae, and Rocheta de Flexo; whatever you possess under the testament of Ung ri [reading uncertain] and his wife Geneva in the valley of Cimina, Mount Morinus, Paderno, and Predalia; and the church of Saint Adrian, with its appurtenances.

[Col. 0599A] Moreover, we confirm for you and your successors all the reasonable and ancient customs of your church, and those which you are known hitherto to have possessed in funeral services, celebrations of Masses, and divisions of offerings, both within the city and throughout the whole bishopric beyond it; likewise the processions established at fixed times, with their customary receptions. We therefore decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of your bishop. If anyone in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Albert, priest cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. [Col. 0599B] I, Bozo, priest cardinal of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Ubald, priest cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, priest cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Hyacinth, deacon cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Arditio, deacon cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Cynthius, deacon cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Hugh, deacon cardinal of Saint Eustace. I, Peter, deacon cardinal of Saint Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Benevento by the hand of the notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the second indiction, in the year 1169 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

[Col. 0599C]

DCXXVI. To the nobles, knights, and all Christ’s faithful.—For the Church of Jerusalem and the defence of that land. (Benevento, 29 July.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 747.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the nobles, knights, and all Christ’s faithful to whom these letters shall come, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Among all things which divine wisdom has appointed in the course of fleeting affairs for the exercise of charity, scarcely anything occurs to us in which charity may be exercised more gloriously for virtue and more fruitfully for reward than by relieving with aid the need of the Eastern Church and of Christian believers, and securing them against the incursions of pagans, so that worship of the divine name may not fail there and the strength of brotherhood may shine forth commendably. For since it rests solely on the will of supreme goodness both to remove the labours of the faithful and to restrain the savagery of barbarians, he sometimes seems to disregard the cry of those who groan, and allows brethren to be afflicted before the eyes of brethren, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God (Psalm 13), and whether the pattern of divine compassion is found impressed upon anyone’s soul.

For if the Creator of men and angels bowed his heavens and came down (Psalm 17), and did not disdain to undergo the cross’s gallows for the salvation of an unprofitable servant, it remains that he who lives should no longer live for himself, but for him who died and rose again for us (2 Corinthians 5), who gave himself for us, an offering to God for a sweet-smelling savour (Ephesians 5). The Christian faithful have often laboured greatly for the defence of that land; and by much shedding of blood, through the favour of divine grace, it was achieved that the worship of the Christian faith could be preserved there. Indeed, when long ago, through the people’s sin, it had fallen into the power of the Saracens, men of valour rose up and, destroying or driving out the nations, restored the land anew to Christ’s faith; raising there the banner of faith, they made the Lord’s tomb renowned through the resort of peoples.

Now, however, since it appears reduced in population, worn down by repeated labours, and exhausted by various turns of war, so that unless brotherly charity comes to its aid it fears extreme dangers are imminent, it again seeks the customary assistance from the West. At our exhortation—as though God were exhorting through us—it humbly appeals to you for aid, through our venerable brethren the archbishop of Tyre and the bishop of Paneas, and our beloved sons G., master of the Hospital, and the nobleman A. of Landast; it hopes that such profit will arise from present assistance as it believes it could never again obtain by any human labour. It also foresees extreme dangers as imminent if the help of brotherly charity is either withheld or delayed. For the moment seems at hand when either its enemies will acquire such strength that it cannot withstand their attack, or Christian valour will be so strengthened that each person may rest secure beneath his own tree and your descendants may remain undisturbed by the need to aid them.

Therefore, deterred by fear of so great a danger and prompted by the prospect of so great a benefit, we warn and exhort you all in the Lord, and enjoin upon you remission of sins: for love of him who by being born, dying, and rising again willed to accomplish the salvation of all in that land, gird yourselves manfully for its assistance. Those who are unencumbered in person, and others in their resources, should, putting aside every obstacle of delay, strive to devote themselves for the salvation of our brethren, so that what is known to have been acquired for the glory of the Christian name by much blood of your fathers may by your labour and diligence be preserved and fortified.

[Col. 0600D] Moreover, pursuing your concern with apostolic favour, we grant, by virtue of the authority bestowed on us by the Lord, to those who undertake the labour of this expedition for the love of God and strive to fulfil it according to their ability, that remission of penance imposed through priestly ministry which our fathers and predecessors Urban and Eugenius, of happy memory, are known to have established in their times: namely, that anyone fit for the defence of the land and free for this service, who, having undertaken penance, remains there for two years in defence of the land and, at the command of the king and the leading men of the land, bears the sweat of conflict for Christ’s love, may rejoice that he has obtained remission of the penance imposed. With contrition of heart and oral confession, he may accept this expedition in place of satisfaction for the indulgence of his sins, unless he is found guilty of robbery, theft, or usury received; in such cases, if he has means, sin is not purged unless what was taken is restored. But if he lacks the means to make restitution, the aforesaid satisfaction shall suffice also for remission of those sins. Whoever remains for one year in this labour shall recognize, by apostolic authority, that he is released from half of the satisfaction imposed.

Moreover, lest the disturbance of wicked persons frighten anyone away from a pious desire, we have received their families and possessions under the protection of blessed Peter and decreed that they remain under the protection of ourselves and the prelates of the Church. By apostolic authority, we decree that no question be raised, after the cross has been taken, concerning anything which those who have taken the cross peacefully possessed, until they return or their death is known with certainty. Whoever is burdened with debt and begins so holy a journey with a pure heart shall pay no interest on past debts. They may freely pledge their lands or other possessions to churches, ecclesiastical persons, or other faithful persons, without any objection, after relatives or lords to whose fief the property pertains have been notified and either decline or cannot lend them money. Furthermore, upon all who desire to visit the Lord’s tomb because of the pressing necessity, whether prevented by death on the journey or arriving there, we impose the labour of the journey as penance, obedience, and remission of all sins, so that after the prison-labours of this conflict they may deserve to attain eternal life.

Given at Benevento, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

DCXXVII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—Likewise concerning the Eastern Church. (Benevento, 29 July.)

[*Ibid.*, col. 750.]

[Col. 0601D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since the groans of those crying out in whatever affliction ought to reach the ears of the Church, it befits us to hear the sufferings of the Eastern Church with all the greater attention and to grieve with it more deeply, because we read that a fuller and greater compassion has flowed to us from the breasts of divine consolation. Since we see that place chosen by God among both the old and the new people, whence, as from a heart, the vein of life might flow through the whole body, people rightly run together from every part to assist that land, because the whole human race seems to have drawn from it the food of life and the drink of salvation.

But now, as is said, it has been brought to such a crisis of necessity that it cannot conceal its impending distress, and we, with the whole Western Church, must think more earnestly of helping it. The moment seems at hand when either the enemies of Christ’s cross will acquire such strength that the Eastern Church cannot withstand their attack, or our people, through divine favour and the help of their brethren, will prosper so greatly that they may rest secure from attack and every anxiety and concern for helping them will be removed from the Western Church.

Now therefore, because our venerable brethren F., archbishop of Tyre, and the bishop of Belmes, the master of the Hospital, and the nobleman A. of Landast are being sent to set forth the need of that land and request the aid of the Western Church, we exhort your brotherhood by apostolic letters and enjoin you by the authority committed to us by God to assist the aforesaid brethren diligently in our stead. By your persuasion, procure that our dearest son in Christ, Louis, the illustrious king of the Franks, convoke together the ecclesiastical and secular persons of the realm and make provision for assisting that land, applying such discernment that those found suitable in person, and others in their resources, may fulfil the debt of charity toward their brethren and hasten to provide aid before the forces of the Turks become stronger against them through foreign resources. You yourself should also strive to convene the persons of your province and deliberate and arrange with them what pertains to God’s honour and the salvation of that land.

Further, we entrust our authority in this matter to your prudence and to that of the other archbishops of the realm, so that, in accordance with the tenor of the letters which we are sending for this purpose, you may proceed to provide for the protection and security of those departing and the indulgence of penitents, and receive under the protection of the Church the households and resources of those who undertake the labour of this journey for the love of God and the aid of the land. If you see that anything should be added for their protection which it befits the Church to provide, carry it out in our stead; and together exercise priestly zeal for the execution of this pious work, so that your ministry may be honoured in all things and the Eastern Church, by God’s inspiration, may receive the customary aid from your realm.

[Col. 0602D] Given at Benevento, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

DCXXVIII. He receives under protection the convent of Saints Fabian and Damian and confirms its possessions and rights, at the request of Galdinus, Archbishop of Milan, and Albert, Bishop of Lodi. (Benevento, 31 July.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 672.]
