ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ, THAIS, abbess of the monastery of St [Col. 0603A] Fabian of Farinate and St Damian of Donaria, and to her sisters, present and future, to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The care of the universal churches has been granted to us by God, the provider of all good things, so that we may cherish religious persons and strive by every means to promote service pleasing to God; for no service is ever rendered acceptably to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved in the purity of religion. Therefore, beloved daughter in Christ, Abbess Thais, we graciously assent to your petition, presented through our venerable brothers G., archbishop of Milan and legate of the Apostolic See, and Albert, bishop of Lodi; and, following the example of our predecessors of holy memory, Paschal, Calixtus, and Innocent, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the churches of the blessed Fabian and Damian over which, by God’s appointment, you preside [Col. 0603B], and decree that they shall henceforth remain free from every burden imposed by mortals. One of these churches, namely that of Blessed Fabian of Farinate, Counts Lantelmus, William, Arditius, Roger, Albicus, Arduin, and Osbert of Bergamo—who built it upon their own estate—offered to blessed Peter and his Roman Church, under an annual rent of twelve denarii of Milanese currency. We likewise confirm the other church, that of Blessed Damian of Donaria, under a like rent.

Therefore, by the present page of privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever goods and whatever possessions the same Church possesses, whether by the grant of the aforesaid counts or by the generosity of any of the faithful, or may hereafter, by God’s generosity, lawfully and canonically acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and those who succeed you. Nor shall the diocesan bishop have authority to burden the churches themselves or the persons serving in their houses, or to exercise judicial power in them, except for the consecration of places, the blessing of nuns, and the ordination of clerics appointed therein—provided that the bishop is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to administer these sacraments freely and without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you shall receive them from whatever Catholic bishop [Col. 0603D] you prefer.

Accordingly, let no person whatsoever be permitted to disturb the aforesaid churches, take away their possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations; rather, let all be kept whole for the benefit of the nuns serving God in the aforementioned churches, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. Upon the death of you, the present abbess of these places, or of any woman who succeeds you, no one shall be set over them through any device of deceit or violence, except one whom the sisters by common consent, or the sounder part of the sisters’ counsel, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff or by someone to whom he entrusts this task.

We also decree that the burial ground of these places shall be free [Col. 0604A], so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final will of those who decide to be buried in the aforesaid places, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken remain reserved. We wholly forbid the exaction from persons living the common life of tithes on newly cultivated land which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the nourishment of your animals. As Blessed Gregory says, we need say nothing here about portions to be made or hospitality to be offered, since everything that remains must be expended upon pious and religious causes. If anyone therefore shall hereafter, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 0604B] I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto. I, Ubald, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Albert, priest-cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina. I, Bozo, priest-cardinal of St Pudentiana, title of Pastor. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of St Lawrence in Damaso. I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Arditius, deacon-cardinal of St Theodore. I, Cinthius, deacon-cardinal of St Adrian. [Col. 0604C] I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of St Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Gerard, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 31 July, in the second indiction, in the year 1169 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

DCXXIX. He confirms the donation made by Gerard, bishop of Padua, to the abbess and monastery of St Zacharias of Venice, concerning tithes of properties on Monte Silice. (Benevento, 16 August.)

[CORNELII, *Ecclesiae Venetae*, XI, 379.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ [Col. 0604D], G., abbess, and to the sisters of the monastery of St Zacharias of Venice: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant consent to the just desires of petitioners, so that vows which do not depart from the path of reason may be fulfilled in effect. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, concurring with grateful assent in your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority for you and your monastery the tithe which you hold at Monte Cilice, reasonably granted to you by our venerable brother Gerard, bishop of Padua, and strengthened by the security of his written instrument; and we fortify it by the protection of this document. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation [Col. 0605A] or in any way oppose it. But should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Benevento, 16 August.

DCXXX. Privilege for the Church of Bologna. (Benevento.)

[SAVIOLI, *Annal. Bologn.*, II, II, 22.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother JOHN, bishop of Bologna, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The most holy Roman Church has always loved the Church of Bologna with special favor and has endeavored to honor it more generously than others. Therefore we, though placed, with insufficient fitness, upon the watchtower of that same Church, love the aforesaid Church of Bologna with customary goodwill and desire, venerable brother John, bishop, to grant favorable assent to your just petitions. Accordingly, brother bishop, embracing your person and the Church entrusted to you in the full arms of charity, we grant and lease to you, your successors, and, through you, to the Church of Bologna, by title of perpetual emphyteutic lease, all the greater and lesser properties both in the city and county of Bologna—namely the *massa primarii*, the other *massae*, and estates in that county—except whatever belongs there to the patrimony of the noblewoman Countess Matilda, and except the *bannum* in the city of Bologna which belongs to the Roman pontiff, according as it has hitherto been and shall hereafter be adjudged [Col. 0605C]. This is done as our predecessor Pope Anastasius of pious memory is known to have granted and leased these things in emphyteusis to Gerard, once bishop of Bologna and your predecessor of good memory, with the common counsel of his brethren, after receiving from him one hundred pounds in assessed payment, which he expended for the benefit of the Roman Church. We strengthen the lease itself by the page of this document.

For this lease, you and your successors shall pay each year to us and our successors two pounds of pure silver in the month of June. Furthermore, we have thought fit to add to this document that neither you nor any of your successors may sell or alienate this lease to any church or person, except to us or to our successors. We and our successors undertake to defend the aforesaid lease for you and your successors against every person. If either party fails to perform what is its obligation, as written above, it shall pay the other one hundred pounds of pure gold as a penalty, and the lease shall nevertheless remain irrevocably in force. Therefore let no person dare, with rash boldness, to infringe this page of our lease or oppose it in any manner. But should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0606A] I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ubald, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius. I, Hildebrand, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Albert, priest-cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of St Peter in Chains. I, John, priest-cardinal of St Pudentiana, title of Pastor. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, priest-cardinal of St Mark. [Col. 0606B] I, Theodinus, priest-cardinal of St Vitalis, title of Vestina. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and St Rufina. I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Arditius, deacon-cardinal of St Theodore. I, Cinthius, deacon-cardinal of St Adrian. I, Manfred, deacon-cardinal of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of St Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa. I, Peter, cardinal of St Mary.

Given at Veroli through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 18 April, in the third indiction, in the year 1169 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0606C], in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

DCXXXI. He grants to Guala, bishop of Bergamo, the church of St Mary of Turre at Suere and the church of St Julian of Sovisio above the Adda. (Benevento, 4 November.)

[LUPI, *Cod. diplom. Bergom.*, II, 1257.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother GUALA, bishop of Bergamo, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

When, out of devotion, you came into our presence to visit us and your mother, the most holy Roman Church, you carefully explained to us and [Col. 0606D] our brethren that the bishopric committed to you was exceedingly small. You therefore urgently requested that we should grant you some of those churches which, within the said bishopric, pertain exclusively to the Roman Church, so that you might in some measure relieve your need. Accordingly, attentively considering the affection of most sincere devotion which you are known to have displayed in many ways toward the aforesaid Roman Church, and also considering how great a labor you have undertaken to advance our affairs and those of that same Church, and what fruit the almighty and merciful Lord has bestowed upon your labor, we grant to you and your aforesaid Church, and also to your successors, by the common counsel of our brethren, the church of St Mary of Turre, situated above the village of Sucre, and the church of St Julian [Col. 0607A] of Sovisio, situated above the Adda, to govern and administer by apostolic authority [lacuna]; and we have invested you therein by a golden ring. You and your successors shall pay from them to us and our successors an annual rent—namely, twelve denarii of old Milanese currency for each church. The clerics of the same churches shall render reverence and obedience to you and your successors as to ourselves and as to the bishop himself, and shall answer fully in parochial right.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid grant [Col. 0607B], etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Ubald, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Albert, priest-cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of St Peter in Chains. I, Bozo, priest-cardinal of St Pudentiana, title of Pastor. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Damaso. I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in [Col. 0607C] Cosmedin. I, Arditius, deacon-cardinal of St Theodore. I, Cinthius, deacon-cardinal of St Adrian. I, Manfred, deacon-cardinal of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of St Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Benevento, through the hand of Gerard, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 4 November, in the third indiction, in the year 1169 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

DCXXXII. He grants Absalon, bishop of Roskilde, in perpetuity the mastership and spiritual preeminence of the island of Rügen, conquered and converted by King Valdemar. (Benevento, 4 November.)

[HASSELBACH, *Cod. Pomeran. diplom.*, I, 64.]

[Col. 0607D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother ABSALON, bishop of Roskilde: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When the religion of the Christian faith is spread through the cooperating grace of God, and the malice of a faithless people is crushed, broken, and restrained, we conceive so much greater joy and gladness in our mind as the worship of the divine majesty is thereby more widely increased and the universal Church receives growth from day to day. From the letters of our dearest son in Christ, Valdemar, illustrious king of the Danes, and of many others, we have manifestly learned that a certain island called Ro, situated near his kingdom [Col. 0608A], had been devoted from the earliest times of the Catholic faith to such idolatry and superstition that it made the surrounding region tributary to itself and continually inflicted many injuries and frequent dangers upon that kingdom and all neighboring Christians. The same king, inspired by heavenly breath, fortified with the arms of Christ and armed with the shield of faith, considered this; protected by divine gift, he overcame with strong and outstretched arm the obstinacy of the people of that island, and most powerfully, resolutely, and courageously brought back their disgraceful savagery to the faith and law of Christ, subjecting it also to his own rule.

Since the leading men and people of that land possess but a small island and consequently cannot have a bishop and pastor of their own, their king, overcome by their prayers and supplication and taking their need into account, has humbly and earnestly asked us to commit to you the spiritual care and administration of that island. We therefore, desiring with most benevolent mind to favor the petitions of the same king in so far as we may do so with God and justice, and wishing to honor you in grace and distinction as a venerable brother and firm pillar of the Church, moved also by the intervention of our venerable brother E., archbishop of Lund and legate of the Apostolic See, of the bishops and princes of the kingdom, by the urgency of our venerable brother the archbishop of Uppsala [Col. 0608C], and of our beloved sons, the Brianensis abbot, Master John, envoy of the same king, and Master Walter, your cleric, grant to you and your successors in perpetuity the mastership and spiritual preeminence of that island, without prejudice to the rights of other churches, should they possess any there. Since its people are untrained in the faith and are still ignorant of our law, announce to them the word of salvation, show them the way of truth, and instruct them by salutary regulations and Christian teaching.

Given at Benevento, 4 November.

DCXXXIII. He enters Canute, duke of the Danes, in the catalogue of saints. (Benevento, 8 November.)

[THORKELIN, *Diplom. Arna-Magn.*, I, 27.]

[Col. 0608D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren, the archbishop of Lund, legate of the Apostolic See, the bishops, and to the beloved sons, abbots, priors, and prelates of other churches established throughout Denmark: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the letters of our dearest son in Christ, W., illustrious king of the Danes, from your writings, and from the careful account of our venerable brother the archbishop of Uppsala and those who came with him, we have learned how Canute, duke of the Danes, of revered memory, father of the aforesaid king, while yet living [Col. 0609A], was a man of honorable and praiseworthy life and conduct; and how, after his death, a certain spring burst forth beside his tomb, a blind man received sight, and the almighty and merciful Lord deigned to perform many other miraculous works around him. The aforesaid archbishop and his companions were prepared, if we wished to receive it, to confirm this under the sanctity of an oath.

Therefore, having received the petition of the aforesaid king and of ourselves concerning his canonization, and trusting in the mercy of God and the merits of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we have, with the common counsel of our brethren, judged him worthy to be enrolled in the catalogue of saints. By apostolic authority we establish that you shall celebrate the day of his birth into heaven on 25 June. In accordance with your wish and desire, we have judged the body of this saint to be thus glorified and honored on earth with due proclamations, just as the almighty and merciful Lord has glorified him in heaven by His grace; so that hereafter he may be numbered among the saints, since, as we have learned from our own testimony, from that of the aforesaid archbishop and his companions, and from many others, he has merited this through signs and miracles [Col. 0609B]. Since, therefore, it becomes the prudence of our sincerity to honor with pious devotion and to venerate with all zeal him whom your whole community asks us to honor by apostolic authority, we ask, admonish, and exhort your devotion in the Lord through apostolic writings that henceforth you should endeavor to honor him with fitting honors and venerate him with due service, so that through this you may receive a manifold reward from the recompender of all good things and be aided in many ways before the Most High by his merits and intercessions [Col. 0609C].

Given at Benevento, 8 November, in the year of the Lord 1170.

DCXXXIV. To all parishioners of the Church of Uppsala.—That they obey [Stephen], archbishop. (Benevento, 8 November.)

[LILJEGREN, *Diplomatarium Suecanum*, I, 89.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all parishioners of the Church of Uppsala [Col. 0609D]: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported and shown to us by the testimony of certain persons that some among you, stirred by diabolical persuasion, have been accustomed to rise against the prelates of churches and, imputing diverse crimes to them, to compel them to submit to the judgment of laymen. Since it would seem astonishing to all if a sheep ought to slaughter its shepherd or pronounce a sentence of condemnation against him, we command and enjoin your whole body by apostolic writings that henceforth you shall in no way attempt such things, to the peril of your souls. Rather, humbly render in all things due obedience and reverence to our venerable brother S., your archbishop, whom we have sent to those regions for your salvation and advancement [Col. 0610A], as to your father and shepherd. Nor presume to accuse him or any other prelate of the Church before laymen, or to bring him before a secular tribunal. For the person of the aforesaid archbishop is known to be subject to the examination of no one save the Roman pontiff [lacuna]. Therefore, what is by no means lawful for any king or prince to do, you ought not in any way to usurp against your own salvation, since you might thereby most justly fear the indignation of almighty God.

Given at Benevento, 8 November.

DCXXXV. Privilege for the church of St Vincent at Bergamo. (Benevento, 11 November.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 466.]

[Col. 0610B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ADELARD, archdeacon, and his brethren, present and future, canonically living in the mother church of St Vincent at Bergamo: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever a request is made to us that is known to accord with religion and propriety, it befits us gladly to grant it and to render fitting support to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your reasonable requests and, after the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Innocent, Lucius, and Adrian, Roman pontiffs, receive under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See the church of Blessed Vincent the martyr, in which you are devoted to divine service [Col. 0610C], together with the community of your congregation and all that belongs to the same church; and we fortify it by the page of this document. We establish that whatever possessions and goods the same church presently lawfully and reasonably possesses in churches, villages, towns, tithes, offerings, market revenues, or other things, or may hereafter reasonably acquire, with the Lord’s help, through the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors forever. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

The church of St Mary, situated in the castle of Calcinate; the church of St Martin, situated in the village of the same place; the church of St Michael of Carpeneto; the church of St Mary of Gorlo; the church of St George of Spalanico; the church of St Christina of Albegno; and the church of St Cassian, situated in the city of Bergamo. We therefore decree that, so long as you remain in the observance of canonical discipline, no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass them with oppressive exactions or rash vexations [Col. 0611A]. Rather, let all be kept whole, for the complete benefit of those uses for whose governance and support they were granted. We also forbid the bishop, the archbishop, or any person to divert the goods of your community to private uses, to grant them in benefices to others, or in any way to alienate them from the prebend of the brethren or from the common good. Leases, exchanges, or investitures of estates shall in no way be carried out without the counsel of all the brethren or of the sounder part; nor shall this right be invaded by the bishop or by any persons whatsoever. Nevertheless, the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the Catholic bishops of Bergamo remain reserved.

If, therefore, any archbishop, bishop, emperor, king, prince, duke, margrave, count, viscount, or any ecclesiastical or secular person shall knowingly attempt rashly to violate this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offense by appropriate satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that same church, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0611C], so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Albert, priest-cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of St Peter in Chains. I, Boso, priest-cardinal of St Pudentiana, title of Pastor. [Col. 0611D] I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Damaso. I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Arditius, deacon-cardinal of St Theodore. I, Cinthius, deacon-cardinal of St Adrian. I, Manfred, deacon-cardinal of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of St Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Gerard, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 11 November, in the third indiction, in the year 1167 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

DCXXXVI. To Valdemar, king of the Danes.—He commends the abbot and brethren of Calve.

[LANGEBEK, *Scriptores Rerum Danicarum*, V, p. 243.]

[Col. 0612A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, VALDEMAR, illustrious king of the Danes: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We greatly rejoice that, by divine grace inspiring you, you persevere in devotion to blessed Peter and to us, strive to anticipate religious men with honor and favor alike, and grant them help and support out of piety; and we pray with devout supplication to the most high and almighty Lord that He may grant you perseverance in this. We offer especial and more worthy thanks to your serenity because you look with a kindly eye upon religious men, especially the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Calve [Col. 0612B], and deign, in pious compassion, to love them and provide them with the aid of welcome consolation. We trust that you will reap with multiplied fruit the seed of good work which you have sown in them, and we do not doubt that from this will come to you the reward of blessed recompense.

Since it is fitting and particularly becoming to your highness that, the more the pious and merciful Lord has exalted you on earth and placed you in a higher rank of honor, the more attentively you ought to give heed to works of piety and zealously accomplish with ardent desire those things that are pleasing and perfect to Him, we ask, admonish, and exhort your royal excellency in the Lord that, as you have well begun, you may steadfastly persevere in devotion to blessed Peter and to us, and with devout heart and pure mind attend to the honor and exaltation of your only mother, the most holy Roman Church [Col. 0612C]. Furthermore, we hold ratified and confirmed the transfer of the monastery, which the aforesaid abbot and brethren are known to have made from one place to another by the authority of our venerable brother Eskil, archbishop of Lund, and the bishops of the land, and with your consent; likewise, the exchange which they made with you. We ask your greatness to show yourself favorable and kind to the aforementioned brethren and to be their protector, helper, and defender.

DCXXXVII. To Briennus, abbot of Calve.

[LANGEBEK, *ibid.*, p. 244.]

[Col. 0612D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BRIENNUS, abbot, and the brethren of Calve: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is our purpose and desire to attend with fatherly solicitude and diligent care to the peace and quiet of religious persons, and to afford their vows and petitions kindly favor and free effect. For it has been brought to our attention that, by the authority of our brother Eskil, archbishop of Lund, and the bishops of the land, and with the consent of our dearest son in Christ, Valdemar, illustrious king of the Danes, you have transferred your monastery from Weng, where it formerly stood [Col. 0613A], together with its possessions, to the place called Calve, leaving only the village of Weng in the king’s hands in exchange for the land which you received from that same king. Since transfers and exchanges made for the benefit of churches ought to be approved and held ratified, we approve, as is fitting, the transfer of your said monastery; we establish that it shall remain ratified and firm; and we confirm by apostolic authority for you and your church the exchange which you made with the aforesaid king in the course of that transfer, fortifying it by the protection of this document. We establish that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. But should anyone [Col. 0613B] presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

CIRCA THE YEAR 1169.

DCXXXVIII. To Boniface, master of the knighthood of the Temple in Lombardy.

[TIRABOSCHI, *Memor. Moden.*, III, Proofs, p. 54.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BONIFACE, master, and the brethren of the knighthood of the Temple in Lombardy: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whereas a dispute had long been conducted between you and our beloved sons William [Col. 0613C], abbot, and the brethren of Fraxinoro, concerning the church of St Stephen, situated in the suburb of the city of Reggio, the hospital [lacuna] its possessions, the same dispute was settled by an amicable agreement. We hold that agreement [lacuna] ratified and firm; the aforesaid church with its hospital and other appurtenances, subject to a reserved rent [lacuna] of ten solidi [lacuna] to the abbot and his monastery and [lacuna] pounds of oil, which the aforesaid [lacuna] that the diocesan bishops [lacuna] let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page [lacuna]. [Col. 0613D] [lacuna]

IN THE YEARS 1162–1170.

DCXXXIX. He commands Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to compel the monks of Boxley to pay tithes to the church of St Mary.

[Gilbert Foliot, *Epistles*, ed. GILES, II, 66.]

ALEXANDER Pope III, to THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury.

The office of the dispensation entrusted to us by God repeatedly admonishes and exhorts us that we should make beneficial provision for all Christ’s churches and preserve their entire rights unimpaired. It has indeed come to our attention that the monks of Boxley do not pay in full the tithes owed to the church of St Mary, in whose parish they reside, and refuse to render them in accordance with the canons. Therefore, brother, we command and enjoin you by apostolic writings, by our authority and with all strictness, without impediment of appeal, to compel the aforesaid monks to pay those tithes in their entirety to the aforesaid church—even from those cultivated lands upon which houses had formerly been built—which they used to pay before they resided in the same church [Col. 0614A]. For just as tithes were formerly paid from pasturelands, so now we will that tithes be paid without diminution from those same lands after their conversion to the fertility of crops [Col. 0614B].

DCXL. To Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury.—Concerning appeals to the Apostolic See.

[Gilbert Foliot, *Epistles*, ed. GILES, II, 62.]

It has been reported to us that whenever your suffragan bishops or the archdeacons of your province appeal to our hearing concerning some definite matter, they place their bishoprics and archdeaconries under the protection of us and the Roman Church; and when they appeal for a year, in the meantime they do not permit you to take cognizance of their own offenses or those of their subjects, thus nullifying and suspending all your jurisdiction [Col. 0614C]. Therefore, wishing in pastoral solicitude to provide that the pretext of an appeal may not give occasion for committing serious offenses, we have thought fit to grant you, by apostolic authority, that if the aforesaid bishops and archdeacons appeal to our hearing and place their bishoprics and archdeaconries under apostolic protection, you shall by no means, because of their appeal, refrain from taking cognizance of cases and offenses of their subjects, and of their own offenses if these are manifest and notorious—excepting only those matters concerning which an appeal has been made—and from determining concerning them what you judge ought to be determined according to justice.

DCXLI. To R., son of Henry. (Fragment.)

[Epistles of St Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 146.]

[Col. 0614D]

To the beloved son R., son of Henry.

To the just desires of petitioners, etc., as far as “assent.” The land on the island of Thanet which our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, restored to you, just as he granted it to you and your heirs to hold with its appurtenances, to your devotion, etc.

DCXLII. To Philip, abbot of Prémontré, etc.—For the peace of the Church of Prémontré.

[MARTENE, *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 816.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to [Col. 0615A] PHILIP [Note: [Col. 0615] Philip, having become abbot of Prémontré from being abbot of Belleval, died in the year 1170.], of Prémontré, and to the other abbots gathered at Prémontré in God’s name.

It has come to our attention that, owing to certain measures which you have recently established among yourselves, the minds of no small number of your converts have been troubled—so much so that many of them would more readily return to the world than be brought to accept those enactments. Therefore, since those set over others must weigh matters carefully and take heed lest by authority they scatter the Lord’s flock, which ought to be kept by gentleness and charity, we counsel and admonish your whole community that, avoiding disturbance of the order with all the diligence you can, you defer to another time every novelty from which some division might arise among you. Keep yourselves within the bounds of your fathers; and see to it that, while you desire to reach out toward things new and uncertain, you do not, at very great loss, forfeit the things which you hold certain and have found beneficial. We do not deny that both you and all who submit themselves to divine service must always strive for higher things, and that, with the blessed Apostle, forgetting what lies behind, they ought continually to stretch themselves toward what lies before (Phil. III). Yet all things have their season. There is a time to speak and a time to be silent; a time to cast stones and a time to gather them; a time to sow and a time to reap (Eccles. III). Indeed, all labour is easily lost if the fitting opportunity is not observed.

Certainly, how greatly the evil of discord must be avoided in religious communities, we would rather have you learn from another’s example than from your own experience. For you see that, as small things have grown through concord, so even the greatest have fallen apart through discord. It is better to meet coming evils before their time than, after they have arrived, to labour in seeking remedies, as Solomon says: “The wise man, seeing evil, turns aside; the little ones, passing on, have borne losses” (Prov. XXVII). Therefore, by our counsel, until the peace of the Church is restored and until your fellow abbots can assemble more fully from every side, avoid all innovations that could cause division; and preserve with fatherly affection your little ones, whom, like a hen her chicks, you ought to guard and cherish beneath the wings of charity. But when He has restored peace to His Church and your abbots have gathered more fully from all quarters, you will then be able more usefully and firmly to establish what is salutary. For if anything of strength should perhaps be lacking to your constitutions from yourselves, it may be supplied by the authority of the Apostolic See. Meanwhile hold fast what you have begun, and so adhere to the ancient enactments confirmed by the Apostolic See that the peace of the order may no longer be disturbed under the pretext of greater austerity.

## A.D. 1164–1170

### DCXLIII. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—Concerning the profession of Gilbert of Hereford, later Bishop of London.

[Letters of St Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 19.]

[Col. 0616A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When you were present before us at the celebration of the Council of Tours, we remember that you wished to obtain that our venerable brother Gilbert, formerly Bishop of Hereford but now Bishop of London, should also make to you, for the Church of London, the profession which he had made to your predecessor in the name of the Church of Hereford, just as his predecessors had made it to your predecessors. But, considering that the profession which he had made to the Church of Canterbury in the name of Hereford could and ought sufficiently to suffice, especially since, if he were compelled to make another, that same bishop might appear liable to the charge of having violated his profession, and since it is not the custom of the Roman Church that anyone be compelled, on the occasion of his translation, to make profession twice, we remember that we answered and advised you to be content with that first profession which he had made in the Church of Hereford to your predecessor and his successors, and not burden him with another profession beyond this.

Therefore, since you have taken care humbly to obey our admonitions and counsel in this matter, by the authority of the present letters we decree that no prejudice to you or to your church may henceforth arise from this, so as to prevent those who succeed the aforesaid bishop in the Church of London from being bound to render the customary and due profession both to you and to your successors.

## A.D. 1166–1170

### DCXLIV. To all the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury.—That Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, presides over them not only by metropolitan right but also by right of legation.

[Ibid., p. 62.]

Since you are not ignorant that our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, presides over you not only by metropolitan right but also by right of legation, it is quite astonishing that some of you, as we have heard, dare to maintain that the same archbishop ought to hear no cause concerning your bishoprics either by metropolitan or legatine right unless it is brought before him by appeal. Certainly, although perhaps by metropolitan right he ought not to hear a cause concerning his bishoprics unless it is referred to him by appeal, nevertheless, by reason of his legation he can and ought to hear every cause concerning those bishoprics which comes before him, whether by appeal or by someone’s complaint, since he is known to exercise our authority in his province.

We therefore command and direct you that you leave to the judgment of that archbishop the causes which are brought to him from your bishoprics; and that you do not attempt to hinder or prevent any cleric or layperson subject to your jurisdiction from transferring his cause, should he wish, to the aforesaid archbishop.

## A.D. 1168–1170

### DCXLV. He commands the judges of Velletri that, “when any cause concerning wills left to the Church has been brought before their examination, they shall handle it not according to the civil laws but according to the provisions of the decrees, and shall be content with three or two lawful witnesses.” (Benevento, Jan. 1.)

[BORGIA, *History of Velletri*, p. 240.]

[Col. 0617B]

### DCXLVI. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of the knights Goslen and O. (Benevento, Jan. 2.)

[MARTEN., *Amplified Collection*, II, 771.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You are to know that from the complaint of the knights Goslen and O. it has come to our hearing that, when formerly Herl., a canon of Reims, had received from his kinsman Ric. certain revenues in pledge for thirty pounds, upon the condition that, after he had recovered from those revenues his principal apart from expenses, the said revenues should return without contradiction to the right and ownership of that same R., R. having died, the aforesaid G. and O., who succeeded to his goods by nearness of blood, have been unable to possess the aforementioned revenues, although the same canon is said to have recovered his principal in full after deduction of expenses.

For Herl. asserts that the aforesaid R. had bestowed the said revenues upon his wife Ada as a marriage-gift; and thus not only he himself, but also A. and P., the vice-lord, grievously oppose the same knights in this matter. Therefore, since we can and ought to fail no one in his justice, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, when you are requested concerning this, having summoned both parties before you, you diligently hear the cause and, within forty days after receipt of these letters, set it at rest by the means of justice, all contradiction and appeal ceasing. But if either party, lawfully cited, should scorn to obey your judgment, strike that party with ecclesiastical censure, appeal set aside, until due satisfaction has been made.

Given at Benevento, on the fourth Nones of January [2 January].

### DCXLVII. He confirms gifts bestowed on the monastery of Longpont by the bishops and chapter of Senlis. (Benevento, Jan. 2.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, X, Documents, 432.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HUGH, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Longpont, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother Henry, Bishop of Senlis, and also the canons of his church, have informed us by letters sent that they have liberally granted to you the whole alms-gift which Peter, Theobald, and Amalric, bishops formerly of Senlis, of good memory, with the assent of their chapter, granted to you—especially all the lands, meadows, and vineyards which, both in the days of those bishops and in modern times, you have acquired in the territory of Soissons at the place called Pratella—and have confirmed these, together with the *vinagium* [vineyard due] of the lands and vineyards which they possess there, subject to an annual rent.

Moreover, the aforesaid bishop and his canons have granted you whatever you may be able to acquire in the aforesaid territory by purchase or alms-gift, and have strengthened this grant under the protection of a written instrument in a fixed form. This concession, as it is known to be contained in the authentic instrument made on the matter by the said bishop and his church, we confirm to you and, through you, to your monastery by apostolic authority, and secure by the protection of the present writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Benevento, on the fourth Nones of January [2 January].

### DCXLVIII. He confirms for the monastery of Le Bec the privileges granted by William, formerly Archbishop of Rouen. (Benevento, Jan. 7.)

[Works of LANFRANC, ed. GILES, I, 332.]

[Col. 0618C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROGER, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Le Bec, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the text of certain letters of William, formerly Archbishop of Rouen, of good memory, it has become known to us that he granted many liberties to you, your monastery, and the parish of that place; and that he freed that church, together with its parish, from every episcopal exaction, as is known to be set out more fully in his instrument made upon this matter. This concession, therefore, since it was reasonably made and reduced to an authentic written instrument, we ratify and confirm by apostolic authority, and secure by the protection of the present writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Benevento, on the seventh Ides of January [7 January].

### DCXLIX. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—Against the lepers of Cambrai. (Benevento, Jan. 8.)

[MARTEN., *Amplified Collection*, II, 772.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having received the complaint of the lepers of Cambrai, that the abbots of Saint Andrew of the Castle [Note: [Col. 0619D] Saint Andrew of the Castle, a Benedictine monastery in the diocese of Cambrai.] and of the Holy Sepulchre [Note: [Col. 0619D] The Holy Sepulchre, another Benedictine monastery in the city of Cambrai. Compare this letter with Letters 155 and 156.], the canons of Saint Gaugericus, and the noble man Manasses of Ruriniac, were extorting tithes from them upon their newly cultivated lands and upon the sustenance of their animals, we commanded your brotherhood at their request that, if the aforesaid abbots and canons would not comply with our commands in this matter—that is, if they did not within forty days after receipt of our letters restore in full to those said infirm persons the tithes which they had rashly presumed to take away, or make a peaceful and amicable agreement with them on the matter, and did not thereafter cease troubling them concerning it—you should strictly restrain them from entering churches and declare the abbots suspended from the administration of their churches by apostolic authority.

But now, from a report sent by the said abbots, it has reached our ears that the aforementioned infirm persons are attempting to withhold from them tithes which they have paid continuously for thirty years up to this year, and which our father and predecessor Pope Eugenius of holy memory and our other predecessors confirmed to them. What is serious, after an appeal had been made to us, they did not hesitate to despoil those persons by the violence of laymen; and when their messenger met the messenger of these persons on the road and, in our name, instructed them to return with him to us, they refused in any way to consent.

Therefore, although we wish to uphold and support the aforesaid infirm persons, nevertheless, since we neither ought nor wish to diminish the rights of others, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth of this matter. If it is established to you that the said abbots and canons possessed the aforesaid tithes without dispute for thirty years up to this year, and that our predecessors confirmed them to those parties, compel the infirm persons to desist from molesting them and to pay them the said tithes, all contradiction and appeal ceasing; and if they should perhaps produce before you letters of ours against this and wish to rely upon them, you are not in any way to defer to those letters.

Nevertheless, concerning the lands which those same infirm persons have newly brought under cultivation within the last three years, and concerning the sustenance of their animals, they are to be compelled to pay tithes to no one. Whatever the others received by violence from those tithes after the appeal to us was made, they are to be compelled to restore. Certainly, the said Manasses is not to be required to answer them in any respect concerning these matters. We do not, however, wish them under this pretext to presume in any way to clear up other persons’ lands against their will.

Given at Benevento, on the sixth Ides of January [8 January].

### DCL. To the same.—On behalf of the Church of Prémontré. (Benevento, Jan. 9.)

[Ibid., col. 773.]

[Col. 0620A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that John of Burgundy has been bound by the bond of excommunication for the losses and injuries which he rashly inflicted upon the Church of Prémontré. Therefore, since an ecclesiastical sentence pronounced against evildoers for their offences ought to remain valid and unshaken, and must retain the strength of firmness until due satisfaction has been made, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you ensure that the same sentence is inviolably observed until due satisfaction has been made.

Given at Benevento, on the fifth Ides of January [9 January].

### DCLI. To . . . .—On behalf of the Church of Saint Remigius of Reims. (Benevento, Jan. 12.)

[Ibid., col. 774.]

ALEXANDER, etc.

Our beloved son, the abbot of Saint Remigius, has informed us that certain people of Châlons presume to take from him a certain house and thirty pounds in the money of Châlons, concerning which they scorn to render him justice. Therefore, since we are bound to preserve more earnestly for religious persons and places the justice which we owe to all, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and strictly compel the said men, your parishioners, either to restore without delay the aforesaid house and money to the said abbot and leave him in peace, or without delay to render him full justice thereon before your tribunal, appeal set aside. If both of you cannot be present in these matters, one of you shall nonetheless proceed, as stated, in hearing the cause.

Given at Benevento, on the second Ides of January [12 January].

### DCLII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of Huldewin, vice-lord of Reims. (Benevento, Jan. 16.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0620D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son Holduin, vice-lord of your church, has shown us in a detailed account that you yourself, at your own pleasure, withdrew from him the benefice which he had customarily held in the church of Saint Sixtus through S., the former treasurer of good memory, as many others before him had held it, although he was prepared, as he asserts, to submit to justice concerning this. Therefore, since he maintains that he has knowingly offended you in no respect for which you ought to despoil him of the aforesaid benefice, and since before us he has not detracted from you in any matter or uttered, so far as we have been able to discern, a single improper word, we earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort your brotherhood by apostolic letters to consider what is more fitting for you rather than any person’s suggestion or impulse of mind; and, setting aside all resentment, for reverence of blessed Peter and ourselves and in consideration of the devotion which he bears toward you, restore without difficulty the aforesaid benefice to the said vice-lord and leave him in peace to hold it as he has customarily done.

Thus he shall be bound to be more faithful to you at all times, and shall rejoice that he has complied with our prayers to your sincerity rather than with a command; and we too shall be bound to regard this as altogether welcome and acceptable and to offer abundant thanks for it to your affection.

Given at Benevento, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February [16 January].

### DCLIII. He gently rebukes Henry, Archbishop of Reims, concerning certain matters. (Benevento, Jan. 18.)

[Ibid., col. 775.]

ALEXANDER, to HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, etc.

Mindful of the long-standing devotion and sincerity which you have shown toward us and the Roman Church, we cherish your person with a closer charity in the Lord, although afterward you have conducted yourself in many matters otherwise than was fitting; and we often recall the fruit which we received long ago from your devotion. But if reports are at times made concerning you of things directed against us and the Roman Church, we bear them more grievously and with greater distress because we believed less that such things could at any time be done by you.

For this reason, not at all forgetting the fatherly affection which we bear toward your person, we thought certain matters should be conveyed orally to your discretion through our beloved son, the abbot of Saint Vincent of Senlis [Note: [Col. 0621D] Saint Vincent of Senlis, a celebrated monastery of the Order of Saint Augustine, of the Gallican Congregation, founded in 1159 by Queen Anne, wife of Henry I.], whom we know to be in every respect faithful and devoted to you—matters which we did not wish to entrust to the credit of a letter. By the present writing we command your brotherhood diligently to hear the same matters from him and to apply yourself promptly to their correction, so that men of the present day may find in you nothing which they can censure or which may be deemed worthy of reproof; nor may a bad example be transmitted through you to posterity—from whom the fruits of good works are expected to proceed.

However great may be the distinction of your office and your nobility of blood, henceforth we shall not be able to spare you, consistently with the duty of our office, as we would rather make known to your devotion in person, if that could be done, than by letter. But since we cannot speak with you mouth to mouth, we preferred to admonish you through the aforesaid abbot, your intimate associate, concerning those things which need correction, rather than commit them to writing or communicate them to you through another. Your prudence ought assuredly to observe this carefully and to place such faith and trust in the word of that abbot, which he received from our own mouth, that by sure evidences of deeds we may prove that you have faithfully committed our admonition to memory and humbly received fatherly correction, so that those who see your actions may find rather something to commend than anything that is deservedly to be censured.

Given at Benevento, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February [18 January].

### DCLIV. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims, and the Bishop of Laon.—On behalf of the church of Noveio, that land violently taken from it be restored. (Benevento, Jan. 18.)

[Ibid., col. 776.]

[Col. 0622B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, and the Bishop of Laon, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved sons, the prior and brethren of the church of Noveio, have complained to us that G. of Château in Porcien and R. of Rause, your parishioners, after holding a certain piece of land violently for a long time, finally restored it to that church. But now, returning to their vomit, they have again laid hands upon it. The aforesaid R. has resumed the part which he used to hold, while G. has relinquished part of what he held there and is striving to retain a part. Moreover, the said G. seized men of the aforesaid church and compelled them to ransom themselves. The men of R. also, with diabolical audacity, carried off five horses belonging to the said prior and brethren, led them into the territory of that same R., and are said to have sold them there.

Therefore, since it pertains to our office more diligently to preserve the rights of religious persons and to foster them above others, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters carefully and earnestly to admonish the aforesaid G. and R. either to restore in full and without any delay the land to the aforementioned prior and brethren and leave them in peace, or to render them full and sufficient justice concerning it before you, appeal set aside. If they refuse to comply with your admonition, pronounce upon them, all excuse and appeal set aside, a sentence of excommunication; and if they do not amend even then, prohibit all divine services from being celebrated in their lands, except baptism of infants and the penances of the dying.

Concerning the other things taken from the said prior and his brethren both by them and by their men, ensure that full and strict justice is rendered to them, with the remedy of appeal removed, so that they may recover their rights through you and we may have reason more fittingly to commend your diligence in this matter. Moreover, by the authority of the present letters we enjoin you strictly to forbid, under threat of anathema, the knights and other parishioners under your jurisdiction, on account of the noble Count of Registe, to harm, plunder, or disturb the lands or men of the oft-mentioned prior and his brethren. If they do anything contrary to your prohibition, each of you shall compel your parishioners by ecclesiastical censure to render justice for this.

Furthermore, you shall strictly compel G. of Taisy—who is said to have appealed to us against the prior of Noveio already more than a year ago—to submit before you to the equity of law concerning the matters from which he appealed, appeal set aside, unless he can show a reasonable cause why he has not pursued his appeal. If he has a canonical excuse, compel him either to pursue his appeal within a suitable time or to submit to justice before you, the appeal being withdrawn.

Given at Benevento, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February [18 January].

### DCLV. To the same.—On behalf of the church of Noveio concerning the church of Braguen. (Benevento, Jan. 18.)

[Ibid., col. 778.]

[Col. 0623C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We remember that we have already committed, appeal set aside, the cause known to have long been disputed between our beloved sons, the prior and brethren of Noveio, and the clerics of Braguen, to our venerable brother H. [Note: [Col. 0623D] Hugh.] Bishop of Soissons, and our beloved son P. [Note: [Col. 0623D] Peter.] Abbot of Saint Remigius of Reims. After summoning the parties before them and fully investigating the cause, they rendered judgment in favour of the said prior and brethren and adjudged the church to them. In opposing this judgment, the aforesaid clerics deserved to be bound by a sentence of excommunication, especially Goze and his son J., because they retained the provostship of Braguen together with its prebend contrary to the judgment given.

Therefore, since the authority of law decrees that a matter adjudged must stand, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to ensure that the aforesaid judgment, as rendered by the said bishop and abbot, is firmly observed and carried into execution, all contradiction and appeal set aside. Those who have presumed to act against it and have thereby incurred a sentence of excommunication—which you yourself are also said to have pronounced—are, with appeal withdrawn, to be diligently avoided throughout your entire province as excommunicated persons, [lacuna] until they restore in full all things taken away to the aforementioned prior and brethren, render fitting satisfaction for the losses and injuries inflicted, and leave them in peace in accordance with the judgment rendered.

Nevertheless, if our beloved sons Fr., the dean, and the canons of the Church should perhaps at some time wish to proceed against that same prior and brethren, we do not wish the sentence of the aforesaid men to prejudice them in any respect, unless it is established to us that the aforesaid prior and brethren possess such an instrument bearing subscriptions as the text which they showed us. But if those clerics of Braguen, namely Jo. and R., whom we caused to be absolved in our stead, do not make worthy satisfaction to the prior and brethren both for the things taken and for the losses and injuries inflicted, or do not wish the judgment to be observed, you shall restore them, all delay and appeal ceasing, to the same bond of anathema by which they had been bound, and ensure that all avoid them as excommunicated persons until due satisfaction has been made.

Given at Benevento, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February [18 January].

### DCLVI. To . . .—On behalf of the abbot and brethren of Trois-Fontaines. (Benevento, Jan. 18.)

[Ibid., col. 779.]

ALEXANDER, etc.

Our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of Trois-Fontaines [Note: [Col. 0623D] Trois-Fontaines, a monastery of no little distinction of the Cistercian Order, in the line of Clairvaux, founded in the diocese of Châlons.], have shown us by a repeated complaint that, when S., vice-lord of Châlons, was passing by one of their granges, he urgently asked the brethren who were there to receive as a guest his servant, whose horse was too tired to proceed farther. The servant was received by the brethren, and the said vice-lord had already gone on; meanwhile robbers burst into that grange and, after despoiling its workers, took the said servant’s cloak. On this pretext Albert, then provost of that same vice-lord, took one horse from the said brethren. When, because of this, he was brought before the tribunal of the Bishop of Châlons, he answered that he had neither taken the horse nor received a cauldron in place of the horse.

But since Albert is said afterward to have acknowledged in the presence of the same bishop what he had previously denied, having great confidence in your prudence and integrity, we entrust to you the determination of this matter. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, after summoning both parties before you, if it is lawfully established or can be proved before you that the said Albert acknowledged in court what he had previously denied, relying upon our authority you shall admonish and strictly compel him to restore, appeal and pretext set aside, the horse and the cauldron to the said abbot and brethren. If he does not do so, do not delay to bind him with the bond of excommunication; and let your notification be sent to our venerable brother the Bishop of Châlons, that he may observe the sentence firmly and unshakenly and cause it to be observed throughout his bishopric.

Given at Benevento, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February [18 January].

### DCLVII. To the abbot and monks of Saint-Vaast.—That they promise obedience to no one but the Bishop of Rome. (Benevento, Jan. 19.)

[MARTEN., *Amplified Collection*, I, 880.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, to his beloved sons the abbot and brethren of Saint-Vaast, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0625B]

It has not escaped our memory how our brother A. [Note: [Col. 0625D] Andrew, formerly abbot of Vaux-de-Sernay, was ordained Bishop of Arras and died in 1771.] Bishop of Arras, when he was formerly present before us, raised, in the presence of certain of your brethren, a question concerning the obedience to be rendered him by your church. But, after diligently and carefully examining the privileges of your church, we were wholly unable from their tenor to conclude that you, son Abbot, owe obedience to anyone other than the Roman Church.

Therefore, since the aforesaid bishop did not subsequently pursue his claim, and since it is improper that, while other abbots dwelling outside the diocese of Arras—whose churches do not specially belong to the Roman pontiff—promise no obedience to the Bishop of Arras for the churches which they hold in his parish, you, son Abbot, should be bound by a promise of any obedience to him, we command you by apostolic letters and strictly prohibit you from promising, or attempting for any reason to render, any obedience or subjection to any archbishop or bishop except the Roman pontiff. And to you, sons, the monks, we firmly and strictly enjoin by the authority of the present letters that you never allow your abbot, whoever he may be at the time, to promise any obedience or subjection to any archbishop or bishop except the Roman pontiff; especially since your church belongs only to the Roman Church and is subject by parochial right to no other.

[Col. 0625D]

Given at Benevento, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February [19 January].

### DCLVIII. To . . .—On the cause of the abbess of Avenay. (Benevento, Jan. 21.)

[MARTEN., *Amplified Collection*, II, 780.]

ALEXANDER, etc.

The cause known to be in dispute between the abbot of Trois-Fontaines and the abbess of Avenay [Note: [Col. 0625D] Aveniacum, in French Avenay, a distinguished convent of Benedictine nuns, situated five miles from the city of Reims.], concerning a certain house, we entrust to your experience, in which we have full confidence, to hear and bring to a fitting conclusion, the remedy of appeal having been removed. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, when you have been requested concerning this, you assemble together in one place, summon both parties before you, hear and investigate fully the arguments on either side, and determine the same cause by the means of justice, as stated, with the impediment of appeal removed.

Given at Benevento, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February [21 January].

### DCLIX. To the Bishop of Cahors.—Concerning relief of the monastery of Moissac from debts. (Benevento, Jan. 21.)

[MARTEN., *Treasury of Anecdotes*, I, 456.]

[Col. 0626B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the Bishop of Cahors, greeting and apostolic blessing.

How heavily the monastery of Moissac is burdened with debts, and how it is subject to want and poverty, your discretion ought not in any way to be unaware. Since we ought to devote our whole effort to relieving the burdens and necessities of the monastery and, as far as we can, lightening its hardships, we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and earnestly exhort the burgesses of Moissac that, if they have recovered twice over their principal from the fruits received, they resign to that monastery, setting aside every pretext, the lands, revenues, and dignities which they hold by way of pledge; and that henceforth they do not under any circumstances presume, without the common consent of the abbot, the chapter, and the sounder part, to receive the treasury, possessions, dignities, or revenues of the monastery in pledge.

They are not to delay restoring to the brethren the lands and revenues which they have occupied, or rendering full justice concerning them in your presence. But if they should perhaps refuse to comply with your admonitions, compel them by our authority to do so; strike them also with ecclesiastical censure; and place their land under interdict.

Given at Benevento, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February [21 January].

### DCLX. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of John, a priest, that he may minister in his church. (Benevento, Jan. 26.)

[MARTEN., *Amplified Collection*, II, 780.]

[Col. 0626D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the tenor of certain of your letters, and from the statement of John, priest and bearer of the present letter, we have learned that, when he had been presented to a certain church, you refused to admit him thereto, because he is said to have been ordained by O., formerly bishop of Metz, who, although at first Catholic, later fell into the error of schism.

> [Note: Col. 0625D: Here a scribal error has crept in, for in the list of bishops of Metz [Col. 0626D] none is found whose name begins with the letter O. At that time Stephen was in office, who governed the Church of Metz from 1120 to 1163. Meursius, bishop of Madaura, in his *History of the Bishops of Metz*, and Wasseburgus in his *History of Verdun*, maintain that he adhered indeed [Col. 0627D] to Emperor Frederick, but not with a schismatic intention. This letter, however, proves them wrong. For Stephen was excommunicated because of the schism and, later coming to his senses, was released from that bond.]

Since we have no certainty concerning the time of his ordination, we have instructed by our letters our beloved son, the bishop-elect of Metz, to investigate carefully and diligently whether the aforesaid John received the rank of priesthood from him while the aforesaid bishop was Catholic, or after he had fallen into schism and deserved to be bound by excommunication, or after that bishop’s absolution; and to endeavor swiftly to inform you by his letters of whatever he may discover.

> [Note: Col. 0627D: Theoderic of Bar, elected from the office of primicerius [chief chanter] [Col. 0628D] in 1164, was not consecrated.]

Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your fraternity that, once you have learned more fully through the letters of the same bishop-elect the truth of this matter, if it is certain to you that the aforesaid John was ordained by the said bishop while he was Catholic, or after his absolution, you are mercifully to receive him into the aforesaid church in the office of priest. Otherwise, you are in no way to permit him to minister in the order received from that bishop.

Given at Benevento, the seventh day before the Kalends of February.

DCLXI. To Gerard, Archbishop of Salona. (Benevento, January 31.)

[Farlatus, *Illyricum sacrum*, III, 191.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G[ERARD], Archbishop of Salona, legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Concerning what your fraternity asked of us—namely, what should be done regarding bigamists—we reply to your inquiry by these present letters: both those who ordain them are to be deprived of the power and office of ordaining, and those ordained, if they have been promoted to sacred orders, must be wholly deprived of those orders. For, contrary to the Apostle, no dispensation may be granted in the case of bigamists (1 Tim. 3), so that they may be promoted to sacred orders or, if promoted, may in any way remain in them. In the case of the ordainer, however, a dispensation may be granted, so that he is not deprived of the power and office of ordaining.

Concerning those ordained simoniacally, we cannot give you a definite answer in accordance with your request unless we learn more fully how they were ordained. For some, although they are ordained simoniacally in a certain respect—for example, where the persons ordained themselves are ignorant—may nevertheless remain in their orders, because they are not simoniacs.

But concerning those who, it is said, are joined in the fourth and fifth degrees of consanguinity in your province: because of the hardness of the people, pass over such marriages, although contracted against the ordinances of the sacred canons, in silence and forbearance. Yet strive in a general synod to forbid all persons, under threat of anathema, from contracting similar marriages in future; decreeing that such marriages, if contracted after your prohibition, must be invalid. Thereafter, if you find marriages contracted within the prescribed degree of consanguinity, you must not fail to annul them.

Moreover, let no one presume to put away his wife except for the sole cause of fornication, in accordance with the command of the divine word and the Apostle’s admonition. If anyone puts away his wife for another cause, strive by our authority and yours to compel him, by the stricter constraint of ecclesiastical discipline, promptly to receive her back. If he puts her away for the cause of fornication, let him either be reconciled to her, or compel him, while she lives, to observe continence.

Given at Benevento, the second day before the Kalends of February.

DCLXII. He commands the Abbot of Flavigny to render obedience to Bartholomew, Bishop of Beauvais. (Benevento, February 2.)

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 781.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the Abbot of Flavigny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

> [Note: Col. 0628D: The monastery of Flaiacum or Flaviacum, commonly called Saint-Germer, named from Saint Germer, its abbot and founder, is four hours’ distance from Beauvais.]

A complaint from our venerable brother B., Bishop of Beauvais, has reached our hearing: although the church committed to you is established within the bounds of his diocese, you disdain to render him the obedience and subjection due to him, alleging no other reason than that our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Rheims, withdrew you from his jurisdiction. This we can scarcely believe of so great a man, since that archbishop could not have done it without the authority of the Roman pontiff.

We, however, desiring to preserve entire and unimpaired for that bishop, as for our venerable brother, his rights, command your discretion by apostolic letters: if your church is situated within the diocese of the Church of Beauvais and has not been withdrawn from his jurisdiction by the authority of the Roman pontiff, render to the aforesaid bishop the obedience and reverence due to him, without any objection—unless your church has otherwise prescribed against that church by possession of long duration.

Given at Benevento, the fourth day before the Nones of February.

DCLXIII. To …—On behalf of the youth P. (Benevento, February 5.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, etc.

It becomes us to devote ourselves to works of mercy, and to grant assistance and aid, and to bring relief by the hand of our solicitude, to those who seek the support of our beneficence and suffer want through necessity. Moved by this consideration, we earnestly ask and exhort your charity, on behalf of P., a youth of good promise, that, for love of God and out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, you mercifully and charitably provide him with food and clothing until the Lord shall make better provision for him in some place. Thus you may receive an everlasting reward from almighty God and expect abundant thanks from us.

Given at Benevento, on the Nones of February.

DCLXIV. He confirms to the Abbey of Saint-Denis at Paris the church of Saint-Médard of Tremblay. (Benevento, February 8.)

[Doublet, *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 508.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and brothers of the church of Saint-Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0629B] It is fitting that we readily grant the just desires of petitioners, and that requests which do not depart from the path of reason be fulfilled by the ensuing effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting favorably to your just petitions, we confirm to you, and through you to that monastery, by apostolic authority, and fortify with the protection of this present writing, the church of Saint-Médard of Tremblay, with the chapel of Ville-Peinte and the tithes of that village, as your monastery now justly and lawfully possesses it. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly act against it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the wrath of almighty God and of His apostles, the blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Kalends of April.

DCLXV. To …—On behalf of the Abbot of Saint Mary of Vertus. (Benevento, February 9.)

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 782.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, etc.

We recently received complaints from our beloved son J., abbot of Saint Mary of Vertus, concerning certain burdens imposed upon his church. We desire that these be settled with all the more due effectiveness because the church suffers greater poverty and the abbot is less able, because of his lack of strength, to bear the church’s business.

> [Note: Col. 0629D: The Abbey of Blessed Mary of Vertus belongs to the Canons Regular of the Order of Saint Augustine; besides it there is there another abbey of Saint Saviour, of the Order of Saint Benedict.]

For he complains that the priest Man. presumed violently to take from him the church of Alvéziol, granted to the Church of Vertus by B., formerly bishop of Châlons, of good memory; and that, in regard to restoring it, he is said to have resorted to an appeal, yet has taken no care to appear before us either personally or through another.

> [Note: Col. 0630D: Boso.]

He also complains that Eut. of Coulon unjustly holds the tithes of his labours and the annual rent of his house; that R. of Coulon and his brothers hold lands belonging by right to the same church; and that G. of Bergeres presumes to take from it twelve sestarii of grain from a mill near Clamanges and, though often admonished, refuses to restore them.

Since we have great confidence in your discretion, and since the aforesaid abbot greatly needs the protection of the Church, we command you by these letters to summon the above-mentioned men and the representative of the same abbot before you. Having carefully investigated and understood the church’s complaint and the parties’ arguments, impose such a proper settlement upon them that the aforesaid abbot is not compelled longer to suffer through the failure of justice. If they disdain either to appear or to abide by your judgment, compel them by ecclesiastical censure, informing their bishop on our behalf that he is to have the sentence pronounced against them observed until fitting satisfaction is made. Further, because the above-named priest M. is said not to have pursued his appeal, we command that cause, if this proves to be so, to be settled with the appeal set aside.

Given at Benevento, the fifth day before the Ides of February.

DCLXVI. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims—Concerning the tribute due to the Roman Church. (Benevento, February 11.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since many churches situated in your province are tributary to blessed Peter and to us, and neither we nor our predecessors remember receiving from them their due tribute for a long time now elapsed, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, when you are approached by our said beloved son Brother Rostaim, you shall urge the aforesaid churches by letter and messenger and compel them to pay their due tribute to us to the aforesaid R. We have thought it proper to record below the names of the churches: the church of Saint Nicholas of the Isle of Lours owes ten sous of that currency; and many others, whose names we do not have expressly. Concerning them we charge your discretion diligently to admonish and compel those churches to pay the due tribute to us to the aforesaid R., according to the reduction.

Given at Benevento, the third day before the Ides of February.

DCLXVII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims, and Hugh, Bishop of Soissons—For peace between King Louis of France and King Henry of England. (Benevento, February 11.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, and HUGH, Bishop of Soissons: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because our beloved sons W., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, and O., cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have remained for a long time in the lands beyond the mountains, we had no slight hope and confidence that our dearest sons in Christ, Louis and Henry, illustrious kings of the French and English, would through their care and diligence, yours, and that of other religious men, be reconciled and maintain firm peace and concord with one another. But, to our sorrow, we have been disappointed in this hope and desire; and your diligence is by no means unaware how great and continual losses ensue to all Christendom and to the Eastern Church, especially from their discord, since this is evident to everyone.
