Therefore we ask, admonish, and exhort your fraternity in the Lord by apostolic letters: strive with all your strength, through yourselves and other religious men whom you know to be fit for this purpose, to restore peace and concord between them. Work in every possible way, again and again, so that by this means, with the Lord’s cooperation, you may provide a beneficial remedy for the people of both kingdoms, who are treated cruelly enough amid this turmoil; and may thereby receive a worthy reward before God, and no slight praise and glory before humankind. We too shall be bound to commend in many ways in the Lord your care and diligence on this account. Even if once or twice you have suffered rebuff in this matter, we nevertheless do not wish you to desist in any way because of it, but to repeat your efforts more frequently.

Given at Benevento, the third day before the Ides of February.

DCLXVIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims—On behalf of the Count of Soissons concerning wine measures. (Benevento, February 11.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Let your diligence know that we have instructed our beloved sons, the dean and canons of Soissons, either to reach an amicable and peaceful agreement with our beloved son, the noble Count of Soissons, concerning the complaint which they have against him about the wine measures of the city of Soissons, or to have the matter decided before you by judicial process. Therefore we command your fraternity by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and strictly compel the aforesaid dean and canons either to make an amicable settlement with the aforesaid count concerning the case pending between them, or to have the matter judicially determined with him in your presence within forty days after receiving these letters. You, however, are to hear the case carefully and decide it through the administration of justice.

Given at Benevento, the third day before the Ides of February.

DCLXIX. To Girard, Archbishop of Split. (Benevento, February 12.)

[Farlati, *Illyricum sacrum*, III, 189.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GIRARD, Archbishop of Split, legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having learned of your anxieties and concerns, by which you are strongly pressed in preserving the rights of your church, we have been rather surprised at your prudence, because you have begun far too suddenly to raise disputes concerning the bishopric and other matters. A bishop ought, for a year, to see all things as though he did not see them, and in simplicity to overlook what otherwise would have to be pursued more harshly.

Therefore we admonish, counsel, and exhort your prudence to refrain from these matters for the present; strive to learn more fully the condition of the land and the character and customs of its people; and gradually investigate carefully the claims of your Church. When you have been informed on these matters, if any question or doubt arises, report it to us confidently, certain and assured that, in matters in which we can do so with a clear conscience, we shall gladly yield to your fraternity, attend to your rights as to those of our venerable brother, and grant favour and assistance.

Moreover, we earnestly commend to your sincerity S., the bearer of the present letters, who is returning to you. We ask and admonish you that, when you have [lacuna] a suitable opportunity—which, God willing, will be soon—you provide for and treat the aforesaid S. so well that he may be more devoted and faithful to you, and may perceive that our prayers have benefited him with you.

Given at Benevento, the second day before the Ides of February.

DCLXX. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims—On behalf of the clerk Robert. (Benevento, February 18.)

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 784.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the detailed statement of the clerk Robert, bearer of the present letters, we have learned that Hu., formerly archdeacon of your church, had his mother as a slave, but emancipated her for the remedy of his soul and granted that she should remain forever, as a free woman with her heirs, under the lordship of the monastery of Novy. Since the prior of that place, as we have heard, is attempting to reduce her to servitude and to alienate her as a slave into lay control, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters carefully to investigate the truth of the matter. If it is established that the mother of the aforesaid Robert was thus emancipated, do not permit her in any way to be reduced to servitude; but, with every objection and appeal removed, ensure that she remains free with her heirs, just as the aforesaid Hu. is known to have ordained.

Given at Benevento, the twelfth day before the Kalends of March.

DCLXXI. To the Archbishop of Split. (Benevento, February 18.)

[Farlatus, as above, vol. IV, p. 11.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G[ERARD], Archbishop of Split, legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

In the register of our father and predecessor Pope Eugenius, we found recorded that Demetrius, formerly Duke of Dalmatia and Croatia, had offered to the Roman Church, in the time of our predecessor blessed Gregory VII, the monastery of Saint Gregory, called Urana, with all its movable and immovable property. Since a dispute has arisen over the aforesaid monastery between our brother L., Bishop of Skradin, and our beloved sons of the knighthood of the Temple, especially as that bishop maintains that it belongs to him by diocesan right, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters to ensure that the said monastery remains free, as it was offered to blessed Peter and the Roman Church by the aforesaid duke; and on this matter you are by no means to permit the aforesaid brothers henceforth to be harassed by that bishop. We send you, enclosed with the present letters, a transcript of the document which we found in the above-mentioned register.

Given at Benevento, the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, namely in the year 1169.

DCLXXII. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury—That he punish with ecclesiastical severity Owen, prince of Wales, who refused to receive his letters concerning his “female cousin, whom he is said to keep as a wife,” and the Archdeacon of Bangor, who defied his letters. (Benevento, February 24.)

[*Letters of Saint Thomas*, ed. Giles, II, 36.]

ALEXANDER, pope, to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

You are to know that it has come to our ears that Owen, prince of Wales, refused to receive the letters which we sent him concerning his female cousin, whom he is said to keep as a wife, and did not dismiss that same female cousin in accordance with our admonition. The Archdeacon of Bangor also defied our letters and was unwilling in any respect to obey them. Since it pertains to your office to punish their presumption in this matter with ecclesiastical severity—especially since their deeds are better known and more evident to you than to us—we leave to the judgment of your discretion what you deem should be decided in the matter. For we shall hold ratified and firm the sentence which you have canonically pronounced against them for their offences, and we command that it be observed without challenge until fitting satisfaction is made.

Given at Benevento, the sixth day before the Kalends of March.

DCLXXIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims—On behalf of Richard, priest. (Benevento, February 2.)

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 785.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the letters of our venerable brother Hu., Bishop of Soissons, and of religious persons, we have learned that, at the presentation of the prior of Saint Remigius of Brana, with the consent of the Abbot of Saint Evodius, the same bishop instituted Richard, priest, in the church of Algeco and Cersolio, and entrusted to him the care of souls.

> [Note: Col. 0633: The Abbey of Saint Evodius of Brana, of the Premonstratensian Order, is in the diocese of Soissons.]

When this came to the knowledge of Albert, priest, who is said already to have renounced the said chapel before you because of many accusations brought against him by the parishioners of that church, he came into our presence and obtained from us letters of confirmation concerning the same church. On hearing this, Richard lodged a serious complaint against him with the bishop. The bishop summoned him to answer before him to the aforesaid Richard; but he disregarded the bishop’s summons and appealed to your tribunal. When both were brought before your court and he produced our letters before you, you deferred to the letters and suspended the case.

Since letters obtained contrary to justice and by surreption ought to have no validity, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters: if it is lawfully established to you that the aforesaid A. had not been presented to the bishop in the aforesaid chapel, or had renounced that chapel before you; and if the aforesaid Richard subsequently acquired that chapel canonically—unless he later committed something for which he ought by law to lose it—then, with every pretext and appeal set aside, ensure that it is left to him in peace and quiet. Our letters are thus to inflict no prejudice upon him nor procure favour for another.

If the aforesaid A. has violently seized any property of that church, order it restored to Richard. Further, ensure, without delay or appeal, that the benefices which A. received from that church after Richard’s appeal are restored to Richard, and that suitable satisfaction is made for the damages and injuries inflicted—especially if A. did not pursue the appeal made to us by the aforesaid Richard.

Given at Benevento, the fifth day before the Kalends of March.

DCLXXIV. He forbids churches and oratories to be built in the parish of the Church of Prato against the will of the provost. (Benevento, February 25.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, III, 332.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons UBERTO, provost, and the canons of Prato: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of the administration entrusted to us urges and admonishes us to love humble and devoted sons, to grant their just requests with kindly favour, and to bestow our consent. Giving more earnest consideration, therefore, to the devotion which you laudably show toward blessed Peter and ourselves, we grant you by apostolic authority that within the parish of your church no one may, without the consent of you and your successors, build an oratory or church, saving the privileges of the Roman Church. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever, etc.

Given at Benevento, the fifth day before the Kalends of March.

## YEAR 1170

DCLXXV. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Peter at Modena. (Benevento, January 10.)

[Tiraboschi, *Memorie istoriche modenesi*, III, *Proofs*, p. 51.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GEMINIAN, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter situated near Modena, and its brothers, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

A pious request ought to be fulfilled by a favorable result, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth worthily and the requested benefit may undoubtedly obtain its force. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions. Following the example of our father and predecessor of holy memory, Pope Eugenius, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter, to whose service you are bound, and fortify it with the privilege of the present writing. We decree first of all that the monastic order, known to have been established in that monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Further, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. We have thought it proper to specify among them the following in their proper names:

Namely, the land upon which that monastery stands, bounded as follows: on the north, by the Salicitan road as far as the military ditch, and beyond that ditch by the land extending to Cenosa, and by the new ditch running into the said military ditch; on the west, by the stream issuing from the aforesaid ditch and running as far as the Mutinella ditch, and thence to the said Salicitan road; and eight jugera of land beside the military ditch, having the monastery itself to the east and [a second boundary is uncertain in the source], and Saint Geminianus to the south and west; one mill above the city itself called Gajolinum; and below it land with houses and vineyards, bounded thus: a canal to the east, the little court of Saint Madri to the south, the place called Formigine to the west, and below, the land of the hospice which Lanfrancus Galdemanus held; and the other possessions held by the aforesaid monastery around Modena, both within and outside it; and certain mills which it possesses, or other things which could be made for the use of the aforesaid brothers; and whatever right it has in the waters flowing around Modena, especially in the stream called Motinella, which runs between the land of blessed Peter and the land of Peter of Saint Donatus; and, within the city, the church of Saint John the Baptist; and the tithes and burial rights which you have held from ancient times inside and outside the city; the church of Saint Nicholas with the hospital situated near the city; the church of Saint Mary of Massa; the church of Saint Mary of Mugnano; the church of Saint Anastasius of Savignano; the church of Saint Mary of Ambiliano; the church of Saint Geminianus of Curre; the church of Saint Mary near the old castle; the church of Saint Mary of Silva; the church of Saint Michael of Palude; the castle of Adiano, with the churches of Saint Michael and Saint Mary; the little court called Abrica, in its entirety; the church of Aliano; the stronghold called Cornitulum, with the church of Saint Martin; the church of Saint Michael of Sorbitulo; the monastery of Saint Michael of Candiana; the land which you hold in Crespellano and in the court of Pragatali; and whatever else you possess in the bishoprics of Reggio, Ferrara, Verona, and Padua.

> [Note: Col. 0635D: I have not discovered when or by what means the monastery of Candiana in the Paduan territory became subject to that of Saint Peter of Modena. Certainly it had been so at least from the year 1113, when Ponzio, abbot of Modena, granted Peter, abbot of Candiana, investiture of half of that church and its goods, etc. [Col. 0636D] This act is preserved by Signor Abbot Giuseppe Gennari, a most diligent collector of Paduan antiquities, together with another similar investiture granted in 1136 by Placido, abbot of Modena, to George, abbot of Candiana.]

You shall have free authority, without anyone’s objection, to receive into conversion clerics or free and emancipated laypersons living in the secular state. Further, no one whatsoever may presume to demand tithes from you for your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals. When you, the present abbot of the place, or any of your successors dies, no one may be set over the monastery by any trick of surreption or by violence, except the person whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers, shall provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery or take away its possessions, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Hubald, Bishop of Ostia.  
I, Bernard, Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Ildebrand, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles.  
I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina.  
I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains.  
I, Boso, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana, called Pastor.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark.  
I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of Saint Vitalis, of the title of Vestina.  
I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.  
I, Manfred, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.  
I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace near the Temple of Agrippa.  
I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Benevento by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1169, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

DCLXXVI. To Rotrou, Archbishop of Rouen, and Bernard, Bishop of Nevers—That they approach King Henry and exhort him not merely, as he promised through envoys, to restore Thomas of Canterbury fully, but also to “receive him with the kiss of peace.” If the king does not restore Thomas’s seized possessions within forty days, they are to subject his land on this side of the sea to a sentence of interdict. They are to excommunicate those who have inflicted injuries upon Peter, Archdeacon of Pavia. (Benevento, January 19.)

[*Letters of Saint Thomas*, ed. Giles, II, 55.]

ALEXANDER, pope, to ROTROU, Archbishop of Rouen, and BERNARD, Bishop of Nevers.

Our dearest son in Christ, Henry, illustrious King of the English, informed us by letters and messengers that he had granted our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, that, for the love of God and of ourselves and likewise of the Roman Church, he might safely return to his church and peacefully hold and possess it and all his possessions, as he held them before he departed, while he was in the king’s favour; and likewise his own men who had departed with him.

But the said messengers further represented to us that the aforesaid king, having been grievously provoked, had firmly declared that he would by no means receive the aforesaid archbishop with a kiss; nevertheless, his firstborn son would offer the kiss in his stead, for love of God and of us. Master Vivian, too, having returned to our presence, reported to us carefully that, as he had learned at the conference held at Montmartre, the king would grant the said archbishop his favour and affection; would cause him to possess his goods as his predecessor had ever possessed them best; and would also presently grant him one thousand marks for his equipment.

Therefore, placing in every respect full hope and confidence in your prudence, discretion, and integrity, and observing likewise that you are bound to us and to the Roman Church by most sincere devotion, we have decided to send you to the aforesaid king and archbishop for the execution of this peace. Accordingly, we command and enjoin your fraternity by apostolic letters, and impose this upon you by virtue of obedience: after coming together, within one month of receiving these letters, undertake your journey to that king. Diligently and earnestly admonish him on God’s behalf and ours, and strive by every means to persuade him to grant the aforesaid archbishop his peace and security; and, in reverence for the divine majesty, for the honour of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and for his own salvation, receive him with the kiss of peace.

Restore mercifully to the archbishop and all his people all their possessions, as he has ever held them best, as we have learned that the king promised to do through many of our messengers, especially through our beloved son William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, and through the aforesaid Vivian. Cause the archbishop to return safely to his church and remain there in peace. Exhort the archbishop earnestly on our behalf to accept that peace, and urge him insistently to humble himself toward the king as far as he can without prejudice to the liberty of the Church and without danger to himself or his people.

Nevertheless, if the king cannot be induced to pay the thousand marks of which we have spoken above, we do not wish peace to be hindered on that account in any way, provided that the king is willing to fulfill the other terms. But if, within forty days after our admonition, he is unwilling to carry out what he promised us—especially the complete restoration of the possessions taken away—and also what we have signified to him concerning the kiss, unless perhaps the archbishop [Col. 0638D] is willing to be content with the kiss of the son, you shall subject all his lands on this side of the sea to a sentence of interdict by the authority of blessed Peter and ourselves, all contradiction and appeal being set aside; and therein you shall forbid the celebration of every divine office except the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying—unless you are altogether certain that the often-mentioned King Henry will fulfill these things shortly after the forty days have elapsed, or that the archbishop is willing to accept the kiss of the son in place of his own.

But if peace is concluded through the Lord’s cooperation, you shall approach the same king not immediately upon the making of peace, but after a short interval, to be determined by your discretion; and on God’s behalf and by your admonition [Col. 0639A] you shall impose upon him, for the remission of his sins, that he utterly abolish and condemn the evil customs—especially those newly introduced by himself—which are contrary to his salvation and to the liberty of the Church; that he release bishops and the other persons of the realm from observing them; and that he restore to the archbishop and his people the proceeds of revenues received. If he does not comply with your admonition in this matter, you shall inform us by letter, as fully and swiftly as possible, together with the archbishop himself, what of those customs ought to be abolished, and what the king is willing to do concerning restitution of the proceeds received. But if you conceive a certain hope that peace and reconciliation will be made, absolve all those excommunicated persons [Col. 0639B] who ought to be absolved, on the condition that, unless peace follows, you immediately restore them to their former excommunication, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal.

Moreover, if the king can by no means be induced to grant the kiss, endeavor to induce the archbishop, if he recognizes that this can be done without danger to his own person and his followers and can find it advisable in counsel, to be content with the kiss of the son. If either of you cannot or will not be present to carry these matters out—which we do not believe—the other shall nevertheless not delay in carrying out the aforesaid measures.

Furthermore, we command you sternly to rebuke the aforesaid king because certain of his men, at his instigation, as is said, and by his command, seized and dishonorably mistreated our beloved son Peter, archdeacon of Pavia, who had been sent to him by our beloved son Gratian, subdeacon and notary, and Master Vivian; [Col. 0639C] they also deprived him of certain belongings. Those whom it is established laid violent hands upon that same Peter and his clerical companions, you shall publicly declare excommunicated, all appeal being set aside; and you shall command all to avoid them as excommunicated persons until they restore what was taken, make fitting satisfaction to those injured, and come to us, with your letters, to make satisfaction. You shall also carefully impress upon the king that the said Gratian could not, consistently with our command, have done anything other than what he did. Had he attempted otherwise, we would without doubt have annulled it [Col. 0639D]. If anyone has suggested to the king that he or his companion might have acted otherwise in accordance with our command, he has by no means told him the truth.

Given at Benevento, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February [19 January].

### DCLXXVII. To Rotrod, Archbishop of Rouen.—That he should vigorously administer the legation to Henry, king of the English.  
*(Benevento, January?)*

*[Ibid., p. 54.]*

ALEXANDER, pope, to ROTROD, Archbishop of Rouen.

Because, above your fellow bishops and other ecclesiastical persons living in the land [Col. 0640A] of the illustrious king of the English, we have special confidence in your person, and know you to be bound to us and to the Roman Church by most sincere devotion, we have entrusted to you the task of carrying out the affair of the peace and reconciliation of our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and, in virtue of obedience, enjoin upon your brotherhood that, in the aforesaid affair, setting aside all fear and doubt, you show yourself so steadfast and diligent that the aforesaid king may find in you episcopal maturity and constancy, and may recognize that you revere God and the duty of your office more than any human being. Thus neither may we be disappointed in the hope which we long ago conceived, and have often [Col. 0640B] experienced, concerning your person; nor may we have reason deservedly to regret that we selected you in particular, above the other persons known to be in the land of the said king, for the execution of this affair. Rather, we should be bound on this account to commend your solicitude and diligence in many ways.

### DCLXXVIII. To Bernard, Bishop of Nevers.—Concerning the legation entrusted to him and the Archbishop of Rouen by apostolic letters (Epistle 676).  
*(Benevento, January?)*

*[Ibid., p. 103.]*

ALEXANDER, pope, to BERNARD, Bishop of Nevers.

Because we have conceived complete confidence in your prudence, integrity, and steadfastness, and have had certain experience of these qualities in many matters, we have decided to associate you with the Archbishop of Rouen in carrying out the peace of our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. We have appointed him as your fellow executor because he is known to be from the land of the illustrious king of the English, lest that king should seem to have any occasion to complain against us on the ground that we had entrusted the affair to persons foreign to, and living outside, his land.

And because, as we have said, we know you to be a man of episcopal maturity and constancy, distinguished among your fellow bishops in integrity and learning, we command and, in virtue [Col. 0640D] of obedience, enjoin upon your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid Archbishop of Rouen should be unwilling or unable to proceed with you in the matters which we enjoin upon you, you shall proceed without delay in the aforesaid business, setting aside all fear and doubt, according to the tenor of our letters. Show yourself herein so careful and diligent that you may deserve to receive from God a worthy reward, and may win no small praise and glory among humankind; and that we may be bound to commend your diligence in many ways and may be able, as we desire, more fully to prove in this matter the devotion and constancy which we have experienced in you in other matters.

### DCLXXIX. To Henry, King of the English.—He commends to him Rotrod and Bernard, his legates, on behalf of Thomas of Canterbury.  
*(Benevento, January?)*

*[Ibid., p. 131.]*

[Col. 0641A]

ALEXANDER, pope, to HENRY, King of England.

Our beloved sons John, dean of Salisbury, Giles of Rouen, and John of Séez, archdeacons, your envoys, appearing before us brought letters from your royal highness. From their tenor we learned that, regarding the matters which they should state to us on your behalf, we ought to believe them as though they were you yourself. Together with Reginald, archdeacon of Salisbury, they indeed laid certain matters earnestly and carefully before us in the presence of ourselves and our brethren, to which we considered that we could not in any respect consent, as indeed we ought not to have consented.

At length, when—as was unfitting—we were in no way inclined to heed what had first been intimated to us, they carefully set before us that you had granted, as we saw in the written memorandum, to our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, that, for the love of God, of ourselves, and of the Roman Church, he should return safely to his church and should peacefully hold and possess it and all his possessions as he had held them before he departed, while he was in your favor; and likewise his followers who departed on his account. This [Col. 0641C] we hold most welcome and altogether acceptable, hoping in Christ’s mercy that he who has begun this will bring it to a better conclusion and will move you to complete what remains lacking. Therefore we ascribe this to the immense and overflowing mercy of him from whom all good things proceed, and render manifold thanksgivings to your generosity on this account.

When, however, we questioned the aforesaid envoys closely concerning the form of the security, and especially concerning the granting of the kiss, they answered us that, having been grievously provoked, you had declared that you would by no means receive the aforesaid archbishop with the kiss of peace; yet your firstborn son, on your behalf, would offer him the kiss for the love of God and of ourselves. Accordingly, because one of our envoys—Master Vivian—on his return to our presence carefully informed us that, as he had understood at the conference held at Montmartre, you would grant favor and affection to the aforementioned archbishop and would cause him to possess his lands as his predecessor had ever possessed them to better advantage, and would also presently grant him a thousand marks for his equipment, we, placing complete trust in the clemency of your royal highness, considered that we should address our prayers and exhortations to your excellency concerning the granting of the kiss, even though your aforementioned envoys resisted more than was proper.

And because it accords with royal dignity and honor, and is known greatly to conduce to your salvation, that you bring to the desired and God-pleasing fulfillment what has been divinely inspired in your heart concerning these matters—so that you may deserve to receive from him a full and perfect reward—we ask, warn, and exhort your serenity in the Lord by apostolic letters. Further, absolving you altogether by the authority of blessed Peter and ourselves from the binding of an oath, if at any time you made one while carried away by the heat of anger, we enjoin upon you, for the remission of sins, that, out of reverence for the divine majesty, regard for blessed Peter and ourselves, and for your own salvation and honor, you receive the aforesaid archbishop with the kiss of peace; graciously restore to him your peace and security and all his possessions, as he ever held them to best advantage; and thus heed us in this matter—or rather, God within us—who will grant you an everlasting reward in heaven for this and, bestowing abundant praise and glory on earth, will make you and your heirs co-heirs with his own. [Col. 0642B]

If any more important matters are being negotiated between you through our dearest son in Christ Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, through our venerable brethren the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Soissons, or through others; or if you have since promised anything more acceptable to the aforesaid archbishop, fulfill and carry it out more fully and carefully for the remission of your sins.

For we are sending the said Archbishop of Rouen and our venerable brother Bernard, Bishop of Nevers, to your presence for the execution of the aforesaid peace. Through them we make known to you our will and what we know greatly conduces to royal salvation and honor, earnestly asking and warning your highness that, if anything must be added or changed, you correct and amend it at their admonition for the love of God and of ourselves. Hear what they lay before you on our behalf and, giving a kindly hearing, deign to fulfill it so effectively that the almighty and merciful Lord may grant true peace to you and your heirs, royal honor may thereby be increased in many ways, and you may obtain from God an unfailing reward, and no small praise and glory in the sight of humankind. [Col. 0642D]

The aforesaid archbishop and bishop, if they conceive certain hope of peace and reconciliation, shall absolve those excommunicated persons who ought to be absolved, provided that, if peace follows through the Lord’s working, they incur no peril to their honor, rank, or office, nor any mark of infamy, because they had been excommunicated. On our behalf they shall induce the archbishop to accept peace; and if he alleges any just fear in some respect, they must diligently admonish you to remove it and must in many ways urge you, on God’s behalf and ours, to fulfill what we make known to you through ourselves.

But if peace does not follow—may God avert it—and those who state that they have appealed choose to pursue their appeal, we shall carefully hear their arguments in the matter and, once the case is known, judge as God may grant us to do. Let them pursue their appeal in the next octave of Saint Michael, or at the next feast of Saint Luke, provided that this postponement shall not in any respect prejudice the justice of either party. [Col. 0643A]

### DCLXXX. To Gilbert, Bishop of London.—He states that he has ordered the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Exeter [or Nevers?] to absolve him from the sentence of excommunication pronounced against him by Thomas of Canterbury.  
*(Benevento, 12 February.)*

*[Ibid., p. 93.]*

[Col. 0643B]

The fact that we do not at present bestow upon you the greeting of apostolic blessing must be ascribed not to our harshness but rather to the merits of your case. For, since we have heard that your metropolitan pronounced sentence against you, it would be wholly unworthy and altogether foreign to the propriety of our office for us to greet you in our letters.

This is indeed most grievous and altogether distressing to us, because we embrace you, as our venerable brother and as a man whom we know to excel in no small degree in religious devotion, learning, and integrity, with the closer arms of charity in the Lord. In all matters, so far as we can with God and justice, we wish readily to show you deference and more willingly to display honor and favor toward you.

But, in order that you may experience our disposition toward you through sure evidences of action, and may know that we have withheld our blessing from you not by choice but rather from necessity, we have instructed our venerable brethren the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Exeter that, upon receiving from you an oath that you will obey our command concerning those matters for which sentence has been pronounced against you, they shall absolve you in our stead—if, having lost confidence in the appeal which you say you made, you prefer to be absolved, as we believe is more expedient for you than pursuing your appeal. But if you choose to pursue the appeal, we shall gladly receive your person, carefully hear your arguments, and, once we have examined the matter, judge as the Lord grants us to do. [Col. 0643D]

If you wish to be absolved by the aforesaid archbishop and bishop, they shall absolve you by our authority, on the condition that, because you had been excommunicated, you incur no danger to your rank, office, or dignity, nor any mark of infamy. But if both cannot be present to carry this out, the other shall nevertheless do so as stated; and he shall command, and in virtue of obedience enjoin, our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, on our behalf, to keep your absolution concealed and entirely secret until it can be made public without danger to you.

And since our beloved son Master David, canon of your church—a learned, prudent, and discerning man, and also most faithful to you—has earnestly pressed your case before us and our brethren, both privately and publicly, and has taken care to apply to its execution all the diligence and effort he could, and even more than he was bound to apply, we earnestly ask and warn your discretion by apostolic letters that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, and in consideration of his own service in having proved so faithful and devoted to you, you hold him in more particular favor. Do not believe malicious suggestions against him or distrust his fidelity in any respect; rather, reward his service in such a way that he may be bound always to remain faithful and devoted to you and yours, while we, holding this welcome and acceptable, [Col. 0644B] are bound to render manifold thanks to your affection on that account.

Given at Benevento, on the second day before the Ides of February [12 February].

### DCLXXXI. To Rotrod, Archbishop of Rouen, and Bernard, Bishop of Nevers.—That they should absolve Gilbert, Bishop of London.  
*(Benevento, February?)*

*[Ibid., p. 62.]*

ALEXANDER, pope, to ROTROD, Archbishop of Rouen, and BERNARD, Bishop of Nevers.

Let your discretion know that we have informed Gilbert, Bishop of London, by our letters that, if he wishes to be absolved from the sentence pronounced against him by our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, he is to come into the presence of yourselves—or of one of you, if both cannot be present—and, after taking an oath that he will obey our command, receive absolution from you.

Therefore, wishing to show him deference in all matters, so far as we can with God and justice, as a religious, learned, prudent, and discerning man, and moved by the petition of our beloved son Master David, canon of the Church of London, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the said bishop comes to you to receive absolution, you shall absolve him, after receiving from him an oath that he will obey our command concerning the aforesaid sentence, with the remedy of appeal removed. This is on the condition that he shall suffer no peril to dignity, rank, or office, nor incur any mark of infamy on that account. [Col. 0644D]

Once the absolution has been performed, inform the aforesaid archbishop of it by your letters, and firmly command him on our behalf, and enjoin him in virtue of obedience, to keep that absolution hidden and altogether secret until it can be made public without danger to the bishop himself. If both of you cannot be present to carry this out, the other shall nevertheless carry it out as we have said. Farewell.

### DCLXXXII. To the Bishops of Kent.—That they should ensure observance of a sentence of interdict if the legates Rotrod and Bernard pronounce it “over all the land of King Henry which lies on this side of the sea.”  
*(Benevento, 18 February.)*

*[Ibid., p. 42.]*

[Col. 0645A]

ALEXANDER, pope, to all the bishops of Kent.

Let your diligence know that we have sent our venerable brethren, the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Nevers, to the king of the English for the peace and reconciliation of our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. We have instructed and firmly commanded them that, unless the king can be induced by their admonition to peace and concord according to what he promised us through his letters and envoys, they shall subject all his land lying on this side of the sea [Col. 0645B] to an interdict, all contradiction and appeal being set aside, and shall forbid there the celebration of every divine office except the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command, direct, and enjoin you, under penalty affecting rank and office and in virtue of obedience, that you firmly observe throughout your dioceses, all excuse and appeal being set aside and notwithstanding any fear, favor, or prohibition, whatever sentence in this matter may be pronounced by the aforesaid archbishop or bishop, or by one of them if both cannot or will not be present; and that you cause it to be inviolably observed by all, so far as lies in your power.

[Col. 0645C]

Given at Benevento, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March [18 February].

### DCLXXXIII. To Roger, Archbishop of York, Legate of the Apostolic See, Hugh, Bishop of Durham, etc.—On the same matter.  
*(Benevento, 18 February.)*

*[Ibid., p. 47.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren ROGER, Archbishop of York and legate of the Apostolic See; HUGH, Bishop of Durham; and his beloved sons, the prelates of churches established throughout the archbishopric of York.

Let your diligence know that we have sent our venerable brethren Rotrod, Archbishop of Rouen, and Bernard, Bishop of Nevers, to the illustrious king of the English for the peace and reconciliation of our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. We have instructed and firmly commanded them that, unless the same king can be induced by their admonition to peace and concord in accordance with what he promised us through his letters and envoys, they shall subject all his land situated in the kingdom of the Franks to an interdict, all contradiction and appeal being set aside; and there they shall forbid the celebration of every divine office except the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and enjoin you, under penalty affecting rank and office and in virtue of obedience, that, notwithstanding any fear, favor, or prohibition, you firmly observe throughout your dioceses, all excuse and appeal being set aside, the sentence which the aforesaid Archbishop of Canterbury may pronounce upon his province for this reason, and cause it to be inviolably observed by all so far as lies in your power. [Col. 0646A]

Given at Benevento, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March [18 February].

In the same form he writes to all archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches established throughout the land on this side of the sea of the illustrious king of the English: “Let your diligence know,” etc.

### DCLXXXIV. To Joscius, Archbishop of Tours, and his suffragans.—On the same matter.  
*(Benevento, February?)*

*[Ibid., p. 73.]*

[Col. 0646B]

ALEXANDER, pope, to the Bishop of Tours and his suffragans, and also to his beloved sons, the prelates of other churches established in the Church of Tours.

Let your diligence know that we have sent our venerable brethren, the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Nevers, to the illustrious king of the English for the peace and reconciliation of our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. We have instructed and firmly commanded them that, unless the same king can be induced to peace and concord, in accordance with what he promised us through his letters and envoys, [Col. 0646C] or unless, by some artifice or device, whether personally or through his agents, he causes them to be unable to approach him according to our command and to set before him in complete freedom and security the matters which we have enjoined upon him concerning these things, they shall subject all his land situated in the kingdom of the Franks to an interdict, all contradiction and appeal being set aside. Therein they shall forbid the celebration of every divine office except the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and, in virtue of obedience, enjoin upon you under penalty affecting rank and office that you firmly observe throughout your dioceses, notwithstanding any fear, favor, or prohibition and with every excuse and appeal removed, whatever sentence the aforesaid archbishop and bishop, or either of them, may pronounce upon the land of the aforesaid king in accordance with our command; and that you cause it to be inviolably observed by all, so far as lies in your power. [Col. 0646D]

### DCLXXXV–DCLXXXVIII.

In the same form, to the Archbishop of Bourges and his suffragans, and also to the other prelates of churches.

In the same form, to the Archbishop of Bordeaux, legate of the Apostolic See, and his suffragans.

In the same form, to the Archbishop of Auch and his suffragans.

In the same form, to all bishops and other prelates of churches established throughout the province of Rouen. [Col. 0647A]

### DCLXXXIX. To Rotrod, Archbishop of Rouen, and Bernard, Bishop of Nevers.—He states that it has been reported to him that King Henry has crossed into England. He commands them to hasten to him within twenty days and carry out the instructions given in the earlier letters.  
*(Benevento, February?)*

*[Ibid., p. 59.]*

ALEXANDER, pope, to the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Nevers.

Because we have complete hope and confidence in every respect in the ardor of your devotion and sincerity, and also in your discernment, maturity, and prudence, we selected you, above the other persons of the kingdom of the Franks, to carry out the peace of our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. As we informed you by other letters, we therefore sent you to our dearest son in Christ, Henry, illustrious king of the English.

Since we have afterward heard that the same king has crossed the sea into England, and lest the affair of the aforesaid archbishop be hindered or delayed in any way because of this, we command and, in virtue of obedience, enjoin upon your brotherhood by repeated letters that, as you value the favor of blessed Peter and ourselves, and wish that we and the Roman Church should henceforth have some ground to trust in your integrity and constancy, you shall, laying aside every excuse, assemble together and set out to go to the said king within twenty days after receiving these letters—unless perhaps you have already done so—and make haste to him. [Col. 0647C]

When you have come into his presence, you yourselves shall urgently set before him the matters which we specified in our other letters, as befits men of episcopal constancy, with every doubt and fear removed; and on our behalf you shall strive by every means to induce him to carry them out. If the king does not, within forty days after your admonition, fulfill what he promised us—especially the complete restoration of the possessions taken away, the restoration of full peace to the archbishop and his followers, and the granting of the kiss to him, unless perhaps he is willing to be content with the kiss of the son—or if by some artifice or device, personally or through his agents, he makes it impossible for you to approach him according to our command and set before him in complete freedom and security the matters entrusted to your solicitude concerning these points, then by the authority of blessed Peter and ourselves, all contradiction and appeal being set aside, pronounce a sentence of interdict over all his lands on this side of the sea. There you shall forbid the celebration of every divine office except the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying, as was expressly set forth in the other letters which we sent you on this matter. [Col. 0648A]

You shall also send, without any excuse, our letters concerning the observance of the interdict, which we are transmitting to the archbishops and bishops of his land lying on this side of the sea; and on our behalf firmly enjoin upon them that they keep our interdict inviolably throughout their dioceses, notwithstanding any fear, prohibition, or appeal, and that they do not presume to act against it in any way. If any archbishop, bishop, or other person whatever scorns to observe your interdict, suspend him from the exercise of his office, setting aside the remedy of appeal. If he does not even then come to his senses, pronounce a sentence of excommunication against him.

In addition to the matters stated above, you shall set before the aforesaid king, verbally or by your letters, most firmly: that if he does not even then come to his senses, we shall by no means spare his person, as neither did we spare Frederick, the so-called emperor, but shall without doubt pronounce a sentence of excommunication against him. We wish, moreover, and strictly enjoin upon you under the consideration of God’s favor and ours, that you apply all fitting and necessary diligence and effort in carrying out what we have said. If either of you cannot or will not be present—which we do not believe, and which would be neither fitting nor tolerable—the other shall nevertheless carry out the aforesaid measures, all doubt and fear being removed. [Col. 0648B]

### DCXC. To the same persons.—He prescribes to whom, among those excommunicated by Thomas of Canterbury, they should restore communion and to whom they should deny it.  
*(Benevento, February?)*

*[Ibid., p. 61.]*

[Col. 0648C]

Because we recall that, in our other letters which we sent you concerning the affair of our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, we gave your discretion an express command concerning his excommunicated persons: that, once a certain hope of peace had been conceived, you ought to absolve them, we command and direct your brotherhood by repeated letters that, if they are absolved by you, you shall absolve them according to the form and custom of the Roman Church.

But to those who have held, or still hold, the possessions of the aforesaid archbishop or of the church committed to him, or the benefices of his clerics; who have also received, or still receive, their proceeds; and especially to Geoffrey, Archdeacon of Canterbury, if it is established that he has taken and holds the church of Otford from a lay hand, as we have heard, grant the benefit of absolution on no account unless they first provide sufficient security that they will restore without delay to the said archbishop the benefices which they hold and will pay over, without deduction, the proceeds received therefrom. If, after providing security and receiving absolution, they refuse to fulfill this, restore them to their former sentence of excommunication, setting aside every excuse and appeal; and by our authority cause all to avoid them as excommunicated persons until due satisfaction has been made. [Col. 0649A]

### DCXCI. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—That he should use the counsel of Rotrod, Archbishop of Rouen, William, Archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See, and Bernard, Bishop of Nevers.  
*(Benevento, February?)*

*[Ibid., p. 27.]*

ALEXANDER, pope, to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

We recall that through our venerable brother the Archbishop of Sens, legate of the Apostolic See, and through our other letters, we informed your discretion that the illustrious king of the English had sent us envoys and written copies concerning your peace. We have sent our letters to our venerable brethren the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Nevers concerning the execution of that peace, as the said Archbishop of Sens may more fully recount to your prudence in person.

Since your beloved sons Alexander and John, your envoys, wished to remain for some of your business after the departure of the aforesaid archbishop, we considered that we should communicate our will and counsel to you more privately and swiftly through that archbishop. By apostolic letters we earnestly ask and warn your brotherhood [Col. 0649C] that, as we have informed you by other letters, you comply with the counsel and admonition of the aforesaid Archbishops of Sens and Rouen and of the Bishop of Nevers.

### DCXCII. Privilege for the Church of Saint Mary of Viborg.  
*(Benevento, 21 February.)*

*[THORKELIN, Diplomatarium Arna-Magnæanum, I, 24.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons SUENO, provost of the Church of Saint Mary of Viborg, and his brethren, both present and future, forever.

A pious request ought to be fulfilled by an effective outcome, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth worthily and the benefit requested may undoubtedly gain force. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Innocent of pious memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of Saint Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, we establish that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, the Lord granting it, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offering of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

We confirm to your devotion by apostolic authority the Church of Blessed Margaret the Virgin, which our venerable brother Nicholas, your bishop, as we have learned from his letters, resigned to you; and also the Church of Saint Martin, which is on the island of Fur, so that henceforth each of those churches shall remain under your governance and administration.

Concerning also the Lenten sustenance which the bishop formerly had at times in your church, and on account of which your religious community has customarily been disturbed by no small disputes, we decree that, just as the aforesaid bishop is known to have resigned it to you by his privilege with equitable consideration [Col. 0650B] and thereafter remitted it, so it shall henceforth be maintained, and neither he nor his successor may at any time demand sustenance from you contrary to this. Moreover, we forbid the bishop to receive from the offerings made at the bodies of the saints in your church anything beyond the fourth part which he has customarily received. Furthermore, by the tenor of the present letters we grant you that no one may unjustly presume to seize or retain, contrary to your disposition, the estates or possessions of your church, whether situated within or outside your city. In the election of your bishop, moreover, since you are canons of the cathedral church, you shall have the first voice, as is known to belong to you by the law of the canons and by ancient custom observed down to [Col. 0650C] these times; nor shall anyone from elsewhere be chosen as your bishop so long as a suitable person is found in your cathedral church who may, according to the statutes of the canons, be selected with the canonical and unanimous consent, without any impropriety. Let no perverse person dare to alter for the worse the cloister customs which are known to have been laudably maintained hitherto in this your place; rather, let them always endure unshaken in their strength.

Adding these provisions, we decree that no prince whatsoever may, without the consent of the provost and brethren, introduce anyone into the cloister or into the newly cleared lands. We also grant that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will [Col. 0650D] of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, the rights nevertheless being preserved of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Further, upon the death of you, the present provost of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of intrigue or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall, according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine, determine ought to be elected.

Therefore we decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of your bishop. If, therefore, anyone in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. [Col. 0651A] I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius. I, Hildebrand, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, cardinal priest of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, Boso, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana, of the Shepherd. [Col. 0651B] I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Vitalis, of Vestina. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Manfred, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Agro.

Given at Benevento, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0651C] 1169, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### DCXCIII. To Waldemar, King of the Danes.—On behalf of the brethren of Calve. (Benevento, February?)

[LANGEBEK, *Script. Dan.*, V, 246.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, WALDEMAR, illustrious king of the Danes, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Let your Excellency know that we have instructed our venerable brethren, Sueno, bishop of Aarhus, and Nicholas, bishop of Viborg, diligently and earnestly to admonish the noblewoman Margaret to restore without delay, and to leave in peace, to our beloved sons Briennus, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Saint Mary of Calve, the land of Culsne, which she is said to have taken from them by force; and likewise her ornaments in the church of Weng, which, as we have heard, she presumed to seize and carry away by armed hand. Otherwise, under examination by the aforesaid bishops, she is not to delay, all appeal set aside, in rendering sufficient justice concerning these matters to the said abbot and brethren. Therefore, since He through whom kings reign (Prov. 8) granted your Highness the sword for the punishment of evildoers [Col. 0652A] and the praise of the good (1 Pet. 2), by apostolic letters we ask, warn, and exhort Your Serenity in the Lord: if the aforesaid woman, setting aside the fear of God, should refuse to be constrained by ecclesiastical censure to do the things set forth above, let royal majesty, by the power committed to it by the Lord, compel her to restore what she has taken or, in accordance with our mandate, to render justice before the above-named bishops. Thus the aforementioned abbot and brethren may recover their right through you, and we may have occasion to commend your magnificence in the Lord in many ways. But if the above-mentioned possession should at any time have passed to another, who has presumed to deny his justice to the often-mentioned abbot and brethren, let your Excellency restrain its holder from such presumption and, by royal power, compel him to render the monastery its due justice.  

[Note: [Col. 0651D] Abbot Briennus was at Rome in November 1169, and perhaps until the spring of 1170, together with Stephen, archbishop of Uppsala. Hence one may conclude [Col. 0652D] that this diploma was issued at the beginning of 1170.]

### DCXCIV. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—What is to be required of King Henry before his son’s coronation. (Benevento, February 24.)

[*Epistolae S. Thomae*, ed. GILES, II, 26.]

ALEXANDER, pope, to THOMAS, archbishop of Canterbury, and to all the bishops of England.

By the obligation of the office entrusted to us, our concern is bound to preserve the churches of God and their rights, and to apply care and diligence lest they be oppressed or destroyed by anyone. Moved by this consideration, and wishing to preserve to the Church of Canterbury its dignity and right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, and moreover enjoin you by virtue of obedience, that if Henry, the illustrious king of the English, wishes his son to be crowned and anointed king, you, brother of Canterbury—to whose office, we have heard, this belongs by the ancient dignity of your church—shall by no means lay hands upon him, nor permit anyone else to do so, unless he first takes the oath which his predecessor kings have customarily rendered to the Church of God and especially to Canterbury; [Col. 0652D] and unless he wholly absolves everyone from observance of his customs and from those oaths which were last extorted from the men of England.

And to you, brother bishops, we strictly prohibit by apostolic authority that you presume in any way to attend that coronation unless he has taken the oath. Rather, you are to absent yourselves and depart from it with all speed, notwithstanding any contradiction or prohibition whatsoever.

### DCXCV. To Roger of York, Hugh of Durham, and all the bishops of England.—That they must not presume to crown the king’s son when this is due to Canterbury. (At Cerumar [or: at Cisrinarium], February 26.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, I, 25.]

[Col. 0653A]

ALEXANDER, pope, to ROGER of York, HUGH of Durham, and all the bishops of England.

Since it has long since come to our hearing through the report of many that the coronation and anointing of the kings of England belongs, by the ancient custom and dignity of his church, to the archbishop of Canterbury, we strictly forbid your brotherhood by the present letters, under apostolic authority, that if the illustrious king of the English wishes his son to be crowned and anointed king while our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, is in exile, [Col. 0653B] none of you may presume to lay hands upon him or dare to involve himself in this matter in any way. If any of you should presume to attempt this, let him know that it will undoubtedly redound gravely to the peril of his office and order. In these matters we wish the remedy of appeal to be denied to all, and every occasion of malicious obstruction excluded.

Given at Cerumar, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March.

### DCXCVI. To Roger, Archbishop of York, and all the bishops of England.—That they must not presume to injure the rights of the Church of Canterbury.

[*Epistolae S. Thomae*, ed. GILES, II, 46.]

[Col. 0653C]

ALEXANDER, pope, to ROGER, archbishop of York, and to all the bishops of England.

Your brotherhood can know from certain indications what a prerogative of authority and dignity has adorned the Church of Canterbury from ancient times, and how we wish, in accordance with the duty of our office, to preserve for it its dignities and rights. Wherefore, by apostolic letters we command you—and in commanding, direct you—that you never attempt in any manner to do anything against the authority and dignity of that church, nor presume with rash daring to proceed against it. If you do so, [Col. 0653D] it will be grievous to us, nor shall we be able to endure it with equanimity.

### DCXCVII. To . . . . .—On behalf of Haideric, whose nephew had been struck by an arrow. (At Saint-Germain, March 5.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 821.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, etc.

From the bearer of the present letters it has come to the hearing of the Apostolic See that, while his ten-year-old son was shooting arrows with other boys, a nephew of that same Haideric was struck by an arrow and died. The said son is reported to have done this by accident while playing among the other boys, though the matter is uncertain. But because, as he himself informed us, you were insistently demanding from him one hundred solidi on behalf of the aforesaid Haideric, according to the custom of that land, he appealed to our hearing. Therefore, since what is customarily left unpunished in children the laws of men decree to be corrected more severely in men of mature age, we command your affection by apostolic letters either to desist from his prosecution or, when summoned by him, to appear before the bishop of Noyon, firmly to accept and observe, all appeal set aside, whatever that bishop shall decide concerning the matter.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the third day before the Nones of May [read: March].

### DCXCVIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of the priest Baldwin. (At Saint-Germain, March 7.)

[Ibid., col. 820.]

[Col. 0654B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We have received the complaint of Baldwin, priest of the church of Saint Martin, who came into our presence: Harduin, your parishioner, and his son, with wicked daring laid violent hands upon him and presumed to drag him by the hair and beat him. B., moreover, the brother of the aforesaid Harduin, and B.’s son, as the priest himself asserts, provided them assistance in committing so great a crime and were likewise associates and accomplices in this wrongdoing. Therefore, because pontifical authority ought not to be negligent or lax in punishing the misdeeds of the wicked, we, although unworthy, preside over the Apostolic See and do not wish to leave the offense of such grave temerity in any degree unpunished, as we ought not. By apostolic letters we command your brotherhood diligently to investigate the truth of the matter and, all appeal set aside, publicly declare excommunicated all whom you ascertain to have laid violent hands upon the aforesaid priest; and cause them to be cautiously shunned by all as excommunicated persons [Col. 0654D] until they make suitable satisfaction to the injured party and present themselves before us with your letters.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the Nones of March.

### DCXCIX. To the same.—That he cause A., the bearer of the present letters, to have restored to him his church, seized by others. (At Saint-Germain, March 7.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

From the complaint of A., bearer of the present letters, we have learned that when T., formerly abbot of Dervensis, had long ago lawfully given him a certain church, [Col. 0655A] the priests G. and Hu. presumed to take it from him and still hold it thus seized. Therefore, because we recognize ourselves to be debtors to every person in respect of his right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to admonish the aforesaid G. and Hu. and strictly to compel them either to restore without delay the said church to the aforementioned A. and allow him to hold it in peace, or, before you, without appeal, not delay in rendering to him whatever the form of law shall prescribe in this matter.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the Nones of March.

### DCC. He directs B., dean, and the chapter of Saint Martin of Tours firmly to observe “everything which William, archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See, and Stephen, bishop of Meaux, shall determine concerning the revenues and provostships of the chapter”; and he enjoins them that “henceforth the procession of the Purification of Blessed Mary shall be celebrated forever, with the return of the candles, as is customary.” (At Saint-Germain, March 10.)

[*Recueil sur Saint-Martin de Tours*, documentary appendices, p. 21.]

[Col. 0655B]

### DCCI. He commands certain persons to judge between Gerard and Ar., who are litigating over an inheritance. (Verberie, March 18.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 822.]

We have received the complaint of Gerard, bearer of the present letters, who came to the clemency of the Apostolic See not without much labor: a certain kinsman of himself and Ar., named Manger, died without children and bestowed his land as alms upon them; thereafter the said Ar. began to inflict much trouble and injury upon him concerning this. Therefore each party appealed to our hearing. But when the aforesaid Gerard, as we have said, came into our presence, because the opposing party neither came nor sent a representative, we could not bring the matter to its due conclusion. We therefore commit it to your experience to be heard and decided by the means of justice. Wherefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion, after summoning both parties before you, to hear more carefully the case pending between them and [Col. 0655D] to decide it, with the remedy of appeal removed and the order of law observed.

Given at Verberie, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### DCCII. To the same.—That he refrain from vexing his suffragans, especially Bartholomew, bishop of Beauvais. (Verberie, March 18.)

[Ibid., col. 823.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Just as you desire that the rights of the church entrusted to you by your predecessors be kept whole and inviolate in your hands, so it befits your diligence to leave unimpaired and preserve uninjured the rights belonging to the churches and persons subject to you. We remember having already commanded your discretion in other letters that you claim nothing for yourself in the bishoprics of your suffragans, and especially of our venerable brother B., bishop of Beauvais, contrary to the form of the canons and beyond ancient and reasonable custom. Therefore, since it is unworthy that you should unjustly burden your subjects or occupy their rights with insufficient reason, by repeated letters we command and direct your brotherhood that you inflict no burden upon your suffragans, and especially upon the aforesaid bishop of Beauvais, contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers or beyond the ancient and reasonable custom of your predecessors; [Col. 0656B] that you do not presume, without consulting them, to determine or judge anything concerning the clerics or churches of their bishoprics, unless perhaps a cause has been brought before you by appeal; and that you demand from them nothing which they do not owe you by right. We also prohibit you in every way from burdening the person of the aforesaid bishop of Beauvais without the judgment of his fellow bishops. If you have anything against him, let it be decided according to the form of the sacred canons by the judgment of the bishops of the same province.

Given at Verberie, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### DCCIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of the brother of the priest Walter, and on behalf of Walter himself, that he may treat them kindly. (Verberie, March 19.)

[Ibid., col. 822.]

[Col. 0656C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of the men of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

From the report transmitted to us by Walter, a priest, we have learned that, at the beginning of this disturbance, he could not remain in the bishopric of Toul, where he was born, because of the malice of the schismatics; he therefore came into the region of Rheims with his mother, brother, and sister, and has hitherto conducted himself there quite commendably.  

[Note: [Col. 0655D] In Lorraine, under the metropolitan see of Trier.]

Therefore, since, as is said, his brother, although educated and upright, has not yet been designated for the clerical state, we ask, warn, and exhort your brotherhood [Col. 0656D] in the Lord by apostolic letters: for the sake of divine love and out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, ordain the aforesaid G.’s brother as a cleric, and provide for him somewhere suitably, so that he may receive the necessities of life and faithfully serve almighty God. Thus we too may be bound to commend your charity in the Lord in many ways and to regard this as pleasing and acceptable. Moreover, we ask and warn your sincerity that, at our intervention, you hold the often-mentioned G. so commended that he may find our prayers on his behalf effective with you, and that we may be bound to return abundant thanks to your affection on that account.

Given at Verberie, on the seventeenth [read: fourteenth] day before the Kalends of April.

### DCCIV. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—That he again excommunicate Arwin, absolved from excommunication by the abbot of Saint-Remi, unless he restores to Roland what was taken within fifteen days. (Verberie, March 20.)

[Ibid., col. 823.]

[Col. 0657A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of the men of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Upon the complaint of Roland, bearer of the present letters, we learned that, when we had formerly entrusted to the judgment of your prudent discretion for decision the case pending between him and Arwin concerning certain things taken from him, you subjected the said Arwin to a sentence of excommunication because he refused either to restore the things taken to the said R. or to submit with him to justice concerning them. Now, however, as the same R. asserts that he has been informed, our beloved son, the abbot of Saint-Remi, unlawfully absolved the aforesaid Ar., though no satisfaction had been rendered, from the bond of excommunication. Therefore, since a sentence pronounced upon any evildoers for their offenses ought to retain its force until worthy satisfaction has been made, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters: if the said abbot—which we do not believe—has absolved the aforesaid Ar. from the sentence by which he was bound, admonish and diligently induce him to restore to the above-named R., within fifteen days after receipt of these letters, [Col. 0657C] the things taken, or to submit before you to the equity of law, according to the tenor of the other letters. If he does not do so, restore him to the same sentence, all contradiction and appeal ceasing. But if he has not been absolved, do not relax the prescribed sentence until he is compelled fully to carry out one of the two alternatives which we have stated.

Given at Verberie, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### DCCV. To the bishops established in the March.—On the property of the monastery of Saint Clement. (Verberie, March 25.)

[*Chron. Casaur.*, in MURATORI, *Rer. Ital. Script.*, II, II, 912.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Fermo; likewise to the bishop of Ascoli; likewise to the bishop of Camerino; likewise to G., our subdeacon and procurator of Osimo; likewise to the beloved son, the prior of Fonte Avellana, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The more closely our beloved sons Leonas, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Saint Clement of Pescara are bound to us and to the Roman Church by devotion, the more earnestly we are bound to assist them in their right and preserve it for them. Accordingly, wishing to provide for their justice, we command and direct you by apostolic letters to restore, all pretext and excuse ceasing, to the aforesaid abbot and brethren the possessions in your parish known to belong to the said monastery which you or any of your parishioners hold occupied; or otherwise render them full justice concerning these matters, so that henceforth they need not bring a complaint to us because their right has failed. If those holding the properties should perhaps refuse to comply with your admonition in this matter, strike them with a sentence of excommunication and cause them to be avoided by all as excommunicated persons until worthy satisfaction has been made.

Given at Verberie, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

### DCCVI. To the chapter of Soissons.—That they restore to P., clerk of King Louis, the prebend withheld for two years. (Verberie, March 26.)

[Ibid., col. 824.]

[Col. 0658B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to P., dean, and to the whole chapter of Soissons, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your discretion, we believe, is not unaware how great is the kindness in Christ of our dearest son Louis, the illustrious king of the French, and how praiseworthy and pious is his devotion toward ecclesiastical men. Therefore both you and all who serve the Lord Jesus Christ in clerical office ought to respond to his kindness in such a way that his benevolence toward ecclesiastical men and churches may be increased and grow. It has come to us, and has been represented on behalf of our aforementioned most serene son the king, [Col. 0658C] that for two years you have withheld from our beloved son P., bearer of the present letters and his clerk, the revenues of his prebend; and, although requested, you have altogether refused to restore what was withheld. Since we can neither suffer nor ought to suffer the aforesaid son of ours to lose what is known to belong to his prebend, by the present letters we command you—and in commanding, direct you—to restore in full, within half a month after receipt of these letters, with every pretext and excuse removed, whatever you have withheld from his prebend either in the present year or in the preceding year; and henceforth you are not to presume to withhold anything from him.

Given at Verberie, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April.

### DCCVII. To the provost, dean, archdeacon, and entire chapter of Auxerre.—On behalf of Master P. (Verberie, March?)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 882.]

[Col. 0658D]

The duty of our office invites and exhorts us to attend more diligently to those persons whom we know to be zealous in devotion and readier in the service of the Church. Therefore, having certain hope and confidence in your sincerity, we offer earnest prayers to your devotion on behalf of our beloved son Master P., your fellow canon. Since he is pleasing and devoted to us, we hold him dear and acceptable; and by apostolic letters we more fully ask [Col. 0659A] that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves and in consideration of our dearest son in Christ Louis, the illustrious king of the French, in whose service he is engaged, you grant him the benefice of his prebend which he holds in your church for up to three years, or at least for two years. Thus he may become more devoted to you because of your devotion, and we may be obliged on that account to render fullest thanks to your devotion.

### DCCVIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of the Church of Compiègne. (Verberie, March 29.)

[Ibid., col. 825.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of the men of Rheims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved abbot and brethren of Compiègne have complained to us that the servants of their monastery and the burgesses of Compiègne withhold from them the rights due and refuse to submit with them to justice concerning these matters.
