The abbot of Saint-Memmie at Châlons, the abbot of Charleul [Note: [Col. 0659D] It seems that *Caroli-loci* should be read. Charleul was a notable Cistercian monastery in the diocese of Senlis, one day’s journey from Compiègne. There is, however, another Cistercian monastery, Cherlieu, in the county of Burgundy, in the diocese of Besançon.], and the abbot of Thenolles presume to invade certain possessions belonging to them and endeavor to take them away. Since we are specially bound to preserve the rights of the monastery of Compiègne, which has no bishop other than ourselves, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you diligently admonish, on our behalf and yours, the said servants and burgesses to pay without any delay or diminution their rights to the aforesaid monastery; and that you admonish and strictly compel the abbots either promptly to restore the tithe and the occupied possessions to that monastery or, under your examination and with appeal removed, to render full justice concerning them to the aforesaid abbot and brethren of Compiègne. Furthermore, by the authority of the present letters we enjoin your discretion diligently to admonish the lord of Tornelle, patron and advocate of the monastery of Compiègne, who is excessively burdening and trying to ruin certain villages of that monastery, to render full justice in this matter to the abbot and brethren; and to constrain him under the severity of anathema. [Col. 0659D]

Given at Verberie, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April.

### DCCIX. To . . .—On behalf of Nicholas, citizen of Châlons. (Verberie, March 29.)

[Ibid., col. 826.]

It has been represented to us, and we have learned from the complaint of Nicholas, a citizen of Châlons, that the master of the house of Saint James did not hesitate violently to take from him land which he had possessed for a long time by hereditary right, with no one making a claim. [Col. 0660A] Therefore, because such oppressions and injuries ought not to be committed by religious men, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, when you have been asked concerning this matter, to assemble together, summon both parties before you, hear and ascertain fully the arguments on both sides, and decide the case by means of justice, with appeal removed.

Given at Verberie, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April.

### DCCX. He commands the archbishops of Rheims and Rouen and their suffragans to protect the church of Saint Peter of Silincurt from its adversaries’ injuries. (Verberie, March 29.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0660B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren [HENRY], archbishop of Rheims, and [ROTROD], archbishop of Rouen, and to their suffragans, greetings and apostolic blessing.

By the Lord’s providence, the care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us and the concern of pastoral governance laid upon us, so that we may take care to uproot, destroy, and eradicate what we recognize ought to be uprooted and destroyed. Certainly, since the increasing wickedness of men upon the earth disturbs the peace and tranquility of the churches and impedes the rest and quiet of religious persons, we must strive with all earnestness to extirpate vices and repress their wickedness, and arm ourselves with pontifical constancy and strength. Thus, through the urgency of our concern, those devoted to the repose of contemplation may endure no annoyances or persecutions from evil men and may be able to devote themselves to good works and virtue. It has come to our hearing that the church of Saint Peter of Silincurt [Note: [Col. 0660D] Selincourt was a notable Premonstratensian abbey in the diocese of Amiens, commonly called Saint-Tear because, as they say, a tear of the Savior was preserved there.] is harassed by many injuries and assailed by oppressions. When it brings a complaint against its wrongdoers before ministers of the churches and seeks reparation for the losses inflicted upon it, those wrongdoers, in order to evade justice and as a means of escape, raise the cry of appeal, but do not pursue the appeal in any way. Since the remedy of appeal ought by no means to aid those known to appeal in deceit and fraud, we command and direct your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when the religious brethren of that church bring their wrongdoers before any one of you concerning injuries or losses inflicted upon them, or property taken from them, each of you is to admonish and compel them to render full and sufficient justice. If they raise the cry of appeal but do not within the prescribed time come to the Apostolic See to pursue the appeal, or send suitable representatives, you are to bind them with the bond of excommunication, the appeal set aside, [Col. 0661A] and cause that sentence to be observed inviolate until worthy satisfaction is made.

Furthermore, since it has been reported to us that the viscount of Pincinay, Bernard of Saint-Valery, and Walter Tirel, with their men, have inflicted grave losses upon that church and taken animals and many other things, for which they have not yet been willing to make satisfaction, we likewise command you by the authority of the present letters, if the matter stands thus, to admonish and strictly compel them to restore all that has been taken to the aforesaid church, repair the losses inflicted, make full satisfaction for the injuries committed, and henceforth wholly cease from harassing it. Should they perhaps refuse to do this, you are to bind them, with every obstacle removed, in the bond of excommunication and cause them to be treated as excommunicated until full satisfaction; and if even then they do not come to their senses, you are to prohibit the celebration of divine offices in their lands, except for the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying. But those proved to have killed a lay brother of the aforesaid church and burned its houses and granges, you are publicly to declare excommunicated with lighted candles, and command all to avoid them until they offer suitable satisfaction and amendment for so great a wrongdoing, and the killers come to the Apostolic See with your letters to make satisfaction. [Col. 0661B]

Given at Verberie, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April.

### DCCXI. Privilege for the Church of Saint Mammes of Langres. (Verberie, March 30.)

(*Gallia Christiana*, new ed., IV, documents, 184.)

[Col. 0661C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons MANASSES, dean, and the entire chapter of Saint Mammes of Langres, to the canons now present and those to be instituted in the future, forever.

The authority of our office admonishes and invites us to labor for the condition of the churches and, with the Lord’s help, to provide beneficially for their peace and tranquility. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the protection of the present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the Lord’s favor, through grants of popes, gifts of kings and princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms: [Col. 0661D]

The high altar in the same church, likewise all the altars within that church, freely held, together with the benefices conferred there and the presentations; likewise the chapel of the Blessed Mary between the two towers; also the parish of Holy Cross with its appurtenances, namely the chapel of Bourona and the chapel of the Holy Trinity in the porch of the church of Langres, together with the election and appointment of priests in the aforesaid churches, free and exempt from every exaction; the church of Barium with its appurtenances; the church of Perceio with its appurtenances; the church of Curto-Campo with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Mosteriolo with its tithes and appurtenances. In the church of St. Martin [otherwise, Maurelius] on the river Vienne, two bezants; in the church of Villa in the district of Dijon, two bezants; in the church of Bure, two bezants; in the church of Villania, two bezants; the church of Dampetra on the river Saône; the church of Polesot with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Laniaco with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Vivaco with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Anceio Franco; the churches of Taliceio and Blaceio; the church [Col. 0662B] of Merone [otherwise, Nerone] with its *paratae*; the church of Nancile [otherwise, Nuile] in the district of Dijon; the church of Ageio and of Gypseio; the churches of Barbire and Coion; whatever you possess in the church of Rumille; the church of St. Hilary with its appurtenances; the church of Buxeria; the church of Provencheriis; the church of St. Calixtus; the alms-gift of Alberic, canon of Langres, at the village of Calinas [otherwise, Chalmi], and the church of that same village with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Audeliaco with its appurtenances; the churches of Marcilliaco and Planiaco; the church of Monte-Landonensi with its appurtenances; the church of Chalandre; the church of Annulle; and all other churches which you lawfully possess.

We also confirm to you by apostolic authority the provisions which the bishop is bound to furnish annually to the chapter of Langres [Col. 0662C], namely: at the Nativity of the Lord, at the Lord’s Supper, at Easter, annually on the day of his consecration, on the feast of St. Mammetus, and one further provision from the church of St. Martin of Langres on the very day of the feast; and the right of election over all your churches and priests, as you have possessed it hitherto. Moreover, we likewise confirm to you the ancient and reasonable customs concerning the administration and observance of justice in your church and in the other churches of the city of Langres. We decree that the customs or revenues called “the Crosses,” from the whole bishopric of Langres—except those granted by the bishops of Langres to churches [Col. 0662D] or monasteries of that bishopric and known to have been confirmed by their written instruments—are to be confirmed to you.

We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations whatsoever; but that all shall be preserved unimpaired and whole, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the bishop of Langres. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

Given at Veroli, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of April [30 March], in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1170, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### DCCXII. Privilege for the Canons of Pisa.  
*(Veroli, April.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 405.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the canons of Pisa, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The manner in which the monastery of Sexto, which belongs in a special way to the right of blessed Peter and to our disposition, has been ruined through that intruder—who, like one to whom none of the sheep belonged, consumed its possessions and goods by selling and squandering them [Col. 0663B]—and has fallen very far from its former condition, is not, we believe, unknown to your prudent discernment; rather, owing to the proximity of the place, it ought to be clearly apparent to you. But since, by the duty of our office, we are bound to exercise care for all the churches of God, we ought to attend with more earnest concern to those which look directly to our care and protection, without any intermediary; and it is fitting that we render them the aid of the Apostolic See, lest their rights be diminished or unlawfully withheld by anyone.

Accordingly, by apostolic authority we annul the sales, enfeoffments, alienations, and pledges which that intruder made from the treasure, possessions, or other property of the aforesaid monastery, and decree that they are utterly without force [Col. 0663C], as they are known to be void by the strict rule of law. By these apostolic letters we command and direct your discretion diligently to warn and induce the holders of those possessions and goods, who are your parishioners, to relinquish them to the aforesaid monastery free and unencumbered, with every contradiction and appeal set aside, within forty days after receiving these letters; nor are they thereafter to presume to retain them at the peril of their souls. If they contemptuously refuse to comply with your admonition, then, relying on apostolic authority and setting aside recourse to appeal, publicly pronounce upon them a sentence of excommunication, by which you shall hold them bound until they make fitting satisfaction.

[Col. 0663D] Given at Veroli, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April [16 March].  
[Note: [Col. 0663] The words “XVII Kal. April.” contain an error. JAFFÉ.]

### DCCXIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—He orders him to compel John, canon of Laon, and the woman He., who are disputing an inheritance, to appear before [Theobald], Bishop of Amiens, for judgment.  
*(Veroli, 2 April.)*

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 827.]

We committed for hearing and for due final determination, with the impediment of appeal removed, to our venerable brother the bishop of Amiens the case known to have long been litigated between John, canon of Laon, and the woman He., his stepmother, concerning the inheritance and other property of John’s father. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, when requested in this matter, you compel both parties to appear before the aforesaid bishop, and cause what he shall judge between them in this matter to be firmly and inviolably observed and put into execution, appeal set aside.

Given at Veroli, on the fifth day before the Nones of April [1 April].

### DCCXIV. To the same.—On behalf of Stephen, canon of Reims.  
*(Veroli, 2 April.)*

[Ibid., col. 828.]

The less frequently we lay petitions before you and burden you in matters of this kind, the more fitting it is that your diligence should hear our requests—and especially honourable ones—more willingly and promote them more effectively, so that by performing the deed we may further demonstrate that affection which we have long found you to bear in many ways toward us and the Roman Church. Your diligence knows that our beloved son Stephen, a canon of your church, is a man noble by birth, discreet and upright; therefore, out of regard for himself as well as for his kinsmen, we hold him dear and acceptable, and we willingly wish, insofar as we can with God, to advance his interests.

Accordingly, having full confidence in the sincerity and devoted affection of your heart, and being moved by the urgent entreaties of our beloved daughter in Christ, the lady B., widow of R., of happy memory, formerly king of Sicily [Col. 0664C], we earnestly request and admonish your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you generously grant and assign to the said Stephen some dignity in your church, if one is vacant, or the first which happens to become vacant there, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves and in consideration of his nobility and merit. Thus we shall be bound to render manifold thanks to your devotion and to promote your prayers and petitions more willingly and effectively when an opportunity arises; and the said Stephen shall be bound always to prove more faithful and devoted to you and more zealous in your service.

[Note: [Col. 0663] Roger.]

Given at Veroli, on the fifth day before the Nones of April [1 April].

### DCCXV. To the same.—On behalf of the same man.  
*(Veroli, 2 April.)*

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0664D] Some time ago, our beloved son Stephen, canon of Reims, appearing before us, obtained from us, as we well remember, that the case between himself and our beloved son P., abbot of St. Remigius, concerning certain customs of Stephen’s men—and concerning which Stephen had appealed to our hearing—should be committed to our venerable brothers, the bishops of Amiens and Beauvais, for determination, recourse to appeal having been removed. But afterwards, as we recall, other letters were obtained from us, because we did not remember that the aforesaid case had already been entrusted to the said judges. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, if because of the later letters a sentence of interdict or excommunication has been pronounced against the aforesaid men, you shall, with delay and appeal set aside, relax it, provided that Stephen gives security that he is willing to submit to justice before the aforementioned judges.

Given at Veroli, on the fifth day before the Nones of April [1 April].

### DCCXVI. To John, Bishop of Bologna, and his successors, he affirms that property was granted by Anastasius IV to Bishop Gerard by emphyteutic lease for one hundred pounds, on condition that the bishops annually pay two pounds of pure silver to the Roman See.  
*(Veroli, 18 April.)*

[SAVIOLI, *Annali Bolognesi*, II, II, 27.]

[Col. 0665B]

### DCCXVII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans.—In favour of the Church of Vicogne.  
*(Veroli, 22 April.)*

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 829.]

Many of you have heard, we believe, by how great burdens and how heavy a load of debts the Church of Vicogne has been afflicted; and we ourselves, both because of the care of governance entrusted to us and because of the devotion of our beloved son S., abbot of that place, whom we hold dear in our inmost heart [Col. 0665C], would in every way wish that church to be relieved of such straits and, with the Lord’s help, restored to its former condition. Therefore, lest it be said of her in your sight: “All her friends have despised her; there is none to comfort her in her distress” (Lamentations 1:2), by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, whenever the needs of that church are made known to you by the aforesaid abbot, or by its brethren and messengers, you apply priestly diligence to relieving them. When asked, exercise against its wrongdoers such zeal in your pontifical office, and carry out so fully whatever belongs to ecclesiastical censure in restraining them, that the church itself need not suffer [Col. 0665D] through lack of justice, and that you may receive both our commendation and the abundance of reward from God for supporting the needs of religious persons and repressing the malice of the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 0665D] Compare this letter with letter 719.]

Given at Veroli, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April].

### DCCXVIII. To the Chapter of Soissons.—On behalf of Peter, canon.  
*(Veroli, 24 April.)*

(Ibid., col. 830.)

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Po., dean, and to the whole chapter of Soissons, greetings and apostolic blessing.

When you, son dean, and our beloved son Peter, your canon, were present before us, you and your fellow-brother Nevelo, who was with you, stated that the said Peter had been excommunicated by the chapter and expelled from your church because, after giving you his pledge that he would swear the customs which you wished him to swear, he later contemptuously refused to perform this. Peter, on the other hand, replied that he had given that pledge on the condition that he could take the oath with a sound conscience; he added that, because the things which he was required to swear seemed unjust to him, he could not take the oath without prejudice to his conscience. Since, therefore [Col. 0666B], it was not through any fault of his that he did not remain continually in your church, he urgently sought restoration of his prebend, including the fruits already received.

Accordingly, since he denied that he had given his pledge unconditionally, and because no one ought to be compelled to take an oath against his conscience, we absolve him from the sentence by which he was said to have been bound, and send him back to you absolved. By these apostolic letters, commanding and directing you, and directing and commanding you, we order that within fifteen days after receiving these letters, setting aside every excuse and appeal, you restore to him his prebend with the fruits already received, and treat him honourably and kindly as your brother. But if, in this matter—which we by no means believe—you presume to oppose our command [Col. 0666C], know that we have instructed our venerable brother Henry, archbishop of Reims, to restore to the aforesaid Peter his prebend and the withheld fruits, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, without diminution, and to ensure that he possesses them in full.

Given at Veroli, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May [24 April].

### DCCXIX. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims, and the Count of Flanders.—For the Church of Vicogne, that it may be relieved from usury.  
*(Veroli, 24 April.)*

[Ibid., col. 831.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HENRY [Col. 0666D], archbishop of Reims, and to the count of Flanders, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Neither the magnitude of the afflictions of the Church of Vicogne nor the proximity of the place permits you to be ignorant of them. But because, as we have learned from the report of our beloved son S., abbot of that place, you have compassionately shared its suffering, we hold this grateful and welcome, and desire that your compassion may result in its relief. For we found that church burdened by such a weight of debts [Col. 0667A] that, unless your authority and power come to its aid in response to apostolic exhortation, it is to be feared that it will soon be reduced to desolation. Thus, where a multitude of religious men has hitherto dwelt, there may come to be, God forbid, a wilderness or a habitation of laymen.

We, indeed, desire all the more vigorously to meet so great an evil because we ought to be especially solicitous for the needs of religious persons, and because the aforesaid abbot, whom obedience alone subjected to these burdens, has proved more devoted and faithful to us and to the Church of God. Since, therefore, it does not readily appear how it can be relieved of such grave burdens unless it is released from payment of interest, by these letters we command you that, for the love of God and reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves [Col. 0667B], you extend the right hand of your office and power to relieve the needs of that church. Cause the exactions of moneylenders to cease against it in such a manner that they can extort from it nothing beyond the principal. For thereby you will not only lighten the church’s burden, but the souls of those moneylenders may also be delivered from the fires of hell. And if they must be compelled to this even against their will, it will eventually be beneficial to them, when, someday stricken with compunction and returned to their senses, they begin to value the benefit that had once been conferred upon them unwillingly.

Therefore, venerable brother archbishop, exercise the authority of your pontifical office against them by rebuking, reproving, entreating, and, if they remain obstinate, excommunicating; and you, son count, restrain them with the authority granted you from above, so that the church itself may, by God’s gift, be restored to its former condition [Col. 0667C], and that you may obtain both our commendation for the help given it and, from almighty God, the abundant reward of everlasting recompense.

[Note: [Col. 0665D] Vicogne, a distinguished monastery of the Premonstratensian Order in the diocese of Arras; for its beginnings, see the history in volume XII of the *Spicilegium*.]

[Note: [Col. 0665D] Stephen, called “of Ursina-valle,” who was the fourth head of the monastery and freed it from debts which it had incurred through the oppressions of Baldwin, count of Hainaut, and through the fire at Harcies, as we learn from the manuscript Chronicle of Vicogne.]

Given at Veroli, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March [read: May; 24 April].

### DCCXX. To the People of Nonantola.—That a privilege granted to the Bishop of Modena was not bestowed to their injury.  
*(Veroli, 26 April.)*

[TIRABOSCHI, *Storia di Nonantola*, II, p. 103.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons A., abbot, and the brethren, and to all the clergy and people of Nonantola, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0667D] Having learned from the report of Alb., B., and M., your messengers, that our brother the bishop of Modena has boasted that he obtained from us a privilege by which the dignity or liberty of your monastery would be diminished, we were alike astonished and disturbed, nor could we ever believe that the bishop would have attempted this. [Col. 0668A] For since your monastery belongs, without intermediary, to the right and ownership of blessed Peter and likewise to our care and protection, it never entered our mind, nor, God willing, shall enter it, that we ought in any way to diminish the rights and liberties of that monastery. On the contrary, we wish you to know that, when that bishop earnestly pressed us to renew an ancient privilege of one of our predecessors, we were altogether unwilling to renew it because it derogated from your monastery’s liberty. Thus he departed from us without the renewal of the privilege.

[Note: [Col. 0667D] Here there is mention of a bishop of Modena who had gone to Rome and who on that occasion had sought to obtain from the pontiff a bull contrary to the privileges of the abbey of Nonantola. It therefore seems that the bishop meant here is Ardizzone, who in fact, as has been seen in the series of bishops, attended the general Lateran council held at the beginning of May 1179. But the brief published here is addressed to Abbot A., [Col. 0668D] that is, Alberto; and we have seen that as early as February of that same year he had been succeeded by Abbot Boniface. One may nevertheless believe either that, since Boniface had not yet gone to Rome to receive the pontiff’s blessing, his election was unknown, or that the writer of the brief, accustomed for many years to naming Abbot Alberto, named him by mistake instead of Boniface.]

We therefore admonish and command all of you to preserve the aforesaid monastery in its ancient condition and proper strength, and diligently to uphold [Col. 0668B] and foster its rights, so that through this you may find praise and glory in the sight of God and of men.

Given at Veroli, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May [26 April].

### DCCXXI. He confirms the judgment issued by Odo, apostolic legate, concerning the church of St. Benedict, between the monks of Nonantola and Offredus, Bishop of Cremona.  
*(Veroli, 26 April.)*

[Ibid., p. 293.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Alberto, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Nonantola, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0668C] Matters judicially determined and duly decided by the legates of the Apostolic See ought to be endowed with perpetual firmness and strengthened by the protection of apostolic guardianship. Therefore, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we hold ratified and firm the definitive judgment which our beloved son Odo, cardinal-deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison and legate of the Apostolic See, judicially pronounced between you and our venerable brother Offredus, bishop of Cremona, concerning the church of St. Benedict of Cremona. As it is contained in his authentic instrument prepared on this matter, we confirm it by apostolic authority and fortify it with the protection of this written document [Col. 0668D], decreeing that absolutely no person may violate this page of our confirmation or in any way act contrary to it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Veroli, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May [26 April].

### DCCXXII. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of Peter, canon of Soissons.  
*(Veroli, 26 April.)*

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 832.]

[Col. 0669A] We wish it to come to the knowledge of your discretion that we have firmly commanded our beloved sons, the dean and chapter of Soissons, to restore to their beloved son Peter, their canon, his prebend with the fruits already received within fifteen days after the receipt of our letters, every excuse and appeal having ceased, and to ensure that he possesses it in full. Since we do not wish our command in this matter to be defrauded of its due effect, especially since we have received urgent petitions for the said Peter from our dearest son in Christ, Louis, the most illustrious king of the Franks, whose clerk he is, and since we have also been not a little moved by Peter’s justice [Col. 0669B], we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the chapter of the aforesaid church contemptuously fails to perform this within the time prescribed to it, you shall without delay restore to the aforesaid Peter his prebend with the fruits already received, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, and ensure that he has it without diminution—unless perhaps you know this to conflict with the sworn custom of the Church of Soissons. But if it is established that this would be contrary to the oath of its canons, you shall strictly compel the aforesaid chapter, with delay and appeal set aside, to make suitable compensation to the aforesaid Peter for the lost fruits [Col. 0669C].

Given at Veroli, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May [26 April].

### DCCXXIII. He thanks the canons of Pisa for electing G., his notary, as a canon of the Church of Pisa. Their dispute with the monks of St. Savinus has been entrusted to the judgment of the archbishop.  
*(Veroli, 27 April.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 404.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons V., archpriest, and the canons of Pisa, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Having received your letter with our customary kindness and gladness of heart, we regard it as most grateful and welcome that, as we had earlier learned from the report of our beloved sons Gualandus, our subdeacon, and P., your canons, and afterwards learned from the same letter of yours, you have willingly elected our beloved son G., our notary, at our request and intervention, as a brother and canon of your church [Col. 0669D]. For this we render most abundant thanks to your affection, intending and wishing on this account to hear your petitions more willingly and effectively and henceforth to show ourselves especially more ready to promote your advantage and welfare.

We therefore request and admonish all of you that, holding firm and unshaken what you have done concerning him at the urgent instance of our prayers [Col. 0670A], when he comes to you, you receive him with a joyful countenance as your brother and canon and treat him fraternally and honourably. Furthermore, concerning the case between you and the abbot and monks of St. Savinus about the body of Count Tancred: because those monks presented the facts very differently from you, we committed the matter to your venerable brother, your archbishop, to determine under a specific form, ordering him that, unless the aforesaid count chose burial at that monastery, if he otherwise belonged to burial in your church, he should cause our interdict to be inviolably observed—especially if this was attempted after an appeal—until the body of the aforesaid count is restored to you [Col. 0670B] and fitting satisfaction has been made for the injury inflicted.

Given at Veroli, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May [27 April].

### DCCXXIV. He forbids the entire chapter of abbots of the Premonstratensian Order to allow palfreys to be given to archdeacons for the installation of an abbot.  
*(Veroli, 29 April.)*

[LE PAIGE, *Biblioth. Praem.*, 630.]

In rooting out dishonourable and wicked customs, we ought to apply pastoral foresight, and employ vigilant care and ready concern lest they should be able to flourish in the churches of God. Now, since at the blessing of abbots and their reception of pastoral care, archdeacons demand a palfrey because they install abbots in the stall—a demand proceeding from no reasonable cause but solely from the root of greed and issuing in the wickedness of simony—we command and direct all of you by apostolic letters that, if a palfrey is demanded in this manner from any one of you by the archdeacon of his diocese, that person is not to presume to give it to him on any grounds, lest both giver and receiver suffer divine punishment because of the sin of simony.

Given at Veroli, on the third day before the Kalends of May [29 April].

### DCCXXV. To Po., Dean, and the Chapter of Soissons.—On behalf of Peter, canon.  
*(Veroli, 1 May.)*

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 832.]

[Col. 0670D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Po., dean, and to the whole chapter of Soissons, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The office of the apostolate entrusted to us and the authority of the administration we have undertaken earnestly exhort and admonish us to look with a gracious countenance upon ecclesiastics and to make careful provision that their rights are not harassed by undue vexations. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and direct all of you to ensure that our beloved son P., your canon, possesses in full and without molestation the fruits of his prebend; and, for as long as he is in the service of your church or bishop, or in the schools, you are in no way to presume, without judgment and lawful summons, to deprive him of the fruits of that prebend [Col. 0671A].

Given at Veroli, on the Kalends of May [1 May].

### DCCXXVI. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of Baldwin, Chancellor of Noyon.  
*(Veroli, 1 May.)*

[Ibid., col. 833.]

It has not escaped our memory how diligently and affectionately we once admonished your prudence by our letters not to harass our beloved son Baldwin with any undue vexations concerning the chancellorship of the Church of Noyon, thereby preventing him from obtaining his right in the matter. Since, therefore, it befits you diligently to attend to the duty of your office, by which you are bound to assist rather than harm each person in his right [Col. 0671B], we request, admonish, and command your brotherhood by repeated letters that, carefully considering and attending to the fact that not only those who bear the office of pontifical dignity, but all persons, ought to prefer reason to will, you inflict upon the said B., out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, no molestation or burden concerning the aforesaid chancellorship; rather, according as your office requires, show yourself to him and to all alike as a defender of justice.

Given at Veroli, on the Kalends of May [1 May].

### DCCXXVII. To the same.—That he absolve certain persons excommunicated by the Bishop of Châlons.  
*(Veroli, 3 May.)*

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0671C] It has come to us that, when P. Berengaud had some time ago dangerously and severely wounded Guido, the kinsmen of the said G., disturbed by violent indignation, broke into his house in the heat of anger. Therefore our brother, the bishop of Châlons, subjected the violators of the house to a sentence of anathema, and entirely refuses to absolve them without payment, although they are prepared to repair the house which they broke into. Since, therefore, if this is true, he ought not to have punished them so severely for this, we command and direct your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the matter stands thus, after they have made satisfaction to the person to whom they caused damage, you shall wholly absolve the aforesaid men without a *bannum* [fine], every contradiction and appeal set aside, and publicly announce throughout your province that they are completely absolved [Col. 0671D].

Given at Veroli, on the fifth day before the Nones of May [3 May].

### DCCXXVIII. Privilege for the Monastery of Casa-Marii.  
*(Veroli, 9 May.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 1392.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GREGORY, abbot of the monastery of Saints John and Paul called Casa-Marii, and his brethren, present and future, professing the religious life, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0672A] A pious request ought to be brought to effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth worthily and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire force. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, the Roman pontiffs Calixtus, Anastasius, and Adrian; and we fortify it with the privilege of this written document. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that place according to God, the Rule of St. Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall be inviolably observed there for all time.

[Col. 0672B] Moreover, whatever possessions or goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by name:

Namely, the church of St. Michael the Archangel; the church of St. Hippolytus; and whatever you possess in the church of St. Vitus, which are in the territory of the city of Veroli; the church of St. Angelo on the hill of Corneto; the church of St. Saviour; and the church of St. Mary of Regimenio in the territory of the hill of St. John; the church of St. Nicholas [Col. 0672C] in the Castle of Babucus; the church of St. John and the church of St. Sylvester, with the amphitheatre commonly called Appretiatum; in the territory of Frosinone, the church of Holy Cross; in the territory of Anagni, the church of St. Vincent beside the castle of Morrei in the valley of Orbetana; and the church of St. Manno beside the castle of Castuli in the territory of Marsica, together with all the estates of the aforesaid churches; mills at Arinula and those which you possess in the territory of Castrum; likewise the peasants and hereditary lands which we see that you have hitherto peaceably possessed in the city of Veroli, the Castle of Babucus, and the hill of St. John.

Pastures and use of woods throughout the territory of Castrum and of Monte Negro; pastures and use of woods, and the whole castellany of that same Monte Negro; and, outside the walls [Col. 0672D], one hundred paces of adjacent land, as it descends thence on either side to the stream and, in its circuit northward, follows the very precipice of the hill; and land in the territory of the aforesaid hill sufficient for two ploughs to cultivate; the church of St. Benedict with all its appurtenances; and the church of St. Angelo of Meruleto with its chapels and appurtenances. All these things Pope Eugenius, our father and predecessor of happy memory, granted to you at the dedication of your church, and the Roman pontiffs Anastasius and Adrian strengthened by their privileges; we likewise confirm them to you and your successors. We also command that the exchange which you lawfully made with the bishop of Veroli and the canons of St. Erasmus, and with Gregory, formerly keeper of the castle called Castrum, be inviolably observed in future times [Col. 0673A].

We further decree that your monastery, which is recognized as belonging to the right and property of Blessed Peter, shall be subject to no ecclesiastical or secular person other than the Roman pontiff. Moreover, taking this into consideration, we decree that no archbishop or bishop may place the aforesaid monastery under interdict, or pronounce upon you a sentence of interdict or excommunication without authorization from the Roman pontiff. Likewise, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone to dare to subject to an interdict any church belonging to that monastery which has no congregation, so that, if [Col. 0673B] any one of your brethren wishes there to sing out of devotion, he shall have full freedom to sing, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded.

Furthermore, by this decree we have thought it proper to establish that your brethren, wherever they may be situated, shall be free and immune from every obligation of secular service and from every burden of worldly oppression. Certainly, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the foodstuffs of your animals. And, wishing by paternal provision to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone to dare to cross the boundaries established by our predecessor around the precinct of your monastery, extending five hundred paces from it [Col. 0673C], or within them to commit theft or robbery, seize a person, or perpetrate any violence. But if anyone does so and, having been warned a second or third time, contemptuously refuses to make suitable satisfaction, let him be judged a sacrilegious person and punished by the disciplinary censure of the Church.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of monks who are to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic and is willing to provide these things freely and without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer; supported, indeed, by our authority, he shall grant what is requested. Nor shall that bishop [Col. 0673D], or any officer of bishops, have authority unjustly to claim for himself anything in chapels belonging to the aforesaid monastery beyond the quarter of tithes and offerings properly due to him.

Upon the death of yourself, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any device of deceit or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, have elected according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, whether from their own community or, if necessary, from another community of the Cistercian Order, to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff.

We therefore decree that absolutely no person, etc. Amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
[Col. 0674A] I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Ubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius.  
I, Aldobrandus, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia.  
I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina.  
I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains.  
I, Boso, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, [Col. 0674B] title of Pastor.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark.  
I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of Saint Vitalis, title of Vestina.  
I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.  
I, Cynthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian.  
I, Manfredus, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil.  
I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa.  
[Col. 0674C] I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Veroli, by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of May, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1170, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

## DCCXXIX. To F., dean, and the chapter of Reims.—Against J., chancellor, and Giles, dean of Villa Dominica, on behalf of Robert, priest of Sacey.  
*(Veroli, 12 May.)*

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 834.]

You should know that the complaint of Robert, priest, has been brought before our hearing: J., procurator of the archdeacon of Reims, and Giles, dean [Col. 0674D] of Villa Dominica, alleged against him that, knowingly associating with a certain excommunicated person, he had incurred the stain of anathema; and they said that they would prove this through lawful witnesses. Yet when the day appointed for proof arrived, they did not prove it as they had promised. Instead, the aforesaid J. ordered the same man to clear himself by the oath of a seventh hand, adding that he must have the three priests whom J. had named for him, together with the others in the purgation according to J.’s own will.

Although the aforesaid priest had often been ready to clear himself with his witnesses, the aforementioned J. and the dean unjustly prolonged the case. The priest, having placed both his person and property under the protection of the Apostolic See, appealed to our hearing; but, although his messenger was present before us, the other party neither came nor sent anyone to answer for it. Therefore, since it is unworthy and unjust to condemn innocent blood, we command you by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid J. and the dean can prove their accusation, you shall receive from the priest an oath that he will abide by your decision in this matter, absolve him without demanding any money, and impose upon him a suitable penance. But if you do not consider that he should be absolved without a monetary exaction, we decree by apostolic authority that he is absolved. If, however, they fail in their proof, then, having received from the priest only the purgation of his own hand, you shall wholly absolve him by apostolic authority from their accusation in these matters. For so slight an offence [Col. 0675B] ought not to require such a severe purgation.

Given at Veroli, on the fourth day before the Ides of May.

## DCCXXX. He exhorts Robert, prior, and the chapter of Saint Victor of Paris to obey Abbot Ervisius.  
*(Veroli, 13 May.)*

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, VI, col. 264.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROBERT, prior, and the chapter of Saint Victor of Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have repeatedly warned and commanded our beloved son Ervisius, your abbot, and now again by our letters command him, to administer and transact the affairs of your church, both internal and external, with the counsel [Col. 0675C] of the greater and sounder part of the chapter; and to apply prompt care and diligence to your advancement according to the institution of your order.

[Note: From this it appears that Ervisius, while relinquishing the dignity of abbot, was not stripped of all government, but retained certain matters to administer.]

Since, therefore, we believe and hope that the same abbot will gladly do this in accordance with our warning and command, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters to render due obedience and reverence to that abbot, assist him prudently and effectively in ordering and disposing of your church’s affairs, and, according to the institution of your order, show yourselves so ready both for the cultivation of religious life and for the increase of temporal resources that, by your zeal and care, with the Lord’s help, the same church may grow in spiritual things and [Col. 0675D] also advance in temporal prosperity. But if anything in your church requires correction which cannot be corrected in the council of the greater and sounder part of the chapter, we will and command that it be more suitably corrected at the direction of those to whom we have entrusted the governance of that church’s condition.

Given at Venice, on the third day before the Ides of May.

## DCCXXXI. He approves the peace established by Hugh, bishop of Rodez, and his brother Hugh, count of Rodez.  
*(Veroli, 14 May.)*

[MANSI, *Concil.* XXI, 1045.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, bishop of Rodez, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever matters concerning peace are requested to be confirmed by the Apostolic See, it is fitting that we grant a more gracious assent in proportion as more and more welcome benefits accrue to all from the good of peace. For, from a certain document sent to us by your brotherhood, it has come to our hearing that you, having held a council of your abbots, provosts, archdeacons, and the barons of your land, established the following peace and agreement with your noble brother Hugh, count of Rodez:

“All movable and immovable property, and all persons, clerics as well as laypeople, shall at all times be secure under this peace. No one, except armed knights and retainers, may bear any weapons; knights may carry swords only, and retainers individual staffs, who, like the rest, must enjoy the security of the peace. Except in the case of those who refuse to confirm and inviolably observe this peace as established, permission shall not be denied to distrain upon the property of those who publicly commit perjury, or deny a pledge for a manifest debt or an acknowledged suretyship—yet you yourselves are excepted.”

For the support and defence of such peace and security, it has been decreed that abbots, archdeacons, archpriests, monks, canons, priors, all clerics who govern churches of their own, as well as knights, merchants, [Col. 0676C] and burgesses possessing means; and also all persons, clerics and laypeople alike, who have a yoke of oxen or other animals with which they can plough, or more than this, or who have a pack animal—that is, a horse or mare, mule or she-mule—which they hire out for carrying burdens, shall pay twelve deniers of Rodez, or other coinage of equal value. When they have a sheepfold of sheep, they shall pay six deniers of the same currency, or an equivalent sum. The same amount shall be paid by those who own only one ox or another animal with which they can plough, or an ass which they can hire out. Retainers and craftsmen—that is, smiths, tailors, furriers, and all labourers—shall pay six, eight, or twelve deniers according to the judgment of their chaplains.

But if a father and his sons, brothers, or kinsmen have not yet separated from one another and their goods have not been divided, one shall pay for all; otherwise, each shall pay for himself. This common levy shall be rendered through each parish, with a written record by one of the parishioners, whom the chaplain, with the counsel of his archpriest and the consent of his parishioners, has elected. On the appointed day it shall be carried by that parishioner, with the same written record, to the church of Rodez.

Whoever loses his property after paying the common levy as aforesaid shall be restored in full, provided that he can identify a definite person who has taken his goods or the place where they are; otherwise, not at all. If it should happen that enemies plunder or destroy villages or towns, movable goods shall indeed be compensated from the common fund, but damage to immovable property shall not be restored, except insofar as it can be recovered from the wrongdoers. Clerics who do not have churches of their own are not compelled to contribute, unless they own a yoke of oxen, if they do not wish to do so; but, if they do not pay the common levy and should lose their goods, no compensation shall be made to them.”

It was added to the aforesaid peace “that chaplains of churches and all laypeople aged fourteen and above must affirm and observe the peace and the common levy. Those who contemptuously refuse obedience in this matter must be barred from the thresholds of the church [Col. 0677B] and made strangers to every peace. The parish churches in which violators of the peace reside shall cease from divine offices until they are compelled to make amends.”

We hold this institution of peace, established by you and confirmed by an authentic instrument, firm and ratified; we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the present writing, decreeing that absolutely no person may infringe this page of our confirmation or oppose it in any way. But should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at Veroli, on the second day before the Ides of May, [in the second year of our pontificate [Note: The words enclosed in brackets were added by another hand.]].

## DCCXXXII. To Walter, bishop of Tournai.—Concerning the establishment of forty canons in the Church of Tournai.  
*(Veroli, 14 May.)*

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, III, Instr. 48.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Tournai, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us and shown on your behalf that the church entrusted to you has few clerics assigned to its service, although it is said to enjoy a great abundance of possessions. Since it is unworthy that so distinguished a church should not have an abundance of clerics serving it, by the authority of these present letters we grant your brotherhood apostolic permission, with the counsel of prudent and religious men of your diocese, to establish forty from thirty prebends, provided that the possessions of the aforesaid church are sufficient for this, so that the canons of your church will not be compelled to seek other prebends, but may have an honourable livelihood from the benefice of that church itself.

Given at Veroli, on the second day before the Ides of March [read: May].

## DCCXXXIII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of P., a priest, that he be kindly received by the lord of Reims.  
*(Veroli, 21 May.)*

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 835.]

[Col. 0678A]

We inform your affection that our son P., appearing in our presence, told us that he was born in the archbishopric of Reims and was there ordained subdeacon. Afterwards, as he asserts, setting out for Jerusalem in good devotion, he received there the order of deacon; returning to his native land, he served God for a long time in that order of deacon, and was afterwards promoted to the priesthood. But now he has recently been summoned to answer concerning his diaconal order, and, perceiving the burden placed upon him, he has fled to the remedy of the Apostolic See.

Since it is our duty to have compassion upon the poor who take refuge with us, diligently investigating the truth concerning the order of his diaconate, we have learned from certain testimonies that the aforesaid P. was ordained deacon of Sidon. And because the Roman Church, in which by Christ’s ordination we serve, ought to be a safeguard of counsel and assistance to those who humbly seek it, we ask, warn, and command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, in consideration of divine love and fear, kindly to receive the said P.; since the fact of his diaconal order is sufficiently well established before us, allow him to serve God peacefully in the priestly office, and, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, do not delay to assign him an ecclesiastical benefice from which he may live honourably.

Given at Veroli, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June.

## DCCXXXIV. To the same.—That he decide the controversy between U. and his brother Nicholas, on the one hand, and the monks of Anchin, on the other; and the controversy between the brethren of Saint Foillan and the canons of Saint Vincent.  
*(Veroli, 21 May.)*

[Ibid., col. 835.]

U., bearer of this letter, coming to the clemency of the Apostolic See, showed us by his statement that, when he and his brother Nicholas had lodged a complaint before the court of the Church of Cambrai against the abbot and monks of Anchin, because they were unjustly disinheriting them, and the case concerning this had been heard, the aforesaid Nicholas appealed to our hearing; but the abbot and monks neither came nor sent anyone to answer for them.

[Note: I conjecture that “Auncinos monks” means the monks of Anchin [Aquicinctenses], in the diocese of Arras, from the French word *Anchin*.]

Since we are bound to all God’s faithful in their justice, we entrust this case to your judgment, to be heard and brought to its due conclusion with the appeal set aside. We command you by apostolic letters that, when you are requested in this matter, you summon both parties before you and, having fully heard and examined the arguments on both sides, decide the same case by the mediation of justice, without recourse to appeal, so that neither party may have legitimate cause to complain of a defect of justice.

We also entrust to your experience the hearing of the case being litigated between the aforesaid brethren and the abbot of Saint Foillan [Col. 0679A] and the canons of Saint Vincent concerning a certain portion of their inheritance. By these letters we charge you to hear that case and decide it, with appeal removed and the equity of law preserved.

[Note: Saint Foillan is a monastery of the Premonstratensian Order in Hainaut, in the diocese of Cambrai.]

Given at Veroli, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June.

## DCCXXXV. To the same.—On behalf of the church of Cercamp, that the viscount of Pinchey cease troubling it.  
*(Veroli, 23 May.)*

[Ibid., col. 837.]

[Col. 0679B] From the complaint sent by the abbot and brethren of Cercamp, it has come to the hearing of the Apostolic See that the viscount of Pinchey does not hesitate to inflict many burdens upon them and their house in their property and possessions, although, because of the renown of their religious life and uprightness, he ought with attentive care to defend them, so far as he can, from the oppression of others.

[Note: Cercamp is a notable monastery of the Cistercian Order, founded from the line of Pontigny in the diocese of Amiens, not far from Hesdin, about 1140, by Hugh, count of Saint-Pol.]

Since it is our duty especially to love religious persons and their houses with charity in Christ, and to apply attentive concern and diligence to their defence, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to approach the said viscount and compel him by ecclesiastical coercion either to restore, with fitting satisfaction, whatever damage he has inflicted upon those brethren, and wholly desist from burdening and troubling them; or to render them complete justice before you in this matter, without recourse to appeal. Thus the aforesaid brethren may be secure from his molestation under the protection of your authority and rejoice in peacefully possessing what is theirs.

Given at Veroli, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June.

## DCCXXXVI. To the same.—On behalf of the church of Cercamp.  
*(Veroli, 23 May.)*

[Ibid., col. 838.]

Although by the obligation of our office we are bound to preserve the justice of all God’s faithful, we ought to assist religious men, fervently devoted to divine service, with all the readier zeal because, by the purpose of the religious life they have undertaken, it is less fitting for them to engage in litigation.

The abbot and brethren of Cercamp, our beloved sons, have complained to us, and you should know that it has come to our hearing that the nobleman B. of Saint-Valery refuses to restore to them eight marks of silver which, as he says, their cellarer lent him. Moreover, when the same Bernard became surety to those brethren for a certain knight in the sum of sixty pounds, he by no means causes those pounds to be repaid to them as he is bound to do, and he does not cease to inflict many other burdens upon them and their monastery.

[Note: Indeed Henry had been a monk professed in the Cistercian Order at Clairvaux; and monks who were formerly raised to episcopal dignity did not lay aside their monastic habit while bishops.]

Therefore, because the pontifical authority conferred upon you by the Provider of all things, as well as the religious habit which you wear, should more urgently urge and induce you to preserve the rights of the aforesaid brethren, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to warn and exhort the said B. to restore, without trouble or difficulty, to those brethren the eight marks lent to him by the aforesaid cellarer; to pay, or cause to be paid, to them the sixty pounds for which he made himself their surety; and wholly to desist from molesting them. Otherwise, without delay, he shall render them full and sufficient justice under your examination in this matter, without appeal. If he refuses to comply with your warning, pronounce against him a sentence of excommunication, appeal being set aside; and, if even then he does not come to his senses, subject his land to interdict.

Given at Veroli, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June.

## DCCXXXVII. To the same.—On behalf of Her., that he be absolved from interdict.  
*(Veroli, 25 May.)*

[Ibid., col. 839.]

Her., bearer of this letter, coming to the Apostolic See, humbly represented to us that, when he had long ago had a case concerning certain possessions with his stepmother and the father of that stepmother, he and his sister appealed to our hearing. Because they did not pursue the appeal lodged within a suitable time, J., your vice-archdeacon, caused them to be bound by the bond of anathema. However, the same Her., appearing in our presence, firmly asserted that they had been entirely unable to pursue the appeal both because of his youthful age and because of pressing necessity.

We therefore, yielding with paternal affection to their necessities, caused the aforesaid Her. to be absolved from the sentence of excommunication. By the authority of these letters we command your brotherhood wholly to absolve his sister from the same sentence, without exacting any ban-payment, after receiving sufficient security from them that, in the aforesaid case, they will submit to justice before our venerable brother [Theobald], bishop of Amiens, and our beloved son F., dean of Reims, together with the said stepmother and her father. Thereafter, when requested in this matter, compel both parties to appear before the same judges and firmly to observe their judgment in the aforesaid case, appeal being set aside.

Given at Veroli, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.

## DCCXXXVIII. To F., dean, and the chapter of Reims.—On behalf of Vivien, priest, against the bishop of Châlons, lest what he did in good faith be turned to his loss or discredit.  
*(Veroli, 25 May.)*

[Ibid., col. 839.]

[Col. 0681A]

Vivien, a poor priest and bearer of this letter, coming before us, humbly related that, when a certain person had stolen goods belonging to a church, he entrusted them to Vivien in secret confession, earnestly requesting him not to delay returning the goods to the chaplain of that church on the following day. Then the thief deceitfully approached the same chaplain, alleging that, under pretext of five shillings which he was to receive from him on that account, the aforesaid priest had those goods.

Accordingly, on the appointed day, as the priest carried the aforesaid goods with him in order to return them to the chaplain, he encountered the chaplain and the thief on the road. Drawing the chaplain aside in secret, he privately returned the goods to him, stating that they had been disclosed under confession. But the chaplain, insistently asserting this to be false, summoned the priest and began to accuse and severely harass him as a thief. Therefore our venerable brother G., bishop of Châlons, deprived him of the church which he had possessed for forty years and pronounced against him a sentence of excommunication, although on another ground: namely, that he had neglected to appear before the bishop after twice being summoned concerning this matter by the bishop’s messenger.

Since what he did in good faith must not be turned to his loss or discredit, and we cannot readily believe that a man of such office and age committed that theft or sacrilege, we have caused him to be absolved from the sentence of excommunication. By apostolic letters we command and enjoin your discretion, after summoning the parties before you, diligently to hear this case and bring it to its due conclusion without contradiction or appeal, taking careful care that the justice of this poor man does not perish under your examination. If he is found innocent, cause the church, together with the revenues received from it, and his office to be restored to him by our authority, appeal being set aside, and allow him to remain in peace.

Given at Veroli, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.

## DCCXXXIX. To the same.—Against Thomas and John, on behalf of Theobald, clerk.  
*(Veroli, 27 May.)*

[Ibid., col. 840.]

Theobald, clerk and bearer of this letter, coming to the clemency of the Apostolic See, showed us with tearful complaint that Master J., vicar of the archdeacon, and Thomas, priest, laid violent hands upon him and his brother with diabolical boldness, and, after an appeal had been made to us, committed him to prison, where they were detained for forty days [Col. 0682A] and could not leave until they were forced to ransom themselves for one hundred and twelve shillings. Afterwards, through a certain provost, they were compelled to swear that they would in no way pursue their appeal.

Since this redounds most gravely to the injury of the Roman Church, and we can no more tolerate it patiently than we ought, we command and enjoin you by apostolic letters, and charge you under obedience, to set aside all fear, favour, and affection, carefully investigate the truth of the matter, and, if this is established, suspend the said T. and J. from every ecclesiastical office and benefice, without recourse to appeal. Publicly proclaim excommunicated both them and those who compelled the aforesaid T. and his brother to swear not to pursue the appeal, and cause all to avoid them carefully as excommunicated persons, until they restore in full everything taken from the said T. and his brother, make satisfaction for the losses and injuries inflicted, and come to us with your letters to make satisfaction.

If, however, T. and his brother cannot produce clerics or priests as witnesses for their allegation, receive three or two lay witnesses if they are produced; and, both in this and in the other matters we have mentioned, proceed no less according to the form of our command even if an appeal is made.

Given at Veroli, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

## DCCXL. He remits sins to those who visit the church of the monastery of Pescara on the day of the translation of the body of Pope Saint Clement.  
*(Veroli, 28 May.)*

[*Chron. Casaur.*, in MURATORI, *Rer. Ital. Script.*, II, II, 907.]

[Col. 0682C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons LEONATUS, abbot, and the convent of Saint Clement of Pescara, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although all who visit pious and religious places out of devotion, and there render almighty God favourable to themselves by devout prayers and the vowed affections of their hearts, deserve to receive pardon for their sins, nevertheless, on solemn and principal feast days these places ought to be visited more ceremoniously by all God’s faithful and venerated with greater devotion and reverence, in proportion as ecclesiastical men then devote themselves more devoutly to divine worship and almighty God is more especially and fervently implored for the offences of the people.

Since, therefore, it is pious and just, and instituted by the holy Fathers, that on principal and solemn days all faithful should flock to God’s churches with contrite hearts and ardent desire, and in the offering of praise and appeasement implore indulgence for their sins, we, yielding to your pious desires and just requests, grant, on behalf of almighty God and by the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul and our own, remission of their sins to all who, on the day of the translation of the body of Pope and martyr Saint Clement—which, as ancient writings state, rests in that church—devoutly flock to your church and there, together with you, render offerings of praise and appeasement in veneration of that glorious martyr.

Given at Veroli, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May.

## DCCXLI. To a certain bishop.—That Herbert, citizen of Châlons, be absolved from the excommunication pronounced after his appeal.  
*(Veroli, 29 May.)*

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 843.]

From the complaint sent by Herbert, citizen of Châlons, it has come to our hearing that his chaplain Roland pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him after an appeal had been made to us. Since whatever is attempted by anyone against an appeal ought to have no force of validity, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters, after careful investigation of the facts, that, if it is established to you that the same Herbert was excommunicated after his appeal, you shall declare him absolved and cause him to be regarded as absolved, without contradiction or appeal. Thereafter, diligently hear and bring to its due conclusion, without appeal, the case pending between the same chaplain and the aforesaid Herbert.

Given at Veroli, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June.

## DCCXLII. To William, bishop of Sens, legate of the Apostolic See.—He clears himself of the accusation that the bishop of London had been absolved at his command.

(MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 900.)

[Col. 0683C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WILLIAM, bishop of Sens, legate of the Apostolic See, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have gratefully received the letters which your devotion sent us concerning the affair of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Canterbury, and have taken care to hear them diligently and attentively. But because the bishop of London did not come to us, we have determined nothing concerning his case. Yet, had he come to us, we would have endeavoured to preserve for the said archbishop—that is, the archbishop of Canterbury—his justice so far as could be done with a safe conscience.

We believe that he has already learned in part how we proceeded in this case, as has also our dearest son in Christ Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, according to the oral charge we gave you. For after your departure we changed nothing in this matter, nor have we judged that anything should be changed in the future, although the aforesaid king of the English most urgently pressed us concerning it through the consuls of Lombardy, who were present before us together with his messenger, and also through the messengers of our dearest son in Christ Manuel, illustrious emperor of Constantinople, asking that we should grant him a somewhat longer time.

Since we regard the cause of that archbishop as our own and that of the Church, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to admonish our venerable brothers, the archbishop of Rouen and the bishop of Nevers, concerning the diligent and speedy execution of our command; and to exhort them more urgently either orally or by letter, if you cannot have both present. But if they have not yet proceeded at all in that affair, rebuke them more severely on our behalf and do not omit sternly to reprove them. If, however, it should happen that they pronounce in the land of the aforesaid king a sentence of interdict in accordance with our command, you shall [observe] it throughout the land of the same king; if it should happen that they pronounce a sentence of interdict in accordance with our command, you shall [observe] it throughout the land of the same king which is known to lie within your province, all excuse and appeal being removed, and shall cause it, insofar as lies in your power, to be inviolably observed by all. [The source repeats this clause corruptly.]

## DCCXLIII. He commands the archbishops of Bourges, Reims, Tours, and Rouen to ensure the complete abolition of the erroneous doctrine that Christ, insofar as he is man, is not something.  
*(Veroli, 2 June.)*

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 843.]

[Col. 0684C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishops of Bourges, Reims, Tours, and Rouen, and to their suffragans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Note: Peter of La Châtre, who occupied the see of Bourges for about thirty years; he died in 1171.]

[Note: Henry, to whom almost all the letters of this codex are addressed.]

[Note: Joscius, transferred in 1157 from the bishopric of Saint-Brieuc to the Church of Tours; he died in 1175.]

[Note: Rotrou, likewise transferred in 1164 from Évreux to the see of Rouen; he died in 1183.]

Those who, by the Lord’s ordering, are endowed with pontifical rank are bound to take care and to watch most diligently lest unsound doctrine gain strength in the Church of God, appearing to run contrary to the Catholic faith; for the negligence of the prelates of the Church might be charged if they did not take care to root out what must be wholly cut away by all the faithful. Therefore, urging your charity earnestly to exercise the duty of your office, we command and enjoin your fraternity by apostolic letters that each of you, in his province, having summoned prudent and religious men, [Note: [Col. 0684D] Against this unsound doctrine James of Cornwall wrote a small work, published by us in vol. V of the *Anecdota* (*Patrologia*, vol. CXCIX). He dedicated it to Alexander III, who had already condemned this perverse doctrine at the Council of Tours in 1163.] take care utterly to abolish the unsound doctrine which certain persons still hold and preach: namely, that Christ, in so far as he is man, is not something; and that you command all men to hold and preach Christ as perfect God and likewise perfect and true man, consisting, in so far as he is man, of soul and body [Col. 0685A]; firmly forbidding everyone, under threat of anathema, ever again to presume to hold or teach that doctrine, but rather to detest it utterly.

Given at Veroli, 2 June.

### DCCXLIV. To William, Archbishop of Sens: he renews the order formerly given at Paris that, having summoned his suffragans to Paris, he should ensure the suppression of the proposition of Peter, former Bishop of Paris, “that Christ, in so far as he is man, is not something,” and should command the masters to teach that “Christ is, as perfect God, so perfect man, and a true man consisting of soul and body.” (Veroli, June?)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 119.]

[Col. 0685B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to WILLIAM, Archbishop of Sens, greeting.

When you were formerly present before us, we orally enjoined you, after summoning your suffragans to Paris, to devote yourself wholly to the abolition of the unsound doctrine of Peter, formerly Bishop of Paris, by which it is said that Christ, in so far as he is man, is not something, and to apply effective effort thereto. Therefore we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that you summon your suffragans to Paris, as we commanded you when you were present, and that, together with them and other religious [Col. 0685C] and prudent men, you strive utterly to abolish the aforesaid doctrine. Command that the masters and scholars there studying theology be taught that Christ is, as perfect God, so perfect man, and a true man consisting of soul and body; firmly and expressly enjoining all that they must by no means presume henceforth to teach that doctrine, but must utterly detest it.

### DCCXLV. Bull for the Hospital of Saint Blaise near Monza. (Veroli, 5 June.)

[GIULINI, *Memorie di Milano*, VI, 542.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ARDICUS, master of the hospital situated near [Col. 0685D] Saint Blaise, adjoining Monza, and to his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed in succession, forever.

For this purpose in the governance of the Apostolic See [lacuna] we ought to respond to petitions. Therefore, beloved son Ardicus in the Lord, considering your praiseworthy devotion, following the example of our predecessor of blessed memory Pope Innocent, we strengthen by the protection of the Roman Church and our own [lacuna] the aforesaid hospital with all its appurtenances. It was offered to Blessed Peter by your predecessor Adam, with the assent and counsel of Arnold and John and the other neighbours of that place, subject to an annual payment of six denarii in old Milanese currency to us and our successors. We decree that [Col. 0686A] whatever possessions and goods the same hospital now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future be able to acquire, by grant of pontiffs, gifts of kings, generosity of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by God’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. We decree therefore, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone therefore shall in future, etc.

“Show me thy ways, O Lord.” In the monogram: “Fare well.”

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme. [Col. 0686B] I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, James, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace near the Temple of Agrippa.

Given at Veroli by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of June, in the third indiction, in the year 1170 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### DCCXLVI. To the dean and chapter of the Church of Chartres: that they restore his prebend to Philip, son of Count Robert. (Veroli, 15 June.)

[MARTEN., *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 844.]

[Col. 0686C]

The prudence of your discretion ought carefully to consider how noble and powerful Philip, son of our beloved son Count Robert, is by reason of his father, our dearest son in Christ Louis, illustrious King of the Franks, and our venerable brother the Archbishop of Rheims; and how many advantages and benefits may in time accrue to the Church of Chartres through him. In consideration of these great men, you ought to grant him a prerogative which you do not grant to others.
