And because we ourselves are greatly indebted to him in consideration of the aforesaid men [Col. 0686D], and ought to be watchful and solicitous for his benefit and advancement, and to invite others to the same by earnest exhortations, we earnestly ask and carefully admonish your charity that, for reverence for Blessed Peter and ourselves, and in respect of the men mentioned, you restore to the aforesaid Philip the revenues of his prebend in full, not as to an outsider but as to an insider; and that you grant him in this matter a prerogative which you would not otherwise grant to anyone, so that the aforementioned men may thereby be readier and more zealous toward the advantage and advancement of your church, and that we too may be bound to render most abundant thanks to your sincerity.

Given at Veroli, 15 June.

### DCCXLVII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims: that he has written to the Archbishop of Sens and the chapter of Chartres on behalf of Philip, his nephew. (Veroli, 15 June.)

[Ibid., col. 845.]

[Col. 0687A]

The tried faith and steadfast devotion which, from the beginning of this disturbance, you have shown toward the most holy Roman Church and our person with unwavering constancy urge and induce us in every way to desire to love you with pure charity as a most dear brother and an immovable pillar of the Church; to aspire with all our heart’s desire to your honour and advancement; and, so far as we can with God and justice, to grant your petitions a favourable [Col. 0687B] effect. For we might deservedly be reproached with the fault of inhumanity if we should ever consign to oblivion the fervour of the sincerity and constancy you have shown us. Therefore, although it seems burdensome to us to make a request contrary to the reasonable statute of the Church of Chartres which we had confirmed, nevertheless, out of regard for our affection for you, we have written most warmly—something we would not otherwise have done—to our venerable brother the Archbishop of Sens, legate of the Apostolic See, and to the chapter of Chartres, on behalf of our beloved son Philip, your nephew. We are wholly ready and prepared, both in this matter and in others, to defer to your fraternity and to hear your petitions gladly. Yet we admonish and earnestly exhort your prudence [Col. 0687C] to provide for churches and ecclesiastical affairs through mature, discreet, and honourable persons, and, setting aside secular concerns, to devote yourself to the cultivation of virtue and upright conduct; so that, if you are great by birth, you may be proved greater by virtue and character.

Given at Veroli, 15 June.

### DCCXLVIII. To the same: he gives thanks for ten marks of gold given to him and “assigned at Paris to Eustace, master of the Knights Templar”; he commends the brethren of the Knights Templar. (Veroli, 16 June.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0687D]

For the assistance which your generosity took care to give us in ten marks of gold, and for having caused them to be assigned at Paris to our beloved son Eustace, master of the Knights Templar, we give abundant thanks to your liberality. Moreover, for the favour and kindness which your fraternity shows our beloved sons, the brethren of the Knights Templar, we render you thanks. We ask and admonish you that, for piety’s sake, reverence for Blessed Peter and ourselves, and consideration of their religious order, you love, support, and honour these beloved brethren; show them your customary favour and goodwill; and protect and preserve their rights against the assaults of evil men. Thus you may receive our commendation for this [Col. 0688A] and expect an unfailing reward from almighty God.

Given at Veroli, 16 June.

### DCCXLIX. At the request of Gerard, Archbishop of Split, he confirms the rule that journeys made by archbishops to the emperor of Constantinople and to the king of Hungary are not to impose an expense upon the clergy of Split. (Veroli, 20 June.)

[FARLATI, *Illyricum Sacrum*, III, 192.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all the clergy of Split, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever confirmation by the Apostolic See is requested concerning any matter, we ought readily to grant it and to afford favourable support to reasonable requests. Our venerable brother G., your archbishop, appearing before us, stated that when a serious dispute had arisen between you and the laity concerning churches which you hold, and the laity maintained that you ought to give assistance to our archbishop when he was going to the emperor of Constantinople or the king of Hungary, the aforesaid archbishop, having examined and understood your arguments, settled the controversy by a suitable decision. By absolving you from such an exaction, he confirmed by pontifical authority, following the example of Gaudius, the late archbishop of good memory, the liberty which you possessed. We therefore, assenting favourably to your devotion and just requests, confirm this liberty by apostolic authority [Col. 0688C] and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing, decreeing that no one whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the wrath of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Veroli, 20 June.

### DCCL. Bull for the monastery of Saint Stephen of the Valleys, in Saintonge. (Veroli, 25 June.)

[*Gallia Christiana Nova*, II, *Instrumenta*, 476.]

[Col. 0688D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER WILLIAM, abbot of the monastery of Saint Stephen of the Valleys, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever, etc.

Accordingly, beloved sons in the Lord, we willingly assent to your just requests. We receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, be able to acquire by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors [Col. 0689A]. We have thought fit to set these down in their proper names:

The village of Vallibus and the free and unrestricted lordship of that village, with the cemetery of the same place, its tithes, jurisdictions, and all its appurtenances; the right which you have in the village of Arces; the church of Saint Saturninus; the church of Saint Palladius; the church of Saint Augustine; the church of Saint Sulpicius; the church of Saint Eparchius; the church of Saint Martin of Arces; the church of Banella; the church of Saint Peter of Graia; the church of Saint Martin of Bots; and the church of Saint Germanus of Langoira. We also grant that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are [Col. 0689B] excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Furthermore, no one may presume to exact tithes from you of your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals. When a general interdict has been imposed, you may celebrate the divine offices with closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of deception or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall determine ought to be elected from among themselves or from the Church of Maillezais, according to the fear of God [Col. 0689C] and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. In the parish churches which you hold, you may elect priests and present them to the bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them, so that they shall answer to the bishop concerning the care of the people, but to you concerning temporal matters. We also confirm in perpetual right to the same church the lands, meadows, and all other things which the late Arnold of Mauritania and his successors gave your church by pious gift, as well as the meadows, lands, and *terragia* [land-dues] which Arnold Gamno and his provosts—namely Ramnulfus Gunbaldus—gave. We decree therefore that no one whatsoever may, etc.

[Col. 0689D]

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Bernard, bishop of the church of Porto. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint [name omitted in the source] near the Temple of Agrippa.

Given at Veroli by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 25 June, in the third indiction, in the year 1170 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander.

### DCCLI. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims: that he should not permit the goods of the brethren of the Knights Templar to be violated. (Veroli, June–July.)

[MARTEN., *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 846.]

[Col. 0690A]

The brethren of the Knights Templar, because of their religious profession and honourable conduct, and because they fight bravely and vigorously against the Saracens in defence of Christendom, ought to be loved with fuller charity by the prelates of churches and more willingly supported in their rights. But, since we have learned from the report sent by those brethren that there are persons in your province who plunder their goods and are not restrained by the ecclesiastical sword, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, when you receive a complaint from the aforesaid brethren concerning their wrongdoers, [Col. 0690B] you yourself and your bishops admonish and strictly compel those wrongdoers to make due satisfaction to the said brethren, as reason dictates, for the damages and injuries inflicted and the goods taken away. If, after your and your bishops’ admonition, they refuse to do so, bind them with the bond of excommunication; and wherever they may come within your province, have them avoided there as excommunicated persons.

Given at Veroli, 2 July.

### DCCLII. To the same: that he should declare Radulf of Cociaco excommunicated for breaking into the Knights Templar’s chapel. (Veroli, 17 July.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0690C]

From the report of the brethren of the Knights Templar, we have learned that Radulf of Cociaco, after breaking into their chapel, violently dragged a man out of it. Since we can neither may nor ought to leave unpunished so great an outrage of presumption and sacrilege, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, if the matter is as stated, you publicly declare the aforesaid R. excommunicated with lighted candles, and have him avoided by all as an excommunicated person until he has made full satisfaction to the brethren for the injury inflicted and you take care that he is reconciled to the Church by worthy satisfaction.

Given at Veroli, 17 July.

### DCCLIII. To the same: on behalf of a certain knight who had been disinterred. (Veroli, 21 July.)

[Ibid., col. 847.]

[Col. 0690D]

The brethren of the Knights Templar have informed us that, after they had buried a certain knight in their cemetery—one who humbly received penance and the body and blood of Christ before his death—they later removed him from the cemetery out of fear of you, although they maintain that it is false and cannot be proved by any argument that he had been excommunicated. But if he was not excommunicated, and neither committed evil with his son nor consented to it, on account of which you assert that he incurred the bond of excommunication, then before God and [Col. 0691A] the Church he is absolved, and you must not deny him ecclesiastical burial. Therefore we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid knight did not commit with his son the offence for which the son was excommunicated, did not consent to it, and was not otherwise excommunicated, you shall, setting aside all pretexts, have him buried again in the cemetery where he had been buried.

### DCCLIV. To the same: that Guy, a canon of Saint John of Soissons, a repentant apostate, should be received by his abbot. (Veroli, 25 July.)

[Ibid.]

The authority of our office urges us, and the duty of charity requires, to assist the poor and to recall those who have strayed and wandered to the way of truth. Guy, the bearer of this letter, was long a canon under the Rule of Saint Augustine in the church of Blessed John at Soissons, but at the devil’s malicious instigation he abandoned his habit. Having come before us, and promising amendment with tears, he obtained from us letters of intercession to his abbot, that he might receive him. As we have heard, the abbot utterly disregarded them. He has also confessed to us his fault: that he had received priestly ordination without the permission of his abbot. We therefore dismissed him free and absolved. Wherefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you carefully admonish the aforesaid abbot to receive [Col. 0691C] his brother. But if he should perhaps refuse to do this, relying on our authority, do not delay, within thirty days after receipt of our letters and with every excuse and appeal set aside, to bring back to its fold the sheep which has strayed, lest it perish.

Given at Veroli, 25 July.

### DCCLV. To the abbot of Saint Remigius and Fulco, dean of Rheims: he delegates to them the settlement of a dispute between N., a cleric, and certain laymen. (Veroli, 30 July.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 925.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of Saint Remigius and FULCO, dean [Col. 0691D] of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the letters which the provost and chapter of Saint Symphorianus [Note: [Col. 0691D] A college of canons still distinguished at Rheims. Flodoard, book II, chapter 4, on the basilicas to which Archbishop Lando made various bequests: “Likewise, to [Col. 0692D] the basilica of Saint Symphorianus, which is called ‘at the Apostles.’” Jac. SIRM.] sent us, know that the following has been brought to our hearing. A dispute had arisen between N., a cleric, and H. and E. with their associates, concerning a certain rent-paying house of the same church. The aforesaid cleric asserted that it had been given him as alms, while the aforesaid men said that it belonged to them by hereditary right. Those men appealed to our venerable brother Henry [Col. 0692A], Archbishop of Rheims, and the aforesaid N. appealed to our hearing. Since we could not bring the matter to its due conclusion while the parties were absent, we have thought fit to commit it to your discretion. Therefore we command your prudence by apostolic letters that, when you are requested in this matter, you summon the parties before you, diligently hear and examine the arguments on both sides, and bring the case to its proper conclusion, setting aside appeal.

Given at Veroli, 30 July.

### DCCLVI. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims: that he should restrain the exactions of Thomas, burgess of Saint Remigius. (Veroli, 30 July.)

[MARTEN., *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 848.]

[Col. 0692B]

It has been brought to the hearing of the Apostolic See that Thomas, an evil burgess of Saint Remigius, some time ago exacted ten pounds from the mother of Milo, asserting that he had lent them to her husband during his lifetime. After half a year, the same T. urgently demanded twelve pounds from the aforesaid woman as a debt formerly owed him by right, and repeatedly harassed both her and her said son heavily concerning these sums. Because of this wholly unjust harassment, since they said that they owed him no such money, the aforesaid M. appealed to our hearing. Thomas, however, disregarding the appeal, rashly seized him and committed him to prison, keeping him in captivity until he extorted sixty shillings from him. [Col. 0692C] Since we do not wish to leave uncorrected the audacity of such presumption, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that you have all that you ascertain was taken from the aforesaid M. after the appeal restored to him with due satisfaction, without delay or appeal, and have him released in peace; and that you inflict upon Thomas an appropriate penalty for so great an offence. Then diligently hear the case between them concerning the aforesaid money and, setting aside appeal, decide it by its due conclusion.

Given at Veroli, 30 July.

### DCCLVII. To the same: he entrusts to him for settlement the pending case between the abbess of Saint Peter and the abbot of Saint Remigius. (Veroli, 30 July.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0692D]

The abbess of Saint Peter at Rheims informed us that, when a certain man of Saint Remigius had taken in marriage a certain woman belonging to the church of Saint Peter, the abbot of Saint Remigius summoned that man and sought violently to take his property from him on that account. He appealed to our hearing because of this burden. Therefore, committing the matter to your experience, we command your fraternity by [Col. 0693A] apostolic letters that, after summoning both parties before you, you hear the case and decide it by due judgment, while observing this equity: that each church may rejoice that it has obtained its right, and that their lawful marriage may not be dissolved.

Given at Veroli, 30 July.

### DCCLVIII. To the same: concerning Hubald, a burgess of the castle of Saint Remigius, on the violation of the peace. (Veroli, 30 July.)

[Ibid.]

It has come to us that J., the procurator of your archdeacon, exacted from Hubald, burgess of the castle of Saint Remigius, the penalty for bloodshed and breach of the peace, on the ground that he had shed blood and violated the peace. But the same H. wholly denied before J. the charges made against him. John, on the other hand, asserted that the matter was notorious and could not be denied on any ground, since a certain priest said that he had learned in penitential confession from the wounded man that the aforesaid H. had inflicted the wounds upon him. Hubald, however, perceiving that he was being oppressed by J., appealed to our hearing. Therefore, placing great confidence in your prudence and integrity, we delegate the case to your examination. By the authority of this letter we command your fraternity, after summoning the parties before you, to hear the matter carefully and decide it by due judgment, setting aside appeal, so that the aforesaid H. may suffer no loss [Col. 0693C] of his right under your examination.

Given at Veroli, 30 July.

### DCCLIX. Privilege for the church of Saint Andrew of Musciano. (Veroli.)

[LAMI, *Ecclesiae Florentinae Monumenta*, II, 1311.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ANGEL, prior of the church of Saint Andrew of Musciano, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

The authority of our office urges us to labour for the condition of churches and, with the Lord’s help, to provide wisely for their peace and advantage. For it is recognized as worthy and fitting to honour that we, who have been appointed to govern churches, should protect them from the malice of evil men and fortify them by the patronage of Blessed Peter and the Apostolic See. Accordingly, beloved son Angel in the Lord, prior of the aforesaid church, assenting to your reasonable requests, we receive under the guardianship of Blessed Peter and the protection of the Apostolic See the church of Saint Andrew of Musciano, over which, by God’s appointment, you are known to preside, and confirm it by the page of our writing. We decree therefore that whatever possessions and goods the aforesaid church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future be able to acquire, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors [Col. 0694A]. We have thought fit to set down the following in their proper names:

The estate on which your church is founded, with its appurtenances; everything which you possess in Poio and Campo Silvano, and in Campo de Navilo; everything which you possess in Villa Obscura, in Costa de Musinuli, Fontanella, Diffranico, Rio Pascoli, Castagnito, Villanova, and in [lacuna]; and in Saint Paul and Piscina; everything which you possess in Vallese and in the whole village of Tornioni, in Lama de Cannito; everything which you possess in the places called Godesoli, on the hill of Montilli and at Poio de Novole; everything which the Galleffi and the men of Carcarelli with their associates hold from you; everything which those men generally called “of Lebiano” hold from you; and everything which you possess in Plano de Septimo. In particular, everything which you justly and reasonably possess in the church of Saint Peter of Soliciano and its appurtenances, the vineyard which you hold there, and everything which you possess at Lisceto, Caselle, Rospaldi, Strata, Muricia, and Carcarelli, and any other things which you reasonably possess in the aforesaid or other places.

Moreover, we confirm the tithes of the estates of your patrons, which they possess, or which others possess through them, or may acquire in future, throughout the territory of the parish church of Saint Julian at Septimo, the parish church of Saint Martin at Brozzi, the parish church of Saint Vincent at Peza, throughout the whole valley of Greve and at Villanova, throughout the whole chapel of Saint Paul, and at Casignano—excepting the *Mosiis* of Cucillatico [Col. 0694C], the tithes of which they must pay to the Florentine canonry. We also confirm all tithes of the estates formerly belonging to Bentius, son of Petrus of Radda, situated at Godosole, Saint Paul, Casignano, and other places and localities throughout the parish of the church already named; further, all tithes of newly cleared land from the woods of the aforesaid patrons, wherever they are or shall be cultivated, and from all other woods whatsoever which are or shall be cultivated throughout the whole territory of that church, as you have held them peacefully for forty years past, by apostolic authority.

Likewise, we confirm all first-fruits of the people of the aforesaid church and the bequests reasonably conferred upon you by God’s faithful. We grant that the burial of your patrons and others who resolve to be buried among you shall be free, and that no one may oppose their devotion and last will, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Upon the death of you, the present prior of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any craft of deception or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, determine should be elected according to God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine. We also confirm to you, by the page of this present writing, the ordering and administration of your church and the presentation of your clerics [Col. 0695A] to be ordained by the bishop of Florence, so long as canonical order is observed in that church. We decree therefore, etc.

Given at Veroli by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, in the third indiction, in the year 1170 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### DCCLX. He appoints Henry, Archbishop of Rheims, and P., abbot of Saint Lucian, judges between Adelelm and his wife. (Veroli, 2 September.)

[MARTEN., *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 850.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, and [Col. 0695B] beloved son P., abbot of Saint Lucian, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0695] Saint Lucian’s monastery is a noteworthy monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict near Beauvais; it still survives under the Congregation of Saint-Maur.]

We have thought fit to commit to your discretion and determination the case known to be pending concerning the marriage of Adelelm and his wife. Therefore we command your prudence, in which we have full confidence, by apostolic letters that, when requested in this matter, you summon the aforesaid A. and his wife before you. Since, as has been represented to us, A. and his wife are known to have been bound by a sentence of excommunication after an appeal was made to us, absolve them from the bond of anathema by our authority. And because, as we have learned from the writings and testimony of religious persons, those attacking A.’s marriage are found to have been moved by the poison of hatred and the ardour of greed rather than by love of justice—since, while B., A.’s brother, still lived, no question whatever was raised concerning his marriage, wholly similar to A.’s—within twenty days of receiving this letter, on our behalf, cause A.’s marriage to remain in its established state. Carefully observe that it is safer for some persons joined together contrary to human ordinances to remain together than, on any pretext, to separate those whom God has joined together. If both of you cannot be present, the one of you shall nevertheless proceed to hear the case.

Given at Veroli, 2 October.

### DCCLXI. Privilege for the church of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem. (Veroli, 9 September.)

[ROZIÈRE, *Cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre*, 296.]

[Col. 0695D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Peter, prior of the Holy Sepulchre, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

Whenever we are asked for something known to accord with religion and honour, it is fitting that we grant it gladly and afford suitable support to the desires of those who ask. Accordingly, beloved sons in the Lord [Col. 0696A], we assent to your just requests and, following the example of our predecessors of pious memory—Honorius, Innocent, Celestine, Lucius, and Eugenius, Roman pontiffs—we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that church according to God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future be able to acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors [Col. 0696B]. We have thought fit to set down the following in their proper names:

The half of all offerings that belong or are brought to the Lord’s Sepulchre; but of wax the church shall always have two shares, one for the church’s lights, the other for the canons’ service; only the third shall accrue to the use of our venerable brother Amalric, your patriarch, and his successors. Likewise, all offerings of the life-giving Cross, which is assigned to your custody, except only on Good Friday, or when necessity compels that same patriarch or his successors to carry it on campaign; likewise [Col. 0696C] the high altar situated in your choir, together with all offerings accruing to it; also the prison and altar with everything offered there; the altar of Saint Peter and Saint Stephen, and the Invention [of the Cross], with all its altars and offerings; the parish altar at the head of the Holy Sepulchre, with its offerings; the chair behind the high altar, and everything offered there, whether at the patriarch’s hand or foot, or when he celebrates Mass at any of the aforesaid altars; also all offerings of the compass [compassus], which is in the middle of your choir; the square between the church gate and the columns, and the other square between those same columns and the Hospital of Saint John, as it extends in length and breadth; furthermore, [Col. 0696D] the houses, shops, lands, and whatever you possess in the quarter of the church and patriarch, and may henceforth be able justly to acquire; and all other houses, shops, and lands which you possess within or outside Jerusalem. Likewise, all the ovens of Jerusalem, except two, one belonging to the Hospital and one to the Latina; and especially that one which the patriarch restored to you on the testimony of Peter, Archbishop of Tyre, and which he had held from you on loan. Further, the church and cemetery outside David’s Gate beside the road leading to Bethlehem; also half of that estate which King Baldwin I gave to the aforesaid church of the Lord’s Sepulchre in exchange for the bishopric [Col. 0697A] of Bethlehem; all tithes of the city of Jerusalem and of the entire bishopric, except the tithes of funde [term/read­ing uncertain], reasonably granted to you by Arnulf of good memory, formerly patriarch of Jerusalem, as you now possess them peacefully; and likewise all other tithes which you may lawfully be able hereafter to acquire in that city and bishopric—we confirm these to you and to your said church by apostolic authority.

Neapoliterra, which Amalric, illustrious king of Jerusalem, gave you in the new borough; the church which you began to build there, with a cemetery, by concession of our venerable brother Amalric, patriarch of Jerusalem; and whatever right [Col. 0697B] you have at Neapolis and in its territory. [We confirm] the twenty-one villages which Duke Godfrey gave, with their appurtenances, to your church; likewise the settlements you have built—namely Greater Machomaria, Lesser Machomaria, and Bethsuri—and all others which you are to build where Latins shall dwell, with churches and the full integrity of justice and parochial right; likewise Thecue with all its appurtenances, and the church of the Quarantine with all its appurtenances; Geladia; the land which you bought from John Gomman; and all villages with their appurtenances which you bought from Hugh of Ibelin. [We confirm] the church of Saint Peter at Joppa, with the full integrity of its honour and dignity, as you now peacefully possess it; and the tithe [Col. 0697C] which you receive throughout that entire county from the king, religious persons, and all Christians; whatever right you have at Ascalon and in its territory; whatever right you have, under the authority and lordship of the lord of Assur, at Caesarea and throughout its whole archbishopric; the castle of Feniculus, the house near Caiphas, Jebul, Lecara; and likewise everything which you reasonably possess or shall possess throughout the archbishopric of Nazareth, the bishopric of Acre, and the entire archbishopric of Tyre; and all, moreover, which you have or may hereafter, God granting, lawfully acquire throughout the patriarchate and kingdom of Jerusalem. Likewise, whatever right you have at Mount Pilgrim and throughout the bishopric of Tripoli, and whatever you have in Antioch and throughout its patriarchate and principality, or may hereafter, God granting, [Col. 0697D] lawfully acquire. Further, all possessions which you hold overseas in the kingdom of the king of Sicily, namely in Sicily itself, Calabria, and all Apulia: first, the church of the Holy Sepulchre and Saint Lawrence at Brindisi, with all its appurtenances; at Barletta, the church of the Holy Sepulchre with all its appurtenances; the church at Troia with all its appurtenances; at Benevento, the church of Saint Theodore with all its appurtenances; whatever right you have, or shall have, at Rome and throughout its territory, in Tuscany, and in all Italy; moreover, everything which the aforesaid church of the Lord’s Sepulchre is known lawfully to possess, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s bounty, acquire throughout the whole kingdom of France and all provinces lawfully subject to it, as well as in all kingdoms and counties of Spain, or anywhere in the lands beyond the mountains [Col. 0698A]. We likewise confirm in perpetuity to you and your successors all the ancient and reasonable customs of your church.

Certainly, concerning these and your other possessions and goods, you shall have free power, though by common counsel, to dispose of them for the honour of God and the advancement of your church. Upon the death or sea-crossing of the patriarch of Jerusalem, the prior and canons then serving in the same church shall faithfully guard and administer, as is just, the patriarch’s house and household, and all things belonging to his right, within and without, until another has been appointed according to the Lord, or until he returns, [Col. 0698B] should he have crossed the sea.

Moreover, we confirm to you one half of the possessions held in common between you, as in England, Denmark, Germany, Poland, Ruthenia, Avagia, Hungary, Constantinople, and throughout all its territory, in which you are bound to bear one half of the expenses. We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations whatsoever; but that all things shall be preserved unimpaired and entire, for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right and due reverence of the patriarch of Jerusalem. If anyone therefore in the future, [Col. 0698C] etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, John, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Boso, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. [Col. 0698D] I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of Saint Vitalis, of the title of Vestina. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Veroli, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman [Col. 0699A] Church, on the fifth day before the Ides of September, in the third indiction, in the year 1170 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

DCCLXII. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—If he seems to have acted too leniently in Thomas’s cause, this arose because he believed that patience must be employed. He suspends Roger of York from episcopal rank; he anathematizes Jocelin of Salisbury and Gilbert of London, who took part in crowning the new king. (Veroli, 10 September.)

*Letters of Saint Thomas*, ed. Giles, II, 32.

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, [Col. 0699B] greeting and apostolic blessing.

Among the many anxieties which, owing to the evil of the times, press themselves upon our mind, your suffering, which you have undertaken in defence of ecclesiastical liberty, troubles us greatly: for we earnestly desire to assist you, yet the obstacle of clamorous causes on every side delays our purpose. For where many dangers rush upon us, the mind cannot easily determine to which side it ought rather to incline, especially when it cannot be known from which course it may gain greater advantage or avoid greater harm and danger.

For if sailors themselves are sometimes rendered so uncertain by conflicting winds that they cannot agree among themselves whether they should proceed to their intended destination [Col. 0699C] or be carried back to the harbour they had left, it is neither surprising nor blameworthy if, on this great and wide sea—where creeping things without number impede our course, and where dangers are feared not so much for bodies and bodily merchandise as for souls and spiritual virtues—it does not readily occur to him who steers the ship of the Church to which side he should rather give assent. For divergent counsels proceed from divergent wills: one view appears right to him who advances a particular cause, another to him who must provide and take counsel for the common good.

Therefore, dearest brother, if we seem to have acted too leniently in your cause and that of the English Church, and have not answered your petitions according to your wish, [Col. 0699D] this has not arisen because we do not believe that the cause itself is common to us with you and the English Church, or because we wish to fail you in any respect, but because we believed patience should be employed, so that we might overcome evil with good. We also feared that, should a greater schism arise in the Church, it might be imputed to our severity.

But now, because the disturbers of peace and oppressors of ecclesiastical liberty seem to be moved by no compunction to correct past evils, but rather, drawing sins like a long rope, rage ever more fiercely both to your injury and to the oppression of the Church of Canterbury, and seem almost to have cut off from you every hope of repentance, we direct canonical sentence against our brother Roger, Archbishop of York, [Col. 0700A] and the remaining bishops who took an oath to preserve those wicked customs and are instigators of such great evil; and we suspend them from episcopal rank. But the bishops of Salisbury and London, who seemed to owe a greater debt of gratitude and are said to have repaid favour with ingratitude, if they gave their presence and service to the crowning of the new king contrary to the dignity of the Church of Canterbury, we restore to the sentence of anathema from which they had been released.

Certainly, the bishop of Rochester, your vicar, who ought to have contended more steadfastly for your right and that of your church; Geoffrey Ridel, Archdeacon of Canterbury, who, as is said, rages more grievously against his mother [Church], [Col. 0700B] and scorns the sentence of excommunication pronounced against him by you—which we hold valid and confirm by apostolic authority; his vicar Robert; and G . . . . . . , bishop of Saint Asaph, a contemner of our command, and David, archdeacon of the same church—we leave to your authority and power, so that, if something more severe must be decreed against them, you may carry it out by the power entrusted to you, the obstacle of appeal being removed. Whatever you shall canonically do concerning their punishment, we, with the Lord as author, shall hold ratified and firm.

And these measures seem sufficient for the present. But if we see such obstinacy in evildoers that they are not moved to repentance even by this penalty, then, with the Lord as author, we shall still take up against them the armour of faith and exercise, to the degree we judge expedient, pontifical zeal for the house of the Lord. [Col. 0700C] Furthermore, since Solomon teaches us that in every matter we must attend to the opportunity of the time, and we have heard that the enemies of the Church, who also lie in wait against the kingdom of France, have invaded the city of Mâcon, you are to know that it is our will and counsel that you seek the advice of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Franks, concerning these matters, and proceed, in accordance with his will, to send our letters; lest, if perhaps—God avert it—some disturbance should arise in his kingdom, your cause and that of the Church be made more burdensome by the kingdom’s disturbance, or, if peace should be restored to you and the Church, you might consider it liable to be disturbed [Col. 0700D] by this event.

Given at Veroli, on the fourth day before the Ides of September.

DCCLXIII. To several bishops of England.—He suspends from every rank those who took part, contrary to the rights of Canterbury, in crowning the king’s son; moreover, he anathematizes the bishops of London and Salisbury. (Ferentino, 16 September.)

*Ibid.*, p. 82.

ALEXANDER, pope, to the bishops of London, Salisbury, Exeter, Chester, Rochester, Saint Asaph, and Llandaff.

You ought, when our dearest son Henry, your king, first proposed to you under the pretext of royal dignity and fealty the enactments which he also demanded in writing and requested to be confirmed by oath—enactments which plainly enough oppressed both the liberty of the Church and the authority of the priestly office—to have raised your eyes to heaven and stood up in opposition for the house of the Lord, so that ecclesiastical dignity might not be shipwrecked before your eyes while you remained silent. Indeed, if any zeal for righteousness arising from pastoral care had possessed you, you would have recognized that you were set over nations and kingdoms in order that, in great matters and small, you should uproot the plantings of vices and graft in the shoot pleasing to the Lord.

But now, because reverence for an earthly ruler has prevailed more with you than fear of the Lord and the honour of episcopal dignity, you have, to our grief, despised your birthright for a paltry dish of lentils, like Esau; and you have fulfilled in yourselves what Jeremiah laments concerning the Jewish people: [Col. 0701B] “The elders sat upon the ground; they kept silent; the virgin daughters of Judah sprinkled their heads with ashes” (*Lamentations* 2).

Certainly, if, terrified by threats and intimidation, you proceeded to accept and confirm those wicked customs by oath, ought you not, after so long an interval, to have resumed priestly steadfastness and, with repentance for the former transgression, protested in a priestly manner against such enormities? Yet you have added obstinacy to a detestable deed: you persist in observing those usurpations, and seem so to follow the will of the aforesaid king in oppressing the Church that ecclesiastical laws appear, as though outlawed, already to have been banished from a great part of your kingdom.

And we indeed have waited until now, hoping that divine grace might visit the prince’s heart either through your office or through its own inspiration and our waiting, and make him a lover of heavenly glory rather than his own. For this too had frequently been urged upon us and, given the state of the times, seemed highly desirable: that his harshness should be softened by patience and gentleness rather than otherwise. But while we awaited correction and repentance for the past, he altered nothing of his former severity; instead, he persists immovably in those wicked customs.

For a considerable time now, your venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, because he wished to oppose those usurpations—although earlier, through weakness of the flesh, he had appeared to consent to them—has been exiled from the church entrusted to him, together with his clerics and kinsfolk. You recognize this even while we are silent; and would that you sympathized with him with that affection of charity with which you ought to sympathize in such a cause. Yet you have not only withheld from him fraternal aid, but have added to the pain of his wounds. For when the said king recently wished to have his son crowned, although this is asserted by ancient right to belong to the Archbishop of Canterbury, you, setting aside the authority and reverence due to the aforesaid brother of ours and to his church, furnished your favour and service for that coronation, without having given or, as is said, even demanded any assurance that the Church’s liberty would be preserved. Indeed, you even allowed [Col. 0702A] an oath to be exacted from him for the preservation of the customs of the realm. . . .

Certainly, we have laboured repeatedly for their reconciliation through letters and persons sent from our side, and through many other men deemed worthy of being heard; but of whatever hope has been given us, we have thus far been able to bring back nothing but an empty display of words. We do not say this, however, as though, while we were still in France, we had not experienced that same king as generous and devoted toward us in many respects. But for that reason we ought not to refrain from opposing ourselves with zeal for righteousness to such great transgressions, for the glory of God and for his salvation and ours.

Now, therefore, because the faults of laypeople look to none more than to idle and negligent prelates, who often foster a great pestilence when they neglect to apply the necessary remedy, and because after long waiting you rise with no sorrow against yourselves and no fervour against those wicked usurpations, by the power committed to us by God and the authority of the Apostolic See, which, though unworthy, we serve by God’s ordinance, we suspend you from every episcopal rank. But those among you—the bishops of London and Salisbury—who, because of the favour obtained from us, ought in accordance with our expectation to have laboured more for reconciliation and refrained from burdening the aforesaid archbishop, if they lent the service of their favour to the said coronation, we restore to the sentence of anathema and command that they be avoided as excommunicated persons.

Concerning the bishop of Rochester and Geoffrey Ridel, Archdeacon of Canterbury, who, although they stand under greater obligation to the Church of Canterbury, are said to hold the aforesaid archbishop in less reverence and honour—and one of them, namely the bishop of Rochester, attended that coronation, while the other scorns the sentence of excommunication pronounced against him by the aforesaid archbishop—we command you, appeal having been removed, to observe what he shall canonically decree. For we determine that the more grievously they seem to offend, the more severely they are to be punished. Moreover, whatever the same archbishop has decreed, or shall hereafter reasonably decree, against Robert, vicar of the Archdeacon of Canterbury and a contemner of his sentence, we command to be observed firmly and inviolably, no appeal being allowed to aid him. [Col. 0702D] But the clerics of Count Hugh—Nicholas, Thomas, William, and the rest—who, while knowingly excommunicated by the aforesaid archbishop, have presumed to celebrate divine offices, if this is so, we command to be bound by the bond of anathema and that their company be avoided as that of excommunicated persons.

Given at Ferentino, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October.

DCCLXIV. To Roger, Archbishop of York, and Hugh, Bishop of Durham.—Of the same purport. (Ferentino, 16 September.)

*Ibid.*, p. 48.

ALEXANDER, pope, to ROGER, Archbishop of York, and the Bishop of Durham.

Although you are commendable and pleasing to us in many respects, and we embrace you with the arms of sincere charity, we nevertheless ought not on that account to omit to call you to account for, and correct with zeal for righteousness, those deeds which, when committed and uncorrected, bring forth death. For the Lord says through the prophet: “If, when I say to the wicked man, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not announce it to him or speak to him, he indeed shall die in his sin, but I shall require his blood from your hand” (*Ezekiel* 3).

The oppression of the English Church and the diminution of its liberty, which is known to have been brought about by your king, whether of his own motion or, rather, at the suggestion of others, has long afflicted our mind greatly and caused us no small anxiety and grief. For whereas he ought to have considered correcting those things wrongly done by his predecessors, he instead, adding transgressions to transgressions, both enacted and confirmed under the pretext of royal dignity such wicked statutes that under them the Church’s liberty perishes and the ordinances of apostolic men, so far as he is able, are stripped of their force. Nor did he believe it sufficient that the divine laws should suffer silence and suspension through him in the kingdom of England, unless he also transmitted sin to his heirs and caused his kingdom for a long time to sit without ephod and without shoulder-piece.

Thus he caused those wicked usurpations, without any exception, to be confirmed by the oath of you and your other brothers and fellow bishops, and judged that anyone who wished to dissent from those wicked customs should be punished as an enemy. This is shown by the exile of the venerable Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury; it is also demonstrated by the lamentable proscription of his clerics and kinsfolk, even of those who, still hanging from their mother’s breasts, cried in their cradles. Fear of death is instilled if anyone should raise his mind to this end: that he might wish, against those enactments, to obey the divine laws.

We ourselves, whose judgment ought to have corrected or punished those transgressions, were urgently pressed, under the pretext of unsettled times, to confirm them; and no little effort was made with us to induce us to confer the authority of the Apostolic See upon those usurpations before they had even been set forth to us. This happened at the beginning. But as time went on, when the aforesaid archbishop was in exile in fulfilment of his pastoral office and repeatedly sought from our office the customary aid of the Roman Church, we sent to the said king some of the better and greater among our brethren, and we also sent other ecclesiastical persons. We thought that his hardness would be broken by our humility and gentleness, and that Solomon’s saying would come to pass: “By patience a ruler is softened, and a gentle tongue breaks wrath” (*Proverbs* 15).

But the king, deceiving our forbearance by the manifold skill of his envoys, seems to have hardened his heart against our warnings to such a degree that he neither ceases to rage against the aforementioned archbishop nor permits anything to be diminished from those perverse statutes. Indeed, he also afflicts the Church of Canterbury with very great loss of its possessions and despoils it, in its very ecclesiastical ministry, of its ancient dignity. For recently, wishing to have his son crowned, he disregarded that same archbishop, to whom this office is known by ancient right to belong, and through your hand, brother archbishop, had the crown of the kingdom placed upon him in another province.

At that coronation, no assurance concerning preservation of the Church’s liberty was given according to custom or, as they say, required; instead, it is said that an oath was confirmed that he must preserve forever inviolate the customs of the realm, which they call ancestral and under which the dignity of the Church is endangered. Though the violence of the aforesaid king deeply troubles us in this matter, we can be moved still more by the weakness of you and your other fellow bishops, who—what we say in sorrow—“became rams without horns; you went forth without strength before the face of the pursuer” (*Lamentations* 1).

And even if it might perhaps have been lawful for you, brother archbishop, to act in your own province, yet how it could have been lawful for you to do so in another province, and especially that of the man who chose to go into exile for righteousness and, almost alone, to depart and give glory to God, we can find neither by reason nor in the ordinances of the holy Fathers. If anyone should object in excuse of so great a transgression that many grave and enormous acts are committed in other kingdoms as well, we may truly answer that we have not yet found any kingdom fallen into such contempt for the divine law as to have caused such manifest enormities to be sanctioned by written instruments and the oaths of bishops—unless one shamelessly alleges what schismatics later committed, after being cut off from the communion of believers, in unheard-of and condemnable pride.

Therefore, because, according to the prophet’s word, something more perverse than in all other provinces has occurred among you in these usurpations, and after those most wicked customs were confirmed by oath, you did not further take up the shield of faith to stand for the house of the Lord on the day of battle, but “laid your body upon the ground, that you might become a way for the passer-by,” lest, if we remain silent longer, we be entangled with you in the sentence of condemnation on the day of judgment: by the authority of the most holy Roman Church, in whose service we minister by God’s will, we suspend you from every office of episcopal rank. We hope that, placed at least under discipline and paternal correction, you may at length return to your senses and strive to defend the Church’s liberty. [Col. 0705A] But if not even thus you resume zeal for the episcopal office, we shall yet, with the Lord as author, do what is incumbent upon us.

Take care lest what was said to a certain man through the prophet be said to you: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I shall reject you from ministering to me as priest” (*Hosea* 4). For since we see that we hold, by God’s disposal as it pleased him, the place of that Peter whom neither blows nor chains could restrain from preaching God’s word, we ought not, in uncertain expectation of peace, to put away in a napkin the money of the divine word entrusted to us and keep it bound up until the hour for gaining profit gradually passes and the creditor comes to call us to account for its return.

Given at Ferentino, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October.

DCCLXV. To Rotrou, Archbishop of Rouen.—That he should see to the delivery of his preceding letters to the Archbishop of York and the bishops of England, and inquire carefully whether Henry, Bishop of Bayeux, and Froger, Bishop of Sées, attended the coronation. (Ferentino, September [?])

*Ibid.*, p. 64.

ALEXANDER, pope, to ROTROU, Archbishop of Rouen.

Since those who hold higher rank ought to be so fortified by strength of virtue and faith that, for righteousness and the defence of ecclesiastical liberty, they set themselves up as an impregnable wall, we grieve exceedingly [Col. 0705C] that reverence for an earthly prince has prevailed more among the bishops of England than the honour of episcopal dignity. They not only swore to the customs proposed to them by the king, contrary to ecclesiastical reason, but also placed the crown upon his son, to the detriment of the dignity and right of our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, and of his church.

Because we can neither can nor ought to leave so grave and enormous an offence unpunished, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, and order you in virtue of obedience, to send, without delay or excuse, through your messenger and have delivered the letters which we address to the Archbishop of York and the bishops of England. Furthermore, make careful inquiry whether the bishops of Bayeux and Sées attended the coronation of which we have spoken. If you find that they did attend, inform us, so that we may punish them.

Certainly, compel the aforesaid bishop of Sées—who, neglecting the ministry of God, has, as is said, become like a courtier, a despoiler of country people and avenger of crimes—if this is so, to renounce either royal service or his bishopric. For if courtiers are forbidden to be promoted to holy orders, much less should those who are established in holy orders be admitted among courtiers.

DCCLXVI. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, and Gilbert, Bishop of London.—That they deliver the archdeaconry of Derby to Master W. de Lega. (Ferentino, 1 October.)

*Letters of Gilbert Foliot*, II, 67.

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers T., Archbishop of Canterbury, and G., Bishop of London, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Seated in the chair of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by the decision of divine dispensation, we ought so to administer everything in God’s Church that no one, so far as lies within us, may be compelled to suffer long through want of justice, but that each person may, through our care, obtain the fulfilment of his right. Now our beloved son Master W. de Lega, bearer of this letter, appearing before our apostolic presence, stated to us that Walter of good memory, formerly Bishop of Coventry, canonically invested him in and granted him the archdeaconry of Derby with its liberties, by book and golden ring.

Therefore, since we wish what is reasonably ordained by our brother bishops to remain in unshaken force, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this assertion is supported by truth, you shall, without delay, deliver and assign the aforesaid archdeaconry with its appurtenances to the said master. If one of you cannot be present to carry out this business because of urgent necessity, the other shall nonetheless proceed in the matter.

Given at Ferentino, on the Kalends of October.

DCCLXVII. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, and the other bishops of England.—That divine offices are not to be celebrated in the lands of excommunicated persons. (Anagni, 8 October.)

*Letters of Saint Thomas*, ed. Giles, II, 31.

ALEXANDER, pope, to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury, and the other bishops of England.

Because the enormities and crimes of the wicked are not opposed with pontifical authority as they ought to be, the insolence and audacity of evildoers increase daily, fear of God is despised, and due reverence and devotion are denied to churches and ecclesiastical persons. Since we must oppose such great evils by the priestly ministry and apply vigilant foresight and care lest they grow, we command your brotherhood through apostolic letters, and by commanding we order, that you publicly declare deprived by our authority of every ecclesiastical office and benefice all priests, deacons, and subdeacons who knowingly celebrated divine offices contrary to our special interdict or that of their bishops, or who henceforth celebrate divine offices in the lands of excommunicated persons while those excommunicated persons are present, or compel anyone to celebrate them, until they come to us and receive [Col. 0707A] our command. If they are contemptuous of our command in this matter, excommunicate them. And if excommunicated persons sing [the offices], seize those whom you can apprehend and confine them in monasteries, so that they may there perform perpetual penance and their punishment may be a warning to others.

Given at Anagni, on the eighth day before the Ides of October.

DCCLXVIII. To Louis, King of the Franks.—That he should not communicate with excommunicated persons. (Anagni, October [?])

*Ibid.*, p. 142.

ALEXANDER, pope, to LOUIS, King of the Franks.

[Col. 0707B] It is recognized as especially conducive to the welfare of kings and princes that, the more richly they are adorned with power, dignity, and the gift of divine grace, the more zealously and devoutly they should carry out those things that pertain to works of piety and justice; that they should distinguish churches and ecclesiastical persons, in whom God is especially honoured, with reverence and honour alike; and that they should observe the ordinances of the holy Fathers with a more devout mind and purer heart.

We do not believe that it escapes your royal discernment how wicked and detestable it is, and how forbidden by the Church and the holy Fathers, knowingly to associate with excommunicated persons and to foster the evil of their perversity—especially since those who knowingly extend favour to persons stained by their own fault and crimes make themselves participants in their condemnation. For excommunication, in the manner of leprosy which corrupts the whole body, defiles and disfigures the entire person. Lepers, as is read in the Old Testament, were cast outside the camp. In like manner, excommunicated persons must be altogether excluded from the fellowship and communion of God’s faithful.

Therefore, lest your royal serenity be contaminated even slightly by the filth of such great corruption, or the authority of ecclesiastical censure be diminished through your occasion, we ask, admonish, counsel, and exhort the prudence of your discernment, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of your sins: that you shall in no way knowingly associate—especially in food and drink, prayer, or the kiss of peace—with those whom you know from the prelates of churches to be excommunicated and separated from the communion of the Church; nor, out of personal affection or under the pretext of any embassy which he may conduct to you, furnish them favour or the privileges of familiarity. And firmly and devoutly observe the sentences of archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches, so that you may thereby deserve to receive eternal reward from almighty God, and the shamefulness and wickedness of evildoers may not be able to stain the virtue of your integrity.

DCCLXIX. To William, Archbishop of Sens, and Rotrou, Archbishop of Rouen.—That, under pain of censures, they cause the peace which the king of England promised in words to be carried out. (Anagni, October 9.)

[Ibid., p. 72.]

[Col. 0708A]

Pope ALEXANDER to the Archbishops of Sens and Rouen.

Whenever we recall to mind the troubles, straits, anxieties, burdens, and afflictions which our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, endured with unconquered fortitude and bore with an even mind for the honour and liberty of the Church, our spirit rejoices anew at the constancy of his admirable virtue and patience; and day by day the affection of our love toward him grows ever greater. Therefore, wishing to provide him, as a most dear brother and a principal member of the Church, with a remedy of fitting consolation amid his various troubles and pressures, and desiring more wisely to provide for the salvation of our dearest son in Christ, Henry, illustrious king of the English—who sinned the more grievously in proportion as he inflicted greater persecutions and troubles upon that archbishop and more heavily burdened Christ, nor can he make adequate expiation for so great an offence unless what was taken away is restored—we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, and enjoin you in virtue of obedience, that within twenty days after receiving these letters you diligently approach that king on our behalf, earnestly admonish and exhort him to fulfil in deed the peace which he made verbally with the same archbishop.

Moreover, you shall urge the king thereafter to restore everything taken away, repair the damage inflicted, and utterly cut off the wicked and detestable customs. But if within thirty days after your admonition he refuses to bring to completion the peace which he established and promised, you shall prohibit throughout all his lands on this side of the sea the celebration of all divine offices, save baptism for infants and penance for the dying, setting aside every impediment of appeal; and you shall cause that sentence to be observed inviolably until fitting satisfaction has been made. If either one of you, some necessity preventing him, cannot or will not take part in carrying this out—which we would not wish, nor would it be expedient—the other shall nevertheless carry out what has been said.

Given at Anagni, the seventh day before the Ides of October.

DCCLXX. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—Concerning the renewed excommunication of those excommunicated persons who, though absolved by the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Nevers, have not restored possessions taken from the Church of Canterbury. (Anagni, October 9.)

[Ibid., p. 28.]

Pope ALEXANDER to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

If the enormities and crimes of the wicked were left unpunished, the virtue of the good could readily succumb, and vices would seem, with due order overturned, to prevail over virtues. But it was established and ordained by the very Creator of the world that virtues should hold pre-eminence and always occupy the higher place and order.

Accordingly, we commanded our venerable brothers, the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Nevers, by our letters that, once they were certain that peace between you, brother archbishop, and our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the English, was to be restored, they should absolve, according to the form prescribed to them, those whom you had excommunicated. But because we doubt whether those whom your excommunication had bound had made satisfaction according to the terms of our mandate, lest they be able to glory in their malice and vainly congratulate themselves, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters and enjoin you in virtue of obedience: unless those who were excommunicated have obtained, through the aforesaid archbishop and bishop, or through someone acting by their command, the benefit of absolution according to our prescribed form, and have, within twenty days after your admonition and that of your people, surrendered the churches and possessions of the Church of Canterbury and of all its dependants, together with all revenues received from them, then within fifteen days after our letters on this matter have reached the aforesaid archbishop and bishop, you shall treat them, restored to the same sentence, as excommunicated persons, all excuse and appeal being set aside; and throughout your parishes you shall cause them to be avoided as publicly excommunicated persons, until they have fully performed all the aforesaid requirements.

If any clerics among them presume to celebrate the divine offices, to attend their celebration, or to compel any priest to celebrate, declare them deprived of every office and benefice, and cause them to be declared deprived throughout the whole land of the king. If they are laymen, excepting the king and his son, who presume such acts, give them a stern warning and instil fear and terror into them: unless they desist, they shall be visited with a heavier punishment, and until they make satisfaction they shall be excluded from giving testimony.

Given at Anagni, the seventh day before the Ides of October.

DCCLXXI. To Rotrou, Archbishop of Rouen, and Bernard, Bishop of Nevers.—On the same matter. (Anagni, October 9.)

[Ibid., p. 63.]

[Col. 0709D]

Pope ALEXANDER to ROTROU, Archbishop of Rouen, and BERNARD, Bishop of Narbonne.

Having heard and understood that our dearest son in Christ, Henry, illustrious king of England, inspired by divine grace and overcome by the urgency of our admonitions and exhortations, has restored his favour and peace to our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, we have rejoiced and exulted greatly. From this, with God’s help, we believe that great good and growth will result for the universal Church.

Nevertheless, since certain persons, clerics as well as laymen, established in his kingdom, favouring an earthly prince more than the eternal King, unlawfully and outrageously occupied both churches and other rights of the Church of Canterbury, and were therefore bound by the archbishop with the bond of excommunication—persons whom we ordered your brotherhood to absolve under a definite form if there were certain hope that peace would be completed—we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters and enjoin you in virtue of obedience: unless those who were excommunicated and have been absolved by you, or at your command, according to our form, surrender within twenty days after the admonition of the said Archbishop of Canterbury and his people, whether they have peace or not, the churches and possessions of the Church of Canterbury and of all its dependants, together with all revenues received from them, you shall, fortified by our authority and setting aside every excuse, restore them within fifteen days after you have been required concerning this matter to the same sentence in which they were formerly held, until they have fulfilled all the aforesaid requirements.

If any clerics among them presume to celebrate the divine offices, to attend their celebration, or to compel any priest to celebrate, declare them deprived of every office and benefice, and cause them to be declared deprived throughout the whole land of the king. If they are laymen, excepting the king and his son, who presume such acts, give them a stern warning and instil fear and terror into them: unless they desist, they shall be visited with a heavier punishment, and until they make satisfaction they shall be excluded from giving testimony.

Given at Anagni, the seventh day before the Ides of October.

DCCLXXII. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—Concerning the coronation of the son of Henry, king of the English. (Anagni, October.)

[Ibid., p. 30.]

Pope ALEXANDER to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

Carefully considering the constancy of virtue and faith and the courageous spirit which you are known to have assumed in preserving the liberty of your Church, we willingly offer you, as a most dear brother, counsel and assistance in matters known to concern the preservation and advancement of your Church. Against those who endeavour to diminish or disturb the rights and dignity of that Church, we desire with diligent concern to furnish the protection of apostolic guardianship.

We have heard and learned by certain report that the Archbishop of York, contrary to our prohibition and interdict, placed the crown upon Henry, son of the illustrious king of the English, within your province. Since you maintain that by this act the right and dignity of your Church have been gravely and outrageously impaired, and since we wish in this matter to provide both for you and for that Church, we decree by apostolic authority that the act of the aforesaid archbishop can in no way hereafter generate prejudice against you, so as to prevent you from holding the possession of the coronation and anointing of the kings of England in the manner in which your predecessors and that Church are known to have held it for the past forty years.

Given at Anagni, the twentieth day before the Kalends of October.

[Note: [Col. 0711D] Thus in the text, but erroneously.]

DCCLXXIII. To Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.—Concerning censure to be imposed upon the king unless he grants full peace together with restoration of possessions. (Segni, October 13.)

[Ibid., p. 26.]

Pope ALEXANDER to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

We are oppressed by anxiety of heart and bitterness whenever we recall and diligently ponder the straits, burdens, and afflictions which you have borne with an even mind and unconquered fortitude through zeal for justice and in support of the liberty of the Church. Yet, in order that you might fulfil in yourself the perfection of virtue, you could not be broken by adversities or moved from the purpose of your steadfastness. We commend your admirable virtue in this respect, and rejoice greatly with you in the Lord over such patience.

Moreover, since we have long awaited our dearest son in Christ, Henry, illustrious king of the English, in patience and kindness, and have often admonished him with gentle and sweet words, and sometimes with hard and harsh ones, that he should return to himself: if he does not fulfil in deed the peace which he made with you, and does not restore to you, to your people, and to your Church the possessions and honours that were taken away, we grant you full authority to exercise ecclesiastical justice, according to the obligation of your office, upon persons and places belonging to your legation, every impediment of appeal notwithstanding—excepting, however, the person of the king, his wife, and his children—provided that you employ the prudence and circumspection required by priestly moderation.

Given at Segni, the third day before the Ides of October.

DCCLXXIV. To all prelates throughout the lands of the king of the English on this side of the sea.—That they observe the sentence which William, Archbishop of Sens, and Rotrou, Archbishop of Rouen, may pronounce in the king’s lands on this side of the sea. (Segni, October 13.)

[Ibid., p. 81.]

[Col. 0711D]

Pope ALEXANDER to all prelates established throughout the lands of the king of the English on this side of the sea.

The care of the pastoral office which, by the Lord’s providence, though unworthy, we bear, urges and exhorts us earnestly to extend the gaze of our concern to all persons and to exercise more assiduous care for the salvation of all. Therefore we command all of you by apostolic letters and enjoin you, under pain of loss of order and office and in virtue of obedience, that if the king of England does not fulfil the full peace and security which he repeatedly promised us by letters and messengers to grant to our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, and to his people—peace and security which he offered, through the mediation of our venerable brothers the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Nevers, later in the presence of many persons—and if he does not restore to him his archbishopric together with full restitution of possessions and honours taken away, then you shall firmly and unshakenly observe throughout your parishes, all appeal and excuse set aside, the sentence which our venerable brother William, Archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See, and the aforesaid Archbishop of Rouen, or either one of them, may on this account promulgate in his lands on this side of the sea; and you shall cause it to be observed inviolably by others.

Given at Segni, the third day before the Ides of October.

DCCLXXV. Privilege for the Church of St Mary of Gubbio. (Tusculum, October 30.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 638.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BENEDICT, provost of the episcopal church of Blessed Marianus in the city of Gubbio, and his brethren, both present and future, canonically established, for ever.

Whenever a request is made to us which is recognized as fitting religion and uprightness, it befits us willingly to grant it and to give appropriate support to the desires of the petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, and following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, the Roman pontiffs Innocent and Celestine, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Blessed Marianus, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing that whatever possessions, etc., among which we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The parish church, namely, of St John in the city of Gubbio; the parish church of St Mary of Sorvita; the parish church of Lisiano; the parish church of St Mary of Algnana; the parish church of St Mary of Glodiano, together with the parish churches of St Donatus and St Virianus; the parish church of St Gervasius; the parish church of St Paternianus of Modiano; the estate of Lavari; together with all other churches belonging to the goods of the aforesaid church—namely, the chapel of St Bartholomew, the chapel of the Holy Cross, the chapel of St Verecundus, the chapel of St Angelus, the chapel of St George, the chapel of St Sabinus, the chapel of St Angelus, the chapel of St Christopher, the chapel of the Saviour, the chapel of St Mary of Modiano, the chapel of St Bartholomew of Castro Venali, the chapel of St Mary and the chapel of St George of Cortina, the chapel of St Mary of Scarafajo, the chapel of St Margaret with all its appurtenances, the chapel of St Mary of the Francolini in the city of Perugia, and the chapel of the castle of Monte Aureo; [Col. 0713A] the chapel of Poggio dei Figli d’Armanno; the share which you possess in the castle of Castiglione and in the church of the same castle; a share of the castle of Carestelli and in the church of that castle; the church of Poggio Glodiano and one-third of the same Poggio; the castle of Monte Giuliano with its estate; the castle of Monte Analdo with its estate; the castle of Goligata with its estate; the castle of the valley of St Marcula, with its church and estate; the castle of Agnania; and the castle of Agello, with its church. We confirm these to you as you now peacefully possess them.

We also forbid anyone, without your permission, to presume to build a church within the ancient boundaries of the greater or baptismal church; nor may anyone dare take away from you anything granted within the boundaries of the greater and baptismal church, or compel persons dwelling within those same boundaries to go elsewhere for burial. We grant you free authority to receive clerics or free laymen who desire to leave the secular habit and live religiously in your church.

We also decree that the burial-place of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, without prejudice to the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Furthermore, by this present decree we ordain that the Bishop of Perugia may not impose new and undue exactions upon the church which you have at Perugia, nor subject that church to interdict without just and manifest cause.

DCCLXXVI. To Gilbert of London and Jocelin of Salisbury.—He declares them removed from the exercise of their offices and anathematized until they make satisfaction to Thomas of Canterbury. (Tusculum, November 24.)

[*Letters of St Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 102.]

[Col. 0713C]

“Although the duty of pastoral care,” etc., down to: “Know, therefore, that by the authority entrusted to us by God you are suspended from episcopal office so long as [this lasts], and, if peace has not been completed, restored to the sentence of anathema, because, after favour had been obtained [the text reads *apud gratia*, uncertain], you ought, in accordance with our hope, to have laboured more for reconciliation and refrained from burdening the aforesaid archbishop, until you come to the Apostolic See to make satisfaction for so great an offence, unless this depends upon the aforesaid archbishop. But if you take care to make satisfaction to that archbishop and the Church of Canterbury in such a manner, etc.”

In the same terms to the Archbishop of York, except concerning relaxation of the suspension, which the lord pope reserves to himself.

DCCLXXVII. To [Richard], Bishop of Chester; [Walter], Bishop of Rochester; [Geoffrey], Bishop of St Asaph; [Nicholas], Bishop of Llandaff; and [Hugh], Bishop of Durham.—On the same matter. (Tusculum, November 24.)

[Ibid., p. 85.]
