Although the duty of pastoral care requires us to act both with the gentleness of oil and the harshness of wine, and to set before those who appear subject to us now mild things, now severe ones, yet it would be our will and desire that every occasion of severity should so withdraw itself in all matters, and especially in relation to our brethren and fellow bishops, that we should always need only to strengthen them in good and exhort them to better things with gentle and sweet words.

But because, as the charity of many grows cold and wickedness abounds, the iniquity of these unhappy times has advanced so far that even those appointed to lead and govern others can scarcely at times be recalled from their own wills except by every severity, we are sometimes compelled to extend the rod of discipline against those whom we ought to have as helpers in correcting others.

There is no need to record in the present letter what cause compelled our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, to live in exile from his see, since you saw it in person and widespread report proclaimed it throughout nearly the whole Western Church. For him, indeed, thanksgiving and a voice of praise ought in common to resound to our Creator, who, as we believe, having been tried in few things, will be well disposed in many; for God tested him and found him worthy of Himself. But concerning you we report with no little astonishment that, having lost the spirit of compassion, you have so turned away the eye of pity from his tribulation that he might have said what that just and God-fearing man Job complained of amid his sufferings: “My brethren have passed me by, like a torrent which rushes swiftly through the valleys” (Job 6).

The terror of divine judgment might sufficiently have been impressed upon you by the fact that you did not go up to meet the enemy, nor set yourselves as a wall, to stand for the house of the Lord in the day of battle; that you became like rams without horns before the face of the pursuer (Lamentations 1). Moreover, you turned battle against him who alone out of so great a multitude had been zealous for the law of the Lord; and, as the prophet says, “You took away the tunic and cloak from above” (Micah 2). For although Theobald, of blessed memory, predecessor of that archbishop, is said to have placed the crown upon our dearest son Henry, king of the English, and although the predecessor of that king received the crown from him, so that the Church of Canterbury possessed this dignity as it were by right of possession, you nevertheless presumed, without consulting him and within his province, to render your ministry or assent to the coronation of a new king, although we had forbidden it by apostolic authority and letters.

You ought to have alleviated his exile by whatever consolations you could; instead, you aggravated his cause and, grievous to say, added to the pain of his wounds. Though in this act we may not proceed against your persons with a severity equal to the guilt, we ought not to pass it over in silence, lest—God forbid!—the sentence of divine severity condemn both us and you if, while you build a wall, as the prophet says, we plaster it with mud without straw, and open the way to similar offences; if we neglect to punish acts which were wrongly done even in the eyes of all.

Know, therefore, that by the authority entrusted to us by God you are suspended from episcopal office until you come to the Apostolic See to make satisfaction for so great an offence, unless this is prevented by the aforesaid archbishop. But if you take care to make satisfaction to that archbishop and the Church of Canterbury in such a manner that he considers this penalty should be remitted, we wish our authority to be exercised through him.

Given at Tusculum, the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

DCCLXXVIII. To Henry, king of the English.—He congratulates him on having restored his favour and love to Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury; he urges him to return what was taken away, etc.

[*Letters of St Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 135.]

[Col. 0715B]

Pope ALEXANDER to HENRY, king of England.

Having learned from the letters of our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, that, putting aside all disturbance and resentment, you had restored to him your favour and love, we conceived so much joy and gladness as this is more pleasing and acceptable to God, more honourable to you, and more fruitful for your salvation. For we know that the same archbishop excels so greatly in religious devotion, prudence, integrity, and strength of faith that we do not doubt that he is faithful and devoted to you and your kingdom, applies himself with all his strength, ability, and will to your honour and advancement, and faithfully and diligently watches over the increase of your glory and exaltation.

Moreover, since sin is not forgiven unless what has been taken away is restored, and although that archbishop may perhaps keep silent about this because of the patience and affection he has toward you, nevertheless we, who earnestly desire your salvation, must by no means be silent. Nor does it become your magnificence—whom the Lord has made so great and powerful—to retain the rights and goods of the Church of Canterbury. We therefore beseech, admonish, and earnestly exhort the clemency of your royal serenity that, following the example of Zacchaeus, of whom the Gospel says: “Lord, behold, I give half my goods to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19), you strive promptly to restore what you have taken away to the aforesaid archbishop and his Church and to repair the harms and losses which you have inflicted upon them. Thus, in the matter in which you sinned, you may appease God, we may fittingly pardon you so great an offence, and the same archbishop may be found most ready for your service and devotion, for the increase of the honour of you and your heirs.

Give favourable assent to those who wish peace to be restored between yourself and him; but do not henceforth listen to those whom you know have hitherto incited this dissension. Furthermore, admonish and exhort your son, concerning the matter of the oath which he omitted—namely, to preserve the right and liberty of the Church of Canterbury, as the kings and princes of England are known to have done—to make fitting satisfaction to that archbishop and his Church, and cause what was omitted to be fulfilled. Let both you and your son freely and peacefully leave to the aforesaid archbishop and to other ecclesiastical persons the appointment of churches and other matters belonging to churchmen, so that by acting thus you may worthily offer the sacrifice of praise to the Lord and gain for yourselves an eternal kingdom.

DCCLXXIX. To the clergy and people of the king of England.—That they do not disturb the concord and peace concluded between King Henry and Thomas.

[Ibid., p. 74.]

Pope ALEXANDER to the clergy and people of the king of England, on this side of the sea and beyond the sea.

Your wisdom does not fail to know how pleasing and acceptable it is to God to restore peace and concord among persons at variance, and how grave and detestable it is to disturb the good of peace and stir up quarrels and disputes among any persons. Since, indeed, from the concord and peace which, by divine grace cooperating, has been restored between the king of the English and our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, not only the Church but the kingdom itself will, God favouring, receive great good and increase, we command all of you by way of admonition and order you under threat of excommunication that none of you presume to hinder or disturb the aforesaid peace, but rather that you devote yourselves by every means to its advancement and observance.

DCCLXXX. He grants to Stephen, Bishop of Meaux, that, if the chapter is divided among itself, he may take cognizance of the case. (PETIT, *The Penitential of Theodore*, II.)

[Col. 0716C]

The care of pontifical government requires that you endeavour, as far as you are able and with justice, to recall dissident brethren to concord. Therefore, by these present letters, we grant you that if discord should arise—God forbid!—among your canons concerning matters belonging to your chapter, and if they cannot reach agreement within a suitable term which you have fixed for them, you shall be free to take cognizance of the case or entrust its determination to another . . . .

YEAR 1171.

DCCLXXXI. He commands [Lando], elect, the archpriest, and the canons of the Church of Lucca not to injure the brethren of St Frigdianus. (Tusculum, January 8.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanies*, IV, 596.]

[Col. 0716D]

Our beloved sons, the prior and canons of St Frigdianus, have sent us a grave complaint against you, alleging that you show yourselves toward them excessively inhuman, harsh, and unyielding; and, what is more serious and deeply pierces our spirit with bitterness, that you have publicly declared that the body of Blessed Frigdianus rests in your church and have not feared, under threat of anathema, to forbid your citizens [Col. 0717A] henceforth to frequent their church on the principal solemnities, as they had been accustomed to do. You have taken this occasion, as we have learned from them, because this year they celebrated the feast of Blessed Abraham on the day of the dedication of your church.

Even if the aforesaid canons appear in this respect to have acted toward you with less brotherliness and friendliness, you are nevertheless said to have disparaged to such an extent our father and predecessor Pope Eugenius, of holy and venerable memory—who, in the presence of yourselves, G., your former bishop of blessed memory, and almost the whole city, touched the body of Blessed Frigdianus with his own hands and caused it to be placed in the altar which he himself dedicated—that, unless the customary clemency of the Apostolic See restrained the emotion of our mind, we would punish you so severely that punishment itself would teach you how dangerous it is to disparage the authority of the Roman Church, and even yourselves, who then consented to this act, or in any manner to impugn what it did.

But because we neither wish nor ought on any account to allow the Church of Blessed Frigdianus—whom, as our predecessors did, we desire to cherish and foster especially, and with still greater devotion because it endured persecutions and graver dangers for the Church of God and in devotion to us—to be deprived in any degree, by your word or deed, of its dignity or of the customary veneration of the people of Lucca; and because you ought, on account of the religious devotion and integrity in which it excels, not to oppress it but rather to foster it in many ways, we command all of you by apostolic letters, ordering and reiterating our order, that you shall not henceforth allege, on the basis of any frivolity or any reason whatever, that the body of Blessed Frigdianus lies in your church; nor shall you celebrate his feast more solemnly than customary; nor shall you in any way dare forbid clerics or laymen to visit their church, as usual, on the principal solemnities. Rather, entirely relaxing your interdict, you shall preserve for them their rights and honours in these and other matters, so that they shall no longer have just ground for complaint against you.

Unless you obey our command and should henceforth attempt such acts, we shall annul them, and, with the Lord’s aid, shall take care to punish and chastise your disobedience and transgression by strict correction. For we have commanded the same prior and canons not to celebrate in any manner the feast of Blessed Abraham on the day of the dedication of your church, but to appoint another, more suitable day for its celebration.

Given at Tusculum, the sixth day before the Ides of January.

DCCLXXXII. Privilege for the Church of St Mary of Seckau. (Tusculum, February 10.)

[PUSCH and FROEHLICH, *Diplomata of Styria*, I, 157.]

Pope ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WERNHER, provost of the Church of St Mary of Seckau, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

[Col. 0718A] Whenever a request is made to us which accords with reason, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we assent to your just petitions and, following the example of our father and predecessor Pope Innocent of holy memory, receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of Seckau, over which, by God’s help, you are known to preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine shall be kept there inviolably for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods you now justly possess, etc., among which we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid Church of St Mary of Seckau is situated, with all its appurtenances, as that place was granted to you by Conrad, Archbishop of Salzburg, of blessed memory, in exchange for the place called Feistritz. By gift of the nobleman Alram and his wife Richenza: Feistritz, Altdorf, V . . . . . Plesche, with all its dependent people. In Bavaria: Waltenstein with its estates and dependent people, namely Shelz, Willendorf, and Geroldsdorf, with vineyards and all other appurtenances; the estate called Chambe and Erla. In the March: Chunberg, Arberdorf, Hainrichsdorf, and Lower Pozendorf, with all that belongs to it. By gift of Ulrich, kinsman of the aforementioned Alram, founder of that place: Henneberg with all estates belonging to it and the alpine pastures of Lichtst[ei]g [Liechtsteig] and Predegai. In Carinthia: an estate near St Stephen, a manor-house and twelve holdings; an estate near Jaun and the mountain where silver and lead are mined, with every right. Near Glan: six holdings. By gift of the aforesaid archbishop: the parish of Cumbenz with all its rights; tithes at Henrichsdorf, Erbendorf, Chunberg, and Jeringen. By gift of the noble margrave Otakar: the forests and alpine pastures adjoining that monastery—Undrim, Setall, Gotestall, Forwiz, and Teufental. By gift of the noblewoman Gisela: the alpine pasture called Zecue [probably Zeirice], and the election and presentation of clerics in the church of Schönberg. By gift of Burchard of Murz and his wife Judith: an estate and two holdings at Talheim.

(Thus far are the properties; there follows the authority to receive converts, to receive ordinations from another bishop if the diocesan bishop is lacking, to admit burials, and to elect provosts.)

Given at Tusculum through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1170, and in the twelfth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

DCCLXXXIII. He orders that all estates and privileges of the monastery of Admont, which he enumerates individually, remain secure. (Tusculum, February 10.)

[PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, III, 666.]

Pope ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Liutold, abbot of the monastery of St Blasius called Admont, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

The authority of our office admonishes and invites us to labour for the welfare of churches and, with the Lord’s help, beneficially to provide for their peace and tranquillity. For it is deemed worthy and fitting to integrity that we, who by the Lord’s ordering have been appointed to govern them, should both protect them from the wickedness of evil men and fortify them by the patronage of Blessed Peter and the Apostolic See.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, and following in the footsteps of our predecessors of blessed memory, Paschal, Innocent, and Lucius, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the gift of kings or princes, the offering of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain whole and unimpaired for you and your successors; among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

From the gift of Gebhard, of blessed memory, Archbishop of Salzburg, founder of the same monastery: in [Col. 0719C] the valley of Admont, the estate of the church of St. Blaise, and whatever Countess Hemma possessed there. A salt-pan near the monastery at Halle, and the greater part of the adjoining woodland. From the gift of Archbishop Thiemo, his successor: the manor on the other side of the stream called Admont, the church of St. Amandus the bishop, and the remainder of the woodland. The parish and the right of public proclamation (*praeconium*) beyond the river Enns, with the church of St. Amandus. A salt-pan at Halle, with the meadow adjoining the aforesaid river. From the gift of Conrad the Elder, Archbishop of Salzburg: salt-pans and saltworks at Halle, and the entire forest belonging to Wenge, with newly cleared lands and tithes. The manors of Rudindorf, Arnieck, Rute, Chrumpowe, and what the aforesaid bishops gave for the [Col. 0719D] various uses of the Alps and mountains, where salt is boiled and iron mined, with fields, meadows, woods, waters, and watercourses, from the brook Zedelze to Frodnize and from Luzahe to Staiphe. From the gift of Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg: the church of St. Gall in the New Forest, with tithes, newly cleared lands, all its rights, and the saltworks there. From the gift of Conrad I: the church of St. Mary Magdalene and the hospice at Friesach, with tithes, estates, and all their legal rights. From the gift of certain nobles—namely Rainer, Petrissa, and other kinsmen of Liutold, Abbot of Admont—the allodial estates of Tovernick and Chirchaim, with all their appurtenances. One half of the church of St. James, with the estate of Cholmenzi. From the gift of Archbishop Gebhard: tithes [Col. 0720A] at Tivene, Flatsach, Chrapfeld, and Michtendorf, with all their appurtenances. From the gift of Archbishop Conrad II: the tithe-manor at Wertse, with the estate of Rapotendorf, Guttenprunnen, and other possessions of the lady Mathilda. The church of St. Michael, with the estate of Zezen. The church of St. John, with the estate of Zozzen, its tithes, and all its rights.

From the gift of Margrave Otakar: the alpine pasture of Scoberen belonging to the same estate. Whatever you possess at Grazlup and Pals. From the gift of Archbishop Gebhard: the tithes of Chatse, Welze, and Lungowe, with their appurtenances. From the gift of the same archbishop: the church of Tiufenbach and Aichdorf, and Preitenfurt, with all their appurtenances. At Wenge, the church of St. Agatha [Col. 0720B] with all its appurtenances. The church of St. Andrew and the manor of Trieben, with all their appurtenances. The church of Dietmarsdorf and its manor, with the adjoining estates—namely the two Griez, Perndorf, Strechowe, and Puhel—with all their appurtenances. From the gift of Albert, Archbishop of Salzburg: the parish of Palte, with all its rights. From the gift of Archbishop Conrad I: the church of St. Mary, with the estate called Lower Jaeringen. From the gift of Archbishop Gebhard: Upper Jaeringen, with all their appurtenances. The estate of Nazowe, with many other adjoining estates. From the gift of Archbishops Conrad and Eberhard: the church of St. Nicholas and the estate of Gottfried Mokkernowe, with newly cleared lands and tithes. The church of St. Martin, with [Col. 0720C] the estate of Strazganch, formerly belonging to Margrave Gunther and Count Conrad of Pilstain, with all its appurtenances. The estate of Radlach, formerly belonging to Count Bernhard. Whatever you possess at Lusniz, Chamere, and Mutarn.

From the gift of the nobles Treboche and Tunewiz: five manors at the bridge of St. Stephen; in the same parish, from the gift of Archbishop Eberhard, tithes. Whatever estates and tithes you possess at St. Benedict, Puchowe, Lobenich, and Chrowat. From the gift of Conrad I: tithes at Murz. From the gift of nobles: the estates of Muterndorf. From the gift of Archbishop Eberhard: two holdings in the village of Teschanschirchen, with the entire tithe-district between Pincha and Lavenze. [Col. 0720D] From the gift of nobles: whatever you possess at Wurvelach, Potsach, Gomvarn, Phaphenstain, and Aichowe. From the gift of Archbishop Gebhard: Ruste, Arnsdorf, and Welmnich, with their appurtenances. At Wachowe, whatever Count of Wolfrathusen gave you; at Brunnen, whatever Frederick the advocate gave you. Whatever you possess through the gift of nobles at Chremse, Ense, and Ulsburch. At Treswiz and Liuzen, estates with their tithe-rights. The church of St. John and the estate of Hagenberg, and Winzenbach and Gundachringen.

From the gift of archbishops: whatever you possess at Sundrmaeringen, Prukkarn, Aiche, and Eberhartingen. The great allodial estate at Hoveheim, which you purchased from the nobles of Abensberg. From the gift of nobles: [Col. 0721A] the estate at Upper and Lower Hus, with the church of St. Paternian and all its appurtenances. At Enswalde, Schratengastei, and Tricenwald. The church of St. Martin, with newly cleared lands and tithes as far as Horgenbrucken. From the gift of Archbishop Gebhard: the estates of Mittrehoven, Wenge, and Elinowe. From the gift of Archbishop Conrad I: the estate at Chuchil, the manor at Salzburg, and Hirsehalm, with their appurtenances. In the village of Beirhalle, whatever you acquired by gift or exchange from Count Berthold and Otto the Count Palatine. From the gift of nobles: whatever you possess at Pergen, Brichaim, and Haselbach. The church of St. Martin, with the great estate of Elsindorf, formerly belonging to Udalric; and the other church, with Bernhard’s estate; and everything that you purchased there.

[Col. 0721B] Neither the bishop, nor the abbot himself, nor any person whatsoever shall have authority to give the goods of the same monastery to anyone as a fief or benefice, without the consent of the better and more discerning brethren, or to alienate them by any other means. We decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the last wishes of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while the rights of the mother church are preserved. No opposition by any bishop or provost shall prevent you from receiving free and unencumbered laypersons or clerics into conversion. We also forbid any brother, after making his profession, to depart from this cloister without the permission of the abbot and the whole community; and no one shall dare to retain one who has departed [Col. 0721C] without a guarantee in letters issued by the community. No one shall presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the produce of your animals. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over the monastery through any cunning of intrigue or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the council, in accordance with the fear of God and the Rule of St. Benedict, shall determine ought to be elected.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, etc., with the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical reverence due to the Archbishop of Salzburg preserved; he shall nevertheless have no right [Col. 0721D] whatever to impose upon it any harassment or custom harmful to the peace of religious persons. If therefore anyone in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and St. Rufina. I, Conrad, Archbishop of the See of Mainz and Cardinal of Sabina. I, Odo, Bishop of Tusculum. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St. Mary. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian. I, Manfred, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of St. Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. [Col. 0722A] I, John, cardinal priest of the title of SS. John and Paul of Pammachius. I, Hildebrand, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of St. Peter in Chains. I, Boso, cardinal priest of St. Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Damaso.

Given at Tusculum by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth Ides of February, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1170 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twelfth year of the pontificate [Col. 0722B] of Pope Alexander III.

### DCCLXXXIV. Privilege for the Church of St. Peter at Treviso.  
*(Tusculum, February 11.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 525.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons DRUDO, provost of the church of St. Peter at Treviso, and his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that just petitioners be granted their requests, especially when piety supports the will of those now living and does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, [Col. 0722C] graciously assenting to your just petitions, after the example of Pope Eugenius, our predecessor of holy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church of St. Peter, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. By apostolic authority we confirm the common life which you have promised to observe in that church; and we forbid any of you, after making this promise, to turn back except on religious grounds. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him be deprived of the benefice of the same church; nor shall anyone henceforth be instituted canon in that church unless he has promised to observe this common life. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods the same Church now justly and canonically [Col. 0722D] possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have judged that these should be specified by their own names.

(The possessions are enumerated.)

Given at Tusculum, by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and cardinal notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the third Ides of February, in the year 1170 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### DCCLXXXV. For the nuns of Blasiliensis (diocese of St. Flour)

There exists a bull of Pope Alexander III for the nuns of Blasiliensis, in which he mentions privileges granted to them by the supreme pontiffs Sergius and Calixtus, and enumerates the principal possessions of the monastery: the village in which the monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the churches of St. Saturninus and St. Stephen, with everything belonging to them; and, in addition, the tithe of their newly cleared lands. Given at Tusculum by the hands of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the year 1170 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, II, Instruments, 158.]

[Col. 0723A]

### DCCLXXXVI. To Peter, Abbot of St. Remigius, and Fulk, Dean of Rheims.—That they should decide the case of two abbots.  
*(Tusculum, February 25.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 923.]

[Col. 0723B]

We entrust to you for hearing and final determination according to due process the case known to be in dispute between the Abbot of St. Urban [Note: [Col. 0723D] It is a monastery of the same order as that of Dervense, and in the same diocese of Châlons; but it is in the town of Jouisville, or, as it later came to be called, [Col. 0724D] Joinville. The church of St. Desiderius is that which gave its name to a town of some consequence in that district, and belongs by right to the monastery of Dervense. Jacques SIRM.] and the Abbot of Dervense, concerning the church of St. Desiderius and certain other matters. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your experience that, when requested in this matter, you shall meet together and summon both parties before you; and, after carefully hearing and examining the arguments on both sides, you shall decide the same case [Col. 0723C] according to justice, with appeal excluded.

Given at Tusculum, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March.

### DCCLXXXVII. He erects the Church of Cefalù into an episcopal see and confirms its goods and rights.  
*(Tusculum, April 9.)*

[PIRRI, *Sicilia sacra*, II, p. 801.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BOSO, Bishop of Cefalù, and his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0723D] Since, as the record of events and the venerable ordinances of the holy Fathers clearly declare, the Apostolic See has always had authority not only to establish new episcopal sees in suitable places, but also to separate united sees and unite those which have been separated: we, who by the office of the supreme pontificate imposed on us by God ought, so far as God grants, to give diligent thought to the condition of all Churches, have determined that the Church of Cefalù—to whose governance, by the Lord’s disposition, you were recently called [Col. 0724A] and consecrated bishop—shall be established as an episcopal see. Thus the cathedral see there shall be inviolably maintained for all time.

We also decree that whatever possessions and goods the same Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have judged that the following should be specified by their own names:

The city of Cefalù itself, as it was granted with all its appurtenances to the aforesaid Church of Cefalù by the kings of Sicily and confirmed under the authority [Col. 0724B] of their privilege; the hamlet of Arsa with all its appurtenances; the hamlet of Polla with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Lucy of Syracuse, with hamlets and all its appurtenances; the church of St. Mary of Camerata, with all its possessions and appurtenances. Likewise, we confirm to the same Church, by apostolic authority, the diocese, with tithes and every episcopal right, as it was granted by the Church of Messina to the Church entrusted to you: namely, the aforesaid city of Cefalù with all its appurtenances; Mistrectum with its dependencies; Thusum with its dependencies; Pollina with its dependencies; Grattera with its dependencies; Rocca d’Asino with its dependencies; Collesano with its [Col. 0724C] dependencies; Polizzi with its dependencies; Colatabuturum with its dependencies; Sclefana with its dependencies; Ascusa with its dependencies; and the territory beginning where the river Tortae begins and descending to the sea, and from the sea as far as Cefalù.

Furthermore, we decree and establish by the page of this document that churches situated in your diocese, on account of temporal service which they are known to render to others, shall not dare to deny you obedience in spiritual matters. Moreover, we hold valid and firm the lawful gifts made to the aforesaid church by Roger and William, kings of Sicily of illustrious memory, and confirm them by apostolic authority. In addition, we confirm by our privilege the reasonable immunities and liberties granted by the aforesaid illustrious kings of Sicily and by your successors. We further decree [Col. 0724D] that no archbishop or bishop may harass you or the household entrusted to you with undue and unprecedented exactions or burdens. We also add and forbid by apostolic authority that no church may receive your canons or converts into religious life without your consent or that of your successors, unless perhaps they wish to enter a stricter religious order.

We therefore decree, etc., with the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right and reverence due to the Archbishop of Messina preserved. If therefore anyone in the future, etc.

[Col. 0725A] I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Bernard, Bishop of Porto and St. Rufina. I, Odo, Bishop of Tusculum. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of SS. John and Paul of Pammachius. I, Hildebrand, priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of St. Peter in Chains. I, Boso, cardinal priest of St. Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Damaso. [Col. 0725B] I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of St. Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa.

Given at Tusculum by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth Ides of April, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1171 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### DCCLXXXVIII. To Stephen, Archbishop of Bourges, and Bernard, Bishop of Nevers.—That they should absolve the Bishops of London and Salisbury, excommunicated by Thomas.  
*(Tusculum, April 24.)*

[*Letters of Gilbert Foliot*, II, 59.]

[Col. 0725C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the Archbishop of Bourges and the Bishop of Nevers, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not believe that it is unknown to your brotherhood how Thomas, of holy memory, formerly Archbishop of Canterbury, by our command pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the Bishop of London and the Bishop of Salisbury, [Col. 0725D] a sentence which we have held valid and firm and have taken care to confirm by apostolic authority. Since the aforesaid bishops, worn down by old age and bodily weakness, and one of them afflicted by illness, cannot come into our presence, we have decided to entrust their absolution to you, whose prudence and integrity we trust; the envoys of King Henry of England and of the same bishops have pressed us most earnestly for it.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, within a month after those envoys have returned home, if you have not learned that our legates—whom we have resolved to send into those regions to investigate the enormity [Col. 0726A] of that crime and wicked deed which was perpetrated, and to effect the king’s reconciliation—have crossed the Alps, you shall publicly absolve the bishops from the bond of excommunication, once they have taken an oath according to the custom of the Church that they will abide by our command; while the sentence of suspension, for the cause on account of which they were last brought into excommunication, shall remain in full force.

If it becomes known to you that the Bishop of Salisbury, being ill, cannot come to you, you shall go to him in person, if that can be done with our approval; or, if you cannot go, you shall send suitable persons in whom both we and you may have confidence, to absolve him publicly in the sight of the Church after receiving his oath that he will obey [Col. 0726B] our command. But if you, brother archbishop, cannot be present for this matter, then you, brother bishop, shall yourself carry out the foregoing with the Abbot of Pontigny, with the greatest care.

Given at Tusculum, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

### DCCLXXXIX. To Jocelin, Bishop of Salisbury.—He grants that he need not undertake the journey to him.  
*(Tusculum, April [?])*

[*Letters of St. Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 104.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JOCELIN, Bishop of Salisbury, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0726C] Although it was our purpose, and that of our brethren in counsel, that we should not absolve you unless you appeared before the Apostolic See, your beloved son Robert, dean of the church of Évreux, has repeatedly reported to us your old age and infirmity; and formerly our beloved son Reginald, your archdeacon, likewise carefully and diligently set forth the same matter to us. At the request of the same dean, at the prayers of your dearest sons in Christ, William, illustrious King of Sicily, and his mother Queen Matilda, who earnestly interceded with us for you, and also out of regard and affection for our dearest son in Christ, Henry, King of England, we have more graciously accommodated ourselves to your inability and have mercifully remitted to you the labour and danger of so long a journey. [Col. 0726D] Therefore, by the authority of these present letters, we enjoin you to send to us five, or at least four, religious, reputable, and trustworthy persons from your diocese, who shall, according to the tenor of your mandate concerning the accusations made against you in the case of Thomas, of holy memory, formerly Archbishop of Canterbury, and concerning the matters for which you were suspended and excommunicated, make your defence and clear you.

Given at Benevento, on the third day before the Kalends of April. [Note: [Col. 0725D] This clause is undoubtedly erroneous. JAFFÉ.]

### DCCXC. To Joscius, Archbishop of Tours, and his suffragans.—He confirms the sentence of interdict pronounced against the king of England’s lands on this side of the sea because of violence inflicted on St. Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.  
*(Tusculum, May 14.)*

[MARTEN., *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 569.]

[Col. 0727A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren John, Archbishop of Tours, and all his suffragans and ecclesiastical persons established in his province, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although unworthy, we are placed upon the watchtower of the Apostolic See; through ourselves or through those appointed to share the responsibility entrusted to us, we must correct all offences with prudent vigilance [Col. 0727B] and oppose each person’s errors with pontifical moderation, lest, through our neglect, vices seem to prevail over virtues. For we have not forgotten how, being solicitous and vigilant in fulfilment of our office for the peace of Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, of holy memory—whose soul, consecrated to God, as we believe, by precious martyrdom, dwells in heaven with the saints—we commanded our venerable brethren William, Archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See, and Ro[trodo], Archbishop of Rouen, that, if the King of England did not leave that archbishop and his church in complete peace and liberty, restore what had been taken away, and firmly preserve the peace he had made with him, they should place the king’s lands on this side of the sea under interdict; [Col. 0727C] and that, if either could not or would not be present for any reason, the other should nevertheless carry out our command with diligence.

Since, however, the aforesaid Ro., Archbishop of Rouen, refused to execute our command, it was carried out by the said Archbishop of Sens. Therefore, with the common counsel of our brethren, holding valid and firm the sentence which that archbishop is known to have pronounced, by our command and authority, upon all the lands on this side of the sea of the aforesaid King of England, and confirming it by apostolic authority, we command you by apostolic letters and, by virtue of obedience and under penalty affecting your order and office, require that you firmly and inviolably observe the same sentence in the lands subject to the said king, [Col. 0727D] and cause it to be inviolably observed by others. None of you shall presume to relax it or, contrary to it, to celebrate divine offices without a mandate from the Roman pontiff or from a legate sent by him.

Given at Tusculum, on the second Ides of May.

### DCCXCI. Bull for Mainard, Abbot of Aquistris (diocese of Bordeaux).  
*(Tusculum, May 15.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, II, Instruments, 310.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons MAINARD, abbot of the monastery of St. Mary [Col. 0728A] of Aquistris, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may quickly attain its effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, we decree that the monastic order, known to have been established in that place according to the Rule of the Lord and of blessed Benedict, shall there be inviolably observed for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically [Col. 0728B] possesses, or may hereafter acquire by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have judged that the following should be specified by their own names:

In the district of Bordeaux: the church of St. Peter of La Landa; St. Genesius of Lugon; the churches of Fronsiac, St. Peter and St. Martin; the church of St. Peter of Gorcia; the church of St. John of Coutras; the church of St. Peter of Porchiers; the church of St. Stephen of Camedel; the chapel of St. Mary of the Island; the chapel of St. Mary of Fronsiac; the chapel of St. James of Malmico; the chapel of St. Mary of Egypt at Bayas; the chapel of St. James [Col. 0728C] of Rotellans; the chapel of St. Vincent of Picturis; the chapel of St. Nicholas of Fecie; and the chapel of St. Mary Magdalene of Las Artigas. In the district of Saintonge: the church of St. Mary of Barda; the church of St. Martin of Cruc; the church of St. Martin of Aria; the church of St. Vivian of Cleirac; the churches of Saints Saturninus and Nazarius of Sercou; the chapel of St. James of Triac; the chapel of St. Giles of Casis Solis; the chapel of St. Leodegar of La Clota; the chapel of St. Paul of Monte Ebrioso; the chapel of St. Mary of Bedenac; and the chapel of St. Valeria of Frainel.

No one shall presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate either by your own hands or through others, without harm to your souls. When a general interdict shall be [Note: [Col. 0727D] Something is missing in the original.] in force, you may celebrate the offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. [Col. 0728D] We also grant that the burial-place of the same house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken shall be preserved. In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose priests and present the chosen men to the bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust to them the care of souls, so that they shall answer to the bishop for the care of the people, but to you for temporal matters. Furthermore, we likewise confirm the procession which your church holds on the last day of August, reasonably granted from ancient times by the archbishops and bishops of the province of Bordeaux; and we forbid anyone to presume to inflict injury or molestation upon those who attend the same procession out of devotion, either while going or returning.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person, etc. Amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, Bishop of Ostia. I, Hildebrand, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. John, cardinal of St. Anastasia. William, cardinal of St. Peter in Chains. Boso, cardinal of St. Pudentiana. [Col. 0729B] Hyacinth, cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin. Manfred, cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Tusculum, by the hand of Granerius, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of May, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1171 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

### DCCXCII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—That he should report what was done at the meeting between Emperor Frederick and his brother Louis.  
*(Tusculum, June 1.)*

[MARTEN., *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 936.]

When we recall and weigh in studious reflection how fervent the devotion of your charity was at the beginning of the schism [Col. 0729C] and at the outset of our elevation, when you were bound to us by no obligation of duty or honour, it seems that your most fervent devotion has in large measure grown cool; do not take this amiss. Although we can never doubt in any respect our dearest son in Christ, Louis, the illustrious King of the French, your brother—since we have learned that his devotion toward us and the Church is singular and special among all the kings and princes of the world, and in every way anxious and fervent for the welfare of the universal Church—yet it would have been greatly advantageous for your brotherhood to have communicated to us some certain information through yourself concerning the conference which he is known recently to have held with F., the so-called emperor. But because we do not doubt that the prudence of your discretion is earnestly directed toward the peace of the universal Church, and because we hold it to be unquestionably true that the aforesaid king ought not to conceal from you anything which ought to be entrusted to anyone, we ask, advise, and command your brotherhood that, in accordance with what our venerable brother, the Bishop of Troyes, and our beloved son, the Abbot of Pontigny [Note: [Col. 0729] Guarinus, who afterwards became Archbishop of Bourges.], or either of them, shall communicate to you on our behalf, you shall, as we trust in your devotion, devote diligent and effective effort with the said king to advance the honour and welfare of the Church; and whatever you discover in this matter, you shall endeavour to communicate to our care through a faithful and discreet person as swiftly [Col. 0730A] as you can, since not everything should be committed to letters.

Given at Tusculum, on the Kalends of June.

### DCCXCIII. To the suffragans of the Church of Tarragona.—He grieves at the murder of Hugh, Archbishop of Tarragona, and advises and urges them to elect another as quickly as possible.  
*(Tusculum, June 19.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1068.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, the bishops suffragan of the Church of Tarragona, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having heard of the death of Hugh, of good memory, formerly [Col. 0730B] your archbishop, we have been deeply troubled, and we sympathize with both you and the Church of Tarragona in paternal affection, since we know that his care and governance of that Church of God were fruitful and beneficial. That our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King of Aragon, expelled from his kingdom those wicked and criminal men who put the aforesaid archbishop to death is pleasing and acceptable to us; and for this we commend, in the Lord and as it deserves, the king’s foresight.

Since the mother of those criminals is said to have given favour and counsel to her sons in so great a crime and to have plotted so atrocious and monstrous an outrage, if the matter is so, compel her to enter a strict religious order; [Col. 0730C] or, should she perhaps refuse to comply in this, strive with the said king that she, together with her husband, sons, and grandsons, if she has any, may be expelled from the bounds of his kingdom. Furthermore, since the absence of a shepherd undoubtedly brings bitter dangers and temporal losses upon Churches, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to confer diligently and earnestly with the chapter of the aforesaid Church concerning the appointment of your archbishop. Assemble at that church with the same chapter, take unanimous and concordant action in favour of a suitable, reputable, learned person worthy of so great an office, elect him as your master, and present him [Col. 0730D] to the Apostolic See within a suitable period, so that we may be more fully informed about the election. Publicly declare those criminals excommunicated, with lighted candles; and, in places of your province to which they come, forbid the celebration of divine offices as long as they are present there.

Given at Tusculum, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.

### DCCXCIV. To Herbert [of Bosham], living in exile after the martyrdom of his lord St. Thomas.—A letter of consolation.  
*(Tusculum, June 24.)*

[*Works of Herbert of Bosham*, ed. GILES, II, 303.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0731A] son Master HERBERT, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received your letter with paternal kindness; and, having understood the anxieties, distresses, troubles, and pressures that you endure with an even spirit, we sympathize with you, as with a devoted and special son of the Church, with sincere affection of heart, and willingly grant, insofar as we can, the comfort of welcome consolation.

Indeed, we regard as pleasing and acceptable the fact that you adhered with such constancy of mind to Thomas, of holy memory, formerly archbishop of Canterbury, that you would not abandon him in the exile of his persecution, and that now you steadfastly preserve his memory in word and deed. We commend the constancy of your devotion in this respect with the fitting praises in the Lord, [Col. 0731B] firmly purposing and intending to cherish you with closer affection as an honourable and learned man, and to consider with watchful care and concern your advancement and welfare. Therefore, being very watchful and solicitous for your position, we have firmly directed our beloved sons Albert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and Theodwin, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Vitalis, legates of the apostolic see, to obtain for you and the other clerics and laymen of the aforesaid archbishop the favour and peace of the king of England, and to procure your return to that land and your secure residence there. But if perhaps they cannot, according to our desire, prevail with the aforesaid king and obtain for you his peace and favour, it will be for you to inform us [Col. 0731C] how we may more conveniently provide for you, and in what manner we may honourably and beneficially make provision for you. For we desire willingly to attend to your necessities; and, as to a special and devoted son of the Church, we shall, God being the author of it, effectively take care to provide for you in whatever befits us and seems expedient to us. Be strong, therefore, in the Lord, and place your hope and trust in him, who does not forsake those who hope in him, but after cloudiness makes calm, and with temptation provides an outcome.

Given at Tusculum, the eighth day before the Kalends of July [24 June].

DCCXCV. To the archdeacon, dean, and other clerics of Nottinghamshire.—That they preserve the rights of the church of Saint Mary of Southwell. (Tusculum, 28 July.)

[Monastic. Anglic., III, appendix, p. 10.]

[Col. 0731D]

Since the office of government entrusted to us and the duty of charity move us to labour for the condition of churches and to preserve, with attentive care, the dignities and rights proper to each church of God, we therefore, desiring to provide for the church of Southwell in its right and dignity, command and enjoin your whole body by apostolic letters that you render to that church the due and customary honour and reverence which our predecessors and we ourselves are known hitherto to have shown it; and that you preserve unimpaired and intact the rights and ancient liberties of that church: namely, by carrying the chrism [Col. 0732A] from the church of York before Easter to the aforesaid church through you, sons, the dean; by distributing it thence in the customary manner through the other churches to the monasteries of that archdeaconry; by assembling at the annual synod at the appointed time and at the procession at Pentecost with customary solemnity; and in other respects.

But to you, archdeacon, we forbid by apostolic authority that you, or your officials or clerics, should attempt unduly to burden the churches or clerics of that archdeaconry under pretext of visitation or frequent chapter-meetings; that you should cause great and costly banquets for yourselves to be prepared from the poverty of the clerics through your churches; or that you should exact from those clerics an undue payment for the redemption of men, contrary to the decrees of the holy [Col. 0732B] Fathers and the custom of our predecessors. Rather, according to the resources of the place, where reason requires it, take care so to moderate your hospitality that your visitation ought to be more welcome to them than burdensome. Also strive to provide the aforesaid clerics with prudent and honourable deans, who may be seen to instruct them by their conduct and morals, and who seek not so much temporal gain as correction of morals and the advancement of souls. Moreover, provide carefully that you appear to carry out our command in this matter in such a way that no complaint against you need be brought to us; for if you are disobedient to us in this, we shall, with divine authority, take care to chastise your disobedience with the due rod of correction. [Col. 0732C]

Given at Tusculum, on the Ides of July [15 July].

DCCXCVI. He grants the church of Southwell various immunities and privileges, and confirms its goods and possessions. (Tusculum, 28 July.)

[Monastic. Angl., III, 10.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the church of Saint Mary of Southwell, both present and those canonically appointed in the future: for perpetual remembrance.

We have been appointed by divine providence, though inadequate in merit, to the government of all churches, so that we ought to devote more earnest care to the welfare and advancement of each, [Col. 0732D] and watch with unwearied concern for their condition, lest we may deservedly be reproved by the heavenly householder for negligence, if, God forbid, we have been insufficiently diligent in governing the Church. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Saint Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting it, by concession of popes, gift of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 0733A]

Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority the ancient customary liberties—namely, those which the church of York is known to have possessed from ancient times and still to possess—as the archiepiscopal church, the chapter of York, and the illustrious kings of England have, by pious and reasonable provision, granted them to you and your church and confirmed them in their authentic writings; under threat of anathema against anyone who should … infringe them or presumptuously act against them in any respect.

In addition, we decree that, if any of your parishioners should presume to inflict violence or injury upon you in lands, houses, or other property belonging to your church, [Col. 0733B] you may pronounce a sentence of excommunication against him without anyone’s opposition.

Moreover, if any of your parishioners, or even of the parishioners of the church of York, shall lay violent hands upon anyone within the cemetery of your church, or forcibly drag him away from there or from your houses, or shall act against the peace of the Church in those places, you may restrain him by the censure of the Church granted to you. We further forbid that anyone should have the power or licence to bestow the benefit of absolution upon persons who, as stated, have been placed by you under interdict or bound by anathema for their excesses and injuries inflicted upon your church and yourselves, unless satisfaction has first been duly made to you and your church regarding the matters for which they were interdicted or excommunicated by you. [Col. 0733C]

Likewise, by decree of this present writing we establish that the churches of the prebends and of the common fund shall be wholly free and exempt from every episcopal right and custom; and that in those churches you may institute suitable vicars without any opposition, just as the archbishops and chapter of York are known to have permitted this to you and your predecessors, and as it is now peacefully observed in the church of York and in yours. Furthermore, as has been granted to you by the same archbishops and observed by long custom, we decree that both clerics and laymen of the county of Nottinghamshire shall come to your church at Pentecost [Col. 0733D] in solemn procession; that a synod shall be held there every year according to the ancient and reasonable custom of that church; and that chrism shall be brought there from the church of York by the deans of that county, to be distributed thence through the other churches.

We also decree that the following, as it is known to have been observed by ancient and reasonable custom, shall henceforth remain unshaken: namely, when any one of your canons dies or changes his religious habit and manner of life, the revenues that would have belonged to him in that same year shall be distributed, with the counsel of the chapter, for his soul or for payment of his debts.

We therefore decree, etc.

[Col. 0734A] Given at Tusculum through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August [28 July], in the fourth indiction, in the year 1171 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the twelfth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

DCCXCVII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Mary of Morimondo. (Tusculum, 28 July.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 146.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JAMES, abbot of the monastery of the church of Saint Mary of Morimondo, situated near the Ticino, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

[Col. 0734B] Apostolic protection ought to be present for those who choose the religious life, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that place according to God, the Rule of Saint Benedict, and the institutions of the Cistercian brethren, shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions, whatever goods, etc., among which we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the same place called Morimondo, [Col. 0734C] formerly called Fulcher’s Field, with its waters, watercourses, and all its appurtenances; the grange where the abbey formerly stood, called Morimondo; the grange of Fara Basiliana; the grange of Old Fara; the grange of Castelletto, with all its rafts (*ratis*), waters, watercourses, pastures, woods, and all its immunities and appurtenances on this side of the Ticino and beyond it, including fishing in the Ticino; likewise, the exchange canonically made concerning the territory of the aforesaid grange of Fara Basiliana between you and the parish church of Saint Stephen of Roxiace, as is contained in the authentic instrument made concerning it; and the agreement made between you and the provost of the parish church of Casolata concerning tithes and the territory of Old Fara, and confirmed by an authentic instrument—we confirm these to you by apostolic authority. Yet no one may presume to exact tithes from you on the produce of your labour, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the nourishment of your animals. [Col. 0734D]

Also, desiring by paternal provision to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority that anyone within the enclosure of your places or granges should dare to commit violence, robbery, or theft; set fire; seize or kill persons. You may also receive into your monastery clerics or laymen fleeing the world, provided that they are free and absolved, and retain them without any opposition. Moreover, we forbid that any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, may on any pretext leave the cloister without permission of the prior or abbot. No one may dare to retain one who departs without letters of assurance from the community. [Col. 0735A]

We therefore decree, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, John, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul and of Pammachius. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Boso, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, priest of the title of Saint Mark. [Col. 0735B] I, Ardico, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Theodore. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius near the Temple of Agrippa. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Magrugio.

Given at Tusculum through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August [28 July], in the fourth indiction, in the year 1171 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the twelfth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

DCCXCVII bis. Privilege granted to Robert, bishop of the church of Catania, at Tusculum, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September [20 August], fourth indiction, in the year 1171 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the twelfth year of the pontificate. (These details only in PIRRI, *Sicilia sacra*, I, 531.)

DCCXCVIII. To [Rothrod], archbishop of Rouen, and [Theobald], bishop of Amiens.—That they restore Roger of York fully to his former position if he clears himself by oath of the charges made against him. (Tusculum, 23 October.)

[*Epistolae S. Thomae*, ed. GILES, II, 65.]

[Col. 0735C]

POPE ALEXANDER to his venerable brothers, the archbishop of Rouen and the bishop of Amiens.

Both the proximity of the place itself and the report spread throughout the world do not permit you to be ignorant how our brother Roger, archbishop of York and legate of the apostolic see, was suspended from pontifical office when certain causes intervened. From this matter, as many have said and proclaimed, it came about that that most monstrous crime and unspeakable outrage was perpetrated against Thomas, of holy memory, formerly archbishop of Canterbury. For when it had been reported to the illustrious king of England that the aforesaid archbishop of Canterbury had inflicted so great an injury upon him, his kingdom, and the bishops, the king was so disturbed and angered that certain of those standing around him, perceiving his agitation and wishing to please him, at the devil’s instigation attacked the aforesaid archbishop of Canterbury with armed force and, as you know, cruelly killed him in his own church—a place where even murderers indeed ought to be safe. [Col. 0735D] This, certainly, fills the minds of those who hear it with all the greater horror, and brings greater infamy upon those said to have been the occasion of so great an atrocity, inasmuch as the crime is judged more cruel and the deed more grave.

But because the envoys of the aforesaid king could by no argument obtain from us, despite their insistence, that we should entrust in those regions the purgation of that archbishop or of the other bishops who had been excommunicated or interdicted for a similar cause, the same archbishop informed us, through the king’s own envoys and through letters sent to us by himself and other great men, that Frederick, called emperor and persecutor of the Church, because of the fervour of devotion and fidelity which he had shown toward us and the Church from the beginning of this disturbance, was unwilling to grant him safe-conduct to come to us, although he was willing and prepared to come and clear himself before us, had not obstacles on the roads delayed him. Therefore, since we have found the faith and devotion of this archbishop toward us and the Church to be pure, sincere, and unchanging, moved by consideration of his devotion and also inclined out of regard for the aforesaid king of England, to whom we desire to show favourable deference insofar as we can with God and justice, we have graciously and kindly remitted to him, by the common counsel of our brethren, the journey of coming to us, and have judged it right to entrust his case to you, in whose prudence and honour we have confidence. [Col. 0736A]

Accordingly, we command your brotherhoods by apostolic letters that, assembling together as soon as you can at the border of the lands of the king of France and the king of England, namely in the March, you summon the aforesaid archbishop; and, having called to your side religious and prudent men, if the same archbishop, together with the two greatest and best persons of his church, who are of good reputation and unimpaired standing—or, if that cannot be done, with two other of his canons, not regarded as inferior in life, conduct, and faith to the persons, namely Master Vacarius and Master Angerus, or two others equal to them in merit; or, if he cannot have them present, with two priors or abbots of approved life and conduct, of whom it is likely that they would not commit perjury—shall swear before the holy Gospels placed before them that he neither confirmed those wicked customs by oath taken, faith pledged, or written instrument, nor promised to observe them; that he did not knowingly provoke the king by writing, word, or deed, on account of which the aforesaid archbishop was killed or suffered bodily punishment; that he did not receive your letters commanding him not to place the crown upon the king’s son; nor knew that they had been presented to him, nor knowingly prevented their being presented: then, relying on your authority, you shall without delay restore to him the full exercise of his office. [Col. 0736B–D]

But if, in carrying this out, you both cannot be present because of some evident and necessary impediment, then the one of you who is present shall carry it out as stated, with religious, prudent men and men of great authority from that province.

Given at Tusculum, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November [23 October].

DCCXCIX. To the same.—He does not wish the archbishop of York henceforth to establish his innocence in any way other than this: if he does so, he may exercise his office in the regions on this side of the sea. (Tusculum, October?)

[Ibid., p. 67.]

[Col. 0737A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers ROTROD, archbishop of Rouen, and the bishop of Amiens: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because it sometimes happens, as Scripture says, that ease of pardon provides an incentive to wrongdoing, we do not wish the venerable [Col. 0737B] archbishop of York henceforth—although he has repeatedly and urgently requested that we should act otherwise—to establish his innocence except in such a way that, if he does so, he may exercise his office in the regions on this side of the sea. Otherwise, we fear that the ulcer already formed may fester into pus. We therefore command you by apostolic letters that, after the truth of the present purgation has been investigated with particular care, the examination before you be made so manifest that nothing at all is derogated from the command recently sent to your brotherhoods concerning this matter. For whenever the truth of matters so serious and so great must be established, unless more diligent caution or investigation of the case comes to aid, the rewards of one who knows may be endangered and reputation may easily suffer harm.

DCCC. To Henry, king of England.—He commends Master D., English by birth. (SAVIOLI, *Annals*.)

[Bologn., I, II, 268.]

[Col. 0737C]

Among the other envoys of your magnificence who came into our presence, our beloved son Master D., having left the scholarly disciplines and studies to which he was devoted at Bologna, presented himself before us. As a learned, prudent, and discreet man, he took as much care and labour as he could to advance your affairs, and demonstrated by clear proofs that he is faithful and devoted in all things to your highness. We, moreover, [Col. 0737D] who by the obligation of our office ought to assist ecclesiastical men, and especially those who shine above others in learning, honour, and discretion, and to attend to their welfare with more earnest care, have carefully recalled to mind the learning, poverty, and prudence of the said D. and have judged it right to commend him most earnestly to your munificence. Although your clemency ought to have been moved by us on his behalf, nevertheless, because we know more fully his person, position, and resources, we have anticipated your highness with our prayers for him.

Therefore, since, attracted by the sweetness of his native soil, he desires to remain in your kingdom, where he was born, rather than in a foreign land, we have taken care to provide for him in that kingdom. For we believe [Col. 0738A] and hope that it ought not to displease your munificence if, by the authority of the ministry common to us, we have provided for his need: with pious discretion we have granted him the first prebend that happens to fall vacant in the church of Lincoln, especially since we believe him worthy not only of a canonry but even of a bishopric, and judge him suitable for these things, so far as we have been able to discern. Since the aforesaid church is at this time deprived of its own pastor, trusting in royal devotion and sincerity, we have supplied the bishop’s functions there by authority of our office, and have instituted the said D. a canon in the first prebend that becomes vacant there, lest the effect of our provision should perhaps be obstructed by some intervening circumstance and he should be deprived in vain of the desired gift of your favour. [Col. 0738B]

For it undoubtedly belongs to the enhancement of royal magnificence to retain in benefices and other gifts of favour men distinguished by learning and honour, especially those born in your kingdom, lest poverty compel them to transfer themselves to the realms of foreigners. We therefore ask, advise, and exhort your serenity in the Lord by apostolic letters to be willing that what we have done in this matter, insofar as it concerns your highness, be held valid and firm and put into execution; and not to allow it to be maliciously disturbed by anyone, nor to permit it to be hindered in any manner on account of a grant or promise made by anyone to another person. Rather, hear our prayers in this matter as you would wish yours to be heard by us when opportunity is offered, and insofar as we can with God. For in this, as we believe, you will receive a worthy reward from God and will deservedly carry away manifold praise before men. [Col. 0738C]

DCCCI. To the same.—He commends R., archdeacon of Salisbury, Richard Bar, and Master D., who served the king’s interest with the utmost zeal not only before the arrival of the other embassy, but also when they brought the news of the new legate, more welcome than the former. (Ibid., 269.)

DCCCII. He annuls gifts sealed with the seal of the monastery without the authorization of the monks of Saint Augustine of Canterbury, and decrees “that their seal shall be kept in such a manner that no person, except by the common consent and will of the brethren or of the sounder part of the convent, may dare to seal with the aforesaid seal any charter containing contracts of gift or obligations concerning the possessions of the monastery.” (*Hist. Angl. Script. decem*, II, 1817.)

[Col. 0738D]

DCCCIII. To A., provost of Reichersberg.—He congratulates him that amid the persecutions of heretics he has adhered steadfastly to the pope. (JAFFÉ, *Regesta Rom. Pont.*, 738, from a twelfth-century Reichersberg manuscript.)

To his beloved son A., provost of Reichersberg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0739A] Having received the letters of your affection with cheerful spirit and glad mind, we give devout thanks to him who granted you a spirit able to bear grave things and who, by his condescending favour, poured grace into your breast, because you have so fastened the anchor of your hope in reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves that, set amid a perverse nation, you have not allowed the right and Catholic faith to suffer loss in you; and because the wall of your faith, shaken by repeated blows, many batterings, and the blaring trumpet of threats, could not be broken, nor did you fear the strong wind rushing upon you or the storms of the raging sea. We pursue with fitting thanksgiving the constancy of your admirable virtue. Therefore we have all the greater will and desire to love you and your church with sincere charity and to promote your welfare and advancement, inasmuch as you are known to have laboured more steadfastly and firmly for the Catholic faith. [Col. 0739B]

But you, in devotion to blessed Peter and to ourselves, advance and grow stronger day by day more and more, so that you may appear to offer to God in your sacrifice “the tail together with the head.” Furthermore, abstain, in greeting, prayer, drink, and food, from communion with those schismatics who are expressly excommunicated or who received orders from the head of the schism. But you may without hesitation associate with the princes, since we have excommunicated by name none of those who remain except F., the head of this wickedness, and O. [Col. 0739C] Indeed, if you should on occasion associate under necessity with incendiaries—concerning whom, as we believe, the decrees command that they be excommunicated, although the Church causes them to be absolved as excommunicates in order to inspire fear—you need not fear on that account a judgment of condemnation before God.

IN THE YEAR 1170–1172.

DCCCIV. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—That provision be made with some benefice for Walter, a priest, and his brother, who had moved from the diocese of Toul to that of Reims because of the schismatics. (Tusculum, 20 October.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 851.]

[Col. 0739D]

It has not slipped from our memory, nor do we believe that you have forgotten, how formerly we earnestly asked your brotherhood on behalf of Walter, a priest, and his brother, who, leaving the bishopric of Toul because of the perfidy of the schismatics, from which place they had originated, as we have learned, withdrew to the region of Reims; and how we earnestly judged them worthy of your recommendation. But now, because by our letters we have asked our venerable brother, the bishop of Soissons, on behalf of that priest, to grant and assign him freely the church which the canons of Saint Gervais of Soissons are said to have freely promised at the request of our dearest son in Christ Louis, illustrious king of the French, [Col. 0740A] or another of equivalent value, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters earnestly to urge and induce that bishop to strive promptly and effectively to put our request in this matter into effect. You also are henceforth to hold the aforesaid priest and his brother commended to you through our intervention, so that you may seem to sympathize with their necessities in paternal affection and that we may therefore owe manifold thanks to your charity. Moreover, if you find the brother of the aforesaid priest suitable, do not delay to ordain him according to the tenor of our other letters.

[Col. 0740B] Given at Tusculum, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November [20 October].

DCCCV. To the same.—Against John, a priest who troubled the brethren of Mari. (Tusculum, 20 October.)

[Ibid., col. 852.]

You are to know that we have received the complaint of the abbot and brethren of Mari [Note: [Col. 0739D] The monastery of Mari, which seems formerly to have belonged to the diocese of Reims, is not found today.] that, whereas a certain altar had been granted to them by Hugh, formerly archdeacon of Reims, with the will and assent of Saint [Note: [Col. 0740D] Samson.] your predecessor of good memory, John, priest of the church in which that altar is situated, presumes to trouble them concerning it and does not permit them peacefully to possess the aforesaid altar, as the said archdeacon is known to have possessed it. [Col. 0740C] The same abbot and brethren further added that the aforesaid priest altogether refuses to pay them two parts of the offerings said to belong to those brethren. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to restrain, by the authority entrusted to you, the aforesaid priest from improperly burdening and troubling the said brethren, both concerning that altar and concerning other matters. But if the same priest believes himself protected against the petition of those brethren and decides to enter into a case with them, then, after you have carefully heard and examined the arguments of both sides, decide the case yourself, not through others, with its due conclusion. Furthermore, because the aforesaid brethren complain that their plough-team was driven off from land belonging to them by that priest, and assert that he has violently occupied the same land, we likewise wish this case to be examined by you and concluded with due judgment. [Col. 0740D]

Given at Tusculum, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November [20 October].

DCCCVI. To the same.—That he order a vineyard formerly given to the brethren of Mari to be restored. (Tusculum, 20 October.)

[Ibid.]

It has been brought to our ears on behalf of our beloved sons, the abbot [Col. 0741A] and brethren of Mari, that a certain citizen of Reims, who had assumed the religious habit in their monastery, left them a vineyard.
