A fellow citizen of his, named H., had held that vineyard as a pledge from him for the past twenty years. When the said H. died, his son nevertheless retained the aforesaid vineyard, contrary to God and his own salvation, although his father had, it is said, received from it his principal and more besides, apart from expenses; and, though repeatedly asked, he altogether refused to surrender the vineyard to the aforesaid monastery. But after he was suddenly removed from the present light by death, Odo, his brother-in-law, as is said, occupied the same vineyard as though it were his own and presumes violently to retain it. Since it is altogether unworthy [Col. 0741B] and unjust that the same monastery should be defrauded of what is its own, especially since the same abbot and brethren assert that they repaid to the aforesaid H. the principal for the recovery of the aforesaid vineyard, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to cause the said vineyard, together with the fruits received from it, to be restored and left in peace to that monastery within forty days after receipt of these letters; or else to cause full and sufficient justice to be rendered to it concerning the matter before you, with objection and appeal set aside. Nor are you to refuse to receive the testimony of the brethren themselves, through whom the said abbot intends to prove that he repaid the aforesaid H. his principal for the said vineyard.

[Col. 0741C] Given at Tusculum, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November [20 October].

DCCCVII. To the bishops established throughout the kingdom of France.—Concerning the governance of schools. (Tusculum, 20 October.)

[Ibid.]

The more the Gallican Church shines in the learning and honour of its leading persons, and the more carefully it strives to avoid things which appear to bring ecclesiastical honour into disgrace, the more worthy of vehement astonishment it seems that those who assume the name and dignity of master of the schools in your churches do not grant churchmen licence to teach others without a fixed payment. Since, however, such a wicked and excessive custom has sprung from the root of greed [Col. 0741D] and grievously disgraces ecclesiastical honour, it is for you to take thought and to strive with all earnestness that this custom be utterly uprooted from your churches; for it is especially and particularly credited to you if anything worthy of praise or blame is found in those churches. We also, who, although unworthy, exercise supreme authority by the dispensation of the Creator’s mercy, unwilling to leave uncorrected so great a vice of greed and rapacity, command your brotherhoods by apostolic letters to take care, under threat of anathema, that those exercising that dignity—if it can be called a dignity—may no longer dare to demand or extort anything from anyone for granting licence to teach others. [Col. 0742A] Rather, strictly command them to permit any suitable and learned men who wish to direct literary studies to govern schools without any harassment or exaction, lest learning should henceforth seem to be put up for sale when it ought to be bestowed freely upon all. But if any prove transgressors of your prohibition or command, deprive them by our authority and yours of the aforesaid offices and dignities. Moreover, if you neglect to correct this in accordance with our command, we shall regard your negligence as grave and troublesome and shall be compelled to extend our hand to correct these matters, so that, if they choose to persist in this purpose of rapacity, they will not be able to do so.

Given at Tusculum, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November [20 October].

DCCCVIII. To Peter, abbot of Saint Remigius, and B., archdeacon of Reims.—He entrusts a lawsuit to their judgment. (Tusculum, 23 October.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 947.]

[Col. 0742B]

We entrust to your experience for hearing and for determination by an appropriate judgment, with appeal set aside, the case which has long been litigated in the presence of our venerable brother the archbishop of Reims and brought before us by appeal, between Warin of Wimericourt and his wife’s sister, concerning a certain rent, part of which the aforesaid woman asserts belongs to her by hereditary right. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, when requested concerning this matter, you summon both parties before you and, after carefully hearing and examining the arguments on both sides, decide the same case, appeal set aside, either by agreement or through justice. [Col. 0742C]

Given at Tusculum, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November [23 October].

DCCCIX. To Henry, archbishop of Reims, and Theobald, bishop of Amiens.—He commends to them R., a woman who was suffering various injuries from many persons. (Tusculum, 27 October.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 854.]

From the complaint of R., a woman, we have learned that Gerard, a wealthy canon of St. Fursey, took from her her house at Péronne and certain other things, and inflicted many losses upon her. Drogo of Chameis and Peter of Glosabocca likewise caused her no small losses in connection with that house [Col. 0742D], and still presume to cause them. Since, therefore, by the office of apostolic ministry entrusted to us, we are bound to render justice to all, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and strictly compel the aforesaid G. to restore to the said woman the aforementioned house, together with everything taken and full compensation for the losses; and Drogo and P. to make good the losses inflicted and thereafter desist from harassing and troubling her; or else to render her justice in this matter before you, without recourse to appeal. But if they scorn to obey your admonitions, exercise canonical justice against them.

Given at Tusculum, 27 October.

DCCCX. To the same.—On behalf of the same woman, who suffered loss of property at the hands of the officials of Philip, Count of Flanders. (Tusculum, 27 October.)

[Ibid., col. 855.]

[Col. 0743A]

Because R., the bearer of these letters, has complained to us concerning the officials of our beloved son, the nobleman Ph., Count of Flanders, that they violently took her property, we have requested and admonished the same count to have all that was taken restored to the said woman, or to see that full justice is rendered her in the matter. But if the aforesaid count does not do justice to that woman regarding his officials, admonish and strictly compel those officials to restore in full all that was taken to the said woman [Col. 0743B], or, without appeal, not delay in rendering her full justice in the matter before you. If they are unwilling to do either, bind them with the bond of excommunication.

Given at Tusculum, 27 October.

DCCCXI. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—Concerning the correction of abuses in the bishopric of Tournai. (Tusculum, 29 October.)

[Ibid.]

When in the Church of God we hear that something is springing up from the root of avarice and breaking forth into Simoniacal depravity, it is fitting that we apply ourselves diligently to cutting it down swiftly [Col. 0743C], lest anything be found in the Church that offends the eyes of the divine Majesty or conflicts with ecclesiastical propriety. For report has informed us—and we could not hear it without being moved—that in the bishopric of Tournai unbridled avarice reigns to such an extent that abbots and monks, canons, and other ecclesiastical persons to whose presentation the churches of that bishopric belong, presume to impose unlawful exactions upon the priests ordained in those churches, contrary to the rigor of the canons and the ordinances of the holy Fathers. Unless those priests take the churches at farm or for rent, and serve the aforesaid persons at their pleasure, they are violently expelled from the said churches [Col. 0743D], and other priests who offer more are installed there. In appointing clergy to those churches, moreover, they disregard the integrity of the persons appointed and demand, unwilling as we are to say it, an amount of money.

Since it belongs to our office to root out utterly the vice of so great an abomination, we have commanded our venerable brother T., Bishop of Amiens, to investigate diligently the truth of the matter; and, should he find the Church of Tournai, in head or members, entangled in this vice of such depravity, to notify you on our behalf, so that you may correct and amend such abuses with pastoral solicitude. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when you receive that bishop’s letters concerning the correction of these matters, you cut away and uproot to the quick the root of so great an iniquity [Col. 0744A] and the vice of rapacity, so that not even a trace of so great an evil may remain, nor any report of such Simoniacal depravity henceforth circulate concerning the aforesaid persons. But if you should be negligent or remiss in correcting these matters, we would be compelled to extend our own hand to their correction.

Given at Tusculum, 29 October.

DCCCXII. To the same.—That he restrain the Bishop of Amiens from demanding obedience from the abbot of St. Riquier. (Tusculum, 31 October.)

[Ibid., col. 856.]

[Col. 0744B] Since we know you to be diligent and zealous in preserving the right and honor of the Roman Church, we confidently urge your brotherhood in matters which we know concern the increase and advancement of that Church. Since the church of Blessed Riquier is said to belong specially to the right and property of Blessed Peter, and equally to our governance and protection, and since, as you well recall, while it lacked a pastor we provided it with an abbot through your care, the venerable brother, the Bishop of Amiens, after that abbot’s death, has now installed an abbot there by his own authority and compelled him to render obedience to himself.

Because we neither can nor ought on any grounds to allow the rights of the Roman Church to be diminished [Col. 0744C], and because in that bishop—if he did this knowingly—such an act of presumption would deserve severe punishment, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, after you have fully ascertained the truth of the matter, that, if you find it to be so, you earnestly admonish and induce the bishop not to delay in releasing the abbot from obedience to him. If he fails to do so, release the abbot from that obedience by our authority; and, having learned from the monks whether any payment is owed to Blessed Peter in this matter, order it to be rendered to us in full. Whatever you do in this matter, take care to notify us as quickly as possible by your letters; and be so diligent and watchful in accomplishing it that we may deservedly commend your care and diligence in this respect.

[Col. 0744D] Given at Tusculum, 31 October.

DCCCXIII. To the same.—Concerning the dispute between Roger and his father-in-law Guiard. (Tusculum, 4 November.)

[Ibid., col. 857.]

We have learned from Roger’s transmitted complaint—Roger being a man of the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem—that, when an appeal in the case pending between himself and Guiard, his father-in-law, had long since been made to our hearing, the same G., forestalling the day set for the appeal, obtained the commission of that case to our beloved sons R., Archdeacon of Châlons, and the abbot [Col. 0745A] of All Saints on the Island.

[Note: [Col. 0745] All Saints on the Island is an abbey of regular canons of the Order of St. Augustine in the city of Châlons.]

When both parties appeared before them, the aforesaid R., because he was being compelled to answer concerning articles not contained in our letters of commission, appealed from them to our hearing. But they, disregarding the appeal, presumed to receive witnesses against him and to subject him to excommunication. Since those judges were not permitted to exceed the limit and form of our letters, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth of the matter; and, if you find it to be so, publicly declare, without delay and without appeal, that the sentence has no force. Thereafter hear more diligently the case pending between them [Col. 0745B], and determine it to its proper conclusion, without recourse to appeal.

But if the matter stands otherwise, we command and will that the sentence be observed, unless it contains manifest injustice. And because the aforesaid R. has complained to us that the same G., his father-in-law, keeps his wife from him by force, we command your discretion, if the matter is so, to compel G., under the coercion of an anathema, to restore his wife to the aforesaid R., unless G. alleges a just fear; if he alleges such fear, provide that adequate security be furnished to the woman.

Given at Tusculum, 4 November.

DCCCXIV. To the same.—That he remove P., priest of Curtismunt, guilty of many offenses, from his church. (Tusculum, 7 November.)

[Ibid., col. 858.]

[Col. 0745C]

The parishioners of the village of Curtismunt have sent us a serious complaint against their priest P.: though he was the son of a priest and begotten during his father’s priesthood, he obtained letters from us by deception, and by means of them acquired the parish which his father had held. Added to this is the fact that, although while seated at table he was repeatedly asked to go to a certain parishioner of his who was near death in order to give her penance, he refused to go; and thus, through his fault and negligence, the said woman died without confession and without receiving the body of the Lord.

It is also charged against him that at Christmas, after all the offerings had been made [Col. 0745D] by each of his parishioners, he exacts by coercion two loaves from each, contrary to ancient and reasonable custom, and that he is publicly a concubinary. Since these matters, if true, ought not to be passed over with closed eyes, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, strictly enjoining you, after a careful inquiry into the truth of the matter, that if the aforesaid woman died without penance and reception of the Lord’s body through his sloth and negligence; or if, being begotten during his father’s priesthood, he possesses the church in which his father ministered and obtained it by our letters while concealing the truth [Col. 0746A]; or if he is publicly a concubinary, you are not to delay in removing him from the aforesaid church, without pretext and without appeal.

Given at Tusculum, 7 November.

DCCCXV. To Peter, Abbot of St. Remigius, and Fulk, Dean of Rheims.—Concerning students of Rheims unjustly excommunicated by a priest and subjected to other injuries. (Tusculum, 8 November.)

[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 956.]

We have heard from the transmitted complaint of certain students living in the borough of St. Remigius that, when I., priest of the Borough of St. Remigius, on a Sunday, before clergy and laity and disregarding clerical modesty, led dances, those students rebuked and mocked him for it. Thereupon, supported by certain persons, the same priest, in rage and fury, rashly broke down the students’ door and windows [Col. 0746B] and laid violent hands upon some of them. Not content with these injuries, without the knowledge of our venerable brother Henry, Archbishop of Rheims, or his officials, he pronounced a sentence of excommunication the next day against persons neither cited nor having confessed; that sentence the archbishop, as he ought, caused to be relaxed.

The students maintain that their liberty was seriously infringed in this respect, asserting that they possess the privilege that no one may lay violent hands upon them or dare pronounce an ecclesiastical sentence against them until they are willing to submit to justice before their master. Therefore, provoked by this and other injuries, the students, as they assert, appealed against the same priest to our presence; but neither in person nor through another did he present himself before us.

Since the same priest seems, if this is true, to have committed multiple offenses, and since we do not wish—as we ought not—to leave his offenses uncorrected, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, strictly enjoining you to summon the parties before you and investigate diligently the truth of the matter. If you find that the said priest led dances before clergy and laity and, on that account [Col. 0746D], inflicted so grave an injury on the said students, or so rashly subjected them to anathema, punish him sternly and severely by our authority, without appeal, for such frivolity, presumption, and audacity. If it is established to you that he or his accomplices laid violent hands upon any of the aforesaid students who were clerics, then, relying upon apostolic authority and setting aside every objection and appeal, publicly declare them excommunicated and ensure that they are cautiously avoided as excommunicates, until they make suitable satisfaction to those injured and, with letters testifying to this from you, present themselves before the apostolic presence [Col. 0747A]. Prohibit all persons from daring to molest or burden the aforesaid students in any way contrary to their liberty, so long as they are prepared to submit to justice before their master.

Given at Tusculum, 8 November.

DCCCXVI. To the same.—That losses inflicted on the monastery of Anchin be repaired, and that the abbess of St. Michael’s not provide burial to excommunicates; if she has done so, that she disinter them. (Tusculum, 9 November.)

[Ibid., col. 950.]

Our beloved son A., Abbot of the church of Anchin—

[Note: [Col. 0747D] Alexander. In Miraeus’s edition of the Supplement to Sigebert: “In the year 1170 Baldwin IV, Count of Hainaut, died and was buried by Alexander, Abbot of Anchin, in the church of St. Waltrude.” The monastery is of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Arras, in which also lies the district of Vicoigne. Jacques Sirmond.]

—has informed us by letters that [Col. 0747B] the monks of Garde, among the oppressions and injuries which they are said irreverently to inflict upon him and his church, presume unjustly to take from them a certain tithe of land in the district of Vicoigne, which rightfully belongs to them. The abbess and nuns of St. Michael of Vurles also despoil one of his churches, namely St. Martin’s, of its parishioners; unlawfully usurping its rights for themselves, they admit to divine offices parishioners of the said abbot who have been excommunicated for their offenses and excluded from the threshold of the church, and grant burial to them when dead.

Since it is dangerous for religious persons to commit acts that bring peril to souls, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, strictly enjoining you, within twenty days after receiving these letters, to admonish and strictly compel the aforementioned persons to leave the aforesaid abbot and his church their rights whole and unimpaired, and restore what they have taken without harassment or difficulty; or to render them full justice before you, without appeal [Col. 0747C]. Moreover, because ecclesiastical sacraments must be wholly denied to those who, because of their sins, have been separated from the communion of the faithful, we further enjoin by the authority of these letters that, under penalty affecting their order and office, you forbid the aforesaid abbess and nuns of St. Michael to dare admit any excommunicated persons to divine offices or burial. If they have buried any persons bound by the bond of excommunication, they are not to delay, without appeal or pretext, to disinter them [Col. 0747D] and cast them out of the cemetery.

Given at Tusculum, 9 November.

DCCCXVII. To the same.—He commits a case to them for judgment. (Tusculum, 16 November.)

[Ibid., col. 955.]

From letters sent to us by our venerable brother Henry, Archbishop of Rheims, we have plainly learned that Baldwin of Aigne, intending to set out for Jerusalem, granted to a widowed sister of his, named Agnes, who lived in his house, three measures of wheat and one of oats, to be received annually from his tithe [Col. 0748A]. After the death of the same B. on pilgrimage, Gerard of Landas, who had married Baldwin’s daughter, did not hesitate to take by force from Agnes the aforesaid measures of wheat and oats. When Gerard had been summoned to the archbishop’s court and both he and the woman appeared before that archbishop, the woman produced lawful and suitable witnesses. The aforesaid four measures, concerning which the controversy was pending, having been adjudged to her, she was placed by the archbishop in possession of them.

Furthermore, as we have learned from the same letters, the said Agnes brought another claim against the same Gerard: namely, that the aforesaid Baldwin had a son born outside lawful marriage. Since he could not convey his inheritance to that son, he purchased a certain piece of land with his own money and gave it to him. When the son set out on a journey with his father, he granted that land to the said Agnes, to hold and possess forever should he fail to return. The aforementioned Gerard afterwards presumed shamelessly to take it from her. The same woman further complained that unlawful violence had been inflicted upon her concerning land left to her by her nephew. When Gerard, having been summoned, and the woman met on the appointed day before the archbishop, and she wished to produce her witnesses [Col. 0748C], Gerard appealed to our hearing.

But when the woman came before us, the other party neither came nor sent a representative to answer for him. Therefore, trusting in your prudence and integrity, we commit this case to you for hearing and due determination. We command your discretion by apostolic letters to summon both parties before you and, having fully heard and examined the arguments on both sides, endeavor to determine by justice, without recourse to appeal, the controversies and questions concerning those articles which you ascertain were appealed to us; so that neither party may rightly complain that its right has failed, nor may the aforesaid woman be compelled any further to seek our assistance in this matter [Col. 0748D].

Given at Tusculum, 16 November.

DCCCXVIII. To the Abbot of St. Remigius of Rheims and the Prior of St. Martin of the Fields.—He commits for judgment the case of two abbots. (Tusculum, 23 November.)

[Ibid., col. 950.]

From the transmitted complaint of G., Abbot of Garde—

[Note: [Col. 0748D] Of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Amiens, to which also belongs the abbey of Sérancourt, of the Premonstratensian Order. ID.]

—we have learned that the abbot and canons [Col. 0749A] of the church of St. Peter of Sérancourt unjustly despoiled his monastery of a certain tract of land because of a change of ministers, and unlawfully retain it in occupation. Since no scruple of discord or material for quarrels should remain among religious men, who ought to devote themselves to the repose of heavenly contemplation, trusting in your prudence and integrity we commit this case to you for hearing and due determination.

Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, when you have been asked to do so, you meet together, summon both parties before you, and, after fully hearing and examining the arguments on each side, determine the case within two months, without recourse to appeal, either by agreement or by means of justice [Col. 0749B]. In particular, if it is established to you that the aforesaid abbot was expelled contrary to right from possession of the said land, first cause that possession to be restored to him without appeal. But if both of you cannot be present in the matter, let one of you proceed no less fully in the case.

Given at Tusculum, 23 November.

DCCCXIX. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—That he absolve the brothers Reiner and Walter from excommunication for violently laying hands upon a priest. (Tusculum, 24 November.)

[MARTÈNE, Amplified Collection, II, 858.]

[Col. 0749C] From the transmitted account of Reiner and his brother Walter, we have learned that, when a dispute arose between a brother of theirs and a priest, inflamed by anger they laid violent hands upon that priest; but since he was not injured, they made satisfaction to the chapter of Cambrai and to the priest. Since, because of the hazards and dangers of the journey, they hesitate to come before us in order to obtain the benefit of absolution, and since we wish to accommodate them and defer to your brotherhood, we have entrusted their absolution to your judgment. Therefore we command your discretion that, after receiving from them the oath customary in the Church, you absolve them by our authority; and afterwards command them, under the force of the oath, that henceforth [Col. 0749D] they are never to lay violent hands upon a cleric, monk, or lay brother, or upon Templars or Hospitallers, except in self-defense, or by command of their bishop or other prelate, or unless they find such persons with their wife, sister, or daughter. Nevertheless, compel them to make suitable satisfaction to the priest for the injury inflicted, if they have not yet done so; and have whatever they would have spent in travelling to us given to the lepers of Cambrai.

Given at Tusculum, 24 November.

DCCCXX. To the same.—That he protect G., a poor cleric, from the harassment of Richard the canon. (Tusculum, 24 November.)

[Ibid., col. 859.]

[Col. 0750A]

From the complaint of G., a poor cleric, we have learned that, after he had long served a certain canon named Ric., and had advanced him more than ten Valenciennes pounds, both from his own means and on credit from others, when the term of his service was completed the canon not only refused to repay what had been advanced to him, but also presumed wrongfully and fraudulently to dispute five measures of wheat and more, which G. had bought with his own money. Afterwards, when G. brought suit against the said canon concerning these matters, the latter, compelled by justice, acknowledged the aforesaid debt. Yet when G. pressed him to pay the debt, he appealed to our hearing but neither came nor sent a representative to answer for him.

Since we are bound to render justice to every person, and especially to ecclesiastical men, and since it is unfitting that the aforesaid G. should suffer so great a loss from his own property in return for a service from which he ought to receive profit, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to admonish and strictly compel the said canon to restore G.’s debt in full, make good the losses inflicted, or render him full justice in the matter before you, without appeal. But if he presumes to deny the amount of the debt or of the accounting, said to have been made between them concerning both wheat and money [Col. 0750C], compel him, since the question concerns money, to take the oath against vexatious litigation.

Given at Tusculum, 24 November.

DCCCXXI. To the brethren of Nonantola.—He adjudges to them the place of Lovoletus, occupied by the Bishop of Modena. (Tusculum, 25 November.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *History of Nonantola*, II, 276.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and brethren of Nonantola: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Matters settled by the authority of the Roman Church through agreement or judgment ought to remain firm; and, lest they be changed by anyone’s rash presumption, they must be strengthened by the protection of apostolic confirmation [Col. 0750D]. Since a controversy had long been pending between you and our venerable brother the Bishop of Modena concerning possession of Lovoletus before our beloved son Hildebrand, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles and legate of the Apostolic See, the same bishop appealed to our hearing.

We committed the determination of this case to our beloved son O., deacon-cardinal of St. Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano and legate of the Apostolic See—

[Note: [Col. 0749] Cardinal Oddo of Brescia, raised to that dignity by Eugene III in the year 1150.]

—who, after hearing the arguments and allegations of both parties and receiving witnesses as well [Col. 0751A], fixed a date for both parties to present themselves before the apostolic presence with their attestations and allegations. But when your messenger arrived and the aforesaid bishop did not come before us either personally or through others, we sent the allegations and witness depositions under our seal to our beloved son Manfred—

[Note: [Col. 0751D] Manfred of Siena, appointed cardinal by Alexander III in the year 1163.]

—deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil and legate of the Apostolic See, and commanded him to settle the case without appeal. Although that bishop, as we have learned from the letters of Cardinal Manfred, had been peremptorily summoned and was unwilling to appear personally or through an adequate representative, Manfred had nevertheless learned by the lawful testimony of many witnesses [Col. 0751B] that your church had held peaceful possession of the said place for forty years and more, and that the bishop himself had occupied it on his own authority during the six previous years. Therefore Cardinal Manfred, after taking counsel with prudent men, adjudged to you free restitution of possession of Lovoletus, so that henceforth you may enjoy the advantage of a possessor, while the bishop, if he wishes to litigate concerning ownership, bears the burden of a claimant.

We hold that sentence, pronounced by the said Cardinal M. and confirmed in an authentic written instrument, ratified and firm; confirming it by apostolic authority, we fortify it with the protection of this present writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it [Col. 0751C]. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Tusculum, 26 November.

DCCCXXII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of G., deacon, concerning the church of Undescota. (Tusculum, 27 November.)

[MARTÈNE, Amplified Collection, II, 860.]

Our venerable brother the Bishop of Thérouanne informed us that, when we had previously addressed earnest requests to him to provide for G., deacon and bearer of these letters, in the church of Undescota, he summoned B., priest [Col. 0751D] of that church, and began carefully to investigate his ordination. At length, from B.’s own confession in court, he learned that B. had been ordained priest by the schismatic and intruded bishop of Arras, namely Gero; but B. said that this ordination took place before Gero fell into schism, and asserted that he himself had acquired that church canonically.

When the aforesaid deacon urgently pressed the bishop to provide for him in the said church according to the tenor of our letters, B. appealed against the deacon to our hearing and fixed the approaching feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary as the term for his appeal [Col. 0752A], so that he might retain that church and avoid the danger which he knew was imminent. Since there is no doubt that the aforesaid Gero, intruded bishop of Arras, was a schismatic and excommunicated, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the matter with the aforesaid bishop and others who know the truth. If it is established to you that the said B. acknowledged in court before that bishop that he had been ordained priest by the aforesaid G., depose him permanently by our authority, without appeal, from the order which he received from him; remove him from the said church; and admonish and induce the aforesaid bishop [Col. 0752B] not to delay in providing for the said deacon in the same church according to the tenor of our request.

Given at Tusculum, 27 November.

DCCCXXIII. To the same.—On behalf of the brethren of the Church of Maurimont. (Tusculum, 27 November.)

[Ibid., 86.]

We have heard from the serious complaint of our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the Church of Maurimont—

[Note: [Col. 0751D] The monastery of Maurimont, of the Order of St. Benedict, [Col. 0752D] in the diocese of Châlons, still belongs to the congregation of St. Vitonus.]

—that the priest of Sainte-Menehould violently invaded their house with an armed band, beat their household, and with diabolical audacity wounded P., a monk and bearer of these letters [Col. 0752C], cruelly shedding his blood. Since these things, if true, are not the deeds of a Christian and deserve all the more severe punishment because they should less readily have been undertaken by a priest, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the matter is so, you do not delay, without appeal, to bind the said priest, his assistants, and his supporters—by whose counsel and aid you ascertain this was done—with the bond of excommunication. Cause them to be avoided as excommunicates until they have made suitable satisfaction to those injured, restored what was taken, and compensated the losses inflicted; and until both the priest, suspended from office and benefice, and all others known to have laid violent hands upon the monk present themselves before the apostolic presence with letters testifying to this from you [Col. 0752D].

Given at Tusculum, 27 November.

DCCCXXIV. To the same.—That he restrain certain persons who exacted tithes of newly cultivated land from the sick of Cambrai. (Tusculum, 29 November.)

[Ibid.]

We have received the repeated complaint sent to us by the brethren of the sick of Cambrai: the abbots of St. Andrew of the Castle and of the Holy Sepulchre, the canons of St. Géry, and Phil., knight of Ruminiaco, presume to demand and violently extort from them tithes of their newly cultivated lands and of fodder for their animals [Col. 0753A], contrary to the writing which we granted them. They cannot in any way be restrained from exacting those tithes, despite our commands and injunctions on this subject, so often repeated.

When you wished to proceed in this case, which had long since been entrusted to your judgment, certain letters seeming to have been issued by us were, as we have learned, read before you. Those letters, sent on behalf of the brethren themselves, appeared more openly to conflict with their claim. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, setting aside every delay, objection, and appeal, to restrain the aforesaid knight by our and your authority from exacting those tithes. If he has perhaps seized any by violence, compel him through ecclesiastical censure to restore them within eleven days after receipt of these letters [Col. 0753B].

Moreover, we will and command that you diligently admonish both the aforesaid abbots and the canons, and, by the authority conferred upon you, compel them: if they are known rashly to have taken from the said brethren any tithes from fodder for their animals or from newly cultivated lands which the brethren cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense, they are not to delay, without appeal, to restore them in full within the prescribed term, and are to cease henceforth demanding or taking tithes from them on these grounds. But if they possess newly cultivated lands brought under cultivation by others, from which tithes had customarily been paid to the aforesaid abbots [Col. 0753C] and canons, we do not wish those abbots or canons to be deprived of their tithes; rather, they are to receive tithes from those lands just as they had customarily received them from others who held the same newly cultivated lands before the brethren.

Given at Tusculum, 29 November.

DCCCXXV. To [Henry], Bishop of Senlis, and [Peter], Abbot of St. Remigius.—That the brethren of Corbie restore to the brethren of St. Mary of Brana a tithe they have taken; likewise, that a tithe once sold by an abbot be restored to the same monastery. (Tusculum, 30 November.)

[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 944.]

[Col. 0753D] Our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the church of St. Mary of Brana, have shown us in a report sent to us that our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of Corbie—

[Note: [Col. 0753D] This is an especially distinguished monastery on the river Somme, in the diocese of Amiens. It is called Old Corbie, to distinguish it from the Saxon Corbie, which was founded much later than the French one. Sirmond.]

—have not hesitated, contrary to equity and justice, to take from them a certain tithe. Since, therefore, as by the will of divine Providence the care of all churches rests upon us, so too we are bound to provide for each in its own right, and are compelled by consideration of the office entrusted to us to restore to a state of rectitude those things done irregularly or outrageously, we command your discretion by apostolic letters [Col. 0754A] to admonish and strictly compel the Abbot of Corbie and his brethren to restore the aforesaid tithe to the said abbot and brethren, setting aside all pretext, and leave them in peace; or else to render them full justice in the matter before your judgment.

But if they resolve to enter into litigation rather than restore the tithe, meet together, summon both parties before you, and, having fully heard and examined the arguments on both sides, determine the case, without recourse to appeal, either by agreement or through justice.

Moreover, as has come to our ears from the report sent by the same abbot and brethren, Rodulf, formerly abbot of the aforesaid church, sold a certain tithe to the monks [Col. 0754B] of St. Leodegar [Note: [Col. 0754D] Of the Order of St. Augustine at Soissons. ID.], whereby that church suffers grave and enormous loss. Since that contract was petty and simoniacal, and the principal persons—the seller and the buyer—would, if still living, deserve condemnation to perpetual deposition, we nevertheless enjoin upon you to make every effort to admonish and strictly compel those monks, upon receiving back the price, to restore that tithe to them, all appeal set aside, and to leave them in peace. For it is neither fitting nor consonant with reason that one church should be enriched through another’s loss. Inflict upon those who made so ruinous and detestable a contract, if they survive, such punishment that others who hear of it may fear to presume upon similar acts.

[Col. 0754C] Given at Tusculum, the second day before the Kalends of December [30 November].

DCCCXXVI. To the same persons.—That the monks of Saint Remigius of Braine are not to molest the brethren of Saint Mary of Braine [Note: [Col. 0754D] A town on the river Vesle, in the district of Soissons. There, therefore, are the monasteries mentioned, as well as the dignity of a countship. ID.]. (At Tusculum, 30 November.)

[Ibid.]

You should know that it has been reported to the hearing of the Apostolic See that the monks of Saint Remigius of Braine strictly forbid the religious men, the abbot and brethren of Saint Mary of Braine, to administer any sacraments to the household of the count and countess of Braine. Since it is unseemly and dishonourable for those who have chosen, in the religious habit, to serve the Lord to harass anyone with undue vexations, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to admonish the aforesaid monks and, by our authority, compel them either not, on any pretext, to forbid the established household of the count or countess, the knights of the castle, newcomers, their wives, children, or households, to attend that church and receive ecclesiastical sacraments there; or not to defer carrying out before you whatever justice shall dictate. For we have directed them to carry out one of the aforesaid alternatives before you.

Given at Tusculum, the second day before the Kalends of December.

DCCCXXVII. To the abbot and brethren of Corbie.—That they restore to the monastery of Braine the tithe taken away. (At Tusculum, 30 November.)

[Ibid., col. 946.]

[Col. 0755A]

Our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the church of Saint Mary of Braine, have shown us by a report sent to us that you do not hesitate, contrary to the equity of law, to take from them a certain tithe. Therefore, since by the will of divine Providence the care of all churches rests upon us, and we are likewise bound to provide each person with his right, and, in consideration of the office entrusted to us, are compelled to restore to a state of rectitude matters done disorderly or outrageously, we commit the hearing of this matter to our venerable brother, the bishop of Senlis, and to our beloved son, the abbot of Saint Remigius of Rheims, and its settlement, with appeal set aside, by the administration of justice. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command you to restore the aforesaid tithe to the said abbot and brethren and leave them in peace; or to render them full justice concerning it before the aforesaid judges, all appeal set aside, accepting and inviolably observing their judgment in this matter.

Given at Tusculum, the second day before the Kalends of December.

DCCCXXVIII. To the bishops of Amiens and Tournai, and the abbot of Saint Remigius.—That they judge the disputes of the abbot of Braine and a certain knight. (At Tusculum, 30 November.)

[Ibid., col. 945.]

[Col. 0755C]

From the complaint sent by our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the church of Braine, it has come to our ears that John, knight of Hostel, violently took from them four muids of wheat, nine muids of oats, and five setiers by the measure of Soissons; and that he rashly presumed to take twelve muids of wine in their court and two in his own vineyard. Moreover, because he prevented them from harvesting their vineyard in its proper season, he caused them a loss of six muids of wine; he made them lose, for three years, one and a half setiers of wheat which the monks of Saint Nicholas of the Wood paid them annually; and, causing them damage in his wood estimated at sixty pounds, he did not hesitate unlawfully to take the land in which they were accustomed to sow two muids less one setier, as well as the land of Robert son of Widela, and seven setiers of vinagium (wine-dues), which that Robert, with the consent of Berner, lord of the land, had given them for an annual rent of one muid of wheat.

[Col. 0755D]

Further, he violently occupied certain land which they had possessed for a long time and had cleared at an expense of forty pounds; and he did not fear to inflict on them many other vexations, injuries, burdens, persecutions, and losses.

Since it was formerly reported to us on behalf of the aforesaid John that, when he and the aforesaid abbot had jointly submitted to certain persons the matter of certain possessions—namely, meadows, lands, and vineyards—and those persons had made an award between them, the abbot accepted their award in part and rejected it in part, we, wishing to uphold each in his right, commanded you, brother bishop of Tournai, to admonish the aforesaid abbot to observe that award without disturbance. But since it has now been intimated to us that it was not the abbot but the knight who withdrew from the award, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you assemble together, summon both parties before you, earnestly admonish and direct them firmly and without disturbance to observe the award concerning those possessions for which they voluntarily submitted themselves to arbitrators.

If they refuse to abide by the award, and their sureties cannot compel them by law to observe it, then diligently hear the case both concerning the matters adjudicated between them and concerning the other matters disputed between them, and take care to settle it by amicable composition or through justice, without respect of persons. In particular, compel the said John, all appeal set aside, to restore whatever he violently took from that abbot and brethren concerning which no award was made. If, however, the aforesaid John, having been cited by you, should disdain either to appear before you or to obey your judgment, bind him, all appeal and pretext set aside, with the bond of excommunication; and in the land where he lives prohibit the celebration of all divine offices, except baptism of infants and penitence for the dying.

If either party considers that an appeal should be made, diligently and carefully hear the arguments and allegations produced on either side; receive, all appeal set aside, the witnesses produced by each party; faithfully cause the depositions of those sworn witnesses to be written down; and endeavour to send them to us sealed under your seal, setting a suitable term for both parties by which they must appear before the Apostolic See with those attestations. Moreover, if the three of you cannot all attend this matter together, you, brother bishop of Tournai, together with one of the others, shall carry out the foregoing more promptly.

[Col. 0756D] Given at Tusculum, the second day before the Kalends of December.

DCCCXXIX. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of the monastery of Saint Medard in a case of usury. (At Tusculum, 2 December.)

[Marten, *Most Ample Collection*, II, 862.]

At the representation of our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of Saint Medard, you should know that it has come to our hearing that, when a certain Godoin had lent them a sum of money and had received from them two hundred marks of silver beyond the principal under the name of interest, he at length died intestate, as his sins deserved. Since it is altogether unworthy and unjust that, if the matter stands thus, that monastery should further be burdened concerning interest or principal, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, after diligently investigating the truth of the matter, that, if this is established to your satisfaction, you do not henceforth permit the aforesaid monastery to be molested for the recovery of principal or interest. Rather, the heirs of the aforesaid G. ought fully to restore to the said brethren what was extorted from them beyond the principal.

[Col. 0757A]

But if the heirs of G. presume to molest the aforesaid monastery concerning the aforementioned money, restrain them from their presumption by ecclesiastical coercion, all appeal set aside.

Given at Tusculum, the fourth day before the Nones of December [2 December].

DCCCXXX. To the same.—On behalf of the monastery of Maurimont concerning grain. (At Tusculum, 2 December.)

[Ibid., col. 863.]

[Col. 0757B]

A complaint has been brought to our hearing on behalf of the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Maurimont: Milo, surnamed Arrivatus, does not fear unreasonably to take forty setiers of grain from that monastery. When called to account concerning this, he gave his pledge that he would restore the aforesaid grain to the monastery; nevertheless, disregarding the sanctity of his pledge, he shamelessly continues to retain it. Therefore, wishing that due justice be rendered to the said brethren, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, if this is so, to admonish the aforesaid M. and strictly compel him, all appeal set aside, to restore the said forty setiers of grain to the brethren within twenty days after receipt of these letters, without diminution, and to leave them in peace.

[Col. 0757C]

Correct his offence in this respect so that he may recognize that he has grievously transgressed, and others, taking warning from his example, may guard themselves more carefully against so dangerous an offence.

Given at Tusculum, the fourth day before the Nones of December [2 December].

DCCCXXXI. To all the faithful established throughout the kingdom of France.—That they assist the Church of Nazareth. (At Tusculum, 8 December.)

[Ibid.]

Although your whole community may have learned from the accounts of travellers about the desolations, tribulations, hardships, and sufferings of cities, castles, and other places in the Eastern land, we have nevertheless judged it necessary, not without sorrow, to inform you and earnestly to stir your charity to compassion for such great evils. For, by divine and hidden judgment, an earthquake has destroyed and utterly uprooted many cities and towns, some wholly and some in part; and in their ruins a vast multitude of people has been suffocated.

[Col. 0757D]

Accordingly, certain enemies and adversaries of Christ, taking courage, have occupied by tyrannical invasion several places of Christians. Among these, having seized, through their sins, a large and populous village belonging to the Church of Nazareth, they carried off the clergy and other inhabitants into captivity. Thus the canons of that church, both from this and from other evils and hardships that have befallen them, have fallen into such need and poverty that, unless they are helped by God’s faithful people, they will not be able long to remain in their church in the service of the supreme Creator.

Moreover, since the Gospel Scripture testifies, “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2), and since all who desire to attain the splendour of unbounded light and that glory of eternity which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2:19), and where thieves neither break in nor steal (Matt. 4:20), must strive to sow upon earth that seed of good work which they may reap in heaven with multiplied fruit, we ask, admonish, and exhort you in the Lord, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of sins, that you receive as devoutly as humbly the brethren and messengers of the aforesaid canons sent to you to set forth their burdens and needs.

[Col. 0758B]

Extend to them the consolations of charity and the aid of assistance, so that from almighty God, who leaves no good deed unrewarded, you may receive the rewards of eternal recompense and, God being gracious, may deserve to attain the joys of heavenly blessedness.

Given at Tusculum, the sixth day before the Ides of December [8 December].

DCCCXXXII. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—He commits a case to him for examination and settlement. (At Tusculum, 9 December.)

[Ibid., 865.]

[Col. 0758C]

From the representation of Theobald, bearer of the present letter, we have learned that his sureties of Appy, after they had stood surety for him in the sum of fifteen pounds, told him that, if he wished and consented, they would satisfy from that sum the person to whom he owed those pounds. Because they refused to do this and pursued him for sixty-one shillings and six pence, he appealed to our hearing. Since the truth of this matter is known to us, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid T. can prove by lawful witnesses that the said sureties had from his property as much as the sum for which they stood surety for him, you admonish and compel them either to release him from that obligation or to render him full justice before you.

[Col. 0758D]

If they refuse, strike them with ecclesiastical censure, all appeal set aside. But regarding the sixty-one shillings and six pence which they demanded from him, hear the case and decide it through justice, all appeal set aside.

Given at Tusculum, the fifth day before the Ides of December [9 December].

DCCCXXXIII. To the same.—That he receive the monastery of Corbie under his protection. (At Tusculum, 9 December.)

[Ibid., col. 869.]

From the report sent to us by our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the Church of Corbie [Note: [Col. 0759D] Corbie, an ancient and distinguished monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, four hours from Amiens, founded by St. Bathild, wife of Clovis II, king of the Franks [Col. 0760D]], we have learned that you have anticipated them with favour and affection and have endeavoured to do them good. We are greatly delighted by this, and more warmly moved toward love and affection for you, judging it all the more welcome and acceptable because we love that monastery especially and are bound to protect, foster, and preserve it, by more solicitous provision, as our own special possession.

[Note: [Col. 0760D] The monastery of Corbie acknowledges no bishop other than the pope.]

[Col. 0759A]

Therefore, while rendering abundant thanks to your sincerity for what has gone before, we ask and earnestly admonish your brotherhood, for the sake of that monastery, to love, support, protect, and preserve it in its rights, for love of God and reverence for blessed Peter and for us. Do not in any way diminish its rights and liberties, nor, insofar as lies in you, allow them to be diminished by anyone. Instead, when you receive a complaint concerning this from those of your diocese, see that full justice is rendered, so that in this matter we may abundantly commend the diligence of your solicitude and return you plentiful thanks.

[Col. 0759B] Given at Tusculum, the fifth day before the Ides of December [9 December].

DCCCXXXIV. To the same.—That he restrain Guy, archbishop of Châlons, from harassing the widow M. (At Tusculum, 10 December.)

[Ibid.]

There would be no end to litigation if matters settled by judgment or agreement were drawn into the difficulty of renewed consideration [f. contention]. For it has been reported to our ears that, although the case between the widow M. and our brother G., bishop of Châlons, had been suitably concluded, that bishop now causes it to be revived through a certain townsman of his, and thus causes the aforesaid woman to be wearied by costly litigation.

[Col. 0759C]

Since it is unjust and contrary to reason to reopen, on any pretext, matters known to have been lawfully decided, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to admonish the aforesaid bishop on your behalf and ours, and strictly compel him not, either personally or through a subordinate, on any ground improperly to molest the said woman concerning her case, if it has been settled by agreement or judgment. If he rashly attempts this, restrain his rashness by suitable punishment.

[Col. 0759D] Given at Tusculum, the fourth day before the Ides of December [10 December].

DCCCXXXV. To Peter, abbot of Saint Remigius.—That he not prohibit men of his monastery from taking wives from another lordship. (At Tusculum, 11 December.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 926.]

It has been brought to our hearing that you are prosecuting Robert and Martin, men of your monastery, because they have taken wives from another lordship. Since such a pretext seems frivolous and empty, and it is not fitting for you to impose an undue burden upon anyone on that account, we command your discretion by apostolic letters not to harass the aforesaid men with any vexations, nor presume improperly to burden them, for the reason stated.

[Col. 0760A]

Nevertheless, if you wish to proceed against them concerning this matter, pursue it in your court according to judicial procedure.

Given at Tusculum, the third day before the Ides of December [11 December].

DCCCXXXVI. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—He commits to him the settlement of the case between the priests Lambert and Bartholomew. (At Tusculum, 11 December.)

[Marten, *Most Ample Collection*, I, 870.]

When Lambert and Bartholomew had appeared before the Apostolic See concerning the case disputed between them over the church of Octave, Lambert asserted before us that the aforesaid church had been canonically granted to him, and that William, the archpriest, had entrusted it to Bartholomew until his return, when Lambert went to Paris for the sake of study. Bartholomew, on the other hand, alleged that he had found the said church vacant, had canonically obtained it, and had possessed it peacefully for more than two years.

[Col. 0760B]

Since neither party could establish before us the matters they alleged, we, placing great confidence in your integrity and discretion, commit the case to your judgment, to be heard and brought to its due conclusion. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood, when you are asked concerning it, to summon both parties before you and, after fully hearing and ascertaining the arguments on both sides, decide the case with the impediment of appeal removed, through justice. Use such foresight and diligence that neither party can rightly complain of a deficiency of justice.

[Col. 0760C] Given at Tusculum, the third day before the Ides of December [11 December].

DCCCXXXVII. To the dean and chapter of the Church of Paris.—On the residence of non-resident canons. (At Tusculum, 12 December.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 1067.]

In accordance with the duty of our office, we desire diligently to promote what concerns the growth of churches and the beauty of their adornment, and we wish to give prompt care and attention to matters that we know concern your advancement and that of your church. From the letters sent to us by your devotion, however, we have plainly learned that certain among you, occupied with other business, seldom appear in your church; and that, because the rest desire to enjoy the same licence of absence, you have, by common counsel, designated as non-resident canons those of your canons who have not been regularly present in the service of your church for half the year.

[Col. 0760D]

You have provided, nevertheless, that they are to receive annually about four marks of silver from their prebend, except those remaining in our service or that of the king of France; and you have confirmed this under the imposition of anathema. Therefore, wishing, as we have said, to provide by paternal mediation for your peace, tranquillity, and welfare, we regard the aforesaid ordinance, made by the greater and sounder part of the chapter, as ratified and firm. So that it may not be altered by anyone’s presumption, we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it with the protection of this present writing, decreeing that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it.

[Col. 0761A]

But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0761B] Given at Tusculum, the second day before the Ides of December [12 December].

DCCCXXXVIII. To Peter, abbot of Saint Remigius, and Fulco, dean of Rheims.—That an abbot who received a man belonging to another abbot, with his goods, be compelled to restore him. (At Tusculum, 18 December.)

[Ibid., col. 927.]

Our beloved son, the abbot of Humularia [Note: [Col. 0761D] Now Humblières, in the diocese of Noyon; in the same diocese is the Augustinian monastery of Saint Mary of Ham. Jacques Sirmond.], informed us by letters sent to us that the abbot of Ham had received a certain man belonging to him, together with his goods, into the religious habit, whereby the aforesaid abbot of Humularia complains that his rights have been considerably impaired.

[Col. 0761C]

Since, by the office entrusted to us, we must uphold each person in his right, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to admonish the aforesaid abbot by our authority and strictly compel him either to restore the named man with his goods to the aforesaid abbot, or to make an amicable and peaceful settlement with him, or to render sufficient justice concerning the matter before you, all appeal set aside.

Given at Tusculum, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January [18 December].

DCCCXXXIX. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—That he prevent the interest which Bernard the leper demanded from Gerard of Joëcourt. (At Tusculum, 18 December.)

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 870.]

[Col. 0761D]

From the complaint sent by Gerard of Joëcourt, it has been represented to us that he borrowed on interest one hundred shillings from Oda, sister of a certain leper named Bernard; and that he had paid her up to one hundred shillings in accrued interest. Nevertheless, after the death of the said sister, the same leper urgently demands that G. pay him the aforesaid hundred shillings. Since, as your discretion knows, usury is reckoned among the gravest crimes and, because there is no doubt that it endangers souls, is held hateful to God and the faithful, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to bring both the said leper and Gerard before you.

[Col. 0762A]

If it is lawfully established to your satisfaction by Gerard’s proof that the said leper or his sister received from Gerard one hundred shillings as interest, strictly compel the said Bernard by our authority to desist from his claim against Gerard for either principal or interest, and to leave him in peace and quiet.

Given at Tusculum, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January [18 December].

DCCCXL. To the same.—That he absolve the excommunicated Albert and secure to him the church of Angey and Cersouil. (At Tusculum, 18 December.)

[Ibid., col. 871.]

[Col. 0762B]

Albert, bearer of the present letter, came before the clemency of the Apostolic See and showed us in a humble complaint that, while the Church of Soissons was vacant, our beloved son N., archdeacon of that church, granted him the church of Angey and Cersouil according to the ancient and reasonable custom of his church; and that he possessed it peacefully and quietly for a long time. At length, when he came to our court and obtained our letters of confirmation concerning that church, our venerable brother Hu., bishop of Soissons, during Albert’s absence granted that church to a certain familiar of his, named Ric., which Ric. was quite unable to enter because the countess of Braine and the parishioners forbade him.

[Col. 0762C]

Long afterward, when the said Ric. brought Albert into court concerning this before the aforesaid bishop, and Albert appealed to your jurisdiction, you, having seen our confirmation and the lawful witnesses whom he produced, and having received assurance concerning N., the archdeacon, that Albert had canonically obtained the church, left him in peace. But when Ric. appealed to our hearing and came, while Albert neither appeared nor sent anyone to answer for him, we wrote to you in this manner: if it were established that Albert had not received the church from the bishop’s hand, you were to deprive him of it. Thus it happened that you adjudged the aforesaid church away from him and declared him excommunicated, both throughout the bishopric and in that church, unless he relinquished it.

[Col. 0762D]

But since we wrote not to an unlettered man, but to one learned and discerning, and since archdeacons, as we have said, while the principal church is vacant, may freely make appointments to the churches of their archdeaconries, and since one seems sufficiently to receive a benefice from the bishop’s hand when one receives it from the hand of him who acts in the bishop’s place, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the matter stands thus, you declare him absolved by us and cause his church to be left to him in peace. But if the matter stands otherwise, cause what our venerable brethren the bishops of Beauvais and Amiens shall determine, all appeal set aside, to be accepted and firmly observed. For although we gladly wish to defer to you as to a most dear brother, we could not remit the case to your examination because an appeal had been made from you to our hearing.

[Col. 0763A] Given at Tusculum, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January [18 December].

DCCCXLI. To the same.—Against Peter, called elect of Cambrai, and Drogo, chancellor of Noyon. (At Tusculum, 18 December.)

[Ibid., col. 872.]

Since the matters which you have reported to us concerning P., called elect of Cambrai [Note: [Col. 0763D] Peter of Alsace, son of Thierry, count of Flanders, and Sibyl, daughter of Fulk, king of Jerusalem. He relinquished the bishopric unordained in 1170, having married a daughter of the count of Nevers, by whom he had no offspring.], and Drogo are grave and many, deserving punishment, although we grieve for the Church of Maroilles [Note: [Col. 0764D] The monastery of Maroilles, of the Order of St. Benedict, on the river Helpe in the diocese of Cambrai.], we nevertheless rejoice that God is in this matter now punishing your offences, and that from their conduct you plainly recognize that you acted wrongly.

[Col. 0763B]

You ought carefully to recall how great gravity, circumspection, and purity must be shown in appointing persons to episcopal sees; how you yourself have sometimes erred in these matters; how you pressed us to confirm Drogo in the chancellorship of the Church of Noyon; and how the matter of the aforesaid man of Cambrai occurred to you, since he ought not, because of his age, to have been called to episcopal dignity. Indeed, even under secular law, if he had been a lay person, he would have had his father as guardian in his own case. You must ponder these things with diligent reflection, be zealous to make satisfaction to your Creator for them, seek forgiveness for this offence in heart and mind, and make such prudent and careful provision that the Church may not incur graver losses.

[Col. 0763C]

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and direct your brotherhood strictly to compel the aforesaid D. to return to his church and there to bewail his sins and crimes in worthy penitence; he is not to go out or transfer elsewhere under obedience. If, within a month after your admonition, he refuses to return to the cloister from which he departed [Note: [Col. 0764D] Ham, of the Order of St. Augustine, in the diocese of Noyon.] and to remain there constantly, publicly excommunicate him with lighted candles and have him excommunicated by his abbot.

[Col. 0763D]

Strictly restrain the aforesaid called elect of Cambrai from molesting the Church of Maroilles and its possessions; compel him to restore what he has taken from it and amend what he is unlawfully doing against it. If he does not come to his senses, apply the punishment due, according to the circumstances of the time and the person.

Given at Tusculum, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January [18 December].

DCCCXLII. To Philip, count of Flanders.—That he exhort his brother, the elect of Cambrai, to obey his archbishop and not harass the Church of Maroilles. (At Tusculum, December ?)

[Ibid., col. 873.]

[Col. 0764A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the noble man PHILIP, count of Flanders: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us and demonstrated by certain assertion that the man called elect of Cambrai, relying on your power and nobility, has already begun to be contumacious and rebellious toward his archbishop, to despise his admonitions and commands, and to rage violently against the holy churches of God and ecclesiastical persons.

[Col. 0764B]

Since no one, however powerful or strong, ought to presume upon his own strength and power or stretch forth the hand of his power against God, we earnestly ask and command your greatness: rebuke, correct, and chastise your aforesaid brother severely for his offences; give him no boldness or favour in matters against God; rather, withdraw from him every hope and assistance. Also earnestly admonish, exhort, and induce him to endeavour, at his archbishop’s command, to amend the acts which he is said wickedly to have committed against the Church of Maroilles; and to show himself humble, devoted, and obedient to that archbishop, and to be formed by ecclesiastical instruction, so that in him nobility of conduct may adorn nobility of blood.

[Col. 0764C]

If he acts otherwise, know for certain that neither his strength nor his nobility can protect his boldness or presumption; for the hand of the Lord is mighty, and no counsel, wisdom, or strength prevails against God.

DCCCXLIII. To the abbot of Ham.—That he recall to his monastery his wandering canon Drogo. (At Tusculum, 18 December.)

[Ibid., col. 874.]

Since it is written, “A good name is better than great riches” (Prov. 22:1), we must exert ourselves and strive by every means to ensure that the reputation of your good name and honour is kept uninjured and cannot lawfully be darkened by the fault of dishonour or corroded by hostile interpretation.

[Col. 0764D]

But because the deeds and acts performed by your canon Drogo disgrace both him and your order, and tarnish your reputation and honour, which above all you ought to preserve, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to recall the aforesaid D. to the cloister, without pretext or delay, and not permit him to go out on obediences or to remain there. If he disdains to obey your admonition, publicly excommunicate him with lighted candles, and cause all persons to avoid him as excommunicated.

[Col. 0765A]

For gain acquired at the cost of honour is shameful, and he accumulates true riches who preserves for himself a good name and reputation. If you do not speedily recall him at our command and restrain his presumption and insolence, know for certain that we have ordered him to be excommunicated by our venerable brother H., archbishop of Rheims; and, with God as author, we shall be compelled to take vengeance more severely and harshly than you perhaps believe upon you and your church.

Given at Tusculum, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January [18 December].

DCCCXLIV. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—That he compel Odo the butcher to pay Richer the seventeen pounds owed. (At Tusculum, 21 December.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0765B]

From the report sent by Richer, it has come to our ears that Odo the butcher owes him seventeen pounds, which he refuses to pay. Since by the office entrusted to us we are debtors to all, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to admonish the said O. and strictly compel him either to pay Richer the aforesaid money, provide a pledge for it, or render full justice concerning it before you, all appeal set aside.

[Col. 0765C] Given at Tusculum, the twelfth day before the Kalends of January [21 December].

DCCCXLV. To Peter, abbot of Saint Remigius, and Fulco, canon of the Church of Rheims.—That they investigate the case of a usurer. (Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 922.)

It has come to our hearing that Jo. of Soissons holds in pledge land belonging to wards whose guardian is Th., a citizen of Rheims; and he is said to have received his principal and as much again. Since the crime of usury and every kind of excess are wholly to be abhorred by all persons professing Christianity, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if it is established that the aforesaid Jo. has received from the said land his principal and as much again beyond expenses, you strictly compel him by our authority, all pretext and appeal set aside, to restore that land to the said wards and their guardian and leave them in peace.

[Col. 0765D]

But if you learn that he has not received from it his principal or more, compel him, once he has received his principal, to return the land to the wards, delay and appeal set aside. Carry this out diligently within forty days after receipt of these letters.

DCCCXLVI. To Peter, abbot of Saint Remigius.—That he investigate the case of certain wards. (Ibid.)

[Col. 0766A]

On receiving the complaint of T., a citizen of Rheims, that God., formerly of Soissons, was withholding from the wards whom the same T. has in his custody a house which is said to belong to them by hereditary right, we recall having instructed your discretion to admonish and more strictly compel the said G. either to restore the detained house to the aforesaid wards or to render justice before our venerable brother, the bishop of Noyon. But since the said G., as is reported, was removed from this world before our letter reached you, and you admonished his wife to carry out one of these alternatives, she replied that the cause of the children did not concern her and that, because of their minority, the children could not bring suit. Therefore, since this delay and waiting may bring the aforesaid wards many losses and disadvantages in respect of their right, and since, according to the office committed to us, it is incumbent on us to provide for the wards of both parties, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, under injunction, that within forty days of receiving these letters you admonish and strictly compel the aforesaid woman either to answer before you, on behalf of her children whose guardianship she holds, to the guardian of the aforesaid wards concerning the house already mentioned; or to appoint an agent who ought to answer for them; or to leave the same house to the wards freely and peacefully. But if she wishes to proceed to trial, summon both parties before you, hear the case, and decide it by the means of justice, all appeal being excluded.

## In the Year 1171–1172

### DCCCXLVII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—That he suspend from priestly office Willard, a priest widely defamed, if the facts are established. (Tusculum, 20 January.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 878.]

The venerable brother T., bishop of Amiens, informed us that one of his priests, named Willard, had been denounced by his parishioners and publicly disgraced concerning a certain married woman with whom he is said to have a spiritual kinship, namely that he had begotten two daughters by her and, after renouncing her, had again had a daughter by her. The same bishop brought the aforesaid priest to trial on account of so great an infamy and imposed upon him a purgation for so serious an offence, which the priest offered to undergo. When, at his own request, canonical delays had been granted to him once and twice, and at last, on the day appointed for the purgation, the aforesaid priest stated before the bishop and many others in a public confession that he could not clear himself of so great an infamy, the bishop, after taking counsel with several prudent men, suspended the aforesaid priest from office and benefice on this account.

But many days later the priest appealed to our hearing. Finally, coming into our presence, he represented that he had been suspended after his appeal and obtained our letters to you, directing that, if matters stood thus, you should restore to him his office and benefice before he was compelled to undergo his purgation. Although, before you heard our letters, the aforesaid bishop had appealed the same priest to our presence, as he asserts, on the ground of false representation, you nevertheless restored to that priest his office and benefice. If the assertion rests equally upon truth, we cannot but wonder at this; for our letters are customarily always qualified by the words “if this be so.” And even if, as we do not believe, that condition was omitted from those letters, it ought nevertheless to be understood, and inquiry should always be made whether the report accords with the truth.

Therefore we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, after summoning both parties before you, you diligently investigate the truth of the matter. If it is established to you that the said bishop truthfully represented these things to us, restore the aforesaid priest, without delay or appeal, to the same sentence of suspension. Or, if he confessed before the bishop and many others that he could not clear himself of that infamy, and offered no reasonable cause why he could not undergo the purgation except that he was conscious of this wickedness, remove him permanently from priestly office.

Given at Tusculum, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February [20 January].

### DCCCXLVIII. To the same.—He commits a certain case to him for decision. (Tusculum, 21 January.)

[Ibid., col. 879.]

On the representation of our beloved son R., archdeacon of Châlons, we learned that, when the case between V., bearer of these letters, and J., a priest, concerning the church of St. Mary was being tried in your presence, the said V. produced his witnesses, namely Herm. and Henry, priests, to testify to the truth known by them in that case. The opposing party, alleging them to be insufficiently qualified, appealed them to our hearing as persons accused of crime. Thereupon, when both parties appeared before the aforesaid archdeacon and the said J. acknowledged that he had charged those witnesses with crimes solely out of anger, the archdeacon, since they could not pursue the appeal because of the shortness of the time allowed, arranged the matter by mutual pledges and with the consent of both sides as follows: if the aforesaid J. acknowledged in your presence what he had confessed before the archdeacon, they would desist from the appeal.

On the day appointed, however, the said J. contemptuously failed to appear before you. Accordingly V. presented himself before us with his witnesses; but J. neither came then nor sent an advocate to answer for him. Since an appeal had been made in the principal matter, we remitted the same case to your examination, commanding that, after both parties had appeared before you, if it were established that the said J. had violated the pledge he had given, you should impose upon him a fitting penance for breach of faith, admit the aforesaid witnesses with the appeal set aside, and, within fifteen days after receiving our letters, determine the case, all remedy of appeal being removed.

[Col. 0768B] But after the said V. had departed from our presence and, in accordance with the form prescribed above, carried our letters to you, his adversary came into our presence and, because, as we believe, we did not remember that the same V. had carried our letters, obtained letters concerning the same case differing from the earlier ones. On his return, both parties appeared before you; but you refused to proceed in the case according to the earlier letters, asserting that the latest intention must always prevail and that later letters ought to prejudice earlier ones. Yet the same V. waited a month for his adversary at our court and appears to have been greatly harassed; moreover, earlier oaths take precedence over later ones, and the same holds in contracts of sale and purchase. Therefore we command your fraternity by these present letters, under injunction, that the later letters, especially since they were obtained with the truth concealed, have no force; and that, in accordance with the tenor of the earlier letters—that is, after examining the witnesses and admitting those found qualified, with every pretext and appeal removed—you proceed in the same case within fifteen days after receipt of these letters. Take especial care not to commit the same case to John, by whom great detraction is made from your reputation and honour; rather, you yourself ought to decide it with maturity and diligence.

[Col. 0768D] Given at Tusculum, the twelfth day before the Kalends of February [21 January].

### DCCCXLIX. He commands Henry, Archbishop of Rheims, [Guy], Bishop of Châlons, and [Arnulf], Elect of Verdun, to restrain the castellan of Vitry from harassing Caladia. (Tusculum, 23 January.)

[Ibid., col. 881.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, the Bishop of Châlons, and his beloved son the Elect of Verdun, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we defend religious men from the attacks of the wicked with more watchful care, and support them promptly and diligently in their rights, so that, when their peace has been secured by attentive concern, they may more freely devote themselves to divine service.
