Our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of Caladia [Note: [Col. 0769D] An abbey of the Cistercian order in the diocese of Verdun, which, if Wassebourg is to be believed, was formerly inhabited by three hundred monks, but now by very few.], have sent us a complaint showing that the castellan of Vitry violently took away their plough-teams, and that he himself and certain other parishioners of yours have no scruple about plundering their goods and taking booty from them.

Since it accords with your office to restrain the insolence of laymen from oppressing religious men, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you take care to admonish and strictly compel the said castellan to make suitable satisfaction to the aforesaid brethren for the damages inflicted and injuries done; and that you strictly forbid, under threat of anathema, both him and your other parishioners to plunder the goods of those brethren by violence, presume to take booty from them, knowingly receive booty taken from their goods, or attempt to purchase it. If the aforesaid brethren lodge a complaint against any of them, administer such strict justice that, aided by the support of your protection, the brethren may rejoice in peacefully possessing what is theirs, and that we may deservedly commend your zeal and diligence in this matter.

Given at Tusculum, the tenth day before the Kalends of February [23 January].

### DCCCL. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—For the monks of Noyon against the canons of Braques. (Tusculum, 27 January.)

[Ibid., col. 882.]

When our beloved sons, the prior and brethren of Noyon, monks of La Sauve-Majeure [Note: [Col. 0769D–0770D] La Sauve-Majeure, formerly a celebrated monastery of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Gerard, a monk of Corbie, in the diocese of Bordeaux; it still remains under the Congregation of St. Maur.], complained to us that the clerics of the church of Braques—which your predecessor Samson of blessed memory, with the assent of the Count of Rethel, granted to the aforesaid monks, on the condition that, as the secular clerics died, monks should be substituted in their place—had unjustly despoiled them of the provostship, certain prebends, houses, and other goods, we committed the case for determination under a specified form to our venerable brother the bishop of Soissons and to our beloved son the abbot of St. Remigius at Rheims. We ordered that if the clerics would not obey their judgment, they should be bound by a sentence of excommunication, notwithstanding any appeal.

But, as we learned from the letters of those judges, when they had decided the case, they bound the clerics, because they refused to obey their judgment, with the bond of anathema. Thereafter one of them came into our presence, and we caused them to be absolved, directing that the sentence of the aforesaid judges should remain ratified and unshaken. Yet we have been told that, using as a pretext the letters which we granted for their absolution, they presume to harass the aforesaid monks and rashly attempt to contravene the sentence, although such conduct deserves punishment. We therefore command your fraternity by apostolic letters that you cause the prescribed sentence to be firmly and inviolably observed, with the obstacle of appeal removed; and if the clerics presume to harass the same monks contrary to the tenor of that sentence, punish their presumption with due severity.

If those clerics have brought back from us any contrary letters—which we do not believe—such letters are in no way to prejudice these letters. Nor may the monks in any degree despoil those clerics who held prebends there before the aforesaid church was granted to them.

Given at Tusculum, the sixth day before the Kalends of February [27 January].

### DCCCLI. He admonishes Conrad, Archbishop of Mainz, legate of the Apostolic See, not to reopen the controversy between the monastery of St. Zeno of Verona and the citizens of Ferrara concerning the castle of Ostiglia, adjudicated by Oberto da Orto; for it is his duty “to establish peace and concord between the cities of Lombardy and their citizens, especially at this time, and to work toward their unity.” (Tusculum, 28 January.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, V, 794.]

[Col. 0770C] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother C., Archbishop of Mainz, legate of the Apostolic See, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved sons G. . . . , the Podestà of Verona and the commune of that city, informed us by letters that, whereas the controversy long conducted between the monastery of St. Zeno and the citizens of Ferrara concerning Ostiglia had been decided by a definitive sentence rendered by a certain arbiter, Ubertus de Orto, whom each side had chosen as arbiter and had sworn to abide by in this matter, and whereas the aforesaid Ostiglia had been adjudged to the said monastery, you are endeavouring to revive the controversy and have ordered the abbot of the aforesaid monastery and likewise the people of Ferrara to answer concerning it.

But it is unfitting to reopen a settled dispute—especially one from which, as is known, so many murders and evils have arisen—or to set aside a judgment which both sides are said to have sworn to observe. Indeed, no end would exist to lawsuits if cases already decided returned to the vexation of renewed contention. Moreover, it is especially necessary for us at this time to establish peace and concord among the cities of Lombardy and their citizens, and to labour with watchful diligence and reflection for their unity. We therefore admonish and command your fraternity that, carefully considering and observing how grave and dangerous the present times are . . . , you raise no dispute against the aforesaid abbot concerning the aforesaid Ostiglia, nor in any manner strive, under any inducement, to harass him with molestations or burdens on that account. For if that controversy were revived, many evils, grave dangers, and very many murders would follow, and the state of peace and unity in Lombardy, which we desire you to preserve with all zeal and labour, would be seriously disturbed.

Given at Tusculum, the fifth day before the Kalends of February [28 January].

### DCCCLII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—For the Templars of Jerusalem. (Tusculum, 31 January.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 883.]

We have been informed that G. and R. Gozo have presumed violently to take from the brethren of the Knighthood of the Temple lands, vineyards, and no small amount of their movable property. Since it pertains to our office to defend the aforesaid brethren from the injuries of evil men and to support them by apostolic protection, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that you endeavour to admonish and strictly compel the aforesaid men either to restore without delay, and intact, to those brethren the lands, vineyards, and other things taken away, or to render them full justice under the examination of your discretion. If they should perhaps refuse to do so, let them be bound by you with the bond of anathema.

Given at Tusculum, the second day before the Kalends of February [31 January].

### DCCCLIII. To William, Archbishop of Sens, legate of the Apostolic See; S[tephen], Bishop of Meaux; and the Abbot of Val-Secret.—That they restore the fallen discipline of the monastery of St. Victor. (Tusculum, 1 February.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 993.]

[Col. 0771C] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers W., Archbishop of Sens, legate of the Apostolic See, and S., Bishop of Meaux, and to his beloved son the Abbot of Val-Secret, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Repeated reports concerning the condition of the Church of St. Victor have long struck our ears, and we fear that at the final judgment we shall be judged more severely if we are slow or remiss in investigating and correcting the matters reported. For Scripture says: “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from bloodshed” (Jeremiah 48).

Formerly, through the teaching of salvation flowing from that place and the fragrance of good conduct breathed by that Church, in many churches crooked things were made straight and rough things were turned into level ways. It was truly a well of living waters, from which the parched hearts of many drew the draught of life to quench the heat of worldly desires. But now, as is said, while the guardian’s watch has gradually fallen asleep and love of religion has grown cold in the head, a deadly torpor has spread also to some part of the members; and there has come about there what the prophet says of a certain man: “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he knew it not; indeed, grey hairs are scattered upon him, and he is unaware” (Hosea 7).

Yet we do not say this because we do not believe that very many wise and distinguished men may be found there, able to be for many “a fragrance of life unto life.” But even with a strong crew of rowers it is not easy to steer a ship into port if the helmsman holding the rudder is unskilled or negligent. Therefore, lest what the Prophet lamented concerning himself should perhaps happen to that church, saying, “My friends and my neighbours drew near and stood against me, and those who were close to me stood afar off” (Psalm VII), since we cannot visit that church in person, we have decreed that the office of visitation be performed for it.

We command you by apostolic letters that, going there, you investigate with the maturity and diligence fitting to the task its condition and the conduct of the abbot and brethren, and that whatever you learn there requires correction you correct in our stead. Thus, by your endeavour and by divine grace, religion may flourish there anew, and we may not be held to render an account on the Day of Judgment for the dissolution of so great a house. If, however, you see that the condition of the church cannot be reformed unless one or more persons are removed, let not your sword spare even in this matter. Receive from us full authority, all appeal being excluded, to uproot what ought to be uprooted and, with the Lord’s aid, to plant what ought to be planted. For we wish by means of you to be found excusable before God, so that at the final judgment nothing may be demanded of us concerning the spiritual loss of that Church. If all three of you cannot be present to carry this out, let no fewer than two of you diligently execute what has been said.

Given at Tusculum, on the Kalends of February [1 February].

### DCCCLIV. He informs the abbot and canons of St. Victor of the preceding letters. (Tusculum, 1 February.)

[Ibid., 994.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and canons of St. Victor at Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0772D] It has long since reached us concerning your condition that it ought to be strictly examined and corrected. Since your Church, by God’s grace, has for a long time flourished in religion and learning, so that many have gathered at the fragrance of your ointments and seen light in your light, we have waited until now to see whether you would at last return to yourselves and remove from among you the material of dissension and scandal. But because in our waiting we observe not so much any correction following as your weakness becoming more severe, we have judged it fitting to send certain persons to your church: namely, our venerable brothers W., Archbishop of Sens, legate of the Apostolic See, and S., Bishop of Meaux, and our beloved son N., Abbot of Val-Secret. They are to investigate the state of your community and, all appeal being excluded, correct and amend what they discover requires correction.

We therefore command you by apostolic letters, under injunction, that when they come to you, you set before them whatever your need and correction require to be set forth; and that you humbly accept and firmly observe whatever they, or two of them, determine among you, whether concerning the restoration of the discipline of the order or, if circumstances require, the removal of persons.

Given at Tusculum, on the Kalends of February [1 February].

### DCCCLV. He informs Louis, King of the Franks, what he has ordered concerning the correction of discipline in the monastery of St. Victor at Paris. (Tusculum, 1 February.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, VI, 249.]

[Col. 0773B] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LOUIS, most Christian King of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we consider the exceptional renown of your glory, scarcely anything appears capable of rendering you worthy of so great praise and so secure concerning eternal reward as the proven fact that you love religion with sincere devotion and willingly devote yourself, as befits the office of royal dignity, to planting it in your kingdom. Would that those in the priestly order proceeded with such disposition and care toward the establishment and preservation of religion as royal favour follows them with help in its defence! For we believe that the condition of the whole Church throughout your kingdom would then be such that the name of the Lord would be honoured in all things and the multitude of faithful peoples would find many guides on the way of life.

But now, while priests sleep—though they ought to give attention to the guardianship of others—holy religion grows lukewarm in many places; and, to use the words of one poet, in place of the tender violet and purple narcissus,

> Unhappy darnel and barren oats hold sway.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* I.153)

We grieve greatly that this has happened in the Church of St. Victor. Although it formerly flourished in religion, it is now, sadly, said to have grown lukewarm in the observance of its profession, so that it, which once extended a hand to many running on the way of salvation, now needs another’s help and finds none to lift it up. Yet this is not reported to occur because there are not many there who possess both knowledge and love of religion; rather, as certain members languish together with their head, the fervour of religion in that Church is known to have grown cold.

When reports from many persons concerning their lukewarmness had long ago reached us, we delayed until now to give heed and apply the necessary medicine to so grave a sickness, waiting for them at some time to turn their eyes back upon themselves and more zealously consider the restoration of religion. But since the head is executing too negligently the matters that concern the amendment of himself and his subjects, we must at last devote ourselves to carrying out what has been said. If the rumour which has so often reached our ears is true, we must discover this through others, since we cannot do so in person; and, if the allegations are substantiated, let the same persons apply without delay the medicine they judge necessary.

We have therefore provided to entrust our authority in this matter to our venerable brothers William, Archbishop of Sens, Stephen, Bishop of Meaux, and N., Abbot of Val-Secret. The fuller and easier their knowledge of this matter may be, the more they will provide remedies for salvation with less harm. Since it contributes to the fullness of your reward if, through their diligence and with royal favour assisting, the condition of the aforesaid Church is set in order, we admonish and exhort your highness in the Lord to lend your favour to the execution of this business and suffer no opposition to be made that might prevent the measures which those men judge should be established from being established there. Otherwise, if the remedy is perhaps delayed too long and, through our dissimulation, the sickness begins to worsen, even the perception of pain may perish, and afterward health will scarcely return, and only with great difficulty.

Given at Tusculum, on the Kalends of February [1 February].

### DCCCLVI. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—He commends to him the Knights of the Temple. (Tusculum, 2 February.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 883.]

How especially the Knights of the Temple situated at Jerusalem are devoted to the service of almighty God and dedicated to the heavenly knighthood is indicated by their venerable habit and clearly declared by the sign of the Lord’s cross which they constantly bear upon their bodies. For they are established for this purpose: that they may not fear to lay down their lives for their brethren. Since it is fitting that we take care to provide in every way possible according to God for such illustrious champions of Christ, we ask, admonish, and command your fraternity that, out of regard for divine love, reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, and the salvation of your soul, you love, support, and honour them; preserve their rights whole and unimpaired; extend to them the protection and favour of your patronage; and do not delay to render them full justice against their wrongdoers.

We especially command your fraternity urgently to admonish and strictly compel your parishioner Guitterius to restore without delay to the aforesaid brethren, if it is so, the booty which he is said formerly to have taken from the village of Onisvisner, and not to postpone making suitable satisfaction for the violence inflicted. If he refuses to obey your admonition, bind him with the bond of excommunication.

Given at Tusculum, the fourth day before the Nones of February [2 February].

### DCCCLVII. To Peter, Abbot of St. Remigius, and B., Archdeacon of Rheims.—They are to admonish the Bishop of Soissons no longer to refuse to invest the subdeacon presented to him with the church of St. Medard; otherwise they themselves are to invest him. (Tusculum, 3 February.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 948.]

O., a subdeacon and bearer of these letters, appearing in our presence, represented to us in a humble petition that, when our beloved son the abbot of St. Peter of Châlons, with the assent of his chapter, had presented him to our venerable brother the Bishop of Soissons for ordination in the church of St. Medard, which is said to belong to his church, so that the bishop might invest him with the aforesaid church and commit to him the care of souls, the said bishop refused to do so. But since it is unfitting and wholly contrary to reason that the care of a people should be denied to the said subdeacon except for a manifest and reasonable cause, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, under injunction, that within forty days after receipt of these letters you endeavour to admonish and earnestly induce the said bishop either to invest the aforesaid subdeacon with the prescribed church and commit the care of souls to him, or to show before you a reasonable cause why he ought not to do so.

If he refuses to obey your admonitions, then, relying on our authority, you yourselves shall invest the often-mentioned subdeacon with the aforesaid church, without any delay or appeal, and commit to him the care of souls; provided that he is answerable to the said bishop concerning the care of the people, but to the aforesaid abbot concerning temporal matters.

Given at Tusculum, the third day before the Nones of February [3 February].

### DCCCLVIII. To the priests and clerics of parishes belonging to the monastery of St. Peter of Montibus.—That they not bury their parishioners in their own churches, but that they be buried at the monastery of St. Peter of Montibus. (Tusculum, 5 February.)

[Ibid., col. 957.]

ALEXANDER Pope III, to the priests and other clerics of parish churches belonging to the monastery of St. Peter of Montibus.

It has come to us that, although the inhabitants of your parishes have customarily been buried from ancient custom at the monastery of St. Peter of Montibus, you, contrary to that custom, bury the bodies of the dead in your own churches. Since it is not fitting that you withdraw from the aforesaid monastery anything of its right, when as devoted sons you ought to preserve its rights whole, we command you by apostolic letters, under injunction, that, if this is so, you do not presume to receive for burial in your churches any of those inhabitants, unless they have chosen to be buried with you. Nor are you henceforth to attempt to bury any lay person within the walls of your churches, since this would be unworthy and wholly alien to ecclesiastical institution.

Given at Tusculum, on the Nones of February [5 February].

### DCCCLIX. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—That he cause Araldus the priest’s church to be restored to him. (Tusculum, 8 February.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 884.]

Araldus, priest and bearer of these letters, informed us that the prior and chapter of the church of Sarmel had granted to Dominic, a deacon, during the lifetime of the priest of that church, the church of St. Remigius of Masdeio, which is known to belong to their jurisdiction. In the presence of many people, the said deacon renounced it into the hands of the aforesaid prior. After some time had passed, the priest who was in that church resigned it to the prior and chapter. With the assent of the chapter, the aforesaid prior granted it to Araldus, presented him to our venerable brother the Bishop of Châlons, and Araldus, receiving the care of souls from him, afterward possessed the prescribed church peacefully for seven years.

After this, however, as the same priest asserts, the aforementioned deacon came into our presence and obtained our letters to you, providing that if he could prove by lawful witnesses that the aforesaid church had previously been canonically granted to him, you should not delay to restore it to him. Although the priest objected and appealed the deacon to our presence, you restored the church to him. But since by the duty of our office we are bound to preserve each person’s right unimpaired, especially that of ecclesiastical persons, and to restore to the path of rectitude what is known to have been done through some error, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters, under injunction, that within forty days after receipt of these letters you summon both parties before you. Having diligently investigated and ascertained the truth, if it is established that the aforesaid deacon renounced the prescribed church into the hands of the aforesaid prior, and that afterward the aforesaid A. canonically acquired and freely possessed it, remove the deacon and restore it to the aforesaid Araldus, the priest, without delay or appeal, causing him to possess it peacefully.

Given at Tusculum, the sixth day before the Ides of February [8 February].

### DCCCLX. To the same.—He commends to him the brethren of the monastery of Virtus. (Tusculum, 9 February.)

[Ibid., 885.]

We ought, with pastoral concern, diligently to attend to the peace and quiet of religious men and take more attentive care that they are not disturbed by undue vexations. From the representation of our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Virtus, we have learned that Laudatus, a citizen of Châlons, continually harasses them over a certain sum of money which he unjustly demands from them, although the aforesaid abbot and brethren firmly assert that they owe him nothing whatever.

Therefore, since by the office entrusted to us we are bound to defend ecclesiastical men against the injuries and vexations of all persons, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that you admonish and strictly compel the said man not to demand anything undue from the aforesaid brethren, nor henceforth presume to harass them or unjustly trouble their goods. But if he trusts in the right and wishes to proceed against them concerning the money already mentioned, let him proceed before you in due judicial order; hear the case and decide it with a proper conclusion.

Given at Tusculum, the fifth day before the Ides of February [9 February].

### DCCCLXI. To Peter, Abbot of St. Remigius, and Fulk, Dean of Rheims.—He commits a case for judgment. (Tusculum, 12 February.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 926.]

Our beloved son the abbot of St. Theodore, sending us a complaint, showed that the woman Helisendis and her husband harass him in many ways concerning a certain piece of land and presume to trouble him with undue vexations. When proceedings had been initiated concerning this matter, they finally appealed to our hearing. Since, by the office entrusted to us, we are debtors to all God’s faithful and must assist each person in his right, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you admonish and strictly compel the aforesaid woman and her husband altogether to cease harassing the said abbot concerning the prescribed land and to leave it to him peacefully and undisturbed; or, if they rely upon a right, to proceed before you in due judicial order. If they decide to enter the case, summon the parties before you; hear and ascertain the arguments on each side; and decide the same case by the means of justice, with the obstacle of appeal removed.

Given at Tusculum, the second day before the Ides of February [12 February].

### DCCCLXII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—He commends to him F., Archdeacon of Ostrevant. (Tusculum, 13 February.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 885.]

[Col. 0777D]

Those whom we believe to excel in uprightness and learning, we commend to your solicitude with all the greater care because it pertains especially to your brotherhood to cherish honourable and learned men and to show them honour and favour. Accordingly, considering the prudence and integrity of our beloved son F., archdeacon of Ostrevant, we love him with sincere affection of heart as a worthy, honourable, and discreet man, and have thought fit earnestly to commend him to your brotherhood. Wherefore we ask and admonish your charity, [Col. 0778A] for reverence for blessed Peter and for us, and in view of his worth and integrity, to love, support, and honour him; to grant his requests effectively and graciously; and in no way to burden him in his honour and benefices, nor permit anyone else to burden him. Thus may he rejoice that he has been commended to your affection by our prayers, and may we likewise be bound to return abundant thanks to your sincerity.

Given at Tusculum, on the Ides of February.

DCCCLXIII. To the same. — On behalf of the clerk Stephen against the canons of Châlons. (Tusculum, 20 February.)

[Ibid., col. 886.]

[Col. 0778B] Formerly, upon the complaint of Stephen, a poor clerk and bearer of the present letter, we entrusted to our beloved sons, the archdeacon and dean of your Church, for determination, appeal having been set aside, the case between him and the canons of the Church of Châlons concerning lands belonging to the endowment of the altar of Cortoismunt, which those canons held. As we have learned from their letters, they adjudged by sentence that those lands belonged to the endowment of that altar and should be restored to the said clerk. Yet the aforementioned canons refused either to carry out the sentence or, at the admonition of the judges, to restore to the said clerk the revenues which they had received from them.

Therefore, holding that sentence to be valid and firm, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters [Col. 0778C] that, by both our authority and your own, you admonish and strictly compel the said canons to leave the aforesaid lands in the peaceable and undisturbed possession of the abovementioned clerk, as they were adjudged to him by the aforesaid judges, appeal having ceased; and that they do not delay restoring to him, without delay or any deduction, whatever revenues they have received from them since the sentence was pronounced.

Given at Tusculum, 10 Kalends of March [20 February].

DCCCLXIV. To Guido, abbot of Saint Nicaise, and Master Radulf, canon of Reims. — That they compel certain persons who had inflicted losses on the monastery of Saint Remigius to make reparation. (Tusculum, 21 February.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 942.]

[Col. 0778D]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Guido, abbot of Saint Nicaise, and Master Radulf, canon of Reims.

It has been represented to us that Galcherus of Châtillon, inflamed with diabolical fury, destroyed the village of Belloi, which belongs to the monastery of blessed Remigius, and so despoiled two other villages of the same monastery that the plunder carried away from them is estimated at forty pounds. Moreover, Milo Malus-Vicinus is said to have inflicted many losses and injuries upon that monastery, yet he refuses either to make satisfaction there or to render what justice requires. Simon of the borough also does not cease to inflict many losses and injuries on the aforesaid monastery at Wandrecicurt. Furthermore, Burdinus [Col. 0779A] of Besanes is endeavouring to take away from two men land that had been given in alms to the aforementioned monastery and which the abbot of that place had granted them by hereditary right. Likewise, the priest of Alem. presumes to build a certain house in a village of the aforesaid monastery, to the detriment of that church.

In addition, a certain man of Saint Remigius, inflamed by the ardour of divine love and charity, gave himself, together with a portion of his inheritance, to the hospital of Saint Mary of Reims, for the service of guests and for the remedy of his soul. Although he gave his relatives a great part of his goods, they came from afar and are seeking to harass the aforementioned monastery and the Church of Reims over the said alms. Therefore, since it is our concern to defend the rights of churches [Col. 0779B] and to provide them the protection of apostolic guardianship against their wrongdoers, we command your discretion by apostolic letters, on our behalf, to admonish the aforesaid persons and to compel them more strictly: to make suitable satisfaction to the said monastery for the losses and injuries inflicted; to restore what they have taken; and thereafter entirely to desist from harassing it and its possessions—or else to render it full justice in this matter under the examination of your discretion.

Moreover, the abbot of the oft-mentioned monastery has sent us a grave complaint against the treasurer of Laon, because at Créon he diminishes and wholly withholds the abbot’s justice; against William, marshal of the noble Count Henry, because he took ten pounds from one of the abbot’s men and inflicted many evils upon him; and against the abbot of Tenaliis, who, though said to inflict many losses upon him, refused, as we commanded, to answer him concerning this before our venerable brother, the archbishop of Reims. Therefore, by the authority of these presents, we lay upon you the duty [Col. 0779C] to endeavour, by our authority, to admonish and strictly compel the aforesaid men to repair the losses inflicted upon the said abbot, restore what has been taken, render satisfaction for the injuries done, or fulfil the requirements of justice. In all the foregoing, proceed with such maturity and prudence that your diligence and solicitude may deservedly be commended, and that we may be able more confidently to entrust ecclesiastical business to your discretion. [Col. 0779D]

Given at Tusculum, 9 Kalends of March [21 February].

DCCCLXV. To the same. — Entrusts for determination the case between the abbots of Saint Urban and of Der. (Tusculum, 21 February.)

[Ibid.]

We entrusted to our beloved sons P., abbot of Saint Remigius, and F., dean of Reims, for hearing and due determination the case pending between our beloved sons the abbot of Saint Urban [Note: [Col. 0779] The abbey of Saint Urban, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Châlons, under the congregation of Saint-Vanne, as is also that of Der.] and the abbot of Der concerning a certain chapel. But [Col. 0780A] because the abbot of Der, on a false allegation, appealed, as we have learned, to our hearing, although the same case had been entrusted to them with appeal set aside, and because he wishes to pursue that appeal made to us, we entrust the same case to you, in whose prudence and integrity we have confidence, for hearing and suitable determination.

Therefore, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when you are requested concerning this matter, you summon both parties before you and, having fully heard and examined the arguments on both sides, decide the same case by concord or justice, appeal having been set aside.

Given at Tusculum, 9 Kalends of March [21 February].

DCCCLXVI. To Peter, abbot, and the brothers of Saint Remigius. — Holds valid the remission of *frescengiae* made to their monastery by the archbishop of Reims. (Tusculum, 22 February.)

[Ibid., col. 943.]

[Col. 0780B]

We ought to admit reasonable and honourable petitions with a willing mind, and to bring to effect the requests that do not depart from the path of reason. It has indeed been reported to us that, whereas each year you were obliged to pay the archbishop of Reims two procurations—one on the feast of the deposition of Saint Remigius and the other on that of his translation—and whereas no valuation had been made of the price of the *frescengiae*, each being separately specified according to fixed numbers and measures, our venerable brother Henry, archbishop of Reims, [Col. 0780C] in pious consideration of the burden and disturbance which you suffered from this, wholly remitted the *frescengiae* to you and your monastery. This remission was made on the express condition that, on the deposition of blessed Remigius, you are bound to pay fifty sols of Reims currency each year to the archbishops of Reims, and the same amount on his translation.

We therefore confirm by apostolic authority, and fortify with the protection of the present writing, that remission as made by the aforesaid archbishop and ratified by the protection of his seal, so that you may hold it firm and valid. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way act contrary to it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul. [Col. 0780D]

Given at Tusculum, 8 Kalends of March [22 February].

DCCCLXVII. To the same. — Entrusts for determination the case between the canons of Saint Nicholas of Châlons and the abbot of Der. (Tusculum, 22 February.)

[Ibid.]

It has come to our hearing that, while the case pending between our beloved sons the canons [Col. 0781A] of Saint Nicholas of Châlons and the abbot of Der concerning the church of Champ-Aubert was being heard before our brother the bishop of Châlons, an appeal was made to us. Since neither party came prepared to litigate, we entrust the same case to you, in whose prudence and integrity we have confidence, for hearing and due determination, appeal having been set aside.

Therefore, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when you are requested concerning this matter, you summon both parties before you and, having fully heard and examined the arguments on both sides, decide that case within two months by justice, the obstacle of appeal having been removed.

Given at Tusculum, 8 Kalends of March [22 February].

DCCCLXVIII. Entrusts to the bishops of Bourges and Amiens the marital case of S. and R. of Guise. (Tusculum, 22 February.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0781B]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the bishops of Bourges and Amiens [Note: [Col. 0781D] Theobald.], greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since certain experience has taught us that you are cultivators and lovers of justice and utterly abhor in every way those things known to proceed from the root of wickedness, we formerly entrusted to you, whose faithfulness and integrity we have proved, for hearing and due determination the matrimonial case pending between the noblewoman S. [Col. 0781C] and her husband R. of Guise. But because, as we have learned from your letters, the case has not yet been brought to a suitable conclusion, we command your brotherhood by repeated letters to meet together, summon both parties before you at a suitable place and time, and, after fully hearing and examining the arguments on both sides, decide the same case with episcopal maturity and gravity, setting aside every favour and partiality, purely and sincerely, in accordance with the tenor of our other letters, observing the equity of the canons and removing the obstacle of appeal. Your judgment should thereby deservedly be approved both before God and before men. [Col. 0781D]

If any letters have been obtained from us on the husband’s behalf which are contrary to these letters or to our former letters, give them no credence whatsoever, but regard them as fraudulently procured. Moreover, if the aforesaid husband refuses, in accordance with your command, to give the woman full security that he must receive her and treat her with marital affection, then, appeal having been set aside, strike him with sentence of excommunication. By our authority, cause him to be avoided as excommunicate throughout the whole diocese of Laon; and intervene effectively with the noble Count Philip of Flanders [Col. 0782A] so that he may cause the land which the woman’s husband received from her side to be restored to her without molestation and left in peace, until the said husband more fully recognizes his offence and humbly and devoutly fulfils the Church’s command.

We further will that you execute the aforesaid more promptly within eleven days after receipt of these letters.

Given at Tusculum, 8 Kalends of March [22 February].

DCCCLXIX. To Galdinus, archbishop of Milan. — On behalf of the subdeacon Obertus. (Tusculum, 26 February.)

[FRISI, *Memorie storiche di Monza*, vol. II, p. 67.]

[Col. 0782B] Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G., archbishop of Milan, legate of the Apostolic See, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son, the subdeacon Obertus, archpriest of the Church of Monza, informed us by a report sent to us that the nobles and vavassors of Sesto refuse to pay tithes to his church and thereby do not hesitate to provoke against themselves the eyes of the divine Majesty. For since tithes have been instituted by God, not by man, those who presume to withhold them from the places to which they are assigned incur God’s offence.

Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command and enjoin your brotherhood that you earnestly admonish [Col. 0782C] and strictly compel the aforesaid nobles and vavassors henceforth to pay to the said priest and his church, without diminution or difficulty, the tithes due from their animals and other goods from which it is customary to give a tenth; nor may they any longer presume, to the destruction of their souls, to retain them. If any contemptuously refuse to obey your admonitions, strike them with ecclesiastical censure.

Given at Tusculum, 4 Kalends of March [26 February].

DCCCLXX. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — That no letters against him were granted to the abbot of Cheminon. (Tusculum, 27 February.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0782D]

It has been reported to us that the abbot of Chimeignon [Note: [Col. 0781] Chemino, a Cistercian abbey in the diocese of Châlons.] boasts and glories that he has obtained letters from us enabling him to summon before our venerable brother William, archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See, appeal having been removed, any persons whom he wished to sue from within your archdiocese. You are to know that this is false; and we greatly wonder with what face he makes this boast, since we do not believe that we have granted such letters either to him or to others, unless perhaps this happened through error.

We therefore will and command that, if he shows you such letters, [Col. 0783A] you wrest them from him and send them to us, so that, if they were issued through error, we may correct them; or impose a penalty, if one should be imposed.

Given at Tusculum, 3 Kalends of March [27 February].

DCCCLXXI. To the same. — In favour of Leo, elected abbot of Saint-Ghislain, whom the schismatics had expelled. (Tusculum, 27 February.)

[Ibid., col. 889.]

It has come to our hearing that, after Leo had been canonically elected abbot of Saint-Ghislain [Note: [Col. 0783D] The monastery of Saint-Ghislain, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in Hainaut, two miles from Mons, in the diocese of Cambrai.], he was afterward expelled by schismatics because he refused to take that nefarious and detestable oath; and another was intruded in his place by the said elected bishop of Cambrai [Col. 0783B] [Note: [Col. 0783D] namely Peter of Alsace, mentioned above.]. Since, by preserving the virtue of Catholic faith and unity, he deserved to acquire glory and praise and to expect the reward of worthy recompense, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, once the truth of the matter has been ascertained, if it is established to you that the election of the aforesaid L. was canonically made and that he was removed for no other reason than that he would not assent to schismatic depravity or be defiled by that detestable oath, you are to confirm his election, provided that he is otherwise suitable, notwithstanding any appeal. Remove the intruder and cause him freely and without molestation to have the administration of the aforesaid Church. If anyone should presume rashly to harass him in this matter, do not delay exercising against him the censure of ecclesiastical correction. [Col. 0783C]

Given at Tusculum, 3 Kalends of March [27 February].

DCCCLXXII. To the same. — That he prevent a marriage between the daughter of King Louis and the son of Emperor Frederick. (Tusculum, 28 February.)

[Ibid.]

It has been represented to us that our dearest son in Christ, Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, has been asked to betroth his daughter in marriage to the son of F., persecutor of the Church. Since this could be dangerous to the kingdom and harmful to the Church, we admonish and command your brotherhood [Col. 0783D] to use every means to dissuade the said king from allowing that marriage to take place, and entirely to prevent it.

For, if it pleases the king, he may give her in marriage to the son of the emperor of Constantinople, because, with God’s help, we shall work at an opportune time to bring the matter swiftly to completion. Certainly, with the emperor, the kingdom and the maiden’s relatives will always find an inexhaustible treasury.

Given at Tusculum, 2 Kalends of March [28 February].

DCCCLXXIII. Commands the bishop of Tournai [Note: [Col. 0784D] Walter, who died in 1171.] to restore to the priest Daniel what was taken from him. (Tusculum, 1 March.)

[Ibid., col. 890.]

[Col. 0784A]

From the representation of Daniel, priest of Saint John at Ghent, we have learned that, while you imposed upon him and certain others an unreasonable annual exaction of money and turned it into a custom, they humbly and devoutly begged you to refrain from such an exaction. But you, violently angered and disturbed, suspended the aforesaid D. from office because he raised an objection; you induced the others by threats to permit you to take, at your will, whatever you decreed concerning their property; and, what is grave, [Col. 0784B] you strictly ordered the abbot of Saint Peter at Ghent [Note: [Col. 0784D] Commonly called Blandinien; a distinguished abbey of the Order of Saint Benedict.] to expel him altogether and appoint another priest in his place.

If these things are true, you would realize by certain experience and prove by evident indications how grave and harshly deserving of punishment they are, were we not to love your person with great warmth of charity. Yet the dignity and office which, by the Lord’s providence, you hold ought to make you moderate and restrained toward your subjects, and render you kindly and benevolent. You should always heed what is read in the Epistle of blessed Peter: “Not as lording it over the clergy, but made an example to the flock.” Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, and strictly order you under peril to your order and office, that, if this is so, you restore to the said priest [Col. 0784C] his benefice and office unimpaired, in peace and quiet, and desist from exactions of this sort, which are known to be wholly incompatible with the dignity of your administration.

For this proceeds from the root of greed and avarice; from it simoniacal wickednesses break forth, very many enormities are committed, and destructive examples are undoubtedly generated. Therefore, having regard to your honour, correct and amend your excesses and presumptions in this matter so that hereafter we need hear no complaint from the said priest or others concerning you on such points. Know and recognize for certain that, if any further complaint concerning these things is brought to us, however much we may love your person, [Col. 0784D] we shall punish you so severely that others who hear of it will fear in any way to attempt similar actions.

Given at Tusculum, on the Kalends of March [1 March].

DCCCLXXIV. To the bishops of Meaux and Amiens. — Entrusts to them the examination of the matrimonial case between Count Robert and the daughter of Hugh of Broyes. (Tusculum, 4 March.)

[Ibid., col. 891.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brothers the bishops of Meaux [Note: [Col. 0785D] Stephen of the Chapel, made bishop in 1164.] and Amiens [Note: [Col. 0785D] Theobald.], greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been represented to us that, when our beloved son, the noble Count Robert, proposed to give his daughter in marriage to Hugh of Broyes and join her to him in matrimony, the noble Count Henry alleged that between them there was such a degree of affinity that they could not be united with God and according to law. An appeal from the examination of our venerable brother, the bishop of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0786D] Henry of Carinthia, made bishop from being a monk of Morimond; he lies buried in the monastery of Boulancourt.], was made to our hearing. Count Robert sent his messenger, but the other party neither came nor sent anyone to answer on its behalf.

Therefore, placing full confidence in your prudence and integrity, [Col. 0785B] we have thought fit to entrust the same case to your competence. We command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if any persons appear who lawfully wish and are able to contest the marriage, you diligently hear the arguments and allegations produced on either side; receive, appeal having been set aside, such suitable witnesses as deserve credence; carefully commit the sworn testimony of those witnesses to writing; and send it to us, enclosed under your seals, after appointing a suitable term for both parties to present themselves before the apostolic presence with those attestations. Nevertheless, if there has been no appeal in the same case, we do not wish you to proceed in any way with its execution. [Col. 0785C]

Given at Tusculum, 4 Nones of March [4 March].

DCCCLXXV. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — That he receive humanely the bishop of Beauvais, to whom he had ordered all due obedience to be rendered, when the latter makes satisfaction to him. (Tusculum, 4 March.)

[Ibid., col. 892.]

We received with due kindness our beloved sons S., the master, and Brother D., of the Order of the Temple, your messengers, who came to us with your brotherhood’s letters. From their faithful and prudent statement, we learned that our brother, the bishop [Col. 0785D] of Beauvais, having been disobedient to you in certain matters, had not responded in two synods which you held with the reverence and humility proper to him; that, before requesting your brotherhood, he had represented to us that he had been burdened by you; and that, although you summoned him for this and he personally set out to come before us, he had not taken care to pursue the appeal. His clerks excused him, saying that he had abandoned it not through contempt or contumacy, but solely because of illness.

We were angered and troubled against him, and took care to rebuke him by our letters concerning this, as we judged expedient [Col. 0786A] and as befitted us without prejudice to his honour. We remember the most sincere devotion and faith which, since the time of our promotion, you have shown toward the most holy Roman Church and especially toward our person with unconquerable constancy. We therefore have the most ardent desire and will to love you with the sincerest affection of heart as a dearest brother, a great member and a most firm pillar of the Church, and willingly to promote your honour and exaltation insofar as we can with God and justice.

Nevertheless, because it is fitting for you, both on account of the nobility of blood in which you excel and because of the dignity which you hold, to show a spirit of kindness and gentleness toward your subjects, and especially toward your suffragans, and to be kind and merciful, we, greatly relying on your clemency and gentleness and desiring readily to defer to you as a dearest brother, directed the aforesaid bishop humbly to beg mercy and pardon from you; [Col. 0786B] to make satisfaction to you, as to his father and lord, with all humility and reverence concerning matters which are manifest and from which an appeal has been made to us; and to present himself as humble, devoted, and obedient.

We therefore ask, counsel, and admonish your brotherhood that, once the bishop has humbled himself in your presence and sought mercy and pardon from you, and has rendered suitable satisfaction—as you ought to require and he to offer—you remit your anger and indignation; graciously restore to him your favour and affection; and show yourself kindly and appeased toward him. Treat him with such gentleness and kindness that the clemency of your mildness may be especially commended as a result, and that we too may rejoice with him because we referred him to your mercy and kindness, and may be bound to render abundant thanks to your affection. [Col. 0786C]

Given at Tusculum, 4 Nones of March [4 March].

DCCCLXXVI. Commands Henry, archbishop of Reims, and P., abbot of Saint Remigius, to cause the restoration to the clerk Richard of his prebend in the church of Saint Pharaïldis. (Tusculum, 4 March.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0786D]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Henry, archbishop of Reims, and Peter, abbot of Saint Remigius, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the complaint sent to us by Richard, a poor clerk, it has come to our hearing that G., a clerk of Ghent, presumed unlawfully to take from him a prebend granted to him in the church of Saint Pharaïldis. Since we are bound to render justice to ecclesiastical men, and especially to those burdened by poverty, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you earnestly admonish and more strictly compel the aforesaid clerk [Col. 0787A] to restore to R. the said prebend without molestation or difficulty, and leave him in peace and quiet; or else, in your presence and appeal having been set aside, not delay to render him full justice in this matter.

Given at Tusculum, 4 Nones of March [4 March].

DCCCLXXVII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — Confirms the election of Robert, bishop-elect of Arras, and grants him time to receive holy orders. (Tusculum, 4 March.)

[Ibid.]

As has become known to us from the letters of the dean and canons of the Church of Arras, when that Church was vacant of a pastor, they unanimously agreed upon our beloved son R. [Note: [Col. 0787D] Robert, who was also provost of Aire, of Saint Donatian at Bruges, and of Saint Amatus at Douai; he was also bishop of Cambrai, and died miserably, having been killed in 1172, according to Alberic in his *Chronicle*.] [Col. 0787B], provost of Saint-Omer, and elected him as their bishop and master. Although confirmation of their election belongs to you as their metropolitan, because that provost is below the orders and the dispensation for such an election pertains to the Roman pontiff and to no other, they urgently and humbly requested us to ratify their election by apostolic authority through dispensation.

Accordingly, yielding to their prayers, considering the prudence and discretion of the same provost, and believing that welcome benefits would accrue to the aforesaid Church through him, we have thought fit, by the common counsel of our brethren, to grant a dispensation in this matter and confirm the election by apostolic authority, without prejudice to the dignity and right of you and the Church entrusted to you. Furthermore, considering how many affairs of the said elect are pending with the noble Count Philip of Flanders, from which he cannot readily or quickly be released, we have thought fit, at the request of that count’s prayers, to grant him that from the approaching feast of Pentecost until one full year has elapsed he shall not be compelled against his will to receive orders. [Col. 0787C] Thus, when those affairs have been settled, he may receive orders and consecration with a more devoted mind and more freely devote himself to the episcopal office.

We therefore will and command that you do not burden that elect concerning the reception of orders within that term, since the sacred canons allow a far longer interval to those who are to be promoted from one order to another. [Col. 0787D]

Given at Tusculum, 4 Nones of March [4 March].

DCCCLXXVIII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims, and Walter, bishop of Tournai. — That they abolish an evil custom in the parish of Dudassel. (Tusculum, 5 March.)

[Ibid., col. 894.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers Henry, archbishop of Reims, [Col. 0788A] and G., bishop of Tournai, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us from the complaint transmitted by the parishioners of the church of Dudassel that, when one of them is accused by the tithe-inspectors of failing to pay his full tithes, and has not, after the third Sunday, produced what is said to have been withheld from the tithes, then on the weekday immediately following the third Sunday he is required to confirm by oath that he has paid his tithes in full, unless perhaps he chooses to make up what he is alleged to have withheld from the tithes. But if, in taking the oath, he trembles in hand, countenance, eyes, or any other part, so that the trembling can be noticed; or if one or more fingers of his hand are absent and are not placed upon the relics without any trembling, then by an evil and unjust custom he is compelled to pay two sols and twice the tithe which he is said to have withheld. [Col. 0788B]

That custom is altogether wicked and detestable, contrary to both divine and human law, and is known to have arisen only from the root of excessive greed. For those who approach with trembling are more to be commended than those who approach sacred relics irreverently—indeed, not to say shamelessly. Therefore, since evil customs must be wholly uprooted and ought to find no place among clergy or laity, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the matter is so, you remove and wholly extirpate by our authority and yours such a horrible and detestable custom. You are not to allow those compelled to take an oath to be fined hereafter on account of their trembling in taking it, or because they have not laid their whole hand upon the relics. [Col. 0788C]

If any persons impose any penalty on this account, restrain them from so great a presumption by ecclesiastical censure, with the remedy of appeal removed. Strictly prohibit tithes from being exacted from laymen, paid to them, or any excuse or oath whatsoever concerning the withholding of tithes being required from them.

Given at Tusculum, 3 Nones of March [5 March].

DCCCLXXIX. Entrusts to Henry, archbishop of Reims, and G., bishop of Laon, the determination of the case concerning certain offerings between the canons of Bruges and R., priest of Dudassel. (Tusculum, 6 March.)

[Ibid., col. 895.]

[Col. 0788D]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers Henry, archbishop of Reims, and G. [Note: [Col. 0788D] Walter of Mauritania, made bishop from dean.], bishop of Laon, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When our beloved son L., acting for the canons of Bruges, and R., priest of the church of Dudassel, were present before us, they began to dispute before us concerning certain [Col. 0789A] offerings. To assert his claim to those offerings, the same priest presented to us a certain privilege in the name of the provost of Bruges and the aforesaid canons, which he earnestly requested us to confirm. He added that, because he and his church had been despoiled of the aforesaid offerings without judicial process, he had appealed to our hearing.

But the aforesaid L., who spoke for the aforementioned canons, asserted that the agreement made concerning those offerings could not and ought not to stand in law, and that the aforesaid privilege should not be confirmed, because the contract was wrongful: temporal things had been given in compensation for offerings which are spiritual. Therefore, wishing to bring the matter to an end, since neither party could establish before us the matters alleged, we entrust the same case to your competence. We command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, with both parties summoned before you, you diligently investigate the truth of the matter. If you find that the aforesaid priest and the church under his care were despoiled of the said offerings without judicial process or after appeal, cause the offerings to be restored to them, with the remedy of appeal removed. Then, if the aforesaid canons wish to proceed concerning the matter, hear the case and bring it to due conclusion, appeal having been set aside. [Col. 0789B]

Given at Tusculum, 11 Nones of March [5 March].

DCCCLXXX. Entrusts to the archbishop of Reims for determination a case between a man and a woman. (Tusculum, 6 March.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0789C]

A beloved son of ours, W., dean of St. Saviour’s, informed us that a certain parishioner of the church of St. Mary at Bruges had had relations with a woman; at length the woman claimed him as her husband, while the man denied that she was his wife, though he admitted that he had carnally kept her for some time. When this dispute was being heard before him, the woman failed, at the first and second summons, in proving the marriage; afterwards, when a delay had been granted, the aforesaid woman produced her mother, her brother’s servant, and her sister’s own maidservant to prove the marriage. But when the same dean wished to pronounce judgment upon the case, the aforesaid woman appealed to our venerable brother, the bishop of Tournai, appointing a day on which she would come to the church. The man, however, raised an appeal to our hearing. Therefore, since because of the parties’ absence we could not proceed in the case, we entrust it to your experienced judgment, commanding your brotherhood by the authority of these present letters that, when you are requested concerning it, you summon both parties before you and, having fully heard and examined the arguments on both sides, decide the case by a canonical judgment within eleven days after receipt of these letters, with any remedy of appeal removed.

Given at Tusculum, 25 February.

DCCCLXXXI. To the same. — That he shall cause property taken from P. and from the priest T. by Count Rainald and Henry of Grandpré to be restored. (Tusculum, 7 March.)

[Ibid., col. 897.]

We have received the complaint of the priest P., who came to us, that Count Rainald refuses to pay him seventeen solidi, which he is bound to deliver upon the security given by a surety. He further added that Henry of Magnopratum, through his servant, violently caused a certain beast of burden to be taken from him, and caused the same priest, by laying violent hands upon him, to be treated shamefully and dishonourably. He likewise set before us that the same H. unjustly took twenty-five solidi from the priest T., his nephew, and scorns to restore them. Since, therefore, we cannot and ought not to endure that laymen should violently invade the rights of clerics or, with rash boldness, commit violence against them, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you cause all things taken from the said priests to be restored in full within forty days after receipt of these letters, or that full and sufficient justice concerning them be rendered to the priests before you, with appeal set aside. If the aforesaid knights do not otherwise comply with you, strike them with ecclesiastical censure. But if it is established to you that the servant of the aforesaid Henry, by Henry’s command, wickedly dared to lay violent hands upon the above-mentioned priest, your discretion knows more fully what you ought to do in consequence.

Given at Tusculum, 7 March.

DCCCLXXXII. To the same. — That he should urge the bishop of Soissons, content with the bishopric alone, to relinquish the chancellorship. (Tusculum, 7 March.)

[Ibid.]

It befits us to apply ready care and diligence to those matters which concern the increase of virtues and the salvation of souls, and with ardent desire and solicitude to promote the welfare and advancement of churches. Certainly, it is not unknown to your prudence, but certain and manifest, how necessary it is for a bishop to exercise vigilance and solicitude over the care of the flock entrusted to him, and, lest it be exposed to the bites of wolves, to keep watch with the eye of more attentive concern. Moreover, since our venerable brother, the bishop of Soissons, cannot suitably exercise at once the office of chancellor and the responsibility of pontifical administration, because each office requires the whole and undivided person, we have commanded him, having relinquished the chancellorship,

> [Note: There is no doubt that Hugh, bishop of Soissons, obeyed Pope Alexander’s admonitions by relinquishing the chancellorship; for, as Mabillon observes in Book II of *De re diplomatica*, chapter 12, the chancellorship was vacant in the years 1171 and 1173; Hugh died in 1175.]

to devote himself diligently and earnestly to the care and administration entrusted to him, and to stand watchful and attentive over the protection of the Church and people committed to him, so that he may be able to render a full account thereof before the Master of the Household. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you admonish the same bishop concerning this matter and, if it can be done with the assent and peace of our dearest son in Christ, E., illustrious king of the Franks, compel him strictly.

Given at Tusculum, 7 March.

DCCCLXXXIII. To the same. — Concerning the case between the priest James and the abbot of St. Saviour of Virtus. (Tusculum, 10 March.)

[Ibid., col. 898.]

The priest James, appearing in our presence, showed us in a humble complaint that, when the abbot of St. Saviour of Virtus had presented him to our venerable brother, the bishop of Châlons, for the church of St. Stephen in the village of Senior, and the bishop had invested him with that church, the abbot subsequently began to deny that he had given him the church or had presented him to it, because the same priest would not, at his command, increase the rent. And when both he and the clerk W., to whom, the abbot asserted, he had granted the aforesaid church, had appeared before the said bishop concerning this matter, although the bishop admitted that he had not entrusted the cure of that church to the said W., the aforesaid priest nevertheless feared that he would be overborne by his adversary’s power and appealed to our hearing. When he appeared before us on this account, neither he nor the abbot’s representative had come prepared to litigate; therefore we could in no way proceed with the case or bring it to its due conclusion. Accordingly, fully trusting in your prudence and integrity, we entrust the same case to your experienced judgment, to be heard and concluded in due form. We therefore command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you summon before you the abbot, the priest, and the clerk; and, having fully heard and examined the arguments on both sides, if it is lawfully established to you that the aforesaid church was conferred upon the above-named priest through the abbot’s presentation and the bishop’s grant, and that he has not subsequently committed anything for which he ought deservedly to be deprived of it, cause it to be peacefully and quietly relinquished to him, with appeal and pretext removed. Otherwise, hear the case and judge what is just, with the remedy of appeal set aside.

Given at Tusculum, 10 March.

DCCCLXXXIV. To Henry, archbishop of Reims, and G., bishop of Laon. — Concerning the case between the canons of Bruges and the priest R. (Tusculum, 11 March.)

[Ibid., col. 899.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers HENRY, archbishop of Reims, and G[ALTER], bishop of Laon: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Although in the letters which we sent to your discretion concerning certain offerings, over which there is a dispute between the canons of the church of St. Donatian at Bruges and R., priest of the church of Dudasselle, it was stated that our beloved son L. had spoken on behalf of the canons, nevertheless we remember, and our brothers likewise recall, that the same L. declared himself to be only the representative of the aforesaid provost. Therefore, the statement in the other letters that he was the representative of the canons remained uncorrected because of the excessive press of business. The above-mentioned priest said that he had no case against that provost, but only against the canons. We therefore will and command that, notwithstanding the statement in the other letters that the aforesaid L. was the canons’ representative, you inquire more diligently into the truth of the matter concerning this same case, according to the tenor of our other letters. If you find that the said priest and his church were deprived of the aforesaid offerings without judgment or after an appeal, cause those offerings to be restored to them, without delay and with appeal set aside. Thereafter, if the aforesaid provost or the canons should wish to proceed against the same priest or his church concerning this matter, hear the case and conclude it by canonical judgment, with appeal removed.

Given at Tusculum, 11 March.

DCCCLXXXV. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — That he shall publicly declare excommunicated Roger Tokell, Guy, and others who laid violent hands upon clerics. (Tusculum, 13 March.)

[Ibid., col. 900.]

We have received a complaint on behalf of the chapter of Châlons against Roger Tokell, Guy son of the seneschal, and their other accomplices: with rash audacity laying violent hands upon the treasurer of its church and its clerics, they treated them shamefully and dishonourably. Since an offence of such presumption must be punished with severe correction, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, strictly enjoining you to inquire diligently into the truth of this matter. If you find it to be so, publicly declare the aforesaid men excommunicated, with lighted candles and appeal set aside, and cause them to be carefully avoided until they make fitting satisfaction to the same treasurer and his clerics for the injury inflicted, and appear before the apostolic presence with your letters to make satisfaction for so great an offence.

Given at Tusculum, 13 March.

DCCCLXXXVI. To the bishop of Châlons. — That he shall cause a priest, unknowingly ordained though the son of a priest, to retain his church. (Tusculum, 13 March.)

[Ibid., col. 900.]

Since it is written in the Book of Psalms: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10); and elsewhere: “Mercy and truth shall go before thy face” (Psalm 88:13), we formerly considered it proper to refer P., bearer of these letters, to your mercy, since you had ordained him priest without knowing that he was the son of a priest: if you found him otherwise suitable and honourable, you were to receive him to the church to which he had been presented. We regard it as welcome and acceptable that, at our suggestion, you assigned him the aforesaid church. We admonish and command your brotherhood that you maintain him in that church and in no way permit that church to be troubled or disturbed there on that account. Yet the dispensation which we wish to grant in this man’s case must not establish a rule for others; nor are you to take from it an example for henceforth promoting to orders sons of priests born in priesthood, unless they have been proved, in a cloister of regular canons or monks, to be of worthy conduct.

Given at Tusculum, 13 March.

DCCCLXXXVII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — He deprives the bishop of Senlis, who had divided a prebend, of the power of granting prebends. (Tusculum, 13 March.)

[Ibid., col. 901.]

When Henry, archdeacon of Senlis, was in our presence, our beloved sons S., Master S., and D., brothers of the Order of the Temple, your messengers, lodged before us and our brethren a serious complaint on your behalf against our brother the bishop of Senlis,

> [Note: Henry, formerly abbot of St. Quentin of Beauvais, who became bishop.]

namely that, after he had at your request granted your clerk G. the first prebend which should become vacant in his church, he did not fear to divide, between G. and the aforesaid archdeacon, the prebend which became vacant, contrary to our decree issued in the Council of Tours:

> [Note: Thus in the Council of Tours, chapter 1: “While the greater benefices of the Church remain intact, it seems most unbecoming that the lesser prebends of clerics should suffer division. Therefore, in order that the churches may retain firm unity in their greater as in their lesser members, we prohibit the division of prebends or dignities through alteration.”]

Although you had admonished him by letter and orally to correct what he had done, and he refused to comply with your admonition, you appealed to our hearing. The archdeacon, preserving moderation and humility in the manner of his speech, did not deny what your messengers had alleged; rather, he firmly maintained that the bishop had forgotten our decree when he halved the prebend, and prudently added that he had failed to pursue the appeal not from contempt for you but because illness prevented him.

Desiring to defer, insofar as we can with God and justice, to your honour and dignity, and to take more diligent care lest others acquire boldness to offend and an occasion to violate our decree, we suspend the bishop from the authority to grant prebends until our mercy, or that of our Catholic successor. By the deliberate counsel of our brethren, we have deprived the archdeacon of the half-prebend which he received contrary to our decree, while leaving him by our authority in his archdeaconry and canonry, so that he shall lack that half-prebend perpetually. But either the half which he now has shall be made whole by his bishop after the bishop, through the mercy of the Apostolic See, has had the authority to grant prebends restored to him, or else it shall be made whole by the bishop’s successor, or another whole prebend shall be assigned to him. Truly, although your aforesaid clerk G. ought on the same ground to have been deprived of his half-prebend, nevertheless, for your honour, in consideration of your brotherhood, and because he was absent, we have left it to him by dispensation; provided that, when a whole prebend in the same church becomes vacant, he is to be assigned it after relinquishing the half.

Henceforth we earnestly commend the aforesaid bishop to your charity, asking and admonishing you that, mercifully restoring to the bishop your favour and affection, you love, support, honour, and treat him kindly and gently as your own creation. For we have instructed him to render you, as to his father and lord, the obedience and reverence due to you; and we do not doubt that he is ready and willing to do so.

Given at Tusculum, 13 March.

DCCCLXXXVIII. To the same. — Concerning Master Gerard’s absolution from excommunication. (Tusculum, 14 March.)

[Ibid., col. 902.]

When our beloved sons Brother Simon and Master Stephen, your messengers, and Master Gerard, bearer of these letters, appeared before us, your said messengers declared that G. had been excommunicated and ought to be avoided as excommunicated. The aforesaid G., however, maintained that, when a certain woman, against whom another party was bringing a claim concerning eighteen pounds, had died, our beloved son Bos., archdeacon of your church, who acted in your stead in cases, took occasion against him. Since the case had been committed to you and the same G. had acted before us for the aforesaid woman in obtaining letters of commission, the archdeacon summoned him to answer in his presence as surety in that case. But he, not acknowledging that he was a surety, and observing that the letters themselves contained nothing about suretyship, refused to answer concerning this before that archdeacon; indeed, he appealed to our hearing. Yet he said that he was wholly unaware that the same archdeacon had excommunicated him, except that the aforesaid messengers asserted that he had been excommunicated. Although the sentence would not have bound him if it had been issued against him after the appeal, since it was unknown to us whether he had been excommunicated before or after the appeal, we caused him to be absolved from that sentence and send him back absolved. We earnestly admonish and command your brotherhood to regard him as absolved, cause all to regard him as absolved, demand nothing from him nor allow anything to be demanded from others on account of that excommunication, and inflict or allow no penalty to be inflicted upon him for this reason.

Given at Tusculum, 14 March.

DCCCLXXXIX. To the same. — He writes in favour of the deacon D., to whom the brothers of St. Eugendus had granted the church of Masdeium. (Tusculum, 16 March.)

[Ibid., col. 903.]

D., a deacon and bearer of these letters, coming to the clemency of the Apostolic See, showed us in a tearful complaint that, although the abbot and brothers of St. Eugendus had canonically granted him the church of Masdeium,

> [Note: St. Eugendus, a noble and very ancient abbey in the diocese of Besançon, founded by St. Romanus, first called Condat, then named after its third abbot, St. Eugenius; today it is known by the name of St. Claude, whose body it preserves to this day incorrupt.]

our brother the bishop of Châlons refused to receive him upon their presentation and, against their wishes, installed another in that church. The same deacon was therefore compelled to appeal to the Apostolic See. Since the truth of this matter is not established for us, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to inquire diligently into it. If you find it to be so, and if the bishop cannot show a reasonable cause why he refuses to receive him to that church, cause the aforesaid church to be assigned to D., with pretext and appeal set aside, so that he may not be compelled further to suffer through lack of justice. But if on this ground he is to be removed from his portion, then, once the man who was installed against the will of the abbot and brethren has been removed, do not delay in ordaining there another suitable man upon their presentation.

Given at Tusculum, 16 March.

DCCCXC. To the abbots of St. Remigius and St. Denis at Reims. — He commits a case to them for judgment. (Tusculum, 17 March.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 957.]

We entrust to your experienced judgment, to be heard and concluded by a suitable decision with appeal set aside, the case which has long been litigated between G. of Reims and the woman A. concerning a certain house before our beloved son B., archdeacon of Reims, and which, as is said, has been brought before us by appeal. Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, when requested concerning it, you summon both parties before you; and, if you ascertain that the case was brought before us by appeal, having heard and examined the arguments on both sides, bring the same case to an end, with appeal removed, either by settlement or by judgment.

Given at Tusculum, 17 March.

DCCCXCI. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — That he shall suspend from office the bishop of Châlons, who demanded money for absolving an excommunicated woman. (Tusculum, 17 March.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 904.]

It has been reported to us that, when our brother G., bishop of Châlons,

> [Note: Guy of Joinville.]

had struck his parishioners—namely Evannus, certain others, and their households—with sentence of excommunication for their offences, after our mandate had been received and, as we believe, suitable satisfaction rendered, he absolved all except the wife of the above-named E. from the sentence by which they were bound. He scorned to absolve E.’s wife because she would not pay him the nine pounds which the bishop demanded for her absolution, although she was prepared to submit to the equity of law concerning the matter for which she had been excommunicated. When the aforesaid bishop persisted in his intention, penance, the viaticum, and also burial were denied the said woman in her death. Therefore, if the reports brought before us concerning the said bishop are true, many matters deserve grave punishment. We command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you diligently inquire into the truth; and, if it is established to you that the bishop denied the benefit of absolution to that woman, though she sought absolution, through greed for money, and that through his avarice she died without penance, suspend the bishop from the exercise of his pontifical office until our command. Cause the body of the aforesaid woman to be committed to ecclesiastical burial, since punishment and guilt ought to fall upon him who denied the benefit of absolution to one seeking it at the point of death.

Given at Tusculum, 17 March.

DCCCXCII. To the same. — That he shall declare excommunicated two canons of his church who laid violent hands upon a deacon. (Tusculum, 17 March.)

[Ibid.]

Whenever ecclesiastics commit acts which, if committed by laymen, ought to be punished by severe correction, we must correct their transgression all the more promptly because others are more readily prompted toward good or evil by their example. From the complaint of M., a deacon and bearer of these letters, it has come to our attention that John Brieter and his uncle Erlewinus, canons of your church, reviled him with insults and abuse within the chapter before our beloved sons the dean and canons of that church; and, laying violent hands upon him, did not fear to treat him shamefully and dishonourably. Since such a great and grave offence deserves to be punished with much severity not only in clerics but in any others whatsoever, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to investigate the truth of the matter diligently through those who were present. If you find it to be so, declare the aforesaid canons excommunicated, with appeal set aside; and until they make fitting satisfaction to the same deacon for the injuries inflicted and appear before the apostolic presence with your letters, cause them to be carefully avoided as excommunicated persons.
