Given at Tusculum, 17 March.

DCCCXCIII. To the same. — That the canons of Laon shall make satisfaction to the nuns of St. Peter at Reims for the injuries inflicted. (Tusculum, 17 March.)

[Ibid., col. 905.]

A complaint has been brought to our hearing on behalf of the abbess and sisters of St. Peter at Reims: although a division had long ago been made by judgment between them and our beloved sons the canons of the Church of Laon concerning a certain wood and common land to be divided, the same canons inflicted serious losses and injuries upon the said sisters within that division. Although those sisters had introduced the impediment of an appeal in defence of their right, the canons nevertheless, disregarding the appeal, inflicted losses and injuries upon them. Provoked by these losses and injuries, they were compelled to send their complaint to the Apostolic See. Since what is attempted contrary to the order of law in contempt of us and of the Church by anyone, much less by ecclesiastics, must not be left in silence, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to investigate the matter diligently. If you find it to be so, admonish the aforesaid canons and, by the authority granted you, compel them to make full reparation to the above-mentioned sisters within eleven days after receipt of these letters for the losses inflicted, with appeal set aside, and to give appropriate satisfaction for the injuries committed. For their contempt of the appeal, impose upon them, with the remedy of appeal removed, such penalty as, by common report, ought to come to our hearing.

Given at Tusculum, 17 March.

DCCCXCIV. To the same. — He commits to him the case of the widow Elisendis. (Tusculum, 17 March.)

[Ibid.]

It has been reported to us that, when the widow Elisendis and her sons brought a claim before your discretion against John of Aculum and his sister concerning a debt of twelve pounds which they were bound to pay her, they, wishing to evade justice, appealed to our justice; but after two years had elapsed, they have in no way pursued the appeal, either personally or through others. Since it would be unworthy and wholly contrary to reason that justice for the said widow or her sons should fail under the pretext of a frivolous appeal, we refer the same case to your examination and command you by apostolic letters that, if it is established to you that J. and his sister have not pursued the appeal, personally or through another, during so long a time, admonish them and compel them with all strictness either to pay the aforesaid money to the said widow and her sons, without trouble or deduction, within eleven days after receipt of these letters, or to render them before you full justice concerning it, with appeal set aside.

Given at Tusculum, 17 March.

DCCCXCV. To the same. — That he shall protect the men of St. Remigius from the vexations of the canons of Soissons. (Tusculum, 21 March.)

[Ibid.]

A complaint has reached the hearing of the Apostolic See on behalf of the church of St. Remigius that the canons of Soissons and Nicholas of Bazoches compel the men of St. Remigius to redemption-payment and presume to harass them with many vexations and unjust exactions. Therefore, since it is unworthy that the aforesaid church should suffer from them an unlawful loss of its men, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and strictly compel the said men to abstain altogether from demanding redemption from the men of the above-named church and from molesting or exacting from them. But if they are confident that they possess any right in this matter, they may establish it in your presence.

Given at Tusculum, 21 March.

DCCCXCVI. To the archbishop of Tours and the bishop of Autun. — That they shall examine the sentence of excommunication pronounced by the archbishop of Reims against Count Henry. (Tusculum, 22 March.)

[Ibid., col. 907.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the archbishop of Tours,

> [Note: Joscius, who governed the Church of Tours from 1157 to 1175.]

and the bishop of Autun,

> [Note: Henry, brother of Odo II, duke of Burgundy.]

greeting and the apostolic blessing.

When our beloved sons Master Stephen and Milo of Châlons, messengers of our venerable brother H., archbishop of Reims, came into our presence with his letters, they urgently entreated us to confirm by the protection of the Apostolic See the sentence of excommunication which he had pronounced against the nobleman Count Henry for his offences. But our beloved sons John Salvalupus and Master Melior, who had come concerning the same matter on behalf of the count, firmly asserted before us that the sentence was not binding, declaring that it had been pronounced after an appeal had been made to the Apostolic See. The said messengers of the archbishop acknowledged that the sentence had been pronounced against the count after the obstacle of appeal had been raised, as the other party firmly maintained; but they added that the same count, exceeding the limits of the appeal, invaded after the appeal the lands of the Church of Reims through his provosts and by his malice; and that, after some of the people there had been killed and others taken captive, he caused a certain church within the archbishop’s jurisdiction to be burned at his pleasure. Nor did he wish, at the entreaty and admonition of the aforesaid archbishop, to release the people whom he held captive until he unjustly compelled them to ransom themselves.

Against this, the messengers of the said count answered that, if his provosts and soldiery had committed such acts after the appeal, this had not proceeded from the count’s knowledge or command. They wholly denied that he had been asked concerning the captives, adding that the count’s men had not invaded the archbishop’s land; rather, when the provosts and soldiery of that archbishop invaded the count’s land, the count’s men met them and, fortune favouring them, put them to flight, killing some and taking others captive.

Although various things were said before us by both sides concerning this matter, neither party could prove them to us. Since only two points were established for us by the confession of each party—that an appeal had been made to us, and that after the appeal the archbishop subjected the above-named count to excommunication—we could not and ought not, in accordance with his prayer and petition, confirm or hold valid that sentence. Nevertheless, we desire readily to defer in every matter in which we can do so with God to him as our venerable brother, distinguished both by the office of his dignity and by nobility of blood, unless we could first obtain certainty concerning what his messengers had laid before us.

Therefore, lest we seem to leave either party material for complaint through a defect of justice, we have thought fit to commit the examination of these matters to your experienced judgment, in which we have full and undoubted confidence. By apostolic authority we command you to meet together and diligently investigate the truth of all these matters within eleven days after receipt of these letters. If it is established to you that the said provosts and soldiery, by the command or with the knowledge of the above-mentioned count, after the appeal and before the excommunication, attacked the aforesaid archbishop’s land—not repelling injury but inflicting it—or that the count himself, when asked by the archbishop, refused either to restore the persons whom he held in chains or to render justice concerning them, then, unless in the meantime they have come to an amicable agreement, which we prefer, hold the sentence pronounced against him valid and confirm it by our authority, with the impediment of appeal removed; and command that it be observed inviolate.

Moreover, declare excommunicated until fitting satisfaction those arsonists who dared set fire to the aforesaid church, and cause all carefully to avoid them. Otherwise the sentence ought not to bind, because a sentence pronounced after an appeal, as your brotherhood knows, can and ought to have no force unless it is known or proved that the person subsequently committed an act for which he ought to be held under the bond of anathema. We further command you by the authority of these present letters, if you receive a mandate concerning the building of castles from our dearest son in Christ L., illustrious king of the Franks, to exercise our authority effectively and strive to conclude the case, if possible by settlement, or otherwise by judgment. What we have commanded concerning excommunication, we order to be observed likewise concerning an interdict of the land.

Given at Tusculum, 22 March.

DCCCXCVII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — That he shall not burden the bishop of Beauvais and his other suffragans, and shall settle his disputes with Count Henry. (Tusculum, 22 March.)

[Ibid., col. 909.]

That ardor of sincerity and devotion, and that constancy of integrity, which from the beginning of our elevation you have shown magnanimously toward your sole and singular mother, the most holy Roman Church, and especially toward our own person—we always bear it in our heart; and likewise, weighing the strength of your admirable faith in careful reflection, we hold a firm resolve and a most fervent will to love your person with abundant charity as that of a dearest brother and an immovable pillar of the Church, and to strive with ardent desire for your honor and advancement. For since you have set yourself up as an impregnable wall and a tower of strength for the house of the Lord and the Catholic faith, and have labored according to your powers to advance the business and cause of the Church, you may deservedly trust and be fully assured that we love your person from purity of heart, and wish in every way to be solicitous and diligent for your honor.

Therefore, if we sometimes write to your fraternity things which perhaps seem burdensome to you, we do this not from lesser affection; rather, the more fervently we love you, the more willingly we urge upon you those things which concern the preservation of your honor and reputation and the increase of your virtues. By setting before you matters sometimes harsh and hard, we always intend to recall you from things which might obscure the renown of your good name with some cloud of detraction. For since a father corrects and chastises the one whom he loves, and the blows of a friend are better than the flattering kisses of an enemy, you could by no means have full confidence in us if we did not carefully advise you concerning what is expedient for your honor and welfare, and what is especially known to concern preserving the integrity of your reputation—particularly since it is written: “He who neglects his reputation is cruel.”

Accordingly, since a rule has been laid down for both us and you, according to which we ought to deal with subjects with prudence and moderation, your fraternity ought not to be troubled or disturbed for any reason if, by our admonitions and commands, we suggest that you not burden your suffragans—especially the bishop of Beauvais—beyond the limit fixed by the holy Fathers; rather, that you treat them with gentleness and kindness. You should also have about you persons so mature, honorable, and discreet that your reputation may be fragrant through their manner of life, the excellence of your integrity may shine forth more praiseworthily, and you may confidently rely on their counsel in conducting ecclesiastical business and, in your absence, unhesitatingly entrust to them the affairs which arise for execution.

[Col. 0801C] Certainly, if the clerics of the bishop of Beauvais have boasted—which we do not believe—that we have thereby derogated from your right and dignity, you ought not readily to have believed them, since our charity toward you burns so strongly that we would knowingly derogate in no respect from your right and dignity for anyone’s sake. But we granted him what we could not lawfully deny him: namely, that you are not permitted to dispose or order his churches and rights contrary to the form of the canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers, or to burden his person. Otherwise, you must not at all believe that we had derogated from your right or dignity on behalf of the bishop of Beauvais.

Moreover, we abound toward you with such purity of mind and sincerity of heart that you may be as secure and certain of the fullness of the love and favor of the Apostolic See and of ourselves, and may rely upon us as confidently, as any person could ever better trust or hope; nor should you give ear or attention if anyone should ever presume to whisper the contrary. Yet we do not wish you, because of the favor which, as your merits require, you have found in the sight of ourselves and of the whole Church, to burden the aforesaid bishop of Beauvais or any others in such a way that episcopal maturity or priestly moderation should seem to suffer a defect in you.

For the future, we ask, admonish, advise, and exhort your prudence that, in accordance with the counsel and exhortation of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Franks, your brother, and of your other friends, you make a peaceful and amicable settlement with the noble Count Henry concerning the dispute between you and him over the Castle. Consider, as a prudent and discerning man, how great losses and inconveniences may result from that discord for you, your Church, and the same count. But if you cannot settle the matter with him, submit it to the judgment of the king or another person to whom the king himself shall think fit to commit the case.

Given at Tusculum, the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

DCCCXCVIII. To the same. — He replies concerning various matters on which the archbishop had consulted him. (Tusculum, March 22.)

[Ibid., col. 911.]

Since the most holy Roman Church has, by God’s ordering, been established as the head and teacher of all Churches, and consultations and questions are rightly referred to it from diverse parts of the world, we rejoice that you have consulted it on various questions of law, and we deservedly commend your prudence. Therefore we have considered it fitting to answer your fraternity by the present letter.

If an appeal has been made before judgment or afterward for the sake of delaying in vain, or even from necessity, a year is customarily allowed to such appellants; or, if pressing and evident necessity appears, two years are allowed, unless the judge from whom the appeal was made has set a shorter period according to the distance of places and provinces and the amount of time. If the appellant has not prosecuted the appeal within that period, the judgment shall stand if he appealed after the judgment; and he appears to have fallen from his case, nor shall the appellant thereafter be heard upon the same matter.

But if the appeal was made without any grievance and before the commencement of the suit, such an appellant shall be heard, because the sacred canons everywhere permit appeals. Nevertheless, if he appealed before judgment, he shall be compelled to stand by the judgment of the person from whom he is known to have appealed. If, however, an appeal was made in the field or otherwise before the case began, such proceedings are not usually called appeals but summonses to court.

Furthermore, if the appellant is a robber or otherwise a violent possessor of another’s property, an appeal of this sort made in court before ecclesiastical persons is customarily heard—unless, perhaps, he is an evident robber or fornicator, like the man whom the Apostle excommunicated while absent and not summoned.

Further, if someone appeals in one case and, while the appeal is pending, commits some crime, or is said to have committed one earlier, or is now accused of one, or is sued over another matter concerning which no appeal has been made and which does not concern the judge from whom he appealed in the other business, he may, if he wishes, avoid that judge as suspect. Otherwise he must stand by the judgment of the one from whom the appeal was made, especially if that judge is his ordinary judge.

Likewise, if two persons litigating before a judge, one appeals to our hearing and the other to the hearing of his own judge concerning the same matter, and the one who appealed to his own judge, appearing on the day fixed for the appeal, states that he has appealed to him while concealing the fact that his adversary had appealed to the hearing of the Roman pontiff: if the latter, having been lawfully cited, neither appears nor sends a representative, or otherwise refuses to obey, and the judge pronounces a sentence of excommunication against him, the sentence of excommunication shall indeed stand for contumacy, unless the judge learns that he had appealed to the hearing of the Roman pontiff.

Finally, you ask at the end of your questions whether, if an appeal has been made from a civil judge to our hearing before or after judgment, such an appeal is valid. It is valid indeed in the cases of those subject to our temporal jurisdiction; but with respect to others, even if it is valid by the custom of the Church, we do not believe that it is valid according to the strict rule of law.

Given at Tusculum, the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

DCCCXCIX. To the illustrious king of the Franks. — That he should settle the dispute between the archbishop of Reims and Count Henry. (Tusculum, March 22.)

[Ibid., col. 912.]

When the messengers of our venerable brother Henry, archbishop of Reims, your brother, and of the noble Count Henry appeared before us and pleaded against one another in our presence, we learned from their assertions that a dispute had arisen between the same archbishop and count—not slight, but exceedingly grave. This is all the more grievous and distressing to us because we wish all persons in your kingdom, and especially the noble and powerful, to enjoy the fullest peace; for we regard your peace and that of the same kingdom, as you have well deserved, not as foreign but as specially and properly our own and the Church’s.

Desiring, as our office requires, to calm their contentions, we yielded, insofar as reason permitted, to the requests of both. We committed the case concerning both the appeal and the excommunication, which specially belonged to us, to our venerable brothers the archbishop of Tours and the bishop of Autun—men certainly prudent and discreet—to examine and bring to its proper conclusion.

But since the aforesaid count complains that certain castles have lately been built by the archbishop, to his no small harm and detriment, and since so great and grave a root of dissension seems to draw nourishment from this, we are greatly disturbed concerning that dissension and are, as we ought to be, solicitous for their peace. We ask, advise, and admonish your royal majesty to intervene effectively between them to restore peace and concord, to endeavor to remove from their midst every cause of quarrel, and to decide the case by judgment or, what we prefer, by amicable settlement. For it is better and more salutary to meet a disease at its beginning than, once it has hardened, to seek a remedy.

But if, concerning the building of the aforesaid castles, you should perhaps be unwilling—which we do not believe—to involve yourself, commit the case to discreet persons who will apply diligence and labor to it and endeavor, if possible, to bring it to an end by amicable settlement or even by judgment. For it greatly benefits you and your kingdom that peace and concord be restored more swiftly between persons so great and powerful.

Given at Tusculum, the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

CM. To Bartholomew, bishop of Beauvais. — That he had not granted him letters exempting him from the jurisdiction of the archbishop of Reims, and that he should render him due obedience. (Tusculum, March 22.)

[Ibid., col. 913.]

[Col. 0804B]

The clerics and messengers of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Reims, stated before us that your clerics had asserted, with provocative behavior on the road, that they had obtained from us letters by which you had been exempted from the jurisdiction and reverence due to that archbishop. We therefore greatly wonder and are exceedingly disturbed at the presumption with which they attempted this, since it is altogether remote from the truth.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your fraternity to render due obedience and honor to the aforesaid archbishop, to show him full devotion and reverence, and to compel your clerics to ask pardon for so great a presumption—or, if they are guiltless, to clear themselves. For we have asked and admonished the same archbishop not to burden you or anyone else on account of the favor which he has for us, in such a way that episcopal maturity or priestly moderation should seem to suffer a defect in him.

Given at Tusculum, the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

CMI. To William, archbishop of Sens. — That he should grant an archdeaconry in his church to the nephew of the archbishop of Reims.  
[Note: [Col. 0803D] In the manuscript this letter bears no inscription; but we infer that it was written to the archbishop of Sens, because elsewhere it is established that Alexander directed letters to that same bishop of Sens on behalf of Philip, nephew of Henry, archbishop of Reims [Col. 0804D].] (Tusculum, March 22.)

[Ibid., col. 914.]

[Col. 0804D]

Our venerable brother, the archbishop of Reims, informed us in a report sent to us that, out of pure and spontaneous generosity, you granted to his nephew the archdeaconry of your Church when it became vacant. But your prudence ought carefully to consider how great the aforesaid archbishop is in the Church of God, with what reverence and devotion you ought to honor him beforehand, how we stand indebted to him who has set himself as a wall and bulwark against enemies for the defense of the Church, and how we are bound to defer to his will. You should display ready diligence and effective assistance in fulfilling his desire.

Therefore, we ask, admonish, and exhort your fraternity that, for reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, and out of regard for the aforesaid archbishop, you generously grant and assign to his nephew, as you are known to have promised, the archdeaconry which becomes vacant in your Church. Thus the same archbishop ought to love both you and your Church more sincerely on that account, attend with more devoted care to your honor and advancement, and we ought thereby to render fuller thanks to your sincerity.

Given at Tusculum, the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

CMII. To Peter, abbot of Saint-Remigius, and Fulk, dean of Reims. — That they should investigate the case of certain persons who had appealed from the bishop of Amiens, appointed judge by the pope. (Tusculum, March 24.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 925.]

[Col. 0805B]

Formerly, when the case between Warin and his son, citizens of Reims, on the one hand, and Oldewin and John, burgesses of Reims, on the other, concerning a certain house, had been brought before us, we committed that case, if we remember correctly, to our venerable brother the bishop of Amiens for decision. Now, however, as has reached our ears through the transmitted complaint of the aforesaid Oldewin and John, when they had approached the same bishop in accordance with our command, they appealed to our hearing, avoiding the judge as suspect, because the aforesaid Warin and his son are said to have familiarity with that bishop, and one of them is reported to be of his household.

[Note: [Col. 0805D] Both were inhabitants of Reims. Yet he distinguishes *burgenses* from *cives*, because he calls *cives* those whose dwelling was within the city walls, and *burgenses* those whose dwelling was in the borough or castle of Saint-Remigius. Jac. Sirmond.]

Since, therefore, the aforesaid burgesses appeared before us through their representative, while the other party neither came nor sent any representative on its behalf, and since we consider that a judge ought not to be appointed in a case when he may reasonably be suspect to either party, we commit the case to your experience. We command that, once both parties have been summoned before you, you hear the case more diligently and, if it is established to you that an appeal was made, bring it to its proper conclusion, with contradiction and appeal set aside.

[Col. 0805D] Given at Tusculum, the ninth day before the Kalends of April.

CMIII. To the same. — He commits to them for judgment the case of two women. (Tusculum, March 25.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 949.]

From the transmitted complaint of the poorhouse of Vitry it has reached our hearing that R., a woman, had brought M., a woman, before the archdeacon of Châlons in a suit concerning a certain house which the same poor persons assert rightfully belongs to them; and that the archdeacon rendered a definitive judgment in favor of the said R. M. appealed to the hearing of our venerable brother Henry, archbishop of Reims, whereas R. appealed to our hearing.

But since, when R.’s representative appeared, the other party neither came nor sent any representative on its behalf, we commit the case to your experience for hearing and proper final determination. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your discretion that, when you are requested concerning this matter, you assemble together, summon both parties before you, hear and fully investigate the arguments on both sides, and, with the remedy of appeal removed, decide the case through justice.

Given at Tusculum, the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

CMIV. He rebukes the bishop of Arras because he had not yet granted R., a cleric, a prebend in his church. (Tusculum, March 25.)

[MARTEN., *Amplified Collection*, II, 914.]

[Col. 0806B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the bishop of Arras, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0806D] Andrew, who succeeded Godescalc upon his resignation in 1164 and died in 1171.]

It has not fallen from our memory, nor do we believe that you are forgetful, how we wrote to you once and again on behalf of R., nephew of Robert Bug., the bearer of the present letter. Yet you have shown yourself so hard in admitting our requests that, as his repeated complaint shows, you have refused to comply with our letters. We take this as exceedingly grave and distressing and cannot but be moved thereby, since you seem to close your ears to our requests, which you ought reverently and humbly to heed.

We know, indeed, that your predecessor G., at our request, generously granted that cleric the first prebend that should become vacant in the Church of Arras and assigned him, for our sake, ten shillings each month for as long as he remained bishop. But when you succeeded that bishop, although several prebends had also become vacant in the same Church, he was unable to obtain any; thus frustrated in his hope and expectation, he is compelled to return to us not without labor and seek our assistance.

Since, therefore, it is unworthy and wholly improper that you should overturn what is known to have been done at our request, we admonish and command your fraternity to grant and assign generously to the aforesaid cleric a prebend, if one is now vacant or when one first happens to become vacant in your Church, every occasion and excuse ceasing. Otherwise, lest you be reproved for disobedience or we be compelled to be more seriously angered against you, show before our venerable brother, the lord bishop of Thérouanne, within forty days after receiving these letters, a manifest and reasonable cause why you do not fulfill our command. If, however, you should perhaps be unwilling to do either of these things, we have commanded that bishop promptly to inform us of it by his letters, so that we may punish you according to your deserts.

Given at Tusculum, the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

CMV. To Peter, abbot of Saint-Remigius. — That one who had seized the land of a man departing for Jerusalem should be compelled to restore it. (Tusculum, March 30.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 923.]

It has been reported to us that, after O., a citizen of Saint-Theodoric at Reims, had taken up the Lord’s cross to depart for Jerusalem, Gerard of Rosay violently seized a certain piece of his land and still holds it occupied. Moved by the tearful petition of O.’s wife, and more readily inclined by the obligation of our office—which binds us to defend with especial care all who are engaged in God’s service and their goods—we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the matter is so, you diligently admonish the said Gerard and, by our authority under excommunication, compel him to restore to the wife of the aforesaid O. the aforesaid land, with the fruits received from it, all contradiction and appeal set aside, and to leave her in peace.

Thereafter, if the aforementioned Gerard believes that any right in the same land belongs to him, let him pursue the matter in judicial order before you against the aforesaid O. after he returns from the regions of Jerusalem.

[Col. 0807C] Given at Tusculum, the third day before the Kalends of April.

CMVI. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — On behalf of the abbot of Saint John of the Vines against R., a priest who had seized the church of Bonnis. (Tusculum, April 3.)

[MARTEN., *Amplified Collection*, II, 915.]

We have received a complaint from the abbot and brethren of Saint John of the Vines that, although the church of Bonnis belongs to them, R., a priest, presumes to celebrate the solemnities of Mass and other divine offices there without the knowledge and presentation of the abbot and contrary to the tenor of the privileges of the Roman Church. Therefore, since we wish the rights and dignities of the aforesaid Church to be preserved unimpaired, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the truth of the matter within twenty days after receiving these letters. If you find it to be so, do not delay, by our authority and your own, to remove the said priest from the same church of Bonnis, all delay and appeal set aside.

Given at Tusculum, the third day before the Nones of April.

CMVII. To the same. — Against Aalis, a female moneylender. (Tusculum, April 3.)

[Ibid., col. 916.]

From the transmitted complaint of the noblewoman Helvidis of Sonunt, a widow, it has reached our ears that, having borrowed money at interest from a certain female moneylender named Aalis, she paid her nineteen pounds as interest beyond the principal and lodged a complaint against her before the Church for recovery of the interest. When the said moneylender had been summoned to judgment, she, distrusting the law and seeking evasion, appealed to our hearing.

But since she neither appeared at the date appointed for her nor sent a representative concerning this matter, and since, by the obligation of pastoral care, we ought to uphold all persons, especially widows and orphans, in their rights, we command you by apostolic letters to summon both parties before you within twenty days after receiving our letters. If the matter is established to you, compel the aforesaid moneylender by ecclesiastical censure to settle with her or, with the remedy of appeal removed, to restore to the aforesaid widow whatever she is found to have exacted in interest—or the greater part of it.

Given at Tusculum, the third day before the Nones of April.

CMVIII. To Peter, abbot of Saint-Remigius, and Fulk, dean of Reims. — That they should be judges in the case of the abbot of Dervensis and the clerics of Saint Nicholas of Châlons. (Tusculum, April 4.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 947.]

Our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of Dervensis, informed us that, although we had committed to our venerable brother, the archbishop of Reims, for decision the case between them and the clerics of Saint Nicholas of Châlons concerning the church of Champ-Albert, the same archbishop delegated the case to Master R., canon of Reims. When both parties had appeared before that canon, the aforesaid clerics produced less than suitable witnesses concerning the tithes of Champ-Albert, which they sought to claim for themselves.

The aforesaid abbot, however, produced before the same canon other suitable witnesses to disprove the aforementioned witnesses; but, as he asserts, the canon refused to receive them and intended to prolong the case and weary both parties with costly disputes. Therefore, believing himself aggrieved in this respect, the abbot appealed to our hearing and fixed for his appeal the octave of the Purification of Blessed Mary most recently past.

Since, therefore, because of the absence of the parties we were unable to examine the case, we commit it to your experience, commanding your discretion that, after both parties have been summoned before you, you hear the same case more diligently and bring it to its proper conclusion within eleven days after receiving these letters, with the remedy of appeal removed. If, however, the same case has perhaps been committed to another, you two—or one of you—shall meet with that person or those persons to whom it was committed; and, after carefully examining these letters, or any others obtained concerning the same case, without either set of letters prejudicing the truth, bring the case to an end by agreement or judgment, appeal being set aside.

Given at Tusculum, the second day before the Nones of April.

CMIX. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — He commends to him D. and G., who had left the diocese of Toul because of schismatics. (Tusculum, April 6.)

[MARTEN., *Amplified Collection*, II, 916.]

[Col. 0809A]

You ought to receive with readier mind petitions which seek an effect of charity; and we should the more willingly be heard in them, the more we desire your devotion and charity to be commended. We remember having earnestly petitioned your fraternity on behalf of our beloved sons D. and G., who, when the error of schism was gaining strength there, are said to have left the bishopric of Toul—where they were born—and all their property, out of devotion to the Roman Church.

You, as we have heard, wishing to grant our request in this matter, commanded our venerable brother, the bishop of Soissons, to grant one of them a certain church; but because it was in litigation and dispute, he could not confer it upon him. Therefore, since it belongs especially to the obligation of our office to bestow care and concern upon the necessities of the needy and, with paternal provision, to assist above all those who endure poverty and hardship for the Catholic unity of the Church, we ask, admonish, and command your fraternity by repeated letters, for the sake of divine mercy and in reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, diligently and charitably to attend to providing for those clerics. Through yourself and our brother bishops, your suffragans, provide suitably and honorably for each of them in the bishopric of Reims or in your province, so that on this occasion we may more fully experience the sincerity of your devotion toward us and the Roman Church, may owe you a greater fullness of love and favor on that account, and they may rejoice to have found with you a worthy and welcome consolation in their exile.

Given at Tusculum, the eighth day before the Ides of April.

CMX. To the same. — Concerning the bishop-elect of Cambrai, who had ordered the abbot of Mareolis to be thrown from a horse. (Tusculum, April 7.)

[Ibid., col. 917.]

[Col. 0809D] It has been reported to us that the man who is called bishop-elect of Cambrai ordered the abbot of Mareolis to be thrown from his horse and treated shamefully and inhumanely.

[Note: [Col. 0809D] Mareolae, or Mareolum, is an abbey of regular canons of the order of Saint Augustine, for whom Alvisus, bishop of Arras, substituted secular canons [Col. 0810D].]

Therefore, since it seems most shameful and grievous that religious men should suffer injuries and indignities from those by whom they ought to be defended, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that, if the matter is so, restrain the aforesaid man of Cambrai from entering churches, even if for this he deserves to be entangled in the bond of excommunication. Further, publicly pronounce excommunicated, with lighted candles, those who threw the aforesaid abbot from his horse, and cause all persons carefully to avoid them, until they have made suitable satisfaction to him for the injury inflicted and, intending to make satisfaction for so great an offence, have presented themselves before the Apostolic See with testimonial letters from you.

Given at Tusculum, the seventh day before the Ides of April.

CMXI. He confirms certain laws of the Church of Chartres, written by William, legate of the Apostolic See. (Tusculum, April 8.)

[PETIT, *Theodore’s Penitential*, II, 429.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons . . ., the dean and chapter of the Church of Chartres, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The providence of pontifical authority demands and pastoral concern requires that we watch over the advancement of all and strive with the whole effort of our solicitude toward those things which concern the increase of the Churches. For the foresight of prelates is praiseworthy and commendable when they provide for Churches by wholesome government and endeavor to direct their condition and preserve it unimpaired.

We have learned that our venerable brother William, archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See, recognizing the deceit and fraud committed by unfaithful officials in administering and disposing of your Church’s revenues, established and ordered, with the advice and approval of your chapter, that two, three, four, or more persons, according to a proper assessment of the income of the prebends, should be joined together. They are to administer honorably the portions assigned to their lot and take most faithful care to protect, foster, and assist the peasants on the lands under their jurisdiction.

And lest they be insufficiently attentive or negligent in the care imposed upon them, he transferred to the rights of the canons all jurisdictions called secular which customarily belong to provosts, whether concerning lands or peasants. Thus, for no offence whatever may a provost expel or punish any peasant. But if any peasant is so rash as not to pay his revenue when it is due, the provost shall punish him and claim for himself payment of the amends for the offence. Certainly, if any peasant wrongs an outsider, the complaint shall be brought to the canons.

The presentation of priests in the churches to which they shall summon them shall belong jointly to the canons and the provost. If the provost is unwilling or neglects to be present, the canons shall nevertheless carry out what belongs to them. The priest who is presented shall pledge fidelity to both parties.

The aforesaid archbishop, wishing this constitution to remain ratified and firm, decreed that all the foregoing should be observed in the provostship which he held; and he likewise judged that the same should be observed in the other taxable and precarious provostships when those who hold them depart this life or happen in any manner to relinquish them.

Furthermore, he established and ordered that those made canons before this institution who have not resided in your city as *mansionarii* for at least half a year shall receive annually one hundred shillings less than resident canons. He further established that those who are canons, if they are not resident canons, shall receive nothing from the prebend—forty shillings [the syntax is corrupt or elliptical]—excepting those whom you have excepted. It was also added that this division of prebends should remain in force for five years, and that those to whom authority has been given and granted should deal moderately with their subjects, should not bring vexatious claims against them, nor oppress them with compulsory services or burden them excessively.

We hold this constitution, as set forth above, ratified and firm, and confirm it by apostolic authority. Furthermore, we likewise confirm by the authority of the Apostolic See the liberty of your cloister, as it is contained in the privileges of the kings of France, and the ancient and reasonable custom of your Church: namely, that men and guests of that Church, selling or buying throughout your city and bishopric anything belonging to their own use and that of their household, shall pay no customary due or toll upon any merchandise.

We decree that absolutely no person may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. But should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0811C] Given at Tusculum, the seventh day before the Ides of April.

CMXII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — On behalf of G., a poor priest who, while ill and not in possession of his faculties, had been clothed in the monastic habit. (Tusculum, April 8.)

[MARTEN., *Amplified Collection*, II, 918.]

G., a poor priest and bearer of the present letter, came to us and carefully related that, when he was suffering from so severe an illness that he was not in possession of his faculties, the monks of Saint Peter of Châlons carried him and all his belongings with them to their monastery and moreover clothed him in the monastic habit. When he had recovered consciousness and was astonished at what had been done to him, he immediately protested and, when opportunity was given, cast off that habit.

Although the said monks have, as he asserts, now dismissed him, they nevertheless refuse to restore to him the church which he had held through A., formerly bishop of Soissons of good memory, upon their presentation, and the other things taken from him.

[Note: [Col. 0811] Ansculf of Pierrefonds, who presided over the Church of Soissons from 1152 to 1159.]

Since the truth of this matter is not clear to us, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters diligently and carefully to investigate it within twenty days after receiving these letters. If it is established to you that the aforesaid priest was not in possession of his faculties when the said monks clothed him in the monastic habit, and that after recovering consciousness he did not ratify what had been done to him, cause both the church and the other things taken from him to be restored to him in full, all delay and appeal set aside, and leave him in peace.

But if he was in possession of his faculties when he was clothed in monastic garments, or if he was not then in possession of his faculties but, after recovering consciousness, ratified the act, compel him by our authority and your own to resume in the same monastery the habit he cast off; and compel the monks to receive him and treat him with brotherly charity, because they ought to seek not so much the milk and wool as the salvation of the sheep.

Given at Tusculum, the sixth day before the Ides of April.

CMXIII. To the same. — That he should cause the vicarage of Suast to be restored to the priest B. (Tusculum, April 9.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0812B]

The Apostolic See, like a pious and kindly mother, has customarily been present with compassionate favor to all who are unjustly oppressed, and has offered them the shield of its protection against their adversaries. It has been reported to us that, when B., a priest, had canonically and perpetually obtained the vicarage of the church of Suast, Aicardus, a priest, by his power and force expelled him from that vicarage and holds it unjustly occupied. Therefore, since oppressions and acts of violence of this kind are detestable and wholly abominable in any layman, much more in a cleric, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters [Col. 0812C] that, if the vicarage of the aforesaid church was granted to the said B. so that he should be its perpetual vicar, you shall earnestly admonish and strictly compel the aforesaid A. to restore to the same B., without delay or pretext, the vicarage of the aforesaid church together with everything taken away, and to leave him in peace and quiet; or, in your presence, and with recourse to appeal removed, to render him full justice in the matter. But if he should perhaps refuse to do this, do not delay to deprive him of office and benefice.

Given at Tusculum, on the fifth day before the Ides of April.

CMXIV. To the same. — That he compel Robert of Bove to restore what he had taken from A., canon of St. Peter’s at Laon. (Tusculum, April 10.)

[Ibid., col. 919.]

[Col. 0812D]

From the complaint of our beloved son A., canon of St. Peter’s at Laon, it has come to our hearing that Robert of Bove, while exercising the sentence of his tyranny in the province of Laon, among the other violences of his rapine violently carried off his cows and sheep, which he does not hesitate to retain at the peril of his salvation, heedlessly failing to consider that it is written: “God has condemned robbers and evildoers.” Therefore, since by virtue of the office of the supreme pontificate which we have undertaken, we are bound to take care that robbers cannot glory in impunity, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters [Col. 0813A] that you admonish the said R. and compel him with every strictness, within forty days after receipt of these letters, to restore to the aforesaid canon the assessed value of the said cows and sheep, or without delay to render him full justice in this matter under the examination of your discretion, with the impediment of appeal removed. But if he should refuse to do this, strike him with the sword of excommunication, and place his land under interdict until due satisfaction is made.

Given at Tusculum, on the fourth day before the Ides of April.

CMXV. To the same. — That he restrain the harassments inflicted by Hugh of Junceriac upon the land of St. Medard. (Tusculum, April 10.)

[Ibid., col. 920.]

[Col. 0813B]

Our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of St. Medard at Soissons, have shown us through a complaint sent to us that Hugh of Juncheri

[Note: Junceriac is a town two miles from Sedan, where the monastery of St. Medard once possessed a very rich cell.]

plunders and violently invades their land and does not cease to weary them with unlawful harassment on this account. Therefore, since we are bound to defend the goods and possessions of that monastery with proportionately greater care because they are known to pertain more especially to the right and property of Blessed Peter and ourselves, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you diligently admonish the aforesaid evildoer and compel him with every strictness to restore the aforesaid land to the brethren mentioned, make good the damages done, [Col. 0813C] and henceforth entirely cease from molesting them. But if he should disdain to obey your commands in this matter, then, within twenty days after your admonition, with every pretext and appeal set aside, place him under excommunication and his land under interdict.

Given at Tusculum, on the fourth day before the Ides of April.

CMXVI. To the same. — That he settle the case between the abbot of St. Medard and the abbot of St. John of the Vines concerning the tithes of Espiers. (Tusculum, April 11.)

[Ibid.]

Because the abbot and brethren of St. John of the Vines and the priest of Espiers have complained to us that our beloved son J., [Col. 0813D]

[Note: Ingramnus, a monk of Corbie, afterwards abbot of Marchiennes, then made abbot of St. Medard at Soissons in 1148, resigned in 1177; from the *Chronicle of St. Medard*, *Spicilegium*, vol. II.]

abbot of St. Medard at Soissons, unjustly takes from them a share of the common tithe and the tithe from newly cleared lands which the cultivators of the parish of Espiers cultivate, we, wishing to preserve each party’s right, entrust the case itself to your experience to be heard and brought to its due conclusion. We therefore command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when you have been asked concerning this matter, you summon both parties before your [Col. 0814A] presence and, after fully hearing and examining the arguments on both sides, decide the case within thirty days after receipt of these letters, with contradiction and appeal set aside. You shall take particular care not to entrust this case to another, but shall hear it yourself, having associated with yourself prudent and discerning men, and shall strive to settle it with every diligence and seriousness.

Given at Tusculum, on the third day before the Ides of April.

CMXVII. To Peter, abbot of St. Remigius, and Fulk, dean of Reims. — Concerning money bequeathed by testament to churches and the poor. (Tusculum, April 14.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 948.]

[Col. 0814B]

It has been made known to us on behalf of the dean of Amiens and S., formerly nephew of I., formerly a canon of Amiens, that money which the prior of Abbatis Villa

[Note: Abbatis Villa was originally called Villa Abbatis; it was a possession of the abbot of St. Riquier, with the rank of a priory, in the district of Ponthieu, in the diocese of Amiens, on the Somme. Now, after growing into a town of proper size, it still retains its ancient name. Jacques Sirmond.]

had borrowed was left by the same canon, through the hands of the said dean and his nephew, to be distributed to churches and the poor for the remedy of his soul. After his death, when the dean and S. demanded the aforesaid money from the aforementioned prior, he refused to return it; rather, seeking evasions, he appealed to our hearing, but neither came himself nor sent anyone to answer on his behalf. Since it would be dangerous for anyone, and especially for a religious man, violently to retain another’s money—particularly money directed to be bestowed upon churches or the poor for the souls of the dead—we command your discretion by apostolic letters [Col. 0814C] that you admonish the aforesaid prior and strictly compel him by our authority either wholly to restore the aforesaid sum, namely one hundred and sixty pounds, or a little less, to the said dean and S., for distribution to churches and the poor according to the disposition of the said canon; or, within two months, with appeal removed, to render them full justice under the examination of your discretion. But if, after lawful admonition, he is unwilling to do either of these things, do not delay to exercise canonical censure against him.

Given at Tusculum, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May.

CMXVIII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — That he restrain the knight Gilo from the harassment he inflicted upon the brethren of St. John of the Vines. (Tusculum, April 17.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 921.]

[Col. 0814D]

On behalf of our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of St. John of the Vines, we have received a grave complaint against the knight Gilo: namely, that he presumes to trouble them and their church concerning a certain tithe which, in the time of their predecessors, they are said to have possessed peacefully at Vernolium, [Col. 0815A] although, as they assert, he received four pounds from those brethren for the sake of peace, so that he would not thereafter vex them with this harassment. Therefore, since we neither wish nor ought to endure that these brethren should suffer molestation or injury, through the rash invasion of anyone, in respect of benefices bestowed upon them, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to investigate as diligently as swiftly; and, if you find that this is so, within thirty days after receipt of these letters, diligently admonish the said knight and compel him with every strictness to permit the aforesaid brethren to possess the same tithe in peace and quiet. But if, upon your admonition, he refuses to fulfil this, bind him, with excuse and appeal [Col. 0815B] removed, by the bond of excommunication; cause him to be carefully avoided throughout your province as excommunicated; and on no account relax that sentence until he has made suitable satisfaction to the aforesaid Church in this matter.

Given at Tusculum, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

CMXIX. To the same. — That Adam of Corbie restore his money to John the cleric. (Tusculum, April 17.)

[Ibid., col. 922.]

John, a cleric and bearer of these letters, has complained to us that Adam of Corbie refuses to repay him three marks of silver which he had lent him. Therefore, since it is dangerous and contrary to the order [Col. 0815C] of law that anyone should violently retain the rights belonging to another, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you admonish the said A. and, under the strictness of excommunication, compel him, within thirty days after receipt of these letters, either to restore the aforesaid money in full to the said John or, with recourse to appeal removed, to render him before you full and sufficient justice in the matter.

Given at Tusculum, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

CMXX. To the same. — On behalf of Maria, a citizen of Châlons. (Tusculum, April 17.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0815D]

From the complaint sent by Maria, a citizen of Châlons, it has come to our hearing that, although the case concerning her inheritance between herself and our brother, the bishop of Châlons, and Radulf, a burgess, had been examined by the Apostolic See, determined by sentence, and put into execution now for five years and more, the same R. now presumes to revive the same complaint and is not ashamed to trouble the woman with manifold harassment on that account. Therefore, since matters which have been decided and settled by the judgment of the Apostolic See ought not to be brought into the uncertainty of renewed litigation, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the matter stands thus, you strictly [Col. 0816A] compel the aforesaid burgess, with pretext and appeal set aside, firmly to observe the aforesaid sentence, henceforth to desist from harassing the said woman on this matter, and wholly to compensate her for damages of twenty pounds; or to render before you full justice in the matter, with every strictness.

Given at Tusculum, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

CMXXI. To the same. — Concerning the case between the canons of St. Peter’s at Laon and the canons of the cathedral church. (Tusculum, April 17.)

[Ibid., col. 923.]

From a complaint sent by the canons of St. Peter’s at Laon, we have received the grievance that our beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Laon, strive to hold by force the freehold [Col. 0816B] of Vallibus, which the former assert belongs to their jurisdiction. Therefore, since it is unworthy and altogether indecent that ecclesiastical persons should trouble men of the same profession with unjust harassments, when they are bound rather, so far as lies in their power, to defend them from the assaults of others, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you admonish the aforesaid canons of Laon and strictly compel them, within twenty days after receipt of these letters, either to restore the aforesaid freehold to the said canons of St. Peter and leave them in peace and quiet, or to render them before you complete justice in the matter.

Given at Tusculum, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

CMXXII. To the same. — That the clerics of Holy Trinity may be permitted to have a cemetery. (Tusculum, April 20.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0816C]

On behalf of the clerics of Holy Trinity, we have received a repeated complaint that the administrator of the hospital of St. Stephen, in a rash act of presumption, closed their cemetery—which had been jointly established outside the city walls, within the bounds of their parish, for their parishioners and the poor of the aforesaid hospital—and does not permit them to bury their parishioners. Therefore, because the aforesaid clerics complain that they suffer grave loss and injury from this, and because it is unworthy that they should be deprived of their right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters [Col. 0816D] that you earnestly admonish the aforesaid administrator and strictly compel him to permit the aforesaid canons freely to possess that cemetery of theirs and to bury their parishioners there, without any contradiction or appeal; or, with recourse to appeal removed, diligently and fully to carry out under the examination of your discretion whatever shall be just and equitable in the matter. Moreover, as for the altar which he is said to have erected within their parish without the consent of themselves and of his proper bishop, if this is so, unless he is fortified in this matter by the authority of an authentic written instrument of the Roman Church, cause it to be removed, with the impediment of appeal removed—unless perhaps you can peacefully and amicably bring about an agreement between them.

Given at Tusculum, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.

CMXXIII. To the canons of the Church of Laon. — That he entrusted to their dean for correction only those matters in their Church which required correction. (Tusculum, April 20.)

[Ibid., col. 324.]

[Col. 0817A]

Although formerly we commanded by our letters both you and our beloved son, the dean of your Church, that you should apply yourselves unanimously to correcting those things in your Church which required correction, and nevertheless commanded the same dean that, if you neglected these matters, he himself, with the counsel of the bishop and the consent of the chapter or its sounder part, and with appeal removed, should correct them, it was not our intention that, in any cause other than that which was then pending in your [Col. 0817B] Church, he should be able to correct canons with appeal removed. For this reason, indeed, we commanded the aforesaid dean utterly to absolve Stephen, your fellow canon, from the sentence which he pronounced against him after an appeal, once suitable satisfaction had been rendered. Moreover, we forbade him to presume to suspend any of you from office or benefice without a manifest and reasonable cause—and then only with the counsel and consent of the chapter or its sounder part, as is contained in our letters. Rather, with the seriousness and moderation stated, and having taken the counsel of his brethren, he must be seen to proceed in the office committed to him in such a way that his discretion cannot deservedly be impugned and his acts cannot lawfully be annulled. So that you may more fully know the command which we gave to the same dean, we have thought fit to send you these present letters as testimony.

Given at Tusculum, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.

CMXXIV. To Peter, abbot of St. Remigius, and B., archdeacon of Reims. — That money owed to a cleric be restored. (Tusculum, April 26.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 949.]

We have received the complaint of I., a cleric and bearer of these letters, that I. of Hospitio refuses to pay him about six pounds, which in the presence of many persons he publicly acknowledged that he owed him, and does not hesitate to inflict many other injuries upon him. Therefore, because by the obligation [Col. 0817D] of our office we are bound to assist all persons in what is theirs, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you take care to admonish the aforesaid I. of Hospitio and strictly compel him by our authority either to restore to the said cleric the aforesaid money without harassment or diminution and make suitable satisfaction for the injuries inflicted, or, with recourse to appeal removed, not to delay rendering him the fullness of justice under your examination; and that you hear the case and, with appeal set aside, bring it to its due conclusion.

Given at Tusculum, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May.

CMXXV. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — On behalf of B., a regular canon, to whom two altars at Troisly were granted for life. (Tusculum, April 29.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 925.]

[Col. 0818A]

Our beloved son B., a canon of St. John of the Vines, appearing before us, set forth in a detailed account that, since he had long continued faithfully in the service of A., of good memory, formerly bishop of Soissons, that bishop granted him for his possession during B.’s life two altars at Troisly, namely St. Peter’s and St. Martin’s, together with their tithes. He also presented to us, for greater certainty, the written instrument of that bishop’s grant, authenticated with his seal, [Col. 0818B] so that we might more readily give credence to his statements in this matter. After some time had elapsed, however, the aforesaid bishop granted those same altars by proprietary right to the canons of Soissons, on the condition that the said B. should pay the aforesaid canons five shillings yearly from them during his lifetime. Finally, after the death of the same bishop, Herbert, a canon of Soissons, by the favor and power of P., archdeacon of the Church of Soissons, began seriously to attack B. concerning those altars, to such an extent that he compelled him, not without great labor and expense, to come before our predecessor of pious memory, Pope Adrian. And while the said archdeacon, who was conducting Herbert’s case, and the said B. were litigating against one another before our venerable brother, the bishop of Ostia, there was made between them before him, as we have learned from a certain written instrument and from the bishop’s own oral statement, the following agreement: the said Herbert was to possess in full two parts of those altars, and the said B. was to receive the remaining part without any contradiction; and whichever of them should die first, the survivor was to obtain the whole revenues of the same altars. Now, however, as the said B. has set forth to us, since Herbert has departed this present life, the canons of the Church of Soissons, failing to observe the aforesaid agreement, have violently occupied all the revenues of those altars and strive to retain them by their own authority. Therefore, since [Col. 0818D] we must take care that the aforesaid B. does not suffer injury to his right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you cause that third part which was granted by the agreement to the said B., then as now a regular canon, to be restored to him without molestation or diminution, with every delay and appeal set aside, together with the fruits received from it since the canons’ occupation. Then, diligently investigating the truth of the matter concerning the other two parts, you shall carefully admonish the said canons and compel them with every strictness, within thirty days after receipt of these letters, either to restore the aforesaid two parts to the said B., together with the fruits which they are known to have received from them since their occupation, and permit him to possess them [Col. 0819A] in peace; or, with every pretext and appeal set aside, not to delay rendering before you full and sufficient justice concerning them.

Furthermore, within the aforesaid period, diligently admonish and strictly compel the brethren of the Premonstratensian monastery either to restore to the same B., with appeal removed and without any difficulty, two measures of wheat and one of oats, which for ten years and more they had rendered to him annually without dispute or contradiction; or to render full justice before you. Likewise compel the priests of Troisly, by ecclesiastical strictness, within the same period and with the impediment of appeal removed, either to pay the said canon the customary rent, and especially twenty-two shillings which they are said to have received from the offerings and small tithes of the preceding year belonging to him, as he asserts; or to stand before you to answer justice.

Given at Tusculum, on the third day before the Kalends of May.

CMXXVI. To Peter, abbot of St. Remigius, and Fulk, dean of Reims. — That they hear the case between the abbot of All Saints and the canons of Holy Trinity.

[Note: Their collegiate body is in the city of Châlons itself, in which, as we have noted in connection with Peter of Celle, letter 14, book VIII, the monastery of the Isle of All Saints is also situated. Jacques Sirmond.]

(Tusculum, May 1.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 924.]

We entrust to your experience, to be heard and brought to its due [Col. 0819C] conclusion, the case pending between the abbot of the church of All Saints on the island of Châlons and the canons of Holy Trinity concerning a certain cemetery. We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters that, when you have been requested in this matter, you summon both parties before you and, after fully hearing and examining the arguments on both sides, bring the same case to its due conclusion within forty days after receipt of these letters. Moreover, you shall also hear more diligently the case known to be litigated between those same parties concerning certain lands of the vicedominus, and shall strive to decide it by means of justice.

Given at Tusculum, on the Kalends of May.

CMXXVII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — That the church of St. Maurice be restored to G., a priest. (Tusculum, May 1.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 927.]

[Col. 0819D]

A complaint has been brought to us on behalf of G., a priest of Arras, that the canons of the Church of Arras violently expelled him from the church of St. Maurice, where he asserts that he ministered peacefully for fifteen years. Since it is altogether foreign to ecclesiastical men to dispossess anyone violently of his possession, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters [Col. 0820A] that you diligently admonish the said canons and compel them with every strictness either to restore the aforesaid church, together with everything taken from it, to the said priest without molestation, or, within forty days after receipt of these letters and with recourse to appeal removed, to render him before you the fullness of justice in the matter.

Given at Tusculum, on the Kalends of May.

CMXXVIII. To Bartholomew, bishop of Beauvais, and Peter, abbot of St. Remigius. — That they reform the monastery of Flaiac.

[Note: St. Geremarus of Flaviac. Thus they call it today, partly from the place and partly from its first founder. Nicholas I calls it the monastery of Flaviac in his letter to Odo, bishop of Beauvais, in whose territory it is situated. A monk of this place was Ralph of Flaviac, who wrote on Leviticus. ID.]

(Tusculum, May 4.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 921.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BARTHOLOMEW, bishop of Beauvais, and his beloved son PETER, abbot of St. Remigius at Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0820B]

It has been brought to our hearing that the monastery of Flaiac, because of an abbot who is said not to have been canonically elected there, has been so diminished in spiritual and temporal matters that, where there was customarily, as is said, a pattern and example of religious life, scarcely any traces of decency or religion now appear to remain. For it is alleged that after the same abbot, by means of certain cloistered and unlearned monks—persons unacquainted with and ignorant of the external business they conducted—had acquired the administration of that monastery in a less than canonical manner, he did not blush to devote his concern and diligence, not to preserving religion or increasing the goods of the Church, but to alienating [Col. 0820C] what he found there preserved by his predecessors. Therefore, since we must provide and keep watch diligently lest the aforesaid monastery fall into a worse condition if prompt provision is not made for it, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, within thirty days after receipt of these letters, you go together to that place, or summon the abbot and monks before you at another suitable place; diligently investigate the condition of the monastery; and prescribe for them the means and manner by which it may be reformed in spiritual and temporal matters. But if it appears likely that it cannot suitably be restored through the abbot, then, setting aside appeal, remove him from the administration, [Col. 0820D] and, if one is found in that monastery itself, or from another religious house, provide for that monastery, with the counsel of religious men, another suitable and religious person as abbot, through whose effort and diligence there may be hope that the same monastery can be reformed in spiritual and temporal matters—if the aforesaid monks cannot, upon your admonition, agree upon a person of the kind we have described.

Given at Tusculum, on the fourth day before the Nones of May.

CMXXIX. To Peter, abbot of St. Remigius, and Fulk, dean of Reims. — He entrusts a case for judgment. (Tusculum, May 4.)

[Ibid., col. 954.]

[Col. 0821A]

It has been communicated to us on behalf of a certain woman, stepdaughter of the nobleman R., knight of Villers, that she had long ago pledged to G., her uncle, a canon of the church of Amiens, for thirty pounds, certain revenues called *terragia* [land-rents]; but that the same canon refuses to restore her revenues to her, although he is said to have received much beyond his principal, expenses having been deducted. Therefore, since the crime of usury is detestable and dreadful in laymen, much more in clerics, being condemned by the pages of both Testaments, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after summoning both parties before you, you diligently investigate the truth of the matter; and, if this is established to you, admonish the said canon and strictly compel him by our authority, without delay or appeal, to restore the aforesaid revenues to the woman mentioned above without any exaction, and to leave her in peace. Any other complaints, however, which may be pending between the parties, you shall hear diligently and decide by agreement or through judgment.

Given at Tusculum, on the fourth day before the Nones of May.

CMXXX. To the same. — He entrusts a case for judgment. (Tusculum, May 4.)

[Ibid., col. 955.]

[Col. 0821C]

We entrust to your experience, in which we have full confidence, to be heard and brought to its due conclusion, the case long disputed between R. of Vilers and Amilius, knight of Becloi, concerning the dowry of the wife of the aforesaid R., and brought before us, as is said, by appeal. We therefore command your discretion by apostolic letters that, after you have been asked concerning this matter, you summon both parties before you and, after fully hearing and examining the arguments on both sides, decide the same case—if it is established to you that it was brought before us by appeal—by agreement or through justice, with recourse to appeal removed. Moreover, by the authority of these present letters, we command you to hear the other complaints which they may submit to you against one another and to settle them by agreement or judgment. But if both of you cannot be present in this case, let one of you not delay to impose an end upon it as stated.

Given at Tusculum, on the fifth day before the Nones of May.

CMXXXI. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — He entrusts for examination the case of Hilard, a priest, whom he had absolved from the censures of the bishop of Amiens. (Tusculum, May 4.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 927.)

[Col. 0822A]

Hilard, bearer of these letters, appearing before us, set forth in a supplicatory account that our brother T.,

[Note: Theobald, related by affinity to William of Champagne, cardinal and archbishop of Sens; from archdeacon, elected bishop about the year 1170.]

bishop of Amiens, because Hilard confessed before him that on the vigil of St.

[Note: St. Fuscian, a martyr under Rictiovarus, is numbered among the chief patrons of Amiens; and not far from the city of Amiens there is a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict under the name of St. Fuscian.]

Fuscian he had eaten meat, although, as he asserts, the observance is not established in his region, forbade him the divine office; nor could he obtain mercy from him. Added to this is that when the bishop charged him with the crime of adultery and gave him a period of grace in which to clear himself, fear of the bishop prevented his fellow and neighboring priests from standing with him in his purgation. Yet the bishop, disregarding his appeal, nevertheless forbade him office and benefice, violently expelled him from the Church, and bound him with the bond of excommunication. We therefore command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, under the power of obedience, that, if he can clear himself in your presence through lawful witnesses, you assign to him both office and benefice, with every appeal and contradiction removed, and cause him by our authority to possess them peacefully. But since we ought not to set the unarmed against the armed, we first command that everything taken from him be restored in full, and only afterwards that, after the canonical period of grace, he be cleared of the charges brought against him. We send him to you absolved.

Given at Tusculum, on the fourth day before the Nones of May.

CMXXXII. To the same. — That his church be restored to Wibaud, a cleric. (Tusculum, May 9.)

[Ibid., 928.]

Wibaud, a cleric, complaining in our presence, showed us in his own account that Savem and Hugh Vitulus, canons of Arras, unjustly took from him the church of St. Maurice, which they had granted him for an annual rent, although, as he asserts, they had received from that cleric a surety guaranteeing payment of the rent. Therefore, since it was not fitting [Col. 0822D] for those canons to withdraw the aforesaid church from him without examination of the case, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you diligently admonish the said canons and, by the authority conferred upon you, strictly compel them, within forty days after receipt of these letters, either to restore the aforesaid church to the said Wibaud without delay or difficulty, as they granted it to him, or, with recourse to appeal removed, not to delay doing before you what the rule of law shall require in the matter.

Given at Tusculum, on the seventh day before the Ides of May.

CMXXXIII. To the Premonstratensian canons. — He disapproves the election which they had made contrary to the form of the order, and commands them to elect another abbot. (Tusculum, May 10.)

[Ibid., 929.]

[Col. 0823A]

It had been reasonable to expect, beloved sons in God, that, when Philip [Note: [Col. 0823D] Philip, who died in 1170.], your former abbot of blessed memory, had been called away, the contentions having been quieted, the various party interests set aside, and the counsel of the elders employed, such a pastoral election would take place among you as would not kindle anew the fire of dissension which had long since arisen in your house, but would bring about concord and fraternal union. If you were truly wise and disciplined, you would accomplish your works in meekness and show by good conduct that you possess love of religious life and a desire for peace. But now, since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not, as the Apostle says, carnal and walking according to man?

Certainly, although it is written, “Do nothing through contention or vain glory,” you proceeded to that which ought always to be done in the Church of God with fuller deliberation and maturer counsel in an impulse of spirit and heat of mind. Neglecting the institution of your order, and without awaiting the counsel and assent of those abbots who had assembled with you according to custom for holding the election, and who, together with some of you, were discussing the election from a common purpose, you wished to take the abbot of Belli-locus as your pastor—a man of whom we have heard long ago and concerning whom you need by no means trouble yourselves to instruct us.

[Note: [Col. 0823D] This was John, brother of the count of Brienne. Nevertheless, his election prevailed, since his name is found in the catalogue of the abbots of Prémontré immediately after Philip, [Col. 0824D].]

For we have learned that your church is both inwardly wearied by scandals and outwardly burdened by a mass of debts. It ought to be restored to its former condition upon shoulders long worn by regular discipline. Therefore, attending not so much to what pleases you as to what is expedient for you and for the whole order, we have decided, with the common counsel of our brethren, that that abbot shall return to his own place without delay, and that you, released from obedience to him, shall proceed to another election according to the institution of your order.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your whole community that, having summoned our beloved son G., abbot of Saint Martin, together with those others who on the previous occasion, with him and some of your brethren, undertook the task of electing an abbot, you shall proceed to hold an election by their counsel and concurrence.

[Note: [Col. 0824D] Garin, the second abbot of the celebrated monastery of Saint Martin of Laon, of the Premonstratensian order.]

Know that, if you attempt to do anything otherwise, it will be frivolous and void and will be able to have no force. For in granting you an abbot, we consider the welfare of souls, not the patronage of persons; and we wish that alone to be ratified which shall be judged to accord with regular institutions and the advancement of the order.

Moreover, although the aforesaid abbot formerly fostered and promoted schism, and although he has returned to our obedience and to the unity of the Church, and although we have restored our favor to him and wish to preserve it toward him paternally, unless he himself withdraw from it, nevertheless both we and your whole order might suffer serious detriment if we allowed him at this time to hold mastery over that Church which is the head of the order. You must also consider jointly that neither in your order nor in the Cistercian order has there hitherto been said to exist a custom or institution under which disputes were raised and sought for a higher office, when many have preferred to yield not only because of fault but even because of suspicion alone, rather than seek an occasion for disputation under the pretext either of obtaining rule or of demonstrating innocence.

Given at Tusculum, on the sixth day before the Ides of May.

### CMXXXIV. To Peter, abbot of Saint Remigius.—That he grant a prebend to a certain Hubert. (Tusculum, May 12.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 924.]

We are bound to provide for learned and devout men with so much the more ready concern, and to attend more diligently to their interests, insofar as a more fruitful benefit and advantage may accrue to God’s holy Churches from making provision for them. Therefore, giving more attentive consideration to the learning of our beloved son Master Hubert and to the devotion which he bears toward you, we earnestly commend him to your charity, asking—and by asking commanding—you, for reverence toward Saint Peter and ourselves and in view of his devotion and learning, generously to grant and assign to him a prebend in the church of Saint Timothy, if one is now vacant or when one first becomes vacant.
