Thus we shall owe abundant thanks to your sincerity on this account and shall commend your prudence and devotion in the Lord in many ways.

Given at Tusculum, on the fourth day before the Ides of May.

### CMXXXV. To the bishop of Senlis and the abbot of Saint Medard.—That injuries done to the monastery of Saint Remigius be repaired. (Tusculum, May 12.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Senlis and his beloved son the abbot of Saint Medard: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has come to our attention on behalf of our beloved son, the abbot of Saint Remigius of Rheims, that, although a certain maidservant and certain possessions had been restored to his monastery by judgment of the Church of Rheims, he afterward suffered very many losses in this matter on the pretext of certain letters of ours, as he asserts. Since matters known to have been reasonably settled by judgment ought not to be drawn back into renewed litigation, we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently and carefully to investigate the truth of the matter. If it becomes clear to you that the said monastery was reasonably restored to the aforementioned possessions and maidservant, you shall cause that restitution to remain ratified and firm, and shall cause the losses inflicted upon the monastery in respect of these matters to be made good, relying on our authority and setting aside every pretext and appeal.

Given at Tusculum, on the fourth day before the Ides of May.

### CMXXXVI. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—Against the nuns of Malbodium, rebellious against their abbess. (Tusculum, May 12.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 931.]

They incur the stain of guilt and deserve to be struck by severe punishment who not only fail to obey their prelates, but also dare rashly to rise against those by whom they are corrected for their offenses and do not fear to drive them from their own seats. From the report sent to us by our beloved daughter C., abbess of Malbodium, it has been brought to our attention that her nuns, whom she was correcting for their offenses according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, inflamed with diabolical fury, were not ashamed, after an appeal had been made to us, disgracefully to expel her by lay force, though she had been convicted of no crime.

[Note: [Col. 0825D] From this letter it is clear that nuns of the Order of Saint Benedict still existed in the church of Malbodium in the time of Alexander III; their place is now occupied by secular canonesses. But by what authority?]

But because we are bound by the office of correction entrusted to us to restrain the contumacious and rebellious with the bridle of chastisement and correction—and because news of punishment rather than of guilt for so great an offense ought first to have reached us—we command your fraternity by apostolic letters to ensure that the truth of the matter is diligently and carefully investigated. If you find it to be so, do not delay, setting aside pretext and appeal, to restore the aforesaid abbess in her monastery to the full exercise of administration and rule. Endeavor to punish those persons by whose violence she was expelled from her monastery in such a way as to inspire fear in others and make them afraid henceforth to attempt similar acts. If afterward they wish to proceed against her, hear the case and decide it according to justice, setting aside appeal.

Given at Tusculum, on the fourth day before the Ides of May.

### CMXXXVII. To Peter, abbot of Saint Remigius, and Fulk, dean of Rheims.—That they hear the case of a certain William, who complained that he was oppressed by usury. (Tusculum, May 17.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 929.]

From the statement of William, bearer of the present letters, we have learned that, having bought from a citizen of Rheims for sixty-nine solidi a crop which was worth sixty solidi, the latter refuses to receive the principal and is endeavoring to extort excessive interest from him. Since, as we have learned, an appeal in this matter has been made to our hearing, we commit the hearing of the case to you, in whose prudence and integrity we have confidence. By the authority of the present letters we command your discretion urgently to admonish and strictly compel the said citizen to accept the agreed price and not presume on any ground to harass the same William in the exaction of interest. But if he alleges some other just and reasonable cause, hear him and, setting aside appeal, decide the matter by a due judgment.

Given at Tusculum, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June.

### CMXXXVIII. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—He reproves him for harassing his own people. (Tusculum, May 17.)

[Ibid., 931.]

The more closely we embrace your person with the arms of purer charity, the more strongly we are moved and troubled by the matters brought against you by many persons. To omit for the present the serious complaint which we recently received against you on behalf of the monastery of Saint Basolus, the common complaint, as it were, of all your suffragan bishops is this: that you oppress them as though they were simple clerics, and treat their Churches and clerics as your own according to your will. Yet your discretion ought to show itself so benevolent and kind toward the said bishops that you may appear both to love them with fraternal charity and to hold firmly in your heart what Saint Peter says in his Epistle: “Not as lording it over [them], but setting forth an example of life to the flock.”

[Note: [Col. 0825D] The monastery of Saint Basolus, three or four hours distant from the city of Rheims, where Archbishop Artald in 961 expelled the clerics and installed monks of the Order of Saint Benedict, still survives under the Congregation of Saint Maur.]

Since we love you as a most dear brother, we admonish your prudence with paternal affection and enjoin upon you by the authority in which we are preeminent diligently henceforth to abstain from these practices; to love and honor the aforesaid bishops more devotedly as your brothers and fellow bishops; and, preserving their rights and dignities whole and unimpaired, not to summon their Churches or clerics to cases unless these have been brought before your hearing by appeal. If they are at times to be reproved for delay, reprove them kindly, urge them to render justice to their subjects, and endeavor to show them deference both in word and in the performance of deeds.

Given at Tusculum, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June.

### CMXXXIX. To the same.—On behalf of Jordan, a citizen of Laon. (Tusculum, May 17.)

[Ibid., col. 932.]

It has come to our hearing that when Jordan, a citizen of Laon, appealed from your tribunal to our hearing, and the messenger whom he had sent to pursue the appeal on his behalf died on the road, Master John, then your vicar, bound him with the bond of excommunication as though he had failed to pursue the appeal. But because the same J., so far as lay within his power, did pursue the appeal, we directed our venerable brother the bishop of Amiens that, if the matter were so, the aforesaid J. should be completely absolved. And when, in the presence of our beloved son R., a canon of your church, the same Jordan proved by suitable witnesses that the matter was so, the said R., by command of the aforesaid bishop, absolved him from excommunication and directed our venerable brother the bishop of Laon, on our behalf, to regard him and his household as absolved.

Therefore, since the truth of the matter is unknown to us, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters diligently and carefully to inquire into it. If you find it to be so, cause the said J. and his household to be regarded as absolved by the aforesaid bishop, strictly forbidding—and taking care yourself—that the household be excommunicated for the wrongdoing of its lord and head of household, unless perhaps it consented to his wickedness. For it is expressly provided in the sacred canons that households ought not to be excommunicated for the offenses of their lords, nor compelled to avoid their communion. Furthermore, urgently admonish and strictly compel the men of Martegni, namely Wer., William, R., and G., to restore to the said J. seven and a half pounds which they are said unlawfully to have taken from him, and to render him full justice concerning this in your presence, setting aside appeal.

Given at Tusculum, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June.

### CMXL. To the abbots of Saint Remigius and Saint Nicasius.—He commits a case to them for judgment. (Tusculum, May 20.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 958.]

From the report sent by E., a woman, we have learned that when G. urgently demanded from her fifty-five solidi in money of Rheims, she alleged that the same G. had forgiven that sum to her husband while he was in the country. The case was therefore brought before the hearing of our venerable brother the archbishop of Rheims, from whose tribunal the woman appealed to our hearing. But since the woman sent her messenger and the other party neither came nor sent any representative to answer for him, we commit the hearing and due determination of this case to your experience, in which we have full confidence. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your discretion that, when you are requested in this matter, having associated with yourselves prudent and honorable men, you summon both parties before you; and, after fully hearing and examining the arguments on either side, decide the same case according to justice, setting aside appeal. If, however, G., the opposing party, though lawfully cited, scorns either to come before you or to obey your judgment, compel him by ecclesiastical censure under our authority.

Given at Tusculum, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June.

### CMXLI. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—That he may promote to holy orders the penitent clerk Robert, who had unwillingly taken part in a homicide. (Tusculum, May 23.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 933.]

From the report sent by Robert, a clerk, it has been brought to our attention that he took part in a homicide unwillingly and under compulsion, and afterward performed worthy fruits of penance. Therefore, since the medicine of penance is not to be denied to transgressors if they wish to correct and amend their offenses, nor are the bowels of mercy to be closed against them in any way, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, observing his learning, you shall not delay at a suitable time to promote him, absolved by our authority, to holy orders. If provision has been made for him in any benefice by anyone, we grant by apostolic authority that he may receive it without hindrance or challenge and thereafter freely serve the Church. But if anyone presumes to infringe or attack this grant, strike him with ecclesiastical censure.

Given at Tusculum, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June.

### CMXLII. To the same.—He commits for decision a case between Odierius, citizen of Laon, and the clerk Maurice. (Tusculum, May 26.)

[Ibid., col. 936.]

We commit to your experience for hearing and, setting aside appeal, for due determination the case known to be in dispute between Odierius, burgess of Laon, and the clerk Maurice concerning 113 solidi, which the same Hodierius demands from the same clerk on account of the suretyship of Reiner, whose estate he has succeeded to. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your fraternity that, when you are requested in this matter, you summon both parties before you and, after fully hearing and examining the arguments on either side, decide the same case according to justice within forty days after receipt of these letters, removing the remedy of appeal.

Given at Tusculum, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June.

### CMXLIII. To the abbots of Clairvaux and Saint Remigius.—That they reform the monastery of Der. (Tusculum, May 28.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 952.]

When we called our beloved son, the abbot of Der, to account concerning the dissipation of his monastery’s goods and the laxity which we had long heard had occurred through that abbot, he prudently and commendably excused himself before us and our brethren. He asserted that, when a multitude of Brabançons had invaded part of his monastery’s land in hostile fashion and were intending to occupy the remainder, he was compelled to contract many debts so that he might free the land of the monastery from the hands of that wicked people.

[Note: [Col. 0829D] These men, whether roaming of their own accord or hired under another’s auspices, were at this time plundering everything in their incursions, sparing neither churches nor monasteries, as appears in the Lateran Council of Pope Alexander, chapter 27. Jac. Sirmond.]

He added further that he had assigned the revenues of the same monastery to certain persons so that those debts might be paid from them, and that the monastery had been burdened by no fault of his in these matters nor rendered lax in others. But since these things are not established for us, we have thought fit to commit their investigation and correction to your experience, in which we have full confidence. By the authority of the present letters we command your discretion that, going together to the monastery itself, you diligently and carefully investigate the truth of the matter; and that what you find needing correction in the abbot or monks you correct under our authority, setting aside appeal and employing seriousness and moderation.

If you know it to be expedient for the monastery that some of the monks of that place be removed, do not delay to remove them thence under our authority, setting aside appeal, and establish other religious persons there. In these matters be so diligent and provident that, through your zeal and diligence, the said monastery may, by God’s help, be reformed into a better state, and that your care and vigilance may deserve the praise of great commendation. If the persons to whom the revenues of the monastery have been assigned for payment of the debts do not suitably attend to payment of the debts or do not administer those revenues well, remove them by apostolic authority and take care, with the counsel of the abbot and brethren of the monastery, to assign them to other persons more provident and prudent, through whose zeal and care those debts may be paid more promptly and suitably.

But if any of the abbot and monks are contumacious or rebellious toward you in these matters, so that you cannot carry out our command in this respect, pronounce a canonical sentence against them under our authority, setting aside appeal; for, with God’s help, we shall hold ratified and firm the sentence which you canonically pronounce against them.

Given at Tusculum, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June.

### CMXLIV. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—That he cause Vivien, a priest, to be restored to his church. (Tusculum, June 4.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 937.]

Coming before the clemency of the Apostolic See, Vivien, a priest and bearer of the present letters, showed us in a tearful complaint that, although he had possessed peacefully and freely the church of Saint Memmius of Cosantia, our brother G., bishop of Châlons, despoiled him of the same church without judgment or justice. Since we ought to remove to the form of equity matters done contrary to legal order, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters, after diligently inquiring into and ascertaining the truth of the matter, that, if it becomes clear to you that the aforesaid priest was despoiled of the specified church without judgment and justice, you admonish—and, if necessary, compel—the same bishop within thirty days after receipt of these letters, setting aside pretext and appeal, to restore to him the said church with the fruits received from it and leave him in free and peaceful possession. If he should perhaps refuse to do so, do not delay, relying on our authority and your own, to accomplish it yourself.

Given at Tusculum, on the second day before the Nones of June.

### CMXLV. To the same.—For the sick people of Sparnacum. (Tusculum, June 7.)

[Ibid.]

It is humane and consonant with piety to attend by paternal provision to the needs of those struck by the disease of leprosy and to assist them with a hand of solicitude. We have heard, moreover, that the sick people of Sparnacum often incur grave dangers because they lack a chaplain and die without receiving the viaticum.

[Note: [Col. 0830D] Sparnacum, a town on the River Marne, in the diocese of Rheims, five hours distant from the city.]

Therefore, because they live in your parish, you ought to extend to them the aid of your provision where they are known to need it. We admonish and command your fraternity to grant the said sick people, within twenty days after receipt of these letters, a chaplain solely for their use and that of those dwelling with them, and to bless a cemetery, so that henceforth they may not suffer want of spiritual ministrations.

Given at Tusculum, on the seventh day before the Ides of June.

### CMXLVI. To the same.—That he cause Lambert, a priest, to be restored to his church, if no canonical impediment stands in the way. (Tusculum, June 9.)

[Ibid., col. 938.]

Lambert, a priest, appearing in our presence, showed us in a tearful complaint that our venerable brother the bishop of Châlons had violently and without judicial process taken away the church of Saint Memmius of Cosantia, which his predecessor of blessed memory had canonically granted him and which he himself had peacefully and quietly possessed for five years. But because it is unseemly and wholly foreign to the sacred canons that anyone be deprived, without reasonable and manifest cause, of a church reasonably granted to him, we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that within forty days after their receipt you diligently inquire into the truth of the matter. Unless it becomes clear to you that the father of the aforesaid priest was a priest and begot him, as is said, while in the priesthood—or that he was removed from his church for some other just and reasonable cause—cause the church to be restored to him, setting aside pretext and appeal, and leave him in peace. Thereafter, if the aforesaid bishop or another person wishes to proceed against him concerning the said church, hear the case and decide it by a due judgment.

Given at Tusculum, on the fifth day before the Ides of June.

### CMXLVII. To the provost and dean of Rheims.—That tithes be restored to a clerk to whom his father had given them as alms, having purchased them long ago. (Tusculum, June 11.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 951.]

From the complaint sent by Stephen, clerk of Roi, we have learned that, when his father, wishing to avoid the stain of sin, gave him as alms certain tithes which he possessed by hereditary right, Ralph the traitor presumptuously dared to claim them for himself. When the said clerk summoned the aforesaid R. before your venerable brother the archbishop in order to obtain justice before him, he was compelled to appeal to our hearing.

But although his father could not have given them to him by right, nevertheless, because it is safer for the same clerk to possess them than for them to devolve upon a layman, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if this is so, within forty days after receipt of these letters, you admonish and strictly compel the said R. to restore without diminution the tithes he has received to the aforementioned clerk and to inflict upon him no trouble or burden concerning tithes yet to be received. This is to be understood, however, on the condition that after the death of the said clerk, the specified tithes must be restored and peacefully relinquished to the person to whom they are known to belong by right. If he scorns to obey our admonitions, bind him with the bond of excommunication until their restoration, setting aside every appeal.

Given at Tusculum, on the third day before the Ides of June.

### CMXLVIII. To Henry, archbishop of the people of Rheims.—He commends to him the canons of Saint Maurice of Tours. (Tusculum, June 11.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 939.]

If you are willing to weigh by right consideration the office of pontifical dignity which you hold through the generosity of the heavenly gift, you will know that by that office it is fitting for you to defend and protect more zealously the rights of churches against your parishioners, since you have been called to share in the duty of defending churches. Therefore we command your fraternity by apostolic letters that whenever you receive a complaint from the chapter of Blessed Maurice of Tours concerning your parishioners, you shall render them full and sufficient justice in such a manner that they find in you no deficiency of justice whatever and that the rashness or presumption of your parishioners does not remain unpunished.

[Note: [Col. 0831] That is, the cathedral church, which has Saint Maurice as its patron.]

For it is very expedient for you to restrain more strictly the offenses of your parishioners from all injuries or annoyances done to Churches or clerics. If any of your parishioners prove contumacious or rebellious toward you in these matters, pronounce against them a sentence of excommunication, removing delay and appeal.

Given at Tusculum, on the third day before the Ides of June.

### CMXLIX. To the same.—He admonishes him to restore Septem-salices to the brethren of Saint Basolus and to cease harassing them. (Tusculum, June 16.)

[Ibid.]

Both nobility of blood and the dignity of the pontifical office in which, by God’s ordering, you excel ought with more earnest care to restrain you from actions in which your honor may deservedly be impugned or your nobility in any degree diminished. For the more you shine in dignity and distinction of birth, the more seriously you are reproved if you undertake anything worthy of reproof or any censure.

For it has come to our attention on behalf of the abbot and brethren of Saint Basolus that you violently took from their monastery a village named Septem-salices, which the predecessors of the noble Count Henry had granted to that monastery in perpetual alms, and which your ancestors, the illustrious kings of the Franks, had confirmed by authentic charters, as had Roman pontiffs by their privileges. After driving out, at the prompting of your own will, two monks assigned to serve the church of that place, you built in that village a castle from lime and stones gathered for restoring the aforesaid church, despite the opposition of the said brethren. In the forest belonging to them, on the pretext of building that castle, you inflicted on them losses of three hundred pounds—an injury wholly unworthy to be inflicted by you.

Moreover, where that castle was built, its castellan and his accomplices oppressed the said monastery in its goods and possessions to such a degree that, violently breaking open the monks’ own granaries, they carried off the grain, hay, straw, and chaff; they plundered the monastery’s land and even consigned men to prison. In addition, you compelled the aforesaid abbot to pay you one hundred pounds, commanding him, while he was in your city and under force of obedience, not to leave that city before payment of the said money. You mercilessly extorted sixty pounds from the men of one of their villages, named Verzei, after their seizure and imprisonment. And, what is worse—and reprehensible in every way in any man, much less in an archbishop—you forced those same men into an unlawful customary payment: namely, that each of them should pay you every year a single measure of oats. Nor did you hesitate to extort forty pounds from another village belonging to the same brethren.

Since it is in every way deemed worthy of reproof and censure if the aforesaid brethren experience as an enemy the man whom they ought to have as a protector, although we wish to show you every deference, we neither wish nor ought to close our ears to such grave outcries. We wish you, rather than another, to correct and usefully amend these things for the present, because we love your person with such fervor of charity that, although we could commit their correction to others, we prefer to defer to you in this and other matters in which, with God’s help, we can do so with ready will, as to our venerable brother.

We therefore admonish, command, and enjoin your fraternity that, if the matter is as stated, you yourself correct and amend with all speed, as your prudence requires, the things we have set forth; or else reach such an amicable and peaceful agreement with those brethren that you cannot incur a mark of blame concerning this matter and no renewed complaint need be brought to us. But if you delay amendment so long that a complaint about it is again brought to our hearing, then, with God’s help, we shall support the same brethren more zealously in their right.

Given at Tusculum, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.

### CML. To the same.—He commends B. and R., clerks whom he had absolved from a sentence of excommunication. (Tusculum, June 16.)

[Ibid., 941.]

We earnestly commend to your devotion B. and R., clerks and bearers of the present letters, whom we caused to be absolved from the sentence of excommunication by which they were bound because they had laid violent hands upon God’s friend, the deacon of Laon. We ask, admonish, and command your fraternity by apostolic letters, in view of divine love, reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, and because it belongs to our office more zealously to defend all persons—and especially ecclesiastical men—from the disturbances of the malicious, to maintain and defend them. Endeavor to reconcile them with the aforesaid deacon and with the others whose hatred they incurred on account of that deacon. If you see it expedient, compel the said clerks to make satisfaction to the aforesaid deacon, and him to make satisfaction to those clerks. Forbid all persons of the diocese of Laon, under threat of anathema, to inflict any annoyance or injury upon the said clerks in their persons or property on the ground that they laid hands on the said deacon. If anyone, after your prohibition, presumes on that ground to harass the said clerks, strike him with ecclesiastical censure, setting aside appeal.

Given at Tusculum, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.

### CMLI. To the same.—He grants him power to absolve Arnulf of Landast from excommunication. (Tusculum, June 18.)

[Ibid.]

Since we wish with ready mind to defer to you as our venerable brother and gladly to admit both your prayers and those of our dearest son in Christ L., the illustrious king of the Franks, yielding to the prayers of that king and of yourself, we grant you by apostolic authority permission to absolve, in our stead and according to the custom of the Church, Arnulf of Landast, who incurred a sentence of excommunication for violently laying hands upon a priest, after receiving from him an oath; and to impose upon him a penance appropriate to the character and extent of the offense. When he has been absolved, command him, under force of the oath, not again to lay violent hands upon a cleric, monk, Templar, Hospitaller, or lay brother of any religious order, unless in self-defense or by command of his prelate.

Given at Tusculum, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July.

### CMLII. To William, bishop of Auxerre, and Matthew, bishop of Troyes.—He commits to them for determination the controversy over the election of Seguin as abbot of Saint Potentian of Château-Censoir, an election opposed by Stephen, bishop of Autun. (Tusculum, June 23.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 921.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren W[ILLIAM], bishop of Auxerre, and M[ATTHEW], bishop of Troyes: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When our beloved sons Amelinus, canon of St. Potentian of Château-Censoir, and Werric, canon of Avallon, messenger of our venerable brother the bishop of Autun, had appeared in our presence, the aforesaid Amelinus stated before us in a firm account that, when the same bishop had been called from the said church to the office of episcopal dignity, the canons of that church informed that bishop that, since the liberty of holding an election—which by common law is due to all conventual churches—had formerly been granted to them by his predecessors, the bishops of Autun, they wished to hold an election in that church, lest the church suffer serious loss and no slight inconvenience through the absence of a pastor. But the aforesaid bishop refused to give the same canons his consent in this matter, asserting that he had not yet resigned that church, and that they had jointly agreed upon him and decreed that they would have him as abbot.

When certain of the said canons saw that the will of the same bishop was not inclined toward holding an election, but saw rather that he wished to retain the care of that church, they placed both that church and themselves under our protection and that of the Roman Church, and moreover appealed to our hearing. The aforesaid A[melinus] further asserts that, when the resident canons wished to deliberate concerning the election, the non-resident canons asked that they appoint another day for the election, so that they might obtain from the above-mentioned bishop permission to hold an election, promising that, whether they obtained permission from that bishop or not, at the appointed time they would not oppose their election. Since they could not obtain that permission from the said bishop, at the appointed time all the resident canons save one, having received, as we have said, the permission of the non-residents that they would not oppose their election, unanimously chose our beloved son Seguin, their fellow canon, as abbot.

> [Note: Seguin was the nephew of Hugh of Moncelles, abbot of St. Germain at Paris; through whose favor he was confirmed in the abbey to which he had been elected.]

But the aforesaid messenger of the said bishop firmly maintained that this election ought to have no force, since, after the aforesaid canons had jointly agreed upon the aforesaid bishop, certain of them, whom that bishop had excommunicated while the others appealed to our hearing, presumed to elect the aforesaid Seguin. He added that, at the request of the canons, he had subjected to excommunication all who should attempt to elect an abbot in that church without the consent of the often-mentioned bishop, and also on account of the mills and other possessions which they had taken from that bishop. Amelinus, answering these objections, asserted that they had never agreed upon the said bishop in such a way that he should have special care of that church, but rather that, as their bishop, he should protect that church and defend it from the injuries of others. He added that the sentence of excommunication did not hold, because it had been promulgated against them after an appeal had been made to us. He further firmly asserted that, after they had held the election, they took the mills and other possessions from the often-mentioned bishop, and that the excommunication pronounced before the appeal had not in the least come to their knowledge.

We therefore, considering in this matter the transgression of that bishop, and observing how he had forbidden the holding of this election by power rather than by law—although for this reason he was not permitted to pronounce sentence against the same canons or in any way to prohibit them from their common and private right (since the liberty of election, which by common law is due to conventual churches, had been granted to them by the predecessor of that bishop as a private right)—decree that the said excommunication or appeal is of no force; not in order to establish a precedent for others, but in order to restrain the ambition and transgression of that bishop.

Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, assembling together, you summon both parties before you and, having fully heard and examined the arguments on both sides, bring the same case to a canonical conclusion, with the remedy of appeal set aside, within forty days after receipt of these letters. If it is established to you that all the resident canons then present except one, having received the non-residents’ permission that they would not oppose their election, chose the often-mentioned Seguin for themselves, then, notwithstanding any appeal or excommunication issued by the bishop on this account, you shall, setting delay and appeal aside, confirm that election by apostolic authority. Nor shall it be an obstacle that the canons are said to have agreed upon the bishop after his promotion; although the other party wholly denies this, for even if they had agreed upon him, that would be contrary to the sacred canons, which provide that each church ought to enjoy its own pastor.

But if either party, before or after receipt of our letters, breaks out into an appeal, you shall nevertheless proceed in the same case as stated above, setting the appeal aside. If both of you cannot be present to carry this out, one of you, associating prudent and discerning men with himself, shall proceed in the same case as stated above, appeal being removed.

Given at Tusculum, 23 June.

### CMLIII. To Stephen, bishop of Autun

He commands him “not in any way to set his authority against the canons of St. Potentian of Château-Censoir, but to regard as valid their canonically conducted election.”

[Ibid., p. 923.]

### CMLIV. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims—On behalf of the abbess of St. Peter at Rheims.  
(Tusculum, 25 June.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 942.]

From the report sent to us by our beloved daughter, the abbess of St. Peter at Rheims, it has come to our attention that, when we had entrusted to our venerable brothers the bishops of Beauvais and Amiens for due settlement the controversy pending between her and the abbot of Calade concerning the revenues of a certain estate which that abbot holds in the land of St. Peter, they, having heard and examined the arguments of each side, put the abbess in possession and adjudged that the same abbot must compensate her for the damages. Yet the abbot, infected with schismatic perversity, did not restore what had been adjudged, and presumed still unjustly to retain those revenues. Although our brother the bishop of Châlons had received our command that, since the aforesaid estate lay in his parish, he should cause the abbess likewise to possess what had been adjudged, he entirely failed to carry it out.

Therefore, since we do not wish the fact that the aforesaid abbot is tainted by schismatic contagion to hinder the said abbess in any way from obtaining her justice, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, if the matter stands thus, you shall cause the damages adjudged to the said abbess to be compensated from the revenues which the said abbot has in your province, all excuse and appeal being set aside; and that the revenues which the aforesaid bishops are known to have adjudged shall, by our authority and yours, be left to her in peace and quiet.

Given at Tusculum, 25 June.

### CMLV. To the same—On behalf of the church of St. John of the Vines at Cervenniac.  
(Tusculum, 26 June.)

[Ibid.]

Our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of St. John of the Vines, have complained to us that certain knights of the diocese of Soissons have, by their own authority, taken from them the tithe of Cervenai, confirmed to that church by the seal of blessed memory G., formerly bishop of Soissons, and subsequently strengthened by the protection of our predecessors and by our own written grant; nor do they cease to harass them over this matter. Since, therefore, if this is true, there is no doubt that it redounds to our injury and to the loss of the aforesaid church, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, after summoning the parties before you within twenty days after receipt of these letters, if you find the matter to be so, you shall carefully admonish and induce the aforesaid knights to restore to the said brethren, without harassment or difficulty, the aforesaid tithe together with all proceeds and offerings received from it, and to leave them in peace and quiet.

If they perhaps refuse to comply with your admonition in this matter, bind them by the bond of excommunication by our authority and yours, all excuse and appeal ceasing; and if they do not come to their senses even then, subject their lands to interdict, appeal being removed.

Given at Tusculum, 26 June.

### CMLVI. To the same—Concerning exactions which the abbot of Compiègne demanded from certain villages, and property of the abbot alienated by him.  
(Tusculum, 8 July.)

[Ibid., col. 943.]

The inhabitants of three villages of the Church of Compiègne—namely Prunastrum, Fabarolum, and Mesvilers—have sent us a complaint against our beloved son, the abbot of that Church. They assert that, when the nobleman Peter of Tornella, advocate of those villages, was extorting from them unlawful tallages and exactions, we instructed you to restrain that man from these things by ecclesiastical discipline. At last, though only with difficulty, he confirmed before our venerable brother T., bishop of Amiens, under oath, that he would by no means extort tallages or exactions from the said inhabitants; and the same abbot, under pain of excommunication, prohibited anyone thereafter from burdening them with the same tallages and exactions.

But now that abbot, not fearing to incur the peril of excommunication, supported by the favor and power of the aforesaid P., has presumed to extort from the said inhabitants such a heavy tallage that very many of them have been compelled to abandon the said villages and move elsewhere. Since he grievously exceeds all bounds who oppresses his subjects—especially contrary to the obligation of an oath and a sentence of excommunication—with violent condemnation and vexes them by unlawful exaction, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to summon the aforesaid abbot and P., together with R., P.’s son, before you. Having diligently investigated and ascertained the truth, admonish them and, supported by apostolic authority, compel them to leave the aforesaid villages, all contradiction and appeal ceasing, in that liberty and immunity in which they are known to have been in the time of the canons, as is known to be contained in the authentic document which the same abbot and P. are said to possess.

> [Note: The Church of Compiègne had indeed been founded for canons by Charles the Bald; Suger, abbot of St. Denis and administrator of the realm, replaced them with monks by order of Pope Eugenius III.]

So that you may more suitably and effectively provide for the men of the aforesaid Church and for the indemnity of the said inhabitants, compel that abbot and P. by apostolic authority to produce before you the documents just mentioned, and according to their tenor cause both parties to be content with their respective rights. Moreover, since the same abbot is said unlawfully to have alienated much of the property of that Church and, without cause, to have contracted many debts, we will and command that you call him to account on these matters. Having more fully learned the truth, take care to inform us in your letters, fully and expressly and without any admixture of falsehood, of whatever shall be established to you in this matter, so that, if we find him guilty and culpable, we may punish him with due correction.

Given at Tusculum, 8 July.

### CMLVII. To the same—Concerning damages inflicted upon G., canon of Châlons, by the knight Wermund.  
(Tusculum, 11 July.)

[Ibid., col. 944.]

We have learned from the complaint of G., canon of Châlons, that the knight Wermund, nephew of the archdeacon, unreasonably plundered him and the inhabitants of the village of Alnetum and inflicted serious losses upon them. When the said knight had therefore been bound by a sentence of excommunication, the aforesaid archdeacon caused him to be absolved from that sentence, binding himself to the said men to make good without diminution the damages inflicted by him, and making himself their principal debtor in this matter. Afterwards the said knight took the cross and set out to visit the Lord’s sepulchre; and the same archdeacon restored part of what had been taken, but refuses to restore the remainder.

Since, by the duty of the office committed to us, we are bound to render to each person what is due to him and to defend the less powerful from the oppressions of the powerful with the shield of apostolic protection, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, if the assertion of the aforesaid canon rests on truth, you shall admonish the said archdeacon and, if necessary, compel him by ecclesiastical discipline, appeal being removed, to compensate the said canon and inhabitants for the damages inflicted, as he bound himself to them and constituted himself principal debtor; to restore without diminution what was taken; or to make a peaceful and amicable settlement with them concerning it.

Given at Tusculum, 11 July.

### CMLVIII. To the same—On behalf of Sebert, citizen of Rheims, concerning a certain house.  
(Tusculum, 14 July.)

[Ibid., col. 946.]

We have received the complaint sent to us by Sebert, citizen of Rheims: whereas he had bought a certain house from Galvinus and his wife, and they had firmly promised him on their pledged faith that at no time would they bring him trouble or burden concerning it, they now, despising the sacred obligation of faith, presume to harass the aforesaid S. over the said house. Since it is exceedingly dangerous and detestable to violate pledged faith, and it belongs to our office to assist everyone in his right, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to admonish and strictly compel the aforesaid G. and his wife not henceforth to presume to inflict upon the said S. any trouble or burden concerning the aforesaid house. Take care to punish them for the violated pledge in such a way that, instructed by punishment, they may know how wicked it is knowingly to violate pledged faith.

Given at Tusculum, 14 July.

### CMLIX. To the same—On behalf of John Multo.  
(Tusculum, 14 July.)

[Ibid.]

Since our beloved son John Multo, to the extent of his ability, was most diligent and zealous for your honor while present in our court, and since we do not doubt that, insofar as we can understand, he is bound to you by great devotion, we have confidently thought fit to commend him to your affection. We hold as undoubtedly true that, even without our prayers, you ought, in consideration of his devotion and worth, to protect him and support him in his rights.

Therefore we earnestly request and admonish your brotherhood that, for God’s sake, and for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, and in consideration of his devotion and worth, you love him more especially, uphold and defend him in his right, and do not allow him to be wrongfully harassed in any respect. Rather, hold him commended to you, in consideration of us and of his service, in such a way in his rights that, under the wing of your protection, he may be secure from the attacks of malicious persons, may always become more fervent in his devotion to you, and may give us cause to render abundant thanks to your affection.

Given at Tusculum, 5 July.

### CMLX. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims—That every qualified person may be permitted to direct schools.  
(Tusculum, 15 July.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 952.]

Our beloved son, the abbot of St. Peter of the Mountains, has shown us in a report sent to us that the master of schools of the Church of Châlons claims for himself authority over the schools in the land of the said abbot and permits no one appointed by the abbot to direct schools there. Therefore, since knowledge of letters is a gift of God, every person should be free to distribute without charge the talent entrusted to him, to whomsoever he wishes.

> [Note: What Alexander III rules here concerning teachers, Alexander IV likewise established concerning students in the schools of the Dominicans, writing in these words to the bishop of Paris: “Moreover, we establish that all students—both religious, residing at Paris at any time for the sake of study with permission of their prelates, and secular—may freely attend, wherever they wish, lectures or sermons, or disputations of questions.” Jac. Sirmond.]

By these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to order both the abbot and the master of schools not to prohibit, or presume under any pretext to forbid, any upright and learned man from directing schools in the city or suburbs, wherever he wishes. For that which is acquired by the gift of heavenly grace ought not to be set out for sale; rather, it ought to be offered freely to all, that what is written may be fulfilled: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew 10). Yet although the same master of schools may perhaps claim that privilege for himself in the city itself on the pretext of an evil custom, he cannot claim it in the abbot’s land in any way.

Given at Tusculum, on the Ides of July.

### CMLXI. To the same—That he protect the clerk T. from the burdens imposed by the bishop of Châlons, and subject A. of Possessa to excommunication.  
(Tusculum, 16 July.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 947.]

From the complaint of the poor clerk T., bearer of these letters, we have learned that, when our brother G., bishop of Châlons, wished wrongfully to burden him with harassment concerning his church of Acciti-curia, the same clerk, foreseeing the burden, placed himself, his church, and his goods under our protection and that of the Church, and moreover appealed to the Apostolic See. Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, after diligently investigating the truth of the matter, if it is established to you that the same bishop wishes wrongfully to harass him concerning the said church, you shall restrain him from that bishop’s harassment by our authority and yours, appeal being removed. But if he sees anything in the clerk requiring correction, let him correct and amend it in a fatherly manner.

Moreover, since it has come to our hearing that the nobleman A. of Possessa, after an appeal had been made to us, burned the church and houses of the same clerk, and the entire village of that place, we likewise command your discretion by the authority of these letters that, if the matter is so, you shall publicly declare the same man excommunicated, delay and appeal being removed, until he has compensated the said clerk and his church for the damages inflicted and has offered suitable satisfaction for the injuries done to God and the Church. If he cannot be compelled by excommunication to make the satisfaction which we have stated, do not delay in subjecting his land to interdict.

Given at Tusculum, 16 July.

### CMLXII. To the same—That he permit the canon Drogo to live with the bishop-elect of Cambrai.  
(Tusculum, 25 July.)

[Ibid., col. 948.]

Having heard grave and difficult complaints which were made to us against Drogo, we, wishing to bar him from an opportunity for wrongdoing, instructed you, if we remember correctly, to compel him, if necessary by ecclesiastical censure, to return to his cloister as soon as possible.

> [Note: A regular canon of the monastery of Ham in the diocese of Noyon, against whom Letter 540 appears above.]

But since we have received earnest prayers for the same Drogo from our beloved son P., the noble count of Flanders, and many others, who excuse him concerning those matters previously reported to us about him, and since his abbot and brethren have earnestly commended him to us, we, yielding to their prayers, command your brotherhood by repeated letters wholly to desist from carrying out the mandate which we sent against him in other letters. Permit him to remain with our beloved son, the bishop-elect of Cambrai; do not pronounce a sentence against the same D. on the occasion of our letters; and we strictly prohibit your brotherhood in every way from carrying out in any respect the tenor of those letters which we sent you against him. For we permit both the same D. and other religious men to be with the aforesaid bishop-elect, provided, however, that they have the consent of their prelates.

> [Note: Philip, son of Count Thierry.]

Given at Tusculum, 25 July.

### CMLXIII. To the same—He entrusts to him for settlement the case between Odo of St. Denis and Pagan the Englishman and his wife.  
(Tusculum, 26 July.)

[Ibid.]

We entrust to your experience, in which we have full confidence, for hearing and due settlement, the case between Odo of St. Denis and Pagan the Englishman and his wife, formerly the daughter of Genevieve of St. Germain, concerning a certain window situated above the Great Bridge, first litigated for a long time in the presence of our venerable brother M., bishop of Paris, and afterwards before the venerable W., archbishop of Sens, legate of the Apostolic See, and brought before us by appeal.

> [Note: That Odo seems to be Odo, abbot of St. Denis, who succeeded Suger and died in 1169.]

> [Note: Maurice, who succeeded Peter Lombard in the year 1160.]

> [Note: William, cardinal, who was transferred from the Church of Sens to the see of Rheims after the death of our Henry.]

Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, when requested concerning this matter, you summon both parties before you and, after diligently hearing and examining the arguments on both sides, if it is established to you that the case was brought before us by appeal, decide it by agreement or by justice, the remedy of appeal being set aside.

Given at Tusculum, 26 July.

### CMLXIV. To the same—He commends the canons of Compiègne.  
(Tusculum, 26 July.)

[Ibid., col. 949.]

It is fitting that we should cherish with a special prerogative of affection and favor, and defend with more earnest care from the injuries of the malicious, those who are known principally to belong to our care, provision, and protection. Therefore, considering that the canons of Compiègne have no bishop or master other than the Roman pontiff, and considering also that it is incumbent upon us to exercise care and solicitude concerning them and to preserve them unharmed from the attack of the wicked, we have thought fit to commend them to your protection all the more earnestly because, by reason of your rank and dignity, you stand nearer to us, and are known and proved to be more closely bound to us by fervor of devotion and sincerity of faith.

Therefore we admonish and command your brotherhood that, as special sons of the Roman Church, you uphold, protect, and defend those canons in their rights on our behalf, without prejudice to the right of the abbot and brethren of Compiègne. If any controversy arises between them and the abbot of Compiègne, labor with diligent care and solicitude to settle the dispute and restore peace between them, so that they may rejoice in your assistance and we may be bound to render manifold thanks to your affection for this.

Given at Tusculum, 26 July.

### CMLXV. To the same—That he persuade the king to have his son crowned.  
(Tusculum, 3 August.)

[Ibid., col. 950.]

When we consider and carefully recall how our dearest son in Christ L., the illustrious king of the Franks, his forebears, and the kingdom entrusted to him have been devoted to blessed Peter; how they have always adhered to him in inseparable faith and love; and how, especially in our time, they have taken care to assist the Roman Church in all its necessities and distresses with the arm of strength and to support it kindly, we cannot be unmindful of such devotion and faith. We desire always to be found watchful and solicitous for the welfare of that king and of the son whom the Lord has granted him in His mercy and compassion, and to direct the whole desire and affection of our heart to those matters which ought to contribute to the peace of the kingdom and the glory and exaltation of the king himself. Thus may we appear to be all the more eager to repay that king and kingdom worthily in word and deed according to their merits, the more sincere their faith and purer their devotion toward us are known to be.

Now, since it is the part of a prudent and wise man to observe with provident circumspection the changes of times and affairs, and to foresee from afar adversities which may occur, we admonish, advise, and command your brotherhood by apostolic letters—you whom, above others, by the office of your dignity and by ties of blood, it especially becomes to be solicitous for the welfare of the king and kingdom—that you carefully admonish and exhort the king, and with every urgency induce him, providing for himself and his son, to cause that son, by the sounder counsel of yourself and other great persons of the realm and with the help of heavenly grace, to be crowned and anointed king, and to bind the whole kingdom to him by an oath of fidelity.

> [Note: Philip, the firstborn son of Louis the Younger, born in 1165, was not crowned until some years after this letter was written, namely in 1179. In that year, says the Chronicle of St. Denis, “Philip, the boy, son of King Louis, was consecrated king on the Kalends of November by William, archbishop of Rheims, and by William, abbot of St. Denis, who after his consecration received from him the crown, the shirt, and the other royal garments—the tunic, spurs, and sceptre.”]

For we hope, with the Lord as author, that from this there will accrue to the king and the whole kingdom glory, exaltation, and the greatest increase; and with laudable zeal those measures ought to be carried out which can be useful and beneficial and are known in no way to be harmful. For the illustrious emperor of Constantinople, wishing to provide that his empire might not be disturbed by any change, has already caused his son, though scarcely three years old, to be crowned and the whole empire to be bound to him by an oath of fidelity; and we have seen other exalted persons do the same.

Given at Tusculum, 3 August.

### CMLXVI. To the same—Concerning satisfaction to be made to a canon of St. John of the Borough at Laon for injuries inflicted.  
(Tusculum, 5 August.)

[Ibid., col. 951.]

From letters sent to us by our venerable brother the bishop of Laon, having more fully understood the enormity of the crime and excess committed by the clerk B. and his companion R. against the canon, a friend of God, of St. John of the Borough, although we caused them to be absolved, we nevertheless instructed the said clerk, who was still in our presence, that he and his companion should make suitable satisfaction to the injured party, and restore without diminution whatever the same canon could prove had been taken from him by them, or its value.

We further ordered the same clerk to abstain for three years from entering the bishopric of Laon, unless he had obtained permission from the aforesaid bishop or canon, or unless he came in order to make satisfaction to the said canon, if the latter should wish to receive their satisfaction. But if the aforesaid canon wished to exceed in his demand for satisfaction the measure proper to him, you shall cause satisfaction to be made to him as seems best to you. Through this clerk we gave orders to the layman that, after making satisfaction, he should take the cross and, visiting the Lord’s sepulchre, remain there for one year in the service of the poor of the Jerusalem hospital.

But because it is fitting for us, who preach mercy, to exercise it more kindly toward offenders, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood, treating them as absolved, earnestly to admonish and endeavor to induce the said canon, upon receiving from the aforesaid men suitable satisfaction for the injuries inflicted and redress for those things which he can prove were taken from him by them, to forgive them this offense for love of Him who prayed for His persecutors and commanded that offenders be forgiven from the heart; to restore to them his favor and affection; and not, personally or through others, to inflict upon them any trouble or burden on this account.

Given at Tusculum, 5 August.

### CMLXVII. To . . . .—He entrusts a case for judgment.  
(Tusculum, 8 August.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 954.]

From the complaint sent by Euronius, we remember that we entrusted to your experience the case pending between that Euronius and Roland. But because, as we have learned, you had not yet proceeded in that case according to the tenor of our mandate, the aforesaid R. obtained letters from the Apostolic See by false representation; and Master John bound the aforesaid Euronius with the bond of excommunication. Since, therefore, that sentence cannot, and ought not, to hold, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion to declare publicly, supported by our authority, that the aforesaid Euronius is absolved. Do not thereafter hear the aforesaid R., nor in any manner receive his appeal to our presence. Having diligently investigated the truth of the matter through our venerable brother the bishop of Châlons, earnestly admonish and strictly compel R. and his wife Susanna, within twenty days after receipt of these letters, to restore to the said Euronius his property and expenses, all contradiction and appeal being removed. If they disdain to obey your admonitions, bind them with the bond of excommunication.

Thereafter, if the same R. wishes to proceed against Euronius, let him pursue the case in due judicial order before our venerable brother the bishop of Châlons; and let that bishop hear the case and decide it with due finality.

Given at Tusculum, 8 August.

### CMLXVIII. To Peter, abbot of St. Remigius—That he prohibit an orphan from being disturbed concerning his inheritance, and be judge of the case.  
(Tusculum, 9 August.)

[Ibid., col. 930.]

We have received a grave complaint on behalf of the orphan Guido: while his father G. lay at the point of death, he left him, by hereditary right, a house, fields, vineyards, and whatever movable property he possessed, for his possession; and he acknowledged the same in the presence of our venerable brother the archbishop of Rheims. Yet now N. and his nephews presume to draw the said orphan into litigation and wrongfully harass him concerning this. Since, therefore, by the care of government we have undertaken, we are bound to be patrons and defenders of orphans, by these apostolic letters we command your discretion, if it is established to you that an appeal was made to us in this case, to admonish N. and his nephews and strictly compel them by our authority to desist from harassing the said orphan concerning the aforesaid inheritance and permit him to possess it in peace and quiet, as granted by his father and acknowledged in the presence of the aforesaid archbishop. Or, if they claim to have any right in it, let them pursue it before you in due judicial order, the obstacle of appeal being removed.

Given at Tusculum, 9 August.

### CMLXIX. To the abbot and chapter of St. Remigius—That they provide M., a clerk, with some ecclesiastical benefice.  
(Tusculum, 9 August.)

[Ibid., col. 951.]

The pastoral care and solicitude which, although unworthy, we exercise by the Lord’s disposition, more earnestly admonishes and exhorts us always to be solicitous and diligent for ecclesiastical persons, especially for those who have no ecclesiastical benefice and are of good reputation and character, and more earnestly to urge prelates of churches to provide them with suitable benefices. Moved by this consideration and also trusting in your devotion, we offer earnest prayers to your charity on behalf of our beloved son M., a clerk and bearer of these letters, who asserts that he is wholly devoted to your church and whose morals and manner of life are highly commended by our beloved sons, the brethren of the Knights Templar, among whom he has lived.

By these apostolic letters we earnestly request, admonish, and command your devotion that, for the love of God and reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, you generously provide the same clerk with a suitable ecclesiastical benefice, from which he may honorably receive the necessities of life while remaining in your devotion. Thus your generosity and devotion may appear commendable, and we, rendering you abundant thanks on this account, may more willingly and effectively grant your prayers and petitions whenever an opportunity arises.

Given at Tusculum, 9 August.

### CMLXX. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims—That he restore a priest to the church from which he had been expelled, and declare excommunicated those who had shamefully expelled him.  
(Tusculum, 22 August.)

[Ibid., col. 930.]

R., a priest, appearing before us, set forth to us in a tearful complaint that R. and William, canons of the church of Saint Donatian at Bruges, because a dispute had arisen between him and the dean and canons of the aforesaid church concerning the offerings belonging to that priest’s church, laid violent hands upon him; and, after an appeal had been made to us, expelled him from his church and did not shrink from intruding another into it. Moreover, Walter, cantor of the aforesaid church of Saint Donatian [Note: [Col. 0845D] The archbishop of Rheims, whose relics were conveyed there. Flodoard, book I, chapter 5: “From here Donatian became bishop; his relics too, carried to the maritime regions by the bishops of Noyon or Tournai, are remembered as having been adorned with the varied splendor of miracles.” Bruges of Flanders, which now also has its own bishop, then belonged to the diocese of Tournai, which was joined to Noyon. Jac. Sirmond.], and Gillenus, a canon, on a Sunday, before all the [Col. 0846D] people, tearing his vestments in the midst of the procession, presumed shamefully to expel him from the choir.

Since we neither can nor ought to leave unpunished an outrage of such presumption, lest laymen take from it an occasion to rise against clerics, we command you, brother, by apostolic letters, to investigate the truth of the matter diligently within forty days. If you find that it is so, publicly declare the aforesaid men, who have burst into such audacity, excommunicated, with candles lighted; and [Col. 0847A] cause them to be carefully avoided by all as excommunicates, until they make suitable satisfaction to the injured party and, in order to make satisfaction for so great an offence, present themselves before the apostolic presence with your letters containing the truth of the matter.

Remove from that church, once the appeal has ceased, the man who is said to have been intruded into the aforesaid church after an appeal had been made to us; and do not delay restoring it to the aforementioned priest, together with the revenues received from it. Thereafter, if anyone wishes to proceed against the aforesaid priest concerning the said church, let him pursue the matter before you in judicial order; hear the case and determine it by a due judgment.

Given at Tusculum, 11 Kalends of September [22 August].

CMLXXI. To Peter, abbot of Saint Remigius, and Fulco, dean of Rheims.—He entrusts a lawsuit to them for judgment. (Tusculum, 27 August.)

[Ibid., col. 953.]

[Col. 0847B]

Constantius, a subdeacon and bearer of these letters, appearing before us, stated in his complaint that G. of Poigny had violently taken from him a certain house of his, situated in the village of Poigny, and unjustly holds it occupied. Since both parties had on this account appeared before our beloved R., canon of Rheims, the aforesaid subdeacon, fearing that he would be prejudiced, appealed to our hearing. But because, when he appeared, the other party neither came nor sent any representative [Col. 0847C] for himself, we commit the case to your experience, in which we have full confidence, to be heard and concluded by a due judgment.

Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters, enjoining you that, when you have been requested in this matter, you summon both parties before you and, after diligently hearing and examining the arguments on both sides, settle that case within forty days after receipt of these letters, all remedy of appeal being removed, by agreement or by justice.

Given at Tusculum, 6 Kalends of September [27 August].

CMLXXII. To the brethren of Corbie (diocese of Amiens). (Tusculum, 29 August.)

[Gallia Christiana, X, Instruments, 318.]

[Col. 0847D] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the whole chapter of Corbie: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When John, your former abbot of good memory, came to us with our beloved sons H. and H., your fellow-brethren, we received that abbot with due kindness, in view of his devotion and in consideration of the special status by which your monastery is directly attached to us without any intermediary; and we took care kindly and paternally to treat him as a devoted and special son.

Having examined the privilege of the Roman Church concerning the immunity [Col. 0848A] and liberty of your monastery, which the said abbot presented to us, and having heard from his careful report that the same monastery is not within the boundaries of the bishopric of Rheims but is situated in the bishopric of Amiens; and that, in the two villages of Folly and Neuville adjoining Corbie, the bishop of Amiens has only two churches, one at the entrance and the other at the exit; and that, whereas the other three parish churches of the village of Corbie belong properly and specially to that monastery, the archbishop of Rheims or any other person has not customarily had there any jurisdiction, as is said to be public and notorious: we have instructed our venerable brother, the archbishop of Rheims, that he is not, by means of appeals or otherwise, violently to hinder or disturb you in your possession. But if he is confident of his right, willing both to receive and to render justice, he may present himself before the apostolic presence through his representatives from the next feast of Saint Luke until the completion of a year.

Therefore we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if the same archbishop decides on this account to send his representatives to our presence, you too are to come without delay with your documents and arguments, or send sufficient representatives to the apostolic see; for, insofar as the Lord grants us power, we shall take care to preserve the rights and liberty of your monastery whole and inviolate.

Given at Tusculum, 4 Kalends of September [29 August].

CMLXXIII. To William, bishop of Strängnäs [Note: [Col. 0847] In Sweden, under the bishop of Uppsala, whom he indicates by the title of his metropolitan. In the *Notitia episcopatuum* it is called Strängnäs.—Jac. Sirmond.].—He receives his church under his protection and confirms its possessions. (Tusculum, 7 September.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 940.]

[Col. 0848C]

It befits us to love with a closer charity our brothers and fellow bishops, especially those placed amid a perverse nation and established in remote parts of the world; and, that they may be able to make greater profit from the talent entrusted to them and to devote themselves more vigorously to the cultivation of justice and the adornment of God’s house, it befits us to grant them the grace and favor of the apostolic see.

Therefore, observing the constancy of your devotion and the purity of faith by which you are seen to cling with unshaken firmness to blessed Peter and to us, we desire to love and honor you as our venerable brother, and with due kindness to favor your reasonable requests and desires. Accordingly, receiving your Church under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to that Church, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, those things which it now peacefully and lawfully possesses, and especially Neeric, as it has been confirmed to you by the king, by your metropolitan, and by our venerable brother Eskil, archbishop of Lund and legate of the apostolic see, and secured by the guarantee of his writing.

We decree [Col. 0849A] that no person whatsoever may violate this charter of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles, the blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at Tusculum, 7 Ides of September [7 September].

CMLXXIV. To Kol, bishop of Linköping [Note: [Col. 0849] A suffragan of Uppsala. It is a well-known city of Sweden, in which Nicholas, the English cardinal and legate of Eugenius III, is recorded to have held a synod in 1148.—Jac. Sirmond.].—He approves his election in place of another who had voluntarily resigned and sought a monastery. (Tusculum, 8 September.)

[Ibid., col. 939.]

By reason of the care entrusted to us and by the obligation of charity, we are bound to love with sincere charity men endowed with the pontifical office [Col. 0849B] and adorned with upright conduct, and to bring to effect, by an answering deed, their requests which do not depart from the path of reason. Thus they may strive more earnestly to seek the ornaments of virtue and to persevere in honorable conduct, in proportion as they recognize themselves to be anticipated by greater honor and favor from the apostolic see.

It has indeed been reported to us that, when our beloved son Stenar, formerly bishop of Linköping, preferred monastic repose to episcopal honor and freely and voluntarily resigned both pontifical dignity into the hands of our venerable brother Eskil, archbishop of Lund and legate of the apostolic see, and the regalia before the king and the leading men of the kingdom, the clergy and people of that place, with the assent [Col. 0849C] of the said archbishop, king, and duke of the land, unanimously and harmoniously elected you as their father and bishop.

Yet although he was not permitted to renounce episcopal dignity without the authority of the Roman pontiff, nevertheless, wishing by paternal provision to meet the need of your Church and to defer to the upright judgment of so many men, we accept this equably. Holding your election and consecration valid and firm, we confirm them by apostolic authority and grant you full power to correct vices and cut away excesses among your subjects.

You, however, are to pursue the faults of those subject to you with such zeal in rebuking them that those who are guilty may swiftly correct and amend their offences, while others, seeing this, may not aspire to commit like acts. Yet observe this consideration: correct the vices of your subjects sternly and severely, gently and mildly, according to the natures and circumstances of the persons involved. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may violate this charter of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles, the blessed Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0849D] Given at Tusculum, 6 Ides of September [8 September].

CMLXXV. To the archbishop of Uppsala and his suffragans.—Concerning mothers who procure the death of their offspring; incest and other foul lust; those who celebrate Mass with dry wine-lees and crumbs of bread dipped in wine; and marriages contracted without a priestly blessing. (Tusculum, 9 September.)

[Ibid., col. 937.]

[Col. 0850A]

In the place of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by the gift of God and our Lord, who says, “I have appointed you a watchman over the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 3), established, though unworthy, upon the watchtower of the apostolic see over nations and kingdoms, we are compelled by the obligation of the pontifical office to exercise care for all. By pastoral foresight we must withstand the ancient enemy, who prowls about like a most savage lion seeking whom he may devour, [Col. 0850B] lest he invade the Lord’s flock and tear it with the various bites of vices.

Accordingly, our heart is pierced by a keen pang of grief upon hearing that in your regions cruel and shameful lust has so increased that certain women procure the death of their offspring, while those who corrupt them presume not only to consent to so horrible and detestable a crime but even to urge it upon them; others defile themselves with incestuous union, and many with an abominable pollution involving beasts. How grave these things are, and how utterly hostile to our Creator, the very atrocity of the crime sufficiently shows; even the ears of those who hear of it cannot receive it without profound horror.

For if the man who, by spilling his seed upon the ground, did not wish to receive offspring from [Col. 0850C] his wife is known from the narrative of the Old Testament to have been struck by the Lord, what punishment is shown to be due to one who does not shrink from killing his own child once born and prefers it to perish rather than to live? Saint Augustine shows that those who urge or consent to this crime are likewise involved in its penalty, saying:

> They dangerously deceive themselves who suppose that only those are murderers who kill a human being with their hands, and not rather those through whose counsel, deceit, and exhortation human beings are destroyed. For the Jews did not kill the Lord with their own hands, as it is written: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone”; yet the Lord’s death is imputed to them, because they killed him with the tongue, saying: “Crucify him, crucify him.”

How greatly the sacred canons abhor incest is shown by the Council of Lleida:

> “With those,” it says, “who defile themselves with incestuous pollution, so long as they persist in that detestable and unlawful cohabitation of the flesh, no Christian at all may take food, as the Apostle commanded.”

Moreover, Moses the lawgiver declares with what severity the crime of those who copulate with beasts is to be punished, when he commands even the animals themselves to be killed, because, contaminated by such a disgraceful act, they renew the shameful memory of what was done.

Therefore, since it is fitting to pursue with sufficiently severe rigor the abominable presumption of these offences, take care to restrain under the yoke of stricter penance the aforesaid killers of their own offspring, those who urge or consent to the crime itself, all parricides, those who have relations with mother, daughter, female cousin, or niece, and those who copulate with beasts. Unless they are worn out by old age or burdened by bodily infirmity or poverty, compel them to come to the apostolic see and visit the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, so that by the sweat of their brow and the toil of their journey they may escape the wrath of the heavenly Judge and find his mercy.

Furthermore, those who are found to have smothered their children while sleeping—not by intention but by accident—are to undergo penitential discipline for three years if the children were baptized; but if they died without sacred baptism, for five years. [Col. 0851B] Priests, who ought especially to beware of these things, are to be deprived permanently of the exercise of their office. But if parents were absent when their children were suffocated, or if it happened while the children were in another’s care, they shall be free from blame, provided that they believed they had entrusted them not to insane but to suitable custody.

Moreover, not without bitterness of heart have we heard that certain priests, contrary to apostolic ordinances, celebrate Mass with dry wine-lees or with crumbs of bread dipped in wine; and that lay believers, not in the Christian manner, contract marriage without priestly blessing and Mass. Hence unlawful marriages frequently occur, and divorce arises between lawful [Col. 0851C] persons.

Indeed, since every crime and every sin is removed by sacrifices offered to God, what henceforth will be given to the Lord for expiation of offences when error occurs in the very offering of the sacrifice? For when the Teacher of truth entrusted to his disciples the sacrament of our salvation, he did not take dry wine-lees or crumbs of bread dipped in wine, but bread and a cup, and, having blessed them, gave them to his disciples.

Therefore, because to act otherwise is contrary to evangelical and apostolic teaching and wholly opposed to ecclesiastical custom, we forbid by apostolic authority that anyone henceforth presume to offer sacrifice with dry wine-lees, crumbs of bread dipped in wine, or in any manner other than that instituted by the Lord. Rather, according to the form of the most holy Roman Church, [Col. 0851D] which you ought to imitate in all things, offer in the sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood bread alone and wine mixed with water.

Furthermore, the authority of many holy Fathers declares that marriages ought not to be contracted clandestinely or without priestly blessing, nor except between lawful persons whom no line of consanguinity joins within the seventh degree; and that marriages once contracted may not be dissolved except canonically and with the bishop’s consent. [Col. 0852A] Therefore, strengthened by the ordinances of the holy Fathers and ecclesiastical institutions, observe diligently these matters which have been stated, and command others to observe them inviolate. Use the moderation of dispensation, so that you do not separate those joined in the fifth or fourth degree, but by episcopal authority and rigor forbid any further unions of that kind.

Given at Tusculum, 5 Ides of September [9 September].

CMLXXVI. To the archbishop of Uppsala, his suffragans, and Duke Gutherm.—That they are no longer to assist against their enemies the Finns, who deceitfully promised to become Christians. (Tusculum, 9 September.)

[Ibid., col. 940.]

[Col. 0852B]

ALEXANDER, Pope III, to the archbishop of Uppsala and his suffragans, and to Duke GUTHERM [Note: [Col. 0851D] Of the Swedes. Gutherm is mentioned by Saxo Grammaticus, book XIV, where he treats of the baptism of Canute, son of Valdemar, king of Denmark: “The performance of this religious office was graced by the presence of Gutherm, duke of the Swedes, who had come on an embassy to bring the king, Charles, a niece of Valdemar betrothed to him.” Jac. Sirmond.].

A very serious and difficult complaint has been brought to the apostolic see: that the Finns [Note: [Col. 0851D] The Finns, northern peoples of Sweden, who inhabit Finland or Finningia. Id.] always, when an army of enemies threatens them, promise to keep the Christian faith and eagerly seek preachers and instructors in Christian law; but when the army withdraws, they deny the faith, despise the preachers, and persecute them severely.

Since in this they appear to mock God and deride the Christian religion, and since, making themselves twice the children of Gehenna, their whole salvation and life appear to consist in earthly things with heavenly things neglected, it is not fitting that the Christian name should afford them [Col. 0852C] defence in adversity when they are shown in prosperity to despise and abhor it.
