We therefore admonish and command you all to guard henceforth so prudently and discreetly against their deceit and fraud that, if necessity arises, they may not have recourse to your aid and defence unless they assign to you for occupation the fortifications which they possess, if any; or otherwise provide such sufficient surety and security that henceforth they can by no means draw back or deceive your prudence. Rather, let them be compelled firmly to maintain and observe the teachings of the Christian faith, so that they may no longer appear among those of whom it was said: “He will praise you when you have done him good.”

[Col. 0852D] Given at Tusculum, 5 Ides of September [9 September].

CMLXXVII. To the archbishop of Trondheim and A., bishop formerly of Stavanger.—That they should send the monk Nicholas as companion to Fulco, apostle to the Estonians. (Tusculum, 9 September.)

[Ibid., col. 941.]

ALEXANDER, Pope III, to the archbishop of Trondheim [Note: [Col. 0852D] In Norway. Some call Trondheim the metropolis of Norway. Saxo, book X, at the end: “His body, that of King Magnus, having been brought back to Norway, was buried at Trondheim in a coffin among the royal monuments.” The bishop of Stavanger is likewise a suffragan of this metropolitan see. Jac. Sirmond.], and to A., formerly bishop of Stavanger.

[Col. 0853A] Divine and human law desires, and the obligation of charity requires, that we should give attention to the common good and employ every effort and care for the recall and conversion of unbelievers. We therefore earnestly ask and admonish your prudence to grant as a companion to our venerable brother Fulco, bishop of the Estonians—who, inspired by divine grace, proposes to undertake the ministry and labor of preaching for the conversion of that people—the monk Nicholas, a man who, as we have learned, is native to that people, religious and discerning. Thus he may accomplish so great a good and, with the Lord’s help, call that people by the word of preaching to the knowledge of the true light and to the worship and teaching of the Christian faith; and from this there may accrue to you [Col. 0853B] an abundance of eternal reward.

Given at Tusculum, 5 Ides of September [9 September].

CMLXXVIII. To the bishop of Amiens and the abbot of Saint Remigius.—That they are to investigate the case of the priest from whom the bishop of Tournai had taken his church. (Tusculum, 9 September.)

[Ibid., col. 927.]

When Daniel, a priest [Note: [Col. 0853D] Priest of Saint John at Ghent. That town, together with the monastery of Saint Peter, concerning which the next letter treats, was at that time in the diocese of Tournai; it now has its own bishop. Jac. Sirmond.], had formerly come to our presence and lodged before us a grave complaint against our brother, the bishop of Tournai, alleging that the bishop had deprived him of his office [Col. 0853C] and church because he would not pay him what had been demanded, and had granted that church to Walter, a priest, we sent our letters to that bishop on this matter, as seemed fitting to our office and to reason.

At length the bishop sent us his own envoys and writings, reporting that the aforesaid church had not been granted to Daniel permanently but had been entrusted to him on probation for a year, on the understanding that, if he were not suitable and not of the conduct and life he ought to be, he would be removed, so that the church might freely be granted to an honorable person. Finally, when the same Daniel was accused before the bishop of frequenting a tavern and of having often spent the night there in such a manner that, without having slept, he celebrated Mass on the following day, and when he had failed in the purgation which the bishop had imposed upon him, the bishop suspended him from office and granted the church in which he ministered, upon presentation by the abbot to whom it belongs, to Walter, a priest.

After this was done, Daniel appealed first to the hearing of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Rheims, and afterward to ours. Daniel, however, denying all these things, steadfastly maintained that he had received the aforesaid church from the bishop’s predecessor, upon presentation by the aforesaid abbot; and that the bishop had deprived him of office and benefice for this sole reason: that he would not furnish what the bishop had demanded and had boldly forbidden him, on behalf of himself and his fellow priests, to practice extortions against them so frequently.

He further alleged that, when he had appealed on this account, the bishop afterward charged him with the crimes written above, which had not initially been charged against him; and that, although he was prepared to clear himself of them, the bishop withdrew his compurgators by threats and intimidation. Yet he could not be convicted of those crimes by any evidence. When Daniel and Walter had appeared before us and made varied and conflicting allegations against one another, we could not proceed in their case or bring it to an appropriate conclusion, because they lacked sufficient witnesses and arguments.

Therefore, trusting in the prudence of your integrity and discernment, we commit this case to your prudence to be heard and determined by a due judgment. We accordingly command you by apostolic letters that, when you have been requested in this matter, you are to assemble together at a suitable place and time, summon both parties before you, and, after more fully hearing and examining the arguments on both sides, settle the case through justice, all obstacle of appeal being removed. This is to be done such that, if it is lawfully established before you that the oft-mentioned Daniel was not granted the aforesaid church permanently but was entrusted with it for a time; or that he has been reasonably convicted of drunkenness and of having spent the night in a tavern in such a manner that on the next day he sang Mass without any preceding sleep; or that, in a judicial proceeding, namely before his bishop or archbishop, he was accused or called to account and, without compulsion, confessed before several persons: then, notwithstanding any appeal, impose perpetual silence upon him concerning that church and compel him to desist from his claim against Walter.

But if that church was canonically conferred upon Daniel, and he was afterward neither convicted nor confessed of any crime for which he ought by law to have been deprived of it; or if, as he at one time alleged, he was deprived of that church after his appeal, cause it to be restored to him and allow him to retain it peacefully and quietly. Thereafter, if Walter or anyone else wishes to proceed against him, hear the case and bring it to a due conclusion, appeal having been removed.

[Col. 0854D] Given at Tusculum, 5 Ides of September [9 September].

CMLXXIX. To the archbishop of Uppsala and his suffragans.—That they should ensure the correction of simony and many offences against ecclesiastical discipline. (Tusculum, 10 September.)

[Ibid., col. 931.]

ALEXANDER, Pope, to the archbishop of Uppsala [Note: [Col. 0854D] Others call him “Upsellensis,” and Uppsala the metropolis of the kingdoms of Sweden and Gothia. Letters 973 and 975 were likewise written to him and his suffragans.], and to all his suffragans established both in Sweden and in Gothia.

Established by the Lord, although with insufficient merits, [Col. 0855A] over nations and kingdoms, we are compelled by the office of administration imposed upon us and by its obligation to extend the gaze of our concern over the whole body of the flock entrusted to us, and to drench the hearts of all believers with the rain of apostolic instruction and saving doctrine. Thus, just as “the sound of the apostles went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world,” so we also, who preside over their chair—not succeeding to them in merit of life or holiness of works, but in pastoral care and dignity—may proclaim the word of salvation, the Gospel of Christian and Catholic truth, to those far away and those near; bearing the apostolic name neither vainly nor merely in word, but fulfilling it in the execution of our office and in the truth of our work, insofar as God grants us power.

For we have heard, and could not hear without grief, that among you, both in Sweden and in Gothia, through the excessive and perverse—not liberty, but rather abuse and insolence—of laymen, a most evil and detestable custom has taken root. From it many unlawful things have resulted, and evils have sprung up that are not merely outrageous but intolerable. For, as is said, the laymen, without consulting you or in contempt of you, grant and confer churches upon whomever they wish, doing everything simoniacally, whether for money, private favor, or hatred. From this, many things harmful and destructive are said to occur both in the act itself and by its example.

Any priest whatsoever, arriving from anywhere, even though he has no proof of his ordination, presumes, at the mere command or nod even of laymen, to celebrate the divine offices at peril to their salvation and his own. Hence it sometimes occurs that fugitive monks, murderers, persons entangled in and marked by any crimes whatsoever, or men not advanced to the order of priesthood, do not fear, with utterly wicked and condemnable presumption, to exercise the priesthood. Likewise, any man who has no church at all, or has a poor one and seeks a richer, does not blush, by giving or promising money to the more powerful persons of the parish, to supplant another as impudently as unlawfully.

Furthermore, when clerics wish to pursue litigation against laymen, or laymen against clerics, they are compelled to submit to laymen’s judgments and to prosecute or defend themselves according to laymen’s enactments or laws. Nor are clerics of the lower orders alone harassed by such wrongs. Even you yourselves, if at any time, aflame with zeal for God, you exercise the rigor of justice, are summoned, through the envy of a disobedient flock devising some accusation against you, either to the ordeal of red-hot iron or to some other judgment equally forbidden and abominable; no reverence or honor being shown to the canons which prohibit this or to pontifical dignity. To increase and crown these evils, clerics throughout that kingdom are beaten with impunity, and at times even killed. These things are indeed grave; they must be reckoned not as works of Christian profession but rather as tares of the enemy.

[Col. 0856A] To root out and utterly extirpate these things from your midst, you ought and are bound to rise up all the more vigorously because the vices of subjects reflect the negligence and sloth of their prelates. The offence committed so frequently, freely, and with impunity by those over whom they preside—and for whom they must also render an account at the final judgment—is imputed to the prelates as a crime. Especially since the prophet says: “Cry aloud; do not cease; declare to my people their crimes” (Isaiah 58); and elsewhere: “Unless you announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I shall require his blood at your hand” (Ezekiel 3). And in the sacred canons, which it does not become your prudence to ignore, it is written:

> “To neglect, when one can, to disturb wicked persons is nothing other than to encourage them; nor is he free from the taint of secret complicity who ceases to oppose a manifest crime.”

Now, because sins have through excessive and long-standing license already become customary—although, according to a certain philosopher, it is perfected wretchedness, and there scarcely seems room for remedy where what were vices become customs; and although, according to the Gospel, one who was dead in sin already stinks—there is much greater need of effort, with the Lord and not without tears and compassion, to raise the dead man, lest they be despaired of. As with one four days in the tomb, those whom it is possible to help through the invocation of God’s name and his assistance must be helped.

Therefore, that God may also be glorified in them and wisdom honored by her children, take up the charity of Moses beseeching the Lord for the people, the zeal of Phinehas executing vengeance, the contrition of David praying, and the mercy of Jesus Christ weeping over Jerusalem and shedding tears for Lazarus. Having, according to the Apostle, the shield of faith, the breastplate of righteousness, and the helmet of the hope of salvation, put on the armor of God and fight the ancient serpent: expelling him from bodies possessed through sins dwelling in them, plundering all things in which he has confidence, and, with the help of heavenly grace, cleansing from the filth of vices those whom he strives to make his dwelling-place, so that they may deserve to be called and become the house of God, that is, the holy temple of the Lord. Let no terror hinder you in carrying out the pastoral office; remember—and profess not in word only but in deed—what the supreme and first Shepherd is recorded both to have taught and to have done: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10).

And because, through error and ignorance both of divine and human law, the evils we have described appear to have taken root among you and have hitherto been exercised with impunity by laymen as though lawful, you must use the ordinances of the holy Fathers as weapons, rely upon them, and, together with those Fathers, oppose what is unlawfully committed. Thus things which have grown up through excessive abuse and ignorance may perish through their knowledge and authority.

Indeed, the ordinances of the holy Fathers forbid laymen, as a sacrilege, to confer churches, ecclesiastical benefices, or dignities, or to dispose of them in any way. They nevertheless condemn clerics [Col. 0857A] who receive from or through laymen, for a price or gratis, a church or the investiture of a church or ecclesiastical dignity, not only to peril of their order but also to the penalty of excommunication.

For in the synod of Pope Symmachus [Note: [Col. 0857D] Roman Synod of 502.] it is recorded as decreed:

> “It has not been deemed proper that a layman should have any power of appointment in the Church; necessity requires him to obey, not authority to command.”

Likewise:

> “No power to dispose in any respect of ecclesiastical dignities is recorded as having been granted to laymen, even though religious.”

Likewise Pope Callixtus:

> “If any prince or other person claims for himself the disposal, donation, or possession of ecclesiastical property, let him be judged a sacrilegious person.”

Likewise Paschal:

> “Let no layman occupy or dispose of the goods of churches; whoever acts otherwise is, according to the chapter of blessed Alexander, to be excluded from the thresholds of the Church.”

Likewise Alexander:

> “By no means may any cleric or priest hold a church through laymen, neither for a price nor gratuitously.”

Likewise Paschal:

> “If any cleric, abbot, or monk obtains a church through laymen, he is subject to excommunication according to the holy canons of the apostles and the chapter of the Council of Antioch.”

Likewise:

> “Following the constitutions of the sacred canons, we decree that any cleric who from this hour receives investiture of a church or an ecclesiastical dignity from the hand of a layman, and he who imposes his hand upon him, shall be liable to the loss of his rank and deprived of communion.”

Many other canonical ordinances and decrees of the holy Fathers concur in this judgment.

[Col. 0857C] Moreover, to confer churches or ecclesiastical benefices through the intervention of a price or of any gift whatever is simoniacal and undoubtedly savors of Simoniacal perversity. How detestable, how dreadful Simon’s crime is, its notorious enormity itself does not permit you to ignore. It certainly involves both giver and receiver in the condemnation of Simon, as the sacred reading of the Acts of the Apostles attests. Although many writings of the holy Fathers, besides the ordinance of the apostles, have been issued for its condemnation, we believe that a few out of many will suffice.

Among these, let the first be that of Blessed Gregory: “If a priest has obtained a church by money, let him not only be deprived of the church, but also stripped of the honor of the priesthood; [Col. 0857D] for no believer is ignorant that to buy or sell an altar, tithes, and the Holy Spirit is the Simoniacal heresy.” The same elsewhere: “We have heard, most beloved, what it was necessary for us to hear, though certainly we had no wish to have heard it: namely, that certain professed members of the sacred orders, through giving or receiving gifts, appropriate to themselves churches of God, or appropriate their offerings to themselves; and we are astonished that you did not long ago sharply correct this crime. For both are rightly to be rebuked and removed from the thresholds of the holy Church: both the man who bestows gifts in pursuit of a church and the man who presumes to receive something in order to grant a church. The former [Col. 0858A] presumes to buy the gift of God, the latter to sell it. Nor would I call this deed greatly different from sacrilege, since that which ought freely to have been done voluntarily and by the sacred discretion of deliberation is made dependent upon a monetary bargain. Therefore, dearest brethren, carefully refute things so done; prevent their being carried out; and do not hesitate to strike those who resist your commands with the fitting bond of anathema.” Likewise: “If anyone, whether giver or receiver, buys by giving or sells by receiving churches of God or ecclesiastical benefices—which some call prebends—through the intervention of money, he is not excluded from Simon’s perdition.”

Moreover, not money alone, but every sort of service or gift criminally intervenes in such matters. Hence the same Blessed Gregory says: “Well, when Scripture described the just man with regard to a prebend, it says: ‘Blessed is he who shakes his hands free from every gift.’ It did not say merely ‘from a gift,’ but ‘from every gift.’ For one kind of gift comes through service, another through the hand, another through the tongue. A gift through service is improperly rendered servitude; a gift through the hand is money; a gift through the tongue is favor. Therefore, when one confers sacred orders, then he shakes his hands free from every gift, when in divine matters he seeks not only no money, but not even human favor.”

That a priest or any cleric coming from elsewhere, or unknown, ought not to be received or permitted to minister in another diocese without testimony and at least letters from his own bishop, is laid down in the Council of Chalcedon in these words: [Col. 0858C] “No foreign cleric or reader may anywhere whatsoever minister outside his own city without letters of recommendation from his own bishop.” Likewise, in the Council of Carthage: “Let no one dare retain or promote in the church entrusted to him a foreign cleric without the consent of that cleric’s bishop.” Likewise, Blessed Augustine in a certain sermon to the people: “We exhort your Christian devotion that, in accordance with the ordinances of the holy canons, no priest coming from elsewhere be received in churches founded by you unless he has been ordained by your bishop or is received by him through letters of recommendation.”

Further, lest clerics be dragged before secular courts, the laws of the Roman emperors also prohibit this; these are to be observed as canons wherever they do not conflict with the canons. The authority of the holy Fathers and of our predecessors also forbids it. For Pope Gelasius, of blessed memory, writes: “Let no one ever presume to accuse a bishop or other clerics before a secular judge.” Likewise Alexander, to all the orthodox: “It has been reported to the summit of this holy and apostolic see, to which the disposition of the highest causes and all affairs of the Churches were entrusted by the Lord himself, as to a head—for He says: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build the Church’ (Matt. 16)—that certain rivals and plotters against this holy Church presume to accuse priests of God before [Col. 0859A] public judges, whereas the Apostle rather commands that Christians’ causes be brought to the churches, so that they may be decided there. Those who thus transgress have transgressed against their God and do not obey His commands.”

The Catholic Church admits neither the judgment of boiling water or red-hot iron nor the duel called monomachia, against anyone at all, much less against a bishop. Hence Pope Stephen V says: “The sacred canons do not judge that a confession may be extorted from anyone by the testing of red-hot iron or boiling water; and what has not been established by the teaching of the holy Fathers must not be presumed upon through superstitious invention.” Likewise Pope Nicholas: “We do not adopt monomachia as law, since we find that it was not commanded; although we read that certain persons entered into it, as sacred history relates of Saint David and Goliath, nevertheless divine authority nowhere ordained that it be held as law, since those who follow this and similar practices appear merely to put God to the test.”

Furthermore, we add this command: diligently and earnestly admonish the people committed to your rule and government faithfully and devoutly to pay tithes to the churches, as is known to have been instituted by the Lord himself; and, if necessary, compel them under the constraint of anathema, according to that saying of the prophet Malachi speaking in the person of the Lord: “Bring all the tithe into my storehouse, that there may be food in my house” (Mal. 4).

Hence in the Council of Mainz: “That tithes are to be given to God and to God’s priests is indicated by Abraham’s deeds and Jacob’s promises, and is recalled by all holy priests.” Likewise, from the Council of Rouen: “All tithes of the land, whether from crops or from the fruits of trees, belong to the Lord and are sanctified to Him. But because many are found unwilling to give tithes, we decree that, according to our Lord’s command, they be admonished once, a second time, and a third. If they do not amend, let them be struck with anathema until they make fitting satisfaction and amendment. Yet those who wish on that account to revoke, or withdraw from the disposal of ecclesiastical persons, what they or their parents are known to have bestowed on churches—indeed, on God himself—are in no way to be heard; for even if they had bestowed such things on a man, [Col. 0859D] they would be unable to reclaim them.” Hence Ambrose, in his book *On Penance*: “There are those who, when they have bestowed their wealth upon the Church through a sudden impulse of mind rather than through settled judgment, later think it should be reclaimed. Neither their first act nor their second gains them a reward: the first had no judgment, and the second involved sacrilege.” Likewise, from the Council of Agde: “Clerics or laypersons who persist in withholding obligations made by their parents, whether given or left by will, or who think that what they themselves gave to churches or monasteries ought to be taken away, are, as the holy synod has decreed, to be excluded from the churches as murderers of the poor until they restore it.”

Those, however, who lay violent hands upon clerics—unless perhaps in self-defense—incur the penalty of excommunication, as the most holy Roman Church long ago established [Col. 0860A] and inviolably maintains; nor does it suffer or permit them to be absolved by anyone whatsoever except the Roman pontiff or by his command.

You therefore, following in the footsteps of that Church which is the head and teacher of all Churches, comply with its and our ruling in all the matters stated above. Observe what, as we have said, was established by the holy Fathers and our predecessors; and, insofar as lies within you, cause it to be firmly and inviolably observed by all throughout your bishoprics. We command that those who despise ecclesiastical authority be struck with punishment until they have performed worthy penance. But upon the obedient may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good conduct [Col. 0860B] and in the future find the rewards of eternal peace.

Given at Tusculum, 10 September.

### CMLXXX. To the northern kings and princes.—That they should fight bravely against the Estonians, enemies of the Christian name. (Tusculum, 11 September.)

[Ibid., col. 936.]

Pope ALEXANDER III to the kings and princes and other faithful of Christ established throughout the kingdoms of the Danes, Norwegians, Geats, and Goths.

Our spirit is greatly afflicted, and we are tormented by no small bitterness and grief, when we hear that the savagery of the Estonians and of the other pagans of those regions rises more grievously and rages more fiercely against God’s faithful and cultivators of the Christian faith, and assails the power of the Christian name. Yet we praise and bless the Lord because you persist with unshaken firmness in the Catholic faith and in devotion to the most holy Roman Church, which is the head of all Churches and, appointed by the Lord as their teacher, holds primacy over all other Churches by a heavenly privilege; and because you preserve the bond and unity of the Christian religion. Therefore, since it pertains to our office to set before you by earnest exhortation, and more diligently to commend, those things known to concern the strengthening of the faith and the salvation of your souls, we admonish and exhort [Col. 0860D] you all in the Lord: devote yourselves to divine worship; love mercy, justice, and judgment; abstain from robbery and wicked deeds; render to God devoted and acceptable service; show due honor and reverence to the aforesaid most holy Roman Church as to your mother and teacher; humbly obey your bishops, priests, and other prelates; render to them their tithes, first-fruits, offerings, and other dues; honor them in every way as fathers and shepherds of your souls; zealously defend, uphold, and preserve their rights. Armed with heavenly weapons and strengthened by apostolic exhortations, gird yourselves with the spirit of fortitude to defend the truth of the Christian faith, [Col. 0861A] laboring with strong arm to spread the religion of the Christian name, so that you may gain victory over your enemies and, by the Lord’s working, obtain the crown of righteousness laid up for you.

For those who fight powerfully and courageously against the pagans often mentioned, we grant, trusting in the mercy of God and the merits of the apostles Peter and Paul, remission of one year from the sins which they have confessed and for which they have received penance, as we customarily grant to those who visit the Lord’s sepulcher. But to those who die in that conflict, provided they have received penance, we grant remission of all their sins.

Given at Tusculum, 11 September.

### CMLXXXI. Bull for the monastery of Corbie (diocese of Amiens). (Tusculum, 11 September.)

[Gall. Christ., X, Instr. 318.]

[Col. 0861B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and brothers of Corbie, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are bound to extend special protection to those churches and persons known to belong directly, without any intermediary, to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter and ourselves; and, by the authority and duty of the apostolic see, we are compelled to exercise more ready care and concern for the preservation of their condition. But we have heard—and are greatly disturbed—that, although your monastery is known to belong so properly and specially to blessed Peter that it has no prelate or master other than the Roman pontiff, our venerable brother Henry, Archbishop of Reims, receives appeals made without justification by your burgesses and presumes, against your will, to hear or handle their causes. For if he would not receive appeals from parishioners of the Archbishop of Tours or of Sens, much less ought he receive those from your parishioners. He is bound to preserve and protect the rights of the Roman Church with proportionately greater zeal, inasmuch as, by reason of the dignity entrusted to him, he is more strictly bound and is known to be joined to us in a closer devotion. Therefore [Col. 0861D] we have admonished, ordered, and commanded him henceforth on no ground to judge concerning the burgesses of your aforesaid monastery, or claim any jurisdiction over them. If any of them should judge it proper to appeal to him, he is in no way to admit the appeal, but in these matters and in others is to leave the rights of the aforesaid monastery whole and unimpaired, so that he may thereby deserve our commendation and the said monastery may suffer no burden from him or his agents. But if ever—may God avert it!—he should attempt to act contrary to this, we grant you these present letters, according to the customary clemency of the apostolic see, for the defense and preservation of your right and liberty [Col. 0862A].

Given at Tusculum, 11 September.

### CMLXXXII. To the bishop of Amiens and the abbot of Saint-Remi.—That they should investigate the case of the bishop of Tournai, accused of exactions. (Tusculum, 16 September.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 929.]

Pope ALEXANDER to [THEOBALD], bishop of Amiens, and the abbot of Saint-Remi.

From the representation of Daniel, priest of Saint John at Ghent, it had been made known to us that our brother, the bishop of Tournai, extorted from him and certain others an intolerable annual exaction of money and had turned it into a customary practice. They had humbly and devoutly asked him to desist from such an exaction; but, violently angered and disturbed, he suspended the said Daniel from office because he had raised the matter, and by threats induced others to accept, at his pleasure, whatever he should determine concerning their property. Moreover—and this is serious—he ordered the abbot of Saint Peter’s at Ghent, after the complete expulsion of Daniel already mentioned, to ordain another priest in his place.

However, the aforesaid bishop, by letters sent to us, stated that the church in question had been temporarily entrusted to Daniel; that Daniel, addicted to drunkenness, frequently spent the night in taverns; and that, without any sleep having preceded it, he had not feared rashly to celebrate Mass. Since he had confessed this when he failed in his purgation, the bishop suspended him from office and nevertheless deprived him of the church, which he did not hold permanently but only in commendam. Since Daniel denies all this, and there is a common and almost general complaint by all that the said bishop treats his priests and clerics worse than hired servants and extorts from them heavy and unbearable annual exactions, we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently and carefully to investigate all these matters, and to report to us in your letters the plain and unalloyed truth of whatever you find, without admixture of falsehood, so that, once the facts are established, we may more confidently and safely correct [Col. 0862D] what we recognize ought to be corrected.

Given at Tusculum, 16 September.

### CMLXXXIII. To all the faithful of God established throughout Denmark.—That they should relieve the poverty of Fulco, bishop of the Estonians, with their resources. (Tusculum, 17 September.)

[Ibid., col. 936.]

All who desire to live devoutly in Christ and to attain the radiance of unbounded light and that heavenly homeland which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the human heart (1 Cor. 2), where neither thieves [Col. 0863A] break in nor steal and moth does not destroy (Matt. 6), ought to anticipate their last day by works of mercy and, with eternity in view, sow on earth what, through the Lord’s generosity, they may gather again in heaven with multiplied fruit. For it is written: “He who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessings shall reap eternal life from blessing” (1 Cor. 10). We believe that it has become known to you all how our venerable brother Fulco, bishop of the Estonians, is pressed by want and poverty, labors with all his strength to convert the people of his bishopric, who are ignorant of the Christian faith, and endeavors to apply as much care and diligence as he can. Since he who supplies counsel and assistance to him for accomplishing so pious and holy a work becomes a sharer in the reward, we admonish and exhort your devotion in the Lord, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of your sins, that, relieving the said bishop’s poverty from the goods bestowed on you by God, you extend to him a helping hand and provide the comforts of charity out of regard for divine love. Thus, through these and other good works which, by God’s inspiration, you perform, may you deserve, through the Lord’s favor, to obtain from the Most High pardon for your sins and to attain the joys of eternal blessedness [Col. 0863B].

Given at Tusculum, 17 September.

### CMLXXXIV. To the clerics and laypeople of the diocese of Linköping.—That they should obey their bishop. (Tusculum, 17 September.)

[Ibid., col. 941.]

[Col. 0863C]

Pope ALEXANDER III to all clerics and laypeople of the diocese of Linköping [Lincopiensis].

It is fitting that you all devote your whole effort to considering what pertains to the perfection of virtues and the salvation of souls, and voluntarily perform those things through which you may acquire the grace of the Most High and, with the assistance of divine power, attain the glory of eternal blessedness. Moreover, since without the virtue of obedience no one can perfectly please God or render acceptable service, we command you by these apostolic letters, commanding and command by commanding, [Col. 0863D] that you render every obedience and reverence to our venerable brother C., your bishop, just as you are known to have done to Gilo, his predecessor of good memory. In matters which concern God and the salvation of your souls, take care humbly to obey his counsels and commands, and render to him his dues wholly and fully, so that through your humility and obedience [Col. 0864A] you may obtain from God pardon for your sins and eternal glory. But if any among you prove contumacious or rebellious toward him, we shall, with the Lord as author, hold valid and firm the sentence which that bishop reasonably pronounces upon them for this reason.

Given at Tusculum, 17 September.

### CMLXXXV. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—For Hodeard’s widow and children against three abbots. (Tusculum, 29 September.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 952.]

From the complaint sent to us by Hodeardis of Maderies and her sons, we have learned that Baldwin, formerly husband of the same woman, had lent, without interest, eighty pounds and forty-six solidi of Châlons currency to the abbot and brothers of Saint Paul at Verdun; yet those brothers refuse to repay them that money.

[Note: [Col. 0863D] The abbey of Saint Paul, formerly of the Order of Saint Benedict, passed in the twelfth century to the Premonstratensians.]

Her sons further stated that the brothers of the church of Vallis Regis likewise refuse to pay them the sixty-three pounds they owe them, although they had pledged to pay that money to them by specified terms; and that the abbot and brothers of Trois-Fontaines refuse to repay them the hundred pounds and more which they had deposited with him. Since we are bound to assist each person in his right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to admonish the abbots and brothers of those churches and strictly compel them by our authority either to restore the said money in full to the aforesaid woman [Col. 0864C] and her sons, or without delay to render them the fullness of justice in the matter before you.

[Note: [Col. 0863D] Vallis Regis: a Premonstratensian abbey founded by Rainard, Count of Bar, in the diocese of Toul.]

[Note: [Col. 0863D] Trois-Fontaines: a Cistercian monastery, the first daughter-house of Clairvaux, in the diocese of Châlons.]

Given at Tusculum, 29 September.

### CMLXXXVI. To the same.—Of similar matter. (Tusculum, 29 September.)

[Ibid.]

A complaint has reached our ears on behalf of Hodeardis of Maderies and her sons: she had lent, without interest, one hundred and thirty-three pounds and five solidi to the abbot and brothers of Saint Benedict at Vepre, seventy pounds to the abbot and brothers of Villers, and fifty-five pounds of Châlons currency, less fifteen solidi, four denarii, and one obol, to the abbot and brothers of Saint Leo at Toul; yet she cannot recover that money from them. Therefore, because we can and ought to deny no one his right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to admonish the said abbots and strictly compel them by our authority either to restore in full the prescribed money to the aforesaid woman and her sons or, without delay, to render them the fullness of justice in the matter before you.

[Note: [Col. 0864D] Saint Benedict at Vepre: a Cistercian house in the diocese of Verdun.]

[Note: [Col. 0864D] Villers, two hours distant from Metz: a Cistercian abbey.]

[Note: [Col. 0864D] The abbey of Saint Leo, Pope Leo IX’s namesake, in the city of Toul, belonged to the Order of Regular Canons of Saint Augustine.]

Given at Tusculum, 29 September.

### CMLXXXVII. To the same.—Of similar matter. (Tusculum, 29 September.)

[Ibid., col. 953.]

A complaint has reached our ears on behalf of Hodeardis of Maderies and her sons: she had lent without interest twenty-six pounds of Châlons currency to the abbot and brothers of Île, and thirteen pounds to the abbot and brothers of Prisney; yet she could not recover that money from them. Therefore, because we can and ought to deny no one his right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to admonish the said abbots and brothers and strictly compel them by our authority either to restore in full the prescribed money to the aforesaid woman and her sons or, with appeal set aside, without delay to render them the fullness of justice before you.

[Note: [Col. 0865D] Called the Isle of Bar, this abbey was formerly of regular canons of the Order of Saint Augustine, of the congregation of Arrouaise; in the twelfth century it passed to the Cistercians in the line of Morimond.]

[Note: [Col. 0866D] I am wholly ignorant what monastery Prisney was, and I especially doubt whether it still exists.]

Given at Tusculum, 29 September.

### CMLXXXVIII. He commands the bishops of Marsi, Penne, and Valva, and the clerics of Chieti and Forcona, to observe the excommunication pronounced by Leonas, abbot of Pescara, against Berardus Gentilis and his brothers, and against Roger, son of Riccardus, and his brothers; and to declare excommunicated the schismatic clerics of Farfa monastery who performed divine offices in the territory of San Sano against Leonas’s interdict. (Tusculum, 4 October.)

[MURATORI, *Rer. Ital. sacra*, II, II, 909.]

[Col. 0865C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the bishops of Marsi, Penne, and Valva, and to his beloved sons, the clerics of the Churches of Chieti and Forcona, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You are aware that various and numerous complaints have reached our hearing on behalf of our beloved son Leonas, abbot of Saint Clement at Pescara, against the noble men Berardus Gentilis and his brothers, Roger, son of Riccardus, and his brothers: they withhold from him and his monastery the due and customary rent from the territory of San Sano; they do not fear to divide among themselves the churches of that territory and their possessions, and to appoint and send priests from them. In addition, when the same abbot pronounced a sentence of interdict upon that territory and of excommunication upon a certain Simoniac, who is said certainly to have bought a church from the aforesaid men for a price, those same men do not cease to support the excommunicated man and, contrary to the abbot’s interdict, have divine services celebrated in the aforesaid territory by clerics of Farfa monastery, who are schismatics [Col. 0866A].

Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, setting aside every delay and objection, you declare excommunicated and cause to be avoided as excommunicated those clerics who knowingly sang in the prescribed territory against the abbot’s interdict. When the said abbot has pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the aforesaid men for such great offenses, in accordance with our command, you are firmly to observe it and cause it to be inviolably observed, with every pretext and appeal set aside. Do not permit divine offices to be celebrated in your churches while they are present, and forbid clerics of your bishoprics to go into that territory in order to celebrate offices there.

Given at Tusculum, 4 October.

### CMLXXXIX. To Leonas, abbot of Pescara, he signifies that he has exhorted Berardus Gentilis and his brothers, and Roger, son of Riccardus, and his brothers, to make good within fifteen days the damage inflicted upon him; should they fail to do so, he is to excommunicate them. (Tusculum, 4 October.)

[Ibid., col. 908.]

[Col. 0866B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LEONAS, abbot of Saint Clement at Pescara, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received your messenger and letters with the due gladness of heart. Recognizing the concern which, as a devoted and special son, you are known to have for our condition and that of the Church, we inform your affection by these present letters that we and our brethren are, by God’s grace, sound and well, and that, as the Lord enables us, we keep pastoral watch over the welfare and advancement of the universal Church. Furthermore, having heard from the mouth of your messengers of the burdens and injuries which the noble men Berardus Gentilis and his brothers, Roger, son of Riccardus, and his brothers, … [lacuna] … should not delay to make suitable satisfaction to you and your monastery, as you will learn more fully from the written instruction which we send them.

We therefore command your discretion that, if the men already mentioned refuse to comply with our admonitions and commands within fifteen days after receiving our letters, you declare them excommunicated by our authority and cause them diligently to be avoided as excommunicated—unless perhaps you judge that they should be tolerated longer. For we have instructed the neighboring bishops firmly to observe your sentence and cause it to be inviolably observed; and to excommunicate, and cause to be avoided as excommunicated, clerics who knowingly sang in the territory of San Sano against your interdict. We indeed have the will and fervent desire to love your person with sincere and special charity in the Lord, and to preserve with attentive concern the rights of your monastery as our special and proper possession. We give thanks to your affection [Col. 0867A] for your solicitude concerning our well-being.

Given at Tusculum, 4 October.

### CMXC. To the people of Nonantola.—On relieving their debt and reforming discipline in the monastery. (Tusculum, 15 December.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *Storia di Nonantola*, II, 274.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and brothers of the monastery of Nonantola, its nobles and other vassals and men of the same monastery, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Considering the burdens and pressures by which the monastery already mentioned is severely afflicted, and also observing how it has been diminished and worn down both spiritually and temporally—though it formerly flourished in great religious devotion and respectability and abounded in great wealth—we sympathize, from a special affection demanded by our office, with its distress and need, and are stirred to more earnest care and solicitude for its relief. Therefore we have instructed our beloved son I[ldebrand], cardinal-priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles and legate of the apostolic see, to go to that place, summon together there such of you as he judges it most expedient to assemble, and, after deliberation and counsel with them, so provide and arrange that all the monastery’s debts may be paid and the monastery restored to religious order.

[Note: [Col. 0867D] This is Cardinal Ildebrand, believed to have belonged to the Bolognese de’ Grassi family. He was created cardinal of the title of Saint Eustachius by Eugenius III and was subsequently, according to Ciaconius and Oldoinus, transferred in 1161 to the title of the Most Holy Twelve Apostles. He died on 8 November 1178. (See Trombelli, *Memories of Saint Mary of Reno*, p. 223.) He is the same man to whom the administration of the Church of Modena was entrusted when Eugenius III deprived it of the rank of episcopal see.]

Accordingly, we command you all by apostolic letters that, at his summons, you … [lacuna] … come, and that all of you provide him with counsel, support, and aid for the reform of the same monastery and the relief of its debts; take care humbly and without objection to obey his commands and ordinances in this matter. You, sons, abbot and monks, must take care that henceforth, through your negligence or lack of foresight, the same monastery may not fall into so great a loss.

Given at Tusculum, 15 December.

### CMXCI. He grants to Ubaldo, bishop of Ostia, and to the archpriest and canons of Velletri that wills “which their parishioners make in their last will before their priest and three or two other suitable persons shall remain valid.” (See Gregory’s *Decretals*, book III, title 26, chapter 10.)

[Col. 0867D]

### ANNO 1172.

### CMXCII. He receives the Church of Zaragoza under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Tusculum, 22 January.)

[ARRUEGO, *Cathedral of Zaragoza*, 674.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Peter, bishop of Zaragoza, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Established by the Lord’s disposition upon the watchtower of the apostolic see, we ought to love with fraternal charity our brother bishops, whether near or far away, and, with the Lord’s help, beneficially provide for their peace and tranquility. Moved by this consideration, venerable brother in Christ, bishop, and following in the footsteps of our predecessors Eugenius and Adrian, Roman pontiffs of holy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of Zaragoza, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside; and we fortify it by the privilege of the present document. [Col. 0868B] We decree that whatever possessions and goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the bounty of kings or princes, or other just means, obtain through the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper names:
the church of Saint Mary, which is within the walls of the city; whatever right you have in the church of the Holy Masses; the churches of Torocha, both within the town and within its boundaries, with all their appurtenances; the churches of Monreal with their appurtenances; the churches of Arodenes, of Saint Mary of Benaein, and of Pennagolosa, of Torol, and of Alambra, with all [Col. 0868C] their appurtenances; the churches of Castellot; the churches of Alcanica and Moditerrania, with all their appurtenances; the churches of Cosp, Nonasp, Michinentia, Scatron, Sastago, Vilella, Pina, and Alfaxarin; the churches of Rosera, Salz, Gorreia, and Espanes, with all their appurtenances; the churches of Luna, Exea, Baio, and Escoron, with their appurtenances; the churches of Noveles, Rozazol, Cortes, Mestit, Frescano, Mogalon, Alberit, Borota, Ajaccione, and Crocle, which are situated on the stream Burge, with all their appurtenances; the churches of Ricla, Cappanis, Epila, Rota, Orrea, Alagon, Gallus, and Petrola, with all their appurtenances; [Col. 0868D] the churches of Codo, Ferrera, Bardones, Monfort, Osa, Martin, Monte Albano, Belgit, and Saint Peter, with all their appurtenances; the castle of Cotanda and the castle of Albalat, with all their boundaries, and the churches built there.

We likewise decree that, on the side bordering the Saracens, all the boundaries of that bishopric, as they are known lawfully to have existed in antiquity, shall henceforth be preserved for you and your successors in peace and undiminished. Moreover, we confirm in perpetuity for you and your successors that agreement canonically made at Calahorra between you and Lupus, formerly [Col. 0869A] bishop of Pamplona, in the presence of our beloved son Hyacinth, cardinal deacon, then legate of the Apostolic See. By that agreement the churches of Luna, the church of Exea, the church of Toust, the churches above Zaragoza, the church of Baio, and the church of Escoron, with all their appurtenances, are known to have come to you.

Furthermore, we confirm in perpetuity for you and your successors the boundaries of the bishopric of Zaragoza, according to the division made by King Wamba in the Council of Toledo, and whatever is known to belong to the right of your church within those same boundaries. Likewise, by apostolic authority we confirm in perpetuity for you and your successors the donations and grants reasonably made to the Church of Zaragoza by King Ildefonsus, [Col. 0869B] by King Ramiro his brother, and by the illustrious Ildefonsus, king of Spain. We also confirm by the present charter the liberties and immunities granted in pious devotion to that same Church by the aforesaid King Ildefonsus and by the nobleman Raymond, count of Barcelona, and secured by their written instruments; and we decree that the same Church is free from every secular yoke and lordship.

Moreover, whatever goods or possessions our dearest son in Christ, Ildefonsus, illustrious king of Aragon, formerly son of R., count of Barcelona, is known to have bestowed upon you and your Church by pious generosity; likewise, the liberties of the clergy and the tithes of the Saracens in your bishopric granted to you and your Church by that same king, as is contained in the king’s authentic instruments drawn up on this matter: all these we confirm to you by apostolic authority.

Further, desiring with paternal solicitude to provide for your peace and tranquillity, and for that of the Church entrusted to you, we have judged that the agreement between you and the abbot of Pina concerning the churches of Luna and Taust—reasonably made by the action of Bernard, of good memory, formerly archbishop of Tarragona, in the presence of our venerable brothers William, now archbishop of Tarragona but then bishop of Barcelona, William bishop of Lérida, and R., of revered memory, formerly count of Barcelona, together with certain barons and other persons of the kingdom of Aragon, [Col. 0869D] by the agreement and good pleasure of both parties—should be strengthened by the safeguard of our charter and confirmed by the present privilege, as is known to be contained in the authentic instrument made concerning it.

We decree, therefore, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone, therefore, in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul at Pammachius. I, John, cardinal priest of Saint Anastasia. I, Buil, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter, etc.

[Col. 0870A] Given at Tusculum, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, in the fifth indiction, in the year 1171 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

CMXCIII. To Ildefonsus, king of Aragon.—He thanks him for expelling Robert from the kingdom; he urges him to exclude Robert’s entire offspring from the same kingdom and to assign their goods to the treasury. (Tusculum, January 26.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1076.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, ILDEFONSUS, illustrious king of Aragon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0870B] It has been reported to us that, girded with the weapons of justice, you have sternly punished Robert and Berengarius, together with their mother and heirs, for the atrocity of the crime and the most savage wickedness perpetrated, at the Devil’s instigation, in the death of the archbishop of Tarragona of pious memory; and that by royal edict you caused them to be banished from your kingdom. We regard this as welcome and acceptable, and therefore commend more highly in the Lord the prudence of your royal majesty with praises.

And because their crime was so detestable that they deserved to be punished with perpetual condemnation and ought throughout their lives to remain in tears and penance in expiation of so great an offence, we admonish, earnestly exhort, and command the diligence of your royal serenity [Col. 0870C] that, excluding the aforesaid evildoers and their mother, together with their offspring, from your whole kingdom and land forever, you receive them henceforth in your land at no one’s instigation; and that you freely restore, without molestation, to the Church of Tarragona, and permit it to hold in peace, one half of the possessions situated at Tarragona or in its territory, according to the terms of the agreement made between it and Raymond, of good memory, formerly your father. Thus the same Church, which laments the great injury inflicted by the death of its archbishop, may feel itself relieved in that respect, and you may not appear to act against your father’s pact or to defraud that Church of its right—which would be exceedingly dangerous for you.

But if any persons subject to your jurisdiction receive the aforesaid traitors [Col. 0870D] in your land, utterly take away their goods, and, instilling fear into persons, add another punishment. Moreover, if—what we do not believe—you pass over our admonitions with deaf ears, we command that your kingdom be placed under interdict. And if even thus our admonitions are not obeyed, we shall by no means spare your person either.

Given at Tusculum, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February.

CMXCIV. Privilege for the Church of Tarentaise. (Tusculum, February 15.)

[Gallia Christiana, XII, Documents, 385.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PETER, archbishop of Tarentaise, and his canonically appointed successors [Col. 0871A] in perpetuity.

Established by the Lord’s disposition upon the watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought to love our brother bishops, both near and far, with fraternal charity, and, with the Lord’s aid, beneficially provide for their peace and tranquillity. Therefore, venerable brother archbishop, in consideration of this matter, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church over which, by God’s authority, you preside; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present charter. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of popes, generosity of kings [Col. 0871B] or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. We have judged that the following should be expressly set down by their proper names:

the bishoprics of Aosta and Sion; Musterium, with all its appurtenances; the castle of Saint James and the church of that place, with tithes and all its appurtenances; the church of Campagniola, with tithes and all its appurtenances; the village of Allodiis and its church, with tithes and all its appurtenances; the village of Saint John and its church, with tithes and all its appurtenances; the village of Flacheria, with all its tithes and appurtenances; the village of Comba, with tithes and its appurtenances; [Col. 0871C] the village of Saint Martin of the Deserts, with tithes and all its appurtenances; the church of Monte Pontio, with tithes and all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Maurice, with all tithes and appurtenances; the church of Ayma, with tithes and its appurtenances; the church of Viletta, with tithes and all its appurtenances; the valley of Saint Desiderius and the churches of that valley, with tithes and all their appurtenances; the share which it has in the castle of Conflens and the churches of that castle, with all their appurtenances; the church of Venthone, with all its appurtenances; four churches of Luciaco, with tithes and their appurtenances; the church of Saesarchiis, with tithes and all its appurtenances; the church of Clariaco, [Col. 0871D] with all the churches belonging to it, their tithes, and their appurtenances.

Moreover, we decree that the aforesaid Church shall never be subject by right to any archbishop or primatial church, but shall be subject directly, without intermediary, to the Holy Roman Church alone, as it is known to have been hitherto. We likewise confirm by apostolic authority for you and your successors the jurisdictions, court, and good customs which you and your predecessors have hitherto reasonably possessed in the land of the Church of Tarentaise. We also judge that the fiefs and estates which you reasonably hold directly, or which others hold in your name, and which belong to the aforesaid Church, should be confirmed for you and your successors under threat of anathema. We forbid any [Col. 0872A] holder of fiefs in the name of yourself or your Church to presume to withhold from you the good customs of the fiefs, or to conceal those fiefs or customs, or rashly to alienate them in any manner from that Church.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved unimpaired and entire, to benefit the uses and needs of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone, therefore, in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina. [Col. 0872B] I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John, Paul, and Januaria. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Boso, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, Ardico, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Theodore. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa. I, Peter de Bono, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary [Col. 0872C] in Aquiro.

Given at Tusculum, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the fifth indiction, in the year 1171 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

CMXCV. To [Rotrou], archbishop of Rouen, and [Theobald], bishop of Amiens.—That they are to restore the fullness of office to Gilbert, bishop of London, if he swears with a sixth hand that he knowingly provoked the king neither by writing, word, nor deed to the death of Saint Thomas. (Tusculum, February 27.)

[Letters of Saint Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 68.]

[Col. 0872D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishop of Rouen and the bishop of Amiens: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not believe that it is unknown to your brotherhood, since report has spread it abroad through a great part of the world, how our brothers Gilbert, bishop of London, and the other bishops of England, certain causes having intervened, were formerly suspended from their office by our authority, and others were bound by the bond of excommunication. When, through Thomas, formerly archbishop of Canterbury, of holy and revered memory, our letters concerning their suspension [Col. 0873A] and excommunication were published in the kingdom of England and this was reported to the king of England, he conceived such indignation, bitterness, and disturbance against that archbishop, and displayed it so much in face and gesture, that some of those about him, [thinking] that they were rendering him a service worthy and acceptable to him and would thereby more fully gain his favour and goodwill, fell upon the aforesaid archbishop of Canterbury with the weapons of injustice and impiety and atrociously and cruelly killed him in his church before the altar, not considering how heinous it is to lay hands upon the anointed of God and to stain Christ’s bride with his blood.

But the horror of the crime has brought all the greater infamy upon those who are said to have furnished the occasion of so great an atrocity and wickedness, and has more deeply blackened their honour, insofar as the offence is judged more cruel and the crime more detestable. [Col. 0873B] Moreover, when the aforesaid king had earnestly petitioned us through his envoys that we should entrust to be received in those regions the purgation of those whom infamy had stained in this matter, we were unwilling to consent to this in any way; for if persons appeared who wished to accuse them, we had determined to examine the case in our presence, while if no accusers appeared, we had determined to call them to account concerning this and to impose upon them such purgation as we should know necessary to abolish so great an infamy.

But since no one appeared who wished [Col. 0873C] to accuse them, and the aforesaid bishop of London, because of bodily weakness, was unable to undertake so great a labour, while many dangers and perils threatened upon the journey, he sent to our presence his beloved sons R., his archdeacon, Master Richard, and Master Hugh, his clerks, so that they might make purgation before us on his behalf. After we had carefully deliberated with our brethren whether his purgation should be received before us, we finally decreed to entrust the receipt of that purgation to you, because we judged it more honourable and expedient for you and that bishop that the purgation should be received in the place where the infamy was more widely spread and that the bishop should demonstrate his innocence.

Therefore, placing the fullest confidence in your religion, prudence, and integrity, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you meet together as soon as you can after inspecting our letters, on the frontier of the king of France and the king of England, namely in the March; summon the aforesaid bishop before you; and, having summoned religious and discerning men, if that bishop swears, upon the holy Gospels set before him, with a sixth hand of religious abbots and priors of monks and regular canons of proved life and conduct, or of monks whom he has with him and canons of his own Church, who are of unblemished reputation and standing and concerning whom it is likely that they would not wish to commit perjury, [Col. 0874A] that he knowingly provoked the king neither by writing nor word nor deed, on account of which the aforesaid archbishop of Canterbury was killed, nor imposed a corporal punishment upon him, then, relying upon our authority, restore to him without delay the fullness of his office, without diminution of his reputation and good name.

But if, through some manifest and necessary impediment, both of you cannot be present for carrying this out, let whichever of you is present execute the matter more promptly with religious, discerning, and highly authoritative men of that province.

Given at Tusculum, on the third day before the Kalends of March.

CMXCVI. To Galdinus, archbishop of Milan.—Concerning the election of a primicerius. (Tusculum, March 25.)

[SAXIUS, *Series of the Archbishops of Milan*, II, 574.]

[Col. 0874B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GALDINUS, archbishop of Milan and legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From your letters and those of the *decumani* of your Church, who are known to have a dispute with you concerning the election of the primicerius, and from the writing sent to us by our beloved sons Manfred, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil and legate of the Apostolic See, and the consuls of Milan, it has become clear to us that, although the case concerning the primicerius had long been disputed and discussed before us and others between you and the same *decumani*, you finally sent us the arguments and allegations on either side and urgently requested us to endeavour to impose a due conclusion upon the case, which had long been handled before delegated judges and arbitrators, and to remove every cause of contention.

Having received your allegations and arguments, we held lengthy and careful deliberation about them with our brethren, because the allegations themselves were quite prolix and diffuse. If the entire case had been brought before our examination, we might perhaps have deliberated otherwise; but because sentence had been given in the same cause by delegated judges and had not been suspended by appeal—indeed, had been accepted by both sides—we did not judge that it should be annulled in what is manifest [Col. 0874D] and evident.

Now, since the same judges had pronounced sentence that the priests and clerks of the *decumani* might choose from their college eight whom they considered most suitable and devoted to peace and concord, who, together with the archbishop, should treat him with honour and reverence as a father and lord, while he should treat them as sons; and that they, together with him, and he together with them, should unanimously, harmoniously, and sincerely make the election of the primicerius: according to the tenor of the sentence they chose eight electors from their college. These repeatedly deliberated concerning the election of a primicerius.

At last, the eight electors reverently sought your will and, wishing to make the election with you according to the tenor of the aforesaid sentence, saw, as they say, that you were acting under the direction not only of priests but of certain members of your household. Without your consent, as may be understood from their allegations, they nominated Master Gibuinus, provost of Saint George, supposing, as we believe, that you ought to comply with them as with sons, as established in the sentence; and that, because they were eight in number while you were but one, even if you disagreed with them, their election would nevertheless have binding force. But after they had made their nomination, you immediately nominated Master Nicholas, provost of Saint Nazarius, as primicerius—indeed, as your allegations stated, you nominated three persons—believing, as we suppose, that the word contained in the sentence permitted you to do so, because they ought to render you honour and reverence as father and lord in the election of the primicerius.

Having examined the arguments alleged on these matters, we deliberated quite carefully and at length concerning them with our brethren. After prolonged deliberation, we annulled both elections by apostolic authority, not on account of the persons or their merits, but because of the defect of the elections themselves; for we found that neither had been made according to the tenor of the aforesaid sentence or according to the common law. Since the sentence provided that you should make the election of the primicerius with the aforesaid electors, and they with you, unanimously, harmoniously, and sincerely, it is clear that neither election was made according to that tenor, because neither was made harmoniously: neither you with their consent, nor they, as we believe and as appears from their allegations, after seeking yours.

According to the common law, moreover, neither election ought to stand. For although the electors on the part of the *decumani* are eight in number, they nevertheless appear to represent only one person in that election. Since the dispute was between you and the college as between two persons, the delegated judges decided that election should belong to each side, ordering that eight electors from the whole college should be selected to celebrate the election with you, because it seemed burdensome and difficult for all to assemble together for the election. Just as they decreed eight, they could equally have decreed one or several, and fewer. Since, as we have said, these eight represent only one person, while you represent the other, neither you could make an election without them nor they without you.

But as to how the election should henceforth be made, and which election should be held valid, we wish, setting aside the dispute over those two questions—namely, whether it was permissible for arbitrators to interpret, and whether they interpreted justly—to determine by this present writing. By common counsel of our brethren, we judge that, since those eight appear, as stated above, to represent one person, and the election has been adjudged to you and them, if they make an election without you, or you without them, each election must be of no effect—just as, if two judges were delegated in the same cause and one of them pronounced one judgment while the other pronounced another, neither judgment would stand.

But if you and the same eight electors make the election jointly and harmoniously, that election must without question be held valid, unless it should be rejected on account of a defect in the person elected. If, however, you cannot agree jointly upon a person, but at least two or more of those eight electors agree with you in the election, we decree that the election is valid. For since they appear in this matter to represent one person, while you represent the other, after two of them have agreed with you, who represent the more worthy person in the election, the election should rightly be held valid. It is as though the chapters of two churches, having an equal number of persons to whom it belongs to make an election, cannot agree harmoniously in the election, and two persons—or even one—from one chapter agree in the election with the other: that election stands, especially if the more worthy chapter has made it.

Further, as we have understood from the aforesaid allegations, the arbitrators decreed that, whenever the college must be summoned to make an election of a primicerius, it should be summoned after permission has been requested from the archbishop; and if the archbishop refuses to grant permission, the priests may nevertheless summon the college to make the election. Conversely, if the priests refuse to summon the college for this purpose, then the archbishop shall sincerely and paternally summon the college and cause the eight who must make the election with him to be selected. We have not judged that this arrangement, established by the same arbitrators, should be altered; rather, holding it valid and firm, we confirm it by apostolic authority and decree that it shall have the strength of perpetual validity.

And in order that this judgment of our determination may be inviolably observed for all time, we confirm it by apostolic authority and fortify it by the protection of this present charter, decreeing that no person whatsoever may infringe this document of our determination and confirmation or in any way oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his apostles, blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at Tusculum, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

CMXCVII. To the canons of Saint Victor.—He confirms the resignation of Abbot Ervisius and the promotion of Guarinus. (Tusculum, April 11.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, VI, 254.]

[Col. 0876D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the church of Saint Victor of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more greatly your Church has hitherto flourished in religious observance and shone with ampler glory of merit, the more we rejoiced and were glad on hearing of its reformation, and were cheered by its welfare and progress. We have heard that, through the cooperation of our venerable brothers the archbishops of Bourges and Sens, who laboured toward this end with all diligence according to the tenor of our mandate, your Church has been restored to its former state and [Col. 0877A] rank. Ervisius, formerly abbot, freely resigned the administration in the presence of our beloved sons Alexander, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and Theodoric, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Vitalis, legates of the Apostolic See; through his fault its condition had been deformed to no small degree. You then unanimously chose a suitable, honourable, and learned person as your abbot and took care to provide yourselves with a shepherd.

We, whose duty it is reasonably to grant favourable support to worthy wishes and enactments and to desire their growth, hold and confirm, with the common counsel of our brethren, both your recent election and his resignation as valid and firm. We admonish and command your whole community to render due reverence and obedience to the abbot whom you have elected, and to take care to show yourselves so devoted and humble toward him that, through your obedience and his governance, the order of religious observance and integrity may flourish anew in your church and, with the Lord’s aid, be preserved more fully.

Given at Tusculum, on the third day before the Ides of April.

CMXCVIII. To Guarinus, abbot of Saint Victor.—He congratulates him on his election and urges him diligently to discharge a shepherd’s office. (Tusculum, April 11.)

[Ibid., col. 255.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0877C] son GUARINUS, abbot of Saint Victor of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having learned and ascertained that, when Ervisius, formerly abbot of the Church over which you are known to preside, freely and voluntarily resigned the administration, the brethren of that Church elected you as their abbot by their common vote and desire, we rejoice and are glad all the more because we had been more deeply grieved by the tribulation of that Church and were oppressed by greater anxiety and concern for its condition.

Therefore, because it befits you to consider carefully how great the religious observance and integrity of the Church to which, by the Lord’s providence, you have been called has hitherto been, and how regular discipline flourished there in its rigour, we admonish and command your discretion [Col. 0877D] to attend prudently and steadfastly to the administration entrusted to you. Exercise the office committed to you effectively and diligently, with the help of heavenly grace, for God’s honour and for the edification of yourself and those entrusted to you, so that through your prudence and solicitude the order of religious life may always flourish anew there and may receive ever greater increase from day to day. For we wish to love and support you and that Church, and, when occasion requires, to furnish you with the protection of apostolic defence.

Given at Tusculum, on the third day before the Ides of April.

CMXCIX. He receives under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Saint Mary of Monte-Laeto, and confirms its privileges and rights. (Tusculum, June 24.)

[AGUIRRE, *Councils of Spain*, III, 387.]

[Col. 0878A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons VIBIANUS, abbot of the church of Saint Mary of Monte-Laeto, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

The immaculate Virgin Mary, Mother of God, who surpasses the merits of the saints by her own excellence, purer and more exalted than all the angels, ought to be honoured continually by all the faithful with all the greater devotion and special reverence inasmuch as she deserved to be happily exalted above all angels by the very author of immortality. We, desiring to be aided before the Most High by the help of her intercession, wish to favour with a certain special prerogative those churches built in honour of that singular Virgin and to fortify them with the safeguard of apostolic protection, lest they be harassed by undue vexations.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present charter. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by grant of popes, generosity [Col. 0878C] of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. We have judged that the following should be expressly set down by their proper names:

Yegui with all its appurtenances; Hugar with all its appurtenances; Surbac with all its appurtenances; and San with all its appurtenances; Yrugium with all its appurtenances; Ollonium with all its appurtenances; Urriatciriaga with all its appurtenances; Villaria with all its appurtenances; the little monastery of Saint Clement with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Just with all its appurtenances; Yart with all its appurtenances; the estate of Arcubus with all [Col. 0878D] its appurtenances; Turres with all its appurtenances; Turellas with all its appurtenances; Mendavia with all its appurtenances; Sotogarria with all its appurtenances; Althesa with the church of Saint Saviour; Legarda with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Eulalia with all its appurtenances; Monarisgustia with all its appurtenances; Oivartum with all its appurtenances; Tafalia with all its appurtenances; Olith with all its appurtenances; Harroniz with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Aemilianus with all its appurtenances; Luquing with all its appurtenances; Loyen with all its appurtenances; Subice with all its appurtenances; Cirria with all its appurtenances; Rotas of Puente la Reina; Arbescaa with all its appurtenances; Subjelcaa [Col. 0879A] with all its appurtenances; Hisquidia with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Estella; Saint Martin of Arria; Saint Emeterius; Saint James of Aloru; the church of Melche; the village of Sabaal; and Saint John of Sada.

We also grant that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the final wish of anyone who has decided to be buried there, unless he is excommunicated or under interdict; saving, nevertheless, the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.
