When a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a low voice.

Moreover, no one may presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands and at your own expense, or from the fodder of your animals. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any cunning of deception or by force, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent or the sounder part of their counsel, provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved unimpaired and entire, to benefit in every way the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone, therefore, in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia. I, John, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul and Januaria. I, Boso, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina. I, William, cardinal priest of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in [Col. 0879D] Damaso. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon beside the temple of Agrippa. I, Peter de Bosi, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Vitellus, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at Tusculum through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, in the fifth indiction, in the year 1172 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

M. He confirms all the rights and goods of the monastery of Saint Mary of Tremiti. (Tusculum, July 25.)

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, V, 441.]

[Col. 0880A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ANASTASIUS, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Tremiti, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

By the authority and duty of the Apostolic See we are compelled to concern ourselves for the condition of all churches, and, with the Lord’s help, especially to provide for the peace of those which adhere more particularly to that See and are subject to it as by proper right. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your truly just petitions; and, following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, Innocent and Paschal, Roman pontiffs, we have received under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to the Lord’s service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order, known to have been established in that monastery according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s favor, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

In the county of Chieti, the church of Saint Mary in Frisa with its appurtenances; the castle of Rivo Maris, with the church of Saint Peter and its appurtenances; the castle of Aquaviva, with its churches and their appurtenances; the castle of Senella with its appurtenances; the castle of Turricella; the castle of Planati; one third of the Castle of Linari; and the castle called Sparpaglia with its appurtenances.

In the county of Molise, the church of Saint Paul with its hill; the church of Saint Nicholas, and another church of Saint Nicholas, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint John of Montenegro with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Sylvester of Terramala; the church of Saint Leotherius with its appurtenances; the castle of Guillionisi; and, in its territory, the church of Saint Nicholas, the church of Saint Lucy, the church of Saint Vitus of Vallesurda, and another church of Saint Vitus of Biferno, with all their appurtenances; the castle of Vetrana; the church of Saint Mary in Arcora; the castle of Campo dell’Abbadessa; and the church of Saint Quiricus, with all their appurtenances.

In the principality of Benevento, the churches of Saint Lucy, Saint Martin, Saint Nicholas, Saint John, Saint Mary in Corneto, and Saint Nicholas of Sapione, with all their appurtenances; the castle of Tora; the castle of Petraficta, with all their appurtenances; the church of Saint Andrew with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter in Puliano; the city of Mari; and the castle of Vena de Causa, with all their appurtenances.

In the territory of Ripa Alta, the churches of Saint John, Saint Angel, Saint Paul, and Saint Lawrence, with all their appurtenances. In the territory of Lesina, the churches of Holy Cross, Saint Mary, Saint Anthony, and Saint Andrew, with their appurtenances. In the territory of Città, the churches of Saint Felicitas and Saint Simeon, with all appurtenances. And in the territory of the Castle of Serra, the church of Saint John with its appurtenances. In the territory of Tragonaria, the church of Saint Angel with all its appurtenances. In the territory of Dénia, the church of Saint Mary of the Sea with its appurtenances, the church of Saint Angel of Rocca, the church of Saint Nicholas of Lauris, and another church of Saint Nicholas of Gregory, with all their appurtenances. In the territory of Monte Sant’Angelo on Gargano, the church of Saint Mary of Calana with all its appurtenances. In the territory of Trani, the church of Saint Blaise with all its appurtenances, and Saint Mary of Calenella. In the city of Bestia, the church of Saint John outside that city, and the churches of Saint James, Saint Lawrence, and Saint Thecla, with all their possessions. In the city of Troia, the church of Saint Vincent with all its appurtenances.

You may receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of churches or altars, and ordinations of monks or clerics to be promoted to sacred orders from whatever bishop you choose, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these things to you freely and without any improper demand.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any stratagem of usurpation or by force, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall judge according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict to be elected. The person elected, moreover, shall go to the Roman pontiff for consecration.

Know, moreover, that this place is so special and proper to our Apostolic See that no archbishop, abbot, duke, marquis, count, viscount, castald, or any other person great or small may claim for himself any lordship whatsoever in that place or inflict any injury upon that monastery.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole and undiminished for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, etc.

[Col. 0882A]

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius, have subscribed.  
I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, have subscribed.  
I, Boso, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso, have subscribed.  
I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore, have subscribed.  
I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, have subscribed.  
I, Ugo, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius beside the Temple of Agrippa, have subscribed.  
I, Vitellius, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.  
I, Peter de Bono, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquirio, have subscribed.

Given at Tusculum by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 25 July, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1171, and in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

## MI. He confirms the agreement made between Dominic, abbot of Cassino, and John, bishop of Fondi. (Tusculum, 12 September.)

[GATTULA, *History of Cassino*, 262.]

[Col. 0882C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons D., abbot, and the brethren of Cassino: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Matters reasonably settled between persons by judgment or agreement ought, lest they be torn from their firmness by anyone’s malice or altered by rash presumption, to remain ratified and unshaken; and they ought fittingly to be strengthened by apostolic protection. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by this present writing so that it may be observed inviolate for all time, the agreement which our venerable brother R., bishop of Aquino, and our beloved sons G., abbot of Fossanova, A., abbot of Saint Lawrence of Aversa, and G., abbot of Casamari, are known reasonably to have made between you and our venerable brother, the bishop of Fondi, concerning the churches of Saint Magnus, Saint Honuphrius in the field of Melle, Saint Elias in Ambrifo, and Saint Martin in Terelle, granting to that bishop the church of Saint Martin in Ynula and a certain tract of land called *limata*, as is contained in the authentic instrument made concerning it. …

We decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever to infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Tusculum, 12 September.

## MII. To Henry II, king of England.—He urges him, by his power, to bring back and preserve in the worship of the Christian faith the people of Ireland, stained by very many impurities and abominations. (Tusculum, 20 September.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, etc., I, 45.]

[Col. 0883B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, HENRY, illustrious king of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Through widespread report and trustworthy testimony we have learned, not without great gladness of heart, how you, like a devout king and a magnificent prince, have triumphed wonderfully and gloriously—by the Lord’s working, and, as we firmly believe, with the purpose that you might extend the power of your serenity against that uncultivated and undisciplined people—over that Irish nation which, setting aside the fear of God, wanders everywhere like an unbridled creature through the precipices of vices, rejects the religion and virtue of the Christian faith, destroys itself by mutual slaughter, and inhabits that kingdom which, as we have learned, the Roman princes, conquerors of the world, left inaccessible in their time.

For, to pass over for the present other enormities and vices to which that people, abandoning the religion of the Christian faith, devotes itself with considerable irreverence: as our venerable brethren Christian, bishop of Lismore and legate of the Apostolic See, and the archbishops and bishops of that land have informed us by their letters, and as our beloved son R., archdeacon of Llandaff, a prudent and discerning man especially bound to your royal majesty by a bond of devotion, who saw these matters with eyewitness certainty, has carefully and wisely explained to you orally, that people has perhaps thus become more fully known to your royal serenity: they publicly take their stepmothers and are not ashamed to beget children by them; a brother has intercourse with his brother’s wife while the latter is alive; one man has sexual relations with two sisters as concubines; and many, putting aside their mothers, take their daughters. All alike eat meat openly during Lent; they do not pay tithes; and they show no due reverence whatever to God’s holy churches and ecclesiastical persons.

Therefore, because, as we have learned from the reports of those same archbishops and bishops and from the fuller and more explicit account given us by the aforesaid archdeacon, you have, by divine inspiration, raised your mind to assemble your magnificent naval and land force in order to subject that people to your rule and eradicate the foulness of so great an abomination, we regard this as pleasing and acceptable, as we ought; and we offer devout thanksgivings to Him from whom every good proceeds and who, in His saving good pleasure, orders the pious acts and purposes of His faithful. In earnest prayers we beseech almighty God that, just as through the power of your greatness the unlawful deeds committed in that aforesaid land have already begun to cease and the shoots of virtues to spring up in place of vices, so also, with the Lord’s cooperation, through you that people may, casting aside the foulness of sins, receive in every respect the full discipline of Christian religion, to the unfading crown of your eternal glory and the advancement of its own salvation.

We therefore ask, admonish, and exhort your royal excellency in the Lord, and impose this upon you for the remission of sins: that you should more earnestly strengthen and confirm your purpose in the undertaking which you have laudably begun, and by your power bring back and preserve that people in the worship of the Christian faith; so that, as you have undertaken so great a labor against it, as we believe, for the pardon of your sins, you may also deserve to receive an eternal crown from the advancement of its salvation.

And because, as your magnificent excellency knows, the Roman Church has a different right in an island than on a large and continuous mainland, we, holding hope and confidence in the fervor of your devotion—that you desire not merely to preserve that Church’s rights but also to enlarge them, and that where it has no right you ought to confer such right upon it—ask and earnestly admonish your magnificence to take care diligently to preserve for us in the aforesaid land the rights of blessed Peter; and, if it has no such rights there, that your greatness establish and assign those same rights to that Church, so that we may owe abundant thanks to your royal highness, and you may appear to offer to God the first fruits of your glory and triumph.

Given at Tusculum, 20 September.

## MIII. To the kings and princes of Ireland.—He urges them to ensure that they preserve firm and unshaken, with due submission, the fealty which they made to Henry II, king of England, under the sanctity of an oath. (Tusculum, 20 September.)

[Same source.]

[Col. 0884D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the noble men, kings, and princes of Ireland: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When common report and certain testimony made it very fully known to us that you had received our dearest son in Christ, H[enry], the illustrious king of England, as your king and lord and had sworn fealty to him, we conceived so much the greater joy in our hearts because, through the power of that king and with the Lord’s cooperation, there will be greater peace and tranquillity in your land, and the Irish people, which by the enormity and foulness of its vices appeared to have wandered so far away, will be more earnestly instructed in divine worship and will receive a better discipline of the Christian faith.

Accordingly, for having freely subjected yourselves to so powerful and magnificent a king and such a devoted son of the Church, we commend your prudence with fitting praise, since no slight benefit is expected thereby to come to you, to the Church, and to the whole people of that land. We therefore earnestly admonish your nobility and command that you take care to preserve firm and unshaken, with due submission, the fealty which you made under the sanctity of an oath to so great a king; and that you show yourselves toward him subject and devoted in humility and gentleness, so that you may always receive his ampler favor and we may be bound to commend your prudence worthily on that account.

Given at Tusculum, 20 September.

## MIV. To Christian, bishop of Lismore, legate of the Apostolic See, and to the archbishops of Ireland.—Concerning support for the Catholic king of England and most Christian prince. (Tusculum, 20 September.)

[Same source.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren CHRISTIAN, bishop of Lismore, legate of the Apostolic See, and GEL[ASIUS], archbishop of Armagh, DONATUS, archbishop of Cashel, LAURENCE, archbishop of Dublin, and CATHOLICUS, archbishop of Tuam, and to their suffragans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

How greatly the Irish people is infected with enormities of vice, and how, setting aside the fear of God and the religion of the Christian faith, it pursues those things which bring danger to souls, has become known to us from the series of your letters and has also frequently come to the knowledge of the Apostolic See through the truthful testimony of others.

Thus, having learned from your letters that, through the power of our dearest son in Christ, H[ENRY], the illustrious king of the English—who, moved by divine inspiration, assembled his forces and subjected to his rule that barbarous, uncultivated people ignorant of divine law—the unlawful things committed in your land have already begun to cease, with the Lord’s cooperation, we rejoiced with joy. And to Him who granted so great a victory and triumph to the aforesaid king we render immeasurable thanksgivings, humbly praying that through the vigilance and care of that king, with your assistance, that undisciplined and untamed people may in every respect and in all things be encouraged toward the worship of divine law and the religion of the Christian faith, and that you and the other ecclesiastical men may enjoy due honor and tranquillity.

Since it is fitting that you should apply careful diligence and favor to the pursuit of what has been begun with so devout a purpose, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic writings that, insofar as you can, without prejudice to your rank and office, you diligently and manfully assist the aforesaid king—as a magnificent man and a son most devoted to the Church—in maintaining and preserving that land and in uprooting from it the foulness of so great an abomination.

And if any kings, princes, or other men of that land should rashly attempt to act against the obligation of their oath and the fealty shown to the aforesaid king, then, unless he speedily comes to his senses at your admonition as he ought, relying on apostolic authority and laying aside every occasion and excuse, strike him with ecclesiastical censure. You are to execute our command faithfully and effectively, so that, just as the aforesaid king, as a Catholic and most Christian prince, is said kindly and graciously to have heeded us in restoring to you tithes and other ecclesiastical rights, and in all matters concerning ecclesiastical liberty, so you also may firmly preserve for him those matters which concern royal dignity and, as far as lies in you, cause them to be preserved by others.

Given at Tusculum, 20 September.

## MV. He receives the Church of Padua under his protection and confirms its goods and possessions. (Tusculum, 10 October.)

[ORSATO, *History of Padua*, 333.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILFRED, archpriest, and the canons of the Church of Padua, present and future, canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

Although unworthy, we have been entrusted with the care and concern of all churches, so that we ought diligently to labor with watchful care for their condition and exercise the solicitude of apostolic circumspection. Since by the office of our assumed administration we are bound to attend carefully to the peace of the churches, the patronage of apostolic protection ought on no account to be lacking to you and your Church. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church, in which you are devoted to divine service, strengthening it by the privilege of this present writing.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods assigned to your benefit and necessities it justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s favor, through the grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors. Of these goods, those which the bishops of Padua of former times, of good memory, assigned by pious liberality and reasonable provision to the use of the canons of the aforesaid Church, we have judged ought to be confirmed by apostolic authority to you and your successors and recorded by their proper names:

The chapel of Saint Lucy of Padua; all the tithes of that city, especially those from mills situated within the district of Padua, together with all villages and hamlets adjoining it; whatever right you have in the tithe of Limena; the tithes of the village of Aggeris; the tithe of Bussilago belonging to the commune of the village of Altichiero; of Torre, Milianiga, Cacintaga, Noenta, the village of Bergani; half of the tithes of Scandolato; of Fovea Liutara, Casale, Leone, Albinasico, Roncone, Mandria, Spasiano, Volta, Burzigana, Tencharola, Sermedaula, on both sides of the Storta, and of Bibano; likewise the tithes of the parish church of Pernumia with its villages and dependent churches; and the tithes of Cartura, Arzere, Gazo, and Gurgo; and the tithes from all cleared lands which, in the time of Bellino, your late bishop of good memory, were cleared, or shall henceforth be cleared in the aforesaid places.

Excepted, however, is the tithe from the demesne of the monastery of Saint Peter, which it possesses at Volta, according to the grant which the canons formerly made to that monastery; and excepted is the tithe from a certain part of the wood of Brenta, called Choatia, which was offered or granted to that monastery together with ownership of the land itself by the aforesaid Bishop Bellino. Also, the chapel of Saint Saviour of Camino; the chapel of Saint Peter of Strata; the chapel of Saint Martin of Savonaria; and the tithes from cleared lands which your Church has cleared, or will cause to be cleared, in the wood called Purpura or known by other names, bounded on one side by the river Brenta and on the other by the ditch of Stalvetere.

Also, the chapel of Saints Nicholas and Basil of Roncalia; the chapel of Saint Fidentius of Roncaliutari; the chapel of Saint Fidentius of Pulveraria, with all tithes of the place called Pulveraria; the chapel of Saint Michael at the Well of the Vitaliani, with all the lands which you hold there and their tithes; the chapel of Saint Mary of Spasiano; the chapel of Saint Bartholomew of Tencarolia; the chapel of Saints Fabian and Sebastian of Bruzigona; the chapel of Saint Fidentius of Sermendaula; and the chapel of Saint Bartholomew of Fossato.

Furthermore, we likewise confirm to you and, through you, to your Church, all lands of Padua and Roncalia with their tithes and fourth parts which Ildebert and Gauslin, bishops of Padua, and their other predecessors granted to your Church; the lands of Lignario with three tithe-rights; and all offerings or grants reasonably made to the aforesaid Church.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole and undiminished for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the due reverence owed to your bishop.

If, therefore, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Gualterius, bishop of Albano.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, John, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius.  
I, Roto, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor.  
I, Pegus, cardinal priest of Saint Lawrence in Damaso.  
I, Adicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.  
I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian.  
I, Hugh, cardinal deacon and custodian beside the Temple of Agrippa.

Given at Tusculum by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 10 October, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1172, and in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

## MVI. To Hugh III, duke of Burgundy.—He accepts the estate given to himself and the Roman Church near Dijon for building a church answerable only to the Roman pontiff. (Tusculum, 8 November.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 927.]

[Col. 0888C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman HUGH, duke of Burgundy: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we should graciously yield to the petitions of noble and powerful men when they are known to rest upon reason and propriety, and willingly grant them effective hearing, so that they may be more fervently encouraged toward the advantage and advancement of the churches when they know that their just petitions are readily heard by the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, moved by the fervor of your devotion and the urgency of your petition, we have received into the right and property of the Roman Church the estate which you have generously offered to blessed Peter and to us at Dijon for building a church and its offices.

> **[Note: Col. 0887D]** When Duke Hugh was returning from his journey to Jerusalem, as he himself relates in a letter of 1172 concerning the foundation and endowment of the chapel at Dijon: “I, Hugh, duke of Burgundy, wish it to be known to those present and future that, as I was going to Jerusalem, because of the excessive turbulence of the sea and the severity of the impending peril, both I and all who were aboard the ship were grievously terrified. Therefore, making a vow, I promised God that I would build on my estate near Dijon a church in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and Saint John the Evangelist. It consequently happened that, on my return, coming to Rome, I offered to God through the hand of Alexander, supreme pontiff of good memory, what I had vowed, and caused it to be confirmed by apostolic authority, as is contained in the authentic instrument which I obtained from him,” etc.]

And we grant you the authority and permission to build there a church which shall answer only to the Roman pontiff, prohibiting by apostolic authority any bishop or other ecclesiastical person from claiming for himself any right whatsoever in that church or in the clerics serving that church.

Given at Tusculum, 8 November.

## MVII. He receives the monastery of Cona under his protection and enumerates and confirms its goods and possessions. (Tusculum, 16 November.)

[D. MARRIER, *History of Saint Martin of the Fields*, book IV, 304.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior of the monastery of Cona and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

A pious request should be fulfilled with a corresponding result, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth laudably and the requested benefit may undoubtedly gain strength. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, strengthening it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s favor, through the grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of Saint Peter of Cona with all its appurtenances, and whatever you possess there; whatever you possess in the territory of Foissy; whatever you possess on Mount Arlais; the church of Saint Martin of Dormella with all its appurtenances; and the mill of Mont-Moret, situated in the parish of that church. Whatever you possess in the church of Saint Martin of Miri; in the church of Savius; in the church of Saint Valerian; in the church of Saint Lupus of Ville-Thierry; in the church of Saint Martin of Truisi and in that same village; in Varennes, Valentiis, and Lavile; namely, the water surplus to the monastery, with the right of passage; the meadows of Milleris given to your monastery by Ata, countess of Blois, of good memory; a fourth part of the *salagium* of Masteriolo and the rent of Moncellis; whatever you possess in the *stasmi* mill of Saint Valerian; the land of Chasnet; whatever you possess in the village of Emanti; the land which you possess on Mount Machoi; whatever you possess at Palai and in the wood of Arlais; whatever you possess in the wood of Saint Maurice and in the viscount’s wood of Saint Peter; and the land which you possess in the parish of Blena—meadows, a mill, alder-grove, and woodland; a fourth part of the territory of Villafrod; and the allod of Saveniaco.

We also decree that the burial-place of the same house shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; saving, nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose priests and present them to the bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust to them the care of souls, so that they shall answer to the bishop for the care of the people and to you for temporal matters. Furthermore, no one shall presume to exact tithes from your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the fodder of your animals.

When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. Upon the death of you, the present prior of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any stratagem of usurpation or by force, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall judge according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict to be elected.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole and undiminished for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical person, etc.

Given at Tusculum by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 16 November, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1172, and in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

## MVIII. Privilege for the nunnery of Saint Mary of Sinningthwaite. (Tusculum, 18 December.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, I, 828.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, CHRISTIANA, prioress of the monastery of Saint Mary of Sinningthwaite, and her sisters, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Whenever we are asked for something known to accord with religion and propriety, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and bestow suitable support upon the desires of those who ask. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of blessed Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, in which you are devoted to divine service, strengthening it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the observance of the Cistercian brethren shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s favor, through the grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; Haget, by the gift of Geoffrey son of Bertrand; two carucates of land, by the gift of Simon Ward, Matilda his wife, and William her son; and the place called Essholt, with its appurtenances in woodland, plain, arable land, and water, free and quit from every exaction, as is contained in their authentic instrument made concerning it.

Further, desiring to provide for your peace and tranquillity with paternal solicitude, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone, within the enclosures of your monastery or granges, from daring to commit violence, robbery, or theft; set fire; seize or kill a person. You may also receive into your conversion clerics or laypersons fleeing the world who are free and absolved, and retain them in your monastery without anyone’s opposition. Moreover, we prohibit, etc.

Given at Tusculum by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January [18 December], in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1172, and in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

## MIX. To the convent of Saint Augustine at Canterbury he confirms “the churches of Minster and Faversham for the repair of the church consumed by fire”; and grants “that they may choose clerics in their parish churches and present them to the diocesan bishop.”

[Chronicle of W. Thorn, in TWYSDEN, *Writers of English Affairs*, II, 1815.]

**YEAR 1170–1173.**
MX. To Theobald and the clerics of the church of St. Anastasia [also St. Lucy] at Verona: he declares that the sentence pronounced against him by Hildebrand of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles and by Raymond, bishop of Brescia, “according to the custom of the city of Verona,” has been annulled by himself.

[Decretals of Gregory, book II, title 27, chapter 8.]

[Col. 0891D]

**YEAR 1171–1173.**

**MXI. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—That Agatha be restored to R. of Adversa, her husband.** (Tusculum, January 4.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 875.]

Agatha, the woman bearing these letters, having come before the clemency of the apostolic see, showed us by her humble complaint [Col. 0892A] that, although she had been lawfully betrothed to R. of Adversa in the sight of the Church, had lived with him for eighteen years, and had borne him three children, R. of Sablois, lord of the land, made him and his relatives swear that he would dismiss and separate himself from her. Thus it came about that he dismissed her without just cause, deprived her for three years of the comfort of married life, and compelled her to suffer much want and distress. Since a husband neither can nor ought to dismiss his wife without just cause, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, under injunction, that, if this is so, you urgently admonish the aforesaid R. and compel him by our authority to receive the said A. kindly as his sister and treat her with marital affection, and to repay in full the money which she borrowed for her necessities [Col. 0892B].

Moreover, if she has doubts concerning the man, you shall cause him to give her complete security, so that she need no longer have any doubt on that account. But if he scorns to obey your admonitions, bind him, the aforesaid R., and the other principal supporters of this wrongdoing by the bond of excommunication, without impediment from appeal; place their lands under interdict; and cause her dower to be restored to that woman, every pretext and appeal being set aside. Nevertheless, if, after he has received her back, persons appear who wish, and are lawfully able, to challenge the marriage contracted between them, hear the case and, employing episcopal deliberation, decide it by a canonical judgment.

Furthermore, if they have been together for so long a time, no persons are readily to be admitted to accuse this marriage unless certain indications and suspicions appear that their kinship is so close that, according to God and justice, they cannot and ought not remain together. We also will that, within eleven days after receipt of these letters, you carry out our command with the greatest diligence in the manner stated above; and that you admit as witnesses none of those who were present at their betrothal and, having testified, advanced no objection against the marriage. Know that it is safer to leave persons who have been joined together less lawfully than to separate those who have been joined lawfully.

Given at Tusculum, the second day before the Nones of January.

**MXII. To the same.—For the abbot of Maroilles against C., knight of Taisnières.** (Tusculum, January 6.)

[Ibid., col. 876.]

[Col. 0892D]

From the complaint transmitted to us by the abbot and brethren of the church of Maroilles, we have learned that C., knight of Taisnières, and his sons violently withhold the tithes of their houses, which are known to belong to the aforesaid church; and that they presume unreasonably to take from that church the land-rent of one ploughland situated in the wood of Becloiz. Worse still, although the abbot and brethren object, they hold the altar of the said church and do not fear to receive its offerings at peril to their souls [Col. 0893A].

The same abbot and brethren also informed us that, although B., knight of Romeries, holds from them in fief one half of the revenues of that same village, he acknowledges that he ought to collect and guard the other half; yet he forbids the same abbot and brethren to build a house in the said village, does not permit their custodian to be there, and presumes to withhold sixty Hainaut pounds from the property of the same church. Since, by the duty of the dignity entrusted to us, we are bound to preserve their rights for all churches and to defend them more earnestly from the assaults of evildoers with the shield of apostolic protection, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you admonish and strictly compel the said C. and his sons to restore to the aforesaid abbot and brethren the tithes withheld, or their value, and the aforesaid land-rent; that henceforth they inflict upon them no annoyance or burden concerning that land-rent or the collection of the tithes; or else, within forty days after receipt of these letters, that they provide complete justice in your presence, with recourse to appeal removed [Col. 0893B].

They shall likewise restore to the aforesaid abbot and brethren the custody of the altar and the offerings taken away, and shall in no way thereafter interfere in the matter. Do not delay diligently to admonish and compel the aforesaid B., knight of Romeries, not to prevent on any ground the aforementioned brethren from collecting the half of the revenues of the said village, from building a house in that village, or from having their custodian there; and to restore to the same abbot and brethren, without deduction, the aforesaid sum of sixty pounds; or else, in your presence and within the prescribed term, with impediment from appeal removed, do not delay to require him to render full justice [Col. 0893C]. But if he and the others whom we have mentioned scorn to obey your admonitions, bind them by the bond of excommunication, appeal set aside, until restitution of what was taken and suitable satisfaction have been made.

Given at Tusculum, the eighth day before the Ides of January.

**MXIII. To the same.—For the same, against Lambert of Nigella and Oilard of Landrecies.** (Tusculum, January 6.)

[Ibid., col. 677.]

[Col. 0893D]

We have received the complaint of the abbot and brethren of the church of Maroilles: Lambert of Nigella and Oilard of Landrecies presume violently to take the tithe of Fustor, which belongs to that church, asserting that they hold that tithe from the said church in fief, although, as is said, the abbot and brethren are wholly unaware of this. Certain of their neighbours also do not fear violently to take wheat and oats from the church’s own granaries, asserting that they ought to receive them as a fief.

Since wrongdoers of this kind must be sharply punished for their presumption by the sword of ecclesiastical correction, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you admonish and strictly compel the aforesaid men and those of their neighbours whom the aforementioned abbot and brethren name to you to restore, without deduction, the tithe, wheat, and oats taken from them, or their value; and that henceforth they presume in no way to take anything from the same brethren; or else, within forty days after receipt of these letters, with appeal set aside, they shall provide complete justice in your presence [Col. 0894A]. If at your admonition they are unwilling to fulfil either of these requirements, bind them by the bond of excommunication, appeal set aside, until they carry out one of them.

Given at Tusculum, the eighth day before the Ides of January.

**MXIV. To B[artholomew], archbishop of Exeter.—What penances are to be imposed upon those who confess that they came, short of or at the laying on of hands, with intent to kill, strike, or seize Thomas, formerly archbishop of Canterbury; those who assert that they inflamed the king’s mind to hatred, from which the homicide may have followed; those who say that after his death they seized the spoils of that holy man and of his people; those who know themselves guilty solely by association with excommunicated persons; clerics known to have been armed participants in so great a crime; and clerics who advised that the holy man should be seized.**

[Letters of Gilbert Foliot, ed. GILES, II, 80.]

[Col. 0894B]

ALEXANDER the Third, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother B., bishop of Exeter, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as it is fitting and wholly consonant with reason that grave and difficult questions should be referred to the judgment of the apostolic see, so too, by the office of care which we have undertaken, it is incumbent upon us to resolve those questions, insofar as God grants us to do so, and to answer each person seeking counsel from us; so that, through the providence of the Roman Church, which by the Lord’s ordering holds primacy throughout the world, questions may be resolved and uncertainty in these matters removed from everyone’s hearts [Col. 0894C]. Although, concerning the questions which your discernment has sent to us for decision, we do not doubt that you are prudent and circumspect, nevertheless the ministry of our service compels us to answer you concerning them according to our discernment and judgment.

Indeed, since you are learned, wise, and discerning, and highly experienced in these matters, you know more fully that, in the offences of individuals, not only the nature and seriousness of the crime, but also age, knowledge, sex, and status must be considered [Col. 0894D]. For penance ought to be imposed upon each person not merely according to the nature and seriousness of the offence, but according to the considerations already mentioned, and according to the place and time in which the offence was committed; since, as you yourself know, the same offence must be punished more severely in one person than in another.

Those who confess that they came, short of or at the laying on of hands, with intent to kill, strike, or seize that holy and venerable man, formerly archbishop of Canterbury—if his death had followed from that seizure—are to be punished with an equal or almost equal penalty. Those also who came not to strike, but to aid the assailants should the violence which some were about to undertake be resisted, are to be punished with a somewhat lighter penalty. For, since it is written, “He who was able to save a man from death and did not save him, killed him,” it is plain that those who came to assist murderers against others are not free from the guilt of homicide. Nor is he free from the taint of secret complicity who, though able to do so openly, fails to oppose the crime [Col. 0895A].

Those, however, who assert that they inflamed the king’s mind to hatred, from which the homicide perhaps followed, are to be punished sufficiently harshly and severely, though not so strictly—unless perhaps by their suggestions they had provoked the king himself to that homicide. Nor were those free from guilt, nor should they be exempt from punishment, who, although ignorant of that wicked plot, nevertheless, if they knew the men to be hired assassins, assisted by guarding their baggage [Col. 0895B].

As for those who say that after his death they seized the spoils of that holy man and of his people: if they committed no other offence in so great a crime, we judge them free from punishment for his death. Yet they are bound to restore in full what they seized to those to whom it belonged, if they have means from which they can make restitution; and a moderate penance is nonetheless to be imposed upon them for this. For although some of them confess that they distributed what they seized to the poor, they ought not to have given other people’s property to the poor when they could have restored it to its owners.

For those who know themselves guilty solely through association with excommunicated persons, penance must be imposed according to the length of time during which they remained in that wrongdoing, and after inquiry whether they associated knowingly or unknowingly, through fear or affection [Col. 0895C].

We judge that clerics known to have been armed participants in so great a crime, and those clerics who advised that the same holy man should be seized, must be permanently deposed not only from service at the altar, but in such a manner that they may never in any way read lessons in churches or sing responsories separately in the choir. Rather, in the psalms they are to strive before God to implore pardon for what they have done. Moreover, these clerics are to be confined, if possible, in the strict cloister of monks or regular canons, in such a way that for seven or five years they must be barred from entering churches [Col. 0895D].

Concerning the matter on which you sought our counsel—whether students who strike one another, whether under age or of full age, and clerics or religious men in cloisters, must according to that canon which decrees that those who lay violent hands upon clerics are to be sent to the apostolic see for absolution, come to that same see for their absolution—we answer your inquiry as follows. If clerics below the age of puberty strike one another, or if one strikes another, they are not to be sent to the apostolic see, because their age excuses them. Nor are clerics to be sent there if, being of full age, they happen to strike one another not out of hatred, envy, or anger, but in playful frivolity [Col. 0896A].

Nor is a master to be sent there if he strikes a student who is a cleric for purposes of discipline or correction, because in such cases the laying on of violent hands cannot be imputed. But if the same students or secular clerics strike one another out of hatred, they must come to the apostolic see for absolution. Monks and regular canons, however they strike one another in the cloister, are not to be sent there, but are to be subjected to discipline according to the judgment and discretion of their abbot. If the abbot’s discretion does not suffice for their correction, the judgment of the diocesan bishop must be employed.

If a doorkeeper of some authority, acting maliciously under pretext of his office, injures a cleric, he may be absolved by his bishop, unless perhaps he has gravely wounded that cleric [Col. 0896B]. An official who has laid hands upon a cleric cannot obtain the benefit of absolution without a mandate from the Roman pontiff, because no layperson is given such authority over a cleric—unless, while repelling an onrushing crowd, he injures a cleric not deliberately but by accident. If, however, a person repels by force or injures a cleric who is using force against him, he ought not on that account to be sent to the apostolic see, provided he immediately repels force by force, since the laws and all rights permit force to be repelled by force. Nor is a person to be compelled to come to that see if he has laid violent hands upon a cleric found committing indecency with his own wife, mother, sister, or daughter. But if he catches him in fornication or adultery, where the woman with whom the fornication or adultery is committed is not related to him in so close a degree of blood, or if he otherwise lays violent hands upon him, he is not exempt from the sentence of that excommunication [Col. 0896C].

**YEAR 1173.**

**MXV. To the same.—Against the dean of St. Quentin and those subject to him, who demanded money for the blessing of marriages.** (Signia, February 2.)

[Ibid., col. 953.]

We remember having written to E., dean of St. Quentin [Col. 0896D], that he should celebrate the divine offices at women’s betrothals freely, as is proper, and without any exaction, and should compel the priests subject to him to do the same. As we have learned, he did not hesitate to disregard our command, and he appealed to our hearing, together with three priests who supported him, against R., the priest bearing these letters, because the latter reproved him on this account; thus under this pretext he could exercise his wrongdoing more freely.

When the matter came before us, the aforesaid dean and the said priests neither appeared nor sent anyone to answer on their behalf. Since it is known to be incumbent upon our office to root out utterly simoniacal depravity both in the blessing of marriages and in burials, as well as in all ecclesiastical sacraments whatsoever, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, relying on apostolic authority, you compel the aforesaid dean to demand nothing in the blessing of marriages, at burials of the dead, or in any other ecclesiastical sacrament [Col. 0897A]. If it becomes known to you that, after the aforesaid appeal, he has presumed to make an exaction, do not delay, all appeal being set aside, to send him to us suspended from ecclesiastical office and benefice, together with your letters containing the truth of the matter, there to bear the penalty he deserves for so grave an offence of depravity.

Correct and punish severely the aforesaid priests who, having raised the cry of appeal, scorned to pursue that appeal, so that they may henceforth cease from such presumption and others may be deterred by their example [Col. 0897B]. We likewise command you by the authority of these letters to compel the said dean, all objection and appeal being set aside, to restore in full to the aforesaid priest all expenses which he incurred on the journey because of him.

Given at Signia, the fourth day before the Nones of February.

**MXVI. To the same.—Against G., dean of Unacort, accused of simony.** (Signia, February 2.)

[Ibid., col. 954.]

We ought to uproot simoniacal depravity with ever more earnest care by the sickle of apostolic provision, insofar as the prelates of churches may be corrupted more extensively by such a plague and ecclesiastical honour may be stained [Col. 0897C]. It has indeed been reported to us that G., dean of Unacort, seeking temporal profit rather than the salvation of souls, has so loosened the reins to the vice of avarice that, at the betrothals of women, putting aside all fear of God, he does not permit the divine offices to be celebrated in the church of Joi unless two or three solidi in the coinage of Cambrai are assigned to him as the price of wine. If any woman is betrothed and he has not received this stated price, he causes both bridegroom and bride to be bound by the bond of excommunication.

Since this is improper and wholly foreign to the sacred canons, and wounds which do not respond to the fomentations of medicine must be cut away with iron [Col. 0897D], we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, under injunction, that, if this is found to be so, you cause the aforesaid priest, suspended from office, to be brought before the apostolic presence with your letters containing the truth of the matter, there to bear the penalty he deserves for so grave an offence of depravity.

Given at Signia, the fourth day before the Nones of February.

**MXVII. To the same.—For the monastery of St. Saviour of Virtu.** (Signia, February 18.)

[Ibid., col. 955.]

We have received a complaint from our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the church of St. Saviour of Virtu [Col. 0898A], that G., priest, P. and R., knights, R. of Cismai, and certain others presume to harass the aforesaid church with many annoyances and burdens, and do not fear to stretch forth violent hands to plunder its possessions. Since it is our concern to provide with pastoral care that religious places are not exposed to the attacks of evil men, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this is so, within eleven days after receipt of these letters you urgently admonish and most strictly compel the aforesaid men not to delay restoring, without any objection, whatever they are known to have unjustly and unreasonably taken from the said abbot and brethren, and to leave them thereafter in peace and quiet [Col. 0898B]. Otherwise compel them to do this by ecclesiastical censure.

Given at Signia, the twelfth day before the Kalends of March.

**MXVIII. Privilege for the monastery of St. Saviour and St. Rotrude of Andres.** (Signia, February 25.)

[D’ACHERY, *Spicilegium*, folio edition, II, 812.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot of the monastery of St. Saviour and St. Rotrude, situated in the parish of Thérouanne, and to his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life: in perpetuity.

Whenever this is requested of us, etc. First, indeed, establishing that the monastic order which is known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall there be observed inviolate for all time [Col. 0898C]. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, acquire by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to state the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with its houses, lands, and other appurtenances. Furthermore, no one whatsoever shall presume to demand tithes from you of your newly cultivated lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or of the sustenance of your animals [Col. 0898D]. You may also receive free and unencumbered clerics or laymen fleeing from the world into your conversion, and retain them in your monastery without anyone’s opposition. We further forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your house, to depart from it without the permission of his abbot or master; and no one shall dare retain one who departs without the security of your common letters, unless he wishes to transfer to a stricter religious observance.

We also grant that the burial place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict [Col. 0899A]; saving, however, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Moreover, when there is a general interdict upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices with closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding those under interdict and excommunicated persons, and in a subdued voice.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of fraud or violence, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, etc., saving the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop [Col. 0899B]. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, etc.

Given at Signia, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, the fifth day before the Kalends of March, sixth indiction, in the year 1172 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

**MXIX. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—Against the abbot of Anchin, who had despoiled a priest of his church.** (Signia, March 4.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 955.]

[Col. 0899C]

From the complaint of Hugh, priest and bearer of these letters, we have learned that our beloved son, the abbot of Anchin, despoiled him, without judgment or reasonable cause, of a certain church which he had held by grant of that abbot. Since ecclesiastical men ought not unreasonably to be ejected from possession of their churches or improperly troubled regarding them, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, after summoning both parties before you, you diligently investigate the truth of the matter. If the assertion of the said priest rests upon truth, cause that church, together with all things taken and received from it, to be restored to him without appeal [Col. 0899D]. Further, if this is so, punish severely the priest Jesse, who is said to have received that church after an appeal was made to us, so that he may henceforth fear to act contrary to appeals. Then, if the aforesaid abbot or the same priest should wish to bring an action against the aforesaid Hugh concerning the said church, hear the case and, appeal set aside, decide it with a due conclusion.

Given at Signia, the fourth day before the Nones of March.

**MXX. To the same.—Concerning the case between the canons of St. Martin and St. Mary of Laon.** (Signia, March 8.)

[Ibid., col. 956.]

We entrust to your experience, in which we have complete confidence, for hearing and for settlement by agreement or judgment, appeal set aside, the case known to be in dispute between our beloved sons the canons of St. Martin and the clerics of St. Mary of Laon [Col. 0900A] concerning two parts of the tithe of Mont-Cavillo. We therefore command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when you are asked concerning this matter, you summon both parties before you; and, after fully hearing and examining the arguments on both sides, decide the case within forty days after receipt of these letters, with remedy by appeal removed, through agreement or through justice.

Given at Signia, the eighth day before the Ides of March.

**MXXI. To Albert and Theodwin, legates of the apostolic see: he announces that Thomas, formerly archbishop of Canterbury, was enrolled among the ranks of saints on Ash Wednesday.** (Signia, March 10.)

[Letters of Gilbert Foliot, ed. GILES, II, 58.]

[Col. 0900B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ALBERT, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina, and THEODWIN, priest-cardinal of St. Vitalis, legates of the apostolic see: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although some accounts of the miracles of that holy man Thomas, formerly archbishop of Canterbury, had been brought to our attention by very many persons to whom we are accustomed, and bound, to give credit, we nevertheless awaited your testimony, so that we might proceed more freely in canonizing him, once through you we had become more certain concerning the miracles of that holy man [Col. 0900C]. Therefore, having received the testimony of your letters, on Ash Wednesday, with a multitude of clerics present in the church, we solemnly canonized that holy man and decreed that he should be enrolled in the glorious fellowship of martyrs.

Since we are sending letters about this matter not only to the English Church but also to the kings themselves, we direct your discretion to deliver those letters yourselves to the same kings, if possible, and to cause the letters which we send to the monks of Canterbury and to the English Church to be delivered.

Given at Signia, the sixth day before the Ides of March.

**MXXII. To the same.—Concerning the reconciliation of the church of Canterbury.** (Signia, March [?].)

[Letters of Gilbert Foliot, II, 58.]

[Col. 0900D]

We command you to have the church of Canterbury reconciled, provided, however, that the sacrament of its former dedication is not to be repeated. Rather, as is customary in the church of St. Peter, it is only to be sprinkled with holy water. Fare well.

**MXXIII. To the chapter of Canterbury.—Concerning the canonization of blessed Thomas, archbishop.** (Signia, March 12.)

[Letters of St. Thomas, ed. GILES, II, 39.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior and monks of the church of Canterbury [Col. 0901A]: greeting and apostolic blessing.

All the faithful ought to rejoice at the miracles of that holy and venerable man Thomas, your archbishop. But you ought to be filled with still greater joy and exultation in this matter, inasmuch as you more often behold his miracles with the faith of eyewitnesses, and your church has been particularly honoured by the presence of his most sacred body. Having considered the glory of his merits, by which he shone magnanimously in his lifetime, and having full certainty concerning his miracles not only from common and widespread report but also from the testimony of our beloved sons Albert, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina, and Theodwin, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Vitalis, legates of the apostolic see, and of many other persons [Col. 0901B], we solemnly canonized the aforesaid archbishop on Ash Wednesday, with a multitude of clerics and laypeople present in the church, after deliberation with our brethren; and we decreed that he should be numbered among the fellowship of holy martyrs.

Accordingly, by apostolic authority, we command you and all the faithful of England to celebrate every year with due veneration his birthday—the day on which he ended his life in glorious suffering. Since it is fitting and greatly expedient for you that his holy body be placed with the reverence and honour due to it, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, on some principal day, after a solemn procession and with clergy and people assembled, you reverently and devoutly place his body honourably in an altar [Col. 0901C]; or, placing it as is fitting in some worthy shrine, raise it aloft; and strive by your devout prayers to obtain from the Lord his patronage for the salvation of the faithful and the peace of the universal Church.

Given at Signia, the fourth day before the Ides of March. Farewell.

**MXXIV. To the clergy and people of England.—On the same subject.** (Signia, March 12.)

[Ibid., p. 75.]

ALEXANDER, pope, to the clergy and people of all England, concerning the canonization of St. Thomas.

[Col. 0901D]

England is fragrant with the sweetness and power of the signs which almighty God performs through the merits of that holy and venerable man Thomas, formerly archbishop of Canterbury; and everywhere the whole Christian religion of the faithful rejoices, because He who is wonderful and glorious in His saints has glorified His saint after death. His praiseworthy life shone with much glory of merits and was at last perfected by the martyrdom of a glorious contest. Although no one who considers his praiseworthy manner of life and his glorious passion can doubt his holiness, nevertheless our Redeemer and Saviour willed to illumine the tokens of his holiness with magnificent miracles, so that all might know that he who, for Christ, bore hardships and dangers with the constancy of unconquerable courage [Col. 0902A] had received in eternal blessedness the triumph of his labour and contest.

Having heard the innumerable and great miracles which the whole body of the faithful relates as continually occurring through the merits of that holy man, and having been especially assured concerning these matters, not without great joy, by our beloved brethren Albert, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina, and Theodwin, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Vitalis, legates of the apostolic see—who learned of those miracles with greater certainty because they were nearer to the place—and having given credence, as we ought, to the testimony of many other persons, we solemnly canonized the aforesaid archbishop in the church, with a great assembly of clerics and laypeople present there, on Ash Wednesday, after deliberation with our brethren [Col. 0902B]; and we decreed that he should be entered in the catalogue of saints.

We therefore admonish all of you and, by the authority which we exercise, strictly command you to celebrate solemnly each year the day of the passion of the aforesaid glorious martyr, and to strive through devout prayers to him to obtain forgiveness of sins; so that he who for Christ endured exile in life and the martyrdom of suffering in death with steadfast courage may, moved by the faithful’s unceasing supplication, intercede for you with the Lord.

Given at Signia, the fourth day before the Ides of March.

**MXXV. To the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches established throughout England.—On the same subject.** (Signia, March 13.)

[Radulf of Diceto, *Imagines Historiarum*, in TWYSDEN, *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, I, 569.]

[Col. 0902C]

“England is fragrant,” etc., as in the preceding letter. Given at Signia, the third day before the Ides of March.

**MXXVI. He takes the church of St. Stephen of Dijon under his protection and confirms its possessions and rights.** (Signia, March 14.)

[History of Saint-Étienne of Dijon, Preface, 112.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HER., abbot of St. Stephen of Dijon, and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life: in perpetuity.

[Col. 0902D]

It befits the clemency of apostolic governance to cherish religious men and strengthen their houses with pious protection. For it is recognized as worthy and consonant with propriety that we, who by the Lord’s ordering have been raised to the governance of churches, should both defend them from the malice of wicked men and fortify them with the patronage of the apostolic see. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of the present document.

First, indeed, establishing that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall there be observed inviolate for all time [Col. 0903A]. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, acquire through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state the following by their proper names:

The place itself, in which the aforementioned church dedicated in honour of blessed Stephen the protomartyr stands, with the cemetery inside the castle wall; the church of St. Medard, with the chapel of St. Vincent, cemetery, and tithes; the church of St. James of Tremoleto, with the chapel of St. Mary of the Market; the church of St. Martin of Fixius, with the chapel of St. Symphorian of Breschon and cemeteries [Col. 0903B]. We further add that the regular canons of the aforesaid church shall be instituted freely and without opposition in parish churches where three or four of them reside, one of whom shall undertake the care of souls. Furthermore, no one shall presume to demand tithes from you of your newly cultivated lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or of the sustenance of your animals.

We decree, therefore, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop.

If anyone therefore in future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 0903C] I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Gualter, bishop of Albano. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius. I, William, priest-cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Boso, priest-cardinal of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marius. I, Ardicio, priest-cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Cinthius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of Saint Justus beside the Temple of Agrippa. [Col. 0903D] I, Vitellius, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Aquiro. I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of Saint Angelo.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 14 March, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1172, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### MXXVII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims—On behalf of the abbot of Saint Medard against Elizabeth, a widow accused of usury. (Segni, 20 March.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 956.]

[Col. 0904A]

The beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of Saint Medard, have complained to us, and it has come to our hearing that Elizabeth, widow of Codin, Thomas her son-in-law, and the other successors of the aforesaid C., are attempting, by secular force, to extort from their church eleven marks of silver as interest; although the aforesaid E. and her husband are said to have received from that church, under the name of interest and to the peril of their souls, five hundred marks of silver beyond the principal. Since, therefore, [Col. 0904B] we can neither endure nor ought to permit that the aforesaid church be burdened, to the detriment of its salvation, by the aforesaid moneylenders in respect of an exaction of interest, when they ought rather to restore what they have wrongly received from that church, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, after summoning the parties before you within twenty days after receipt of these letters, you diligently and carefully investigate the truth of the matter. If the aforesaid brethren can prove that these same moneylenders have received their principal in full, admonish and induce them henceforth to presume to demand nothing from those brethren, either as principal or as interest; and, with all remedy of appeal removed, cause them altogether to desist from troubling them in this matter.

But if they refuse to comply with [Col. 0904C] your admonition, publicly excommunicate them, with all remedy of appeal removed, and cause them throughout your province to be carefully avoided until they have made fitting satisfaction. Nevertheless, admonish and induce them also to restore without difficulty to the said brethren whatever the aforesaid C. or his wife received from the aforesaid church beyond the principal; or, without delay, to reach a peaceful and amicable settlement with them.

Given at Segni, 20 March.

### MXXVIII. To the same—Concerning an annual payment of wax which he demanded from the priests of the deanery of Virtus. (Segni, 21 March.)

[Ibid., col. 957.]

[Col. 0904D]

The priests of the deanery of Virtus have informed us that, when formerly, at the prayers and admonition of G. [Note: [Col. 0903] Guy of Montaigu, who was elected in 1143, or Geoffrey, who preceded him.] formerly bishop of Châlons, they had induced their parishioners by diligent warnings and exhortations to contribute forty pounds of wax for the lights of the church of Saint Stephen, and later, through the intervention of Bishop Boso, had added ten pounds, the treasurer is attempting to convert what was bestowed as a gift into a debt, and to make profit from a work of piety. He compels them to exact one obol from each of their parishioners, poor and rich alike, and to assign it to him for wax. But the dean [Col. 0905A] and chapter of the church of Châlons, by letters sent to us, have stated that the prescribed payment ought to be rendered not as a free gift but as a debt.

Since the truth of the matter is not known to us, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when requested concerning this, you assemble together in one place, summon both parties before you, and, after fully hearing and ascertaining the arguments on both sides, decide the case by means of agreement or justice, with all remedy of appeal removed, so that neither party may complain of a failure of justice.

Given at Segni, 21 March.

### MXXIX. To the same—That he is not to absolve the priest P. from excommunication unless he makes amends. (Segni, 25 March.)

[Ibid., col. 959.]

[Col. 0905B]

If we remember correctly, we entrusted to our venerable brethren, the bishops of Amiens and Senlis, for hearing and due determination, the case concerning a certain house which is being litigated between A., priest of Saint Maurice, and P. Having summoned both parties before them, as we have learned, and having heard and examined the arguments on both sides, they adjudged that house to the aforesaid P. according to the order of law. They bound the aforementioned priest with the bond of anathema because he resisted surrendering that house to him. When he came into our presence, he was not, as he ought not to have been, absolved by us. [Col. 0905C] And when he had returned home, as has been reported to us, he presumed, as a contumacious and disobedient man, to celebrate the divine offices.

Since it belongs to our office to punish such presumption with due punishment, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you cause the aforesaid priest firmly and inviolably to observe the sentence of excommunication pronounced against him, until he has made fitting satisfaction for so grave an offence and gives firm security that he will comply with the sentence of the aforesaid bishops.

Given at Segni, 25 March.

### MXXX. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Sabinus of Piacenza. (Anagni, 28 March.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, II, 218.]

[Col. 0905D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons SAVINUS, abbot of the monastery of Saint Sabinus, situated near Piacenza, and his brethren, present and future, regularly appointed, for ever.

The duty of our office admonishes us, etc. Therefore, etc. Moreover, whatever possessions, etc., among which we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms:

In the city of Piacenza, the church of Saint Mary, the church of Saint Victoria, and one hospital with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Bartholomew; the church of the Holy Trinity; the church of Saint Ambrose with its hospital; the church of Saint Saviour, with a certain [Col. 0906A] hospital and all its appurtenances; the estate of Robiano with two churches, tithes, and everything belonging to it. Whatever you possess within and outside the castle of Arcuato, we confirm to you by this present writing. The castle of Besentioni with two churches and all things belonging to it. In the estate of Albiano, two churches with all their appurtenances. At Pontepuro, the church of Saint Martin with its appurtenances. The estate of Paterna with two churches. The estate of Torre with one church and its appurtenances. The estate of Conio with its church and the other things which you justly possess there. In the March of Genoa, namely in the valley of Segesta, the monastery of Saint Victoria with three chapels. Further, whatever Sigifred, bishop of Piacenza of good memory, is known to have bestowed upon your monastery in churches, tithes, *rationalia* [rights or revenues], and administration at Monte Arxizio. [Col. 0906B] At Visilano, the church of Saint George and whatever else you have there; the estate of Reggiano with the church of Saint Sabinus and all that belongs to it; the estate of Fabiano with the church of Saint Stephen; the estate of Saints Nabor and Felix with the church of Saint Sabinus; at Tavernaco, the church of Saint Mary; in the estate of Fontana Petrosa, the church of Saint Sabinus and the church of Saint Gregory, with all else that you justly possess there. At Suprarivo, the church of Saint Mary with its tithes; the hospital of Tretia with the church of Saint Nicholas; the estate of Moze with the church of Saint Sabinus and all things belonging to it.
