Also the tithes of the vineyard and of the bishop’s Broglio, and of another vineyard which is outside the gate of Saint Anthony; [Col. 0906C] and the fisheries which you possess in the Po, from the port of Portario as far as the mouth of the Cold Stream; the castle of Calenzano with everything you have there; the chapel of Saint Sabinus of Lechi with the other things you have there.

Moreover, of your newly cultivated lands, etc. In addition, by this present decree we enact that, according to ancient custom, you may ring the bells on the night of the Nativity of the Lord, at the beginning of Mass on Holy Saturday, and at Vespers. By this decree also we prohibit the bishop of Piacenza from imposing new and undue exactions upon you, your monastery, or your churches, or from inflicting undue burdens. We further prohibit anyone from building a new church or oratory within the bounds of your parish without the consent [Col. 0906D] of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, without prejudice to the privileges and authentic writings of the Roman Church. We decree, therefore, that it shall be permitted to no person whatever, etc., saving, etc. If anyone therefore, etc. Amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Gualter, bishop of Albano. I, John, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Bozo, priest-cardinal of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. [Col. 0907A] I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint . . . . I, Oddo, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Cinthius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Manfred, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of Saint Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Vitellus, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 28 March, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1172, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### MXXXI. He receives the church of Saint Eustorgius of Milan under protection and confirms its goods. (Anagni, 28 March.)

[GIULINI, *Memorie storiche di Milano*, VI, 544.]

[Col. 0907B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PHILIP, provost of the church of Saint Eustorgius, and his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed, for ever.

Whenever that which is known to accord with religion and uprightness is requested of us, it is fitting that we grant it with willing mind and give suitable assistance to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously [Col. 0907C] consent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. We enact that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms:

The hospital constructed in honour of God and for the support of the poor in the suburb of the Ticinese gate: its ordering and establishment, [Col. 0907D] governance, lordship, and investiture of the hospital and its supervision; all these, as they were granted to you by our venerable brother Galdinus, archbishop of Milan and legate of the Apostolic See, and confirmed by the protection of his writing, we confirm to you. The church of Saint Peter; the church of Saint Stephen with its tithes and other appurtenances.

We decree, therefore, that it shall be permitted to no person whatever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all shall be preserved unimpaired and entire for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority [Col. 0908A] of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If anyone therefore in future, etc.

In the circle:

“SHOW ME THY WAYS, O LORD.”

In the monogram: Fare well.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Gualter, bishop of Albano. I, John, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, of Saint Anastasia. I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Boso, priest-cardinal of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. [Col. 0908B] I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark. I, Oddo, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Cinthius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Manfred, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of Saint Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Vitellus, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Aquiro.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 28 March, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1172, in the fourteenth year [Col. 0908C] of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### MXXXII. Bull for the canons of the Church of Lausanne. (Anagni, 31 March.)

[*Mémoires de la Société d’histoire de la Suisse Romande*; Lausanne, 1838, octavo; vol. VII, p. 20; Gilliéron manuscript, vol. I, p. 83, drawn from Ruchat.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Lausanne, and their successors canonically appointed, for ever.

Whenever that which is recognized to accord with religion and uprightness is requested of us, it is fitting that we grant it with willing mind and give suitable [Col. 0908D] assistance to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously consent to your petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of Lausanne, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We enact that whatever possessions or goods which you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms: the church of Saint Mary and the altar of the Holy Cross, with all offerings throughout the year; the church of [Col. 0909A] Crans; the church of Saint Rothasius; the church of Telochino; the church of Juolene, with all its appurtenances; the church of Cavornaco with its appurtenances; the church of Crisi; the church of Grangia; the church of Rota; the church of Albaco; the church of Bullo; the church of Viviaco; the church of Orba with its appurtenances; the church of Morsiaco; and the church of Danusiaco with its appurtenances.

We decree, therefore, that it shall be permitted to no person whatever rashly to disturb you or the aforesaid Church, to take away your possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass you by any vexations; but that all be preserved entire for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical reverence due to your bishop. If any ecclesiastical or [Col. 0909B] secular person hereafter, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to contravene it, let that person, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict punishment at the last judgment. But to all who preserve the rights of that place, may the peace of the Lord Jesus Christ be granted, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

(Seal.) (Monogram.)

[Col. 0909C] I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Boso, priest-cardinal of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Gualter, bishop of Albano. I, Oddo, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, etc., etc.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 31 March, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1173, in the fourteenth year [Col. 0909D] of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### MXXXIII. He informs William, Archbishop of Sens, and his suffragans that Thomas, formerly Archbishop of Canterbury, was enrolled among the saints “at the beginning of Lent.” He orders the day on which he was slain to be celebrated each year. (Anagni, 2 April.)

[Sirmond, *Opera*, III, 886.]

“England is fragrant,” etc., as in Epistle 1024 above.

Given at Tusculum [read: Anagni], 2 April.

### MXXXIV. To Walter, Bishop of Aversa—That he is to celebrate yearly, with great veneration, the feast of Saint Thomas. (Anagni, April [?])

[*Letters of Saint Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 88.]

[Col. 0910A]

POPE ALEXANDER to the bishop of Aversa.

Because, though unworthy, we hold in the Church of God the supreme place in the stead of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we ought, by virtue of the office of the apostolate entrusted to us, all the more diligently to venerate on earth the most glorious martyr Thomas, formerly archbishop of Canterbury, who strove unto death for the justice of God and the liberty of the Church and, as though founded upon a firm rock, did not fear the words of the ungodly, [Col. 0910B] because it is certain that, as his merits require, he rejoices in eternal blessedness among the rejoicing choirs of saints.

For you have heard, and the greater part of the world knows through the revelation of divine grace, how Almighty God, who is wondrous and glorious in His saints, has gloriously magnified him on earth by the power of His might from the day when, through the palm of martyrdom, he entered heaven as victor—as we firmly believe without doubt—and does not cease daily to work many miraculous signs in his name. Therefore, after deliberation with our brethren, following earnest petitions from archbishops and bishops, and especially at the urging of our beloved sons Albert, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and Theodwin, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Vitalis, legates of the Apostolic See, who had more fully investigated the truth of the matter and had learned it by sight and hearing, [Col. 0910C] we have canonized him. Enrolling him in the catalogue of Saints, we establish that the day of his Passion—the day immediately after the feast of the Holy Innocents—is to be solemnly celebrated each year in honour of God and counted among the feasts of the holy martyrs. Through the aforesaid cardinals, as well as through the archbishops and bishops established in England, France, and other regions, we command that it be celebrated with the fullest devotion.

Since that which is known to have been ordained by the most holy Roman Church—constituted by the Lord Himself as head and teacher of all Churches—with such holy and provident deliberation, must be observed by all Christ’s faithful with great veneration, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to celebrate yearly with great veneration the solemnity of the aforesaid martyr, and to command your parishioners generally to celebrate it. Diligently admonish them to devote themselves so fervently to the veneration of this saint that, through the intervention of his merits, they may be able unfailingly to obtain the grace of their Redeemer. Furthermore, by the authority of these presents we enjoin upon you that you inform your fellow bishops of your province, on our behalf, that you have received this command from us, and carefully invite [Col. 0911A] and exhort them to celebrate the feast of that precious martyr, so that through your effort and diligence they may be more ardently moved to this and cause it to be observed each year by their parishioners with great devotion. Through whose merits may heavenly grace join us to him. Amen.

### MXXXV. He receives the monastery of Belloloco under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Anagni, 8 April.)

[*Gallia Christiana vetus*, IV, 152.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GIRALD, abbot of the monastery of Belloloco, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

[Col. 0911B]

Those who choose the religious life ought to receive apostolic protection, lest an assault of any rashness either turn them from their purpose or—God forbid—weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously consenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, which Fulk, former count of Anjou of illustrious memory, offered from its foundation in perpetual right to blessed Peter through our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Sergius; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We enact that whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just [Col. 0911C] means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms:

The church of Saints Peter and Ursus at Loches, with tithes, lands, meadows, vineyards, and its other appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Vine-Mount; Saint Medard of Dedra; Saint Mary of Crusillis; Saint James of Mose; Saint Peter of Belesma; Saint Mary Magdalene; Saint Peter of Dolis; Saint Leubacius of Senapariis; Saint Lawrence of Langiaco; Saint Martin of Fontanis; one half of the gift of the churches of Salone and Cherceii; Saint Stephen of Canaiis with the fief which it possesses in Bosogerio; Saint Loth of Mostello; [Col. 0911D] Saint Peter of Mimia; Saint Martin of Perol; five solidi of rent from the abbey of the monks of [lacuna]; the church of Saint Peter of Veschero; the house of Rochanescia; the freehold of Plessiacum; Trionem; Tressortem; the land of Archebaud; the land of Chavancio; the island and house of Sorpilleriis; and the house of Villepaganus. Moreover, we confirm to you by apostolic authority the ancient and reasonable customs and liberties granted to your monastery by the founders of that place, as they are contained in the authentic charter of the aforesaid count.

I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. [Col. 0912A] I, Boso, priest-cardinal of Saint Pudentiana. I, Pegus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark. I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Gualter, bishop of Albano. I, Luchrius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Manfred, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, William, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Peter, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary.

Given at Anagni, 8 April, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1173, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Alexander [Col. 0912B].

### MXXXVI. He confirms to the monks of Saint Peter of Modena all their rights and goods. (Anagni, 8 June.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, V, 349.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GEMINIAN, abbot of Saint Peter of Modena, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

Those who choose the religious life ought to receive apostolic protection, lest an assault of any rashness either turn them from their purpose or—God forbid—weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously consent to your just petitions [Col. 0912C] and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, etc. Moreover, we confirm to you and your monastery by apostolic authority the judgment of settlement known to have been issued concerning the case long contested between you and our venerable brother G., bishop of Padua, over the monastery of Candiana, by our venerable brethren the bishops of Pavia and Piacenza and our beloved son B., elect of the Holy Sepulchre, as it is contained in the authentic writing made concerning it; and we enact that it shall remain firm and ratified for ever. Further, we have thought fit to confirm in full by apostolic authority to you, son abbot, and your successors, and through you to that monastery, the correction, ordering, and disposition of that monastery itself and of all things belonging to it, [Col. 0912D] according as they were granted to you by the judgment.

We also enact that no one may presume to build a church or oratory within the parishes of your monastery and churches without the consent of the bishop and yourselves. Moreover, of your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, and of the increase of your animals, let no one presume to demand tithes from you. We further prohibit any layman from daring to demand tithes from you or to extort them in any manner. We decree, therefore, that it shall be permitted to no person whatever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, [Col. 0913A] or harass it by any vexations; but that all shall be preserved unimpaired and entire for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore, etc.

“SHOW ME THY WAYS, O LORD.”

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina. I, Gualter, bishop of Albano. I, William, priest-cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Boso, priest-cardinal of Saint Pudentiana [Col. 0913B] of the title of Pastor. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark. I, Oddo, deacon-cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Cinthius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Manfred, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of Saint Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Vitellus, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in [Col. 0913C] Aquiro.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 20 June, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1172, in the nineteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

Mark of the lost hanging lead bull.

### MXXXVII. He confirms the goods and privileges of the Church of Saint Donatian at Bruges. (Anagni, 4 July.)

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, III, 53.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROBERT, provost, AKETTO, dean, and the canons of the Church of Blessed Donatian at Bruges, and their successors canonically appointed, in perpetual memory.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that just petitioners be granted their requests, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wishes and truth does not oppose them.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously consent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

We enact that whatever possessions or goods the same Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through grant of pontiffs, [Col. 0914A] bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Further, we confirm in perpetuity to you and your church the free election of your provost, as you are known to have had it hitherto.

Moreover, graciously yielding to the prayers and earnest request of our beloved son, the noble Philip, count of Flanders, we enact by this present decree that, as has been established from the earliest times, whoever is constituted provost by the common election of the dean and chapter of your church shall be appointed chancellor by the count of Flanders.

We also confirm by apostolic authority the reasonable customs of your church, [Col. 0914B] its constant and most devout care for divine worship, and the community of refectory and dormitory established with pious and provident consideration; and, as these have hitherto been maintained, so we command that they be observed inviolably hereafter.

We also grant that the burial of the counts of Flanders and their notaries and officials, as you have hitherto possessed it, and likewise the burial of others who choose burial among you—unless they are excommunicated or under interdict—shall be free, so that none may oppose their devotion and final wishes; the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken being nevertheless preserved.

[Col. 0914C] When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

We decree, therefore, that it shall be permitted to no person whatever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all shall be preserved unimpaired and entire for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and reverence due to the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore in future, etc.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on 4 July, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1173, in the fourteenth year [Col. 0914D] of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### MXXXVIII. To William, Archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See; to the Archbishops of Tours and Bordeaux; and to Arten. (Guarin?), elect of Bourges—He commands them “to compel their parishioners, under pain of excommunication, to pay the rights and tithes of the Church of Blessed Martin.” (Anagni, 23 August.)

[*Defence of Saint Martin of Tours*, 3.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren W[ILLIAM], Archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See; the archbishops of Tours and Bordeaux; the bishops of Le Mans, Poitiers, Angers, [Col. 0915A] Agen, Troyes, and Langres; and to his beloved sons the elect of Bourges, Arten., and the canons of the Church of Bourges: greeting and apostolic blessing.

In preserving the rights of Churches—and especially of those which belong particularly to blessed Peter and to us—you ought to be diligent and attentive, lest through your lukewarmness and negligence the rights of Churches perish, though you ought to preserve them with vigilant care. Therefore, since the Church of Blessed Martin of Tours has no bishop except the Roman pontiff, you ought to be so much the more solicitous to preserve its rights, because you ought with special care to defend and foster the rights of the Roman Church, and in these matters your zeal can appear all the more worthy of praise.

Accordingly, [Col. 0915B] we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, under obedience, diligently to admonish your parishioners who owe tithes or other dues to the aforesaid Church of Blessed Martin; to enjoin upon them, under threat of excommunication, that they pay to that church, in full and without any contradiction or appeal, the tithes and other dues they owe. If any of them, after your admonition, should presume to withhold from that church its due tithes or other rights, pronounce them excommunicated in your synods, with all remedy of appeal removed, and cause them to be avoided as excommunicated until they make fitting satisfaction.

[Col. 0915C] Given at Anagni, 3 August.

### MXXXIX. Privilege for the Church of Saint Martin of Tours. (Anagni, 7 August.)

[Ibid., p. 18.]

Although we are bound, by the authority and benevolence of the Apostolic See, to all Churches and ecclesiastical persons, it is nevertheless fitting that we provide with more earnest care for those persons known to be especially subject to the Holy Roman Church. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of Blessed Martin of Tours, in which you devote yourselves to the divine [Col. 0915D] office and which is known, without any intermediary, to belong especially to the right and property of the Roman Church; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing, etc.

Given at Anagni, 7 August, in the sixth indiction, in the year of Christ 1173, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### MXL. Privilege for the Church of Chartres. (Anagni, 9 September.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, VIII, Documents, 339.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Geoffrey, dean, and the canons of the Church of Chartres, both present and future, canonically appointed, forever.

Although unworthy, we have been appointed by divine providence to the governance of the universal Church, etc.; decreeing that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s help, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings and princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The wood of Saint Stephen, with its church and all the tithes of that wood; the village called Disconfectura, with the church established there; the church [Col. 0916B] of Fontanella; the church of Boseri; the church of Poli, with its chapels and all appurtenances belonging to them, and the tithes of Chartres; the church of Saint Saturninus with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Leodegarius of Alberiis, as it was freely and absolutely given and granted in perpetuity to the chapter, exempt from every jurisdiction of the archdeacon, by William, archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See, while he held the care and administration of the Church of Chartres, with the consent and assent of Milo, the archdeacon in whose archdeaconry it lay; the provostship of Alvers; the provostship of Unigradu; the provostship of Masengi; the provostship of Normandy, with its people, villages, territories, churches, chapels, tithes, land-dues, other customary rights and liberties, [Col. 0916C] and everything belonging to the same provostships.

Moreover, by the present decree we enact, and by apostolic authority more strictly forbid, that anyone in your city or its adjoining suburbs presume, without the authority and consent of your bishop and yourselves, to build a church, chapel, oratory, or cemetery, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. Furthermore, by this present document we strictly forbid anyone to receive at divine offices or for burial parishioners of the Church of Chartres whom you have excommunicated or specifically placed under interdict, or to grant them the benefit of absolution without suitable satisfaction. We also confirm the liberties and immunities granted to you and your church either by Roman pontiffs, [Col. 0916D] by your bishops, or by kings and princes, together with the ancient and reasonable customs of that church; and we decree that they shall possess perpetual validity.

We therefore decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Very many cardinals follow.]

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth Ides of September, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1173 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MXLI. Privilege for the Church of Blessed Thomas of Chieti. (Anagni, September 28.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VI, 707.]

[Col. 0917A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Andrew, bishop of Chieti, and to his successors canonically appointed, forever.

Established by the Lord’s ordinance upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, etc. Therefore, venerable brother bishop, we graciously assent to your just requests; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of holy memory, Nicholas II, Paschal II, and Eugenius III, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of Blessed Thomas of Chieti, over which, by God’s appointment, you are known to preside, [Col. 0917B] and strengthen it by the privilege of this document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, etc., among which we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

The parish territory of the Church of Chieti, as it is bounded by ancient and just limits: namely, from Staffilo between the mountains and the mountain itself called Ursa; then as it proceeds to Coza, and sets its boundary in the water below as far as the water of Sonulano; then as it goes to Mount Reste and passes by Mount Crinis; and as it continues as far as Mount Selani; and as it runs in the river called Trinium as far as the seashore; and along the seashore as far as Pescara; and returns to the former boundary, namely to the aforesaid Staffilo.

[Col. 0917C] Further, the city of Chieti itself; the castle of Trevelliano; Villa Magna; Mount Filardi; the castle of Orni; the castle of Scurcula; the castle of Saint Paul; the castle called Furca; the castle of Genestrula; and the castle of Saint Cosidius, with their appurtenances. Beyond Pescara: the castle of Montesilvano; the church of Saint Mary at Rigoli; the castle of Sculcula; the castle of Lastiniano; the church of Saint Mary of the People; the church of Saint Justa with its appurtenances; on the Aterno, the parish church of Saints Leguntianus and Domitianus; the church of Saint Thomas; the church of the Savior; the church of Saint Jerusalem; and the church of Saint Nicholas, with all their appurtenances; the tithe of the bridge and port of the Aterno at Buclanico; the church of Saint [Col. 0917D] Savior and Saint Angel, with the count’s tithes; the parish church of Saint Sylvester; the count’s tithes in the castle of Saint Angel of the Three Boundaries; the tithes of the castles which were in the episcopate of Chieti under the lordship of Count Robert of Rotello; and what the Church of Chieti holds in the castle of Septi; the church of Saint Mary at Bari; the church of Saint Blaise.

At Lanciano: the monastery of Saint Martin of Pallitta; the church of Saint Lentius at Atissa, with all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint John at Arclano; the monastery of Saint Angel at Cirnaclano, with all its appurtenances. On Mount Odense: the church of Saint Nicholas and one half of the church of Saint Mary; the church of the Savior and the church of Saint Peter, with their appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Maurus with its benefice; the monastery of Saint Salvi; the church of Saint Nicholas [Col. 0918A] of Heremitano. At Ortona: the churches of Saint Mary and Saint George, with their appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Mary in Basilica. In the city of Luparelli: the parish church of Saint Peter, with its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Mary in Palatio; the church of Saint James of Turcella, with their appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Pancras; the monastery of Saint Mary de Letto, with Casale and other properties belonging to it; the monastery of Saint Martin in Valle; the church of Saint Justin at Casule. In the castle of Bissi: the parish church of Saint Mary with its appurtenances; the parish church of Saint Martin of the sons of Tresidius; the church of Saint Mary of Casa Candidella; the church of Saint Peter in the castle of Lori; the church of Saint Mary at Biano; the church of Saint Basil; the monastery of Saint Peter in Campis; the church of Saint Nicholas of the hamlet [Col. 0918B] of Sunnio; the church of Saint Mary de Latro.

At Abbatejo: the parish church of Saint Martin with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Francis of the parish; the parish church of Juliano; the parish church of Saint Cecilia; the parish church of Pizzocortano; the church of Saint Lucy of Argelli; the church of Saint Linus; the parish church of Ovele; the parish church of Saint Mary of Caramanico; the parish church of Saint John of Abbatejo; the church of Saint Cosidius; and the church of Saint Pontius of Saint Valentine in the castle of Jocco; the church of Saint Mary at Percle; the church of Saint Eustasius; the church of Saint Martin of Fara.

Between the mountains: the church of Saint John of Pedara; the church of Saint John of Cantalupo; the church of the Savior of Limari; the church of Saint Mary of Sparpalia; the church of Saint Nicholas of Ilice; the church of the Savior of Valle Surda; the church [Col. 0918C] of Saint Mary of Valle Caruncli; the church of the Holy Trinity of Faragine; the church of Saint John in Valdo, with all their appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter of Troja; and the church of Saint Mary of Tasso.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved entire for the use and benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the right of ownership of Blessed Peter and the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone therefore in future, etc.

[Col. 0918D] I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Boso, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Manfred, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. [Col. 0919A] I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Vitellius, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Angel.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1173 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MXLII. He grants various privileges to Oddo, master of the military order of the Temple at Jerusalem, and to his successors and brethren. (Anagni, October 26.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, etc., I, 27.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0919B] sons Oddo, master of the religious military order of the Temple situated at Jerusalem, his successors, and the brethren, both present and future, who have professed the regular life, forever.

“Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change, nor shadow of turning” (James 1). Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concerning you and for your sake we praise almighty God, because throughout the whole world your religious order and venerable institution are proclaimed.

For whereas by nature you were children of wrath and devoted to the pleasures of the world, now, through the grace breathed into you by the Gospel, you have not become deaf hearers. Having abandoned worldly pomp and private possessions, and having likewise left [Col. 0919C] the broad way which leads to death, you have humbly chosen the steep path which leads to life; and, to prove that you are specially numbered among the soldiery of God, you continually bear upon your breast the sign of the life-giving cross.

There is added to this that, as men of Israel and warriors most thoroughly trained for the divine battle, inflamed by the flame of true charity, you fulfill in deed the saying of the Gospel: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15).

Therefore, according to the word of the supreme Shepherd, you do not fear to lay down your lives for your brethren and to defend them from the incursions of pagans; and, though you are designated soldiers of the Temple by name, you have been appointed by the Lord as defenders of the Catholic Church and assailants of Christ’s enemies.

Although your zeal and praiseworthy devotion labor with all body and mind in so sacred a work, nevertheless we exhort your whole body in the Lord and, for the remission of sins, by the authority of God and of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, enjoin upon both you and your servants that, in defending the Catholic Church and rescuing from pagan tyranny that Church which lies under their filth, you labor boldly, calling upon Christ’s name, to overthrow the enemies of the cross. Whatever you take from their spoils, confidently apply to your own uses; and we forbid anyone to compel you, against [Col. 0920A] your will, to give any share thereof. We decree that the house or Temple in which you are gathered for the praise and glory of God, for the defense of his faithful, and for the liberation of God’s Church, together with all its possessions and goods which it is known now lawfully to hold, or may in future acquire, with the Lord’s help, through grants of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, or other lawful means, shall remain in perpetual future times under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See.

By this present decree we also enact that the religious life established in your house through divine inspiration shall there be observed inviolably, and that the brethren serving almighty God there shall live chastely and without private property, proving their profession by word and conduct, and shall be subject and obedient in all things and through all things to their master or to those whom he commands.

Furthermore, just as this house has deserved to be the fountain and origin of your sacred institution and order, so it shall likewise be held in perpetuity as the head and mistress of all places belonging to it.

Adding this, we command that, upon the death of you, beloved son Oddo in the Lord, or of any of your successors, no one be placed over the brethren of the same house unless he is a military and religious person who has professed the habit of your way of life; nor shall the person to be appointed be elected by others, but only by all the brethren together or by the [Col. 0920C] sounder part of them.

Moreover, no ecclesiastical or secular person may lawfully infringe or lessen the customs jointly established by the master and brethren for the observance of your religion and office. Nor may the same customs, observed by you for some time and confirmed in writing, be changed except by the master, with the consent of the sounder part of the chapter.

Indeed, we prohibit and wholly forbid any ecclesiastical or secular person to presume to demand from the master and brethren of that house fealties, homages, oaths, or other securities commonly exacted by secular persons.

[Col. 0920D] Know this: just as your sacred institution and religious military order were established by divine providence, so likewise it is not fitting that you transfer yourselves to another place under the pretext of a more religious life. For God, who is unchangeable and eternal, does not approve changeable hearts; rather, he wills that the sacred purpose once begun be brought through to the end of its proper action.

How many, and how great, were those who pleased the Lord under the military belt and cloak of earthly rule and left for themselves an everlasting memorial! How many, and how great, being engaged in warfare, fought bravely in their times for the covenant of God and the defense of their fathers’ laws, and, consecrating their hands to the Lord in the blood of unbelievers, after the labors of war attained the prize of eternal life! Therefore consider your calling, both knights and servants, and, according to the Apostle, let each one of you remain in the calling in which he was called (Ephesians 4).

Accordingly, we command that your brethren, once devoted and received into your sacred college, after making profession in your military order and taking the habit of religion, have no power to return to the world. Nor may any of them, after making profession, cast aside the Cross of the Lord once assumed and the habit of your religion, or transfer to another place or even to a monastery under the pretext of a greater or lesser religious observance, without the consent or knowledge of the brethren or of whoever is master; nor may any ecclesiastical or secular person have permission to receive or retain them.

And because those who are defenders of the Church ought to live and be supported from the goods of the Church, we wholly forbid tithes to be demanded from you against your will from movable goods, livestock, or anything whatsoever belonging to your venerable house.

So that nothing may be lacking to you for the fullness of salvation and care of your souls, and so that ecclesiastical sacraments and divine offices may be more conveniently supplied to your sacred college, we similarly enact that you may receive upright clerics and priests, ordained according to God and, so far as concerns your conscience, coming to you from wherever they may be; and that you may keep them with yourselves both in your principal house and in your obediences and dependent places—provided that, if they come from nearby, you request them from their own bishops, and that they are bound to no other profession or order. If the bishops should perhaps refuse to grant them to you, nevertheless you shall have, by the authority of the Holy Roman Church, permission to receive and retain them.

If any of these, after making profession, should prove disturbers of your religion or house, or even useless, you may remove them with the sounder part of the chapter, grant them leave to pass to another [Col. 0921D] order where they wish to live according to God, and appoint other suitable persons in their place. These also shall be tested in your community for the space of one year; when this is completed, if their conduct requires it and they are found useful for your service, then at last they shall make profession to live under rule and obey their master. They shall nevertheless have the same food, clothing, and bedding as yourselves, except that they shall wear closed garments.

Nor may they themselves involve themselves in the chapter or administration of your house except insofar as you require of them. Moreover, they shall be subject to no person outside your chapter; and they shall render obedience in all things and through all things to you, beloved son Oddo in the Lord, and to your successors, as to their master [Col. 0922A] and prelate.

Furthermore, we command [lacuna] that you receive the ordinations of those clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, provided he enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See; supported by our authority, he shall grant what is requested.

We forbid them to preach for money or profit, and forbid you to send them to preach for such a cause, unless perhaps the master of the Temple then in office should judge, for certain reasons, that this ought to be done.

Whoever of these is received in your college shall promise, by a written undertaking placed upon the altar, stability of place, conversion of manners, [Col. 0922B] and that he will serve the Lord in military service for all the days of his life under obedience to the master of the Temple; this being without prejudice to episcopal right, both in tithes, offerings, and burials.

We likewise grant you authority to build oratories in places granted to the sacred Temple where your household resides, in which that household may hear divine offices; and there, if anyone among you or your household dies, he may be buried. For it is unseemly and close to peril for souls that religious brethren, on the occasion of going to church, should mingle with crowds of men and gatherings of women.

Moreover, the tithes which, with the counsel and consent of bishops, you can obtain from the hands of clerics or laymen through your exertions, and also those which, with the consent of bishops and their clerics, you acquire, we confirm to you by apostolic authority.

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we decree that wherever you happen to come, you may receive penance, anointings, and any other ecclesiastical sacraments from upright and Catholic priests, lest anything perhaps be lacking to you for the reception of spiritual goods.

Since in Christ we are all one and there is no distinction of persons with God, we will that your household and servants also share in the remission of sins, other beneficence, and apostolic blessing granted to you.

When your brethren appointed to receive collections arrive at a city, castle, or village, if that place happens to be under interdict, then in joyful recognition of their arrival, for the honor of the Temple and reverence for those knights, the churches shall be opened once a year, excommunicated persons being excluded, and divine offices shall be celebrated.

Let no one whatsoever therefore rashly disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be kept entire for your benefit and for the benefit of the other faithful of God. If anyone knowingly should rashly attempt to contravene the terms of this our [Col. 0923A] constitution, after being warned a second or third time, unless he corrects his offense by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed, be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But those who observe these provisions shall obtain the blessing and grace of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. [Col. 0923B] I, Vic., cardinal priest of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Boso, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Peter, of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, cardinal priest of Saint Mark. I, Manfred, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. [Col. 0923C] I, Vitellus, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of Saint Angel.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1173 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MXLIII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims—On behalf of the abbot of Maricoles against William, castellan of Saint-Omer. (Anagni, November 18.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 993.]

[Col. 0923D] From the complaint forwarded to us by the abbot of the monastery of Maricoles, it has become known to us that the nobleman William, castellan of Saint-Omer, presumes violently to take away certain tithes and land-dues belonging to the aforesaid monastery. Since it pertains to our office alike to preserve and defend the rights of that monastery, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to warn the said William; and, if necessary, setting aside appeal, compel him by ecclesiastical censure either to restore without diminution to the aforesaid monastery the tithes and land-dues taken away, or their value, and henceforth to inflict no molestation or burden upon it concerning their receipt; or, in your presence within forty days after receipt of these letters, with appeal set aside, to render justice in full.

Given at Anagni, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December.

MXLIV. He receives the Church of Castello under protection and confirms its goods and possessions. (Anagni, November 20.)

(HUGO, *Ann. ord. Praem.*, I, 381.)

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Ralph, abbot of the Church of Castello, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

To those choosing the religious life, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, [Col. 0924B] in which you are devoted to divine service, strengthening it by the privilege of this document. First, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that church according to God, the Rule of Blessed Augustine, and the institution of the Premonstratensian brethren shall be observed there inviolably in perpetuity. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s help, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these [Col. 0924C] we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

(It enumerates their possessions.)

Indeed, let no one presume to exact from you tithes of the newly cultivated lands which you till by your own hands or at your own expense, or of the feed of your animals. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. We likewise decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; saving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. In parish churches, moreover, you may appoint [Col. 0924D] three or four of your canons, one of whom shall be presented to the bishop in order to receive from him the cure of souls; and he shall answer to the bishop in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. You may also receive into your conversion clerics or free laymen fleeing from the world, and retain them in your church without anyone’s objection. Furthermore, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to leave the cloister through levity without the permission of the prior or abbot; and no one may presume to retain a departing brother without letters of guarantee from the community. We further decree that no ecclesiastical or secular person may burden or improperly harass your churches [Col. 0925A] and the clerics residing there with undue and unaccustomed exactions. Above all, we prohibit anyone from presuming to demand or extort anything for the election or blessing of your abbot, because the election and blessing of an abbot must be free and gratuitous. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be installed through the cunning of any intrigue or through force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine determine should be elected.

We therefore decree, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, bishop of Ostia. [Col. 0925B] I, Bernard, bishop of Porto. I, Walter, bishop of Albano. I, John, cardinal priest of the Church of Saint Anastasia. I, William, cardinal priest of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Boso, cardinal priest of the Church of Saint Pudentiana. I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon. I, Witellius, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. [Col. 0925C] I, Wanfredus, cardinal priest of Saint Cecilia. I, Peter, cardinal priest of Saint Chrysogonus.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, of the Holy Roman Church [lacuna], on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1173 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MXLV. To Henry, archbishop of Reims—On behalf of Master Ralph. (Anagni, November 30.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 994.]

We have learned from the representation of Master Ralph that, although a case between him and John [Col. 0925D] of Nouvelles-Maisons concerning thirty pounds in Reims currency had long been litigated in your court, and restoration of the aforesaid money had been adjudged to the same Ralph, the aforementioned John, contumaciously withdrawing from your court, scorned to comply with the equity of the law. Therefore you pronounced against him, as a contumacious person, a sentence of excommunication. Since we hold that sentence, as having been reasonably issued, to be ratified and confirmed, we command that it be inviolably observed until suitable satisfaction is made.

Given at Anagni, on the second day before the Kalends of December.

MXLVI. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the Abbey of Saint John of Valenciennes, of the Order of Regular Canons of Saint Augustine. (Anagni, December 4.)

[MIRAEI, *Opp. dipl.*, II, 829.]

[Col. 0926A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Gilbert, abbot of the Church of Saint John the Baptist of Valenciennes, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

A desire shown to concern the purpose of religion and the salvation of souls ought fittingly to be granted by us with a willing mind, and petitioners’ desires supplied with appropriate assistance. Therefore, beloved [Col. 0926B] sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and Paul the aforesaid church in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this document. First, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that church according to God, the Rule of Blessed Augustine, and the institution of the brethren of Arrouaise—that is, of Arrouaise Abbey—shall be observed there inviolably in perpetuity. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s help, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other [Col. 0926C] lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself where the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter in the marketplace; the churches of Alneto and Saltem, with their possessions and all the tithes of those same villages; the altar-right of Struem, with five small gardens in the same village; the altar-rights of Elpines and Presel; the altar-right of Sepmeries; the schools of the whole castle of Valenciennes, which your church has held from ancient times; the dwellings of the canons around the church, with one brewery; the dwelling of Gervase of Provins before the church doors; the house which belonged to Master Adam; the house of Gonteri of Putero, with the house of Fredesendis and other houses belonging to them, with an oven; the rent-paying houses which you have in Valenciennes; the land of Mortrui; the mill called Fossart; the vegetable garden of the brethren within the castle enclosure; etc.; the count and his household, his official likewise, and all who live from your bread; the castellans and peers with their households and officials; clerics, scholars, and the households of the canons.

Indeed, let no one presume to exact from you tithes of the newly cultivated lands which you till by your own hands or at your own expense, or of the feed of your animals. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, without ringing bells and in a subdued [Col. 0927A] voice. We likewise decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; saving nevertheless the right of the mother church.

In the parish churches which you hold, moreover, you may appoint four, or at least three, of your canons, one of whom shall be presented to the bishop to receive from him the cure of souls; and he shall answer to the bishop in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters, etc.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the second Nones of December, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1173 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord [Col. 0927B] Pope Alexander III.

MXLVII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans—On the needs of the Eastern Church, and that they should seek peace between Kings Louis of France and Henry of England. (Anagni, December 23.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 994.]

Not without grave sorrow and sadness of heart do we hear that that Holy Land, in which the feet of the Lord stood, is exposed to extreme dangers, and that against it the accursed race of pagans is arming with detestable strength and power. So great is the multitude and might of that people that, unless He with whom it makes no difference whether He conquers by many or by few comes to the aid of that land, we and the whole body of the faithful must fear lest the sanctuary of God be exposed—God forbid!—to the plunderings of the pagans, and lest there the faith of the Christian name be endangered. To defend and preserve that faith, the prelates of the churches ought to stand watchfully alert and to encourage their parishioners more fervently: so that, just as that land was wrested from the hands of the wicked by the power of kings, princes, and other faithful of Christ, and not without much shedding of blood, so also by their strength and labour it may, with the Lord’s assistance, be preserved unharmed from their attack—as hitherto it has been preserved through God’s mercy. Indeed, in order that this accursed people may accomplish what they have wickedly conceived in their hearts, those who formerly seemed to disagree among themselves have become unanimous and united. Their fury and iniquity have increased so greatly that, on one side Egyptians and Turks, and on the other Persians and Medes, have gathered together for the confusion and destruction of the faithful. This year, for two months, they boldly persisted in devastating that land with an army in the field—although formerly they were accustomed to fear, within their own borders, the strength of the faithful coming there from regions beyond the mountains. [Col. 0927C–D]

For what chiefly gives that accursed people the audacity and vigour to dare this, among other things, is that war and strife have arisen almost everywhere among Christian kings and princes. Thus, because our sins deserve it, those who formerly used to wage war upon pagan and foreign nations now destroy one another by the reciprocal disaster of wars. [Col. 0928A]

Although the wars waged among other Christian princes make the enemies of Christ’s cross bold in pursuing what they have conceived, yet that war which is being carried on with hostility between our dearest sons in Christ, L., the illustrious king of the Franks, and Henry, the illustrious king of the English, makes them still stronger and bolder. For they see them held back by mutual wars and disputes—those by whose strength they recall that they have often been routed and crushed. Therefore, since it is greatly advantageous both to those kings and to Christendom that they should have peace between themselves, seeing that each is known to suffer grave losses and dangers from their war, while the Eastern Church is worn down by the harsh afflictions of the pagans: considering how, by reason of the ministry of service entrusted to us, it is incumbent upon us to devote ourselves to the peace and concord of all, and with pastoral solicitude to provide for the dangers threatening the aforesaid land; and considering also how it concerns you and all ecclesiastical persons to apply diligent effort together with us in these matters—we invite your prudence to this all the more confidently because we know you to be especially solicitous in matters pertaining to God’s honour and the common advancement of Christendom. [Col. 0928A–B]

Accordingly, we earnestly admonish and command your brotherhood that, devoting yourselves diligently to restoring peace between the two kings, you, brother archbishop, carefully admonish and endeavour to induce the same king of the Franks, your brother, mercifully to incline his mind toward making peace with the aforesaid king of the English, so far as this may be done without prejudice to his honour; and that he speedily aid the Eastern land by the power of his kingdom. Encourage more earnestly also the people of your province, so that, in accordance with the exhortation of our venerable brother the bishop of Lydda and of the beloved son, the subprior of the Lord’s Sepulchre—religious and honourable men who are acting as envoys in the regions beyond the mountains for this purpose—they may faithfully and diligently apply themselves to the defence of that land and not delay to bring speedy aid to its clergy and people. Thus may both you and they, by the Lord’s gift, deserve to obtain an unfading crown, and may that land, aided by the protection of the faithful, not succumb to the violence of the unbelievers. [Col. 0928C–D]

Given at Anagni, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

## YEAR 1160–1174

### MXLVIII. Reply to William, bishop of Norwich

He replies: “If vicars, falsely assuming to themselves the status of a parson, set themselves up against the incumbents, they are not to be admitted to exercise their office in the same diocese.” (See Gregory’s *Decretals*, book V, title 31, chapter 6.)

### MXLIX. To W[illiam], bishop of Norwich.—Concerning vexatious appeals, etc.

[*Letters of Gilbert Foliot*, ed. Giles, II, 95.]

[Col. 0929A]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Norwich, greeting.

From the tenor of your letters and from the report of certain persons we have learned that many of your subjects, attending not to their own right but rather persisting in obstinacy, harass you with lawsuits and contentious and wearisome words—especially sons of priests and vicars of churches. When their fathers or masters die, they defend themselves in the churches and in their possessions by vexatious appeals, disregarding the sacred obligation of oaths or of faith; and thus they presume to occupy by their own authority places in which they previously served on behalf of others, before suitable persons can be appointed to vacant churches. Then, when they are summoned to court, they produce as witnesses of their own wrongdoing persons fallen into a similar offence and joined in conspiracy with them or with other such people, and thus they try to make the falsehood they allege appear plausible. Some, moreover, having procured letters under our seal, do not fear to forge them; and, after altering the writings to suit their will, they repeatedly attempt to deceive judges delegated by us. [Col. 0929A–B]

Therefore, since it is fitting that we apply an appropriate remedy to such practices and restrain the aforesaid quibblers more severely, as is proper, from such presumptuous litigation, we answer your concern by the present notification as follows: fortify the incumbents of churches situated in your diocese by your authentic documents and those of the lords of the land in such a way that, should any one of them happen to die, the deceased person’s son or vicar, or anyone else, may not by any trickery forestall your right of conferring the incumbency of the vacant church upon a suitable man. If any such person appeals to our hearing in order to procure a vexatious delay and fixes a long term for his appeal, assign him a day within which he can suitably come to the Apostolic See. If he scorns to appear on that day, compel him thereafter, all excuse and appeal ceasing, strictly to abide without objection by your judgment regarding the matters in dispute. [Col. 0929C–D]

But if anyone fixes a fitting term for his appeal and nevertheless does not pursue it by the appointed day, compel him nonetheless thereafter, appeal set aside, to obey your sentence, as we have said concerning the other. If, however, such cases are tried before you or before anyone else, we do not wish persons suffering from a similar fault to be admitted as witnesses if it is certain, or if they can lawfully be convicted, concerning such matters, when they are produced by either party. Further, concerning that priest who forged our letters which you sent us, by the authority of these presents we command your discretion that, if he can be found, you deprive him forever of every priestly office and ecclesiastical benefice and confine him in some monastery of strict observance, so that there, suffering the penalty for so great a crime, he may lament having committed such acts, and others may henceforth be deterred from similar conduct. If you can subsequently discover any other persons guilty of like offences, commit them to the strictest custody, with recourse to appeal removed, until you receive an apostolic command concerning them. [Col. 0929D–0930A]

## YEAR 1163–1174

### ML. To Roger, bishop of Worcester.—Concerning those who pretend to belong to the ecclesiastical profession and contract marriages; concerning fornicating priests.

[*Letters of Gilbert Foliot*, ed. Giles, II, 97.]

[Col. 0930B]

Among the other concerns entrusted to your care, it befits your prudence to attend diligently and carefully to appoint and set over the churches committed to your government such ministers as know how fittingly to order the house of the Lord and can usefully preside over and benefit God’s people. Yet it has reached our hearing that certain persons dwell in your diocese who, while pretending to belong to the ecclesiastical profession and nevertheless holding ecclesiastical benefices, contract marriages and still strive to retain the benefices they have acquired. Others, although they are sons of priests, succeed their fathers in churches as if by hereditary right; and, having afterwards been instituted in them, are promoted to holy orders less than lawfully. [Col. 0930B–C]

Since this is unworthy and is known wholly to conflict with the ordinances of the sacred canons, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you permit no one who has contracted marriage below the subdiaconate to be separated from his wife on any ground, unless by common consent the wives wish to enter religious life and the men themselves remain continually in God’s service. But if they live with their wives, they ought in no way to retain ecclesiastical benefices, which are known to belong only to those who persevere constantly in God’s service. Those, however, who at the subdiaconate or above have entered into marriages can and ought to leave the women even against their will and resistance; for such a union is to be called not marriage but rather concubinage. [Col. 0930C–D]

By the authority of these presents we also command you not to permit sons of priests to minister in their fathers’ churches or to obtain them on any pretext whatever. Rather, endeavour wholly to remove them, with every obstacle of appeal ceasing, from the churches in which their fathers are known to have ministered. Concerning priests who publicly commit fornication, we likewise command your discretion that you diligently visit and earnestly admonish them to dismiss and utterly put away their concubines. If they scorn to comply with your admonition and decide to persist in their uncleanness, do not delay, without recourse to appeal, to deprive them of every ecclesiastical office and benefice.

## YEAR 1173–1174

[Col. 0931A]

### MLI. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—He answers one asking whether he may receive homage from the schismatic bishop of Liège. (Anagni, 27 March.)

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 959.]

Since we wish you to preserve whole and inviolate the rights and dignities of the Church entrusted to you, and to impart to you, as to a most dear brother whom we love with more abundant charity than others, counsel and aid in spiritual and temporal matters, and willingly to show you every deference that we can with God and justice, it seems burdensome and unfitting to us to give you counsel by which the dignity of your Church might in any way be diminished or by which your brotherhood might do something that would offend the eyes of the divine Majesty. You have indeed sought our counsel through our beloved son M., clerk and your messenger, whether you ought to receive homage from the intruder of Liège—

> **[Note: Col. 0931D]** This appears to be Radulf, brother of Berthold, duke of Thuringia, Conrad, and Albert. Expelled from the see of Mainz because of avarice, he was elected bishop of Liège in 1167 through the favour of Henry, count of Namur, and other relatives. [Col. 0932D]

—who is polluted by the contagion of schism. Hitherto you have delayed receiving this homage lest perhaps, contrary to what is forbidden by the holy Fathers, you should be obliged to communicate with him and thus incur the stain of participation in his fellowship, gravely offending God thereby. The same M. asserted, however, that you fear that, through such delay, the rights and dignity of your Church will be impaired—which we by no means wish—and that you fear otherwise offending your Creator, something which above all things your prudence and all Christ’s faithful ought most carefully to avoid. [Col. 0931B–C]

Concerning this, we have thought fit to reply to your brotherhood as follows: unless that intruder returns from schismatic perversity to the unity of the Church and devotion to blessed Peter and to us, do not communicate with him in any respect, if you can refrain without prejudice to the right and dignity of the Church of Rheims; and, so long as he persists in schism, do not receive homage from him, if you can omit it without grave loss to that Church. Otherwise you may offend almighty God in this matter, and others may take an example from you by participating with persons polluted by the contagion of schism. But if you learn that your Church would suffer grave loss if you delayed receiving his homage, we leave the matter to your judgment. Yet we admonish your honour and earnestly exhort you to use temporal things in such a way that you do not neglect the eternal and spiritual.

Given at Anagni, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April.

### MLII. To the same.—Against [Guy], bishop of Châlons, who did not defer to appeals made by him to the archbishop of Rheims. (Anagni, 27 March.)

[Ibid., col. 960.]

You should know that it has reached our hearing from your brotherhood that whenever appeals are made from the bishop of Châlons to your hearing, the bishop of Châlons does not defer to those appeals, whereby, you complain, you are greatly burdened. But because we are greatly troubled and disturbed if the said bishop or any of your suffragans fails to defer to you as his prelate and scorns to obey, we have commanded the bishop of Châlons that in appeals and in other matters he humbly defer to you as his metropolitan, to whom he is bound to answer in spiritual matters. Otherwise he may fear lest those beneath him scorn to obey and defer to him; and if at last he presumes to persist in such contumacy, by the Lord’s authority we shall take care severely to avenge upon him your injury and contempt as though done to our own person. [Col. 0932A–B]

### MLIII. To the same.—That he is not to restore communion to the abbot of Dervent until he has done what was ordered. (Anagni, 28 March.)

[Ibid., col. 961.]

Our beloved sons, the canons of St Nicholas of Châlons, informed us by a communication sent to us that you had bound our beloved son, the abbot of Dervent, by the bond of excommunication, because he had scorned to obey your command—which he had promised on oath to observe—concerning the determination of the judgment which you had pronounced in the case pending between him and the aforesaid canons. Therefore, since we neither wish nor ought to pass over such an offence with our eyes shut, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you keep the aforesaid abbot bound under the sentence of excommunication until he firmly accepts and observes your command, as he swore to do. [Col. 0932B–C]

Given at Anagni, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April.

### MLIV. To the same.—For the monastery of Cuissy, against the canons of St Peter of Laon. (Anagni, 2 April.)

[Ibid.]

Our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the church of Cuissy—

> **[Note: Col. 0932D]** Cuissy, a monastery of the Premonstratensian order in the diocese of Laon.

—have shown us in a complaint transmitted to us that the canons of St Peter of Laon do not fear unjustly to demand tithes from them contrary to the privilege of our predecessor of pious memory, Pope Innocent. Since it pertains to us to preserve with pastoral solicitude the rights of religious persons, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and induce the aforesaid canons not to presume to demand the specified tithes from the aforesaid abbot and brethren. But if they rely upon a legal right, let them pursue their claim against them in your presence by judicial procedure; and hear the case carefully and decide it through concord or justice. If they are unwilling to do either, compel them by ecclesiastical censure to do one or the other. [Col. 0932D–0933A]

Given at Anagni, on the fourth Nones of April.

### MLV. To the same.—Concerning the church of Arcy, to be adjudged to the subdeacon Henry. (Anagni, 8 April.)

[Ibid., col. 962.]

When it had formerly been represented to us that the priest Radulf, barring our beloved son Henry, subdeacon, from access to the church of Arcy—which Radulf maintained had been canonically granted to him by our beloved son the abbot of St Peter of the Mountains after the incumbent of that church had entered upon the way of all flesh—had appealed the same Henry to our hearing, alleging that the prior of that place had instituted him in that church and that, at the presentation of the archdeacon and of the prior himself, the bishop of Soissons had committed its administration to him: we entrusted the case to our beloved sons, the provost, dean, and chapter of the church of Rheims, to hear and bring to its due conclusion. [Col. 0933A–B]

As they informed us by their letters, having summoned both parties before them and heard and examined the arguments fully on either side, they ordered the aforesaid R. to be removed from the said church and the aforementioned Henry to be put into possession of it. They also notified the bishop of Soissons by their letters to commit the care of souls to the said Henry. Yet the bishop, putting forward the appeal made to us by R. and the fact that he had committed the care of souls to him at the presentation of the prior, refused to receive the said Henry into the aforesaid church. At length, when the aforesaid Henry and Radulf had come into our presence, the same Henry [read perhaps: Radulf], as it pleased the Lord, was removed from the midst and paid the debt of nature. Therefore, considering the labours and anxieties of the same Henry, and considering how the aforesaid church had been adjudged to him by the said authority, we hold the judgment of the aforesaid provost, dean, and chapter valid and firm, and have taken care to confirm by apostolic authority the aforesaid church to the said Henry and to strengthen it by the force of our writing. [Col. 0933B–D]

Since it is fitting that the aforesaid bishop defer reverently and devoutly to the decrees of the Apostolic See and in no way oppose its authority, we commanded that bishop to commit to the said Henry the care and administration of the aforesaid church within twenty days after receiving our letters, and not permit any annoyance or burden to be inflicted upon him on that account. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid bishop does not fulfil our command within the prescribed term, you yourself execute it without difficulty or delay, notwithstanding any objection or appeal. [Col. 0933D]

Given at Anagni, on the sixth Ides of April.

### MLVI. To the same.—That he grant an oratory and cemetery to the sick of Osdayn. (Anagni, 9 April.)

[Ibid., col. 963.]

[Col. 0934A]

The suffering and misery of the sick brethren of Osdayn ought to move everyone to compassion for them, so that they may more easily and conveniently attend to their needs and welfare when they have considered with fraternal reflection the brethren’s incurable illness.
