Since some of them are so debilitated and disfigured that they cannot, and do not dare, mingle in any way with the healthy, it befits your prudence to provide them with an oratory and cemetery where they may attend the divine offices and have burial when they die. Therefore we earnestly request and command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to allow the aforesaid sick persons, without any objection, to have a chaplain and construct an oratory with a cemetery. [Col. 0934A–B]

Yet their chaplain is not to admit parishioners of other churches to daily offices or to the principal solemnities, nor receive them for burial, nor demand tithes or offerings from them in any way. Rather, he is to provide carefully and minister fervently only to the sick persons and their household, as he knows to be expedient for the salvation of their souls. Moreover, we will and command that you in no way demand tithes from those sick persons, nor permit anyone to demand them on any ground, from newly cultivated lands which they cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense, or from the increase of their animals. [Col. 0934B–C]

Given at Anagni, on the fifth Ides of April.

### MLVII. He confirms to the monastery of St Remigius of Rheims its rights concerning the church of St Martin in the village of St Remigius. (Anagni, 10 April.)

[Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, VI, 645.]

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and brethren of St Remigius, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Matters concluded by judgment or amicable settlement ought to remain valid and firm; and, lest a recurrence of dispute should arise, it is fitting that we strengthen them by the protection of our authority. We have learned, moreover, and have known from the authentic document of our venerable brother G., bishop of Avignon, that when a dispute concerning the parochial right of a certain village arose between you and the monks of Montmajour, dwelling in the diocese of Avignon, it was finally settled, with the consent of the parties, in the following manner by the same G., to whom our father and predecessor of holy memory, Pope Eugenius, had committed the case: namely, that the whole parochial right of the said village should remain peacefully and quietly with the church of St Martin of St Remigius, which is under the jurisdiction of Rheims, and be preserved forever entire. [Col. 0934D–0935A]

If, nevertheless, women rising after childbirth should come to the chapel of the monks of Montmajour out of devotion to the glorious and ever-virgin Mary, they are to discharge their vows there in accordance with the tenor of the privilege of Pope Callistus of pious memory; provided, however, that the aforesaid monks receive only the offerings of those women and of their midwives. He also forbade the bell to be rung more than once, and then only as much as sufficed to rouse their own household. The aforesaid G. further added, in order to settle forever the controversies of both parties, that the monks of Montmajour should neither appoint nor admit in their chapel anyone, male or female, except members of their own household and the women mentioned above, as determined, to any divine office. [Col. 0935A]

We confirm by apostolic authority that settlement, which, as is contained in the authentic document of the oft-mentioned bishop, is known to have been observed until now, and strengthen it by the protection of the present writing. Let no one, therefore, etc. [Col. 0935B]

Given at Anagni, on the fourth Ides of April.

### MLVIII. To Henry, archbishop of Rheims.—That he cause the already concluded case of the abbot and brethren of Humblières to be observed. (Anagni, 13 April.)

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 964.]

Our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of Humblières, informed us that, when the case pending between them and the abbot of Ribemont, the abbess of Monasteriolum, and G., knight of Bresnoy, had received its due conclusion under the examination of the bishops of Laon and Noyon, to whom we had entrusted the matter for final determination, afterwards a certain monk of Ribemont, coming into our presence on business of the treasurer of Laon, asked that the same case be committed to the bishop of Tournai, concealing that it had been concluded. Yet the sentence had been pronounced by those bishops, although many objected or appealed. [Col. 0935C]

Therefore, since we, who are bound to put an end to lawsuits and contentions, do not wish to revive a dispute that has been settled, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to investigate the matter from the aforesaid bishops and others who know the truth. If it is established to you that the said case was concluded by those bishops and that their sentence was not suspended by appeal, hold that sentence valid and cause it to be observed inviolate. Nor permit the aforesaid bishop of Tournai to proceed in the same case under pretext of our commission. [Col. 0935C–D]

Given at Anagni, on the Ides of April.

### MLIX. To the same.—Concerning a prebend in the church of St Peter at Douai, to be given to the clerk Walcher. (Anagni, 14 April.)

[Ibid.]

Our beloved son Walcher, clerk and bearer of these presents, coming to us, stated with diligent assertion that Hu., provost, and the canons of St Peter at Douai had some time ago unanimously and concordantly received him as their brother and canon, and, freely granting him the prebend which should first become vacant in that church, confirmed their grant by an authentic writing. When the said prebend had become vacant and the aforesaid provost objected to assigning it to him, the said clerk appealed to our hearing and pursued the appeal he had lodged at great labour and danger to his body. [Col. 0936A]

Wishing therefore to provide carefully for that clerk in this matter, we commanded the said provost and canons that, just as they received him as their canon and granted him the prebend now vacant, they should assign it to him without delay, within fifteen days after receiving our letters, all pretext and appeal ceasing. If, after the appeal made to us, they have bestowed that prebend upon another—which we do not believe—they are to revoke it within the same term, appeal set aside, and without delay assign it to the aforesaid clerk. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the same provost and canons have not carried out our command, you are not to delay strictly and diligently to investigate the truth of the matter. If it is established to you that the same provost and canons received the aforesaid clerk as their canon, granted him the prebend when it first became vacant, and confirmed this by authentic writing, you are strictly to compel them, by our authority and yours, with recourse to appeal removed, to execute our command within another fifteen days. [Col. 0936A–C]

Given at Anagni, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May.

### MLX. To the same.—That the lepers of Épernay be exempt from tithes on newly cultivated lands, etc. (Anagni, 14 April.)

[Ibid., col. 965.]

We have received the complaint of the lepers of Épernay. They assert that, although they had obtained from us letters of protection for their house, and although the clemency of the Apostolic See had exempted them from payment of tithes on their newly cultivated lands, which they cultivate at their own expense, and on the increase of their animals, the canons of Épernay became angered and disturbed against them on that account. Indeed, when the master of the lepers, with certain brethren and servants, was gathering hay in their own meadows, eight of the aforesaid canons rose up against them, severely beat the master and the brethren with him, inflicted many wounds on their servants, and violently caused that hay to be carried away from the meadows. [Col. 0936C–D]

Therefore, since we are very gravely offended when things ordained by us are overturned through anyone’s rashness, and since we might be charged with negligence if we left so great an offence unpunished, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you permit no tithes to be demanded or exacted from the aforesaid sick persons from their newly cultivated lands which they cultivate at their own expense, or from the increase of their animals. Having investigated the truth of the facts more diligently concerning the matters we have stated, if you find it to be so, publicly pronounce excommunicated—recourse to appeal removed—those who committed so great a crime, and cause them to be avoided as excommunicated persons until they make fitting satisfaction to those injured, restore the hay taken away, and those who laid violent hands upon the aforesaid master and his brethren, if they are clerics, present themselves before the Apostolic See with your letters containing the truth of the facts. [Col. 0937A]

Given at Anagni, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May.

### MLXI. He commends to him Milo, apostolic messenger. (Anagni, 17 April.)

[Ibid., col. 966.]

[Col. 0937B]

Our beloved son Milo, whom you sent to us, showed such concern in your affairs and pressed us so earnestly for the advancement of those affairs that we have plainly recognized him to be exceedingly faithful and devoted to you. Therefore, commending him carefully to you in consideration of his devotion and service, we earnestly request and admonish your brotherhood that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and for us, and in view of the service which he is known to have rendered you by coming to us now for the second time, you love and honour the same M. more warmly and confer benefits upon him so suitably and usefully that he may more easily and willingly expose his own person to dangers for you. Thus we shall be bound to render you abundant thanks for this and shall be able worthily to commend your prudence in the Lord. [Col. 0937B–C]

Given at Anagni, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

### MLXII. To the same.—That he excommunicate An. of Loos, who had put the subdeacon R. in chains. (Anagni, 17 April.)

[Ibid.]

The subdeacon R. laid before our hearing a grave complaint: An. of Loos, at the instigation of the devil, committed him to prison and shamelessly extorted money from him. Since we neither can nor ought to leave unpunished the audacity of so great an iniquity—an offence for whose more severe punishment we are compelled to gird ourselves with apostolic authority—we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, after diligently and carefully investigating the truth of the matter, that if you find this to be so, you pronounce the aforesaid An. and the principal accomplices in the same crime excommunicated, appeal set aside, and cause all to avoid them as excommunicated persons, until the said A. makes fitting satisfaction to the aforesaid subdeacon for so grave an injury, restores without diminution all that he extorted or caused to be taken from him, and comes to the Apostolic See, with letters from you testifying to the truth of the matter, to make satisfaction for so great an offence. [Col. 0937C–0938A]

Given at Anagni, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

### MLXIII. To the same.—That the parish of Nizy be restored to the priest A. (Anagni, 18 April.)

[Ibid., col. 967.]

We have received the complaint of A., priest and bearer of these presents, that although he had canonically acquired the parish of Nizy and had possessed it peacefully for a long time, the priest G. presumed unreasonably to take it from him and unjustly holds it under occupation. Since it is unseemly and contrary to reason that the said priest should be deprived of the aforesaid parish without manifest and reasonable cause, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, after summoning the parties before you, you admonish and strictly compel the said G. either to restore to the aforesaid A. the said parish together with the revenues received from it and leave him in peace, or, in your presence and with recourse to appeal removed, to render him full justice without delay. [Col. 0938A–B]

Given at Anagni, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May.

### MLXIV. To the same.—For the priest Evrard. (Anagni, 19 April.)

[Ibid., col. 968.]

We have received in writing the complaint of the priest Evrard that Matthew, a citizen of Châlons, unjustly took from him a certain street or plot of ground, which he holds occupied by his own power. Since we are bound to give the said priest, who is said to be poor and to have a case against a rich man, more ready assistance in vindicating his right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to admonish the said M. and, appeal set aside, compel him under penalty of excommunication either to restore the aforesaid property to the said priest without difficulty and leave him in peace, or, under your examination and with appeal set aside, without delay render him complete justice concerning it. [Col. 0938B–C]

Given at Anagni, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May.

### MLXV. To the same.—He writes that he has granted no privilege to Philip, count of Flanders, contrary to the rights of the church of Rheims. (Anagni, 19 April.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0938D]

Since we possess the clearest proofs and indications of your devotion and fidelity, and have always found it beneficially displayed toward the honour and exaltation of your mother, the most holy Roman Church, we should seem to derogate considerably from our own honour and to forget all humanity unless we loved your person most sincerely as that of our dearest brother and a chief member of the Church, and endeavoured to preserve fully for you your honour and dignity. Lest, therefore, any doubt or scruple of uncertainty remain in your mind on this point, we wish you to know that we have granted no immunity to the noble man Ph., count of Flanders, against your right and dignity; nor have we exempted him from your authority, so as to prevent you from exercising over him that jurisdiction and authority which your predecessors are known to have exercised and which the sacred canons permit. [Col. 0938D–0939A]

Given at Anagni, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May.

### MLXVI. To the same.—He entrusts for examination the case between the abbot of Humolaria and F. of Nigella. (Anagni, 20 April.)

[Ibid., col. 970.]

Jam pridem, si bene meminimus, venerabili fratri nostro B., bishop of Beauvais, we committed for hearing and for due settlement the case between the abbot and brethren of Humolary and T. de Nigella concerning a measure of salt. As we have learned from the statement of the said brethren, he indeed put the aforementioned T. into possession; wherefore the brethren maintain that they have been greatly aggrieved, both because they regarded that judge himself as suspect, being their adversary, and because, the same bishop forbidding it, they were not allowed to see the tenor of the letters which had been issued by us on this matter. But since those brethren are confident that they have justice against the aforesaid T., and since we can neither, nor ought to, deny them what we are bound, by the office committed to us, to afford to all, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the aforesaid brethren wish to proceed concerning title, you, having summoned the parties, shall hear the case more diligently—if it has not been settled by him or committed to another—and, with appeal set aside, shall decide it through justice in such a manner that your discernment may deservedly be commended thereby.

Given at Anagni, the twelfth day before the Kalends of May [20 April].

MLXVII. To the same.—On behalf of certain merchants of Flanders against the abbot of Dervensis. (Anagni, 21 April.)

[Ibid.]

Ric. and Arn., Flemish merchants, appearing in our presence, showed us by their statement that they had some time ago lent thirty marks of silver to the abbot of the monastery of Dervensis [Col. 0939D], which money they afterwards could in no way recover from him, although he had received our mandate concerning it. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, upon receiving these present letters, you shall admonish the said abbot and strictly compel him by our authority to restore the aforesaid money without delay to the said merchants, and to make such settlement with them concerning that which he is bound to pay in addition, that those merchants may not be compelled on this account to bring any complaint to us.

Given at Anagni, the eleventh day before the Kalends of May [21 April].

MLXVIII. To the same.—Against the canons of Compiègne, who were troubling the monks. (Anagni, 28 April.)

[Ibid., col. 971.]

[Col. 0940A]

From the representations of our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of Compiègne, you should know that it has come to our hearing that, although they have held peacefully for ten years certain shares in the granges of Hortiis and Borcherra, the canons of that church now do not cease unjustly to harass them concerning these matters. Nor are they willing to leave that grange in the condition in which it is known to have been when the monks were admitted to it. Therefore, since we neither wish nor ought to tolerate the aforesaid abbot and monks being burdened by undue harassment in this or other matters, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, enjoining you that you shall not allow the same abbot and monks to be harassed by the said canons concerning those portions; rather, setting appeal aside, you shall cause those monks peacefully to possess the same portions, as they were reasonably granted to them by the canons. But if they harass the same abbot and monks contrary to the tenor of our mandate, you shall restrain them from their presumption by ecclesiastical coercion under our authority, all contradiction and appeal ceasing.

Moreover, we command your discretion to preserve whole and unharmed the liberties and rights of the aforesaid monastery and the privileges which it is known to possess from the Apostolic See, as we trust of you and as becomes your prudence. And if at any time you receive from the abbot and brethren of that place a complaint against persons within your province, take care so to restrain their wrongdoers from their iniquity that the diligence of your solicitude may deservedly be commended thereby, and that the monastery itself may be kept safe under your protection from the attacks of evil men.

Given at Anagni, the fourth day before the Kalends of May [28 April].

MLXIX. To the same.—He thanks him for fostering and commends to him the brethren of Compiègne under his protection. (Anagni, 28 April.)

[Ibid., col. 972.]

[Col. 0940D]

Our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of Compiègne, have carefully reported to us through their messenger, with much thanksgiving, how earnestly you love their monastery, diligently protect and preserve the rights of that place, and generously show your favor and support to the aforesaid abbot and brethren. Accordingly, earnestly commending your prudence in the Lord for this, and rendering abundant thanks to your affection, we attentively request and admonish your brotherhood that, as you have begun well, you may love more earnestly the aforesaid monastery, the abbot, and the brethren serving the Lord there; preserve their rights whole and unharmed; and so protect that monastery from undue burdens that the aforesaid abbot and brethren may rejoice to possess their rights peacefully under the patronage of your protection, and that we may be bound to render still fuller thanks to your affection.

Furthermore, since the canons who remain there still hold, as we have learned, the ancient common seal in their own control, the aforesaid abbot and brethren state that they fear lest documents be sealed with that seal which may turn to the detriment of the aforesaid monastery. By the authority of these presents we enjoin upon your brotherhood that, under threat of excommunication, you forbid the said canons to presume to seal with the aforesaid seal any document harmful to the monastery just mentioned. If, however, those canons have sealed any document concerning the goods and possessions of the aforesaid monastery without the assent and will of the aforesaid [Col. 0941B] abbot and brethren, you shall, by our authority and with appeal set aside, declare that document wholly void and of no effect.

Given at Anagni, the fourth day before the Kalends of May [28 April].

MLXX. To the same.—That he should ensure the inviolate observance of the settlement made between the brethren of Compiègne and Tenolay. (Anagni, 28 April.)

[Ibid.]

From the communication sent to us by the abbot and brethren of Compiègne, it has come to our attention that, after the abbot and brethren of Tenolay—

> [Note: [Col. 0941D] The abbey of Tenolay, in French *Tenaille*, of the Premonstratensian Order in the diocese of Laon.]

—had, without the knowledge or consent of the brethren of Compiègne, cleared and brought under cultivation certain woods belonging to the right of the monastery of Compiègne [Col. 0941C], an amicable settlement was at last made between them, with the consent of the parties, in your court before our beloved sons the abbots of Saint-Remi and Saint-Crépin and other worthy men. Since matters settled by amicable agreement ought not to be undone by any presumption whatever, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, enjoining you that, with the remedy of appeal removed, you shall cause the aforesaid settlement, as made with the assent of the parties, to be inviolably observed on both sides, and shall not permit either party rashly to act against that settlement. But if either party presumes to act against the same settlement [Col. 0941D] and, after admonition, does not desist, restrain it from its presumption by ecclesiastical coercion, with appeal set aside.

Given at Anagni, the fourth day before the Kalends of May [28 April].

MLXXI. To the same.—On the case between the canons of Saint-Laurent of Beauvais and the bishop of Beauvais. (Anagni, 30 April.)

[Ibid.]

From the complaint sent by the canons of the church of Saint-Laurent of Beauvais [Col. 0942A], it has come to our hearing that our venerable brother Bartholomew, bishop of Beauvais, has unjustly withdrawn from them more than seven bakers who used to frequent their mill, and has compelled them to grind elsewhere according to his will rather than according to right. He has also presumed to take from them the church of Franc-Castel, which they maintain belongs to them by the gift of the aforesaid canon. Therefore, since by the authority of the Apostolic See we are bound to preserve ecclesiastical persons in their rights, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you earnestly admonish and exhort the aforesaid bishop to permit the said bakers freely to grind in the mill of the aforesaid canons, as they were accustomed to do, and to restore the aforesaid church quietly and peacefully to those canons; or else, in your presence, not delay to render them full justice concerning it.

Further, because the predecessor of the aforesaid bishop is said to have taken from the vicars the annual distributions due upon the deaths of canons of the aforesaid church, we likewise enjoin upon you by the authority of these presents that you firmly require that bishop either to restore those annual distributions to the vicars, or not delay to render full justice on this matter under the examination of your discretion.

Given at Anagni, the second day before the Kalends of May [30 April].

MLXXII. To the same.—He entrusts for settlement the case of H., a woman of Suune. (Anagni, 1 May.)

[Ibid., col. 974.]

[Col. 0942C]

From the complaint sent by H., a woman of Suune, it has come to our hearing that, when Master G. of Laon had stood surety to her, on behalf of A., formerly lady of Rochenies, for eighteen pounds, that lady died and the aforesaid H. has not yet been able to recover her money. Since it seems unworthy and unjust that the aforesaid H. should be defrauded of the money owed to her, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, enjoining you that you admonish and compel the aforesaid G. to pay the above-mentioned money in full to the aforesaid H., or else not delay to render her full justice concerning it in your presence. But if he chooses instead to enter into litigation, you shall hear the case with diligence and, with appeal set aside, decide it by agreement or through justice.

Given at Anagni, on the Kalends of May [1 May].

MLXXIII. To the same.—For the monks of La Sauve-Majeure against Wiscard and Ralph of Coucy. (Anagni, 4 May.)

[Ibid.]

Our beloved son, the abbot of La Sauve-Majeure, informed us—

> [Note: [Col. 0941D] The abbey of La Sauve-Majeure, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Bordeaux. It once possessed a rich cell not far from Codiciacum—or, as Alexander here calls it, Coceium (Coucy)—which Wiscard and Ralph were harassing.]

—that Wiscard and Ralph of Coucy, and certain others, repeatedly trouble the monks of La Sauve concerning woods and other possessions of theirs [Col. 0943A], and do not cease to inflict great injuries and burdens upon them. Since it belongs to us, by the office committed to us, to provide for the security of churches, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, enjoining you that you earnestly admonish and with every diligence induce the aforesaid men and such others as the said abbot shall name to you; and, if necessary, compel them by excommunication, with appeal set aside, in no way to trouble the aforesaid abbot and monks concerning the woods just mentioned or their other possessions. Rather, they must restore in full everything taken from them and wholly desist from burdening them; or, if they wish to bring anything against them, they shall proceed in your presence by judicial process. You shall hear the case diligently and, with appeal ceasing, decide it by a canonical judgment.

Moreover, if the aforesaid abbot or monks lodge with you a complaint concerning other persons of your parishes, render them such full justice against those persons that we may deservedly commend your solicitude and zeal for justice.

Given at Anagni, the fourth Nones of May [4 May].

MLXXIV. He bids Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen, who is “grieving over the various fortunes of wars and the scandal of the kings and the land,” to be of strong spirit. He commands him “to attend diligently to restoring peace between the kings, and to correct with the customary pontifical severity the transgressions of bishops, deans, archdeacons, clerics, and laymen.” He adds other commands. He forbids him to “lend his pallium to another metropolitan if it happens that the latter comes without his pallium to the church of Rouen for some principal solemnity; for the pallium,” he says, “does not pass beyond your person, but each man ought to be buried with it.” (Anagni, 11 May.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1071.]

[Col. 0943C]

Although the times are dangerous and the various fortunes of war afflict your region, it does not therefore become you to grieve without measure or cast down your spirit into bitterness, so as to seem forgetful of courage and fortitude. Rather, the greater the adversity and turmoil threatening you and the land, the more resolutely you ought to rise against those tribulations and put on the strength of greater fortitude and courage, because the constancy of a prudent man is tested in adversity. Although you grieve, as you may rightly grieve, over the scandal of the kings and the land, it is nevertheless not expedient that you be so affected by sorrow or overwhelmed by grief that it may be attributed to faint-heartedness; for the Lord is able to make calm after the storm and to grant rest after tribulation.

We especially commend you because you display such devotion toward us and the Roman Church that you cannot be negligent or slack in matters pertaining to that Church’s advantage and advancement; rather, as a noble, prudent, and wise man, you devote yourself fervently in every way to the honor and exaltation of that Church. Thus, the more we love your person, the more attentive we make you in matters belonging to your office. We admonish and strictly command your brotherhood that, setting aside that excessive sorrow and bitterness of heart by which, as we hear, you are afflicted because of the land’s turmoil, you strive prudently to exercise the office of solicitude entrusted to you. Whenever opportunity presents itself, devote careful attention to restoring peace between the kings; and correct and amend more diligently, with customary pontifical severity, the transgressions of bishops, deans, archdeacons, abbots, and others, both clerics and laymen, entrusted to your governance. Do not so follow the compassion of a mother that you appear to set aside the severity of a master.

We commend your gentleness and patience, as they deservedly commend you to us. But you must not show yourself so gentle and kind to your subjects that they can abuse your patience and kindness, or take from your excessive gentleness boldness to commit unlawful acts; for unlawful acts are committed more freely when wrongdoers see themselves secure in their impunity. Restrain, with the diligence appropriate to you and by the authority granted to you, the canons of your cathedral church—especially those holding some office of dignity therein and thus found to be eminent—from their transgressions; and more earnestly encourage and instruct them in virtue and uprightness, so that, as they excel in dignity in your province, they may likewise flourish in moral uprightness [Col. 0944C] and provide others with a model and example of right living. Do not reject those who appeal to the hearing of your metropolitan see and who, through the remedy of appeal, seek refuge in your protection. Instead, hear patiently and impartially all who come to you; afford protection and favor, as your office requires, to those unjustly oppressed; uphold them in their right with pastoral solicitude; and show yourself a father to all, so that you may appear to be not merely a father, but an archbishop and teacher.

Furthermore, we command your brotherhood that if any layman of your province, of his own will or by command of secular authority, lays violent hands on a cleric not yet condemned by the Church [Col. 0944D], throws him into chains, or keeps him in prison, then, setting aside favor and affection, and with contradiction and appeal removed, you shall publicly declare him excommunicated—or cause him to be so declared—with lighted candles, and he shall be avoided as excommunicated. But if a cleric has been arrested for his faults by the officials of ecclesiastical prelates, do not allow him to be consigned to public custody or shut up in a lay prison. Instead, have a suitable place of custody provided in your own house or that of another ecclesiastical person, where he may be kept according to the character and gravity of his offence. As for matters known to belong to the right of your church, strive vigorously and lawfully to reclaim them, setting aside every favor and fear, so that your solicitude and foresight may deservedly be commended thereby, and the church entrusted to you may suffer no prejudice from your silence.

We have also thought it necessary to enjoin more strictly upon you that, on account of the aforesaid conflict among the kings or for any other reason, you must not presume to abandon your pastoral care; for, according to the Lord’s saying, the man who abandons the guardianship of the flock entrusted to him when the wolf comes, exposing it to the wolf’s bites, is proved not a shepherd but a hireling. If any bishop subject to your jurisdiction has, by his own authority, transferred himself to another church, or has presumed by lay authority to appropriate to his own use the goods of a church or monastery [Col. 0945B], recall him from his purpose by ecclesiastical coercion under our authority and yours. Do not delay to compel restitution of the alienated property, or wholly release the former church from his obedience. In these matters, as a prudent and wise man, be diligent and zealous; exercise your office so wisely in all things that you may govern and benefit the clergy and people entrusted to you, and that the Church over which you preside may, through the Lord’s cooperation, receive welcome increase in spiritual and temporal matters from your care and governance.

Moreover, from the ardor of your sincere love proceeds our granting you permission and authority to restrain from the audacity of their rashness those who presume to oppose the dignity of the Roman Church. Accordingly, wishing in all things possible with God to show deference to you as to our dearest brother, we grant by apostolic authority that, if any of your suffragans presumes to act contrary to an appeal made to our hearing or yours, you may restrain his transgression with pastoral solicitude by our authority and your own.

Further, because you have asked us whether you may lend your pallium to another metropolitan should he happen to come without his own pallium to the church entrusted to you on some principal solemnity, and celebrate therein the solemnities of Mass: although we do not recall having seen an express canon on this point, we answer your inquiry as follows. It does not appear fitting that you should lend your pallium to another, since your pallium does not pass beyond your person, but each man ought, as your discernment knows, to be buried with it. However, after confirmation of his election, the suffragans of a metropolitan may, at that metropolitan’s command, consecrate an elect who belongs to his jurisdiction, even if the metropolitan has not received the pallium. And if the metropolitan is suffering illness or is otherwise prevented, his suffragans may, at his command, confer the gift of consecration upon the elect after the metropolitan’s reception of the pallium, and even before it, if his election has been confirmed.

Given at Anagni, the fifth Ides of May [11 May].

MLXXV. To Henry, archbishop, and all bishops and abbots established throughout the archbishopric of Reims.—He commends to them the brethren of Saint-Remi of Reims. (Anagni, 15 May.)

[MARTEN., *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 975.]

[Col. 0946A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishop of Reims and bishops, and to his beloved sons the abbots and other prelates of churches established throughout the archbishopric of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, by reason of the solicitude laid upon us, we ought to be concerned for preserving the condition of each person, we are especially bound to attend to the preservation and protection of those devoted to religion and more strictly dedicated to divine service, and to keep their rights whole and inviolate. Moved by this consideration, we command all of you by apostolic letters, enjoining you that wherever, within your parishes, wrongdoers against our beloved sons the abbot and brethren of Saint-Remi of Reims are found—or persons who presume unjustly to withhold the chief rents owed to them—if, after being admonished by those among you whose parishioners they are, they refuse to repent or render justice, you shall bind them with the bond of excommunication and subject their lands to interdict. You shall observe that sentence inviolate until worthy satisfaction is made, and cause it to be firmly observed throughout your provinces.

[Col. 0946C] Given at Anagni, on the Ides of May [15 May].

MLXXVI. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of Alagrin, a citizen of Anagni. (Anagni, 18 May.)

[Ibid., col. 976.]

After Paganus and Rainald, burgesses of your city, had stayed with us for a long time, they finally borrowed, from a certain faithful citizen of Anagni named Alagrin, sixteen pounds in Provins currency, with Walter, priest of the infirmary of Sparnac, as surety. Both the said burgesses and that priest gave sworn security for payment of the aforesaid money, as they themselves acknowledged before our beloved son V., cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus [Col. 0946D]. In their oath they added that they would not leave our court until the aforesaid money had been paid to the said creditor. Since, in breach of their oath and without paying the money, they have returned home, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, enjoining you that you compel the said burgesses and priest, by ecclesiastical and, if necessary, temporal coercion, with appeal set aside, to pay in full to the aforesaid creditor and to his messenger, who will come to you with these letters, the aforesaid money and the necessary costs of the journey within fifteen days after receipt of these letters. By apostolic authority, decree that letters which they have obtained from us shall have no force until the debt has been paid and the travelling expenses restored.

Given at Anagni, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June [18 May].

MLXXVII. To the same.—That he should cause Rainald’s land to be restored to him. (Anagni, 19 May.)

[Ibid.]

From the complaint sent by Rainald, it has come to our hearing that, after Adam de Villari had some time ago granted him a certain piece of land in fief and homage, and he had possessed it quietly and peacefully for a long time, the aforesaid A. despoiled him of that land without judicial process and presumed to invest a certain brother of his with it [Col. 0947B]. Therefore, since we acknowledge ourselves bound to all God’s faithful in their right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you diligently investigate the truth of the matter. If you find that it is so, admonish the aforesaid A. and his brother by our authority to restore that land to the said R., together with the fruits received from it, and to make satisfaction to him for the losses and injuries inflicted. Once restoration has been made, if they are confident of their brother’s right, let them proceed against him in your presence by judicial process. You shall hear the case and endeavor to settle it through justice or amicable agreement. But if the said men contemptuously refuse to obey your admonitions, do not delay, relying on our authority, to subject them to excommunication, with every excuse and appeal removed.

Given at Anagni, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June [19 May].

MLXXVIII. To the same.—Against the canons of Compiègne, who had installed a chaplain in the church of Saint Clement against the abbot’s will. (Anagni, 20 May.)

[Ibid., col. 977.]

It has come to us from the complaint sent by the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Compiègne that, although the church of Saint Clement belongs to that monastery, upon the death of its chaplain the canons of that church presumed to intrude a chaplain there against the will of the aforesaid abbot and brethren [Col. 0947D]. Contrary to their prohibition made in our name, and after an appeal, he did not fear to celebrate divine offices in that church, although the appointment of the chaplain there is said to belong to the abbot himself. Since so grave and outrageous a presumption ought not to be left uncorrected, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, enjoining you that, after summoning both parties before you, you carefully investigate the truth of the matter. If it is established that appointment of the chaplain in the aforesaid church belongs to the said abbot and that the aforesaid chaplain was installed there against his will, then, relying on apostolic authority and with appeal set aside, remove him from it. Duly punish and correct both him and the aforesaid canons for the excess of this rashness, and grant the same abbot full power to appoint a chaplain there.

Compel the canons of the aforesaid church by ecclesiastical coercion, with appeal set aside, to restore to the said abbot the authentic documents of that church which they are known to have concealed. Command them under threat of anathema never to presume to dispose of or alienate from that church its treasury or ornaments. Rather, they are to strive faithfully to preserve them under the abbot’s oversight and to render the abbot the obedience they owe with reverence. In these matters proceed as becomes your prudence, with such integrity and diligence that we may deservedly commend the diligence of your solicitude thereby.

Given at Anagni, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June [20 May].

MLXXIX. To the same.—That he should arrange for the church of Saint-Médard of Barleus to be given to the priest W. (Anagni, 21 May.)

[Ibid., col. 978.]

When W., a priest, bearer of these letters and representative of the priest Robert concerning the church of Saint-Médard of Barleus, was present before us, we carefully heard and considered the arguments on both sides and adjudged that church to the said W. We commanded and enjoined our beloved sons, the dean and treasurer of the church of Noyon, not to delay in assigning the aforesaid church to the same W., removing the priest R. from it by our authority, with every contradiction and appeal set aside [Col. 0948C]. We also commanded that they cause the fruits received from it in the meantime, if any have been placed in sequestration, to be delivered to him likewise, with appeal set aside. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to cause whatever that dean and treasurer do in this matter in accordance with our mandate to be inviolably observed, with every excuse and appeal set aside.

Given at Anagni, the twelfth day before the Kalends of June [21 May].

MLXXX. To the same.—For G., a poor cleric, against R. de Thori, canon of Beauvais. (Anagni, 26 May.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0948D]

From the complaint sent by G., a poor cleric, we have learned that Ro. de Thori, a canon of Beauvais, unjustly retains in occupation the house of his uncle, which ought to devolve upon that cleric by right of succession. Since we acknowledge ourselves bound to rich and poor alike in their right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you admonish the said R. and compel him under the coercion of excommunication either to restore the aforesaid house to the said cleric without harassment or difficulty and leave him in peace, or not delay to render him full justice concerning it under your examination, with appeal set aside. But if he prefers to enter into litigation, you shall hear the case diligently and, without respect of persons, with appeal set aside, as we have said, decide it by due judgment.

Given at Anagni, the seventh day before the Kalends of June [26 May].

MLXXXI. To the same.—For the lepers of Tours-sur-Marne against the monks of that place and the priest Evirvinus. (Anagni, 1 June.)

[Ibid., col. 979.]

We have received the complaint of the lepers of Tours-sur-Marne that the monks—

> [Note: [Col. 0949D] Of the Cluniac Order.]

—of that village and the priest Evirvinus pronounced a sentence of excommunication against some of them after an appeal had been made to us; and that they caused three of their brethren, who died after that sentence, to be buried outside the cemetery [Col. 0949B]. Since we can neither, nor ought to, pass by the grievances of the aforesaid lepers with deaf ears—being so afflicted by the just judgment of God that, beyond the common duty, we are not without reason bound to assist them—we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, after summoning the parties before you, you diligently investigate the truth of these matters. If they are established before you, declare the aforesaid sentence invalid, with appeal set aside; cause the bodies of the aforesaid persons to be buried within the cemetery; and cause the aforesaid monks and priest to be avoided as excommunicated for as long as the aforesaid lepers and their brethren are known to have been avoided on account of the aforesaid sentence.

[Col. 0949C] Given at Anagni, on the Kalends of June [1 June].

MLXXXII. He informs the Carthusian brethren that he has undertaken protection of the monastery of Gyrio, founded by Henry, bishop of Gurk. (Anagni, 2 June.)

[PUSCH and FROELICH, *Diplomata ducatus Styriae*, II, 135.]

It becomes us to apply the full diligence of our solicitude to matters that appear to concern the practice of religion, and diligently and carefully to foster what is known to pertain to the glory of the Lord. We have learned from the letter of our venerable brother Henry, bishop of Gurk, that, touched by the grace of divine inspiration, he established, with the counsel and assent of the provost and canons of his church and of that church’s ministeriales, a community of your congregation in an estate named Gyrio, situated in the March and belonging by right to the aforesaid church. To the brethren living there he assigned so much in revenues and possessions as might honestly suffice for the necessities of their life [Col. 0949D].

Accordingly, considering your religious life to be pleasing and acceptable to God, at the request of the aforesaid bishop we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid place, with its boundaries and its cultivated and uncultivated possessions assigned to that place by the bishop, as stated above. We decree that what the aforesaid bishop has done in this respect shall remain firm and stable forever [Col. 0950A], establishing that no person whatsoever may infringe this charter of our protection and confirmation or in any way act against it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, the fourth Nones of June [2 June].

MLXXXIII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—That he should ensure reparation of the injuries inflicted upon the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem. (Anagni, 3 June.)

[MARTEN., *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 979.]

On behalf of our beloved sons, the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem dwelling in the diocese of Châlons, you should know that it has come to our hearing [Col. 0950B] that, after James de Port-sur-Marne had given them a certain house of his in alms for the remedy of his own soul and those of his parents, certain men of those parts, stirred by diabolical fury, presumed to expel the brethren from that house and destroyed the enclosure around the place belonging to it. They further added that Lambert Blundus, Clarembald, and certain others made an armed attack upon a house of the aforesaid brethren called Fraisnoi, situated near Cambrai, and carried away forty sheep from it, none of which they have yet restored to those brethren.

Since we are bound to preserve the rights of the said brethren—whom, in consideration of their religious life, we embrace with the arms of sincere charity—and since, by the office committed to us, we acknowledge ourselves debtors to all in their right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you carefully admonish and induce the aforesaid men and the other wrongdoers whom those brethren shall name to you to restore everything taken from them, make reparation for the damage done, render fitting satisfaction for the injuries inflicted, and wholly desist from injuring and burdening them; or else, with appeal set aside, to render full justice in your presence. If, after your admonition, they do none of these things, bind them with a sentence of excommunication, with appeal and excuse set aside; and do not relax that sentence without suitable satisfaction.

Given at Anagni, the third Nones of June [3 June].

MLXXXIV. To the same.—That he should grant some benefice to the deacon G. (Anagni, 4 June.)

[Ibid., col. 980.]

Although we ought to be concerned for the provision of all, it is fitting that we look with a more kindly eye upon, and make effective provision for, those who, though promoted to holy orders, hold no place or benefice in the Church of God, lest, if they should begin to suffer disgraceful want, the dignity of their order itself seem to be cheapened along with them. Therefore we have thought fit earnestly to commend to your brotherhood G., the bearer of these letters, who [Col. 0951A] was formerly ordained deacon by your predecessor S. of good memory and has no ecclesiastical benefice; asking and commanding that, for the love of God, reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, and the duty of your office, you make generous provision for him from some benefice by which he may obtain the necessities of life. Thus you may receive an unfailing reward from almighty God, and G. himself may rejoice that he has found with you a welcome support for his maintenance.

MLXXXV. To the same. — That he restore to the priest J. the church of Villa Senior. (Anagni, June 4.)

[Ibid., col. 981.]

[Col. 0951B]

J., a poor priest and bearer of these letters, returning to us, recalled to our memory how proceedings had taken place in his case concerning the church of Villa Senior. He asserted that, since the presentation of a chaplain to that church belongs to the abbot of St. Saviour’s, he was presented through the abbot’s prior to our venerable brother, the bishop of Châlons, and received from that bishop the care of souls.

[Note: [Col. 0951] St. Saviour’s, outside the city of Vertus, is a monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Châlons.]

But when a clerk named William, through the favour of the aforesaid abbot, harassed the said priest concerning that church, the priest came to us and obtained from us letters to you. In them we commanded you that, if it were established to your satisfaction that he had been invested by the aforesaid bishop [Col. 0951C] with the aforesaid church upon the presentation of the aforesaid prior, you should cause him to possess that church peacefully. Afterwards, when you had sought information from the said bishop, he asserted that, when the aforesaid prior presented that priest, he had first obtained the permission of his abbot, who declared that he ratified whatever the prior should do in the matter; accordingly, the bishop received him into the said church and entrusted the care of souls to him. Therefore, both because of that bishop’s assertion and because of the depositions of the witnesses presented to you on this matter, you allowed the priest peacefully to retain the aforesaid church.

Yet after a long time, the same William came into our presence and obtained from us letters to you, [Col. 0951D] on the occasion of which the aforesaid priest was again drawn into litigation. Since the abbot and prior in question denied that they had presented the aforesaid priest, you deprived him of the aforesaid church on the strength of their assertion, and invested the same G. with it. Since, therefore, no greater credence should be given to the abbot and prior than to the bishop, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if you deprived the aforesaid priest of that church solely upon the assertion of the said abbot and prior, without witnesses having been heard or sworn on the matter, you shall restore that church to him, without appeal; and, if the aforementioned G. has several prebends [Col. 0952A] and churches, you shall entirely release the priest from his claim and cause him peacefully to possess the aforesaid church.

Given at Anagni, on the second day before the Nones of June.

MLXXXVI. To William, archbishop of Tarragona, and his suffragans. — That they admonish the king of Aragon not to permit Robert, who had conspired in the murder of Hugh, archbishop of Tarragona, to reside in his kingdom. (Anagni, June 7.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 1069.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers William, archbishop of Tarragona, legate of the apostolic see, and his suffragans, [Col. 0952B] greeting and apostolic blessing.

It accords with our office to correct the crimes and enormities of criminals and to punish offenders’ faults with due severity, lest impunity for wickedness leave others emboldened to offend. Certainly, the prudence of your brotherhood cannot be unaware how gravely and monstrously those have sinned who plotted the death of Hugh, formerly archbishop of Tarragona, of good memory. We have learned that Robert, at the devil’s instigation, conspired in the death of the aforesaid archbishop and poured upon him the poison of wickedness which he had conceived.

Since we cannot and ought not leave such an unjust and cruel crime unpunished, we command and enjoin your brotherhood, by these apostolic letters, that on behalf of ourselves and yourselves you admonish our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Aragonese, and labour by every means to induce him not, under any circumstances, to receive the aforesaid Robert into his kingdom, nor in any way consent to keep him there, nor show him any grace or favour. But if he should perhaps refuse to comply with your admonitions, throughout his kingdom, with every excuse and appeal removed, prohibit the celebration of divine offices, except baptism for infants and penances for the dying; and, setting aside all fear and favour, pronounce against the king himself a sentence of excommunication and cause that sentence to be observed inviolably until fitting satisfaction has been made.

[Col. 0952D] Given at Anagni, on the seventh day before the Ides of June.

MLXXXVII. To Ildefonsus, king of Aragon. — On the same matter. (Anagni, June 9.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ILDEFONSUS, illustrious king of Aragon, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since it is written, “The honour of a king loves judgment” (Psalm 98:4), it greatly concerns both your honour and your salvation to love justice and to preserve it for every person according to the dignity bestowed on you by God; for the glory of a ruler is happy when the condition of his subjects is secure. Certainly, the prudence of your royal highness cannot be unaware how gravely and monstrously those have sinned who plotted the death of Hugh, formerly archbishop of Tarragona, of good memory. We have learned that Robert, at the devil’s instigation, conspired in the death of the aforesaid archbishop and poured upon him the poison of wickedness which he had conceived.

Therefore, because so monstrous a crime ought to be punished by the most severe vengeance, lest others be emboldened to offend if his transgression remains unpunished, we earnestly admonish and command your royal highness not, under any circumstances, to receive the aforesaid Robert into your kingdom or permit him in any way to remain there, so that at least in this manner he may correct and amend his transgression. But if [Col. 0953B] you should decide not to comply with our admonitions, we have instructed our venerable brother, the archbishop of Tarragona, legate of the apostolic see, and his suffragans, to place your kingdom under interdict and also to pronounce against you, by our authority, a sentence of excommunication.

Given at Anagni, on the fifth day before the Ides of June.

MLXXXVIII. To Fulk, dean, and the canons of the Church of Reims. — He exhorts them to resume the common life which they had abandoned. (Anagni, June 11.)

[MARTENE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 458.]

The more churches fix their eyes upon you [Col. 0953C] and hope to learn and maintain the way of salvation through your teaching and example, the more it is fitting that you exercise yourselves in God’s commandments, showing those who follow you, in your own persons, by what virtue and caution they ought to walk in the way of life. Certainly, in times past, as the widespread report of many affirmed, and as was laudably observed by your predecessors, they seemed to make it their concern that, just as they surpassed neighbouring churches in rank of dignity, so they should also excel them in the pattern of honourable conduct and in the power of their deeds; and, just as they stood at the summit by virtue of their office, so likewise they should be foremost in examples of virtue. Among them shone forth a pattern of propriety in dress, and, in accordance with canonical tradition, they took their daily meal from a common refectory with thanksgiving.

From this there resulted no small assistance for the poor, and, where there was less substance, provision for the needy was greater. This was because common property was valued more highly than private property, and rivalry among them concerned not so much worldly ostentation and riches as the ordering of morals and uprightness of life. But now, as we say only with grief of heart, morals have gradually been corrupted by abundance and the common good consumed by private pursuits. Each of you has withdrawn to his own upper room, and you have abandoned the common table, hospitality, and provision for the poor. In this we greatly fear that, with the separation of your bodies, a separation of minds has followed or preceded; and that, just as you have not thought it good to take your meal together in one place, [Col. 0954A] so you may not walk in the concord of one will. There may befall you what the Lord says through the prophet: “I called your name a fair olive tree, fruitful and beautiful; at the sound of a great utterance fire was kindled in it, and its branches were burned” (Jeremiah 11). We also fear that what is written may be said of you: “How the gold has grown dim, how the finest colour has changed! The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lamentations 4).

Therefore, lest on the day of judgment we ourselves be condemned with you if we remain silent, we have thought fit to stir up all of you by our exhortation, admonishing, commanding, and enjoining by apostolic letters under threat of divine judgment that, taking up your spirit anew, you return to your former condition, and restore to a seemly pattern and their earlier state what is known to have fallen away among you through creeping vanity: fellowship at table, provision for the poor, moderation of dress, diligence in office, and other honourable works. Consider that the Church which was falling away is commanded in the Apocalypse: “Remember from where you have fallen, and do the first works; otherwise I shall come to you quickly and remove your lampstand from its place” (Apocalypse 25 [materially uncertain citation; evidently Revelation 2:5]). Consider, therefore, how many there are whose care looks to you and who imitate your deeds, whether for good or for evil. See to it that, to those for whom you ought to be “an aroma of life unto life,” you may not instead prove “an aroma of death unto death”—may the Lord avert it. Do not put it off from day to day or allow yourselves to be drawn along by the multitude of offenders; rather, bloom anew into grace [Col. 0954C] and bear such fruit as does not perish with the flesh, but lives with the Spirit of God and remains for ever.

Given at Anagni, on the third day before the Ides of June.

MLXXXIX. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — That he recall his canons to the common life and cause the customary alms to be given. (Anagni, June [?].)

[Ibid.]

If, according to the word of Holy Scripture, more will be required of him to whom more has been entrusted, you do not doubt, dearest son, that much will be required of you on the day of the final harvest, since in the course of time you see that great power has been conferred upon you for the advancement [Col. 0954D] of the Church. Although by the authority of your office you must provide for many, you ought always to give more careful attention to those specially committed to you, preparing yourself daily, in fear and trembling, to render an account of them on the day of judgment.

The frequent report of your sons does not permit you to be unaware how greatly the Church of Reims, entrusted to your governance, once flourished in the honourableness of its life and the ordering of its morals. Yet although it ought to have made much progress under your governance—since both the authority by which you are known to preside and the exercise of discipline under which you had laboured for so long gave reason to hope for this—it is now seen not to have happened thus, whether because of your many occupations or the hardness of your subjects. For although through your zeal and authority it has greatly advanced in temporal matters, spiritually it is said, to our sorrow, to have declined very greatly from its former condition. Thus, with the increase of temporal goods, there has followed no small loss of morals.

For although your canons once had a common table, making generous provision not only for their own proper dignity but also for the poor’s support; although they conducted themselves with sufficient propriety in dress and order of life, and came reverently to church for the sacred offices; they have now turned to private pursuits and, as is said, abandoned the custom of the common table. Having discontinued aid to the poor, they do not preserve their approved gravity of conduct, but have for the most part declined into themselves. Thus the younger men have become impatient of [Col. 0955B] discipline, and the older men have relaxed the reins of instruction, so that what once was among the churches of Gaul, their subject churches, and other churches, a model of life that spread the fragrance of its honourableness far and wide, has now failed of its former renown [lacuna] and now in itself, now in others, to bring the desired [lacuna] that in the church there are more persons [lacuna] grave, but that such ease in [lacuna] of souls [lacuna] a multitude [lacuna] the word of reading scarcely any place among them [lacuna]. From this we greatly fear that it comes to pass because your brotherhood, occupied with external affairs, perhaps does not attend to the administration of these men with the diligence that it ought.

Therefore, lest the fire of the altar be utterly extinguished among them, if there is none to lay wood upon it each day, and lest on the day of judgment your brotherhood be required to answer for the deficiency of virtue found in your sons, we admonish and command your charity by apostolic letters to be more vigilant concerning your sons’ spiritual advancement. Whatever seems to have been abolished in fellowship at table, aid to the poor, and other works of piety, whether through creeping negligence or growing wickedness, strive to recall to its former state and pattern of honourableness. Thus, as is your name, so may your praise be; and the greater the authority you possess in the Church, the more perfect may you appear in deed and virtue.

And because, according to the word of Solomon, who says, “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Ecclesiastes 11), you have already provided many things for the use of this present life, may you be found at the end of time to have prepared things that avail still more for the state of eternal life. Having rendered a good account of the administration you have undertaken, may you deserve to hear from Him who will require the account: “Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.”

MXC. To the same. — For the monastery of St. Medard against the canons of St. Gervasius. (Anagni, June 16.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 982.]

Our beloved sons, the abbot and brothers of the church of St. [Col. 0956A] Medard, have shown us by a complaint sent to us that our beloved sons, the canons of the church of St. Gervasius, presume unjustly and violently to take from them tithes which the aforesaid church is known to have possessed from ancient times.

[Note: [Col. 0955] That is, the cathedral church of Soissons, which is dedicated to the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius.]

Since it is our office to preserve with special care the rights of all churches, and especially those which are known especially to belong to the provision of the apostolic see, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you earnestly admonish and strictly compel the aforesaid canons not to delay restoring the said tithes to the aforementioned abbot and brothers. Thereafter, if they believe that they have any right in those tithes, let them pursue it in due judicial order before you; and you shall hear the case and, without appeal, bring it to its proper conclusion.

Given at Anagni, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July.

MXCI. To the same. — Against the count of Regiteste, who was harassing the brothers of Jungeriac. (Anagni, June 16.)

[Ibid.]

It has come to our hearing, on behalf of our beloved sons, the abbot and brothers of St. Medard of Soissons, that a nobleman, the count of Regiteste, and his nephews impose unlawful exactions upon their men of Jungeri and presume continually to harass them; indeed, they do not hesitate to seize them and compel them to pay ransom. Since by the duty of our office we are bound to preserve ecclesiastical persons in their rights and to defend them more earnestly against the injuries of evildoers, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to admonish and induce the aforesaid count and his sons to restore all that they have taken from the said men and never again presume to harass them; or else, within twenty days of receipt of these letters, to render full justice before you, without appeal. If they despise obedience to your admonitions, bind them, without appeal, in the bond of excommunication until restitution of what was taken and fitting satisfaction have been made.

Given at Anagni, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June.

MXCII. To the same. — That he cause the land pledged by Phy. de Petrafonte to be restored. (Anagni, June 17.)

[Ibid., col. 983.]

[Col. 0956D]

A complaint has been brought to our ears on behalf of Phy. de Petrafonte that, although Peter, knight of Compiègne, has received from the proceeds of a certain piece of land which Phy. had pledged to him more than his principal, expenses having been deducted, he nevertheless still holds that land in occupation. Since vices which bring peril to souls must be rooted out, [Col. 0957A] we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, after summoning both parties before you, carefully to investigate the truth of the matter. If it is established to your satisfaction that the aforesaid Peter has received his principal from the proceeds of the said land, admonish him and, without appeal, compel him under the constraint of excommunication to restore that land to the said Phy. without any delay or exaction, and to leave him in peaceful and undisturbed possession.

Given at Anagni, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

MXCIII. To the same. — That he declare excommunicated Ernald, who had laid violent hands upon B., a canon of Laon. (Anagni, June 17.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0957B]

From the report of our beloved son B., a canon of Laon, it has come to our hearing that Ernald, inflamed by diabolical fury, laid violent hands upon him; and, although he had sworn on this account to abide by his mandate, he afterwards refused to do so. Since we cannot and ought not leave unpunished the transgression of such presumption, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the matter is so, you publicly declare the aforesaid E. excommunicated, with lighted candles and without appeal, and cause him to be carefully avoided by all, until he has made fitting satisfaction to the aforementioned B. for the injuries inflicted and presents himself before the apostolic presence with your letters.

[Col. 0957C] Given at Anagni, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July.

MXCIV. To the same. — For John, a clerk, and Ralph, his brother, against Lambert, their brother. (Anagni, June 18.)

[Ibid., col. 984.]

John, a clerk, and Ralph, his brother, the bearers of these letters, came to us and lodged before our hearing a complaint against their brother Lambert. They asserted that the same L. unreasonably presumes to harass them concerning a certain house situated within the cloister of the church of Châlons, movable goods, and a certain sum of money. They further added [Col. 0957D] that the same L. violently holds in occupation a share of the inheritance that falls to them by paternal and maternal right, together with a vineyard belonging to them.

Since we, who by the ministry of the service we have undertaken are bound diligently to assist everyone in his right, are especially obliged to provide for ecclesiastical persons in their claims of justice, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters earnestly to admonish the aforesaid L. and compel him by ecclesiastical censure either to restore to his aforementioned brothers, without harassment, everything taken from them, together with the fruits received therefrom, or, without recourse to appeal, to render them sufficient and full justice before you in the matter. Likewise, take care to admonish the same L. and compel him by ecclesiastical constraint altogether to desist from harassing his aforesaid brothers concerning the said house, movable goods, and sum of money; or, if he is confident of his right, to pursue the matter with them before you in judicial order, without appeal.

Given at Anagni, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July.

MXCV. To the same. — For John, a clerk, and Ralph, his brother, whom the bishop of Châlons had unjustly excommunicated. (Anagni, June 20.)

[Ibid., col. 985.]

[Col. 0958B]

You should know, from the complaint made to us by John, a clerk, and Ralph, his brother, that it has come to our hearing that, although they had appealed from the presence of our venerable brother the bishop of Châlons to our hearing, the bishop, paying no heed to the appeal, declared them excommunicated by our authority and ordered them to be treated as excommunicated, although he did not possess our letters by which that authority had been granted to him. Although, if this is so, that sentence could not have bound them, nevertheless, because the matter was unknown to us, we caused them to be absolved from that sentence. We command your brotherhood, without appeal, to declare them absolved and to cause them to be treated as absolved. If it is established to your satisfaction that the aforesaid bishop acted in this against the appeal, compel him, by our authority and yours and with every contradiction and appeal removed, to repay in full the necessary expenses which they incurred in coming to us, staying, and returning; and report the truth of the matter to us, so that, with God as author, we may be able on another occasion to punish his presumption.

Given at Anagni, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July.

MXCVI. To the same. — Concerning the dispute between the monks of Lessines and Malbodium over the church of the village of Anor. (Anagni, June 23.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 0958D]

It has been reported to our ears that, when a certain church and village named Anor were formerly newly built on the boundary of the estates of the monasteries of Lessines and Malbodium, a question arose between these monasteries concerning the said church: to which of those monasteries it ought to be subject.

[Note: [Col. 0957D] The church of Lessines, or Lesnes, is a distinguished abbey of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Cambrai, [Col. 0958D] over which Louis of Blois presided, famous for his writings and devout character.]

When the dispute had been heard before the diocesan bishop, he decided it in this manner: the church should be perpetually subject to whichever monastery’s estate it was found to lie in after the division of the boundaries. After the division of the boundaries, it was found [Col. 0959A] in the freehold estate of the monastery of Malbodium; but the abbot of Lessines refused to relinquish the church as had been adjudged and instead maintained that he should retain it contrary to justice.

Since it does not befit religious men to inflict on another what they would not wish to suffer from another, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, after summoning both parties before you, carefully to investigate the truth of these matters. If this is established to your satisfaction, admonish the aforesaid abbot and compel him by ecclesiastical constraint, without contradiction or appeal, to restore the aforesaid church to the monastery of Malbodium and leave it in peace. This is to be done notwithstanding any letters of confirmation of ours which the aforesaid abbot is known to have obtained concerning that church, unless the sentence of the aforesaid bishop was suspended by appeal. But if it was suspended by appeal, and the party which appealed did not pursue the appeal lodged within two years, you shall nevertheless cause that sentence to be put into execution, without appeal.

Given at Anagni, on the ninth day before the Kalends of July.

MXCVII. To the same. — For G., a canon of Laon. (Anagni, June 25.)

[Ibid., col. 986.]

It has been reported to our ears that, when certain shares of the Church of Laon were assigned to the canons of that church, from which they might receive their prebends, the chapter of the same church eventually granted and assigned prebends to three [Col. 0959C] of the canons in the village called Tavaux, out of the greater and lesser tithe and the revenue of the mill. It retained for itself the collections, house-rents, head-payments, the oven, and a certain nearby wood belonging to the same village. These were customarily granted to one of the canons for five years under a fixed rent, such that the person who possessed them with the chapter’s consent had as full authority over them as the chapter itself, and was permitted to sell the wood by its surface growth, from which he might pay part of the rent due.

Now, when this year the aforesaid possessions had been assigned to G., a canon of the aforesaid church, as stated above and according to the custom of that church, part of the aforesaid wood had been cleared and reduced to arable land. Yet the aforesaid three canons do not hesitate, in respect of that land, to exact tithe and *terragium*—a land-dues payment—beyond the shares assigned to them. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to call those three canons back without delay from exacting the aforesaid tithe and *terragium* beyond the shares assigned to them, and to cause anything which they have thereby taken from the said G. to be restored to him. Or, if they are confident of their right, hear the case and, without appeal, decide it by agreement or by justice.

Given at Anagni, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July.

MXCVIII. To the same. — For the brothers of St. Nicasius against the monks of Élan. (Anagni, July 8.)

[Ibid., col. 987.]

[Col. 0960A]

Our beloved sons, the abbot and brothers of St. Nicasius, having sent us letters, informed us that the brothers of Élan had received from them, under an annual rent of two measures of wheat, to be paid to them at Reims measure on the feast of St. Remigius, a certain court or estate of theirs called Singlis, with its buildings and other appurtenances.

[Note: [Col. 0959D] St. Nicasius was a monastery of no little distinction of the Order of St. Benedict in the city of Reims, founded by Archbishop Gervasius.]

[Note: [Col. 0960D] Élan was a monastery of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Reims, where St. Roger, abbot, is renowned for miracles.]

The agreement made on this matter by reciprocal charters, with the consent of both chapters, had also been strengthened by your privilege. Yet, after the aforesaid brothers had paid the said rent quietly and peacefully for seven continuous years, they have ceased to pay it for the last four years. Since it does not befit ecclesiastical men, by an exercise of their own will, to withhold from anyone that which they acknowledge they owe him, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to admonish the aforesaid brothers and strictly compel them to restore the withheld rent in full to the aforementioned abbot and brothers, without any harassment or difficulty, and thereafter to observe the aforesaid agreement firmly and without infringement; or else to render them full justice concerning the matter before you, without contradiction or appeal. But if they should decide rather to enter into litigation, summon the parties before you, hear the case with diligence, and decide it by agreement or justice, without appeal.

Given at Anagni, on the eighth day before the Ides of July.

MXCIX. To the same. — Concerning the suit between the vidame of Pinconium and the abbot of Anchin. (Anagni, July 11.)

[Ibid., col. 988.]

It has come to our ears from the vidame of Pinconium that, when he had brought the abbot of Anchin into litigation before our venerable brother the bishop of Amiens concerning certain possessions which the abbot is said unlawfully to hold, the abbot appealed to our hearing. But while the other party appeared through his messenger, the abbot neither came [Col. 0960D] himself nor sent an advocate on his behalf.

Trusting, therefore, in your prudence and integrity, we commit this case to your careful discretion, commanding by the authority of these letters that, after summoning both parties before you, you hear the aforesaid case diligently and, without recourse to appeal, decide it by agreement or justice. If, however, the aforesaid abbot, having been cited to appear before you, should refuse to come or to obey your judgment, do not delay, without appeal, to put the aforesaid vicedean into possession of the matters in dispute, [Col. 0961A] so that the aforesaid abbot, wearied by this, may be compelled to submit to justice.

Given at Anagni, on the fifth day before the Ides of July.

MC. To the same. — That he arrange for a cemetery to be blessed for the sick at Mellent. (Anagni, July 18.)

[Ibid.]

The sick brothers at Mellent have informed us that they have no cemetery in which they can commit their bodies to burial, humbly and devoutly asking us to address prayers to your devotion for the blessing of their cemetery. Since it is fitting that we sympathize with their afflictions and distresses, lest those who suffer continual pains be deprived of human help, we earnestly ask and command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, for the love of God and reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, you cause a cemetery to be blessed by any one of your suffragans, for the use only of the aforesaid sick brothers and their household, so that these brothers may not be compelled on this account to make the journey to our presence, either in person or through a messenger.

Given at Anagni, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August.

MCI. He takes under protection the house of sick brothers residing near the city of Reims, and confirms “the fairs which Archbishop Henry has granted to be held annually near that house.” (Anagni, July 21.)

[D. MARLOT, *Metropolis Remensis*, II, 400.]

[Col. 0961C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved faithful, the sick brothers residing near the city of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting and consonant with reason that we, who are bound to exercise the ministry of the dispensation entrusted to us toward all, should not fail in your necessities. With paternal affection we sympathize with your misfortunes and continual pains, and willingly impart the aid which, with God and justice, we are able to provide.
