Therefore, beloved sons, yielding to your just requests and moved by the office of compassion, we receive your house, with all that it now rightfully possesses or may in the future acquire, [Col. 0961D] under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves.

Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to your house, the fairs which our venerable brother Henry, archbishop of Reims, granted for the benefit of your house to be held annually near that house, and confirmed by his charter: namely, from Easter Day until the evening of the following Sunday. We prohibit anyone from daring to inflict injury or molestation upon any person coming to those fairs or returning from them, in his person or possessions. Moreover, let no one presume to demand tithes from you of your newly cultivated lands, or of those products which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense—namely, from your gardens, the fruits of your trees, and the increase of your animals.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this charter of our protection. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August.

MCII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims. — That he strive to establish peace between Louis, king of the Franks, and Henry, king of the English. (Anagni, July 21.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 989.]

[Col. 0962B]

Since we see that, from the discord and conflict which, through the prompting of diabolical deceit, has arisen between our dearest son in Christ L., the illustrious king of the French, and Henry, king of the English, and that king of England’s sons, most grave dangers threaten all Christendom and especially the Eastern land—and unless it is speedily, by the Lord’s action, quieted, we fear (may the Lord avert it!) still graver ones—we wish, as the duty of our office requires, to devote diligent attention to restoring peace between those kings, and to invite them to the same end by earnest admonitions and exhortations.

[Col. 0962C] For you know, and all the kingdoms of the world know, how that Eastern land was freed from the filth of the pagans by the strength and labours of Christ’s faithful who went there from the realms of the French and the English, and has until now, by God’s grace, been preserved from their attacks. Unless the aforesaid dissension is quickly stilled, we have great fear—as indeed we may reasonably fear—that the boldness of the unbelievers against Christ’s faithful may increase, and that, in accordance with the perverse purpose of their wickedness, to the dishonour of the Christian name, they may presume to invade that Holy Land—that land, indeed, for whose defence and preservation the devotion of all Christians ought to gird itself—since it is surrounded on every side by the enemies of Christ, was twice overrun by them in the preceding year, and, as we believe you have heard, [Col. 0962D] burned and devastated in many places.

We therefore, foreseeing not only these but many other dangers, as required by our office, and considering how, on the occasion of the aforesaid discord, the order of religion is perishing in their realms and elsewhere, and the vigour of ecclesiastical discipline and the condition of the churches have been disrupted and disturbed, have instructed our venerable brothers the archbishop of Tarentaise, [Note: [Col. 0961D] This was that great Saint Peter, formerly abbot of Tamié, who was made archbishop of Tarentaise and who, by his prudence, even reconciled Emperor Frederick with Pope Alexander, as is evident from the letters which we saw at the end of his Life in the Hardenhousan manuscript and which are printed by Bolland.] the bishop of Clermont, [Note: [Col. 0962D] Pons, who before becoming bishop had been abbot of Clairvaux, and who laboured greatly to reconcile Emperor Frederick with the legitimate pope, as may be seen in Frederick’s letter, which we published in volume I of the *Anecdota*.] and our beloved sons the abbot of Cîteaux, [Col. 0963A] [Note: [Col. 0963] Alexander, who in 1174, together with Peter of Tarentaise, reconciled King Henry with his sons.] the prior of the Carthusians, and Brother G., master of the house of the militia of the Temple in the regions on this side of the sea, that they all, or some of them, having associated with themselves you and our venerable brother W., archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See, should strive to bring the aforesaid discord to a peaceful settlement with the help of heavenly grace and to establish firm peace and concord between the aforementioned kings.

Since, therefore, we know you as a prudent and honourable man who loves peace, and believe that you wish to labour most earnestly for it, lest above all the bond of catholic unity be broken—a unity for preserving which we know you to be watchful and wholly circumspect—we earnestly admonish and command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that [Col. 0963B] you diligently and prudently apply yourself, together with all or some of the religious persons whom we have mentioned, to the restoration of peace; and that, before the aforesaid king of the French and his barons, you intervene on your part, with regard to God and for the sake of your salvation, so effectively that through your diligence and solicitude and that of those whom we have mentioned, the aforesaid discord may, with the Lord’s cooperation, be brought to a peaceful settlement. Thus you may obtain from the Most High the fruit of eternal reward and gain among men the glory of abundant praise.

Indeed, you could accomplish nothing from which greater honour and glory, and a fuller fruit of eternal reward, could come to you than if you devoted care and effective effort to restoring peace between those kings. We send you and the aforesaid archbishop of Sens a copy of the letter [Col. 0963C] which we are directing on this matter to the same king of the French, for your inspection, so that, if you judge it expedient, you may have it presented to the king; otherwise, retain it.

Given at Anagni, the fifth day before the Kalends of September [28 August].

MCIII. To the same [Henry, archbishop of Reims].—He entrusts to him the settlement of a certain case. (Anagni, 3 August.)

[*Ibid.*, col. 990.]

From the complaint submitted to us by F., a citizen of Reims, we have learned that S., a burgess of Saint-Remi, does not cease grievously to harass him concerning a certain house which he sold to him for four pounds and [Col. 0963D] twelve shillings. At the sale he had pledged his faith and promised that neither he himself nor others would cause F. any harassment or burden concerning the aforesaid house; yet on this account he has inflicted upon him many losses and burdens. Since it is dangerous for anyone, and contrary to salvation, to violate faith once pledged, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, after summoning the parties before you, you carefully investigate the truth of the matter; and, if you ascertain that this is so, earnestly admonish the aforesaid S. and, if necessary, compelling him by ecclesiastical coercion with appeal set aside, require him henceforth to inflict no harassment or burden upon the said F. concerning the aforesaid house [Col. 0964A], but to permit him to possess it peaceably, as he promised on his pledged faith. He must also make suitable reparation to him for the losses occasioned by the aforesaid house, or reach a peaceful and amicable agreement with him concerning this matter, or, in your presence and with recourse to appeal removed, render full justice.

Given at Anagni, the eleventh day before the Kalends of September [22 August].

MCIV. To the same.—That he should strive with all his strength to prevent a marriage between the son of the king of France and the daughter of Emperor Frederick. (Anagni, 6 September.)

[*Ibid.*, col. 991.]

Since, as we have heard, the talk long since laid to rest concerning the contracting of a marriage between the son of our dearest [Col. 0964B] son in Christ L., the illustrious king of the French, and the daughter of that F. called emperor, is being revived, and since we fear that scandals and dangers will result from this for us, for the Church, and also for the kingdom of the French, we make your prudence attentive and concerned in every way, holding it as certain that this cannot be brought to completion without the counsel of yourself and our venerable brother W., archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See.

Therefore, because we have special confidence in you, and know that the said king readily accepts your counsels and admonitions, we earnestly admonish and command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, carefully considering and attending to how your own interests are involved in this matter, [Col. 0964C] you labour so effectively that either the said undertaking is revoked or, if it cannot be revoked, provision is made in such a manner that the Church of God suffers no loss or detriment from it and that your care and vigilance may deservedly be commended.

We also wish you to urge the aforesaid king effectively to seek help from heaven against his enemies, not from man; for divine help is altogether fruitful and effective, whereas human help is often found ineffective. Be so concerned and diligent in these matters that your words may be proved by the effectiveness of your deeds and that the Church of God may feel in this, as in other matters, relief and advancement from your diligence and solicitude.

[Col. 0964D] Given at Anagni, the eighth day before the Ides of September [6 September].

MCV. To the same.—That G., bishop of Châlons, should admit Horricus to the church of Saint Julian of Helissia. (Anagni, 10 September.)

[*Ibid.*, col. 992.]

It befits us to give diligent attention to the provision of churches and to invite other prelates of churches to do likewise by earnest admonitions and exhortations. It has been reported to us that, when our beloved son, the abbot of Muremont, moved by regard for God and affection, presented the clerk Horricus to our brother [Col. 0965A] G., bishop of Châlons, for the church of Saint Julian of Helissia, the bishop refused to receive him, alleging no other reason than that Horricus was not in priestly orders.

Since it is not fitting that the provision of clerics who lack an ecclesiastical benefice should be hindered for such a reason, especially when, after obtaining churches, they are willing and able to be promoted to the rank of priest, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to enjoin upon the aforesaid bishop, by your letters in our name and your own, that, unless a manifest and reasonable cause prevents it, he restore Horricus to the aforesaid church, with occasion and appeal removed, and entrust him with the care of souls, provided that he is willing personally to serve [Col. 0965B] that church and is able to be promoted to the priesthood within a suitable period.

Given at Anagni, the fourth day before the Ides of September [10 September].

MCVI. To the same.—On behalf of H., treasurer of Auxerre. (Anagni, 26 October.)

[*Ibid.*]

Our beloved son H., treasurer of the church of Auxerre, bearer of the present letter, appearing before us, stated that certain of his father’s serfs had fled from his land to inhabit other places, and that his father had granted him those serfs to hold. He therefore humbly requested that we should give him the support of the Apostolic See for obtaining his right over them. Since, so far as lies within our power, we ought in no way to permit the same treasurer to be defrauded of his right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if you learn that the aforesaid serfs are living anywhere within your diocese, [Col. 0965C] you admonish them and, with appeal set aside, strictly compel them either to come to the aforesaid treasurer and render him the service due to him as their lord, or to render full justice under your examination. You shall hear the case and decide it by means of justice.

But if the aforesaid serfs, having been lawfully summoned, refuse to appear before you or to obey your judgment, subject them—and likewise those who presume to harbour them contrary to your command—to excommunication, and cause them to be carefully avoided as excommunicated persons throughout your diocese.

Given at Anagni, the seventh day before the Kalends of November [26 October].

MCVII. To the priests and clerics established throughout England and the lands on this side of the sea of the king of England.—That the king of England should restore their wives to his sons.

(MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1032.)

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishops and bishops, and to his beloved sons the abbots and other prelates of churches, and to all the clergy established throughout England and the lands on this side of the sea of the illustrious king of England: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0966A] It is not unknown to you, as we suppose, how Henry, the illustrious king of the English, because of the discord which, through the exaction of sins, has arisen between himself and his sons, is holding their wives—namely, the daughters of our dearest son in Christ Louis, the illustrious king of the French. The king of France and the sons-in-law of the aforesaid king of England, his sons, have presented to us earnest petitions for the wives’ restoration.

We, therefore, earnestly considering it just and honourable that husbands ought to reclaim their wives, and wishing readily to comply with the prayers of the same king of France and his sons-in-law, not only in those matters which we are bound by the duty of our office to accomplish but also in all matters not at variance with justice, have sufficiently [Col. 0966B] and earnestly admonished the aforesaid king of England and commanded him that, at the admonition of our venerable brothers the archbishop of Tarentaise, the bishop of Clermont, and our beloved son the prior of the Carthusians—or, if he cannot be present, the prior of Mont-Dieu in his place—or of two of these if all three cannot be present, he should not delay restoring the wives to his sons within forty days after receiving our letters.

But if he has not restored them to their husbands within the prescribed term, we command by apostolic authority that the whole province in which they are detained, and to which they may be transferred, shall, so long as they are there and until they are restored to their husbands, cease from all divine offices except the baptism of infants and penance for the dying.

Accordingly, we command and, in commanding, direct all of you by apostolic letters that you induce the same king of England by earnest admonitions and exhortations to restore them, setting before him that it is no less advantageous to him to restore them than it is to their husbands to receive them. If, in accordance with our admonition and command, he does not restore the wives to his sons within the appointed term, then in whichever of your provinces they are detained or to which they are transferred, so long as they remain there, [Col. 0966C] celebrate no divine offices, nor permit them to be celebrated by others, except the baptism of infants and penances of the dying, all contradiction and appeal in these matters ceasing. Know for certain that, if any persons—though we do not believe it—attempt to act against our interdict, [Col. 0966D] they will, by the Lord’s authorship, incur the punishment due to their rashness and transgression.

IN THE YEAR 1174.

MCVIII. To Gerard, abbot, and the whole convent of Clairvaux.—He announces that Abbot Bernard has been enrolled among the saints.

(Anagni, 18 January.—This bull is extant among the appendices to the *Works of Saint Bernard*. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXV, col. 624.)

MCIX. To all abbots of the Cistercian Order.—Of the same subject. (Anagni, 18 January.—See *ibid.*, col. 623.)

[Col. 0967A]

MCX. To the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and other prelates of churches established in the kingdom of the French.—Of similar subject.

(Anagni, 18 January.—See *ibid.*, col. 622.)

MCXI. To Louis, king of the French.—Of the same subject.

(Anagni, 18 January.—See *ibid.*, col. 623.)

MCXII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of the monastery of Cluny. (Anagni, 21 January.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 999.]

[Col. 0967B]

The more especially the monastery of Cluny is shown to belong to the jurisdiction of Saint Peter and to our care and protection, the more readily are we bound to uphold and preserve its rights and defend them from the assaults of malicious persons. For we carry out an appropriate function of our office when we diligently attend to matters known to fall under our care.

Accordingly, we command and, in commanding, direct all of you by apostolic letters that you most urgently admonish those clerics or laymen who hold, without the consent of the chapter of Cluny or of its greater and sounder part, priories, churches, and [Col. 0967C] other possessions belonging to the monastery of Cluny, whether leased or entrusted to them. Labour by every means to induce them to restore those possessions to the monastery of Cluny—if they concern leased properties, after deducting the expenses, whatever they have received from them beyond what they gave for their lease—without occasion or contradiction, and thereafter to leave them in peace and quiet.

If they disdain to obey our admonitions, pronounce them excommunicated by apostolic authority, with no appeal or opposition prevailing, and cause that sentence to be inviolably observed until worthy satisfaction has been made.

Given at Anagni, the twelfth day before the Kalends of February [21 January].

MCXIII. To the same.—That the schools of Rigue-Tesse should be preserved for the monks of Saint-Remi. (Anagni, 28 January.)

[*Ibid.*]

[Col. 0967D]

The abbot of Saint-Remi has informed us that the noble count of Rigue-Tesse presumes, in rash boldness, to take away the school of that castle, which his father, after the death of Gal., who had held it, left by pious generosity to his monks residing in that same castle. Therefore, since we ought to support all God’s faithful, and especially religious men, in their rights, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you earnestly admonish the aforesaid man and, if necessary, compel him, with appeal set aside, [Col. 0968A] under the severity of anathema, to restore the aforesaid school to the said monks and to cause them no further harassment or burden concerning it.

Furthermore, carefully admonish and induce the nobleman Anselm of Possessa not to presume, on any account, to impose new or unlawful customs upon the men of the aforesaid abbot living in the village called Aisencella. If in wicked boldness he should presume to do so, punish and correct his presumption with due severity.

Given at Anagni, the fifth day before the Kalends of February [28 January].

MCXIV. To the same.—On behalf of the abbot of Saint-Remi against men subject to him. (Anagni, 29 January.)

[*Ibid.*, col. 1000.)

[Col. 0968B]

It has been represented to us on behalf of our beloved son the abbot of Saint-Remi that, since he has very wealthy men in the city of Châlons, they have risen to such obstinacy and pride that they disdain to serve him as they and their predecessors customarily served his predecessors. Since it is unjust, and in no way tolerable, that the aforesaid abbot should be defrauded of services due to him, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you admonish the aforesaid men and, under the severity of anathema and with appeal set aside, compel them to render reverently and devotedly, without harassment or contradiction, to the aforesaid abbot the services which they and their predecessors were accustomed to render to him and his predecessors [Col. 0968C].

If, however, they show a reasonable cause why they ought not to serve him, hear it carefully and decide the matter according to what the principle of equity dictates.

Given at Anagni, the fourth day before the Kalends of February [29 January].

MCXV. To the same.—Against several persons who were harassing the monastery of Saint-Remi. (Anagni, 29 January.)

[*Ibid.*, col. 1001.]

It has been reported to us that Geoffrey of Joinville and his son unjustly oppress the village of the monastery of Saint-Remi called Corcelles, and presume to inflict many injuries and losses on the abbot of that monastery. William of Meallen, Josbert of Calmont and his son, and G. of Noelli do not hesitate to cause injury to the aforesaid monastery. Ralph of Cuzeio, moreover, imposes hateful and evil customs upon the same monastery and delays, each year beyond the appointed term and not without loss to the monastery, the payment of sixty shillings which he is bound to pay annually for the castle of Cuzeio on the feast of Saint Remi.

Since, therefore, by the Lord’s providence, although unworthy, we have been placed in that office in which we ought to preserve with diligent care the rights of all persons, and especially of religious men, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters [Col. 0969A] that you urgently admonish and induce the said G. and his son, W., and Josbert his son, and G. of Nuelli, not in any way to diminish or disturb the rights of the aforesaid monastery or harass it with unlawful vexations, but to repair the losses inflicted, restore everything taken away, and make suitable satisfaction for the injuries done; or, with appeal set aside, to render it full justice in the examination of your discretion.

Strive carefully to admonish and induce Ralph of Cuzeio not to impose hateful or evil customs upon the monastery and to pay the due rent in full at the appointed time. But if he and the others whom we have mentioned should perhaps disdain to comply with these admonitions, bind them by the bond of excommunication, no appeal prevailing, and cause that sentence to be inviolably observed until worthy satisfaction has been made.

Furthermore, it has been reported to us on behalf of the aforesaid abbot that Gal. Bertot took great possessions from his monastery, for which he was bound by the sentence of excommunication on the authority of our predecessor, Pope Eugenius of holy memory. Since an ecclesiastical sentence pronounced against evildoers for their offences by authority of the Roman pontiff ought to stand valid and firm, and must retain the force of firmness until worthy satisfaction, we likewise enjoin upon your care by this present notice that, if this is so, you publicly declare the said G. excommunicated in your church [Col. 0969B], cause him to be carefully avoided until worthy satisfaction has been made, and firmly and strictly enjoin upon our beloved son, the elect of Cambrai, by our authority and your own, that he do the same in his church.

Moreover, as has been reported to us, Count Gisebald of Ruceio has for the past fifteen years withheld from the aforesaid monastery twenty shillings which he owes it annually in rent; he has inflicted a loss of sixty pounds and more; and he presumes to impose intolerable burdens upon the monastery’s men by frequent plunderings and exactions. With every earnestness, admonish and diligently induce him to restore what he has withheld from the fixed rent, to pay that rent in full thereafter, to make good the loss of sixty pounds, and [Col. 0969C] to restore the other things which he is known to have extorted by plunderings and exactions, or to render justice concerning these matters. If he should perhaps refuse to do either, strike him with the sword of anathema until he corrects his offence by worthy satisfaction.

Given at Anagni, the fourth day before the Kalends of February [29 January].

MCXVI. He takes under protection the church of Saint Mary of Mont-desir, of the Cluniac Order, and confirms all its possessions and rights. (Anagni, 1 February.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, p. 73.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BERENGARIUS, prior of the church of Saint Mary [Col. 0970A] of Mont-desir, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

The administration of the office entrusted to us compels us, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions, take your church, in which you are dedicated to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, we decree that the monastic order established in your church according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the brethren of Cluny shall be inviolably observed there in perpetuity.

Moreover, whatever possessions, etc., among which we have thought fit expressly to specify the following:

First, the place itself on which the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances: namely, the church of Blessed Mary with the thirteen prebends formerly held by secular canons; and the prebend formerly held by the masters of the schools in the castle of Mont-desir, who governed the schools—or, in place of that prebend, thirty shillings of Provins currency; the direction of the schools; the oil for anointing; the church of Saint Peter, with its churchyard, tithe, and rent of seventeen shillings, which the priests of that church must pay every year. Concerning the offerings of Saint Peter’s altar, it has for many years been established that five parts of those offerings—namely, those made at masses for the living—should go to the monks, and the sixth part to the priests [Col. 0970B]; but of those made at masses for the dead, one half should belong to the monks and the other to the priests. Xarinus, bishop of Amiens of good memory, also forbade any alteration of this arrangement under anathema.

Likewise, the church of the Holy Sepulchre, with altar, churchyard, and tithe; the church of Farelli, with its court, altar, churchyard, and whole tithe; the church of Villa, with the chapel of Maisnil, with altars, churchyards, and tithes; the church of Nova Villa, with altar, churchyard, and the whole tithe; the church of Fretcio, with altar, churchyard, and tithe; the church of Dommalich, with altar, churchyard, and whole tithe; the church of Esteltay, with altar, churchyard, and whole tithe; [Col. 0970C] the church of Domna Petra, with altar, churchyard, and whole tithe; the church of Brach, with altar, churchyard, and whole tithe; the church of Souviller, with the dependent chapel of Aubviller, with altars, churchyards, and tithes; the church of Contorium, with altar, churchyard, and the whole tithe; half the churches of Annethi and Fenerii, and of their altars and small tithes; the church of Cais, with altar and churchyard and two parts of the whole greater tithe; likewise, the village of Curcellis with its appurtenances; at Mont-desir, the mill by the bridge and, each week, three denarii of Vermandois currency at the toll; bread at Contorium; half the mill of Prato; at Forsenviller, the entire allod in lands and woods given by Elizabeth Rabies; likewise the tithe of Spatenis, received by you through the hand of our venerable brother Odo, bishop of Beauvais, at the request of Ralph, count of Vermandois, and also of Ivo, count of Soissons; likewise, in the diocese of Amiens, the greater tithe of Septemfortis, the land-rent of Plenivilla, five modii of grain from the new mill, given as alms by Robert of Tournella, and the income of the harvest from Corbeii.

At Contorium, half the upper mill and the water and pools pertaining to its right; at Le Plessis of Ralph Vitalis, three parts of the land-rent of Goy; at Mont-desir, half the mill called Engelran’s. We further decree that the burial-ground of the place itself shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will [Col. 0971A] of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken nevertheless being preserved.

When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. Let no one presume to exact tithes from you on your newly cultivated lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals.

We therefore decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If anyone in the future, etc.

Given at Anagni, by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Nones [1 February], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1173 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCXVII. He confirms all the possessions of the monastery of Saint Mary of Liskes. (Anagni, 12 February.)

[HUGO, *Annals of the Premonstratensian Order*, II, 31.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ROBERT, abbot of the church of Saint Mary of Liskes, and his brethren of the Premonstratensian Order, in the diocese of Thérouanne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of the Apostolic See, in whose service we labour by the Lord’s bounty, and brotherly love urge us to consent to the just desires of religious persons and graciously to grant their reasonable requests. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, giving favourable assent to your just petitions, after the example of our predecessor Pope Adrian of blessed memory, we take the aforesaid church, in which you are dedicated to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document.

First, we decree that the canonical order known to be established in that place according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the custom of the church of Prémontré, shall be inviolably observed there in perpetuity. Moreover, whatever possessions [Col. 0972A] and whatever goods you at present justly and canonically possess, or may in future, by the Lord’s favour, acquire through grants of pontiffs, benefactions of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit expressly to specify the following:

The place itself in which the said church is situated, with all its appurtenances, by the gift of Drogo, formerly bishop of Thérouanne; the altar of Liskes, with a third part of the tithe of that parish and with the other shares which you rightfully possess there through the gift of Robert of Hamis and his son Baldwin; lands in the same parish; lands given by Eustace of Liskes, both in the said parish and in the village of Lostinguee; [Col. 0972B] etc.

Given at Anagni, by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Ides of February [12 February], in the second indiction, in the year 1173 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCXVIII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—That, if the count receives Countess C. of Toulouse honourably, he should persuade her to return to the husband whom she had left. (Anagni, 14 February.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 1003.]

As our beloved daughter in Christ, the noblewoman C., countess of Toulouse and your sister, reported to us, she had resolved to live chastely because the noble count of Toulouse, her husband, does not keep faith with her but unlawfully joins himself to other women. We earnestly admonished the same countess to return to her husband. But because she was unwilling to comply with our admonitions in this matter until the aforesaid count abandoned this path of depravity and dissipation, we sent letters of apostolic exhortation to that count, requiring him, wholly abandoning such a course, to recall the aforesaid countess, his wife, honourably and as is fitting, by distinguished and honourable envoys and by letters sent to her and to you, after giving full security that he will treat the same countess decently and honourably, as is appropriate for so great and noble a lady.

We have also instructed our venerable brothers [Pons], archbishop of Narbonne, and [Adalbert], bishop of Nîmes, and our beloved son R., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, [Col. 0972C] to strive to admonish and diligently induce the same count to do this, and not to omit in any way to inform us and you by letter of whatever they discover concerning the matter.

We therefore ask, admonish, and earnestly exhort your brotherhood that, if the aforesaid count has honourably invited the said countess to return to him, as we have stated, you admonish her by brotherly exhortation and diligently induce her to return to the aforesaid count. For it is neither fitting nor honourable for a wife to remain without her husband, provided that she is so honourably treated by him [Col. 0973A] that she has no just cause to leave him.

Given at Anagni, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March [14 February].

MCXIX. To the same.—He declares that F., his parishioner, never spoke ill of him in the curia. (Anagni, 22 February.)

[*Ibid.*, col. 1004.]

F., bearer of the present letter and your parishioner, represented to us in tears that you were gravely angered against him because a false report had suggested to you that he had spoken ill of you in our curia. Since it is altogether wicked and unjust that an innocent person should be joined to the guilty or innocent blood condemned, and since we wish to provide that he suffer no punishment for which he has incurred no stain of wrongdoing, we admonish and command your brotherhood that, if you have conceived against the same F.—which we do not believe—any indignation or resentment, especially since he is not worthy of Caesar’s anger, you graciously forgive him for God’s sake and out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, restore to him your favour and affection, and neither obstruct him nor permit him to be obstructed from obtaining his right, both concerning half of the house and concerning the other matters of which he complains, under the examination of delegated judges.

Indeed, we have no recollection whatever that he spoke ill of you or said anything against your dignity.

[Col. 0973C] Given at Anagni, the eighth day before the Kalends of March [22 February].

MCXX. Bull concerning the church of Saint Peter at Auxerre, recently endowed with the title of abbey. (Anagni, 25 February.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, XII, documents, 134.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons O., abbot, and the brethren of Saint Peter of Auxerre: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting for us to approve those measures which are established by reasonable foresight for the honour and advancement of churches, and to strengthen them by apostolic authority so that they may obtain due force. We have heard that our venerable brother William, bishop of Auxerre, at your request and that of our venerable brother the archbishop of Sens, legate of the Apostolic See, [Col. 0973D] changed your church from a deanery into an abbey and firmly established that in future an abbot, not a dean, should be appointed in it. Since that establishment was reasonably made, we hold it ratified and firm and strengthen it by the protection of this present document. We decree that the canonical order known to be instituted in the same church according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be inviolably observed there in perpetuity.

Likewise, we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to your church, the church of Venosa with the chaplaincy of Rouvre, as you now rightfully possess them. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our constitution, etc.

Given at Anagni, the fifth day before the Kalends of March [25 February], in the seventh indiction.

MCXXI. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—That satisfaction be made to the monastery of Gorze for the injuries inflicted by G. of Aspremont. (Anagni, February 28.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 1004.]

The beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Gorze [Note: [Col. 0973] The monastery of Gorze, a distinguished house of the Order of St. Benedict in the diocese of Metz, was founded by Bishop Chrodegang.], have shown us in a complaint sent to us that the nobleman G. of Aspremont does not fear repeatedly to harass their churches [Col. 0974B] and villages, to compel their men to ransom themselves, and, besides this, has damaged the aforesaid monastery to the amount of one hundred marks of silver. Since, therefore, by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us we are bound to defend with pastoral solicitude the rights of all, and especially of religious persons who, established in the midst of schismatics, do not depart from the unity of the most holy Roman Church, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you diligently admonish and carefully induce the aforesaid G. to restore in their entirety to the aforementioned abbot and brethren all that has been taken away, make good the damage inflicted, render appropriate satisfaction for the injuries done, and thereafter leave them in peace and quiet. But if [Col. 0974C] he should perhaps refuse to obey your admonition, relying on apostolic authority, place his land under interdict; so that you permit no divine offices to be celebrated in it, except the baptism of infants and the penitence of the dying; and if he does not amend even thus, bind his person and those who are the chief supporters of his wrongdoing with the bond of excommunication, until you hold them bound to make fitting satisfaction.

Given at Anagni, the second day before the Kalends of March.

MCXXII. Privilege for the Church of Capua. (Anagni, March 1.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VI, 327.]

[Col. 0974D] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ALFANO, Archbishop of Capua, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Since by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us by God, etc. Therefore, in consideration of this matter, venerable brother in Christ, Archbishop, we graciously assent to your just requests, receive under the protection of St. Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid Church, over which, by the Lord’s authorisation, you are shown to preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document; decreeing that whatever possessions and whatever goods [Col. 0975A] that Church now justly and canonically possesses, etc., among which we have thought fit to specify these in their proper names:

The bishopric of Aquino; the bishoprics of Venafro and Isernia; the bishopric of Theano, of Sessa, and of Calin [Calinensem]; the bishopric of Calven. [Calven.], of Caiazzo, and of Caserta. In Capua: the abbey of St. Mary Major; the church of the Lord Saviour; the church of St. John at the Court; the church of St. Michael; the church of St. Mary of the Arch; the church of the Holy Apostles; the church of St. James in the Castle. In the diocese of the Church of Theano: the church of St. Erasmus, the church of St. Mary, the church of St. Helena, and the church of St. Nicholas, which are in the territory of Scarpato. In the place called Baulano: the church of St. Elijah and the church [Col. 0975B] of St. Martin. At Fontana de Corregiis: the church of St. Mary. In the diocese of the Church of Sessa: the church of St. Lucy at the place called Sorbello. In the diocese of the Church of Calvi: at Rocca Montis Draconis, the church of St. Rufinus and the church of St. Pancras. In the diocese of the Church of Calvi [Calven.]: the church of St. Andrew at Cementa; the church of St. Germanus at Palera; the church of St. Tammaro of the mountain; the church of St. Paul of Formello; the church of St. Peter of Borlerano; the church of St. Symmachus; the church of St. Erasmus of Mostardino; the church of All Saints at the place called Sanguinarii. At Sclavi: the church of St. Michael, the church of St. Peter, the church of St. Mary, the church of St. Nazarius, the church of St. Angel of Jano, and the church of St. Mary. At Camillano: the church of St. Angel, the church of St. [Col. 0975C] Mary, and the church of St. Nicholas. In the diocese of the Church of Caiazzo: the church of St. Angel of Melanito and the church of St. Peter at li Bagnatori. In the diocese of the Church of Caserta: the church of St. Vitus of Hercole; the church of St. Nazarius in Campo Puzan; the church of St. Peter at Goffolli; the church of St. Secundinus; and the church of St. Felix. In the territory of Murrone: the church of St. Mary, the church of St. Felix, the church of St. Peter, and the church of St. Stephen. Near that diocese: the church of St. Euphemia, the church of St. John at Gajanum, the church of St. Mary at Lupinum, the church of St. Felix, and the church of St. Priscus. At Casapuli: the church of St. Nicholas, the church of St. Arpius, and the church of St. Peter of Sarzano. At Marzanisi: the church of St. Angel and [Col. 0975D] the church of St. Martin. At Campurcipi: the church of St. Caesarius, the church of St. Procopius, and the church of St. Venera. At Airolo: the church of St. Juliana and the church of St. Nicholas at Ronulas. In the territory of Castellammare: the church of St. Adjutor, the church of St. Marcellus, and the church of St. Blaise; the church of St. Stephen; another church of St. Blaise; the church of St. John; the church of St. Nicholas; the church of St. Severina; and the church of the Holy Cross. At Cancello: the church of St. Angel and the church of All Saints; the church of St. John and the church of St. Apollinaris of Patrazzano; the church of St. George; the church of St. John of the Tower; the church of St. Vitus; the church of St. Peter; the church of St. Nicholas; the church of St. Martin; the church of St. Castrensis; the church of St. Martin of [Col. 0976A] Rosella; the church of St. Flavian; the church of St. Barbara; the church of St. Juliana; and the church of St. Andrew. At Arnona: the church of St. Mary, the church of St. Blaise, the church of St. Paulinus, and the church of St. Erasmus of Cazoli. At Grazzanisi: the church of St. John, the church of St. Mary, the church of St. Maximiliana, and the church of St. Nicholas. We therefore decree, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ubaldus, Bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, Bishop of Porto and St. Rufina. I, Gualterius, Bishop of Albano. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Anastasia. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of St. Peter in Chains. [Col. 0976B] I, Boso, cardinal priest of St. Pudentiana, title of Pastor. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Damaso. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Mark. I, Manfred, cardinal priest of the title of St. Cecilia. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Chrysogonus. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Cynthius, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of St. Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Vitellius, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of St. Angel. [Col. 0976C] I, Laborans, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of March, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1173 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCXXIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—He commends to him the brethren of the monastery of Mairimont. (Anagni, March 1.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 1005.]

Since the Church of Mairimont, as you know, is surrounded by wicked men, the provision of pastoral solicitude ought to be readier to protect it [Col. 0976D] in proportion as it might more easily succumb to the violence and plundering of malicious persons unless it were defended from their attacks by the rigor of ecclesiastical discipline. Therefore, desiring with paternal solicitude to attend to the peace and tranquility of that Church, we commit it to your protection; and, earnestly admonishing your brotherhood, command that whenever you receive a complaint from the abbot and brethren of that Church concerning their wrongdoers, you assist them wisely and strive so to restrain those wrongdoers from the audacity of their presumption that, through the care of your solicitude, those brethren may enjoy their due tranquility, while their wrongdoers cannot rejoice in their impunity.

Given at Anagni, on the Kalends of March.

MCXXIV. To the same.—On behalf of the abbot of Mairimont against the harassment of several nobles. (Anagni, March 6.)

[Ibid., col. 1006.]

[Col. 0977A]

On the complaint of our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the Church of Mairimont, you should know that it has come to our hearing that the noblemen the Count of Grandpré, Engobrand of Altri and his son, Peter of Liri, Thomas of Suen, Dudo Ferrandus, his nephew Guerric, and Albert, advocate of Warno, have violently inflicted serious losses on that Church and do not cease to afflict it to the peril of its salvation. Since, therefore, it could be ascribed to the negligence of prelates if the vigor of ecclesiastical discipline were lukewarm in repressing [Col. 0977B] the audacity of wicked men who rage against the holy Churches of God, we command your brotherhood, by apostolic letters and under injunction, that, if the matter stands thus, you admonish the men named with earnest exhortation to repair in full the damages inflicted upon the aforesaid Church within thirty days after receipt of these letters, without appeal, and thereafter desist from similar acts. But if they refuse to comply with your admonition, forbid divine offices to be celebrated in their lands, the remedy of appeal being removed; and if they do not amend even thus, bind their persons with the bond of excommunication. And if the aforesaid Albert has been excommunicated for another cause, as is represented to us, pronounce him excommunicated also on this account, [Col. 0977C] and cause both him and all the others to be shunned throughout your province as excommunicated persons until fitting satisfaction has been made.

Given at Anagni, the second day before the Nones of March.

MCXXV. To the same.—Against several persons who harassed the monastery of St. Remigius. (Anagni, March 8.)

[Ibid.]

Our beloved son, the abbot of St. Remigius of Rheims, has shown us in a complaint sent to us that Hugh of Risnel has presumed to take from him the village of Domno-Remigio; that Milo of St. Margaret and Anselm of the court [Col. 0977D] of Hilbercunt, as well as the provosts of Busey, Juniac, Marolles, Châtillon, and Vitry, and certain other officials of the noble Count Henry, have presumed violently to withhold certain revenues belonging to the treasury of the monastery of St. Remigius, as well as other revenues, and presume unjustly to harass its men. Moreover, Garin of Boob presumes, by interposing an appeal, to prevent payment to the aforesaid abbot of a certain sum of money bequeathed to him in alms; and Adam of Capis does not fear to seize a certain piece of land by force. Since, therefore, by the obligation of our office we are bound to defend and preserve the rights of the aforesaid abbot and of the monastery entrusted to him, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you [Col. 0978A] diligently admonish the aforesaid men, if they belong to your province, suitably to satisfy the aforesaid abbot concerning the matters stated, to desist thereafter from harassing and troubling him, or to render him complete justice in this matter before the judgment of your discretion. But if they should refuse to do this, bind them with the bond of excommunication until fitting satisfaction has been made. Furthermore, cause that right which he asserts he has in the property of Nicholas of Châlons, formerly his man, who died without an heir, to be fully preserved to him, or that complete justice in the matter be rendered under the judgment of your discretion, appeal being set aside.

Given at Anagni, the eighth day before the Ides of March.

MCXXVI. To the same.—He exhorts him to gentleness toward A., a citizen of Laon. (Anagni, March 10.)

[Ibid., col. 1007.]

[Col. 0978B]

The dignity of the pontifical office which, by the disposing grace of God, you are known to hold ought to induce you to appear mild and gentle toward your subjects. And if anything should at any time be alleged to you concerning one of them that might move you to indignation, it does not become your discretion suddenly and indiscreetly to move against him; but if the offence is such as may, without injury to conscience, be remitted without punishment, you ought mercifully to pardon the offender; or, if it requires correction, to correct him with such humanity that you do not appear to exceed in severity or, in your gentleness as bishop, to set aside [Col. 0978C] due gravity. For from the representation of O., a citizen of Laon, we have learned that, when, on the perverse suggestion of certain persons, you charged him with having spoken evil of your person, and he in your presence steadfastly offered to clear himself through ten lawful men, you refused to accept his purgation. Fearing, therefore, that he would be oppressed by you, the same O. appealed to our hearing. Since, accordingly, it is not fitting that you should burden less reasonably one who seeks to establish his innocence before you, we admonish and earnestly exhort your brotherhood by apostolic letters mercifully to remit your indignation toward the aforesaid O. without requiring purgation, or, after accepting his purgation, [Col. 0978D] not to delay to restore to him your favor and affection, so that the moderation of your discretion may thereby deservedly be commended.

Given at Anagni, the sixth day before the Ides of March.

MCXXVII. To the same.—Concerning the provision of a priest for the lepers of Épernay. (Anagni, March 16.)

[Ibid., col. 1008.]

Having formerly heard the complaint of the lepers of Épernay that, since they had no priest, many of them were dying without confession and viaticum, we directed our letters to you, if we remember correctly, that you might provide against so great a danger to them. But now, since, as the same lepers have informed us, a certain priest named Walter, of good reputation and life, has attached himself to their house, [Col. 0979A] we again earnestly admonish and command your brotherhood to appoint that priest to the chapel which they have there, and not delay to entrust to him the care of souls for the aforesaid sick persons and their household; and, when you have been asked to do so, without appeal, not delay to dedicate that chapel for himself alone and his household; and wisely and diligently protect the aforesaid priest from the undue harassment of the canons of Épernay. Thus may your charity and affection be deservedly commended in this matter, and may the aforesaid lepers, under your defence and protection, be secure from the molestation of malicious persons.

[Col. 0979B] Given at Anagni, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of April.

MCXXVIII. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims, and [Desiderius], Bishop of Thérouanne.—That tithes not be demanded from Cistercians for lands which they cultivate by their own labour. (Anagni, March 21.)

[Ibid., col. 1009.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brethren HENRY, Archbishop of Rheims, and the Bishop of Thérouanne, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The prudent judgment of your discretion is not ignorant, as we believe, how all the brethren of the Cistercian Order were granted by the Fathers and our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs—and the concession was also renewed by us—that they should be bound to pay tithes to no one from the produce of lands which they cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense, or from the sustenance of their animals. Yet, as we have learned, the canons of the Church of Thérouanne, the provost of Loos and his canons, the abbot of Mont-Saint-Éloi [Note: [Col. 0979D] Mont-Saint-Éloi is a monastery of regular canons of no little distinction, two hours’ distance from Arras.] and his canons, the abbot and monks of the church of St. John of Thérouanne [Note: [Col. 0979D] The monastery of St. John of Thérouanne, or called “on the Mount,” of the Order of St. Benedict, formerly situated in the suburb of Thérouanne, has now been transferred to Ypres.], the abbot and monks of Ham [Note: [Col. 0979D] The monastery of Ham, of the Order of St. Benedict, in the diocese of Saint-Omer.], the provost and canons of Cassel, and certain others established in your regions, despising in this respect the ordinances of the Apostolic See, do not hesitate to demand tithes from the religious of Clairmarais [Note: [Col. 0979D] Clairmarais, a distinguished monastery of the Cistercian Order, two hours’ distance from Saint-Omer.], not only from other produce, but also from certain newly cleared lands and from the sustenance of their animals—something which was permitted to no one, however religious. Since, therefore, [Col. 0980A] we can neither suffer nor ought to suffer anyone to act contrary to the ordinances of the Apostolic See, we command your brotherhoods by apostolic letters and under injunction, relying on apostolic authority and without contradiction or appeal, to restrain the aforesaid men by ecclesiastical censure from demanding tithes from the labour or from the sustenance of the animals of the brethren just mentioned; and throughout your bishoprics cause the other concessions granted to the aforesaid brethren by privileges of the Apostolic See to be observed inviolate.

Given at Anagni, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

MCXXIX. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims.—On behalf of the brethren of St. Martin of Laon. (Anagni, March 23.)

[Ibid., col. 1010.]

[Col. 0980B]

We have received the complaint of the abbot and brethren of St. Martin of Laon: when Garin of Cherchi had uprooted certain of their vineyards and was at last brought to judgment, he appealed to our hearing. But because, though the other party appeared, the aforesaid G. neither came nor sent an advocate to answer for him, we commit this case to your experience, commanding you by the authority of the present letters to admonish the same G. and compel him, under the constraint of excommunication, either to repair the damages inflicted upon the aforesaid brethren or to render them full justice in the matter before you, the remedy of appeal being removed.

Given at Anagni, the tenth day before the Kalends of April.

MCXXX. To Guigo, Count of Forez.—He recites and confirms by his authority the settlement and exchange of rights made between him and the Church of Lyons. (Anagni, April 1.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 942.]

[Col. 0980C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GUIGO, Count of Forez, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the Church of Lyons has often been afflicted by you [Note: [Col. 0979D] “At that time,” says the author of the *Life of St. Anthelm, Bishop of Belley*, “the Count of Forez devastated the city of Lyons, which he had taken by treachery, and, despoiling everything, displayed the fury of his malice especially against the Church. For when the clergy, by God’s favour, had escaped his hands like fugitives and exiles, he angrily demolished their houses. But Lord Heraclius, Archbishop of that city, and the venerable persons of the other dignities, went to the wilderness of Portes.” We learn when this occurred from a charter of the monastery of Savigny, which begins thus: “In the year 1161 of the Lord’s Incarnation, while Frederick, the most victorious emperor, reigned in Italy, while Louis was king in France, while Heraclius governed the archbishopric of Lyons, and while he and his clergy were in conflict with the Count of Forez,” etc. MENESTRIER, *Hist. de Lyon*, p. 35; he also prints Guigo’s charter, from which it is clear that peace was made between them on the borders of Anse and Villefranche, “at the conference held between the Archbishop of Lyons and myself concerning our war,” not, indeed, in 1158, on the Wednesday, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, as is there stated, but in 1162, when 18 July fell on a Wednesday.], at length a certain settlement has been made between you and your son Guigo, on the one hand, and our venerable brother Guichard, Archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, and our beloved sons the canons of Lyons, [Col. 0981A] on the other, for the good of peace, and has been confirmed by your oath. In order that it may be inviolably observed for all time, we have thought fit to record it word for word.

> “In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, for the stability of perpetual peace between Lord Guichard, Archbishop of Lyons, and the Church of Lyons, and Guigo, Count of Forez, the following exchange was made by common consent:
>
> “The lord archbishop and the Church granted to the count whatever they, or another in their name, possessed beyond the Loire: namely, the obedience of Nervieu [Note: [Col. 0981D] Nervieu.] and of Saltrenen [Note: [Col. 0981D] Souternon.], as far as Amion [Note: [Col. 0981D] Amions.] and as far as Ulphiacum [Note: [Col. 0981D] Urphé.], and beyond, if they possessed any right belonging to the aforesaid obedience; and whatever [Col. 0981B] they possessed from Ulphiacum as far as Cervières [Note: [Col. 0981D] Cervières.] and from Cervières as far as Thiers. They retained for themselves the revenues of St. John of Lavastris [Note: [Col. 0981D] Saint-Jean de la Vestre.], while granting to the lord count lordship over the castle of Rochefort, which the lord of Thiers holds in the name of the Church. They also granted him whatever right they had in the castle of St. Roman of Puy, and thence as far as Le Puy and Auvergne. But from Amion and the other aforesaid boundaries northward, whatever right the archbishop and both the Church and the count had, they retained for themselves. Nevertheless, in the district of Roanne beyond the Loire and about the Loire, as far as the lordship of the lords of Roanne extends, the Church may not make or [Col. 0981C] acquire a fortification; or, if it makes or acquires one, it shall belong to the count, who shall hold it from the Church. The Church may acquire open lands for a canonry or in alms, provided that this is done without payment of money; and in its obediences it may acquire tithes, wardships (*gardas*), vicariates, and all other things pertaining to obedience.
>
> “On this side of the Loire, they granted to the count, from Balbigny [Note: [Col. 0981D] Balbigny.] and Poilly [Note: [Col. 0981D] Poilly.] as far as Old Caneva [Note: [Col. 0981D] Ville-Nève.], which lies within the count’s boundaries, whatever right they had in the district of Donzy as far as the district of Chamosset [Note: [Col. 0981D] Chamosset.], and from the district of Cornillon [Note: [Col. 0981D] Cornillon.] as far as the district of St. Symphorian; so that Maringes and Mais should remain within the count’s boundaries. And whatever right the archbishop or Church has from the district of St. Symphorian [Col. 0981D] on this side of the Loire toward the count’s land, and beyond the Loire from Amion and Ulphiacum, and from Cervières as far as Thiers, and from Thiers as far as Le Puy, they [Col. 0982A] granted to the count. They also granted to the count St. Eugendus [Note: [Col. 0981D] Saint-Héand.] and whatever the archbishop possessed at Chevrières [Note: [Col. 0981D] Chevrières.]; Castelluttum [Note: [Col. 0981D] Châ elus.] and Fontanesium [Note: [Col. 0982D] Fontanez.] lie within the count’s boundaries, except for the obedience of Grandmont, which the Church retains for itself. They remitted to the count the oath concerning St. Priest [Note: [Col. 0982D] S. Priest.] which he owed the Church, and that which Gaudemar of Jarez held there in the name of the Church, provided that he holds the castle from the Church. They granted to the count the castle of Fougeroles [Note: [Col. 0982D] Fougeroles.] and that which Guichard of Jarez owed for it; likewise, that which Briannus held from the Church in the castle of Grangens, saving the right of both Church and count at Sorbières [Note: [Col. 0982D] Sorbières.]. St. John of Bonofonte, St. Genesius [Note: [Col. 0982D] S. Genis.], Villars [Note: [Col. 0982D] Villars.], and St. Victor remained freely to the Church.
>
> “It must further be noted that in all these matters both the archbishop and the Church retained for themselves the churches, notwithstanding the royal right or other right granted to the count; they likewise retained the customary dues and rents of churches, with offerings and burials, and whatever right is known to belong to chapelries; while granting to the count all possessions and their revenues, both from tithes and otherwise, except those belonging to chapelries.
>
> “In return for all these things granted by the archbishop and Church to the count, Guigo the count and his son Guigo, on oath, granted to the Church by perpetual right, by way of exchange, [Col. 0982C] the things set down below. Namely, whatever right the count himself had in Lyons, or another possessed in his name, and in its dependencies. Beyond the Rhône, likewise, whatever he himself or another in his name possessed from Vienne as far as Anthon [Note: [Col. 0982D] Anthon.] and as far as Bourgoin [Note: [Col. 0982D] Bourgoin.], unless a succession should devolve upon him by hereditary right and line of consanguinity, all other claims being excluded. Beyond the Saône, likewise, the castle of Pérouges [Note: [Col. 0982D] Peroges.], which Guichard of Anthon held from him in fee, and half of Montaney [Note: [Col. 0982D] Montaney.], which Peter of Montluel held from him; also Giriacum [Note: [Col. 0982D] Giry.], which Hugh the Barefoot held from him in fee, together with their fealties. On this side of the Saône, the castle of Châtillon [Note: [Col. 0982D] Châtillon.] and whatever he possessed both in the castle and its district, for which the lord of the castle owes liege homage and fealty; the castle of Liconium [Note: [Col. 0982D] Château-d’Oin.] as far as Old Caneva, and the homage and liege fealty [Col. 0983A] owed for it; likewise Chamosset [Note: [Col. 0983D] Chamosset.] and its district, and its homage and liege fealty; Iseron [Note: [Col. 0983D] Iseron.] with its district and the liege fealty of its lords. St. Symphorian and its district remain within the Church’s boundaries. He granted to the Church Greziacum [Note: [Col. 0983D] Gressieu.] and Argentoria [Note: [Col. 0983D] Argentières.] as far as the district of Mais, as well as the fief of the lord of Riverie and homage and liege fealty. The castle of Riverie [Note: [Col. 0983D] Riverie.] and its district, and all that is contained as far as the district of Châlus, are held within the Church’s boundaries. From Alepin toward the count’s land, the Church must make no fortification. Likewise Changy [Note: [Col. 0983D] Changy.] with its district, and the two castles of St. Annemundus [Note: [Col. 0983D] Saint-Chanmond.] with their districts, are within the Church’s [Col. 0983B] boundaries, saving the count’s road from the cross of Mont-Viole [Note: [Col. 0983D] Mont-Viole.] as far as Forez. Berard of Pisaits and his holding remained to the Church, to which he owes homage and fealty. Everything contained from the district of Rochetaillée [Note: [Col. 0983D] Rochetaillé.] as far as Maleval [Note: [Col. 0984D] Maleval.] is within the Church’s boundaries; in particular, he granted to the Church whatever Aymar of Fernay held in fee from the count at Chavagnieu [Note: [Col. 0984D] Chavagnieu.], together with his fealty. Within these boundaries the same count also gave the Church the castle of Montagny [Note: [Col. 0984D] Montagny.] and what he possessed in its district, together with liege homage and fealty; and what he possessed at Félines [Note: [Col. 0984D] Félines.], and whatever right he or another in his name possessed within the said boundaries.
>
> “It must indeed be understood that within the Church’s aforesaid boundaries [Col. 0983C] the count may neither possess nor acquire anything, nor make a fortification; and if, by violence or injury to the Church, he makes one, it shall be the Church’s own property. Nor ought he to maintain or assist against the Church any person dwelling within those boundaries. Likewise, within the count’s boundaries, the archbishop or Church may neither make nor acquire a fortification; and if anyone acquires or builds one, it shall be the count’s own property, provided that he holds it in the Church’s name. Nor ought the Church or archbishop to maintain or assist against him anyone dwelling within the count’s boundaries, except with the spiritual sword. The Church may acquire open lands within the count’s boundaries, given in alms or for the establishment of a canonry, without payment of [Col. 0983D] money. In all the foregoing, however, the archbishop reserved his archiepiscopal rights; but whoever holds the castle of St. Praejectus, Rochetaillée [Note: [Col. 0984D] Rochetaillée.], the castle of Roche, Fougeroles [Note: [Col. 0984D] Fougeroles.], or Grangens [Note: [Col. 0984D] Grangens.], owes the count homage and liege fealty. What the count gave to Briannus in [Col. 0984A] the castle of St. Annemundus [Note: [Col. 0984D] Saint-Chaumond.], in the open country and in the district, that same Briannus shall hold from the Church and shall therefore owe homage and fealty to the Church.
>
> “But if anyone raises a claim or war against either party concerning the matters contained in this exchange, they must in good faith give one another mutual assistance, at their own expense and without restitution for loss, to the best of their ability; and they must in every way take care that, on account of all the matters contained in this exchange, the count is not excommunicated or his land subjected to interdict.
>
> “It must also be understood that the lord archbishop promised the count and his heirs that he would firmly observe this exchange. The canons likewise, having sworn an oath, confirmed that they would henceforth receive no one as a canon until he had confirmed this same oath, nor would they render obedience or fealty to future archbishops until those archbishops had promised firmly to observe it.
>
> “Moreover, it must be understood that the count owes homage and liege fealty to the archbishop. And this is the fief for which he is bound to him by homage and fealty: the castle of Fougeroles, half of Grangent, the castle of St. Praejectus, St. Eugendus, Cambeotium, Poncin, Villadieu, and Nerviacum with its dependencies. When the count or his heirs render fealty to the archbishop, they must promise under the oath of fealty that they will firmly observe the aforesaid agreement. He may assign the tithes from the Church’s fief to religious places and persons for his soul. [Col. 0984C] But if he alienates them under another title, he must receive only land of his own in fee from the Church. The Church’s holding cannot be separated from the county. Chapelries cannot be diminished by obedientiaries. Between St. Annemundus and La Tour, and between St. Annemundus and St. Praejectus, neither may make a fortification.
>
> “We also wish it to be made known that, besides the foregoing, the Church gave the count one thousand one hundred marks of silver for this exchange.
>
> “These things were done in the year 1193 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Pope Alexander III presiding, Frederick reigning as Roman emperor, and Louis, most pious king of the French, reigning.”

[Col. 0984D] We therefore hold this settlement, made as it was by the common agreement of the parties, to be ratified and confirmed; and, confirming it by apostolic authority, we strengthen it by the protection of this present document. Decreeing that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person to infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way to act contrary to it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur [Col. 0985A] the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, on the Kalends of April.

MCXXXI. He receives under protection the monastery of St. Mary of Nogent and enumerates and confirms its possessions. (Anagni, April 4.)

[DU PLESSIS, *Histoire de Coucy*, 143.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, abbot of the monastery of St. Mary of Nogent, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

[lacuna] We receive the aforesaid monastery under the protection of St. Peter and of ourselves and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, decreeing that the monastic order known to have been established in that monastery according to God and the Rule of St. Benedict shall there be preserved inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and whatever goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses or may, with the Lord’s favour, acquire in the future by concession of pontiffs, grant of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other such means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper names:

The church of Coucy, with its prebends and all things pertaining to it; the altar of [lacuna]. From [Col. 0985C] the gift of the wife of Geoffrey of Condrino, four measures of grain, etc. [lacuna] From the gift of Ralph of Coucy, one hundred solidi of good money and twenty solidi arising from the church of St. Remigius of Coucy, to be received from the wine dues, for the soul of his wife, etc.

We therefore decree, etc.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the day before the Nones of April, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1174 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCXXXII. To Lupus, King of Valencia.

(TWISDEN, *Scriptores Anglicani*, I, 580.)

ALEXANDER, pontiff of great and venerable Rome, to LUPUS, glorious king of Valencia, that he may know the heavenly Creator and render Him service pleasing to Him.

Since we all have one God, the Father, in heaven, you ought to worship Him alone with your whole heart and love Him with all your strength, He who has granted you such great power over the nations and kingdoms of the Saracens. But since He created all men free by nature, no one was, by the condition of nature, subject to slavery.

MCXXXIII. To Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury.—He affirms the primacy of England for him and his successors.

(Ibid.)

ALEXANDER, pope, to RICHARD, Archbishop of Canterbury.

[Col. 0986A] The Archbishop of Canterbury has been set upon the candlestick, that he may shine before men; and, chosen from the clergy for the comfort of the clergy, he has been appointed as a special support of ecclesiastical liberty, for the governance, defence, and protection of all Englishmen, since within a few days three offices have converged in one and the same person: archbishop, primate, and legate of the Apostolic See.

Out of regard for charity, and because, although unworthy, we consecrated you bishop with our own hands and conferred upon you the fullness of authority, we have, with the counsel of our brethren, judged that your just petitions should be granted with due kindness. Adhering to the footsteps of our predecessors of pious memory, Paschal and Eugenius, Roman pontiffs, [Col. 0986B] we grant to you and to your lawful successors the primacy of the Church of Canterbury as fully as it is known to have been possessed formerly by Lanfranc, Anselm, and the other archbishops of Canterbury, their predecessors.

### MCXXXIV. To John, bishop-elect of Chichester

He signifies that he has instructed Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, “not to delay proceeding with his promotion because he is said to be a canon’s son.”

(See *Decretals of Gregory*, book I, title 20, chapter 2.)

### MCXXXV. To all the faithful established throughout France

He commends Peter, Cardinal of St. Chrysogonus. (Anagni, 17 April.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 967.]

[Col. 0986C] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishops and bishops, and to his beloved sons the abbots and other prelates of churches, and to all clergy and laity established throughout the kingdom of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since we have plainly experienced the prudence, learning, and integrity of our beloved son P., priest-cardinal of the title of St. Chrysogonus, and since we sincerely love him in the Lord as a learned, prudent, and discerning man, we commit to him with greater confidence those matters which must be carried out by honourable and prudent men, inasmuch as we have fuller confidence [Col. 0986D] in the fervour of his devotion and in his prudence. Therefore, for certain more important and difficult affairs, we have judged that this cardinal should be dispatched especially and principally to your regions. We have granted him authority and power to correct whatever he finds there in need of correction and to determine causes brought before his hearing.

Accordingly, we earnestly admonish and command your whole body that you take care to receive this cardinal with due honour, as a learned, prudent, and honourable man sent from our side, who is exceedingly dear and welcome to us; and that you firmly accept and observe his correction and those measures which he establishes with prudent circumspection. Thus may he find in you the fervour of your customary devotion, and may we commend your prudence and sincerity [Col. 0987A] with worthy praises in the Lord.

Given at Anagni, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May [17 April].

### MCXXXVI. To Henry, Archbishop of Rheims

That he should urge the king to make himself an arbiter of peace between the Church and the Empire, and should also endeavour to induce the kings of France and England to concord. (Anagni, 19 April.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 969.]

Since in all things we have laudably and effectively experienced the fervour of your most welcome devotion, we have a sure hope and undoubted confidence that, even without our urging, you will willingly undertake what pertains to the peace and advancement of the Church. Yet, because it is incumbent upon us to make your prudence attentive to those matters which are expedient for us and for the Church, we ask, admonish, and command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you diligently and frequently exhort our dearest son in Christ, L., the illustrious king of the Franks, your brother, to devote himself earnestly to restoring peace between the Church and the Empire, in accordance with the admonition of our beloved son P., priest-cardinal of the title of St. Chrysogonus—

[Note: [Col. 0987D] Peter, who was made cardinal by Alexander III and in the same year, 1173, was sent by him into Gaul to [Col. 0988D] arrange peace between King Louis of the Franks and Henry of the English, according to Ciaconius.]

—whom we are sending to that king—if in any way Almighty God opens for him an honourable path to peace; and that he proceed in the cause of peace according to the counsel of that cardinal. Let him also bend his mind mercifully, so far as he can without prejudice to [Col. 0987C] his honour, toward making peace with Henry, the illustrious king of the English. For it is to be feared that, if such war should continue longer between these kings, losses of property and dangers to persons may arise in both kingdoms through this conflict, and that the eastern land may be exposed—may the Lord avert it—to the plundering of the pagans.

In these matters, and in others which the same cardinal shall propose to you on our behalf, place undoubted trust in him. Receive and treat him honourably as a learned, discerning, and prudent man, exceedingly dear and welcome to us; and show him such favour and affection that we may be bound to render most abundant thanks to your goodwill.

Given at Anagni, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May [19 April].

### MCXXXVII. To the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury

Concerning appeals. (Anagni, 14 May.)

[*Letters of St. Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 40.]

[Col. 0987D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, the suffragans of the Church of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother the Archbishop of Canterbury, legate of the Apostolic See, has informed us that whenever you, or your archdeacons, appeal to our presence from his presence concerning some [Col. 0988A] specified affair, you place your bishoprics and archdeaconries under apostolic protection and appeal for a year; and meanwhile you do not permit him to take cognizance either of past offences or of your new excesses, or of the offences of your subjects, but suspend and wholly nullify all his jurisdiction.

Since, therefore, we must provide that manifest offences do not remain uncorrected under the pretext of an appeal, and that your subjects do not rejoice in the impunity of their transgressions, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if you subject your bishoprics, or your archdeacons their archdeaconries, to apostolic protection and appeal to our hearing, you must by no means attempt on that account to hinder the said archbishop [Col. 0988B] from being able to take cognizance of the causes or offences of your subjects and punish them according to the gravity of their deserts with due correction. He may also duly correct your own offences, if any are manifest and notorious—excepting only those concerning which an appeal has been lodged—and restore to the path of rectitude whatever has been unjustly done.

Given at Anagni, the second day before the Ides of May [14 May].

### MCXXXVIII. He takes the monastery of St. Andrew under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges

(Anagni, 15 May.)

[HUGO, *Annals of the Premonstratensian Order*, I, 147.]

[Col. 0988C] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WALTER, prior of the church of the Premonstratensian Order, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Whenever something is requested of us which is recognized as consonant with religion and integrity, it is fitting that we grant it with a willing mind; and first we decree that the canonical order, known to have been established in that place according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the Premonstratensian brethren, shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions, etc., among which we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:
