[Col. 0988D] The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the field of Aurea Vallis; Alajot; half the tithe and lordship of St. Vincent; Bizant and the grange of Mont-Leon; the land of Tarnat; the enclosed land of Assonat near Plaudiacum; Valleriae near St. Germanus; the mill of St. Andrew; [lacuna] of the marriage-property of Clermont, of Camalerica, of Bellomont, of Montferrand, of Gorzat, of St. Avitus, of Pompinat, of St. Vincent, of Romagnat, of Albiriat, of Sayra, of St. Maximinus, of Gergoia, of Noanon Dorcinet, and of St. Leodegarius.

[Col. 0989A] Further, desiring with paternal diligence to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosure of your places or granges from daring to commit violence, robbery, or theft, to set fire, or to seize or kill persons. Moreover, when a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a low voice. We likewise grant that the burial-ground of the place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while the right of the mother church is nevertheless preserved.

Further, you may receive into your religious community free and unencumbered clerics or laymen fleeing the world, and retain them in your church without anyone’s opposition. We further prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving the cloister without the permission of his abbot; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without letters of the community guaranteeing his standing.

Indeed, no one may presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your animals. On the death of you, the present prior of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any trickery or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of their counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of May, in the indiction, in the year 1174, in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

### MCXXXIX. He takes the Church of St. Mary of Luffeld under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges

(Anagni, 10 June.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, I, 521.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons RALPH, prior of St. Mary of Luffeld, and his brethren, present and future, [Col. 0989D] professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

It is fitting that apostolic protection should be at hand for those choosing the religious life. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the safeguard of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions, etc., among which we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Mary of Lodeford with all its appurtenances; the place of St. Mary; the chapel of St. Thomas the Martyr; the place of St. Mary of Stlechamstude with all [Col. 0990A] its appurtenances; the place of Eradetnel with all its appurtenances; the vill called Obersawe with all its appurtenances; the land which you hold in Langeport; the land which you hold in Waveduns; the land which you hold in Saldene; two parts of the tithes of the lordship of that same vill; the land which you hold in Lechamstude; the land which you hold in Westburt; the land which you hold in Bedford, with a certain dwelling before the archdeacon’s gate; the land which you hold in Selveston; the bread tithe from the house of Hamo son of Manfelin; the bread tithe from the house of William de Brun; the bread tithe from the house of William de Brun; the bread tithe from the house of William de Lillingstan; and the house which you hold in Storhampton.

Moreover, when a general interdict of the land has been imposed, [Col. 0990B] you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a low voice. Indeed, no one may presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your animals. You may also receive into your religious community free and unencumbered laymen or clerics fleeing the world and retain them without anyone’s opposition. We prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving the cloister through any levity without the permission of his prior; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without letters of the community guaranteeing his standing. Nor may anyone impose upon you or your churches new and unlawful exactions; but we confirm by apostolic authority for you and your church the ancient and reasonable customs, liberties, and immunities of your church.

We decree also that the burial-ground of the place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; the right, however, of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken is preserved. On the death of you, the present prior of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any trickery or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed [Col. 0990D] Benedict.

We decree therefore, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore, etc.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of June [10 June], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1174 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

### MCXL. He takes the Church of Stokes under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges

(Anagni, 30 June.)

[Ibid., p. 1010.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0991A] sons NICHOLAS, prior of the church of Stokes, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift result. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, etc., as above. First, we decree that the monastic order, known to have been established in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods, etc., among which we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the church [Col. 0991B] of Hunedena; the church of Baisse; the church of Clara; the church of Little Bradelea; the church of Trillame; the church of Bures; the church of Caveham; the church of Cremplisham; the church of St. Clement of Norwich; and the church of Frisentuna, situated in the diocese of Norwich; in the diocese of London, the church of Bertedeld, the church of Tartede, the church of Essa, the church of Belham, and the church of Stamburnia; in the diocese of Winchester, the church of Wakinges; in the diocese of Rochester, the church of Peccham; the tithes which you hold in Sancford, Berdefeld, Pitelinge-kege, Stinchingefeld, Toppesfeld, Wicham, [Col. 0991C] Badeleja, Nertstert, Deseninge, Baisse, Stanesfeld, Clara, Hunedena, Namstede, Bomestede, Nowerelle, Bucheshale, Slinestede, Deleford, Chippelec, Culinges, Poselingeworde, Belilee, Seham, and Corneres; the tithes in Belcham Petri; the tithes in Belcham Rspertes [reading uncertain]; the tithes in Delham, Bestingetorp, Kedeswele, Chodham, Steinglingeherste, Beneclee, Nalstede, Atveredesfeld, Denordestune, Nanchesdune, Cavenedis, Sturemare, Barve, Tillebere, Chediatune, Nalesford, Naveringeland, and Witervele; the tithes of William de Bisnai; the land of Roger the carpenter in Stokes, exchanged for your land of Clara; the land of Sterneham, given to you by Geoffrey son of Alinand; the land of Neni, given to you by Adam son of Guarin; the mill of Waldnigefeld, given to you by Helinand, steward of the count of Clara; [Col. 0992A] the land in Trillawe, given to you by Robert the butler; the land of Bridebroc; the land of Naverelle; the land of Polee; the land of Bradelece; the land of Belcham; the land of Esse; and one hundred shillings’ worth of land, which you hold by the gift of Roger, count of Clara, when he was at the point of death.

We likewise decree that the burial-ground of the place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken is preserved. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a low voice. [Col. 0992B] You may also receive into your religious community free and unencumbered clerics or laymen fleeing the world, and retain them in your monastery without anyone’s opposition. We further prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving the cloister without the permission of his prior; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without letters of the community guaranteeing his standing, unless he wishes to transfer to a stricter life.

In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose priests and present them to the bishops; if they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust to them the care of souls, so that they shall answer to the bishop concerning the care of the people, but to you concerning temporal matters. We also prohibit strangers from introducing new and unlawful customs [Col. 0992C] into your churches. Indeed, no one may presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your animals.

We decree therefore, etc., saving, indeed, the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of July [30 June], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1174 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander II.

### MCXLI. Privilege for the Abbey of St. Martin of Chora

(Anagni, 17 July.)

[MABILLON, *Benedictine Annals*, VI, 722.]

[Col. 0992D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BASIL, abbot of the Church of St. Mary and St. Martin of Chora, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

It is fitting that apostolic protection should be at hand for those choosing the religious life. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions, etc., decreeing that whatever possessions, etc., among which we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the [Col. 0993A] vill called Chora itself; ovens, mills, and the whole jurisdiction of the vill with its inhabitants; the woods, namely Fraite-chaloet, and its share of Rogeo; and the water from the stream [lacuna] from Cholistri as far as the stream of Prisciac; the church of Domeziac with all its appurtenances; the church of Bazochiis with all its appurtenances; the church of Montezabo with all its appurtenances; the church of Novemfontes; the church of Montevigneo with all its appurtenances; the church of Sancta-Christiana with all its appurtenances; the church of Petrapertusa with all its appurtenances; the chapel of Curte for celebrating divine office; the church of Vassiac with its dependencies; and one [lacuna] rent-payment from every house in the whole [Col. 0993B] parish: the chapel of Chora, and the church of St. Andrew; the church of Castelud; the church of Epure; the church of Montezabo; the church of Sassiac; the church of Venus; the church of St. Mary of Maer; the church of Dornachiac; the church of Briva; the church of Cersi; the church of Petrapertusa; the church of Domitiac; the church of Bazochiis; the church of Montevineo; and the right of use which the Church of Chora has in the woods of the lord of Petrapertusa, at Faiis, Herbert, Batert, Brolio, Chaneio de Veles, and its Battitiae, at Sauvezea; its share in the wood of Cumbis; a site for a grange in that same wood, free from every service owed to the castle called Petrapertusa, and likewise its keeper; and the free gift, sale, and pledging of any possession within the entire castellany of the said castle, whoever makes it, from his own right to the aforesaid church; half the *cosduma* of each house of Uziac and of the town, if it lies within the castellany of Pons of Petrapertusa; land; thirds; rents; *cosdumae*; inhabitants; and the tithe of the cultivation of the monks of Minoda, according as it pertains to the aforesaid abbey; land, thirds, rents, *cosdumae*, tithes, inhabitants, and woods of Oziac, Ciriac, Ochis, Urbiniac, Ateis, Mullet, and Empuriac, with all the jurisdictions and *cosdumae* which the aforesaid abbey holds in them; land, thirds, *cosdumae*, tithes, rents, meadows, [Col. 0993D] vineyards, and inhabitants of Domitiac, Basochiis, Flaiac, Cistriac, Dormitiac, Monteadversiac, Carentiac, Chalauro, Seobreo, and Petrapertusa, with all the jurisdictions and *cosdumae* which the aforesaid abbey holds in them.

Also the priory of Curte, with the whole jurisdiction of the vill, tithes from the monks’ cultivation, lands, thirds, rents, *cosdumae*, inhabitants, and a portion of the wood of Arvial; land, thirds, rents, *cosdumae*, and meadows of St. Columba, Massiac, Boisum, Antiiac, and Montoliblo, with all jurisdictions and *cosdumae* belonging to the aforesaid priory. Also the priory of Vasiac, with all lands and meadows; thirds, rents, tithes from the monks’ cultivation; [Col. 0994A] the general court; the wood of Sarreia; and all jurisdictions and *cosdumae* which the aforesaid priory holds in the aforesaid vill; lands, thirds, rents, and all rights which the aforesaid priory holds in the vill of Berriaco.

When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a low voice. On the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any trickery or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

[Col. 0994B] We decree therefore, etc.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August [17 July], in the sixteenth indiction, in the year 1173 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

### MCXLII. Privilege for the Church of St. Martin of Tours

(Fragment.) (Anagni, 3 August.)

[*Works of Launoy*, III, II, 67.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc.

Since the Church of blessed Martin of Tours has no bishop except the Roman pontiff, instructions are given to the archbishops and bishops, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the third day before the Nones of August [3 August], in the fifteenth year of [Col. 0994C] our pontificate.

### MCXLIII. To Conrad, Archbishop of Mainz and legate of the Apostolic See

He writes that the Bishop of Gurk, together with Richer, whom he had unlawfully consecrated Bishop of Brixen at Regensburg, had transferred the archbishopric of Salzburg, taken away from Adalbert, to the provost of Berchtesgaden (Henry). He is to declare that crime void. He commands him to recall both bishops and the provost, clergy, and people of Salzburg to obedience to Adalbert. (Anagni, 8 September.)

[*Chronicle of Reichersberg*, in LUDEWIG, *Writers of German Affairs*, II, 310.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son CONRAD, Archbishop of Mainz and legate of the Apostolic [Col. 0994D] See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more fully we know the purity of your faith and devotion toward us and the Roman Church, and the more we have experienced your prudence and diligence in all things, the more confidently we entrust to you matters requiring a prudent and resolute man and demanding execution with much circumspection. Certainly, the proximity of the places, your rank, and your prudence do not permit you to be at all ignorant of that monstrous act which we have lately learned, not without great bitterness of heart, to have been undertaken against our venerable brother Adalbert, Archbishop of Salzburg, by men whose fidelity we did not appear to have any reason to doubt.

[Col. 0995A] We have heard that when our venerable brother, the Bishop of Gurk, had conferred upon the bishop-elect of Brixen the gift of consecration at Regensburg—something which he was not permitted to do, against the prohibition of the aforesaid archbishop—the same Bishop of Brixen, together with the said Bishop of Gurk, presumed to convene against that archbishop. On the day immediately following his own consecration, he pronounced against the archbishop a sentence of deposition; and, with rash audacity, he intruded into the Church of Salzburg the provost of Berchtesgaden, a man who had indeed formerly been regarded as religious and Catholic. Nor did he hesitate to absolve the clergy from obedience and the laity from fidelity to that archbishop.

We are astonished—and cannot be sufficiently astonished—at the said Bishop of Gurk and Bishop of Brixen. The former, namely the Bishop of Gurk, from the beginning of his promotion and even before, as we believe, showed by letters and messengers fervent devotion toward us and the Roman Church. The latter, namely the Bishop of Brixen, while he was engaged with us in scholarly studies, was bound to us by a certain especially close familiarity; he is shown to be a man of great religious seriousness and integrity, and professes himself Catholic. How then did they burst into so novel, monstrous, and unheard-of a crime? They neither could nor ought to have dared to pronounce sentence against any bishop, much less against the aforesaid archbishop, to whom they owe obedience and reverence, without a mandate of the Roman pontiff. This is especially so because that archbishop, as you know, was canonically [Col. 0995C] elected, confirmed by us, and received the pallium from your hand in the fullness of the pontifical office.

Although the said Bishop of Gurk and Bishop of Brixen assert that the aforesaid bishop has been established in the aforesaid Church under obedience and devotion to us, we nevertheless do not see—and no one can see—how it can or ought to be that one who was instituted archbishop in that Church by our mandate and authority should, without our knowledge, be removed from that Church, and another be set over him through the favour of an earthly prince. Therefore, since that Church has never at any time been infected by the stain of schismatic depravity, we and all who love that Church must take care that it not be newly besprinkled with the defilement of some contagion. Accordingly, we have thought fit to urge and most earnestly admonish your prudence, in which we place every hope and confidence, to correct [Col. 0995D] this enormity.

Therefore, annulling so monstrous a crime, we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters publicly to declare the act itself void and without effect. Setting aside every human favour and influence, you are to strive as swiftly as possible to recall the said Bishop of Gurk and Bishop of Brixen, and the Provost of Salzburg, who undertook this act, from so foolish a purpose. Set them a term neither too long nor too short, within which time the intruded man must return to his own church, there to serve God henceforth, and return to the obedience and devotion of the said archbishop. Among other things, you shall tell the intruded man that he must not prefer ambition for rank and honour to religious seriousness and integrity, but serve God in simplicity of heart. By our authority, command both clergy and people belonging to his church to render to the aforesaid archbishop every obedience and honour as to their master and prelate. Take care to inform us fully by your letters how you have progressed in this matter.

Given at Anagni, the sixth day before the Ides of September [8 September].

### MCXLIV. To Siboto, provost, and the choir of the Church of Salzburg

That they return to obedience to Adalbert. (Anagni, 8 September.)

[Ibid., p. 311.]

[Col. 0996B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Siboto, provost, and the clergy of the Church of Salzburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard, not without much pain and bitterness of heart, how you, provost, have undertaken a monstrous act against our venerable brother, your archbishop, to whom you are bound to render obedience and reverence as to your master and prelate. That illustrious renown for praise and reputation which that Church has everywhere acquired before God and men by preserving Catholic unity ought especially to have recalled you from so dishonourable a purpose.

Certainly, you ought to have considered with anxious care and diligence, and reflected with earnest meditation, in what condition the man of holy memory Eberhard, formerly your archbishop, and his successor Conrad of good memory, as well as their predecessors, governed that Church. You should not have been able to depart in any manner from their path, but ought by every means to strive to adhere to their footsteps. We do not see—and no one can see—that the election, confirmation, or bestowal of the pallium upon the aforesaid archbishop should have been annulled, especially without the authority of the Roman pontiff, and another set over him. For that archbishop, as you know, was confirmed by us and received the pallium—that is, the fullness of the pontifical office—and our commands concerning the obedience to be rendered him have often been issued [Col. 0996D] to you and to others subject to his jurisdiction.

We are all the more astonished and disturbed over this because we love your Church with a more ample charity on account of the fervour of your devotion, and are affected with greater sadness and pain if anything should ever occur which appears in any way to detract from your praise and reputation, or to redound to the dishonour of reproach. Although, as we have heard, you allege our devotion and obedience in this very act, we nevertheless do not see—and no one can see—how this could have been done consistently with obedience to us and with integrity.

Since, therefore, the act itself is wholly contrary to divine and human law, we neither ought nor can endure it. Annulled as it is, and void by the law itself, we annul it by apostolic authority, [Col. 0997A] and command your whole body, under obedience, that you return to yourselves as swiftly as possible; consider carefully what your reputation and salvation require; abandon without any delay such a dishonourable purpose; and return to the obedience and devotion of the said archbishop. Be devoted and subject to him as to your master and prelate. Take care to conduct yourselves in this and in other matters in such a way that your actions may furnish others with examples of virtue.

But if, contrary to what we do not suppose, you act otherwise, then the more fervently we love you and your Church, the more vigorously, with the Lord’s help, we shall take care to recall you from so unlawful an act. For we would not seem to love you sincerely if we did not provide with paternal affection for your reputation and integrity.

Given at Anagni, the sixth day before the Ides of September [8 September].

### MCXLV. To Adalbert, Archbishop of Salzburg

He informs him of the foregoing letters. (Anagni, 8 September.)

[Ibid., p. 309.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ADALBERT, Archbishop of Salzburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having heard and understood that enormous deed which has been wickedly undertaken against you, not without offence to God and derogation from our authority [Col. 0997C], we were greatly astonished and disturbed. For, because of the fervour of your devotion, we love your person with sincere charity in the Lord; and we desire your peace and tranquillity, regarding the disturbance which threatens you and your Church as in no way foreign to ourselves, but as our own particular and proper affliction. Therefore, since the deed itself is contrary alike to divine and human law, we have annulled it by apostolic authority; we have sent our letters to those men who were the authors of so great a presumption, recalling them with pastoral concern from so unjust a design; and concerning this matter we have written to our venerable brother Conrad, Archbishop of Mainz, legate of the Apostolic See, as you will learn more fully from copies of our letters [Col. 0997D].

Therefore be strengthened in the Lord and act manfully, putting your hope in him who can deliver you from pressures and distresses and, after so great a disturbance, will by his grace give you peace and tranquillity. And, that you may have almighty God more favourable and propitious, strive to submit yourself to him with all devotion and zealously apply yourself to those things which are pleasing and acceptable to him. As a prudent, provident, and discerning man, devote all your effort to recovering the patrimony of the Church and to preserving that Church itself in faith and Catholic unity. We, moreover, bear toward you a firm purpose and ready will: to love your person with more abundant charity as that of a most dear brother, and in your persecutions and distresses [Col. 0998A] to offer every counsel and assistance which, with God, we are able to give.

Given at Anagni, 8 September.

**MCXLVI. To the dean and chapter of Paris.—He confirms the possessions of the Church of Paris; likewise concerning the prebend of St Geneviève in the Church of Paris. (Ferentino, 28 October.)**

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 1058.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons B., dean, and the chapter of the Church of Paris: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

The more honourably and effectively we have experienced in many matters the fervour of your devotion, the more willingly we wish to preserve and protect the rights and liberties of your Church [Col. 0998B], and more graciously to yield to your just petitions, so that you may experience more abundantly our favour because of the sincerity of the devotion which you show toward us and the Roman Church. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by the obligation of our office and graciously induced by your petitions, we hold valid and firm the liberties and ancient reasonable customs of your Church, observed from the time of the holy memory of our father and predecessor Pope Eugenius until our own times; and, confirming them by apostolic authority, we decree that they shall possess perpetual force hereafter.

Moreover, since certain monasteries and churches possess prebends in your Church, and the prebend of St Geneviève [Col. 0998C] has been granted to our beloved son Master Mainerius, you have feared lest, by gradual encroachment, such a practice may take root in your Church, to the detriment of the aforesaid monasteries and churches and to your own burden. You therefore asked us to provide with pastoral care for your right and for the immunity of those monasteries and churches in this matter. Accordingly, by this present writing we strictly forbid your being compelled to make any person a canon in respect of any of the prebends which the aforementioned monasteries or churches possess in your Church.

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation and constitution, or in any way to oppose it. But should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation [Col. 0998D] of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Ferentino, 28 October.

**MCXLVII. To Peter, Cardinal of St Chrysogonus, legate of the Apostolic See.—Concerning payment for the administration of the schools. (Ferentino, 29 October.)**

[Ibid., col. 971.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St Chrysogonus, legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Although we have directed that those wishing to teach should exact nothing from anyone for administering schools, according to the saying, “Come and hear,” nevertheless, wishing, so far as may be done without impropriety, to show ready kindness in consideration of the honour and learning of Master Peter, chancellor of Paris—whom we love with special favour and wish to honour—we command your discretion, after consultation with our venerable brothers William, Archbishop of Sens, legate of the Apostolic See, and the Archbishop of Reims, and with other worthy and honourable persons, to provide and arrange, with circumspect diligence, whatever seems right to you concerning the administration of the Parisian schools, provided that what you do in this matter does not exceed what concerns the person of the aforesaid Peter. You are to employ such caution and moderation that you may not appear to exceed due measure, and that those who administer the schools [Col. 0999B] may not be burdened immoderately.

Given at Ferentino, 29 October.

**MCXLVIII. To the dean and chapter of Paris.—Concerning the stipend of canons. (Ferentino, 11 November.)**

[Ibid., col. 1059.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the dean and chapter of the Church of Paris: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Justice demands and reason persuades that we should bestow more abundant favour and more graciously grant our support to the just petitions of those known to burn with great devotion toward us and the Roman Church, and who more readily carry out [Col. 0999C] our will. Thus, since at our request you have generously added six pounds yearly for our beloved son Robert of Beelei, vicar of St Peter of Fossat, in addition to the eight pounds which he was accustomed to receive annually in your Church, apart from distributions and small revenues, we, wishing to ensure that what you did with ready devotion out of reverence for us should not turn to your damage or prejudice, establish by apostolic authority that, on account of the addition which you made to the said Robert or to our beloved son Master Macarius, to whom the prebend of St Geneviève has been granted, you may not in any way be troubled by the aforesaid churches, so that after the death of Robert and Mainerius those prebends shall return to the same condition [Col. 0999D] in which they are known to have been before the addition was made.

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our constitution or in any way to oppose it. But should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Ferentino, 9 November.

**MCXLIX. He confirms the regular discipline, possessions, and privileges of the canons of Pistoia. (Ferentino, 19 November.)**

[Zacharia, *Anecdota medii aevi*, 232.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Heudinus, provost, and the other brethren of the canonry of Pistoia [Col. 1000A], present and future, who shall remain in the observance of the regular life: in perpetuity.

“Whenever that is requested of us which is recognized as fitting religion and honour,” etc., as in the bull of Eugenius III issued for the same persons on 11 December 1151 (*Patrologia*, vol. CLXXX, col. 1480), except for the following variant readings: “[of] Lucius and our father and predecessor Eugenius of holy memory . . . . You, son provost, or your successors, are to restrain . . . . The chapel of St Vitalis and the church of Vico Fario at the Lucchese gate . . . . Gerard, son of Baroncius . . . . To the glory of heavenly blessedness.”

The subscriptions, however, are these:

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 1000B] I, Hubaldus, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and St Rufina. I, Gualterius, bishop of Albano. I, John, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, title of Pammachius. I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of St Peter in Chains. I, Ardicio, deacon-cardinal of St Theodore. I, Cinthius, deacon-cardinal of St Adrian. I, Laborans, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Portico.

Given at Ferentino, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, 19 November, indiction VIII, in the year 1174 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

**MCL. He receives under protection the monastery of St Mary of Monreale and confirms all its possessions and privileges. (Ferentino, 30 December.)**

[Margarini, *Bullarium Casinense*, II, 185.]

[Col. 1000C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ William, illustrious king of Sicily, and his heirs, in perpetuity: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

By the duty of the government entrusted to us, we are obliged to consider the qualities and merits of individuals, so that we may exercise toward all the ministry of the dispensation committed to us in such a manner [Col. 1000D] that devoted sons of the Church, according to their rank and merit, may receive from the Apostolic See over which, though unworthy, we preside by the Lord’s disposition, the welcome fulfilment of their petitions. For this reason we are the more willing and gracious to show favour to your royal serenity and comply with your will, especially in matters pleasing and acceptable to our Redeemer and profitable to your salvation and renown, because we love your person with more abundant charity as that of a most dear son and most Christian king. We recall that most welcome benefits have come to us and to the Church of God from the ardour of your most welcome devotion, and, with the Lord as author, we continually believe that they will come; so that you may always possess greater devotion and reverence toward God and his holy churches, and may apply yourself more ardently to the worship of justice and works [Col. 1001A] of piety, when you have effectively obtained through the special prerogative of our love and favour that which you desire with pious and fervent longing.

Accordingly, as we have heard, not only from the letters of your highness but also with great joy and gladness of heart from the certain report of others, you have, through the inspiration of divine grace, begun to build at Santa Ruriacia, at royal and most generous expense, a monastery in honour of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God and Virgin; and, with the Lord’s cooperation, you have resolved to endow it with very extensive possessions, so that the place may be renowned and a community of monks established there to serve God. We extol your pious vow and purpose in this matter with the highest praise, and grant to your petitions, for carrying out the pious work [Col. 1001B] which you have begun at the Lord’s prompting, an effect as gracious as it is welcome.

Therefore, dearest son in Christ, because of the singular and spiritual affection which we have for you as a most Christian king, with the counsel of our brethren we establish by apostolic authority that this monastery shall at no time be subject to any archbishop, bishop, or other ecclesiastical person, but only to the Roman pontiff; rather, it shall always remain free and exempt from every obligation and subjection to other ecclesiastical persons. We further decree by this present writing that everything bestowed or to be bestowed, exchanged or to be exchanged, upon the aforesaid monastery outside your kingdom shall remain perpetually in the power of the abbot and convent of that monastery [Col. 1001C]. But whatever has been bestowed or shall be bestowed, exchanged or shall be exchanged, upon the same monastery within your kingdom shall remain unimpaired with the consent of you and your heirs.

The abbot and convent of the aforesaid monastery may also summon whichever Catholic bishop they wish for the ordination of clerics or monks to be ordained in the monastery or its dependencies, and may receive from him their ordinations, chrism, holy oil, and the consecration of altars or churches. By our authority he shall grant what is requested freely and without any opposition. In all parochial churches of the same monastery we grant that the font may be blessed by its own clerics [Col. 1001D] and that sacred baptism may be celebrated.

Moreover, we forbid and, by apostolic authority, strictly prohibit any archbishop or bishop from daring to forbid Christian people to enter the churches of the said monastery or the monastery itself and to make there some offering from their own goods, as is customary in pious devotion. If, however, any church or holding is bestowed upon the aforesaid monastery, concerning which tithes or another right are owed to a bishop or another ecclesiastical person, and that bishop or person has granted to the same monastery by episcopal right the tithes and other right which they are known to possess in another church or holding, we permit that gift and grant to remain inviolate for all time [Col. 1002A]. We further establish that no archbishop, bishop, or any other ecclesiastical person shall dare demand a tithe or a fourth from holdings and possessions granted to the same monastery or its cells with episcopal right, or from lands which the brethren of that monastery cultivate at their own expense in the monastery or its cells.

We forbid anyone to presume to subject the people living in those holdings to excommunication or interdict, or to summon the clerics of the monastery or of its holdings to a synod. We grant and bestow upon the abbot of that monastery full authority [Col. 1002B] and permission to convene a synod of both monks and other clerics dwelling in the monastery’s holdings. We strictly forbid any person to be placed over the abbot in administration, unless the abbot has been convicted of such crimes as ought to be punished under the censure of the sacred canons. We forbid any monk to be removed from that monastery against the abbot’s will in order to establish other monasteries.

Further, that the ardour of your devotion and desire may be more greatly enkindled, we grant to the abbot of the same monastery who is canonically established there, and to his successors, the use of the mitre, gloves, sandals, tunic, and dalmatic; the pastoral staff; and likewise the daily use of the ring. And we grant them full authority, after Mass and the other divine offices, to bless the people in the manner of a bishop [Col. 1002C].

The abbot and brethren of the aforesaid monastery and its cells may also receive, without the opposition of any bishop or other ecclesiastical person, and retain without anyone’s interference, clerics of every order or laypeople fleeing the secular world, free and absolved persons who come, whether healthy or sick, with their goods and possessions for conversion of life. It shall also be lawful, by our authority, for brethren placed in the cells of the aforesaid monastery in cities or other places to ring bells whenever they wish for the divine offices. No archbishop or bishop may presume to forbid the people of God to enter the aforesaid monastery or its cells [Col. 1002D] to hear the word of God, except under a general interdict of the whole city or parish.

We decree that burial in the monastery itself and in all its churches and cells shall be free, so that none may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict. Nor may any archbishop or bishop excommunicate or place under interdict anyone choosing burial in that monastery or its cells, or deny them penance or viaticum, save for manifest cause. We likewise have judged it proper to grant by apostolic authority that everyone canonically elected abbot of the aforesaid monastery may receive blessing from whichever archbishop or bishop he prefers [Col. 1003A]. If an abbot is accused or impeded in any matter, his case shall be handled, examined, and concluded, with the consent of you and your heirs, by ecclesiastical persons and discerning, suitable persons of the same kingdom.

Furthermore, we establish by apostolic authority that no archbishop, bishop, or other person may dare enter the monastic enclosure without the permission and will of the abbot or convent, or celebrate divine offices in that monastery or its churches without the permission of the abbot and convent and of the prelates of those churches. We likewise grant to the abbot of the aforesaid monastery that he may canonically regulate the monastery and its churches. Moreover, it shall be lawful for that abbot [Col. 1003B] to hear the confessions of all his clerics and laypeople, of whatever order or sex, and to judge all crimes and causes belonging to an ecclesiastical judge. The aforesaid abbot and his brethren shall also be free to construct oratories in any places of their holdings for their own use and that of their people.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away or diminish its possessions, harass it by any vexations, infringe this page of our constitution, or in any way oppose it. But should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 1003C] I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Balthasar, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and St Rufina, have subscribed. I, Gualterius, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, John, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, title of Pammachius, have subscribed. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St Anastasia, have subscribed. I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of St Peter in Chains, have subscribed. I, Boso, priest-cardinal of the title of St Susanna, have subscribed. I, Ardicio, deacon-cardinal of the title of St Theodore [Col. 1003D], have subscribed. I, Vitellus, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

Given at Ferentino through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of January, indiction eight, in the year 1174 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

The sign of Pope Alexander III:

[“Show me your ways, O Lord.”]

**MCLI. To Marsilius, abbot, and the brethren of Cara Insula, who “had transferred their monastery from two less suitable places to a most suitable place called Om,” he confirms those same two places.**

[Langebeck, *Scriptores rerum Danicarum*, V, 248.]

[Col. 1004A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Marsilius, abbot, and the brethren of Cara Insula: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

It has come to our hearing that, compelled by great necessity and reasonable cause, you transferred your monastery from two places less suitable for your order to a fitting and most suitable place called Om, with the counsel and consent of your own bishop and the favour of the king of the land. You therefore humbly and earnestly asked us [Col. 1004B] to confirm those two places to you and your monastery. Accordingly, since it is fitting that, considering your religious life and honour, we should graciously assent to your reasonable vows and desires and carefully consider in the Lord your welfare and advancement, we confirm by apostolic authority those aforesaid two places to you and your monastery, as you reasonably possess them, and protect them by the safeguard of this present writing.

We establish that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. But should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

**IN THE YEAR 1161–1175.**

[Col. 1004C]

**MCLII. To the Cistercian abbots and brethren established in England.—He forbids them to seek rights of patronage in churches or churches themselves. (Ferentino.)**

[Letters of Gilbert Foliot, ed. Giles, II, 106.]

ALEXANDER III, pope, to his beloved sons, the abbots and brethren of monasteries of the Cistercian Order established in England: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that, contrary to the ancient custom and institution of your order, you are striving to obtain by purchase and other means the right to present clerics to churches [Col. 1004D], so that under such a pretext you may be permitted to possess churches and hold them yourselves or through others. Since it is not fitting that, upon any occasion or pretext, you should depart from the ancient institutions of your fathers or do anything for which you may be reproved for the vice of greed, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you cease to acquire rights of patronage in churches or churches themselves. It is neither expedient for you nor are we willing to tolerate that you or your order should be disparaged under such a pretext. Indeed, we love you and your order so much that we in no way wish to encourage you in matters contrary to your religious life and honour; concerning you [Col. 1005A], we wish to hear nothing disadvantageous or adverse.

Given at Ferentino.

**MCLIII. For the prioress of Broburg, concerning ten pounds. (22 January.)**

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 821.]

On behalf of Helwidis, prioress of Broborg, we have received a complaint that, when her mother died, she had formerly bequeathed ten pounds to her by will and entrusted them to the prioress’s aunt to hold for her use; but the heirs of that aunt refuse to pay her the aforesaid money and instead presume unjustly to retain it. Since, moreover, by the office of the supreme apostolate which, although unworthy, we exercise through the disposition of divine providence, we are bound to render to each person his right, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to admonish the heirs of her aforesaid aunt and diligently compel them by ecclesiastical censure either to restore the aforesaid money to the said prioress without any objection or deduction, or, within forty days after receiving these letters, to render to her before you, without delay and without appeal, what is just in the matter. Thus she is not forced, contrary to the religious habit she has received, to be worn down by prolonged litigation, when she can obtain her right through you.

Given 22 January.

**MCLIV. To the bishop of Beauvais.—For A., dean of Châteauroux.**

[Ibid., col. 798.]

[Col. 1005C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother [Bartholomew], bishop of Beauvais: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son A., dean of Châteauroux, has informed us that, when he was seriously prosecuted concerning certain causes before our venerable brother the Archbishop of Reims, to whom an appeal had first been made from our brother the bishop of Châlons, he appealed thence to our hearing. Since, when the representative of the aforesaid dean was present before us, his adversaries neither came nor sent representatives on their behalf, we commit the aforesaid causes to your experience to be concluded definitively [Col. 1005D], without recourse to appeal. Therefore, by the authority of these present letters, we command your brotherhood that, when requested in this matter, you summon the parties before you, hear the same causes more carefully, and decide them, appeal set aside, with justice as mediator.

**MCLV. To G., bishop of Châlons.—For the cleric Milo, that he may be provided with a benefice.**

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 842.]

The office committed to you and the duty of charity require you to make useful provision for ecclesiastical persons, especially those who have not yet been able to obtain any benefice in the Church, and to provide them with suitable benefices. Therefore, commending to your discretion more earnestly Milo, a learned and, as we hear, honourable cleric, who is native to your diocese, we ask, command, and exhort your brotherhood through apostolic letters [Col. 1006A] that, out of reverence for St Peter and for us, in consideration of his worthiness, and also from the duty of your office, you provide the said Milo in some church sufficiently decently and honourably that he may have the necessities of life in adequate measure and faithfully serve almighty God in his order; thus we too shall be bound, not undeservedly, to commend your care in this matter.

**MCLVI. To Henry, Archbishop of Reims.—Concerning the absolution of a certain citizen M. of Châlons.**

[Ibid., col. 703.]

If we remember correctly, we entrusted to you the case of a certain woman named E., so that you might render her justice against those of whom she complains. Accordingly, when proceedings were brought against M., a citizen of Châlons, and you wished to compel him to answer the aforesaid woman in your presence, fearing injury he appealed to our hearing. Nevertheless, as he asserts to us, you proceeded in judgment, and, more seriously, after the appeal had been made, you declared him excommunicated. Since we do not clearly recall whether that case was delegated to you with appeal excluded or with the obstacle of appeal reserved, we will and command that, if you undertook to handle the said woman’s case with recourse to appeal reserved [Col. 1006C], then—because it did not become your prudence to excommunicate him or proceed in judgment after an appeal had intervened—you shall regard him as absolved. The case is to receive its due completion of justice before our venerable brother the bishop of Laon, to whom we have entrusted it. You shall also compel both the man and the woman to appear before that bishop’s tribunal and show him the letters we sent you concerning the same case, so that from them he may understand the truth of the matter more fully.

But if you undertook to determine the aforesaid woman’s case with appeal excluded, you shall nevertheless receive the oft-mentioned M. as absolved and, after giving him free opportunity to call witnesses and allege whatever he wishes on his own behalf, endeavour to end that controversy, with appeal excluded [Col. 1006D], by a canonical conclusion, so that neither party may henceforth be compelled to complain of a failure of justice. We also ask that, on his journey to and from, and while staying with you, you permit no injury to be inflicted upon him.

Given 13 March [the printed *Mergolii* is apparently *Martii*].

**MCLVII. To the same.—That he compel the canons of St Ursmar and of Antoing to dismiss all concubines; those below the order of subdeacon who have wives, to adhere to their wives; but those in that order and above, to adhere to their churches and dismiss their wives.**

[Ibid., col. 794.]

It has come to us that the canons of St Ursmar and of Antoing [Col. 1007A], who are known to be subject to the prelate of the Church of Lobbes, live scandalously and dissolutely, presume to keep concubines in their own dwellings, and that some of them, as we have heard, have contracted marriages. Since this is known altogether to conflict with the institutions of the holy Fathers—so that those who ought to offer others an example of goodness, by living badly provoke them to unlawful acts through depraved deeds—we command your discretion by apostolic letters that you strictly compel all who are known to keep concubines either to relinquish their ecclesiastical benefices or to dismiss those women entirely. Those who are below the order of subdeacon and have wives, you shall cause to adhere to their wives and to be wholly deprived of ecclesiastical benefices. But if they have been promoted to the subdiaconate [Col. 1007B] or a higher order and have dared to take any woman into cohabitation, you shall compel them with every strictness to withdraw entirely from such union and faithfully serve almighty God in their churches.

Furthermore, Lambert, cleric and canon of St Ursmar, who, by unjustly harassing our beloved son [Note: [Col. 1007D] John, who succeeded Franco in 1159 and presided for twenty years, namely until 1179, when he resigned the abbacy.] J., abbot of the Church of Lobbes, appealed to our hearing . . .

**MCLVIII. To the same.—For Matthew, citizen of Châlons.**

[Ibid., col. 817.]

By these present letters we wish to make known to your brotherhood that our dearest son in Christ, Louis, illustrious king of the French, your brother, has quite affectionately asked us on behalf of M., a citizen of Châlons [Col. 1007C], that at the intercession of his love and prayers we absolve him from the bond of excommunication, with which, it is said, you bound him for no other reason than because he appealed to our hearing. Your discretion ought not in any way to be ignorant how fitting it is for both us and you to show deference to the said king and, where we can do so with God and justice, to grant his petition. For as a most Christian king, he shows St Peter in our person great devotion and reverence and frequently [variant: fervently] promotes the honour and exaltation of the Church and of us. There is no doubt that very many benefits have proceeded, and continually proceed [Col. 1007D], to that Church from his devotion. It is therefore fitting that we make due return to him, and that we should not be reluctant, at his request, to do whatever we would ever have done for anyone.

Accordingly, we admonish and command your prudence that, out of regard for the said king and in fulfilment of our command, you absolve from the sentence by which he is bound the aforesaid M.—whom we send back to you for this purpose, because we entrusted his case to your care for determination with appeal excluded—setting aside pretexts; and that you demand nothing from him in any way for his absolution. Nevertheless, have him furnish sufficient security [Col. 1008A] that, in the case between him and the woman of Herdes, he will abide by the judgment already given or yet to be given by you. If, moreover, in pronouncing judgment something less than complete or improper occurred, we will and command that you endeavour to correct it more fully according to judicial procedure.

**MCLIX. To the same.—That he hear and determine the case between M. and A., if the custom of the land permits it; otherwise, that he refer it to a secular judge.**

[Ibid., col. 841.]

We commit to your experience for hearing and due determination the case known to be contested between Martin and Adam concerning a certain vineyard, which the said M. claims by reason of his wife’s cousin. [Col. 1008B] Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, when requested in this matter, you summon both parties before you and, having fully heard and examined the arguments on either side, decide the same case, appeal set aside, with justice as mediator, if the custom of the land permits it to be determined before an ecclesiastical judge. Otherwise, refer it to the secular judge to whom it belongs.

**MCLX. To the same.—For the abbot and brethren of Sarnai.**

[Ibid., col. 850.]

From the complaint transmitted to us by the religious men, the abbot and brethren of Sarnai [Note: [Col. 1008D] Commonly called Vallis Sarnaii, of the Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Paris.], it has come to our attention [Col. 1008C] that the woman Rossa and Phy. of Castris violently took from them a certain vineyard, which they refuse to restore. Since it especially belongs to our office to defend the rights of all, and particularly of religious men more strictly dedicated to divine service, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and compel the said woman and her son either to restore the aforesaid vineyard without disturbance or difficulty to the said brethren and leave them in peace, or, within forty days after receiving these letters, to render them full justice concerning it before your tribunal, with appeal excluded. If they do neither, compel them by ecclesiastical censure, all appeal set aside, until one or the other has been carried out [Col. 1008D].

**MCLXI. To the same.—That authority be given at Valenciennes to the hospital for the poor to build a church, and that ecclesiastical men not be judged by secular persons.**

[Ibid., col. 868.]

The matter has been brought to our attention that a certain hospital at Valenciennes was long ago established for the aid and reception of Christ’s poor, where many works of charity are continually provided for the sick and needy. But since there is no church there in which the sick and the brethren residing there may hear the divine offices [Col. 1009A], or in which the dead may be buried, the bodies of those who die are carried elsewhere, not without expense. Therefore, because we have been earnestly petitioned to provide for this religious house in this respect, moved by mercy and likewise inclined by the obligation of our office, we admonish and command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the matter stands thus, you urgently admonish and induce the canons of the Church of Cambrai to grant the brethren of the aforesaid place free permission to build there an oratory and cemetery, after receiving from them sufficient security that they will not presume to receive parishioners of other churches either for the daily offices or for burial.

Moreover, because it has been reported to us that in the aforesaid town of Valenciennes [Col. 1009B] there are ecclesiastical men who possess no ecclesiastical benefices and who are judged by secular persons as though they were laymen, without considering how thereby Almighty God is offended and the liberty of the churches suffers harm, we nevertheless command your discretion that you permit no ecclesiastical man in your province to be judged by secular persons, restraining by our authority and your own those who have presumed to summon clerics before a secular court.

### MCLXII. To the same and to the abbot of Jouy.—On behalf of J., a poor man and priest, formerly a novice in the monastery of Jouy.

*(Ibid., col. 945.)*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Reims, and to his beloved son, the abbot of Jouy: greeting and apostolic blessing.

J., a poor priest and chaplain of our beloved sons, the sick brethren of Tours-sur-Marne, came before the clemency of the Apostolic See and set forth to us in a humble petition that, formerly, in his childhood, he remained for two months on probation in the novices’ cell of the monastery of Jouy.

> [Note: [Col. 1009D] Jouy is a monastery of the Cistercian order in the diocese of Sens.]

But, suffering from a serious illness of the head, he freely left that monastery with the permission of the abbot of that place. Thereafter, advancing through the several orders, he was ordained priest and joined the aforesaid house of the sick. Now, however, certain persons wishing to trouble him assert that, because he departed from the aforementioned monastery, he is excommunicated [Col. 1009D] and ought to be removed from orders.

> [Note: [Col. 1009D] From this passage it is clear that novices who voluntarily departed through their own fault during the period of probation, even before it had been completed, were formerly regarded as apostates. For this novice, though he left after two months because of illness and with the abbot’s blessing, could scarcely escape the stigma of excommunication—a point which I could establish by other examples.]

Therefore, since not all contend with equal strength in the tabernacle of the Lord, and he who cannot remain upon the mountain should descend into the valley so that he may be saved there, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you declare that the aforesaid priest is free from their accusation and ought to continue in holy orders; provided, however, that he serve the aforesaid sick brethren perpetually according to the vow he made, lest, with Lot’s wife, he look back—she who, because she looked back, is known to have been turned into a pillar of salt [Col. 1010A].

### MCLXIII. To …—On behalf of F., a cleric, that a prebend be restored to him.

*(Ibid., col. 806.)*

On behalf of our son F., bearer of the present letters, we long ago requested you very earnestly that you ought to grant and generously assign him one prebend in the church of Saint Stephen or in the church of Blessed Mary of the Valleys. We further wrote that you, brother bishop, should ordain him a cleric and should thereafter not delay to institute him as a canon of one of the churches just mentioned. But you, as you are accustomed to do, have passed over our requests in this matter with deaf ears [Col. 1010B], and have taken no care to provide for the aforesaid F. in any respect.

Since it is unworthy that men who have long devoted themselves to scholarly disciplines should possess no benefice from which they may suitably obtain the necessities of life, by repeated letters we ask, admonish, and, in asking, command all of you that, for the love of God, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, and in consideration of his worthiness, you take care to give and assign to the said F. the first prebend that becomes vacant in either of the aforesaid churches after that which we ordered to be assigned to our beloved son, the abbot of Clairvaux.

> [Note: [Col. 1010D] Clairvaux, a monastery of the Cistercian order in the diocese of Sens, founded in 1127 by Artaldus, abbot of Preuilly.]

Thus at least on this occasion may he find that our requests and command have benefited him in some measure; and may we be bound to render you abundant thanks for accepting our requests [Col. 1010C], and to advance your petitions more readily. You, brother bishop, should diligently tonsure and ordain him a cleric, as we commanded you on another occasion; and, once ordained, assign him to one of the aforesaid churches. Bring this about so that he is not compelled to return to us again, for that would be exceedingly burdensome and altogether troublesome to us.

### MCLXIV. To the abbot of Corbie.—Concerning the right of the archbishop of Reims in the borough adjoining the monastery of Corbie.

*(Ibid., col. 924.)*

Our venerable brother, the archbishop of Reims, has shown us by a report sent to us that the borough adjoining your monastery is subject to him and to his church in spiritual matters as well as temporal [Col. 1010D], and that the men of that place have customarily appealed to his church in ecclesiastical causes. Yet you, contrary to ancient custom and to the rights of that church, have obtained from the Apostolic See a rescript concerning this matter and have seriously impaired the right and dignity of that church.

Since we wish and ought to preserve your rights in such a way that we in no respect diminish what belongs by right to the archbishop and his church, we command and enjoin your belovedness by apostolic letters [Col. 1011A] that, if for the preceding forty years the predecessors of the aforesaid archbishop and his church have possessed episcopal jurisdiction in the town of your monastery, you shall in no way withdraw it from him under pretext of any privilege or writing obtained from us, nor presume in this respect to derogate from his dignity. For we cannot or ought not, because of the special favor which we have toward your monastery, to deprive the aforesaid archbishop of his dignity or right.

Nevertheless, if you are able to defend yourself by lawful prescription or by the privileges of our predecessors, you shall pursue the matter judicially in the presence of our venerable brother, the archbishop of Bourges, together with that archbishop; and you shall strive to protect the liberty of your monastery by reasonable moderation.

## Year 1164–1175

[Col. 1011B]

### MCLXV.

*(Ibid., col. 842.)* To the bishop of Châlons.—That his priests may not demand money for the baptism of infants or for the burial of the dead.

*(Ibid., col. 842.)*

It has come to us that the chaplains of your city demand payment for the baptism of infants and for the burial of the dead, and refuse, for any reason, to administer the sacrament of regeneration to those to be baptized or the benefit of burial to the deceased unless a sum of money is paid to them. Since this is judged utterly detestable in the sight of God [Col. 1011C] and before men, and is wholly contrary to our decree issued long ago at the Council of Tours—

> [Note: [Col. 1011] In 1163 the Council of Tours was held, whose canon 6 forbids any charge to be demanded for the burial of the dead.]

—we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you wholly restrain all priests of your diocese from such wicked presumption, and that, lest this be done hereafter, you publicly forbid it in every parish in our name and your own, under penalty of deprivation of office. Against those found to have received money in such a case, you should endeavor to punish the ardor of so great a greed, not by a monetary penalty but by a spiritual one so severe that others, hearing of it, may deservedly be terrified of like conduct.

### MCLXVI. To Theobald, bishop of Amiens.—On behalf of John Aculeus against his stepmother: that he hear and decide the case between them.

*(Ibid., col. 836.)*

[Col. 1011D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother T[HEOBALD], bishop of Amiens: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We remember that we formerly committed to our venerable brother Hu., bishop of Soissons, the case long known to be in dispute between John, canon of the Church of Laon, and Hel., his stepmother, concerning the inheritance and other property belonging to the share of the same J. Since the said woman [Col. 1012A], although she made an amicable settlement with the aforesaid J. and confirmed it by the giving of her pledge, afterwards presumed to withdraw from it contrary to her pledged faith, the same J. appealed to our hearing. The woman, moreover, caused his house to be broken into by force by her accomplices, and caused whatever could be found there to be carried away.

Since there would be no end to lawsuits if it were permissible to depart from settlements made in good faith, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that you investigate the truth of the matter; and, if it is established that this is so, cause the aforesaid settlement to be firmly observed and carried into execution by both parties, all contradiction and appeal removed. Those things which are found to have been taken from the aforesaid J. or his sister after the appeal was made to us [Col. 1012B], you shall, relying on our authority, restore to them before hearing the principal case, with delay and appeal set aside; and you shall order suitable satisfaction to be made to him for the damages inflicted and for those who broke into his house.

If the aforementioned woman does not otherwise obey you, strike her and her sureties with sentence of excommunication, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal, and cause that sentence to be observed by all without resistance until due satisfaction has been made. Carefully carry out all these matters within twenty days after receipt of these letters.

### MCLXVII. To Henry, archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of Theobald against Guy of Appia.

*(Ibid., col. 866.)*

[Col. 1012C]

On behalf of Theobald, your parishioner, we have heard a sufficiently grave and pitiable complaint: though he is a man of Saint Remigius, Guy of Appia rashly seized him after summoning him to himself under a pledge of good faith, bound both his hands and neck with iron chains, and wickedly committed him to prison. When the said Guy was asked by certain friends and kinsmen of the aforesaid T. to release and discharge that same T., he utterly refused; indeed, he fiercely threatened him with hanging.

Terrified by fear of so atrocious a penalty, he redeemed himself by giving sureties, for fifteen pounds. Of this sum, after pledging his land as security, he paid eleven pounds, eight shillings, and a half [Col. 1012D]. For the remainder he is being grievously pressed before N., procurator of your archdeacon. Since we neither ought nor can leave unpunished the savagery of such tyranny and the excess of so unjust a presumption, lest others be encouraged to similar acts by its impunity, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, within forty days after receipt of these letters, you diligently investigate the matter. If you find it to be so, diligently admonish the aforesaid wrongdoer and compel him under constraint of anathema to repay without diminution to the said T. everything he extorted from him through such tyranny and oppression [Col. 1013A], make suitable satisfaction for the injuries inflicted, and entirely release his sureties from that suretyship and himself from any oath by which he may be bound to you on that account.

We do not wish you to commit this case, or other grave and difficult matters to be carried out, to the said N.; rather, carry them out yourself with diligence, lest perhaps there happen to you concerning the said N.—God forbid—what we have heard happened to the bishop of Noyon of blessed memory concerning Drogo.

## Year 1175

### MCLXVIII. He confirms to the nunnery of Saint Mary at Palermo certain tithes bestowed by Tustinus, bishop of Mazara.

[Col. 1013B]

Given at Florence [read: Ferentino], on the Kalends of February (1 February), in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1174, in the sixteenth year of his pontificate.

*(PIRRI, Sicilia sacra, II, 844.)*

### MCLXIX. He takes the monastery of Vallis Christiana under protection and confirms its possessions and rights.  
*(Ferentino, 14 February.)*

*[Hugo, Annals of the Premonstratensian Order, II, 631.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BARTHOLOMEW, abbot of Vallis Christiana, and his brethren, present and future, professing the religious life: in perpetuity.

It is fitting that apostolic protection [Col. 1013C] be present for those who choose the religious life, etc. First, we establish that the canonical order, known to have been instituted in that place according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the Premonstratensian brethren, shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods, etc., among which we have thought certain matters should be specifically noted:

The place itself on which the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances: lands, vineyards, gardens, meadows, pastures, waters, watercourses, mills, granges, and their appurtenances. We also decree that the burial-ground of the place shall be free, so that none may oppose the devotion and last will [Col. 1013D] of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving, nevertheless, the right of the mother church.

No one may presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, nor on the sustenance of your animals. You may receive into your conversion clerics or laymen who are free and absolved, fleeing the world, and retain them in your community without anyone’s opposition. In your parish churches, after the death of the priests who hold them, you may appoint four, or at least three, of your canons, one of whom shall be presented to the diocesan bishop to receive from him the care of souls. He shall answer to the bishop in spiritual matters [Col. 1014A], but to you in temporal matters.

Further, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your house, to leave that cloister without permission of his abbot; and no one may dare retain a brother who has departed without the security of letters from the community, unless he wishes to transfer to a stricter religious order. Upon the death of yourself, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be appointed there through any artifice of deceit or violence, save the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine.

Moreover, when a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may, with doors closed, excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, bells not rung [Col. 1014B], celebrate the divine offices in a low voice.

We therefore decree, etc., without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore, etc.

Given at Ferentino, by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1175 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

### MCLXX. To Peter, cardinal-priest of Saint Chrysogonus, legate of the Apostolic See.—That those who killed the bishop-elect of Cambrai be publicly declared excommunicated.  
*(Ferentino, 11 March.)*

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 969.]*

[Col. 1014C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Not without great sorrow and bitterness of heart have we heard of the horrible and detestable crime lately perpetrated by diabolical daring in the killing of R., bishop-elect of Cambrai, of good memory. Since we ought not to leave so great and grave an outrage uninvestigated or unpunished, but ought rather to employ every diligence and care in judging it, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters [Col. 1014D] that you diligently admonish and induce our venerable brethren, the archbishop of Reims and his suffragans, to do as we commanded them: publicly declare excommunicated, with lighted candles, those who so cruelly killed the aforesaid bishop-elect or caused him to be killed, and likewise those who assisted in killing or capturing him; and cause this to be announced in every church of their bishoprics, until they make worthy satisfaction to God and the Church for so great and grave an offense and present themselves before the apostolic presence with their letters.

But if they perhaps refuse or delay to do this, then you, having summoned the suffragan bishops of the Church of Reims and other ecclesiastical persons of that province, shall, publicly and with appeal set aside, declare excommunicated with lighted candles [Col. 1015A] those whom we have named, until they come to the Apostolic See with your letters in order to make satisfaction.

Given at Ferentino, on the sixth day before the Ides of March.

### MCLXXI. He confirms the privileges and rights of the monastery of Saint Stephen of Bañolas.  
*(Ferentino, 13 March.)*

*[AGUIRRE, Collection of Spanish Councils, III, 388.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons RAYMOND, abbot of the monastery of Saint Stephen of Bañolas, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Apostolic protection ought to be present for those choosing the religious life, lest an assault of anyone’s rashness [Col. 1015B] either draw them back from their purpose or—God forbid!—weaken the strength of holy religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, fortifying it by the privilege of this present document.

First, we establish that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s favor, acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the gift of kings or princes, the offering of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among them we have thought it fitting to set out the following by their proper names:

The parish surrounding the monastery itself in the valley of Bañolas; the churches of Saint Mary, Saint Benedict, Saint Peter of Agemal, Saint Romanus of Millanicis with its cemetery, Saint Christopher, and Saint James, with their tithes and first-fruits and with half the tithes or first-fruits of the village of Figeroles and of the Hermitages; the churches of Saint Mary and Saint Lawrence at Porqueres, with its cemetery; the churches of Saint Maurice of Calvis, Saint Cyricus, Saint Julian of Meritatz [Col. 1015D], and Saint Martin of Campo Majori.

In the valley of Miliarias: the churches of Saint Peter, Saint Andrew of Ramils, Saint Vincent of Felegoso, Saint Vincent of Saliente, Saint Julian of Augustino, Saint Mary of the village of Azert, and Saint Martial of Quarantella; the cell of Saint Mary of the stream of Azar, with tithes, offerings, and all their other appurtenances. In the county of Empúries: the cells of Holy Cross and Saint Nicholas, with their cemeteries and freeholds, and the castle of Calepodium with its appurtenances. In the county of Petra Latensis: the churches of Saint Martin and Saint Silverius. At Villamala: the cell of Saint John of Crosis; the cell of Saint Cyprian of Pinta, with tithes, offerings, and all their other appurtenances. In the county of Girona: the churches of Saint Mary [Col. 1016A] of Fenestris and Saint Felix of Buada, with tithes, offerings, and all their other appurtenances. In the county of Barcelona: the monastery of Saint Martial of Monte Signi; at Tarilano, the church of Saint Saviour. We also confirm to you and your successors the market customarily held by your monastery, the toll, and all jurisdiction.
