Further, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone, apart from the will of yourselves and the abbot for the time being, to dare subject your lay brethren (*conversi*) to secular judgment or power. Upon the death of yourself, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be appointed there by any artifice of deceit or violence, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel [Col. 1016B], shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordination of the clerics of your house and of monks to be advanced to sacred orders, from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, as this has been granted to your monastery by certain of our predecessors and observed by your fellow-provincial bishops.

We further add that no bishop may place the cloister itself or those serving the Lord there under interdict or excommunication without a hearing before the Roman pontiff or his legate, nor inflict upon the other places belonging to you a penalty of canonical censure without definite cause. We forbid public masses to be celebrated in that monastery by a bishop without the consent of the abbot and brethren [Col. 1016C], or stations to be held there, or popular assemblies gathered for hearing cases, lest the retreats of God’s servants provide any occasion for popular gatherings.

We likewise establish that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We therefore decree, etc.

Given at Ferentino, by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Ides of March [Col. 1016D], in the eighth indiction, in the year 1174 of the Lord’s Incarnation (perhaps 1175), and in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Alexander III.

### MCLXXII. To Conrad, archbishop of Mainz.—On behalf of the community of Lunelac.  
*(Ferentino, 21 March.)*

*[JAFFÉ, Registers of the Roman Pontiffs, p. 762.]*

To C[ONRAD], archbishop of Mainz and legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the transmitted complaint of the abbot and community of the monastery of Lunelac, we have learned that [Theobald], bishop of Passau, has unjustly taken from them certain churches which they assert that they have possessed for a long time and presumptuously holds them by force. [Col. 1017A] Since we are bound to uphold the rights of all God’s faithful, and especially of religious men, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters urgently to admonish the said bishop and compel him by canonical constraint, without delay or excuse, either to restore the aforesaid churches to the said abbot and brethren and thereafter leave them to possess them freely and peacefully, or not delay to render full justice in the matter before you.

Given at Ferentino [Ferentino], on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

### MCLXXIII. To R[ichard], archbishop of Canterbury.—He commands him, under pain of excommunication, to admonish the Hospitallers and Templars that, if they have buried persons who died excommunicated in church cemeteries, they must remove them.  
*(Ferentino, 23 March.)*

*[Letters of Gilbert Foliot, ed. GILES, II, 64.]*

[Col. 1017B]

ALEXANDER Pope III, to the archbishop of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the Lord’s disposition, we have been placed, although unworthy, in the see of the prince of the blessed apostles, in order that we may plant what belongs to the adornment of virtues and strive to uproot and eradicate what is contrary to reason and impedes perfect salvation. We have learned that the Hospitallers and Templars presume, contrary to the prohibition of bishops, to grant ecclesiastical burial to persons expressly excommunicated, without considering how grave it is to communicate in death with those whom the Church, while they lived, separated from her bosom [Col. 1017C] for their offenses.

Therefore, because we neither wish nor ought in any way to tolerate such presumption and rashness, brother, we command you by apostolic letters to admonish and exhort the aforesaid brethren, and command them in our name, that if they have buried in church cemeteries any persons who died excommunicated, they must remove them entirely from those cemeteries. If they refuse, you yourself shall carry this out, by our authority and with the obstacle of appeal removed, in the case of those whom you ascertain to have died excommunicated.

Moreover, concerning those who swear that they will stand by the command of the Church and afterwards, having sworn the oath [Col. 1017D], appeal: let your diligence ensure that you compel them either to observe what they swear or, within forty days after lodging the appeal, to set out in order to prosecute it.

Given at Ferentino, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April.

### MCLXXIV. To W., bishop-elect of Lucca.—That a church usurped by him be restored to the canons of Lucca.  
*(Ferentino, 25 March.)*

*[BALUZE, Miscellanies, ed. Mansi, I, 432.]*

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons W[ILLIAM], bishop-elect, and the canons of Lucca: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having heard how B., formerly provost of Saint George, contrary to the order of propriety and at peril to his soul [Col. 1018A], purchased the church of Saint Matthew of Fossa Natali from the abbot of Monteverde for forty pounds, and how, when he entered upon that bargain at the devil’s prompting, we commanded R., the provost, and the monks of Saint George by a mandatory order to relinquish the said church with all the above-described goods, all excuse and pretext ceasing, and not attempt in any way to interfere with it. For just as our predecessor of good memory, Pope Adrian, when the case was brought before his hearing, annulled this bargain, contrary to the canons, with the common counsel of the brethren, so we too subsequently took care to annul the same contract.

But because, as we have learned, the said provost and monks obstinately resist our command [Col. 1018B] … and you hold by force the aforesaid church and its goods, which you have occupied, we—unwilling to leave unpunished, or in any way tolerate, the audacity of so great a presumption, namely that what was acquired simoniacally should be held in this manner—command and enjoin you by apostolic letters that, if the said provost and monks should perhaps refuse, upon your admonition, to relinquish the aforementioned church with its property, you shall take it by our authority and remove it from them entirely, appeal set aside. If they presume to inflict any violence in this matter, you shall prohibit the celebration of divine offices in their church.

Given at Ferentino, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

### MCLXXV. He commands R., provost, and all the monks of Saint George to relinquish the church of Saint Matthew of Fossa Natali within forty days. He refers to the preceding letter to the bishop-elect of Lucca.  
*(Ferentino, 25 March.)*

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 1081.]*

[Col. 1018C]

Having learned and established that B., your former provost, contrary to the order of propriety and at peril to his soul, bought the church of Saint Matthew of Fossa Natali from the abbot of Monteverde for forty pounds of oil, and further entered into this bargain at the devil’s prompting, we annulled the contract, as it had been annulled by our predecessor of good memory, Pope Adrian. By apostolic letters [Col. 1018D] we commanded you to relinquish that church with all its goods, all pretext and excuse ceasing, and never again presume to interfere with it.

But you, as we have learned, presumptuously retain the aforesaid church … in every way … and to the peril of your souls, and are not afraid in this respect to oppose the divine commands. Therefore, unless the customary clemency of the Apostolic See restrained the movement of our mind, we would punish you so harshly that the penalty itself would teach you how dangerous it is to oppose apostolic commands. Yet, lest we be compelled to punish your disobedience and contumacy with severe correction, … we command and enjoin you by these present letters that, within fifteen days after receipt of these letters [Col. 1019A], setting aside pretext and appeal, you relinquish the aforesaid church with all the above-described goods and presume no longer to interfere with it.

If you decide to persist in your presumption and disobedience, we command our beloved sons, the bishop-elect and canons of Lucca, by our letters, that they enter that church by our authority and in no way delay to take it from you. And if you inflict violence upon them in this matter, they shall prohibit the celebration of divine offices in your church.

Given at Ferentino, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

### MCLXXVI. He takes the abbey of Majella under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges.  
*(Ferentino, 28 March.)*

*[Vatican Bullarium, I, 62.]*

[Col. 1019B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons TRANSMUNDUS, abbot of the hermitage of Majella, and his brethren, present and future, professing the eremitic life: in perpetuity.

The authority of the Apostolic See, which by the Lord’s bounty we serve, and the unity of fraternal charity exhort us to assent to the just desires of religious persons and graciously to grant their reasonable requests. Therefore, beloved son Transmundus, abbot, we graciously assent to your just requests; and, following the footsteps of our predecessors of holy memory [Col. 1019C], Paschal, Eugenius, and Adrian, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the church of Saint Saviour, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document.

We establish that the hermitage in which you dwell shall remain free from every right and power, and that you may enjoy complete tranquility in the Lord’s service. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s favor, acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

[Col. 1019D] The church of Saint Saviour of Angre Castellare, with the adjoining height of Cefalia; the church of Saint Martin at Ranclano, with its dependent cells; the church of Saint Pancras, with its cells; the altar of Pinna, with the adjoining height of Fameclano; the church of Saint Mary of Lavella, with its cells; the church of Saint Angel and Saint Peter of the castle of Larome; the church of Saint [Col. 1020A] Clement, with its cells; the monastery of Saint Andrew, with its cells; the church of Saint Blaise; the church of Saint Agatha; the church of Saint Procopius; the church of Saint Nicholas; the church of Saint Helena of the castle of Saint Angel in Trifinio, and there the villeins, together with landed and vineyard possessions.

Likewise, at Fara, the villeins, mills, and landed and vineyard possessions, and the church of Saint Cantiana. At Vacrum, the church of Saint Agatha and the church of Saint Nicholas, with its lands, vineyards, and possessions. At Praetorum, the church of Saint Candida, the church of Saint Nicholas, the villeins, mills, and landed and vineyard possessions. At Castellione, the church of Saint Justa and Saint Agnes, with villeins, lands, and vineyards. At Buccanicum, the church of Saint [Col. 1020B] Mary of Mirabello, the church of Saint Mary of Bassano, the church of Saint James, and the church of Saint Blaise. [Note: [Col. 1019D] For this church of Saint Blaise, consult the notes to the bull of Eugenius III (*Patrologia*, vol. CLXXX, col. 1444). We add only this: that this chapel, situated outside the walls of Becclari by Conrad in the oft-mentioned manuscript under letter D, fol. 38, in the year 1144, came under the jurisdiction of the abbey of Majella through the gift of Martilius, son of Robert.] The villeins, mills, and landed and vineyard possessions.

At Manoppello, the church of Saint Giles. [Note: [Col. 1019D] Alexander names the church of Saint Giles situated in the territory of Monopelli, which lies within the diocese of Chieti; the preceding pontiffs Adrian and Eugenius omit it. The new enumeration of churches must be explained by their new and recent acquisition. Roamundus, count of Monopelli, granted this church to the abbey of Majella in 1164. This date, later than the time of Eugenius and Adrian, falls within the pontificate of Alexander III. It is therefore no wonder that Alexander’s later bull is richer in the number of churches.] At Saint Vitus, the monastery of Saint Angel, with cells, villeins, mills, lands, and vineyards; at Pollotri, the monastery of Saint Barbat, with cells, villeins, lands, and vineyards. At Gipsum de Domo, the church of Saint Mary, with villeins, lands, and vineyards, and the church of Saint Mary of Caldarari, with its cells. At Monte Morisco, the church of Saint Helena. At Atessa, the church of Saint Juliana. At Casule, the estate called Colle-Milonis, with its appurtenances; one hospital [Col. 1020C] at Plazzano. At Septem, the church of Saint Pastor and one hospital; at Lauzanum, one hospital; at Rocca Morici, the church of Saint Mary and Saint Nicholas; at Ursonia, the church of Saint Martin; at Ilice, the church of Saint Angel, with its cells, villeins, lands, and vineyards; on the bank of the Corvaria, the church of Saint Victorinus, with lands and vineyards.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of your clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders, from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic and is willing to supply these things freely and without any improper charge. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, may grant what is requested.

[Col. 1020D] Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of intrigue or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict; he shall come to the Apostolic See to receive blessing.

[Col. 1021A] Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid hermitage, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it in any manner; rather, all things shall be preserved unimpaired and entire, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you and your successors shall pay one gold piece annually to us and to our successors. If, therefore, anyone in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, [Col. 1021B] have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius, have subscribed. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, have subscribed. I, Boso, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore, have subscribed. I, Cynthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, have subscribed. I, Vitellus, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

Given at Ferentino through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April [28 March], in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1021C] 1175, and in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

## 1177. To the bishops of Penne and Valva.—That they are to declare the clerics of Castellione excommunicated.  
*(Ferentino, 2 April.)*

[MURATORI, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, II, II, 908.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the bishops of Penne and Valva: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been made known to us on behalf of our beloved son Leonatus, abbot of Saint Clement of Pescara, that, when he had pronounced a sentence of interdict against his clerics of Castellione because of their offences, they nevertheless presumed, [Col. 1021D] after the sentence of interdict, to sing; therefore, since they had not ceased to celebrate the divine offices, he bound them with the bond of excommunication. Since an ecclesiastical sentence lawfully pronounced against offenders ought to remain valid and firm, we command and strictly direct your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you shall publicly declare the aforesaid clerics excommunicated throughout your bishoprics, with lighted candles, and shall cause all people carefully to avoid them as excommunicated persons, until they return to the command and obedience of the aforesaid abbot, make suitable satisfaction to him, and present themselves before the apostolic presence with your letters.

Given at Ferentino, on the fourth Nones of April [2 April].

## 1178. To the archbishops of Lyons and Bourges.—That they are to recognize Peter, cardinal of Saint Chrysogonus, as legate.  
*(Ferentino, 12 April.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 967.]

[Col. 1022A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren [GUICHARD], archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, and [GUARIN], archbishop of Bourges; to their suffragans; and to all clergy and people established in their bishoprics and in the bishopric of Le Puy: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The prudent judgment of your discernment is not unaware, as we believe, how we formerly appointed our beloved son [Col. 1022B] Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, as legate of the Apostolic See in the regions beyond the mountains, having weighed his integrity, prudence, and honourable character. We placed such hope and confidence in him that, through his solicitude and foresight, you too might, with the Lord as author, advance in wholesome institutions and the Church of God might receive welcome increase.

We therefore command and enjoin all of you that you take care to receive the aforesaid cardinal, as legate of the Apostolic See and as a prudent, industrious, and discerning man, most dear and acceptable to us, with due honour and reverence; that, when summoned by him, you come without any contradiction; and that in appeals [Col. 1022C] as well as in other matters you show him every reverence and obedience as legate of the Apostolic See, and reverently obey, as is fitting, his most salutary admonitions and commands. Thus may he himself, with the Lord’s aid, be of service to us, and may we render thanks to almighty God for the fruit of his legation.

Given at Ferentino, on the second Ides of April [12 April].

## 1179. He receives Otto, provost of Raitenbuch, under protection. He commands him to receive into the unity of the Church clerics in the German kingdom who renounce schism.  
*(Ferentino, 15 May.)*

[*Monumenta Boica*, VIII, 15.]

[Col. 1022D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son OTTO, provost of the church of Saint Mary at Raitenbuch: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to fulfilment the vows which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord Otto, provost, considering the devotion which you are known to have toward blessed Peter and ourselves, we receive you as a spiritual son of the most holy Roman Church, and the aforesaid church of Raitenbuch over which you preside, with all its appurtenances, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and confirm them by the safeguard of this present writing.

[Col. 1023A] We decree that, if any clerics of the German kingdom wish to renounce schism, during the continuance of this division you may, at your discretion and after suitable satisfaction has been made, receive them in our stead and recall them to the unity of mother Church and to our obedience. We further absolve both you and your aforesaid church, and the clerics of your other churches, from all obedience and fidelity owed to bishops who have withdrawn to the schismatic party, until they return to our obedience and reverence and to the unity of the Catholic Church. We also grant you free authority to withhold tithes or any ecclesiastical revenues from the priests and clerics of your villages who persist in schism, [Col. 1023B] until they come to their senses.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may unlawfully disturb your person or your church, or harass either by any molestations. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Ferentino, on the Ides of May [15 May].

## 1180. He confirms the bishopric of Ciudad Rodrigo, established by Fernando, king of the Spains. He pardons Bishop Peter for receiving consecration from the archbishop of Compostela without authorization from the Apostolic See.  
*(Ferentino, 25 May.—See ESCALONA, *Historia del real monasterio de Sahagun*, Madrid, 1782, folio, p. 549.)*

[Col. 1023C]

## 1181. To the archbishop of Vienne and the bishop of Clermont.—That, under penalty of excommunication, they compel Count Guigues of Forez to observe the settlement confirmed by the pope between him and the church of Lyons.  
*(Ferentino, May–June.)*

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 950.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren [ROBERT], archbishop of Vienne and legate of the Apostolic See, and [PONCE], bishop of Clermont: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We remember—and you have not forgotten, as we suppose—that the church of Lyons formerly suffered many persecutions, burdens, and losses of property at the hands of the noble Count of Forez [Guigues]. At length a certain exchange was made between that church and the count, and was confirmed by the solemnity of an oath; from this the same count now deceitfully seeks to withdraw.

Indeed, as has now been made known to us by another report also, the following settlement was concluded between them: neither party was to acquire anything by any means within the boundaries contained in the agreement, unless perhaps something there should be bestowed upon the church as alms. The same count further agreed that, in the churches granted to him, with all the others reserved to the said church, he would inflict no trouble or injury upon the priests or others [Col. 1024A] concerned. Yet, in violation of that settlement and the sanctity of his oath, he presumes to burden the priests and other possessors of those churches with grave and exorbitant exactions, and seeks to usurp those same churches with all their endowment for himself.

Although the settlement itself is less than honourable, we nevertheless confirmed it by apostolic authority for the sake of peace, fearing greatly that, if we wished to revoke it, more serious disadvantages and even dangers to persons might arise for the aforesaid Church. And now the aforesaid count maintains that the settlement was confirmed by us in order that he might invade the said churches and subject them to his own power. Since, therefore, it would better serve the reputation and salvation of that count to abandon what he retains in the settlement that is less than honourable, [Col. 1024B] than to stretch violent hands toward other things, and since we are unwilling to permit him with impunity to violate in himself the sanctity of his oath or to harass the aforesaid church by unlawful oppression, we command and strictly direct your brotherhood by apostolic letters to take care to admonish and diligently induce the aforesaid count to observe that settlement, as he confirmed it by oath, firm and inviolate, all contradiction and appeal being set aside; and, if he is known to have seized anything contrary to that settlement or extorted anything from priests or others, not to delay restoring it as soon as possible.

But if he refuses to comply with your admonitions, by our authority, and with recourse to appeal removed, prohibit throughout all his land the celebration of every divine office, except baptism for little children and penances for [Col. 1024C] the dying. If even then he does not repent, bind his person with the bond of anathema, and cause the sentence of both interdict and excommunication to be inviolably observed until suitable satisfaction has been made.

Given at Ferentino, on the fifth . . . of June.

## 1182. He commands archbishops and bishops to “compel all who are bound to give vows or other revenues to the Church of Compostela to pay the vows and revenues.”  
*(Ferentino, 30 June.—See FERRER, *Historia del apostol de Jesus Christo Sanct Iago*, Madrid, 1610, folio, p. 279.)*

## 1183. To the master of the military order of Saint James in Spain and his brethren.—He approves their institute.

[Col. 1024D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Peter FERDINAND, master of the military order of Saint James, and his brethren, clerical and lay, present and future, professing the common life: for perpetual remembrance.

Blessed is God in His gifts and holy in all His works: He continually makes His Church fruitful with new offspring; and, just as He causes sons to arise in it in place of fathers, so from generation to generation He spreads knowledge of His name and the light of Christian faith. Thus, as before sunrise the stars follow one another toward their setting in the firmament, so in the ranks of the Church the generations of the righteous may succeed one another through time, [Col. 1025A] before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes and the brightness of the true Sun illumines our darkness. And just as many are often cast down to earth by the dragon’s tail, so through the adoption of the Spirit may there daily be a restoration of the lost, and may many be raised from the depth of hell to seek heavenly things; and may bodies be kept on earth in such a way that, like fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household, people dwell in heaven in thought and desire.

We rejoice that this has been accomplished in our time by divine gift in the regions of Spain, where certain noble men, entangled in the bonds of sins but breathed upon [Col. 1025B] and touched by the grace from above through the mercy of Him who calls things that are not as though they were, have felt inward sorrow of heart for their many transgressions and have done penance for past sins. They have resolved to give not only their earthly possessions but also their bodies to every extreme danger for the Lord. Following the example of our Lord Jesus Christ, who said, “I have come not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 6), they have determined to live in the habit and manner of religious life under obedience to one master.

They have so moderated their purpose and order that, because the whole multitude of believers is divided into married and continent persons, and because the Lord Jesus Christ willed to be born not only for men but also for women from a woman and to dwell among humankind, [Col. 1025C] there shall be in this order those who lead a celibate life and follow the counsel of blessed Paul, who says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Corinthians 7). There shall also be those who, in accordance with the Lord’s institution, make use of their wives to beget offspring and avoid the precipice of incontinence, and who strive with them to pass from the valley of tears and earthly pilgrimage to the dwelling-place of the heavenly homeland, washing away their guilt by tears and works of mercy.

Though it falls to these, because of care for the flesh and affection for children, to build wood, hay, and straw upon their foundation, which is Christ, let others, more unencumbered and continent, build [Col. 1025D] gold, silver, and precious stones. Yet both groups shall serve one king and build one heavenly dwelling upon one foundation, strengthened by the Psalmist’s promise in the Lord—a promise that also comforts the lesser members of the Church—which says: “Your eyes saw my imperfection, and all shall be written in your book” (Psalm 138 [139]).

Among this fellowship of Christ’s faithful, you, beloved son in the Lord Peter Ferdinand, have by God’s will undertaken mastery and oversight over the others. Having come into our presence with certain of your brethren, you humbly requested, as was fitting, that the Apostolic See should receive you as its special sons under our protection, and should receive into the right and ownership of the most holy Roman Church the place in which the head of the order [Col. 1026A] has been established.

Accordingly, considering your devotion and good desire in the Lord, with the common counsel of our brethren we receive you as special and proper sons of the most holy Roman Church. Confirming your order by apostolic authority, we strengthen it by the privilege of the present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods you now justly and lawfully possess, or may in future acquire, with the Lord’s aid, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have considered it proper to specify [Col. 1026B] the following in their own terms. *(It enumerates some of their possessions.)*

It continues: Furthermore, we enact that no one may, on the ground of ancient possession or a written instrument, take away from you things held beyond human memory under the power of the Saracens and now acquired, or to be acquired in future with the Lord’s help, through the generosity of princes or by your own endeavour and labour. For since your one purpose and outstanding concern are always to contend for the defence of the Christian name, readily exposing not merely possessions but your very persons for the protection of your brethren, this pious work and praiseworthy undertaking could be greatly hindered if your labours and stipends, which benefit the community, [Col. 1026C] were snatched away by others, and idle and slothful persons—who in their labours seek not the things of Jesus Christ but their own—received those gains provided by such great labours for you and for the needs of Christ’s poor. As the Apostle says: “Whoever does not work shall not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3).

Among the things established to be observed in your profession of the order, the first is that you must live without private property under obedience to one master, in all humility and harmony. You have the example of those faithful who, converted to Christian faith by the preaching of the apostles, sold everything and laid the price at their feet; it was distributed to each according to need, and [Col. 1026D] none of those who possessed anything called it his own, but all things were common to them.

For the begetting of offspring to be reared in the fear of the Lord, and as a remedy for human frailty according to the Lord’s institution and the Apostle’s allowance, who says: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, let every man have his own wife, and likewise every woman her own husband” (1 Corinthians 7), whoever cannot remain continent may enter marriage and shall keep faith inviolate toward his wife, and the wife toward her husband, so that the continence of the marriage-bed may not be violated. But if the husbands have died and the widows who have entered the order wish to marry, this shall be reported to the master or commander, so that, with his permission, the woman herself may marry whomever she wishes, [Col. 1027A] only in the Lord. The same is to be understood as observed concerning men, for both are bound by one law.

We likewise establish that no brother or sister, after entering your order and promising obedience, may presume to return to the world or transfer to another order without the master’s permission, since there are appointed places in your order where each can live more strictly. No one may dare retain a person departing; rather, the person who has departed shall be compelled by ecclesiastical discipline to return to his or her order.

So that all matters in your order may be handled with greater deliberation, it has been established among you that a place shall be appointed where, each year [Col. 1027B] on the feast of All Saints, a general chapter shall be held. There shall be there a gathering of clerics and a prior who can care for them and for the other clerics belonging to your order, and who, when necessary, shall provide for the souls of the brethren. There shall also be thirteen brethren in the order who, when necessary, shall assist the master in counsel and in the administration of the house, and shall have due charge of electing the master.

When the master departs this life, the prior of the clerics shall take charge of the house and order. They shall obey him as the master of the order until the election of a master has been celebrated through the care of the aforesaid thirteen brethren. When he has heard and learned of the master’s death, he shall summon those thirteen brethren without [Col. 1027C] any delay. If any of them is unable to be present within fifty days because of illness or another reason, he shall, with the counsel of the others who are present, appoint another in the absentee’s place, so that the election of a master may not be delayed in the least by anyone’s absence.

If the master serving at the time appears harmful or useless, those thirteen brethren, with the counsel of the prior of the clerics and the sounder part of the chapter, shall have authority to correct him or even remove him. If disputes arise between him and the chapter, they shall bring them to due conclusion, lest the order decline or its temporal property be dissipated through outside judgments. Yet these brethren shall not be lifted up into any pride by this, but shall remain devoted and obedient to their master. If any of them dies, or is to be replaced because of fault or any other reason, the master, with the counsel of the greater part of those remaining, shall appoint another in his place.

At the chapter which, as we have said, is to be held annually, these thirteen brethren and the commanders of houses shall come without delay to the appointed place, unless an evident and grave necessity prevents them. Together they shall deliberate on what must be established for the advancement of the order, the salvation of souls, and the maintenance of bodies. Above all, they shall be exhorted to devote themselves to the defence of Christians and strictly commanded not to wage war against Saracens from love of worldly praise, desire to shed [Col. 1028A] blood, or covetousness for earthly things, but to aim only, in their fighting, either to protect Christians from Saracen attack or to induce the Saracens themselves to embrace the worship of the Christian faith.

Suitable visitors shall then also be elected to visit the houses of the brethren faithfully throughout the year; whatever they find there requiring correction they shall either correct themselves or refer to the general chapter for correction.

Moreover, the clerics of your order shall live together in villages and towns and remain obedient to the prior appointed over them. They shall instruct in literary learning the sons of brethren entrusted to them by the master, and shall provide the brethren with spiritual ministrations both in life and [Col. 1028B] in death. They shall wear surplices, maintain a community and cloister under their prior, and humbly do whatever he commands them according to God. Brethren whom the master judges suitable shall also live there; they shall not be idle, but shall devote themselves to prayer and other works of piety.

The brethren shall render tithes to the clerics from their labours and other goods granted by God, so that the clerics may provide books and suitable ornaments for the churches and make fitting provision for their bodily needs. If anything remains over, it shall be distributed to the uses of the poor according to the master’s direction.

So that concord and charity may be preserved among you, and all may abstain from the sin of detraction and murmuring, [Col. 1028C] every commander appointed in any place shall, according to the resources of the house, provide whatever is needed in health and illness with care and goodwill, so that he may appear neither stingy in resources nor bitter in speech.

Let the care of guests and the needy be your special concern, and let necessities be generously bestowed on them according to the resources of the house.

Let honour and reverence be shown to the prelates of churches. Let counsel and aid be supplied to Christ’s faithful—canons, monks, Templars, Hospitallers, and others devoted to the observance of holy religion. Let the need of any such person be relieved if resources permit, [Col. 1028D] so that God may be glorified in your works and those who see them may be drawn by the fragrance of your humility and charity.

In addition, we decree that, if any place in which there ought to be a bishop comes into your power, there shall be a bishop there, who, along with his churches and clergy, shall receive the revenues, possessions, and spiritual rights assigned to him. The remainder, however, shall pass to your use and remain under your administration without anyone’s objection. Certainly, in the parish churches which you possess, we do not wish bishops to be deprived of their rights. But if you build new churches in deserted places or in Saracen lands themselves, those churches shall enjoy full liberty and shall not be burdened by any exaction of tithes or other matter by bishops. You may govern those churches and their congregations through suitable clerics of your own; nor shall they be subject to an interdict or excommunication imposed by bishops. Rather, you may always celebrate divine offices in both the greater church that is the head of the order and the other churches, after excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons.

[Col. 1029A] Furthermore, lest you be diverted from the defence of Christians by human harassment and calumnies, we decree by apostolic authority that no one may presume to place your persons under interdict or excommunicate them, except a legate of the Apostolic See sent from the side of the Roman pontiff. We establish the same concerning your households and servants who receive your pay, so long as they are prepared to render justice—unless the offence is such that they incur ecclesiastical censure by the act itself.

You shall receive chrism and holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of your clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders, from the diocesan bishop, provided he is Catholic and has the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is bound to supply these things freely and without any improper charge. Otherwise, you may appeal to whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, may grant what is requested.

[Col. 1029B] Moreover, you may build oratories in your places where there are four brethren or more, in which only your brethren and households [Col. 1029C] may hear the divine office and have Christian burial. We wish to provide for your needs in such a way that neighbouring churches suffer no injury thereby. When, however, there is a general interdict of the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

Nevertheless, by the present decree we enact that, if anyone lays violent hands upon any one of you—that is, a brother or a sister—he shall be bound by a sentence of excommunication. The same provision shall be observed for your protection, both as to sentence and penalty, as is known to have been established by general council under Pope Innocent of happy memory, our predecessor, concerning the protection of clerics.

[Col. 1029D] We therefore decree that no person may rashly disturb your rights or possessions, take away your goods, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass you by any vexations. Rather, let all things be preserved unimpaired and entire, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See.

As a token of this favour received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay ten *malachini* annually to us and to our successors.

If, therefore, any secular or ecclesiastical person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should attempt to act against [Col. 1030A] it, after a second or third warning, unless he retracts his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all of you and all who preserve your rights may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

“SHOW ME YOUR WAYS, O LORD.”

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Walter, bishop of Galuam. [Col. 1030B] I, John, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, Boso, cardinal priest of Saint Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, Manfred, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Sabina. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Corditio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Cynthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Vitellus, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Laborans, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in [Col. 1030C] Portico. I, Rainerius, cardinal deacon of Saint Gregory at the Velabrum. I, Vivian, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

Given at Ferentino through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of July [5 July], in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1175, and in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

## 1184. He receives the monastery of Warivilla under protection and confirms its goods.  
*(Ferentino, 10 July.)*

[LOUVET, *Antiquités du Beauvoisis*, I, 624.]

[Col. 1030D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, MATHILDA, prioress of Warivilla, and her sisters, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

To prudent virgins who, having taken their lamps, strive to go forth to meet Christ through works of piety, the help of the Apostolic See ought to be afforded with all the more ready concern because, on account of the frailty of their sex and the purpose of their adopted religious life, they are known to be less able to defend greater interests. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

[Col. 1031A] We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly possesses, or may in future acquire, with the Lord’s aid, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and those who succeed you. Among these we have considered it proper to specify the following in their own terms:

The place in which your monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; and whatever the noblewoman Adelidis of Bullis, with the consent of her sons—namely Lancelin, Manasser, Renald, and Theobald—and of her daughters Beatrice, Mabilia, and Basilidis, as well as of certain successors, namely [Col. 1031B] William of Merlot and the brothers John and Robert of Conti, gave to that monastery; and whatever she lawfully granted it to possess—namely, everything which the aforesaid monastery may at any time acquire from the fief of the said castle by gift, purchase, or any other title whatsoever. Likewise, the chapel of St. Rimoldus, with the tithe pertaining to it, namely from the valley of St. Denis; likewise the tithe of Boissy and the tithe of Mézières, the tithe of Trussencourt; one modius of wheat annually at the mill of Montreuil, from the alms of Robert of Milly; also the house of William, son of Elias of Gerberoy, which is at Beauvais near the church of St. Peter; likewise the house of William Estivel, which is on the street of St. Lawrence.

[Col. 1031C] Moreover, no one shall presume to demand tithes from you on newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the fodder of your animals. When, however, a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. We likewise decree that the burial ground of that place shall be free; and no one shall oppose the devotion and last will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted, without prejudice, however, to the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We decree therefore, etc., without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop. If anyone therefore in the future, etc.

[Col. 1031D] Given at Ferentino by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth Ides of July [11 July], in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1175, in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCLXXXV. Confirms to the alms-house of St. Gervasius at Paris a house situated beside the atrium of St. Gervasius and an annual rent of four denarii. (Ferentino, 28 July.)

[Dom Félibien, *History of Paris*, vol. III, Documents, p. 66.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the procurator and brethren of the alms-house [Col. 1032A] of St. Gervasius at Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we grant ready assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to completion by effective action those requests which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and to your house the house situated beside the atrium of St. Gervasius, granted by pious benefaction to the same alms-house by Garin the mason; and the annual rent of four denarii, annually paid to the nobleman Robert, count of Brenne, and bestowed by that count upon your house in perpetual alms. We strengthen these possessions, as you reasonably possess them, by the protection of this present writing. [Col. 1032B]

We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way act contrary to it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Florence, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August [28 July].

MCLXXXVI. To Peter, cardinal of St. Chrysogonus, legate of the Apostolic See.—That the abbot of Quintiacus restore to the prior of Lanariacus the tithes which he took from him. (Ferentino, 2 August.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 968.]

[Col. 1032C] From the complaint of our beloved son P., prior of Lanariacus, we have learned that the abbot and monks of St. Benedict of Quintiacus have unjustly taken from him tithes from his fields and vineyards, and in consequence presume to harass him in many ways. Since, therefore, we must support each person in his right, and take especial care that religious men are not unjustly oppressed, we command your discretion by apostolic letters: admonish the aforesaid abbot and monks with all diligence and, if necessary, strictly compel them to restore to the said prior, without annoyance or difficulty, the aforesaid tithes; let them presume on no ground thereafter to exact them; or, setting aside appeal, let them render him full justice in your presence concerning this matter.

[Col. 1032D] Given at Ferentino, on the fourth Nones of August [2 August].

MCLXXXVII. Confirms the privileges granted to the canons of the church of Blessed Mary of Brescia. (Ferentino, 10 August.)

[Gradonici, *Pontificate of Brescia*, 216.]

. . . . . Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your successors all tithes arising both from possessions and from meadows within the boundaries of the parish district of Brescia, and all other tithes from newly cleared lands which are or shall hereafter be within those same boundaries; and especially those from Castenedulo and from the upper part of Campania—excepting those held by another church or ecclesiastical person, and those which religious men have brought, or have already brought, under cultivation—as Raymond, your former bishop of blessed memory, granted those tithes to you by prudent and reasonable provision. [Col. 1033A] Etc.

Given at Ferentino by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth Ides of August [10 August], in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1175, in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCLXXXVIII. To Peter, cardinal of St. Chrysogonus, legate of the Apostolic See.—That he cease to retain the church of Meaux. (Ferentino, 8 September.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 969.]

[Col. 1033B] The higher a place of dignity you have attained by the gift of divine favor, the more cautiously and circumspectly you ought to walk, and to present yourself in such a manner that people may find in you what they should follow, not what they should reproach. We have learned, however, that you still retain the church of Meaux and receive its revenues, so that, as the envoys of our venerable brother William, archbishop of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See, have reported to us, none of those revenues reaches him; and the canons of that church do not dare freely to hold an election. Therefore, since this greatly detracts from your reputation and standing and from the honor of the Church, and is imputed to excessive avarice, we admonish, counsel, and command your discretion: tell the archbishop [Col. 1033C] and canons not to refrain on your account from providing that church with a suitable person as bishop and pastor. In your acts and conduct, moreover, preserve such circumspection and moderation that you may thereby prove commendable in the sight of God and in the eyes of men, and that the Roman Church may receive an increase of honor and glory.

Given at Ferentino, on the sixth Ides of September [8 September].

MCLXXXIX. To Onuphrius, abbot of St. Saviour of Messina, of the Order of St. Basil.—Approves his institution. (Anagni, 19 October.)

[Ibidem, col. 1054.]

[Col. 1033D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ONUFRIUS, archimandrite of St. Saviour of Messina, and to his brethren, present and future.

By the authority of the Apostolic See, over which, though unworthy, we preside by the Lord’s providence, and by the obligation of our office, we are bound to love religious men with sincere charity and to fortify them by apostolic protection, lest the assault of any rash person either turn them away from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion.

Accordingly, favorably inclined by the prayers of our dearest son in Christ, William, illustrious king of Sicily, and graciously assenting to your petitions, [Col. 1034A] we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the monastic order, established in that monastery from ancient times according to God and the Rule of St. Basil, shall be observed there inviolate for ever.

Furthermore, whatever possessions, goods, obediences, and abbeys King Roger of revered memory granted to that monastery by his privilege, secured with a golden seal; and every honor, dignity, custom, and whatever else he bestowed upon you and your successors—as is more fully contained in his privilege—shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 1034B]

Among these we have thought fit to set out the following in their own terms. (It enumerates their possessions.)

In all the aforesaid monasteries, you, son archimandrite, and your successors after you must appoint abbots with the counsel and consent of the monks who are in them. If any abbot proves unworthy of the abbey over which he presides, you and your successors must remove him justly and canonically, and appoint another in his place whom you judge worthy, in accordance with the fear of God and the rule of your monastery. You may likewise examine and judge [Col. 1034C] the abbots, monks, and laypeople of all the aforesaid monasteries and obediences, in spiritual as well as temporal matters, and justly and canonically determine their cases. They, in turn, must show you and your successors the obedience and reverence due to you as their father and archimandrite, and pay you the established dues.

In addition, whatever possessions and goods—whether fisheries, olive groves, woods, mills, lands, reed-beds, orchards, people, or anything else—the monastery now justly and canonically possesses there, or may in future acquire, with the Lord’s favor, through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other means, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and to the monastery itself. [Col. 1034D] On the condition that you, son archimandrite, and your successors must pay annually to the archbishop of Messina and his successors, as a census: twenty solidi, one hundred pounds of wax, twenty [units] of incense, and an equal number of casks of oil. Moreover, no one may presume to exact or extort tithes from you or your people on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from any other of your revenues or from the fodder of your animals.

[Col. 1035A] You may also receive into your monastery clerics or laymen, free and unencumbered, who flee the world, and retain them without any contradiction. Furthermore, we forbid any of your brothers, after making profession in the monastery, to leave that place without his archimandrite’s permission, except in pursuit of a stricter religious life. No one may dare retain one who departs without documentary assurance from the community. We also forbid anyone to place the monastery itself, or its monasteries, obediences, or people, under interdict. We hold valid the ancient liberties and immunities and the reasonable customs granted to your monasteries and hitherto observed, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired for ever.

Upon the death of you, the present archimandrite of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one [Col. 1035B] shall be set over it by any deceitful contrivance or violence, except the person whom the brethren of the monastery by common consent, or the sounder counsel of the greater part of the brethren, shall provide from among themselves to be elected according to the fear of God and the rule of the monastery.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may, etc., without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the annual census owed to the archbishop of Messina, as stated above. If anyone therefore in the future, etc.

Given at Anagni by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November [19 October], in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1175, in the seventeenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCXC. Confirms the possessions of the church of St. Mary of Cagia in the diocese of Meaux. (Fragment.) (Anagni, 16 November.)

[Du Plessis, *History of the Church of Meaux*, II, 60.]

[Col. 1035C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ODO, abbot of the church of St. Mary of Cagia, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

. . . . Whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s favor, through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, [Col. 1035D] or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to set out the following in their own terms:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Saturninus; the church of St. Martin of Fontenay; the church of St. Rigomerus; the church of Blessed Remigius of Vana; the church of Pino; etc. . . . .

Given at Anagni by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December [16 November], in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1175, in the seventeenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCXCI. To the archbishop of Lyons, legate of the Apostolic See, and his suffragans, etc.—Commends to them Peter, cardinal of St. Chrysogonus, his legate. (Anagni, 18 November.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 965.]

[Col. 1036A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the archbishop of Lyons, legate of the Apostolic See, and his suffragans, and to his beloved sons, the abbots and all the clergy and people established throughout the province of Lyons: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We greatly rejoice and exult in the Lord because good and praiseworthy testimony is borne, through God’s grace, concerning our beloved son Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Chrysogonus, whom we have appointed legate of the Apostolic See in your province [Col. 1036B] and elsewhere. His honorable and praiseworthy conduct, integrity, and prudence had long ago led us to form the judgment about him which we have now, with the Lord’s cooperation, more fully learned through the evidence of his acts. For the more abundantly we love you as devoted and special sons of the Church, the more we judged that a person of greater moderation, prudence, and distinction ought to be provided for you as legate. Although we previously sent you other letters concerning his legation, nevertheless, because we love that cardinal with special favor and esteem and cherish him as dear and welcome, we send you repeated letters, [Col. 1036C] admonishing your whole body and commanding you under precept to receive the aforesaid cardinal, as befits so great a man and a legate of the Apostolic See, with due honor and reverence. At his summons, come without any contradiction; firmly accept and observe his enactments and admonitions; and render him the honor and reverence due to a legate of the Apostolic See. Thus, with the Lord’s help, he may profit you and others beneficially, and we may render due thanks to almighty God for the fruit of his legation.

Given at Anagni, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December [18 November].

MCXCII. Takes the monastery of St. Mary of Nogent into protection and confirms its possessions and immunities. (Anagni, 22 November.)

[Du Plessis, *History of Coucy*, 145.]

[Col. 1036D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons John, abbot of the monastery of St. Mary of Nogent, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

. . . . . We receive the aforesaid monastery under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves. . . . . Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s favor, through grants of popes, gifts of kings [Col. 1037A] or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to set out the following in their own terms:

The church of Coucy, canonically granted to you by Bartholomew, formerly bishop of Laon, of blessed memory, as you reasonably possess it; so that, as was established by him and contained in the authentic document made concerning it, upon the death of any canon of that church, a monk shall be substituted in his place. We likewise decree that all immunities, dignities, and liberties bestowed upon your monastery by the said bishop shall remain entire and unimpaired. . . . . Etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. [Col. 1037B] I, Walter, bishop of Albano. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of SS. John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Albert, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina. I, Boso, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Mark. I, Manfred, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Cecilia. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Susanna. I, Arditio, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore. I, Cinthius, deacon-cardinal of St. Adrian. I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of St. Eustachius beside the temple [Col. 1037C] of Agrippa. I, Vivianus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, James, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Laborans, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Portico.

Given at Anagni by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December [22 November], in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1175, in the seventeenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

CIRCA THE YEAR 1175.

MCXCIII. To Robert, bishop of Exeter, and Roger, bishop of Worcester.—That they remove Clarembald, abbot of St. Augustine’s, Canterbury.

[Twisden, *Writers of English Affairs*, II, 1817.]

[Col. 1037D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers ROBERT, bishop of Exeter, and ROGER, bishop of Worcester: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having formerly heard from many persons, and especially from the report sent by you and by our beloved sons of the monastery of St. Augustine at Canterbury, of the enormities and offenses of their former elect; and having also received their complaint concerning the destruction of the monastery, which through the negligence and fault of the aforesaid elect had almost reached utter ruin, we, compassionating with paternal affection the ruin and downfall of that monastery as our own [Col. 1038A] special and particular concern, commanded you to investigate these matters diligently. If you found that the aforesaid elect was so useless and harmful to the monastery that it could not be reformed without his removal, you were to remove him from administration, setting aside the remedy of appeal. Now, however, your letters have made manifest to us that, while in accordance with the terms of our command you diligently investigated the allegations made against that elect, you found him entangled in so many public offenses and crimes that their recital in your letters caused our ears excessive weariness and grief.

For these reasons, as you had received in command from us, [Col. 1038B] you entirely removed him from administration. We therefore hold his removal valid and firm, and confirm it by apostolic authority. By apostolic letters, we command your discretion under precept: if the said Clarembald, in rash and destructive audacity, should presume by the violence of any powerful person to occupy that church or its possessions, or in any manner to alienate or disturb the church, publicly declare him excommunicated by our authority, with lighted candles; and ensure that he is cautiously avoided by everyone as an excommunicate, until he presents himself before us to make satisfaction for his offenses and enormities.

MCXCIV. To Roger, archbishop of York.—That, according to a privilege formerly granted him, he may carry the cross before himself throughout England.

[*Letters of Gilbert Foliot*, II, 71.]

[Col. 1038C]

ALEXANDER, pope, to ROGER, archbishop of York, legate of the Apostolic See.

It has not escaped your memory how, in the first year of our elevation, you caused to be presented to us a document of letters of our predecessor Pope Honorius of happy memory, in which it was stated that apostolic favor had granted to your predecessors, and to their successors, the liberty of having the cross carried before them throughout all England. Following in the footsteps of that same predecessor of ours, [Col. 1038D] we confirmed to you by the protection of our writing what had been graciously granted to your predecessors by our predecessor. Subsequently, however, Thomas, formerly archbishop of Canterbury, of holy and venerable memory, thinking that this tended to the detriment of his right and dignity, began to raise a dispute concerning it and for this reason appealed to the Apostolic See. He maintained, if we remember correctly, that neither you nor your predecessors had ever been permitted to do this. Thus it came about that we prohibited you by our letters from daring, on any ground, to have the cross carried before you in the province of the Church of Canterbury until the case had been examined.

Since, therefore, through our beloved sons J. and A., your clerks, you have lodged before us a grave complaint, alleging [Col. 1039A] that we had deprived you, without judicial examination, of possession of this right, which you and your predecessors had held, and since we wish to show consideration to you as our venerable brother and preserve your rights whole and unimpaired, we establish by these present letters that our letters of prohibition shall cause you no prejudice. Thus it shall remain free to you and your successors, as a privilege has been granted to you through the favor of the Apostolic See and as you and your predecessors have been accustomed to do, to have the cross carried before you throughout all England, until a definitive judgment determines what your church ought by right to possess.

MCXCV. Takes under protection the monastery of St. Thomas of Paraclete (at Æbelholt) and confirms its possessions and privileges.

[Langebeck, *Writers of Danish Affairs*, VI, 435.]

[Col. 1039B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, abbot of the church of St. Thomas of Paraclete, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, in order that we may love religious persons and endeavor by every means to advance religion pleasing to God. No service, indeed, is ever rendered acceptably to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved in the purity of religion. Therefore all lovers of the Christian faith ought to love religion and more diligently foster venerable places together with the persons devoted to divine service, so that they may not be troubled by the molestations of wicked people or wearied by oppressive exactions. Accordingly, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church in which you are devoted to divine service, strengthening it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the canonical order instituted in your church according to God, the Rule of St. Augustine, and the institution of the brethren [Col. 1039C] of St. Victor at Paris, shall be observed there inviolate for ever. [Col. 1039D] Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s favor, through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall be preserved firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to set out the following in their own terms:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is built, with all its appurtenances; the church of Tjæreby with its tithes; one third of the tithes in the church of Alsentorp; one third of the tithes of the church of Anæs; one third of the tithes of the church of Hælsinge; one third of the tithes of the church [Col. 1040A] of Krækkem; Eskilsø; the estate at Syntherby with wood, fields, and meadows; land at Særslev; the estate at Julighe with the church of that village, meadows, fields, and a mill situated beside Værebro; the estate at Hatheløse with woods, meadows, and fields; the whole village of Nævet with woods, meadows, fields, and fisheries; the village of Tjæreby with its church, woods, meadows, and fields; land at Hott with a portion of woodland; land at Tolletorp with woodland; land at Frettoff.

Moreover, no one whatsoever may presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the fodder of your animals. You may receive clerics or laymen, free and unencumbered, fleeing the world [Col. 1040B] for conversion, and retain them in your church without any contradiction. Furthermore, we forbid any of your brothers, after making profession at your place, to leave it; and no one may dare retain one who leaves without documentary assurance from your community. In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose clerics and present them to the diocesan bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them, so that they must answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. We likewise grant that the burial ground of the place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted, without prejudice, however, to the rights of those churches from which bodies of the dead are taken. [Col. 1040C] When, however, a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated or interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any deceitful contrivance or violence, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or that part of the brethren which is of sounder counsel, shall provide to be elected in accordance with God and the Rule of St. Augustine.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved whole and unimpaired for the benefit in every way of the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop. [Col. 1040D]

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall attempt rashly to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he corrects his offense by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; [Col. 1041A] and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance.

But to all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen. Let all the people say—and let all the people say—Amen.

IN THE YEARS 1160–1176.

MCXCVI. To the archbishop of Narbonne and the bishop of Elne.—Confirms, by authority of the Apostolic See, a sentence of interdict pronounced against the abbot of Canigou. (Anagni, 1 March.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 1060.]

[Col. 1041B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the archbishop of Narbonne and the bishop of Elne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that, because the abbot of Canigou would not be subject to the monastery of Cras or render obedience to its abbot, as his predecessors had rendered it to their predecessors, you pronounced against him a sentence of interdict at our command. Therefore, since it is fitting that we hold valid and firm what is established by authority of the Apostolic See, we command and again command your brotherhood by apostolic letters: if the matter stands thus, cause the aforesaid sentence—which we hold valid and firm, as it was reasonably pronounced by you—to be observed firmly and inviolably, all pretext and appeal [Col. 1041C] set aside. If the said abbot does not even then come to his senses, lay your hands more heavily upon him, for we wish to be held valid and firm whatever you shall deem proper to establish canonically against him. If both of you cannot be present to carry this out, one of you, with prudent men associated with him, shall nevertheless carry it out.

[Col. 1041C] Given at Anagni, on the Kalends of March [1 March].

MCXCVII. Privilege for the monastery of St. Bertin at Saint-Omer. (Anagni, 8 March.)

[Collection of Charters, III, 353.]

[Col. 1041D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of St. Bertin: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we grant ready assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to completion by effective action those requests which do not depart from the path of reason. Accordingly, beloved sons in the Lord, favorably assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to the same monastery, the milling of grain from the ministerial of St. Bertin in the town of Saint-Omer, as your monastery is known to have possessed it reasonably for forty years past. We strengthen it by the protection of this present writing, decreeing [Col. 1042A] that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way act contrary to it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, on the eighth Ides of March [8 March].

MCXCVIII. To the rectors of Lombardy.—That they dissuade the citizens of Modena from harassing the monastery of Nonantola, and release twenty of the forty hostages received from the monastery. (Anagni, 23 March.)

[Tiraboschi, *History of Nonantola*, II, 273.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the rectors of Lombardy: greeting and apostolic [Col. 1042B] blessing.

The more particularly the monastery of Nonantola pertains to the jurisdiction of Blessed Peter and to ours, the more bound we are to be solicitous for its preservation and to take more earnest care and concern that nothing be done to its loss or disadvantage; for we could be reproached with excessive negligence if, through any lukewarmness or faint-heartedness, we neglected matters entrusted to our care. Therefore we admonish, direct, and command your diligence to admonish and compel the citizens of Modena wholly to desist from troubling the monastery of Nonantola, and to leave its people and rights in peace and quiet. [Col. 1042C] We further enjoin upon you that, since you have taken forty hostages from the said monastery, and may, given the condition of the place, be satisfied with a smaller number, you shall retain twenty and restore the other hostages. Carry out the aforesaid measures in such a way that we may commend your care and devotion more earnestly in the Lord.

Given at Anagni, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April [23 March].

MCXCIX. To all the bishops of the province of Rouen.—That they do not absolve those whom the chapter of the Church of Rouen has bound. (Anagni, 22 April.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 1068.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 1042D] brothers, all bishops established throughout the province of Rouen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When the Church of Rouen is the mother and teacher of all the churches committed to your governance, it is fitting that you should honour it in every way in matters pertaining to the Lord, and diligently defend and uphold its justice insofar as lies within you, so that you may be shown sincerely to love that church which ought to enjoy your support and humble submission. For we have received from the beloved sons, the dean and canons of that Church, that when they subject certain of their parishioners to excommunication for their offences, or place their land under interdict, those persons against whom the sentence of excommunication or interdict is pronounced sometimes transfer themselves into your bishoprics, and thus commonly disdain to observe the sentence; and, because they are not avoided as excommunicates, they persist longer in their wrongdoing. Therefore, since a sentence of ecclesiastical censure pronounced against wrongdoers for their offences must be inviolably observed until worthy satisfaction has been made, by these apostolic letters we command you, and in commanding enjoin upon you, that whenever the Church of Rouen has pronounced a sentence of excommunication against any of its parishioners who are wrongdoers, or has subjected their land to interdict, upon receipt of letters from the chapter of that Church, you shall publicly proclaim those persons excommunicated and their land placed under interdict, and shall order that they be more cautiously avoided by all until worthy satisfaction has been made.

Given at Anagni, 10 Kalends of May [22 April].
