I, Bobo, priest-cardinal of St. Pudentiana, title of Pastor. I, Theodorus, priest-cardinal of St. Vitalis, title of Vestina. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Susanna. I, Jacinctus, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Arditio, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore. I, Cinthyus, deacon-cardinal of St. Adrian. [Col. 1125A] I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of St. Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of St. Angelo.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, through the hand of Master Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July [28 June], in the tenth indiction, in the year 1177 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

MCCXCIX. He takes the monastery of St. Andrew at Ravenna under protection and confirms its goods and rights. (Venice, at Rialto, 9 July.)

[FANTUZZI, *Monuments of Ravenna*, I, 327.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, CALISWERE, abbess of the monastery of St. Andrew of Ravenna, and her sisters, [Col. 1125B] present and future, forever.

For holy virgins who desire to please the Lord under the religious habit, the support of the apostolic see ought to be present all the more vigorously because, owing to the frailty of their sex and the commitment of the religious life which they have undertaken, they are less able to defend their own rights. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it with the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, establishing that the monastic order which is known to have been instituted in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict [Col. 1125C] shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods the same monastery at present justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s permission, acquire by grant of popes, gift of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and to those who succeed you. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Whatever you possess in the estate of Taibano: Bibiano, Alfiano, Nebulino, and the chapel of St. Mary situated in the estate of the aforesaid Taibano; the things which Lambert, formerly count, relinquished in the county of Populonia; the land which John de Saxo holds from [or: of] your monastery [Col. 1125D] and which pertains to the tower; one hundred *Blancanicum* [uncertain toponym or measure]; Marcianicum; Septanta; and whatever you possess in Galliano and Luco, and in the hamlet of Ebriaco—all of which lie in the county of Imola. Pistrinum; a ground-floor house and a vineyard situated near the church of St. Severinus; Persulino; Manciano; Agello; Armenzano; Galliano; Lacuna; [lacuna]; and whatever you possess in the parish of Zezata, in Monogora, in Fossola, in the meadows, and in the house of Galando [lacuna], and in Mozafrina, now called Gudignola.

Everything that you possess in the parish of Libbe, in the parish of St. Peter Intersilbe, in the parish of St. Mary at Furculae, and of St. Peter at Briseta; at Godo, one whole *mansus*; whatever you possess in the parish of St. Boculus, called Trontola; at Exdate; and in the county of Faenza: [Col. 1126A] namely, the monastery of St. Mary at Celeseum, with all its appurtenances; the monastery of St. Martin beyond the major church, with all its appurtenances; likewise, the place called Nebulino, with all its other estates, hamlets, and other dependencies; a house, formerly called Urbanis, situated near the paved bridge, with the chapel founded there, namely St. Mary’s, and all its appurtenances; one estate called *Vicus reus*, situated in the parish of St. Pancras; one fishery called Busceleta, with its marshes, woods, hunting rights, and other things belonging to it, situated in the parish of St. Mary at the Port, bounded on one side of the said fishery by Gaibana, on another by Sandolo, and on a third by the ditch [Col. 1126B] called that of John Pitulo, the ditch of Medano, and the ditch called Gattuli and Zelle; and whatever you possess at Ficarolis and in its county. At Filo, one hundred *tornaturiae* of land, and a *mansus* situated on the hill called Focariae; in the district of Ponsaro, the place called Triscolo with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Apollinaris at Ronco, with its land, marsh, wood, and mill, together with its two banks as far as the aqueduct wall; at Godoaria, one *mansus*; and whatever you possess in the parish of St. Zacharias, at Cervia, moreover in the city of Ravenna, at Riversano, in the valley of St. Victor, and, further, whatever is known reasonably to belong to your monastery. [Col. 1126C]

We therefore decree, etc.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, through the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of July [9 July], in the tenth indiction, in the year 1177 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCCC. He takes the monastery of St. Mary in Organo at Verona under protection and confirms its goods, possessions, and privileges. (Venice, at Rialto, 10 July.)

[HORMAIR, *History of the Princely County of Tyrol*, I, II, 79.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1126D] sons Opizo, abbot of the monastery of St. Mary in Organo, and his brothers, present and future, who profess the regular life, forever.

The authority of our office exhorts us to take care for the condition of religious places and to make wholesome provision for their peace and tranquillity. For it is recognized as worthy and fitting to propriety that we who have been raised to the governance of churches should both protect them from the malice of wicked men and fortify them by the patronage of the apostolic see and of blessed Peter. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following the example of our predecessor Pope John X of blessed memory, we receive the aforesaid monastery of Blessed Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the guardianship of the apostolic see and [Col. 1127A] our protection, and fortify it with the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, establishing that the monastic order known to have been instituted in the same monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate forever. Moreover, whatever possessions, whatever goods [lacuna]. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is built, with all its appurtenances; the chapel of St. Mary of Sargada, with all its appurtenances; the chapel of St. Syrus in the castle of Verona, with everything belonging to it; the chapel of St. Sophia, with its possessions; the chapel of St. Donatus of Maruno, with all its dependencies; [Col. 1127B] the chapel of St. Michael of Mizoli, with all its possessions; the obedience [dependent priory] of St. Peter of Lunico, with everything belonging to it; the chapel of Ponte Marmoreo and the chapel of St. Syrus of Aquileia; the church of St. Mary in Solario; the church of St. Mary in Siciano and the canonry of St. Lawrence in Siciano; the church of Consecrated St. Mary; the church of the holy martyrs Faustinus and Jovita, with all the churches and hospices belonging to the monastery of St. Mary in Organo and St. Mary in Baro; the estate of Baro, with its appurtenances; the estate of Desargada, with all its dependencies; the estate of Ponte Marmoreo, with its appurtenances; the estate of St. Sophia, with all its appurtenances; the estate of [Col. 1127C] Siciano, with all its appurtenances; the estate of Marono, with all its appurtenances; the estate of Mizoli, with all its dependencies; the estate of Lunico, with all its appurtenances; the estate of Codenola, with all its dependencies; the estate of Ylasio, with all its appurtenances; the estate of Arculis, with all its dependencies; cultivated and uncultivated lands and vineyards.

We likewise confirm by apostolic authority to you and to the same monastery the tithes and other revenues which your monastery is known justly to possess everywhere. You may also receive clerics or laymen fleeing from the world, etc., as in the bull for the monastery of St. Mary of New Port, above no. 1298. You shall receive the consecrations [Col. 1127D] of your monastery and of the churches belonging to it—as is contained in the privilege of our aforesaid predecessor of revered memory—as well as the ordinations of monks and clerics who are to be promoted to holy orders, and the blessing of the abbot, from the patriarch of Aquileia, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the apostolic see, and is willing to grant these things to you freely and without any improper demand, as you have done hitherto. We further prohibit the bishop of Verona from rashly molesting you or your monastery contrary to the tenor of the privilege of our aforesaid predecessor. Upon your death, etc.

We therefore decree, etc.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, through the hand of Gratian, [Col. 1128A] subdeacon and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of July [10 July], in the tenth indiction, in the year 1177 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

MCCCI. He confirms enactments made and to be made by the General Chapter of the Carthusian Order, with authority to appoint and remove priors and correct members of the order, from whose decisions no appeal is permitted. (Venice, at Rialto, 11 July.)

[*Privileges of the Carthusian Order*, 2.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior and brothers of the Carthusians: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, by the Lord’s working, you are devoted to religion and uprightness [Col. 1128B] and intent upon works of charity, beyond the common obligation we wish to love and foster you with a special prerogative, and always to attend to your welfare and advancement. Therefore, desiring that your religious order—which by God’s grace everywhere gives forth the fragrance of virtues—should receive strength and growth from day to day and continually press forward, we confirm by apostolic authority the provisions and ordinances which the General Chapter of your order, in prudent deliberation, has made and shall make concerning the appointment and removal of priors, the enactments which it has made or shall make beneficially for the order, and the discipline which it has imposed upon those found to be rebellious against the order. We decree that these shall remain valid and firm hereafter, establishing that no one may oppose the institution of your chapter by [Col. 1128C] appeal or by any other means.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, on the fifth day before the Ides of July [11 July].

MCCCII. To the monastery of Blessed Mary at Soissons, he confirms the “guarantee of the prebends” of the church of St. Peter. (Venice, at Rialto, 20 July.)

[D. GERMAIN, *History of Our Lady of Soissons*, 440.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, the abbess and sisters of Blessed Mary of Soissons: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that, although the church of St. Peter of Soissons has from ancient times been subject to your church, and it properly belongs to you to confer the prebends [Col. 1128D] of the aforesaid church, the dean and canons of that church, contrary to right and justice and without consulting you, rashly wished to add one prebend from their common fund and confer it upon a certain priest named Ernald. But, at last recognizing their rashness, they made full and fitting satisfaction to you for so great a presumption. Lest what they did should in the future give rise to prejudice against the honor and dignity of your church, we confirm to you by apostolic authority, and fortify with the protection of this present document, the guarantee (*guadio*) of the prebends of the aforesaid church, as you held it from ancient times and are known to hold it now. Establishing that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation, etc.

[Col. 1129A] Given at Venice, at Rialto, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August [20 July], in the first year of our pontificate. [Note: [Col. 1129D] This was added by another hand.]

MCCCIII. He instructs the archbishop of Split, apostolic legate, and Michael, bishop of Trogir, to warn under penalty of excommunication the pirates of Šibenik, who robbed his subdeacon Raymond de Capella, returning to him from King William of Sicily, both of royal letters and of other valuables, to restore them. (Venice, at Rialto, 23 July.)

[FARLATI, *Sacred Illyricum*, III, 197.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the archbishop of Split, legate of the apostolic see, and Michael, bishop of Trogir: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1129B] When our beloved son Raymond de Capella, our subdeacon, was returning to us from the presence of our dearest son in Christ, W., illustrious king of Sicily—to whom he had been sent by us and by our son James, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin—pirates who were at Sagettia of the castle of Šibenik, where two counts were present, namely Nestros and Perlat, presumed to lay violent hands upon him and his companions. They did not hesitate basely and dishonorably to take from him everything that he had in the ship, worth more than sixty marks of silver; also our letters; and also those which the aforesaid king was sending to us, as well as a document concerning the … money of the said cardinal.

On this account we are the more moved and disturbed, [Col. 1129C] inasmuch as this touches more directly upon our injury and contempt; for we could not pass over in quietness and silence so great a loss and injuries done to any cleric, much less to our own subdeacon. Since, therefore, we cannot and ought not to endure such presumption and outrage remaining uncorrected, we command and, in commanding, enjoin your brotherhoods by apostolic letters to warn without delay those two counts, the pirates, and the other robbers who were at the aforesaid Sagettia, that they restore, without diminution or delay, both the letters and the things taken from the aforesaid messenger, our subdeacon and bearer of this letter, together with the expenses which he was compelled to incur on this account. You shall also diligently induce the castle of Šibenik, to which that Sagettia belonged, to restore [Col. 1129D] whatever of these things came into its hands.

But if, upon your duly delivered warning, they fail to do this, then, all contradiction and appeal ceasing, publicly excommunicate by our authority, with lighted candles, those persons and all who were then at the aforesaid Sagettia. And if they do not even then come to their senses within ten days, prohibit the celebration of all divine offices in the city of Šibenik, if the said Sagettia belonged to it, except baptism for infants and penance. As for those who laid violent hands upon our aforesaid subdeacon, publicly pronounce them excommunicated without delay, without recourse to appeal; cause them to be avoided as excommunicates [Col. 1130A] until they restore everything taken; and require them to come to the apostolic see, with your letters, to make satisfaction to us, to the aforesaid cardinal, and also to our said subdeacon. Carefully provide that the same messenger may be able to return safely to us with the things he recovers. Henceforth, if one of you cannot be present for the following proceedings [lacuna], the other shall nevertheless carry them out.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, on the tenth day before the Kalends of August [23 July].

MCCCIV. To Roger, archbishop of York, legate of the apostolic see, and Hugh, bishop of Durham, he reports that on 21 July the son of Albert, margrave of Brandenburg, chamberlain of Emperor Frederick, swore an oath: “that, after the emperor came to Venice, he would have the peace of the Church, the peace of William, king of Sicily, for fifteen years, and a truce with the Lombards for six years confirmed by oath.” He reports that on 24 July the emperor reached the church of St. Nicholas and “there, having renounced the schism, both he himself and the archbishops, bishops, and other princes of the German kingdom obtained the benefit of absolution through bishops and cardinals.” He then reports that at Venice on that day and the following day, 25 July, in the church of St. Mark, the emperor rendered him the honors due to him. (Venice, at Rialto, 26 July.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 181.]

[Col. 1130B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers ROGER, archbishop of York, [Col. 1130C] legate of the apostolic see, and Hugh, bishop of Durham: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The services of most welcome devotion which you are known to have rendered to us and to the Church with such devotion and praise-worthiness require that we should report to you, as special and devoted spiritual sons, the happy successes of the Church in special letters [reading uncertain: *fit spiritualibus, specialibus litteris describ.*]; for it is worthy, fitting, and proper that those whom we have found so firm and steadfast in their devotion to us should be made cheerful and glad at our prosperity and that of the Church itself. Therefore give thanks with us to almighty God, who dwells on high and looks down upon the lowly from above, by whose gift it has come about that his bride, the most holy Church, long and grievously battered by stormy waves and a violent tempest, has at last reached the harbor of salvation and, with the raging storms calmed, rejoices in the peace due to her and long desired.

Indeed, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of the coming month of August [21 July], by order of our dearest son in Christ Frederick, illustrious emperor of the Romans, the son of Margrave Albert—a nobleman, great and powerful, and chamberlain of that emperor—in the presence of the ecclesiastical and secular princes of the German kingdom, publicly swore in his soul, before us and before an innumerable multitude, [Col. 1131A] with his hand upon the most holy Gospels, that, after the emperor came to Venice, all dispute and opposition having been stilled, he would cause the peace of the Church, as arranged and negotiated through our brothers and his princes; the peace of our dearest son in Christ William, illustrious king of Sicily, for fifteen years; and the truce with the Lombards for six years, to be confirmed by oath on his own soul and also by his princes, as is contained in the written peace and truce. And the princes of the German kingdom—namely our venerable brothers the archbishops of Magdeburg and Cologne, and Christian, called of Mainz, together with certain others—caused an oath to be sworn in their own souls on their own behalf.

On the ninth day before the Kalends of August [24 July], the aforesaid emperor, as had been negotiated [Col. 1131B] and arranged, came to the church of St. Nicholas, one mile from Venice. There both he himself and the archbishops, bishops, and other princes of the German kingdom, renouncing the schism, obtained the benefit of absolution through our brother bishops and cardinals, by our command, in the presence of certain others. Thereupon they came to Venice; and there, before the church of St. Mark, while an innumerable multitude of men and women was present and loudly giving thanks and praise to the Most High, the aforesaid emperor humbly and reverently rendered us obedience and reverence as supreme pontiff. Having received from us the kiss of peace, he devoutly took our right hand and led us with fitting reverence and devotion [Col. 1131C] into the church as far as the altar.

On the following day, the feast of blessed James, at the request of the same emperor, we went to the aforesaid church of St. Mark to celebrate the solemnities of Mass. When we arrived there, the aforesaid emperor came outside the church to meet us; taking our right side devoutly, he led us into the church. After the solemnities of Mass had been completed, he took our right hand as far as the door of that church. When we mounted our palfrey prepared there, he held the stirrup and rendered us every honor and reverence which his predecessors were accustomed to render our predecessors. It shall therefore be your concern to rejoice with us and the Church in these prosperous events and to make the achievement of peace known to the other devoted sons of the Church, [Col. 1131D] so that those touched by zeal for the house of the Lord may rejoice and exult in the Lord over the divinely given gift of peace.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, on the seventh day before the Kalends of August [26 July].

MCCCV. To Peter, abbot of Monte Cassino, and the archbishop of Capua, he reports the same things as in the preceding letter to Roger, archbishop of York. (Venice, at Rialto, 27 July.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 918.]

“The services of most welcome devotion,” etc., as in the preceding letter.

MCCCVI. To William, archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans, he announces that Emperor Frederick has returned to obedience to the Church. (Venice, at Rialto, 27 July.)

[D. MARLOT, *Metropolitan [Church of] Reims*, II, 406.]

[Col. 1132A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers WILLIAM, archbishop of Reims, legate of the apostolic see, and his suffragans, and to his beloved sons, the abbots established in the province of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since we acknowledge that glorious and magnificent benefits have come to the most holy Roman Church and to us through the aid, power, and favor of our dearest son in Christ Louis, illustrious king of France, and of his kingdom, it is fitting and consonant [Col. 1132B] with reason that we should report to him and to you, by whose aid we have been powerfully assisted in our necessities, the prosperous and happy outcome of the peace. We hold as indubitable truth that, after God, that king together with his kingdom has cooperated in the honor and exaltation of the holy Church and has bestowed great increase upon it; and as we acknowledge this in word, so, with God as author, we shall acknowledge it in deed and speech at all times.

Let it be known to your solicitude that our dearest son in Christ Frederick, illustrious emperor of the Romans, through the inspiration of divine grace, laying aside the error of vanity and turning to the way of truth, has returned to obedience to the Church and to us [Col. 1132C] reverently and devoutly, as was fitting. He has rendered to blessed Peter in us that reverence and devotion which his predecessors were accustomed to render our predecessors, and has promised that he will render it henceforth. For this indeed we give praise to the Most High; and consequently we return abundant thanks to the king and kingdom, because they in no way abandoned the Church or ourselves in our trials and persecutions, but magnificently aided and defended us to the end. We therefore warn and earnestly exhort your belovedness that, rejoicing with the Church and with us in prosperity, you may persevere, as you have steadfastly done hitherto, in devotion to blessed Peter and to us; and that you may diligently exhort and induce [Col. 1132D] the king to persist therein with his kingdom.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August [27 July].

MCCCVII. To Guy, archbishop of Sens, and his suffragans, he writes the same things in the same words as in the preceding letter to William of Reims. (Venice, at Rialto, 30 July.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 991.]

“Since through the aid,” etc., as above.

MCCCVIII. To the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order: concerning the reconciliation of Emperor Frederick. (Venice, at Rialto, 30 July.)

[MARTENE, *Treasury of Anecdotes*, I, 1847.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 1133A] and beloved sons, the abbots and others assembling for the General Chapter at Cîteaux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks to almighty God, who, though he dwells on high, looks down upon the lowly from above and causes those who believe in him to rejoice in due happiness. We keep before our eyes the purity of that most sincere devotion which you are known to have laudably displayed toward us and the Roman Church during this time of disturbance; and we recognize that you have interceded before the Lord in constant prayers for the peace of the Church. Roused at length by these intercessions, at his command he has, with every storm calmed, delivered Peter’s little ship from the depths of the sea and granted it the harbor of salvation and repose.

Indeed, our dearest [Col. 1133B] son in Christ Frederick, illustrious emperor of the Romans, through the Lord’s inspiration—he in whose hand are the hearts of kings and princes—through the effort and labor of our brothers, of our venerable brother P. [Pontius], bishop of Clermont, and of our beloved son [Hugh], abbot of Bonneval, returned to our devotion and to Catholic unity. Renouncing the schism with the ecclesiastical and secular princes of the German kingdom, on the Sunday immediately before the feast of blessed James the Apostle, while an innumerable multitude of men and women rejoiced in the Lord with loud voices, he came to Venice into our presence. He rendered to us reverence and submission as supreme pontiff; and, having received the kiss of peace, he humbly and devoutly took our right hand into the church of St. [Col. 1133C] Mark as far as the altar.

On the feast of blessed James, at the request of that emperor, we went to the same church to celebrate the solemnities of Mass. When he heard that we were arriving, he immediately came to meet us and, receiving us at his right side with the fitting reverence and humility, led us into the aforesaid church. When Mass, which he heard from us though unworthy, had ended, he took our right hand as far as the church door, and rendered every honor and reverence which his predecessors were accustomed to render our predecessors. We therefore earnestly admonish and exhort all of you that, as almighty God has magnified his mercy toward us in the affair of the Church and has, by his ineffable mercy, directed its affairs in our hand, so you should offer him boundless praise and thanks, knock continually upon him in prayers and petitions, [Col. 1133D] that he may deign to protect and preserve his Church, increase the peace divinely granted to it, and cause it to attain enduring stability.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, on the third day before the Kalends of August [30 July].

MCCCIX. Privilege for the Church of Bonn. (Venice, at Rialto, 31 July.)

[GUNTHER, *Rhenish-Moselle Diplomatic Codex*, I, 428.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons LOTHAR, provost of the Church of Bonn, [Col. 1134A] and his successors canonically appointed, forever.

We have been raised, although unworthy, to the height of the supreme pontificate so that we may exercise pastoral care and concern for all God’s churches, both those nearby and those far away, and take care to cherish them against the assaults of wicked men by the patronage of apostolic protection. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Provost Lothar, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, after the example of Innocent of blessed memory and Eugenius, our father and predecessor among the Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the Church of Bonn, over which you are known, by God’s authoring, to preside, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. [Col. 1134B] We establish that whatever possessions and whatever goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s favor, acquire by grant of popes, gift of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and your successors.

Furthermore, as was established by our aforesaid predecessors and confirmed by an authoritative document, we grant to you and your successors free authority at specified times to visit and make circuits of the deaneries situated in your archdeaconry—namely Archowe and Zulpechowe, Efflemsi, and Sibergensi—as you have hitherto been accustomed reasonably to do. In addition, we have judged it proper to grant to you and [Col. 1134C] your successors that, in the year in which you customarily visit the churches, you may preside over the assembly of priests in two deaneries, namely Archowe and Zulpechowe, and in the third, namely Sibergensi, every year, as your predecessor and you yourself are known reasonably to have presided hitherto. You shall have the seat and place, both in the choir of St. Peter and in public processions or assemblies, as was adjudged by the Church of Cologne and confirmed by our aforesaid predecessors.

Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your successors the ban [jurisdictional right] of the deanery of Siberg, granted by Arnold, formerly archbishop of Cologne, to Gerard, your predecessor, as you canonically possess that ban. We strictly prohibit the abbot of Siberch—whom Herman, formerly archbishop of Cologne, had given authority to grant that deanery—from presuming, contrary to the institution of the aforesaid Archbishop Arnold and the judgment of the Church of Cologne, to grant that same deanery to anyone without the assent and counsel of you or your successors, [Col. 1134D] since the care of souls ought to be entrusted to him through you, who hold the office of archdeacon. We hold valid and firm the other liberties which the same archbishop is known reasonably to have confirmed to the officials of your church, and decree that they shall remain whole and inviolate forever. We likewise confirm by apostolic authority to you and to the same Church the advocacy of Wele, as it was reasonably granted to the Church of Bonn by Philip, archbishop of Cologne. [Col. 1135A] We therefore decree.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, bishop of Ostia. I, Gualterius, bishop of Albano. I, Guillelmus, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Anastasia. I, Boso, priest-cardinal of St. Pudentiana, title of Pastor. I, Theodinus, priest-cardinal of St. Vitalis, title of Vestina. I, James, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary [Col. 1135B] in Cosmedin. I, Ardino, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore. I, Hugh, deacon-cardinal of St. Angelo.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of August, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1177 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

MCCCX. To Louis, King of the Franks.—He writes that Emperor Frederick has returned to his duty. (Venice, Rialto, 31 July.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 990.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious King of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We send back to you with a certain word of peace our beloved son Master I., your cleric, who seems to abound in ardour of devotion and sincerity of faith concerning your honour and exaltation, since he was specially sent to us by Your Highness concerning the word of peace. Although for this purpose we had proposed to send to Your Serenity a great and honourable messenger, whom we know to have proved, beyond all mortals, most useful and fruitful to the Church and to us during the time of our persecution, and to whom, after God, we ascribe whatever prosperity, honour, and glory has befallen the Church and ourselves; nevertheless, considering the devotion, faith, and praiseworthy purpose of your aforesaid cleric, through him we announce to you, as a most dear son and most Christian king, the happy outcome of peace.

Let the serenity of Your Greatness therefore know that our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, together with the princes whom he had with him, especially the ecclesiastical ones, inwardly touched by divine grace and drenched with the shower of heavenly blessing, has utterly laid aside the error of vanity and, humbling himself before God and in the eyes of men, has returned humbly and devoutly, as was fitting, to obedience to the Church and to us. He has shown to blessed Peter in our person that reverence and honour which his predecessors customarily showed to our predecessors, and he has promised firmly and immovably to show it henceforth.

For this indeed we render most devoted praises to the Most High, from whom every good proceeds; and consequently we render manifold thanks to you and to your kingdom, through whose help and power, with heavenly grace going before, we do not doubt that we have attained so great and desirable a good. We therefore ask, admonish, and exhort Your Highness in the Lord that, together with your kingdom, you may henceforth firmly and steadfastly show the reverence and devotion which you have shown in us to your mother, the most holy Roman Church; and that you may so zealously attend to her honour and exaltation that thereby you may obtain the heavenly kingdom and preserve the earthly one more fully for yourself. You may possess the undoubted hope and confidence that the faith and devotion which you and your kingdom have magnanimously shown to the Church and to us at this moment of such necessity can never at any time slip from our memory. Indeed, with the Lord as author, we shall henceforth take care to cherish and embrace you and your kingdom more fruitfully and effectively.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, on the second day before the Kalends of August.

MCCCXI. To the Archbishop of York and the Bishop of Lincoln.—Concerning the nuns of Swine and Cotum. (Venice, Rialto, 2 August.)

[*Monast. Angl.*, I, 834.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the Archbishop of York and his beloved son the Bishop of Lincoln, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved daughters, the nuns of Swine and Cotum, have informed us that, although it has been granted to them, as to the brothers of the Cistercian Order, by the clemency of the Apostolic See, that they are not bound to pay tithes to anyone from the produce of lands which they cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense, certain ecclesiastics have distorted the chapter itself by a perverse and sinister interpretation. They assert that “produce” (*labores*) means newly cleared land (*novalia*), and thus, contrary to the privilege of the Apostolic See, the aforesaid nuns are burdened by the exaction of tithes.

Since, therefore, this interpretation is wholly foreign to our understanding and to that of others who wish to understand it soundly—for according to that chapter they are free and exempt from payment of tithes both from lands which they have brought under cultivation and from cultivated lands which they themselves cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense—we command, by apostolic writings and under obedience, your Fraternity and Discretion that you exact no tithes whatsoever from the aforesaid nuns, who are situated in your dioceses, from their produce or their lands which they cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense; nor permit anyone else to exact them. For it is neither fitting nor honourable that the privileges of the Apostolic See, which ought to retain inviolable force, should be infringed.

If, moreover, any clerics or laymen burden them by demanding tithes contrary to the privileges of the Apostolic See, strike the laymen with sentence of excommunication; and, all contradiction and appeal ceasing, suspend the clerics from office, and cause both the sentence of excommunication and that of suspension to be inviolably observed until due satisfaction is made.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, on the fourth day before the Nones of August.

MCCCXII. He confirms the privileges of the Church of St Peter of Osnabrück and the possessions of its clerics. (Venice, Rialto, 3 August.)

[MOSER, *Osnabrückische Geschichte*, Berlin, 1844, IV, 101.]

[Col. 1137B] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clerics of the Church of St Peter at Osnabrück, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant our assent to the just desires of petitioners, and that vows which do not depart from the path of reason be fulfilled in effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring with your just petitions by a gracious assent, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and to your church the rights and boundaries of your church, as they are defined and contained in the privilege of Philip, formerly Bishop of Osnabrück, and as you are known to have justly possessed them. We strengthen them by the protection of the present writing, decreeing that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed Apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, on the third day before the Nones of August.

MCCCXIII. He takes the monastery of St Ulrich under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Venice, Rialto, 6 August.)

[*Monum. Boica*, XXII, 187.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HENRY, abbot of the monastery of St Ulrich, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

[Col. 1137D] Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized as suitable to religion and honour, it befits us to grant it willingly and to afford fitting support to the desires of the powerful. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this writing.

First, indeed, we decree [Col. 1138A] that the monastic order which is recognized as established in the same monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions [lacuna]. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself on which the aforesaid monastery is built, with its waters, fisheries, woods, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, watercourses, and all other appurtenances; the estate of your stewardship situated within your city, with all its appurtenances. The tithes of newly cleared land adjoining the sands of the river Lech, and whatever you possess around the bridge of that river; the village of Husteten with all its appurtenances, [Col. 1138B] just as Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, together with his son, left you the whole right in its entirety; the sacristy of your monastery with its offerings, the treasury of the church, and every right, as you have reasonably held these down to the present time; the church of Gundolteshaim with all its appurtenances [Note: [Col. 1137D] See the book of traditions, no. LXXIX.]; the tithes of Mendichingen [Note: [Col. 1137D] See no. VI.], the tithes of Robingin, the tithes of Inningen, and the tithes of Kaeckingen [Note: [Col. 1137D] Goeggingen.], with all their appurtenances, granted to you by the Bishop of Augsburg; the church and tithes of Haeder, with the whole village [Note: [Col. 1137D] Heder in the district of Zusmarshausen.]; the church and tithes of Finningen, with the whole village; the tithes of Tottinwis [Note: [Col. 1137D] Thodenweis.] and the castle which you purchased from Count Palatine Otto the Younger, with its other appurtenances; the stewardship estate of Holenbach with all its appurtenances; the lesser tithes of Mandenchingen [Note: [Col. 1137D] Schwabmünchen.] [Col. 1138C] from all the bishop’s fields, and fifteen pigs annually from the bishop’s share; the tithes of Wachenhowen with their appurtenances; the estate and mill of Walishoven with their appurtenances; Rotenbach with its appurtenances [Note: [Col. 1137D] Roettenbach in the district of Schrobenhausen.]; Scehinbach with its appurtenances [Note: [Col. 1138D] Schonenbach in the district of Aichach.]; in the borough of Aichach, an estate and the other things belonging by right to the monastery; at Steten in Bavaria, a stewardship estate with all its appurtenances; at Celle, a stewardship estate, church, and tithes with their appurtenances [Note: [Col. 1138D] Obezzell in the district of Friedberg.]; the estate of Rohelingen with its appurtenances; the church of Pfaffenhoven and whatever the devout Albert there offered you; the church of Lelchuelderdorf with its appurtenances [Note: [Col. 1138D] The Church of St Afra in the plain of the Lech.]; the estate of Mandechingen which Wimar gave [Col. 1138D] to you; Stainbahe with its appurtenances; the stewardship estate of Pacche with its appurtenances [Note: [Col. 1138D] Bacher in the district of Friedberg.]; the village and church of Arnesriet with their appurtenances; the estate and mill of Pridichingen with their appurtenances [Note: [Col. 1138D] Bridrichingen.]; Staindorf, with all that belongs there to your right; the estate which a certain Hailwich gave you; likewise the estate which a certain Berta of Buren gave you; and the church of Wfhusen with its appurtenances [Note: [Col. 1138D] Aufhausen.].

[Col. 1139A] Certainly, from your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, and from the sustenance of your animals, no one whatsoever may presume to exact tithes from you. We also grant that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; saving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose clerics and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them, so that they shall answer to him concerning spiritual matters and to you concerning temporal matters. Further, you may receive clerics or laymen who are free and unbound, fleeing from the world for conversion, and retain them in your monastery without any opposition.

Furthermore, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in your house, from leaving it without permission of his abbot, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain one who leaves without letters of the community guaranteeing him. Whenever a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, and in a subdued voice.

Moreover, we decree that the liberties and immunities reasonably granted to your monastery by kings and princes, ecclesiastical as well as secular, and the ancient and reasonable customs of your monastery, shall remain whole [Col. 1139C] and unimpaired by this present decree. On the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of intrigue or by violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

We therefore decree, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, Bishop of Ostia. I, Galterius, Bishop of Albano. I, Conrad, Archbishop of Mainz and Bishop of Sabina. I, William, Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. [Col. 1139D] I, Manfred, Bishop of Palestrina. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Anastasia. I, John, cardinal priest of St Pudentiana, title of Pastor. I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of St Vitalis, title of Vestina. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St Susanna. I, James, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of St Theodore. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of St Adrian. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of St Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of St Angelo. I, Laborans, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico.

[Col. 1140A] Given at Venice, at Rialto, by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of August, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1177 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

MCCCXIV. To Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury, legate of the Apostolic See, and his suffragans.—Concerning the peace restored with Emperor Frederick. (Venice, Rialto, 6 August.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 918.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren RICHARD, Archbishop of Canterbury, and his suffragans, and to his beloved sons, the abbots specially subject to the Roman Church situated in [Col. 1140B] the archbishopric of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We render immense praises and thanks to Almighty God, who, although He had long permitted Peter’s ship to be shaken by the stormy tempest of the sea, has now at last commanded the winds and the sea, and a great calm has come to pass. Thus, the raging waves of the sea having been calmed, the aforesaid ship has been brought back to the harbour of peace and safety.

Certainly, on the Sunday immediately preceding the feast of blessed James, our dearest son in Christ Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, came with great devotion to Venice into our presence, accompanied by the ecclesiastical and secular princes of the German kingdom. There, before an innumerable multitude of men and women loudly resounding praises to the Most High, [Col. 1140C] he showed us, as supreme pontiff, every reverence and honour. On the feast of blessed James, when at his request we went to the church of St Mark to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass, he came to meet us; and, when the Mass had ended—which he reverently heard from us, though unworthy—he showed us every honour which his predecessors customarily showed to our predecessors.

On the Kalends of the present month of August, in the presence of a great multitude, the aforesaid emperor caused an oath to be sworn upon his soul. The princes whom he had present, ecclesiastical as well as secular, confirmed by their sworn oath that he ought to observe intact and unimpaired the peace of the Church in perpetuity; the peace of our dearest son in Christ William, illustrious [Col. 1140D] King of Sicily, for fifteen years; and the truce with the Lombards from the aforesaid Kalends for six [seven] years, according as that peace and truce were arranged, negotiated, and reduced to writing.

And as the emperor received us as Catholic pope and spiritual father, so we received him as Catholic emperor, his wife as Catholic empress, and their son as Catholic king. Therefore give thanks to our Creator, who has looked with His mercy upon His bride, the most holy Church, and, after the many persecutions by which she was grievously oppressed and worn down, has through His grace restored to her full peace and tranquillity.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, on the eighth day before the Ides of August.

MCCCXV. He informs the choir of the Church of Salzburg, the prelates of its churches, and the ministerials of the aforesaid church that, in the place of Adalbert, who had voluntarily resigned his archbishopric, Conrad, former Archbishop of Mainz, was elected by [Romanus], Bishop of Gurk, and [Theobald], Bishop of Passau, and by the prelates of Salzburg. (Venice, Rialto, 9 August.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXII, 191.]

[Col. 1141A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the choir of the Church of Salzburg, the prelates of its churches, and the ministerials of the aforesaid church established within [outside] the mountains, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother Adalbert, formerly your archbishop, seeing and considering the necessity of [Col. 1141B] your Church, since he could not recover the favour of our dearest son in Christ Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, preferred to yield rather than contend. He freely and without any contradiction resigned your Church and its administration into our hands.

Afterwards our venerable brethren, the Bishops of Gurk and Passau, and the prelates of your Church, who were present with us, having received our command to conduct an election, unanimously agreed upon our venerable brother Conrad, formerly Archbishop of Mainz, a man learned, prudent, industrious, and discerning, very dear and welcome to us, and noble alike in character and birth. They elected him archbishop [Col. 1141C] and master.

The more abundantly we love your Church, because of the ardour of that most welcome devotion which it steadfastly preserved toward us and the Roman Church during this time of disturbance, the more readily we have given our favour and assent to their election. Without depriving him of the honour or dignity which he has held until now, we have granted him to you as archbishop. Out of regard and consideration for him, we wish to love that same Church more warmly in spirit and to attend with more eager zeal to its welfare and growth; and through his industry, nobility, and power, we believe, with God as author, that welcome benefits will accrue to the aforesaid Church.

[Col. 1141D] We therefore do not wish you to take it ill or in any manner to be troubled that those who were with us made the election without awaiting your counsel, since they proceeded to conduct the election by our will and command.

Accordingly, fully absolving all of you from the obedience which you promised to the aforesaid Adalbert, or to the man who had been placed over you, and absolving from that oath those among you who swore fealty to either of them, by the authority in which, though unworthy, we hold pre-eminence, we command your whole community through apostolic writings, and in commanding we enjoin, that, all contradiction and appeal ceasing, you render due obedience and reverence to the said Archbishop Conrad, [Col. 1142A] and take care humbly and devoutly to obey his salutary admonitions and commands. Those among you who have been accustomed and ought to swear fealty to the archbishop are not to delay in giving him fealty.

And whoever holds, under any title, the demesnes of the bishopric of Salzburg which have been occupied since the time of your former archbishop Eberhard of blessed memory shall, without excuse or pretext, restore them without difficulty to the said Conrad or to his messengers. Whoever holds fiefs newly granted shall leave them free and unencumbered. If anyone does not return the aforesaid demesnes and newly granted fiefs to the same archbishop within fifteen days after the issuing of these letters, in accordance with our command, you shall regard them as excommunicated, all contradiction and appeal having been set aside.

Certainly, by the counsel of our brethren, and the emperor by the decision of his princes, we have wholly annulled all alienations of demesnes and all newly made grants of fiefs, and have decreed them void and without effect. Any sentence of suspension, interdict, or excommunication which the aforesaid Archbishop Conrad shall canonically pronounce against the contumacious [Col. 1142B] or rebellious, we shall, with God as author, hold valid and firm, and shall cause it to be observed no otherwise than if it had been pronounced by ourselves. For we love that archbishop so warmly and sincerely in the Lord that we desire, with ready mind, to defer to him in all things which, with God and justice, we can do, as to our dearest brother.

[Col. 1142C] Given at Venice, at Rialto, on the fifth day before the Ides of August.

MCCCXVI. He confirms the Premonstratensian observance of the monastery of St James of Mainz. (Venice, Rialto, 18 August.)

[HUGO, *Annal. Praem. ord.*, II, 848.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons FULBERT, abbot, and the brethren of St James of Mainz, professing the Premonstratensian Order, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother, the archbishop of the holy Church of Mainz, has reported to us that black monks had customarily been in the aforesaid monastery of St James. But because a predecessor of that [Col. 1142D] archbishop had been killed there, the abbot and his monks were expelled from that monastery because of the sinister suspicion which the abbot and certain of his brethren had incurred there concerning that man’s death. You were introduced into that monastery by the aforesaid archbishop, with the consent of our dearest son in Christ Frederick, Emperor of the Romans, after deliberation by many persons.

Considering the ardour of religion with which your whole order is known to be fragrant, we judge that in this matter the proceeding was undertaken with prudent circumspection. We therefore hold valid and firm the transfer and change made by the same archbishop, as we have said, and confirm the monastery itself to you by apostolic authority. We more strictly forbid anyone henceforth to presume to remove brethren of your order from the aforesaid monastery or to inflict upon you any undue annoyance or burden concerning it, or concerning those things which belong to the same monastery.

So that you may serve the Lord there more peacefully and conveniently, we receive the aforesaid monastery, with all its possessions which it at present justly and canonically holds, or may in future acquire by just means through the Lord’s favour, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the protection of this writing. We decree that your order, recognized as established according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the Premonstratensians, shall be inviolably observed there for all time, etc.

[Col. 1143B] We therefore decree, etc.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, by the hand of Gratian, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1177 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

MCCCXVII. To the Archbishop of Split, apostolic legate, he states that he has committed his dispute with the Archbishop of Zadar concerning the bishopric of Hvar to the arbitration of Raymond of Capella, his subdeacon, who is undertaking an apostolic legation to Slavonia. (Venice, Rialto, 25 August.)

[FARLATI, *Illyricum sacrum*, III, 198.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 1143C] brother, the Archbishop of SPLIT, legate of the Apostolic See, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since a controversy is being conducted between you and our venerable brother the Archbishop of Zadar concerning the bishopric of Hvar, we have thought fit to commit the cause itself to our beloved son Raymond of Capella, our subdeacon, whom we are sending as legate of the Apostolic See into Slavonia. For, since he is learned, prudent, and discerning, we hope that the same cause ought under his examination to attain a worthy result.

We therefore command and enjoin your Fraternity that, if you are summoned for this purpose by the same our subdelegate, you shall appear before him, either in person or through a sufficient representative, [Col. 1143D] and shall firmly accept and observe what he decides concerning it. But if either party appeals, we have instructed the same subdeacon nevertheless to hear carefully the arguments and allegations on both sides, receive witnesses with appeal set aside, diligently record the depositions of those sworn witnesses, and send them to us, setting a suitable term for each party to appear before the apostolic presence with those attestations and allegations.

Moreover, if either party absents itself so as not to come into the presence of our subdeacon, or cannot be found when required, we have instructed the same subdeacon nonetheless to receive, with appeal set aside, the witnesses of the other party [Col. 1144A] and transmit their depositions.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September.

MCCCXVIII. He forbids Everard, Bishop of Tournai, in the division of prebends to proceed otherwise than according to the tenor of his writing (see above, epistle 732). (Venice, Rialto, 25 August.)

[MIRAEI, *Opp. dipl.*, II, 976.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother EVERARD, bishop, and to his beloved sons, the dean and chapter of Tournai, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard—and, hearing, could not but marvel—that although we granted to Walter of blessed memory, your predecessor, brother bishop, that out of each three prebends established in your church he should make four, you, acting contrary to our concession, exceed that number and have not hesitated, on the pretext of our writing, to halve certain prebends.

Since, therefore, it neither becomes you, nor can we endure, that you should misuse a concession granted by us, we command you by apostolic writings under obedience that you, brother bishop, shall proceed in the division of those prebends only according to the tenor of our writing. Henceforth, do not ordain a canon in the aforesaid church until you have restored the halved prebends in accordance with the tenor of our concession—especially the prebend of our beloved son G., Archdeacon of Laon, your fellow canon, which, like certain others, is said to have been halved. Nor, sons, may you canons presume to receive anyone as a canon until the halved prebends have been restored in accordance with our command.

But if you act against our command, it will be exceedingly grievous and displeasing to us; nor shall we be able to leave your presumption uncorrected, since it is not lawful for you or for anyone else to transgress the enactments of the Roman pontiff.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September.

MCCCXIX. He takes the Church of St Donatian of Bruges under protection and confirms its goods and possessions. (Venice, Rialto, 6 September.)

[MIRAEI, *Opp. dipl.*, II, 1330.]

[Col. 1144D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GERARD, provost of the Church of St Donatian of Bruges, and his brethren, present and future, to be canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The authority of the Apostolic See entrusted to us urges us to afford the protection of guardianship to places and persons which duly seek its aid with devotion. For just as no effect should be granted to those who seek unjust things, so no petition of those desiring lawful things should be delayed, especially when they rejoice to serve Almighty God with honourable life and praiseworthy [Col. 1145A] conduct.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of blessed Donatian of Bruges, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the protection of this writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 1145B] Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

In the diocese of Tournai: the altars of Dudazela and the offerings of the church of Dudazela, which are made through the devout worship of the faithful in reverence for St Leonard; Utkerca; Horescam with its appurtenances; the altars of St Michael and of the Holy Cross; Sumkerca, Clemeskerca, Suevensela, and Artrica.

In the diocese of Thérouanne: Widelgat; Kemla, with all tithes and lands belonging to it; Hesua with its appurtenances; Dikesmuta and Clarc; two parts of the tithe from the parish of Ypres; likewise two parts of the tithe from Formasela and Diesbuse, and from the newly cleared lands of that territory. The chancery of the Count of Flanders, as it was granted to your church through the devout generosity of Count Robert [Col. 1145C] and confirmed by his charter, and as the church itself has held it peacefully until now.

Whenever a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

On the death of you, the present provost of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any crafty device or violence, except one whom the brethren of the same church shall canonically provide for election according to the Lord. We likewise decree that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are [Col. 1145D] excommunicated or under interdict, saving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole and intact for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops.

If, therefore, in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Ubald, Bishop of Ostia. [Col. 1146A] I, William, Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Anastasia. I, Boso, cardinal priest of St Pudentiana, title of Pastor. I, Theodinus, cardinal priest of St Vitalis, title of Christina. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St Susanna. I, James, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of St Theodore. I, Hugh, cardinal deacon of St Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. [Col. 1146B] I, Laborans, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, Raynerius, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Venice, Rialto, by the hand of Master Gerard, subdeacon and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of September, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1177 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

MCCCXX. He permits Dominic, Abbot of St Justina of Padua, “that at funeral services, in the bishop’s absence, or if he does not wish to sing Mass, he may sing a special Mass in the monastery.” (Venice, Rialto, 16 September.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 441.]

[Col. 1146C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son DOMINIC, Abbot of St Justina of Padua, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have learned from a certain document authenticated by public hand that, between you and the canons of Padua, through the mediation of our venerable brother G., Bishop of Padua, and of Manfred and Bonojohn, whom you and the other party had jointly chosen, the following peace and agreement was made: that, at funeral services, the archpriest of the aforesaid church, if the bishop is absent or unwilling to sing Mass, shall sing the special Mass, if the choir of canons has been invited; or, if the archpriest is not present, you shall sing; and if both you and the archpriest are absent, one of the canons shall [Col. 1146D] celebrate Mass.

But since, as you assert, the aforesaid agreement has been violated by the canons, desiring to provide for you in this matter with paternal care, we have thought fit to grant you apostolic authorization that, at funeral services, if the bishop is absent or unwilling to sing Mass, it shall be lawful for you to sing a special Mass in your monastery, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal.

Given at Venice, at Rialto, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October.

MCCCXXI. He confirms the agreement made between Baldwin, former bishop, and Gerard of Chérisy. (Venice, Rialto, 26 September.)

[MABILLON, *De re diplom.*, p. 276.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 1147A] brother R., Bishop of Noyon, greeting and blessing.

We have seen the letter of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Franks, from whose tenor it became known to us that, when a dispute had arisen before that king between B., your predecessor of blessed memory, and Gerard of Chirisi, at length, in the presence of the king himself and many bystanders, the following agreement was made between him and the said G.: the aforesaid G. did homage to him for the castle of Chirisi, subject to these conditions: whenever the bishop of Noyon summons him concerning the excommunication which, as is said, ought to have been pronounced upon the aforesaid castle, the same G. shall submit to judgment in the court of the bishop of Noyon by the peers who are the bishop’s own men [the text reads: *reddito*]. [Col. 1147B] And if it can be proved that that excommunication was pronounced, the same G. shall surrender the aforesaid castle into the bishop’s hand, to be demolished and utterly destroyed, or dealt with wholly at his pleasure. But if the excommunication cannot be proved, the said G. and his heir shall hold that castle from the bishop of Noyon by homage.

Moreover, the same G. added in the homage which he rendered to the aforesaid bishop that he or his heir, for forty days, with two knights and at his own expense, shall serve the bishop of Noyon within the county of Noyon whenever the bishop wishes and has caused him to be summoned for that purpose. Furthermore, the same G. pledged faith that no loss shall come to the bishop of Noyon from the escort-duty toll of Pont-l’Évêque, or from the other tolls and bridge-tolls through the aforesaid castle; and that no cart carrying wine, nor any merchandise bound for any fair, shall pass through the castle. Or, if this occurs, the bishop shall have the escort-duty toll and the fine from those passing through; and the same G. and his heir shall make amends to the bishop for this.

Likewise, the ten pounds which the father of the said G. claimed to hold from the bishop of Noyon at Pont-l’Évêque, and which Simon, your predecessor, obtained in litigation, the same G. has now quitclaimed and released forever, free and clear, to the aforesaid bishop and his successors. He also promised that, if war threatens the bishop of Noyon, he will hand over the castle to him, to be restored after peace has been made, without any contradiction. And he confirmed before the aforesaid king of the Franks, on his faith, that he would observe all these things; he made that king guarantor under law concerning them; and, so that greater security might be had concerning all these matters, he assigned to that king the castellany of Laon as counter-pledge.

Therefore, wishing that what was established in this matter through the aforesaid king should possess the strength of perpetual stability, we hold the said agreement, made as we have stated, ratified and firm; and, confirming it by apostolic authority, we fortify it by the protection of this present writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 1148A] Given at Venice in Rialto, the sixth day before the Kalends of October.

MCCCXXII. To John, priest and king of the Indians, he writes that he had indeed long heard that John followed the Christian law; but that only then had the physician Philip reported that John wished “to be instructed in Catholic doctrine and to have a church in the City and some altar at Jerusalem.” He therefore sends the same physician Philip, through whom John may be brought to the Catholic faith. (Venice in Rialto, September 27.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 907.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, the illustrious and magnificent king of the Indians, most holy among priests: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See, over which, though unworthy, we preside, [Col. 1148B] is, as the Lord Himself bears witness, the head and teacher of all who believe in Christ. For He said to blessed Peter, whom, though unworthy, we have succeeded: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16). Christ willed this rock to be the foundation of the Church, and He foretells that it will be shaken by no blasts of wind and by no storms. Therefore blessed Peter, upon whom He founded the Church, deserved, not without reason, especially and pre-eminently among the other apostles, to receive the power of binding and loosing. To him the Lord said: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also [Col. 1148C] in heaven” (ibid.).

We had certainly already long ago heard, from many reports and in common rumour, how, since you profess the Christian name, you are unceasingly devoted to pious works and direct your mind toward matters pleasing and acceptable to God. Moreover, our beloved son Master Philip, physician and member of our household, who maintains that in those regions he discussed your pious intention and purpose with great and honourable men of your kingdom, has, as a prudent, discerning, circumspect, and wise man, firmly and carefully reported to us that he heard more plainly from them that it is your will and purpose to be instructed in Catholic and apostolic doctrine; and that you earnestly strive that neither you nor the land entrusted to your exalted rank may ever appear to hold anything in your faith which in any manner differs or disagrees from the teaching of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1148D]

Concerning this, indeed, we rejoice greatly with you as with a dearest son; and we render immense thanksgivings to Him from whom every gift proceeds. Joining desire to desire and prayers to prayers, we ask that He who granted you to receive the Christian name may, through His ineffable mercy, inspire your mind to will wholly to understand those things which the Christian religion ought to hold concerning every article of faith. For one who does not agree with that profession in word and deed cannot truly hope for salvation from a Christian profession. Nor is it enough for anyone to be called by the Christian name if he holds concerning himself something other than what Catholic and apostolic doctrine contains, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 7). [Col. 1149A]

Furthermore, this also adds to the commendation of your virtue: as the prudent Master Philip asserts that he heard from your people, you desired with ardent longing to have in the City a church and some altar at Jerusalem, where prudent men from your kingdom might reside and be more fully instructed in apostolic doctrine, through whom afterward you and the people of your kingdom might receive and hold that doctrine. We, however, who, though with insufficient merits, have been placed in the chair of blessed Peter, recognize ourselves, in accordance with the Apostle (Romans 1), as debtors to wise and foolish alike, to rich and poor alike. We bear every concern for your salvation and that of your people, and we wish, with ready mind—as we are bound by the ministry of government entrusted to us—to recall you from those articles in which you err from the Christian and Catholic faith. For the Lord Himself said to blessed Peter, whom He made prince of all the apostles: “And when you have turned again, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22).

Although it seems exceedingly burdensome and laborious to send anyone from our side into your presence amid so many labours, the various perils of travel and places, and distant and unknown shores, nevertheless, considering the obligation of our office and weighing your purpose and intention, we send to your greatness the aforesaid Philip, our physician and household member, certainly a discerning, circumspect, and prudent man. We trust in the mercy of Jesus Christ that, if you persist in the purpose and intention which, by the Lord’s inspiration, we understand you to have conceived, then, once you have shortly been instructed by God’s mercy concerning those articles of the Christian faith in which you and your people seem to disagree with us, you need fear absolutely nothing that might hinder the salvation of you or yours by error, or obscure in you the Christian name. [Col. 1149C]

We therefore ask, admonish, and exhort your royal excellence in the Lord to receive the same Philip, for reverence toward blessed Peter and toward us, with due kindness, as an honourable, discerning, prudent man sent from our side; and to treat him reverently and devoutly. And if it is your will and purpose—as indeed it wholly ought to be—that you be instructed in apostolic doctrine concerning those matters which the same Philip shall set before you on our behalf, hear and heed him diligently; and send back to us with him honourable persons and letters sealed with your seal, by which we may fully know your purpose and will. For the more exalted and great you are deemed to be, and the less you appear puffed up by your wealth and power, the more willingly we shall take care to admit and effectively grant your petitions, both concerning the grant of a church in the City and concerning the conferral of altars in the church of Saints Peter and Paul, in Jerusalem in the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, and in other matters which you may justly request. For we desire by every means possible to us according to God to advance your desire in this matter, which has proved most worthy of commendation; and we desire to win your soul and those of your people for the Lord. [Col. 1150A]

Given at Venice in Rialto, the fifth day before the Kalends of October.

MCCCXX. He takes the monastery of Saint Mary Magdalene of Lake Joux under protection and confirms its goods and possessions. (Venice in Rialto, September 29.)

[*Memoirs and Documents of the Historical Society of French-Speaking Switzerland*, Lausanne, 1838, vol. I, p. 185.]

[Col. 1150B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WALTER, abbot of the church of Saint Mary Magdalene of Lake Joux, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Those choosing the religious life ought to receive apostolic protection, lest an assault of anyone’s rashness directed against them perhaps recall them from their purpose or, which God forbid, weaken the strength of holy religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, receive the aforesaid church—in which you are devoted to divine service—under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order which is known to be established in that place according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the constitution of the Premonstratensian brethren, shall be observed there inviolate in perpetuity.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future be able to acquire, by grant of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought it proper to specify the following by their own names:

The place itself and the whole valley in which your abbey is situated, on every side, as the mountains slope toward the lake and pour water into it, together with the lake itself and its fishery, from the upper fishpond to Mont Risoux [Note: [Col. 1149D] Mont-Risoux.]; the church of Cuarvens, with the lands, tithes, jurisdictions, and households which you possess there; the land of Valle-Leonis [Note: [Col. 1149D] Vaulion.] and the land which you have at Montevilla [Note: [Col. 1149D] Mont-Taville]; the church of Saint Symphorian [Note: [Col. 1150D] Saint-Saphorin-sur-Morges.], with the lands, vineyards, and tithes which you possess in that village and neighbouring hamlets; the lands and vineyards which you possess at Columbario [Note: [Col. 1150D] Colombier.], Lonay [Note: [Col. 1150D] Lonay sur-Morges.], [Col. 1151A] Echichen [Note: [Col. 1151D] Echchiens.], Trivillin [Note: [Col. 1151D] Trivelin-sur-Aubonne.], Alamand [Note: [Col. 1151D] Allaman.], and Bolgez [Note: [Col. 1151D] Bougy.]; the lands, vineyards, and households which Albert of Becrens [Note: [Col. 1151D] Bettens.], of blessed memory, conferred on you; the land which you have at Bructignie [Note: [Col. 1151D] Bretigny.], Villars Luczon [Note: [Col. 1151D] Villard-Lussery.], and Villars Odon; the place with vineyards at Rivorio [Note: [Col. 1151D] Rivaz à Lavaux.], which you have by the gift of Guy, formerly bishop of Lausanne, of blessed memory, together with the tithe of that same land; the church of Ornys [Note: [Col. 1151D] Orny.] with all its appurtenances; the land and vineyards which Louis of Monte Castro and his sons conferred upon your church at Castanerio [Note: [Col. 1152D] Châtagneria, district of Coppet.]; the land and tithes which you have in the place called Subsilva [Note: [Col. 1152D] Suscevaz.]; the allod of Montericherii [Note: [Col. 1152D] Montricher.], which Aymo of Augusta held from Lord Dalmatius; at that same Montericherii, rights of use and pasture throughout the entire lordship of Vufflens, as you reasonably possess them; [Col. 1151B] likewise the land which the lord of that castle freely granted you for building a house; the pastures of Lantifor, which the common people call the limestone of Jura, given to you in alms by Hugh of Grandson; the land which you have at Oulen [Note: [Col. 1152D] Oulens.]; the land and households which you have at Bectens [Note: [Col. 1152D] Bettens.]; the place called Holy Cross [Note: [Col. 1152D] Sainte-Croix, in the Jura.] and two mills belonging to that place, and a certain parcel of cleared land; the land and vineyards which you have at Bremblens [Note: [Col. 1152D] Bremblens.] and Saint Germanus [Note: [Col. 1152D] Saint-Germain.];
