At Basencourt, two shares of the great tithe; at Bois-Hugues, fifteen tenants; at Wellebove, one *modius* of grain; at Manullebre, two shares of the great tithe; at Fria, twenty solidi of Angers currency from rent; at Avenes, two shares of the great tithe and one cultivated holding; at Cui, the church and its parsonage with tithe; at Dompeter, the church and its parsonage with tithe; [Col. 1179C] at Brevolio, the church, its parsonage with tithe and tenants, and land for one ploughland with two meadows; at St. Stephen’s, three solidi; at Humeth, one *modius* of grain; at Menerual, the church and its parsonage with all tithes, rents, holdings, and tenants, together with land for half a ploughland; at Maurum, one cultivated holding and one tenant, with two shares of the tithe.

At Tilly, the church and parsonage with all tithes; at Rubempré, the church and parsonage with tithes, and land for one ploughland; at Sainte-Beuve, the church and parsonage with tithes; at Noyers, two shares of the tithe; at Landa, two shares of the tithe; at Oriolum, one free tenant with one water-right; at Scurnum, [Col. 1179D] seven tenants; at Rofredum, three *modii* of grain. At St. Albinus, the church and parsonage with the whole tithe; at Amecourt, half the village—in land, tenants, woodland, and tithing-rights, excepting the vavassors—and one meadow; at Jolencourt, one mill and acres of land where *versones* are taken [uncertain term]; at Dodelville, two shares of the great and small tithe, with rent from the cultivated holdings; at Tolon monastery, the church and parsonage with the whole tithe, and one *modius* of grain to be rendered from that same tithe to the priest of the aforesaid church; at Fulcerioles, tenants and holdings; at the village called Jande, the church and parsonage with the whole village and tithe, and half-shares in lands and woods, both cultivated and uncultivated; [Col. 1180A] at Campaioles, eighteen *minae* of grain; at Flavacourt, a third part of the small tithe, a third part of the tithe of the small holdings, and, out of nine vessels of the great tithe, five.

At Erengi, out of nine vessels of the great tithe, five, and one holding for making a barn; at Maserias, half the tithe; at Basencourt, a fourth part of the tithe; at Neuville, half the tithe of the small holdings and, from the great tithe, a seventh *mina*; at Thianville, three shares of the tithe, land for one ploughland, one barn, a mill-site on the water, and six tenants; at Gamericourt, the church and churchyard with two shares of the great tithe and one third of the small tithe, together with lordship.

[Col. 1180B] At Bontacourt, one *modius* of wheat in the lord’s barn; at St. Brice, a third part of the small holdings and a third part of the tithe of Robert the vavassor; at Maisnil-Drogon, half the tithe; at Reliac, half the tithe; at Bois-Garnier, the tithe; at Gaagni, the whole tithe; at Fay, a share in the church with two shares of the great tithe and the whole tithe of the small holdings, excepting the fief of Lord Ingelram of Trie, and eight tenants with full jurisdiction.

At Frames, the whole tithe, and from the same tithe three *modii* rendered to the priest for Masses; at the Assumption of Blessed Mary, half the candles; at Bereville, one *modius* of wheat in the Lord’s barn; at Amerville, six tenants and two shares of half [Col. 1180C] the tithe; at Berceium, one *modius* in the lord’s barn for the soul of his brother; at Cortils, two shares of the tithe and a tract of land.

In the valley of Engeltart, six solidi in rent; at Pontoise, three solidi in rent from the house of St. Geremarus, and one enclosed vineyard; at Gensi and at Gergi, one holding with many vineyards; at Bernecourt, half the revenues in lands and vineyards, and one fish-weir in the water, from which eels are rendered to you.

At Noientel, the church and parsonage, two shares of the small tithe, the customary shares of the bread offered at the altar from Christmas until Epiphany, three shares of the candles at the Purification of Blessed Mary, [Col. 1180D] one *modius* of wine in tithe, and five tenants; one tenant in the other village; at Giencourt, a cellar with presses and many vineyards; at Vals, a fourth part of a *mansus* with vineyards.

At Prinsengi, one *mansus* and two shares of Bertha’s tithe; at Blalmicourt, half the great tithe; at Villers, a fourth part of the entire tithe; at Hameviller, half the tithe; at Clares, a third part of the tithe; at Hecherii, twenty *minae* of wheat; at Anet, the church and parsonage, and a fourth part in all tithes of candles and bread; at Ramercourt, one free tenant with the land-dues of his land; at Lamercourt, rents, capons, pennies, and oats.

[Col. 1181A] At Ponchon, the church, parsonage, house, and winepress, with tithes, vineyards, and lands; at Hodene, an enclosed vineyard and, in the bishop’s enclosure, the whole tithe of wine; in the city of Beauvais, by gift of John, a cleric of Beauvais, a house with an enclosed vineyard at Tardona, the village of Tardona, and its mill with lands, tithes, and jurisdictions; in the city of Beauvais, two shares in the fish vicariate, with several fish-hooks, a free oven, and an oven-house exempt from every exaction.

At Esparburg, the church and parsonage with lands, tithes, and tenants; in the mills, four *modii* of wheat with the other revenues; also, in the forest of Bray, from the aforesaid monastery as far as the stream of Spalburg, both for you and for the men of [Col. 1181B] your land, living timber for lodging, deadwood for burning, and living timber for the fences of cultivated holdings; likewise, any swarm or vessel of bees found there shall be yours. If your men are arrested for an offence and judgment is rendered, half the fine shall be yours; the vice-lords of Gerboredo shall have the other half, together with the jurisdiction over bloodshed and the ban in the whole aforesaid forest, excepting birds and hunting, which belong to the bishop.

At Codretum, a barn with lands and woods; the wood of Puteoli with the soil of that land and its *griagium* [uncertain due or right]; the church of St. Lucian with its parsonage and all tithes; the chapel of St. Mary with its parsonage and two shares of the small tithe, including candles at the Purification and Assumption of Blessed Mary; [Col. 1181C] at St. Peter of the Fields, the church with its parsonage, tithes, tenants, and rents; at the village of Puteoli, a chapel and parsonage with all tithes, tenants, and revenues from the bishop’s mills; at Ferrières, two shares in the tithe, half of the mill of Spina with the milling due from Hanachies; the church of Senentis with its parsonage and other dependencies; the village of Herolcourt with full jurisdiction and half the tithe.

At Gornac, free tenants with rents; at Maltis, two *modii* of grain; at St. Mansuet, a third part of the tithe. At Felcheriae, the church of Blessed Mary, the right to present the priest, two [Col. 1181D] shares of the offerings at that church’s altar with all tithes; at St. Mary of the Fields, a share in annual dues, money, candles, and bread; at Moiliense, the church with parsonage and tithes; at Almas, one tithing; at Romiseans, two shares of the tithe from the fief of Ralph of Gisencourt; at St. Mary of Beaupré, two *modii* of wheat and one of oats; at Neuville, two shares of the great tithe both from cultivated lands and from newly cleared land, and six *minae* of oats from the mill; at St. Mary of the Meadow, ten solidi for the churches of Borenc and Basivual; at Alt., one tenant with arable land; at Lumel, two shares of the great tithe, twenty solidi in the parsonage, and six solidi from one small holding; at Hermenriant, [Col. 1182A] two shares of the tithe from the territory of Count Hugh.

Whatever you have in Normandy by gift of Henry, formerly king of England, of illustrious memory; by gift of Geoffrey, formerly count of Anjou and duke of the Normans, of noble memory; by gift of Henry, the illustrious king of the English; whatever you have in England by gift of William, count of Warenne, by gift of Hugh, lord of Gournay, by gift of Philip de Braiose, and by gift of Richard de Escars. Moreover, whatever you have in the archbishopric of Rouen and in the bishoprics of Beauvais and Amiens. In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose clerics and priests and present them to the bishop; if they are suitable, the bishops shall entrust to them the care of souls, so that [Col. 1182B] they shall answer to those bishops in spiritual matters, but to you in temporal matters.

Certainly, concerning your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or concerning the produce of your animals, let no one presume in any way to exact tithes from you. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laypersons, free and released from worldly life, who flee from the world, and retain them in your monastery without any opposition. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your house, to leave that house without his abbot’s permission, even under the pretext of a stricter religious observance; nor may anyone dare retain one who has departed without the security of your common letters. When, moreover, a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding those under interdict and the excommunicated, and in a low voice.

We also grant that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict. Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it by any device of deception or violence, save the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, shall determine ought to be chosen.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be kept whole and unimpaired for the governance and support of those for whom they were granted, and be of benefit to them in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical person, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Alberic, cardinal and chancellor of the Church of St. Bononia, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July [20 June], in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1178 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the nineteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCCCLIV. To the clergy of Salamanca.—That they obey Peter, bishop consecrated by him. (Lateran, 29 June.)

[AVILA, *History of the Antiquities of the City of Salamanca*. Salamanca, 1608, octavo, p. 160.]

[Col. 1183A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the whole clergy of Salamanca: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received with paternal affection of mind our venerable brother Peter, your bishop, when he came to us—a man learned, prudent, and discerning. Having first advanced him to the office of priest, we afterward consecrated him bishop, invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit; and we have judged that he, consecrated by our hands as by the hands of Blessed Peter, should be sent to you. But since it would seem pointless for persons to have a father and shepherd unless they were subject to him with filial devotion, by these apostolic letters we admonish, command, and enjoin your whole body that you humbly render to the aforesaid bishop, as ruler of your souls, the obedience and reverence due in all things, and obey his commands without any opposition. We strictly warn you not to presume to seize tithes by lay power and on your own authority. If you do so, we shall, by the Lord’s authority, hold valid and firm the sentence which the aforementioned bishop shall canonically pronounce against you on this account.

[Col. 1183C]

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of July [29 June].

MCCCLV. To Alfonso, king of the Castilians.—He commends Peter, bishop of Salamanca. (Lateran, 15 January.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, ALFONSO, illustrious king of the Castilians: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Desiring in every respect to give effect to your prayers and petitions, as far as we can do so with God and justice, and effectively to promote them, and considering the learning and integrity of the letters of our venerable brother Peter, bishop of Salamanca, we advanced him to the priesthood after a definite title had been assigned to him in the city; afterward, having invoked the presence of the Holy Spirit, we took care solemnly to confer upon him the gift of consecration. Accordingly, as a prudent and discerning man, faithful, as we believe in every respect, and devoted to royal excellence, we judged that he, consecrated by our hands as by the hands of Blessed Peter, should be sent to his church. By these apostolic letters we ask, admonish, and exhort Your Serenity in the Lord that, in consideration of us and of his fidelity and devotion, which he has repeatedly displayed toward you, you love, uphold, and honour this bishop; and that you effectively furnish strength and aid for the recovery of the rights of the church entrusted to him. Thus he may be bound to remain ever more devoted and faithful to Your Highness on this account, while you may happily deserve to obtain from Almighty God an unfailing reward thereby, and to expect from us the fullest thanks.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of July [15 July].

MCCCLVI. To [Ubaldo], archbishop of Pisa, and all bishops and abbots established throughout Tuscany.—He invites them to a council to be celebrated at Rome on “the first Sunday of the coming Lent” (18 February 1179). (Tusculum, 21 September.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 211.]

Because in the field of the Lord, which is the Church, shoots of vices daily arise and spring up like thorns and thistles—both because the human disposition is inclined to evil from its youth, and because the hostile man does not cease, out of his malice, to sow tares over the field and strives to choke the good growth—it is necessary that the cultivators be diligent: now to uproot and cut away what has already sprung up; now to bar the way to harmful growths yet to arise; and thereafter to graft in fruitful growth and sow good seed which, God making it fruitful, may bring forth thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold fruit. For those words of the Lord also appear to express this, by which He instructed Jeremiah the prophet—and in him the evangelical priest—saying: “My words [are] in your mouth. Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms, to pluck up, to pull down, to destroy, to scatter abroad, to build, and to plant” (Jeremiah 1).

Although this duty rests upon all rulers of churches, it presses much more strongly upon the bishop of the Roman city, who is known to have received from the Lord Jesus Christ, in Blessed Peter, both the charge to be head of the Church and an express and special command to feed the Lord’s sheep and strengthen his brethren (Luke 22; John 21). Hence, although insufficient in merits, we have been called by God’s ordering, as pleased Him, to the care of the Apostolic See and the ministry of the universal Church. Because we see very many matters in the Church of God requiring correction—both to amend what appears worthy of amendment and to promulgate what may seem conducive to the salvation of the faithful—we have decreed that ecclesiastical persons be summoned from various regions. By their presence and counsel, salutary measures may be enacted, and what is good may, according to the custom of the ancient Fathers, be provided for and confirmed by many; for if this were done in a particular manner, it could not easily have full force.

Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command you to take care to cooperate with all desire in this our arrangement, and, God guiding you, to come to the city of Rome on the first Sunday of the coming Lent, so that, through the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, what must be done may be done by common endeavour, both in correcting abuses and in establishing what is pleasing to God; and that with one shoulder we may lift the ark of the Lord and with one mouth glorify God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Given at Tusculum, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October [21 September].

MCCCLVII. To the archbishops, bishops, and abbots of Hungary. Same subject. (Tusculum, 21 September.)

[FEJÉR, *Diplomatic Codex of Hungary*, II, 193.]

“Because in the field,” etc.

MCCCLVIII. To Guarin, archbishop of Bourges, his suffragans, and the abbots established throughout their dioceses.—Same subject. (Tusculum, September [?].)

[D. BOUQUET, *Collection*, XV, 962.]

“Because in the field,” etc.

MCCCLIX. He takes the church of St. Opportuna at Paris under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Tusculum, 1 October.)

[Dom FÉLIBIEN, *History of Paris*, III, proofs, 34.]

[Col. 1185B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of Saint Opportuna, present and future, canonically appointed in perpetuity.

A pious request of the will, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we take under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this writing; decreeing that whatever possessions, etc., among which we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of the Holy Innocents; the watery land called the marshes, adjoining the city of Paris, as our venerable brethren William, formerly archbishop of Sens and now archbishop of Reims, legate of the Apostolic See, and Maurice, bishop of Paris, and our dearest son in Christ Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, are known to have confirmed to you and your church and strengthened by their writings; likewise the capiceria (office of the capicerus) of that church, as Theobald, of good memory, bishop of the Church of Paris, reasonably adjudged it to you; and also the liberty of your cloister and the increase of the ancient prebends made from the new rent of the marsh, as the aforesaid our brethren the archbishop of Reims and Maurice, bishop of Paris, granted by their authentic writings—we confirm these to you and to your said church by apostolic authority.

We therefore decree, etc.

(The subscriptions follow.)

Given at Tusculum, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of October [1 October], in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1178 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the twentieth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCCCLX. To the bishops of London and Winchester, observing “that judgment concerning possessions belongs to the king, not to the Church,” he commands them to “leave the judgment of possessions to Henry, king of the English.”

(Tusculum, 1 October.—TWISDEN, *Histories of English Writers*, I, 602.)

[Col. 1186A]

MCCCLXI. He takes the monastery of St. Thomas of Paraclete (at Ebelholt) under protection and confirms its goods and rights.

(TORKELIN, *Diplomata of Arne Magnusson*, I, 50.)

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, abbot of St. Thomas of Paraclete, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

A pious request of the will ought to be brought to completion by a corresponding result, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit requested, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and take under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Blessed Thomas of Paraclete, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this writing. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order which is known to have been established in your church according to God, the Rule of Blessed Augustine, and the institution of the brethren of St. Victor of Paris, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, the Lord granting it, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of Eskilli Island, with the island itself and its other appurtenances; the church of Julaechae, with the land and tithe belonging to it and its other appurtenances; the dwelling in that village belonging to the same house, with all its dependencies; the mill situated near Waraebro, with its appurtenances; the church of Tiaereby and the dwelling situated there, with fields, meadows, woods, and its other appurtenances; the dwelling at Hathelosae, with fields, meadows, woods, and its other appurtenances; the whole village called Naeveth, with all its land, meadows, and woods, free and exempt, with its other appurtenances; the fisheries of Clona and the other fisheries which you hold in common with the other inhabitants of that district; a court in the city of Roskilde, with its houses and their appurtenances; a third part of the tithe in the churches of Annesae, Haelsinghe, Craekom, and Alsentorp; and the entire tithe of the church of Tieraeby, which our venerable brother Absalon, then bishop of Roskilde and now archbishop of Lund, reasonably granted you to possess in perpetuity; the village called Fretherslof, with fields, woods, meadows, mills, and other appurtenances; and the church of that village with its tithes.

Certainly, concerning your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or concerning the produce of your animals, let no one presume to exact tithes from you. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laypersons, free and released from worldly life, fleeing from the world, and retain them without any opposition. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your house, through any fickleness, to leave that cloister without his abbot’s permission; nor may anyone dare retain one who has departed without the security of your common letters. When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated or those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a low voice. In the parish churches which you possess, you may also elect clerics and present them to the bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them, so that they must answer to him regarding spiritual matters and to you regarding temporal matters.

Wishing also, with paternal care, to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosures of your houses or granges to commit violence, robbery, or theft; to set fire; or to seize or kill a person. We likewise decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, without prejudice nevertheless to the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be kept whole for the governance and support of those for whom they were granted, and be of benefit to them in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical person in the future, etc.

Given in the year of the Lord 1198, and in the twentieth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

WITHIN THE YEARS 1159–1179

MCCCLXII. To the bishops of Parma and Reggio.—That they are to ensure the restoration of certain goods to the monks of Nonantola. (Anagni, 25 November.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *History of Nonantola*, II, 278.]

[Col. 1187D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, the bishops of Parma and Reggio: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard, and have been astonished, that our venerable brother O. [Omnibonus], bishop of Verona, and R., son of the count, have presumed on their own authority to usurp certain possessions which the monastery of Nonantola held peacefully in the estate of Nugaria [the transmitted syntax is uncertain]. Since we ought not to endure this patiently, we command your discretion by these apostolic letters, with the force of a precept, to summon the parties before you and carefully investigate the truth of this matter. If it is established before you that this is so, take care to admonish and earnestly induce the aforesaid bishop to revoke as soon as possible what has been done so wickedly, restore the abbot and brethren of that monastery without delay to possession of those lands, and not allow them to be unlawfully troubled concerning them. But if that bishop does not do this, do not delay to carry it out yourselves by our authority, all contradiction and appeal set aside. And if the aforesaid R., after the brethren have been restored to possession of the lands, unlawfully troubles them concerning them, bind him, appeals being set aside, with the bond of anathema.

Given at Anagni, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December [25 November].

MCCCLXIII. To the people of Nonantola.—That P., who has given his whole life to God, is to be judged free from his vow. (Anagni, 26 November.)

[Ibid., p. 275.]

[Col. 1188C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of Nonantola, the archpriest, and the canons of the people of Nonantola: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Coming to the clemency of the Apostolic See with your letters, sons archpriest and canons, P., bearer of the present letter, set before us in a humble report—and from those letters themselves we learned—that, inspired by the grace of divine revelation, he built from the foundations the church of St. Mary,

> [Note: [Col. 1187D] Perhaps this is the church of Santa Maria delle Banzole outside Nonantola, frequently named in the records of the abbey.]

which had been demolished because of the war of the Modenese; and there he vowed to serve the Lord perpetually. The same pious and merciful Lord, through P.’s exertion and labour and through the merits of his life, enlarged that church in possessions and other resources, and made it notably celebrated and splendid in the devotion of women and men. But after a long period had passed, because he could not endure the various temptations which came upon him, he left the church by the River Taro,

> [Note: [Col. 1187D] It seems evident that this refers to the bridge over the Taro, of which some ruins may still be seen near Castel Guelfo, beyond the torrent, whose course has now changed. This brief therefore provides the hitherto unknown information concerning the origin of that bridge itself. From a brief of Innocent IV, of 1244, preserved in the archive of the community of Parma, it is gathered that certain brethren were entrusted with its custody, to whom Innocent III had allowed the right to live according to the rule of those of Altopascio. In another brief of the same Innocent IV, of 1253, likewise preserved there, the bridge is called: “At Streta, which is called the Via Claudia,” following the custom of the later ages of calling the road Claudia, though it should properly be called Aemilia. Near that bridge was a hospital or convent belonging to the bishop of Parma; in 1304, at the request of Benedict XI, he ceded it to Cistercian monks of Fontevivo. I owe these notices to the repeatedly praised Father Irenaeus Affò.]

above Parma, where many people used to drown, and with the Lord’s help built a bridge and performed many deeds which appear pleasing and acceptable to God and men. But since you are doubtful and uncertain whether he remains bound by his earlier vow, and whether he was allowed to change the place where he had promised himself to maintain stability, let it be made known to your discretion by these letters that the said P. did not break his vow by transferring himself to another place, where he is able to bear more fruit for the Lord and render worthier fruit. We therefore command you to declare that he is not bound by that vow, but is rather released from it; for one does not violate a vow who changes it for the better.

Moreover, because the same P. has laboured greatly for the building up of the aforesaid church and therefore desires above all things that a suitable person be appointed there, by the authority of this present letter we enjoin you to institute in the aforesaid church, with his counsel, one of yourselves, sons canons, or another person of honourable life and conduct, who is suitable and must comply with P.’s counsel in the ordering of that church.

For we believe that greater benefits will thereby accrue to that church, to which it is evident that very great increase has come through the care and diligence of the aforesaid P.

Given at Anagni, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December [26 November].

MCCCLXIV. He takes the nunnery of St. Mary of Kala under protection and confirms its goods. (Anagni, 28 November.)

[D. DUPLESSIS, *History of Meaux*, II, 48.]

[Col. 1189C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ HELEVISE, abbess, and the nuns of the monastery of St. Mary of Kala: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Apostolic See ought to grant protection to prudent virgins who, under the habit of religion and with lamps lit, continually prepare themselves through works of holiness to go forth to meet the bridegroom, lest perhaps, etc. [lacuna] Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, the Lord granting it, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and those who succeed you. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The village in which your monastery is situated, namely Kala; whatever you reasonably possess in the diocese of Meaux at Mintriacum, together with the patronage of the church; the whole village of Colons [lacuna]; and the church of St. Andrew of Kala, etc. [lacuna]

Given at Anagni, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December [28 November].

MCCCLXV. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the collegiate church of Saints Michael and Gudula. (Anagni.)

[MIRAEUS, *Diplomatic Works*, II, 1179.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GODESCALC, dean, and the canons of the church of St. Michael and St. Gudula of Brussels, present and future, canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that we grant effect to reasonable petitioners, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wish and truth does not fail it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we take the aforementioned church with all its appurtenances under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, the Lord granting it, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The site itself on which your church stands, with its cemetery and adjoining grounds; the chaplaincy of St. James at Caldenberga, with all its appurtenances; the chaplaincy of St. Nicholas in the lower market, with every right and appurtenance; also the three hospitals within the circuit of your town, with all their appurtenances, for which you are bound to provide for the reception of the poor and pilgrims; the church of St. John at Molenbeke, with tithes, lands, and all that you are known to possess within that parish; the church of Melsbroeck, granted to you in perpetuity by Peter, formerly its parson, through the hand of the bishop of Cambrai, with all its appurtenances; likewise the small tithe which you hold within the boundaries of your parish, with meadows, gardens, holdings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and with all churches and tithes which you possess in the diocese of Cambrai.

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we confirm to you the liberties and ancient, reasonable customs of that church. We further decree that no one within the boundaries of your parish shall be buried or baptized except at the mother church, save lepers, to whom you have granted a cemetery with an oratory outside the town according to the tenor of the arrangement made concerning this matter, as has been established from ancient times and hitherto observed.

We also enact that the people of your entire parish shall gather at the mother church on the principal solemnities of the year, to hear and receive the divine offices, as was established and observed from the first foundation of the church. When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices quietly behind closed doors, without ringing bells and excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict.

We therefore decree, etc.

Given at Anagni.

WITHIN THE YEARS 1160–1179

[Col. 1191A]

MCCCLXVI. To the chapter of Blessed Martin of Tours.—That no person of servile condition or born outside lawful marriage be received as a canon. (Anagni, 10 March.)

[*Defence of the Church of Saint-Martin of Tours*, 21.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the dean, treasurer, and chapter of Blessed Martin of Tours: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since we are bound to extend the favour of the Apostolic See to all churchmen in matters pertaining to the adornment and increase of churches, we are the more willing, as we ought, and more readily to comply with you in these matters, the more diligently we are bound to seek the benefit and honour of your church—as of one especially and properly our own. It has indeed been reported to us that, since that church is distinguished and highly eminent among the other churches of Gaul, and enjoys the special privilege of liberty, there has from ancient times been an approved and commendable custom there: that no one of servile condition, or one not born of lawful marriage, is to be received as a canon in that church. We therefore wholly approve this same custom and desire that it have perpetual force. As it has been confirmed by the oath of the canons of that church, we hold it ratified and firm; and, confirming it by apostolic authority, fortify it by the protection of this writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of Blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, on the sixth day before the Ides of March [10 March].

MCCCLXVII. To Hugh, bishop of Genoa.—On behalf of William, lord of Montpellier. He forbids the Genoese to injure the port of Maguelone. (Anagni, 14 October.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Collection*, XV, 947.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the bishop of Genoa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son William of Montpellier represented to us in his complaint that our beloved sons, the consuls and people of Genoa,

> [Note: [Col. 1191D] Men of that age generally wrote “Januenses”; hence the original text of this and the following instrument appears to have been somewhat altered.]

seeking dominion at sea, frequently attack his port, destroy ships by fire, violently despoil pilgrims and merchants of their goods, and compel them to avoid Genoa. Since, however greatly we love the aforesaid consuls and city in the Lord, we can neither endure nor ought to endure that the said nobleman and his people should suffer molestation or injury in their own right—for, owing to his devotion and that of his father, we are bound to assist him with particular zeal—we command your brotherhood by these apostolic letters, with the force of a precept, diligently to warn your consuls and citizens to desist from such presumption. If, once warned, they do not desist, punish them by our authority, all contradiction and appeal set aside, in such a manner that others who hear of it may not presume to do the like.

Given at Anagni, on the fifth day before the Ides of October [11 October], in the tenth year of our pontificate.

> [Note: [Col. 1191D] The tenth year of Alexander’s pontificate fell in 1169, a year in which he did not stay at Anagni. Alexander resided in that city in 1173, 1174, and also 1175 and 1176, as is established from various records.]

MCCCLXVIII. To the consuls and people of Genoa.—He dissuades them from wrongs against William, lord of Montpellier. (Anagni, 11 October.)

[Ibid.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the consuls and people of Genoa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

A frequent and repeated complaint has reached us from our beloved son, the nobleman William of Montpellier, that you, seeking dominion at sea, frequently attack his port, destroy ships by fire, violently despoil pilgrims and merchants of their goods, and compel them to avoid Genoa.

> [Note: [Col. 1191D] In the treaty concluded in 1166 for five years between the Genoese and the citizens of Narbonne, the Narbonese stipulated, among other things: “So long as there is war between the Genoese and the Pisans, we shall receive no Pisan coming from the sea, nor his property; [lacuna] nor shall we carry by sea a person or money belonging to anyone not of our land, unless he is Genoese or the money belongs to a Genoese [lacuna]; excepting pilgrims, whom we may carry in one ship per year, provided that it is not a ship of the Hospital or Temple, and that those pilgrims are not from Montpellier, Saint-Gilles, or the territory from the Rhône to Nice.” Vol. III, *History of the Ocean*, documentary section, col. 114. From these words we understand that hostility long prevailed between the Genoese and the lord of Montpellier, as also with the lord or count of Saint-Gilles or Toulouse, who certainly favoured the Pisans against the Genoese.]

Certainly, the more the almighty Lord has exalted you and your city, and the more graciously He has looked upon you in His mercy, the more earnestly you ought to abstain from acts by which you appear to incur the reproach of men, peril to your salvation, and deserved fear of the judgment of divine vengeance. Since, however greatly we love you and your city in the Lord, we cannot and ought not to endure that the said nobleman and his people should suffer molestation in their own right, for we are bound to assist him with particular zeal owing to his devotion and that of his father. We admonish and command your whole body to desist from such injuries and molestations, because it is not fitting to seek such dominion at sea—dominion which we do not even read that pagans sought. But if you do not desist from such presumption, we have instructed our venerable brother, the bishop, to punish your offenders and violators of our command by our authority in such a manner that others who see it may not presume to do the like.

Given at Anagni, on the fifth day before the Ides of October [11 October], [in the tenth year of our pontificate].

> [Note: [Col. 1193D] The words in brackets were added by another hand.]

MCCCLXIX. To the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Passignano.—He confirms to them the right of patronage in certain churches. (Anagni, 12 October.)

[LAMI, *Monuments of the Florentine Church*, I, 219.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Passignano: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It becomes us willingly to admit, and to bring to effective completion, the petitions of religious men that accord with reason and do not depart from ecclesiastical propriety. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we confirm to you and, through you, to your monastery by apostolic authority, and fortify by the protection of this writing, the right of patronage which you hold in the church of Luviano; whatever you hold in the parish of that church between the two rivers called Cassiani; the right of patronage of the church of Maiano and whatever you hold in that village; the right of patronage of the church of Fonte-Rutuli, its annual rent, and the other revenues which you receive annually from it; whatever you hold in the estate of Travalle; the right of patronage of the church of Matraio; and the right of patronage of the church of Collebono, as you reasonably possess them.

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we prohibit anyone from presuming to alter the ordinances which, in accordance with God, the Rule of Blessed Benedict, and the ancient and reasonable custom of your monastery, you have made or shall make by common agreement in your chapter; rather, we command that they be observed inviolate.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation and constitution or in any way oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, etc.

Given at Anagni, on the fourth day before the Ides of October [12 October].

WITHIN THE YEARS 1166–1179

MCCCLXX. To the provost and chapter of Viborg.—He reports that he has taken the nunnery of St. Margaret of Asmiald under protection. (Lateran, 20 February.)

[TORCKELIN, *Diplomata of Arne Magnusson*, I, 23.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the provost and chapter of the Church of Viborg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1194A] We are moved by the duty of our pastoral office, so that, since by the Lord’s disposition we hold the governance of the Roman Church, we are bound to take care of all churches and to extend apostolic protection to them.

Therefore, dearly beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the church of St. Margaret of Asmiald, in which your sisters are devoted to divine service, together with its appurtenances, and strengthen it by the safeguard of this present writing; decreeing that the canonical order known to have been established there according to God and the Rule of St. Augustine shall be observed there inviolably for all time. This church, moreover, just as you have hitherto reasonably and peaceably possessed it and still possess it at present [Col. 1194B], we confirm to you and, through you, to the aforesaid Church of Viborg, by apostolic authority. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation and protection, or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, 20 February.

MCCCLXXI. To the clerics established throughout the archdeaconry of Berkshire.—He grants them various privileges. (Lateran, 22 February.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, etc., I, 43.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons established throughout the archdeaconry of Berkshire, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although unworthy, the care of all Churches has been entrusted to us; and, just as by the obligation of our office we are compelled to provide that subjects do not withhold from their superiors the reverence and honour due to them, so likewise we wish to prevent subjects from being unduly burdened by their superiors. Therefore, providing with paternal solicitude for your peace, by apostolic authority we grant you that you shall not be compelled to furnish dogs or hawks to your archdeacon, nor to receive him more often than once in a year; on that occasion you are to provide him with necessities for one day and one night, for only seven riders [Col. 1194D], an equal number of persons, and three servants on foot.

Therefore let no person whatsoever infringe this page of our grant or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, 22 February.

MCCCLXXII. To the bishop of Chalon and the abbot of La Ferté.—That they should compel certain knights to restore what they have taken from the monastery of Tournus. (Lateran, 11 March.)

[JUENIN, *Hist. de Tournus*, 177.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Chalon [Col. 1195A], and to his beloved son the abbot of La Ferté, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The complaint of our beloved son, the abbot of Tournus, has reached our ears: the knights of Chabanes are violently holding their port, while Arduin of Sala and Guy Rufus have not hesitated to take by violent hand the mounts of two of his monks. To this is added that R. of Lent has violently occupied Chapiz, an estate of the aforesaid monastery, and refuses to restore it to the said abbot.

Since it is incumbent upon us to defend the goods of that monastery and to restrain, from unlawful oppressions, the insolence of wicked men, we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that you take care to warn and diligently induce the aforesaid men to restore without difficulty to the above-mentioned abbot all that they have taken and withheld, and to leave him in peace; or else that they do not delay to render full satisfaction under the examination of your justice. But if, when compelled, they do neither of these things, then, all pretext and contradiction ceasing, bind them with the bond of anathema, forbidding the celebration of offices in their lands, so long as all matters have not there been settled, except for penances and baptism; and cause both the sentence of excommunication and that of interdict to be inviolably observed.

Given at the Lateran, 11 March.

MCCCLXXIII. To the archbishops of Bourges and Besançon, etc.—He exhorts them to protect the goods of the monastery of Tournus. (Lateran, 13 March.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1195C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishops of Bourges and Besançon, and J[OHN], bishop of Poitiers, legate of the Apostolic See, and to the other bishops in whose dioceses the churches and possessions of the monastery of Tournus are situated, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of Tournus, assert that they endure many oppressions from your parishioners [Col. 1195D], it becomes us to exercise pastoral solicitude, lest through your negligence the goods of the aforesaid brethren be exposed to the plundering of evil men. Therefore we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic letters that, whenever you receive a complaint from those brethren against your parishioners, you admonish their wrongdoers, without fruitless delay, to make suitable satisfaction for their offences or to render justice; and compel them by sentence of excommunication. Carry out our command effectively, so that you cannot be reproached for negligence, nor those brethren be forced, with good reason, to trouble us.

Given at the Lateran, 13 March.

MCCCLXXIV. He grants to Nicholas, prior, and the brethren of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem the church of St. Giles, situated at Rome near the Golden Gate. (Lateran, 14 March.)

[Eug. de ROZIÈRE, *Cartul. du Saint-Sépulcre*, 272.]

[Col. 1196A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons NICHOLAS, prior, and the brethren of the Holy Sepulchre, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Taking most carefully into account the manifold affection of your devotion and sincerity, which you splendidly show toward us and the Church of God, and the fervour of your religious life and uprightness, we willingly and with especial zeal direct our attention to your advantage and advancement; and we apply more ardently care and diligence alike to the enlargement and prosperity of the church entrusted to you [Col. 1196B]. Induced by this consideration, we have granted by apostolic authority to your devotion the church of St. Giles, situated at Rome near the Golden Gate and close to the church of Blessed Peter, together with the hospital house adjoining it, in order that, with the Lord’s aid, religious life may be established there, and that the church itself and the house may be restored through your efforts, as will appear more clearly from our rescript of confirmation and grant. Therefore by apostolic letters we ask, admonish, and command all of you that, in order that a pattern of religious life and uprightness may be established in the aforesaid church as is fitting, you devote yourselves vigorously [Col. 1196C] and swiftly to this task, and promptly appoint to its governance persons among you who are more mature and more upright, continually beseeching Christ’s boundless mercy for us and for the peace of the Church.

Given at the Lateran, 14 March.

MCCCLXXV. To the abbot and brethren of the monastery of St. Denis. (Lateran, 28 March.)

[DOUBLET, *Hist. de Saint-Denys*, p. 508.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and brethren of the church of St. Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we should apply ourselves with greater zeal to the prosperity of your monastery, because that monastery is known to belong in a special manner to the protection and disposition of the Apostolic See and of ourselves [Col. 1196D]. Therefore, wishing to provide with paternal solicitude for the security of your monastery, we forbid by apostolic authority any abbot of that monastery to presume to give to his relatives or to others the lands and revenues belonging to it, houses, or even property arising from escheats, or the domestic offices, except only those which belong to clerical servants; nor may he dare to borrow more than one hundred pounds without the consent of the whole chapter, or of its greater and sounder part. Nor may any monk borrow anything from another without the abbot’s consent; but he who holds a domestic office shall not borrow more than one hundred shillings [Col. 1197A] except with the abbot’s consent. We also decree that the abbot shall have his own seal, since it is neither honourable nor fitting for him to remain without a seal. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 28 March.

MCCCLXXVI. To Simon, bishop of Meaux.—That no parish church be granted to anyone who does not reside. (Lateran, 1 April.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 1080.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Meaux, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as it belongs to our office to prohibit what is improper, so it is especially fitting for us [Col. 1197B] to establish what is right and to strengthen what has been established by the protection of apostolic authority. Induced by this reasoning, we have judged that it should be prohibited by apostolic authority that anyone in your bishopric may hold a parish church unless he is willing to serve it in person, without prejudice to mercy toward those unable to be personally present because illness or another canonical cause prevents them.

Given at the Lateran, … before the Kalends of April.

MCCCLXXVII. He informs certain archbishops that he has taken the monastery of St. Nicholas of Angers under his protection. (Lateran, 12 April.)

[Abbey of St. Nicholas of Angers, p. 80, according to Bréquigny, *Table chron.*, III, 535.]

[Col. 1197C]

MCCCLXXVIII. To the archbishop of Bourges and the bishops of Clermont and Le Puy.—That they should ensure observance of the sentence promulgated for the monastery of Tournus. (Lateran, 23 April.)

[JUENIN, *Hist. de Tournus*, 178.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishop of Bourges and the bishops of Clermont and Le Puy, greeting and apostolic blessing.

No, or only slight, reverence would be paid to ecclesiastical severity if persons excommunicated by one authority were to be admitted by others to the sacraments of the Church without suitable satisfaction [Col. 1197D]; and ease of pardon would more often be an incentive to sin. Therefore, since ecclesiastical bonds are not to be held in contempt—for sometimes a person incurs a greater guilt by contempt than he had previously deserved from the original offence—we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to observe the sentence reasonably promulgated by delegated judges under our authority for the monastery of Tournus or its members, and to cause it to be inviolably observed by all until worthy satisfaction has been made.

Given at the Lateran, 23 April.

MCCCLXXIX. He gives the same command to the archbishop of Vienne.

(Ibid.)

MCCCLXXX. To the consuls and people of Siena.—He confirms the peace concerning boundaries between the Sienese and the Florentines. (Lateran, 17 May.)

[MURATORI, *Antiq. Ital.*, VI, 399.]

[Col. 1198A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the consuls and people of Siena, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the tenor of the public instrument submitted to us, and from the report of our beloved son the plebanus of St. Agnes, we have fully learned that, in the settlement of peace between you and the Florentines, those Florentines surrendered to your Church and city whatever is contained within the boundaries of your bishopric, and strengthened their surrender with oaths and public instruments. [Col. 1198B] So that no dispute concerning the boundaries between you and them may arise in the future, you have earnestly and diligently requested that we confirm them to you by apostolic authority; and we have judged that they should be stated by their proper names: the Sienese Valley, the Road of Poci, Monte Bifurcato, Astrago of Cagnano, where the church of St. Damian stood, Galliano, the castle of Piniungo, the Ditch of Bolsano, the Pool of Strega, Pruno of Campo Tatoli, the Hill of St. Mary, Piumferreum, Druove of George. At Ciparello, two boundary-markers: one beside the church, the other near the house of the sons of Malaven. And the boundaries of the parish church of St. Agnes, namely Donicatum at Uspiano, formerly of Sasso; the Stream of John, which runs at the foot of Mortennano; and the holding of that parish church at Villole; the house formerly of the son of Leolo on the hill, as far as the cornel tree; the spring on the road; and the boundaries designated above at Ciparello, in the Sienese Valley, and the Road of Poci; and the parish church of St. Agnes at Poggio Bonizio, with the people of that same parish church, other properties having been assigned.

Accordingly, graciously yielding to your just requests and rejoicing in your concord, we confirm by apostolic authority to your Church and city the settlement made between you and the Florentines with the agreement of those present, and with the consent of our venerable brother the bishop of Florence and our beloved son the bishop-elect of Siena, and ratified and accepted between the aforesaid parties by mutual oaths and charters, together with everything contained therein, as is set forth in the public instruments; and we strengthen it by the safeguard of this present writing [Col. 1198D]. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, 17 May.

MCCCLXXXI. He confirms the possessions of the canons of the Church of Cesena. (Lateran, 30 May.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, II, 451.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the canons of the church of Cesena, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1199A] It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners, and bring to effect and fulfil the requests that do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, dearly beloved sons in the Lord, concurring with grateful assent in your just requests, we decree that the privileges which the bishops of Cesena are known reasonably to have granted you shall remain valid; decreeing that no person may infringe this page of our confirmation, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 30 May.

IN THE YEAR 1173–1179.

MCCCLXXXII. To the abbot and canons of Lucerne.—He confirms to them a certain tract of land. (Anagni, 11 November.)

[*Neustria pia*, 797.]

[Col. 1199B]

ALEXANDER, etc., to his beloved sons the abbot and canons of Lucerne, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are moved by the office of piety and urged by the obligation of the administration we have undertaken to foster, insofar as we can with God’s help, the freedom of religious houses, so that the persons devoted in them to divine service may apply themselves more freely to the observance which they profess, the more fully they are safeguarded from secular harassment. Induced by this reasoning, and graciously assenting to your prayers, we hold valid the surrender of the land lying between your principal fishpond and the wood, and Thar, and Tharnet, made by Hasculf of Suligney to Achard of good memory, formerly bishop of Avranches [Col. 1199C]; and by apostolic authority we decree that none of Hasculf’s successors, under pretext of the right which he is said to have possessed in the aforesaid land before the surrender, may claim any patronage or jurisdiction in your abbey, known to have been built there. Therefore let no person whatsoever infringe this page, etc.

Given at Anagni, 11 November.

IN THE YEAR 1175–1179.

MCCCLXXXIII. To Richard, archbishop of Canterbury.—Concerning the coronation of the kings of England. (Anagni, November.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, etc., I, 26.]

[Col. 1199D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother RICHARD, archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The greater the devotion which you show toward us and the Roman Church, and the more fully you are known to have deserved the favour of the Apostolic See, the more willingly we wish to preserve intact your dignities and rights, so that you may grow ever more ardent in devotion to us and to the Church, knowing that we are diligent and in every respect attentive to defend your rights.

[Col. 1200A] Therefore, since a controversy has arisen concerning the coronation and anointing of a king, and since we wish to provide that neither you nor your successors suffer in this matter any injury to your right or dignity, we have judged, with the common counsel of our brethren, that we should grant you this: within the boundaries of the province of Canterbury, in churches belonging to the jurisdiction of the Church of Canterbury, or in churches which belong specially to blessed Peter and to us, no one except the archbishop of Canterbury—or, during a vacancy of the see, the person acting in the place of that archbishop by command of the Church of Canterbury—may crown or anoint kings.

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our constitution or in any way oppose it [Col. 1200B]. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, 4 November.

IN THE YEAR 1178–1179.

MCCCLXXXIV. To Master Girard Puella.—He restores revenues voluntarily relinquished during the schism. (Lateran, 15 March.)

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 963.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Master GIRARD Puella, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1200C] Your learning, probity, and uprightness of character urge and exhort us to love you sincerely with the affection of charity as a worthy, upright, and learned man, and to foster you with a special prerogative of love and favour. Induced by this consideration, and wishing to honour your person with the special privilege of our affection, we restore to you, by the customary clemency and kindness of the Apostolic See, and through the intervention of our venerable brother the archbishop of Mainz, the revenues which you voluntarily remitted in the German kingdom during the height of the schism, no one compelling you. We decree that it shall not detract from or stain your reputation [Col. 1200D], nor be able in future to create prejudice against your promotion, that you are known to have held revenues among schismatics for some time.

Given at the Lateran, 15 March.

MCCCLXXXV. He grants to William, abbot of St. Denis, and his successors the use of the mitre, ring, and sandals. (Lateran, 30 March.)

[D. FÉLIBIEN, *Hist. de l’Egl. de St-Denys*, Pr., p. CXI.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WILLIAM, abbot of St. Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

To those whom we love with more sincere charity, and whom we know to be readier in devotion to blessed Peter and to ourselves, we ought to grant a more ample prerogative [Col. 1201A] of honour and favour. Therefore, moved by the sincerity of your devotion and faith, and wishing that your monastery enjoy a special privilege of dignity from the Apostolic See, we grant, by the customary clemency of the Apostolic See, to you and your successors the use of the mitre, ring, and sandals.

Given at the Lateran, 30 March.

MCCCLXXXVI. He confirms to Simon, formerly abbot of St. Mary of Blois, the benefices conferred on him by John, bishop of Chartres, after his resignation of office. (Lateran, 9 April.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, VIII, Instrumenta 425.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SIMON, formerly abbot of St. Mary [Col. 1201B] of Blois, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us on your behalf that, considering the labours and hardships of prelates, you chose to be lowly in the house of God and to serve the Lord without the anxiety of ecclesiastical government rather than glory in the title of prelate, and therefore resigned the administration of the aforesaid church. In view of this humility, our venerable brother J., bishop of Chartres, and our beloved son Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Chrysogonus and legate of the Apostolic See, with the consent of the brethren of that church, granted you for your maintenance, to possess freely as long as you live, the house of Monticelles and Bueron with their appurtenances. Let no one, therefore, etc. Should anyone, moreover, etc.

[Col. 1201C] Given at the Lateran, 9 April.

MCCCLXXXVII. To Simon, bishop of Meaux. (Lateran.)

[DUPLESSIS, *Hist. de l’Eglise de Meaux*.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother SIMON, bishop of Meaux, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as it belongs to our office, etc. … Therefore, induced by this reasoning, we have judged that it should be prohibited by apostolic authority that anyone in your bishopric may hold a parish church unless he is willing to serve it in person, without prejudice to mercy toward those who cannot be personally present because illness or another canonical cause prevents them [Col. 1201D].

Given at the Lateran, …

IN THE YEAR 1179.

MCCCLXXXVIII. He takes the monastery of SS. Flora and Lucilla at Arezzo under his protection, and confirms its goods and privileges. (Tusculum, 2 January.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullar. Casin.*, 194.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HOMINIDEUS, abbot of the monastery of St. Flora, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

[Col. 1202A] A pious petition ought to be pursued to its fulfilment, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth worthily and the benefit sought may assuredly acquire force. Therefore, dearly beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just requests, after the example of our predecessor Pope Innocent of holy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery of St. Flora, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the safeguard of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s assistance [Col. 1202B], shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

(He enumerates their possessions.)

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any deceitful device or violence, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall determine should be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of St. Benedict. We also decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; saving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead [Col. 1202C] are taken.

We decree, therefore, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of SS. John and Paul at Pammachius. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Mark. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Susanna. I, Vivian, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cinthius, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Cecilia. I, Arduin, cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. [Col. 1202D] I, Ardicio, cardinal-deacon of the title of St. Theodore. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of the title of SS. Cosmas and Damian. I, Matthew, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary the New. I, Bernard, cardinal-deacon of the title of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

Given at Tusculum through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of January, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1178 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twentieth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

MCCCLXXXIX. To John, bishop, and the chapter of Chartres.—That dignities be granted only to those who promise residence, and that no one from another diocese be admitted as a canon of the church or parish priest unless released by his own bishop. (Tusculum, 23 January.)

[PETIT, *Theodori Poenitent.*, II, 432.]

[Col. 1203A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother J[OHN], bishop, and his beloved sons the dean and chapter of Chartres, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since more is required from one to whom more has been entrusted, it is fitting and consonant with reason that those honoured above others in your church should serve it more diligently [Col. 1203B] and attend to its interests. Therefore, induced by this reasoning, we have decreed by apostolic authority that henceforth the dignities of the Church of Chartres shall by no means be granted to persons who have not promised to reside, in accordance with ancient and reasonable custom. If, however, after making their promise they do not fulfil it, they shall be deprived of those dignities. Furthermore, by apostolic authority we forbid the admission of anyone from another diocese as a canon of your church or as a parish priest unless he has first been released by his own bishop.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our constitution, etc.

[Col. 1203C] Given at Tusculum, 23 January.

MCCCXC. To Matthew, bishop of Troyes.—Concerning the number of canons, priests, and deacons of the Church of Troyes, etc. (Tusculum, 27 January.)

[MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.*, I, 906.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brother MATTHEW, bishop, and to his beloved sons the chapter of Troyes, present and future, canonically appointed, for ever.

Since your uprightness, brother bishop, and devotion deserve that you should be heard by us in your petitions, we more willingly grant you what you judge should be sought according to God, because you are known to have obtained a fuller favour of the Apostolic See [Col. 1203D]. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, graciously assenting to your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the Church of Troyes, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing; decreeing that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings [Col. 1204A] or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s assistance, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Furthermore, since you state that, on the counsel of prudent and religious men, you have decreed that in the church entrusted to you there shall be permanently seven canons who are at least priests and seven deacons, besides the archdeacons; and that, upon their death, no one shall be substituted in their places except priests or deacons, or others established in such orders, who are to be advanced to those orders at the nearest opportunity afforded by the grades of orders, provided that they have given a promise and profession of maintaining residence in the aforesaid Church:

> [Note: [Col. 1203D] Hato, bishop of Troyes, lamented the absence of canons in his Church; and therefore, in 1145, in a solemn chapter, in the presence and with the consent of Alberic, legate of the Apostolic See, and at the request also of the canons of Troyes, he decreed that, beyond twenty shillings [Col. 1204D] yearly, those who did not present themselves as resident attendants for the Church’s service should receive nothing from their prebendal benefice. Quercetanus reports his decree on this matter in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 104.]

We graciously assent to your petitions as was fitting, hold your constitution made on these matters, as we have stated, valid and firm, and decree that it shall remain unimpaired for all time. We add that, if clerics of lower orders are appointed and, after being warned, do not receive those orders at the first four Ember seasons, you shall have full authority from us to remove them altogether and substitute others [Col. 1204B]. Furthermore, with your knowledge and consent, we decree that resident canons in the aforesaid Church who are in the service of you, of your successors, or of the Church itself, or who with your and the chapter’s permission devote themselves to scholarly disciplines, or who are prevented by illness, shall nevertheless receive the full fruits of their prebends. Other canons, however, who are not continually present in that Church shall, by our constitution, receive only twenty shillings annually.

Furthermore, by authority of the Apostolic See we add that, whenever the aforesaid Church lacks a dean, a priest who is a canon shall be appointed dean by you and your successors; or a deacon, who shall be ordained priest at the first ensuing Ember seasons. If, after being warned, he should perhaps neglect to receive that order during those same Ember seasons, it shall be lawful for you and your successors to bar him from the authority and exercise of that office and from his place both in choir and chapter. And if he does not receive priestly orders in the first following Ember seasons even then, you may remove him and freely appoint another in his place. Moreover [Col. 1204D], in order that the high altar of the aforesaid Church may always be held in greater reverence, we more strictly prohibit by this present writing the admission of anyone to celebrate the solemnities of Mass at that altar, except a bishop, abbot, or canon of the aforesaid Church; or the prior of St. George, who belongs specially to the same Church; or a suitable and upright regular canon sent by that prior,

> [Note: [Col. 1204D] Pope Lucius III later granted the same privilege to the matricular priests [Col. 1205D]. In 1183 the bishop of Troyes, together with the chapter, granted this same permission to four canons whom the dean of Troyes should appoint for service in the chapel [Col. 1206D] of Blessed Mary; it was also granted to the subchanter in 1217.]

who, like the others, shall reverently perform there the office of priest and receive in full the fruit of the prebend [Col. 1205A] which he holds in that Church.

We decree, therefore, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, John, cardinal-priest, etc.

Given at Tusculum through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 27 January, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1178 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twentieth year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

MCCCXCI. To Lupus, king of Valencia.—He thanks him for protecting and honouring Christians. (Tusculum, January?)

[TWISDEN, *Hist. Angl. Script.*, I, 602.]

[Col. 1205B]

ALEXANDER, pontiff of great and venerable Rome, to LUPUS, glorious king of Valencia: may he attain knowledge of the heavenly Creator and render Him acceptable service.

Although the lofty and incomprehensible providence of divine majesty has entrusted dominion over countless peoples to you, and although your Highness has by no means received the sacraments of the Christian faith, nevertheless, as report has reached us, you love and honour the worshippers and faithful of Christ with a certain special prerogative, and are known to extend to them no small favour of familiarity. Therefore we urgently ask and exhort Your Excellence to send back to us, by your favour, free and released the Christians who are now held captive among you, so that the Almighty Father [Col. 1205C], Creator of all, may enlarge and preserve for you your temporal kingdom on earth, and, after the end of this life, the Redeemer of all—whose name is blessed for ever—may grant you in heaven that kingdom which shall endure without end through the sacraments of the Christian faith.

MCCCXCII. Bull for the Church of Béziers. (Tusculum, 3 February.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, VI, Instrumenta 140.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BERNARD, bishop of Béziers, and to his successors canonically appointed, for ever.

Being placed, though with insufficient merits, by the highest providence in this position and office [Col. 1205D], we are bound to assist our brethren and fellow bishops, both near at hand and far away, with the concern of brotherly charity, and to grant them apostolic protection so that they may be able to govern the Churches entrusted to them. Therefore, venerable brother bishop in Christ, we graciously grant your just requests; and, after the example of Pope Adrian, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves [Col. 1206A] the Church of Béziers, of the holy martyrs Nazarius and Celsus, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatsoever possessions and goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter be able to acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The abbey of St. Aphrodisius; the abbey of St. James; and the processions and stations which the clergy of those same abbeys have customarily performed in your church on appointed days; the church of St. Saturninus; the monastery of St. Peter of Juncelles; the monastery of St. Martin of Villamagna; the church of St. Mary of Cassian; and the churches [Col. 1206B] of St. Cyriacus, St. Mary of Frangolano, of Faysen, of Caisano, of Rovinaco, of Avena, of Clementiano, of Diano, and of the Holy Saviour of Podio; of Lodozano; St. Mary of Bello-loco; of Redes; of Caprimon; of Felgeriis; of Gradano; of Coiano; of Albignano; of Caprilis; of Muris; of Monte-Blanco; of Camprinnano; of Valesiis; St. Christopher of Margunc; of Magalacio; of Torves; and of Buada.

The castle of Gabian and the castle of Lignan, with their churches and all their appurtenances; the castle of Vallano; the castle of Beciano; the castle of Casulis; the castle of Cerviano; and the fortified place of St. Baudilius of Silanciano; the village of Badonas; the village of Amiliaco; the village of Paleriis; the village of Pinibus; and the village of Aspiranc, with the church of St. Romanus; the share which you possess [Col. 1206C] in the village called Erignanus, with the tithes of that place; the village of Carnencas; and the whole territory of Podas.

Moreover, whatever rights you possess in the city of Béziers and its suburbs; one third of the tolls both by land and by sea; and the customary annual tax of the Jews. Likewise, we confirm by apostolic authority the agreements made and accepted between your church and the churches of St. Aphrodisius and St. James, and the monastery of St. Peter of Juncelles, concerning episcopal reverence and possessions, by the free and spontaneous consent of the parties, as they are set forth in authentic documents.

We therefore decree, etc.

Given at Tusculum through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman [Col. 1206D] Church, on the third Nones of February, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1178 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the twentieth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### MCCCXCIII. To Simon, bishop of Meaux.—Concerning the election of abbots in monasteries of his diocese. (Lateran, February 18.)

[Du Plessis, *History of the Church of Meaux*, II, 66.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother SIMON, bishop of the people of Meaux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1207A] Because of dissension among the brethren, monasteries in your diocese, as you assert, frequently happen to remain without a pastor for a long time.
