We have heard, and hearing have been astonished, that although the brethren of the monastery of Dunes, like all other members of the Cistercian Order, have been granted by our fathers and predecessors, and subsequently confirmed by us, freedom from paying tithes to anyone upon the labours which they cultivate with their own hands or at their own expense, certain persons nevertheless presume, contrary to the indulgence of the Apostolic See, to demand and extort tithes from them. By a perverse interpretation of apostolic privileges, they distort the chapter, asserting that, where “from labours” is inserted, it must be understood as referring to newly cleared land.

Since it is clear to all who think rightly that such an interpretation is perverse and contrary to sound understanding—for according to that chapter they are completely exempt from payment of tithes both on newly cleared lands and on other cultivated lands which they cultivate with their own hands or at their own expense—therefore, lest anyone have occasion maliciously to attack them or harass them in any manner contrary to justice, we command and order you by apostolic letters [Col. 1234B] to take care, by our authority, to forbid all persons subject to your power from presuming in any manner to extort tithes from the aforementioned brethren of Dunes, or from brethren of other monasteries of the Cistercian Order situated in your bishoprics, either on newly cleared land or on other lands which they cultivate with their own hands or at their own expense, or from the increase of their animals. For if we had intended, where we use the words “from labours,” to refer only to newly cleared land, we would have used “from newly cleared land,” as we do in the privileges granted to certain others.

Because it is not fitting that the ordinances of the Apostolic See, which ought to retain inviolable force, should be rashly violated, we command and order you by apostolic letters that, if any canons, clerics, monks, or laypeople burden the aforesaid brethren with demands for tithes contrary to the privileges of the Apostolic See, then, without appeal, you shall strike the laypeople with a sentence of excommunication and suspend the others from their office; and you shall ensure that both the sentence of excommunication and that of suspension are inviolably observed until worthy satisfaction has been made.

Furthermore, by the authority of this present letter we command and order you that, if any persons lay violent hands upon brethren of the aforesaid monasteries, you shall publicly declare them excommunicated with lighted candles, and shall cause them to be strictly avoided by all as excommunicated persons until they have made suitable satisfaction to the aforesaid [Col. 1234D] brethren and have presented themselves before the Apostolic See with letters from the diocesan bishop setting out the truth of the matter.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

MCDXXI. To Henry, Patriarch of Grado, and Dominic, Bishop of Caorle.—That they shall cause the sentence issued for the monastery of Saint Saviour to be observed by all. (Lateran, 22 April.)

[CORNEL., *Ecclesiae Venetae*, XIV, 103.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers HENRY, Patriarch of Grado, and D., Bishop of Caorle: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1235A] Long ago, brother Patriarch, if we remember correctly, we entrusted to you and to Ildebrand, of good memory, formerly cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, the hearing of the case concerning certain parochial houses disputed between our beloved son, the Prior of Saint Saviour, and the pleban of Saint Bartholomew. Having learned the truth in the matter, as we have received, you pronounced a definitive sentence; but this, as it ought, is said not yet to have been carried into execution.

Since the authority of divine and human legislation firmly decrees that a matter adjudged must be observed, we command and order your brotherhood by apostolic letters to ensure that this sentence, since it was reasonably pronounced, is held ratified and valid. You shall admonish and strictly compel the clerics of the aforesaid church of Saint Bartholomew [Col. 1235B] not to admit to divine offices any persons from those houses concerning which judgment was rendered between them and the aforesaid prior; nor shall they dare to bury them in their cemetery, while preserving the right of the Church of Saint Saviour in the portion of the testament. You shall firmly enjoin those persons to attend the Church of Saint Saviour for participation in divine offices, as has been decreed and ordained, generally prohibiting under threat of anathema their admission to divine offices in other churches contrary to the right of the church to which they were adjudged.

If, in contempt of the Church, they presume to frequent [other churches], publicly declare them excommunicated; and in a church which, contrary to your prohibition, has received them, prohibit the celebration of divine offices until worthy satisfaction has been made. [Col. 1235C] If the clerics of the Church of Saint Bartholomew are contumacious in observing this sentence, suspend them from office, so that, when they come to us with your letters, they may learn from the punishment itself that a definitive sentence must be obeyed and that they must wholly abstain from harassing religious men. We command that these matters be observed without contradiction, as stated above.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.

[Note: [Col. 1235D] We assign this diploma, whose copy lacks the chronological year-date, to 1179 because it mentions Ildebrand with the words “of good memory,” which are customarily applied to deceased persons. [Col. 1236D] Since, as we read in the edition *Italia sacra Veneta*, vol. II, col. 118, Ildebrand died in 1168, these letters of Alexander III which we present were issued after that time.]

MCDXXII. He requests Christian, Archbishop of Mainz, to assist Leonatus, Abbot of Pescara, in recovering the possessions of the monastery. (Lateran, 3 May.)

[MURATORI, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, II, II, 910.]

[Col. 1235D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable Archbishop of Mainz: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more sincerely we love our beloved son, the Abbot of Saint Clement of Pescara, in consideration of the devotion which he shows toward us and the Church and of the monastery over which he presides—which belongs especially to the right of blessed Peter—the more earnestly we have thought fit to commend him to your affection, hoping that, at our intervention, you will promptly accomplish what, for love of justice and without anyone’s urging, ought to be brought into effect.

Since, therefore, the aforesaid monastery suffered grave loss in the March through the occasion of the long-standing discord between the Church and the Empire, the aforesaid abbot particularly needs your assistance in recovering its rights. We desire that assistance to be rendered all the more effectively because we are the more strictly bound to provide for the needs of the aforesaid monastery. Accordingly, we request, earnestly exhort, and command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to receive kindly, for reverence of blessed Peter and ourselves, the aforesaid abbot or his messengers, as we confidently expect of you; and strictly compel those who hold in the March of Ancona possessions belonging to the monastery just mentioned [Col. 1236B] to restore them, so that our letters may obtain their desired effect and we may be able repeatedly to commend your diligence.

We do not wish it to be objected to restitution that they possessed these things during the time of schism, since hostility ought rightly to prevent prescription.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Nones of May.

MCDXXIII. To [Gentile], Bishop of Osimo, [Peter] of Fermo, [Acceptabilis] of Camerino, and [James], Bishop of Senigallia.—He commands them to order the restoration to the monastery of Pescara of possessions seized during the schism. (Lateran, 15 May.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1236C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the Bishop of Osimo, legate of the Apostolic See, and the Bishops of Fermo, Camerino, and Senigallia: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The greater the reverence which you ought to show to blessed Peter and the most holy Roman Church, the more earnestly you are bound to hold in your care the monasteries and churches that look directly to us, without intermediary, and to restrain your parishioners more strictly from harassing them. We have learned that certain of your parishioners hold many possessions of Saint Clement of Pescara, which they rashly invaded on their own initiative while the schism was in progress.

Since, then, the more especially this monastery belongs to the right of blessed Peter, the more strongly we wish its immunity to be safeguarded, we command and order your brotherhood by apostolic letters not to delay strictly admonishing those of your parishioners who are named to you to restore what they unjustly hold contrary to right. Moreover, if anyone should presume either to refuse to restore what was seized or, after restoration, to harass the monastery, then, without delay or appeal, bind him with the bond of excommunication and cause him to be avoided by all as excommunicated until he has made worthy satisfaction. [Col. 1237A] Take diligent care to execute the apostolic command in such a way that the abbot is not compelled to resort to the Apostolic See through a failure of justice, and that you do not have to suffer refusal from us in your own petitions.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of May.

MCDXXIV. To Alfonso, King of the Portuguese.—He takes the kingdom of Portugal under protection. (Lateran, 23 May.)

[Brandão, *Monarchia Lusitana*, Lisbon, 1690, folio, vol. III, 295.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ ALFONSO, illustrious King of the Portuguese, and to his heirs for ever.

[Col. 1237B] Manifest proofs have established that, through the toils of war and military contests, as a fearless destroyer of the enemies of the Christian name and a zealous defender of the Christian faith, you have rendered manifold services to your mother, the most holy Church. Thus, as a good son and Catholic prince, you have left to posterity a name worthy of remembrance and an inimitable example.

It is fitting that the Apostolic See should love with sincere affection that which heavenly providence has chosen for the rule and salvation of the people, and should labour effectively to grant its just petitions. Accordingly, considering your person, adorned with prudence, endowed with justice, and suited to governing the people, we receive it under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves. We grant to your highness, and confirm by apostolic authority, the kingdom of Portugal with the full integrity of honour and dignity belonging to kings, together with all places that, with the aid of heavenly grace, you shall have rescued from Saracen hands, in which the neighbouring Christian princes cannot assert a right for themselves.

And that you may be more fervently moved to the service of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the most holy Roman Church, we have judged it right to grant these things to you and to your aforesaid heirs; and, God willing, in fulfilment of the apostolic office laid upon us, we shall defend them in respect of what has been granted. It is therefore your concern, dearest son, to remain humble and devoted in regard to the honour and service of your mother, the most holy Roman Church, [Col. 1237D] and to exert yourself in her needs and in extending the boundaries of the Christian faith, so that the Apostolic See may rejoice in so devoted and glorious a son and rest in its love for him.

Moreover, as a sign that the aforesaid kingdom belongs to the right of blessed Peter, you have established that two marks of gold shall be paid annually to us and our successors as a fuller token of reverence. You and your successors shall ensure that this payment, for the use of us and our successors, is assigned to the Archbishop of Braga for the time being.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your person or that of your heirs, or the aforesaid kingdom; take away its possessions; retain what has been taken; diminish them; or harass it with any vexations. If anyone, therefore, in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Viceranus, cardinal priest of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cynthius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Luigo, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement. I, Arduin, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Matthew, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. [Col. 1238B] I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina. I, Peter, bishop of Tusculum. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Ardicio, called cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Laborans, called cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Rainerius, called cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Gratian, called cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, John, called cardinal of Saint Angelo. I, Raineris, called cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Matthew, called cardinal of Saint Mary the New. I, Bernard, called cardinal of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

[Col. 1238C] Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.

MCDXXV. Privilege for the Church of Saints Stephen and Willehad at Bremen. (Lateran, 29 May.)

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburgisches Urkundenbuch*, I, 222.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HENRY, provost of the Church of Saint Stephen and Saint Willehad at Bremen, and its brethren, both present and future, canonically appointed for ever.

When, in the holy Churches of God, measures are ordained by their prelates for the strengthening and increase of religion and for the unceasing praise of the divine majesty, we ought to secure them by the authority of the apostolic office, lest they be violated by the rash assault of any persons or, at the prompting of the enemy of humankind, removed through the perversity of persecutors.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions. We hold ratified the transfer of your community, made for God’s honour by Albero, Archbishop of Bremen of blessed memory, together with the liberties and immunities conferred by him upon your Church, as is contained in his authentic document. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and Paul the Church in which you are devoted to divine service, and confirm it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order established in that Church according to the fear of God and canonical decrees [Col. 1239A] shall be inviolably observed there for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through grants of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which your church is situated, with the cloister precincts and its other appurtenances; the parish in the city of Bremen, from the house of Alberic and his wife Dede toward your church as far as the end of the city, and in Uthbremen and in Walle, which [Col. 1239B] the aforesaid archbishop, with the common consent of his chapter, conferred upon your Church, to be administered in every respect by the authority of your provost—except that, in synodal matters, the parishioners are bound to obey only his archdeacon. The estate of Hamedesen, with tithes and its other appurtenances; the estate of Baldinge, with its appurtenances; the estate of Boken, with its appurtenances; the estate of Rammingestorp, with its appurtenances; the estate of Dendorp, with tithes and its other appurtenances; the estate of Wechlede, with the parish church, tithes, and its other appurtenances. The parish church of Estorp, with tithes and other appurtenances. The estate at Winberge, with its appurtenances. The chapel at Hamedese, with its appurtenances; the estate [Col. 1239C] at Merdvelde, with chapel and its appurtenances; the estate at Hiddenstorp, with its appurtenances. At the place called Silva, separate holdings with the tithe. The estate at Sete, with its appurtenances. Two estates at Habehusen, with tithes and their other appurtenances. The estate at Walle, with tithes and its other appurtenances. By gift of the aforesaid Albero, archbishop of Bremen, two and a half Dutch holdings, with the entire tithe of Hemme. The estate at Wittenstide, with tithes and its other appurtenances; the estate at Wedene, with the advocacy, tithes, and all its appurtenances. And, by gift of Count Hermann, forty holdings at Mirica, with all secular jurisdiction.

Moreover, we prohibit the provost of your church from presuming, without the common consent of the brethren, or of the greater and sounder part of them, to grant in fief any possessions or [Col. 1239D] revenues belonging to the chapter, or to alienate them under any other title. We also decree that, according to ancient institution and the custom of both churches, your places shall be reserved for you in the assembly of the greater chapter and in the choir of the greater church, and that the offerings of the faithful shall be canonically apportioned according to observance of the former custom, provided that you render the services due to that church in their proper place and at the appropriate time. We likewise judge that the liberties and immunities reasonably granted to you and your Church, and observed hitherto, shall remain ratified and unimpaired for all time.

Furthermore, we decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final [Col. 1240A] wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless perhaps they are excommunicated or under interdict; the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken nevertheless being preserved. And when you, the present provost of the same place, or any of your successors, die, no one shall be placed over it through any contrivance of stealth or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide, according to God, to be elected.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, or to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, and shall be of use to them in every way, [Col. 1240B] the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop being preserved. If, therefore, in the future, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his fault by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself to be answerable before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the Last Judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of the same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the [Col. 1240C] strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

(S.) (M.)

I, Alexander. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul at Pammachius. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Livianus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cynthius, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Hugh, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Clement. I, Ardericus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. [Col. 1240D] I, Matthew, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Hubaldus, . . . bishop. I, Theodoric, bishop of Porto. I, Peter, bishop of Tusculum. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Berneredus, bishop of Palestrina. I, James, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Ardicis, cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Laborans, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Reinerius, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Rainerus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian. [Col. 1241A] I, Matthew, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary . . . . I, Bernard, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the twelfth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1178 [read 1179], in the eighteenth [twentieth] year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

MCDXXVI. Privilege for the Church of Saint Mary at Fine. (Lateran.—The chronological indications are erroneous.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquities of Italy*, III, 1177.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, prior of the parish church [Note: [Col. 1241D] By this name the college of Canons Regular is denoted.] of Saint Mary the Virgin at Fine, and to his brethren, both present [Col. 1241B] and future, professing the religious life: in perpetuity.

It befits the governance of the Apostolic office . . . . . to love religious persons and to fortify their places with pious protection. For we recognize it as worthy and consonant with honour that we, who have been raised to the governance of churches, should . . . . . protect them from human malice and cherish them under the patronage of the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests . . . . . and, following the example of Anastasius, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the church in which you are devoted to divine service. Decreeing that whatever possessions, [Col. 1241C] whatever goods, that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by grant of pontiffs, gift of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, God being favourable, shall remain firm, whole, and unimpaired. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Namely, the church of Peneto and whatever you justly hold in that village; the church of Gualtiperga and the possessions . . . . . which you have in that place. Whatever you justly and lawfully possess in the estate of Colle, the estate of Saint Regulus, the Old Castle and the estate of that castle, and in the castle and estate of Parrana, we confirm to the same church. We strengthen by the page of this present writing the land, the death-dues, gifts, offerings, [Col. 1241D] and whatever Opitho, archbishop of Pisa of good memory, reasonably granted you. If any person from the surrounding parish churches should give you anything of his right, whether in life or in death, in consideration of devotion, or should decide through religious devotion to be buried at the same church, no one shall oppose this, the rights of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken being preserved. As a token of the protection received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay six denarii of Luccan money annually to us and our successors.

Therefore we decree, etc.

[Col. 1242A] I, John, priest-cardinal of Saints . . . . . Pammachius. I, John, priest-cardinal . . . . . I, Theodinus, priest-cardinal . . . . . I, Vivianus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Hugh, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Clement. I, Arduinus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, James, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, L . . . . . I, R . . . . . at the Golden Veil. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo. [Col. 1242B] I, Rainerius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Matthew, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 9 October, in the indiction . . . . . , in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1179, in the twentieth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCDXXVII. He grants an indulgence of twenty days to the Church of Saint Saviour on the anniversary of its dedication. (Segni, 22 July.)

[CORNELIUS, *Venetian Church*, II, 279.]

[Col. 1242C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons VIVIANUS, prior, and the brethren of Saint Saviour of Rialto: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are moved by the authority of the Apostolic See and called by the duty of our office willingly to receive the petitions of the sons of the Church and effectively to grant assent to their just requests. Induced by this consideration, and trusting in the merits of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we remit twenty days of imposed penance to all who visit your church on the anniversary of its dedication for the sake of devotion, just as we are known to have granted on the day of the dedication of that church.

Given at Segni, on the second day before the Kalends of August.

MCDXXVIII. At the will of the canons, he assigns certain revenues to Lombard, “formerly archbishop of Benevento.” (Segni, 27 July.)

[UGHELLI, *Sacred Italy*, VIII, 122.]

[Col. 1242D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother LOMBARD, formerly archbishop of Benevento: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When certain of the senior canons of the Church of Benevento came into our presence and, on their own behalf and that of others, carefully discussed with us the ordering of that church, we, wishing honourably to provide for your needs in accordance with the means of [Col. 1243A] that church, have, by the common counsel of our brethren, granted you for the whole term of your life: the mill situated at the foot of the suburb, from which come six *coscini* of wheat each month and certain other proceeds—provided that, if anything is lacking from the six *coscini*, it shall be supplied from the cellar or elsewhere; sixty *saumae* of pure wine yearly, together with casks in which it may be stored; forty-eight *romanati* from the garden; and, with the consent of those canons, from the altar so much as will make up twenty-four ounces of gold. Later, in the presence of the aforesaid canons, we added that provisions from the Church should be supplied for the pack-animal which you keep to carry firewood. We further permit you to have full authority to dispose as you please, in life and in death, [Col. 1243B] of your books and garments. We also decree that the house of Turricella shall be assigned to you as a dwelling for as long as you live. That this our grant and arrangement may remain firm and unimpaired, we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing, decreeing that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever to infringe this page of our grant and confirmation or rashly to act against it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed Peter and Paul. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Alberic, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 1243C] on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, in the twelfth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1179, and in the twentieth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCDXXIX. He confirms the peace concluded between the brethren of the Order of the Temple and the brethren of the Hospital. (Segni, 2 August.)

[RYMER, *Treaties concluded*, etc., I, I, 44.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the master and brethren of the Order of the Temple: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more your religious order and that of the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem are believed to be pleasing to God and humankind, and are proved more necessary and suitable to the eastern land, [Col. 1243D] the greater joy and gladness we ought to derive from your unity and theirs, and the more earnestly we ought to labour that the bond of love may always be maintained among you. Moved by this consideration, we not only approve but also ratify, and by apostolic authority confirm, the peace and concord which, with the consent of our beloved sons the master and brethren of the Hospital, you have made concerning all disputes long contested between your house and theirs, whether concerning lands and possessions, money, or any other matters. We decree that it shall remain firm and unimpaired for ever. We have considered it necessary to set it down in these letters word for word:

[Col. 1244A] “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

“Let all, future as well as present, know that by the will of almighty God, and at the command and admonition of Lord Pope Alexander—to whom alone, after the Lord, we are bound to render obedience—I, Brother Odo of Saint-Amand, humble master of the Order of the Temple, and I, Roger of Moulins, minister of the house of the Hospital of Jerusalem, with the counsel and consent of our chapters, have made a firm peace and acceptable concord concerning all disputes which have been aired until this day between the house of the Temple and the house of the Hospital, whether concerning lands and possessions, money, or any other things; all disputes both [Col. 1244B] on this side and beyond being so settled that none may thereafter be raised or renewed.

“We establish and command that this peace and concord, the termination of all disputes, and mutual brotherly love, shall be held, maintained, and fostered by all brethren of the Temple and Hospital; while the goods and possessions which each house is known to hold today, both overseas and on this side of the sea, shall henceforth remain to each house in quiet and peace.

“But if any dispute should hereafter arise between us or our successors, or even among our brethren on this side of the sea or beyond it, we decree, as we have received in command from the lord pope, that it shall be settled by three brethren of each [Col. 1244C] party. That is to say, the commanders of those houses or provinces between which the question has arisen, each taking their more discerning brethren, shall endeavour to resolve that dispute and preserve peace between themselves, avoiding, so far as they are able, fraud and burden to either party.

“If those brethren cannot by themselves put an end to the dispute, they shall jointly call in some of their friends, by whose counsel and mediation the question may be settled. Thus, that upon which the greater part of those brethren or friends agrees shall bring the dispute to an end, and unbroken peace and firm affection shall always endure among the brethren.

[Col. 1244D] “But if they still cannot attain peace by this means, let them send the dispute to us in writing, and we, God willing, shall settle it. The brethren themselves, nevertheless, shall continue to maintain peace and goodwill among one another.

“But if any brother—God forbid!—should depart from this peace and from maintaining peace and love, let him know that he has acted contrary to the command of his master and the ordinance of the chapter of Jerusalem; nor can he make satisfaction for such an offence in any manner until he presents himself before his master and the chapter of Jerusalem.

“To this we have thought fit to add that the brethren of each house shall everywhere love and honour one another, and that each shall seek and preserve the advantage of the other with mutual charity and [Col. 1245A] brotherly unanimity, so that, although belonging to two houses by profession, they may appear to belong to one through love.”

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to act against it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Segni, on the fourth day before the Nones of August.

MCDXXX. (Segni, 4 August.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Collection*, XV, 967.]

He grants to the dean and chapter of Laon “that no one shall presume henceforth to renew or establish the commune of Laon, dissolved by Louis, king of the Franks; nor shall bishops be permitted, without their consent, or that of the greater and sounder part of the chapter, to ordain any commune or general constitution bearing the character of a commune under a disguised name.”

MCDXXXI. To the abbot and convent of Saint Vaast.—He confirms the settlement they made with the count of Hainaut and their rights in the village of Hasprens. (Segni, 18 August.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplified Collection*, I, 906.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, to the abbot and brethren of Saint [Col. 1245C] Vaast: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the tenor of your report we have learned that, when the noble Count of Hainaut was accustomed to harass by unlawful exactions the people of the village of Hasprens, which is recognized as belonging to you, our venerable brother, the bishop of Tusculum, then legate of the Apostolic See, in order to avert danger from you and your people, placed the count’s land under interdict at your complaint. Compelled by the severity of that sentence, the same count, before our venerable brethren the bishops of Arras and Cambrai, acknowledged your right; and under the solemn obligation of an oath he confirmed that he would observe the ancient customs and rights of the aforesaid village and its people. And lest there should thereafter be doubt concerning what had been settled, by the count’s own confession, for your honour and advantage, the customs and rights which you ought to have in the aforesaid village [Col. 1245D] were carefully committed to writing with the count’s consent, and subsequently were solemnly confirmed by both your seal and his. We therefore, wishing with paternal concern to provide for the peace and tranquillity of you and your people, hold ratified the settlement made between you and the same count; and by apostolic authority we confirm to your devotion, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the rights and customs which you have held from ancient times in the aforesaid village and which, by the count’s own acknowledgement, you are still known to possess, as is more fully contained in the authentic instruments made [Col. 1246A] by both sides. Decreeing that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever, etc.

Given at Segni, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September.

MCDXXXII. Privilege for the Church of Acerenza. (Segni, 7 September.)

[UGHELLI, *Sacred Italy*, VII, 33.—The portions here omitted for brevity are to be supplied from the diploma granted to the same Church by Eugenius III on 1 April 1151; see *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXX.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, etc., to his venerable brother RICHARD, archbishop of Acerenza, and his successors, [Col. 1246B] etc.

Following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, Paschal and Eugenius, Roman pontiffs, we strengthen the holy Church of Acerenza by the authority of this decree of the exalted Apostolic See, etc., and confirm to you and your successors whatever is recognized as having belonged to it by metropolitan right in past times: namely Venosa, Gravina, Tricarico, Tursi, and Potenza, so that you and your lawful successors may have authority canonically and by decretal law to ordain and consecrate bishops in them, the authority of the Holy Roman Church being preserved in all things. Furthermore, decreeing, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 1246C] I, Ubaldus, bishop of Ostia. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina. I, Matthew, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Matthew, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of September, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1179, and in the twentieth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCDXXXIII. To the dean and canons of Saint Anianus of Orléans. He exhorts them “to permit the canons of Saint Evurtius, who have a prebend in the Church of Saint Anianus, to celebrate the divine offices there upon the high altar on double feasts.” (Segni, 9 September.)

[*Antiquities of Saint-Aignan of Orléans*, Preface, p. 53.]

[Col. 1246D]

MCDXXXIV. He confirms the privileges of the Church of Cambrai. (Given [at Segni?] on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October [15 September], in the twelfth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1169 [Note: [Col. 1245D] The chronological indications are corrupt.], and in the twentieth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.)

[Memoir of M. de Choiseul against the magistracy of Cambrai, document 14.]

MCDXXXV. He takes the Church of Lausanne under protection and confirms its rights. (Anagni, 17 October.)

[*Memoirs and Documents of French-speaking Switzerland*, VII, 24.]

[Col. 1247A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ROGER, bishop of the Church of Lausanne and legate of the Apostolic See, and to his successors canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

The authority of the supreme pontificate moves us to provide with paternal care for our brothers and fellow bishops both near at hand and far away, and to uphold in their rights the churches entrusted to their governance. But we are compelled to give more attentive support to you and your Church [Col. 1247B] because, through long association and familiarity, we have more plainly experienced your devotion and integrity. Therefore, venerable brother bishop in Christ, we grant willing assent to your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen with the protection of this present writing, the Church of Lausanne, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside. Decreeing that whatever possessions, whatever goods, etc. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Namely, those things which, in the time of Burchard, formerly bishop of Lausanne, were bestowed upon the said church by the pious devotion of Emperor Henry; and those which, in the time of Amadeus, your predecessor, were confirmed by the force of the charter of Conrad, illustrious [Col. 1247C] king of the Romans: namely Muratum and Cubizaca, the authority over Corsiaco and Polliaco, and the valley of Lustriaco. Whatever Duke Rufoldus and his people held, with all its appurtenances, is contained in the charter of the aforesaid Henry. And since all pastors are appointed for building up, not for destruction, we decree by apostolic authority that neither you nor your successors may dissipate or alienate the goods of the Church of Lausanne; rather, let those goods which have been unlawfully alienated be restored to the right of that church by your diligence. By apostolic authority we likewise forbid that you or they should henceforth have licence to give the majoralty of Lausanne in fief.

Furthermore, following in the footsteps of Eugenius, our father and predecessor of happy [Col. 1247D] memory, we annul and declare void all grants made from the goods of that church by Lambert, who, ordained by Viribert the heresiarch, presided over the Church of Lausanne in whatever fashion. Moreover, since the noble Berchtold is said to have sworn the following oath to Amadeus, your aforesaid predecessor, and to his successors: that he would permit a free election to be held in the Church of Lausanne; that he would appropriate nothing of what was held from the bishop; that neither he nor his heir would henceforth demand the service owed for Chebrii and Lustriaco upon a change of bishop, but the bishop would receive these from his hand without any payment, as he received the other regalia; that he would assist to the utmost of his power in recovering in good faith the goods which that church had lost [Col. 1248A] and which had long been alienated; that he would not allow his people to enter the villages of the church for fodder or other necessities, nor lodge in those villages; and that he would neither have lodging in the bishop’s palace or in the houses of clerics or knights against their will, nor forcibly take anything from that palace or those houses. We hold that oath ratified and firm, forbidding under threat of anathema that the aforesaid duke or his heir should presume to act contrary to the matters which we have stated and which have been confirmed by oath.

Further, out of affection we grant you use of the pallium in celebrating the sacred solemnities of Mass, to be used only on the following feasts: namely, at the Nativity of the Lord, the feast of blessed Stephen, Epiphany, the four feasts [Col. 1248B] of blessed Mary, the Lord’s Supper, Holy Saturday and Easter, the Ascension of the Lord, the Saturday before Pentecost and Pentecost itself, the feast of blessed John the Baptist, the feast of the blessed Peter and Paul, All Saints’ Day, dedications of churches, ordinations of clerics, the principal feasts of your church, and the anniversary of your consecration. We also confirm by apostolic authority the rights and reasonable customs of your Church and city.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved unimpaired and whole for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, and shall be of use to them in every way, [Col. 1248C] the authority of the Apostolic See being preserved. If, therefore, in the future, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, etc., etc.

Given at Anagni, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the twelfth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1179, and in the twenty-first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MCDXXXVI. He takes the monastery of Holy Cross at Villa-Bosonis under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Anagni, 18 October.)

[D. CALMET, *History of Lorraine*, II, Preface, p. 386.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brethren WALTER, abbot of Holy Cross at [Col. 1248D] Villa-Bosonis, and his brethren, present and future, professing the religious life: in perpetual memory.

Whenever a request is made to us that is recognized as fitting for religion and honour, it is proper for us to grant it willingly and to afford suitable support to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid monastery in which you are devoted to divine service. First, we decree that the monastic order which is known to have been established in your monastery according to the Lord and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions, [Col. 1249A] whatever goods, that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by grant of pontiffs, gift of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, the Lord providing, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Waldracha, with its ban and appurtenances, building-plots, structures, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, fields, cultivated and uncultivated land, roads, trackless places, exits and revenues, mills, and serfs of both sexes. Also the church of that place, with its chapels belonging to it, namely Britenacha and Hechelingen, and with the tithe. The allod which Abbot Walter bought for twenty-two pounds, called [Col. 1249B] Adelardi. Britecha, with its mills and appurtenances; Fildorf with its mills; also the church of that village and all the appurtenances of the village. The allod in the same village which the aforesaid Abbot Walter bought for eighteen pounds from Gerarhdus, his wife Sophia, and his sons Gerarhdus and Albert; Vrorocoringa, with the church of that place. Albert, count of good memory and first founder of that place, together with his wife Judith, granted this village, with its mills, vineyards, court, and all that belonged to it, to the Church of Holy Cross together with all the aforesaid possessions. Also, the five allods which Count and Margrave Gerarhdus, son of the aforesaid Albert, gave to your church with his wife Gissila: [Col. 1249C] namely Offewilre with its appurtenances; Cisen, with a mill and all the appurtenances of the estate; Datram, with mills and its other appurtenances; Raldinghen and Hergarda, with all belonging to them. Also the churches of the aforesaid allods, namely Offewilre and Cisen; the village of Lualwire, which Duke, Count, and Margrave Theoderic granted to your church; and also the church of that village. The patronage which you hold in the church of Huchenestorff and Altorfig was given by the noblemen William, Godiscalus, and Pirarhdus in the time of Abbot Walter, and was pledged for forty-two pounds that you paid to the creditors. Also the church of that place, and the church of Bectinchen. At Marsele, two small pans (*patellae*) which a certain nobleman Girarhdus [Col. 1249D] granted to the aforesaid church, and three seats which you bought from the heirs for sixteen pounds. The allod of Capiulre, which a certain nobleman gave to the same church. A certain Robert of Frilzdorf, with his wife Euphemia, gave one holding with serfs at Betestorf. Azelinus of Hetesbach and his wife Hiltirgardis gave one holding in the same village. At Lutura they gave nine *jugera*. Udo of Vellespere gave half a holding at Becherdorf. The same man gave half a holding at Seriechinchem. Horicus of Gunsinga gave one quarter-holding at Dilgendorf. Arnold of Britenacha, for the soul of his wife Lucardis, gave one holding at Ramelfinga. Ouldericus of Inne, with his wife Aidalleida, gave one holding at Marchena. Bertrand, [Col. 1250A] a nobleman of Bettinga, with his wife Albiza, gave one and a half holdings at Hesseringa. At Ponteshem, [they gave] one and a half holdings. The same persons gave half a holding at Vilrzdorf. The same persons gave three quarter-holdings at Dala. Walter of Hirnesdorf gave one holding at Noverchinga. Nezel of Latha gave two holdings at Wilre, with *silica* land [perhaps stony land] and woodland for feeding swine. Walter of Uchinga gave half a holding at Runeringua. Giselburgius gave a quarter-holding at Walderfinga. Adeleidis of Tannecha gave half a holding at Direngestorf.

Moreover, he granted to your church and its ministeriales the liberty reasonably conferred by Count Gerard and confirmed by an authentic written instrument: namely, that no one may, without just cause and without the abbot’s consent, bring an action against anyone within the church precinct or against anyone serving the brethren; nor did he grant anyone any right over the church’s own property or over its ministeriales. He also granted to the abbot and brethren, to hold in perpetuity, the ban-right which his fathers held in the district of Niden, from the place called Sucnefwrt as far as the river Sara, over pastures, woods, watercourses, roads and trackless places, exits, and revenues, excepting the hunting-ban.

Likewise, he set advocates over the households of the same church, recently granted freedom, because, occupied as he was, he could not give aid in all temporal matters, on this condition: that they should defend that church’s injuries as their own, and that nothing should be extorted from it beyond the arrangement written below. Summoned by the abbot three times a year to the court, the advocate shall come with one companion and three servants; the abbot shall honourably provide for him on the first night. On the following day, when they sit to hold court, whatever is awarded by the judgment of the scabini, two parts shall belong to the abbot and the third shall go to the advocate. But if, at the appointed terms—that is, after Epiphany, after the octave of Easter, and after the summer solstice—the advocate fails to come to hold court and does not correct matters requiring correction, he shall receive no service from the abbot. For at the aforesaid courts each peasant shall give one obol for daily service. He also granted the church market-right.

On Saturday, when many gather for the market before the gate [lacuna], whatever has been obtained by judicial process from any claim or offence, two parts shall belong to the abbot and the third to the advocate. Moreover, he assigned to the brethren, for buying clothing, from the market of Toul, which he held by hereditary right, one hundred solidi and eighteen denarii every year, which the bearer must spend in going and returning.

Moreover, Stephen and his wife Hedewidis gave the same church half a mansus at Gisengen, paying two solidi at two terms.

Certainly, from your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals, let no one presume to exact tithes from you. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding those excommunicated and under interdict, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing from the world, free and absolved, and retain them without any objection. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to leave the cloister except in order to embrace a stricter religious observance. No one may dare retain one who departs without letters of the community giving assurance. We likewise grant that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; saving, however, the rights of the parish churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. But when you, the present abbot of that place, or any of your successors, die, no one shall be put in authority there by any artifice of fraud or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, shall judge fit to elect.

Therefore we decree, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Theodoric, bishop of the see of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Berneredus, bishop of Palestrina.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Symmachus.  
I, Cinthius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia.  
I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement.  
I, Matthew, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus.  
[Col. 1251C] I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.  
I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo.  
I, Rainerius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian.  
I, Matthew, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New.  
I, Paul, deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1179 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the twenty-first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### MCDXXXVII. Privilege for the Church of Ascoli.  
*(Anagni, 24 October.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 455.]

[Col. 1251D] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons RAYNALD, archdeacon, MATTHEW, archpriest, and the canons of the Church of Ascoli, present and future, canonically instituted, forever.

Whenever that is requested of us which is recognized as consonant with religion and honour, etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just petitions; we receive your canonical body under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing, establishing that whatever possessions, etc.

*(It enumerates their possessions.)*

Moreover, by apostolic authority we grant you this: if anyone imposes any exaction upon your bishopric, or exercises violence or plunder against any other goods of your canonical body, [Col. 1252A] and, after your second or third admonition, contemptuously refuses to amend his presumption, then—whether your bishop is willing or unwilling to correct them after your second or third request, made devoutly and humbly at suitable intervals—you may, by your own authority, pronounce upon them a sentence of interdict and excommunication.

Therefore we decree, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Hubaldus, bishop of Ostia.  
I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Santa Rufina.  
I, Henry, bishop of Albano.  
I, Jo., cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul.  
[Col. 1252B] I, Cintius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia.  
I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement.  
I, Matthew, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus.  
I, Ardictio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.  
I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.  
I, Jo., cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo.  
I, Matth., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New.

Given at Anagni through Lord Dayfen, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of November, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1179 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the twenty-first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II.

### MCDXXXVIII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Aper of Toul.  
*(Anagni, 23 November.)*

[D. CALMET, *Hist. de Lorraine*, II, Preface, p. 383.]

[Col. 1252C] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of the monastery of Saint Aper of Toul and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

The force of equity and the order of reason require that just petitioners be granted effect; especially when piety supports the petitioners’ will and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, we mercifully assent to your just petitions. We receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing; first establishing that the monastic order which is known to have been established in your monastery according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict [Col. 1252D] shall there be observed inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by name:

Namely, the cell of Saint Peter at Castinio, with all its possessions, which Havidis, mother of Duke Theodoric, Duke Theodoric himself, and his son Duke Simon transferred by lawful donation; also land to be cultivated by your oxen, a meadow beneath the cell, and many male and female serfs. Namely, Gisbert and Gislebert with all their household, under this liberty: whoever from any place belonging to your household should dwell there on their land would be subject to no ban whatsoever. But if any of their men dwelt on your land, they would perform one day’s corvée for the duke, if they had oxen; for the rest, throughout the whole year they would remain exempt from all exactions.

[Col. 1253A] We also confirm the retithes of the whole demesne there, both in wine and grain; the right of pasture, water, and wood which the aforesaid donors transferred to you, without any liability to answer for the ban; the toll of the fair held there on the feast of Saint Peter, bestowed upon you by the same donors; and half a sextary of salt from the toll of Neufchâteau, which must be paid to you annually every Thursday by the keeper of the toll of Neufchâteau, together with three further full sextaries: one in the week before the feast of Saint Peter, another in the week before the Nativity of the Lord, and the third in the week before the day of the Lord’s Resurrection; as also its mill and allod at Lifou.

On this condition, that there should be intermarriage of men and women: so that, if your men married women belonging to the duke himself, they should be subject to your lordship. The village of Bundingam (Bodange), entire, with male and female serfs, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, vineyards, and mills; the chapel of the castle of Castiniac, with all its appurtenances; and remission of the service which the ministeriales of Neufchâteau used to exact as though due on the feast of Saint Peter. Ten [Col. 1253C] jugera of vineyard adjoining your vineyard, which Duchess Bertha, sister of our dearest son in Christ F., illustrious emperor of the Romans, and her son Simon, duke and margrave of Lorraine, transferred by lawful donation to Blessed Peter of the cell of Castinio; and the provision that the fair held near the court in the borough of the castle on Saint Peter’s feast may not presumptuously be moved elsewhere.

We also confirm the ordinance of the founders of the said cell, namely Gerard of Flanders and the dukes Theodoric, Simon, Matthew, and Simon. For the salvation of their souls, by divine mercy, they granted to their men, noble and non-noble alike, that they might freely confer their allod upon the aforesaid cell of Blessed Peter, and [granted] fishing in the river Vera (the Vair) for the use of the brethren serving God in the aforesaid cell.

[Col. 1253D] The allod of Lifol, which the noble knight Brocard, with his wife Bertha, gave to the same cell, retaining no advocatial right whatsoever. The tithes of Longchamp; the meadow commonly called Foschalprez, with the allod which Olric of Monuncourt, together with his wife Acelina, freely granted to the aforesaid cell, in lands, meadows, and wherever he possessed property. The allod which the knight Guarsilius gave you in pledge and free of pledge. Another allod which Maria of Longchamp gave to your church, both in pledge and free of pledge. One quarter holding with one mansus, given you by the knight Simon; an allod in meadows, lands, and woods, both in pledge and free of pledge, given you by Otto of Oleinville (Oleinville). One quarter holding given you in the same village by the knight Richard. The quarter holding given you at Roure by Gerard of Flanders. A third part of the tithes in the same village, together with a third part of the tithes at Viocourt, in every respect; all that Bertha of Barleville, with her niece Elizabeth, held at Ramme in lands, meadows, male and female serfs.

[Col. 1254A] One quarter holding which the aforesaid Bertha gave you at Saint-Paul, together with the allod which her nephew Boso gave you, both in pledge and free of pledge. At Morel-maison, a mill free from every claim, and what you possess at Saint-Paul. Moreover, the allod which Drogo of Domno-juliano (Domjulien) gave you, in lands, meadows, and woods, with the mill-site in the same village, together with the other property which he possessed. Six and a half quarter holdings given you by Elizabeth of Castinio, with two quarter holdings which you possess at Fresne and a sixth part of the mill of Van. The meadow given you at Vallencourt by Humbert the priest, with half a field; two quarter holdings given you at Riainville by the knight Richard; and one quarter holding given you in the same village by the knight Roffredus.

[Col. 1254B] Also the gift of the estate which Joffridus of Auzainviller possessed in the same village with his brother Hugh—namely, in meadows, lands, woods, male and female serfs—together with two quarter holdings given you at Morincurt by Theodoric Flatarz; one quarter holding which you have at Marbache; one quarter holding which you have at Parrer; five others which you have at Ulmoy; another which you have at Daswel; three which you have at Mandre; and two which you have at Belmont, together with the allod which you have at Mont and the mill-site.

[Col. 1254C] Moreover, we confirm the peace and agreement made in the following manner between the monks of Saint Peter of Castinio and their vicar: that the vicar shall receive a third part of tithes and alms, and of offerings which come into his own hand while he celebrates Masses; and he alone shall have whatever comes to him from the white garments of newly baptized persons (*albatae*) and from blessed pilgrims’ wallets (*perae*), and from confessions.

> [Note: Col. 1253] The white garments of newly baptized persons and the pilgrims’ wallets that were blessed in the church.

We also establish that the agreement made between the monks of Saint Peter of Castinio and the vicar of their church at Ulmis, with the assent of the whole chapter of Saint Aper, of Henry of blessed memory, formerly bishop of Toul, and of Haimo, archdeacon of the same parish, and also with the dean’s assent, shall remain firm and unimpaired. Namely, the vicar shall receive a third part of all tithes and a third part of the whole endowment of the church, together with a third part of all offerings on the four principal feasts of the year—namely, the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, and Saint Remigius—and half of all alms, movable and immovable. On the day of someone’s death, if he has performed his service, the alms shall be divided equally as stated. But if he cannot perform it, [Col. 1255A] he shall receive three denarii from the common fund out of that alms. Content with these provisions, and imposing no burden whatever upon the monks, the vicar must pay from his own resources all the church’s dues.

Certainly, concerning your newly cleared lands, etc., as in no. 1436 above.

Given at Anagni through the hand of Alberic, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1179 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the twenty-first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

### MCDXXXIX. To the monks of Saint-Germain-des-Prés he grants that, “if the archbishop of Sens should perhaps wish to exceed, in the procuration which he requires from them, the number of persons and mounts fixed by himself, they shall be free to refuse what is demanded.”  
*(Velletri, 18 December.)*

[BOUILLART, *Hist. de Saint-Germain des Prés*, Preface, p. 47.]

[Col. 1255B]

### MCDXL–XLI. To Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours.—He rebukes him because he did not appear at the appointed time, and grants him a new extension.

[MARTEN., *Thes.*, III, 904.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother B. [BARTHOLOMEW], archbishop of Tours and legate of the Apostolic See, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Adrian, directed your predecessor E. [Engebald] to come to the Apostolic See in order to answer Hugh, formerly archbishop of Dol, concerning [Col. 1255C] his suffragans, so we also directed your brotherhood either to reach an amicable settlement with our beloved son, the bishop-elect of Dol, or to present yourself before the apostolic presence by the term which we set for you. But you neither came on the appointed day nor took care to send a representative. And although you sent a certain messenger, alleging through him the reason of your illness and seeking from us an extension until the council, you took no care either to appear in person at the council or to send representatives instructed to conduct the business.

Since we cannot and ought not fail the aforesaid elect in his justice—he has remained with us for a long time and incurred very great expenses—we direct and command your brotherhood by apostolic letters either to settle peacefully and amicably with the aforesaid church, or to appear, fully prepared, in person or through adequate representatives, putting aside excuse and pretext, before the apostolic presence by the next Sunday on which *Laetare Jerusalem* is sung, [Note: Col. 1255D: the fourth Sunday of Lent, 30 March 1180.] or at the latest by the Sunday on which *Ego sum pastor bonus* is sung. [Note: Col. 1255D: the second Sunday after Easter, 4 May 1180.] If you do not then come or send adequate representatives, we shall nevertheless proceed in the case, so far as justice permits, with the Lord as our author. Since we have granted you an extension three times, we have not thought fit to grant a longer one, [Col. 1256A] because the other party appears to have been burdened excessively by this.

### MCDXLII. To the king of the Franks.—That he should endeavour to settle the controversy between the Churches of Dol and Tours.

[Ibid., I, 906.]

We do not believe Your Royal Highness is unaware how the Church of Dol—which Childebert, the illustrious king of the Franks of revered memory, is said to have founded and endowed with great possessions and privileges—has, because of the controversy which it has with the Church of Tours, been afflicted and worn down, and greatly diminished in both spiritual and temporal matters. Therefore, since, as the common father, we are bound to preserve intact, without distinction of persons, the rights of all churches alike, we earnestly ask and exhort your Highness, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of sins, that, looking with a more merciful eye upon the desolation of that church, you make every effort, out of love for God and in consideration of the saints said to have been pastors of the same church—namely Saint Samson, who rests at Orléans; Saint Magloire, who rests at Paris; and Blessed Turiavus, who rests at [Col. 1256B] Saint-Germain, as is said—to bring about a peaceful and amicable settlement between the two churches, through yourself and others.

> [Note: Col. 1256D] That is, at the Parisian abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

For, because of this discord, the possessions of the aforesaid church have already for the most part been seized by barons and other knights. Marriages and the other ecclesiastical sacraments are by no means administered there according to God and the ordinances of the canons; some persons frequently contract marriage within the third degree; one man has three wives; and when a man’s wife becomes leprous, he dismisses her and takes another contrary to ecclesiastical rule. But if a settlement cannot be made, patiently and graciously allow the Church of Dol to proceed against the Church of Tours by judicial order, lest you be regarded—God forbid!—as the cause of such great evils, or deservedly suffer reproach to your name on that account. Certainly, since our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Adrian, wrote concerning this matter, we can neither omit nor ought to omit taking care to support the same Church of Dol in its right.

### MCDXLIII. To (William), archbishop of Reims, he directs that, “having gone to the churches of Lamen. [elsewhere, Laudunensem, i.e. Laon] and Tournai, he should restore for the benefit of a master to govern the schools some benefice which had anciently been assigned for that purpose, or cause another to be assigned, so that, adequate stipends having been provided for the teacher, the poor, who are not aided by their parents’ resources, may through the Church’s mercy rejoice that instruction is available to them, and the wealthy, who can serve the Church’s interests, may not be forced to go far from the Church for the study of letters.”

(MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 1100.)

[Col. 1256D]

## YEAR 1170–1180

[Col. 1257A]

### MCDXLIV. To the prior of the Lord’s Sepulchre at Jerusalem and his successors he grants that, “after archbishops and bishops, they shall hold first place among the abbots and priors of the patriarchate of Jerusalem in assemblies and church offices.”  
*(Tusculum, 12 November.)*

[Eug. de ROZIÈRE, *Cartul. du Saint-Sépulcre*, 270.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior and brethren of the Lord’s Sepulchre, greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the duty of the office entrusted to us, we are bound to preserve sound and unimpaired the dignities and rights of all persons, and especially to foster with more exact diligence in their rights those whom we particularly love because of their religious profession and devotion, and because of consideration for the church which they serve. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously granting effect to your just petitions, we establish by apostolic authority that you, son prior, and your successors shall forever hold first place, after archbishops and bishops, among the abbots and priors of the patriarchate of Jerusalem in assemblies and church offices, just as the earlier priors who preceded you are known to have held it. This shall not be prevented because some who used to be called priors are now, their title having been changed, called abbots; the customary honour shall nonetheless be preserved in this respect for you [Col. 1257C] and your successors.

Given at Tusculum, on the second day before the Ides of November.

### MCDXLV. He commands the abbots of the Temple of the Lord, Mount Sion, and the Valley of Jehoshaphat, and the prior of the Mount of Olives, that, “on the principal solemnities of their churches, if the patriarch of Jerusalem should be absent or ill, or if the Church of Jerusalem should be vacant, they are to receive the prior of that church and his brethren for the solemn procession, and allow them to sing solemn Mass in their churches in the patriarch’s place.”  
*(Tusculum, 13 November.)*

[Ibid., 269.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbots of the Temple of the Lord, Mount Sion, and the Valley of Jehoshaphat, and the prior of the Mount of Olives, and to their brethren, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your prudence ought diligently to consider how necessary it is for all churchmen, and especially for those who serve the Lord under the religious habit, to defer to the ordinances of the Apostolic See and to observe those ordinances without any contradiction, so that you may be shown to be true sons when you take care to submit to your mother’s enactments with filial obedience. Therefore, by apostolic letters we admonish, direct, and command all of you that, on the principal solemnities of your churches, if the patriarch of Jerusalem should be absent or ill, or if the Church of Jerusalem should be vacant, you shall, without objection, receive the prior then holding office in that church [Col. 1258A] with his brethren for the solemn procession, as is contained in our privilege; and in those same churches, putting aside every pretext and excuse, you shall permit the same prior and his brethren to sing solemn Mass in the patriarch’s place. But if—what we do not believe—you scorn to fulfil our ordinances in this respect, know that you will grievously incur the indignation of Blessed Peter and of ourselves and be subjected to fitting punishment for your presumption.

Given at Tusculum, on the Ides of November.

### MCDXLVI. He confirms to the abbot of Saint-Denis and his successors the right of distributing the prebends of the Church of Saint Paul.  
*(Tusculum, 20 December.)*

[DOUBLET, *Hist. de Saint-Denis*, 506.]

[Col. 1258B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those matters which are settled by judgment or amicable agreement ought to remain in their force and stability; and, lest through anyone’s rash presumption they later become the source of renewed contention, they should receive the protection of apostolic confirmation. Since a dispute arose between your predecessors and the canons of the Church of Saint Paul, which is known to be subject to the jurisdiction of your church, concerning the granting and investiture of prebends of that Church of Saint Paul, and remained unresolved until these times, the same canons finally, wholly renouncing whatever right they had in either the grants or the investitures of those prebends—as has become known to us from a document sealed with the seals of great and religious persons—granted, by equal vote and unanimous will, to you and your successors forever the free power to grant the prebends of that church and make their investitures. Holding this ratified and firm, we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it with the protection of the present writing. We establish that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of [Col. 1258D] almighty God and of his apostles Saints Peter and Paul.

Given at Tusculum, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January.

### MCDXLVII.  
*(Tusculum, 20 December.)*

[Ibid., p. 507.]

To the abbot and monks of Saint-Denis he grants that no archbishop, bishop, or other ecclesiastical person, except the Roman pontiff or his legate, may suspend their brethren from divine offices, or condemn them by a sentence of interdict or excommunication, whether they are priors of cells, dwell in cells or in the custody of villages, or reside elsewhere.

## YEAR 1171–1180

[Col. 1259A]

### MCDXLVII *bis*. He exhorts K[nut], illustrious king of the Swedes and Goths, the bishops, the noble duke, and all clergy and people established throughout Gothia, to observe the laws of marriage, honour priests, and pay tithes. He warns them not to “disinherit legitimate sons and leave all their goods to churches,” nor to “venerate as saints, in the manner of unbelievers, men killed in drinking and drunkenness.” He remits to them “the forty-day fast before the feast of Saint Michael, except Friday.” He gives thanks because they “visited him in his many necessities through Richard the priest.”  
*(Tusculum, 6 July.)*

[LILJEGREN, *Dipl. Suecan.*, I, 61.]

[Col. 1259B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ K[NUT], illustrious king of the Swedes and Goths; to our venerable brothers the bishops; to our beloved sons, the noble duke and all clergy and people established throughout Gothia: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The eternal and unchangeable providence of the divine counsel established the most holy Roman Church as head, mother, and teacher of all churches and all faithful, and raised it at the very birth of the Catholic and Christian faith upon its rock. For the Lord said to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys [Col. 1259C] of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16). To this prince of the apostles, in whose chair, though unworthy, we preside, the Son of God committed all his sheep without distinction and principally to be fed, so that whoever belongs to Christ’s fold may be subject to Peter’s teaching and doctrine. For he is reported to have prayed especially for Peter’s faith, saying: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when once you have turned, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22).

Therefore, whenever doubt arises concerning articles of faith or ecclesiastical institutions, recourse is confidently had to the aforesaid Roman Church as mother and teacher of the Christian faith. It belongs to her to feed, instruct, and strengthen peoples tender in the faith by God’s word; for, as the Apostle testifies, without that faith it is impossible to please God (Hebrews 11).

Among the other ordinances of the same Redeemer of all, he chose at the very beginning of human creation to establish the law of marriage himself. He formed woman not from another material but from the very rib of the first man, showing that the two would become one body and flesh. Adam, afterwards recognizing this in the Spirit, himself declared: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2). “Therefore a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Mark 10). The Son of God, afterwards appearing in the substance of our mortality, demonstrated this more plainly and taught in words which shall not pass away though heaven and earth pass away: “It is not lawful [Col. 1260A] for a man to put away his wife except for the cause of fornication; and if, having put her away while she is still alive, he takes another, he shall be called an adulterer—and likewise concerning the wife” (Matthew 19).

Apostolic teaching explains and makes this still clearer: it permits no man to have several wives at the same time, nor a woman several husbands, on any ground. Therefore, while a wife whom he has put away is alive, even on account of fornication, or while a husband is alive, it is not lawful to take another husband or wife, since whoever does so is plainly convicted of adultery. Therefore, dearest sons, flee fornication, because, as the Apostle testifies, fornicators and adulterers shall not possess the kingdom of God.

Ecclesiastical ordinance also provides that, when a wife has died, a man may take no wife from the blood-kindred of his deceased wife; and that, when a husband has died, a surviving woman may take no man from the blood-kindred of her deceased husband, because incest is undoubtedly committed in this case, where no dispensation is applicable. The same is likewise observed, on grounds of propriety, concerning a betrothed woman who has not yet been known by her husband because death or other causes intervened.

Moreover, bishops, priests, monks, and other religious men must be honoured with particular care.
