The Lord taught that they were to be honoured by his word, saying: “He who hears you hears me; he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10); and, “He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye.” Therefore those who persecute them, or plunder or seize their property, undoubtedly persecute Christ and commit the crime of sacrilege by seizing or plundering their goods. For it is exceedingly unjust and a great sacrilege that whatever anyone has bestowed or bequeathed to a church or religious house for the remission of sins or for the salvation or repose of souls should be taken beforehand, carried off, or converted to domestic and private uses, especially by those who ought to preserve it—that is, Christians and God-fearing persons, and above all the princes and magnates of regions—since laymen, however religious they may be, have absolutely no authority to dispose of ecclesiastical resources.

The law of both the New and Old Testaments teaches that tithes must be rendered to priests and other ministers of churches. The Lord says: “Bring all the tithe into [Col. 1260D] my storehouse, that there may be food in my house” (Malachi 3). For God, who deigned to give the whole tithe, deigned to receive it from us, not for himself but undoubtedly for our benefit. Those who faithfully give tithes from their goods will be able to gain both earthly and heavenly things, and they will abound in every good thing. Whenever famine, scarcity, or want of provisions oppresses the world, know that it undoubtedly proceeds from the wrath of God, who complains that he is defrauded in his ministers if he does not receive tithes. And this is, as the eminent teacher Augustine testifies: “The Lord’s most just custom is that those who have not given him a tenth shall afterwards be reduced to a tenth.” Therefore, if you wish to obtain a reward from God or earn forgiveness of sins, render tithes [Col. 1261A] and pay to the Lord alms from the nine parts.

Moreover, it has been reported to us that there are some among you who, disinheriting their legitimate sons, leave all their goods to churches. This is permitted by no law. Rather, one who has two sons may, if he wishes, make one of them Christ by leaving half to the Church; one who has three may make Christ the third; and so in other cases. For the Church ought not to receive everything when sons have been disinherited. Brothers or sisters, however, may do this, passing over brothers or sisters: if they die without children, they may leave everything to churches.

Men taken captive by pagans or Christians may not have their wives joined to other men while the former are alive. If they have been so joined, whenever their first husbands return from captivity they must be restored to them without any question; otherwise, so long as they remain with their second husbands after learning that their first husbands live, they are stained by the crime of adultery. Finally, we have heard something that filled us with great horror: that certain among you, deceived by diabolical fraud, venerate as a saint, after the fashion of unbelievers, a man killed in drinking and drunkenness, although the Church scarcely even permits prayer for persons slain in such drunkenness. For the Apostle says that drunkards shall not possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 6). Therefore, if you desire to possess God’s kingdom, you must abstain from drinking bouts and drunkenness, and on no account presume henceforth to worship that man to the peril of your souls. Even if many signs and miracles were performed through him, you would not be permitted publicly to venerate him as a saint without the authority of the Roman Church. But in all the matters we have mentioned, and in others known to concern your salvation, take care to conduct yourselves in such a way that you may deserve to attain temporal and eternal goods from God, the rewarder of every good thing. If, moreover, by the Lord’s help, you are willing to observe what has been said and to walk in other works of virtue, then, trusting in Christ’s mercy and in the authority and power of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we remit for you the forty-day penance before the feast of St Michael, [Col. 1261D] except Friday, which, in reverence for Christ’s cross, you ought to observe more attentively through fasting and other good works. We give you thanks for the visitation which, in many of your own necessities and those of the Church, you made to us through Richard the priest and his fellow-bearer of the present letters; and we particularly commend to you in the Lord the priest who laboured greatly on your behalf in coming to the Apostolic See.

Given at Tusculum, 6 July.

**MCDXLVIII. To the monks of St Savinus.—That they should obey the abbot.**  
*(Tusculum, 28 July.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus*, I, 457.]

[Col. 1262A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the whole chapter of Saint-Savinus: greeting and apostolic blessing.

How great is the power of obedience is shown by the fall of the first man: though placed in the highest blessedness, through the vice of disobedience he fell from glory into misery and was cast down from incomparable good into the vale of tears. Therefore, lest you may be accused or deservedly reproved for the vice of disobedience—you who ought to be adorned with the virtue of obedience—we command and enjoin your whole community by apostolic letters that you render in all things due obedience and reverence to your beloved son, your abbot, as to your spiritual father and the ruler of your souls. Humbly and devoutly obeying his … admonitions and commands, devote yourselves fervently and unanimously to the cultivation of religion, the keeping of enclosure, and the observance of the order. Thus you may appear commendable before God and men for the virtue of obedience and offer your Creator a worthy and acceptable sacrifice of praise and prayer. But if any among you prove rebellious and disobedient toward the same abbot, we shall, by the Lord’s authority, hold valid and firm whatever sentence he canonically pronounces against them on this account.

[Col. 1262C]

Given at Tusculum, 28 July.

**MCDXLIX. He confirms the rule of the canons of St Regulus: canons who have not served the church for six months of the year, without having obtained leave, are to receive only twenty solidi from their prebends.**  
*(Tusculum, 15 August.)*

[*Vie de sainte Rieule*, 398, attested by Bréquigny, *Table chronologique*, III, 537.]

**MCDL. To the archbishop of Auch and the abbot of Marseille.—That they impose suitable penance upon disobedient monks.**  
*(Tusculum, 22 September.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus*, I, 458.]

[Col. 1262D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the archbishop of Auch, legate of the Apostolic See, and to his beloved son the abbot of Marseille: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has come to the hearing of our apostolate that, although we decreed that the monks of Saint-Savinus should lie under excommunication until they restored those church-fourths which had been adjudged to our venerable brother, the bishop of Bigorre, against their monastery by the authority of Pope Eugenius of blessed memory, they presumed after their excommunication to celebrate the divine offices, and continue unceasingly to presume to do so, not considering how it is akin to sacrilege to oppose apostolic ordinances. Therefore [Col. 1263A] we command and enjoin you by apostolic letters that, if this is so, you send those who are more culpable to the monastery of Marseille to do penance there for so grave an offence, without occasion for or recourse to appeal. Upon the others, who are more suitable [for a lesser punishment], impose an appropriate penance, and make them refrain from celebrating Masses for as long as they are known to have sung while excommunicated.

Given at Tusculum, 22 September.

**MCDLI. To Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen.**  
*(Tusculum, 11 October.)*

[Letter of Gilbert Foliot, ed. GILES, II, 78.]

[Col. 1263B]

Because you have asked us whether it is lawful for you to absolve, before they have appeared before your tribunal, persons bound by a sentence of excommunication imposed by bishops or your suffragans who appeal to your hearing: we answer your inquiry by these present letters as follows. If the sentence of excommunication was pronounced against them after their appeal, they need no absolution, since a sentence delivered after an appeal cannot bind anyone. But if they were excommunicated before the appeal, then before the case is entered upon you ought, after receiving an oath from them according to the custom of the Church, to absolve them—unless you prefer in this matter to defer to the bishop by whom they were excommunicated and remit them to him for absolution. Once they have been absolved by the bishop or by you, you must hear the case [Col. 1263C] and bring it to its proper conclusion; for excommunicated persons are not to be heard before absolution, nor may the case in any way be referred back to those from whom appeal has been made.

Given at Tusculum, 11 October.

**MCDLII. Privilege for the monks of St Benedict at Subiaco.**  
*(Tusculum, 15 October.)*

[MARGARINI, *Bullarium Casinense*, II, 196.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all the brethren of St Benedict at Subiaco: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant consent to the just wishes of petitioners and bring to effect, with the outcome following, those requests which do not depart from the straight path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your just petitions, we grant you by apostolic authority that, whenever you see your abbot Simon or those who succeed him wasting the goods of the monastery, if after admonition they should perhaps refuse to desist, you shall have free liberty to appeal to the Apostolic See and to report matters prejudicial to the monastery. Nor may your abbot at any time, on that pretext, put any of you in chains or inflict unjust burdens upon you, while in all things the Rule of blessed Benedict and the discipline of the monastic order remain preserved.

[Col. 1264A]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our concession or rashly oppose it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Tusculum, 15 October.

**YEAR 1175–1180**

**MCDLIII. To Raynerius, archbishop of Salerno.**

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXII, 381.]

[Col. 1264B]

Furthermore, although that custom is not consistent with reason, according to which a cleric who dies between the Kalends of March and the Kalends of November disposes at his own will of the entire revenue of the benefice which he ought to receive in that year, nevertheless, because it is observed in many churches, you may tolerate it sufficiently in your archbishopric—especially if the cleric is burdened with debts at his death. And it is altogether contrary to reason that a single cleric should hold, in one church or in different churches, an archdeaconry together with a precentorship or a deanery, since each individual office in churches requires the regular attendance of persons [the printed text has *personarum*].

**MCDLIV. He confirms the place called God’s Mercy to the hermit Fulbert.**  
*(Tusculum, 18 December.)*

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, XII, *Instrumenta*, 55.]

[Col. 1264C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Brother FULBERT: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant consent to the just wishes of petitioners and bring to effect, with the outcome following, requests which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your successors, and strengthen with the protection of this present writing, the donation of the place called *Misericordia Dei* (“God’s Mercy”), reasonably made to you and your successors by Hugh [Col. 1264D] of Acrivilla and Heimoris, by Reinald Pelotinus, and by Fecelin Bodinus, and ratified by an authentic instrument of our venerable brother William—then archbishop of Sens, now archbishop of Reims and legate of the Apostolic See—as you justly and peacefully possess that same place. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Tusculum, 18 December.

**YEAR 1180**

[Col. 1265A]

**MCDLV. He confirms the establishment of canons of the Order of St Augustine in the abbey of Cisoing and all their goods.**  
*(Velletri, 10 January.)*

[D’ACHERY, *Spicilegium*, II, 882.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ANSELM, abbot of the Church of St Callixtus at Cisoing, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life.

Since, by the Lord’s inspiration, you have professed the regular life, we provide for your peace with paternal consideration, [Col. 1265B] and, lest you be wearied by the harassments of the wicked, we extend apostolic protection to you. Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid Church of St Callixtus, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the canonical order instituted in your church by Rainald, formerly archbishop of Reims, of good memory, according to the Rule of blessed Augustine and the institution of the brethren of the Church of St Denis at Reims, shall be observed there inviolably for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, the Lord providing, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

[Col. 1265C] The place on which your church stands, with tithes and free tenants, such that no one has advocacy over them; the church, grange, and land of Lovilio, with the full tithe and the tenants of the whole village; the wood of the prebends; Malum Alnetum; the wood called Salrugretum; and the holdings of that same village and of Cisoing in arable land, meadows, woods, marshland, and waters, as it possessed them of old; likewise the watercourse of the spring of Burgella, which the church may conduct through its necessary grounds without anyone’s prohibition; the church of Ask, with the full tithe, arable land, tenants, and the priest’s holding; the church of Baisui, with the full tithe, grange, and tenants; the church of Canfen, with the full tithe and tenants; the church of Bouvines, with the full tithe both in the land and court of St Amand and in other lands; the church of Gruison, with the full tithe; the church of Genes, with the full tithe, holding, and grange; the church of Corberiu; the church of Suminio, with the full tithe, the land-rent of the whole village, tenants, and a free holding; the chapel of [Col. 1266A] Gornen, with the full tithe and land-rent; the estate of Belrepaire, with woods, waters, marshland, fishpond, and arable land; the estate of Vitri, with land-rent, tenants, and the right that you possess in the revenues and tithes of that same village; the church of Cheren; the church of Lis; the church of Tofles; the chapel of Hertelerga; the estate of Crespellanis, with land-rent, tenants, and the whole village, so that none there except the abbot alone may exercise jurisdiction or advocacy; the stone house on the hill at Tournai, so that its revenues may be assigned forever to the needs of the church’s sick; the houses of Messines; and the five solidi which the count of Flanders pays for Arboreta.

Moreover, no one may presume to exact or extort tithes from you on your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate by your own hands [Col. 1266B] or at your own expense, nor upon the fodder of your animals. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a low voice. We also decree that the burial-place of that site shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; yet the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved. We further prohibit any of your brethren, after having made profession in that place, from leaving the cloister without the leave of his abbot, except in order to embrace a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without a guarantee in letters from the community. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the secular world who are free and absolved, and retain them without contradiction. We further prohibit any bishop or archdeacon from pronouncing a sentence of excommunication or interdict against you or your churches without manifest and reasonable cause, or from burdening you with novel and unlawful exactions. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it by any craft of deceit or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the counsel of the sounder part of the brethren, [Col. 1266D] in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Augustine, provide to be elected.

Furthermore, we strictly forbid bishops, archdeacons, their canonical officials, or other clerics to have power or licence, under the pretext of any custom, to require from you a palfrey, a silk cope, or anything else for confirmation, installation, or the blessing of your abbot. If they demand anything from you for these matters, since this is detestable and contrary to reason, you may freely refuse what they ask. Moreover, desiring to provide with paternal solicitude for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone from daring, within the enclosure of your places, to commit violence, robbery, or theft, [Col. 1267A] or to seize or kill persons.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved intact, for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If any ecclesiastical or secular person shall knowingly attempt in future rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of the Lord God and our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of St Clement. [Col. 1267C] I, Matthew, cardinal priest of the title of St Marcellus. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of St Theodore. I, Rainerius, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, John, cardinal deacon of St Angelo. I, Ramerius, cardinal deacon of St Adrian. I, Matthew, cardinal deacon of St Mary the New. I, Paul, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at Velletri, through the hand of ALBERT, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman [Col. 1267D] Church, 10 January, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1179 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twenty-first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

**MCDLVI. He takes the monastery of St Victor under protection and confirms its privileges.**  
*(Velletri, 3 February.)*

[*Saint-Victor en Caux*, 38, attested by Bréquigny, *Table chronologique*, III, 552.]

**MCDLVII. To the archbishops and bishops of Sardinia.—For the monastery of Monte Cassino.**  
*(Velletri, 25 February.)*

[DE TOSTI, *Storia di Monte-Casino*, II, 208.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the archbishops and bishops of Sardinia, in whose bishoprics are churches of the monastery of Monte Cassino: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1268A] We have heard—and, hearing it, have been moved to vehement astonishment—that certain among you, in contempt of our decrees recently issued in council, are attempting to infringe the privileges granted by the Apostolic See to the aforesaid monastery. Acting against the liberty which that monastery has hitherto possessed, by the indulgence of that same see, in its churches and in the clerics of those churches, they seek to compel those clerics to promise them obedience under oath and to attend their synod. They forbid divine offices not only to those clerics but also in the aforesaid [Col. 1268B] churches; they deny them holy oil and chrism; and they forbid the people and servants of those churches to pay tithes there, although they always assemble in them for the divine offices and are baptized there as well. Since, therefore, our decrees do not infringe the privileges of the Apostolic See or derogate from those privileges in any respect, we command and enjoin your brotherhood that, supplying holy oil and chrism to the churches of the said monastery, none of you may presume to act against the privileges of the aforesaid monastery or against the liberty hitherto observed by its churches and clerics. Rather, setting aside every occasion and objection, observe the tenor of those privileges inviolably. Be certain that anyone who attempts otherwise may fear our indignation. For we neither wish nor ought to tolerate any diminution of that monastery in its right and liberty.

Given at Velletri, 25 February.

**MCDLVIII. Privilege for the Church of Monopoli.**  
*(Velletri, 26 February.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 965.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother STEPHEN, bishop of Monopoli, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

[Col. 1268D] By the office of apostolate entrusted to us, we ought to love with sincere affection of heart our brothers and fellow bishops, whether nearby or far away, and to preserve their dignity and rights for the churches in which they are known to serve the Lord. Yet it is equitable and reasonable that those known to be more devoted to blessed Peter and his vicars, and who desire to be cherished by the protection of the Holy Roman Church, should be nourished at the breasts of that pious mother and heard in their reasonable petitions. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, graciously assenting to your just requests, we receive under the guardianship of that apostle and our own protection, after the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, the Roman pontiffs Urban, [Col. 1269A] Paschal, Calixtus, Honorius, and Eugenius, the Church of Monopoli, which by God’s authority you are known to govern and which belongs to the right and property of the blessed apostle Peter; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church presently justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, the Lord providing, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors; among which we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms.

*(It enumerates their possessions.)*

We likewise confirm by apostolic authority to you and your successors the liberties granted to the Church of Monopoli by Roman pontiffs, kings, and princes, as your predecessors are known to have held them from ancient custom, and as you canonically and peacefully possess them. We further decree that the same church shall owe reverence of subjection to no one except the Apostolic See. Therefore we decree that you and your successors, enjoying the benefit of this liberty, shall remain forever under obedience to the Apostolic See alone. Upon the death of you, the present bishop of that city, or of any of your successors, the clergy and people of Monopoli shall have the power, all impropriety removed, to elect a bishop canonically. The person elected shall approach the Roman pontiff for consecration. We decree therefore, etc. To all, etc. Amen.

[Col. 1269C] I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. Ubald, bishop of Ostia. Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. Berneredus, bishop of Palestrina. John, cardinal priest of the church of Saints John and Paul of Pammachius. Vivian, cardinal priest of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill. Cynthius, cardinal priest of the church of St Cecilia. Laborans, cardinal priest of St Mary across the Tiber, [of] Callixtus. Hugh, cardinal priest of St Clement. James, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. Rainerius, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil. [Col. 1269D] John, cardinal deacon of St Angelo.

Given at Velletri through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 26 February, thirteenth indiction, in the year 1180 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twenty-first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

**MCDLIX.**  
*(Velletri, 15 March.)*

[PÉRARD, *Recueil de pièces pour servir à l’histoire de Bourgogne*, p. 255.]

At the request of the abbot and chapter of Cîteaux, he decrees that none of the brethren may leave the cloister without their permission, and that no one may dare receive a brother who has departed without the safeguard of letters from the community.

**MCDLX. To Omnibonus, bishop of Verona, and the bishop of Mantua.—That they compel T. to restore the estate of Nogaria to the monks of Nonantola.**  
*(Velletri, 7 April.)*

[TIRABOSCHI, *Storia di Nonantola*, II, 238.]

[Col. 1270A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers O[MNIBONUS], bishop of Verona, and the bishop of Mantua: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The complaint transmitted to us by our beloved sons, the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Nonantola, has made known that the nobleman T., your parishioner, a Veronese brother, presumes to seize and, at peril to his salvation, retain the estate of Nogaria belonging to their monastery. Since we are bound to defend the rights of the aforesaid monastery all the more strongly because its care is known to rest more specially upon us, [Col. 1270B] we command and enjoin your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to admonish the aforementioned T. and, laying aside appeal, to compel him by ecclesiastical severity either to leave the aforesaid estate in the peaceful possession of the brethren or, without delay, to render full justice in your presence.

Given at Velletri, 7 April.

**MCDLXI. To B[artholomew], archbishop of Tours and legate of the Apostolic See, he writes that, having been persuaded that he would come to him “on the next Sunday on which *Laetare Jerusalem* is sung” (30 March), or on “I am the good shepherd” (4 May), his messenger had arrived. He adds that, moved by the prayers of Louis, king of the Franks, and King Philip, he has “extended until the next feast of blessed Martin” (11 November), though “not without a great and serious burden,” the deadline for R., bishop-elect of Dol, who had been waiting with him for more than a year, and orders him to come by that date.**

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III.—Cf. above, letter 1440.]

[Col. 1270C]

**MCDLXII. To the chapter of the Church of Bremen.—That laymen are not to be admitted to the election of an archbishop.**  
*(Tusculum, 29 June.)*

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburgische Urkunden*, I, 215.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the dean, provost, and chapter of the Church of Bremen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that, because certain laymen and clerics at times indiscreetly insert themselves into the election of your bishop, the election itself cannot sometimes be celebrated as it ought. You have therefore asked us to inform you by apostolic writing to whom the election belongs. Let it therefore be made known by these present letters that, although the favour and consent of the prince ought to be sought in the election of a pontiff, laymen must not be admitted to the election. Rather, the election is to be conducted by the canons of the cathedral church and the religious men who are in the city and diocese. Yet we do not say this in such a way that the opposition of religious persons should obstruct the canons. If, therefore, laymen wish to involve themselves in such matters, then, mindful of that canon [Col. 1271A] which says, “The people must be taught, not followed,” exclude them and proceed unanimously and canonically in the election.

Given at Tusculum, 29 June.

**MCDLXIII. Privilege for the Church of Chalon.**  
*(Tusculum, 2 July.)*

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, IV, *Instrumenta*, 243.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GALTER, dean of the Church of Chalon, and his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed in perpetuity: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although, unworthy as we are, the care of all churches has been entrusted to us, the duty of our office requires us to labour for the welfare of all churches and to fortify them with apostolic protection so that they may be secure from the assaults of the malicious. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid Church of Chalon, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, the Lord providing, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. [Col. 1271C] Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of Fontaines, with the tithe of the lands which you possess there; the church of St Vincent of Bragniac, with its tithe and other appurtenances; the church of St George of Dalmariac, with its appurtenances; the church of Bragniac near Verdun, with its tithe; the church of Tureyo, with its tithe; the church of Viriac [Viriciac]; the church of Cerley; the church of Albignei, with its appurtenances; the church of Brancidun, with the chapel below, with its appurtenances [“with its other appurtenances”]; the church of Bressiis [Brissiis]; the church of St German on the hill; and the annual payment of five solidi [Col. 1271D] which you possess in the church of Ozenay; the church of Arconcey [Arcencey]; the church of St Privatus, with the revenues which you have in and around the city of Chalon; the revenue which you possess at Boyac, with its appurtenances; Rocheta, with its dependencies; whatever you have at Varennes; Montaniac, with its appurtenances; whatever you have at Saint-Désiré; whatever you have at Grevilla; whatever you have at Criciac. We prohibit by apostolic authority any frivolous alteration in the rights, liberty, and ancient reasonable customs hitherto observed by your predecessors and yourselves, and likewise the alienation of possessions except with the consent of the chapter and its greater and sounder part. We also grant full authority to lawfully recover for the church alienations made without consultation of the chapter.

[Col. 1272A]

We therefore decree that no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with vexations in any manner; but that all shall be preserved intact, for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the ordinary right of the diocesan bishop. If any ecclesiastical or secular person shall knowingly attempt in future rashly to contravene this page of our confirmation, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by fitting [Col. 1272B] satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Tusculum through the hand of Aldradus, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 2 July, thirteenth indiction, in the year 1180 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twenty-first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander.

**MCDLXIV. He writes to the bishops of Padua, Vicenza, and Treviso that, after peace with the emperor and a Lombard truce had been achieved with such great labours, the Bolognese had destroyed the castle and church of Montebello; and that, although the truce had been violated by men of the imperial party, the emperor’s legates had already demanded “magnificently” that the damage be compensated under the laws of the truce. He asks them to take care that such deeds do not occur and, if they have occurred, to order reparation of the losses inflicted.**  
*(Tusculum, 8 July.)*

[SAVIOLI, *Annali Bolognesi*, II, II, 103.]

[Col. 1272C]

**MCDLXV. He writes the same to the archbishop of Ravenna and his suffragans.**

[LUPI, *Codex diplomaticus Bergomensis*, II, 1311.]

**MCDLXVI. To the canons of the Church of Alessandria.—He confirms their constitution and possessions.**  
*(Tusculum, 18 July.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 912.]

[Col. 1272D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons O., bishop-elect, and the canons of the Church of Alessandria: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We perform a fitting act of our office when those things which are laudably established by provident care for the adornment and honour of the house of the Lord receive increase through us and are strengthened in the firmness of their stability by the protection of apostolic guardianship. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we approve the canonry which you, bishop-elect, have established there in the church of St Peter with the assent of clergy [Col. 1273A] and people. By prudent deliberation you have assigned suitable persons to hold the dignities of the church: to our beloved son Master Hugh, the provostship; to Master Cataldus, the archpriesthood; and to Master P., the precentorship. We hold this arrangement ratified, and confirm the respective dignities of each of the aforesaid by apostolic authority. Furthermore, we have thought fit to confirm by these present letters the churches assigned to your use, sons the canons: namely, St Mary of Gamundio, St Dalmatius of Maringo, St Michael of Soleriis, St Stephen of Bergolio, Holy Trinity of Wilia, St Andrew of Roverteo, and St Augustine of Foro. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation. [Col. 1273B] If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Tusculum, 18 July.

**MCDLXVII. To the archbishops, bishops, and others established throughout Dalmatia.—He commends his subdeacon Theobald, apostolic legate.**  
*(Tusculum, 4 October.)*

[FARLATI, *Illyricum sacrum*, III, 211.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren the archbishops and bishops, and to the beloved sons, the noble men the counts and barons, [Col. 1273C] and to all the clergy and people established throughout Dalmatia and the whole of Slavonia, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The order of reason and the care of the administration entrusted to us require that we, who must render an account of all things at the supreme judgment, should consider the salvation of all and strive, by ourselves and through others, to provide what pertains to the advancement of the faithful. Since, however, we cannot ourselves extend paternal diligence to those who are far away, it is fitting that we entrust apostolic powers to those who are more especially united to us, and whose prudence and fidelity we have tested.

For this reason, we have committed the office of legation in your provinces to our beloved son T., our subdeacon, a learned and honourable man, most dear and [Col. 1273D] acceptable to us, so that in our stead he may root up and destroy whatever ought to be destroyed, and may build and plant whatever, by the Lord’s instruction, he sees ought to be planted. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and enjoin upon your whole community that you take care to receive him honourably as legate of the Apostolic See; that, humbly responding to his summons, you accept and firmly observe whatever he shall decree by our authority for the state of the Church or the salvation of the faithful. Otherwise, if anyone proves disobedient to him, we shall, by the Lord’s authority, hold valid the sentence which the same legate shall canonically pronounce, nor shall we allow it to be altered by any frivolous pretext.

Given at Tusculum, on the fourth day before the Nones of October [4 October].

MCDLXVIII. Privilege for the monastery of Laetien. (Year 1180.)

[REIFFENBERG, *Belgian Chronicles*, VII, 642.]

[Col. 1274A]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons ELGOTHO, abbot of the church of Laetien, and his brethren, present and future, professing the monastic life, for ever.

To those choosing the religious life, etc.

Given at Tusculum, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of November [24 October], in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1180 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twenty-second year of the pontificate of Pope Alexander III.

MCDLXIX. To the bishops of Scotland.—He confirms the sentence of the apostolic legate, by which the latter confirmed John, lawfully elected, and deposed Hugh, whom the king had intruded into the bishopric of St Andrews.

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 912.]

[Col. 1274B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren, all bishops, and beloved sons, abbots and other prelates of churches established throughout Scotland, and to the prior, canons, clergy, and people of St Andrews, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having learned that some time ago our venerable brother John, now bishop of St Andrews, had been canonically elected, and that after his election [Col. 1274C] Hugh, an appeal having been lodged, had been intruded by lay power into that church and had rashly presumed to be consecrated: annulling his election by apostolic authority, we sent our beloved son Alexius, our subdeacon and legate of the Apostolic See, into your parts to investigate the election of the aforesaid John. Having proceeded sufficiently maturely and canonically, as became known to us through the testimony of many, and having found his election canonical, he confirmed it by apostolic authority after many delays, in which he deferred to the royal majesty; commanding, in our name, all belonging to the church of St Andrews to show John obedience and reverence as the elect. Accordingly, since none dared openly to obey because of fear of the king, the same legate subjected not the kingdom, as he could have done by right, but the bishopric to an interdict.

Therefore, when both ecclesiastical and secular princes had been most strictly adjured to give sound counsel to our dearest son in Christ, William, illustrious king of the Scots, and when the king himself had firmly promised that he would abide by their counsel, all answered as one: that he should no longer disturb the consecration of the aforesaid John, performed before our legate and four bishops—the fifth being ill but consenting in writing—but should allow him to be consecrated peacefully in his see. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command [Col. 1275A] and, under penalty of office and benefice, enjoin upon your whole community that, putting on the spirit of fortitude, within eight days after receiving these letters you honourably restore that bishop to his see, setting aside the appeal; that you labour prudently and courageously to preserve ecclesiastical justice; that you diligently exert yourselves to calm the king’s anger; and that you show the aforesaid bishop all the reverence and honour which you rendered to his predecessors. But if the king wishes otherwise, or has been swayed by the counsel of the wicked, it is more necessary to obey God and the holy Roman Church than men. Otherwise, we shall, by God’s authority, hold valid [Col. 1275B] the sentence which our venerable brother Hugh, bishop of Durham, shall pronounce against the contumacious and rebellious, and shall command it to be firmly observed.

MCDLXX. To William, king of Scotland.—He orders him to allow John, lawfully elected and confirmed bishop of St Andrews, to discharge his office undisturbed; otherwise the kingdom is to be punished by interdict and the king by excommunication.

[MANSI, ibid., col. 914.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to WILLIAM, illustrious king of the Scots, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We remember having laboured diligently for your peace and liberty, hoping that through this you would be more firmly established and grow in devotion to the Apostolic See, and would more willingly preserve ecclesiastical liberty. But [Col. 1275C] observing that you have hitherto refused to yield in the affair of our venerable brother John, bishop of St Andrews in Scotland, we are compelled to judge this contrary to the hope which we had entertained concerning the ardour of your royal devotion. Yet, wishing still to test whether our patience might lead the royal disposition to repentance, we earnestly admonish and command your greatness by apostolic letters that, within twenty days after receiving these letters, you grant peace and security to the said bishop, so that he need not fear royal displeasure. Otherwise know that we have commanded our venerable brother Roger, archbishop of York and legate of the Apostolic See in Scotland, to subject your kingdom to interdict, notwithstanding any appeal, [Col. 1275D] and, if you refuse to desist, to pronounce sentence of excommunication upon your person. Be certain also that, if you decide to persist in your violence, then as we laboured that your kingdom might possess liberty, so we shall endeavour that it return to its former subjection.

MCDLXXI. To the bishops of Scotland.—He confirms the excommunication of Hugh, intruded into the bishopric of St Andrews.

[MANSI, ibid., col. 913.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren and beloved sons, prelates of churches established throughout Scotland, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that Hugh, who had seized the church [Col. 1276A] of St Andrews in Scotland, unlawfully retained the episcopal chapel, staff, ring, and other things which he had wrongfully carried away. Though frequently warned, he despised repentance; therefore our beloved son Alexius, our subdeacon and legate of the Apostolic See, before you and a great body of clergy and people, relying on apostolic authority, bound him with the bond of excommunication unless, within fifteen days, he restored what he had seized or carried away, or made suitable satisfaction. Yet he persisted in the evil of arrogance and complied in no respect with the admonitions of the aforesaid legate. We therefore hold valid the sentence pronounced by our authority, and by apostolic letters command and enjoin upon your whole community that, trusting in God’s grace and setting aside every [Col. 1276B] fear, you publicly declare the aforesaid Hugh bound by the bond of excommunication, notwithstanding any appeal, and diligently avoid him as excommunicated until he restores to our brother John, bishop of St Andrews, and to his church the things which he took from the aforesaid goods, or their valuation, and makes suitable satisfaction for the other things which he destroyed.

YEAR 1159–1181.

MCDLXXII. To Henry, king of England.—That he release William, a chaplain imprisoned by his officials, and restore the benefices taken from him.

[*Letters of St Thomas*, ed. GILES, II, 118.]

[Col. 1276C]

POPE ALEXANDER to HENRY, illustrious king of England.

It has been reported to us that certain of your officials living in England have presumed, without reasonable cause, to arrest and commit to prison our beloved William, a chaplain. There, as we have heard, he is still held captive and, as though he were not a priest, is treated shamefully and dishonourably; and we do not believe that this can in any respect please your excellence. Since it does not become your magnificence to tolerate in any way that priests, ministers of the altar, or indeed any clerics should be so arrested by your officers or [Col. 1276D] committed to prison, but rather to correct such an offence more quickly once it has reached your ears, we ask, admonish, and exhort your serenity in the Lord by apostolic letters that, for love of Him who is also called the true King and Priest, and out of reverence for Blessed Peter and ourselves, you release the said William free and absolved; grant him your peace; allow him without molestation to possess the benefices which he held and which were unjustly taken from him; and cause all other things taken from him to be restored to him in full, so that you may deserve to receive from almighty God a worthy reward for this, and may expect abundant thanks from us ourselves.

MCDLXXIII. To Henry, king of England.—He commends R., son of a citizen of Canterbury.

[*Letters of Gilbert Foliot*, ed. GILES, II, 112.]

[Col. 1277A]

R., son of Henry, a citizen of Canterbury, having come to us, earnestly entreated us to address prayers and send our letters on his behalf to your magnificence, constantly asserting and affirming that he had never committed anything for which he ought deservedly to incur royal displeasure or suffer exile. Therefore, since the aforesaid R., burdened by old age and weakness, is altogether unworthy of Caesar’s wrath, we ask, admonish, and exhort your serenity in the Lord by apostolic letters that, in view of divine mercy [Col. 1277B] and out of reverence for Blessed Peter and ourselves, you mercifully remit your displeasure toward him; permit him to return to his home and wife and to remain there peaceably and freely; grant your peace also to him and his people; and cause all things unjustly taken from his people to be restored to him in full. Thus we may greatly commend your royal clemency in the Lord for this, and be bound to render abundant thanks to your highness.

MCDLXXIV. He takes the monastery of St Ouen of Rouen under protection and confirms its goods and possessions.

[POMERAIE, *History of the Abbey of St Ouen*, 406.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved [Col. 1277C] sons, the abbot of St Ouen and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetual remembrance.

It is fitting for us mercifully to accede to the just petitions of religious men and to fulfil their pious desires by bringing them to effect, so that they may devote themselves all the more fervently to the religious purpose inasmuch as they are more readily heard by us in what they justly request. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, granting favourable assent to your just requests, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves your monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in your monastery according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed [Col. 1277D] Benedict shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by God’s favour, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to name the following expressly:

The church of St Ouen; Wadignac, with the churches of that village and all its appurtenances, villages, and churches; Baillol, with its villages, churches, and all other appurtenances; Dalbodium, with churches, villages, and all other appurtenances; [Col. 1278A] Chevreville, with all its villages and appurtenances; Piris, with all its villages, churches, and appurtenances; Anteum, with villages and churches; the men and rents of Humo; Crovilla, with the church and appurtenances of that village; the tithes from them; the village of St Martin in Oximensis, with its church and dwellings; the church of Roz, the whole tithe of the entire village, and the chapel of Mero; the village of Crovilla with its church and appurtenances; the village of Condé with its church and appurtenances; Sanceium with its church and appurtenances; also the rights and dignities which you have in the church of St Leufred and in the church of St Victor at Calley; in England, Mereseium with its church and appurtenances; Fringingeho with its church and appurtenances; in Normandy, Bellummont; the priory of Bertrand with churches, villages, and appurtenances; Sigeium with villages, churches, and appurtenances; the priory of St Peter of Albret; the priory of St Giles. In the city of Rouen: the church of Holy Cross in the parish of St Ouen; the church of St Vivian; the church of St Peter of the Castle; the church of St Stephen; the church of St Andrew; the church of Holy Cross in the market-place; the church of St Peter; the church of Humo and that same village; the church of Malo Alneto; the church of Imovilla; the village of Wellettes with the church of that village and the chapel of Palluel; and the church of Lireio with the tithes of that village.

[Col. 1278C] We further decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that none may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, without prejudice, nevertheless, to the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. No one shall presume to demand tithes from you of your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or of the fodder of your animals. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed there through any cunning of fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common assent, or the sounder part of their counsel, shall elect from the same monastery, if a suitable person is found there, according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict.

[Col. 1278D] Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be kept intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan archbishop.

If anyone therefore, etc.

Amen, amen, amen.

MCDLXXV. Statute for the monastery of St John of the Vines.

?(LOUEN, *History of the Abbey of St John of the Vines*, 295. Paris, 1712, duodecimo.)

We decree that if you have an abbey or priory in your city, castle, or village, and if any one of your canons happens to be a parish priest, [Col. 1279A] he shall live in the same house with his brethren and, as far as he is able, observe his order as the Rule prescribes, lest he appear to be divided from his head. When a synod is held in your city, your canons administering parishes who have attended the synod shall by no means presume to sit or sleep outside the cloister in that city; nor shall the deans of the bishopric dare to exact anything from them because those canons have not attended their meal. If, however, a parish canon happens to be recalled to the cloister or to depart from the parish, the bishop or archdeacon shall by no means be permitted lawfully to seize or retain any matter belonging to the parish church; rather, provided that he is suitable, he shall receive without contradiction the person whom you present and entrust to him the care of souls, lest the parish church suffer loss through an excessive calling away of spiritual and temporal goods. We also prohibit any bishop or other person from daring, without reasonable cause, to burden any of you or your churches with a sentence of excommunication, interdict, or suspension. Moreover, because at the blessing of your abbot and his reception of pastoral care a palfrey is exacted by the archdeacon, on the ground that he places him in the stall, and because this proceeds not from any reasonable cause but from the very root of covetousness and breaks out into the depravity of simony, we prohibit by apostolic authority [Col. 1279C] that, if a palfrey is thus exacted from any of you by your archdeacon, or if anyone presumes for any reason to give one, both giver and receiver alike shall be punished by divine vengeance for the vice of simony.

MCDLXXVI. Rescript to Hugh, abbot of St John of the Vines.

(Ibid., p. 297.)

[lacuna] Furthermore, by this present writing we have thought fit to grant you that, when your churches are vacant, provided that you do not remain alone, you may appoint to them any of your canons, one of whom shall be presented to the diocesan, so that he may receive from him the care of souls; he shall be accountable to the same diocesan for spiritual matters, [Col. 1279D] but to you for temporal matters and the observance of the order. In the other churches to which you decide not to appoint canons, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust to them the care of souls, so that they shall render due account to the bishop for the care of the people and to you for temporal goods. Moreover, we more strictly prohibit any ecclesiastical person from imposing new and undue exactions upon you or your churches, or from pronouncing against you or those churches a sentence of excommunication or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause; and within the boundaries of the parishes no one shall presume to build a new oratory or church without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, [Col. 1280A] while preserving, however, the authentic writings of the Apostolic See. We prohibit anyone from receiving the tithes of your parishes by lay hand without your consent. When there is a general interdict upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, after excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a low voice. No one shall presume to exact tithes from you of your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or of the fodder of your animals. We further decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that none may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted, while preserving nevertheless the rights of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be installed there through any cunning of fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren by common assent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this rescript or rashly oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

YEAR 1160–1181.

[Col. 1280C]

MCDLXXVII. To [Manasses], bishop of Orléans.

[*Letters of Gilbert Foliot*, ed. GILES, II, 80.]

Our beloved son John, dean of your church, in a report sent to us, showed that he granted you half of his prebend on the promise that you should assign him a full prebend when one became vacant. Therefore, since on account of his uprightness, and because he is connected with you by nearness of blood, you ought to love him and honour him with favour and benefice, we ask, admonish, and command your brotherhood to grant and assign to the aforesaid dean, according to your promise, the first [Col. 1280D] or second prebend that becomes vacant in your church, so that he may be bound to you in greater devotion and may be fervently stirred to your service and honour. For whatever benefice you confer upon him is as though you conferred it upon yourself and cast it from your bosom into your lap.

YEAR 1163–1181.

MCDLXXVIII. To [Gilbert], bishop of London, and R., archdeacon.—That they compel clerics and laypeople to desist from illicit marriages and cohabitations.

[Ibid., p. 89.]

ALEXANDER III, bishop, servant of the servants of [Col. 1281A] God, to the venerable brother G., bishop of London, and beloved son R., archdeacon, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that certain of your parishioners widely contract illicit marriages with their blood-relatives and relatives by marriage, and that very many clerics publicly introduce concubines and do not fear to join them to themselves under the solemnity of an oath. Therefore, because we do not wish such grave and enormous offences to remain unrebuked or unpunished, we command and enjoin upon your discretion by apostolic letters that, in accordance with the duty of your office, you compel the clerics and laity of your diocese wholly to desist from such marriages and cohabitations. But if any clerics, not in the subdiaconate [Col. 1281B] but in minor orders, have joined women to themselves by marriage or after an oath has intervened, compel them strictly, setting aside appeal, to cling to their wives and to leave the churches entirely. As for those who have received the subdiaconate or higher orders and have presumed to join women to themselves, diligently admonish and carefully exhort them to put away their concubines entirely and live chastely and continently. If they neglect to comply with your admonition, deprive them, with all delay and appeal set aside, of the churches which they hold, and suspend them likewise from the exercise of their office.

MCDLXXIX. To [Gilbert], bishop of London.—He is not to allow the sons of priests, and those begotten while their fathers were priests, to succeed in churches in which their fathers previously ministered.

[Ibid., p. 90.]

[Col. 1281C]

ALEXANDER III, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother G., bishop of London, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You should know that it has come to our hearing that certain clerics established in your parish, sons of priests and begotten in priesthood, have succeeded in the churches in which their fathers previously ministered and presume to perform divine service there. Since such successions must therefore be wholly rooted out from the threshold of God’s Church, we command and enjoin upon your discretion by apostolic letters [Col. 1281D] that you take every care that such persons are no longer admitted into their fathers’ churches throughout your parishes, nor are you in any way to tolerate any sons of priests who have been promoted to holy orders to celebrate unless they have first ministered in the cloister of regulars.

YEAR 1166–1181.

MCDLXXX. To Sueno, bishop of Aarhus.

[LANGEBECK, *Writers of Danish Affairs*, V, 252.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother SUENO, bishop of Aarhus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1282A] Since your brotherhood has consulted us whether brethren of the Cistercian order are bound to pay tithes to priests or other secular clerics, we answer your prudence as follows: by the benevolence of the Apostolic See they are wholly free and exempt from payment of tithes upon the produce of their labour which they cultivate with their own hands or at their own expense, or upon the fodder of their animals; thus no one at all, however religious or endowed with dignity he may be—still less a secular cleric—may dare to demand or in any manner extort tithes from them.

MCDLXXXI. To [Bartholomew], bishop of Exeter, and Simon, abbot of St Albans.—Concerning the dispute of Robert de Ber and William, clerk.

[*Letters of Gilbert Foliot*, ed. GILES, II, 84.]

[Col. 1282B]

ALEXANDER III, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother B., bishop of Exeter, and beloved son SIMON, abbot of St Albans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Robert de Ber informed us that William, a clerk, bound his chaplain and a great many other witnesses by oath not to offer testimony, counsel, or assistance to the said Robert against himself. Therefore, by the authority of this letter we enjoin upon you that, if the testimony of those persons has not been published and the witnesses who are not bound by oath have not been objected to, you are not to delay in receiving them and, if necessary, other suitable persons whom Robert himself [Col. 1282C] shall produce as witnesses.

YEAR 1168–1181.

MCDLXXXII. To the consuls of Piacenza.—That they cause property taken from his subdeacon Hugh to be restored.

[CAMPI, *History of Piacenza*, II, 362.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons, the consuls of Piacenza, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the report of our beloved son Hugh, our subdeacon, we have learned that Fulco, your citizen, has presumed, contrary to an agreement made between Hugh, formerly bishop of Piacenza and Tusculum, of pious [Col. 1282D] memory, and his brothers, to seize his *vicedominatus*—his stewardship or jurisdiction—and despoil the men belonging to it. We therefore wonder all the more strongly at your uprightness in tolerating this, since you can perceive with surer consideration how greatly the aforesaid Hugh may prove beneficial to the advancement of your city and, being established in the fullness of our favour, may, with God’s aid, rise to greater things. Accordingly, that his rights among you may remain unimpaired ought to engage your prudence with the greater care, inasmuch as you know that we embrace him with more attentive affection and that he can be more useful to your city. Therefore, since we can and ought not [Col. 1283A] to fail him in any respect in his justice, we ask, admonish, and command your prudence to take care to assist our beloved brother, the bishop of Piacenza, in every matter concerning this; and to constrain the aforesaid citizen of yours and his brothers by temporal penalty, so that they fully carry out and observe everything contained in the document made between them and the aforesaid Hugh, formerly bishop of Piacenza, and restore all that was taken.

MCDLXXXII bis. Privilege granted to Ulrich, patriarch of Aquileia.

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, V, 65.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother ULRICH, patriarch of the Church of Aquileia, and to his successors canonically instituted [Col. 1283B] for ever.

Although the love of all the apostles was equal and they all received the same power of binding and loosing, nevertheless, in accordance with the saying of Blessed Leo, a certain distinction of rank was preserved among them, and one was given authority to preside over the rest. In the same manner, within God’s Church there has been made a diversity of offices and dignities; and for the discharge of greater ministries greater persons have been appointed, who should excel in prerogative of rank and possess a broader care of others. From ancient times the Church of Aquileia has plainly been one of the worthier and nobler Churches of the West: it has shone in excellence of rank [Col. 1283C] and is known faithfully and devoutly to adhere to the most holy Roman Church. Therefore the Apostolic See has always diligently preserved for that Church its rights and dignities, has more generously honoured its prelates, and has customarily admitted their just petitions with particular kindness.

Accordingly, venerable brother in Christ, patriarch of Aquileia, to you, and through you to the holy Church of Aquileia, over which by God’s will you are known to preside, following the example of our predecessor Pope Adrian of blessed memory, we grant metropolitan authority over sixteen bishoprics: Pula, Trieste, Parenzo, Pedena, Emona, Concordia, Treviso, Ceneda, Belluno, Feltre, Padua, Vicenza, Trent, Mantua, Verona, and Como. Likewise, we establish as an episcopal see the Church of Justinopolis, which we nevertheless confirm to you and your Church by the counsel of all our brethren, on these terms: our venerable brother Wernard [Col. 1284A], now bishop of that place, is to retain both that Church and that of Trieste, together with the whole bishopric, as long as he lives; and after his death you may, with the counsel of your suffragans and the authority of the Apostolic See, restore the episcopal see in both places, if you wish and if you find their resources sufficient for this purpose. We have likewise thought fit to confirm to you and your successors the abbeys of Osciac, Rosazzo, Velden, Moggio, Sesto, Prates, St Mary at the Organ, St Euphemia of Villanova, Sittich, and Olvenburg, united to Aquileia; one monastery of nuns and another built in the city of Austria in honour of the Blessed Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary; the provostships of St Michael [Col. 1284B] of Lemine; the city of Aquileia; Taven; St Stephen; St Felix; St Ulrich; and the church of St George situated in the city of Venice beside the episcopal see, with all their appurtenances.

We also confirm to you and your successors the use of the pallium, rightly and truly granted to your predecessors by our predecessors for the dignity of that Church, on the days contained in the privilege of your Church. Wherever you may go, we grant by the authority of Blessed Peter and our own permission for a cross to be carried before you and your successors. Furthermore, we likewise strengthen by the sanction of this present decree the county, march, and duchy granted to your Church by royal or imperial privileges. We decree also that whatever possessions and goods the Church of Aquileia now justly and lawfully possesses, or may hereafter acquire by God’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors, while in all things preserving the right and reverence due to the holy Roman Church. Therefore we decree, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1283D] Although this privilege was drawn from an authentic copy, it lacks a dating clause; but, since three hundred years ago it was confirmed by Bernard, patriarch of Aquileia, in the following decree, it is wholly to be trusted. Bernard’s decree reads as follows after the authentic copy of the privilege itself: “And in order that henceforth full credit may everywhere be given to an exemplar, transcript, or copy of this kind, we, Bernard, by divine mercy patriarch of the holy see of Aquileia, have attached to that exemplar, transcript, or copy both our authority and decree. In testimony of this matter, we caused these present [Col. 1284D] letters to be made and fortified by the attachment of our seal. Given in the city of Austria, in the patriarchal palace, on the eleventh day of July, in the year of the Lord 1335, third indiction.” Furthermore, it certainly appears probable that this privilege was granted by Alexander to Ulrich at Venice in 1177, when the same Ulrich had returned to the favour of the Apostolic See.]

YEAR 1171–1181.

MCDLXXXIII. To the doge of Venice.—He commends Henry, patriarch of Venice, to him, and exhorts him favourably to consent to the transfer of the patriarchate of Grado to the city of Venice. (Tusculum, 21 January.)

[CORNEL., *Venetian Church*, III, 75.]

[Col. 1284D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved son, the noble man the doge of Venice [Note: The diploma of Alexander III is believed to have been issued in the year 1178, and therefore addressed to Sebastian Ziani, who remained alive until 13 April of that same year.], greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1285A] Not without contempt and reproach to your land, the venerable brother Henry, patriarch of Grado, is suffering such distress as we neither see nor have heard bishops established in lesser cities suffer. Certainly, since the land of Venice is greater and more renowned than the other lands under your jurisdiction, it will be an honour to you and to that land if the patriarchal see is transferred to that land itself, as is highly expedient, especially since, as you know, matters of dispute frequently arose between the aforesaid patriarch and the bishops of Castello. We make this suggestion to your discernment not from the affection which we have for that patriarch, but rather for your honour and that of your land, since the patriarch is now so old that his life can scarcely last for two years. [Col. 1285B] Therefore, since that transfer concerns the patriarch’s temporary advantage and your land’s lasting honour, we ask you in this matter [lacuna] to forestall us by taking the initiative. We therefore admonish, advise, and exhort your nobility to give a ready and favourable assent to this transfer, in order to remove such reproach from your land and the cause of disputes that commonly arise between the patriarch and the bishops of Castello; and diligently induce the clergy and people of Venice to do the same, because for the honour of that land we shall willingly lend our authority and favour to this.

Given at Tusculum, the twelfth day before the Kalends of February.

[Note: [Col. 1285D] The year in which the document was issued does not appear from the document itself. Its autograph is said to be preserved among the noble Badoer family, on the reverse of which the year 1178 was entered in a later hand. Nor can a more certain chronological indication be inferred from the addition of the place, since Alexander III issued several documents from the town of Tusculum (Frascati) in different years, as may be seen in the latest edition of the *Roman Bullarium*. In 1178 Alexander III was residing at Rome, within whose territory the town of Tusculum was situated.]

MCDLXXXIV. To [Gilbert], bishop of London.—That he compel Count Alberic to receive his wife with due respect.

[*Letters of Gilbert Foliot*, ed. Giles, II, 90.]

[Col. 1285C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GILBERT, bishop of London: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The noblewoman A., wife of Count Alberic, has sent us a lamentable complaint; and we have also very often heard the same thing from the reports of travellers: namely, that when a dispute concerning their marriage had arisen between her and her husband, and the said woman had presented herself before you, although she repeatedly sought your assistance in the matter, you were unwilling to give her any [Col. 1285D] counsel, nor did anyone afford her advocacy in her case on that occasion. Thus, standing alone in your court, deprived of every aid, she appealed to the hearing of the Apostolic See. Subsequently, she is said to have been taken to a certain castle and shut up in a tower, where she is still kept wholly removed from human society. For if you rightly considered who you were and what office you held, such acts would by no means have been committed with your consent, or even while you tolerated them—acts for which the punishment rather than the fault ought first to have been reported to us. [Col. 1286A] Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command you and enjoin you, under the force of obedience, to admonish and diligently induce the said count, employing episcopal diligence, within twenty days of receiving these letters, to receive his aforesaid wife with due respect and without delay to grant her fellowship at table and sharing of his bed.

If he should perhaps contemptuously refuse to carry out all this within the prescribed term, place his entire land under interdict, all delay and appeal being set aside. If even then he does not amend his ways, bind his person with the bond of excommunication; publicly declare that he is to be avoided by all as an excommunicated man; and, wherever he may arrive and for as long as he is present there, unless he is staying at the king’s court, prohibit by our authority the celebration of all divine offices except the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying. Direct also, strictly and in our name, all bishops established throughout England to announce through their parishes that he is to be avoided by all as excommunicated, and to avoid him entirely themselves.

Given at Tusculum, the third day before the Kalends of February.

MCDLXXXV. To the bishops of Valva, Aprutium, Marsica, etc.—That they compel Gentilis of Raiano to pay the due rent to the monastery of Pescara. (Tusculum, 7 February.)

[*Chronicle of Casauria*, in Muratori, *Writers of Italian Affairs*, II, II, 911.]

[Col. 1286C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers ODERI, bishops of Valva, Abruzzo, Marsica, Penne, and Forcona, and to his beloved sons, the chapter of Chieti and the abbot of St Vincent: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the complaint submitted by our beloved son, the abbot of St Clement of Pescara, it has come to our ears that Gentilis of Raiano refuses to pay the rent owed to his monastery; that he does not permit either clerics or laypeople to render to it, without peril to their salvation, the parochial dues which are owed to it by right from Rocca de Soti; and that he does not allow its churches [Col. 1286D] to be administered as is fitting. Since laypeople must be restrained by ecclesiastical censure from oppressing monasteries, we command and direct your discretion by apostolic letters: if what has been put before us rests upon the truth, bind the said Gentilis with the bond of excommunication and cause him to be avoided by all as excommunicated, until he restores what he has taken and desists from molesting the aforesaid monastery. If he does not amend even then, prohibit the celebration of divine offices in his land for as long as he is present there. [Col. 1287A] If all of you cannot carry this out, let two or three of you nevertheless execute it, without favour or fear being any obstacle.

Given at Tusculum, the seventh day before the Ides of February.

MCDLXXXVI. He entrusts to the bishops of Abruzzo and Penne the task of defending the churches of the monastery of Pescara from injuries. (Tusculum, 7 February.)

[The same, in the same place.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the bishops of Abruzzo and Penne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son, the abbot [Col. 1287B] of St Clement of Pescara, has informed us that certain of your parishioners—Ro. of Malatino, Transmundus of Rocca, Ro. of Troja, and the son of Aton. Theod.—on the pretext of a patronage which they assert that they hold in its churches, plunder its goods and despoil its clerics, although they are said to possess no right at all. He further added that some of them have rashly presumed to lay violent hands upon a certain monk of theirs, who was also a priest. Since we neither wish nor ought to pass by with closed eyes the injury done to churches and the insolence of laypeople, we command and direct your brotherhood by apostolic letters to take care to admonish and diligently induce the aforesaid wrongdoers to restore what they have taken, make good the damage inflicted, and give suitable satisfaction for the injuries done. [Col. 1287C] If they do not comply with your admonitions, strike them with the sword of ecclesiastical severity, appeal being set aside. As for those who laid violent hands upon the monk-priest, cause them to be avoided by all as excommunicated until, having made satisfaction, they present themselves before the Apostolic See to be absolved, with testimonial letters from you.

Given at Tusculum, the seventh day before the Ides of February.

MCDLXXXVII. He grants to Cistercian abbots that each of them may absolve and impose penance upon brothers of his monastery who, when they enter its religious life or afterwards in confession, acknowledge that they are bound by excommunication for arson or for violently laying hands on a cleric or another religious person. (Tusculum, 7 March.)

[Henriquez, *Rule*, 55.]

[Col. 1287D]

MCDLXXXVIII. To all who observe the Rule of Grandmont, he “enjoins the labour which they endure in that observance in place of penance and for the remission of sins,” and confirms the Rule itself. (Tusculum, 8 March.)

[*New Gallia Christiana*, II, documents, 191.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, prior, and the brothers of Grandmont: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more deeply we are bound to rejoice in the progress of religious life, the more willingly ought we to bring to effect, in accordance with our desire for what advances salvation, those things that concern the observance of your Rule. Moved by this consideration, we enjoin upon all who keep your Rule, as it is observed in your order, the labour which they endure in that observance, in place of penance and for the remission of their sins. [Col. 1288A] We also confirm by apostolic authority the institution which, for your correction, you beneficially added to your Rule after its confirmation by our predecessor Pope Adrian of happy memory; and we decree that it shall remain in force in future times. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted, etc.

Given at Tusculum, the third day before the Ides of March.
