MCDLXXXIX. To the abbot of Prémontré.—The abbot of Prémontré may absolve members of his institute from sins and excommunication, and may give the tonsure to his clerical novices. (Tusculum, 13 March.)

[Le Paige, *Bibliotheca Praemonstratensis*, 630.]

[Col. 1288B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Prémontré: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since you are father of all who have professed the Premonstratensian Order, and are bound by duty to visit the abbeys of that order, we wish to grant you apostolic favour for the execution of your office. Therefore, granting your requests, by these present [Col. 1288C] letters we permit you freely, by our authority, to impose penance upon and absolve brothers and lay brothers of the same order who wish to confess their sins to you, even if they happen to be bound by the bond of excommunication; and, provided that you are a priest, to give the tonsure to your clerical novices.

Given at Tusculum, the third day before the Ides of March.

MCDXC. To archbishops and bishops.—That they protect the rights of the monastery of St Denis. (Tusculum, 21 March.)

[Doublet, *History of Saint-Denis*, 509.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the archbishops and bishops in whose dioceses the rights of the monastery of Saint Denis are situated: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the monastery of Saint Denis pertains especially to our care and protection, it is incumbent upon us to provide that it is not subjected to the harassment of evildoers or vexed by the malice of anyone whatsoever. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that whenever the abbot and brothers of that monastery bring before you a complaint against wrongdoers among your parishioners—those shown to be wrongdoers—you shall administer justice to them without frustrating delay, all contradiction and appeal being set aside, so that the same [Col. 1289A] brothers may rejoice in peacefully possessing their rights and that we may deservedly commend your care and diligence.

Given at Tusculum, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

MCDXCI. To Henry, patriarch of Grado.—He commands that the sentence pronounced for the monastery of St Saviour be observed. (Tusculum, 26 March.)

[Note: [Col. 1289D] Since the apostolic document of Alexander III by which the sentence pronounced by apostolic delegates is confirmed anew was issued—as we said above it might be argued—in 1166, it is probable that the document now produced was issued in the following year, 1167, before Alexander III had departed from Rome and its territory. In the *Roman Bullarium*, under the year 1167, documents issued at the Lateran and Anagni may be read, vol. II of the new edition of the *Bullarium*, pp. 390–391; from this it may also be argued that he sometimes lived at Tusculum, from which place he could have sent this document. Besides, in the *Bullarium*, pp. 401 and 404, letters of Alexander III issued at Tusculum belong to the year 1170. The reader is therefore free, as seems preferable, to assign this letter, which bears no chronological indication, to one year or the other.]

[Cornelius, *Ecclesia Veneta*, XIV, 99.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers HENRY, patriarch of Grado, and (VITALIS Michael), bishop of Castello: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the letters of our beloved son Ildebrand, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the [Col. 1289B] Twelve Apostles and legate of the Apostolic See, it has come to our ears that, when he was formerly performing the office of legate in those regions, and you, brother patriarch, had received from us for decision the case between our beloved son, the prior of St Saviour, and the parish priest of St Bartholomew, you pronounced, after hearing the matter, a sentence of decision. Since the authority of divine and human laws has decreed that a decided matter must stand, we command and direct your brotherhood by apostolic letters to hold that sentence ratified and firm and cause it to be inviolably observed. Admonish and strictly compel the aforesaid parish priest and his clerics not to admit to divine offices or burial any persons from those houses concerning which judgment and decision were given between them and [Col. 1289C] the aforesaid prior.

Command those persons firmly, strictly, and frequently to attend the church of St Saviour for divine offices, according to what has been said and established; and generally prohibit them under threat of anathema from being admitted to divine offices in other churches. If, despising the church of St Saviour, they presume to frequent another church, excommunicate them; cause the church which, after your prohibition, receives them at divine offices to cease from such offices; and, should the parish priest and his clerics persist in their contumacy, send them to us suspended, so that they may learn that a settled sentence must be obeyed and that they must entirely refrain from harassing [Col. 1289D] religious men.

Given at Tusculum, the seventh day before the Kalends of April.

MCDXCII. To the archbishop of Tours and to all bishops.—For the church of St Martin of Tours. (*Defence of Saint-Martin of Tours*, 23.)

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the archbishop of Tours and [Col. 1290A] all bishops in whose dioceses possessions of the church of Blessed Martin are situated: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the church of Blessed Martin has no bishop or prelate other than the Roman pontiff, it is fitting for us to preserve its rights whole and unimpaired and by every means to induce and exhort those adorned with the episcopal mitre to maintain and defend the possessions of that church. For we could rightly be reproved for negligence if, through failure to exercise the care and concern we owe, the possessions of the aforesaid church were in any degree lost in our time. Therefore, the more closely you are bound to us and to the Roman Church by a stricter charity, the more we ought to defend and preserve with more earnest care and diligence the rights and possessions that belong to the Roman Church. [Col. 1290B] Accordingly, we admonish and command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to warn and strictly compel those within your dioceses who take away and forcibly hold occupied the possessions of the aforesaid church, and inflict losses, injuries, and burdens upon it, within fifteen days after you have been asked about the matter, to restore those possessions to that church without any delay and leave them in peace, or receive a full measure of justice before your tribunal of discretion. If they contemptuously refuse to obey your admonitions and commands in this matter, excommunicate them, and cause them to be more cautiously [Col. 1290C] avoided by all until they are compelled unwillingly to do what they ought voluntarily to have done.

Given at Tusculum, the second day before the Ides of April.

MCDXCIII. He forbids the dean and chapter of Troyes “that any one of them, when elected or consecrated bishop, retain for his own use a prebend formerly held, or other revenues of the church, except those which are known to belong to episcopal right.” (Tusculum, 20 April.)

[Camuzat, *Promptuarium*, p. 1236.]

MCDXCIV. He grants Peter, abbot of the Neapolitan monastery of Saints Severinus and Sosius, and his successors, the use of the mitre. (Tusculum, 21 May.)

[Margarini, *Casinensian Bullarium*, II, 196.]

[Col. 1290D]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of the monastery of Saints Severinus and Sosius: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The obligation of charity prompts us to bestow a special favour of prerogative upon devout sons of the Church, so that, sustained by the benevolence of the Apostolic See, they may govern the churches entrusted to them more beneficially in proportion as their subjects [Col. 1291A] show them greater obedience and honour. Therefore, considering the devotion which you are known to have toward Blessed Peter and ourselves, we have thought fit, out of the customary benevolence of the Apostolic See, to grant the use of the mitre to you and your successors.

Given at Tusculum, the twelfth day before the Kalends of June.

MCDXCV. To the bishops of Parma and Reggio.—For the monastery of Nonantola. (Tusculum, 27 July.)

[Tiraboschi, *History of Nonantola*, II, 278.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the bishops of Parma and Reggio: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the report submitted by our beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Nonantola, we have been informed that William and Minaboves of Cuv[—lacuna—], Gerard of Ancuila, and certain other of your parishioners presume in many ways to trouble the church of Cellae, which is known properly to belong to their monastery, [Col. 1291B] and violently to occupy the goods of that church. Since, by the office of the apostolate laid upon us, we are bound to defend and preserve the rights of all, and especially of churches, we command and direct your brotherhood by apostolic letters to admonish and strictly compel the aforesaid parishioners to desist entirely from troubling that church and restore intact to it the goods they have taken; or, if they believe that they possess any right in the goods of that church and choose to enter a legal action, to receive a full measure of justice in your presence from the abbot and brothers named above. [Col. 1291C] But if they contemptuously refuse to obey your admonitions in this matter, restrain them by ecclesiastical censure.

Given at Tusculum, the fifth day before the Kalends of July.

MCDXCVI. To Richard, archbishop of Canterbury.—That he suspend from offices and benefices the clerics of Count Hugh who performed sacred rites contrary to an interdict.

[*Letters of Gilbert Foliot*, ed. Giles, II, 70.]

You should know that it has come to our ears that the land of the nobleman Count Hugh, because of an injury which [Col. 1291D] that count had inflicted upon the canons of Panteneia, had been placed under interdict by our command. Nevertheless, because the clerics of that land presumed still to celebrate divine offices, they were bound by blessed Thomas the martyr with the bond of excommunication. Later, when that same martyr was returning from exile, on those clerics’ seeking absolution he ordered them to abstain from divine offices until he could consult us concerning their presumption. But shortly thereafter that martyr passed to heaven through martyrdom; and the aforesaid clerics, just as they had done before, did not fear to celebrate divine offices. Since, therefore, the rashness and presumption of those clerics ought not to go unpunished, we command and direct your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, [Col. 1292A] if the matter stands thus, you suspend the aforesaid clerics from offices and benefices for the excess of so great a presumption.

MCDXCVII. He commands Wichmann, archbishop of Magdeburg, and . . . . . bishop of Brandenburg, under penalty of anathema to enact “that no one lay violent hands upon the canons or lay brothers of the church of St Mary of Magdeburg, or presume to plunder or occupy their goods.”

[Leucfeld, *Antiquities of Prémontré*, 91.]

MCDXCVIII–MD. To Guy, archbishop of Sens.—I. “That he no longer demand, as a matter of right, hospitality-provisioning (*procuratio*) at the monastery of St Germain of Paris.” II. “That he not harass the churches of that monastery with excessive hospitality-provisioning.” III. He rebukes the archbishop because “contrary to the privilege of the monks of St Germain of Paris, he did not hesitate to bring forty horses and seventy men to a certain church of the monastery and receive provisioning for them all.”

[Bouillart, *History of Saint-Germain-des-Prés*, documents, p. 47.]

[Col. 1292B]

YEAR 1179–1181.

MDI. (Tusculum, 20 January.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, VII, documents, 74.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, Eremburg, abbess, and the sisters of Gif: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From an authenticated document read aloud in our audience chamber, we have learned that our beloved daughters in Christ, Eva, abbess, and the sisters of Éder, compassionately grieving over your poverty, granted to our venerable brother M. [Maurice], bishop of Paris, the right to establish an abbey in your aforesaid house, for the worship of God and the reform of religion there. For your house was burdened by debt and its buildings threatened ruin, and your poverty could not be relieved by them; and because, from the beginning of that house’s foundation, an abbey had to be established there in response to the request of benefactors. This condition was retained: whenever an abbess should die, if [Col. 1292D] you or those succeeding you cannot agree upon one of your number as abbess, you must canonically elect her not from elsewhere but from the monastery of Éder. Moreover, they granted in perpetuity to support you and those who succeed you the grange called Wumvillare.

Since we ought diligently to promote what pertains to the increase of religious life, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen with the protection of this present document, the liberty granted to your house by the aforesaid abbess and convent, as it is contained in the authenticated document—our privilege already granted to the said monastery of Éder concerning your house and the aforesaid grange notwithstanding. We decree that no person whatsoever may be permitted to violate this page of our confirmation [Col. 1293A] or rashly contravene it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let that person know that he shall incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Tusculum, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February.

MDII. He confirms the settlement between Bishop Henry and the canons of the Church of Modena. (Tusculum, 8 February.)

[Tiraboschi, *Historical Memoirs of the People of Modena*, III, 77.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the provost and canons of Modena: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whereas, in the dispute between you and Henry, formerly bishop of Modena, of good memory, concerning the provisioning of your archbishop [Col. 1293B] and legates of the Apostolic See, the bishop of Palestrina, cardinal-deacon of the church of St George at the Veil of Gold, legate of the Apostolic See, settled that controversy, as we have learned from his written document, by an amicable composition with the voluntary assent of the parties: namely, that whether your bishop is absent or present, he is bound to provide the whole provisioning for the first day, while you are bound to provide the whole of the second day for the aforesaid archbishop and legates.

[Note: [Col. 1293D] This man and Cardinal Manfred of Siena were present in Venice in 1177 at the reconciliation of Frederick with Alexander III, and he died in the following year. Therefore this brief should be dated about 1179; in accordance with Alexander III’s usual practice in briefs, it bears no year-date.]

Since arrangements established by agreement ought to remain firm and inviolate, lest through anyone’s instability they be brought back into the danger of renewed contention, we confirm by apostolic authority the aforesaid settlement, as it was mutually accepted and has been observed hitherto, and strengthen it with the protection of this present document. [Col. 1293C] We decree that no person whatsoever may be permitted to violate this page of our confirmation or rashly contravene it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let that person know that he shall incur the indignation of Almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Tusculum, the sixth day before the Ides of February.

YEAR 1181.

MDIII. Privilege for the Church of Genoa (fragment). (Tusculum, 13 January.)

[Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, IV, 872.]

[Col. 1293D] In the year 1180, Obertus the provost, Boniface the archdeacon, and the other canons of the Church of Genoa were received by Alexander III under apostolic protection and honoured with a privilege, transcribed in the same words as those previously used by Popes Eugenius and Adrian.

Given at Tusculum, by the hand of Dauferius, sub[deacon] of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of January, indiction XIII, in the year 1180 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twenty-second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. [Col. 1294A] I, Theodevinus, bishop of the see of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Paul, bishop of the Church of Palestrina. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St Susanna. I, Vivianus, priest-cardinal of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Centhius, priest-cardinal of the title of St Cecilia. I, Arduinus, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St Mary in Trastevere, of the title of St Callistus. I, Hyacinthus, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Raynerius, deacon-cardinal of St George at the Veil of Gold. [Col. 1294B] I, Gratianus, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, John, deacon-cardinal of St Adrian. I, Matthew, deacon-cardinal of St Mary the New.

MDIV. To all princes.—He exhorts them to aid the Holy Land. (Tusculum, 16 January.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 915.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, noble men—dukes and princes, counts, barons, and all the faithful of God to whom these letters shall come—greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1294C] Alarming reports, which have reached us concerning the regions of Jerusalem by the common testimony of travellers, deeply trouble our heart and the hearts of all our brethren with excessive grief. For scarcely anyone who bears the Christian name can hear without tears and sighs what is recounted concerning the wretched condition of that land. It has indeed been crushed, as we say with sorrow, by incursions of unbelievers; and it is so bereft of the strength of valiant men and the counsel of worthy men that, unless it receives swift and powerful aid from Christian kings and princes of the world, we fear that its desolation is near at hand—may it never be—for the dishonour of God and the contempt of the Christian faith. There is no king who can govern that land, because he, namely Baldwin, [Col. 1294D] who holds the reins of the kingdom, has been so severely scourged by the just judgment of God, as you believe yourselves to know, that he can scarcely endure his body’s continuous torments.

We recall with no small emotion of heart what grievous loss and what lamentable disaster in persons and property that land, for which our fathers and forefathers shed their own blood, suffered in its former conflict with the nations, as sins required; nor can any who are zealous for the law of the Lord bear so great a slaughter of the faithful with a patient mind. This is especially so because that most wicked race of pagans is said to have taken such boldness from the injuries and perils which they have inflicted upon the Christian people that they shamelessly boast that they will invade that land—may the Lord avert it. [Col. 1295A]

Let zeal for the Lord therefore move you, and let not the Christian religion sleep amid so great a ruin threatening that land. Rather, defend courageously all those places which our Saviour and Redeemer consecrated by his bodily presence; despise the nations that reject the Lord and strive to abolish the Christian name from the earth. He is surely no Christian who is not moved by the calamities of that land and does not gird himself to defend it from the assaults of unbelievers, who labour to occupy it and—may it never be—to profane it with their [Col. 1295B] impurities.

Those among you who are strong and fitted for warfare should take up this undertaking, at once so pious and so necessary, and the labour of this pilgrimage, clothed no less with the shield of faith and breastplate of righteousness than with material arms. Let them defend by mighty strength those places in which the Redeemer of humankind chose to be born for us and underwent temporal death, lest Christianity suffer loss in those regions in our time. Since Christ endured many reproaches for our salvation and at last the gibbet of the cross, in order to offer us to God—dead indeed in the flesh, but justified [made alive] in the spirit—it greatly benefits the salvation of the faithful that we expose our bodies for his sake to dangers and labours, lest we seem to have forgotten the price of the blood [Col. 1295C] which he shed for us.

Consider therefore, beloved sons in Christ, and see how shameful and grief-worthy it would be for Christians if the enemies of Christ’s cross should again prevail against the inhabitants of that land. We greatly fear that they will prevail unless aid from various parts of Christendom swiftly comes to those inhabitants.

Therefore, lest Christendom succumb to paganism, make provision with all your strength; for it is better to meet an approaching evil before its time than to seek a remedy after the wound has been inflicted. To those who undertake for Christ’s sake the labour of this journey, we grant and confirm by apostolic authority that indulgence of sins which our fathers and predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Urban and Eugenius, established. [Col. 1295D] We also decree that their wives, children, goods, and possessions shall remain under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and likewise of archbishops, bishops, and the other prelates of the Church. We strictly prohibit any dispute concerning what they peacefully possess from being raised against them after they have taken the cross, until they return or their death is established with certainty.

Moreover, after their relatives or lords—to whose fief they belong—have either refused or been unable to lend them money, they may freely and without any objection pledge their lands or other possessions, as security for the expenses of this expedition, to churches, ecclesiastical persons, or other faithful people. [Col. 1296A] Furthermore, whoever among fighting men fit for the defence of that land approaches those holy places with the fervour of devotion and fights there for two years against the Saracens in defence of the Christian name: trusting in the mercy of Jesus Christ and the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we grant them absolution from all their offences of which they have made confession with contrite and humbled heart. Excepted, however, are cases in which they have seized another’s goods, extorted usury, or committed theft: all of these must be made good in full. If offenders lack the means to make restitution, they shall nevertheless obtain, as we have said, forgiveness for the acts committed. Those who have remained there for a year, as we have said, shall obtain indulgence for one half of the penance imposed upon them and remission of their sins. [Col. 1296B]

To all who wish, because of the present necessity, to visit the Lord’s sepulchre—whether they die on the journey or reach that place—we assign the labour of the journey as penance, obedience, and remission of all sins, so that from the prison-house of this present life they may attain, by the Lord’s gift, that blessedness which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, which the Lord promised to those who love him (1 Cor. 2).

Given at Tusculum, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February.

MDV. To archbishops, bishops, and abbots, he commends the Templars sent to seek aid for the Eastern land.

[Mansi, in the same place, col. 917.]

[Col. 1296C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, archbishops and bishops, and to his beloved sons, abbots and other prelates of churches, to whom these letters shall come: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the Eastern land is deprived, through the assaults of the unbelievers and the incursions of powerful men, both of military strength and of the counsel of worthy men, the archbishops, bishops, and other princes of that land have resolved to send to your regions, to implore the assistance of the faithful, our beloved sons, the Templars, bearers of these letters—men indeed [Col. 1296D] religious and God-fearing. We, moreover, whom the calamity of that land greatly disturbs with grief, solicitous, after the example of our fathers and predecessors, for its preservation, exhort Christian kings and the princes of the world by salutary admonitions to defend those places in which the feet of the Lord stood. And, as our fathers and predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Urban and Eugenius, decreed, so we also decree remission and indulgence of sins for all who undertake, for Christ’s sake, the labor of Jerusalem and make it their concern to fight the Saracens with faithful devotion.

[Col. 1297A] We therefore earnestly admonish and command all of you that you receive the brethren sent for this purpose with kindly disposition; and, having learned through them the condition and need of the Eastern land, that by frequent and earnest exhortations you strive to induce the princes, counts, and other faithful Christians among your parishioners to go swiftly to that land, for whose liberation their fathers and forefathers shed their own blood, and to fight with strength and valor against the enemies of Christ’s cross. Cause the letters which we are sending generally on this matter to be publicly read in all churches; explain their tenor; announce the remission of sins which we grant to those who undertake so pious and necessary a work; and thus exhort all to carry out what we urge, so that, through your diligence and exhortation, that land may swiftly [Col. 1297B] experience the aid and assistance of the faithful, and that you may thereby obtain everlasting reward from almighty God.

Given at Tusculum, 16 January.

MDVI. To Theobald, abbot of Cluny.—He confirms the agreements made by him with William, count of Chalon, and with Gerard, count of Mâcon, secured by the written instrument of Philip, king of France. (Tusculum, February 9.)

[D. Bouquet, *Recueil*, XV, 974.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons THEOBALD, abbot, and the chapter of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1297C] Since your church is subject to us without any intermediary, we desire, as we are bound to do, to provide for its peace and yours, and diligently to ensure that you cannot hereafter be burdened by anyone’s malicious harassment. Therefore, since between you and the noble man, the count of Chalon—[Note: [Col. 1297D] William, whose charter concerning Paredo, preserved in the Library of Cluny, col. 1441, was made at Lordon in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1180, while Philip, king of France, was reigning in France, in the second year of his reign after his coronation. “Moreover, therein,” he says, “I acknowledged and confessed that in the town of Paredo and its appurtenances, and throughout all its territory, I have no right of tallage, pig-tax, beverage-tax, milling-tax, grain-tax, or corvée; all of which I and my officials had very often taken by force. [Col. 1298D] Moreover, I sometimes compelled the men of the Church to go on my expeditions and forced them to perform labor, namely in raising my ditches and building castles. All these things I wholly renounced and remitted, so that none of the things stated above may ever hereafter be demanded by me, or by my heirs or officials,” etc.]—an amicable agreement has been made, before our dearest son in Christ Philip, the illustrious king of the French, concerning all complaints which you had against him and concerning the exactions which he exercised upon the men and lands of that church, and since it is contained in the authentic instrument of that king, we ratify it and confirm it by apostolic authority.

Likewise, we decree that the agreement which you freely made with the noble man Count Gerard—[Note: [Col. 1298D] Gerard, count of Mâcon, whose charter, likewise dated in the same year, see collected there.]—concerning the exactions by which he oppressed your land and men, as it is confirmed in the written instrument of that count, shall remain inviolate in future times.

Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur [Col. 1298A] the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Tusculum, on the fifth day before the Ides of February.

MDVII. He informs Theobald, abbot, and the chapter of Cluny that he has instructed the bishop of Autun to consecrate the chapel at Belna. If he refuses to execute the command, he permits them to invite the bishop of Belley to perform the consecration. (Tusculum, February 10.)

[Library of Cluny, p. 1444.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons T., abbot, and the chapter of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, as you state, you have at Belna a certain chapel [Col. 1298B] which you ask to have consecrated, we have instructed our venerable brother, the bishop of Autun, that, when requested by you, he shall dedicate that chapel and bless a cemetery beside it, on this condition: namely, that at no time it is to receive non-parishioners either for daily services or for burial, nor is it especially to usurp for itself parish rights in tithes or in other matters. Therefore, lest you be disappointed in this desire, by these present letters we grant that, if the aforesaid bishop, having been respectfully and humbly requested by you a second or third time, has not carried out our command, you may freely invite whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, etc.

MDVIII. He commands Guy, archbishop of Sens, Henry, bishop of Bayeux, S., abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, and the dean of the Church of Bayeux, in the controversy between Roland, bishop-elect of Dol, and Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours, legate of the Apostolic See, to commit the statements of witnesses to writing. (Tusculum, February 25.)

[Marten, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, 907.]

[Col. 1298C]

MDIX. He receives the Church of St. Mary of Flotin under protection and confirms its rights and privileges. (Tusculum, March 10.)

[Morin, *History of the Gâtinais*, Paris, 1630, quarto, p. 291.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, prior of the church of Blessed Mary of [Col. 1298D] Flotin, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting that public protection be afforded to religious men devoted to works of piety, so that they may serve the divine offices more freely in proportion as they perceive themselves to be more strongly defended by apostolic protection. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, establishing that the canonical order which is known to have been instituted in that church, through your provision, beloved son, and with the assent of our beloved sons the abbot and brethren of St. John of Sens, as also through the favor and authority of our venerable brother G., archbishop of Sens, shall be inviolably observed there in perpetuity. We have thought it right to set down that order in this present charter, as it is more fully contained in the authentic document of that archbishop, excepting that we have not thought fit to confirm the provision concerning the prior, because it is contrary to reason and conflicts with sacred institutions, since the pillars of the Church ought to be firm and stable, lest the whole building totter through their weakness.

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

“I, G., by the grace of God archbishop of Sens, to our beloved sons Peter, abbot of St. John, and brother William of Flotin, and all their brethren, present and future, greeting for ever.

“It is everywhere known and understood by all that, just as small things quickly grow through concord, so even the greatest things, when discord enters in, soon fall apart. [Col. 1299C] Therefore, seeing that the church of St. John and its new plantation, still tender—the church, namely, of Blessed Mary of Flotin—were proceeding, if not along a path of perversion, yet somewhat along one of estrangement, we resolved to intervene, lest a spark hidden in ashes should someday through negligence burst forth into a sudden conflagration; and to restore mother to daughter and daughter to mother in friendship and concord. Having therefore taken counsel with our beloved son William and the other brethren of Flotin, and likewise with the venerable Peter, abbot of St. John, and his brethren, we began diligently and carefully to work and provide for their peace and concord.

“Since, then, we heard that the aforesaid brethren of Flotin were wholly unwilling to depart from the good and original foundation of a stricter life, but earnestly loved a scant diet and harsh abstinence from food and drink, and eagerly endured coarse and cheap clothing, being tranquil despisers of secular life and lovers of God; and that, diligently attending to vigils, prayers, and psalmody, they in no way wished to change the good purpose of life which they had begun, but wished to bring it to a better completion, [Col. 1299D] we greatly rejoiced and, regarding the number of brethren which they requested to be increased for the enlargement of God’s service, I and the whole Church of St. John gave joyful assent.

“We therefore established and decreed that they might, according to their wish and the capacity of the place, receive as many brethren as they wished for the service of God, without any objection from the abbot and chapter of St. John. Moreover, when the abbot of St. John wishes and is able to come to that place, the brethren who have been received shall make due profession to him and to his successors, as to their own abbot; and then they shall receive canonical blessing from him in that same place. Thereafter it shall not be lawful to remove them from the place. But if the prior who presides over the place removes any of those brethren from that church because of his fault, as disobedient and rebellious, or if a brother himself leaves thence improperly and without the prior’s permission, it shall not be lawful for the abbot to receive him into the church of St. John, unless, touched by the Spirit of God, he wishes to amend his life and embrace the order of the aforesaid church, so that the brethren of that place may receive him, with every exaction of the abbot and chapter of St. John removed.

“Provided, however, that if he was received as a man of good and praiseworthy life, free and released from the subjection of his first profession, before the new seat of the abbot of St. John he shall make profession of the custom and order of the white church, and promise the stability of his person in that place. [Col. 1300B] This was done and granted by both sides on the condition that, so long as three living brethren received from the church of St. John are found there, a fourth shall not be received except by the will and free consent of the prior and brethren of the place.

“Concerning the appointment of the prior in the same place, it was decreed with the assent of both parties that the brethren of Flotin shall have free election: they shall appoint as prior one from their own community whom they judge suitable, and the remaining brethren shall owe obedience to him. It shall belong to the discretion of his office [Col. 1300C] whose administration [lacuna]. But when the abbot comes to the place for visitation, they shall present to him the appointed prior, whom he shall accept once objection has ceased, and shall impose upon him the entire care of administration. If, however, disagreement should arise concerning the appointment of a prior, as is customary among evil men (*malibus*, sic), and the brethren cannot agree among themselves, the abbot of St. John shall be summoned on a day appointed for the election. If the brethren do not then agree, the abbot, yielding to the better and sounder party, shall appoint a prior there by their counsel and assent.

“Their clothing shall be of this kind: they shall have linen garments; apart from surplices and breeches, they shall use no other garments. They shall have white fur tunics, white cloaks, and black capes; likewise, they shall have neither bedding and mattresses nor linen straw-beds, but only pillows for support of the head. They shall eat no flesh or blood at all, except only in the case of the sick. Permission shall be granted them to eat eggs and cheese, except during the Lent before the Nativity of the Lord. From the feast of the Holy Cross until the Nativity of the Lord they shall fast, except on the feast of All Saints. From the Nativity of the Lord until Epiphany they may eat twice daily. From that day until Easter they shall fast, except on the Purification of Blessed Mary. In church they shall always keep silence, except for confession. At table no brother is permitted to speak, except the master alone concerning necessities. From Compline until chapter, after silence has first been imposed, they shall keep silence everywhere, unless necessity compels otherwise. Women—[Col. 1301A] neither kinswomen nor strangers—shall not eat at their table, nor shall they rest at night within their enclosure, nor enter their workshops without a lawful witness.

“They may possess animals, lands, tithes, and any other possessions given as alms or acquired in any other manner, for the provision of the brethren and the support of the poor and guests. The prior and brethren may travel and ride, if commanded by the prior, according to the Rule of St. Augustine. Neither the prior nor the brethren may sell or mortgage anything from revenues, meadows, vineyards, or other income of the church without the counsel of the abbot and chapter of St. John; and this for the greater benefit of the place. Your brethren of Flotin shall yearly pay St. John twenty shillings on the feast day for oil used in the service.

“And that all the aforesaid provisions may be firmly and faithfully observed for ever to the honor of God and the benefit of the place, we command and prescribe; and, under penalty of anathema, we forbid either party to presume to exceed or demand anything beyond what has been written and established by us, except with our consent and that of both parties. That these things may remain unshaken and ratified, we confirm and corroborate them by pontifical authority and the impression of our seal.

“Done publicly in the chapter of St. John in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1161.”

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we establish that [Col. 1301C] whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Haerveus of Châtillon; the tithe of La Narville and the annual *tractus*; also two portions of the tithe of Montecereado and the vineyards which you possess in the enclosed estate of Montbleum; half an arpent of vineyard at Chaloereth; a fourth part of the tithe of Fratevilla and two *tractus*; a fourth part of the tithe of Varennis and a fourth *tractus*; the tithe on the land of Buchard Gonon, which is near Infermitum, [Col. 1301D] and the *tractus* of that tithe; one modius of wheat, to be received yearly in the grange of Amiliac, by the gift of Holisandis, formerly countess of Joigny; in the enclosed estate of the noble man Gilo of Soliac, one modius of wine to be granted you yearly; at Varennes, in the enclosed estate of Sustan, one modius of wine annually; at Saint-Loup, a rent of twelve denarii; at Boenas, by gift of Hugh Godar, whatever rent he possessed there; by gift of Robert Chivillas and his wife, a house with all its furnishings, situated by the common wood, and their vineyards at Saint-Loup and Chasuet, as well as all other things devoutly bestowed by them upon your church; the granges of Lamervilla, free from every rent; the grange [Col. 1302A] of Monte Leurdo; the grange of Feaville; and the meadow at Nanciet, by gift of Gerard surnamed the Usurer; by gift of Pons, knight of Sosiac, whatever rent he possessed in the allod of Chaleret; the tithe of bread and wine expended at the common wood whenever the king and queen lodge there together, or one without the other—a tithe which Louis, the illustrious king of France of revered memory, granted you as alms and confirmed by the security of his seal.

Furthermore, concerning your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, and concerning the increase of your animals, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you. Moreover, you may receive into conversion clerics and laymen fleeing from the world, free and absolved, and retain them without any objection. We further forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to leave it without his superior’s permission, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; and let no one dare retain one who has departed without letters attesting the community’s consent. We also decree that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that none may oppose the devotion and last wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken remain intact. When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate the divine office behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells [Col. 1302C] and in a subdued voice. And, desiring with paternal solicitude to provide for your peace and tranquility, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone from committing violence, robbery, or theft within the enclosures of your places or granges, from setting fire, or from daring to seize or kill a person.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and support of those concerned shall remain whole and inviolate for their complete benefit, saving the authority of the Apostolic See, the canonical right of the aforesaid archbishop, and [Col. 1302D] the due reverence owed to the Church of St. John.

If anyone therefore, in the future, ecclesiastical, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Peter, cardinal of the church of St. Susanna. I, Peter, cardinal of the church of the see of St. Rufina. I, Vivian, priest-cardinal of the Church of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cencius, priest-cardinal of the Church of St. Cecilia. I, Hugh, priest-cardinal of St. Clement. I, Harduin, priest-cardinal of the Church of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Matthew, priest-cardinal of the Church of St. Marcellus. [Col. 1303A] I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St. Mary in Trastevere, of the church of Callixtus. I, Hyacinth, of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Rainerius, deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, John, deacon-cardinal of St. Angelo. I, Rainerius, deacon-cardinal of St. Adrian. I, Matthew, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary the New.

Given at Tusculum by the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the tenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1180, [Col. 1303B] in the twentieth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MDX. Privilege for the monastery of Monte Cassino. (Tusculum, March 23.)

[D. Tosti, *History of the Abbey of Monte Cassino*, II, 206.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons P., abbot, and the convent of Monte Cassino, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since we embrace with the arms of special affection the monastery of Monte Cassino, in which you are devoted to divine services, and since we wish, as we ought, always diligently to attend to its welfare, we rightly rejoice with you in its prosperity and wish to take diligent care to preserve what has been established for its good by reasonable deliberation. Hence, whenever you request from us matters relating to the welfare of your community, we grant your petitions apostolic favor all the more readily because the aforesaid monastery looks in a special manner to our care and protection.

Now, since the cloistered brethren of that monastery sometimes suffered want of clothing, Gentilis of Palearia, of good memory, who had chosen burial at that monastery, moved by piety and for the sake of his own salvation, gave you, as we have learned, sixteen thousand *tareni* for the provision of felt garments and for purchasing close-fitting fur garments every second year. Since [Col. 1303D] you, son abbot, diverted the aforesaid money to another use of the monastery, you granted in compensation to the brethren, in perpetuity, twenty ounces of gold from Castellone and five from the church of Cinglis, to be expended for the purposes stated above. Therefore, since our office imposes upon us the duty of ensuring that what has been prudently done is not undone by anyone’s rashness, graciously moved by your petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority the aforesaid twenty ounces of gold from Castellone and the other five from the church of Cinglis for the use of the brethren, to which use they were assigned by you, son abbot, as is contained in the public instrument; and we strengthen them by the protection of this present writing. Establishing that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation [Col. 1304A] or rashly oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Tusculum, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April.

MDXI. To Peter, abbot of Monte Cassino. (Tusculum, March 23.)

[Ibid., 207.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son P., abbot of Monte Cassino, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever a request is made of us which accords with law and does not conflict with ecclesiastical propriety, we ought readily to grant our consent to the desires of petitioners and, as the effect follows, fulfill their wishes. Moved by this consideration and inclining to your just requests, by these present letters we grant you permission to have the abbesses and nuns of your monasteries, in which no other person possesses episcopal jurisdiction, blessed and veiled by whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, without objection or appeal. [Col. 1304B]

Given at Tusculum, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April.

MDXII. To Casimir, duke of Poland.—He confirms certain enactments made concerning the property of the Church. (Tusculum, March 28.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 914.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1304C] son, the noble man CASIMIR, duke of Poland, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us on behalf of your highness that, on the counsel of the archbishop and bishops of Poland and the princes of the land, you have removed certain abuses and customary injuries from churches and ecclesiastical persons, establishing that the goods of deceased bishops shall no longer be confiscated. It has also been established that, if anyone lays hands upon the property of a deceased bishop, he shall be bound by the bond of anathema. Nor may any one of the plunderers presume to succeed the deceased bishop until he obtains the benefit of absolution, after restoration of what was taken or prior payment of a suitable valuation for it.

Moreover, you have amended, by the counsel of ecclesiastical and secular men, the custom observed by the princes of the land—namely, that wherever they went in pomp, they would invade and empty the granaries of the poor; and that if some minor affair happened to occur among persons absent, their wicked retainers, running about, would either cripple horses they had seized in the course of riding or utterly destroy them. [Col. 1304D] Therefore, since you ask that your constitution, being alike just and honorable, be confirmed by our authority, we assent to your just requests and confirm the aforesaid constitution by apostolic authority, as it is set forth in the authentic written instrument made on this matter; and we strengthen it by the protection of this present writing, forbidding under threat of anathema that anyone presume to violate it for any reason. Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur [Col. 1305A] the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Tusculum, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April.

MDXIII. He receives the Church of St. Laudus of Bourg-Achard under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Tusculum, April 15.)

[*General Armorial of the Nobility of France*, Register IV, part I.]

In the name of the Lord, amen.

By this present public instrument let it be plainly manifest and known to all that this is a true transcript of certain letters of the late Lord Pope Alexander III, sealed with his genuine leaden bull hanging from cords of silk color, according to the custom then used by the Roman Curia; sound and whole, neither damaged nor cancelled, nor suspect in any part, but wholly free from every defect and suspicion. They were delivered to me, the undersigned notary public, on behalf of the venerable and religious men, the prior and convent of St. Laudus of Bourg-Achard, of the Order of St. Augustine, diocese of Rouen, for transcription in the year of the Lord 1459, eighth indiction, on the second day of October, in the second year of the pontificate of our most holy father and lord in Christ, Pius, by divine providence Pope II. The tenor of those letters follows word for word [Col. 1305C] and is as follows:

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons RODULPH, prior of St. Laudus of Bourg-Achard, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Whenever we are asked for what is recognized as consonant with religion and propriety, it is fitting that we grant it with willing mind and furnish suitable assistance to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church of St. Laudus of Bourg-Achard, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First establishing, indeed, that the canonical order known to have been instituted in your house according to [Col. 1305D] God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine shall be inviolably observed there in perpetuity.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself where the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Mary of Taberville and two chapels, namely those of the Holy [Col. 1306A] Trinity and St. Ouen, with all their appurtenances and liberties; the church of St. Philibert of Bochetot with its appurtenances; the church of St. Mary of Hangemara with its appurtenances; the chapel of St. Mary of the Forest of Henry of Neubourg, with its appurtenances and liberties; also the mill at Pont-Audemer, which you hold from the monks of Jumièges, together with the *motta* of their men at Pont-Audemer, your passage to their port, and the other liberties which they granted and confirmed to you in their charter.

By gift of Count Waleran of Ozelteto and his son Robert: exemption, throughout all their land, from charges on your food and the goods you sell or buy; passage-right for pigs; pasturage for all livestock; wood of your own for fuel; and complete exemption from services, tallages, aids, and all customary dues. Also, the tithe of tolls from Bourg-Achard and from Roger de Platanis’s mills at Pont-Audemer; the tithe of passage dues and of all revenues in Bourg-Achard belonging to that same Roger; the tithe of bread from his house in the same borough; the grove adjoining the aforesaid church; and all land within the circuit of your court.

Also, the thirty acres of land and three acres of woodland which Hugh, your first prior, gave to your church by grant of Roger Gule de Marchia and his son Mark; and, on the other side, forty-four acres which descended on his mother’s side; and all the land which Hubert of Sotevilla, with the assent of his daughter Helixent, granted you; and the service and rents of the land which Anfred, son of Godin, held from Walter of Gloz, namely eight shillings and two denarii, by the gift of that Walter; and six acres of land held by Ralph Crepion, for which four shillings are paid to you on the Ascension of the Lord; the land adjoining your grove, with the entire [ploughed] field and Picot’s grove; the land which Hugh Bubulcus held in tenancy; the house in the courtyard in which Julita lived; and every right claimed in Walter Sorel’s land by Nicholas of Cahisneio and his brother William; the land given you by W. Rossel; and three virgates of land given you by Restold.

Also, five acres given you by William and Ralph, sons of Restold; five acres given to you with Robert of Cosneio; five acres given you by Richard of Bosco Tahon, his son Ralph, and his grandson Robert; two acres given you by Robert and Richard, brothers of Hugh the canon; three acres given you by Richard Dolfai; and twenty Balvacian shillings given you by William, count of Aumale, to be received yearly from his toll at Aumale.

By gift of [lacuna] Alan of St. Peter: half an arpent of vineyard and a tithe of his wine and nuts at Longue-Villone. By gift of Ralph of Frollam Court: six acres of land, ten shillings, six pennies, and two capons. By gift of Mark of Mara: four acres [Col. 1307A] of land. By gift of Gervase of Bochetot: one acre. By gift of Robert of Buchetot and his sons Matthew and William: one acre. By gift of William of Piencuria: one mina of rye. By gift of Hugh, son of Robert: two acres of land. By gift of Ralph Pagan: one acre. By gift of Henry of Cahisneio and his brother William: two acres. By gift of Everard of Londo and his brother Richard: three acres and one virgate. By gift of Roger of Fontenis and his son W.: one acre; and one house in the borough; and one tenement between the cemetery and the house of Richard the merchant; and one virgate held by Robert, priest of Boscogoiet; and one house at Falaise, which sister Basilia gave to your church; and the land given to your church by Walter of Pont-Audemer, Robert son of Baldric, Walter the kinsman, his son Richard, and Osbert of Lendin. By gift of John of Bosco and his wife Matilda: one acre of land between Carresis and the wilderness which is in the wood of plane trees. By gift of Amelin and his son Thomas: five virgates of land. By gift of Helios of Tuito Herberti: one acre.

Furthermore, concerning your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, and concerning the increase of your animals, let no one presume to demand tithes from you. You may also receive into conversion clerics and laymen fleeing from the world, free and absolved, and retain them without any objection. When, however, a general interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them, so that they owe accountability to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. We also decree that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wish of those desiring burial there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken remain intact. Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, [Col. 1307D] or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any cunning contrivance or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If therefore in future, etc.

[Col. 1308A] I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Vivian, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement. I, Arduin, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Matthew, cardinal priest of Saint Marcellus. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of Saint Mary in Trastevere, of the title of Calixtus. I, James, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Rainerius, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. [Col. 1308B] I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Romelius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Matthew, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New.

Given at Tusculum, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the twenty-second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

MDXIV. He takes the monastery of Saint Ruffillus under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Tusculum, 13 May.)

[Bullarium Vaticanum, I, CO.]

[Col. 1308C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BENEDICT, abbot of the monastery of Saint Ruffillus of Foropompilius, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

To grant effect to just petitions accords with the force of equity and the order of reason, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wish and truth does not oppose it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. [Col. 1308D] First, indeed, we establish that the monastic order which is known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically holds, or may hereafter, by the grant of popes, the liberality of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, obtain by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

The very place on which the aforesaid monastery is built, with all its appurtenances, [Col. 1309A] namely the lands, vineyards, and woods situated around the monastery itself: on the first side, the river on which your mills were built; on the second side, the public road leading to Livien; on the third, the *campus donicatus* of the bishopric, where there was formerly a *silva donicata* of the bishopric; on the fourth, Palliata, with all other estates and places which you possess and hold; the chapels of Saint Lawrence of Cumignano; the chapel of Saint Paternian of Donicalia; and Saint John of Runco, with all their appurtenances; and whatever you presently possess in the territory of Pesaro and at Moredano. The parish churches of Saint Peter in Ceretu of Meldola and Saint Apollinaris in Collina, with all their chapels. We order that chrism, holy oil, the consecration of your altars or churches, and [Col. 1309B] the ordination of your monks and clerics who are to be promoted to holy orders, be supplied by the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic and enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, without corruption or any exaction; otherwise, you may receive them from any Catholic bishop.

[Note: [Col. 1309C] *Donicatus*, in Du Cange’s interpretation, signifies lordship; hence a *silva donicata* or *campus donicatus*: that is, woodland or land subject to another’s right and ownership. Nor has the word any other sense in the bull here under discussion.]

[Note: [Col. 1309C] No mention of this chapel occurs in the visitation records which we have thus far examined. It must therefore be supposed either to have been destroyed or, in a later period, separated from the abbey of Saint Ruffillus. [Col. 1309D] It is nevertheless mentioned in the bull of Gerard, archbishop of Ravenna, who lived at the same time as Alexander III. This bull appeared in 1180 and consists wholly in listing the goods, churches, and rights of our abbey, which it confirms as follows.]

[Note: [Col. 1309D] That document mentions two churches bearing the name of Saint Paternian: in the one given in 1192 to the chapter of Saint Peter of Parma, the other is designated Saint Paternian of Farazzano. Both lie in the territory of Meldola, but the former is poor and almost devoid of revenues, whereas the latter is rich and endowed with many incomes. We do not know which the bull identifies. We suspect it indicates the latter church, since the visitor speaks thus of the former at the end of folio 5: “It is found entered neither in the books of the abbey, nor does it pay them rent, nor does it have the form of a church; its revenues are eight scudi.”]

[Note: [Col. 1309D] It lies in the territory of Forlì, and is only two miles from the city. It has considerable ecclesiastical wealth. Hence it became a benefice long entrusted in commendam to the knights of the Order of Jerusalem. Runco, which gave the church its surname, is a well-known river, also called Vitis, which waters a large part of the lands of Popiliensis and Livien.]

[Note: [Col. 1310C] In the territory of Pesaro, the bull of Gerard, archbishop of Ravenna, mentioned above, places two churches, one of Saint Sabinus and the other of Saint Cassian. In Moredano [Col. 1310D] it places the chapel of Saint Anastasius. We have not yet been able to determine the fixed location of either territory.]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole and unimpaired for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in future, any ecclesiastical or secular [Col. 1309C] person, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Paul, bishop of the Church of Palestrina. I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. [Col. 1310A] I, Vivian, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cinthius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement. I, Arduin, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Matthew, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of Saint Mary in Trastevere, of the title of Calixtus. I, James, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Raynerius, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. [Col. 1310B] I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Matthew, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New.

Given at Tusculum, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the third Ides of May, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the twenty-first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III.

[Note: [Col. 1310D] If we compare the years of Alexander’s pontificate with the Christian era and the indiction, we are compelled to admit that an error has crept into their designation. The fourteenth indiction agrees well with 1181, but accords badly with the twenty-first year of the pontificate indicated by the bull. We have already established above that Alexander III was proclaimed supreme pontiff of the Church in September 1159. Let the number of years be carried down to 13 May 1181, and a simple calculation will show that Pope Alexander, when he issued this constitution, had exercised the pontificate for twenty-one years, eight months, and some days. Thus one must add one to the papal years, which the writer’s inconsistency omitted.]

MDXV. To the dean and chapter of Chalon. — That their bishop may not excommunicate or suspend clerics of Chalon unless he has first notified the chapter. (Viterbo, 24 June.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 1041.]

[Col. 1310C]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the dean and chapter of Chalon, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever a request is made to us that does not conflict with reason and accords with propriety, it becomes us readily and willingly to grant it and to bestow favourable support upon the petitioners’ desires. Accordingly, by the authority of these presents [Col. 1311A] we grant you that the bishop of Chalon may not interdict, excommunicate without manifest and reasonable cause, or suspend any cleric of the Church of Chalon, unless he himself or his messenger has first notified the chapter. This applies especially so long as the person summoned is willing, before your tribunal, to satisfy the charges brought against him.

Given at Viterbo, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July.

MDXVI. To the dean and chapter of Chalon. — That they may present to the bishop of Autun persons fit to govern churches whom the bishop of Chalon has refused. (Viterbo, 29 June.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1311B] ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GALTER, dean, and the chapter of Chalon, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You have informed us that our venerable brother Engilbert, bishop of Chalon, when suitable persons are presented by you to your churches, refuses to receive them at his own discretion. Therefore, wishing henceforth to provide for your protection from loss, we decree by the authority of these presents that, if after a threefold admonition, made at appropriate intervals, the aforesaid bishop should perhaps refuse to commit the care of souls in churches known to belong to you to suitable persons presented by you or by the greater part of you, you may [Col. 1311C] present them to our venerable brother the bishop of Autun, who, notwithstanding any rash opposition, shall by apostolic authority commit to them the care of souls.

Given at Viterbo, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July.

MDXVII. To Béla, king of Hungary. — That he should no longer hinder the free election of the archbishop of Split. (Viterbo, 6 July.)

[FARLATI, *Illyricum Sacrum*, III, 212.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ BÉLA, illustrious king of Hungary, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From reports made to us by our beloved sons, the clergy and people of Split, we have learned that, although the Church [Col. 1311D] of Split has long lacked a pastor and until these times has enjoyed free election according to the form of the privileges of the Roman pontiffs and the sacred canons, you do not permit a bishop to be elected there in the customary manner. Therefore, desiring to have regard for the royal welfare and, as our office requires, to provide for the protection of the aforesaid church from harm, we admonish and exhort your royal excellence in the Lord to permit, freely and without opposition, the appointment of a suitable person who can both preside over God’s people and serve them. Otherwise, although we wish to show deference to your royal magnificence, we cannot on any ground fail the aforesaid Church in its right. For we believe it also expedient for your royal serenity that you preserve that city in its liberty, make [Col. 1312A] its inhabitants firmer in loyalty to you, and give them no occasion to speak ill of your lordship.

Moreover, we most earnestly admonish and ask your royal magnificence to require Count Minoslav to restore to the aforesaid Church the money which he formerly took from Raynerius, archbishop of Split of blessed memory, or its equivalent valuation; and to permit those places in which cathedral sees are known formerly to have existed to be provided with ordinaries. If he cannot otherwise be brought to do this, compel him by royal power.

Given at Viterbo, on the second Nones of July.

MDXVIII. He takes the Church of Holy Cross at Metz under protection and confirms its goods and possessions. (Viterbo, 7 July.)

[HUGO, *Annals of the Sacred Order of Prémontré*, I, 473.]

[Col. 1312B]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot of the Church of Holy Cross at Metz, and the remaining brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: for perpetual remembrance.

Those who choose the religious life ought to have apostolic aid at hand, lest perhaps an onslaught of rashness turn them from their purpose or, which God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of Holy Cross situated outside the city of Metz, in [Col. 1312C] which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we establish that the canonical order which is shown to exist in the same church according to God, the Rule of Blessed Augustine, and the institution of the brethren of Prémontré, shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of popes, the liberality of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, obtain by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

[Col. 1312D] The very place on which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the freehold of Burris, which Ida gave you with the consent of her heirs; the rent which Albert the advocate gave you through the hands of the late bishop of Metz; the land of Richard of Rimport; the land of Rosselin Matous and his sister Osanna; the vineyards of Renald, son of Nemericus of Viceto, in the territory of Roseliers; the vineyards of Brunerd in Plantoriis and in Martin’s field; the vineyards of Giler near Saint Julian; the vineyards of Gaulter, surnamed Pagan, of Vantome at Mozin; the vineyards of Otto of Viad Lorcifumos; and of Bartholomew at the gate of Salia; the house at Metz which belonged to the knight Ulric; the rent of five solidi which Bermund gave you in the suburb [Col. 1313A] outside Salia; the freehold of Cavillo, of which Allart, with the consent of Beatrice his wife and his sons, gave you his portion, while Garfelius, Gibert, Gimpa his wife, Theodoret of Perta, Gemosius of Larci, and Hugh of Neufchâteau gave you other portions of that freehold; the land of Saint Peter of the Fountain, which Matthew, duke and margrave of Lorraine, through the bishop of Metz and with the consent of Count Sigibert of Alsace, Cono of Manherch, Cono of Cruenges, Andrew and Richard, brothers of Mosterot, Arnulf the steward, and their heirs, granted you in perpetuity; whatever in the same territory Wiricus, his brother Gilo, and Anselm their nephew held for their own use, from the summit of the mountain facing Later as far as the other mountain [Col. 1313B] facing Thil, they gave you with the consent of Count Hugh of Dusbourch and of Evrard, advocate of the aforesaid duke; and throughout the whole *ban* of Laites, the use of your animals in the unoccupied pastures. [lacuna]

Certainly, no one may presume to exact tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laypersons fleeing from the world, free and unencumbered, and retain them without any opposition. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to depart from it without his abbot’s permission; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without the security of letters common to both parties. When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate the divine offices with closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, and in a subdued voice. Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be placed over it through any artifice of stealth or violence, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. We also decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the judgment and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated [Col. 1313D] or under interdict; saving, nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole and unimpaired for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in future, any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Alexander, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. [Col. 1314A] I, Peter, cardinal priest of Saint Cussanus (sic). I, Vivian, cardinal priest of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Arduin, cardinal priest of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of Saint Mary the New in Trastevere. I, James, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Augustine. I, Matthew, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary.

Given at Viterbo, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of July, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the twenty-second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander [Col. 1314B] III.

MDXIX. Privilege for the Church of Treviso. (Viterbo, 19 July.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, V, 529.]

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons DODO, dean of the church of Treviso, and his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made to us which is known to accord with religion and propriety, it becomes us readily and willingly to grant it and to render fitting support to the petitioners’ desires. Accordingly, beloved sons in the Lord, [Col. 1314C] we graciously assent to your requests, receive your Church, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We establish that whatever possessions or goods the same Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of popes, the liberality of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, obtain by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

The church of Saint Michael of Melma, with its village and mills; holdings at Lugugnano; holdings at Seura; holdings at Rivarotta; holdings at Casale; holdings [Col. 1314D] at Burbilago; holdings at Godenzago; holdings at Cancelada; the church of Saint Andrew of Silvarosa, with its village; holdings at Vedelago; holdings at Montebelluna; holdings at Montel; holdings at Malzago; holdings at Petrarubea; holdings at Fener; holdings at Duno; holdings at Manzagello; holdings at Paderno; possessions at Gonzano; the church of Saint Pelagius of Aurine, with the holdings of that village; the church of Saint Bona, with its mills; holdings at Cormelino; holdings at Quinto; holdings at Saint Christina; the church of Saint Mary of Pratogatzol, with the holdings of that village; holdings at Ger; the church of Saint Vitalis, with the holdings of that village; the church of Saint Gervasius, with the holdings of that village; holdings at Canizano; holdings at Gei, with woodland; possessions at Bassano, Romano, and [Col. 1315A] Tor; holdings at Asolo; holdings at Braida; everything you possess at Mestre; the churches which you possess within the city, namely Saint John the Baptist, Saint Bartholomew, Saint Andrew, Saint John of the Bank, and the church of Saint Sophia situated outside the walls of the city of Treviso; the possessions which you have in the city and the tithes which you have around the city itself.
