CDLVII. He commands certain persons not to follow this custom: “when someone has established his claim by documents or witnesses introduced, an oath is nevertheless tendered to him.” [Col. 1356A] Augustini Tarr. *Opera* IV. 372, Decr. Greg. Book II, title 19, chapter 2.—“As the custom.”

CDLVIII. He grants certain persons that “if they establish a hospital without an oratory, they may freely build that house without the knowledge of the bishop in whose parish it is situated.” Augustini Tarr. *Opera* IV. 399, Mansi XXI. 1098.—“If [they establish] a hospital.”

CDLIX. He writes to certain persons that, “if a settlement concerning tithes has been made between them and an ecclesiastical person with the consent of their bishop or archdeacon, it is to remain binding.” Mansi XXII. 376, Boehmeri *Corpus* II, appendix 206, Augustini Tarr. *Opera* IV. 65, Decr. Greg. Book I, title 36, chapter 2.—“We decree that, if.”

CDLX. He forbids certain persons to presume “to impose *taliae* [arbitrary levies] and unlawful exactions upon priests.” Mansi XXII. 275, Boehmeri *Corpus juris canonici* II, appendix 204, Augustini Tarr. *Opera* IV. 327, Decr. [Col. 1356B] Greg. Book V, title 31, chapter 1.—“It has come to [our] hearing.”

CDLXI. He forbids certain persons to venerate, in the manner of unbelievers, as a saint “a certain man killed while drinking and drunk.” Augustini Tarr. *Opera* IV. 422, Decr. Greg. Book III, title 45, chapter 1.—“We have heard that certain persons.”

CDLXII. He commands certain persons to order certain tithes restored to the cleric G. Augustini Tarr. *Opera* IV. 388, Mansi XXI. 1097.—“Being present.”

CDLXIII. He prescribes to certain persons that they must not prohibit the sons of John and the woman T. “from succeeding to their paternal goods.” Mansi XXII. 389, Boehmeri *Corpus* II, appendix 333, Augustini Tarr. *Opera* IV. 261, Decr. Greg. Book IV, title 17, chapter 2.—“Since between I.”

CDLXIV. He commands certain persons to order Philip, Count of Colombes, to restore the church of Frag. to G., cleric of Nobil. Augustini Tarr. *Opera* IV. 364, Mansi XXI. 1094.—“Coming into [our] presence.”

CDLXV. [Col. 1356C] He writes to certain persons concerning the case of the cleric A. Augustini Tarr. *Opera* IV. 365, Decr. Greg. Book I, title 38, chapter 2.—“The complaint of the cleric A.”

CDLXVI. He decrees that clerics ordained outside their own province in overseas regions “are not to be considered ordained.” Mansi XXII. 372.—“Because certain clerics.”

CDLXVII. He decrees as follows: “The suffragans of a metropolitan may, at his command, after confirmation of his election, even if he has not received the pallium, lawfully consecrate an elect who belongs to his jurisdiction.” Augustini Tarr. *Opera* IV. 356 (Decr. Greg. Book I, title 6, chapter 11).—“For suffragans.”

CDLXVIII. He orders as follows: “Let none of the priests accept a gift or any temporal emolument from any publicly sinful or incestuous person, in order to conceal that person’s sin from the bishop or his ministers.” [Col. 1356D] Boehmer, *Corpus juris canonici*, II, app. 201; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 280. — “Let none of the priests.”

CDLXIX. He writes thus: “If anyone indeed immerses a child, saying, ‘In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,’ but does not say, ‘I baptize you,’ such an immersion cannot be called baptism,” etc. Baluzius, *Miscellanea*, III, 373; Mansi XXI, 1101; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 422; Decretals of Gregory, Book III, title 42, chapters 1–2. “If anyone indeed” — “If anyone [immerses] a child” — “Concerning matters in doubt.”

CDLXX. He writes “concerning infants who are found dead with father and mother.” Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 413; (*Decretals of Gregory*, Book V, title 10, chapter 3). — “Concerning infants.”

ANNO 1161–1181.

CDLXXI. He writes to B[artholomew], bishop of Exeter, concerning the marriage of Hugh and M. Mansi XXII, [Col. 1357A] 311; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 266; Boehmer, *Corpus*, II, app. 328. — “It came to our hearing.”

CDLXXII. He writes to B[artholomew], bishop of Exeter, concerning R., “who had known a certain woman and afterwards took her cousin as his wife.” Mansi XXII, 325. — “Coming into our presence.”

CDLXXIII. He writes to B[artholomew], bishop of Exeter, at the request of the chapter of Bordeaux, concerning a cleric who had unwillingly killed a cleric. Mansi XXII, 370; Boehmer, *Corpus juris canonici*, II, app. 224; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 306; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book V, title 12, chapter 9. — “The bearer of these presents [came] to us.”

CDLXXIV. He praises B[artholomew], bishop of Exeter, because he did not permit a church to be bestowed upon the son of the priest R.; but he denies that the same man, since “he is ordained in the subdiaconate, ought altogether to lack the receipt of an ecclesiastical benefice.” Mansi XXII, 354; Boehmer, *Corpus juris canonici*, II, app. 246; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 35; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book I, title 17, [Col. 1357B] chapter 6. — “He set before us.”

CDLXXV. He directs B[artholomew], bishop of Exeter, and the abbot of Forde to judge between R. and II., who are litigating concerning an inheritance. Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 166; Boehmer, *Corpus*, II, app. 333; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book IV, title 17, chapter 5. — “The bearer, R., of these presents.”

ANNO 1164–1181.

CDLXXVI. He directs the bishops of Exeter and Winchester that, if D., a priest, “held the church of Waplam for a long time before the Council of Tours, they are to absolve him from the claim of the monks of Lentunen.” Mansi XXII, 401. — “D. informed us.”

ANNO 1167–1181.

CDLXXVII. He again urges the bishop of Tournai to “receive M., born among the Jews, who has received the Christian sacraments, as a canon of his church, and assign him a stall in choir and a place in chapter.” Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 354; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book I, title 3, chapter 7. — “That you” — “For indeed long ago.”

ANNO 1169–1181.

CDLXXVIII. He replies to Eberard [or Gerard], bishop of Padua, concerning “a man and woman who, by the command of the lord of each of them, received one another, with no priest present and no solemnity observed,” etc. Mansi XXII, 293; Boehmer, *Corpus*, II, app. 320; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 240. — “But concerning that which.”

CDLXXIX. He replies to Eberard [or Gerard], bishop of Padua, “concerning a woman who, although betrothed to one man, is betrothed to and carnally known by another man.” Mansi XXII, 291–292; Boehmer, *Corpus*, II, app. 319; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 239, 223; *Decretals of Gregory*, [Col. 1357D] Book IV, title 1, chapter 6; title 16, chapter 3. — “The concern of the See” — “Concerning a woman who.”

CDLXXX. He writes to G[ilbert], bishop of London, concerning the removal of married priests. Gilbert Foliot, *Letters*, ed. Giles, II, 88 (Mansi XXII, 349; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 144; Boehmer, *Corpus*, II, app. 335). — “Of the Universal Church” — “Universal solicitude.”

ANNO 1173–1181.

CDLXXXI. He informs [Roger], archbishop of York, and R., a priest, that R., a priest, has been absolved from excommunication by the bishop of Tusculum and P[eter], cardinal of St Susanna. Mansi XXII, 317; Boehmer, *Corpus*, II, app. 291; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 128; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book II, title 28, chapter 16. — “To our presence.”

CDLXXXII. He directs the bishop of Pavia to decide the controversy [Col. 1358A] of A. de Plano and G. de Betolio “in accordance with the attestations authenticated with his seal by P[eter], priest-cardinal of the title of St Susanna.” Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 98; Mansi XXI, 1084. — “Since A. de.”

ANNO 1174–1181.

CDLXXXIII. He writes to the bishops of Winchester, Bath, and Hereford concerning the marriage of R. Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 259; Boehmer, *Corpus*, II, app. 322; Mansi XXII, 295; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book IV, title 16, chapter 2. — “From the letters of the venerable [man].”

CDLXXXIV. He writes as follows to R[ichard], archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See: “We do not see with what face you can consult us concerning points of law, when you are said to overturn the order of law and openly to oppose the liberty of the Church—the cause for which that glorious martyr Thomas did not fear to undergo martyrdom. For you are said now to confirm elections of bishops, contrary to the requirements of law, not in a church, as is canonical and honourable, not in your palace, not in your own chamber, but in the king’s private chamber.” Nevertheless, he replies to his inquiry concerning appeals. Boehmer, *Corpus*, II, app. 296; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 135; Mansi XXII, 384, 385, 405; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book II, title 28, chapter 25. — “With what face [can] we” — “Concerning these matters also” — “But concerning that which.”

CDLXXXV. He replies to R[ichard], archbishop of Canterbury, concerning appeals. Mansi XXII, 315; Boehmer, *Corpus*, II, app. 289; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 126; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book II, title 28, chapter 13. — “It came to us that.”

CDLXXXVI. He replies to R[ichard], archbishop of Canterbury, “concerning those who swear that they will stand by the judgment of the Church and then, after making the oath, appeal.” Mansi XXII, 320; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 131. — “Furthermore, concerning those who.”

CDLXXXVII. He directs R[ichard], archbishop of Canterbury, [Col. 1358C] to forbid the archdeacons of the diocese of Coventry “to demand any further monetary penalty from clerics or laymen for correcting offences or punishing crimes, or money for the ordeal by fire or water.” Mansi XXII, 274; Boehmer, *Corpus juris canonici*, II, app. 204; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 339; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book V, title 37, chapter 3. — “Although, according to the Apostle.”

CDLXXXVIII. He writes to R[ichard], archbishop of Canterbury, concerning the dispute of the clerics G. and E. Mansi XXII, 303; Boehmer, *Corpus*, II, app. 269; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 12; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book I, title 3, chapter 2. — “On the part of the venerable [man]” — “On the part of Coventry.”

ANNO 1177–1181.

CDLXXXIX. He directs Wichmann, archbishop of Magdeburg, and … bishop of Brandenburg, [Col. 1358D] to decree under penalty of anathema “that no one shall lay violent hands upon the canons or lay brothers of the church of St Mary of Magdeburg, or presume to plunder or seize their goods.” Ludewig, *Reliquiae*, II, 336; Leuckfeld, *Antiquities of Prémontré*, 91. — “You do not doubt that those.”

CDXC. He writes that concerning the fiefs of a certain provost it should be decided either by the bishop or “by imperial good pleasure.” Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 368; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book II, title 2, chapter 7. — “But since concerning.”

ANNO 1178–1171.

CDXCI. He grants [Lanfranc], bishop of Pavia, permission to revoke donations made by his predecessor P[eter] without consulting the canons. Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 170; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book III, title 34, chapter 2. — “We believe your brotherhood.”

CDXCII. He replies to L[anfranc], bishop-elect of Pavia, concerning [Col. 1359A] the custom of the church of Pavia: “If any mention is made of the kinship of those who are to be joined in marriage, the priests are publicly to announce in the churches that anyone who knows anything is to come forward and declare it within the specified term.” Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 267; Mansi XXI, 1092. — “To these [points], since.”

CDXCIII. He writes to [Lanfranc], bishop-elect of Pavia, concerning the marriage of Em. de Siderio and the son of R. Canis. Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 105; cf. no. ff.; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book II, title 21, chapter 1. — “The case of the marriage.”

CDXCIV. He replies to the bishop of Pavia concerning a girl “whose marriage had been the subject of a dispute between the Siderii and the Canes, citizens of his city.” Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 230; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book IV, title 1, chapter 14. — “Since there is no place.”

CDXCV. He grants the doge of Venice that, “if a cleric from the land of his jurisdiction appeals to his court against a layman in a monetary case,” the case is to “be entrusted for judgment, according to the law and custom of the Venetians, only to persons who are from the land of his jurisdiction; provided that our indulgence,” he says, “is to last only during our lifetime.” Mansi XXII, 407. — “When we were at Venice.”

ANNO 1179–1181. 1181.

CDXCVI. He replies to the archbishop of Bourges [Vituriensis, perhaps Bituricensis], stating that he had admonished L[ouis], king of the French, not to permit “Christian slaves to be kept by Jews, or new synagogues to be constructed.” “But,” he says, “if old synagogues have fallen down or threaten ruin, you may patiently tolerate their rebuilding; yet not their being raised up or made larger or more splendid than they are known to have been before. Indeed, they ought to regard it as a great favour that they are tolerated in their observances and their old synagogues.” Baluzius, *Miscellanea*, III, 379; Bouquet, *Recueil*, XV, 968; Mansi [Col. 1359C] XXI, 1106, XXII, 441; Boehmer, *Corpus*, III, app. 307; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 379, 412; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book II, title 28, chapter 29; Book V, title 6, chapter 7. — “Your [letter] consulted us.”

CDXCVII. He replies to certain questions of R[ichard], archbishop of Canterbury. Mansi XXII, [Col. 1360A] 336; Boehmer, *Corpus*, II, app. 298, 300; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 148; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book III, title 4, chapter 4; title 38, chapters 5 and 10. — “It was reported to us” — “Henceforth, [we entrust this] to your prudence” — “When laymen [act against] bishops” — “But as to what you ask.”

CDXCVIII. He explains to the bishop-elect and chapter of Cassano the decree of the Lateran council: “that property acquired through the Church is to devolve upon it at the death of clerics.” Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 389; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book III, title 26, chapter 12. — “It was reported to our ears.”

CDXCIX. He replies to the bishop of D[ivelle?] (otherwise Dulmen), that “a man to whom the mastership of a church had been granted before his twenty-fifth year, before the Lateran council had yet been held, is not to be deprived of the church.” Mansi XXII, 366; Boehmer, *Corpus juris canonici*, II, app. 242; Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 32. — “Your [letter] to us.”

D. He urges a certain bishop not to violate the statutes of the Lateran council in making appointments to churches. Boehmer, *Corpus juris canonici*, II, app. 242; Augustinus [Col. 1360B] of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 32; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book I, title 14, chapter 4; Book III, title 38, chapter 22. — “It befits you.”

ANNO 1181.

DI. He instructs P[aul], bishop of Palestrina, and the other heirs of the late J[ohn], cardinal-priest of SS John and Paul, to restore certain scholastic books to the brethren of the church of St Fridianus at Lucca. Baluzius, *Miscellanea*, IV, 596. — “We received letters.”

DII. He informs [Roger], archbishop of York, and [Hugh], bishop of Durham, that “he has determined that the privileges of the monastery of St Augustine, Canterbury, which Archbishop Richard wishes to challenge, are to be produced before them in the brothers’ cloister or another place secure for the brothers, until the next feast of the Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist (24 June).” He adds: “Then, until the Purification of Blessed Mary in the following year [Col. 1360C] (2 February 1182), the archbishop is to appear at the Apostolic See, either personally or through an adequate representative, in order to challenge the privileges.” Chronicle of W. Thorn in Twysden, *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, II, 1832; (Augustinus of Tarragona, *Opera*, IV, 374; *Decretals of Gregory*, Book II, title 22, chapter 4). — “We received letters” — “We received letters.”

[Col. 1359]

## LETTERS OF VARIOUS PERSONS TO ALEXANDER III

(The letters for which the source from which we draw is not prefixed are brought here from the collection of letters of St Thomas of Canterbury and Gilbert Foliot, contained in volume 190 of the *Patrologia*.)

### I. Philip, abbot of La Charité

He congratulates Alexander on his elevation to the highest dignity; he reports that the kings of France and England have embraced the pope’s cause. (Year 1159.)

[*Spicilegium*, folio edition, vol. III, p. 527.]

[Col. 1359D]

To his most beloved father and lord in Christ, ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff and universal pope, brother PHILIP of La Charité: the little that he is.

Upon receiving the letters of your graciousness, [Col. 1360D] my heart breathed again in joy; and, like a crown of hope adorned with glory, cheerful serenity blossomed anew in my spirit. Embracing your enthronement with the arms of true love, I offered devout supplication for you to the Giver of all good things. A common thanksgiving and voice of praise resounded, and for your promotion we sing a hymn to our God: “Woe to the man through whom scandal comes!” (Matthew 18). We trust in the mercy of the Creator that the assault of the opposing party will come to nothing, like flowing water; and that transgressors will be swept away like melting wax, because the fire of abomination has fallen upon them. [Col. 1361A] They will not see Christ, the sun of righteousness, who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (James 4).

Moreover, most blessed Father, I inform your Highness that I have now, with the devotion I owed, the diligence required, and commendation, reverently presented your letters to Lord Henry, king of the English. Receiving them kindly, and after deliberation with his own advisers and with us, he recognizes you most willingly as spiritual Father and supreme pontiff, and humbly conveys through us his service and obedience. He will shortly send his own envoys to you. He has charged my lowliness to anticipate his action by the service of devout diligence, so that what he will subsequently do may reach you more privately and swiftly.

I have also endeavoured to forward the general letters which you sent universally to the prelates of England through a trustworthy man, together with the venerable bishops Gilbert of Hereford and Hilary of Chichester. They support and love your person and your cause, as it is maintained—or, so far as we understand it—and will strive faithfully to promote your cause.

Thereafter I went to the devout son of the holy Roman Church, the lord king of the French, whose faithful affection and ready devotion, as befits a Catholic prince, pursue your person and cause with assured love. He would already have confirmed the judgment of his purpose by action, [Col. 1361C] had grave impediments and numerous affairs not disturbed him. A greeting dictated by his spirit is being conveyed to you through our ministry; but the document is held sealed by the warrant of his prudent conscience, reserved until an opportune time arises, when, as to a Father sincerely beloved—indeed diligently chosen—and when circumstances suitably permit, each of the two kings may profitably offer you his obedience and service, in due charity and with the triumph of joy.

By God’s mercy, this very outcome is at the door. For negotiations are under way between him and the king of England for the restoration of peace, and we believe they will soon be concluded; faithful men are conducting them devoutly and faithfully for the common concord of the kingdoms.

[Col. 1361D] What you commanded, so far as it concerned me, has been done. I have been diligent, and I send you a sure and faithful report of my work. I desire that a returning letter of your graciousness may inform me of your condition and that of our holy mother, the Roman Church. We trust in the assistance of divine mercy, that the Lord will quickly crush Satan beneath your feet; that he will bring sure judgment forth to victory; and that judgment will return unto righteousness, and that all who are upright in heart may follow it. Know further that all archbishops and bishops, and the rulers of the Churches, unanimously consent to your election.

### II. Eleanor, queen of England, wife of Henry II

She gives thanks for letters sent by the supreme pontiff and asks his aid for the abbot of St Maxentius. (Year 1160.)

[Ibid., p. 528.]

[Col. 1362A]

To her reverend father and lord, ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, ELEANOR, humble queen of England: the service owed with all devotion.

The devotion of a humble daughter does not cease to rejoice and praise God for this great dignity of my most serene father. The overflowing ardour of filial and true love often breaks forth in praise of a father. The fervour of such accumulated joys cannot be extinguished, nor can the grace of most just favour perish in untimely silence. Thus, whenever discussion of the parties occurs in my presence, I confidently defend your party and do not fear to attack—indeed, by my arguments to defeat—the hostile power which has dared to oppose it.

Previously I rejoiced most justly and rightly embraced your successes; but the glorious graciousness of your letter and greeting, with its abundant commendation and wholly true promise at the end, has sufficiently won every favour of my lowliness. I know not what spiritual sweetness and intimate delight I drank in; every single word I received most joyfully and devoutly, as though each were a separate gift of divine blessing.

Furthermore, [Col. 1362C] your sons and my lords, the cardinals Henry of Pisa and Master William, have shown me great honour and goodwill, by the grace of God and of yourself. I therefore rejoice that men have been sent from your side who are judged most worthy both by the authority of your election and by the complete reverence owed by subjects. Yet because not my intervention with them, but theirs with me, is necessary and salutary, I now supplicate your Highness for my kinsman P., abbot of St Maxentius. Cast most humbly at the footstool of your feet, I press this request: that your mercy may piously restore to my dearest [kinsman] the practice of his order and free authority to perform his ministry.

I should wish for your coming into our regions, if it pleased God and yourself; but whether absent or present, [Col. 1362D] I am most ready to offer every devotion of a humble and faithful servant. May divine mercy preserve the Father of all the Church’s children in health.

### III. Amalric, minister of the Church of the Holy Resurrection at Jerusalem

He declares that, by the unanimous consent of the Eastern clergy and people, after the rejection of Octavian, John, and Guy, Alexander has been chosen as temporal lord and spiritual Father. (Year 1160.)

[*Works of Gretser*, vol. VI, p. 584.]

To his worthily reverend lord and Father, ALEXANDER, by God’s grace universal pope of the Roman and Apostolic Church, AMALRIC, humble minister of the Church of the Holy Resurrection, together with all his suffragans: both the obedience owed and the devoted service of entire obedience.

We received the letter concerning your holy, Catholic, and chosen election with the veneration we owed. On the appointed day, having summoned together all our venerable brothers and sons—who, with willing and eager mind, either were present or sent executive letters declaring and announcing their assent—we carefully read and reread, in the presence of all, of the bishops of Tyre and Nazareth and of our other brothers and sons, the letter mentioned above.

When we heard of the stubborn and rash perversity—and the perverse rashness—of Octavian and his pseudo-brethren J. and G. [John and Guy], [Col. 1363B] we were afraid; and we grieved because they had departed from the unity of holy mother Church. Yet when we afterwards learned of the concordant, sound, and unanimous will of our venerable brethren and lords, the bishops and the other cardinals, and learned also the assent and desire of the consenting clergy and acclaiming people concerning your most holy and canonical election and consecration, we breathed again and rejoiced with great joy.

Moreover, all of us praised and approved that same most sacred and regular election and consecration of yours; we approve it jointly and in concord. Having excommunicated the schismatics Octavian, J., and G., with their supporters, so far as lies in us, [Col. 1363C] we unanimously chose you as temporal lord and spiritual Father, and freely received you.

### IV. Fastred, third abbot of Clairvaux, to Omnibonus, bishop of Verona

Concerning the Council of Toulouse, at which Alexander was recognized as pope after Victor’s rejection, and concerning the assembly at Pavia. (Year 1161.)

[Labbe, *Councils*, vol. X, col. 1407.]

To his beloved and truly venerable lord and Father O[MNIBONUS], by God’s grace bishop of Verona, brother F., called abbot of Clairvaux: the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

I certainly rejoice whenever, among thorns, I find a lily; and, amid the errors of men pursuing human fears or favours, a lover of truth and a most diligent seeker of the divine will. Therefore, in response to your Dignity’s request, we wish you to be certain, on the grounds and in the manner in which we ourselves are certain, concerning the matter you ask about.

Thus, after the many exhortations which we addressed to kings and princes who, through fear or favour toward the emperor, delayed following the truth; after the many consultations we held with archbishops, bishops, and religious men who repeatedly approached the kings; after the long delay imposed upon the cardinals H[enry] and W[illiam], priests, and O[do], deacon, whom Pope Alexander had sent into Gaul; after the many prayers and tears which the Church poured out to the Lord, especially in our order; and after almost utter despair, the Lord arranged matters better than we ourselves had dared to hope.

The two cardinals whom Octavian alone retained from the Roman curia came with the imperial party in great pomp and splendour to the day and place appointed by the kings of France and England, together with their whole Church, for the aforesaid worldly men to declare their adherence. What more need be said?

First the cardinals of Octavian, Jo[hn] and W[ido], were heard; others replied on the opposite side. It was established, not merely by the assertions of Pope Alexander’s cardinals and by qualified witnesses who were present—whom the others could not contradict on any ground—but also by the statements of the adversaries, whom God himself by manifest miracle caused to utter the truth, that Octavian had had no election. He had enthroned himself; with lay assistance he had seized the papal chair, as W. of Cremona testified in the hearing of all, and in my own hearing. It was established also that the same Octavian, already excommunicated eight days before, had received consecration [from a man consecrated eight days before that excommunication; **[Note: [Col. 1363D] The words enclosed in brackets appear to be omitted.]**] from the bishops of Tusculum and Ferentino, themselves excommunicated with him, and from the bishop of Melfi, already condemned and deposed because of his manifest enormities—as the king of England and his bishops, they themselves and their countrymen, declared.

[Col. 1364C] It was likewise established that Alexander had been elected by all the other cardinals who were present; and that, unless he himself had first humbly resisted by fleeing and then by refusing, and unless John and Guy of Cremona, as he himself testified before all, had violently prevented it, he would solemnly have been enthroned—a matter subsequently completed in its proper place and time. He solemnly received authentic consecration from those upon whom this duty rested by office.

It was also plainly proved that, long before the Council of Pavia, the emperor had received Octavian as pope through his envoys and letters sealed in gold. Though they had written that there were 153 bishops at Pavia, there were only forty-four. At the emperor’s summons, they all deliberated at length with W. of Pavia, priest-cardinal of St Peter in Chains, who had adhered to neither party and was now, together with two others, acting as Pope Alexander’s legate in Gaul. The emperor professed himself a layman, [Col. 1364D] one to whom it did not belong to judge the Roman curia or investigate the elections of supreme pontiffs. They resolved not to receive either claimant, because they were few in number compared with the whole Church, until either a common synod of all or of the greater number of kingdoms should assemble, or it should appear more clearly which claimant the larger and sounder part of the Church followed; and they said they would give the same advice to the emperor.

The emperor, however, did not agree. Instead, he compelled, by threats and entreaties, those whom he could summon one by one to accept the man whom he had already accepted. Yet twenty-four of the above number were absent, as the same Cardinal William plainly stated; one of them was the bishop of Pavia, in whose city these things were being done.

Therefore, by the common counsel of the aforesaid kings and of their entire Church, the schismatic Octavian was rejected, Pope Alexander was received, and his legates received with fitting honour and reverence. The bishop of Trier stands in unity. Some of those who had given their hands to Octavian are returning. Thus we Carthusians have obtained leave for the bishop of Grenoble, through our intercession, to return to favour.

[Col. 1365B] Further, Cardinal Odo of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison stated, without contradiction from his hearers, that the aforesaid cardinals J. and W. had come to him, while he was confined with others, urging him to come to Octavian. They were answered that, if they would swear upon the holy Gospels to judge justly, everyone would submit himself to their judgment. But they replied that the pope ought not to be judged by anyone; and said that, if they would make common cause with Octavian, they would restore the mantle which they accused him of having unjustly received. They would submit themselves entirely to their counsel, and he would receive the mantle a second time from their hands.

### V. Peter of Pisa, dean of the Church of Blessed Anianus at Orléans

Against contumacious bishops. (Year 1162.)

[Duchesne, *Writers of French Affairs*, IV, 575.]

[Col. 1365C]

To the venerable Father and lord ALEXANDER, supreme and universal pontiff, P., by the same grace dean of the Church of St Anianus of the holy Roman Church and of the lord king of the French: the service owed and devoted.

The lords cardinals, who witnessed it with their bodily eyes, know how hard I laboured so that, once the error had been destroyed, the person of the kingdom of France might receive you as Father and shepherd of souls. You were therefore received through the great labour of the cardinals, since, during the time of dissension, the prelates of the churches rejoiced in it. [Col. 1365D] For they plundered their subjects with impunity and wickedly burdened the powerless and poor.

The lords cardinals began little by little to exhort and admonish the bishops to walk in the way of uprightness, not to overthrow the ordinances of the Roman Church so indiscriminately, and by no means to stray so openly from the path of justice. While they were certainly proceeding with this too cautiously—perhaps because remorse for their former conduct troubled them—an occasion for war arrived, and war arose between the kings. It will not easily be calmed, for there is no one even to mention peace.

The bishops desire war, because they understand that the war against the Roman Church is increased by the war between kings. The lord king has indeed been greatly disturbed; and because he has attached himself to new leaders and young men, there is very great reason to fear that his disposition may change. [Col. 1366A] The bishops and other prelates of the churches of France rejoice and exult because the lords cardinals have lost royal favour; consequently, they do not fear to stretch out their hands toward every sort of base act. They evade and despise appeals; and, as though no appeal had been made, after an appeal they destroy everything.

The Roman Church has been far too sparing toward offending bishops, and is therefore now held cheap and in contempt. Let holy Roman Church, then, resume her strength and, walking by the paths of justice, order all things by right judgment. Farewell.

### VI. Henry, archbishop of Reims

For St Thomas of Canterbury. (Year 1169.)

[*Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims*, II, 300.]

[Col. 1366B]

To Pope ALEXANDER, [HENRY], archbishop of Reims.

Our venerable brother and friend, the lord of Canterbury, has now spent a fifth year in exilic banishment among us for the honour of God, the liberty of the Church, and the privileges of the Apostolic See. If it please you, lord, what he has endured until now is already enough; it is now time to have compassion upon him. This is necessary both lest other prelates of the churches be frightened by his example from carrying out their office, and lest what one man has hitherto presumed against him with impunity be drawn by other secular powers into a precedent for evil in the oppression of churches.

We therefore beseech your fatherhood, upon whom the eyes of all are fixed, awaiting what outcome the cause of God will receive under your judgment: aid so great an exile—or rather, so sincere a cause—and provide alike for your own honour, for the liberty of the Church, and for her welfare. For if the defender of God’s honour is tortured on the gallows, what hope remains for the other confessors of the divine name?

How his cause recently proceeded may be learned more fully from the testimony of a man held in the highest repute among us, Simon, prior of Mont-Dieu, who wrote what he saw and heard while carrying out your command. He is a man of exceptionally proven religious character, [Col. 1366D] whom we believe no consideration could induce to say anything contrary to his conscience. Farewell.

### VII. The same writer

For Drogo, chancellor of the Church of Noyon. (Year 1170.)

[*Acts*, ibid., p. 305.]

To the reverend Father and lord in Christ, ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, HENRY, styled archbishop of Reims: greeting and reverence.

No grief is more just for a man than to lose the goodwill earned by his service; nor can any distress more heavily assail the mind of a debtor than to receive the title of offence in return for a benefit deserved. I wonder—and my mind cannot wonder enough—what occasion has intervened, what fault of mine has been added, what action stands between us, that I feel the hands of Moses heavy and the result displays a father’s affection unlike that which I deserved.

For what I desire to foster, your authority discolours; and those whom I oppose through the rigour of justice, your favour raises to advancement. My enemies and yours hear of your action and of my resentment; and they rejoice because you have done it. A filial affection does not hide from a father what causes it pain, but seeks fruits of joy from the plant of sorrow.

You have done two things at which I marvel; and in them I grieve no less for your position than for mine. You promote publicly the incapacity—lest I say something harsher—of that man of Arras; by this both that church is troubled, the rigour of justice is confounded, and the property of the Church is dissipated. You intend, as I have heard, to remove from his rank the chancellor of the Church of Noyon, a man, as I believe, of honour and a lover of religion, a member of my household: one neither summoned, heard, nor canonically convicted, nor made guilty by his own confession. [Col. 1367B] The merit and decree of the holy pontiff ought greatly to have spoken for him with you, since he placed such faith and hope in him that, together with a personate, he entrusted to him the care of souls without scruple of conscience.

All are astonished at this, and the ears of those hearing it ring, when incapacity receives assistance and religion receives degradation as such opposite rewards for their merits. There is another matter besides, by which my mind is more severely wounded and pressed: you do not receive my letters with a serene countenance, nor do they receive with you an acceptable conclusion.

With respect to regular clerics, it is the common practice of the Church that they act as archdeacons in dioceses or hold parochial cures. In the case of our aforesaid brother, the chancellor of Noyon, I cannot without grave compunction of heart endure that the sentence of your will should thus condemn him in advance—especially since you received my prayers for him, and I did not deserve to have a recommendation worthy of favour dismissed without favour. Moreover, I announce to you, whatever others may say, that his promotion had the common consent of the canons, and I heard no contradiction raised.

### VIII. The same writer

That he may not hold the election of the bishop of Cambrai valid. (Year 1174.)

[*Acts*, ibid., p. 310.]

[Col. 1367D]

To the reverend Father and lord in Christ, ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, HENRY, styled archbishop of Reims: greeting and sincere obedience.

The dignity of the apostolic office, as it takes precedence over all others, ought likewise to afford to all the gracious assistance of paternal solicitude. The holy sincerity of Your Sublimity knows perfectly well that advancement to ecclesiastical dignity is not praiseworthy when it has violence as its companion, calculating ambition, fraud as its instructor, and simony as its predecessor. By a novel—indeed monstrously deformed—procedure, Robert of Aria enters upon possession of the Church of Cambrai, despite the appeal made to you. He was designated by the imperial mandate; compelled by the prayers and threats of the Count of Flanders; and, having purchased favour, he obtained suffrages solicited as alms. Through the tunnels of a clandestine scheme he burst, proudly and irreverently, into the eminence of the episcopal chair—not called by the Lord as Aaron was, but through the favour of princes and the decision of a reckless multitude. The sacred discernment of Your Exaltedness knows what reverence is due to appeals, how deserving of punishment such presumption is, how strict a censure befits treachery, and what penalties the canons direct against the destroyer of peace and professed partisan of schism. What the sanction of law does not admit, what the decrees of the holy Fathers reject, what the rule of apostolic constitution has already condemned, ought to be foreign to ecclesiastical sincerity.  

[Col. 1368B] Now the eye of the whole community is directed toward you with intent attentiveness and awaits, from the seat of justice, a just judgment without delay: one in which malice finds no unpunished success, nor the proven remedies of appeals are cast back into the trap of contempt. Vindicate the injuries common to all, and let a penalty proportionate to the quality of the offences answer them, so that your honour may remain intact and contempt for our lowliness may not spread to those who follow. The barren and foul woman is rejected by a writ of repudiation; she does not enter into marriage if the violence of a eunuch overpowers a virgin. Let the seed from this wicked bed be exterminated, and let bastard shoots not put down deep roots; but let them be cut away by the hoe of apostolic severity, so that it may deservedly be said of you: “He has done all things well: he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak” (Mark 7).

## VIII bis. On the rebellion of the monks of Saint-Macarius against the Church of Holy Cross at Bordeaux. (1165–1170.)

*[Gallia Christiana Nova*, II, 816, in the text.]

To the most blessed Father and lord ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme and universal pontiff, BERTRAND, unworthy minister of the Church of Bordeaux, greeting and every reverence, with due submission.

[Col. 1368D] It has pleased you, venerable Father, to hold ratified and firm the sentence which our beloved son Bertrand, abbot of Holy Cross, pronounced against the monks of Saint-Macarius on account of disobedience and rebellion. Yet certain of the aforementioned brothers, still persisting in their customary obstinacy and rebellion, scorn to obey your commands and to render to their abbot and to the Church of Holy Cross the obedience and reverence which they owe; nor do they yet fear to endure the sentence of that abbot—ours, but confirmed by your authority. This must therefore be brought to the notice of your holy discernment, so that, should they perhaps come to the feet of Your Holiness, you may know that they remain under the sentence already mentioned. May it please you, Father, to cherish and uphold, as you have begun to do, in its right the Church of Holy Cross, for which we earnestly entreat you.

## IX. Privilege granted by Ferdinand, king of the Spains, to the Roman Church concerning the gift and concession of the castle of Thoraph. (1172.)

*[MURATORI, Antiquitates Italicae*, III, 789.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Among the matters which seem to adorn royal majesty, foremost and principal is the duty of loving and venerating holy and religious places, enriching them with generous gifts, and enlarging them with estates and possessions, so that, by giving earthly things, kings may deserve to obtain eternal things. Therefore I, Ferdinand, by the grace of God king of the Spains, together with [Col. 1369B] my wife Queen Lady Urraca, by this most binding charter of donation, to remain valid forever, donate and give to Saint Peter and to you, our beloved lord Cardinal Hyacinth, legate in Spain, the castle of Thoraph. By my own ring I invest you with it, so that from this day onward you may hold the aforesaid castle, with its meadows, pastures, mountains, springs, streams, mills, trees, villages and mills or waterworks (*azeniae*), fisheries, and with all its rights and appurtenances, together with every royal right. You may possess, sell, give, exchange, and do all that you wish with it. I donate and concede it to you and to the Roman Church, to be held forever by hereditary right, for the remedy of my soul and those of our parents, and for the love and affection which you have always shown toward me.

[Col. 1369C] This was done at Zamora, in the chamber in which the same lord cardinal lay, in the presence of the lady queen, Bobon, brother of the lord cardinal, Raymond of the Chapel of the Holy Roman Church, and the subdeacon Maibard.

If anyone, whether of my family or another, presumes to violate this my voluntary act, may he incur the wrath of almighty God and of blessed Peter the apostle, and be condemned in hell with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord. For his rash attempt he shall pay one hundred pounds of gold to the royal party and to yours, and shall restore fourfold to you or to your representative whatever he has seized; and this document shall remain forever valid.

The charter was made at Zamora, on the seventh day before the Ides of July, in the era 1210 [1172], [Col. 1369D] while Lord King Ferdinand reigned over León, Extremadura, Galicia, and Asturias, in the year in which the most renowned and pious Lord Cardinal Hyacinth, legate of the Apostolic See, came into Spain.

I, Ferdinand, by God’s grace king of the Spains, confirm this document, which I ordered to be made, by my own authority. I, Peter, by God’s grace archbishop of the Church of Compostela, have confirmed. Stephen, bishop of Zamora, have confirmed. Peter, bishop of Salamanca, have confirmed. Adam, bishop of Ourense, have confirmed. John, bishop of Lugo, have confirmed. Peter, bishop of Coria, have confirmed. John, bishop of Mondoñedo, have confirmed. John, bishop of Tui, have confirmed. [Col. 1370A] Dominic, bishop of Ávila, have confirmed. The Count of Urgell, steward of the king, have confirmed. Bernard Rodríguez, lord in Asturias, have confirmed. Count Gómez in Transtámara, have confirmed. Count Peter, have confirmed. Gunter Rodríguez, the king’s standard-bearer, have confirmed. I, Pelagius Gonter, royal notary, Pelagius the archdeacon being chancellor, wrote and confirmed.

## X. Of Ferdinand, king of the Spains.—He accepts the lordship of the pontiff together with his whole kingdom.

*(Ibid.)*

To the most excellent Father and lord, the supreme pontiff [Col. 1370B] ALEXANDER, FERDINAND, by God’s grace king of the Spains, offers due reverence with all devotion of heart.

Both divine and human law prescribe that children obey the commands of their mother and that a mother diligently endeavour to care for her children. But if the mother seems offended without injury from the son, the son ought not offer conciliatory words until the cause of the offence has first been made known. It is dangerous through ignorance to injure what we wish in goodwill to heal. For this reason I neither showed due reverence to your predecessor nor disclosed to him that I was his, as to a father and lord. For I knew that, through no fault of mine or of my father, he was offended with me, detracted from the dignity of my name, and withheld his counsel as from an enemy.

But when I learned that you were my father, through Merion, your faithful friend, and through the bishop of Lugo, intimate to my father and to me, I immediately and graciously accepted your lordship together with my whole kingdom. I believe it will be a defence against my enemies, assistance to my friends, consolation in my difficulties, counsel and help for the governance of my kingdom; for such, joined with a purpose of mercy, is your office. Therefore, through the bearer of this letter, Lord L., bishop of Lugo, to whom I am accustomed to entrust all that is mine as I entrust it to myself, I commit the whole of my cause. I ask and request that you give complete credence to all that he says. May Your Holiness prosper.

## XI. Of Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Chrysogonus.—He enumerates men then eminent in Gaul for learning and virtue. (About 1177.)

*[DUCHESNE, Rerum Francicarum Scriptores*, VI, 560.]

[Col. 1370D] To the most holy Father and lord ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, PETER, by divine condescension alone priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, greeting and obedience as devoted as it is due.

Some time ago we received letters from Your Blessedness directing us to inquire which persons from the kingdom of France, or from those regions, might be promoted to the Roman Church. Certainly, when we had intended to return to the feet of Your Holiness, we wished rather to set forth orally to your discernment the names of those whom we consider worthy and suitable for this than to commend them in written characters. But since—what we cannot say without sorrow—the Lord has recalled to himself many of our fathers, bishops and cardinals, and the Church has been left bereft of their consolation; and since, in accordance with your command, we must remain for some time in those regions to confirm peace between the illustrious kings of France and England and to uproot heretics, we have thought it right to signify to Your Holiness, so that the Church of God under your holy apostolate may grow both in number and in merit, that . . . of Clairvaux, and the prior of Mont-Dieu of the Carthusian order, are learned men and are distinguished for uprightness and religious life. We have learned so much about their life and conduct that, with purity of conscience and without any scruple of doubt, we dare to advise that they should be promoted by you.

[Col. 1371B] Master Baldwin, abbot of Forde, although we have not seen him, is especially commended by the whole Cistercian order for his manifold learning, uprightness, and religious life. Although the venerable man P., abbot of Igny, is not so learned, since nevertheless the Lord frequently deigns to work miracles through him, there can in no way be doubt about his holiness. Furthermore, the abbots of Saint-Remigius at Reims and Saint-Crispin at Soissons are learned and discreet, and among the other abbots of that land and order they are undoubtedly far pre-eminent in uprightness and religious life. We do not think you are unaware of the learning and uprightness of Master Peter the Eater, dean of Troyes. Master Bernard of Pisa, formerly his provost, possesses such learning and has always conducted himself so honourably and praiseworthily in those parts that all bear sufficient testimony on his behalf and judge him most worthy of the highest honours.

[Col. 1371C] Moreover, Master Gerard Puella is discreet and learned, and all who know him bear testimony to his complete integrity, as apostolic discernment has been able to see and hear. Ivo, archdeacon of the Church of Rouen, and Master Herbert Medecius likewise are believed to shine among the rest with no less probity, since they possess knowledge of letters and, we trust, many adornments of virtues leading to the merit of a more perfect life. In addition, in accordance with the command of Your Blessedness, we have received that cask belonging to W., of good memory, formerly bishop of Porto, and have ordered the candlesticks brought to us. We have also notified our venerable brother, the bishop of Poitiers, Albert, the canons of Limoges, and certain others, that if they have anything deposited with them from the goods of that bishop, they are to deliver it to us without delay. If the matter cannot suitably be accomplished through a messenger, we shall go to them ourselves.

[Col. 1371D] When, God willing, we come to the feet of Your Holiness, we shall take care, with God’s help, to bring you the aforementioned cask and candlesticks, together with any other goods of that bishop which we can find; or, if it please you, we shall send them ahead through a trustworthy messenger.

## XII. Instrument by which Adinulf and Landulf, sons of Gregory, renounced every right which they held in the castle of Falbateria, and received it as a fief from Pope Alexander III. (1178.)

*[MURATORI, Antiquitates Italicae*, I, 630.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

In the year of His Incarnation 1178, the nineteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander III, the eleventh indiction, on 11 January, Adinulf and Landulf, sons of Gregory Paganus, not compelled by force nor induced by fraud, but by free judgment and their own will, renounced whatever right they had in the castle of Falbateria, under any title, whether hereditary—namely by succession from father, mother, or others—or acquired; and every right whatsoever of ownership, possession, pledge, or mortgage. They remitted this right to Lord Pope Alexander and to the Roman Church, in the presence of the lords Cardinal John, priest-cardinal of Saint Mark; Cardinal Peter, priest-cardinal of Saint Susanna; Cardinal Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of Santa Maria in Cosmedin; and Cardinal Cencius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian; with Franco, chamberlain of the lord pope, also present.

[Col. 1372C] The lord pope, for himself and his successors, granted the aforesaid brothers the said castle of Falbateria as a fief until twenty-nine years had passed. When that period has elapsed, the castle shall return wholly free to the Church. The aforesaid brothers, or their successors, shall hold that castle at the command of whichever supreme pontiff is then in office, so that it shall be in the supreme pontiff’s power either to grant it to them or to take it away. The aforesaid brothers promised henceforward to possess the same castle in the Church’s name; for this concession they paid the aforesaid lord pope three hundred pounds of Provins currency, and they further promised to render the service which they were accustomed to pay the Roman Church for that castle. They also promised that, if they held any possessions in the territory of Ceprano concerning which they were challenged, they would restore them without dispute if it were clear to them [Col. 1372D] that they held them unjustly; but if this were not clear to them, they would render justice at the command of the lord pope. They confirmed all the foregoing promises by an oath sworn bodily.

Moreover, the same brothers bound themselves, under a penalty of four hundred pounds of Provins currency, to Brother Franco, who lawfully stipulated it, should they fail to observe everything which they had promised. Present were Peter and Fortunatus, doorkeepers of the lord pope; Cencius Gregory; James of Condomi; and Guido Incisor, who were asked to act as witnesses. Then, on the twenty-seventh day of the aforesaid month, Stultus, brother of the aforementioned two, came and, in the presence of the aforesaid Lord Cardinal Cencius, Lord Hugutio, deacon-cardinal of Sant’Angelo, and Brother Franco the chamberlain, renounced, promised, and swore in every respect as his brothers Adinulf and Landulf had done. The castle was granted to him by the lord pope, as it had been to the former two. Present at his oath were Leo of Segni, Peter Gregory, Oddo Benedicti of Bona, Rainald of Pophe, and Peter the Doorkeeper, all of whom were asked to act as witnesses.

[Col. 1373A] And I, Ilditius, judge and scrivener, having been asked, wrote this instrument with my own hand.

## 1159–1181. XIII. Of Guarin, abbot of Saint-Victor.—He cannot send the brothers requested by Cardinal John, and can scarcely send others.

*(D. MARTENE, Amplissima Collectio*, VI, col. 257.)

[Col. 1373B] To the most holy Father and lord ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the universal Church, GUARIN, humble minister of the Church of Saint-Victor at Paris, greeting in the Lord and the most devoted service of complete submission.

Your Sublimity, at the wish, I believe, of Lord John of Naples, commanded my lowliness to assign to him two religious and learned canons to maintain and preserve the canonical order in a church which he had caused to be built for this purpose. He had once already written to my predecessor concerning this, expressly requesting two men whose names he gave, namely Peter of Périgueux and Hugh of Saint-Germain. One of these has died; the other is continually incapacitated by illness. When the lord cardinal learned that one had died, he wrote to me again, requesting by name the survivor and another whom the latter might himself wish to take with him.

[Col. 1373C] But since neither the one, death intervening, nor the other, hindered by the burden of illness, could be sent, while I had in the meantime received your command, I sought the advice of religious and prudent men. They advised that nothing should be done in the matter; indeed, they observed that, since in both letters he had specified by name the men he wanted, he had reserved the choice to himself, wishing to leave nothing in this matter to another’s will or disposition. It would not be safe to send others, lest they prove more burdensome than welcome, if I sent not those whom he sought but others. Finally, those religious men by whose witness to religious life our church was in some measure honoured and by whose counsel it was governed have for the most part now died, and few have arisen after them. For many venerable and learned persons who could have been a benefit and an honour to the Church, although they devoutly sought admission, were rejected—against our wishes—because my predecessor was unwilling or feigned unwillingness.

[Col. 1373D] The house, moreover, is exhausted by disturbances, burdened with debts, stripped of temporal goods, and somewhat impaired in spiritual matters. If, amid so many pressing anxieties, I am compelled to release the few whom I have found able to support me with help and counsel, especially in this new position, since I am young in years and younger still in religious life; and if I lose the eyes which ought to furnish me with the light of counsel and help on the way of religious life and discipline, I shall surely easily go astray and shall not be able alone to bear the burden and care of the house. Yet whatever Your Authority decrees should be done in this matter, I shall carry out to the best of my ability.

Finally, I speak humanly: the brothers greatly fear death, both because of the unfamiliar harshness of the land and because of the unhealthy quality of the air. Moreover, they object that we cannot compel them to go where the rigor of our order is laxly observed. Therefore I consider it most grievous to impose a command which, if carried out, is accepted against their will, and which, if not carried out, is very dangerously refused. Therefore, holy Father and lord, may the moderation of your discernment spare our weakness and the Church’s pressing necessity.

## XIV. Of Eberhard, bishop of Salzburg.—He commends the elect of Aquileia.

*(Works of GRETSER*, VI, 590.)

To ALEXANDER, most holy and most reverend lord and Father, supreme pontiff, EBERHARD, unworthy minister of the Church of Salzburg, offers most devoted service with obedience and prayer.

Certain simple and less learned people are accustomed to be troubled that the Catholic Church is vexed for so long a time by so many and such great disturbances, failing to consider [Col. 1374C] that, as the furnace tests the potter’s vessels, so the trial of tribulation tests righteous persons. The children of God’s Church are not troubled in this way; to them it is said: “A net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures” (Proverbs 1). They indeed know that God chastises every son whom he receives (Hebrews 12), and that those who are outside discipline are strangers to the lot of God’s children. Thus they are filled with great joy because they are found worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus. Yet divine compassion is accustomed to console the faint-hearted even amid blows. Therefore we rightly cry out with the Prophet: “According to the multitude of my sorrows, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Psalm 93). What greater consolation could there be for the Church than to glory in the number and merit of her children, so that it may be said to her in a voice of congratulation: “Those who slandered you have come to you” (Isaiah 60)?

[Col. 1374D] Indeed, day after day we have seen this taking place in the present affair: although the ark of the true Noah is still tossed by the waves of this great sea, the dove nevertheless returns to the ark, for one of this sort finds nowhere outside it to set his foot. Therefore we earnestly commend, insofar as our insignificance dares, our beloved brother, the elect of Aquileia, to Your Holiness; humbly and urgently entreating that his election may be strengthened by your authority. For we truly believe that he has, by divine will, been taken up for this work of ministry. Although, because his planting is still tender, he cannot yet bear ripe fruit, he nevertheless gives good hope in its flower, faithfully and courageously adhering to your footsteps; yet still, with Nicodemus, hearing Jesus in the night of fear because of fear of the Jews.

[Col. 1375A] Under him the uproar of the malicious has altogether subsided, so that those who formerly were against us now seem to be for us. But because all beginnings are timid, we ask Your Holiness that his obedience not be made public until, by the grace of pontifical blessing, you have brought him to mature strength. The bishop of Concordia is also a vigorous fellow-worker in this undertaking and obedience. Concerning ourselves, most holy Father, understand this: we have set our foundation upon the firm Rock, so that neither the winds nor the floods, which do not cease continually to beat against us, shall, with the Lord’s help, be able to overthrow it.

## XV. Of Hugh, abbot of the Church of Blessed Mary of Adrianople, and Peter, prior of the Hospital of Saint John at Constantinople.—What and how much they accomplished among the eastern peoples, during the expedition of Emperor Augustus [Frederick], for the security and dignity of the Roman Church.

*(BONGARS, Gesta Dei per Francos*, p. 1173.)

To A., by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the Roman Church, HUGH, unworthy though he is, abbot of the Church of Blessed Mary at Adrianople, and PETER, prior of the Hospital of Saint John at Constantinople, offer obedience and the service [Col. 1375C] of obedience.

Since not only the fame of Your Holiness, but indeed the co-operating grace of Christ, compels all worshippers of the holy faith both rightly to venerate you as father and in all things to obey your commands, we too, stirred by the love of due submission and by the fragrance of your good renown, labour in remote regions among strangers for the Church’s stability and the honour of your dignity: lest the present pestilence infect the Church, or the Church, wavering in our time, stumble, or reverence for your dignity among eastern peoples be brought to nothing. Let Your Holiness therefore know that we have arrived at Saint-Gilles, after continuous and innumerable dangers both by land and sea during six months—from the beginning of January to the beginning of July—on the expedition of our holy and ever august lord emperor and on the legation of Your Dignity.

[Col. 1375D] But worn down by bodily exhaustion and the onset of diverse adversities, we are unable to undertake the journey of a longer route without failure of our strength. We therefore urgently entreat Your Holiness, in compassion for the sickness caused by our labour, to inform us what and how we are to act. For we have certain matters suitable to be told to your person and directed toward usefulness, which it is not permitted to reveal to anyone but Your Holiness and the most noble king of France. Farewell.

## XVI. Of Louis, king of the Franks.—Against heretics commonly called Poplicans, wandering through the regions of Flanders.

*(D. MARLOT, Metropolis Remensis*, II, 396.)

[Col. 1376A] To the most holy Father and lord ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, LOUIS, by the same grace king of the Franks, greeting and due reverence.

My brother H., archbishop of Reims, recently travelled into the land of Flanders and there found depraved people, followers of a most evil error, fallen into the heresy of the Manichaeans. They are commonly called Poplicans.

> **Note:** [Col. 1375] The Chronicle of Auxerre speaks of these Poplicans under the year 1198.

Through certain observances which they practise, they appear better than they are; and, should they perhaps prosper, there will be great damage to [Col. 1376B] our faith, especially in those regions, where iniquity has sprung up and struck deeper roots. If the archbishop had merely been willing to spare these wicked persons and tolerate this depravity, he would have received a great sum of money for such a redemption—namely, six hundred marks of silver. Since no refuge was open to them with him, they appealed to your hearing. But may your wisdom examine this matter, so poisonous and so destructive, with closer attention, and may you will that so great a pestilence be uprooted rather than allowed to grow. We therefore earnestly pray, for the honour of the Christian faith, that, with the advice of the archbishop, your most beloved son, you allow the matter to proceed, namely that those who rise up against God may be destroyed, etc.

## XVII. Of the same.—In the case of Saint Thomas of Canterbury.

[Col. 1376C] Your Fatherhood has often deigned to ask us concerning the archbishop of Canterbury. If, prompted by regard for divine mercy, we fulfil the prayers of your authority more abundantly, our conscience thereby glories in the Lord. But most recently a report, widely and publicly spread through our kingdom, has caused scandal. It is not for us to rebuke you, who are lord; yet we cannot at all remain silent about matters which we believe injure your reputation. The king of England, being desirous of empty glory, in the conference which we held together displayed, as is said, your open letters to his own party in a boastful and highly vaunting fashion. In them your authority suspended the mouth and hand of the lord of Canterbury against [Col. 1376D] the aforesaid king, his whole kingdom, and persons of that kingdom, until he had fully obtained the king’s favour.

We have no ready answer to the allegations of the opposing party—namely the emperor and the schismatics, who taunt us because we have not ceased and do not cease to support your cause—nor is it within our capacity to devise one, unless your subtle discernment instructs us in responding. We urge you to remember more firmly that in the prayers which we have often humbly offered you we neither mingled threats nor presumed to distrust you. What these things may mean you can readily understand, and the experience of your discernment has more fully recognized how to interpret them completely. Two men stand at your side, upon whom the blame for this matter is laid. But whatever we may do, it does not befit your exaltedness and discernment to depart in any degree from what you know, through their evil persuasion.

## XVIII. Of the same.—He commends Saint Thomas of Canterbury.

You may recall that Your Holiness asked us concerning the lord of Canterbury and gave thanks. Know that, had it not remained with him, we were prepared to bestow, and would gladly have bestowed, greater honour and kindness upon the old man; and our disposition toward him has not yet in any way diminished. Since we have received your prayers on his behalf, we more earnestly entreat your holy Fatherhood to keep in your heart his tribulation and oppression, which he endures for the Roman Church, of which he is a most faithful servant, and for your person, to whom he is most devoted. He has informed us how far your favour has attended his messengers, and for this we render abundant thanks to the mercy of Your Exaltedness. Bound to the archbishop, your most loving son, by a great bond of goodwill, we write little to you for his sake; yet we understand that, for a wise person, much has been said in few words.

## XIX. Of the same.—He reports that Thomas, while in exile, was honourably received by him.

[Col. 1377C] We hold firmly and recall that you entrusted to us the lord of Canterbury, a proved man enduring exile for the Church of God; and we hold him as one commended by you. We do not benefit him as much as we wish, but gladly and from a devoted heart we honour him. We also recall that, at your departure, we commended him to you and urgently entreated you with many prayers to support him and to look mercifully upon him as your exile. But, as is said, your solicitude has set aside both our commendation and his exile.

Know, however, that we should bear with an exceedingly troubled mind the things said to have been done, as is proclaimed in Normandy, England, and even France, unless your sincerity should strive to remedy them. Know also that many are scandalized and do not hesitate to blame and criticize your Fatherhood for what is said to have occurred. We ourselves, greatly indignant, are astonished, and shall be still more astonished unless your integrity proves false the things that are said. Both for the long calamity of his person and for the removal of this reproach, it would be fitting for you and the Curia soon to do something further in this matter, by fresh and resolute counsel. To speak at greater length and to instruct your wisdom would be imputed to us as presumption, since a wise person has enough said to him in few words.

## XX. Of the same.—On the murder of Saint Thomas.

[Col. 1378A] To ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, LOUIS, by the same grace king of the Franks, greeting and due reverence.

A son departs from the law of human affection when he casts down his mother; nor does he remember the Creator’s benefit when he does not grieve at dishonour done to holy Church. Therefore this is especially to be lamented, and the unprecedented novelty of the cruelty renews the pain: for malice, rising against God’s saint, has plunged a sword into the apple of Christ’s eye and has slaughtered the lamp of the Church of Canterbury—not so much cruelly as shamefully. Let a singular kind of justice be aroused; let Peter’s sword be unsheathed to avenge the martyr of Canterbury, because his blood cries out to the universal [Col. 1378B] Church, demanding vengeance not so much for itself as for the whole Church. And behold: at the tomb of the champion, as has been revealed to us, divine grace is manifested in miracles, and it is divinely shown where his humanity rests, he who fought for that Name. The bearers of this letter, bereaved of their father, will relate the course of events to Your Piety. Give your most gracious ear to the testimony of truth, and believe them, in this matter and in others, as you would believe us.

## XXI. Of the same.—He exhorts the pontiff to cut away vices by his authority.

If it is the Lord’s good pleasure in His people to exalt the meek unto salvation, we believe that the time and hour are at hand [Col. 1378C] when judgment shall come upon the world and the prince of this world shall be cast out (John 12). We waited to see this day; we have seen it and rejoiced. Would that, as the day has breathed forth, so the shadows might also decline (Song of Songs 2), and that the darkness of crimes and the mist of sins which has hitherto covered the whole earth might pass away. We see, and rejoice, that peace has been restored to you; may we also see good days restored through you, in which justice and peace may be joined to one another by the intervening kiss of charity.

Those very days are bounded by the happy issues of your life, through which, by a new and welcome miracle, a longer span of years has been granted to one already advanced in age, so that a fuller tally of merits may arise for you. Nor indeed is it to be believed without cause [Col. 1378D] that the immortal King has granted this gift to His holy Church in your person for this purpose: that, as you surpass your predecessors in length of days, so you may surpass them in the blessedness of eternal ages. Surely that heavenly governor and judge of our mortality has, as we trust, preserved you for this day in order that, in an acceptable time, you may judge righteously, make crooked things straight and rough things into level paths; that you may restore Jerusalem as in ancient days, making her deserts like the garden of the Lord and her wilderness like delights.

Until now the earth mourned and languished; Lebanon was ashamed and withered. But behold, the mildness of spring is being poured forth, and shoots of good hope revive from the bosom of the earth. For the hearts of mortals have been shaken and softened by fear of your judgments [Col. 1379A], so that the clod of a breast hitherto barren, now covered with flowering turf, may burst forth into the fruit of a better life. Behold, the vines are already in flower; already the flowers are bearing fruit. Only let there be one who will catch the little foxes and ensnare every venomous creeping thing in the cunning of its malice. And lest the occasion of the accustomed storm should hinder this: behold, winter has passed, the rain is gone and departed, the time of pruning has come (Song of Songs 2).

Therefore, Lord, let the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts be pruned, let it be pruned and dug about, so that, under the fruitful hoe, it may abound for more ample uses, while it bears no barren branches. The Lord your God has rendered this vineyard peaceful to you. Henceforth it will be your work and labour to restore it to Him clean and fruitful: let the mountains drip sweetness upon it [Col. 1379B] and the hills delight; and, while heaven gives rain, let it also bring forth its fruits. Do you likewise give to your voice a voice of power, that all may hear and understand that the Lord has set you as a light to the nations, that you may be His salvation unto the ends of the earth.

For the power to act stands ready for your pious purpose, to which so great an authority for holy action is granted. And, to comprise much in few words: the power to restore the condition of the Church lies before you; only be willing, and all things are safe. It is near to the point that she herself may cry to you: “Only speak the word, and my servant shall be healed” (Matthew 8). For who does not believe your report? Who does not obey your word? Who does not submit to your command? And if anyone should presume, through his own malice, to resist, let the exaltations of God sound in your throat, and let two-edged swords be taken in hand, to execute vengeance among the nations and punishments among the peoples; to bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron manacles (Psalm 149).

Whatever has hitherto sprung up in the Church of God concerning ecclesiastical institutions has been the result of the times’ impossibility and malice; henceforth, if through your neglect that should perish which the good of all expects, it must in every respect be charged to you. Act therefore, act, so that at last holy Church may gain in unity what she lost in schism, and that the integrity of our actions may repair the losses of preceding times. Until now all things have been permitted to everyone, and the dissolution [Col. 1379D] of life sufficiently shows how much the severity of discipline has been enfeebled.

For our bishops indeed preside, but few are of service; with some, matters go well if they do no harm. For uses—or rather abuses—wholly superfluous, they multiply horses and chariots, so that wherever they arrive, they throw everything into confusion through expense and extravagance. These are not the chariots of Amminadib; this is not the heavenly army of horsemen. Let them beware lest theirs rather be the likeness of the chariots which the Almighty overwhelmed amid the waves, when He cast horse and rider into the sea (Exodus 15). They do not judge the orphan, nor does the widow’s cause come before them. With some of them, indeed, the mere valuation of a gift outweighs equity in the balance.

When a bishop is announced as about to come to some estate or monastery [Col. 1380A], you would suppose that a king, not a bishop, were proceeding forth: so great is the army of horses, so great the troop of attendants, so great the crowd of serving-boys going before. Then the scanty sustenance of the Church is exhausted upon sumptuous suppers for diners, and the food of the poor is transferred to the luxuries of banqueters. Oh, if only there were someone to break through the wall, so that a ray of light might be cast within—someone who would bring the works of darkness to judgment and exact vengeance upon the shadow of death.

Moreover, for correcting all these things, a door is opened to you in the Lord, so that, once every obstacle of difficulty has been removed, the apostolic word may run swiftly—a word which Zion may hear and rejoice in, and at whose judgments the daughters of Judah may exult. Therefore, just as the Lord has magnified His dealings with us, and with the other Catholic kings and orthodox princes [Col. 1380B], to whom in your exaltation He has granted the triumph they desired, so must He Himself be honoured in your works, that we may undertake a celebrated rejoicing over the cleansing of the common order. Certainly the disease of the Church which we have lamented grows and advances into a lasting sickness unless it receives healing in this council.

### XXII. To A. . . , Queen of the Franks, concerning the perjury of John of Oxford; she commends Thomas of Canterbury.

To the most holy lord and dearest Father, ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, his humble and devoted daughter A. . . . . , Queen of the Franks: greeting, and devoted service with sincerity of heart.

I shall speak to you as to a father and lord, whose honour [Col. 1380C] my lord the king, I, and our whole kingdom desire as our own, because your honour is ours, and your disgrace—may God avert it—is ours. Having received you as father and lord, amid the surrounding fury of kings who seek your life, we have for God’s sake and yours despised their enmities. Hear then, if it please you, your daughter; and in what I am about to say, do not despise the female sex, but consider the affection of one who loves.

Last year John of Oxford caused a most grievous scandal in the Gallican Church, he who by his perjury so easily triumphed over the Roman Church. The cardinals followed him, whose good works have not yet been heard of in our land—and would that their evil deeds were covered in silence. Hence scandals have been multiplied. Now, however, through his latest messengers, the King of England has obtained letters patent—if indeed they are not forged—by which you decreed that the Archbishop of Canterbury, who has now been an exile for justice’s sake for four years, could not pronounce sentence against him or his land, nor impose a burden upon any person from his land, until he should be restored to the king’s favour.

Do not these letters, Father, seem to give him authority to sin with impunity and to proscribe the archbishop forever? For henceforth it will lie within his discretion whether to receive him into favour or not. By this the whole Church among us has been so scandalized that it could not be more disturbed, because an evil example has been given to all princes. [Col. 1381A] My lord the king, to whom you entrusted the archbishop, is greatly troubled that, if you persist in this judgment, an innocent man is slaughtered in his hands. The whole kingdom grieves that our enemies prevail with you. My lord the king still awaits the fulfillment of your promise; unless he sees it fulfilled more quickly, he—and his descendants—will learn what he ought to hope from the Roman Church. Farewell, dearest and most holy Father; and, if it please you, assist the Archbishop of Canterbury.

### XXIII. Of Blessed Peter, surnamed Monoculus, eighth Abbot of Clairvaux.—He complains that secular persons harass the Cistercian Order with lawsuits, plundering of goods, and the like, and implores the pontiff’s assistance against these evils.

[Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium, III, 264.]

[Col. 1381B]

The evil of the day increases and the perils of the times grow strong, so that we feel those last days to be at hand which the Apostle foretold (2 Timothy 3), in which, as iniquity abounds, the charity of many grows cold (Matthew 24). But especially against your sons who profess the Cistercian Order does the sea of this world advance and swell; dashing itself against the barrier of your protection, it rises against us in a full tempest. In a manner it roars and murmurs around the bars and doors which you have set, indignant, that is, at its being told: “Thus far shall you come, and no farther; here you shall break your swelling waves” (Job 31 [probably 38:11]).

For behold, the children of this world, whom Truth Himself declares more prudent in their generation than the children of light (Luke 16), envy us the very fact that we live, because their perversity will not allow us to possess the means by which we live.
