Seeing, indeed, that the Lord has blessed the work of our hands, they rage with every malice against the provision for our pilgrimage [Col. 1381C], devising in every way how they may seize the little substance of the poor, either by false accusation or by robbery. They renew lawsuits and intensify disputes; and if they cannot prevail to take our goods otherwise, they resort to the devices of that fraud whereby they sometimes demand back from us their own money, or that of their people, by a wholly malicious and fabricated action for a loan or deposit.

Then, when the suit has been instituted before the judge, testimony against us—purchasable indeed, but not pardonable—is produced; and on every side the sincerity of truth is weakened, shaken by the perjuries of wicked witnesses. If you overlook and endure this hereafter, then “not unto us, O Lord, not unto us” (Psalm 113 [Vulgate numbering]), but for buffoons and gluttons do we labour. It remains only that, in despoiling our meagre resources, all who do not fear to take the name of their God in vain may not run in vain.

Therefore come to our aid, most blessed Father, and apply a remedy while the disease is still fresh, lest dogs eat the bread of the children and the luxury and drunkenness of revellers claim for themselves the wages of the poor. Otherwise, why are we “put to death all the day long”? Why do our brethren, amid very many labours, more abundant heats, and excessive cold, wrest from the deepest bowels of the dug-up earth [Col. 1382A] a slender support for an anxious life? We pray, therefore, that the tenor of the ancient custom may be restored to us by your privilege: namely, that if anyone should demand from any of our monasteries a thing improper or doubtful, the abbot of the place, questioned concerning the truth of the matter at peril to his own conscience, and a monk or lay brother, commanded by the force of obedience, may state the case; and that upon their word of truth the decision of the doubtful cause may stand.

If you do this, you preserve our rights for us without injury to others. But if this course perhaps does not please you, devise some other remedy, whatever it may be, which, by removing perjury from the greed of the wicked, may cause the loss caused us by undue payment to cease.

### XXIV. Of the same [writer].—He gives thanks to the pontiff for benefits conferred, especially upon the monastery of Balernes, a daughter-house of Clairvaux, and desires that its lawsuit already begun against wrongdoers may quickly be concluded.

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1382B]

What are we to do, gracious Father? For neither our strength nor our merits suffice to render you thanks such as your lavish beneficence toward the Order requires. Your magnificence has been confirmed among us; it has been strengthened over us, and we cannot attain to it, since the abundance of blessing and gift is so great that the insufficiency of our poverty vainly raises itself to make recompense. Therefore, turning back to God in humble supplication, we unceasingly ask Him to repay you the reward of your pious deed—He who granted you the disposition of mercy—and to multiply in this head of the Church the ointments of heavenly grace [Col. 1382C], that they may flow down even to the hem of His garment as an unceasing river of inexhaustible consolation.

At present, therefore, lying at your feet, we offer these very small thanks on behalf of the monastery of Balernes: because you restored its justice to it as though free after returning from captivity, when it had been held captive under the unjust lot of plunderers; and you brought it back from the sea of a two-sided contest to the harbour of its former peace. But its adversary, terrified by failure to furnish the proof required of him, has not returned the page of your rescript. That rescript was supported by this provision: if he failed in asserting a prescription of forty years, possession should remain restored to the brethren of Balernes, and the mouth of the accuser and perpetual adversary should be silenced by the bars of perpetual silence.

He has not returned it, then—he has not returned it—waiting, as is said, for the end of your life, so that he may then devise anew a fresh origin for his dead cause. Merciful Jesus, how great is the craftiness which moves in fearful consciences under trembling deliberation! He suspects that justice will die for him unless the bishop of justice dies; and, foreseeing a shadowy advantage from the darkening of falsehood, he awaits the setting of the public light. Therefore, that iniquity may lie to itself, we ask, with the honour due in our greeting, that unless within a fixed term he produces the right which he claims, he may be restrained by the bar of the silence already promulgated; so that, while he suspends the fate of so great a Father upon the pretext of justice which he seeks to profit from by the events of death [Col. 1383A], his own injustice may instead die beneath the blade of your living sentence.

### XXV. The community of Clairvaux.—The community entreats the pontiff not to deprive it of its abbot Henry, who was being sought for the bishopric of Toulouse.

We are guided by the example of Christ’s disciples (Matthew 8): when the storm rises upon the sea of this world and we are terrified, we flee from the waves to heavenly aid, knock with prayers at the vicar of the Saviour asleep in the stern, and awaken him with cries. For we trust that the little ship of Clairvaux, which from long ago has had you as its pilot in every tempest, though struck by surging blows, is not shaken so long as it is guided amid the stormy whirlwinds of this sea by such a great and such a pilot.

And, that you may know the full measure of our confidence in you, we shall not fear shipwreck, with you presiding, amid any commotion; for, if you command it, the spirit of the storms shall stand still. But now, most blessed Father, the crash of a sudden whirlwind has roared forth, and a storm bursting from afar has brought us dread of an imminent disturbance. For the Church of Toulouse, deprived of its own shepherd and the rival of our peace, has irreverently cast its eyes upon our abbot [Col. 1383B], as though it did not suppose that it could rise from its own ruin unless meanwhile it contrived the destruction of our condition. It seeks and strives to repair its own loss from our calamity, without observing or considering how perversely it opposes the divine ordinances if it enriches Egyptians with the spoils of Hebrews.

But we, whose concern it is to weigh the loss entailed by this change, prostrate ourselves at your feet in sorrowful devotion, unanimously entreating with poured-out tears that, against the urgency of this tempest, the tranquillity of your consolation may smile upon us; that you may admit no plan for changing our Father which the calamity of his children would later lament. For you know—and we ourselves have learned by experience—that in changes of superiors, discipline, however firm, is relaxed; and when changes of shepherds are more frequently allowed, the integrity of the flock is commonly scattered.

### XXVI. Of Henry, King of England.—He congratulates the pope-elect and asks that the latter receive him as his own spiritual son.

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1383D]

To his dearest lord and Father, ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, HENRY, King of England and Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine and Count of Anjou: greeting and the due submission in Christ.

Your discretion knows well how faithful my predecessors always were to the holy Roman Church. In a similar case they showed this more than once, when, a schism arising in the holy Church as sins required, they followed Catholic unity. Approving and following, therefore, this devotion of my fathers, because I believe your election to be supported by truth [Col. 1384A], I have received you, through your legates, as Father and lord, as supreme pontiff and Catholic pope, together with all clergy and people entrusted by God to my authority, with due solemnity and reverence.

I therefore ask you most mercifully and beseech you with all humility to receive me as your own spiritual son and, if it please you, to hear me in my petitions. Kindly receive the bearer of this letter, Brother R., in whose mouth I have placed my affairs to be explained to you more fully; and grant assent and effect to the matters which he shall speak to you on my behalf. I am ready to comply with your will, and I place myself and what is mine entirely at your disposal, to be disposed of according to your judgment.

Witness the chancellor, at Rouen.

### XXVII. Of the same [writer].—He requests relaxation of the sentence of excommunication pronounced by the Archbishop of Canterbury against certain persons.

[Col. 1384B]

To the venerable Father and supreme pontiff ALEXANDER, HENRY, King of England, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou: greeting and due reverence.

If, Father, you seek proof of my devotion to your holiness and do not perhaps remember what I faithfully did at the beginning of your promotion in honour of you, I pray that you may at least keep before your eyes what I recently carried out in fulfillment of your command, and may fully recognize, if it please you, my devotion toward you by consideration of that act of mine. For an enemy most hostile to me, wholly ready with all his power for the destruction of myself and mine—God forbid!—ever lying in wait for me in order to contrive evil against me, a man with whom to live, as the present event shows, is death to me, and with whom to dwell in the kingdom is disgrace: him, at your command, wholly prostrating myself at your feet, I received in peace, and I took careful measures to provide him an escort from my side, that he might be conducted peacefully to his own possessions.

That peace was fully granted not only to him but also to his followers. Men who for a long time have not ceased, so to speak, to tear my flesh with bitter bites, who have filled the world in their wanderings with sinister rumours against me [Col. 1384D], I received peacefully into my kingdom, carefully providing that they should not be harmed by those whom they had harmed, nor suffer any hardship at all from those whom they had offended. It was therefore fitting, Father, that your holiness should also have provided for me, lest evil be returned to me for good; lest, at the arrival of one to whom I had given peace and whom I had received in peace, the peace of my kingdom should immediately be disturbed, and the Church of the realm, which had deserved no such thing, should be oppressed without a hearing by so heavy a burden on his false suggestions that some have been subjected to suspension and others to anathema, although, if they are given the opportunity of defense, they are ready, with the Lord’s help, to prove in every respect that they have deserved nothing of the sort.

Therefore I devotedly beseech your holiness that, if there are or can be any remnants of your former affection toward me [Col. 1385A], you may relax the sentence imposed upon persons of my kingdom out of regard for justice and for my petition; and that, if anyone raises a complaint against them concerning any matter, you may examine the case either yourselves or through persons acceptable to your discretion, so that each may answer for himself in law and undergo the judicial penalty which he is proved to have deserved. You would not deny this to another. If it is denied to me, I shall say—though with sorrow—that you repel me with excessive severity and regard me as cast off.

I have entrusted the remaining matters to be made known to you by the bearer of this letter, Master David, whom favour commends to me; if, in compassion for me, you hear him, you will be able to preserve for God both my body and my soul, which I now fear is in danger. May your holiness, Father, prosper and show itself gracious toward its own.

### XXVIII. Of the same [writer].—Concerning the free election granted by him to the English Church. He commends the Bishop-elect of Bath.

The lord king to the lord pope.

The Roman Church knows from the long course of time how great a liberty our predecessors possessed concerning appointments to churches. With God in view and through the intervention of your prayers, following the admonitions of the venerable men Albert and Theodwin, legates of your holiness, we have tempered that liberty to the equity of canonical moderation. At present, therefore, we grant free election to the English Church [Col. 1385C], so that she, who more than we could wish has languished desolate of shepherds through various obstacles, may breathe again under the fuller grace of our liberality, liberty having been bestowed upon her.

When, therefore, the election of the Church of Bath was reported to us, having taken counsel with our bishops and learned that the manner and order of the canonical election had been observed, we thought it worthy to commend to your discretion the person elected, conspicuous for uprightness of character and learning. And although, from your long acquaintance with him, he is especially known to you, and has proved trustworthy with us through the manifold testimony of your holiness, nevertheless we beseech you with all the urgency we can command that you may hold him to be such as you have often declared him to us to be [Col. 1385D]. Let your holiness therefore take care lest envy of our name prevent the completion rightly due to what has hitherto proceeded with such sincerity.

### XXIX. Of the same [writer].—He reports that, out of regard for the pontiff, he has restored peace and his affection to the Archbishop of Canterbury; he complains that Vivian and Gratian, legates of the Apostolic See, did not abide by their promises concerning the removal of excommunication, “alleging that expression by which we had said that the dignity of our kingdom must remain unimpaired.”

To Pope ALEXANDER, HENRY, King of England.

We sent our bishops as envoys to the feet of your fatherhood, asking and beseeching you to put a due end, with justice as mediator, to the disputes between us and the Archbishop of Canterbury. [Col. 1386A] At length your kindness was pleased, in accordance with our request, to send us legates from your side with fullness of power, so that they might fully decide and settle all our controversies, the obstacle of appeal being removed. Although they had been sent with this power—as our envoys reported to us and as was expressly contained in your letters, which we still have in our possession—when they arrived among us, as we learned through those same legates, that power was withdrawn from them to our injury.

Accordingly, when we offered ourselves before them for every form of justice, the aforesaid Archbishop of Canterbury, who behaves toward me as unjustly and maliciously as is known to you and to the whole world, utterly scorned to submit to justice before them. Because of his failure, we subsequently sent other envoys to your majesty, through whom we received your letters, which we still have in our possession, in which you exempted our land and persons of the kingdom from the power of the aforesaid Archbishop of Canterbury until he should return to our favour.

But before our favour had been restored to him, you altered this—for a reason unknown to us—while our other envoys still remained at your court and before your latest legates arrived among us. Vivian and Gratian then pronounced a sentence of excommunication against persons of our kingdom and against certain of our household and servants, who attended us every day. When we had received the aforementioned envoys with due honour, they declared both by your letters and orally [Col. 1386C] that they had come for our honour and the exaltation of our kingdom. First, we dealt with the absolution of those excommunicated, who appeared to have been excommunicated not only to our injury but also to yours and to that of the legates themselves. To the requests which they laid before us on your behalf, we yielded, so far as we were able, with pious assent, out of reverence and love for you.

For your letters proposed that we should restore to the aforesaid Archbishop of Canterbury his bishopric, peace, and our affection. We, setting aside all concern for our own honour, after taking counsel with the Archbishops of Bordeaux and Rouen; the Bishops of Le Mans, Rennes, Bayeux, Lisieux, Coutances, and Sées; the Abbots of Fécamp, Bec, Saint-Wandrille, Caen, Troarn, Cerisy, Rievaulx, Mortemer, Tironneau, Bellême, and certain others; as well as Geoffrey of Auxerre and certain other religious men, granted to the aforesaid Archbishop of Canterbury—although, as we have often informed you, he left our kingdom without our knowledge and without any compulsion—that he might return in goodwill and peace and possess all his possessions as he possessed them when he departed from the kingdom, both he and all who had departed with or because of him, for the honour of God and love of you, while the dignity of our kingdom remained intact.

When your envoys received this answer before the men mentioned above [Col. 1387A], without any objection, they absolved those excommunicated persons who were present. It was then agreed between us that one of them, namely Vivian, should cross the sea to absolve those excommunicated persons who were in England, while Gratian should return to convey these terms to the oft-mentioned Archbishop of Canterbury. But next morning, when we had withdrawn from them, after first obtaining their leave because certain business called us away, they refused—at whose prompting or by what spirit we do not know—to abide by what had been granted, alleging that expression by which we had said that the dignity of our kingdom must remain unimpaired. It seemed to us and to those present with us that they had no legal right to make that allegation.

We have thought it right to refer the course of this affair to your conscience, always trusting in your discretion that you do not wish in any respect to derogate from our honour or the dignity of our kingdom. We earnestly beseech your serenity, therefore, to consider attentively the honour and benefit which we have conferred upon you and your court, and which we shall confer in the future unless it is prevented by you; and to settle the matter so that the malicious flatteries of that faithless traitor of ours may not prevail with you as greatly as the merits of our case, supported by the evident testimony of so many and such great men. In accordance with our request, absolve those who have been excommunicated, and ensure that he cannot pour the poison of his excommunication upon us and others. Otherwise, if we are insufficiently heard in this just petition [Col. 1387C], as though despairing of your goodwill, we may be compelled to provide otherwise for our safety and honour.

And because the individual matters said and proposed by us could scarcely be contained in writing, we send to the feet of your fatherhood our clerks and household officers, Reginald, Archdeacon of Salisbury, and Richard Barre, who will explain to you more fully everything debated on both sides. Give them unquestioning credence in all matters which they shall present to your holiness on our behalf. We pray and earnestly advise that your discretion provide for their return to be speedily arranged, because a longer delay on their part could bring intolerable danger and damage to the Church.

### XXX. Of the same [writer].—He complains that the Bishops of London and Salisbury, after an appeal had been made to the pontiff, were newly bound by a sentence of excommunication by the Archbishop of Canterbury.

[Col. 1387D]

To Pope ALEXANDER, HENRY, King of England: every service of due submission.

Your serenity knows well enough how great a distress afflicts me and my land, and with how many wrongs that Thomas of Canterbury, my adversary, has vexed me, although, as conscience bears witness, I have deserved nothing and done nothing worthy of so violent and injurious an outrage. For I do not believe that it has escaped your memory that I obtained from your fatherhood cardinal judges of the holy Roman Church to hear this cause; but it pleased your holiness that my adversary should be exempted from their jurisdiction, and the sincerity of innocence, impeded by your command, could not come into the clarity of light.

Moreover, I have often—indeed always—been ready, in the face of the Church, to stand by law and judgment. If I had sinned even in the least, which I do not recall having done, I was always prepared to make satisfaction as reason might dictate, and to do for the Church of Canterbury much more than my predecessors, who were greater than I, had done. Accordingly, I cannot sufficiently wonder that your prudence permits a son devoted to the Roman Church and ever most ready to submit to law to be oppressed, as it seems to me, against every justice and harassed by unreasonable and injurious outrages.

Now he who does not cease to afflict an innocent man has added a new injury to countless preceding ones. Supported, as he asserts, by your authority, he has newly bound by a sentence of excommunication the Bishops of London and Salisbury [Col. 1388B], devoted and faithful sons of the Roman Church, who, after appealing to you, were ready in every way to obey the law: men neither cited, summoned, convicted, nor in any way warned. He also threatens certain members of my household with the severity of anathema, having no reasonable cause against them. I bear this no less grievously than if the sentence had been pronounced against my own person. Your prudence, I do not think, can be unaware how intolerable this is to me and how much injury it inflicts upon my reputation and yours.

Indeed, it appears that your fatherhood has cast me aside as though abandoned, since it neither attends to nor cares for the injuries of its son, but, to increase my disgrace and humiliation, permits a shameful enemy to rage against me; nor does the moderation of paternal correction restrain the violence of wrongs. I therefore humbly beseech and adjure your eminence, as is just, to show by the performance of deeds the affection which you owe your son; and to deign, without delay, to redress the injury inflicted without judicial procedure upon me, my people, and my land.

With every devotion I also most earnestly beseech that whatever the aforesaid Thomas, my adversary, has decreed against the order of law, after the appeal made to you, against persons in my kingdom, clerical or lay, you may regard as null and void. Witness G., Bishop of Bazas, at Saint-Macaire in Gascony.

### XXXI. Of the same [writer].—He announces the death of Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. (Year 1171.)

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, from the manuscript of Saint-Michel-au-Péril-de-la-Mer.]

To ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, H., King of the English and Duke of the Normans and Aquitanians and Count of the Angevins: greeting and due devotion.

Out of reverence for the Roman Church and love for you—which, God bears witness, I have faithfully sought and steadfastly maintained until now—I granted Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, peace and full restoration of his possessions according to the terms of your command, and permitted him to cross to England with a proper escort. Yet at his arrival he brought not the joy of peace but fire and sword, since he raised against me a question concerning the kingdom and crown. Furthermore, he began everywhere, without cause, to excommunicate my servants.

Therefore, men unable to endure such insolence—those excommunicated and others from England—fell upon him and, what I cannot say without grief, killed him. Since I fear that the anger which I had long conceived against him furnished the cause of this crime, I testify before God that I am deeply troubled. And because in this deed I fear more for my reputation than for my conscience, I ask your serenity to support me at this critical point with the medicine of sound counsel.

### XXXII. Of the same [writer].—He complains of the rebellion of Henry and his other sons against him, and implores the pope’s aid.

To his most holy lord ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the Catholic Church, H., King of England, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, Count of Anjou and Maine: greeting and the service of devoted submission.

In the straits of great dangers, when domestic counsels find no remedy, the aid of those is sought whose prudence, in weightier affairs, long experience has approved. [Col. 1389C] The wickedness of my sons has been spread far and wide: the spirit of iniquity has armed them for their father’s exile so completely that they count it glory and triumph to pursue their father and to renounce all filial affection, my own sins having gone before them. Where the Lord had granted me fuller delight, there He chastises me more grievously; and—what I cannot say without tears—I am compelled to conceive deadly hatred against my own blood and flesh, and to seek heirs outside my family, lest I see one of my seed sitting upon my throne. Nor can I pass over in silence that my friends have withdrawn from me and those of my household seek my life. For a secret conspiracy has so poisoned the minds of my retainers [Col. 1389D] that they set everything aside for the observance of a treacherous plot. For deserters and beggars would rather attach themselves to my sons against me than reign with me and shine in the highest dignities.

Since, therefore, God has raised you to the eminence of the pastoral office, to give the knowledge of salvation to His people (Luke 1), though absent in body yet present in spirit, I cast myself at your knees, seeking wholesome counsel. The kingdom of England lies within your jurisdiction; and, so far as the obligation of feudal right is concerned, I am bound to you alone. Let England learn [Col. 1390A] what the Roman pontiff can accomplish; and, since he does not employ material weapons, let him defend the patrimony of Blessed Peter with the spiritual sword. I could repel the insult of my sons with rebel arms, but I cannot put off being their father; for, as Jeremiah testifies: “The sea-monsters have bared their breasts; they have suckled their young” (Lam. 4). And although their errors have made me almost mad with rage, I retain paternal feelings, and natural condition imposes upon me a certain compulsion to love them. Would that they were wise, understood, and foresaw their latter end (Deut. 32). Domestic enemies nurse my sons; and, having found an occasion for malice, they do not cease until their strength is reduced to dust and, head turned into tail, their servants rule over them, according to that saying [Col. 1390B] of Solomon: “A prudent servant shall rule over a foolish son” (Prov. 17). Let the spirit of counsel, therefore, awaken your prudence, and turn the hearts of the sons toward their father. For the father’s heart shall, at your good pleasure, turn toward his sons; and, in faith in Him through whom kings reign (Prov. 8), I promise your greatness that I shall obey you and your direction in all things. May Christ long preserve you, Holy Father, unharmed for His Church.

### XXXIII. Robert, Count of Leicester, to the Supreme Pontiff.—He seeks his protection for the monastery of Lyre.

(MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 477.)

To his most reverend lord and Father A., by the grace of God supreme pontiff, R., Count of Leicester, the humble [Col. 1390C] son of his holiness, greeting and blessing.

[Note: [Col. 1389D] Adrian, Anastasius, or Alexander, who successively occupied the apostolic see after the year 1153. We nevertheless believe the letter to have been addressed to Alexander.]

[Note: [Col. 1390D] Robert, son of Robert de Meulan, concerning whom William of Jumièges, *History of the Normans*, book VIII, chapter 41.]

I do not think, most Holy Father, that it has slipped from your memory how faithfully my father, R., Count of Leicester, of blessed memory, adhered to you during his life; how sincerely he loved your exalted rank; and hence how he deserved to receive letters from your holiness wholly full of paternal tenderness. I still carefully preserve them, both in remembrance of that affection and of your promise. For it was promised that this love and kindness should be transmitted to his heirs. Encouraged by that promise, I supplicate the mercy of your holiness with bended knees of heart, that I, who seem to be heir to his earthly possessions, may, through the intervention of your [Col. 1390D] holiness, prove an imitator of his virtues.

Concerning the matter for which the present bearer has been sent to you, I signify to your fatherhood—to whom it is not safe to lie—that John Cn. [lacuna] unjustly harasses the monks of Lyre regarding the tithes from my demesnes of Sapewich and Ringeston. Ever since the Normans subjected England to themselves, my predecessors have always been accustomed to give the aforesaid tithes to whomever they wished. My grandfather R., Count of Meulan, had once given the said tithes to the monks of Préaux; but when they had held them for a long time, they were grievously oppressed by the harassment of the reeves who held those villages. They complained to the Count of Meulan, my grandfather, that in collecting the tithes they were so harassed by the insolence of his officials [Col. 1391A] that they derived little benefit from them. Thus the monks complained repeatedly, until my grandfather, taking the tithes into his own demesne, gave the monks of Préaux a certain village called Expectesberi in exchange for those tithes; they still hold it.

My father Robert, Count of blessed memory, at one time granted those same tithes to his reeves together with his other farm-rent. At length, being a just and God-fearing man, and adopting sounder counsel, he reflected that they had once been tithes; and although, through the exchange subsequently made for the aforesaid village, they had now passed into his demesne, he was unwilling to retain them any longer for his own use. Instead, he granted them to his clerks: first to Peter the physician, then to Adam of Ely. But near the end of his life, wishing to assign them permanently, in my presence and that of many others, and at my own request as well, he gave the aforesaid tithes to the monastery of Lyre and to the brethren there serving God, as a perpetual alms, and confirmed the grant to them by writing and by his seal. Surely so great a man, so prudent and God-fearing, especially at the point of death, cannot be believed to have wished to bequeath them to a venerable and religious house unless he was certain that they had not previously been assigned to anyone. Therefore I earnestly entreat your fatherhood that, in regard for mercy and justice, you may deign to open the ears of your mercy [Col. 1391C] to the just petition of the monks of Lyre; and, after hearing the testimony of religious and worthy men, may they rejoice that by your protection they have been freed from the harassments of unjust accusers. Farewell in Christ.

### XXXIV. William, Cardinal-Priest of St Peter in Chains, to Emperor Manuel.—He urges him to form an alliance with King Louis of France for the defence of the Roman Church.

[DUCHESNE, *Rerum Francicarum Scriptores*, IV, 490.]

To MANUEL, by the grace of God most serene emperor and ever Augustus, WILLIAM, by the same grace cardinal-priest of St Peter in Chains, greeting and the increase of an enduring posterity.

[Col. 1391D] From the deeds of emperors and the enlargement of their works, observing with what great honours the reverence of your predecessors exalted the most holy Roman Church, mother of all Christians, and with what privileges they endowed her; and observing what burdens have been inflicted upon that same Church by the tyranny of barbarians since the imperial title is known to have been usurped by them: we deservedly love your excellence with a singular devotion, wish your empire to be preserved in perpetual stability, and to be ever advanced with unfailing increase.

For this reason we desire that you should love the Roman Church just mentioned as duty requires, and should take care to form a firm league of friendship with the most Christian and truly Catholic lord Louis, the most illustrious king [Col. 1392A] of France, who is bound to that Roman Church and to our most blessed Father Alexander by true faith and undivided devotion. Thus, weaving as it were a threefold cord, which is not easily broken, and uniting the strength of three powers, you might preserve one another’s dignities unimpaired and unshaken, and enlarge your honours by mutual assistance.

Moved by this consideration, because we learned through the venerable Archbishop of Benevento that this was pleasing to your highness, we have taken pains earnestly to persuade the aforesaid king of France that, through the mediation of our most holy Father the Roman pontiff, he should enter into a sure league of affection with you and establish lasting peace. We confidently have no doubt that, if through suitable envoys and letters you should request this as is fitting, that proposal will, by the Lord’s aid, obtain a welcome result. But so that no doubt concerning the apostolic office of our aforementioned Father may remain in your mind, we have caused the letter of the said most excellent king to be sent to your majesty; and what we have learned of his will concerning the establishment of friendship with you, we have taken care to communicate in this letter. It will therefore be for your highness and prudence, if this pleases you, to reply without delay; and apply your care and effort more vigilantly, so that this matter may be more promptly put into effect for the exaltation of God’s Church and the strengthening and elevation [Col. 1392C] of the imperial throne.

### XXXV. Otto, Cardinal-Deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.—For Gilbert, Bishop of London.

Our venerable brother, the Bishop of London, needs no extensive commendation before your majesty. For, dearest Father, as your own experience well knows, his person is honourable and his devotion toward your apostolic see manifest. He labours and would willingly give effective assistance for the honour of God and the Church in the affair of the archbishop, as we believe and partly know. Yet, as we ourselves have experienced, the exhorter’s word bears no fruit unless the power and grace of salvation first work in the royal heart. We therefore beseech [Col. 1392D] your merciful clemency to look upon him with a more gracious eye and to regard him as a faithful, honourable, and religious man. For the adverse reports that we heard concerning him while we were with you, we have found to be utterly false.

### XXXVI. Philip, Count of Flanders.—For Thomas of Canterbury.

To POPE ALEXANDER, PHILIP, Count of Flanders.

I render many thanks to your holiness because you wrote to me with so kindly and fatherly an affection concerning the venerable man, and, as is believed, one beloved of God, Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. From this I hope that you will in every respect be the helper and defender against the enemies of the Church. Therefore I in turn now offer your fatherhood all the prayers within my power, that, setting aside every favour and earthly fear, you may love and support the aforesaid Archbishop of Canterbury. Otherwise a great scandal and a ruinous example would arise for us and for the whole world, and your reputation too would be gravely injured.

But rise up in your wrath and overthrow the enemies of the Church, and thus God will be with you. Let it also move you that the aforesaid archbishop, although while still serving in the world he had been brought up in royal households, nevertheless did not refuse pastoral labours; indeed, he is everywhere said to be in exile for the sake of justice and of faithfulness to the Roman Church. The accumulation of evils is further increased because his brethren have separated themselves from him, as is now proclaimed everywhere; having initiated their suit, they have summoned him before your presence, though he is now in hiding, troubled by the straits of poverty [Col. 1393B]. But it is for you, Holy Father, carefully to consider and observe what sort of appeal this is, which seems to have been made for no other purpose than that justice may be oppressed and the Church’s affliction may have no end.

We all, together with the princes of the kingdom of France, await and desire that you grant fitting aid, as he deserves, to this man who is in exile for the honour of God and of your name; and that, as is just, you repel the enemies of the Church, who by trickery and evasions, even by threats, seek to overthrow justice and to deceive your prudence. We also earnestly beseech your fatherhood to restore the Church of Canterbury, in consideration of its present suffering, to its former and due [Col. 1393C] dignities. May your holiness, Father, prosper.

### XXXVII. William, Bishop of Pavia.—Of the same subject as the preceding letter.

To the Lord Pope, WILLIAM of Pavia.

Most blessed Father, it is fitting, and in some measure we are bound, that the apostolic eminence may learn from our declaration the devotion which we experience through manifest proofs in your children and those of the Church, so that we may discharge the debts of our office and that, having learned their fidelity, you may love such persons more especially.

Since, therefore, we have found our venerable brother, the Bishop of London, devoted and faithful in all things to your apostolic see and to the whole Church of God, we have thought him deserving of earnest commendation to your fatherhood, lest the merit of his sincerity be wholly deprived of grace. For he is the man who, more freely than the others, reproves, exhorts, and rebukes the king; nor is he so afraid on account of his steadfast adherence to truth that he does not always urge and lead him toward better things. Unless he had so far resisted, affairs might certainly have sunk into worse conditions.

But if anything has perhaps been represented to the height of your hearing to the effect that the same bishop had subverted the cause of Canterbury with the king in this matter, my lord, we maintain his innocence, since we have known his intention in this affair sufficiently clearly and have often seen him labouring for the good of that same Church of Canterbury. [Col. 1394A] Accordingly, considering his devotion and disposition, we ask the clemency of your holiness to grant these prayers: that, in view of his fidelity, apostolic gentleness may receive his envoys kindly, and that you may bestow upon that bishop such confidence in your favour that he may pursue his praiseworthy purpose with more earnest zeal.

### XXXVIII. William of Pavia and Cardinal Otto.—Concerning the dispute between Henry, King of the English, and Thomas.

To the most blessed Father and lord, by the grace of God supreme pontiff, WILLIAM and OTTO, cardinals by the same grace, greeting and the offices of submission, as devoted as they are due.

[Col. 1394B] On coming into the land of the most illustrious King of the English, we found the controversy between him and the Archbishop of Canterbury aggravated more severely than we could have wished. For the king, and the better part of his followers, asserted that the same archbishop had grievously incited the most serene King of France against him, and had induced the Count of Flanders, his kinsman, who previously bore him no resentment, suddenly to renounce his fealty and wage war against him to the best of his power, as the king held for certain and as clear indications showed. Indeed, when the same count had departed amicably from the king, the archbishop personally went to the theatres of war and incited both the King of France and the said count to war with all their strength.

When, therefore, we first had an audience with the aforesaid King of England at Caen, we delivered your fatherhood’s letters to the king’s hands as was fitting. Having carefully considered and read them, in the presence of others, he found them less comprehensive and somewhat at variance with letters concerning the same affair which he had previously received from you. The king began to burn with sharp indignation, the more so because he said that he knew beyond doubt that, after we had departed from you, the aforesaid archbishop had received letters by which he had been wholly exempted from our jurisdiction, so that he could in no respect be compelled to answer before us. He further maintained that what had been communicated to you concerning the ancient customs of England rested more upon falsehood than could be supported by truth; this the bishops testified in person. He also offered that, if any customs had been added in his own time in the kingdom of England which conflicted with ecclesiastical enactments, he would willingly annul them at our judgment. [Col. 1394D]

But we, with the archbishops, bishops, and abbots of his land joined to us, took every care that the king should not wholly withdraw hope of peace from us, but should rather permit himself to be inclined to allow us to speak with the archbishop both concerning peace and concerning judgment.

Accordingly, sending our own clerks to him with letters, we appointed for him a definite and safe place where, on the feast of St Martin, we might confer with him. He nevertheless put forward certain excuses and postponed the feast day until the octave; this, indeed, penetrated the king’s heart more deeply than we had supposed. When the often-mentioned archbishop, although we offered him a safe-conduct, would not meet us at all upon leaving the King of England’s land for France, we, wishing to defer to him, went into the land of the King of France, to the place he had directed, lest through us there should be an obstacle to what ought to turn to his advantage.

Once the conference had been announced, we first began with great diligence to persuade and earnestly exhort him to show toward the lord king—who had heaped many benefits upon him—such a manner of humility as might provide us with an opportunity for seeking peace. Then [Col. 1395B], withdrawing aside with his companions and at last holding counsel, he proposed to us that he would humble himself sufficiently before the king, provided the honour of God was preserved, the liberty of the Church preserved, the honour of his own person preserved, the possessions of the churches preserved, and moreover the justice of himself and his followers preserved.

After he had thus listed these conditions, we more carefully urged him that it was unnecessary to descend to particulars, since he was offering nothing definite or specific. We then asked him whether, concerning the questions set down in your letters, he was willing to submit to your judgment, as the king and bishops had previously promised to do. In reply, he promptly told us that he had received no such command from you; but that if he first were fully restored, together with all his people, then he would proceed in this matter according to the commands he received from the apostolic see.

Therefore, on returning from the conference, since his words tended neither toward judgment nor toward agreement and he was unwilling, on any grounds, to enter into the case, we took care to report to the king what had become known to us—keeping back many things, as was fitting, and moderating what we had heard. When we had finished speaking, the king and the great men present with him began to assert that he was henceforth absolved, since the archbishop refused judgment.

After the king’s great disturbance, the archbishops, bishops, and abbots of the kingdom of England, together with no few clerics, earnestly asked us whether by any special mandate or by reason of our legation we could compel the aforementioned archbishop to submit to judgment. When they learned that we lacked power in this respect, they feared that the aforesaid archbishop, casting aside judicial order as he had done on another occasion, might inflict an injury upon some persons of the kingdom; and they saw that our presence was thus useless to them and insufficient as protection against the bishop. With unanimous counsel they jointly appealed to your hearing, fixing the term of appeal at the winter feast of St Martin. Meanwhile, they placed themselves and their possessions under apostolic protection, and by the edict of this same appeal included every person in the kingdom and the entire kingdom itself. [Col. 1396A]

Finally, knowing that this affair was turning to the Church’s great detriment, we commanded the aforesaid archbishop, by your authority and ours, forbidding him henceforth—both because your letters had prohibited it and because a solemn appeal had been made—to attempt any act of injury against the aforesaid kingdom, persons, or churches of the kingdom. It will therefore be for apostolic prudence to take careful measures lest this same affair turn to the Church’s grave harm, as those who consider the Church’s welfare fear and dread.

### XXXIX. The Prior and Convent of Canterbury.—For R., Bishop-elect of Winchester.

To the Lord Pope, the Prior of Canterbury and the convent.

[Col. 1396B] We commend to you more confidently those whom we love more sincerely and whom we believe to bear a more sincere love toward the holy Roman Church. One of these, and almost the first among the foremost, is the father of the poor, consoler of the sorrowful, and protector in our distresses: our venerable brother R., Bishop-elect of Winchester. Christ, as the hope of the faithful is, chose him to govern his church so that he might rise up against its adversaries and set himself as a wall for the house of Israel; might powerfully crush the enemies of justice; and might grant due assistance to the just.

Falling at the feet of your majesty, all of us earnestly beseech you to cause him, with due promptness, to be advanced for the dispatch of the needs of his own Church and the consolation of others; and that the favour of your grace may attend his prayers, which he will make only in the Lord. Farewell.

### XL. Odo, Prior, and the Convent of Canterbury.—Although elections were held by the king’s command and R., a monk of the same convent, was elected abbot by unanimous consent, the young king annulled the election.

To the Lord Pope, ODO, Prior, and the Convent of Canterbury.

The calamities which our Church has endured now for a full decade cannot be unknown to the apostolic see, since the whole Christian world has recognized them. If their cause is sought, justice displays itself; the liberty of the Church declares itself; reverence for the apostolic see—whose authority was being nullified in our regions—proclaims itself: the cause for which the glorious martyr of Christ died; for which the brethren and foster-children of the Church were proscribed and compelled to remain in exile; for which, regarded as sheep for the slaughter, we became a spectacle to men, to God, and to angels, and the song of Christ’s persecutors all day long. The blood of martyrs shed among us testifies to these things, but most especially that blood which cries from the earth to God and is borne by the devotion of the faithful throughout the world.

But blessed be God; blessed be your apostolic office, which, through the zealous efforts of the lord cardinals cooperating with the grace of God, has comforted us in our affliction. Thus, after the anguish of so great a shipwreck, the Church seems to have reached the harbour of its due liberty, so that it may safely offer to its God the abominations of the Egyptians. [Col. 1397A] For they recently issued an order that elections should be held in the kingdom, and the lord king, acceding to their requests, commanded that suitable pastors according to God should be appointed in the churches. All rejoiced, but we above all others by every right, since we were placed in greater danger.

We met repeatedly, summoning the bishops of the province and others to whom the election belonged; and at length, God directing our steps according to His good pleasure, it came about that all had one heart and one soul. This could not have happened without divine direction: that wills so discordant should so easily be united in fulfilling the rule of the sacred canons. Therefore, led by the desire and prayer of the people, we came with equal vote and unanimous consent to the man concerning whom the Lord seems to have said to us: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; choose him” (Matt. 17), because he devoutly served me together with my martyr, whom he himself truly loved while suffering for me, and from early life faithfully dwelt in my house: “I command that he be chosen as vicar and ordained as successor.”

This is R., a monk of our church from his youth, advanced among us through every order, prior of Dover monastery, conspicuous for upright character and learned education; modest in speech, prudent in counsel, discerning in action, and in dress and bearing displaying the true form of a well-governed mind. He performs the priestly office most fittingly; zeal for Christ burns in his heart; he willingly opens his hand to the needy; gladly exercises liberality; and commendably manages outward affairs. What wonder, then, that all most willingly united upon so great and such a man, who indeed ought to have been seized by force if he could not otherwise have been obtained?

When, therefore, his election had been freely celebrated according to the institution of the sacred canons, the royal assent—as is customary—followed. A cry full of favour accompanied those electing him; the whole Church began to resound with due praise of God. With the elect, the provincial bishops and the elect of other churches proceeded to the metropolitan see; according to the rite of the people and the custom of their ancestors, he was solemnly enthroned. His consecration, pleasing to God and desired by men, was imminent when, behold, letters unexpectedly appeared bearing the name of the young king, in which he declared that he had appealed against elections which lacked his assent. [Col. 1397D]

Those letters were judged suspect from various grounds and probable signs; most held that they should not be trusted, especially in so great a crisis, where liberty and the salvation of souls might be endangered, the Church’s desolation prolonged, and loss irreparable. It would take long to enumerate the reasons; yet it ought to have been presumed of that king that he would not wish the Church to remain longer captive, to his own peril and the temporal advantage of his rivals. But although the aforesaid letters seemed to the wiser men of no great weight, yet from the humility and devotion of the elect himself, from the fidelity which we remember our fathers and ancestors always to have borne toward the Roman Church, and from the counsel of a few, it proceeded that the consecration should be delayed out of reverence for your name.

For we unhesitatingly hope that the necessity of our Church will find so much greater favour in the eyes of your clemency as you see that the greater honour has been shown you, even at our irreparable loss. You know, Father, that a cruel and long-lasting calamity has oppressed us beyond measure. You see how sad past times have been, how dangerous the present is, and how much more perilous, as is feared, the times now threatening will be. Irreparable desolation, may God avert it, confronts us; we fear a returning storm; and great necessity desires swift relief.

[Col. 1398B] Therefore, prostrate at the feet of your mercy, we earnestly beseech you—and the whole English Church beseeches with us—that, with the plenitude of power granted to you, you may deign, as your holiness judges most expedient, to strengthen by apostolic authority against those who plot to perpetuate the ruin of churches the pastor provided for us by God. Thus, relying upon the apostolic protection of his predecessors, he may be able to imitate their footsteps as God inspires him. We beseech you, I say; the Church beseeches; the glorious martyrs and confessors, patrons of our Church, beseech; and holy Thomas, with a voice joined to them all, repeats and multiplies his prayers.

Until your most sacred heart pours forth to us a good word, a consoling word, the Bride of Christ shall mourn in squalor, and there is none able to comfort her until she receives her bishop in the plenitude of power. Since we cannot, as we would wish, water your feet with tears, we shall water our cheeks; nor shall they have rest until, by God’s mercy, the right hand of your clemency wipes them away. [Col. 1398C]

### XLI. Roger, Archbishop of York.—He gives thanks for benefits received from Alexander and commends Gilbert, Bishop of London.

If eloquence redolent of Tully’s speech were at my command, sweetest Father, it could never suffice to express the magnitude of the favour which you have lately bestowed upon me through the spontaneous impulse of your innate goodness. For I, imprisoned now for more than a year, whither lying envy had caused me to be cast down, had made my bed in darkness, eaten my bread with sighs, and mingled my drink with tears, until the hand of your consolation drew me out from the pit of misery and the lower hell, restoring me to the land of the living [Col. 1398D] and to the upper air.

Now I do not blush before men clothed in purple as formerly, nor avoid the presence of the powerful. But I who until now did not dare raise my eyes to my lord, restored to my former freedom, boldly open my lips to entreat not only for myself but also for those whom I love—especially since they are men numbered among the foremost for life and learning.

The most distinguished lord Bishop of London, who from the beginning of his promotion has always been held honourable even among those without, and of sweet-smelling reputation—a man indeed abounding in the gifts of nature and the powers of intellect, and not at all content with their limits, but cultivating them through a long and strict observance of religion—has been assailed by envy trying to tear his integrity apart. Yet integrity founded upon a firm rock cannot suffer collapse.

To mention some of the charges laid against him by his rivals: know for certain, my lord, that while the lord Archbishop of Canterbury still lived, in my presence he often asked the lord king in England to incline his mind toward peace according to the tenor of your command. At Caen, when the lord king’s indignation against the aforesaid archbishop had been greatly renewed by reports heard from many, he exerted all diligence, even with tears, to soften that vehement impulse. If it pleases you, my lord, consider his years made burdensome by age; regard the weakness of his body, brought on not only by age but also by continual vigils and frequent fasts. Loosen the bonds by which he is held; restore him to freedom, that he may bear the burdens of the Church together with us. [Col. 1399B]

### XLII. The Canons of Rheims.—For Thomas of Canterbury.

To POPE ALEXANDER, the canons of Rheims.

Scandals gain strength in our times, Father, so that your power may shine more clearly in restraining and crushing their authors. For we trust that He who exercised fitting and glorious vengeance upon the members of Satan—that is, the leaders of schism—will crush Satan beneath your feet. Let your right hand, therefore, if it please you, now that the time has come, wield Peter’s sword against the instigators of schism and tormentors of the Church; and at last let it console with due compassion the venerable lord of Canterbury, known now to have been in exile for justice’s sake for five years.

For his justice is now manifest, as your fatherhood may perceive from the letters of the most holy man Simon, Prior of Mont-Dieu, who testifies to what he saw and heard in carrying out your command. He is indeed a man full of the authority of faith, whose words carry more weight among us and all others who know him than many oaths. Who except the Archbishop of Canterbury has ever been compelled or required by a Christian, under any obligation whatsoever, to suppress the honour of God?

The eyes of all are turned toward you, eagerly awaiting what consolation you will grant the confessor, what outcome you will give to God’s cause, and with what severity you will restrain such great audacity. Therefore, falling at your feet, we earnestly beseech you to provide for your honour and the Church’s liberty, because the raising up of one will be the undoubted consolation of many. For if so sincere a cause is endangered in your sight, who hereafter will dare to withstand worldly powers attempting every kind of wrongdoing? May your holiness always prosper. [Col. 1400A]

### XLIII. Rotrou, Archbishop of Rouen.—He humbly asks that, in St Thomas’s case, the pope deal more gently with the king.

Evoked by our lord the king, when we had come to court and some progress had already been made with your legates concerning your instructions, we learned by report of the most trustworthy archbishops and bishops who had assembled for this purpose—and whom we certainly believe, as we do ourselves by hearsay—that the lord king of the English received your messengers and letters with so much the greater joy and eagerness as they seemed to promise him a greater measure of your kindness.

Accordingly, your request concerning peace with the Archbishop of Canterbury [Col. 1400B] and the return of his people having been received more graciously for love of you, with the counsel of the archbishops, bishops, abbots, religious persons, and magnates of his realm, he granted that the archbishop should return to his archbishopric, that he himself be received with all the integrity which he held when he departed, and that he thereafter possess it well and peacefully, to the honour of God—while, of course, the former dignity of his kingdom remained intact.

When, therefore, a lengthy negotiation had arisen between the lord king and your messengers on this subject, they finally agreed upon language pleasing to both parties: namely, that they should immediately absolve those who were present; that one of them, Master Vivian, should at once cross over to absolve those who were in England; and that the other should agree to remain on this side of the sea for the execution of the peace agreed upon. But afterwards, withdrawing their consent, they refused to accept the wording concerning the future preservation of royal dignity which they had already adopted, declining to carry out what had already been beneficially arranged.

Therefore I, together with the aforesaid persons of considerable authority who were present, was sent to press, with every vigilance and concern, for the good of so great a peace: that, as had been said, with the honour of God set before all else and the ancient dignity of the kingdom remaining as was fitting, your messengers should receive with joy the king’s most excellent and altogether acceptable formulation concerning royal dignity, lest so great a good should fail. When much labour had been spent upon this persuasion of ours and nothing had been achieved, we were deeply grieved—especially because we know for certain that, in preserving royal dignity, ecclesiastical liberty or dignity is in no way burdened.

For ecclesiastical dignity advances rather than diminishes royal dignity; and royal dignity has customarily preserved rather than taken away ecclesiastical liberty. Indeed, ecclesiastical and royal dignity meet, as it were, in mutual embraces, since neither do kings attain salvation without the Church, nor does the Church attain peace without royal protection. Therefore, falling at the knees of your holiness with all the devotion we can muster, we humbly and earnestly beseech you not to consider the mere letters and verbal formulations more worthy of embracing than the thing itself; but, according to the spirit of discernment given you by God, act so that the cause of one man may not be turned to the ruin of many, indeed almost numberless persons. For, at times, the gentleness of grace advances the good of peace more than the severity of discipline.

XLIV. Of the same. — On behalf of Gilbert, Bishop of London.

To Pope ALEXANDER, ROTROD, Archbishop of Rouen: obedience and the fullness of reverence.

The abiding desire in our heart to behold the longed-for presence of your serenity is daily increased by the delay itself. Concerning what currently pertains to our venerable and most dear brother Gilbert, Bishop of London—whose life, learning, and gentleness of character breathe forth sweetly even there [Col. 1401B]—we inform your holiness that, when we were in a most private conference, at which only the king of England and we two were present, and where the salvation of the king’s soul was being discussed, this man laboured manfully, discreetly, and with every urgency to procure peace for the lord Archbishop of Canterbury. In every place, both private and public conferences alike, he employed all diligence and earnestness in seeking this peace and restoring all things.

We therefore greatly wonder that the lord of Canterbury acted in any way against him. For if he did this of his own will, without another’s prompting, he sinned against an innocent brother; but if he acted at someone’s suggestion, we know that he was falsely advised. Hence, with all our strength and with the whole devotion of our soul, we beseech your most benign clemency to open the bowels of your compassion to an innocent brother concerning the injury inflicted upon him by the lord of Canterbury. May God preserve your person, for the good of His Church, unharmed through long ages.

XLV. Of the Suffragan Bishops of the Church of Canterbury. — Taking the king’s side against their metropolitan, they appeal to the Apostolic See and request that the feast of the Lord’s Ascension be assigned to them as the term of their appeal.

To their father and lord, the supreme pontiff ALEXANDER, the bishops of the province of Canterbury and persons established in many places throughout their dioceses: the service owed in charity and obedience to their lord and father.

[Col. 1401D] We believe, Father, that your exaltedness remembers how, through our venerable brothers the Bishops of London and Hereford, you had some time ago addressed letters to your devoted son and our most dear lord, the illustrious king of the English, and in paternal kindness admonished him concerning certain matters which seemed to your holiness to require correction in his kingdom. Receiving your command with due veneration, as is well known, he did not swell in anger at your admonitions, nor in pride disdain obedience. Rather, giving thanks for paternal correction, he immediately submitted himself to the Church’s judgment, declaring concerning each matter carefully set before him in accordance with the form of your mandate that he would obey the judgment of the Church of his kingdom and, with devotion praiseworthy and especially commendable in a prince, would correct by its counsel whatever it decreed ought to be corrected.

He has not departed from this purpose, nor withdrawn his mind from his promise. Let someone sit in judgment—someone who knows and judges with reverence for the fear of God, not displaying majesty before him—and the king stands ready in all things, as an obedient son, to submit himself to judgment, obey a lawful sentence, and show himself a prince bound by the laws. Hence there is no need to compel to satisfaction, by interdict, threats, or the stings of curses, one who voluntarily submits himself to the examination of divine laws. For his deeds by no means withdraw themselves from the light, nor do they seek under any pretext to be hidden in darkness.

For the king, most Christian in faith, most honourable in the bond of chaste marriage, and incomparably vigorous guardian and promoter of peace and justice, strives and fervently desires with all his heart that scandals be removed from his kingdom, sins be expelled with their impurities, peace and justice prevail everywhere, and that all things may rejoice and flourish under him in profound security and tranquil calm. Since he perceived that the peace of his kingdom was at times seriously disturbed by the monstrous excesses of certain insolent clerics, while showing the clergy due reverence he referred their excesses to the bishops, the judges of the Church, so that sword might assist sword, and the spiritual power might establish and strengthen among the clergy the peace which he governed and fostered among the people.

In this matter the zeal of both sides became apparent: the bishops’ judgment was that homicide, and anything of that sort, should be punished in a cleric by deprivation of office alone; whereas the king considered that this penalty did not adequately answer the crime, nor properly provide for the establishment of peace, if a reader or acolyte killed someone and was considered safe merely through the loss of the aforementioned order. Thus, while the clergy deferred to the order established from heaven, and while the lord king pursued sin with a righteous hatred, as he hoped, and intended to root peace more deeply, a certain holy contention arose—one excused before the Lord, as we believe, by the simple intention of each party.

It was therefore not through ambition for dominion or with a view to oppressing ecclesiastical liberty, but from a desire to establish peace firmly, that our lord the king wished the customs and dignities of his kingdom—observed by ecclesiastical persons under the kings before him in the kingdom of England, and peacefully and reverently rendered—to be brought forward and committed to public knowledge, so that a contentious rope might not be drawn concerning them in the future. Therefore, after the older bishops and other great men of the realm had been adjured by faith and by the hope which is in God, the condition of former times was set forth, the dignities were investigated, publicly produced, and made known by the testimony of the greatest men in the kingdom.

This is the cruelty of our lord king toward the Church of God proclaimed throughout the whole world; this is his persecution; this is the malignity of his perverse acts spread everywhere by rumours. Yet in all these matters, if anything should endanger his soul or contain anything disgraceful to the Church, he has long promised, and most steadfastly promises, that when admonished by your authority, out of reverence for Christ, honour for the holy Church which he professes as his mother, and concern for the salvation of his soul, he will correct it by the counsel of the Church of his kingdom.

Indeed, Father, our petition would, as we hope, already have obtained the desired end of peace, had not the fresh provocation of our father, the lord of Canterbury, stirred up angers already calmed and almost wholly extinguished. But he, from whose patience we had hitherto hoped for peace and from whose moderation for the restoration of goodwill, has attacked harshly and quite irreverently the very man whom he ought to have softened by admonitions and overcome by merits and gentleness. By sad and terrible letters, breathing nothing at all of a father’s devotion or a pontiff’s patience, when he had lately led an army against disturbers of the peace, he threatened the king with a sentence of excommunication and his kingdom with the penalty of interdict.

If humility is thus rewarded, what will be decreed against the defiant? If prompt devotion to obedience is thus valued, how will stubborn perversity be punished? Still heavier things were added to grave threats. For he bound by a sentence of excommunication, and publicly declared excommunicated, certain faithful friends of our lord king, principal magnates of the realm, who are especially present at the king’s private counsels and in whose hands the king’s counsels and the affairs of the kingdom are directed—though they had neither been cited, defended, nor, as they say, conscious of guilt; neither convicted nor confessed. He further suspended our venerable brother, the lord Bishop of Salisbury, though absent and undefended, neither confessing nor convicted, from priestly and episcopal office before the cause of his suspension had been established by the judgment of his fellow-provincials or indeed of anyone else.

If, then, this order of judicial proceedings is carried forward against the king and the kingdom so perversely—lest we say disorderly—what, we ask, can we suppose will follow? For the days are evil and offer very many opportunities for malice, unless the bond of peace and goodwill by which kingdom and priesthood have hitherto adhered together is broken, and we, with the clergy entrusted to us, go off into the scattering of exile, or, withdrawing from your allegiance—God forbid!—roll down into the evil of schism, into the abyss of iniquity and disobedience. This, indeed, is the shortest path to every loss of religion, and to the overthrow and destruction alike of clergy and people.

Therefore, lest in the time of your apostolate the Church be so wretchedly overthrown; lest the lord king and the peoples serving him be turned away from your obedience—God forbid!—and lest the anger of the lord of Canterbury accomplish against us all that it plots through the counsel of private persons, imposing upon our lord the king or his kingdom, upon us or the churches entrusted to us, some burden contrary to him and his commands: we have appealed, orally and in writing, to your highness, and have designated the feast of the Lord’s Ascension [Col. 1404A] as the term of our appeal. We choose to humble ourselves before you in whatever may please your holiness, rather than be most wearisomely burdened day by day by the lofty impulses of his mind when our merits do not require it.

May almighty God preserve your safety, to benefit His Church for long ages, beloved Father in Christ.

XLVI. Of the same. — They complain that, contrary to the authority of the canons, after their appeal they have been bound by a sentence of excommunication by the Archbishop of Canterbury. Nevertheless, they request that the feast of the passing of Blessed Martin be fixed as the term of their appeal.

To their father and lord, the supreme pontiff ALEXANDER, the English Church: devoted and due service in charity [Col. 1404B] and obedience.

Reverend and venerable Father, we offer affectionate thanks to your highness because, at the request of your most devoted son and our most beloved lord, the illustrious king of the English, you took care to send to him from afar your most dear sons, so necessary to us in the present storm; and because, with paternal affection, you sought through their labours to spare us and piously relieve our burdens by means of our burdens. Therefore, offering thanks to the sender, we received those sent with due honour and with all gladness of heart, hoping that their arrival would put an end to evils long prolonged and restore, through the cooperation of grace, what had been disturbed among us to the serenity of former peace.

Accordingly, we reverently presented ourselves, together with our lord the king, before them as judges sent for this purpose by your holiness, alike wishing and expecting that all matters between our lord the king and the lord of Canterbury, and those between him and ourselves, should be openly conducted in their presence and fully concluded by their definitive sentence, according to the form of your mandate. We stood before them in this fashion, rendering the reverence due to judicial authority; and behold, confounded by unwelcome news, we fell from our earlier hope of joy into the pit of despair, and could scarcely wonder sufficiently at what we heard.

For when it was heard—and acknowledged by the confession of your legates themselves—that they had no authority at all to judge this cause for which they had come, and did not retain what your holiness had granted and confirmed in writing to our lord king, our lord the king was wholly inflamed with anger beyond what can be expressed. Indeed, even our joint entreaty could scarcely recall him to his customary gentleness of feeling toward you. Thus all the joy we had conceived at the arrival of your legates immediately began to be overshadowed by a cloud of sorrow.

The conversations of the nobles of the kingdom themselves furnished incentives to inflame this anger more fiercely, repeatedly impressing upon the lord king that no aid now remained to him or his kingdom against the lord of Canterbury, since the kingdom’s appeal, made long ago to you, had already expired, and the concern of your legates had in no respect brought it help. Hence so great a disturbance arose among the princes of the realm that, unless according to the wisdom given you, you forestall the dangers now breaking forth, you will shortly grieve to see Christ’s garment most wretchedly torn apart.

For the lord of Canterbury labours with all his efforts to bind our lord king with anathema and his kingdom with the penalty of interdict. He exercises upon his subjects the power which he ought to have received for the building up, not the destruction, of the Church in such a manner that he attempts to draw all men into hatred of the king and of all the nobles of the realm, and earnestly seeks to procure the plundering of their property, the sword for their necks, or exile for their bodies. By frequent letters he lays upon them heavy burdens of commands, which he himself, while present, was unwilling to move with a finger, much less bear upon his shoulders.

He summons us to death and the shedding of blood, although he himself took the greatest care to avoid the death which no one deigned either to inflict upon him or threaten him with, and, preserving his own blood unharmed, has not yet been willing for even a drop of it to be shed. To die for Christ is indeed glorious; but we know that to rush imprudently into death does not please Christ. He preaches the liberty of the Church, though it is manifest that, by forcing himself upon the Church of Canterbury through influence, he has taken it away from that Church. He frequently reproaches us with the customs of the kingdom, which he represents in his writings to your highness far otherwise than the facts stand.

Furthermore, he does not observe toward us the authority of the holy canons: after our appeal to you, he excommunicates appellants; he suspends others without citation or warning; he asserts as notorious matters which are neither known nor supported by truth; and in this fashion he confounds as much as he can by means of the power at his disposal. Moreover, he refuses to pay our lord king forty thousand marks, or more, entrusted to him in good faith, as his own people assert, or to render what is just; and he denies to his king and lord what he ought not to have denied even to a pagan or a tax collector.

Therefore, lest the injuries just mentioned now bind us, and lest through our silence and a certain indiscreet connivance we permit what may cause our lord king, his kingdom itself, and the peoples following them to turn wholly away from your obedience: against the judgments of the lord of Canterbury, suspect to us, and against all his commands which bring any burden upon our lord king and his kingdom, upon our persons, or upon the churches and parishes entrusted to us, committing ourselves wholly to your counsel and submitting ourselves to your protection, we have appealed to your hearing and have fixed as the term of our appeal the feast of the passing of Blessed Martin. Farewell, farewell altogether, beloved Father in Christ.

XLVII. Of the Clergy of Normandy. — They request that, in the case of St Thomas, the pontiff show some indulgence toward the king of the English.

To Lord Pope ALEXANDER, the bishops and clergy of Normandy: greeting and obedience.

Our lord the king [Col. 1406A] of England received your messengers and letters with so much the greater joy and eagerness as they seemed to promise him a greater measure of your kindness. Accordingly, your request concerning peace with the Archbishop of Canterbury and the return of his people having been received more graciously for love of you, with the counsel of ecclesiastical persons and magnates of his realm, he granted that the archbishop should return to his archbishopric, that he himself be received with all the integrity which he held when he departed, and that he thereafter possess it in good peace and security, to the honour, indeed, of God and the Church—while, of course, the former dignity of his kingdom remained intact.

When, therefore, a lengthy negotiation had arisen between the lord king and your messengers on this matter, they finally agreed upon language pleasing to both parties: namely, that they should immediately absolve those who were present; that one of them, Master Vivian, should at once cross over to absolve those who were in England; and that the other should agree to remain on this side of the sea for the execution of the peace agreed upon. Afterwards, withdrawing their consent, they refused to accept the wording concerning the future preservation of royal dignity, declining to carry out what had been arranged, although the archbishops, bishops, abbots, religious persons, and magnates of the realm who were present had earnestly pressed them, with many prayers, for the good of so great a peace. For it did not at all seem to us that ecclesiastical liberty or dignity was burdened by preserving royal dignity.

Indeed, ecclesiastical dignity advances rather than diminishes royal dignity, and royal dignity has customarily preserved rather than taken away ecclesiastical liberty. [Col. 1406C] For ecclesiastical and royal dignity meet, as it were, in mutual embraces, since neither do kings attain salvation without the Church, nor does the Church attain peace without royal protection. Therefore, falling at the knees of your compassion with all the devotion we can muster, we humbly and earnestly beseech you not to consider the mere letters and verbal formulations more worthy of embracing than the thing itself. Rather, according to the spirit of discernment given you by God, act so that the cause of one man may not be turned to the ruin of many, indeed almost numberless persons; for at times the gentleness of grace advances the good of peace more than the severity of discipline.

May the Lord preserve your person unharmed for many ages for His Church.

XLVIII. Of William, Bishop of Auxerre. — Against [Gilbert], Bishop of London.

To Pope ALEXANDER, WILLIAM, Bishop of Auxerre.

If one member suffers, the rest must suffer with it. And what cannot be healed by fomentations or cautery is better cut off than allowed to inflict its stain upon the rest. However distinguished and useful it may be in the body, if it breeds scandals and brings in pestilence, the Lord commands that it be cut off and expelled.

Since, therefore, the Church of Canterbury—a noble member of the universal Church, the first see of the Britains, and mother of the faith in the West—suffers greatly, and has now long suffered, because her sons, abusing the powers of public authority through parricidal crime, have rushed upon her, it is necessary that we too should suffer with her and, with and for her, have recourse to the dispenser of salvation, to the shepherd and bishop of our souls.
