But since an illness is not easily healed unless its cause is first known, investigate the cause, if it please you, and the English Church, with God’s favour, will readily recover.

The cause is indeed before your eyes. For that Londoner—who, if you please to recall it, is known at Sens, while conducting an embassy for his king, to have disclosed in words the fury conceived in his mind—now exerts with all his strength and proves by his deeds the most destructive madness against the Church of God. He is the author of this schism, the sower of discord, the fuel of scandal. The war which he long waged against God and his archbishop, he has now at last turned against his brothers and fellow bishops, because they refused to communicate with him when excommunicated, as he pressed them to do through the king’s officials, and refused to withdraw the obedience owed to their archbishop.

Behold, Father, how great a wolf has hitherto lain hidden in a sheep; how manifest a forerunner of Antichrist and herald of iniquity, who persecutes his father and seeks to overthrow his mother. He does not hesitate to commit the manifest crime of disobedience, which corresponds to the offence of idolatry and divination; through the service of tyrants he proscribes and kills the innocent; he knows no peace; and he tears apart the unity of the Church. What else, I ask, will Antichrist do? Did not Christ send your holiness before his face, in the strength of apostolic power, in the spirit and power of Elijah, for the destruction of such great iniquity? Therefore, if it please you, let your majesty crush both this man and the rest whom the lord of Canterbury has for just causes delivered to Satan, so that he who has offered others a model for wrongdoing may leave behind, for those now living and for posterity, a well-known example of correction, to the glory of God, your honour, and the salvation and peace of the whole Church.

XLIX. Of William, Elect of Chartres. — On behalf of Thomas of Canterbury.

To Pope ALEXANDER, the Elect of Chartres.

As a son of the Roman Church, I rejoice wholly in the prosperity of my mother; so in her adversities my flesh is wasted, [Col. 1407D] my spirit afflicted, and all rest denied to my soul. Since the necessity of obedience to the Apostolic See presses upon all the faithful, devotion in charity binds me, who in Christ’s ministry am your special creature, so that by God’s grace neither death nor life may separate me from the fidelity and service of the holy Roman Church and of you. Therefore I shall speak confidently to my lord what most certainly pertains to his glory and the honour of the whole Church.

Among all the kingdoms of the world, there is none which, in my judgment, has always shown the Apostolic See a purer faith, warmer charity, and more abundant devotion than the kingdom of the Franks. Among kings and princes, there is none who more graciously hears your prayers, more humbly obeys your commands, more devotedly honours and more zealously protects the Church and churchmen than our most Christian king. There is no Church more useful than the Gallican Church to the Roman Church in all its distresses.

The Church, king, and kingdom have entreated you on behalf of the lord of Canterbury, who, in defending the liberty of the Church and the dignity of your majesty, has now completed his fourth year as an exile and outlaw. A tyrant, a manifest persecutor of the Church, and enemy of the kingdom of the Franks, whose iniquity is known to all, acts against him before you; and yet—to my shame in saying it, and my grief that it has occurred—he has hitherto prevailed in his malice and emptiness.

For recently, when he came to a conference with the most Christian king and was urged, through the Count of Flanders, who had brought the lord of Canterbury there, to restore peace to the Church, he caused apostolic letters to be read in the hearing of his bishops and magnates. These decreed that the aforesaid Archbishop of Canterbury should not be able to pronounce sentence against him or his land, or inflict any burden upon any person of his land, until he returned to his favour. On hearing this, the most Christian king was confounded, and the whole kingdom and all the sons of the Church grieved that a righteous man and venerable bishop should be suspended without cause, and that such a pernicious document should issue from the Apostolic See as a precedent.

Last year John of Oxford raised a most serious scandal, but it was nothing compared with this. It is the judgment of the lord king that, if you were unwilling to hear his prayers, the cause of God ought not thus to have been oppressed; nor ought harsher weapons to have been given to the sinner, by which he might harass the Church; nor ought an innocent man to have been slaughtered at the table, indeed in the very hands, of the most Christian king. And what wounds most deeply the minds both of the king and all of us is that the injuries and threats of the English are said to have been more effective than the sincere faith, fervent devotion, and continual service of the French.

You promised, Father, if you please to remember, the lord king, who so often pleaded for the lord Archbishop of Canterbury, that you would render him justice; and, what had made your aforesaid son the king rejoice, you commanded that the bishops of the archbishop’s province should render him obedience. But now, to the king’s boundless grief, you oppress by deeds the same archbishop whom you console with words; and he who is honoured in name alone is deprived of the power due to him.

May it therefore please your clemency to cancel your acts and reverse the positions, by releasing the innocent man and overcoming the torturer of the Church with the condemnation he deserves. Otherwise, it is certain that the scandal which has lately arisen and blackens the honour of the Apostolic See cannot be calmed.

L. Of the same. — On behalf of the same.

To Pope ALEXANDER, WILLIAM, Elect of Chartres.

The vigour of the senses flows to all the members from the head; and from the holy Roman Church, which is the head of all the faithful, welfare is secured for all churches both collectively and individually. A noble member of it is the Church of Canterbury, the first see of the English. By the office of preaching and the dispensation of the sacraments it first converted the whole island to the faith [Col. 1409A], so that all other churches ought to venerate her as their mother, since she begot them in Christ through the Gospel.

The king of the English strives not merely to weaken and divide her, but to overthrow her, so that with her he may—God forbid—destroy the liberty of the whole Church, exclude the authority of the Apostolic See from his territories, and alone be able to do everything in his own realm, since he desires everything for himself alone. Unless his shameless audacity is checked, there is great reason to fear that kings and powers may be provoked by such an example into similar shamelessness against the Church of God. For they commonly think lawful what they do not hear is punished.

The lord of Canterbury, a man renowned for the testimony of every virtue, pleasing and welcome for his piety to the lord king, the churches, and the magnates of the Franks, is an exile among us because he dared to oppose such great iniquity, speak for the liberty of the Church, and keep faith with the Apostolic See in preserving its privileges. This cause, most holy Father, is yours: so presumptuous and destructive an injury rebounds upon you. Victory in restraining this tyranny is owed to your apostolate, and glory is reserved for you through God’s mercy. For if he prevails—may God avert it—the English Church is lost and the Gallican Church is in danger.

Your devoted son, the most Christian king of the Franks, awaits; the churches and magnates of the kingdom await what help you will bring against the raging tyrant to the archbishop exiled for justice and to his fellow exiles: in other words, what comfort you will bring to the Church labouring, indeed already almost falling. They await it, I say, holding as done to themselves whatever mercy may be shown to the lord of Canterbury and his people—if you confound John of Oxford, who rendered an accursed oath to the emperor against the Church of God, and his accomplices; if you examine more carefully the deceits of the king of the English:

> “Do not let minds hidden beneath a fox deceive you.”

With God as author, you will have freed the Church. For all that this king does is so suspect to our people and neighbours that they commonly say: “Blessed is he who dashes his little ones against the rock” (Psalm 136). As he is known to the neighbouring peoples, may he become wholly known to you as well—if only not to your harm—lest he do destructive injury.

Therefore we beseech your majesty with all the devotion we can muster to open the ears of your clemency to the prayers and desires of the peoples, to look upon the need of the Church of Canterbury, and to hear compassionately the pitiable petitions of the archbishop and of those who share exile with him for God and the liberty of the Church. Let your holiness certainly know that the lord king and magnates of the kingdom of the Franks desire these petitions to be advanced for diverse and just reasons.

LI. Of Aegidius, Bishop of Évreux. — He humbly requests that the pontiff deal more mildly with the king of the English.

To Pope ALEXANDER, AEGIDIUS, Bishop of Évreux.

Around the beginning of my appointment, I ought to have cast myself at the feet of your Majesty [Col. 1410A], and sought there remedies for my weakness, where the Angel of the supreme counsel has established the foundation of saving counsel. But, through sins that call for punishment, I am prevented from performing these and other duties incumbent upon me, especially since scandals more grievous than usual are arising among us and around us, beyond everyone’s expectation.

For after many labours, severe troubles of almost the whole Church, and that anxiety which you bore in the sanctuary of your breast like a continual cross, divine mercy had inclined the mind of the glorious king of the English toward peace with the Archbishop of Canterbury, in response to your prayers and according to the tenor of your command; and after peace had been announced, the voices and hearts of all good people rejoiced; and the Archbishop of Canterbury himself had crossed into England with safe, sound, and honourable [Col. 1410B] conduct; and all were awaiting at his arrival a voice of gladness and a song of rejoicing—then their harp was turned into mourning. We have received news of such disturbance in the royal serenity, such affliction of the churches, and such near-despair of the whole people, that we cannot but grieve deeply.

For the king’s displeasure weighs upon and offends alike all who serve the Lord under his dominion; and while he suffers, we neither wish nor ought to remain at rest. Therefore, since I have once begun, I shall speak to my lord, though I am dust and ashes. Let your prudence remember, most holy Father, that the holy living creatures are described as having eyes before and behind; and, in order to signify the purity of animals, [Col. 1410C] the Lawgiver did not pass over the division of the hoof in silence. Thus, in the manifold light, let the subtlety of difficult discernment be signified; and in the cloven hoof, believe us, the most gentle moderation of dispensation.

Nor has it escaped your mind that, where the slaughter of many is apparent, severity toward the greater number must be diminished; nor ought the whole house of the Lord to be shaken and troubled so gravely by the killing of one person. Especially since, if the king, though sinning, recognized the Canterbury man’s path of peace and loved it once recognized, he would provide more for the universal peace of the Church, and more wisely for his own interests through discriminating gentleness, than he can achieve by flashing threats and exercising the full rigour of his power.

Moreover, it is neither new nor surprising that the human mind should be deceived or should deceive. For both dangers the Angel of great counsel gave us a safeguard, saying: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10). I marvel by what effrontery it has been represented to your Serenity that the king of the English—and the son of the king of the English and our prince—did not make, at the time due, the profession required by his consecration, and swore an oath to preserve certain customs. In the denial of the one and the assertion of the other, he has been assailed with equal malice. For I tell you before God, upon my soul, that I heard in public the profession made by the aforesaid lord king. But concerning an oath, neither after the consecration nor at the time of consecration has even the slightest word reached my ears to this day.

In all these matters, holy Father, let your holy discernment watch [Col. 1411A] and provide, seeking and asking for those things which belong to the peace of the Jerusalem that is on pilgrimage, lest a greater and more grievous division arise in the Church of God. It is time, most reverend Father, to show and exercise toward your dearest son, the illustrious king of the English, the tender bowels of apostolic charity, so that his righteousness may answer him in the morning, together with the humble and ready devotion which, at a fitting time, he displayed to you and to the Roman Church; so that, by apostolic moderation, he may return into her bosom.

## LII–LIII. Of Aegidius, Bishop of Évreux

[Warthon, *Anglia Sacra*, preface to vol. II, p. V, from the archive of Christ Church, Canterbury. Around the seal is inscribed: “Of Aegidius, by the grace of God Bishop of Évreux.” On the back is written: “Against the false privileges of St Augustine: how, through a single forger-monk of St Medard, they fortified themselves with forged privileges.”]

[Col. 1411B]

### I.

We do not believe that your discernment is unaware how grave a discord arose at the beginning of our episcopate between King Henry and me, the servant of your Holiness, concerning the restoration of the liberty of the Norman churches, which had for many past ages been trampled underfoot. Driven by the storm of that persecution and compelled to leave the bounds of our diocese, we could find harbour only in the bosom of apostolic mercy. What and how great were the consolations bestowed on us by Pope Blessed Innocent, of happy memory, the mind can scarcely conceive or the tongue utter.

Among them, we have endeavoured to make known to your discernment, through this present written report, one matter that we do not believe has come to the knowledge of people today, as a thing worthy of remembrance. When Blessed Innocent arrived at Reims to celebrate a council, it happened that I, the least of God’s servants, was present as customary with our brethren and sons. Among others whom we brought with us, R., elected but not blessed as Abbot of St Ouen, and W., elected but not blessed as Abbot of Jumièges, presented themselves before the apostolic presence in the rank of abbots.

When I informed the apostolic ears of their election—or rather, their deposition—he in his prudent manner diligently inquired of them whether perhaps they were protected by any authentic privileges, by whose authority their persons or churches might be proved exempt from metropolitan subjection. While this apostolic concern was examining the matter with careful insistence, it happened by God’s gift that the venerable G., Bishop of Châlons, formerly Abbot of St Medard, was present. When the elect of St Ouen hesitated concerning the apostolic inquiry, he ended our uncertainty and checked the swelling presumption of that man by the bridle of an old recollection.

For he said that, while he was performing the office of abbot in the church of St Medard, a certain Guernon by name, one of his monks, had confessed at the last point of confession that he had been a forger. Among other things which he had fabricated and written for various churches, he penitently asserted that he had fortified the church of St Ouen and the church of St Augustine of Canterbury with forged privileges under the apostolic name. [Col. 1412A] Indeed, he confessed that, as the reward of iniquity, he had received certain precious ornaments and brought them to the church of St Medard.

When he heard this, Blessed Innocent asked the aforesaid bishop whether he would confirm on oath what he had plainly declared. The man of God, a lover of religion and truth, undertook to do so. Hearing this, the lord pope said: “Come then, my dearest brother: put on the vestments of your dignity and lay the hand of blessing upon the elect who are present, under the canonical profession.” Having obtained permission, I proceeded to do so. What is remarkable to tell, he deferred entering the assembly of venerable Fathers who were awaiting his arrival until I, about to enter with him, should arrive after the abbots had been duly blessed.

These things, most holy Father, we judged should be written for you, beseeching that, if it is proved that the aforesaid churches have usurped anything contrary to their ancestral constitutions, you may, as is your customary and proper practice, preserve for each church its own equitable rights in every respect.

### II.

To the venerable Father and dearest lord ALEXANDER, by the grace of God supreme pontiff of the Holy Roman Church: Aegidius, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Évreux, servant of your Holiness, devoted obedience and reverence.

What is written in the schedule which the Church of Canterbury presents to you with our seal, we received from the mouth of Hugh, formerly Archbishop of the Church of Rouen, of good memory, my father and uncle; and we sent it, sealed with his seal, to Blessed Thomas and the Church of Canterbury, so that the truth of ancient recollection might restrain the presumption of those who, in a spirit of error and a spirit of falsehood, claim for themselves an undue liberty.

But the privileges which, from the confession of Geoffrey, Bishop of Châlons, were proved forged in the presence of Pope Innocent of holy memory and restored to our aforesaid lord archbishop, we ourselves handed over to the fire to be burned, by command of that same our lord. May God preserve your person unharmed for His Church through longer ages.

## LIV. Of Henry, dean, and the chapter of St Paul’s, London—They commend Bishop Gilbert, who is going to Rome

[Col. 1412D]

After our lord the Archbishop of Canterbury found occasion to leave our land, the English Church, troubled from that time and tossed in many ways, became anxiously concerned, as though suddenly left bereft; and, uncertain of the outcome of so great an abandonment, it was agitated under a manifold burden of fear. Yet the most merciful goodness of almighty God came to its aid. Until now it has not allowed the severity of the king’s indignation against the shepherd to roam widely through the flock; it has also restrained the power of his hand, lest he meanwhile burden the Church, his mother, whose most dutiful son he is.

Yet our church was more anxious than the rest, [Col. 1413A] situated as it is in a city more populous than all the other cities of our land, more exposed to royal attentions, and regarded as worthier and superior to other churches by reason of a particular dignity. Since we justly and not without cause feared its oppression and intolerable burdens—which can be expressed better in spoken words than set down in letters—we, together with our lord Gilbert, our bishop, most devoted to you in all things, formerly appealed in every respect to your Holiness. The ground and tenor of that appeal became sufficiently known to your discernment; but your kindness, through letters sent to the lord of Canterbury, spared our church its labours and expenses on that occasion.

By the benefit of those letters we hoped that we would remain in peace until the anger of our lord king had cooled. Yet suddenly and almost unexpectedly we heard that the restraints upon the lord of Canterbury had been loosened and that the exercise of archiepiscopal rigour had been restored to him by your Highness with full power. Therefore our lord and bishop Gilbert, in whose mind concern for his own church and ours is deeply seated, fearing afresh an oppression directed both against his own person and against the whole flock of his church, although conscious of no fault, appealed again to your hearing. Standing before the altar of Blessed Paul in the presence of the Church, with the religious men the Abbot of Westminster, the Abbot of St Augustine’s, Canterbury, the Abbot of Chertsey, priors of communities, archdeacons, and clerics of many churches present, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April [18 March], [Col. 1413C] he commended the integrity of his own position, of our lord king, of all the magnates, and of the whole kingdom to your most holy judgment, and took precaution for their indemnity.

After this appeal—and indeed before it—although he had neither been summoned nor warned until then for any fault, we are greatly astonished and deeply grieved that the sentence of anathema has been pronounced against him and many others by the lord of Canterbury. We cannot see him suffer an undeserved penalty, a matter that concerns us as his children especially and closely, without great contrition of spirit. This is particularly so since we have found his conduct among us most worthily praiseworthy, and know beyond doubt that he has incurred no fault and has in no way either stirred up or fostered our lord king’s anger against the lord [Col. 1413D] of Canterbury; rather, he has laboured most zealously for his peace and safety, and by his exertions has very often conceived the best hope of it.

Therefore, humbly and with deepest affection, we present earnest prayers to your Sublimity for our lord and shepherd, whom the serenity of your grace has permitted to be transferred to the governance of our church: that you may worthily receive him when he comes to you, relieve his affliction and ours with paternal grace, and, as befits apostolic dignity, may your Holiness deign to maintain and uphold inviolate the remedies of appeals granted either to the oppressed or to those fearful even from some slight suspicion. May Christ almighty, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation (2 Cor. 1), preserve your Holiness [Col. 1414A] in long-lasting safety.

## LV. Of Stephen, Bishop of Meaux—For St Thomas in exile

To Pope ALEXANDER, STEPHEN, Bishop of Meaux.

Although a disciple is not above his master, and the judgments of shepherds should be revered by the sheep, not reconsidered, nevertheless it will not be unfitting if a son pleads with his father in a cause of compassion, and a humble servant urgently entreats a good lord for the good of peace. Not only the Roman Church, but the entire Catholic Church knows how unjustly the lord of Canterbury is exiled, how iniquitously he is beaten, and for how good a work he is stoned; and that, while he strives to be a true son of the Church, he has become a public enemy to the Church’s enemies. Indeed, he has been driven into exile for the very cause for which he deserved most worthily to be recalled from exile.

Yet iniquity has not stopped its mouth, nor has the mouth of those speaking wickedness been closed; rather, it persecutes him as if he were some dead ashes, and strives at the chief point of judgment to tear out the eyes of truth, which has already caused the feet of uprightness to turn aside in certain persons. Therefore, with filial devotion and every effort of earnest supplication, we ask that you exercise toward the lord of Canterbury your unwearied, steadfast, and customary circumspection. And while the crafty, moneyed devices of the English lie in wait for you, let papal constancy in no way be diminished; but, maintaining an unmoved and ineradicable steadfastness, preserve for yourselves the goodwill of the lord king and of the whole Gallican Church, [Col. 1414C] and increase their friendship.

## LVI. Of the same—For the same

To Pope ALEXANDER, STEPHEN, Bishop of Meaux.

Scandals are increasing, Father, in our times; but woe to him through whom scandal comes! (Matt. 18.) For if he who causes one of Christ’s little ones to stumble deserves a precipice, a millstone, and the deep, what judgment does he deserve, what punishments does he call down upon himself, who fills the whole Church of God with scandal and strikes the hearts of the saints, so that, if it were possible, even the elect might be moved away from faithfulness and devotion to the apostolic see?

Indeed, last year John of Oxford grievously wounded the Church by scandal: he caused those excommunicated by the lord of Canterbury, persisting in their crime which is known to all, to be absolved without—not merely, I say, satisfaction—but even the appearance of satisfaction. And, what I cannot say without grief and shame, they still lie upon the possessions of churches, despoil clerics, and plunder the goods of Christ’s poor, boasting that they are securely protected with impunity both by the authority of the Roman Church and by the iniquity of their king.

But that scandal, great though it was, was mere sport beside the things which the envoys of the king of England recently brought, and which were published at the latest conference of kings, to the greater wounding of the hearts of all your faithful people. For letters were read by which the lord of Canterbury—a man worthy of reverence for learning [Col. 1415A] and uprightness of character, but still more for the Lord’s cause and the freedom of the Church, whose defender he is—was deprived of his rightful power to restrain his subjects until he should return to the favour of that king, to whom he cannot be acceptable unless he is unacceptable to God, unfaithful to the apostolic see, and harmful to the whole Church.

The Most Christian King was confounded by this statement; the Gallican Church was astonished; the princes grieved that an open enemy of the French realm, a persecutor of the universal Church, an instigator of schism insofar as he could be, and a supporter of heretics had so much influence with you. But now, by God’s help, he has been brought to such a pass that, although he dares to threaten, he cannot harm in this matter. For he who frightens others is himself more afraid; and, God favouring, he is readier for flight than to dare await an enemy. For nowhere is he secure, and he fears domestic enemies no less than foreign ones.

How greatly our lord king was moved because you yielded so much to a persecutor of the Church and his enemy, I can scarcely tell without risking your Holiness’s displeasure with the reporter. Yet it is certain that this scandal cannot be quieted unless you apply a swift remedy. Nor are there lacking persons who urge him henceforth not to cease, out of reverence for you, to pursue his own and his kingdom’s advantage by making agreements with those who hate your name. Therefore may it please your Majesty, for the consolation of the lord of Canterbury—or rather, for the relief of the Church—to soften his mind and free the Gallican Church from so great a scandal. I do not think this can be done unless the innocent man is absolved and the wicked man defeated, whose power the Most High has already restrained, so that his threats need no longer be feared.

It must be feared lest other princes, by this example of abandonment of the Church, presume to do similar things; and whenever they are rebuked by Christ’s priests, strive to close their mouths and take away the power of their ministry. May your Holiness always be well and flourish.

## LVII. Of the same—On the lamentable slaughter of St Thomas

To the lord pope, the Bishop of Meaux.

Although the magnitude of the present matter, holy Father, calls for many words, nevertheless from the reports of many people and from the writings of a great many eminent men sent to you, we do not doubt that the death—precious in the sight of the Lord—of the archbishop, the new martyr as we believe, has been made known to you in full. We have therefore judged that a brief statement should be made to you on this particular point.

Passing over the tearful narrative of the death of so great a man—how, on the morrow of the Innocents, amid the observance of the Innocents, between the temple and the altar, he was slain by agents of Herodian cruelty, who declared before all the people that they acted in his blood by command of their king—we turn, under the most pressing necessity, to prayers alone. Let the blood of another Abel, unjustly shed by a most wicked Cain, move your fatherhood more deeply, as is fitting: blood which does not cease to cry to you from lands beyond the sea. Let the common sorrow and miserable lamentation of the whole [Col. 1416A] Church move you, and the danger that threatens. Let the sudden disturbance of the French kingdom move you; and above all, let the love of God and zeal for justice move you, by which you ought to burn no little against so great an author of crime.

With whatever heartfelt affection we can, therefore, we beseech your Holiness to regard as valid and order firmly observed the sentence promulgated, according to your command, by the lord Archbishop of Sens with the counsel of the provincial bishops, certain abbots, and a great many prudent and religious clerics, against him in his land on this side of the sea. And what could not be done by him, do not delay to supply yourselves, to whom fullness of power has been entrusted. So that that tyrant may not commit such acts without condemnation, and the new martyr may not be defrauded of his due exaltation, subject him and his entire land beyond the sea forcefully to ecclesiastical censure.

Nor should you in any way overlook the elders of the people from whom iniquity has gone forth—namely, the bishops previously condemned on one side (*ex parte*). Remain watchful lest the spirit of falsehood, pretended humility, the terror of frivolous threats, or a false interpretation of greater danger should in any degree cause your prudence to depart from the path of justice. May your Holiness prosper.

## LVIII. Of Milo, Bishop of Thérouanne—Against Gilbert, Bishop of London

To the most holy lord and dearest Father ALEXANDER, [Col. 1416C] by the grace of God supreme pontiff: MILO, Bishop of Thérouanne, greetings and devoted obedience in all things.

That ambition, the mother of impudence, is blind is clear from the fact that it plunges itself with equal rashness into things to be attempted and things not to be attempted; driven by the spurs of desire, it rushes headlong through right and wrong. Driven by the madness of this impulse, the Bishop of London seeks to overthrow his mother, the holy Church of Canterbury, to which he owes fidelity and obedience by his profession already made; and he boasts that he will acquire for the Church of London, over which he presides, the honour of the archbishopric.

It ought to have sufficed him that he caused his father, the lord of Canterbury, to be proscribed now for five years for confessing the truth, defending ecclesiastical freedom, and defending the privileges [Col. 1416D] of the apostolic see; and that—what is unquestionably decisive—he stirred the minds of the king and his officials to persecute the Church, and, disobeying your command, still retains the goods of clerics who have been despoiled for justice’s sake. For even if, in fraudulent contrivance against those despoiled, he has craftily ceased to possess them—or, as we more readily believe, pretends to have yielded possession to others—he is nonetheless to be condemned. This is especially so since he had previously received both your letters and those of his archbishop, commanding him, at peril of his rank and under anathema, to restore to clerics the property he held after taking it away, and, by ecclesiastical severity, to compel others who had seized the same persons’ goods at the king’s command to make restitution.

But because he still holds deeply in mind that the Church of Canterbury did not elect him as its bishop, as he had aspired to be, and because he has hitherto prospered in his wickedness and committed with impunity what wickedly pleased him, as his actions seem to testify, nothing will satisfy him unless he utterly uproots from the land an innocent and just man, his father, now so often a confessor. Recently, at a solemn assembly, he worked through royal officials to compel his brethren and fellow bishops to communicate with him and withdraw the obedience owed to the lord of Canterbury.

But, by God’s inspiration, the principal men were tested in his furnace; resisting him to his face, with God set before their eyes, they await on the one hand the king’s anger, which he stirs up and threatens, and on the other consolation from God. [Col. 1417B] We are neighbours of the English, and frequent intercourse takes place between our people and theirs; therefore what is carried on so publicly among them cannot easily be hidden from us. For a long time he concealed a wolf beneath sheepskins, and by the deception of his bearing and a feigned religious manner mocked the Church. What then remains, best Father, who by the Lord’s cooperation administer the salvation of the whole Church, except that, heeding the counsel of most wise Solomon, you cast out the mocker, already separated from Christ’s body, and contention will go out with him?

For he is the author and instigator of this whole schism; and, as though he were not sufficiently mad by himself, he incites the king. Therefore, prostrate at the feet of your Majesty, we beseech you to bring aid to the Church of Canterbury, and to crush both the aforesaid bishop and the others whom the archbishop struck with a just anathema, so that posterity hearing that such things were presumed—our sins demanding it—may rejoice that they were vigorously extinguished by you with the same severity of vengeance as befits Peter’s successor and Christ’s vicar. For it will greatly illuminate the titles of your glory, which may God perpetuate, if you leave a fitting example of so just a vengeance upon the reprobate. May your Holiness always prosper.

## LIX. Of Bernard, Bishop of Nevers—He entreats that, in the cause of St Thomas of Canterbury, the pope show some indulgence to the king of England

To Pope ALEXANDER, BERNARD, Bishop of Nevers.

[Col. 1417D] After the departure of your envoys from the lord king, we were summoned to the court. There we learned, from the reliable report of archbishops, bishops, and other magnates of his land who had assembled for this purpose, that the same lord king had received your envoys and letters with due reverence, since they appeared to promise him a ready favour of your kindness. They stated that, when your requests had been put before him, the aforesaid king had replied favourably on the advice of the said magnates: that, for love and honour of you, he would permit the Archbishop of Canterbury to return to his archbishopric and receive in full everything that he held when he left, the former dignity of his kingdom being, of course, preserved; and that henceforth he might possess them well and peacefully to God’s honour.

They also stated that, while a lengthy negotiation concerning this matter took place between the lord king and your aforesaid envoys, it was finally agreed on both sides that those who were present should immediately be absolved, and that one of them—namely Master Vivian—should immediately cross over to absolve those in England, while the other should remain for the execution of the agreed peace.

Later, however, withdrawing the consent they had given, they refused to accept the expression “preserving hereafter the royal dignity,” and declined to carry out the arrangements that had been made usefully and prudently, as though something in that expression detracted from ecclesiastical dignity. Yet to all sound-minded and right-thinking persons it seems that royal dignity promotes rather than diminishes ecclesiastical dignity, just as, conversely, ecclesiastical liberty adorns and honours royal majesty. For in these two things there is a most firm knot and friendly bond: ecclesiastical dignity advances royal excellence, and royal authority preserves ecclesiastical peace.

Therefore, cast at the knees of your fatherhood, with all the entreaty in our power, we implore your mercy not to choose, in so critical a situation, the points of letters and the wording of expressions rather than truth itself. Rather, according to the spirit of discernment and counsel given you by God, let the severity of discipline slumber a little in you [Col. 1418C], so that the kindness and gentleness of grace may have greater effect; and, as befits a compassionate father, prefer to the cause of one man the danger and peril of many, or indeed of countless persons.

## LX. Of Baldwin, Bishop of Noyon—Against Gilbert, Bishop of London

To Pope ALEXANDER, BALDWIN, Bishop of Noyon.

A breast must be iron or stone if it is not troubled by the labours and sufferings of the holy Church of Canterbury. And one has inhuman eyes who can refrain from tears amid so many tears of the Church. “She is lamentable to all good people,” but to none, or to few, in the French kingdom should she be more lamentable than to me, [Col. 1418D] for I have seen her glory, received her benefits, and known more intimately the devotion that she has always shown to the holy Roman Church.

For Canterbury has always had, in a manner unheard of elsewhere or rare, bishops who were confessors, who were either crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ or were exiled and proscribed for justice and the Church’s liberty. And he who now presides over her fills up the measure of his fathers; and, as has now become known to both kingdoms from the public confession of his persecutor himself, he has endured exile and proscription for five years for God’s honour.

Yet his predecessors, as one reads in histories or remembers among the living, bore the wrong of exile or proscription in their own persons alone. This man, however, has been banished with his whole household, all his kinsmen, servants, and friends, with grief so much more bitter as the burdens he endured from the torturers of the Church were more unjust and cruel. But far more grievous are the things he now suffers from brethren and household members.

Their standard-bearer is that Bishop of London, who for a long time, disguising a fox as a sheep, secretly carried fire and sword in his hands, to inflame the minds of the king and his officials against the Church and arm their hands. Because the Church of Canterbury did not elect him as its bishop, he is driven by blind ambition, as if turned to madness, and threatens, by the king’s power, to have the archiepiscopal see transferred to London.

His fellow bishops, recently warned by royal officials and, so far as possible, almost compelled to communicate with him and withdraw obedience from the Archbishop of Canterbury, refuted him, as was right, by the reason of law. They refused to agree any longer to his counsel and schemes, because they too await the kingdom of God and meanwhile consolation from the apostolic see. Therefore may it please your Holiness to crush with such severity both the aforesaid bishop, the author and instigator of this schism, and the remaining wrongdoers against the Church whom the lord of Canterbury, their offences requiring it, bound with the chain of anathema, that others terrified by their example may not dare attempt similar acts.

## LXI. Of the same and of Maurice, Bishop of Paris—After a conference was appointed for the Archbishop of Canterbury at Pontoise, the king of England, abandoning the conference he had appointed in insult to the lord of Canterbury, hastily returned to England

[Col. 1419C]

To Pope ALEXANDER, BERNARD, Bishop of Noyon, and MAURICE, Bishop of Paris.

We remember that we have often offered prayers to your Holiness for the English Church and the venerable Archbishop of Canterbury. Nor, God willing, can our persistence be restrained until you show him mercy and the right hand of apostolic majesty represses the malice of those who endeavour to extinguish Christ in him and destroy the liberty of the whole Church.

The harms which he has long and bravely sustained are indeed great and many; the injuries he patiently received in himself and his people are exceedingly atrocious and without precedent. Yet, by divine grace working with him, they have now, as we firmly believe, resulted in great advantage to the Church. For with that king of the English—whom it does not satisfy to torment his subjects with unlawful servitude, oppress the innocent without cause, deceive contractors, plot against neighbours, and defraud lords, unless he also tramples the Church contrary to right and law—there is now no mention of customs or dignities. He asks only that the aforesaid Archbishop of Canterbury render him what an archbishop owes the king, and that he in turn render the archbishop what a king owes an archbishop.

Recently, receiving fuller hope of reconciliation on the strength of this promise, the same Archbishop of Canterbury went in all humility and devotion as far as Pontoise, trusting that he would have a meeting with the king, as the venerable men, the Archbishop [Col. 1420A] of Rouen and the Bishop of Sées, had promised in their letters, and besides them the Abbot of Cîteaux and Brother Geoffrey of Auxerre, whom the aforesaid king had sent to Sens to the repeatedly mentioned archbishop, in order to arrange this conference.

But the same king, when his envoys—Master Richard Barre and Ralph, Archdeacon of Llandaff—returned from your Holiness, withdrew from the agreements in his customary fashion. He said that he would hasten to England in order to have his son crowned, to the harm and injury of the Church of Canterbury, by the hand of the Lord Archbishop of York or another bishop. And, as is widely reported among us, his aforesaid envoys boasted that they had obtained from you both this coronation of the new king and the absolution of those whom the lord of Canterbury had deservedly condemned by anathema.

Thus the repeatedly mentioned Archbishop of Canterbury returned with the matter unresolved, while the Most Christian King grieved with him and the kingdom sympathized; everyone wondering whether even now the apostolic see could be deceived in so conspicuous a case. For who, and for what cause, will be condemned, if such a great and evident injury to Christ, harm to the Church, and act of contempt are not exacted from that king? Who that is innocent will be delivered from the hand of the slanderer, if help is not given to the lord of Canterbury and those exiled with him?

For the measures which his envoys boast that they have nullified seemed especially suited to restrain the man—or rather, iniquity itself. And he had already learned by the punishment of others what ecclesiastical vigour can accomplish against the malice of powers. The Church’s peace was believed to be at the door; and the king himself, having put aside his fierceness, was thought even by his closest associates to seek it sincerely for God’s honour.

But if these concessions are granted to him even after the injury he inflicted upon you in the person of Blessed Peter’s imitator, your lord Gratian, and the other envoys, this is the same as cutting off every path of peace and every hope of the English Church. But may this be far from the holiness of your pontificate: that such a manifest injury be inflicted upon Christ’s confessors, and that, by a pernicious example, iniquity be armed and strengthened in tyrants against the Church. For all hoped that he could no longer deceive your prudence, mock your Holiness, or escape the hand of just severity.

The misery of the Church and the boundless affliction of the innocent which we see have compelled us to use many words. But the chief desire of ourselves and of the whole Gallican Church is that you remove so great a scandal through swift aid, make the aforesaid king content with the things fitting for a Christian king, and compel him to leave unimpaired to the King of kings His privileges.

## LXII. Of Maurice, Bishop of Paris—For St Thomas of Canterbury

To the most holy Father and lord ALEXANDER, by the grace of God supreme pontiff and universal pope: MAURICE, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Paris, fullness of obedience, service, and devotion.

Your Highness should know, most serene Father, that [Col. 1421A] recently negotiations were held near Paris for restoring peace between the king of England and the lord of Canterbury. And, as I heard Master Vivian declare, the king of England granted peace on these terms: namely, that, in accordance with your command and counsel, for the love of God and of yourself and for the honour of holy Church, he would receive the lord of Canterbury into his favour; grant peace and full security, from himself and his people, to all who were in exile for his sake; restore to him the Church of Canterbury in that fullness and liberty in which he had held it most fully after becoming archbishop; and likewise restore to him and his followers all the possessions which he had held, to be held as freely, peacefully, and honourably as the Church and he himself had held them more freely and honourably after his promotion to the archbishopric. [Col. 1421B] He would likewise permit him to possess, to dispose of as he pleased as of his own, all churches and prebends belonging to the archbishopric which had become vacant after he left the land. All these things indeed he granted.

Nevertheless, he utterly refused to receive him with the kiss of peace. Since this seemed suspicious to many prudent persons present, and since they understood that in this way the lord of Canterbury could neither return into the full favour of the king of England nor obtain a complete peace, the peace remained imperfect. Furthermore, the lord of Canterbury required that one portion of what had been taken from him be restored, while the other should be left for his support until he should have your counsel on the matter from religious men. [Col. 1421C] For it would appear unfitting, highly damaging to himself, and a pernicious precedent for holy Church, if he were to remit completely everything taken from him, as the king of England demanded; since, during his absence, the buildings of the Church of Canterbury had been demolished, he had only a meagre recourse to its scattered possessions, and he was held bound by the gravest debt.

Therefore, with bended knees and with all the devotion of my heart, I beseech Your Holiness—whom I have repeatedly entreated on behalf of the Church of Canterbury—mercifully to consider the miseries of your daughter, so long in danger; to provide for her honour and advantage; and, seeking an honourable settlement, to watch with fatherly affection for his prompt recall from exile. It appears, moreover, that the lord of Canterbury [Col. 1421D] can and ought to require no less from the king of England, especially since the lord king publicly said that full favour was by no means restored to the said archbishop of Canterbury, nor would he in any way enter into this settlement unless it were confirmed by the kiss of peace.

### LXIII. Of the same writer.—Against Gilbert, Bishop of London

To Pope ALEXANDER, MAURICE, Bishop of Paris.

License to sin gives birth to and nourishes offences; and men rush onward to greater crimes while they sin in the security of impunity. For some time that bishop of London—lest I call him a wolf, the forerunner of Antichrist—lay concealed [Col. 1422A] in sheepskins. Since his malice was not restrained during the first devastation of Christ’s fold, together with his prince, whose power he abused, he now, impatient of discipline, plots to tear apart the unity of the English Church. For since, his sins demanding it, he was delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, he has sown dissensions, scattered scandals, plotted schisms and seditions, and openly performed works such as Satan, once released, may be thought to perform.

Through the king’s officials he attempted to induce the bishops to communicate with him and to withdraw obedience from the lord of Canterbury, who in our age has set himself before the western lands as a confessor of truth and an example of virtue. But, by God’s inspiration, their leading men resisted him to his face, because he was blameworthy. [Col. 1422B] He thus advanced to such shamelessness as publicly to say that he owed no obedience to the Church of Canterbury, because, after his translation to the Church of London, he had made no profession to it concerning the rendering of obedience. He even dared boast that he would have the archiepiscopal see transferred to London, so that the city which, he says, had had an archflamen before the time of blessed Gregory, apostle of the English, might now possess an archbishop in Christian times.

Does not one who does and says such things, most holy Father, deservedly seem mad? Certainly this man is not from God: he does not keep obedience, does not know faith, and is the author and instigator of schism. May it therefore please Your Majesty—whom God preserve [Col. 1422C] for long ages—to aid the lord of Canterbury, who, as is well known, has now for five years courageously and cheerfully endured exile for justice, for the liberty of the Church, and for the defence of the privileges of the Apostolic See; and to dash and crush against the apostolic rock both the aforesaid bishop of London and the other evildoers of the Church, whom, though late, he struck with anathema as they deserved, beside which their instigators were swallowed up. Otherwise, there is reason to fear that, if—God forbid—so great a crime remains unpunished, it will swiftly bring about the ruin of both the English and French Churches and the overthrow of religion.

### LXIV. Of Matthew, Bishop of Troyes.—For St Thomas of Canterbury

[Col. 1422D]

To Pope ALEXANDER, MATTHEW, Bishop of Troyes.

I act more confidently before my lord, recalling with what condescension so great a Majesty has always loved, honoured, and elevated my lowliness. Indeed, much honour was added to the rank I held, but far more burden; so that my shoulders must necessarily fail unless the Lord puts forth His hand and your clemency adds its grace. For if your providence deigns to turn the eyes of its vigilance toward our regions, it will see great afflictions attending many good persons and still graver struggles threatening many more. Since I cannot correct these things as bishop, and dare not dissemble them, for fear of divine judgment and because of the office I have undertaken, anyone who doubts that I am [Col. 1423A] in straits is altogether ignorant of my condition.

Yet my hope is in God and in you, to whom I judge that both my own distresses and those of my friends should be referred, especially the distresses of those who labour for the confession of truth and justice. One of these, and most worthy of your aid, is the lord of Canterbury, who has now for five years endured among us a proscribed exile with great patience for God’s honour. Hitherto he has been endangered by the savagery of tyrants and the plots of informers; but now he is more gravely endangered by false brethren. The first among them is that bishop of London, who, under the name of bishop, as will become more fully known from the letters of the lord of Sens, shows himself a raging parricide.

May it please Your Holiness, whose safety may the Lord in His mercy deign perpetually to preserve for His Church, [Col. 1423B] that both the aforesaid bishop and the others whom the lord of Canterbury condemned with anathema for their deserts be crushed with such severity that the rest may be deterred from like audacity by the example of punishment.

### LXV. A. Certesiensis.—For Gilbert, Bishop of London

To his venerable and most dear Father and lord ALEXANDER, by the grace of God supreme pontiff and universal pope, Brother A., unworthy minister of Certesiensis, reverence of sincere love and the obedience due, together with all the faithful.

Most dear Father and lord, we humbly entreat Your Majesty on behalf of the lord bishop of London [Col. 1423C] that you may kindly receive him when he comes to you, for the love of God and in view of your fatherly regard, and may hear him with especial kindness in his affairs. We therefore pray your clemency for him with greater confidence, because for many years we have known him to be a wise, honourable, discreet, and religious man, adorned by God’s grace with so many and such great virtues that he is, and is believed to be, one of the most honourable persons in the whole realm of England. By his example and manner of life many people are restrained from their wicked iniquities and invited to honourable conduct.

Yet the enemy envied his good deeds, and with that enemy many are his enemies, interpreting him maliciously and, having circumvented your ears, putting forward falsehood as truth; nor do they fear, in a certain presumptuous guise of truth, to deceive your ears with false suggestions. [Col. 1423D] For, as we have heard, the enemies of truth say that he was the cause and origin of the whole disturbance and discord which existed between the lord of Canterbury and the king of the English. How utterly false and alien from all truth this is, those men know, and so do we with them, who were frequently present at their conversations.

In truth, lord, we can testify to what we saw and heard: the lord of London worked in every way he could, opportunely and inopportunely, to restore peace and concord between the lord of Canterbury and the king of the English. And if he did not obtain what he desired, he deserves no less praise, because [Col. 1424A] he did what he ought. For the king’s heart was not in his hand but in God’s hand, to incline it wherever He wished. Let therefore our lord and most dear Father open the eyes of his mercy and receive the prayers of our lowliness, together with those of others, for the lord of London, so that he may restore him to the peace of his Church. We believe—and believe certainly—that through him great peace will be restored throughout England, if he returns to his own country with your favour. May God save and preserve our most dear Father, sound and safe, for his Church. Farewell.

### LXVI. Of Rotrou, Archbishop of Rouen.—Of the same purport as Letter 61

To Pope ALEXANDER, ROTROU, Archbishop of Rouen.

[Col. 1424B] Having been summoned by our lord the king, we came to court; and when some progress had already been made with your legates concerning your mandates, we learned by report—through the wholly trustworthy account of the archbishops and bishops who had come for this purpose, and whom we naturally believe, as we ourselves do—that the lord king of the English received your messengers and letters with so much greater joy and eagerness as they seemed to promise him a greater measure of your gracious favour.

Accordingly, having most kindly heeded your request concerning peace with the archbishop of Canterbury and the return of his followers, with the counsel of archbishops, bishops, abbots, religious persons, and the leading men of his realm, he granted that the archbishop should return [Col. 1424C] to his archbishopric, receive it in all the integrity in which he held it when he departed, and henceforth possess it well and peacefully, for God’s honour, while of course preserving the former dignity of his kingdom. When a prolonged negotiation therefore arose between the lord king and your messengers concerning this, they finally agreed upon a formula pleasing to both parties: that they should at once absolve those then present; that one of them, namely Master Vivian, should immediately cross over to absolve those who were in England; and that the other should remain on this side of the sea to carry out the peace that had been agreed.

Afterward, however, they withdrew their consent and refused to accept the formula already adopted for the future preservation of royal [Col. 1424D] dignity, refusing to carry out what had already been beneficially arranged. I therefore, together with the aforesaid persons of considerable authority who were present, being sent for so great a good as peace, laboured with every vigilance and care that, as had been said, with God’s honour set first and the ancient dignity of the realm duly maintained, your messengers might receive with joy a proposal of royal dignity that was excellent and worthy of all acceptance, lest so great a good should fail. When much effort had been spent on our persuasion, but nothing achieved, we grieved deeply—especially since we know for certain that, in preserving royal dignity, ecclesiastical liberty or dignity is in no way burdened.

For ecclesiastical dignity advances rather than diminishes [Col. 1425A] royal dignity; and royal dignity has customarily preserved rather than destroyed ecclesiastical liberty. Indeed, ecclesiastical and royal dignity meet as though in mutual embraces, since kings attain no salvation without the Church, nor does the Church attain peace without royal protection. Falling therefore at the knees of your mercy, with all the devotion we can, we beseech Your Holiness not to think that the strokes of letters and verbal formulations should be embraced rather than the matter itself; but, according to the spirit of discernment given you by God, act so that the cause of one person may not turn to the ruin of many—indeed, almost innumerable—persons. For gentleness of grace sometimes contributes more to the good of peace [Col. 1425B] than the severity of discipline.

### LXVII. Of William, Archbishop of Sens.—He prays that the sentence of excommunication pronounced by the Archbishop of Canterbury against the bishops of London and Salisbury be ratified

To Pope ALEXANDER, WILLIAM, Archbishop of Sens.

Still, Father, we are compelled to beseech your mercy on behalf of the venerable lord of Canterbury—or rather, on behalf of the Church and God’s cause, for which he exposed his life—that you may powerfully wield with him the sword of blessed Peter in defence of the liberty of the Church and the privileges of the Apostolic See. For now, if it please you, it is time [Col. 1425C] to pity him and to take action against those who, while the truth of the Gospel shines throughout the world, labour in the time of your pontificate to strip Christ’s confessors of the mention of divine honour.

He himself, in order to deliver his soul before God and faithfully perform his part of the office entrusted to him, though he judged that the head of error ought still to be spared—waiting for it to be instructed unto repentance through the punishment of the members—bound with the bond of anathema the instigators of schism: the bishops of London and Salisbury, Ranulf de Broc, and others whose names have been specified to you. Your devoted son, the most Christian king of France, as you may observe from his letters, prays that you approve what the archbishop did in condemnation of their rashness and malice. And we beseech you with all the devotion we can [Col. 1425D] muster to add the aid of apostolic majesty as well, because there is hope that the Church will readily be freed if your severity restrains and subdues these men. Otherwise, we fear that your aforesaid son, the lord king, and the whole realm of France may be afflicted by no smaller scandal than that stirred up by John of Oxford at his return.

### LXVIII. Of the same writer.—Against Gilbert, Bishop of London

To Pope ALEXANDER, WILLIAM, Archbishop of Sens.

Impunity, mother of crimes and fruitful in offences, has torn apart the unity of the English Church and filled the French Church with most bitter scandal. The head, cause, and fuel of such great evils [Col. 1426A] is that bishop of London, who, now at last changed from a dragon into a lion, openly exercises the wickedness conceived in ambition, since, though late, his sins demanding it, he was delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. For, having been author and instigator of schism, and having laid snares to proscribe and kill the innocent, he now speaks openly and “utters no proverb.” Yet he seeks, with the powers of his king, to overthrow his mother, the Church of Canterbury, to whom he is bound by his profession to render obedience, boasting that he will have the archiepiscopal see transferred to London.

Recently his brethren laudably resisted him to his face when, through the king’s officials, he shamelessly pressed them to communicate with him and to withdraw due obedience from their archbishop. [Col. 1426B] Is he not a manifest forerunner of Antichrist, striving so openly to divide the Church’s unity, sowing discord among brethren, multiplying scandals, afflicting the Church, and delivering the innocent to tyrants’ hands for proscription and slaughter? If unity is removed from the Catholic Church, who or what prevents heresies from springing up? What place will there be for unity unless the virtue of obedience joins together the members of Christ, and charity strengthens them toward one another in faith and truth?

Therefore, best of Fathers, since he has been caught in the works of his hands and the poisoned fruits produced by this unhappy tree call for Peter’s axe, grant him, if you please, this mercy: that, his malice having been broken [Col. 1426C] and his title of bishop erased—for he bears the mark of the beast—he may no longer be able to do harm, but may be compelled to show in conduct the monk which he promised in clothing. The lord of Canterbury has suffered enough and more than enough. Unless you cause peace and security to be restored to him through the arm of apostolic power, and satisfaction made for what has been taken, there is reason to fear that the Church will soon suffer an irreparable loss and that both the present age and posterity will be provoked and encouraged by a pernicious example to crush the Church. May Your Holiness always prosper and flourish.

### LXIX. Of the same writer.—In the cause of St Thomas of Canterbury

To the lord pope, the Archbishop of Sens, greeting and every obedience with the utmost devotion.

[Col. 1426D] We can testify all the more faithfully as to how the cause of the lord of Canterbury recently proceeded at the second conference of the kings because we were admitted more intimately to all that was done there, and applied effort and diligence that the king of England might comply with your admonitions and obey your commands. But after he had with difficulty received your threatening letters and for a long time evaded the insistence of the religious men whom you had sent by a variety of mutually inconsistent replies, he at last, upon our and their sharper insistence, gave the answer he chose.

For he said that he had not expelled the lord of Canterbury from his kingdom. Yet, if he wished to return, and to observe what his predecessors had observed and what he himself had promised, he could return and have peace there. But unless he promised this simply and [Col. 1427A] absolutely, he would not return to England again. And because his answers frequently contradicted one another, so that your messengers had no idea by what knot they might hold their Proteus, so often changing his face, we advised them to ask him for a reply in letters patent stating what he intended to do in response to your request, so that they might report it safely and faithfully to you. Although they pressed this request strongly with the aid of intercessors, the king utterly rejected it.

He was then asked by many persons at least to allow the innocent people whom he had proscribed to return home. But he could be induced by no argument or persuasion to extend to them any consolation.

When these matters had been reported to the archbishop, he answered [Col. 1427B] that he was ready to do, for the recovery of the king’s favour and the Church’s favour, whatever he ought, whatever he could, and whatever his predecessors had done, with his order preserved in every respect. But he said that it was unlawful for him to enter into a new form of obligation and promise that he would follow anyone’s precedents unless his order were preserved, especially without the authority of the Apostolic See. This was so both because imposing a new form of obligation upon ecclesiastical men would be a pernicious precedent and because, as he asserts, when you absolved him from the obligation of observing the customs—which he had made unwillingly and under compulsion—you specifically forbade him, in the hearing of many, after grave and just rebuke, to bind himself further, especially in matters [Col. 1427C] capable of involving any snare, without expressly stating that the honour of God and his order were to remain unimpaired.

For anyone who promises his subjects a custom or permission for unlawful things seems to renounce a pastor’s office. If a bishop, by consent or dissimulation, waters nurseries of vices so that, as they grow strong, the word of God becomes empty or wholly perishes, who will uproot thorns and thistles from the Church? The shepherds of churches are bound to extirpate perverse customs, while he is now required and compelled to swear to their terms. He added also that he could not preserve the faith due to the Roman Church and the customs required of him, because they openly attack the law of God and the privilege of the Apostolic See.

And because neither our words nor those of the religious men found acceptance with the king, nor did the authority of Your Majesty reap fruits of obedience, we departed from him sorrowful, the lord of Canterbury’s peace unresolved. [Col. 1427D] And he, as we have learned for certain, awaits the return of his messengers. If, as is just and is hoped by your faithful servants, you send them back disappointed, we believe that the Church of Canterbury will soon have peace and that the reputation of the Roman Church will be restored in the French Church and throughout the West.

We put this forward not from any bitterness of mind against the king, who recently returned to our favour and with whom we made true peace. Rather, what we have seen, heard, and handled with our hands, we testify for the truth of justice, for the honour of the Church, and for the faith and reverence which we owe to the Apostolic [Col. 1428A] See. We therefore beseech Your Paternity to exercise courageously the rigour of justice which, pressed by the man’s obstinacy, you have at last laudably taken up. For if he sees your constancy, he is believed likely to yield readily and will not leave to contemporary or future princes the feared example of presumption.

### LXX. Of the same writer.—He laments that Gilbert, Bishop of London, has been absolved. On the coronation of King Henry’s son

To Pope ALEXANDER, WILLIAM, Archbishop of Sens.

Let Your Holiness, most holy Father, hear patiently what we say, for our soul abides in bitterness. Both your most devoted son, the most Christian [Col. 1428B] king of the Franks, and the entire French Church are troubled by the scandals which flow from the Apostolic See in the days of your pontificate. For, as our countrymen say, Satan is there released for the destruction of the whole Church, Christ is crucified anew, and one who is a manifest sacrilegious man and murderer is forgiven.

We pursued before you the cause of the English Church and, on our departure, believed that some aid had been given to it. But when, without our knowledge, you caused the bishop of London to be absolved, matters went in the opposite direction and horns were given to the sinner. For behold: that king, toward whom you were too gracious, has had his son consecrated king—if it is indeed a consecration which is performed by excommunicated persons, enemies of the Holy Spirit, and assailants of the Church—and this to the injury of the Church of Canterbury and of the lord king of France, whose daughter that king, God’s and men’s enemy, refused to have share in this consecration. [Col. 1428C] That man of York performed this consecration, or rather desecration, by your authority, as they say, with the bishop of London and certain others, bishops in name only, assisting him, whose memory is accursed.

Therefore, Father, henceforth provide for that Church which has perished in your hands, lest her blood be demanded of you. We do not believe that your reputation and conscience can otherwise be redeemed unless you crush the aforesaid evildoers by apostolic power.

### LXXI. Of the same writer.—On the lamentable murder of St Thomas of Canterbury

[Col. 1428D]

To ALEXANDER, supreme pontiff, the humble minister of the Church of Sens: the spirit of counsel and fortitude, with every service of obedience.

While writing these things—or rather, before I wrote them—I immediately paused and stood in profound doubt as to what manner of expression could set before the eyes of your clemency the atrocity of the crime lately committed and the savagery of the punishment recently inflicted upon the Lord’s anointed. And indeed I think that the cry of the world has already filled the ears of Your Holiness, seated as you are in the watchtower of the world: how that notorious man—not king of England, but rather enemy of the angels and of Christ—has recently acted wickedly against the saint, against the son of Your right hand, whom You [Col. 1429A] have strengthened for Yourself.

Although you may perhaps have received an account of his departure from this world and the manner of his death from diverse, even contrary reports, I report more certainly and faithfully what became known to me from those who were present, and briefly set forth the sequence of the crime committed—though its enormity cannot be conceived. On the day after the feast of the Innocents, in the Nativity of the Lord, as the sun set, about the hour of Vespers, four armed men who had been admitted first approached that strong athlete of Christ most terribly and insolently. I insert their names here, that their memory may remain in perpetual curse: William de Tracy, Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, and Richard Brito.

At their first approach, though greeted by the holy man, they did not return his greeting, since, having already entered the paths of destruction, they openly rejected salvation. Rather, with excessive obstinacy and harshness, upon entering they demanded whether he would immediately absolve, at the king’s command, bishops who had been suspended or excommunicated. [Col. 1429B] He replied modestly that this belonged to the judgment of your singular primacy and that he claimed nothing for himself where so great an authority intervened. They at once disowned him on the king’s behalf and immediately went out to their company. As they departed, they ordered the knights who belonged to the household of the man of God, in the king’s name, to leave likewise and to await the outcome silently and patiently, under peril of their lives and proscription of all their goods. A similar royal edict was publicly issued throughout the city.

But that singular athlete of Christ in our days despised the threats of princes; and he was with difficulty compelled, after much urging, to leave the very place where he had, as it were, already received the message of death—and this only lest he should seem unwilling to be brought to completion. By God’s better ordering, he entered the metropolitan church, dedicated in honour of Christ Himself; and there Christ’s anointed deserved to be sacrificed for Christ’s name, where Christ is sacrificed every day. Praying, he voluntarily offered himself as a peaceful sacrifice to God between the horns of the cross and the altar. [Col. 1429C] For as the hour drew near, he stretched out his neck, bowed his head, received the cup of salvation, and was scalped by the four aforesaid armed men. Before this, however, he had been assailed with insults and many reproaches, so that he might not be deprived of any feature of his Lord’s Passion. He also gave orders that his household should be kept unharmed. Thus the pontiff alone entered the holy places, not without blood.

And because, after the passing of the holy man, we have heard from the frequent report of many persons that certain memorable things occurred through the Lord’s working, they must by no means be passed over. For it is said, and constantly affirmed, that after his Passion he appeared in visions to many people, to whom he declared that he was not dead but alive; and he showed not wounds, but only the scars of wounds.

Act therefore, O man of God; put on the strength of those whose seat you hold, O son of the “shaken out.” Let mercy move you on this side, indignation on that. You owe the one to the son, the other to the tyrant. Increase on earth the glory of him whom God so wondrously glorifies from heaven. [Col. 1430A] But inflict disgrace upon him who so horribly persecuted God in his own land; who, in the womb of his own mother, slew his own father; who twisted the sides of your own belly, tore out your entrails, and trampled on the ground your son, whom, like a mother, you loved uniquely; and who, through I know not what uncircumcised and unclean men, slaughtered him so faithlessly and inhumanely, neither fearing a father’s offence nor pitying age. Therefore, as you have received their ministry, receive their zeal as well; and because you behold Ahab’s crime, let Elijah’s emulation seize you. For Ahab killed and took possession. But what was Ahab? When the whole character of this crime, so laboriously committed, is weighed, Ahab himself is justified by comparison.

This indeed is the deed which holds by far the first place among all crimes of criminals that are read or reported, [Col. 1430B] surpassing all Nero’s wickedness, Herod’s savagery, Julian’s perfidy, and even the sacrilegious destruction wrought by Judas the traitor. Consider what a person was slain, in what church, and what a time the tyrant chose to perpetrate the crime: namely, the Nativity of the Lord and the day immediately following that of the holy Innocents, so that in our own days a new Herod might be raised up from the old. Even the public grant of peace did not recall the traitor from his crime.

And, as though he were not sufficiently mad by himself, he had instigators of his madness, giving horns to the sinner: namely, those false brethren, to be perpetually detested by the whole world of churches—Roger of York, arch-devil, and [Col. 1430C] those of London and Salisbury, not bishops but apostates—who killed your son, their brother Joseph, not mystically but in truth, neither fearing the curse of their father now old, nor sparing his grief or age. May your holy consolation, holy Father, decree that their present life be in perpetual bitterness and their memory in eternal curse.

I earnestly beg that the bearers of this letter, Master Alexander and Master Gunther, worthy and diligent men who were united to God’s holy martyr in life and cannot be separated from him in death, be commended to your charity. I have more privately instilled into their ears, to be disclosed to you, what I did not wish to commit to the prattling strokes of letters.

### LXXII. Of the same writer.—Of similar purport

[Col. 1430D]

To the most holy lord and Father ALEXANDER, by the grace of God supreme pontiff, WILLIAM, humble minister of the Church of Sens: greeting and the obedience due with every devotion.

To your apostolate, holy Father, all power has been given in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28); the two-edged sword is in your hands (Psalm 149). You have been set over nations and kingdoms, to bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron manacles (ibid.). See then, lord, and consider whom they have thus gleaned (Lamentations 2). For the boar out of the forest has laid waste the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts, and the solitary wild beast has devoured it (Psalm 79). The Church of Canterbury—indeed, the universal Church—[Col. 1431A] pours out before you, from the ends of the earth, tears dripping with blood and bitter with anguish, because she has been made like a target for the arrow (Lamentations 3), and has become a reproach to her neighbours (Psalm 88). Those who see her shake their heads over her (Lamentations 2), saying: “Where is their God?” (Psalm 113).

But she herself, groaning and turned backward, cries in the ears of the Lord of Hosts: “Avenge, Lord, the blood of Your servant and martyr, the Archbishop of Canterbury, who was slain—or rather crucified—for the liberty of the Church.” Holy Father, in your days a dreadful word, a heinous deed, an enormous crime has been done, at which whoever hears of it shall have both ears tingle (1 Samuel 3). It has not been heard of in Teman, nor seen in Canaan (Baruch 3). For another Herod, seed of Canaan and not of Judah, brood of vipers (Matthew 3), having sent executioners from his side, did not shrink from ploughing with deep wounds the sign of the Lord’s Passion borne above upon his head, nor from defacing with foul wishes the heavenly image. [Col. 1431B] Alas! As the whole Church declares, both the cause and the punishment make him a martyr: the punishment, the pain of the Passion inflicted upon him; the cause, the rigour of ecclesiastical censure, because he fought for the law of his God even unto death.

It is therefore your concern, most merciful Father, guardian of the walls of Jerusalem (Isaiah LXXII), to apply a remedy to what has happened and foresight for what is to come. For what place can be safe if tyrannical frenzy stains the Holy of Holies with blood and with impunity tears apart the vicars of Christ, the pillars of the Church? Let ecclesiastical laws therefore rise up; let heavenly laws be armed; let vengeance for the blood of the glorious martyr who cries out from England enter into your presence. For it will cry out and shake not only earth but heaven also. Thus provide for our grief in such a way as also to provide for your honour and for the salvation of the Church.

Moreover, we have deemed it fitting to inform your Holiness that, since you had commanded the lord Archbishop of Rouen and ourselves to place under interdict the king of England’s lands on this side of the sea, if he did not keep the peace which he had promised to the lord Archbishop of Canterbury of glorious memory, adding also that, if either of us could not or would not take part in carrying out the matter, the other should nevertheless execute your command [Col. 1431D]. The aforesaid Archbishop of Rouen, after we had caused your letters to be presented to him, informed us that he would come to Sens and proceed in accordance with the form of the apostolic mandate. But when he had come there with Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, Giles, bishop of Évreux, Roger, bishop of Worcester, and many others, both clerics and laymen of the household of the aforesaid king, after many evasions and excuses he appealed from the matter to the Apostolic See, replied that he had set out upon the road to your presence, and that he did not wish to inflict a harsher exasperation upon the aforesaid king.
