But we, knowing that whoever scorns obedience to apostolic commands incurs the vice of paganism [Col. 1432A], in accordance with the tenor of your mandate, by the common counsel of all our venerable brethren the bishops, and of the abbots of Saint-Denis, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Pontigny, Wall… Cenn…, and of many other religious and wise men, pronounced sentence upon his lands on this side of the sea; and we enjoined the aforesaid archbishop and bishops, on your behalf, to ensure that it was observed. For we know that he neither restored the possessions as he had promised, nor furnished security, as the martyr’s death shows. Moreover, through the Carthusian whom we had sent to him, he informed us that he had caused his death and had killed him. Therefore we beseech your clemency [Col. 1432B] to hold the aforesaid sentence ratified and, as befits your majesty and is expedient for the safety of the Church, to cause it to be observed in such a manner that the honor of God and of yourself may be preserved, and that we, who embrace your Holiness with the devotion which you know, may not on this account be made a mockery of. Farewell, and act as becomes your majesty and holiness.

LXXIII. Of William, bishop of Sens, legate of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 1431] Later archbishop of Reims. See *Patrologia*, vol. CCIX.].—He commends Hugh of Campfleury, bishop of Soissons and chancellor of France. (About the year 1170.)

[DUCHESNE, *Rerum Francicarum Scriptores*, IV, 575.]

[Col. 1432C]

To his most beloved lord and Father A., by the grace of God supreme pontiff, WILLIAM, by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Sens and legate of the Apostolic See, devoted obedience.

Because from the serenity of your fatherhood and the abundant richness of your holiness we presume more upon your grace than upon our own merits, we do not at all hesitate to commend to your apostolic office those whom we love most tenderly and know to have proved most faithful to you; judging that we shall be heard all the more readily in proportion as the urgency of our prayers shines with a more honorable affection. Therefore we commend to your kindness as ourselves our venerable brother, the bishop of Soissons and chancellor of the illustrious king of the Franks, a man discreet, [Col. 1432D] upright, learned, and most steadfast in your affairs. We earnestly ask that in all matters in which you can hear and support him, you may kindly do so, if it please you; so that he may henceforth be more faithful from being faithful, and that those who hear of it may flee more ardently to the bosom of your clemency. For whatever is done to him, we shall regard as done to ourselves. May your fatherhood prosper.

LXXIV. Of an anonymous writer.—On the murder of St Thomas of Canterbury.

I had been about to communicate certain matters to your magnificence with tranquillity of mind, but the unforeseen outcome of a pitiable [Col. 1433A] event interrupted my pen and changed the pleasure intended for so great a lord into matter for tears. For behold: that man Thomas, prelate of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, endowed with every uprightness of character and heart, a man of noble spirit, had returned to pastoral care with this resolve: casting all his thoughts upon the Lord, to strive to order everything according to God and for the honor of the Church; to weigh in the balance of equity not what was his own but what was Jesus Christ’s and what he knew would be Christ’s; and, though his enemies said that he had returned driven by the goads of leonine ferocity, he was manifestly shown to be a lover of dovelike simplicity, softened by lamb-like gentleness. This man, gentle and meek in this manner, a certain people of sacrilegious ferocity—perhaps a criminal sect—forced, alas, into the very church of the undivided Trinity [Col. 1433B], before the altar, though he resisted and wished to set himself against the evildoers, and though his clerics who were with him had compelled him there. With drawn swords they addressed him in these words: “Flee, traitor; behold, cruel death hangs over you.” They had first asked, because of the multitude of monks and clerics present: “Where is the archbishop?” He answered them in this way, in a low but very audible voice: “I am he; and you, Reginald, with your accomplices, go back, for you do not know what you are doing. Yet if you seek to kill me, do not touch the others. In the name of Him who deigned to die for me, His servant, I am prepared to meet death.” Then he offered his head to the striker to be struck; and the latter immediately severed his neck as if making a crown, and, mingling blood with brains, sent his body, bowed as though in prayer, to the pavement, and his spirit to Abraham’s bosom [Col. 1433C].

I certainly was not present at these events; but I came to Canterbury on that very day and saw the lifeless body amid sobbing and tears. So far as the disfigurement wrought by the blood allowed, the expression of his face remained serene and somewhat like that of a living man—indeed, to tell the truth, it seemed to those standing by that he was heard as though complaining in a living voice: “Avenge, Lord, the blood of your servant which has been shed.” Let therefore the provident and settled discernment of good minds consider what times are being changed by the enormity of so great a crime: the evil of its own day does not suffice; for from the earliest rage of persecutors it has been unheard of that so horrible a wickedness should be perpetrated. Only this is lacking from the tales: that a place which protects robbers, thieves, murderers, and criminals of whatever sort in unshaken peace should exhibit an innocent man—a gentle, peaceable ruler of the Church—as the object of an expiatory outrage [Col. 1433D]. Let the keen investigation of your foresight foresee, if there is any grief like that which these falsehoods of frenzy are believed to be about to produce. For if the lord king should ratify this nefarious faction by his approval—which God avert!—for it is wicked to suppose that this criminal act proceeded from his command—yet ratification is equivalent to command, and the whole population of England will succumb to the necessity of one of two evils [Col. 1434A]: either, in the pitiable blindness of its mind, it will renounce the discipline, devotion, and obedience of the Apostolic See, or it will remain irreversibly exiled under interdict alone. For it is far less evil to be punished by the hardship of proscription and the devastation of all one’s property than, after recognizing the truth, shamefully to turn back.

LXXV. Of Matthew, treasurer of Sens.—In favor of Thomas of Canterbury, against King Henry. He urges that the threats of the king of England should be disregarded, “because the nobles of Poitou and Brittany, allied with the lord king [of France], have woven for him an inextricable labyrinth.”

To Pope ALEXANDER, MATTHEW, treasurer of Sens.

[Col. 1434B] Every faithful soul is by necessity of law subject to apostolic majesty; but I am bound to you more intimately by special devotion, and, through the concurrent obligation of charity and necessity, am compelled to be more concerned about matters pertaining to your apostolic office than about the condition of my own lot. I shall therefore speak to my lord, confidently dealing with matters more conducive to your honor and advantage—if you wish to hear the words of your little servant, who is endangered because of your mandate—than to my own deliverance, which, God favoring, will succeed. You commanded, Father, if you please to remember, that I should convey the words of your counsel to our most Christian lord king and raise his spirits by giving hope of relief for the lord of Canterbury, lest he be troubled if perhaps he heard that envoys of the king of England [Col. 1434C] had obtained from you something grievous against that archbishop. For you were keeping his cause unimpaired in your bosom. To him alone, Father, I disclosed your words; and he, returning most abundant thanks, pursued the glory of your Holiness with boundless praises. God knows that I dared not reveal the secret of your counsel either to the archbishop himself or to any mortal person.

But behold: through the occasion of letters which the king of England recently caused to be published in a public conference of bishops, and upon hearing the boast of his envoys, who gloried that they had cast down and irreparably crushed the aforesaid archbishop, citing in support of themselves the rescript of your letters, he has become so confused and troubled that he calls me a liar with respect to your promise [Col. 1434D], and says that he will henceforth hope for no good from the actions of the Roman Church except so far as faith has been persuaded by visible evidence. Nor, he says, would he take it ill if, perhaps offering unjust petitions, he were rejected by you; but he grieves, wonders, and is astonished that petitions or threats, presented against God through utterly base persons on behalf of a manifest persecutor of the Church and enemy of the realm, carry more weight with you than his own faithfulness and service and those of his kingdom, and prayers made for God and according to God, consonant with every law and equity, when they are presented by himself and his whole realm. He therefore declared that henceforward, in the matter of the Roman Church, he would not fail, wherever he saw it advantageous, to pursue his own interest and that of his kingdom. For it is held certain that he is willing to accept the long-sought alliance [Col. 1435A] of the emperor, through a marriage contracted between their children. The matter had indeed hitherto been delayed, but the hope of those promoting it has now been strengthened.

I therefore beg and counsel, in that fidelity which is due to a Father and lord, that by more swiftly fulfilling the promise which you made him through me, in the relief of the lord of Canterbury, you may soothe his mind, showing that you are unwilling longer to tolerate the iniquity of the king of England, who is a public enemy of himself, of the kingdom of the Franks, and of the Church of God. Nor need his threats be feared; for just as the cities of Italy, with a divine miracle leading the way, expelled the German tyrant, so the nobles of Poitou and Brittany, allied with the lord king, have woven for him an inextricable labyrinth. He is now so tightly hemmed in that no one sees by what way [Col. 1435B] he can escape. And, with God’s grace preceding and aiding, he will not escape.

Moreover, the Church of Sens is in a strait. On one side, at the insistence of the lord of Auxerre and under pressure from your mandate, we are to assign our archbishop’s prebend to a certain clerk whose face, to speak from conscience, we do not yet know, nor even his name; on the other, the custom and law of our church stand in the way, which we cannot break without perjury. For every canon of our church is bound by necessity of oath to observe it, and it has been strengthened by privileges of the Apostolic See, against which one may not act. It is not lawful, nor has it ever been lawful, for the chapter to grant a prebend without requesting the archbishop’s consent, nor for the archbishop [Col. 1435C] to do so without us. Nor would it be safe for us to prejudice the archbishop, and it is damnable to act against an oath. May it therefore please your graciousness to provide against so great a peril to the Church, because when, by the Lord’s gift, you have created an archbishop, you will more conveniently arrange whatever seems expedient to your Holiness.

LXXVI. Of C., priest of Lantony.—For Gilbert of London.

To ALEXANDER, supreme pontiff, most reverend lord and his most holy Father, C., priest of the Church of Lantony, greetings and due obedience in all things.

It is written: “The simplicity of the righteous shall guide them, and the subversion of the perverse shall lay them waste. The righteousness of the upright shall deliver them, and the wicked shall be caught in their own snares” (Prov. XI). How true and pure is the simplicity, how magnificent and peaceable the justice, of the venerable man Gilbert, bishop of London, his holy manner of life—lasting not for an hour but continuously—and, together with his life, his knowledge and teaching sufficiently make known. Certain persons, as we have learned by report, have not hesitated in the presence of your reverence to accuse this holy and just man, a lover of peace, alleging that he sowed discord between the king and the lord of Canterbury and disturbed the peace. But who can believe that a man so holy and just created and fostered a schism between kingdom and priesthood? We know, and know certainly, that he employed every possible diligence in every way [Col. 1436A] to reconcile the lord of Canterbury to the king. Since he took such care that the lord of Canterbury should be reconciled to the king, to whom can it seem credible that a man of such holiness labored by word or deed for his death? We therefore humbly request your fatherhood that the reputation of so great a man—unimpaired among us, who know him through living with him—may not be diminished before the authority of your reverence by rumors that have injured it. For “the wicked is brought to nothing in his sight, who has not taken up reproach against his neighbors” (Ps. XIV). May your Holiness flourish and prosper, reverend and beloved Father.

LXXVII. Of Simon, prior of Mont-Dieu, and Engelbert, prior of the Valley of St Peter.—What they did in executing the apostolic mandate for restoring concord between the king and the archbishop of Canterbury.

[Col. 1436B]

To Pope ALEXANDER, SIMON, prior of Mont-Dieu, and ENGELBERT, prior of the Valley of St Peter.

We recently went to the illustrious king of England with Brother Bernard of Corilo, so that by authority of your mandate peace and concord might be restored between him and the lord of Canterbury. And so that this matter might be more easily handled, we brought the lord of Canterbury to the place where, by God’s agency, kings have been reconciled. When your admonitory letters had been delivered to the king of England, and after using such diligence with him as we thought expedient [Col. 1436C], we admonished and advised the lord of Canterbury to humble himself before the king and strive by humble petitions and assiduous service to soften his severity. The most Christian king of France, the archbishops, bishops, and great men who were present unanimously advised the same. Pressed by the counsel of the king and of all the archbishops, bishops, and barons, the archbishop agreed. Before everyone he approached the king of England and, bending his knees, placed himself in God and the king for the honor of God and the king, using this form of words so that he might thus deserve peace and the king’s favor.

But because of the words “for the honor of God,” the king would not receive him, publicly saying before everyone that it must not appear that the archbishop wished to preserve God’s honor [Col. 1436D] and the king did not. After much that he ought rather to have kept silent, the king said that he sought nothing else from the archbishop except that, as priest and bishop, he should promise him before all in a word of truth that, without any evil contrivance, he would observe the customs which the holy archbishops of Canterbury had observed toward their kings and which the archbishop himself had on another occasion promised him. The archbishop answered that he had sworn fealty to the king, by which oath he was bound to preserve the king’s life, limbs, and earthly honor, saving his own ecclesiastical order; and that he was most faithfully ready to fulfill this, nor had anything further been demanded from any of his predecessors or was to be demanded from anyone. When the king pressed this point greatly, the lord of Canterbury added that, although none of his predecessors had done or promised this, and he himself ought in no way by right to do it, nevertheless for the peace of the Church and the king’s favor he promised that he would observe those customs which his holy predecessors had observed toward their kings, saving his ecclesiastical order, so far as he could according to God [Col. 1437A]. And, for the sake of recovering the king’s love, he would do whatever he could without prejudice to God’s honor, maintaining that he had never served him more willingly than he would still do, if it pleased him. But the king would not accept this unless he promised, precisely and absolutely under oath, to observe the customs, since he sought nothing further from him. Because the archbishop, though many urged him, refused to do this, the king departed with peace unmade.

When we urged the king to receive the archbishop back into his favor in accordance with your command, and to restore peace and his church to him, he replied that perhaps the counsel of his friends would be to restore the church at some time; but he said that he would not restore his favor, because then the privilege which you had granted him, by which you suspended the archbishop’s authority until he returned to the king’s favor, would be nullified [Col. 1437B]. And because you had commanded that he should first be approached in a spirit of gentleness through your admonitory letters, we delayed giving him your threatening letters until another time; meanwhile intending to pray to God, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, that He might soften the king’s mind and cause peace to be restored for His honor and the Church’s advantage. Whatever remains to be done under your command, when the appropriate time is received, we shall execute through God’s grace with all diligence, and will take care to report to your majesty the outcome that God grants. When Brother Bernard was asked, as we were, to write to you the course of this business, he replied that it is forbidden in his order for any brother to write to you or another person concerning any matter. But he promised that he would state it before your envoy Master Lombard, who delivered your letters to him and who, as one present at the event, will faithfully report the matter to you [Col. 1437C].

LXXXVIII. Of the same writers.—That, accomplishing nothing through the mandate, they presented the pontiff’s threatening letters to the king.

[Col. 1437D] To Pope ALEXANDER, SIMON, prior of Mont-Dieu, and ENGELBERT, prior of the Valley of St Peter.

In accordance with the command of your Holiness, we delivered your threatening letters to the illustrious king of England, applying our effort and diligence to the limit of our strength, that according to your admonition he might restore the lord of Canterbury to favor, restore to him his see and peace, and allow his church free administration. We waited a long time, hoping and praying that God might soften his mind. But since we made no progress by waiting, and your command pressed us, at the second conference of the kings we presented to him your threatening letters. When at last, and only with difficulty, he had received them at our urging and that of the great men present, after much which it would be too long to recount, he gave us this answer [Col. 1438A]:

“I did not expel the lord of Canterbury from the kingdom; yet out of reverence for the lord pope, if he is willing to do for me what he owes, and to observe for me what his predecessors observed toward mine, and what he himself promised, he may return to England and have peace there.”

After varying his answers, he finally said that he would summon the bishops of England and use their counsel. But he fixed no day, nor did we obtain from him anything that could make us certain regarding the lord of Canterbury’s peace and the execution of your mandate. And because he frequently changed his answers, we asked him whether the archbishop might return to his see and enjoy his peace. He replied that the archbishop would never [Col. 1438B] enter the land until he did what he owed the king and promised to observe what others had observed and what he himself had promised. We then asked him to write and authenticate his answer in letters patent, because we needed to report something definite to you, which we did not yet have because he changed his answers so often. But he would not agree.

When we reported this to the archbishop, he replied that he was ready to do for the king whatever he owed him and to observe what had been observed by his predecessors, insofar as he could while preserving his ecclesiastical order. But to undertake new obligations not rendered by his predecessors, and to promise anything of that sort otherwise than with his order preserved, was unlawful for him without the authority of the lord pope: both because it would be harmful to introduce a new form into the Church and because you had forbidden him ever to promise anything such as this except with God’s honor and his ecclesiastical order preserved. He added that, rebuking him, you had said that he ought not to have bound himself to the observance of such customs even for his own head, except with his ecclesiastical order preserved [Col. 1438C]. But if the king, as you command, restores to him his favor, peace, church, and the things taken from himself and his people, he will gladly do, according to God and with his ecclesiastical order preserved, whatever lies within his power in accordance with the king’s will; and he will strive to serve him with all his strength, most diligently and devotedly. May it therefore please your Holiness to bring aid to the suffering Church and persevere in what you have laudably begun; for, as we have heard from many and believe, if you persevere, the peace and safety of the Church are at the doors. And because it is not the custom of the brethren of Grandmont to write to anyone, we have written this to you with the knowledge and consent of our companion Brother Bernard: what we did with the same Brother Bernard, who testified to the truth in the hearing of many, asking those who were permitted to write to report to you what they had heard from him [Col. 1438D].

LXXIX–LXXX. Of A., minister of St Osyth’s.—For Gilbert, bishop of London.

To his reverend lord and Father ALEXANDER, supreme pontiff, A., humble minister of the Church of St Osyth’s, the affection of sincere prayer and the obedience of due submission [Col. 1439A].

Is it not so, Father ever to be loved: where there is pain, there is the hand? Is not a living pain felt in the members of the whole body? Is this not the Apostle’s saying: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (II Cor. XI.) Since therefore we are constituted in the body of Christ, and since “my dove is one, the chosen of her mother” (Cant. IV), and she must fly through both ill and good report, we who are placed in the body sometimes suffer more grievously when, without cause, one is judged by another. Therefore with all possible humility we earnestly beseech your majesty, after setting before yourselves the balance of equity and justice and weighing in suspended judgment both the outcome of past events [Col. 1439B], the advantages and disadvantages of the present time, the peace of the whole English Church, and especially apostolic fidelity and tranquillity in this matter, that you may receive with fatherly affection and kindness our lord Bishop Gilbert: a man endowed with every upright quality, adorned with virtues, distinguished in learning, resplendent in holiness, graced with religious devotion, an example of justice and truth, and as it were a pillar of the entire English Church.

Let therefore the discernment of the supreme pontiff act for himself and for the universal Church, so that it may choose more readily the course by which it can most certainly remedy the Church’s welfare in the case of a man whose integrity is known to be established by authority; and perhaps may not confuse injustices foreign to him with his own, nor admit against him the stamp of rumor, whose evidence not even the conscience that judges him accepts [Col. 1439C]. For who, with reverence for the supreme pontiff unimpaired, would dare accuse such and so great a man of crime: that he would knowingly wish, before the king of England or anyone else, to be the cause of wrongdoing or discord, when he is himself disposed to lay down his life for his brethren? We therefore, according to a good conscience, are witnesses before your understanding in all truth to the innocence of this so great and religious a man, insofar as he was granted from above to apply his mind to the restoration among us of peace between kingdom and priesthood, in which the universal Church rejoices in its tranquillity. May your Holiness prosper, most kindly Father.

LXXXI. Of the abbot of Ramsey.—On the same subject.

[Col. 1439D]

To Pope ALEXANDER, the abbot of Ramsey.

Whenever testimonies are rendered to the best of men, discourse proceeds without retraction or offence, since the commendation of those whom common estimation holds commendable is always irrefutable. Therefore our venerable Father Gilbert, bishop of London, a man distinguished in merit and in name, shines conspicuously among the chosen persons of our land through a certain prerogative of virtues. For he is known to have attained and ascended almost every rank of religious and ecclesiastical order and dignity, trained to perfection in secular learning and the divine law; and, faithfully and prudently administering pastoral government [Col. 1440A], he passed by a sufficiently worthy promotion from monastery to episcopal chair, first at Hereford and afterward at London through the intervention of your authority, illuminating and honoring both by life and teaching alike. Far therefore be any sinister suspicion from a man of such conspicuous integrity and refined religious devotion; and let any malicious interpretation of him or his works be far from your holy ears. For who could believe that a good, upright, religious man had harmed, in the least and according to his conscience, one good, upright, and religious: a bishop an archbishop, a son his father? So far as we can judge with certainty from what we have heard and seen, and also from the undoubted testimony of our lord king, he earnestly sought and diligently strove for the peace and reconciliation of the venerable archbishop [Col. 1440B] with the king himself. If anything was subsequently done outrageously, we believe that it occurred contrary to his knowledge and will. It remains, therefore, most holy Father, that you gently and mildly receive your honorable son as he comes to the bosom of your gentleness, in accordance with the common wish of all good people, and do not allow his innocence to be injured by uncertain conjectures of suspicion, which ought not to be believed. May almighty God preserve your Holiness unharmed for His Church a long time.

LXXXII. Of William of Ramsey.—On the same subject.

To his lord and reverend Father ALEXANDER, by the grace of God supreme pontiff of the holy apostolic and catholic Church, Brother WILLIAM, unworthy servant of the Church of St Benedict at Ramsey, obedience with due reverence [Col. 1440C].

Your eye sees in clear vision, and your ear perceives by frequent hearing, how great the tribulations with which the primitive Church of God is worn down and how manifold the adversities; and, what is more grievous and more anxious to our heart, the head learns daily by experience what the members suffer. But we, seeing the righteous tormented by the wicked amid this fire, and the poor man consumed while the wicked exults, are bound by the law of charity to offer, according to our measure, to brethren placed in adversity that consolation which we would wish offered to ourselves if we were oppressed by the same adversity [Col. 1440D]. We are bound even more to compassionate the holy Fathers whom we see placed in great distress. Therefore the whole English Church, and especially religious communities, grieves for and sympathizes with the noble man Gilbert, bishop of London. For he has always been an example to the Church of God of every form of religious devotion and uprightness; and in every rank to which the Lord led him, he shone forth as a lamp burning for those who looked upon him. And, what must by no means be passed over in silence, the Lord enriched him so greatly with the treasure of heavenly wisdom that reverence ought freely to be rendered to him by all. And because it is written, “Wisdom shall not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wis. I), the reputation of such great virtues [Col. 1441A] and so many gifts of grace, which bear in themselves testimony to the divine Spirit, set his mind far apart from every suspicion of deceit and malice.

For we have another external testimony, than which none can be more certain: namely, that of our lord king. For no one knows as fully what is in a person as the spirit of that person which is within him (I Cor. II). From the testimony, I say, of his letters we have plainly learned that the lord bishop of London never harmed the lord of Canterbury in the estimation of our lord king of England. Therefore, most holy lord, because the eyes of all Israel look toward you and the judgment of each proceeds from your presence, and because, like an angel of God, you know all things under the sun, so that you are moved neither by blessing nor by curse, we do not doubt the equity of your balance. Yet, with humble petition, supplicant voice, and bodies prostrate at the feet of apostolic mercy, we ask, insofar as we can and dare, that in this affair the piety of your divine charity may exalt mercy above judgment [Col. 1441B]. May God preserve you unharmed for His Church through many years.

LXXXIII. Of Henry, abbot of Stratford.—For Gilbert, bishop of London.

To his Father and lord, Pope ALEXANDER, Brother HENRY, called abbot of the monastery of Stratford, and the humble convent of the same place, due obedience to their Father [Col. 1441C], and continual earnest devotion and prayer before the Lord for your welfare.

By the Apostle’s teaching, lord—namely Galatians VI—we have learned that, bearing one another’s burdens, we should thus mutually fulfill the law of Christ among ourselves. Therefore we bear public testimony concerning the conduct of our venerable Father Gilbert, bishop of London, such as we hope and believe to be true, with public report in this matter agreeing with us: namely, that we know him as a prudent, learned, and upright man, received long ago into the public rejoicing of the Church by the example of his praiseworthy life from its beginning. Since we know him to be gentle and peaceable, ever solicitous to reconcile peace among the discordant [Col. 1441D], we believe that he never in any way gave cause or incentive to the dissension which, through the demands of sins, arose between the lord king and the lord of Canterbury; but rather that he diligently exerted as much effort as he could to calm the anger. Because we believe him worthy of commendation, the command of charity compelling us, we commend him to your Holiness, most humbly presenting prayers that we may rejoice at his being returned to us with favor by your exalted authority, through the appeal made for his protection—since, as we believe, we have heard that he has been injured through no fault of his own. We wish you well in the Lord, Father most beloved in Christ.

LXXXIV. Of the Church of Holy Trinity, London.—On the same subject.

[Col. 1442A]

To the venerable Father ALEXANDER, by the grace of God supreme pontiff, S… , humble servant of the Church of Holy Trinity, London, greetings and obedience of due submission.

When, before the supreme Judge who searches the reins and hearts of all (Ps. 7), human frailty hesitates not to commend a man whom his life recommends, may your exalted Holiness—ever-revered and dearly beloved Father, supreme among men in this world—deign to receive with a father’s tender affection and sincere charity the venerable man, Lord Gilbert, bishop of the Church of London, humbly commended by our lowliness. [Col. 1442B] For not only purity of life, integrity of religion, and love of learning render him commendable, but also, as is recognized among us, his steadfast fidelity especially to the Roman Church and his ever-ready, devoted obedience.

For who in England, in carrying out causes under your mandate according to laws, rights, and canons, has so aided the wretched, restored the expelled, freed the oppressed, and re-established peace? Was it not he who lately, setting aside fear of princes and contemptuous of bodily punishment and of schismatics’ malice, scarcely escaped the perils of the British Sea, while others waited for a time; who, having already crossed the narrow passes of the Alps in order wholly to entrust himself to you, [Col. 1442C] went to meet the grace of the supreme pontiff as a mother is honoured? Returning prosperously, he who, as is believed, had chosen the better part expected from him—who became peace for people of good will (Luke 2)—the Church’s peace upon earth.

That he desired this peace, so far as it was granted him from above, and sought it in mind, deed, and word, is shown not only, as has been said, by the journey to you undertaken so faithfully and steadfastly, but also by the sobs and flood of tears which, as we have learned from lawful witnesses, he shed in the general synod for the dissension between the lord king and the man beloved by God and men, now standing before him: our patron, the lord of Canterbury.

Who therefore, good Father, [Col. 1442D] would so rashly judge this man—such and so great a servant of Christ’s Church—among us your sons, as to presume that he ever fomented discord with the lord king, or wished, as it were, to become a cause of, or accessory to, anyone’s guilt; as though he might thereby throw the kingdom’s peace into confusion, offend the holiness of all, and become a persecutor of the Church—he who loves it and defends truth and justice?

Let then the gracious Father, the most holy Father, the spiritual Father, who judges all things and is judged by none, act, lest, through the contagion of a reputation which spoke concerning Christ, “Some say, ‘He is good’; but others say, ‘No, he deceives the crowds’” (John 7), so great a pillar of the Church should fall through the severity of the supreme pontiff. And especially, as the Lord cooperates and confirms the word among us daily by following signs (Mark 16), let him [Col. 1443A] receive from you a fatherly blessing in the Holy Spirit, through whom perhaps your care for all churches may more effectively heal and more cautiously govern. May your Holiness prosper, good Father, ever dear to us.

LXXXV. Of William, prior of the Church of Holy Trinity, London.—On the same subject.

To his Father and lord, ALEXANDER, supreme pontiff: Brother WILLIAM, cloister-prior of the Church of Holy Trinity, London, and the humble convent of the same place, due filial love and humble obedience in all things.

It is apostolic teaching that, if one member suffers, all the other members suffer with it (1 Cor. 12). Therefore we compassionately share, with due love, in the suffering of our venerable Father, the lord [Col. 1443B] bishop of London; and we grieve deeply, in great affliction of spirit, that he endures a punishment which he has not deserved. The conduct of his life, honourably praiseworthy by many testimonies, ought rather to be honoured than burdened with punishments and unjust oppressions.

Since he has hitherto neither been summoned nor warned concerning any fault, we are exceedingly astonished and amazed that a sentence of separation has suddenly been issued against him; especially since we have heard of neither his contumacy, nor understood that his reputation among us has in any degree suffered from public notoriety or any other evil report. Since, by appealing to your Holiness, he has forestalled that sentence, whatever it may be, it is an honour of apostolic dignity worthily to receive a son who comes to you [Col. 1443C] and to relieve his burdens by fatherly grace.

In this matter, while the whole Church of London makes supplication, we too, together with our suppliant mother, earnestly offer prayers to your exaltedness: by receiving our father and gladdening our mother, may you make the whole … suspended toward you for ever bound to you by devotion and grace, and may you show a father’s affection to your sons. May the Lord preserve your safety, Father beloved in Christ.

LXXXVI. Of R., prior of Saint Victor at Paris, and Ervisius, abbot of Saint Augustine.—For Saint Thomas of Canterbury.

To Pope ALEXANDER: the prior of Saint Victor and E., formerly abbot [Col. 1443D] of Saint Augustine.

While holy men—Simon, prior of Mont-Dieu, and Brother Bernard of Grandmont—were truthfully reporting, with other religious and honourable persons present, we ourselves also heard with our own ears, being there in person, the replies which the king of England gave to the lord of Canterbury concerning the business of peace in the Church. They related, and in relating marvelled, how often the king of England had raised the spirits of the lord of Canterbury, his followers, and ourselves to hope for the recovery of ecclesiastical liberty and peace; and how often he had cast them down into despair of recovering that hope which they had earlier conceived.

At last, after many varied replies, neither consistent with one another nor indeed anything but contrary to one another, and after his proud indignation over the presumed presentation [Col. 1444A] of your letters, they were unable to bring back anything certain. Therefore, after so long an expectation and a judgement so long suspended, it is necessary that apostolic authority now at last wield Peter’s sword against the adversary of holy Church and the despiser of the Apostolic See—by a hand so much the stronger as the enemy has fortified himself more strongly, and, if possible, made himself invincible, for resistance and indeed for prevailing.

If you act promptly and firmly, then, according to what they said they had learned from the king’s close advisers, the Church of God will soon arrive at the haven of tranquil security and the joy of the liberty it seeks; indeed, it would long ago have arrived there had you acted more strictly. But if in this extreme necessity you still dissemble, [Col. 1444B] it will without doubt be trampled under a far greater wrong and humiliation than before, and its latter state will be much worse than its former.

Nor should this escape you: your earlier letters, seeming to contain assent to the requests of the king of England but in truth rather concealing the prudent kindness of your intention toward the lord of Canterbury, greatly scandalized the mind of the lord king of France and many others. But your latest letters, which were also threatening, greatly gladdened that same glorious king of ours, devoted and well-disposed toward all good men, but especially toward the lord of Canterbury; and stirred many others to thanksgiving and words of praise, singing to you of mercy [Col. 1444C] and judgement. Of mercy, because you have undertaken to defend an innocent man’s cause; of judgement, because, so far as lies in you, you will repel the wrong of the violent.

LXXXVII. Of William, abbot of Reading.—For Gilbert, bishop of London.

To the most blessed Father and lord A., by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the Catholic Church: Brother WILLIAM, unworthily called abbot of Reading, the least of your sons, wishes that the ship of Peter entrusted to you may be directed unharmed to the harbour of tranquillity.

Because it would be most useful for your Holiness, which by God’s appointment presides over the whole Church, to know the truth of matters arising daily throughout it in every land, we have judged it right, in our lowliness, to inform your exaltedness, with conscience as witness, what kind of man we know your son the bishop of London to be, and how prudently and faithfully he conducted himself in this storm which arose between the king and the archbishop of Canterbury. We do so lest, God forbid, some malicious suggestion cloud your serenity concerning him. [Col. 1444D]

First, we know that, after taking the habit of religion at Cluny in a manner so holy and irreproachable, he lived there for some time in such a way that he was found entirely worthy of promotion, authority over others, and service to them. Promoted once, twice, and often thereafter, he deserved to rise, in life, character, and doctrine, to the summit of the episcopate. In that office, so far as human judgement extends, [Col. 1445A] he has thus far shown himself not merely irreproachable but a useful minister of holy Church: strict and sparing toward himself, merciful and generous toward others.

We have considered it superfluous to write at length of his sobriety in food and clothing; his frugality in other things necessary for this life; his kindness toward the poor, gentleness toward those subject to him, devotion toward holy persons, and sweetness and humanity toward all. By these he has filled the Church of God with a most fragrant scent. We do not believe that these things are unknown to you, since those who love God never cease to proclaim them, while those who think otherwise may conceal them but cannot deny them.

In this dispute which has arisen between our lord the king and the lord archbishop of Canterbury, we know that he has so conducted himself that, had he been trusted, all discord would long ago have been calmed and concord restored—although some enemies of peace, led by malice, have spread a different report about him and carried it even to the archbishop. [Col. 1445B] Nor have we heard, nor received from anyone who truly heard it, that he has harmed the lord archbishop in any matter before the lord king or elsewhere, except that, compelled by extreme necessity, he appealed to your clemency at the beginning of Lent. The archbishop afterwards, as is said, pronounced sentence against him on Palm Sunday. At this everyone in our regions is astonished.

For an appeal to the Apostolic See is accustomed to provide remedy and assistance to all who are oppressed. This benefit, owed by our mother the holy Roman Church to her children and hitherto afforded them in their need, allows none of her own to despair while under oppression. If it is withdrawn or rendered ineffective, we do not know what refuge may henceforth be hoped for in necessity. [Col. 1445C] We therefore earnestly beseech your Blessedness—may God long preserve you safe for us—that toward your son, the bishop of London, who flees to your mercy, you act and show yourself in such a manner that you furnish your other sons with hope and confidence of fleeing to you in time of need.

LXXXVIII. Lombard to Alexander.—How John of Oxford, returning from Rome, boasted that he had obtained much from the pontiff; on hearing this, the king of France was so violently disturbed that he said “he wished immediately to send envoys to forbid the apostolic legates entry into his kingdom.”

[Col. 1445D]

To the reverend Father and lord ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: Lombard, his clerk, offers the service of faithful obedience.

Since I am in Christ a child of your Holiness and the work of your hands, I can neither be silent nor ought to be silent concerning what is publicly said to disparage our reputation and detract from your name, and what is craftily devised to the injury of the whole Church. John of Oxford, [Col. 1446A] boasting insolently that he has returned from Rome with the honour of a deanery and the fullness of your favour, adds no less arrogantly that he will be protected by a privilege against the lord of Canterbury and every bishop; he declares that he is scarcely less than established in the rank of cardinals, subject only to you and your apostolic office.

Moreover, he boasts proudly that he has obtained for the king what no king has ever been able to obtain: namely, by your authority, confirmation of a marriage between the king’s son and the daughter of the count of Brittany, related in the third degree. He also adds that envoys specially requested by the king are being sent, who, with the remedy of appeal removed, will hear and determine whatever the king chooses to bring against the lord archbishop.

These matters, most holy [Col. 1446B] Father, were spread abroad when John returned from Rome. The more unusual they were, and the more rarely such things occur, the more violently they struck the minds of those who heard them. On hearing them, the king of the French, your devout son and the Church’s, was so violently disturbed that he said he wished immediately to send envoys to prevent your legates from entering his kingdom. He did more still, which I have placed in the mouth of the bearer of this letter.

He also said that he wished to summon archbishops and bishops, in order to lay before them and propose to them how the Roman Church, malignantly acting against him, exalts [those hostile to him] and seeks to humiliate him. He said: “Does he not labour to dishonour me, who craftily seeks to shed the blood of the archbishop of Canterbury—an innocent man rejoicing for justice and the Church’s liberty—impiously delivering him into the hands of his enemies and persecutors? I have firmly resolved to receive and honourably and fittingly support him, so long as he remains in exile, and as it were cherish him in my bosom—as I have already begun to do—not in return for services, though in serving him who now persecutes him he has rather inflicted wrongs upon us, [Col. 1446C] but in view of the most just cause which he supports, in regard for his worth, and also from love for the lord pope, who pressed me earnestly enough on his behalf.”

He further announced and openly declared that it was no less grievous to him that you sent legates for this cause than if you had sent them to take away his crown. Nor were there lacking persons to inflame his mind still more. An opportunity has been given to those whose disposition and desire to harm you was known from the beginning, for maligning us and God’s Church and contriving many things. Your indulgence has not changed their ill-will, though your authority might have restrained their attempt.

I learned these things through a certain clerk faithful and devoted to you, who was present while they occurred and reported them privately to me. This one thing, most holy Father, I know most truly—though I cannot write it without tears—that the reputation of your name is in some measure darkened. For detraction from your fame is like food and drink to slanderers and evil-speakers, who, as though drunk and intoxicated with wine, tear at your reputation and, as it were, gnaw at your whole person with the teeth of cursing. They do this partly from favour toward [Col. 1447A] the lord of Canterbury, partly from hatred in pursuing him; especially because, as many believed, the day of his and your victory was near.

For the king so feared that, when the day set for the appeal had elapsed, he would be excommunicated and his whole land laid under interdict, that he openly said he had neither persuaded nor compelled the bishops to appeal and would therefore take no side in the matter. The bishops, however, were so distressed and fearful of an interdict that some sent envoys to the lord of Canterbury and others were ready to come at his summons. But John of Oxford, acting as though your legate, summoned all the bishops and, by your authority, as rumour has it in France, commanded them not to come at the summons of the lord of Canterbury.

On this occasion Master Robert, bishop of Hereford, having already reached the sea to cross it, was recalled, as he excused himself before the lord of Canterbury through his envoys—religious and well-known men—in my presence. [Col. 1447B] Hence there is such disturbance in many minds. They greatly fear the king’s intrigues, and from them the ruin of the English Church and of all churches in his land, the overthrow of liberty, and a longer and harsher persecution of the archbishop. For I have often heard from many that the king is said to have placed all his hope in adverse fortune and in your death—may God in His most kindly mercy defer it for a long time—firmly asserting, as many report, that he will by no means receive your successor unless he first confirms all the dignities and customs of his kingdom.

For this reason he is believed to have deceitfully and fraudulently requested legates: in order to carry out his will not only against the lord of Canterbury but even against all the bishops of his land; or at least so that the archbishop’s excommunication and the interdict upon his land may thus be postponed. By wasting time in this way, he may nullify the authority of the lord of Canterbury; so that, if he is not bound in your time, he need not fear being bound by your successor, whom, as many say, he has not readily resolved to receive. [Col. 1447C]

Therefore, most prudent Father, those who possess the Spirit of God and desire the peace of the Church earnestly long for the spirit of Daniel to be stirred up in you, to expose Bel’s deceits and slay the dragon; and concerning this they implore God with constant and abundant prayers. May your Holiness flourish for many years.

LXXXIX. Of Theobald, count of Blois.—On the martyrdom of Saint Thomas.

To his most reverend lord and Father ALEXANDER, supreme pontiff: THEOBALD, count of Blois and regent of the kingdom of France, greetings and reverence owed with filial submission.

Your Majesty was pleased that peace should be restored and unbroken concord firmly established between the lord archbishop of Canterbury and the king of England. Accordingly, [Col. 1448A] in accordance with the tenor of your mandate, the king of England received him with cheerful countenance, a joyful brow, and a look promising peace and restoring favour to him.

I was present at this peace and concord; and, in my presence, the lord of Canterbury complained to the king of England concerning the coronation of his son, whom the king, urged by hasty vow and burning desire, had caused to be raised to the height of royal dignity. The king of England, guilty of and conscious of wrongdoing in this injury, gave the archbishop of Canterbury a pledge concerning justice and satisfaction. He also complained of the bishops who, contrary to the right and honour of the Church of Canterbury, had presumed to thrust the new king into the royal seat—not from zeal for justice, nor to please God, but to appease a tyrant. The king granted him free and lawful authority over them, to pronounce sentence upon them [Col. 1448B] at the discretion of your authority and his own.

I saw and heard these things, and I am ready to affirm and establish them for you by oath or by whatever other means you may please. Thus, peace having been made, the man of God, full of the Holy Spirit and fearing nothing, departed so as to submit his throat to the sword and expose his neck to the striker. Therefore the innocent lamb suffered martyrdom on the day following the feast of the Holy Innocents. Righteous blood was shed where the provision for our salvation was accustomed to be offered. Courtly hounds, the intimates and household servants of the king of England, presented themselves as the king’s agents and, being guilty, shed innocent blood.

I would report to you in these words the detestable manner of this prodigy and its unheard-of shamefulness, [Col. 1448C] but I fear that it may be imputed to me as hatred of the serpent—whose hatred I do not fear and whose love I do not desire. The bearers of this letter will make the matter known to you openly and more fully. From their report you will learn how great a mass of sorrow, complaint, and calamity belongs to the whole Church, especially to Canterbury, and also to the entire kingdom of France—indeed, to all parts of the world which this wickedness and sedition has reached.

The Roman Church, mother Church, neither ought nor can, without shame, pass over this. Whatever hostile act is dared against the daughter recoils upon the parent; nor is a daughter made captive without injury to her mother. Therefore the blood of the righteous man and martyr of God cries out to you and demands vengeance. May the almighty and merciful [Col. 1448D] Lord, who gave His Son’s blood to the world in order to wipe away its offences and erase the stains of sins, be present with you and guide you regarding the vengeance to be exacted. May He inspire in you the will for sufficient vengeance and supply the means, so that the Church, confounded by the vastness of an unheard-of and unspeakable crime, may rejoice in a strict, unprecedented vengeance pleasing to the whole world. Farewell; and act as befits your Holiness and the dignity of the whole Roman curia.

XC. Of Master Vivian.—What he did in executing the apostolic mandate entrusted to him.

To the most blessed Father and lord ALEXANDER, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the universal Church: VIVIAN, [Col. 1449A] most devoted servant of his Holiness, offers the service of due submission.

You should know with certainty that our having so long delayed informing your Blessedness both of our condition and of the state of the business for which we were sent to the illustrious king of England must be attributed not to negligent laxity, which is reckoned a fault, but to necessity and the nature of the affair. For he was with an army in remote parts of Gascony, and, most holy Father, we could in no way reach him there without the greatest danger. Nor was it the counsel of the most Christian king of France, whom we met at Silviniacum, presenting to him your letters, which he received most devoutly.

Then we withdrew to Sens, awaiting the king of England’s return. Since he had stayed in Gascony longer [Col. 1449B] than we had believed, he finally returned, and we hastened to his presence in Normandy. He and his princes received us honourably enough, and the next day we presented your letters to him. When he had read them, he set before us, at the beginning of his speech, many charges against the lord of Canterbury, as he had formerly set them before our lords the cardinals.

But because you incessantly enjoined him to receive the archbishop back into his love and favour, with all rancour put aside, for the remission of his sins, he in some sense assented verbally and replied that he would take counsel. Before this, however, he raised the matter of absolving those who had been excommunicated. We pass over an account of what authority we held concerning the absolution of the bishops, since it is not unknown to you. Yet whatever authority might afterward have been received, if God inclined his mind and will toward peace, that would in no way stand in the way, since they had sworn an oath for this purpose.

After leading us about with him through many windings, of places no less than of words, and detaining us for some time, he at length proposed the following in the presence of the archbishops of Rouen and Bordeaux: that the three men present should be absolved; that one of us should enter England and absolve the other excommunicated persons found near the seacoast; and that the other should proceed to the archbishop. On this condition, for the sake of Him through whom kings reign (Prov. 8), and from love for you, he would permit the archbishop to come safely [Col. 1449C] and in good peace and firm security to receive back his church in all its entirety, as he had held it before he departed; and to hold it for the honour of God, of the Church, and of himself and his sons. He granted the same to those who were in exile with and for the archbishop, and was to put in writing all that he promised.

But on the following day, when we were to absolve those three men, he merely changed the term “sons” to “heirs,” in the presence of the aforesaid archbishops and one very eminent bishop of Lisieux. “What then of the kiss?” He answered that peace would not fail even for this small point. His word pleased us, and we accepted it.

After their absolution had subsequently been performed, however, where he had said “the honour of his heirs,” while all the rest remained in their former condition, [Col. 1450A] he added in its place: “saving the dignity of his kingdom.” On hearing this, we were greatly disturbed. The terms of the aforesaid words were not being maintained; and so we withdrew from him on both sides and came as far as Caen, within the dominion of the archbishop of Rouen.

When the king was setting out to meet the count of Flanders at Rouen, he entrusted the matter of reopening negotiations for peace with us to the aforementioned archbishops; to the bishops of Lisieux, Worcester, Séez, Bayeux, and Rennes; to the archdeacons of Canterbury and Salisbury; and to his princes. When they pressed us to accept the phrase “saving the dignity of his kingdom,” we answered: “Then let the king’s word and the Lord’s word alike stand—that is, saving the liberty of the Church.” They did not accept this, nor did the king. Although, as he said, he understood the liberty of the Church to be included in the honour of God, he absolutely refused to add it to the writing.

Since they could no longer prevail over us by argument, they preferred that the archbishop, as already stated, should safely return to his church and receive it back, in good peace and security and in all its entirety as he had held it before his departure, with no condition added on either side; and that his followers likewise should receive back theirs. At their insistence, we accepted this wording. [Col. 1450B]

At last, summoned by the king to Rouen, we came with much difficulty. Finally, through his envoys, he informed us at the archbishop’s court that he would by no means depart from the phrase “saving the dignity of his kingdom.” Thus, as neither the first nor the second wording found by the aforementioned persons pleased him, we withdrew. In this way, most blessed Father, we left.

We also commanded the archbishops, under the obligation of fidelity by which they were bound to you, to command those whom we had absolved, under the obligation of the oath by which they were bound to you, and to put it to the lord king: if peace had not followed before our departure, they were not to enjoy the benefit of absolution but were to observe without challenge the sentence which the archbishop of Canterbury had passed against them. Thus far concerning our dealings with the lord king.

We afterwards presented the king’s proposal to the archbishop of Canterbury. Though he bore all the aforesaid matters patiently, he replied that he would gladly preserve the dignity of the king’s realm, provided his own order and his fidelity to the Roman Church were safeguarded. [Col. 1450C] If anyone presents these matters to you otherwise, believe in every respect that they are as we have said.

The name of Lord Gratian does not appear in this letter, not because he did not see and carefully examine it, but because he was hastening to return and wished the letter to be much shorter. Finally, so that you should not believe anything the king’s envoys might say against us before our return, we resolved, on the advice of the archbishops and bishops, to send an envoy to the king himself.

We chose at last Master Peter, an honourable and well-educated man, archdeacon of Pavia, and sent him to the aforesaid king. He was to humbly entreat him for mercy and, on your behalf, earnestly ask him to admit the petitions for carrying out the peace between himself and the lord of Canterbury according to the tenor of your letters which he himself had received.

Though he was honourably received, he was at last dismissed disgracefully and, as he himself declares, contrary to the honour of God and of the king; and afterwards he was despoiled of some of his possessions in the king’s duchy. One of his principal attendants, who, as he said, had already withdrawn in fear a short distance outside the town, was brutally treated by violent men; but, at the intercession of a knight who arrived [Col. 1451A] and directed him to report this deed to us, he was rescued from their hands by divine grace.

XCI. Of the same.—On a similar subject.

To Pope ALEXANDER: Master VIVIAN.

[Col. 1451B] I devoted every effort and diligence to restoring peace between the king of England and the lord of Canterbury according to the form prescribed by your Holiness. At last, after many labours, this point was reached: at the conference of kings held at Paris on the octave of Saint Martin, the lord of Canterbury presented to the king of England, in the presence of the most Christian king, through the lord of Rouen, the bishop of Séez, and myself, the following written petition:

“We ask of our lord the king, in accordance with the command and counsel of the lord pope, that, for the love of God and of the lord pope, for the honour of holy Church, and for the salvation of himself and his heirs, he receive us into his favour and grant to us and all who left the kingdom with and for us his peace and full security from himself and his people, without evil intent. [Col. 1451C] Let him restore to us the Church of Canterbury in that fullness and liberty in which we held it best after we came to that see, together with all the possessions which we held, to hold and possess them as freely, peacefully, and honourably as the Church and we held and possessed them more freely and honourably after we were promoted to the archbishopric. The same is to be granted to our followers. And let him permit us likewise to possess, as we please, all churches and prebends belonging to the archbishopric which fell vacant after we left the land, so that we may dispose of them as of our own.”

This was put into writing. Concerning the movable goods that had been taken, the archbishop promised that he would act according to your counsel, so that no one ought to accuse him on that account.

When the king heard the written petition, he did not openly oppose it; but, changing its wording, he replied that the archbishop should have his church and possessions in peace, as his predecessors had had them. In this way he excluded certain possessions that had newly accrued to this archbishop by right of his church and that he had possessed and held after becoming archbishop, [Col. 1451D] as well as the churches and prebends that had fallen vacant after he left the land. He did this in order craftily to bind him to observance of the king’s own wicked and accursed customs, as we afterwards clearly discovered, for in almost all his words he is sophistical and deceitful toward God’s Church.

Moreover, no entreaty, although many persons urged him, could induce him to receive the said archbishop with the kiss of peace. I pressed the most Christian king to obtain this tiny concession by the urgency of his prayers. But he was unwilling to trouble the other king in any respect while that king was in his land. Yet he said to the lord of Canterbury, and also to me before many persons who were present, that not for so great a quantity of gold as he himself was would he be willing or dare to advise the archbishop to enter the king’s land unless the kiss of peace came first; for without the kiss, favour was not restored.

Those who were present therefore considered it probable that he was deceitfully negotiating peace, since he refused to accept the public and renowned sign of peace among nations. Nor did he care to give the lord of Canterbury any reply through his representatives; rather, as though seeking an occasion to depart, [Col. 1452A] he went away. It appeared that he wished only to feign favour, not to restore it.

May it therefore please your Holiness, if you hear anything contrary to this, to defer all judgement until you see your servant face to face—who was present at every event—and hear from my own mouth how the Church is trampled down and how unjustly the innocent have been proscribed. May the almighty Lord preserve your safety for long ages, to the glory of His name and in fulfilment of the pious wishes of us and our people, most holy and dearly beloved Father.

XCII. Of Laurence, abbot of Westminster.—For Gilbert, bishop of London.

To Pope ALEXANDER: LAURENCE, abbot of Westminster.

[Col. 1452C] The assertion of truth is then accustomed to proceed freely and without offence when it rests upon certain proofs of facts and is fortified by the testimony of the most widespread reputation. Therefore we commend our venerable Father Gilbert, bishop of London, to your Holiness all the more earnestly because, in our regions, both the merit of his life is renowned and common estimation judges him commendable.

Accordingly, to your exaltedness—whose reverence we have no wish, just as we ought not, to defile with any fabricated falsehood—we state without any ambiguity that the life and conduct of the man mentioned, so far as this could come to your knowledge either from clear evidence of facts or from widespread report, have hitherto shone adorned with abundant virtues, and appeared to set before the eyes of beholders a pattern of religion and integrity. [Col. 1452D]

For who among our countrymen can be unaware that the lord of London is most skilled in both divine law and secular learning, distinguished in uprightness, and proven by long and holy conduct in the practice and observance of religion? Who among them is so foolish as not to recognize this? Know also that we have received the following from the testimony of the lord king: that the same lord of London has never harmed the lord of Canterbury before the royal majesty, whether by word or deed. This may be presumed with a certain assurance and confidence by all who know his life and honourable conduct, since it is grievous even to hear, and unworthy of belief, that so illustrious a mirror of religious devotion and holiness in God’s Church should have been a seedbed or fomentor of any malice. [Col. 1453A]

We pray, therefore, most holy Father and lord, that you mercifully open the bosom of kindness and grace to this devoted and venerable son who brings himself to the lap of your gentleness. Deign, if it please you, to restore him, restored to the fullness of your favour, to his church, thereby satisfying the common wishes of good people. For this, we believe, will serve the honour of your exaltedness and the interests of the Church. May almighty God preserve you safe through long and happy years, dearest Father and lord.

XCIII. Of Anonymous Writers.—Against Thomas of Canterbury.

[Col. 1453B]

The time is for healing rather than for complaint. For, because sins demand it, holy Mother Church has been placed between hammer and anvil; and unless divine mercy looks down upon her, she will feel the hammer’s blow. For as the wickedness of the schismatics grows more frequent, the Father of fathers is exiled from his native land for defending his faith and loving justice; and Pharaoh’s hardened heart prevents him from having a free return open to his own see. Added to this, the Church of Canterbury is grievously diminished alike in spiritual and temporal matters. Like a ship upon the sea, deprived of its proper helmsman, it is tossed about and exposed to the winds, while its shepherd is prevented by royal power from remaining within the bounds of his own nation.

He, aware of danger to himself, his Church, and ourselves, has exposed us with him to the bitterness of punishments and labours, failing to consider that authority must be flattered, not disparaged. Though we sympathize with all our hearts in his labours, he proves ungrateful to us; and although we are condemned on his account in the same condemnation, he does not cease to persecute us. For a certain controversy was being conducted between him and the most serene king of the English. By the will of both, a day was fixed on which, through the intervention of justice, their dispute might be settled. At the king’s command archbishops, bishops, and the other prelates of the Churches were summoned for that same day, so that, the more general the celebration of the council, the more manifest might be the exposure of fraud and malice. [Col. 1453C]

When the appointed day arrived, the disturber of the realm and of the Church presented himself before the catholic prince. Not secure as to the quality of his own merits, he armed himself with the banner of the Lord’s Cross, as though he were about to approach a tyrant. Nor was royal majesty merely offended: he also entrusted the judgment of his case to the faith of the bishops, that he might thus be freed from every suspicion. It remained for the bishops to settle the case by judgment, so that they might reconcile those at variance and bury the cause of their dissension. Yet he intervened and forbade sentence to be pronounced concerning him before the king, so that the king’s mind might be more grievously inflamed to anger.

The greatness of his offence is such that its author ought to expose himself to whatever vengeance may befall, ashamed to deprecate the punishment he has deserved. He did not shrink from offending the prince, especially at a time of persecution of the Church, against the interests of the Church; and that offence increased the hammer of persecution against the Church. It would have been better for him to put a bridle upon his prosperity, lest, while he presumptuously strives to attain the summit of affairs, he be deservedly thrust down to lower things for his presumption. Even if the injuries suffered by the Church did not move him, the advances made to him by the king, in both wealth and honours, ought at least to have recalled him from acting against the king.

But his adversary objects that to stand trial before the king would diminish the apostolic see and dignity. As if he did not know that, even if in that judgment something were derogated from the dignity of the Church, this ought nevertheless to have been overlooked for the time, so that peace might be restored to the Church. Again, assuming for himself the name of father—which seems to savour of arrogance—he objects that sons ought by no means to have assembled for their father’s condemnation. But it was necessary that the humility of the sons should moderate the father’s pride, lest after the father the sons should solemnize the father’s hatred. [Col. 1454A]

It is therefore plain from the foregoing, most holy Fathers, that the empty and ineffectual accusation of our adversary ought to languish away: he attacked us solely through the malice of hatred, supported by no advocacy of reason. And since the care of all Churches is known to rest upon you, it is necessary for you to apply prudence and diligence to the condition of the Church of Canterbury, lest that Church be compelled to suffer shipwreck through the excesses of its shepherd.

### XCIV. Of an Anonymous Writer.—He relates what was done at the court which the Emperor Frederick had summoned for the day of Pentecost in order to negotiate peace between himself and the Roman pontiff.

[Col. 1454C]

**To Pope Alexander, from a certain friend of his.**

When the Emperor had assembled his princes at the court which he had appointed for them on the feast of Pentecost, and the princes themselves had begun on the Saturday before the feast and on the following Monday to negotiate a restoration of peace between you and him, Reginald, called “of Cologne,” arrived. He publicly declared and proposed that neither the Emperor’s labour nor his zeal would avail anything against you for his own honour, nor would he at all then agree with his counsels. For he said that the stronger part of the Empire was with you, mentioning Salzburg, Mainz, and others in Germany who had obeyed your Holiness.

Nevertheless, in order to magnify himself, he said: “I have won over to the obedience of our apostolic one more persons than we are; and the king of England will furnish him with fifty or more, according to the lord Emperor’s pleasure.” Accordingly, when the Emperor promised his assent to the prosecution of his plan, while this man made such promises and personally produced, as assurance of the matter, two envoys of the aforesaid king, he proposed the following plan to the Emperor in the hearing of all the princes: namely, that the Emperor himself should swear with his own hand before the sight of the whole court that at no time in all his life would he receive you, or anyone acting on your behalf, as Roman pontiff, but would always adhere unshakenly and inseparably to the devotion of his pope Paschal. If it should happen that Paschal died before him, his successors should observe this same oath. [Col. 1454D]

Moreover, he was to compel his princes to swear the same; and there was to be added to their oath that, if the Emperor should die first, the princes themselves should crown no one king before the person to be crowned had sworn likewise to uphold and foster that same schismatic and his successors. Further, within six weeks after returning from the court to their own territories, the princes were to compel all abbots, provosts, and other prelates of Churches, as well as knights and all others holding any honours in their lands, to swear the same. Those unwilling to do so, after their goods had been entirely confiscated, were to be deposed and stripped of the belt of their rank; or, if they were private persons, cruelly mutilated in their limbs and compelled to go into exile from the whole Empire.

The form of the proposal pleased the Emperor, but it seemed exceedingly harsh and burdensome to the archbishop of Magdeburg and the other bishops who were present. Thus the same archbishop of Magdeburg replied that he would take no oath on this matter unless the man of Cologne first received orders and consecration, by which he might remove every doubt from his own breast and those of the others. When the latter refused to promise this, the Emperor attacked him sharply; reproaching him with his malice, he angrily continued in words such as these:

“Behold, it plainly appears that, like a traitor and deceiver, you set over me a pope, to my danger and without my knowledge. Even before receiving my letters, so that you might not deliberate concerning the election of a substitute pontiff, you at once, amid the *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, God”), and according to your own pleasure, chose for me a new pope. You have thus proved a greater traitor to me than the elect of Mainz, whom you accused of this crime. Especially since he gave me the salutary counsel that, since God had delivered me from danger from the former pope, I should by no means make myself subject to his successor. Now you must know that you will be compelled first to enter the snare which you prepared; and, if others also refuse to do this, you alone will have to undergo the danger which your malice is known to have prepared for the rest.” [Col. 1455C]

Thus, being very tightly pressed, he could not escape but, with the greatest weeping, first take the oath in the aforesaid form and promise that, after receiving orders, he would also receive consecration.

He also produced the aforesaid envoys of the king of England, who publicly swore before all that whatever the Emperor should swear to observe in this matter, the king likewise would firmly maintain and observe. The Emperor therefore gave the aforesaid oath with his own hand, but with this qualification, determined at the word of the archbishop of Magdeburg: if it happened that you and that schismatic died at the same time, and the cardinals of both parties unanimously agreed upon someone, he would be free to receive him—provided, however, as the man of Cologne caused to be added, that the same election proceeded with the Emperor’s assent. Then the princes present, as stated above, each gave his oath.

But when it came to the bishops, all except the bishop of Verden said that they would rather surrender their royal temporalities than take oaths of this kind. They were answered that, willing or unwilling, they must take the oath and retain the temporalities. Thus, with great weeping and lamentation, the archbishop of Magdeburg was the first to swear, but upon this condition: that all the others who were absent should likewise swear, and that he should be released from the oath whenever he ceased to possess the temporalities. The bishop of Bamberg, after many and various excuses, swore to the Emperor in such terms that, so long as he wished to retain the temporalities, he would provide the Emperor with aid and counsel in the affair according as his own judgment should dictate. [Col. 1456A]

The bishop of Verden and the intruded bishop of Halberstadt swore absolutely, like the man of Cologne. The bishops of Verdun and Freising, excused by the absence of their archbishops, were not compelled to take the oath; having received leave, they returned freely to their own places, obtaining permission until the feast of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Only these princes swore: the duke of Saxony, Margrave Albert, and the count palatine, the Emperor’s brother. These were the archbishops who swore: those of Magdeburg and Bamberg, though under the condition stated above. The man of Cologne and his two suffragans, however, swore absolutely. But the son of Conrad, who had come to the court with fifteen hundred knights, departed when he heard oath-taking mentioned. The patriarch of Aquileia was not present, nor any of his suffragans; likewise neither the archbishop of Salzburg nor any of his; nor the archbishop of Trier nor any of his. Many of the princes were absent as well. [Col. 1456C]

### XCV. Of Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury.—He accuses the abbot of Malmesbury of withdrawing himself from obedience to his bishop. He then laments at length the evils that have followed from exemptions of abbots granted by Roman pontiffs because of the tyranny of certain bishops.

[Col. 1456D]

**To the most holy Father and lord Alexander, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, from R., humble minister of the Church of Canterbury: most devoted service of submission.**

As we profess the pre-eminence of the apostolic see to be the teacher of all Churches, so from it we expect counsel in doubts, consolation in distress, and answers in judicial matters. The monastery of Malmesbury, situated in the diocese of Salisbury, recently elected an abbot. When the bishop of Salisbury appealed, and on your behalf firmly forbade the elect to receive the gift of blessing from anyone but himself, the latter nevertheless secretly went to Wales and, having obtained a clandestine and furtive blessing from the bishop of Llandaff, usurped for himself the office of abbot. We, after carefully investigating the bishop’s complaint and the truth of the matter, suspended the Welsh bishop and the abbot until they should allege a privilege of liberty or dignity in excuse for so great an offence. [Col. 1457A]

Therefore, when the parties were present before us and the privileges of the Churches were produced in evidence, we found nothing why the monastery of Malmesbury should not be subject and humbly obedient to the bishop of Salisbury, except only that the abbot put forward certain letters of exemption, which appeared defective in their thread and seal and did not at all bear the style of the Roman curia; therefore the bishop accused them of falsity.
