The abbot endeavoured through witnesses to assert that his predecessors had received blessings, at their own discretion, from whatever bishops they wished, without the bond of a profession [of obedience]. The bishop, on the contrary, produced many professions of the abbots of Malmesbury, made to himself and his predecessors, by which he claimed for himself the abbot’s obedience and the monastery’s subjection.

Accordingly, after the abbot’s witnesses had been produced and received, and their testimonies put into writing, we fixed another day, because the abbot urgently demanded a second production. On that day, when according to our custom we urged what belonged to peace, the bishop humbly offered himself both to peace and to judgment. But the abbot, following the counsel of a certain advocate and fleeing to the crafty artifices of law, would neither submit to judgment nor admit a word of peace. He declared that henceforth he would answer to no bishop or archbishop, but only to the supreme pontiff, concerning profession or obedience; and he withdrew contumaciously.

“Wretched and miserable,” he said, “are abbots who do not wholly destroy the power of bishops, when for an annual ounce of gold they can obtain full liberty from the Roman see.” [Col. 1457B]

For this reason, reverend Father, we lay these matters before the ears of your pre-eminence in common lamentation, because that pest spreads itself most widely. Abbots swell with pride against primates and bishops, and there is no one who renders reverence and honour to his superiors. The yoke of obedience—wherein lay the sole hope of salvation and remedy for the ancient transgression—has been emptied of force. Abbots abhor having a corrector of their excesses; they embrace the wandering licence of impunity, and relax the yoke of cloistered warfare into every freedom of desire. This is why the resources of almost all monasteries have been given over to plunder and prey. For abbots outwardly care for the flesh in its desires, caring only that they may be sumptuously supplied and that peace may prevail in their days; while cloistered religious, like headless men, devote themselves to idleness and empty talk, for they have no governor to incline them toward the fruit of a better life. If you heard their tumultuous disputes, you would think that the cloister differed little from the marketplace. [Col. 1457C]

All these things, reverend Father, call for the timely judgment of your correction. Unless a remedy is more quickly applied to this evil, it must be feared that, as abbots are exempted from bishops, so bishops may be exempted from archbishops, and deans and archdeacons from their prelates. What kind of justice is this—or rather, what deformity of law—to forbid disciples to agree with their teacher, sons to obey their father, soldiers to follow their commander, or servants to be subject to their lord? What is it to exempt abbots from the jurisdiction of bishops but to prescribe contumacy and rebellion, and to arm sons against parents? Let those who judge the world, I pray, consider and judge these things, lest injuries appear to flow from the source from which laws are drawn.

We shall be accused of rashness and be said to have set our mouth in heaven, though we write these things not from a spirit of pride but from the inkhorn of grief. We indeed feel private distresses while we lament public ones; nor is our strength the strength of stone, nor our flesh of bronze, that we should be able to overlook such enormous injuries. After Uriah’s death and Bathsheba’s adultery, a prophet was sent to David who proposed to him the parable of a poor man with one little ewe-lamb, which a rich man who possessed innumerable sheep took from him. Asked for his judgment, David pronounced the sentence of death upon the rich man, and consequently upon himself. [Col. 1458A]

And who today is the rich man who has innumerable sheep, if not the Roman pontiff, who possesses all the Churches of the world? And who is poorer than the Church of Canterbury, which, when it had one sole abbey—namely, the monastery of St Augustine—which it cherished in the bosom of pastoral care and a fatherly embrace, that prophetic rich man, not to say the Roman pontiff, usurped as his own special and proper possession? If we dare say what we feel: since by the office of justice each person is rendered what is his own, it does not greatly advance the Roman pontiff’s justice if he grants a favour to one person to another’s injury, if he takes away what is mine, if he does in ecclesiastical affairs what worldly power abhors in secular affairs.

The Apostle, speaking to the Romans, says: “Let every creature be subject to the higher powers” (Rom. 13). If the Apostle writes thus to the Roman Church, who in the Roman Church has presumed to oppose apostolic teaching? Writing also to the Hebrews, he says: “Obey your rulers” (Heb. 13). In the human body, one member does not refuse to serve another. Some angels preside over others and do not among themselves admit the pride of emancipation. One of them once wished to exempt himself from divine power, and from an angel became the devil. Today, through liberties of this extraordinary kind, the ruin of many is contrived. [Col. 1458C]

Again we say that we shall be charged with disputing the deed of the supreme pontiff and committing sacrilege; nevertheless, there is no fair disputation where the person suffering is not allowed to reply. There is no contest where you strike and I merely receive the blows. If the mouth speaks from disturbance of spirit and abundance of heart, may you mercifully pardon unconsidered heat, most clement Father; for our grief is before your sight and our groaning is not hidden from you. Would that your indignation in correction extended its hand over my head, if only through my reproaches and sorrows the Church of Canterbury might breathe again into the favour of its ancient dignity.

At some time, through God’s mercy, the Roman pontiff will consider how he may become more favourably disposed. For if he calls the Church of St Augustine his special daughter, the Church of Canterbury is a daughter more special, more beautiful, and far more worthy. If he subjects the monastery of St Augustine to her, he takes away nothing except by restoring what belongs to another. For, as Gregory testifies, nothing is lost to ecclesiastical interests if what belongs to another is restored. We know indeed that Roman pontiffs have often granted these exemptions for the peace of monasteries and because of the tyranny of bishops; nevertheless, the matter has turned to the contrary. [Col. 1459A]

For monasteries which have obtained this boon of most pernicious liberty, whether through apostolic authority or, as happens more commonly, by forged bulls, have incurred more unrest, more disobedience, and more poverty. Therefore many houses most renowned for sanctity and religion have either never wished to possess these immunities or have immediately rejected them when obtained. If, then, the abbot of Malmesbury—whom among us we regard as a barren tree, a foolish fig-tree, and a useless stump—comes or sends to you, weigh his life and reputation in the balance of justice. Do not admit his privileges until it is clearly evident, by comparing the writing and the bulls, at what time and by what Fathers they were granted. For the deceitful malice of forgers has armed itself so greatly to the dishonour of bishops that falsity prevails in the exemption of nearly all monasteries, unless, in conducting decisions and examinations, the strictest exactor, the judge of truth, intervenes. May the Lord preserve you to maintain the liberty due to the Churches. [Col. 1459C]

### XCVI. Of the Same.—He defends the reputation of bishops residing at the royal court from slanders, and shows, by examples of the ancients, how profitably they serve there for the realm.

**To Alexander, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, from Richard, humble minister of the Church of Canterbury: devoted service of humility and obedience.**

Detractors, hateful to God (Rom. 1), have suggested monstrous charges to your serenity concerning our bishops, asserting that our venerable brethren R., bishop of Winchester, G., bishop of Ely, and John, bishop of Norwich, following the scent of gifts and wholly casting aside pastoral care, plunge themselves into the waves of courtly service—or rather, courtly malice. They say that they exercise judgments of blood and therefore, as men of blood, abstain from sacred things and do not approach the Lord’s table. For this reason your indignation has been kindled against them, and you prescribe punishment for us if we do not canonically punish such excesses.

Indeed, it would be disgraceful and most worthy of severe correction if the mouth that speaks iniquity were truthful in this matter; but iniquity has lied to itself. For, to extract a few instances from many: no one is more compassionate toward the afflicted than the bishop of Winchester, none humbler in his own eyes, none more devout at the altar, none more lavish in benefactions. Hence his name is as poured-out ointment, and every church of the saints recounts his alms. [Col. 1459D]

The bishop of Ely, moreover, since—in accordance with the terms of your good pleasure, yet without any stain, and as though beyond what was required—he demonstrated his innocence by canonical purgation, has fully and effectively fulfilled the office of bishop and, by holy and honourable conduct, has proved those who stained the innocent man to be liars. He too, and the bishop of Norwich, whose honourableness and prudence you have often learned through long acquaintance and experience when he was sent to you by the lord king, found their Churches poor; but prudently and vigorously recovering and very greatly enlarging their possessions, they have now raised them to an excellent condition.

It is certainly no novelty for bishops to participate in kings’ counsels. For, just as they surpass others in integrity and wisdom, so they are judged readier and more effective in administering the commonwealth. For, as it is written, a kingdom not governed by the counsel of wise men is ordered less beneficially. You also read: “Woe to the land whose king is a child, and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccles. 10). “Blessed is the land whose king is wise, and whose princes eat at their proper time.” This indicates that those ought to take part in kings’ counsels who know, desire, and are able to sympathize with sufferers; to provide for the peace of the land and the people’s welfare; to instruct kings in justice; to meet approaching dangers; to form subjects by examples of more mature life; and by a certain authoritative power to restrain the presumption of evildoers. [Col. 1460B]

The kingdom of the Hebrews would not have been divided in the days of Rehoboam, nor would the ten tribes have revolted from him, had he chosen wiser men as counsellors. Although Saul was prophesying among those who called upon the name of the Lord, it was Samuel’s instruction that established David’s kingdom and strengthened his throne. When King Hezekiah was oppressed by Sennacherib and placed, as it were, in the utmost distress, he received through Isaiah the deliverance of the city and the benefit of consolation. Elisha brought blindness upon the Syrians, and through his aid the besiegers of Samaria were turned to flight. Jehoiada the priest hid Joash, son of Ahaziah, from Athaliah who pursued him; when he had raised him to the kingship, he trained him in holy morals. [Col. 1460C]

But after Jehoiada’s death, Joash began to turn aside from God’s lawful commands; when Zechariah rebuked him, he overwhelmed and crushed him with stones. In this it is most plainly evident how useful and necessary the companionship and teaching of the righteous are to those who have undertaken government of the people. For in the days of King Zedekiah the kingdom of the Jews would not have been destroyed, had the lies of the false prophets not prevailed against Jeremiah, who took counsel for the public good.

Know this: unless the aforesaid bishops were the king’s householders and counsellors, sinners would today build upon the back of the Church, and lay presumption would oppress the clergy savagely and intolerably. But now, if anything is attempted to the injury of the Church, it is rebuked by pontifical authority; or, if ecclesiastical censure is insufficient for this, the lack of the spiritual sword is supplied by the civil sword, and princely punishment is exercised at their discretion. If at any time, as often happens, the king’s anger burns too fiercely against the innocent, it is moderated by the bishops’ prayers. [Col. 1461A]

Through their intervention, judicial severity becomes gentle toward the simple; the cry of the poor is admitted; the dignity of Churches is raised up; the need of the poor is relieved; liberty among the clergy is strengthened; peace among the people and quiet in monasteries are secured; justice is freely administered; pride is cast down; the devotion of laypeople is increased; religion is fostered; judgments are directed; laws are accepted; Roman decrees obtain force; and ecclesiastical possessions are enlarged.

They attend their respective Churches at every principal feast. There, through lavish almsgiving, consolation of orphans and widows, correction of their subjects, and other works of holiness, they most fully redeem the days which they spent at court. Moreover, archbishops or bishops who frequent the court of the king of Sicily do not leave that court for seven or ten years; and, whether they live or die, it makes no difference to the care of ecclesiastical possessions or the governance of souls. We once wished to forbid our bishops this courtly involvement; but prudent and wise men considered their attendance upon the king beneficial. If we withdrew them from his familiarity, we would withdraw peace from monasteries, consolation from the oppressed, and liberty from the Churches. [Col. 1461B]

Therefore, although because of the various hardships they endure there they may earnestly desire to depart, nevertheless, for the sake of the public good and by the common counsel of our brethren, they ought not merely to endure this military service in this life, but to be drawn and compelled to it. Father, be pleased to weigh in the balance of equity the advantage to the English Church and the malice of the detractors who have suggested to you things contrary to truth; and be pleased to communicate to our littleness, by messenger or letter, what shall be acceptable to your eyes in this matter. The truth of the matter ought first to have been declared to you, so that you may proceed more surely and confidently to its determination. When we have received the oracle of your Holiness, we shall be effective and devoted executors of the apostolic command. May God preserve you for long times for His Church, most holy Father. [Col. 1461D]

### XCVII. Of Bartholomew, Bishop of Exeter.—For Richard, formerly archdeacon of Poitiers, bishop-elect of Winchester.

**To the lord pope, from the bishop of Exeter.**

Just as the most holy Roman Church customarily removes the unworthy from the governance of Churches, so it calls fit persons to the care of the pastoral office and bestows upon them the grace and protection of apostolic guardianship. The Church of Winchester, however, having been exposed to many great dangers through the absence of a shepherd, has at length, as is hoped, been given consolation from heaven, through the election of a shepherd according to God; and it is fitting, if it please you, that the further favour of your grace be granted to him.

He is your most devoted son Richard, formerly archdeacon of Poitiers, whose alms comfort the churches of the saints, whose resources are relief for the needy, whose power is a support of justice and an extermination of iniquity. He is prudent in counsel, discerning in action, restrained in speech, and one who follows the rule of temperance in bearing and gesture. He is so wholly converted to God’s worship—as we speak from our heart’s conviction—that he is prepared to expend not only all that is his, but also himself, for the law of the Lord. We believe this, Father, and have been led by many sure signs to believe what we say. [Col. 1462A]

The whole Church of Winchester freely agreed upon him; after a canonical election had been held, the royal assent was subsequently given to him in our presence and that of our brethren. When this became known to our lords, your legates, they were very pleased, as we have learned from their letters. And rightly so, since no one else appeared able so suitably to restore the ruins of the aforesaid Church or so effectively to strengthen among us the authority of the apostolic see. We therefore beseech your fatherhood to have him promoted with due deliberation, so that when promoted he may more easily and successfully address the Church’s needs and advance its interests. Farewell.

### XCVIII. Of the Same.—For R., bishop-elect of Hereford.

**To Pope Alexander, from Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter.**

Strength comes to the members from the head, and after God the salvation of all Churches comes from the holy Roman Church. Your lord cardinal legates, compassionating the Churches among us that had been left desolate, strictly commanded that, postponing every excuse and delay, they should choose for themselves fathers and shepherds according to God. Thus the Church of Hereford, which had long mourned and languished, bereft of its own shepherd, by an equal vote and unanimous agreement freely elected, according to the institutions of the sacred canons, the venerable R., archdeacon of Oxford and canon of its Church: a man distinguished alike by uprightness of character and learning, noble by birth, skilled in both laws, knowing how to govern his own household and to bear the care of God’s Church, gracious and of good reputation with all. [Col. 1462C]

Royal assent was given to his election in our presence and that of our brethren, who all rejoiced and were strengthened in this action; and the favour of all who heard of it was added. Prostrate at the knees of your piety, therefore, we earnestly beseech you to have him promptly promoted, to deal with the needs both of his own Church and of others. Farewell.

### XCIX. Of the Same.—For Richard, bishop-elect of Canterbury.

**To the most excellent lord and dearest Father A., by God’s grace supreme pontiff, from B., bishop of Exeter: greetings.**

For several reasons the English Church rejoices in your apostolate more than usual; but above all things that win the favour of all, you commanded that Christ’s glorious martyr be enrolled in the catalogue of saints, and, through the effort of your legates, the hope of your consolation has dawned upon desolate Churches, so that they may dare with greater confidence to aspire to full liberty.

Among these is our mother, the holy Church of Canterbury, crowned with the blood of so many and such great martyrs, and from the beginning always exposing itself to dangers for justice, for the Church’s liberty, and for fidelity to the apostolic see. At last, after labours, losses, and countless calamities—which it is superfluous to recount, since the whole Christian world has recognized them—it seems, through divine clemency answering to its merits, to have reached the end of shipwreck. [Col. 1463A]

For recently, when those who dwell in the chief see, the suffragans of the province, and all to whom the election belonged had assembled, the whole Church, guided by desire and the prayer of the people, freely and with unanimous consent elected for itself as father and shepherd, according to the institution of the sacred canons, a man whose life supports his conscience and example, whose learned education supports his pattern of life, and whose eloquence supports his teaching: namely Richard, monk of the Church of Canterbury and prior of the monastery of Dover. For many years he had most praiseworthily exercised its care; and he showed faithfulness in need to the athlete of Christ when the latter had been proscribed and was striving for the Church’s liberty, so that he is now judged worthy to succeed him.

After the king’s assent had been obtained, the provincial bishops assembled in the customary manner at the metropolitan see, to perform from their office the gift of consecration required by necessity. But because the ancient enemy begrudges the advancement of souls, letters unexpectedly appeared in their midst, devised, as it seemed to many, by his contrivance and drawn up in the name of the younger king. In these he declared that he had appealed to your hearing against elections which lacked his assent. [Col. 1463B]

Although the letters seemed suspect for various reasons, too lengthy to report, and although the opinion of many was that they ought not to cause prejudice to the consecration due, especially in so great a necessity, the Church nevertheless considered that it ought to defer to your majesty. It hoped without doubt that it would find the greater favour at the apostolic see because, even at its own peril and in so manifest a necessity, it had humbly striven to show it greater honour and reverence.

Since, therefore, to prolong the desolation of the Church is the same as to procure its ruin and the perpetual desolation of the others, prostrate at the feet of your piety we earnestly beseech you to cause us and the English Church to rejoice in a shepherd chosen by heaven, as is our hope; and to appoint in place of Saint Thomas a man whom he proved faithful in his distresses. Let the sufferings of the struggling Church move you, Father; let the prayers of its children move you; let reverence for the most glorious martyr move you, whom we trust is praying that a worthy successor may be appointed to him in the holy Church of Canterbury. [Col. 1463D]

### C. Of the Prior and Convent of the Church of Canterbury.—For R., bishop-elect of Winchester.

[Col. 1464A]

**To the lord pope, from the prior of Canterbury and the convent.**
We more securely commend to you those whom we love more sincerely, and whom we believe to bear a more sincere affection toward the holy Roman Church. One of these, and indeed almost the foremost among them, is the father of the poor and consoler of the sorrowful, our protector in distress: our venerable brother R., bishop-elect of Winchester. Christ has chosen him for this—and, as the faithful hope, for the governance of his church—so that he may rise up against its adversaries from the opposite side, set himself as a wall for the house of Israel, powerfully crush the enemies of justice, and grant the aid due to the righteous. Therefore, [Col. 1464B] prostrate at the feet of your majesty, we all earnestly beg that, with due deliberation, you cause him to be advanced, both to meet the needs of his own church and for the consolation of others; and that the favor of your grace may attend his prayers, which he will make only in the Lord. Farewell.

CI. Of Odo, prior, and the convent of the Church of Canterbury.—On behalf of R., bishop-elect of Canterbury.

To the lord pope, ODO, prior, and the convent of Canterbury.

The calamities which our Church has now endured for a full decade cannot be unknown to the Apostolic See, since the whole Christian world has recognized them. If the cause is sought, justice declares itself; the liberty [Col. 1464C] of the Church appears; reverence for the Apostolic See, whose authority was being nullified in our regions, bears witness that it is the cause for which the glorious martyr of Christ died; for which the brethren and foster-children of the Church, proscribed, were compelled to remain in exile for a long time; and, regarded as sheep for slaughter, we were made a spectacle to God, to men, and to angels, and the song of Christ’s persecutors all day long. The blood of martyrs shed here among us bears testimony—above all that blood which, crying from the ground to God, is borne throughout the whole world by the devotion of the faithful.

But blessed be God; blessed be your apostolic office, which, through the grace of God cooperating with the diligent efforts of the lord cardinals, has consoled us in our tribulation. Thus, after the straits of so great a shipwreck, the Church seems to have reached the harbor of its rightful liberty, [Col. 1464D] so that it may safely offer to its God the abominations of the Egyptians. For recently an order was issued by them concerning the holding of elections in the kingdom; and the lord king, yielding to their requests, commanded that suitable pastors according to God be appointed in the churches. All rejoiced, but we, by every right, more than the rest, since we were placed in greater peril.

Accordingly, we assembled repeatedly, having summoned the bishops of the province and others to whom the election belonged; and at last, God directing our steps according to His good pleasure, it came to pass that all were of one heart and one soul. This could not have happened without a divine prompting: that wills so discordant should so easily be united in fulfilling the form prescribed by the sacred canons. Therefore, led by the desire and prayer of the people, with equal vote and unanimous consent we agreed upon a man [Col. 1465A] of whom the Lord seems to have said to us: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; choose him” (Matthew 17), because he devoutly honored me together with my martyr, whom he himself truly loved as suffering for me; and because, having lived faithfully in my house from his earliest age, I command that he be chosen beforehand as vicar and ordained as successor.

This is R., a monk of our Church from his youth, advanced among us through every order; prior of the monastery of Dover; distinguished by uprightness of character and learning; modest in speech, prudent in counsel, discerning in action; expressing, in dress and bearing, the true form of a well-governed mind. He performs the priestly office most fittingly. The zeal of Christ burns in his heart; he willingly [Col. 1465B] opens his hand to the needy; he gladly practices liberality; and he commendably administers the care of temporal affairs. What wonder, then, that all most willingly agreed upon so great and such a man—one who would even have had to be carried off, had he not otherwise been obtainable?

Since, therefore, his election had been celebrated freely and according to the institution of the sacred canons, the royal assent, as is customary, followed. A cry full of favor attended the electors, and the whole Church began to resound with the due praise of God. With the elect, the provincial bishops and the elect of other churches likewise proceeded to the metropolitan see; according to the rite of the nation and the custom of their ancestors, he was solemnly enthroned. His consecration, pleasing to God and desired by men, was at hand [Col. 1465C] when, suddenly, letters were produced bearing the name of the younger king. In them he declared that he had appealed against elections which did not have his assent.

Indeed, for various reasons and probable indications the letters were alleged to be suspect, and most held that no credence should be given to them—especially in so great a crisis, when liberty and the salvation of souls could be endangered, the desolation of the Church prolonged, and an irreparable loss of resources incurred. It would take too long to enumerate the reasons. Yet certainly it ought to have been presumed on behalf of that king that, at his own peril and to the temporal advantage of his rivals, he would not wish the Church to remain captive any longer.

But although the aforesaid letters seemed to the wiser men to carry little weight, nevertheless, out of the humility and devotion of the elect himself; out of the fidelity which we recall that our fathers and forebears always bore toward the Roman Church; and on the advice of a few, the consecration was deferred out of reverence for your name. For we hope without doubt that the need of our Church will find so much greater favor in the eyes of your clemency [Col. 1466A] as you see [Col. 1466B] that greater honor has been shown to you, even at our irreparable loss.

You know, Father, that a terrible and long-lasting calamity has oppressed us beyond measure. You see how grievous things have been, how dangerous they are, and how still more dangerous times, as is feared, threaten us. Irreparable desolation confronts us—may God avert it; we fear a returning storm; and great necessity calls for prompt consolation.

Therefore, prostrate at the feet of your compassion, we earnestly beseech you; and with us the whole English Church beseeches you: that, by the fullness of authority entrusted to you, your Holiness may deign, as you shall judge best expedient, to strengthen by apostolic authority against those who contrive to perpetuate the ruin of churches the pastor provided for us by God, so that, relying on the apostolic protection of his predecessors, he may be able, as God inspires him, to imitate their footsteps.

We beseech you, I say; the Church beseeches you; [Col. 1466C] the glorious martyrs and confessors, patrons of our Church, also beseech you; and Saint Thomas, with the harmonious voice of all, repeats and multiplies the prayers. Until your most sacred heart brings forth for us a good word, a word of consolation, Christ’s bride will mourn in squalor, and there will be none able to console her, until she receives her bishop with fullness of authority. Because we cannot, as we would wish, water your feet with tears, we shall water our cheeks; nor shall they have rest until, by God’s mercy, the right hand of your clemency wipes them away.
